France and Germany strike car-industry deal linking 2035 engine rules to ‘Made in Europe’ push
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:36:20 UTC
21:36:20 KST

Under the agreement, carmakers would be required to cut their CO₂ emissions by 90% by 2035, without having to offset the remaining 10%, as initially proposed by the Commission.
France and Germany struck a deal on Friday to soften the European Union’s effective ban on new combustion-engine cars from 2035 in exchange for tougher rules favouring European-made products.
Berlin has long opposed the 2035 rules, seeking to protect its automotive industry, while Paris has pushed for strict “Made in Europe” requirements to counter competition from Chinese manufacturers in the EU market.
The agreement was reached on the sidelines of a gathering of EU leaders in Brussels. It links a revision of the 2035 rules on new petrol and diesel cars to the debate over introducing a European preference in public procurement, proposed by the European Commission in March and championed by France.
The announcement comes as EU lawmakers review a European Commission proposal to amend the legislation that would effectively end sales of new petrol and diesel cars and vans from 2035.
“Our shared ambition is clear: to successfully transform our automotive industry while maintaining our climate ambition and ensuring that the cars of the future are produced in Europe,” the joint statement said.
Under the agreement, 70% of car components, excluding batteries, would have to be produced in Europe, while 10% of battery content would have to come from European sources.
“This creates a European preference to ensure that our factories do not become mere assembly plants,” an Élysée source said.
Carmakers would have to reduce their fleet-average CO2 emissions by 90% by 2035, without offsetting the remaining 10%, contrary to an initial proposal from the Commission.
A joint position to influence EU negotiations
The political compromise reflects shared concerns in Paris and Berlin that European carmakers are being squeezed by high production costs, the expensive transition to electric vehicles and growing competition from Chinese manufacturers.
However, the two countries have different priorities when it comes to addressing these challenges.
“France and Germany propose a comprehensive package that combines an ambitious European decarbonisation pathway with the regulatory flexibility needed to reflect different market realities and technological conditions. It also provides concrete incentives for investment, research and development, European production, and resilient supply chains,” the joint statement said.
Germany, home to major carmakers including Volkswagen, BMW and Mercedes-Benz, has called for greater technological flexibility to protect manufacturers seeking to continue selling some combustion-engine and hybrid models after 2035.
France, which has advocated strengthening Europe’s industrial base, has pushed for a strict European preference limited to the EU’s 27 member states.
“Made in Europe” rules have been central to the debate over the Commission’s Industrial Accelerator Act, proposed in March, which would introduce such a preference.
Germany, however, has advocated a broader approach that would include trusted non-EU countries.
Under Friday’s agreement, several non-EU countries with close ties to the bloc — Norway, Iceland, Switzerland and the UK — would be eligible to participate in the European preference, with products from these countries considered “Made in Europe” for the purposes of the rules.
These countries would have to sign agreements with the EU to ensure that European companies can compete for public contracts and access government funding in their markets on fair terms. They would also have to ensure that other countries cannot use them as a backdoor to circumvent the EU’s “Made in Europe” requirements.
The Franco-German deal establishes a joint national position, paving the way for other member states and EU lawmakers to decide whether to support it.
However, Merz could face resistance at home, as Germany’s Social Democratic environment minister has advocated a 95% emissions reduction target, with the remaining 5% offset through the use of low-carbon steel.
A potential rethink of car emissions rules
The EU’s original rules required new cars and vans to achieve a 100% reduction in fleet-average CO2 emissions from 2035, effectively ending sales of new conventional petrol and diesel vehicles.
Although the rules would not ban existing combustion-engine cars from the roads, they have faced sustained opposition from parts of the automotive industry.
In December 2025, the Commission proposed revising the rules in response to pressure from Germany, Italy and carmakers concerned about weak demand for electric vehicles and competition from China.
The proposal would replace the 100% emissions reduction requirement with a 90% target, leaving room for certain technologies and fuels under specified conditions. The change would not amount to an unrestricted return to conventional combustion engines.
“France and Germany are determined to build on this momentum and work swiftly with their European partners towards an agreement,” the statement said.
MEPs are due to vote on the Commission’s proposal in plenary in Strasbourg on 23 November.
The European Parliament and EU governments will then need to agree on how far to relax the bloc’s planned 2035 target for zero CO2 emissions from new cars, including whether to allow greater flexibility for combustion-engine and hybrid vehicles.

Including AJet's fleet, Turkish Airlines currently operates 96 Boeing 737 Next Generation aircraft powered by CFM56-7B engines and 79 Boeing 737 MAX aircraft equipped with LEAP-1B engines.
CFM has delivered more than 10,000 LEAP engines since the engine family entered service a decade ago, with the fleet accumulating over 100 million flight hours, the statement said.

Poland urges internet firms to act on violent content after school stabbings
WARSAW, Oct 16 - Poland summoned internet companies including Google and Meta to the Digital Affairs Ministry on Friday, demanding they do more to curb the spread of violent content following a series of school stabbing attacks.
Thousands of police were sent to schools this week to ensure security after a series of three attacks in four days triggered a wave of online threats that left pupils and teachers fearing for their safety.
Warsaw says the glorification of violence in corners of the internet, for example in groups devoted to Nazi ideology or idolising serial killers, is having a damaging effect on children and has urged social media firms to do more to prevent content that encourages or threatens violence.
"It is the expectation of every Polish citizen that ... no one should incite others to commit suicide, that there should be no content endorsing or encouraging criminal threats, and that users should not be exposed to situations like acts of murder, physical harm, or mutilation," Digital Affairs Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski told a press conference.
Gawkowski said that between October 7 and October 12 Poland flagged 89 cases of illegal content related to the attacks to internet companies, and in two-thirds of cases they failed to take any action.
The meeting was attended by representatives of Google, Meta, TikTok, Discord and Telegram. Elon Musk's X was invited but did not attend, Gawkowski said.
The companies did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
The government is fast-tracking legislation to make it easier and quicker to remove damaging content.
The latest stabbing occurred on Saturday, when three people were injured at a further education college in Warsaw. It followed an attack on October 8 in Leszczydol-Nowiny, northeast of the capital, where a 15-year-old former pupil wearing a helmet-mounted camera killed a school caretaker and wounded two teachers.
A day earlier, a 19-year-old injured 10 people, including himself, at a school in Ostroleka. REUTERS

5 ways to make Halloween decorations friendlier to wildlife
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:33:03 UTC
21:33:03 KST

Recently, a slender, yellow-striped California whipsnake, small enough to fit in a person’s hand, was brought to the California Wildlife Center in Calabasas. Its lower body was so twisted in fine strands of fake spiderwebs that it was essentially a ball, with twigs and leaves stuck in the mess.
“Had that gone on much longer, it could have started severing into its skin,” says Lauren Michaels, director of animal care at the center. Fortunately, the snake recovered and was eventually released. Not every animal is so lucky, though. Cambria Wells, the center’s education and outreach manager, recalls a hummingbird that was similarly wrapped in webbing and didn’t make it.
Every Halloween season, wildlife rehabilitation centers across the country see cases in which birds, bats, snakes, rodents, deer and other wild animals become injured or entangled in seasonal decorations.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The good news is that you can have a spooky spectacle in front of your house and still protect wildlife. Here are five ways to make your Halloween display friendlier to the creatures that fly, slither and scurry through your yard.
Skip stretchy fake spiderwebs
Of all the Halloween decorations people display outdoors, synthetic spiderwebs are the most dangerous, according to many wildlife experts. Made of strong, stretchy plastic, the webbing’s thin, hard-to-see strands can cling to animals and become wrapped around their bodies, posing a serious entanglement hazard. Trapped animals can go hungry, suffer constriction injuries, or even dislocate their limbs as they struggle to free themselves, Wells explains.
To get the spiderweb look without the stretchy strands, the best option is a solid web decoration made from rigid plastic or metal, she advises. Rope-style webs are safer than stretchy spiderwebbing, but they can still pose an entanglement risk.
If you do use stretchy or rope webbing outdoors, Wells recommends pulling it taut against a solid surface, such as your house, rather than across an open space where an animal could fly or travel through it.
Stick with solid decorations
The same principle applies to other decorations. Choose solid objects over anything with netting, strings, ropes, ribbons or other materials in which an animal could become entangled. Think tombstones, solid skeletons, signs or other decorations that hold their shape and don’t have loose or dangling parts.
Popular inflatables can be a safer alternative to netting or webbing, but you should make sure their anchoring cords and power cords are secured and check regularly for damage.
In general, look for durable decorations you can reuse year after year rather than items that are designed to be thrown away after a single season to reduce the broader environmental impact of your Halloween display, Wells notes.
Turn Halloween lights off when you go to bed
“Lighting is an underappreciated form of impact on wildlife,” Wells says. Artificial light can interfere with wildlife behavior and disorient migrating birds, many of which travel during the middle of the night and the early morning at this time of year, she explains.
If you want lights as part of your decor, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service recommends opting for ones with warmer colors, such as amber, orange or red, rather than blue, white or other cooler-colored lights, whose shorter wavelengths are more disruptive to biological rhythms.
But regardless of the type of lights you use, the simplest and most effective step, Wells says, is to turn them off when you go to bed, giving wildlife darkness during the overnight hours.
Deck your windows
Window decals, creepy figures, glowing jack-o’-lanterns and other decorations displayed on or just inside your windows can still be seen from the street without introducing loose materials into your yard that wildlife could encounter.
Decorate with natural materials
Pumpkins are a Halloween staple, but you should remember that they’re also food. If you want to keep wildlife from chowing down on your carefully carved jack-o’-lantern without harming any creatures, Wells says, try bringing it in in the evening or coating it with a bitter apple spray or cayenne pepper diluted with water.
When spooky season is over, you can then compost your pumpkins or dispose of them according to your local food- or yard-waste guidelines. You can also check whether a local wildlife center or animal sanctuary accepts intact, untreated pumpkins for animal feed.
Other natural materials, such as gourds, hay, and cornstalks make for festive decor, but Wells suggests choosing materials from your local area to reduce the risk of introducing invasive plants or seeds.
If you find an entangled animal, call for help
If you discover an animal caught in or injured by Halloween decorations, resist the urge to untangle and release it. Injuries may not be obvious at first, and the animal may need medical care.
Instead contact a local wildlife rehabilitation center for guidance. You can find nearby resources through Animal Help Now.

EU unveils new strategy to step up fight against human trafficking
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:31:02 UTC
21:31:02 KST

Melike Pala
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
The European Commission unveiled a new strategy to combat human trafficking on Friday, setting out six priorities, including the use of technology, cooperation with the private sector, tackling organized crime, and plans to strengthen partnerships with non-EU countries.
More than 20,000 victims of human trafficking were registered across the European Union in 2023 and 2024, marking a 16.1% increase, according to a Commission statement.
Women and girls accounted for 63% of registered victims, most of whom were trafficked for sexual exploitation, while children represented 15% of the total.
Men made up 74% of victims trafficked for labour exploitation.
The first priority focuses on harnessing modern technology to improve the prevention, detection and investigation of human trafficking.
The second priority aims to strengthen cooperation with the private sector to reduce exploitation risks and improve early detection.
Under the third priority, the EU will step up efforts to disrupt transnational trafficking networks linked to organized crime through cross-border cooperation, intelligence-led policing, financial investigations and asset recovery.
The bloc also called on member states to expand cross-border operational cooperation through joint investigation teams, with support from Europol and Eurojust.
The fourth priority addresses trafficking risks linked to migration by strengthening screening procedures, border processes and safeguards in reception conditions.
The fifth priority focuses on improving preparedness and rapid responses during crises, while the sixth priority aims to strengthen the protection of people vulnerable to trafficking.
The strategy will be discussed by the European Parliament and the European Council.

Nobel Peace Prize: the message behind Navi Pillay’s win

Opinion
Nobel Peace Prize: the message behind Navi Pillay’s win
With global institutions under attack and Trump’s power politics on the rise, the award is a firm rejection of the ‘might is right’ doctrine
4-MIN READ4-MIN
1
 Listen
Commodore C. Uday Bhaskar is director of the Society for Policy Studies (SPS), an independent think tank based in New Delhi. 
The awarding of the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize to South African jurist Navanethem “Navi” Pillay matters for reasons that go well beyond the laureate herself.
The award does three things at once. First, it restores credibility to the prize. Second, it rejects in unambiguous terms the Thrasymachian doctrine that might is right, which has become the operating philosophy of major powers. Third, it highlights a warning of what happens when a hegemon decides it is above the law.
The correction was overdue. Last year, the Norwegian Nobel Committee gave the Peace Prize to Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, in what was widely read as a political signal. Machado, however, then gave her prize to US President Donald Trump.
Whatever one’s view of Venezuelan politics, that act made a mockery of an institution founded on Alfred Nobel’s will: that the prize go to the person who has done the most for fraternity between nations, for the abolition or reduction of standing armies, and for the promotion of peace congresses. A Nobel Prize cannot be re-gifted like a souvenir. As the organisers made clear, “a medal can change owners, but the title of a Nobel Peace Prize laureate cannot”.

"Before the final, I knew I could win the match because I felt my opponent wasn’t as well-prepared as I was," he said. "My opponent was tall and I may have trouble taking him down and controlling him on the mat. So, I focused most of my effort on the standing exchanges. I could tell that my opponent was starting to get tired in the last 30 seconds of the first period, so in the second period I put even more pressure on him."

Albanian protests turn violent: What we know
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:26:15 BST
21:26:15 KST

Albanian protests turn violent: What we know
- Published
Protesters and anti-riot police have clashed in Albania's main cities in scenes not witnessed for a long time.
Government buildings have been attacked and some private businesses, too.
So what is happening?
How big and unusual are these protests?
Albania's capital Tirana has seen months of protests from an anti-government "Flamingo" movement, but what started on Tuesday this week was on a different scale.
And the clashes have spread beyond Tirana - to include the main cities of Durrës, Shkodër, Korçë and Vlora.
The new demonstrations were announced as a student movement, ostensibly demanding action by the government to help with the high cost of education fees and books - and the higher cost of living.
Secondary schools joined in, swelling the numbers.
Before too long, masked protesters threw stones at police, and they responded with water cannon, tear gas and batons.
Many were incensed by scenes of a young man being carried away, his broken leg dangling with him in agony.
Apologies were expressed but failed to calm the situation.
A floor of the education ministry was set on fire, with other government institutions ablaze, too.
Every evening, throughout the summer for some 140 days in a row, Albanians in central Tirana would hold pictures of a pink flamingo, calling on Prime Minister Edi Rama - now in his fourth term - to resign.
The protests began over a mega-tourism project on the Adriatic coast linked to US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner. Demonstrators said the bird would become extinct on an island near the coastal city of Vlora, if the plans for a luxury development went ahead.
The public anger comes as allegations of corruption among ministers and other senior officials grow louder.
One deputy prime minister has fled the country, another has been ordered to step down as investigations continue.
- Student protesters attack government buildings in Albania 
  - Published1 day ago
- Kushner-backed luxury resort plan sparks protests in Albania 
  - Published4 June
So has the Flamingo movement radicalised?
The flamingo protesters say they have no links to any political party - one of their slogans being "Rama in jail, Berisha in jail". While Rama is prime minister, Sali Berisha is Albania's main opposition leader - as well as a former prime minister and president.
They were attended by young and old, parents with children and sometimes their grandparents. Some of the participants took pride in cleaning up after every night.
But after months and an unusually hot summer, their numbers dwindled - with no sign that the government was meeting their demands.
The current movement appears far more violent. Dozens of police have been hurt, and the eyes of Europe are now watching what happens next in a country viewed as one of the top candidates for EU membership.
Several young protesters told the BBC that what was going on now was a new phase born of the previous movement.
Five months of peaceful protest had been "met with humiliation, ridicule, mockery," complained one young woman called Livia. "That was a clear message from the government that our voice will not be allowed to be heard."
Another called Brunela said she was worried about what might happen next: "I am very terrified because the media and the government is reacting, especially now. It was not just my voice, it is the voice of Albanian youth."
An overlap between the two sets of protests may well have occurred, even though flamingo leaders have not publicly stated so and no representative of the student movement has come forward.
After all, their main concerns relate to corruption, which the prime minister says must be investigated by the justice system.
How is the government handling the unrest?
Rama has been touring some of the damaged buildings and blaming Sali Berisha for instigating chaos.
"All of this is the work of the very same hand - the hand that has gripped the Albanian opposition by the throat, the hand that has burned and destroyed Albania more than once, and is now prepared to burn and destroy it again to prevent any progress. It is a blind struggle, fuelled by the most irrational hatred," he said on Friday.
The prime minister has ruled out resigning, promising to "listen, address legitimate concerns and keep Albania moving forward".
Berisha's Democratic Party has often tried to get people out to oust Rama.
But the number of his loyal supporters, who have also protested for months and at times clashed with police, has been low in comparison to the current attendance.
So there is some scepticism about Berisha's ability to mastermind the trouble, though he may well seek to capitalise on it.
On the other hand, the Albanian media have suggested that secret services of foreign countries may be involved.
Unfounded allegations have been made against Serbia, with commentators suggesting Belgrade is envious of Albania being often cited as potentially next in line to join the EU.
Indeed, without mentioning names, Prime Minister Rama echoed the allegation on Friday.
"These are foreign hands that do not wish for Albania to be at peace... they do not want Albania to be part of the united European family," he said, adding: "Do you think it is a coincidence that every time Albania receives another green light... or draws closer to that great ambition - that historic objective - flames suddenly erupt? It is no coincidence at all! None of what is happening now is a coincidence."
Is Albania safe to visit?
Although the street violence has taken place in many cities, it remains contained for the time being.
The UK government has urged visitors to check media, external for latest information, stay away from "demonstrations, large-scale gatherings or political rallies" and follow advice of local authorities.
Albania is a popular tourist destination, and the government in Tirana has warned that violence tarnishes the country's image, affecting both tourism and its European path.

MP: Eesti 200 should 'lick its wounds' and sit out 2027 elections
Eesti 200 MPs Ando Kiviberg and Toomas Uibo say their struggling coalition party should skip next March's Riigikogu elections and instead focus on rebuilding for 2031.
Kiviberg told ERR he has not decided whether to run for reelection in March, but if the party decides to run, he would have to act as a team player.
Still, he sees little sense in the party throwing money away at this point, believing Eesti 200 should sit out the 2027 elections instead.
"The party should lick its wounds, do a little soul-searching and commit to preparing properly for 2031," Kiviberg said. He added that he has already discussed the issue with other party members but expects a final decision to be made at Sunday's party council meeting.
Party whip Toomas Uibo, meanwhile, said voters have already made up their minds about Eesti 200, as their rating hit a historic 1.3 percent low in Norstat polls earlier this month.
"I don't know if miracles like this happen, but right now I don't see any point in wasting taxpayer money on running in the elections," he admitted.
While members may still decide on a different course on Sunday, Uibo likewise believes Eesti 200 should instead regroup and focus on the 2031 elections.
Potential Greens merger raises questions
Eesti 200 and the nonparliamentary Estonian Greens are discussing a possible merger, but Kiviberg said this may not necessarily be the right move. "Several party members I've spoken with share my views," he said.
Uibo noted he was unsure whether the two parties have enough in common to unite.
"Of course, you can't expect two different parties to come together and agree on absolutely everything," he said, adding that the question is whether both parties are willing to set enough aside and compromise. "It's still unclear how much common ground we have."
Kiviberg nonetheless ruled out running on another party's ticket next spring and said he has received no such offers. He said he remains committed to Eesti 200 because he believes its ideas are necessary and sound, and will ultimately benefit the country. The question, he said, is how effectively the party has put those ideas into practice.
While Uibo and Kiviberg argued that Eesti 200 should sit out the upcoming elections, fellow MP Peeter Tali told ERR he currently intends to run.
"A politician has to run," Tali said. "If they're no longer a politician, then they don't have to."

Russian strikes and winter hardship may drive more Ukrainians from homes, UN agency warns
GENEVA, Oct 16 - Millions of Ukrainians face another winter of hardship as attacks on critical infrastructure, damaged housing and rising living costs threaten to force more people from their homes, the United Nations migration agency said on Friday.
With temperatures set to fall in the coming months, many families are struggling to secure reliable heating, electricity and water after years of war, the International Organization for Migration said.
This week, Russian missiles and drones have rained down on Ukrainian cities, amid fears that the US could pull back intelligence sharing and weapons support from Kyiv.
"Winter is fast approaching in Ukraine, and for many Ukrainians, the months ahead could be the most difficult since the full-scale war began," Dejan Keserovic, IOM deputy chief of mission in Ukraine, told reporters in Geneva via video link from Kyiv.
Nearly 3.6 million people remain internally displaced across Ukraine since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, while an estimated 3.8 million have returned after displacement, often to damaged or partially destroyed homes, according to the latest IOM figures.
Ukrainians who returned to their homes within the last three months are the most likely to say they intend to leave again, reflecting growing concerns about deteriorating living conditions, the IOM said.
European countries such as Poland, Germany and the Czech Republic currently host around 6 million Ukrainian refugees.
Keserovic said he expected host countries to be preparing for more Ukrainians to leave if the situation got worse.
Repeated Russian strikes on energy and other critical infrastructure have put increasing pressure on Ukraine's electricity, heating and water systems, while drone and missile attacks continue to kill and injure civilians across the country, the IOM said.
Reliable access to water is emerging as a major concern because water systems depend heavily on electricity, the IOM said. The UN agency has installed 31 solar power stations to support water systems across Ukraine, but warned that needs remain immense.
The IOM also warned that funding shortages could hamper aid efforts, with less than 7% of its 2026 Ukraine response plan funded so far, and said urgent resources were needed to improve insulation as households face freezing conditions. REUTERS

American journalist, Palestinians injured in clashes with masked Israeli settlers in West Bank
Several Palestinians and an American photojournalist working for the Washington Post were injured after a group of masked Israeli men clashed with Palestinians harvesting olives in the West Bank, according to videos, eye-witnesses and Palestinian authorities.
Video of the incident obtained by CBS News showed a group of around 20 masked men clad in black or grey clothes descending a hill from the area of an Israeli settlement outpost into an olive grove near the Palestinian village of Abu Falah.
Another video from the incident showed two vehicles set on fire and a Palestinian man with a bloodied face being escorted away from the area by a woman and a man.
Among the injured was Heidi Levine, a veteran American photojournalist working with the Washington Post.
Video shared by the Foreign Press Association showed Levine was surrounded by masked men, pushed to the ground and beaten, and her camera equipment taken from her.
While Levine was on the ground, the masked men launched stones with their arms and slingshots at Palestinians and the Palestinians threw stones at the masked men, the video showed
Levine was taken to a hospital in Ramallah for medical treatment.
Footage of Levine in her hospital bed showed she had a large wound on one of her legs and one of her hands had been bandaged.
"I was attacked, pushed to the ground. Luckily I had my flak jacket and helmet, otherwise I probably wouldn't even be here, because they just kept kicking and kicking me," Levine said from her hospital bed.
The Israeli military said it was looking into the incident and would soon issue a statement.
The Palestine Red Crescent Society said it treated three Palestinians for injuries at Abu Falah. The wounded included a man who had been shot in the thigh, according to WAFA, the official media arm of the Palestinian Authority.
Clashes between Israeli settlers and Palestinian olive pickers also took place near the villages of Burqa and Turmus Ayya, which are located in the central West Bank, WAFA reported. The Palestine Red Crescent treated four people for injuries sustained at the clashes near Burqa, WAFA said.
Attacks against Palestinians in the West Bank have surged in recent years, particularly after the establishment of Israel's current hard-right government in late 2022, according to statistics released by the United Nations humanitarian office.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has condemned the violence and vowed a crackdown against what he says is a small group of several hundred wayward youths responsible for attacks on Palestinians.
Despite those public promises by Netanyahu, the violence has continued in recent weeks.
Over the past 18 days, Yesh Din, an Israeli settlement monitoring group, says it has documented 486 violent incidents against Palestinians across 181 different Palestinian localities, and that 234 of these incidents were related to the olive harvest.
In August, three journalists from NBC and a Palestinian woman they were interviewing were attacked by Israeli settlers in the IWest Bank.

Defence official: Front heats up, energy truce fails as US-Kyiv strain grows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:24:00 UTC
21:24:00 KST

Defence official: Front heats up, energy truce fails as US-Kyiv strain grows
The recent US–Russia diesel deal and a failed energy truce have strained ties with Kyiv at a time when fighting has been escalating at the front, the defense ministry said.
The ministry's intelligence review points to growing friction between Washington and Kyiv as battlefield intensity rises alongside the stalled energy ceasefire.
Speaking at the regular Ministry of Defense Friday press conference, Gert Kaju, head of the ministry's defense readiness department, said a number of significant events had taken place at the strategic level over the past week. He said it became known last Friday that the U.S. had issued the Russian Federation a temporary permit to supply diesel fuel to its market and to the global markets. "According to the expectations of the U.S. leadership, Russia should supply 3 million tons of diesel fuel as quickly as possible, which the U.S. leadership believes should lead to a decline in fuel prices on the U.S. domestic market," Kaju said.
Just over a week earlier the U.S. president had announced a ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia so far as attacks on energy facilities went, but it later emerged that this was a ceasefire arrangement which neither side had agreed to.
Ukraine did attempt to observe the energy ceasefire and refrained from striking Russian oil refineries for three days on the condition that Russia stop attacking Ukraine's electricity generation facilities and transmission networks.
Russia, however, interpreted the agreement as a suspension of attacks only on oil refineries and fuel transportation infrastructure only, and continued striking Ukraine's energy infrastructure. According to Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov, the energy ceasefire proposed by President Donald Trump had not been specified in detail.
The U.S.-Russia diesel supply agreement drew international criticism, some of it from Kyiv. In response, the U.S. raised the question of the need to hold elections and change the government in Ukraine. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy agreed to hold elections on the condition that a 60-day ceasefire be established, but Moscow refused. Russia's leadership believed Ukraine would use the ceasefire to rebuild its forces, and according to Peskov, Moscow was prepared to establish a ceasefire for only 24 hours.
Since Russia had not observed the energy ceasefire, President Zelenskyy announced on October 15 that Ukraine would resume strikes against Russian oil refineries, saying it would be prepared to consider suspending such strikes only if it received assistance in strengthening its missile defense capabilities.
Ukraine counterattacked in the Lyman and Sloviansk sectors in Donetsk oblast
Nearly 230 combat engagements took place per day on the front line over the past week, a rise on the previous week. The most intense fighting took place in Donetsk oblast in the Pokrovsk and Kostiantynivka directions, followed by the Huliaipole direction in Zaporizhzhia oblast, the Southern Slobozhanshchyna direction in Kharkiv oblast and the Lyman sector in Donetsk oblast.
Ukrainian counterattacks took place mainly in the Lyman and Sloviansk directions in Donetsk oblast, the Oleksandrivka area in Dnipropetrovsk oblast and in Sumy oblast. Ukrainian forces pushed back Russian units in the Sloviansk and Kramatorsk sections and strengthened the front line in that sector.
The Russian armed forces' objective remains to reach the borders of Donetsk, Luhansk and Zaporizhzhia oblasts and restore their positions in Dnipropetrovsk oblast, while simultaneously attempting to expand the territory under their control in Sumy and Kharkiv oblasts. At the same time, the Russian Federation lost an average of 1,600 military personnel per day. Russian armed forces' losses remained above 10,000 troops per week, marking the seventh consecutive week that losses had reached this level, the ministry said.
The fighting was also accompanied by extensive airstrikes despite the recent stalled truce. The Russian Federation attacked various targets in at least 19 Ukrainian oblasts (out of a total of 24). Targets of long-range precision strikes included critical infrastructure, residential buildings, government, commercial, educational and medical institutions, the transportation system, the fuel industry and the energy system.
Russia intensively attacks energy infrastructure
The number of strikes against Ukraine's energy infrastructure has steadily increased in recent weeks and multiplied in Kyiv. Between October 4 and 11, Russia attacked Ukraine's energy infrastructure 196 times and its fuel infrastructure 20 times, while Ukrainian energy workers restored electricity supplies to 1.9 million households.
Intensive attacks continued overnight on October 13-14 in Kyiv and Kharkiv oblasts, where 26 energy infrastructure facilities were damaged, including three combined heat and power plants in Kyiv, and according to President Zelenskyy, 600,000 people were left without electricity.
Ukraine responded with extensive long-range strikes. Between October 8 and 10, attacks hit Russian oil refineries in Omsk oblast, Bashkortostan and the Komi Republic, an oil terminal in Rostov oblast and a distribution station in Samara oblast. Attacks resumed on October 15, when a long-range strike hit the Ryazan oil refinery.
In the 242nd week of the war, Ukrainian long-range strikes targeted Yandex data centers in Ryazan, Kaluga and Vladimir oblasts and a Sberbank data center in Saratov oblast for the first time.
Ukraine also attacked companies important to Russia's military-industrial complex in Tver, Nizhny Novgorod and Rostov oblasts, as well as military targets and transport routes in occupied and border areas.
Away from the front line, Russia continued its hybrid activities against countries supporting Ukraine. The Danish Security and Intelligence Service also warned that Russia had launched operations against Danish companies supporting Ukraine in repelling the aggression.
"At the same time, the Finnish Security Intelligence Service noted that Russia poses a real, although not yet immediate, threat to the country's defense industry, which the agency considers an expected development, as Finnish companies operate in the same security environment as the rest of Europe," Kaju added.

Iranian president warns US-Israeli war damaging ecosystems
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:22:28 UTC

Kanyshai Butun
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Friday that the US-Israeli war against Iran is causing serious damage to the country’s ecosystems and called for international mechanisms to protect biodiversity, according to Armenian news agency Armenpress.
Addressing the COP17 Leaders’ Summit in the Armenian capital Yerevan, Pezeshkian warned of the devastating environmental consequences of war, saying military aggression threatens biodiversity, natural resources and future generations.
He said wars destroy forests, fertile lands, wetlands and water resources, while weapons release hazardous chemicals and heavy metals into the environment.
“The destruction of the natural environment is a direct consequence of war. This issue poses a serious threat to the well-being of future generations in our region, including Iran. The environmental consequences of military aggression require urgent security measures from the international community,” he said.
Meanwhile, Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev called for environmental commitments to be translated into practical results, warning that desertification and water scarcity threaten sustainable development and global stability.
He emphasized that environmental issues must take precedence over political differences and that decisions must lead to practical results.
“For millions of people, water shortages and degraded land have already become a daily reality. The most difficult consequence is that this process extends beyond borders, undermining sustainable development and threatening global stability,” Tokayev said.
Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov similarly called for addressing global challenges by strengthening international cooperation and the concerted efforts of all states.
He reaffirmed his country’s support for Armenia’s initiative to establish the Yerevan Platform on Mountain and Freshwater Ecosystems, expressing the readiness to actively engage in its work.
Armenia holds the presidency of COP17, which takes place in Yerevan from Oct. 19 to 30, bringing together government delegations, international organizations, and civil society representatives to assess progress in biodiversity conservation and discuss further action.

Iran says Strait of Hormuz will reopen if U.S. leaves region

Live Updates: Iran says Strait of Hormuz will reopen if U.S. leaves the region
What to know about the Iran war today:
- The Strait of Hormuz will reopen if the U.S. leaves the Middle East, a spokesman for Iran's army said Friday. "If it does not leave, we will expel it," Mohammad Akraminia wrote on X.
- Ships remain exposed to "indiscriminate attacks" in the Strait of Hormuz, even if they try to hide their movements by switching off tracking systems, a maritime monitor warned Thursday, confirming three strikes on vessels in the waterway this week.
- The Iran-backed Houthis launched a strike Thursday on the presidential palace in Yemen's government-held de facto capital of Aden. The attack caused multiple deaths and injuries among the security staff, according to the internationally recognized government.
Iranian navy says a tanker is burning in the Gulf of Oman
The Iranian navy said Friday that it had identified a tanker on fire in what it called a prohibited area in the Gulf of Oman, east of the Strait of Hormuz.
The navy's public relations office said in a statement that military surveillance teams "discovered and identified a violating oil tanker that had caught fire in a prohibited area."
The vessel had "switched off its tracking systems and was attempting to pass through a prohibited area in the Gulf of Oman."
The navy did not say how the tanker "caught fire" but added that "the consequences of uncoordinated movements along routes and in prohibited areas are the creation of insecurity and serious hazards for other vessels."
At least three commercial vessels have been struck in the region in suspected Iranian attacks this week.
Iran says the Strait of Hormuz will reopen if the U.S. "leaves the region"
The Strait of Hormuz will reopen if the U.S. "leaves" the Middle East, an Iranian army official said Friday.
"If the United States leaves the region, the Strait of Hormuz will reopen and collective security will be established with the participation of the countries of the region, and the global economy will improve," army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia wrote on X. "If it does not leave, we will expel it."
He did not elaborate on whether he was calling for a withdrawal of military forces sent during the current war, all U.S. military forces across the region, or military and non-military U.S. government personnel.
Though there were credible reports earlier this month of oil exports from the Persian Gulf ramping back up to near pre-war levels, Iran and the U.S. continue offering conflicting narratives, with the Trump administration insisting the Strait of Hormuz is open, but Tehran claiming it is closed to all traffic unless Iranian authorities grant permission.
Greek maritime risk firm Marisks warned Thursday that ships continue to face "indiscriminate attacks," even if they turned off their tracking systems, which many ships have been doing to avoid detection.
Iran president says conflict in Mideast amounts to "ecocide"
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on Friday urged countries to condemn what he called "ecocide" in the Middle East caused by "wars of aggression" against his country.
Pezeshkian said the conflicts in Gaza and the wider Middle East had taken a significant toll on nature that extended beyond national borders and required "international solutions."
"What has occurred in our region as a result of wars of aggression is ecocide, or environmental genocide, and it must be condemned," Pezeshkian said at a nature summit in Armenia that was attended by United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres.
Pezeshkian decried an "atmosphere of distrust" between Iran and the U.S. in a recent interview with CBS News.
"As long as they don't cease doing what they're imposing on us every day, it's difficult to trust them," he said. "Every day, they increase the sanctions against us. Every day, they threaten us. Every day, they strike us, and they don't honor what they have put in writing. So, if they engage in talks, will they actually follow through?"
CBS/AFP
White House prepares plans to use weapon dubbed "mother of all bombs" on Iran, sources say
The White House and Pentagon have prepared plans to use a Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb to hit military sites in Iran if ordered by President Trump, sources familiar with the matter told CBS News.
A Pentagon official told CBS News: "The Department of War plans for a wide range of operational scenarios to execute Presidential and Secretary level direction and to ensure mission success in any operational environment."
A White House spokesperson said: "We do not comment on sensitive military plans that may or may not exist. President Trump keeps all options on the table to ensure that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon."
Last week, Mr. Trump said the U.S. would not attack Iran before the midterm elections. He also touted "productive conversations" with Iran, though he did not provide specifics.
CNN first reported Thursday on the plans to use the Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb, or MOAB, on Iran.
Mr. Trump set a precedent for using the MOAB, also known as the "mother of all bombs," when it was used in 2017 to attack an Islamic State cave complex in Afghanistan. The bomb is the largest U.S. non-nuclear weapon, weighing upwards of 30,000 pounds at a cost of $170,000 per unit.

Pakistan orders school inspections following deadly roof collapse
Families demand justice for the 35 people killed; relatives say they had warned that the roof was leaking.
Authorities in Pakistan have ordered inspections of regional schools after the collapse of a classroom roof killed at least 34 children and a teacher.
Reports on Friday said that the government has ordered the administration of the northeastern province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa to launch the checks after the deadly incident at Al-Khair school on Thursday.
At least 34 students aged 13 or younger, as well as a teacher, were killed in the roof collapse.
There are conflicting reports about whether the inspections will cover both public and private schools or only private schools. The province’s education department has been given three days to report its findings, according to The Associated Press news agency.
Schools are to be classified as safe, in need of repairs or improvements, or potentially unsafe. Various structures will be assessed, including roofs, ceilings, walls and staircases.
Police arrested Mohammad Khan, the owner of Al-Khair school, shortly after the roof of mud and bricks collapsed.
The building was structurally weak, according to Peshawar Police Chief Saeed Ahmed, who also said that Khan had told officers that recent rains had weakened the structure.
Bereaved families are demanding justice, with some of the victims’ relatives maintaining that they had warned Khan about rainwater repeatedly seeping into classrooms.
Dozens of mourners gathered outside the school on Friday to remember those who died.
Pakistan’s construction standards are widely reported to be poor and builders commonly use substandard materials.

Russia seizes more EU companies’ assets over Ukraine support
- Russia seized assets of four EU companies, including Tarkett, Menshen, Sverige International Holdings and Ontex, in retaliation for Europe’s support for Ukraine.
- The Kremlin said the move was linked to “illegal expropriations of Russian property” and was “reversible”, while Putin warned of “certain downsides” for taking Western assets.
- The companies said they were assessing the impact, as EU leaders backed Zelensky and Russia criticised the EU for freezing about €210 billion of its sovereign assets.
AI generated
MOSCOW – Russia has seized local assets of four companies from France, Germany, Sweden and Belgium, according to a decree by President Vladimir Putin, in retaliation for Europe’s wartime support for Ukraine.
The decree on Oct 15 listed assets belonging to French flooring maker Tarkett, German packaging maker Menshen, Swedish packaging maker Sverige International Holdings and Belgian hygiene product company Ontex.
The decree also listed Russian assets of former European metal-packaging business Eviosys acquired by US packaging group Sonoco in December 2024. The decree listed the assets as owned by Sonoco’s Dutch unit.
EU leaders rallied around President Volodymyr Zelensky at a summit on Oct 16 at one of the most difficult moments for Ukraine amid fears that the US could pull back intelligence sharing and weapons support from Kyiv.
The Kremlin said that the assets’ takeover continued a trend after a similar move in September against food giant Nestle and retailers Auchan and Metro.
“Their country of origin was one of the factors taken into account in making the decision,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said, adding that these countries were involved in “illegal expropriations of Russian property”.
Temporary administration of the European companies’ properties was handed to Russian companies that had been largely unknown.
Putin notes ‘downsides’
Ontex, which employs 350 people in Russia and operates a factory outside Moscow, said it has been informed about the decree and will “consider appropriate actions to safeguard its assets and the continuity of Ontex Russia’s operations”.
Sonoco said in its 2025 report that it had finalised its own exit from Russia in 2022 but acquired more assets, making up 0.5% of the company’s total, as part of the Eviosys deal.
Tarkett said it was “losing effective control over its operations in Russia” and was assessing the situation.
The Kremlin said the measures responded to EU nations’ involvement in “direct battlefield hostilities” but were also “reversible”.
Speaking to Russian businessmen just before the decree was published on Oct 15, Putin acknowledged that taking Western assets had “certain downsides” without giving more details.
He urged the Russian businesses taking over the assets to seek domestic financing sources instead.
Putin cited the 2008 global financial crisis, which had a profound impact on the Russian economy, as an example of the risks of excessive exposure to global markets. He said foreign countries pursued their own interests through investment.
There have been some reports that the US could seek control of some Russian assets frozen in Europe as part of efforts to provide incentives for Russia to negotiate with Ukraine.
Russia criticises the EU for freezing about €210 billion (S$302 billion) of its sovereign assets in response to the war and for targeting assets belonging to Russian companies in Europe and other Western countries. REUTERS

Self-employment declines as freelancers quickly find new jobs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:14:18 UTC
21:14:18 KST

Self-employment declines as freelancers quickly find new jobs
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
After two decades of mostly uninterrupted growth, self-employment in the Netherlands has declined this year for the first time, with former freelancers quickly finding new jobs, according to the Dutch central bank (DNB).
There are 10% fewer self-employed workers this year than in 2024. Their numbers have fallen by some 131,000 since the end of 2024, when they peaked at almost 1.3 million.
In mid-2026, around 12% of the workforce was primarily self-employed, still a substantial share by international standards.
Little impact on unemployment
But according to the DNB, the decline has had little impact on unemployment, with half of former freelancers finding paid work within three months. About a third move to permanent positions or to jobs with prospects of a permanent contract. Others move into flex work. Only 7% become unemployed, which is comparable to previous years.
“Leaving self-employment therefore mainly results in movement within the labour market rather than a greater flow into unemployment,” the DNB said.
About half of former self-employed workers move to different sectors entirely, especially healthcare and social care, education and government, retail, transport and hospitality.
The DNB says this confirms that the Dutch labour market is dynamic. However, its research does not show how people’s income, productivity or employment conditions change after they leave self-employment for new work.
The DNB says it cannot say definitively why the decrease is happening. It does note that stricter enforcement against so-called false self-employment since 2025 may play a role.
“We observe relatively high levels of movement between self-employment and employment in sectors where false self-employment is frequently debated, including healthcare, construction, facility services and business services,” it said.

Ukrainian embroidered clothing brand Etnodim has partnered with British content creator of Ukrainian origin Max Klymenko to launch a charity shirt inspired by his popular TikTok series Career Ladder, with profits from sales going toward supporting Ukrainian children affected by Russia’s war.
The collaboration brings together Klymenko’s internationally recognized social media project, which has helped him attract nearly 10 million TikTok followers, and traditional Ukrainian craftsmanship.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
In his Career Ladder series, Klymenko interviews people from a wide range of professions, including public figures such as Will Smith, Gordon Ramsay, French President Emmanuel Macron, and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
The concept of exploring different careers inspired Klymenko and the Etnodim team to highlight traditional Ukrainian occupations, some of which are gradually disappearing.
The resulting shirt features embroidered representations of historic crafts and professions, including blacksmithing, pottery, harvesting, and milling, reflecting the importance of preserving Ukraine’s cultural heritage.
“We wanted to convey the idea of equal opportunities without stereotypes and remind people that every profession has its own value. The embroidery features traditional Ukrainian crafts that are gradually disappearing, including blacksmithing, pottery, harvesting and milling. The composition on the shirt’s side panel is inspired by Apple Picker, a work by Ukrainian artist Oleksandr Saienko,” the Etnodim team explains.
Beyond its connection to the TikTok series, the design also draws on Klymenko’s personal memories of growing up in Ukraine, particularly his childhood experiences with his grandmother.
According to the press release, conversations about his upbringing, family memories, and current work helped shape the creative direction of the collaboration.
“When I think about my childhood, I immediately think of my grandmother: the time I spent with her, the little forts made of yarn I used to build when visiting her, and all the wonderful things in her house that have stayed in my memory. Decorative plates, a large wooden spoon with classic red and colourful Ukrainian patterns, and a knitted picture of Mykolaiv landscapes hanging on the wall—that picture is probably the most vivid work of art I remember from childhood,” Klymenko said.
The partnership also reflects Klymenko’s continued involvement in charitable initiatives supporting Ukraine and his efforts to introduce Ukrainian culture and experiences to international audiences.
As part of the initiative, profits from sales of the Career Ladder shirt will be donated to Kids of Ukraine to support its SviTY programme, which assists teenagers affected by the war.
The programme focuses on emotional recovery, education, and personal development, helping young people acquire new skills, identify their strengths, and explore future career opportunities.
Through the collaboration, Etnodim and Klymenko aim to combine the promotion of traditional Ukrainian crafts with practical support for children and teenagers navigating their futures amid the ongoing war.
In another recent collaboration, German sportswear brand PUMA joined forces with Ukrainian fashion label CHER’17, marking its first partnership with a local fashion brand in Ukraine.
According to a press release, the CHER’17 x PUMA collection explores the unpredictability of everyday life under the campaign slogan “No plan is a plan.” The collection reinterprets PUMA’s signature designs through details inspired by unexpected mishaps and everyday imperfections.

Ukraine Could Get Starlink Deep Inside Russia in Exchange for 100-Day Oil Strike Pause, WSJ Says

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Could Get Starlink Deep Inside Russia in Exchange for 100-Day Oil Strike Pause, WSJ Says
Two Republican US senators have proposed expanding Starlink coverage roughly 300 kilometers, or 186 miles, inside Russia in exchange for Ukraine suspending strikes on Russian oil refineries for 100 days, The Wall Street Journal reported on October 15, citing people familiar with the discussions.
Senators Roger Wicker and Kevin Cramer presented the proposal to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy during an October 9 visit to Kyiv as part of a bipartisan congressional delegation, according to the report.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Zelenskyy indicated that he was prepared to accept such an arrangement, the sources said.
The expanded coverage could give Ukrainian forces reliable satellite connectivity during operations against Russian ballistic missile launchers located deeper behind the border.
That would potentially allow Ukraine to target the systems before they launch missiles rather than relying solely on air defenses to intercept incoming weapons after they are fired.
Zelenskyy has publicly said Ukraine could also consider halting strikes on Russian refineries in return for additional US-made Patriot interceptors. The Starlink proposal would offer a different form of protection by helping Ukrainian forces target the launch platforms themselves.
According to the WSJ, the senators viewed the proposed arrangement as a possible first step toward reviving a stalled diplomatic process.
The discussions come amid growing pressure from Washington for Kyiv to halt attacks on Russian oil infrastructure. US President Donald Trump announced an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine on October 11, after which Ukraine temporarily suspended strikes on Russian energy facilities.
Despite Kyiv observing the pause, Ukrainian forces subsequently stopped receiving US early warnings about Russian ballistic missile launches, according to Ukrainian officials. The military version of Starlink, Starshield, was also restricted, complicating frontline operations and middle-strike missions against Russian military targets.
Reuters separately reported that the instruction to restrict Starshield came from the White House, although its sources did not identify who specifically ordered the measure. A senior US official said Trump personally had not issued the order.
Previously, Ukraine lifted restrictions on strikes against Russian oil refineries and other energy infrastructure after observing a three-day pause requested by Washington, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated.
“The ban has been lifted. We’ve had enough,” Zelenskyy said.

Joaquim Letria, regarded as one of the leading figures in Portuguese journalism, died this Friday at the age of 82.
Veteran journalist and writer Joaquim Letria died on Friday at the age of 82. The news was first reported by the newspaper Observador, quoting a source close to him.
Joaquim Letria is regarded as one of the leading figures in Portuguese journalism. He founded the weekly newspapers O Jornal and Tal & Qual and later served as director of news at the public broadcaster RTP in the years following the 25 April revolution. Letria was also elected president of the Journalists' Union.
He began his journalism career in 1963 at the Diário de Lisboa and went on to build an international track record, first at the news agency The Associated Press and later as a correspondent for Deutsche-Presse Agentur until 1970. Letria also worked for the BBC in London.

EU summit: European leaders pledge support for Ukraine's Zelenskyy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:10:00 UTC
21:10:00 KST

EU summit: European leaders pledge support for Ukraine's Zelenskyy
October 16, 2026
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy attended the final day of an EU summit in Brussels on Friday as European leaders pledged continued support for the Ukrainian leader and his country in a turbulent week.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa both took the fore in calling on allies to continue their support of Kyiv as it faces increased Russian attacks and detrimental US foreign policy decisions.
What did EU leaders say about the bloc's support for Ukraine?
"This is no time to withdraw support to Ukraine," said Costa as he stood next to the Ukrainian president. "This is no time to relieve Russia's sanctions. Now it is time to increase our support, to increase our pressure."
"One thing is absolutely clear," pledged von der Leyen, "we will not lift any sanctions unless Russia stops this war."
The EU leaders' remarks come just one week after Ukraine and its European allies were blindsided by US President Donald Trump's unilateral decision to lift sanctions on Russian oil exports and purchase diesel from the Kremlin after a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
On Wednesday, a US official said Washington was also considering easing sanctions on Russia's shadow fleet — unflagged tankers that turn off transponders to transport and transfer illicit oil while circumventing international export sanctions.
After undermining years of Western sanctions against Russia over its illegal invasion of Ukraine, Trump is now seeking to increase pressure on Ukraine — calling for Zelenskyy to be replaced as its leader and blasting Kyiv's targeting of Russian energy infrastructure as a "disgrace."
Trump seeks to deflect blame for high energy prices onto Ukraine
Upon arrival at Friday's Brussels summit, Zelenskyy said, "We want to end this war as quick as possible. We don't see now signals from the Russian side that they are ready for this, to end this war, that's why we have to prepare for the winter."
"The winter package is not only energy, it's also air defense and funding," he added.
When asked after his meeting with EU leaders if Trump was scapegoating him for troubles in the US, Zelensky gave a knowing smile and stayed mum. "This is my answer," the Ukrainian president said, as journalists broke into laughter at a press conference in Brussels.
Trump last week justified his calls for Zelenskyy to be removed from office by claiming the Ukrainian leader did not want to stop the war — which Russia launched on February 24, 2022 — as well as attempting to divert anger over high global fuel prices away from his own war in Iran, which triggered the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and sent global oil and gas prices through the roof.
"All he's doing is making the world oil price higher," Trump told far-right US media outlet Newsmax on Thursday. Asked about Ukraine resuming attacks on Russian energy infrastructure, Trump said, "Well, I think that's a disgrace."
Earlier this week, Kyiv reported restrictions on its use of Elon Musk's Starshield system, Starlink's military-grade satellite service which Ukraine relies on for its battlefield communications, mid-range strikes on Russian-occupied territories and interceptor drones.
Zelenskyy hails 'very good' meeting with Hungary PM
The Ukrainian president also praised his first bilateral meeting with Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar on the sidelines of the summit.
"We had a very good meeting," Zelenskyy told reporters in Brussels. He added that he and Magyar had discussed "many things, including relations, the economy, and logistics — all of which are important to our two countries."
Zelenskyy also said that he "won't mind" visiting Budapest.
After meeting, Magyar announced that Budapest and Kyiv had agreed to put their relations on a new footing.
"I assured the Ukrainian president of my full solidarity over the inhuman Russian aggression against his country," Magyar wrote in a Facebook post. He also said that Hungary was ready to assist Ukraine by all possible diplomatic means to reach a ceasefire and lasting peace.
The meeting occurred just days after Kyiv passed legislation addressing Budapest's long-standing concerns regarding the rights of the ethnic Hungarian minority in western Ukraine.

Europe's far right has a Putin problem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:09:43 UTC
21:09:43 KST

Europe's far right has a Putin problem
Rassemblement National (RN) candidate Marine Le Pen in Paris, France, on Sept. 28, 2026. (Anne-Christine Poujoulat / AFP via Getty Images)
Europe's far-right parties grow increasingly divided on something that once united them — sympathies for Vladimir Putin's Russia.
As nationalists and right-wing populists across Western Europe move closer to power, many are seeking to distance themselves from their past admiration for a country waging Europe's largest war since 1945 while conducting hybrid attacks against much of the continent.
Despite finding common ground on dislike of liberalism, NATO, and the EU, Europe's far right is being forced to rethink its relationship with Moscow — much like it had to do with U.S. President Donald Trump.
France's National Rally (RN) and the U.K.'s Nigel Farage now harden rhetoric on Russia while signaling a more conditional, rather than simply hostile, approach to Ukraine, as part of a strategy to cast a wider net of voters.
But the Alternative for Germany (AfD), which has emerged as Europe's largest and most extreme nationalist party, is moving in the opposite direction.
The split comes at a critical moment. The National Rally's Marine Le Pen is a frontrunner for the French presidential election next April, the AfD is leading the German polls, and Farage's Reform party was, until very recently, a favorite to win the next elections in Britain.
Experts who spoke to the Kyiv Independent explain the reasons behind this divide and what the coming string of European elections could mean for Ukraine.
Farage, Le Pen seek Russia detox
For years, far-right leaders have been ranked among the most Moscow-friendly voices in European politics.
In 2014, Farage, the man who later led a campaign to push the U.K. out of the EU and whose Reform party now polls second at 22%, expressed his admiration for Putin as an "operator."
As recently as 2024, while Russia’s full-scale invasion had already been raging for two years, he suggested that the eastward expansion of the EU and NATO provoked the war.
Comments like these have made it easy for his opponents to blast him as a Putin fan.
Now, Farage seems intent on proving he is no such thing.
"Russia in general and Putin in particular are extremely unpopular with Brits, so why would they want to convey the impression that they have any sympathy with them?"
Last year, the Reform leader called the Russian dictator a "very bad dude" and said NATO should shoot down Russian jets intruding into its airspace.
On Ukraine, he has cautiously affirmed support for Ukraine — even backing the idea of using frozen Russian assets for Kyiv's benefit.
And while he criticized plans for a post-war "reassurance" force in Ukraine as outlined by the Labor government, Farage backed sending British troops to the country, if on a temporary basis and as part of a U.N. peacekeeping mission.
Reports have emerged that Farage is even considering a trip to Ukraine as part of his quest to brush off his Russia-friendly image.
A similar shift is taking place across the English Channel.
Prior to 2022, Le Pen said that the Russian occupation of Crimea was not illegal, and her party took out a loan from a Russian bank.
But after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, she backpedaled.
Now, the three-time failed presidential candidate sees she has a real chance to win, with a court clearing a path to her candidacy despite last year's embezzlement conviction.
As the vote nears, she is treading cautiously on foreign policy.
Le Pen has condemned Russian aggression and has backed continued military assistance to Ukraine, even as she wants Paris to cut financial aid — citing France's own budget constraints — opposes Kyiv's EU membership, and is skeptical about future EU aid if it burdens France.
She also said she would be happy to visit Ukraine for talks with President Volodymyr Zelensky.
The RN's younger co-leader, Jordan Bardella, has taken a tougher stance on Russia, naming the country a threat — something that Le Pen avoided in a recent interview with the Financial Times.
Both party chiefs also blasted Moscow in September over its seizure of European business assets in the country and denounced Russian interference and destabilization efforts.
Elsewhere in Europe, far-right parties have proved they can tone down their views on Russia and Ukraine in exchange for government seats.
Matteo Salvini, head of Italy's League party, remembered for once sporting a T-shirt with Putin's likeness, has largely fallen in line behind Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's firmly pro-Western, pro-Ukraine course, save for some symbolic resistance.
And the former Dutch government also maintained its support for Kyiv, even though Geert Wilders's far-right Party for Freedom (PVV) was the strongest party in a short-lived coalition.
Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis, a right-wing populist, while expressing his disdain for EU plans to earmark billions of euros of support for Ukraine, echoed Zelensky's take on a set of recent pro-Russian moves made by the U.S.
"Trump effectively betrayed us by concluding the business deal with Putin, and we have to do something," Babis said on Oct. 16.
Elsewhere, the far right doubles down
This shift is far from uniform, however.
As Meloni, Italy's right-wing, anti-immigration prime minister, prepares for the 2027 elections, she faces a new pro-Kremlin challenger.
Roberto Vannacci, a retired army general, left the League in February to found his own nationalist party, National Future.
Vannacci, a former military attaché in Moscow, has famously said he prefers Putin over Zelensky.
With support reaching as high as 8% in recent polls, National Future has already surpassed Meloni's junior coalition partners.
But the most striking example is the AfD, currently the strongest opposition party in Germany, nearing 30% in polls.
The AfD was seen as so extreme that the far-right European Parliament group expelled it at the RN's urging in 2024, prompting the AfD to form a new ultranationalist coalition, Europe of Sovereign Nations (ESN).
The party campaigns on a halt to military and financial aid to Ukraine, the lifting of sanctions against Russia, and the resumption of Russian energy purchases.
Given the AfD's particular brand of extremism and Berlin's role as the leading military donor to Ukraine, this is an especially worrying signal for Kyiv and Europe.
Like in the U.K., the next German parliamentary elections are expected no later than 2029.
Why the difference
With Russia's full-scale war nearing its fifth anniversary, many countries have seen the public's support for Ukraine cool — but not collapse.
Politicians vying for victory in upcoming elections have to take this into account, with the U.K. being a prime example.
Farage's party certainly has a reputation to fix, after its former leader in Wales, Nathan Gill, was sentenced to prison for taking bribes from pro-Russian Ukrainian politicians.
"Russia in general and Putin in particular are extremely unpopular with Brits, so why would they want to convey the impression that they have any sympathy with them?" Tim Bale, a professor of politics at Queen Mary University of London, comments on Reform's strategy.
A poll from last fall shows that 59% of Brits support continued assistance to Ukraine, and slightly over half back sanctions even at the cost of paying more for energy and food.
The support is somewhat cooler in France, where 47% favor continued arms deliveries to Ukraine, down from 65% in 2022.
Yet this is not an insignificant number, and the majority of French people — including a little over half of RN voters — see Russia as an enemy, according to polls.
Anton Shekhovtsov, a visiting senior fellow at Central European University in Vienna, notes that Le Pen likely remembers well the "reputational nightmare" her Russian loan has caused.
"Everybody just pointed to that loan and said, 'you're all Russian Trojan horses in France,'" Shekhovtsov said in comments for the Kyiv Independent.
Now, Le Pen likely sees an example in Meloni — a politician who emerged from a similar far-right background but maintained a pro-Western course, the expert notes. Meloni's government has been Italy's longest-serving since World War II.
But the AfD has doubled down on its pro-Russian course, despite the majority of Germans continuing to support Ukraine. It does not seem to be hindering its rise.
Jakub Wondreys, a researcher at the Hannah Arendt Institute for the Research on Totalitarianism in Dresden, offers an explanation.
"The key factor is the party's internal division, which we don't see elsewhere. It is specific to German politics, and to the AfD itself," Wondreys tells the Kyiv Independent.
While all parties have different wings, the AfD is notably decentralized, with the former border between West and East Germany surviving as a key divide.
The AfD's extremist, more Moscow-friendly wing is rooted in East Germany, a former Soviet satellite state. The "moderates" are stronger in the west, the researcher explains.
The AfD is growing nationwide, but the east remains its main stronghold — as evidenced by its recent victories in regional elections there. This means that the more extreme wing of the party is also its loudest and most influential one.
This split was laid bare when the AfD's two leaders, Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla, disagreed over a trip by a group of their colleagues to Sochi last November.
Weidel, who hails from what was West Germany, criticized the visit, while Chrupalla, himself born in socialist East Germany, downplayed it, adding that he does not consider Russia a threat.
Recent polls show that 54% of Germans from what was East Germany think aid to Ukraine has gone too far, compared to 39% in the west. Eastern Germans are also less likely to see Russia as a threat.
Yet even an RN or Reform victory would not bode well for Ukraine, regardless of their change of rhetoric, experts warn.
As Bale points out, no matter its public posturing, a Reform government "might try to spend less money on defense aid behind everyone's back."
Just on Oct. 12, Farage pledged to take a "keen look" at whether British aid to Ukraine is being swallowed up by corruption there and signaled that London's support cannot be limitless.
The RN's victory might not end military support for Ukraine, but it will likely curtail the financial assistance and weaken the European sanctions push against Moscow.
And Shekhovtsov warns that even if Le Pen does not adopt overtly pro-Russian positions after the elections, her victory could be such an upset for France and Europe that it might shift political attention away from supporting Ukraine.
The coming election season has the potential to shake the European pro-Ukraine coalition to its core.

Tokayev calls for greater international cooperation to preserve biodiversity
Head of State Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has addressed the COP17 Leaders’ Summit on Biodiversity in Yerevan, Armenia, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing the press service of Akorda.
Welcoming the Summit participants, the Head of State thanked the Prime Minister of Armenia, Nikol Pashinyan, for a warm welcome and a high level of organization of the event.
In his remarks, the President emphasized the need to coordinate international efforts and uphold a shared responsibility to future generations for preserving the environment
"We have gathered here to expand international cooperation aimed at preserving our shared natural heritage. This is a collective responsibility to future generations, who may face serious challenges and threats. It is also a matter of survival for our civilization, as biodiversity is vital to human well-being, economic resilience, and long-term security. Healthy ecosystems play a crucial role in food production, the protection of water resources, and the livelihoods of millions of people.
At the same time, desertification, water scarcity, and other environmental challenges pose a serious threat to the fragile balance between people and nature. For millions, water shortages and land degradation have already become an everyday reality. Most concerning is that these processes transcend national borders, undermining sustainable development and threatening global stability.
Environmental agenda, based on a balanced approach and concrete action, must take precedence over political differences. Our shared priority should be international cooperation based on true partnership, impartiality, and, above all, a commitment to achieve practical results," the President said.

Tokayev highlights Kazakhstan's success in restoring rare animal populations
