Tokayev highlights Kazakhstan's success in restoring rare animal populations
President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said Kazakhstan has achieved significant progress in biodiversity conservation, citing the recovery of populations of the saiga antelope, snow leopard, Turan tiger, Przewalski's horse and Caspian seal, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing the press service of Akorda.
The President described the revival of the saiga population as one of the country's greatest conservation achievements.
“This ancient animal survived the last Ice Age and remains very essential to the natural balance of our steppes. Today Kazakhstan is home to around 98 percent of the world’s saiga population. In 2003, just 21,000 species remained in our country. By the spring of this year, their numbers had reached an estimated 4.7 million,” Tokayev said.
He also noted encouraging signs in the recovery of the snow leopard, “a proud symbol of our mountain heritage.”
“Around 70 percent of its range in our country are within protected areas. Reliable and sustained protection and systematic scientific monitoring have helped its population grow from critically low levels of 90s last century to nearly 190 animals today. Behind all these recoveries are years of hard and dedicated, determined work by the authorities, scientists and international partners,” he noted.
Kassym-Jomart Tokayev expressed his gratitude to the Russian Federation and its President, as well as the United Nations Development Programme, the World Wildlife Fund, and other international partners, including NGOs, for their assistance in restoring the population of the Turan tiger.
He emphasized that in July this year, a tiger was released into the wild for the first time in 70 years, marking a milestone for Kazakhstan.
The Head of State also noted that efforts are underway, in cooperation with Czech, German and Hungarian partners, to reintroduce the Przewalski’s horse to Kazakhstan.
The President also highlighted the need to protect the Caspian Sea and its unique biodiversity.
“At the recent first Caspian Environmental Summit in Turkmenistan, I called for urgent, coordinated action to prevent fatal damage to this fragile ecosystem. The future of Caspian seals causes a particular concern. Its population has fallen from one million to 270,000 over the past century. In Kazakhstan, the Caspian seal has been officially listed as a rare and endangered animal. We urge all five littoral states and international community to increase efforts to protect these species. The tragedy of the Aral Sea is a stark reminder of the devastating cost of reckless exploitation of nature and we must not allow the Caspian Sea to suffer the same fate,” Kassym-Jomart Tokayev emphasized

Evening newswrap: CJP's Dipke detained, Rajnath alleges regime change bid and Rahul's cryptic Rubio post

Millions of Ukrainians who fled Russia’s full-scale invasion and later returned home are at risk of being displaced again over the coming winter, the United Nations warned Friday.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Winter is fast approaching in Ukraine and for many Ukrainians the months ahead could be the most difficult since the full-scale war began,” said Arthur Erken, the IOM’s regional director for Europe and central Asia.
“Millions of Ukrainians who fled and returned are now at risk of being displaced once again, as conditions deteriorate by the day and people face desperate choices in the struggle to survive.”
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of neighbouring Ukraine in February 2022, triggering the biggest refugee crisis in Europe since World War II.
- Fragile existence -
The agency estimates that nearly 3.6 million people remain internally displaced within Ukraine. Around 3.8 million people have returned to their homes, which are often damaged.
It said an estimated 1.45 million returnees lived in frontline districts, including 565,000 in the Kharkiv region alone.
Erken said Russian drone attacks “tend to attack civilian infrastructure”, and repeated strikes had damaged Ukraine’s electricity, heating and water systems.
He said reliable access to water was an urgent concern because water systems depend on electricity.

The IOM has developed 31 solar power stations across the country to support water systems, as these were “harder to attack and harder to destroy completely”.

UN says Gaza malnutrition gains fragile as commercial supplies halt
GENEVA, Oct 16 - Gains in tackling malnutrition in Gaza remain fragile and could be undermined by disruptions to supplies entering the Palestinian enclave, the UN children's agency UNICEF said on Friday, urging that all crossings remain open.
Israel said on Wednesday commercial goods were no longer entering Gaza because of what it described as a dispute over taxes between local merchants and militant group Hamas.
That has cut off a vital source of food and other goods in a territory where most depend on humanitarian assistance after three years of war, repeated displacement and stringent Israeli restrictions on aid deliveries.
Although the ceasefire has improved aid access and reduced large-scale fighting, humanitarian agencies say ongoing strikes, continued displacement and widespread destruction have left civilians highly vulnerable.
Speaking to reporters in Geneva, UNICEF spokesperson Ricardo Pires said the flow of both commercial and humanitarian supplies must remain predictable and continuous.
“The impact on children obviously will be felt if this situation is not resolved," he said.
"We can't go back to a situation where children and families are not getting all the supplies, goods, and services that they require."
A new UNICEF report published on Friday found that while the ceasefire since October has allowed more humanitarian aid and commercial supplies to enter, acute malnutrition remains a risk.
The report said progress in pushing back the threat of famine, confirmed by a global food security monitor in August last year, had been achieved through a scaled-up food and nutrition response, the easing of restrictions on the entry of food and nutrition supplies, and the ceasefire.
However, those gains remain fragile, it said.
“Acute malnutrition rates have fallen, but only one in three children under the age of two is currently achieving minimum dietary diversity,” the report stated. A survey conducted by UNICEF in June also found a significant prevalence of chronic malnutrition, affecting one in eight children under five.
UNICEF also called for improvements in living conditions in the largely devastated enclave, where some 800,000 children are still displaced and most live in tents or unsafe buildings as winter approaches, saying better shelter and basic services are essential to support a lasting recovery. REUTERS

Explainer-Why is the battle for Yemen's Taiz so important?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:05:27 UTC
21:05:27 KST

Explainer-Why is the battle for Yemen's Taiz so important?
Oct 16 - The city of Taiz is rapidly emerging as the most important battlefront in Yemen's reignited civil war, pitting the Iran-allied Houthis against the internationally recognised government, which is backed by a Saudi-led coalition.
Houthi forces have encircled Taiz in recent weeks by cutting its main road south to Aden, causing widespread displacement and worsening a humanitarian crisis.
Here's what you need to know:
WHY IS TAIZ SO IMPORTANT?
Any Houthi victory in Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city, would mark one of the biggest turning points in the country's long civil war, which resumed this summer after a four-year truce.
Taiz city has an estimated population of almost 600,000, said Katja Juric, Aden-based head of programmes for the International Organization for Migration (IOM). Government sources said 80,000 had fled in the latest fighting.
Taiz has been on the frontline between the Houthis and the government since the first days of the conflict that started in early 2015 and has long been seen as a bastion of opposition to the Iran-allied group.
It is the last major urban stronghold of anti-Houthi forces in the southern highland area of Yemen: the rugged hills above both Aden, where the internationally recognised government is based, and the flat coastal plain around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
A Houthi takeover of Taiz would make it much harder for government forces to maintain their counterattack around Bab el-Mandeb and keep the Houthis at arm's length from Aden.
It would also mean a resounding symbolic defeat for the government and the military coalition of Saudi-backed Yemeni forces fighting the Houthis.
WHAT'S THE MILITARY SITUATION AROUND TAIZ?
For years the city has sat at the tip of a government salient stretching north into Houthi territory.
The Houthis held areas to the north, east and west of Taiz, while government forces had the city and its immediate surroundings including Jebel Sabar, the high mountain rising above it to the south.
As fighting in Yemen resumed in recent weeks, the Houthis began making advances to cut off Taiz by seizing territory to the south of Jebel Sabar along the road to Aden, which snakes about 200 km (125 miles) through rugged hills where fighting is slow and difficult.
Sections of the road are now under Houthi control, including at the towns of al-Turbah and Mudiriyat al-Misrakh, leaving Taiz encircled since early October, with the Houthis sometimes shelling government positions in and around the city.
Government forces, backed by airstrikes from the Saudi-led coalition, are trying to drive the Houthis back from their recent gains and reopen the road, but were still losing ground around Taiz rather than recapturing territory in mid-October.
WHY IS TAIZ A STRONGHOLD OF OPPOSITION TO THE HOUTHIS?
Taiz had a long history of difficult ties with rulers from north Yemen and was a hotbed of the 2011 Arab Spring uprisings that toppled veteran former president Ali Abdullah Saleh.
While the Houthis adhere to the Zaydi school of Shi'ite Islam, Taiz is predominantly Sunni Muslim.
Saleh and the Houthis joined forces to seize the capital, Sanaa, in 2014, derailing a political transition that arose out of the Arab Spring and had led to a proposal for a federal, democratic state.
In early 2015, army units loyal to Saleh seized positions in the city, leading to big protests there followed by armed clashes. Protesters accused Saleh and the Houthis of mounting a coup d'etat.
Months of fierce fighting in and around the city followed, with the Houthis and Saleh's army units battling local fighters and army brigades from Yemen's now fragmented military that backed the government.
Taiz citizens endured shelling, sniper fire and terrible shortages in a long siege before government forces eventually drove the Houthis and their allies from the city and re-established a land route to Aden.
The fighting in the city lasted throughout 2015 and parts of 2016, and the siege ran for long stretches until 2017.
WHAT IS THE HUMANITARIAN SITUATION IN TAIZ?
The latest fighting has displaced at least 121,000 in Taiz province, according to the IOM, though many of these are from rural areas outside the city.
Inside Taiz, residents have told Reuters about the shortages they now face of basic items and the huge increase in prices they see in the city markets since the Houthis cut the road to Aden.
Aid agencies have reported widespread shortages of fuel, food, medicines and clean water. Wheat flour stocks in the city are nearly exhausted, the World Food Programme said in mid-October.
The situation risks worsening existing health problems. The UN children's agency UNICEF recently found that one in three of the children it screened in Yemen was malnourished. Cholera, dengue and malaria are all present in Yemen too.
WHAT HAPPENS NEXT?
Government forces backed by Saudi airstrikes are still trying to take back territory to reopen the road, but there is no guarantee they will succeed.
The Houthis, who have upped their attacks on Saudi targets while showing themselves better armed and organised than in earlier phases of the war, are meanwhile trying to cement their siege of Taiz and move closer towards the city.
That might lead to a prolonged siege of the kind that Taiz experienced in the earlier phase of the war.
It's also possible the Houthis might try to take the city. Local opposition means resistance could be fierce and any such attempt could cause a long, bloody battle. REUTERS

Starvation killed 466 Palestinians since 2024, says Gaza Health Ministry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:05:11 UTC
21:05:11 KST

- More than 1.4M people are expected to face crisis-level food insecurity or worse through end of 2026.
- More than 158,000 cases of acute malnutrition recorded among children under 5
At least 466 Palestinians, including 157 children, have died from malnutrition and starvation since 2024, Gaza's Health Ministry said Friday.
The figures were released on World Food Day, observed annually on Oct. 16.
At least 189 elderly people died of starvation, representing 40.5% of the deaths, it said.
In August 2025, the UN declared famine in Gaza.
More than 1.4 million people are expected to face crisis-level food insecurity or worse through the end of 2026, the ministry added.
 
Starvation as a weapon
Israeli authorities have used starvation as a weapon during the genocide in Gaza since October 2023, according to Palestinian government bodies and rights organizations.
Israel tightened restrictions on crossings in March 2025, preventing thousands of aid trucks waiting at border crossings from entering the enclave.
The restrictions followed widespread hunger in northern Gaza caused by the blockade and limits on food and relief supplies, forcing some residents to eat animal feed and wild plants.
In late May 2025, Israel allowed 87 aid trucks to enter Gaza for the first time after 81 days, according to Gaza’s government media office.
Aid later continued to enter on a limited and intermittent basis under strict restrictions until February 2026, when Israel allowed a limited increase in the number of trucks entering the enclave under a ceasefire agreement.
Palestinian officials said the shipments still lacked sufficient quantities of essential food items.
According to Gaza’s government media office, Israel has allowed in only about 34% of the humanitarian aid trucks agreed upon.
 
Malnutrition reaches 'catastrophic levels'
“Malnutrition and starvation rates in Gaza have reached catastrophic levels that are killing children, the elderly and vulnerable groups,” the Health Ministry said.
More than 1.4 million Palestinians, around 67% of Gaza’s population, are expected to face crisis-level food insecurity or worse through the end of 2026.
More than 158,000 cases of acute malnutrition were recorded among children under 5 from 2024 through August 2026, the ministry added.
Of them, 18% of children were suffering from severe acute malnutrition that threatened their lives, while 12.2% of children were affected by stunting, indicating the impact of food shortages on their development.
The mortality rate among children under 5 rose from 13.6 to 33.4 deaths per 1,000 live births between 2022 and 2025, the ministry said.
It estimated that 74,200 children will need treatment for acute malnutrition through April 2027.
 
Pregnant women
Among pregnant women, the ministry said the prevalence of anemia rose to 61% in 2026, compared with 41% before the war.
“Around 4,000 pregnancy losses were recorded during the first half of 2026, more than three times the number recorded during the previous six months,” it added.
“One in three pregnancies in Gaza is now classified as high-risk,” the ministry continued.
“The figures show that the health consequences of the food crisis are increasingly affecting mothers and unborn children, in addition to children,” it said.
 
Calls for urgent international action
“The right to food is a fundamental human right that does not cease to exist during war,” the ministry said.
It called on the international community and the UN to take immediate action to ensure the safe, sustained and unrestricted entry of food, therapeutic nutritional supplements and medicines into Gaza.
The ministry urged that children, pregnant and breastfeeding women, and the elderly be given priority as the groups most vulnerable to malnutrition.
It also called for support to revive local food production to help curb the worsening humanitarian crisis.
The figures come amid the humanitarian consequences of Israel’s genocide in Gaza, which has caused widespread destruction to infrastructure, health facilities and food production sources.
The war has also damaged farmland, food production facilities and water networks, undermining residents’ ability to meet their basic needs locally.
Repeated displacement, loss of income and soaring prices have further increased families’ dependence on humanitarian aid, while access remains irregular.

The decision comes amid opposition criticism of the amendments adopted earlier this year.
The announcement was made by Abdikarim Ahmed Hassan, chairman of the National Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission, during an appearance on state television. Elections for both chambers of parliament will take place on April 15, one month before the presidential vote, he said.
The commission also released a timetable for preparations, with voter and political party registration set to begin on November 1, 2026, according to the Somali National News Agency (SONNA).
Mohamud’s presidential term was originally due to expire in May 2026. However, constitutional amendments approved by parliament in March extended the presidential and parliamentary terms from four to five years, pushing elections back to 2027. Opposition leaders, including former presidents and prime ministers, rejected the changes and called for elections to be held as originally scheduled.
Former President Sharif Sheikh Ahmed has challenged the constitutional amendments in the Supreme Court, arguing that they were adopted without proper legal procedures or broad political agreement. He also rejected the new election timetable, warning that it could lead to “parallel elections, political divisions, internal conflict and a threat to Somalia’s statehood,” Somalia Today reported on Thursday.
Somalia last held a presidential election in 2022, when lawmakers elected Hassan Sheikh Mohamud for a second term, defeating Mohamed Abdullahi Mohamed. The vote followed months of delays and was conducted through an indirect system in which members of parliament chose the president.
The country also faces continuing security challenges from Al-Shabaab, an armed group affiliated with Al-Qaeda that has fought Somalia’s federal government since 2007. The terrorist group conducts raids, bombings, and targeted assassinations in an effort to destabilize the Somali government and regional security structures, and also establish its own rule based on a hardline interpretation of Sharia law.

World Insights: Shoring up power, eroding public trust: Takaichi takes hit over minister's resignation

TOKYO, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi on Thursday appointed ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) lawmaker Arata Takebe as the new farm minister to succeed Kazuo Yana, who resigned a day earlier in what was effectively a dismissal over a string of scandals.
Yana, who joined the cabinet for the first time when Takaichi reshuffled it on Sept. 17, served less than a month, becoming the first cabinet minister to step down over scandals since Takaichi took office last October.
Analysts said Takaichi had prioritized consolidating her own power in making personnel appointments while disregarding appointees' political integrity. The latest controversy has not only dealt a heavy blow to her political credibility but could also affect the implementation of related policies.
If the Takaichi administration remains fixated on right-wing policies and relies on stoking populist sentiment to maintain its approval ratings while failing to address the public's concerns, its governing prospects will only grow dimmer, analysts warned.
"CUTTING LOSSES" UNDER PRESSURE
Japanese media reported in late September that Yana had told a local LDP meeting in May that fiscal 2026 road budgets had been sharply cut for Nasukarasuyama City and Nakagawa Town, two municipalities in his constituency whose mayors did not support him in the House of Representatives election in February.
He was also quoted as saying it was "only natural" to allocate more funds to places that rely on LDP lawmakers.
The remarks sparked a widespread backlash. Yana initially declined to comment on his activities before taking office, saying the issue was outside his ministerial jurisdiction. However, as the controversy escalated and opposition parties pressed him on the matter in the Diet, Japan's parliament, he retracted the remarks and apologized on Oct. 5.
More trouble soon followed. On Oct. 7, Japanese media reported that Yana had arranged free shuttle bus rides for supporters during the 2024 and 2026 House of Representatives election campaigns, possibly in violation of the Public Offices Election Act, which prohibits the provision of benefits and vote-buying.
Answering questions at a House of Representatives session Tuesday, Yana claimed his camp had confirmed with local electoral authorities in advance that the arrangement was lawful. After opposition lawmakers exposed the claim as false, however, he backtracked the following day.
Takaichi had initially made clear that Yana would stay in his post. But as the scandals snowballed and opposition parties stepped up pressure for his resignation, the prime minister shifted her stance, criticizing Yana's remarks and saying she "will not hesitate" to dismiss him "if illegality is found" in his conduct.
With both Takaichi and Yana already scrambling to contain the fallout, fresh media reports emerged on Wednesday that a woman who had helped with Yana's campaign in the 2024 lower house election was paid to call voters and urge them to vote for him, another possible violation of the Public Offices Election Act.
Following the series of allegations and mounting criticism, Yana submitted his resignation at a meeting with Takaichi on Wednesday night, and the prime minister accepted it.
According to analyses by Japanese media, opposition parties, which hold a majority in the Senate, or the upper house of the Diet, have recently moved toward a consensus on submitting a censure motion against Yana.
Although such a motion is not legally binding, its passage would inevitably disrupt parliamentary deliberations and hinder the Takaichi government's legislative agenda, including a bill to temporarily cut the consumption tax on food. Under this pressure, Takaichi had no choice but to let Yana go.
CRONYISM UNDER FIRE
Although Takaichi has tried to contain the damage by cutting Yana loose, questions over her judgment in personnel appointments persist.
Opposition parties and Japanese media commentators argued that Yana's remarks demonstrate that he is unfit to serve as a cabinet minister, or even as a lawmaker, and that Takaichi has made light of the issue, downplaying its gravity.
Kyodo News quoted an LDP lawmaker as saying that Yana believed he would not be replaced because he enjoyed Takaichi's favor, leading him to treat the scandals dismissively. The lawmaker described this as "a downside of (Takaichi's) cronyism."
In fact, Yana is not the only member of Takaichi's reshuffled cabinet embroiled in scandals.
On Tuesday, education minister Yoshihiro Seki admitted that an LDP branch he heads had held political fundraising events within parliamentary office facilities in 2020 and 2024, in breach of the rules.
Because the revenue from both events far exceeded their expenses, and the format of such events makes it easy to conceal the identities of those who bought tickets, a Japanese law scholar described the practice as an egregious form of fundraising that exploits loopholes in the system.
Moreover, both Seki and Yana had previously been disciplined by the LDP over a high-profile political slush fund scandal that came to light in late 2023.
Separately, Hiroshi Nakatsuka, the minister in charge of regulatory reform from the Japan Innovation Party, the LDP's junior coalition partner, was reportedly arrested and indicted in 2007 over a bid-rigging case involving a public construction project while serving as mayor of Hirakata in Osaka Prefecture. He was subsequently convicted.
The string of controversies has cast serious doubt on Takaichi's personnel decisions.
Toshiko Takeya, former Komeito party leader, criticized the LDP for still failing to get to the bottom of the systemic problems behind the slush fund scandal.
Akira Koike, head of the secretariat of the Japanese Communist Party, said the new cabinet lineup showed no sign that Takaichi had reflected on the scandal.
CONSOLIDATING POWER AT EXPENSE OF LIVELIHOODS
Japanese media reports suggested Takaichi's appointment of "scandal-tainted" politicians was intended to shore up her own power base.
In its coverage of the September cabinet and LDP executives reshuffle, Fuji Television Network noted that Takaichi has long struggled with a weak power base within the party. As a result, it said, she relied on the faction of Taro Aso, whose backing helped her win the party leadership race, in making personnel appointments, while bringing in lawmakers implicated in the slush fund scandal to win over members of the former Abe faction.
So far, however, the strategy appears to have backfired.
A poll released by the Asahi Shimbun in late September found that 68 percent of respondents considered the appointment of lawmakers implicated in the slush fund scandal problematic, a view shared by more than half of cabinet supporters and LDP supporters.
The latest poll by public broadcaster NHK, released on Tuesday, showed the Takaichi cabinet's approval rating falling to its lowest level in NHK polling since the prime minister took office.
The top two reasons respondents gave for not supporting the cabinet were that they "don't expect its policies to work" and "cannot trust the prime minister."
While seeking to consolidate her power base by appointing scandal-tainted politicians, Takaichi has not done much to improve people's livelihoods.
The same Asahi Shimbun poll found that 76 percent of respondents considered it problematic that the government had repeatedly promised a consumption tax cut on food without clearly explaining how the measure would be funded.
Meanwhile, a quarterly survey released by the Bank of Japan on Tuesday showed that nearly 90 percent of households polled expected prices to continue rising over the coming year, underscoring persistent public pessimism about the price outlook.
An editorial in the Shimbun Akahata argued that the root of the Takaichi administration's problems lies in a policy agenda focused more on military buildup and constitutional revision. Unless the administration changes course, the editorial warned, the rift between the government and the public will only deepen. ■

====================================================================================================

Oxytocin amplifies negative childhood memories for anxiously attached adults
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:00:12 UTC
21:00:12 KST

Oxytocin is often called the “love hormone,” but it can actually make childhood memories seem more negative for people who struggle with relationship anxiety. A new experiment demonstrates that oxytocin amplifies the emotional intensity of social cues rather than simply promoting warm feelings. The findings were published in the journal Emotion.
Human infants rely entirely on caregivers for survival, leading to an innate drive to form close bonds. These early childhood experiences shape a person’s attachment style, which acts as a mental blueprint for future relationships. Psychologists refer to these blueprints as internal working models. They represent a person’s core beliefs about whether other people will be available and responsive when needed.
Securely attached people generally expect others to be reliable and supportive. Anxiously attached people crave closeness but constantly fear abandonment, often hyper-focusing on relationship threats. Avoidantly attached people distance themselves from intimacy to prevent disappointment, shutting down their emotional needs when they feel vulnerable.
Researchers have long studied the biological systems that drive these social bonds. Oxytocin is a hormone and chemical messenger heavily involved in childbirth, nursing, and pair bonding. In studies of mice and sheep, oxytocin proved necessary for mothers to recognize their offspring and for adults to remember other members of their species.
Early human experiments suggested the hormone universally enhanced trust, cooperation, and empathy. This research helped popularize the idea that oxytocin is a simple prosocial booster.
More recent evidence suggests a nuanced view called the social salience hypothesis. This concept proposes that oxytocin acts as an emotional amplifier, highlighting social information regardless of whether that information is positive or negative. For instance, in animal models, oxytocin has been shown to enhance the fear response in mice after they experience a social defeat by a more aggressive cage-mate.
Researchers at McGill University, led by Melissa Shemirani and Jennifer A. Bartz, wanted to test this hypothesis by examining how oxytocin influences the emotional quality of attachment memories in humans. They sought to replicate and expand upon a previous experiment that only tested men. The research team recruited 77 male and female participants for a two-part study.
During one visit, participants received a dose of oxytocin via a nasal spray. On their other visit, they received a placebo spray. Neither the participants nor the experimenters knew which spray was administered on a given day. This crossover design allowed the researchers to compare how the same individual responded under both conditions.
After waiting for the hormone to take effect, participants were prompted with attachment-related words, such as “protect” or “upset.” They were asked to retrieve specific childhood memories involving their mothers based on these cues. The experimenters then selected one positive and one negative memory and asked the participants to elaborate on them verbally for a few minutes.
Independent human evaluators read transcripts of the recorded narratives and rated them for positive and negative emotional content. For participants with high attachment anxiety, oxytocin caused them to describe their mothers with more negative and less positive emotion compared to when they received the placebo. This suggests that the hormone amplified their underlying insecurities about relationships.
The researchers also analyzed the memory transcripts using two different computer programs designed to detect emotional tone in written text. One program counted the frequency of emotional words based on a vast dictionary, while the other evaluated grammatical context, such as whether a negative word was modified by another word. These automated tools matched the human evaluators in finding that attachment anxiety shaped how oxytocin affected negative emotional language. In the software analyses, however, the significant effect appeared among participants with low anxiety, for whom oxytocin reduced the negative emotional tone of their memories. The computer programs did not find any measurable differences in positive emotional language.
The research team also looked at participants with avoidant attachment styles, who typically suppress their desire for closeness. Oxytocin did not alter the emotional content of their maternal memories. Following the memory task, participants filled out a questionnaire about how much information they shared with the experimenter and how comfortable they felt doing so.
The results showed that avoidant individuals were generally less willing to reveal personal information. When given oxytocin, these participants became even more reluctant to open up emotionally. The hormone appeared to heighten their natural defensive tendency to distance themselves from intimate disclosures.
Readers should note that these results center entirely on recollections of mothers, who were historically viewed as primary caregivers in early psychology research. The study does not address whether oxytocin would alter memories of fathers or other childhood guardians in the same way. The participant group was also relatively young and predominantly White and Asian, meaning the patterns might look different in older adults or other racial groups.
The discrepancy between human evaluators and computer programs highlights the current limitations of automated text analysis. Software tools often struggle to interpret the mixed emotions typical of personal family histories. A memory about being comforted after a scary event contains negative words, but a human listener can easily recognize the overall positive meaning of the caregiver’s response. Spoken language is also full of tangents and structural quirks that confuse software designed for short written texts.
Finally, the findings indicate that oxytocin is not a universal treatment for relationship struggles or social difficulties. Because the hormone acts as a magnifier for pre-existing social fears, using it in therapeutic settings might require customized supervision. Administering oxytocin without proper guidance could inadvertently increase distress for those who already experience high anxiety in their personal connections.
The study, “Attachment, Oxytocin, and Maternal Recollections: Further Evidence for the Salience Hypothesis,” was authored by Melissa Shemirani, Willis Klein, Jonas P. Nitschke, Sonia A. Krol, Signy Sheldon, and Jennifer A. Bartz.

Cocktail of the week: Àclèaf’s PX martini – recipe | The good mixer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:00:10 UTC
21:00:10 KST

This is our twist on the much-loved classic. It takes inspiration from a classic espresso martini, with the addition of vanilla vodka bringing with it an oaked edge that cuts the sweetness of the sherry.
PX martini
Serves 1
50ml vanilla vodka – we use Absolut Vanilia
 
35ml pedro ximénez  
  
35ml freshly brewed espresso 
  – we use Jamaican Blue
Fill a cocktail shaker with ice, then add the vodka, PX and espresso – for the best texture, measure in the espresso last, so the ice doesn’t melt too quickly and over-dilute the cocktail. Shake vigorously for at least 20 seconds, so the mix emulsifies and produces that classic, creamy, frothy, off-white layer on top. Fine strain into a chilled martini glass or coupe and serve.
- Andréa Nuninger, restaurant manager, Àclèaf, Plympton, Devon

Sorry, Darwin: Chinese fossil shows that not all early birds evolved to fly
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Sorry, Darwin: Chinese fossil shows that not all early birds evolved to fly
Discovery suggests that adaptation branched out into more diverse, terrestrial non-flying niches much earlier than previously thought
Chinese scientists have unearthed a fossil of the earliest known flightless bird, offering compelling evidence that not all early birds evolved to take to the skies.
The discovery could also challenge long-held assumptions – including ideas dating back to evolutionary theorist Charles Darwin – that flightlessness in birds arose only as a secondary adaptation after earlier species had mastered flight.
The 150 million-year-old fossil of the Late Jurassic avialan Yuezhuornis yangyuanensis found in China’s southeastern Fujian province suggests that early bird adaptation branched out into more diverse, terrestrial non-flying niches much earlier than previously thought.
“Selection for powered flight has been viewed as the main driver of early avialan skeletal modifications,” the researchers said in a paper published in the peer-reviewed journal Nature on October 14.

Heavy cost for US to return to confrontation with Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:00:03 UTC
21:00:03 KST

The experience of recent conflicts has demonstrated that possessing advanced weaponry and massive firepower does not necessarily equate to achieving strategic objectives. Factors such as depletion of military stockpiles, damage to military equipment, need to procure replacement ammunition, and Iran’s capacity to restore its defensive capabilities all serve to complicate the White House’s calculations regarding a potential re-engagement in military confrontation with powerful Iran.
In a report citing the financial and military costs of past US strikes against Iran, the British newspaper “The Times” highlights the significant strain this conflict has placed on Washington’s military resources. According to the report, US expenditures have exceeded $43 billion in this war, dozens of American aircraft have sustained damage, and the US stockpiles of interceptor missiles have come under pressure. Regardless of the final assessment of the conflict's military outcomes, these figures indicate that sustaining large-scale operations against Iran requires substantial financial and material resources, the resources that cannot be replaced or replenishment in the short term is impossible.
The significance of this issue becomes even greater when the direct costs of military operations are weighed alongside their strategic consequences. In military calculations, the number of attacks carried out or the volume of ammunition expended is not, in itself, the definitive measure of victory. What truly matters is the ratio between the costs incurred and the objectives intended to be achieved through those expenditures. If a military operation entails the extensive use of ammunition and damage to equipment, yet fails to eliminate the adversary’s capacity to continue their resistance, persisting with the same approach may simply lead to mounting costs with no guarantee that the desired outcome will ever be attained.
Erosion of Military Stockpiles: Washington’s Hidden Challenge
One of the most significant consequences of a military conflict is the strain placed on stockpiles of weapons and ammunition. The extensive use of interceptor missiles to counter threats from missiles and drones, particularly when attacks are sustained, can deplete ready-to-use stockpiles, thereby increasing the need for production and resupply. This issue is of particular importance to the United States. In addition to its military commitments in West Asia, Washington must also ensure its forces remain prepared to address potential crises in other parts of the world.
Replenishing arms stockpiles is not merely a matter of securing funding. The production of certain advanced systems and the ammunition they utilize requires complex supply chains, specialized raw materials, and specialized industrial capacity. However, even if new budget allocations are made, rapidly replacing expended stocks is not necessarily feasible. The higher the rate of ammunition consumption in a conflict, the greater pressure placed on production schedules, the prioritization of arms deliveries, and the allocation of resources toward other military missions.
Under such circumstances, Washington’s decision to launch a new round of strikes is not limited merely to an assessment of operational capability; rather, it must also account for the opportunity cost of expending munitions and the subsequent impact on US military readiness. In other words, every missile used in an operation must be evaluated within the context of the United States’ broader defense requirements.
Iran’s Capacity for Recovery and Difficulty of Achieving a Definitive Outcome
On the other side of this equation lies Iran’s capacity to maintain and restore its defensive capabilities. In a report, “The Times” notes that, despite military attacks and pressures, Iran has managed to recover a portion of its missile and drone capabilities. This is significant from the perspective of military calculations, as the effectiveness of an offensive operation depends, to a large extent, on the degree of its lasting impact on the adversary’s capabilities.
If military strikes fail to permanently dismantle a nation’s defensive capacity, inflicting damage at a specific point in time does not necessarily equate to eliminating that nation’s ability to continue its resistance. The potential to repair equipment, restore certain operational capabilities, and maintain the capacity to produce or deploy weaponry can alter the conflict’s equation over time. In such a scenario, the aggressor may be compelled to repeatedly expend further munitions and equipment to sustain military pressure—all while the ultimate outcome of this process remains uncertain. The strategic implication is clear: as long as the adversary retains the ability to continue resisting, one cannot conclude that their defensive capacity has been exhausted based solely on the volume of attacks carried out.
Why could a renewed attack be more costly?
The United States re-engaging in a confrontation with Iran could trigger a repeat of that same costly cycle. New operations would require ammunition, logistics equipment, fuel supplies, the movement of troops, and the protection of military bases and facilities. Should equipment sustain damage or the scope of the conflict expand, costs would rise accordingly. Furthermore, a prolonged crisis could impact energy markets and economic expectations, extending the repercussions well beyond the military battlefield.
On the other hand, the United States must also consider the possibility of a prolonged conflict and the need to remain prepared for unforeseen scenarios. Military operations might begin with limited objectives, but reciprocal responses and shifting conditions could expand their scope. Under such circumstances, the final cost will not necessarily align with initial estimates.
The fundamental question for the White House is whether the costs of a new confrontation would yield commensurate gains. If the objective is to durably weaken Iran’s defensive capabilities, the persistence of its missile and drone capacities could make achieving this goal more difficult. Furthermore, if the aim is to compel Tehran to accede to Washington’s demands, it remains to be seen whether military pressure would truly lead to such an outcome, or if it would merely generate additional costs.
The White House’s Strategic Calculus Test
A report by “The Times” once again draws attention to the gap between military superiority and the achievement of strategic outcomes. Possessing extensive military capabilities enables the infliction of damage, but it does not, in itself, guarantee that the adversary will cease resistance or that the aggressor’s political objectives will be realized. When assessing a conflict, one must simultaneously consider the costs incurred, the resilience of the parties involved, and the extent to which objectives have been achieved.
For Washington, returning to a confrontation with Iran—without regard for the lessons of past costs—means re-entering a path with a predetermined outcome. The strain on U.S. military stockpiles, combined with Iran’s ability to restore parts of its defensive capabilities, suggests that repeating such attacks will not necessarily shift the equation in favor of the aggressor.
Ultimately, the primary challenge for the United States is not merely the capacity to launch a new operation, but the ability to achieve a sustainable outcome at a manageable cost. If previous strikes failed to realize Washington’s intended objectives, any decision to follow the same path requires a clear answer to the question: what will be different this time? Absent such an answer, a renewed attack risks becoming less of a solution to the crisis and more the beginning of another phase of resource depletion and escalating strategic costs for the United States.
MNA

The main building of the Bulgarian Academy of Sciences in central Sofia
PHOTO bas.bg
Font size
A total of 64 scientists affiliated with the Bulgarian Academy of Sciences (BAS) have been ranked among the world’s top 2% of researchers in the latest edition of the Stanford ranking, which assesses scientists’ career-long impact and is compiled by Stanford University in the United States.
Twenty of these scientists are BAS academicians and corresponding members, while the remainder are professors at the Academy’s institutes. The latest Stanford ranking includes a total of 102 Bulgarian researchers, BAS announced.
The ranking is compiled annually based on an analysis of scientometric indicators for more than 12 million scientists whose publications are indexed in Scopus. It reflects the impact individual researchers have had on the advancement of science.
A separate ranking assesses scientific impact over the previous year. It includes another 10 BAS scientists and members who do not feature in the career-long ranking. This brings the total number of scientists affiliated with BAS included in the two rankings to 74.

Likud MK Boaz Bismuth accuses media of targeting Netanyahu over Egypt intel. reports, Qatargate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16

20:56:22 KST

Likud MK Boaz Bismuth accused the media on Wednesday of conducting a campaign against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, claiming that reports concerning a possible pre-October 7 visit by former Egyptian intelligence chief Abbas Kamel and leaked private messages belonging to Netanyahu adviser Yonatan Urich were being used to politically undermine the prime minister.
Speaking in an interview with 103FM, Bismuth, chairman of the Knesset Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee, strongly defended Netanyahu and criticized former Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) chief Yoram Cohen, who is second on former IDF chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot's party list, for comparing the prime minister to Shabbetai Zevi, the 17th-century Jewish false messiah.
"I could put together an entire case about the media's conduct toward the prime minister, and it would all be based on lies," Bismuth said.
"You can say anything, and you can even compare the prime minister to Shabbetai Zevi. That sounds absurd to me," he added.
Bismuth said Netanyahu supporters were being subjected to offensive comparisons involving their political leader, arguing that the rhetoric reflected hostility toward the prime minister rather than legitimate criticism.
"People who vote for Netanyahu hear their leader being compared to someone whose name is followed by the expression 'may the name of the wicked rot,'" he said, referring to a traditional Hebrew condemnation. "A false messiah is someone who joins the 'Anyone but Bibi' camp."
Bismuth defends Netanyahu amid Egyptian intelligence warning controversy
The interview came amid renewed scrutiny of reports that Egyptian intelligence chief Abbas Kamel had traveled to Israel shortly before Hamas's October 7, 2023 attack.
Netanyahu previously denied meeting or speaking with Kamel in the months leading up to the attack, but confirmed this week that an Egyptian aircraft had landed in Israel in September 2023. He maintained that he did not know whom Kamel had met, if the intelligence official had visited.
Asked why Netanyahu had acknowledged the aircraft's arrival only after previously rejecting reports surrounding the alleged visit, Bismuth defended the prime minister's handling of sensitive intelligence matters.
"Prime Minister Netanyahu is a very responsible person," Bismuth said. "Believe me, as chairman of the Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee, who is exposed to certain information, I know he does not disclose material that could benefit him and support his arguments."
He argued that the public debate had been dominated by a politically motivated effort to discredit Netanyahu, including through interviews with former senior security officials.
"What does this shallow campaign do from morning until night?" he asked. "It searches for arguments in interviews with former officials, through stories about Egypt and the Emirates that never happened."
The circumstances surrounding the Egyptian aircraft's arrival and the reported warnings remain disputed. While several international media reports have alleged that Egyptian officials sought to alert Israel to a possible escalation before October 7, Netanyahu has denied receiving such a warning directly from Kamel.
Bismuth condemns publication of Yonatan Urich's private WhatsApp messages
Bismuth also criticized the publication of private correspondence attributed to Yonatan Urich, a senior Netanyahu adviser whose communications have come under scrutiny amid the ongoing political controversies surrounding the prime minister's office.
"My conclusion is that when people want Netanyahu's head, they try to attack him through everyone close to him," Bismuth said.
"The public knows this, and people are already tired of it."
Bismuth alleged that the messages had been obtained through unauthorized access to Urich's WhatsApp account and claimed that some of the published correspondence had been altered. Those allegations have not been independently established.
"Whoever hacked Yonatan Urich's WhatsApp and published private correspondence, while adding and changing things, will pay the price," he said. "The same will happen to anyone who publishes it or cooperates."
He also accused journalists who reported on the messages of celebrating what he described as a criminal violation of an individual's privacy.
"Media figures who celebrate a criminal offense committed against someone should be ashamed of themselves," Bismuth said.
He recalled previous cases involving unauthorized access to mobile phones, including an alleged incident involving former prime minister Naftali Bennett, and suggested that similar privacy concerns had not received sufficient attention.
"Yonatan Urich did not harm Israel's security. I have absolutely no doubt about that," Bismuth said.
"Israel, under Netanyahu, attacked in Qatar, so perhaps it's time to stop with this nonsense?"
Urich has also publicly alleged that his phone was hacked and has threatened legal action against those responsible for distributing the correspondence. The allegations about the messages' authenticity and the circumstances of their release remain contested.
Likud MK rejects questions over loyalty to Netanyahu and party ranking
During the interview, Bismuth was also asked why he continued to defend Netanyahu so strongly despite being placed 21st on the Likud electoral list, after previously securing a higher position in the party's internal rankings.
Bismuth rejected suggestions that the placement had affected his relationship with the prime minister, saying he was satisfied with the party's reserved positions and the broader composition of its list.
"I was elected in 13th place, and that is a very respectable position," he said.
He also referred to his previous professional relationship with political commentator Yaakov Bardugo, noting that he had been Bardugo's employer when both worked at the Israel Hayom newspaper.
Bismuth insisted that his support for Netanyahu was based on his political preference rather than considerations about his own parliamentary position.
"This has nothing to do with me. A seat in the Knesset is a seat you hold temporarily. Netanyahu is the prime minister I want."

Sony debuts US$5,900 gold-plated Walkman player for audiophiles

Sony debuts US$5,900 gold-plated Walkman player for audiophiles
- Sony has launched three new premium Walkman players, its first new hardware in years, with prices from US$1,900 to US$5,900 for audiophiles.
- The flagship NW-WM1ZM3 uses a gold-plated oxygen-free copper chassis, while all models add better sound processing, run the Android operating system, and support high-resolution audio.
- Sony faces cheaper rivals such as Astell & Kern and Chinese brands, but says the new Walkmans offer its “finest portable sound experience”; shipping dates are not yet set.
AI generated
NEW YORK CITY – Sony Group introduced a trio of premium digital music players priced from US$1,900 (S$2,400) to US$5,900, marking the first new hardware in several years carrying the storied Walkman name.
The new Walkman devices aim to deliver the “finest portable sound experience” for audiophiles, the company said in a statement on Oct 15.
Across the line, the hardware benefits from an improved “DSD Remastering Engine” that can make digital music files sound warmer and more analog, Sony said.
When users are streaming compressed, lower-quality music files, the Walkmans use artificial intelligence to identify music genres and enhance both high frequencies and subtle sounds. Fortunately for enthusiasts, major platforms like Spotify and Apple Music already let subscribers stream or download high-resolution, lossless audio.
The three new devices are available for preorder now, though Sony has not yet said when they will start shipping.
To make the most of these players, which are designed for focused listening, shoppers will also need high-end headphones capable of reproducing even the smallest details of their favourite songs.
The Walkman brand is core to Sony’s heritage, and the new products are an example of the more niche consumer segments that the company serves outside of its much bigger personal audio business.
But competitors like Astell & Kern, along with some Chinese brands, offer their own so-called hi-fi players at significantly lower prices than Sony.
Sony’s middle- and top-of-the-line WM1-series players, the NW-WM1ZM3 (US$5,900) and NW-WM1AM3 (US$3,000), both have 5.5-inch, 1080p-resolution screens that are slightly larger and sharper than their predecessors from 2022.
The lowest-end NW-ZX900, which has a 5-inch display, has been upgraded with 1080p resolution, an improvement over 720p on the prior model.
The flagship product offers several additional features meant to justify the nearly US$6,000 price.
That includes a gold-plated oxygen-free copper chassis that the company says will help elevate the sound quality. The screws also have a gold-plated treatment providing a “stable ground connection that delivers powerful bass, an expansive soundstage and smooth, extended high frequencies,” according to Sony.
The two less expensive models, meanwhile, have an aluminum-alloy main enclosure with a gold-plated rear chassis.
All three players run the Android operating system. The lowest-end NW-ZX900 (US$1,900) is making a particularly big leap to Android 16, up from the much older Android 12 software found on its predecessor.
Notably, Sony’s battery life estimates are for low-quality, 128-kilobit-per-second MP3 files, an unlikely usage scenario for enthusiasts.
The NW-WM1ZM3 and NW-WM1AM3 can last through up to 31 hours of streaming or 35 hours when music is stored on the device. The more affordable NW-ZX900 promises the longest endurance: as much as 35 hours of streaming or 40 hours of local playback.
Walkman hardware has not been the only focus for Sony’s pro audio division: Earlier in October, the company introduced a unique spatial audio microphone for smartphones, priced at US$250, that can capture immersive audio for recorded videos.
In 2023, the company bought boutique headphone maker Audeze, a purchase that so far has mostly benefitted its PlayStation division. In September, Sony announced its latest line of gaming headphones that incorporate Audeze’s planar magnetic driver technology. BLOOMBERG

FM Sybiha: Black Sea could become second Strait of Hormuz for global food security
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said this in an interview with Ukrinform.
“Russia is using food as a weapon. We see this, just as we see it exploiting migration policy. Russia is well aware of how vulnerable certain countries are to such actions, particularly efforts to undermine global food security,” the Foreign Minister said.
According to Sybiha, Russia’s blockade of the Black Sea is aimed not only at disrupting shipping but also at creating food shortages in certain African countries, which could trigger new waves of migration to Europe.
“This is a deliberate and clear strategy on Russia’s part. We must have our own strategy for restoring freedom of navigation in the Black Sea, unblocking it, and securing ceasefires in both the energy sector and at sea. We have concrete proposals and new participants who have joined this process for the first time. These include India and Egypt,” the Minister stressed.
Sybiha recalled that in 2022, when navigation in the Black Sea was blocked, global food prices rose by 25%.
“We are once again on the brink of such an increase. The food security of many countries around the world depends on Ukrainian grain, and this is about more than grain alone. Because of Russia’s blockade of the Black Sea, those countries are not receiving products on time,” the Ukrainian Foreign Minister emphasized.
He added that some agricultural land could remain unsown because of the risks created by Russia, which would also affect prices next year.
“Therefore, the consequences are already being felt, and they will only intensify. The Black Sea could become a second Strait of Hormuz, this time in terms of food security,” Sybiha stressed.
He noted that all mediators actively involved in the process were now awaiting a response from Russia, while Ukraine was working with all its European partners to maximize the transit of Ukrainian grain through their countries to designated destinations.
“This will be difficult because Ukraine is one of the world’s largest agricultural producers and can feed up to 400 million people. Collective pressure is therefore needed to force Russia to unblock the Black Sea,” the head of Ukrainian diplomacy concluded.
As Ukrinform reported, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said that European partners are becoming increasingly aware of the threat posed by Russian escalation and the need to counter the “shadow war” Moscow is waging against the West. They also recognize Ukraine’s important role in strengthening European security.

‘Trying to dominate’: How Israel is embedding itself in the Cypriot state
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:54:10 UTC
20:54:10 KST

‘Trying to dominate’: In Cyprus, some fear Israel’s growing influence
Israel now reaches into Cyprus’s water, gas, health and defence and a number of Cypriots fear their island is losing control.
Nicosia and Limassol, Cyprus – Heavily bearded and wearing a loose shirt collar, Christos Achniotis speaks about the history and demographics of Cyprus and runs off dates from memory.
He was 16 when Turkish troops landed in Cyprus in mid-1974. At one point, Limassol has long had a large Russian community, he said, but that revolved around property investments.
Now, he believes there is pressure from Israel, which he says is “trying to dominate as much as possible, land-wise, company-wise”, as well as politically and militarily.
Israel’s reach in Cyprus now runs through the state’s most vital systems.
Mekorot, Israel’s state water company, helps supply the island’s water. Israel Aerospace Industries, a state-owned arms maker, is supplying its new air defences. And Israeli firms run a growing hospital network and hold a stake in the country’s largest gasfield.
Israel’s economy is about 15 times Cyprus’s, according to the World Bank, and Israel’s military spending is about 73 times that of Cyprus.
Cyprus’s government presents the ties as a security alliance against Turkiye, but several Cypriots interviewed by Al Jazeera said they feared their country is handing another state control of systems it cannot live without.
Israel is “a small area with big money and a big military”. Cyprus is strategically placed in the Mediterranean and, just a 35-minute flight away, is an attractive piece of land, said Achniotis.
‘Our resources’
Cyprus gets about 80 percent of its drinking water from the sea.
With its dams just 21 percent full in March, desalination plants supply most of what comes out of its taps, according to the Water Development Department.
Agriculture Minister Maria Panayiotou said in June that desalination would cover almost all domestic demand by next year.
Mekorot has joint ventures with Cypriot firm Netcom that run two of the island’s five permanent plants, at Larnaca and Episkopi, according to the Water Development Department. In August, Mekorot expanded its cooperation with Cyprus, signing a memorandum with the Nicosia District Water Board to help manage water and sewerage in the capital.
For Danae Laou, who works in hospitality in Limassol, the water deals crossed a line.
“It’s terrifying to see, but at the same time, we have no power,” she said.
Today’s occupation of Palestine is in part facilitated by control of vital resources. “I can see the same thing happening here”, she said.
Palestinians know Mekorot well.
In the occupied West Bank, the company is on the United Nations list of businesses linked to illegal Israeli settlements.
Najla Abdellatif Vallander, a Swedish-Palestinian environmental advocate who founded Zero Waste Palestine, has tracked Mekorot’s work in Palestine and abroad and told Al Jazeera that its operations in the West Bank are akin to “water theft”, diverting Palestinian sources to illegal Israeli settlements.
“Israeli settlers are able to enjoy almost unlimited amounts of water while Palestinians are not allowed to use their own water sources,” she said.
Palestinians “have to buy back their own water sources from Mekorot”, and are mostly barred from digging their own wells. “This is water apartheid,” she said.
At the time of publishing, Mekorot had not responded to Al Jazeera’s request for comment.
‘Leverage’
Israel’s economic footprint has grown fast.
Investors in Israel held 5.1 billion euros ($5.7bn) of investment in Cyprus at the end of 2024, more than six times what they held in 2017, according to the Central Bank of Cyprus.
The true figure may be higher as the data excludes Israelis living in Cyprus or elsewhere, and may miss money routed through companies whose owners are hard to trace.
The Tel Aviv Stock Exchange is also weighing a bid for the Cyprus Stock Exchange, which the government is privatising, Cyprus Mail and the Israeli business daily Globes reported this month.
The Cypriot exchange’s European Union licence would give Israel “greater access to the Eurozone market”, a source close to Cyprus’s Ministry of Finance told the Cyprus Mail.
Health is the newest.
Hadassah Medical Centre Limassol, the Israeli hospital group’s first centre in Europe, began seeing patients in July and was formally opened on Thursday.
Its opening was ratified in Israel by Hadassah’s governing bodies, including the Hadassah Women’s Zionist Organization of America.
Offshore, Israel’s NewMed Energy owns 30 percent of the Aphrodite gasfield, according to its filings to the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange.
The two governments are also negotiating over the field, which Israel says extends into its waters.
‘Create a problem’
Israel has also been flexing its military muscle.
Israeli special forces have trained in Cyprus’s Troodos mountains, whose terrain resembles southern Lebanon, according to Israel’s Institute for National Security Studies.
In 2022, the two armies held their largest joint exercise yet, simulating a war with Hezbollah, The Jerusalem Post reported.
Cyprus is replacing its Russian-made air defences with the Barak MX, built by Israel Aerospace Industries, with deliveries beginning in late 2024.
Israel presents itself as a guardian against Turkiye.
Following a coup in Cyprus backed by Greece’s military government in July 1974, Turkiye invaded the island and has occupied its northern part ever since. Only Turkiye and its Turkish Cypriot leadership recognise Northern Cyprus.
In late December 2025, Israeli and Cypriot military officials signed a 2026 cooperation plan covering joint exercises, training, and “strategic military dialogue”, the Israeli military said.
On Tuesday, a pro-Israel advocacy group, the Israel Allies Foundation (IAF), launched a caucus of six Cypriot lawmakers from three parties in Nicosia. Its president, Josh Reinstein, told reporters after the group’s meeting with the Cypriot president at the presidential palace on Wednesday that Turkiye is a “common adversary”, according to the Cyprus Mail.
The opposition party AKEL called it “extremely provocative”, asking what credibility Cyprus has in demanding pressure on Turkiye while backing “another occupying and settler state”, the Cyprus Mail reported.
Last month, Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told the United Nations General Assembly that Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan “illegally occupies northern Cyprus, an EU member”.
Netanyahu “knows what he’s doing”, said Ioanna Lamprou, a writer in Limassol.
Cypriots who feel the world has forgotten the occupation, she said, will “become more sympathetic to Israel and to Netanyahu’s government because of this”, but they “don’t understand that what’s happening in the West Bank is illegal occupation as well”.
Laou understands the government’s reasoning; from its perspective, she said, “Cyprus can’t protect itself from anything.”
Ceylan Hassan, a Turkish Cypriot researcher and environmental social scientist, said the British had won over Cypriots the same way, by promising to keep them safe from a bigger threat.
Israel is doing “the whole colonial thing of let’s create a problem and then be the solution to it and never let it go”.
‘Athens or Crete’
In 1902, Theodore Herzl, the founder of political Zionism, presented a pamphlet to a British Parliamentary Committee with the idea of establishing a Jewish homeland in Cyprus. He offered a pamphlet with the title: The problem of Jewish immigration to England and the United States solved by furthering the Jewish Colonisation of Cyprus.
Britain’s colonial secretary refused, saying Greeks and Muslims lived there, according to Herzl’s diary.
Herzl mused, “The Greeks will gladly sell their lands at a good price and migrate to Athens or Crete.”
Achniotis has thought about that history more since the genocidal war on Gaza began.
Watching what is happening to Palestinians, he said, “I think it can happen to anyone.”
As the onslaught happened so easily, with the acceptance of the US and European governments, “you feel a kind of insecurity,” he said. “Why are they going to respect you?”

Spain’s conservative People’s Party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo on Friday demanded that the navy be sent to Ceuta following unconfirmed reports of a Moroccan patrol boat in the exclave’s waters Thursday.
“Morocco’s repeated incursions into Spanish waters are not isolated incidents, but rather a pattern of aggression that demands a firm response: Deploy the navy to the area. Summon the Moroccan ambassador. Recall our ambassador in Rabat for consultations. Demand explanations from the highest levels of the Moroccan authorities,” Feijóo wrote on X Friday, adding that “Spain is not for sale. Spain defends itself.”
The opposition leader is currently bidding to replace Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez after the embattled socialist announced snap elections for Nov. 29.
Advertisement
Feijóo’s calls for a “firm response” are the latest in a wave of criticism of Sánchez’s government after more than 70,000 migrants arrived in the Spanish exclave of Ceuta on the Moroccan border in late July. Migration ministers across the European Union have in recent months repeatedly demanded tough new EU migration policies.
His comments also come after unconfirmed reports that a Moroccan patrol boat remained in Spanish waters off the coast of Ceuta for hours Thursday, which the Spanish Civil Guard has denied. Moroccan warships also allegedly entered Spanish waters in July, though a European Commission spokesperson told Spanish press agency EFE Wednesday that it was “up to the Spanish and Moroccan authorities to clarify the facts.”
Feijóo spent Thursday morning at a summit of the center-right European People’s Party — of which the PP is a member — in Brussels, during which the EPP lashed out at the Spanish government over the Ceuta crisis in its closing statement, according to POLITICO’s Madrid Playbook. “Europe as a whole must recognize the failure of the Spanish government and exert the necessary pressure to prevent this crisis from becoming entrenched, spreading, or happening again,” Feijóo said in an opinion piece earlier this month.
Tensions over Ceuta and Melilla — which Morocco considers occupied territories — are becoming increasingly strained: A POLITICO poll earlier this week revealed that 58% of respondents believe an armed conflict between Madrid and Rabat is “likely” within the next decade.
In a landmark visit to the exclaves also this week, King Felipe VI said that Ceuta and Melilla were “an inalienable part of the political and national reality that is Spain. The sovereignty and territorial integrity of our country are not negotiable.”
The last time a Spanish head of state visited the territories was in 2007, when former king Juan Carlos I traveled to Ceuta and Melilla amid a diplomatic spat with Morocco.

Norwegian teen sentenced for Iran-linked gang murder plot in UK

Breadcrumb
Norwegian teen sentenced to 20 years in prison for plotting murder in UK for Iran-linked gang
A Norwegian teenager convicted of traveling to Britain to carry out a contract killing on behalf of an international crime gang linked to Iran was sentenced Friday to 20 years in prison.
Johannes Kongsnes Natland, 19, was found guilty in July of conspiracy to murder for agreeing to shoot an unknown target for 25,000 euros (21,500 pounds) last year. He was arrested at a hotel in Huddersfield in northern England with two guns and ammunition two days after arriving in the UK.
The target is not known.
Natland, who was working part time at a pizza restaurant at the time of his arrest, was recruited by a Swedish organised crime group known as the Foxtrot Network while he was playing a game online. The group has links to the Iranian government, according to counterterrorism officers from London’s Metropolitan Police.
Natland admitted possessing the firearms and ammunition but claimed he did not want to go through with the plan.
"You agreed to be the enforcer and pursued it, despite numerous opportunities to extricate yourself," Justice Bobbie Cheema-Grubb said at his sentencing hearing at Woolwich Crown Court in southeast London. "Although the fact that no one was shot dead or physically harmed is important, I am sure had the intervention of the police not prevented the plan from proceeding, you would have done what you had agreed to."
Natland was hired by a 17-year-old known as "Generalen." A court in Norway last year convicted the teenager of attempting to “contribute to murder” and sentenced him to 14 years in custody. A 16-year-old is awaiting trial in Norway for his role in the conspiracy.
The UK government last year announced sanctions against Foxtrot Network and its leader "due to their involvement in violence against Jewish and Israeli targets in Europe on behalf of the Iranian regime."
The sanctions include an asset freeze that bars UK businesses from handling funds or other economic assets controlled by the organization.

Tensions in Rome's Jewish Ghetto on Nazi roundup anniversary, insults at ANPI
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:53:30 CEST
20:53:30 KST

Tensions erupted at the anniversary
of the Raid on the Ghetto of Rome in which Nazis rounded up over
1,000 Jews on October 16, 1943 to send them to
concentration camps, and insults were directed at members of the
Italian Partisans Association ANPI, whose delegation was then
excluded from the commemoration over its recent pro-Palestinian
stances and condemnation of an alleged Israeli 'genocide' in
Gaza.
                                    
Some members of the Roman Jewish community began shouting at and
insulting the ANPI delegation.
                                    
"You need to leave," "Get out, get out," and "Shame on you!"
they shouted at the association of former partisans.
                                    
"We were attacked," said Marina Pierlorenzi, president of the
Rome branch of ANPI.
                                    
"They don't want ANPI here, claiming we are 'pro-Palestine' and
that we have no business being in this square."
In the days leading up to the event, the president of the Roman
Jewish community, Victor Fladlun, had asked ANPI not to
participate.
                                    
Following the tensions with the Jewish community, the ANPI
delegation was moved away from the area designated for the
anniversary ceremony commemorating the roundup, and placed
behind "some barriers," as explained by provincial president
Pierlorenzi.
                                    
In a gesture of solidarity, other associations followed the
partisans and took their place alongside them.
                                    
These included the ANED (National Association of Former
Deportees to Nazi Camps), the FIAP (Italian Federation of
Partisan Associations), and the National Association of War
Victims.
                                    
Rome's Jewish Community said ANPI should not have attended the
event as a matter of propriety.
                                    
"We asked the ANPI not to attend, out of respect. We have a
profound respect for the history of the partisan struggle—it is
our own history, too. It is worth remembering that 5% of Italian
Jews fought in the Resistance—a figure ten times higher than the
national average.
                                    
"We were deeply hurt to see the Jewish Brigade excluded from the
April 25th [Liberation Day] march, and we were deeply hurt once
again by the ANPI's indulgent attitude toward pro-Palestinian
demonstrations.
                                    
"We believe the ANPI should not act as a political party or
engage in politics; instead, it should return to its core
mission: preserving the memory of the partisan struggle and the
Resistance, said the president of the Jewish Community of Rome,
Victor Fadlun.
                                    
"We believe in—and have full respect for—[civil discourse], and
we oppose any form of violence, even if it is merely verbal," he
clarified.
                                    
"Ours is a peaceful and respectful community. But today, it is a
matter of propriety," he emphasized.
                                    
When asked whether it had been a mistake for the Municipality of
Rome to invite the ANPI, Fadlun replied: "I believe that October
16th represents a profound bereavement for our community. There
are direct relatives of those who were deported present.
                                    
Therefore, sensitivity and respect are required."
The Gestapo detained 1,259 people - 363 men, 689 women, and 207
children - during the raid 43 years ago today.
                                    
Of these, 1,023 were identified as Jews and deported to
Auschwitz.

Latvia’s anti-corruption watchdog investigates large cash gifts to Stepaņenko from father living in Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:53:07 UTC
20:53:07 KST

Latvia’s Corruption Prevention and Combating Bureau (KNAB) is conducting a preliminary administrative inquiry into substantial financial gifts received by Jūlija Stepaņenko, leader of the Sovereign Power/Young Latvians Alliance, from her father, who lives in Russia.
KNAB previously announced that it would assess information concerning the financial gifts but did not specify what form the examination would take.
The bureau has now confirmed to news agency LETA that the publicly reported information is being assessed as part of a preliminary administrative inquiry.
Under Latvia’s Criminal Procedure Law, information concerning a possible legal violation may be referred to a competent authority for such an inquiry if investigating the suspected violation does not require the use of criminal procedural powers or investigative methods.
Within the meaning of the law, this type of inquiry involves a state institution and its officials examining a potential legal violation using powers granted under the legislation governing that institution, rather than criminal procedural powers.
As previously reported by LETA, 
Stepaņenko’s declarations as a public official show that she received substantial financial gifts totalling nearly 420,000 euros from her father,
 who lives in Russia and works in the construction industry.
Stepaņenko’s father, Sergei Fedotov, and his company Forma ZhBI have provided material support to Russian troops fighting in Ukraine over several years, according to an investigation published by independent online media outlet The Insider.
The report stated that the company was already producing anti-tank obstacles and stoves in 2022. Fedotov later reportedly donated vehicles to a foundation involved in supplying Russian military forces.
Latvian Television reported that Fedotov established the Forma group of construction companies in Solnechnogorsk, Russia, more than 30 years ago.
He has also served as a municipal deputy.
This summer, Fedotov was awarded an honorary distinction for his contributions to the Moscow region.
In August 2026, during Russia’s State Duma election campaign, the manufacturing facility managed by Fedotov was visited by Viktor Bout, an arms dealer previously convicted of arms trafficking in the United States.
Bout was running for parliament as a candidate for the Liberal Democratic Party of Russia, which was led for many years by Vladimir Zhirinovsky.
Footage broadcast on Russian television showed Fedotov sitting alongside Bout during a party campaign event held at his company.
Bout was released from US imprisonment in 2022 as part of a prisoner exchange negotiated by the Kremlin.
Meanwhile, Latvian Foreign Minister Baiba Braže (New Unity) recently added Fedotov to Latvia’s list of undesirable persons, imposing an indefinite ban on his entry into the country.
Summary: Latvia’s anti-corruption watchdog is examining nearly 420,000 euros in financial gifts received by politician Jūlija Stepaņenko from her Russia-based father, Sergei Fedotov, whose company has reportedly supported Russian troops in Ukraine and who has been banned from entering Latvia.

“I’m not sure it’s necessarily legal in all jurisdictions,” Musk said, adding that the prototype was “not necessarily a safety optimised car but it takes the fun meter to 11”.
In 2014 Musk expressed his scepticism about a future with flying vehicles.
