Tehran hosts 8th national conference on soil conservation and watershed management
TEHRAN – Tehran played host to the 8th national conference on soil conservation and watershed management on October 13 and 14, under the theme ‘successful experiences, national and international lessons learned’.
The conference was hosted by the International Center for Integrated Management of Watershed and Bio-Resources in Arid and Semi-Arid Regions (ICIMWB), as one of the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) category 2 centers in the field of water and natural sciences, the Agricultural Research, Education, and Extension Organization, and Iran’s National Commission for UNESCO.
Bringing together researchers, experts, executive managers, and representatives from national and international institutions, the 8th conference served as a platform for the exchange of knowledge and experience, and the enhancement of collaborations for the conservation of fundamental resources and the sustainable management of watersheds.
Addressing the event, Secretary-General of Iran’s National Commission for UNESCO Hassan Fartousi, highlighted the protection of water and soil as the fundamental requirement for food security and sustainable development.
Referring to challenges such as water scarcity, soil erosion, drought, and land degradation, the official emphasized the importance of integrated watershed management and the use of scientific and interdisciplinary approaches.
The conservation of natural resources needs to be integrated into the country’s development plan. The realization of the goal requires connecting research, policymaking, and practical implementation, as well as promoting the participation of responsible agencies and local communities, he noted.
For his part, Levan Bouadze, the newly appointed Resident Representative of the United Nations Development Program (UNDP) in Iran, said soil erosion and land degradation are among the major environmental challenges whose consequences extend beyond the natural environment, affecting the economic and social well-being of human societies.
Highlighting that soil health and food security are interconnected, the official said that the loss of soil resources not only threatens food security, but also impacts the livelihood of local communities and the sustainability of ecosystems.
The official called for enhancing management capacities and utilizing scientific knowledge to identify natural hazards and mitigate the vulnerability of ecosystems.
Referring to the UNDP’s cooperation with Iranian institutions, the official said the implementation of joint projects aimed at protecting natural resources and combating land degradation provides a great opportunity for the exchange of expertise and the development of practical solutions.
The official went on to say that researchers and scientists can facilitate precise decision-making by generating knowledge and providing scientific solutions, while the government can translate these findings into actionable plans and measures.

Norwegian teen 'hitman' detained for UK murder plot
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:48:44 BST
20:48:44 KST

Norwegian teen 'hitman' detained for UK murder plot
- Published
A teenager who travelled from Norway to the UK to carry out a "hit" for an organised crime group has been sentenced to 20 years' detention.
Johannes Natland, 19, was arrested in a hotel room in Huddersfield, West Yorkshire, with two working guns and 19 rounds of live ammunition in March 2025, the Old Bailey previously heard.
During his retrial, a jury heard the teen was "recruited" by the Foxtrot Network, which was described as a Swedish organised crime group backed by the Iranian regime.
Natland, who had admitted to possession of the firearms and ammunition, was unanimously found guilty of conspiracy to murder and sentenced at Woolwich Crown Court on Friday.
The Foxtrot Network has been sanctioned by both the UK and the US for its close links to the Iranian government, with Natland's target remaining unclear.
Commander Helen Flanagan, head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said: "We haven't been able to establish exactly who the intended victim was."
The Foxtrot Network is known for pioneering a relatively new phenomenon of hiring teenage killers that Europol has called "violence-as-a-service" (VaaS).
At the sentencing hearing, Mrs Justice Cheema-Grubb told Natland: "The Foxtrot Network is an organised crime group which has developed an arm's-length method of recruiting young people to carry out violent crimes.
"You were recruited to travel to England to kill an unidentified target."
Natland had been offered 270,000 Norwegian Kroner, about £21,000, to carry out the killing.
He flew into Manchester Airport on an emergency passport on 17 March 2025, shortly after his 18th birthday.
Natland was guided by videos on the messaging app Signal to Huddersfield, where the guns, a stolen car and a stash of cash were hidden.
He was prevented from carrying out the hit after Norwegian police arrested the teenager who had recruited him for the Foxtrot Network and found messages about the UK plot on his phone.
There was then a race against time to find Natland before he located his unknown target in England.
Addressing Natland, the judge said: "At the heart of this case is a stark fact. You agreed to assassinate another human being, a stranger to you, in a foreign country.
"You knew nothing of that person's life or circumstances. You were just 18 years old when you placed yourself in readiness to murder for money."
He was told: "Although the fact that no one was shot dead or physically harmed is important, I am sure had the intervention of the police not prevented the plan from proceeding, you would have done what you had agreed to."
Natland was at the Briar Court Hotel with two handguns hidden under his bed when he was arrested by police.
When he saw officers at the door, he mimed shooting one of them with his hands before he was pushed against the wall and handcuffed.
"There was pressure because he'd come into the country, and we knew his intention was to carry out a murder on UK soil," said Flanagan.
"We had to move at pace and we intervened really quickly, and just before he sort of moved towards committing that murder."
Natland grew up in the oil city of Stavanger in south-west Norway.
Despite being a promising young footballer, he started taking drugs aged 13 and later dropped out of school.
He previously told the Old Bailey that by last year he was taking drugs "pretty much every day".
He became paranoid his parents were trying to kill him and he ended up in a psychiatric unit with drug-induced psychosis.
Natland's barrister, Paul Hynes KC, said the "mental illness was exacerbated, if not created, by the self-induced consumption of drugs", which had "affected his ability to make rational, good decisions".
The defendant said he spent a short period in a "home for problem children" where he met one of those who later recruited him to the Foxtrot Network, a teenager with the username UnknownHustler.
Mrs Justice Cheema-Grubb told Natland: "You agreed to be the enforcer and pursued it, despite numerous opportunities to extricate yourself."
Within two days of being recruited, Natland flew from Stavanger to Manchester, using the emergency passport as his normal one had expired.
He was stopped by Border Force officials in Manchester and was told to return to the airport to catch the next direct flight home.
Instead, he took a taxi to the hotel in Huddersfield before taking another taxi to a wooded area.
He picked up £2,000 in cash, two guns and bullets, and was directed to a stolen Nissan with false plates to be used in the killing.
The judge added at sentencing: "You returned to the hotel with two guns and 19 bullets.
"You were sent directions to where a stolen car bearing false number plates was parked with its key, after which you bought rubber gloves, took photos and made videos of what you had acquired, including with the money spread out on the hotel bed."
From his hotel room, Natland bragged to his girlfriend he had the "bangs in the bag" and took selfies in his room.
At his trial, one of Natland's footballer friends recalled him talking about the "Swedish Foxes" and telling him: "I'm going to get a lot of money and somebody is going to die."
Natland also confided in his girlfriend before leaving for the UK, saying in a message: "I'm going on crazy mission."
According to her, he said: "Now I can finally kill someone and it's perfect as I get money to do it.
"I can kill someone and life will be wonderful."
Giving evidence, Natland said he wanted to look "cool" to his peers but it was just "bravado" and inside he was "terrified".
He told jurors: "I wasn't an international assassin. I thought people had this impression and expected me to be this guy. I knew I wasn't."
Natland admitted possessing the firearms and ammunition but claimed he would have shot himself in the foot to get out of the "pickle" he was in.
Flanagan said: "Natland was clearly being tasked by someone in the Foxtrot Network, an organised criminal group sanctioned by the UK and the US due to its involvement in orchestrating violence against Jewish and Israeli targets in Europe on behalf of the Iranian regime.
"The intended target of this specific assassination has never been identified, and we found no evidence of any direct link to Iran in this case.
"However, as recent events have shown, Counter Terrorism Policing will seek to proactively disrupt any attempts by hostile states to carry out criminal acts in the UK."
Natland was told he will have to serve at least two thirds of the 20-year sentence behind bars.

Energy shock pushes major central banks toward higher rates as growth risks mount
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:48:13 UTC
20:48:13 KST

- Fed, ECB and Bank of Japan tighten policy as UK policymakers weigh further rate increases amid higher inflation forecasts
- Economist Huw Dixon warns growth could stall heading into 2027, with recessions probable in several G7 economies
Rising energy costs are renewing inflation pressures across major economies, prompting interest-rate increases and complicating central banks’ efforts to contain prices without undermining growth.
The US Federal Reserve, European Central Bank and Bank of Japan raised borrowing costs in September, while the Bank of England held its benchmark rate steady despite growing concerns about the inflation outlook.
Huw Dixon, emeritus professor of economics at Cardiff University, told Anadolu that the energy crisis triggered by the Iran war had substantially changed expectations for inflation and monetary policy since the beginning of the year.
He warned that growth could stall heading into 2027, with recessions probable in several Group of Seven economies.
“Interest rates will have to rise to control inflation, but perhaps we will see policy rates high but below inflation again so as to limit damage to the real economy,” he said.
Dixon argued that central banks would not repeat the shift toward zero interest rates seen during the 2008 financial crisis unless a conflict with Russia broke out.
His assessment highlights the competing pressures facing policymakers as higher energy bills squeeze spending while also raising businesses’ costs.
 
US and eurozone inflation accelerate
US annual consumer inflation rose to 3.7% in September from 3.4% in August, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
Prices increased 0.6% month-on-month, with a 9.1% jump in gasoline prices accounting for more than half the overall rise. 
Annual core inflation, excluding food and energy, accelerated to 2.6% from 2.4%.
Energy prices were 20.4% higher than a year earlier. Gasoline prices rose 34.2% annually, while fuel oil prices climbed 74.2%.
Price pressures also extended beyond energy. Shelter costs increased 0.4% over the month, while recreation, used vehicles, education and airline fares also became more expensive.
The Fed raised its benchmark federal funds target range by 25 basis points to 3.75%-4% on Sept. 16 in a unanimous decision.
It said inflation remained elevated and the increase would support a timelier return to its 2% goal. However, its assessment of activity remained relatively firm, pointing to resilient domestic spending, strong productivity growth and robust capital investment.
In the euro area, annual inflation accelerated to an estimated 3.8% in September from 3.2% in August, according to Eurostat’s flash release.
Energy inflation climbed to 18.8% from 14.3%, while services inflation increased to 3.2% from 3%. Inflation excluding energy, food, alcohol and tobacco edged up to 2.5% from 2.4%.
The ECB raised its three key rates by 25 basis points on Sept. 10, taking its deposit facility rate to 2.5%.
It warned that the Middle East conflict was generating inflation pressures likely to keep price growth well above target for an extended period.
Its September projections put average inflation at 3% in 2026, 2.5% in 2027 and 2.1% in 2028, with the latter two forecasts revised upward from June.
The ECB nevertheless projected continued growth of 0.9% this year and 1.4% next year, distinguishing its baseline outlook from Dixon’s warning of possible recessions. It identified upside risks to inflation and downside risks to growth, while avoiding a commitment to a particular rate path.
 
UK expectations shift toward tighter policy
The Bank of England maintained its benchmark rate at 3.75% on Sept. 17 by a 6-3 vote, with three policymakers favoring an increase to 4%.
UK inflation reached 3.1% in August. The bank’s updated assessment indicated inflation could reach around 3.75% in the fourth quarter, compared with the 3.2% projected in July, and slightly above 4% in early 2027.
Policymakers reported little evidence of substantial spillovers into wage and price-setting so far, but judged that the risk would grow the longer energy costs remained elevated.
Dixon said that before the US-Israeli attack on Iran, UK inflation had been expected to fall to 2% by April and interest rates to decline to a range of 3%-3.5%.
He now expects inflation to reach 4% by year-end and potentially rise further in 2027 if the war resumes.
“Bank of England rates will rise,” he said, describing a similar shift in the outlook for Western Europe and the US.
The bank’s September minutes showed that survey respondents anticipated a prolonged period of unchanged rates, while market pricing pointed upward.
Policymakers cautioned that risk premiums partly explained the market curve, meaning it did not simply represent expectations of future rate decisions.
Higher market borrowing costs were already reaching households: quoted two-year fixed mortgage rates were around 95 basis points above their pre-conflict level.
 
Japan tightens despite lower headline inflation
Japan’s annual headline inflation stood at 1.9% in August, while inflation excluding fresh food was 1.7%, according to the Statistics Bureau.
The Bank of Japan nevertheless raised its overnight policy-rate target to around 1.25% on Sept. 18 by a 7-2 vote.
It cited rising medium- to long-term inflation expectations and the risk that underlying inflation could exceed its 2% target as companies increasingly passed higher wages and input costs into selling prices.
The bank also identified high crude oil prices, yen depreciation and demand for artificial intelligence-related products as sources of price pressure.
It expected inflation excluding fresh food to accelerate clearly above 2% in the second half of fiscal 2026, while signaling further rate increases depending on economic and price developments.
Dixon warned that prolonged uncertainty could undermine confidence in central banks’ ability to maintain price stability.
“Expectations have been anchored in recent years, but there is so much uncertainty I suspect this may break down if central banks let inflation get out of control again,” he said.

By international convention an attack against civilian shipping in territorial waters of a sovereign state, if launched by another state, is a definable act of war. The internationally-recognized extent of a country’s territorial waters is 12 nautical miles, a standard used by NATO member states.
NATO’s Article 4 gives member states the right to consult and request assistance in case of a threat to its territorial integrity. Article 5 of the NATO stipulates that an armed attack against any NATO state constitutes an armed attack against all NATO members and could trigger the use by NATO of armed force in collective defense.

James McAvoy revealed which film brought him a "crazy" fee
Kyiv • UNN
James McAvoy candidly revealed that he regularly receives royalties from one of his films. According to him, the first cheque arrived right after the opening weekend.
Actor James McAvoy spoke candidly about his earnings, including the project for which he was paid "insane" residuals. UNN reports this, citing The Hollywood Reporter.
Details
In a recent interview on the podcast Happy Sad Confused, the actor acknowledged that, although his income from residuals is usually inconsistent, he cannot say the same about M. Night Shyamalan’s 2016 film "Split."
"The only film I get paid really consistently for is ‘Split,’" he told the host. "Well, I think it was made for approximately $6 million or so. Let’s say they spent $30 million on advertising, and we made $40 million on the opening weekend."
"So we were in profit. Therefore, our first residuals check came at the end of the opening weekend. It was madness," McAvoy added.
The film "Split" tells the story of three girls who try to escape after being kidnapped by a man (McAvoy) diagnosed with 23 different personalities. He reprised the role in the 2019 film "Glass."
The actor, who starred in "Atonement," praised Shyamalan, calling him "very smart in many ways."
"What impressed me most was how prepared he was because, you know, he made this film and ‘Glass’ on incredibly modest budgets and was very focused," he said, adding that the director made the most of the shooting time "by being incredibly well prepared" and "maintaining communication with the crew."
Although McAvoy received residuals from "Split," he also acknowledged that he "doesn’t get too much money from [the 2008 film] ‘Wanted.’"
"You always have good residuals, and they’re written into your contract; you get residuals here and there. I very rarely see anything from anything," he added. "Sometimes there are checks for a couple of hundred pounds, and sometimes for 25 cents, and you think: it literally costs more than my check."

Pärnu named European City of Sport for 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

20:46:00 KST

Pärnu named European City of Sport for 2027
Pärnu has been awarded the European City of Sport 2027 title by the European Capitals and Cities of Sport Federation, the city announced.
This means a second Estonian city has been awarded the title in three years, after Tallinn held the role last year.
Mayor Siim Suursild said the recognition reflects work done so far but that the most important work lies ahead, with a focus on getting more people active.
"We are very pleased and have reason to be proud! The European assessment committee has given Pärnu the European City of Sport 2027 title. This is recognition of our work so far and confirms that we are moving in the right direction. But the most important work is still ahead," Suursild said via the city's website.
"For us, the European City of Sport title is not an end in itself. What matters is what we can do better in Pärnu through it — bring more people out to move, support our sports community and create opportunities for an active lifestyle to be a natural part of everyday life," he continued.
The title is awarded by the European Capitals and Cities of Sport Federation, which works as a partner of the European Commission. It recognizes cities with strong sports infrastructure, the capacity to host sporting events and diverse opportunities for residents to take part in sport.
In early October, the federation's assessment committee visited Pärnu, toured its sports facilities and met local sports representatives.
"We got a very good overview of Pärnu and its sporting opportunities. Both the sports facilities and Pärnu's superb natural environment impressed me, creating very good opportunities for movement. Pärnu has a lot to offer as a sports city," said committee member and federation secretary general Hugo Alonso.
The European City of Sport is an annual recognition awarded by ACES Europe, a Brussels-based non-profit that works with EU institutions to promote sport, and is one tier of a scheme that also names European Capitals of Sport for larger cities and Towns or Islands of Sport for smaller communities. Tallinn was European Capital of Sport in 2025.

How many planets could fit in the solar system?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:44:48 UTC
20:44:48 KST

When I was a kid, I once watched a science-fiction flick called Journey to the Far Side of the Sun. The story’s main conceit was that scientists discover an Earth-like planet directly opposite our own in the same orbit around the sun, always hidden from our vantage point. The plot itself was somewhat silly, but the idea of a counter-Earth really stuck with me.
We know no such planet exists in real life, though; its gravitational effects on other worlds such as Mars and Venus would be obvious. Also, we’ve sent probes all through the solar system, and they’ve never spotted such a planetary arrangement.
But is this possible? Could two planets physically share the same orbit? The circumstances would have to be just right, and such a situation would be incredibly unlikely to occur. But the answer, surprisingly, is yes. In fact, many planets can technically share the same orbit! And when they do, their behavior gets pretty weird.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The basic physics of how one object orbits another—say, a planet revolving around a star—has been known since Isaac Newton’s day. The math for such a simple system is pretty straightforward. And it’s deterministic; once you write down the equations, you can predict what the system will look like as far into the future or past as you like.
Throw in a third massive object, though, and the math gets ridiculously more complicated and difficult to solve. Under some circumstances, however, solutions exist that allow for a stable system even if two such planets interact. One of those solutions is a bit of weirdness called a horseshoe orbit, and it relies on a quirk of orbital mechanics.
Imagine that two planets orbit a star on very similar paths, but one (call it Planet 1) is just barely closer to the star than the other (Planet 2). This inner planet, being closer, will move more rapidly around the star than the outer planet. Eventually it will catch up to Planet 2. What happens next is counterintuitive: instead of smashing into each other, or one of them getting flung away on a high-speed slingshot trajectory, they will start to interact gravitationally while they are still hundreds of thousands of kilometers apart. Looking just at Planet 1 for a moment, it will be pulled ahead by Planet 2’s gravity, giving it more orbital energy.
This is where the oddity of orbital mechanics really factors in: if you give an object more energy (say, by accelerating it), it will naturally move to a higher orbit, one with a larger radius. So as Planet 1 accelerates, it moves slightly outward from the star. But objects in larger orbits move slower. Thus, Planet 1 slows down and begins to lag behind Planet 2, widening the gap between them. As seen from Planet 2, Planet 1 will appear to approach on the inside lane, slow down, move to the outside lane and then fall away once again. It’s as if Planet 2 has repelled its sister world! In reality, both objects orbit the star in the same direction, just at different, changing speeds.
But what about Planet 2? It’s affected by Planet 1’s gravity during the encounter as well. Planet 1 pulls Planet 2 backward, stealing some of the latter’s orbital energy. That drops Planet 2 into a smaller orbit, where it speeds up and moves ahead of Planet 1. So now Planet 1 is on the outside path, and Planet 2 on the inside. They’ve swapped orbits!
Eventually they meet again, and this time the roles are reversed: they swap orbits once more, and we’re back to the original situation.
This is not just theoretical; we see this happening in the solar system. Saturn has a pair of moons called Janus and Epimetheus, which orbit the planet on paths that are only 50 kilometers different in radius, and they undergo exactly this orbit swapping every four years or so. So not only does this occur in real life, but it’s actually a stable configuration.
That means two planets can indeed share (or nearly share) the same orbit. And while they will encounter each other, they can do so safely.
But what about an arrangement with more co-orbital planets, such as, say, three? Does that work?
According to research by a team of international scientists published in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society (MNRAS), yes, you can have more than two planets share an orbit. Astonishingly, many more can coexist!
First, the researchers used the mathematics of orbital mechanics to simulate the physics of two Earth-sized planets orbiting a sunlike star at 150 million kilometers (the real life Earth-sun distance) and showed they can persist in such horseshoe orbits for billions of years! Then the team added more and more planets to see what would happen.
When two planets meet up with each other, they swap orbits, as is already understood. But eventually one will then approach the third planet. When it does, they swap orbits and move apart. Eventually one of those two meets up with the first planet, and the whole situation repeats. This happens with every planet-on-planet encounter.
Incredibly, the scientists found this to be true if they had as many as 24 Earth-sized planets packed into a single orbit! Twenty-four! That shocked me. Still, it seems to work in the simulations; any planet can’t get very far along its path without meeting another, and when the two do so, they swap positions and continue on until the next encounter with the next planet down the line, constantly sliding around and jockeying for position.
The scientists even tried this in a simulation of our own solar system, which, they found, could support the addition of an extra couple of Earths or Venuses—or another Mercury or Mars.
Creating a system like this isn’t easy. It’s possible that a very thick ring of dust around a star could form several planets in the same orbit simultaneously, though conditions would have to be rather fine-tuned to allow that to happen. Also, planets can migrate toward and away from their host star on much grander scales as they interact gravitationally. And if enough smaller planets get tossed around by this process, they could also end up in shared orbits.
Detecting such planetary systems from Earth is possible, too. One way we find planets now is through the transit method, in which a planet passing directly in front of its star creates a mini eclipse, as seen from Earth. If several transits occur in sequence when we should only see one for that particular orbit, that would be a sign. Also, the fact that planets in this arrangement slide along their orbit and swap positions means that their positions in that orbit change, which, in turn, changes the timing of the transits. That would be detectable, too, even if all of the planets don’t actually join the transit parade.
Delightfully, the authors of the MNRAS study speculate that there is another way to form these systems: building them on purpose. Having multiple worlds all in one orbit might be handy for interplanetary travel. And while moving them around physically is a daunting task, a sufficiently technologically advanced alien civilization might feel that it’s worth the effort. If we ever were to find such a system, well, that would be interesting, wouldn’t it?
What a way to discover aliens exist! And it would really make me reassess my opinion on Journey to the Far Side of the Sun—possibly

White House ordered limits on Ukraine’s military satellite service, Reuters reports. Who made the decision remains unclear
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:44:06 UTC
20:44:06 KST

Pentagon leaders received instructions from within the White House to slow Starshield, the military-grade version of SpaceX’s Starlink that Ukrainian forces use for battlefield communications and drone operations, Reuters reported on 15 October, citing two US officials and one Western official briefed on the matter. A day earlier, a senior US official told Axios the Trump administration had nothing to do with the alleged Starlink restrictions.
Ukrainian forces rely on US-controlled satellite technology for battlefield operations and for intercepting Russian drones aimed at Ukrainian cities, so the latest restrictions have raised questions about how reliably they can depend on it.
Senior US official denies president requested restrictions
Asked about the order, a senior US official told Reuters, “No such request was ever made by the president.” The White House did not respond to questions about whether other administration officials might have made the request.
Ukrainian officials contacted the White House, State Department, and Pentagon on Tuesday and Wednesday and were told it was a White House decision, a senior Ukrainian official told Reuters.
Berlin and London seek clarity
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul criticized the throttling and said Ukraine must continue to receive full support, Spiegel reported, citing his remarks on ZDF’s Maybrit Illner on Thursday evening. He also said Germany had questions for the US, adding that Germany finances part of the Starlink technology used in Ukraine.
UK Defense Secretary Wes Streeting said US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had assured him in a face-to-face meeting that Starlink was back up and running, according to the Guardian. A person in Ukraine’s Defense Ministry told Reuters on Thursday that military-grade terminals were working in motion again, but only at speeds up to 160 km/h.
New data-speed restrictions disrupted drone missions
The military Starshield package previously had no data-speed restrictions, Ukraine’s 7th Rapid Response Corps told Novynarnia. Ukrainian officials told Axios that after the restrictions were imposed, terminals disconnected when drones exceeded 160 km/h and sometimes at 80 km/h.
The Corps also reported 10–20-second connection drops at 110–120 km/h on the Huliaipole front, which made drones harder to control. One unit had to cancel some missions.
The restrictions came as US President Donald Trump pressed Kyiv to stop striking Russian oil refineries, blaming them for soaring energy prices ahead of November’s midterm elections. Ukrainian officials told Axios they suspected SpaceX imposed the restrictions to pressure Kyiv over the refinery strikes, but that motive has not been confirmed.

Russian attacks kill at least 3, injure 53 across Ukraine, as Moscow hammers energy infrastructure
At least three people were killed and 52 others injured across Ukraine over the past day, as Russian attacks targeted energy infrastructure in several oblasts, regional authorities said on Oct. 16.
In western Volyn Oblast, Russian attacks injured two people and left 370,000 people without electricity, regional governor Roman Romaniuk said. Russian attacks with jet-powered Shahed-type drones across 20 locations destroyed civilian and critical infrastructure, the governor added.
Ukraine's Air Force said Russia attacked Ukraine overnight with 149 Shahed-type drones, 108 of them jet-powered. The Air Force said it neutralized 114 of the Russian drones, 108 of them jet-powered, across 24 locations.
In Kyiv, a Russian drone crashed in Kyiv's Pechersk District on Oct. 15, injuring seven people and causing damage to a residential building, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said. Three of the injured people were hospitalized, Klitschko said. The Russian drone crashed near a five-story residential building, damaging the facades of nearby buildings, as well as setting a car on fire, he added.
In Kyiv Oblast, two people were injured over the past day, according to regional governor Tymur Tkachenko. One person was injured during a morning attack in the Fastiv District that also damaged eight residential buildings on Oct. 14, while another person was injured after a Russian attack in the Buchan District on the morning of Oct. 15.
In Kharkiv Oblast, three people were injured in Russian attacks over the past day, regional governor Oleh Syniehubov said. Among the three injured was a 105-year-old woman, Syniehubov said. Russia attacked the oblast with glide bombs, missiles, and FPV-drones across four settlements, the governor added.
In eastern Donetsk Oblast, Russian attacks over the past day killed one person and injured six others, according to regional governor Vadym Filashkin. One person was killed and three injured in Kramatorsk, while three others were injured in Sloviansk, Filashkin said. Russian attacks also damaged private houses, infrastructure, shops, and cars.
In Cherkasy Oblast, Russian attacks on the city of Uman injured five people, regional governor Ihor Taburets said. Three injured people were hospitalized, and a Russian attack elsewhere led to a fire in a warehouse, the governor said.
In southern Kherson Oblast, two people were killed and six others injured over the past day, regional governor Oleksandr Prokudin said. Russia struck the oblast with artillery fire and drones, Prokudin said, damaging residential areas and social infrastructure.
In Rivne Oblast, seven people sought medical help after a Russian attack on civilian infrastructure, including residential buildings, according to regional governor Oleksandr Koval. None of the seven injured had to be hospitalized, Koval said.

In southern Odesa Oblast, four people were injured in Russian attacks over the past day, according to regional governor Oleh Kiper. Russia struck private houses, a manufacturing enterprise, as well as energy infrastructure, the governor added.

Homeless man reportedly insults Erdogan to get food, bed in jail

- He was detained in Alanya and jailed pending trial, after three failed attempts to get pre-trial detention, according to Sozcu.
- The case highlights Turkey's insult laws, which have been used against critics. Justice ministry data show nearly 83,000 cases since 2016 under articles 299 to 301.
AI generated
ANKARA – A Turkish homeless man admitted to intentionally committing the offence of insulting President Recep Tayyip Erdogan in order to get access to food and a bed in jail, media reports said on Oct 16.
The 66-year-old was detained for the offence in a park in the southern resort town of Alanya, near the city of Antalya.
“I have nowhere to stay, I sleep in rubbish dumps. That is why I did it,” he told a court, which jailed him pending trial for the offence, according to newspaper Sozcu.
He had reportedly tried three times before but until now had not succeeded in being placed in pre-trial detention.
Insulting the president is a criminal offence in Turkey that has often been used against critics.
The authorities have charged many thousands with the crime, from journalists to teenagers and even a former Miss Turkey.
Although the offence has been part of Turkish law for decades, its use has risen significantly since Turkey transitioned to a presidential system in 2018.
Between 2016 and the end of 2025, justice ministry statistics show prosecutors opened nearly 83,000 cases into offences under articles 299 to 301 of the Turkish penal code, which cover insulting the president, insulting the Turkish flag and state symbols, and insulting the Turkish nation and state institutions.
Under article 299, the offence of insulting the president carries a prison term of between one and four years. AFP

Why is China buying up gold?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:38:11 UTC
20:38:11 KST

Why is China buying up gold?
Beijing’s gold purchases reflect a shift away from reliance on US dollar assets, experts say.
China is increasing its gold reserves in a bid to reduce its dependence on US dollar assets and protect against financial and geopolitical risks, analysts say, while households are turning to the precious metal amid uncertainty over the domestic economy.
The People’s Bank of China reported buying gold for a 23rd consecutive month in September, when the country’s central bank also made its largest monthly purchase in nearly three years. The sustained buying points to a longer-term effort to spread risk associated with its vast reserves, experts say.
Among concerns is high US debt and Western governments’ freezing of assets, which has highlighted the inherent risk in holding money overseas, particularly for emerging market and Global South economies. Gold bought and stored domestically offers protection against that risk because access does not depend on the will of another government.
But central bank buying and household demand for gold in China have different drivers. While Beijing is managing its financial exposure, private investors are seeking somewhere to preserve their savings. Here is what we know.
How much gold has China bought?
China’s central bank added approximately 23 tonnes of gold in September, bringing its reported holdings to about 2,410 tonnes, according to the World Gold Council. That was its largest monthly purchase since October 2023. Gold accounted for 8.5 percent of China’s total official reserves at the end of September, compared with 5.5 percent at the end of 2024.
Reserves are assets central banks hold to ensure they can meet international payments and respond to financial disruption. They usually include foreign currencies, foreign government debt and gold.
Private demand for gold within China has also risen, with purchases of gold bars and coins 28.4 percent higher in the first half of 2026 than during the same period last year, according to the China Gold Association. The buying of gold has continued amid falling prices, with gold down around 8.5 percent over the month.
The World Gold Council attributed the decline in gold prices partly to a stronger dollar and higher returns on US government debt. With interest rates going up in an attempt to curb inflation, these investments are attractive for buyers as they pay interest, making them more attractive to private investors than gold, which does not.
Why is China buying more gold?
A key objective is to reduce dependence on US government debt, known as Treasuries, according to Thu Lan Nguyen, head of commodity research at Commerzbank in Frankfurt.
China holds substantial reserves in dollar-based assets and, therefore, buying gold reduces its exposure to decisions taken in Washington. “China’s gold purchases are part of a broader effort to make its reserves more resilient,” Nguyen told Al Jazeera.
The freezing by Western countries of roughly $300bn in Russian Central Bank overseas assets following Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 demonstrated how reserves held abroad can quickly become inaccessible.
The concern for China may be that a future confrontation with Washington could expose some of its overseas assets to similar restrictions. “Gold held domestically has a crucial advantage in this respect: it does not represent a claim on another country and is therefore much less exposed to sanctions or asset freezes,” Nguyen said.
“I would interpret it primarily as risk management,” she added, pointing to increased geopolitical tensions and economic and fiscal risks.
America’s rising debt, which hit $40 trillion for the first time in history earlier this year, adds another source of uncertainty. In February, the US Congressional Budget Office projected that federal debt held by the public would rise from 101 percent of the size of the US economy in 2026 to 120 percent in 2036. That provides context for concerns about Washington’s ability to repay that debt going forward should an economic crash occur. Much of this debt is held by China. Gold, therefore, offers a less volatile and risky asset to hold.
Chinese households have different motivations for buying gold. When confidence in other investments weakens, gold can become more attractive as a way to hold savings. “Strong demand for gold can partly reflect a search for alternative stores of value,” Nguyen said.
The World Gold Council has identified weak Chinese share markets as one factor supporting domestic demand for gold, while its property market is burdened by heavy borrowing and overbuilding, contributing to a fall in housing prices, making it a poorer investment.
What this means for the US dollar
Analysts warned that China’s increased buying of gold does not signal an imminent end to the dollar’s global dominance. “I would be cautious about describing this as a major shift away from the dollar,” Nguyen said. “The dollar remains by far the dominant global reserve currency.”
But a gradual shift could still matter if China and other central banks put more of their new reserves into gold, buying fewer US assets than they normally would. That could weaken one source of demand for US government debt. But the effect would depend on how widely and quickly the shift developed.
“The key point is, therefore, that this is likely to be a slow diversification process rather than a sudden abandonment of the dollar,” Nguyen said. She added that the consequences for the US economy would remain limited unless the trend broadened and accelerated substantially.
Central banks also need readily available foreign currency to support international payments and the dollar remains central to those transactions. So gold can provide financial protection, but it cannot directly replace all the functions of dollar reserves.
Who else is buying gold?
China is part of a wider trend, particularly among central banks in emerging economies, Nguyen said.
“The trend is particularly visible among emerging market central banks,” Nguyen said. “But sanctions are only part of the story.”
Poland has also become a more prominent buyer. Its central bank purchased 31 tonnes in the first quarter of 2026 and another eight tonnes in July, according to the World Gold Council.
Large holdings do not necessarily indicate recent purchases. India, for example, confirmed in June that its physical gold stock remained unchanged at about 880.5 tonnes. India’s gold reserves have changed little since mid-2025, according to the World Gold Council. It bought about four tonnes in 2025, down from 73 tonnes in 2024.
Despite China’s sustained buying, its reserves remain far smaller than those of the United States. Its holdings of about 2,300 tonnes at the end of 2025 amounted to less than one-third of the US stockpile of approximately 8,133 tonnes.

Two Israeli women accused of smuggling 100 kg of khat released on bail in Poland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:37:04 UTC
20:37:04 KST

After three and a half months in detention, a court in Krakow has released on bail two young ultra-Orthodox Israeli women arrested on suspicion of smuggling 100 kilograms of khat, a plant classified as an illegal drug in Poland and the European Union.
The court accepted an argument from their Polish lawyer, Wit Steidler, in favor of their release. The women must report to police weekly and are prohibited from leaving Poland until the legal proceedings are concluded.
Steidler said that under Polish law, the amount of khat found in their suitcases was enormous. "This is a very serious crime in Poland," he explained. "Khat is included on the list of prohibited substances and is classified as a drug. If they are convicted, they could face between three and 23 years in prison. We managed to convince the court that it was inappropriate to continue holding them in detention.
"Even I, as their lawyer, was surprised by the court's decision to release them. But they are young women, this is the first time they have done something so foolish, and there is no point in keeping them isolated. We proposed bail and weekly police supervision. I was lucky the judge listened to me."
The two women, ages 23 and 24, were arrested on June 19 after arriving in Krakow on a flight from Israel. Each was carrying 50 kilograms of khat in her luggage.
There is considerable demand for khat in Europe among immigrants from Ethiopia and Eritrea. According to the report, individuals in Israel recruit young people, usually from the ultra-Orthodox community, to transport the plant in exchange for airfare and a payment of 5,000 shekels. They tell the recruits that if they are caught, the worst they can expect is a small fine or confiscation of their luggage.
However, Poland is considered one of the strictest countries when it comes to khat smuggling. In practice, the immediate consequence is often harsh pretrial detention. As soon as suitcases containing khat are discovered, typically weighing between 40 and 80 kilograms, the couriers are arrested and sent to detention facilities in Poland for periods ranging from several weeks to several months while their cases are examined.
For young people with no previous involvement in crime, the experience can be extremely traumatic: harsh detention conditions in a foreign country, separation from family, a lack of kosher food for those who observe Jewish dietary laws, and language barriers. Polish law enforcement authorities use detention as a form of shock treatment and as a punitive measure in itself, even before a trial begins.
Attorney Mordechai Tzivin, who represents Israelis facing legal difficulties abroad and assisted one of the women voluntarily alongside the Polish lawyer, said the Polish law enforcement authorities deserved thanks for the humane treatment they had shown his client, recognizing that numerous mitigating circumstances should be taken into account.

 Zelenskyy expressed concern that the US is siding with Russia, warning that the Americans and their president are on the wrong side of history. Orpo agreed. EU prosecutors asked to investigate advisory body
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:35:09 UTC
20:35:09 KST

The EU’s antifraud watchdog said it has passed on to prosecutors allegations of potential corruption at the European Economic and Social Committee, a Brussels-based body that advises the EU on proposed legislation and policy.
OLAF, the antifraud office, received a report from whistleblowers earlier this year saying there was a conflict of interest in the management of funds at the EESC, which is financed by the EU. It has now passed the case to the European Public Prosecutor’s Office.
OLAF’s press office told POLITICO it had sent the case to EPPO but added that it could not comment further.
Advertisement
The EPPO did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
“The EESC was informed by OLAF yesterday that this case has been transmitted to the EPPO,” an EESC spokesperson told POLITICO.
“Under these circumstances, the EESC cannot comment further except to re-confirm that when these matters first arose, the EESC president immediately and proactively referred the allegations to OLAF. The EESC will continue to respect fully the independence of this process.” Séamus Boland of Ireland was elected president in October 2025.
“The EESC and its senior leadership take this matter very seriously and remain fully committed to integrity, transparency and accountability,” the spokesperson added.
The EPPO has significantly stronger enforcement powers than OLAF. Whereas OLAF conducts administrative investigations, the EPPO investigates crimes against the financial interests of the EU, and can search private homes or seize evidence.
OLAF has also been investigating a report that EESC executives tried to smoke out a staff whistleblower who raised the alarm about the funding concerns, the EU Ombudsman told POLITICO.
Anonymous letters, seen by POLITICO, say that IT workers at the EESC were asked by senior managers to identify which staffers had connected to the OLAF website in previous weeks.
The EESC said those anonymous letters contained “serious personal threats” and added that they were not made through the EESC’s “robust formal whistleblower process.”

Turkey's Istanbul hit by worst floods in 80 years, with at least 4 dead
Catastrophic flooding in Istanbul was the worst in more than 80 years, Turkey’s interior minister said Friday as the death toll rose to four.
Istanbul, Turkey’s largest city with 16 million residents, was hit by more rain in the 48 hours up to Thursday morning than the combined historical average for September and October, the state-run Anadolu Agency reported.
“We are trying our best to help our citizens, but we are also experiencing the biggest flood disaster since 1942,” Mustafa Ciftci said during a visit to one of the areas hit hardest by Wednesday night’s downpour.
The body of a 66-year-old man was found Friday under a bridge in Istanbul's Sariyer district. Three other deaths were previously reported, including a teenager who was electrocuted in the storm.
Homes and businesses were flooded as water covered streets and parks across the city. Vehicles were washed away and many ended up piled up at the bottom of hills.
Before the discovery of the body on Friday, Ciftci told reporters in Sariyer’s Ayazaga neighborhood that four people remained missing.
He said there were 9,850 reports of damage and other issues related to the floods and that 46,000 personnel were working to clean up debris and help residents in Istanbul.
Murat Kurum, the minister for the environment, urbanization and climate change, accompanied Ciftci to the flood-hit neighborhood.
Addressing concerns that the floods were exacerbated by urban development close to waterways, he said that dealing with the problem was “essential.”
Kurum, who will chair the UN climate change conference, COP31, next month in the Turkish city of Antalya, also linked the floods to the effects of climate change. “Combating climate change is not a choice, but a necessity,” he said.

Malaysia’s welcome for Min Aung Hlaing undermines its stand on justice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:32:50 UTC
20:32:50 KST

Malaysia’s welcome for Min Aung Hlaing undermines its stand on justice
As the US attacks the ICC, Kuala Lumpur welcomes a leader the court’s prosecutor wants arrested. Middle powers must defend international justice.
On October 8, Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim received Myanmar’s President Min Aung Hlaing in Putrajaya with a guard of honour and an official luncheon, in the military chief’s first visit since the 2021 coup. Nine days earlier, Malaysia sent 1,476 Myanmar nationals back by sea in the first phase of a plan to return 5,000 people.
Kuala Lumpur calls this pragmatic diplomacy. In reality, it lends a middle power’s credibility to the Trump administration’s retreat from international accountability, weakening the laws and institutions smaller states rely on most.
Domestic pressures
Since May, a surge of online hate speech and misinformation has targeted the Rohingya, Malaysia’s largest refugee community. By late July, at least nine Rohingya community schools had closed or faced closure orders, and more than 100 Rohingya told UNHCR that residents of their Penang village had driven them out.
The hostility ignores the facts: Malaysia’s police chief says Rohingya account for 0.02 percent of crime. Yet research by INITIATE.MY and the Center for the Study of Organized Hate found AI-generated content amplifying anti-Rohingya disinformation across Malaysia, Indonesia, India and Bangladesh, casting refugees as a threat and legitimising vigilante violence.
Electoral politics plays a part. After heavy losses in three state elections, and with a general election due by February 2028, Anwar’s coalition may see a hard line on Rohingya returns as a show of control, though voter disillusionment and right-wing rivals make any electoral gains uncertain.
Impunity goes mainstream
Malaysia is not acting alone. Mongolia hosted Vladimir Putin in 2024 despite an ICC arrest warrant, and Hungary welcomed Benjamin Netanyahu in 2025 despite another. Kuala Lumpur denies this is recognition, yet Anwar says Malaysia will work towards Myanmar’s full reintegration into ASEAN, and Min Aung Hlaing wants a seat at the bloc’s November summit in Manila. Each welcome makes the next easier and tells leaders accused of atrocities, from Netanyahu to Min Aung Hlaing, that diplomatic rehabilitation is possible without accountability.
ASEAN has tried this before. In April 2021, Min Aung Hlaing agreed to the Five-Point Consensus, then ignored it: The violence continued, the ASEAN special envoy never met Aung San Suu Kyi, and inclusive dialogue never began. The bloc’s one real lever was excluding military leaders from its summits. Myanmar Specialist, Arkar Hein, said “Welcoming him back with nothing asked in return rewards that defiance and tells Naypyidaw that time and a staged election can achieve what
compromise would otherwise require. Each handshake abroad also makes the regime less willing to offer its opponents real concessions, and convinces them that only the battlefield will decide Myanmar’s future.”
A question of consistency
Malaysia has spent decades building its credibility as a regional peacemaker, a hard-won reputation it now puts at risk. It has facilitated the Bangsamoro peace process since 2001, helping negotiate a landmark peace agreement in the southern Philippines, and has facilitated talks in southern Thailand since 2013. In November 2024, Anwar welcomed the ICC’s arrest warrants for Netanyahu and his former defence minister, saying they “should be arrested even if they are visiting other countries”. That same month, the ICC prosecutor sought an arrest warrant for Min Aung Hlaing for alleged crimes against humanity targeting the Rohingya, and an Argentinian court has since issued its own.
The Gambia’s genocide case against Myanmar at the International Court of Justice centres on the 2016-17 operations Min Aung Hlaing commanded, which killed thousands of Rohingya, included mass rapes and burned hundreds of villages, driving more than 700,000 people into Bangladesh. UN investigators called for him to face genocide charges. Malaysia is not a party to the Rome Statute and has no legal duty to arrest him. But its credibility as a peacemaker and on Palestine rests on applying one standard to everyone.
Returns without safeguards
The returns rest on assurances no independent body can verify. UNHCR says it was not involved in the returns and had no access to verify that they were voluntary, and that safe conditions do not exist. Those returned reportedly included 27 children. Though not a party to the Refugee Convention, Malaysia is bound by the customary principle of non-refoulement, and the UN Special Rapporteur on Myanmar has warned of substantial risks.
Naypyidaw says no Rohingya are involved because it does not recognise them as citizens, but other returnees also risk arbitrary detention, prosecution and forced recruitment. The military does not even control Rakhine State, where the Arakan Army holds more than 90 percent of the territory. On September 28, a day before returns began, a military air attack reportedly killed at least 50 civilians there, following more than a dozen other mass killings by the military earlier this year.
Nor can the military-backed government deliver the peace that safe return requires. Its election saw no voting in 67 of 330 townships, and when Min Aung Hlaing offered peace talks in April, the National Unity Government (NUG) and major ethnic armed groups refused. Without a ceasefire and an inclusive political process, assurances of safe return ring hollow.
Malaysia’s frustration is nonetheless legitimate. It has hosted refugees for decades with little international support, and resettlement has shrunk since the Trump administration suspended United States refugee admissions in January 2025. But failed burden-sharing cannot justify returns without safeguards.
Pressure on the court
The ICC exists so that victims of genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity can find justice when their own states fail them. That mission now faces unprecedented pressure. On October 9, hours after former ICC judge Navi Pillay won the Nobel Peace Prize, the Trump administration sanctioned the court itself. Burkina Faso, Mali, Niger, Chad and Venezuela have announced their withdrawal.
Yet middle powers can push back. Seventy-nine ICC members, including Canada, Brazil, Mexico and South Africa, backed the court after the first US sanctions in February 2025, and in May Hungary’s new government reversed its predecessor’s withdrawal. In Southeast Asia, the Philippines surrendered former President Rodrigo Duterte to The Hague, and on October 8 judges found him fit to stand trial for crimes against humanity, with proceedings due to begin on November 30.
Middle powers should say no
Middle powers like Malaysia, and blocs such as ASEAN and the European Union, cannot stop US sanctions, but they need not follow the Trump administration’s lead. As Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney told the World Economic Forum in January, middle powers “must act together, because if we’re not at the table, we’re on the menu”.
Malaysia and its neighbours should lead by saying no: No to efforts to weaken the court, no to treating Min Aung Hlaing’s presidency as a clean slate, and no to Rohingya returns into an active conflict. Malaysia should back efforts to hold him accountable if ICC judges issue a warrant, and reconsider acceding to the Rome Statute, a move it abandoned in 2019.
Saying no does not mean disengaging. Kuala Lumpur should tie Myanmar’s reintegration into ASEAN to real progress on the Five-Point Consensus, starting with an end to violence and inclusive dialogue involving the NUG and ethnic armed organisations. At home, it should pause returns until an independent body confirms they are safe and voluntary, and hold accountable those who evict, threaten or attack refugees.
Malaysia should not carry this burden alone. ASEAN partners, members of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation and donors should fund refugee registration, education and integration, and resettlement countries should restore their commitments. Governments should also hold tech platforms accountable for amplifying anti-refugee disinformation and require swift action against incitement.
For years, Malaysia has offered refuge to the Rohingya and others fleeing Myanmar when few countries would. That record gives it the standing, and the responsibility, to defend the system of international justice it has long championed.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

Guterres urges faster action and financing to stop biodiversity loss
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:32:14 UTC
20:32:14 KST

Guterres urges faster action and financing to stop biodiversity loss
The United Nations Secretary-General appealed on Friday for governments, businesses and communities to accelerate efforts to protect biodiversity for future generations and all life on Earth.
Guterres was speaking in Yerevan, Armenia, ahead of the opening of the COP17 UN biodiversity conference next week.
“The food we eat, the water we drink, the very air we breathe – all are the gifts of biodiversity,” he told the Leaders’ Summit. “Yet every day, humankind saws another branch off the tree of life.”
Extinction risk
The UN chief said factors such as climate disruption, overgrazing and excessive use of fertilisers and pesticides “are driving the triple planetary crisis of pollution, biodiversity loss and climate chaos”.
As a result, more than a million species face the risk of extinction, “edging us ever closer towards an uninhabitable world,” he warned, adding that “it doesn’t have to be this way”.
Progress falling short
Mr. Guterres said the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, agreed four years ago, had inspired action worldwide.
Nearly 90 per cent of parties have established national biodiversity targets, while more than half have developed national road maps. Since 2022, an additional 1.3 million square kilometres of land and six million square kilometres of ocean have received formal protection.
However, “progress is uneven, and far too slow”, he said. Even if countries fulfil their current commitments, only 26 per cent of terrestrial ecosystems and 12 per cent of marine ecosystems would be protected by 2030 – “well short” of the Framework’s goal of conserving 30 per cent of the world’s land and sea by that date.
He also highlighted “major gaps” in national targets linked to economic systems, including commitments to reduce incentives that harm nature. Finance, technical capacity, cooperation and data collection remain inadequate, he said, noting that biodiversity financing is less than half of the $200 billion agreed under the Framework.
He stressed that biodiversity cannot be treated separately from conflict, food insecurity, disease threats or climate change. “Addressing any of these crises requires addressing them all,” he said. “And there is no time to waste.”
Government leadership required
The Secretary-General first called for government leadership, urging countries to meet the “30 by 30” target and “shift from policies that destroy nature, to practices that sustain it”.
Priorities include zero-waste and circular economies, sustainable farming, regenerative agriculture, stronger monitoring and transparency and firmer enforcement of existing laws.
He welcomed the Yerevan Declaration and its commitment to integrate biodiversity into government policies, budgets and regulations.
Redirect finance towards nature
His second appeal focused on finance as “the stark truth is, we are spending money on the wrong things”. He noted that for every dollar invested in protecting nature, $30 is spent on activities that damage it.
“In 2023, $7.3 trillion flowed into nature-negative industries,” he said, including polluting heavy industry, destructive agribusiness and fossil fuels.
“I urge governments everywhere to end these handouts once and for all, and to use the savings for people and planet instead.”
The Secretary-General said that meeting global biodiversity, climate and land-restoration goals would require annual investment in nature-based solutions to reach $571 billion by 2030 – equivalent to about 0.5 per cent of global gross domestic product.
Private sector involvement
“But governments cannot do this alone,” he said, calling for the private sector to step up. He pointed to the UN-backed Cali Fund as a mechanism through which companies benefiting from nature can help finance its protection.
Mr. Guterres also cited the rapid growth of renewable energy. The cost of solar power has fallen by almost 90 per cent since 2010 and investment in clean energy is now nearly double investment in fossil fuels. Moreover, renewable energy prevented emissions last year equivalent to the combined emissions of the United States, the European Union and Japan.
“But these benefits are not shared equally around the globe,” he said, noting that many developing countries have been unable to invest sufficiently in both nature and human development due to debt burdens, limited public budgets and an inequitable international financial system.
Participation from across society
The Secretary-General’s final appeal was for broad participation, particularly from young people, civil society, women, Indigenous Peoples and local communities.
“Environmental decline often falls hardest on the most vulnerable, and those who did the least to cause the problem. But the solutions often arise from these same groups,” he said.
With 76 days remaining until he leaves office, Mr. Guterres said that confronting climate change, biodiversity loss and pollution had been among his highest priorities.
“Let us act with the urgency this moment demands,” he said. “For our children. For our future. And for all life on Earth.”

These are the most underrated travel destinations in Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:31:54 UTC
20:31:54 KST

A little known region in Romania – Bucovina – topped the list for 2027 in a new ranking of underrated travel destinations by Time Out.
Major tourist destinations like Venice or Barcelona are popular for a reason, but when our love for certain cities is negatively impacting the locals who made it great in the first place, it’s time for a rethink.
The world is a big ol’ place, and there are plenty of lesser-known spots crying out for more visitors. Plus, you’ll have a far better time without having to constantly battle crowds.
Which is where Time Out’s list of the world’s most underrated travel destinations comes in.
Updated annually, the latest ranking has 41 cities and regions on it – and this year’s number one spot is in Europe.
Romania’s Bucovina topped the list for 2027, with Time Out drawing a comparison to the better known Translyvania, saying the region has “the same wild mountain scenery, age-old traditions and mind-boggling architecture”, but without the crowds.
Bucovina has been growing in popularity in recent years as the gateway to Via Transilvanica, the 1,400 km-long hiking trail that our writer Rebecca Ann Hughes took on earlier this year.
Europe’s most underrated travel destinations
The next highest-rated underrated travel destinations in Europe are Spain’s Asturian cities, which placed third.
Coastal spots here have already proven popular, but Time Out suggests heading to cities like Oviedo, Gijón and Avilés, particularly if you’re a foodie.
If you’re looking for a crowd-free beach escape, look no further than Zambujeira do Mar, which ranked sixth overall.
The cliffside town in Portugal’s Alentejo region is home to a Blue Flag-listed beach, and with the exception of the weekend of the MEO Sudoeste music festival, you won’t find many other tourists here.
Placing ninth overall is Carry-le-Rouet in France. The magazine compared the seaside resort to more popular spots like St. Tropez and Cannes, declaring it to be “just as idyllic with sea-to-cliff landscapes, turquoise waters and fresh seafood at a fraction of the cost”.
Just outside of the top 10, The Azores ranked 12th overall. The remote Portuguese archipelago has been attracting more attention in recent years, having been dubbed the “Hawaii of Europe”, but it has been working to ensure its tourism develops sustainably.
A destination certified by the Global Sustainable Tourism Council, there are numerous policies in place to protect the nine islands’ cultural, historical and natural assets.
The top 10 most underrated spots globally
- Bucovina, Romania
- South Dakota, US
- Asturian cities, Spain
- Osa Peninsula, Costa Rica
- San Martín, Peru
- Zambujeira do Mar, Portugal
- Bisbee, Arizona, US
- Shenzhen, China
- Carry-le-Rouet, France
- Tioga Pass, California, US

====================================================================================================

‘Subsidising suicide’: UN chief urges governments to stop propping up polluting fossil fuels
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:31:33 UTC
20:31:33 KST

Fossil fuels are 'boiling our planet', says Guterres. Yet COP31 hosts Türkiye and Australia are expanding them, a new report shows.
"Subsidising fossil fuels is subsidising suicide," UN chief Antonio Guterres told leaders today (16 October) ahead of next week's UN biodiversity summit, COP17.
At an event in Yerevan, Armenia, Guterres said governments were still "spending money on the wrong things" and singled out incentives for fossil fuels.
He urged countries to stop subsidising the production of fossil fuels that are "boiling our planet and are the scourge of biodiversity".
"I urge governments everywhere to end these handouts once and for all, and to use the savings for people and planet instead," he said.
EU finance ministers earlier this month called for a phaseout of fossil fuel subsidies at the COP31 climate negotiations taking place in November.
Slow progress on pulling funding for nature-harming activities
Nations have made little headway since pledging in 2022 to reduce public spending on activities that harm nature such as mining, fossil fuel extraction and intensive farming.
Countries have vowed to reduce harmful subsidies by $500 billion (€447b) a year by 2030 but little progress has been made.
"Nature won't thrive on good intentions," Guterres said.
The United Nations says that for every dollar invested in protecting or restoring nature, about $30 (€27) still goes into activities that degrade it.
This includes an estimated $2.6 trillion (€2.3t) a year in public subsidies that negatively impact nature and the climate.
Nearly 200 nations are participating in the UN biodiversity negotiations in Yerevan starting on 19 October where a lack of finance for nature will be a core focus.
Guterres launched a report on 15 October showing that the world was off track to achieving the 2030 biodiversity targets enshrined in a landmark pact dubbed the Paris Agreement for Nature.
"The war on nature has not yet ended," he said.
What is the Paris Agreement for Nature?
Signed by nearly 200 countries and territories, the nature pact laid out 23 targets for halting and reversing nature loss by 2030. These included reducing pollution, protecting threatened species and conserving 30 per cent of the world's land and oceans, known as 30x30.
"It's not all bad news... There is progress, but not enough," Guterres told reporters in Yerevan. "We are far from what is necessary."
The report showed that government policies were insufficient to meet the centrepiece 30x30 biodiversity goal. Taken together, government pledges would cover only 27 per cent of land and inland waters by the end of this decade if enacted in full. For oceans, the figure would be just 12 per cent.
Other targets were lagging further behind. Guterres said countries must honour their financial pledges to developing countries.
The lack of finance has been identified as a particular barrier to achieving the biodiversity goals.
"Biodiversity is in crisis. Species are disappearing and ecosystems are collapsing," said Sue Lieberman from the Wildlife Conservation Society.
"Governments and all stakeholders must see that investing in nature is not a luxury, it is the very key to our survival."
He also emphasised tackling government spending that harms nature, pointing to the "very strong influence" of some sectors that had "too much power" over government including industrial fishing, fossil fuels and logging operations.
COP31 hosts ramp up fossil fuel production
A Global Witness report released this week reveals the power of that influence.
Using data from independent energy consultancy Rystad, the environmental NGO's investigation found that the two COP31 hosts Türkiye and Australia are ramping up fossil fuel production ahead of the major international climate negotiations taking place next month.
Turkish national oil firm TPAO is set to nearly triple gas production. Two of Australia's biggest fossil fuel firms are also on course to hike oil and gas production: Woodside are set to double liquefied natural gas production by 2032 while Santos is on course to increase crude oil production eight-fold by 2035, according to the report.
Türkiye has come under scrutiny for its centrepiece COP31 electrification target. While it aims to raise the global share of energy demand by electricity to 35 per cent, up from around 20 per cent, by 2035, it stops short of specifying how the electricity should be generated. This, critics say, could allow governments to count expanded gas-fired generation as progress towards electrification targets
Efforts to reach a global consensus on setting concrete targets or pathways for phasing out fossil fuels have stalled and the contentious issue is not an official item in the COP31 negotiations.
Earlier his year, about 60 nations demanding faster action on fossil fuels staged their own breakaway conference outside the United Nations process.
Separately from the COP talks, which operate on a consensus-based decision-making process, some countries – including Germany, France and the Netherlands – have released voluntary roadmaps away from fossil fuels. Brazil is expected to follow suit in November.

IMF: UK should cut spending rather than raise taxes on banks
Heather Stewart
Heather Stewart is the Guardian’s economics editor, reporting from Bangkok this week:
We’ve just been in the IMF’s Europe press conference, where the topic of bank taxes in the UK came up [following our report that the chancellor is poised to tax Britain’s banks].
Asked about the possibility at JohnHealey’s upcoming budget, HelgeBerger, the economist who is deputy director in the IMF’s European department, suggested there might be better places to look to balance the books.
Berger pointed out that Healey’s predecessor, RachelReeves, had raised taxes in her budgets, saying:
“The last two budgets involved increasing government revenue, and ultimately there’s a moment where this becomes less productive but there’s still areas where Britain can make additional headroom available: modernising the property taxes or VAT, these are good examples. We wouldn’t recommend labour tax.”
Berger added:
“Ultimately, with taxes roughly at 40% of GDP - historically, for Britain, a high number - then of course balancing these measures on the fiscal side, doing a bit more there, makes good sense.”
He pointed to cost-cutting measures including removing the pensions triple lock, and “better targeting social benefits,” adding, “so I think that’s where you would put the emphasis, rather than the tax that you mentioned.”
Audit, tax and business advisory firm, Blick Rothenberg argues that increasing the bank corporation tax surcharge from 3% back to 8% might backfire.
Artur Vorobyev, a director at Blick Rothenberg, says:
Although this may sound like a reversal of a tax cut, when the surcharge was reduced in 2023, corporation tax increased from 19% to 25%. The combined rate on bank profits went up from 27% to 28%. Increasing the surcharge to 8% now would bring the combined rate to 33%. This is a significant rise and is counterproductive if the Government wants banks to invest and lend more to aid growth.”
Bloomberg: UK banks warn Healey’s tax plan will curtail economic growth
Bloomberg are reporting that the UK’s banking industry has “ramped up lobbying” against extra taxes planned by Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey.
They are apparently warning that a hike could shrink economic output by £6bn over five years and hit areas outside London the hardest.
Bloomberg add:
Pushing a surcharge banks pay on top of a standard corporation tax to 8% from 3% would also cut lending by about £10 billion by 2029 and reduce investment into the UK, according to a letter sent earlier this week to Healey by David Postings, chief of industry lobby group UK Finance.
Demonstrators have been protesting against the IMF and the World Bank at their meeting in Bangkok today, for the second day running.
According to the Bangkok Post, they encountered a police blockade which prevented them walking to Queen Sirikit National Convention Center, where the annual meetings are being held.
The Assembly of the Poor put the number of local and international protesters at 1,000 but the Metropolitan Police Bureau estimated about 800.

We will need to wait for the Budget to get the details of this tax, afterall, this is the Labour Party and they are well known for their U-turns. The Chancellor may need to water down plans for a tax if he wants to avoid denting both the economy and the FTSE 100.

Pensioners could suffer if the government hikes taxes on banks, points out Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell:

In other banking news, the UK government reportedly tried to persuade UBS to shift its headquarters and stock market listing to London in the event of the bank relocating out of Switzerland.

The EU is discussing the use of frozen Russian assets for Ukraine again — who is for it and who is against it
