The EU is discussing the use of frozen Russian assets for Ukraine again — who is for it and who is against it
Kyiv • UNN
EU leaders have resumed discussions on using Russian assets to support Ukraine. Belgium stated that its position remains unchanged.
European leaders on Friday, October 16, resumed discussions on using frozen Russian sovereign assets to support Ukraine, despite Belgium's continued opposition to the scheme, which it successfully blocked last year. Rapporteur reports, as cited by UNN.
Details
"The frozen assets are there: they should be used to support Ukraine. It's that simple," Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs said ahead of the second day of the EU summit in Brussels on Friday, where Ukraine's financial needs were to be discussed with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen also noted that these assets, the vast majority of which are located in Belgium, are the "most obvious place to turn to" in order to support Ukraine, which, according to the publication's estimates, will face a $78 billion funding shortfall next year.
These assets "serve a dual purpose: they will finance Europe's defense, but they will also mean that Russia, which is currently causing so much destruction both in Ukraine and in Europe, will itself pay for everything it is doing," Frederiksen said.
The EU's chief diplomat, Kaja Kallas, also proposed using Russian assets to cover Ukraine's impending budget shortfall. "I am sure that [the leaders] will raise this [issue] today," she said. "Ukraine needs this money right now."
The comments came several weeks after Sweden, Spain, Poland and the Netherlands wrote to the European Commission, urging it to revive last year's heated debate on using these assets to support Ukraine.
Belgium rejected Germany's initiative last year to provide a "reparations loan" backed by the assets, citing legal and financial risks for Euroclear, the Brussels-based securities depository that holds €190 billion in Kremlin funds intended for use in the loan.
Ultimately, EU leaders decided to issue €90 billion in joint debt to finance Ukraine, as well as to freeze the Russian assets indefinitely.
The remarks also came several hours after Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever told reporters that his country's position remained unchanged.
"At the end of a conflict, there is always a peace agreement, and part of that peace agreement is the use of immobilized assets," De Wever said at a press conference that began after midnight on Friday.
"Are there people on this planet who might dream of doing this differently this time and using these assets earlier for certain purposes? The answer to that question is: yes, there are. Are they in this building? They are. Are there [some] outside this building? Yes, there are. Do I want to talk about it? No, I don't," he said.
Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin also hinted that he did not want to resume discussions on the frozen assets on Friday.
"We strongly supported the issue of seizing [these] assets and the possibility of using them, but ultimately it produced no results," said Martin, whose country currently holds the presidency of the Council of the EU.
"I recognize the amount of energy and effort that went into this last time. I would be more supportive of doing something effective, efficient and as quickly as possible on this issue," Martin said.

Nuremberg at 80: How do you put a death machine on trial?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:29:28 UTC
20:29:28 KST

Nuremberg at 80: How do you put a death machine on trial?
On the night of October 16, 1946, 10 individuals were hanged in the Nuremberg prison. These were the main Nazi criminals who had been captured and brought to trial.
Despite the horrifying scale and brutality of the crimes, the Nuremberg Trials remain one of the most controversial proceedings in world history.
Justice instead of revenge
The idea of an international tribunal to address Nazi atrocities had been considered for some time. In 1942, the Soviet Union established a special Extraordinary Commission that gathered information about these crimes. Tragically, it had a lot of work to do. The USSR became the primary battleground for the bloodiest and most brutal war in Europe.
The range and nature of the crimes committed on Soviet soil were staggering: genocide against multiple peoples, mass killings on various grounds, all sorts of war crimes, deliberate attacks on medical facilities and civilian infrastructure, arbitrary executions, economic exploitation, and sexual violence. Essentially, every town liberated from the Nazis had enough evidence to warrant its own tribunal. When the concentration camps were liberated, it became clear that Allied propaganda had not exaggerated but rather understated the extent of Nazi atrocities.
In addition to the Soviet government, the exiled governments of occupied countries – Belgium, Czechoslovakia, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Poland, Norway, France, and Yugoslavia – also wanted to hold the Nazis legally accountable for their crimes.
The outlines of the future tribunal began to take shape in the fall of 1943 during a conference in Moscow attended by the foreign ministers of the ‘Big Three’ – the USSR, the UK, and the US. The three powers agreed that Nazi leaders who committed crimes across multiple nations should be tried by an international court.
At that time, even the idea of lynching Nazi leaders seemed valid. Benito Mussolini was executed along with his mistress by Italian partisans on April 28, 1945, without any trial. Their mutilated bodies were publicly displayed. No one mourned Mussolini; similarly, no one would have objected if a Red Army soldier had shot Hitler.
Sporadic acts of vigilante justice also occurred as the war neared its end. A well-known incident involved American soldiers executing the staff of the Dachau concentration camp. Polish troops beat to death Oscar Dirlewanger, the commander of a punitive brigade responsible for countless deaths in Belarus and Poland.
Yet vigilante justice was not what the Allied leaders envisioned.
The men in the dock – and those who escaped it
It became clear that the crimes committed were not only widespread but complex. Determining individual responsibility was not always an easy task. The Nazis had taken measures to conceal their atrocities whenever possible; for example, they buried the remains of over 100,000 people, mostly Jews, after executing them at Babi Yar ravine near Kiev. Furthermore, once the Reich collapsed and arrests began, everyone began shifting blame onto one another, particularly onto those who had already died.
By April and May of 1945, most of the individuals who would eventually be tried at Nuremberg had been apprehended. Of course, many key figures were never tried.
For obvious reasons, Minister of Propaganda Joseph Goebbels and Hitler himself were absent from the trial: both had committed suicide before they could face justice. Heinrich Himmler, the head of the SS, was captured by two freed Soviet prisoners, yet during a medical examination, he swallowed a poison capsule and died. Heinrich Müller, the leader of the Gestapo, likely shot himself in late April or early May 1945. His body was discovered months later in a temporary grave.
The fate of Martin Bormann, Hitler’s private secretary and head of the party chancellery, was unknown for many years. He went missing, which in 1945 could imply that he had fled under an assumed identity. However, today we can say with certainty that Bormann was killed in the final hours of the defense of Berlin, while attempting to break out of the encircled city alongside a column of German troops.
Twenty-four people were tried in Nuremberg. The most prominent among them was Hermann Göring, the commander of the Luftwaffe, who held numerous official and unofficial positions, served as Hitler’s close associate, and was considered the second most powerful man in the Reich.
Other figures included the Minister for Occupied Eastern Territories and the Nazis’ chief ideologist Alfred Rosenberg; Chief of the Armed Forces Command Wilhelm Keitel; Minister of Foreign Affairs Joachim von Ribbentrop; and the head of the security service Ernst Kaltenbrunner.
Nuremberg’s Palace of Justice was chosen for the trials for several practical reasons. It had direct access to the prison, was in relatively good condition, and was well-equipped to accommodate large numbers of people.
Unprecedented crimes, untested law
The decision was made to conduct the trials according to established legal standards, allowing the defendants the right to defend themselves. The Nazis found attorneys to represent them. Admiral Karl Dönitz took an interesting approach: he secured a maritime law specialist as his lawyer, but said that if he were not allowed to work with him, he would choose the admiral of the Allied forces who commanded submarines as his lawyer.
Rosenberg pursued a different strategy by trying to recruit Hans Frank, who was also being tried for war crimes as the governor of occupied Poland, and happened to be a lawyer by training. However, this request was denied. Furthermore, since the court needed to address the criminal status of certain organizations, and Martin Bormann was absent from the trial, the court appointed its own attorneys. The judges were from the USSR, the US, the UK, and France.
A significant challenge arose from the fact that some legal norms were developed during the trial itself. As a result, defense attorneys argued that the court was fundamentally unlawful since it relied on laws that did not exist at the time the defendants committed their crimes. Certain participants stated that Nuremberg represented “victor’s justice.” This sentiment partly fueled Winston Churchill’s earlier wartime suggestion to execute the political leadership of the Reich outright. The problem was that such a trial was unprecedented – nothing similar had ever been attempted before – and required the unveiling of many layers of guilt to find the responsible persons.
For example, one of the most repugnant acts leading to the mass death of people was the so-called Barbarossa Decree issued in May 1941. This document was signed by Field Marshal Wilhelm Keitel, chief of the German armed forces. It effectively removed accountability for crimes committed by Wehrmacht soldiers and officers against Soviet civilians. Such actions could only be punished if they harmed German interests. If a soldier looted and killed a peasant, Keitel technically bore no responsibility, as the soldier operated within the legal framework that existed at the time.
Additionally, during the trial, Keitel’s attorney attempted to shift all blame onto the dead Hitler, citing that Keitel “was just following orders.” Moreover, the fact that the USSR did not sign several international agreements designed to protect war participants, especially prisoners of war, compounded the issue. The mortality rate among Soviet POWs during WWII exceeded 50%; in absolute terms, 3.3 million out of 5.7 million documented prisoners died. And this was just a small part of the challenges faced by the judges at Nuremberg.
The prosecution comprised four categories of crimes: crimes against humanity, crimes against peace, war crimes, and general conspiracy crimes. There was a significant challenge in aligning the legal positions of the USSR, the UK, and the US. Soviet law existed as an independent branch but was rooted in continental legal principles; meanwhile, the British and Americans relied on their own legal frameworks; for instance, the concept of ‘conspiracy’ was unique to these countries and was not typical in Soviet or German law.
Additionally, the Allies often favored a compromise stance whenever they could have been held accountable for similar actions themselves. This enabled Admiral Dönitz to mitigate his own sentence: although German submarine forces under his command fought ruthlessly, British and American submarine forces could have been accused of similar conduct.
Witnesses, evidence and Göring’s defiance
In some cases, the Allies had to make real compromises with their conscience. One such case involved Erich von dem Bach-Zelewski, who participated in the proceedings as a witness. This man had directly overseen mass killings during counter-partisan operations in Belarus, Russia, Ukraine, and Poland.
A horrifying tactic employed by his subordinates involved rounding up villagers in partisan areas into one building, which was then set ablaze. The mass slaughter of Poles during the Warsaw Uprising in 1944 is another example of his policy – about 15 civilians were killed for every lost insurgent.
Zelewski understood that his survival depended on betraying others, so he turned on everyone, revealing their darkest secrets. Hermann Göring shouted from the defendant’s stand, “You disgusting traitor, swine!” but there was nothing he could do. Ultimately, a German court sentenced him to life in prison, not only for his wartime actions but also for murders committed during the power struggles in Germany in the 1930s.
The tribunal had volumes of documents to examine. American judge Robert Jackson later recalled that he had approached stories of Nazi atrocities with skepticism before the trial, but was horrified by the reality that unfolded before him. He was particularly struck by an SS report detailing the destruction of ghettos – Jews leapt from burning buildings, and some attempted to crawl away on broken legs; they were hunted down like game.
While most defendants tried to speak evasively, Hermann Göring stood his ground until the very end. He was informally dubbed ‘Fuhrer of the Defendants’. Göring urged his co-defendants to remain defiant and not to confess. He showcased his skills as an orator, made sarcastic remarks, and effortlessly parried the initial accusations.
According to him, Gestapo actions and concentration camps were just a response to the terrorist actions of the communists; and the extermination of Jews was merely harsh rhetoric, there were no actual plans for their annihilation. He claimed to have had no hand in any acts of aggression, insisting he was always taken by surprise by such acts. He also maintained that the Reich had to strike preemptively against the USSR to defend itself from potential Soviet aggression. As for the humanitarian catastrophe in occupied territories – that was the fault of the Soviet authorities and their scorched-earth tactics; and any crimes committed by German soldiers were merely isolated incidents.
Göring steamrolled over Justice Robert Jackson with his shameless demagoguery. However, the Allies had seized enough documents to bring down the Reichsmarschall. Soviet prosecutor Roman Rudenko and British prosecutor David Maxwell-Fyfe hammered Göring with his own orders that led to mass starvation. Göring knew that he intended to starve millions and openly discussed it in his circles.
In contrast, Albert Speer, the Minister of Armaments, didn’t plead for mercy; he acknowledged his guilt and presented himself as a humble technocrat, successfully avoiding the gallows.
The defense generally argued that the Nuremberg Tribunal established no new legal norms, yet the entire legal framework had been crafted specifically for this trial. Moreover, the conspiracy concept (one of the four main charges) allowed individuals to be condemned for being affiliated with criminal organizations. This was an unprecedented model in continental European law, including German law, and many lawyers deemed it inapplicable.
Even the term ‘genocide’ was used retroactively, having only emerged during the trial itself. Additionally, the defense reduced the discourse to the notion that the defendants were either uninformed or inadequately aware of the crimes being committed, while the actual perpetrators were presumably already in their graves.
The verdicts and the gallows
Out of 24 defendants, only 12, including Göring and Keitel, received death sentences. In reality, there were only 11, as the fate of Bormann remained unknown. Three others received life sentences – including naval commander Erich Raeder and Minister of Economics Walther Funk – but both were released in the 1950s. Rudolf Hess, one of Hitler’s associates, was sentenced to life in prison and committed suicide in 1987 at age 93. Albert Speer and the leader of the Hitler Youth organization Baldur von Schirach both received 20-year sentences. Interestingly, three people were acquitted: propagandist Hans Fritzsche, diplomat Franz von Papen, and financier Hjalmar Schacht.
Two others managed to evade justice altogether. Party official Robert Ley committed suicide before the trial even began, while Göring somehow obtained poison and took it just hours before his execution.
On the evening of October 15th, three gallows were erected in the prison gymnasium. Before midnight, the condemned were roused from their cells and led out. Execution began just after one o’clock, and by 2:45 AM, it was all over. The bodies were transported to Munich for cremation, and their ashes were scattered.
But that wasn’t the end of it. Following the main trial, there were 12 ‘mini-trials’ which focused on Nazi doctors, judges, and the case of the Einsatzgruppen (paramilitary death squads), among others. In total, 142 more individuals were found guilty, with 13 sentenced to execution. Many of these defendants were just as monstrous as those hanged in the primary trial. For instance, doctors were accused of a range of inhumane experiments on human subjects, including frostbite experiments, the deliberate poisoning of victims, and intentional infection with deadly diseases, among other atrocities.
Among those hanged was Waldemar Hoven, the chief physician at the Buchenwald concentration camp, who conducted gas poisoning experiments on inmates. A whole team of SS officers was convicted in connection to the Einsatzgruppen case. For unclear reasons, out of 24 individuals, only a few were actually executed, despite all being directly responsible for the murders. Among those executed was Paul Blobel, who organized the mass killings at Babi Yar. Additionally, separate trials occurred in various countries under their national laws. In Norway, 12 Germans and 25 collaborators were executed. In Poland, Rudolf Höss, the commandant of Auschwitz, was hanged following a separate trial.
***
The Nuremberg Tribunal was an impressive judicial process, and the Allies’ decision to hold it deserves commendation. The trial wasn’t perfect and it’s true that it departed from traditional methods of justice. Many legal norms were established retroactively; moreover, in the subsequent trials, many Nazi criminals managed to escape justice. However, Nuremberg wasn’t merely about ‘victor’s justice’. No one would dare say that those horrific criminals were hanged unjustly. Most importantly, while the principles of justice established in Nuremberg may have been imperfect, they are still effective in situations reminiscent of the horrors perpetrated by the Nazis.

German parliament backs tobacco tax hike for revenue, public health

Ayhan Simsek
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
Germany’s lower house of parliament late Thursday approved a phased-in increase in the tobacco tax that is expected to raise the average price of a pack of 20 cigarettes from roughly €8 ($9) now to about €9 next year and nearly €12 by 2030.
The Bundestag backed the measure with votes from the governing coalition of Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s center-right CDU/CSU alliance and the center-left SPD. Officials project the step will generate roughly €12 billion in extra federal revenue over the four years.
The increases will take effect step by step each January from 2027 through 2030. Brand cigarettes could cost as much as €14 by the end of the period. Fine-cut tobacco used for rolling cigarettes will also become significantly more expensive.
The figures are average projections based on the higher rates the coalition approved; manufacturers will set the actual retail prices, which can vary by brand.
The government has cited both the need to consolidate the federal budget and protecting public health. The additional revenue is not earmarked and will enter the general budget. Past tobacco tax rises have mainly helped close fiscal gaps.
Health experts see higher prices as an effective way to encourage people to quit. The German Cancer Research Center has reported that about 131,000 people died in Germany in 2023 from tobacco-related diseases. A 2025 survey found that 19% of people age 15 and older in the country smoke.

US in ‘denuclearisation’ talks with Russia and China: Trump
The US and Russia each have more than 4,000 warheads. China is set to catch up with them within five years, Trump says.
The United States is engaged in talks with Russia and China regarding nuclear disarmament, President Donald Trump has announced.
Trump said on Thursday that China – which lags behind the US and Russia in terms of the number of warheads it has – is racing to catch up. He added during an interview with US broadcaster Newsmax that Washington is discussing with its peers a route to “denuclearise”.
China’s nuclear stockpile of about 620 warheads is dwarfed by those of the US and Russia, which each have more than 4,000, but Trump said he thinks China will “catch up” within five years.
“The whole thing is a shame because I’d love to denuclearise if possible,” Trump said. “We’re actually talking to Russia about that, and we’re talking to China about that denuclearisation.”
China doesn’t seem willing to disarm, he noted, but said talks have continued. Newsmax reported that Trump spoke with Chinese President Xi Jinping on the subject, but no further details regarding the talks with either Russia or China were revealed.
Russia has the world’s largest stockpile of nuclear warheads, and the US is close behind, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI).
The two countries together possess an estimated 86 percent of all nuclear weapons globally.
China has the third largest nuclear arsenal, according to SIPRI, having expanded it to 620 warheads in the past year.
Trump’s claims came shortly after the expiration of the Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty, an arms control agreement between the US and Russia to limit their nuclear arsenals.
A month after the treaty expired, French President Emmanuel Macron announced the Forward Deterrence Initiative as Russia’s nuclear sabre-rattling during its war on Ukraine has spooked Europe.
Former Australian Minister of Foreign Affairs Gareth Evans told Al Jazeera that the world’s interest in the risk of nuclear weapons has waned.
“[The] world … has become alarmingly complacent about the risks of nuclear war with every major nuclear arms control agreement dead, dying or on life support and the longstanding taboo against threat or use eroding,” he said

Europe’s best party cities for a Halloween night out, according to a new ranking
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16

20:26:02 KST

From Edinburgh’s fiery Samhuinn festival to Dublin’s Gothic celebrations, Europe has plenty of ways to get into the Halloween spirit.
Halloween falling on a Saturday in 2026 means plenty of us will be keen to make the most of the spooky holiday, even travelling abroad to celebrate it.
Now, a new ranking has revealed the best party places to experience All Hallows' Eve across the globe.
Travel experts at Adventure360 analysed some 113 cities worldwide to uncover where travellers can find the biggest Halloween celebrations this year.
Each individual city was scored on the number of Halloween events happening between 30 October and 1 November, as well as the size of its nightlife offering and late-night restaurant scene.
The safety of the city was examined, too, and the report noted whether or not the destination hosts a signature Halloween or Day of the Dead event. In the end, each city was given a score out of 100.
In first place was New York, with a score of 91.1 out of 100, and it was followed by another US city, Chicago, which got a score of 80.1.
In terms of countries, the US had the most showings in the top 10, with New Orleans coming in at number nine but, continent-wise, Europe was revealed to be far and away the best Halloween destination, with five spots on the list.
Edinburgh is in third place, thanks in part to its legendary Samhuinn Fire festival, while Dublin follows close behind, partially because of its Bram Stoker festival.
Madrid, London and Prague also feature in the top 10, despite none of them actually offering a signature Halloween event; they’re just that spooky!
Within the Halloween top 20, other European cities included Rome, Berlin, Amsterdam, Barcelona, Budapest, and Lisbon
The world's best Halloween party cities 2026
How the cities rank out of a score of 100, according to the Adventure360 study:
- 1. New York, USA – 91.1/100

Europe’s top five cities for Halloween parties
Following the ranking, these are the five best cities to spend Halloween in Europe this year – and the reasons why.
Edinburgh, United Kingdom
Scotland’s capital Edinburgh may only have a relatively small number of nightlife venues and late-night restaurants, but it boasts plenty of Halloween-themed events, not least the Samhuinn Fire festival.
The event brings a dramatic twist to Halloween, with Calton Hill transformed by fire, drumming, acrobatics and elaborate costumes.
Taking place on 31 October, the event reimagines ancient Celtic traditions marking the end of summer and the arrival of winter, with performers acting out the battle between the Summer King and Winter Queen.
Dublin, Ireland
Dublin has just seven Halloween-themed events – one of the lowest amounts in the top 10 – but it makes up for it with its legendary Bram Stoker festival.
This year, the celebration of the city’s Gothic heritage will take place from 23-26 October, with four days of spooky events inspired by the author of Dracula.
Expect haunted walking tours, horror theatre, candlelit library visits and a spectacular parade. There’s family-friendly fun, too, including Stokerland, a free gothic-themed park at St Patrick’s Park.
Madrid, Spain
Madrid may not have one big signature Halloween celebration, but there’s plenty to get stuck into.
For a dose of horror, head to MADHORROR at IFEMA Madrid, running from 30 October to 2 November, with haunted houses, horror films, gaming and comic-book events.
After dark, join a ghost and legends walking tour through the old town, or head to Malasaña for costume parties and late-night drinks and eats.
London, United Kingdom
Although England’s capital doesn’t have a signature Halloween event, it does have some 22 themed happenings, as well as more than 1,000 nightlife venues and 2,600 late-night restaurants, which is the highest number in the top 10.
Head to Kew Gardens for its illuminated Halloween trail, featuring Dracula’s Lair, live performers and a Headless Horseman, or explore the capital’s darker history on a Jack the Ripper walking tour.
For something quirky, the London Transport Museum is holding a Halloween silent disco among its historic trains and buses.
Prague, Czechia
Prague’s Gothic streets make a fitting backdrop for Halloween, with plenty of ways to get into the spooky spirit.
While the Czech capital doesn’t have a signature event, Wonderland Halloween takes over the historic Lucerna Great Hall on 30 October for a night of elaborate costumes, live performances, DJs and theatrical decorations.
For something more low-key, join a ghost tour through the Old Town’s narrow lanes and medieval underground passages, where guides share tales of murder, alchemy and restless spirits.
On 30 October and on Halloween night itself, the legendary five-floor nightclub Karlovy Lázně will play host to its annual Wicked Weekend event.

Swiss journalist risks court sentence for exposing top banker
ZURICH, Oct 16 - Zurich prosecutors this week charged Swiss journalist Lukas Haessig with violating banking secrecy over reporting that set off a high-profile corporate criminal trial of the former boss of Raiffeisen Bank Switzerland, Haessig said on his financial blog Inside Paradeplatz.
• Zurich-based Inside Paradeplatz published a series of articles in 2016 about Pierin Vincenz, former CEO of Raiffeisen Bank Switzerland, and his business partner Beat Stocker, who were found guilty of fraud in April 2022
• That verdict is currently under review by a higher court expected to rule in January 2027
• Police in June 2025 searched the blog's Zurich office and home of its founder, seizing evidence linked to suspected violation of Swiss banking law
• Prosecutors had dropped the case in December 2025, but Zurich's High Court in April said a court must decide how the banking secrecy provision should be interpreted after a complaint by Stocker
• Article 47 of the Swiss Banking Act criminalises disclosure of confidential information leaked by bank insiders, with penalties of up to three years in prison or a fine
• Press freedom group Reporters Without Borders Switzerland called the charges troubling and said Article 47 of the Swiss banking act must not be used to prosecute journalists
• Inside Paradeplatz's reporting was clearly in the public interest, Reporters Without Borders said, adding the banking secrecy law had a chilling effect and pointing to "legal shortcomings" in Switzerland on press freedom
• Prosecutors said the presumption of innocence applies to Haessig. No court date has yet been set REUTERS

Coercive diplomacy: What does the call between Netanyahu and al-Sharaa really mean?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:24:04 UTC
20:24:04 KST

The phone call between Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Syrian interim leader Ahmed al-Sharaa—following months of firing salvos via fighter jets, missiles, and third-party intermediaries, alongside strikes that targeted the courtyard of the Syrian Ministry of Defence and the perimeter of the presidential palace—was no ordinary diplomatic formality. Rather, it was a condensed moment signalling a tectonic shift in the geopolitics and power balance of the Middle East.
When Netanyahu and Sharaa speak directly to discuss sectarian tensions in the Druze-majority province of Sweida, we are not merely witnessing a localised security arrangement dictated by geography and overwhelming force. We are standing before a series of uncomfortable questions shaping the region’s future: Is Syria capitulating entirely to the rhythm of Israeli power, which has established itself as an unyielding arbiter in the new Syrian landscape? Or is this a pragmatic response from Damascus to pressure from an Arab bloc seeking regional normalisation—a bloc that views any effort to rebuild and reintegrate Syria as passing, one way or another, through the neutralisation of active fronts with Tel Aviv?
Furthermore, who granted Israel and Netanyahu the political and international mandate to act as the self-appointed custodian over Syria’s Druze minority?
The most realistic answer lies elsewhere: in a devastated economy, a shattered state apparatus, and a transitional authority that has come to realise that rebuilding Syria requires, above all, zeroing out external hostilities. States emerging from the crucible of war do not enjoy the luxury of managing multiple conflicts at once. Today’s Syria looks far closer to this exhaustion model than to the legacy slogans of traditional “Resistance.”
Yet, the phone call poses far larger strategic dilemmas than it answers: Is this a tactical manoeuvring aimed at preventing escalation and buying time, or the beginning of a structural shift redefining Syria’s place on the regional map? Is Sharaa treating Israel as an unalterable geopolitical reality, or is the entire region entering an era where ideological mantras surrender to the imperatives of economic survival, reconstruction, and stability?
Anticipating an answer requires reading this new Syrian stance not as absolute surrender, but as a tightrope walk driven by a “survival mindset.”
Sharaa lacks the military capacity to engage an adversary that strikes the heart of Damascus with international impunity. Conversely, he understands that total compliance with Israeli terms risks sparking domestic fragmentation and delegitimising his rule regionally.
Hence, the most plausible regional scenario is Damascus moving toward ending the “active state of war” without entering the formal fold of political normalisation—establishing a security framework for borders and minorities that satisfies regional patrons while isolating Syria from radical axes to minimise reconstruction costs.
On the Israeli side, Netanyahu is attempting to engineer an advanced “politico-security belt” reaching deep into Syria’s social fabric.
By asserting proxy guardianship over minority populations like the Druze, Tel Aviv aims not only to secure its northern border, but to institutionalise a model of a “regional patron” holding the keys to stability in broken neighbouring states.
This style of power projection forces any future government in Damascus—whether led by Sharaa or another—to operate within a security architecture drafted in Tel Aviv long before it reaches the halls of the United Nations.
Ultimately, what transpired was not the announcement of a new alliance, but a mutual acknowledgment of a new balance of power. It is an equilibrium in which Netanyahu realizes his security influence remains incomplete without ordering his immediate Syrian backyard, while Sharaa recognizes that reclaiming statehood may require, for the first time in decades, managing relations with Israel through state pragmatism rather than ideological rhetoric.
The significance of the call lies not in its brief duration, but in its role as a barometer for a Middle East where yesterday’s political impossibilities have become today’s negotiating points.
Yet, all these calculations could swiftly evaporate or invert should Netanyahu lose power in the upcoming Israeli elections.
READ: Damascus rejects Israeli politicisation of Syria’s Druze after Netanyahu’s brief call with al-Sharaa
The core dilemma rests not solely within Syria, but in the nature of the Israel that Netanyahu embodies today. Under his tenure, Israel has transformed from a state seeking security-driven compromises into an actor behaving as the region’s absolute power, backed by an unprecedented surplus of self-confidence—perceived by its adversaries as military hubris and by its leadership as earned strategic dominance. Thus, any potential Syrian opening cannot be disentangled from the persona of the man wielding power in Tel Aviv.
Is Damascus reaching out to Israel as a permanent state institution, or is it coercively adapting to an extraordinary “Netanyahu moment” and the hard facts it has established on the ground? This question is no less vital than the issue of normalisation itself. If Netanyahu departs the political stage and Israel reverts to more conventional, less aggressive security calculus, the strategic weight of these contacts may shift overnight. They may well be reinterpreted as fleeting security arrangements dictated by temporary power dynamics rather than enduring strategic realignments.
When the dust settles, we may discover that the true historical event was not the phone conversation between Sharaa and Netanyahu, but the historical epoch that produced the phenomenon of Netanyahu itself—an era that compelled the entire region to redefine power, deterrence, and sovereignty under the weight of a prolonged war that has not yet ended, but will not forever remain governed by the logic of a victor who believes history moves by his will alone.

India's young workers have a new colleague: AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:22:00 UTC
20:22:00 KST

India's young workers have a new colleague: AI
October 16, 2026
Across India, young workers are increasingly turning to artificial intelligence (AI) to speed up routine tasks, whether researching news stories, translating copy, analyzing business data or sorting legal documents.
But the technology can get things wrong, and relying on it too heavily carries risks.
Journalist Farah Kazmi, 28, who works for a news portal in New Delhi, used AI while reporting on rules governing stray animals and feeding them in gated communities. She asked an AI model to find the Supreme Court's latest guidelines, earlier court rulings and recent dog-bite cases.
"Since it can take quite a lot of time to search Google for specific articles about court rulings, previous judgments or recent dog-bite cases, I asked AI to find them for me," Kazmi told DW.
It gave her a starting point for relevant articles and cases, which she then read and cross-checked herself.
Kazmi also uses AI to translate English copy into Hindi for the Hindi news team, and Hindi quotes into English. But translations need careful checking, Kazmi said, pointing out that in one case, AI interpreted the name "Suraj" as "sun," changing the sentence's meaning.
"Before using AI, I mostly relied on Google Translate. It was more literal and did not always understand the context. AI gives a much better and more context-based translation, although it still needs to be checked and corrected," she said.
AI has not fundamentally changed journalism, which still involves talking to people and reporting from the field, Kazmi said.
"Ultimately, I see AI as a tool that helps with research and saves time," she said, "but the actual verification and reporting still has to be done by the journalist."
Yajatt Misra, 28, business strategy and international markets manager at Kanoria Chemicals and Industries, uses AI to analyze data, summarize large volumes of information, prepare first drafts and structure ideas.
It also helps him turn financial and business information from different sources into management updates and presentations.
"Things like summarizing information, preparing first drafts, analyzing data and putting together presentations take less time now," Misra told DW.
Misra said the challenge was knowing when to trust the output. AI can miss business context or get details wrong, so its numbers, logic and conclusions need checking.
"There is less need to spend time on repetitive tasks and more focus on analysis, problem-solving and providing useful insights to the business," Misra said.
A 'junior colleague'
Rakshanda Deka, a 30-year-old lawyer, uses AI to sort large bundles of client documents chronologically or by theme and produce a first list of important dates. Some systems link information to the original documents so lawyers can check the source.
AI can also help prepare standard applications and petitions using a lawyer's own format and style.
"If used sensibly, and without outsourcing the substantive legal thinking, AI is basically like having a sincere fresher or junior colleague," Deka told DW.
But AI can confidently produce false information — making human checking essential.
"AI often gives you false information dressed up very confidently as fact," Deka said. "So it is imperative that you double-check everything."
Deka is concerned that some young lawyers may use AI as a substitute for their own thinking. "A lot of the youngest lawyers are beginning to use AI as a substitute for themselves," she said.
Widespread AI use
The use of AI is widespread among younger Indians, with a survey by Deloitte this year finding that 93% of Gen Z respondents and 95% of millennial respondents used artificial intelligence in their day-to-day work.
An Emeritus survey found that 82% of respondents aged 15 to 28 used AI tools at least weekly to learn or develop new skills.
Dimple Khubchandani, founder of recruitment firm Synoverge Consultants, told DW that employers increasingly want young professionals who can think critically, solve problems and check AI-generated work rather than simply handle basic research or drafting.
"AI is not necessarily eliminating entire job categories, but it is creating leaner teams and raising expectations," she said.
Khubchandani said a marketing agency that once might have hired four junior copywriters could now hire one to use AI for initial drafts, leaving more time to edit, refine the tone and shape strategy.
"AI is raising the baseline capability expected from employees on day one," she said.
Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), one of India's largest IT services companies, said in its 2025-26 annual report that it had scaled up its "Human+AI" operating model and was embedding artificial intelligence across services and software development.
Changing job market
Shrijay Sheth, co-founder of LegalWiz.in, an online legal and compliance service, sees the shift across the economy.
"AI's impact on job profiles isn't an anticipation," Sheth told DW. "It is a reality now. From basic research to strategy, operations, marketing, design and development, AI is changing how work gets done."
In software development, Sheth said, developers are spending less time writing code from scratch and more time monitoring, testing and refining AI-generated output.
"Business, product and problem-solving ability, coupled with skills around working with AI platforms, is valued over mere technical ability to work with any particular coding language," Sheth said.
By the numbers
The question of what happens to entry-level work is becoming harder to ignore.
A 2025 report by NITI Aayog, the Indian government's public policy think tank, cites data from the Center of Advanced Study in India suggesting that more than 60% of formal-sector jobs could be susceptible to automation by 2030 — particularly in IT and business-process services.
It also warns of slower hiring for entry-level software engineers and identifies junior quality-assurance and Level 1 support roles as vulnerable.
The World Bank's October 2026 India Development Update says AI's long-term impact on the country's labor market remains uncertain.
India could benefit from its technical workforce, IT sector and digital infrastructure, the report found, but stronger workforce skills and wider access to AI capabilities will be needed if the gains are to be broadly shared.
"The productivity enhancement and job loss are both real," Sheth said.
Deka said lawyers would increasingly be distinguished by how rigorously they check AI's work. "I think the differentiation is increasingly coming from the thoroughness of post-AI verification and confirmation," she said.

Once upon a time, the Nobel Peace Prize was founded to award genuine efforts to further world peace. Or so the legend goes.
Last week’s announcement that the 2026 prize is being awarded to South African judge, and strident critic of Israel, Navanethem “Navi” Pillay, proves how far it’s come – in the wrong direction.
Pillay, a former International Criminal Court judge, served as UN high commissioner for human rights from 2008 until 2014 – a position she used to promote an anti-Israel agenda – and last year she oversaw the publishing of a UN-commissioned report that concluded that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza.
Hamas, the Iranian-backed terrorist organization that literally committed an act of premeditated genocide during the October 7, 2023 invasion and mega-atrocity, in which 1,200 people were murdered in southern Israel and 251 abducted to Gaza, barely merited a mention.
The focus is on Israel, always on Israel. It’s part of the technique of delegitimization and demonization, with the aim of eventual elimination of the Jewish state.
What did Navi Pillay do?
In 2021, the UN launched an unprecedented, open-ended war-crimes probe against Israel. The “UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem, and in Israel” (COI) is tasked with submitting a report twice a year, in addition to the mandated sessions on Israel held by the UN Security Council every three months. Having uniquely granted the Palestinians “perpetual refugee” status, the UN needs to subject Israel to perpetual blame.
Pillay chaired the three-member COI, despite having already called for the boycott and sanctioning of Israel. She was joined by two members with equally problematic backgrounds, Miloon Kothari and Chris Sidoti. The three resigned last year, apparently fearing they could face US sanctions like UN Special Rapporteur for Palestinian rights Francesca Albanese, another UN official with a proud anti-Israel bias.
The Norwegian Nobel Peace Prize committee announced its decision on October 9, as Israel was deep in a week commemorating the barbaric frenzy of terrorist murders, rapes, and abductions three years ago – the worst attack on Jews since the Holocaust.
Pillay beat a list of contenders reported by Time magazine to have included, among others: Sudan’s Emergency Response Rooms (acting to provide relief in the war that few notice because Israel can’t be blamed), and Mykola Kuleba, co-founder of Save Ukraine, an organization dedicated, among other things, to reuniting Ukrainian children kidnapped and held by Russia during the ongoing war.
Israel’s Foreign Ministry dropped the diplomatic language to post on social media: “If there were an award for lies, hatred, and blood libels, Navi Pillay wouldn’t just be a contender. She’d be a frontrunner. Her role in the relentless, politically motivated demonization of Israel and promotion of the genoLIE speaks volumes.
“Awarding Pillay the Nobel Peace Prize isn’t a recognition of justice. It’s the grotesque weaponization of an award to legitimize anti-Israel hatred and prejudice.
“Now that the Nobel committee has rewarded the biggest lie of the 21st century, Joseph Goebbels is certainly applauding from hell.”
Chess grandmaster Garry Kasparov posted on X: “Maybe next year they will award the Chemistry Prize to a Hamas bomb maker.” Kasparov later clarified that he knows that the peace prize is granted by Norwegian committees while the other Nobel awards are given by Swedish institutions – but the joke’s on all of us.
In 2012, the Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to the European Union – another body that collectively promotes a Palestinian narrative at Israel’s expense. The irony that Norway isn’t even a EU member state was pointed out by Swedish editorial writer Henrik L. Barva, a brave supporter of Israel, Ukraine, and Taiwan.
I first met Barva, along with a very mixed group of international journalists, on a press tour of Taiwan (the Republic of China) to celebrate Double Ten Day, the October 10 national day.
We were together when the decision to award the prize to Barack Obama was announced in 2009, before he had even taken office, and had fun thinking up other Nobel categories in which he could have won the award, including literature for his books and the prize for physics, for defying the laws of nature and becoming the first superman to be elected president of the US.
As it happened, Obama missed the chance to further world peace by failing to support the courageous Iranian Green Movement protesters trying to overthrow the Iranian regime in 2009, and later promoting the disastrous Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action nuclear deal. The results are still being felt globally today.
When the 1994 peace prize was given to Yasser Arafat (along with Yitzhak Rabin and Shimon Peres) for the Oslo Accords, I didn’t find it funny.
I attended this year’s festive Taiwanese national day reception hosted by the Taipei Economic and Cultural Office in Tel Aviv last week. Chief representative Ya-ping (Abby) Lee noted the reception also marked 30 years since Taiwan’s first direct presidential election, and highlighted a shared commitment to democracy and freedom.
She also emphasized, “Taiwan’s global role in technology and the potential for closer cooperation with Israel in innovation and AI, while reaffirming our support for Israeli communities recovering and rebuilding.”
Taiwan was ousted from the UN in 1971 and replaced with the People’s Republic of China. Hence, democratic Taiwan – an economic powerhouse with much to contribute to the fields of health and technology, for example – is unable to share its knowledge through UN bodies, while Communist China – still threatening to invade Taiwan – has a permanent seat (alongside Russia) on the UN Security Council.
JUST AS I wasn’t shocked by Pillay’s Peace Prize award, I was not surprised by the announcement last week that the Palestinian Authority elections had been postponed – yet again. The PA had promised several countries, including France, that it would hold elections in return for gaining recognition as “The State of Palestine” last September. (The UN also recognizes the borderless, failed state.)
The elections – the first in 20 years – were scheduled to be held next month. They have been tentatively rescheduled for September 11, 2027, but don’t hold your breath.
The date 9.11 will be forever remembered for the jihadist attack on the US rather than Palestinian democracy and good governance. PA head Mahmoud Abbas, now in the 21st year of his four-year term, also pushed off the presidential elections, blaming Israel, of course, for the delay.
Israel, unlike the Palestinian territories, is gearing up for elections on October 27, but democracy is no guarantee of winning praise, let alone awards, as both Israel and Taiwan can testify.
US President Donald Trump blasted the decision to award Pillay the prize he has been eyeing for years, but he didn’t stand a chance. If he wasn’t considered worthy of the award for creating the Abraham Accords in 2020, peace agreements that have proven themselves over the years, then he won’t get it now, after tackling Iran.
In 2024, reported peace prize contenders included the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East (UNRWA) and UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, probably for the same reason that Pillay won it this year – dedicated criticism of Israel. It obviously wasn’t for creating peace.
Guterres gracefully complimented Pillay on her award, saying: “It has shown that the force of law must prevail over the law of force…”
Law professor Yuval Elbashan met Pillay in Nepal in 2009 and wrote in Israel Hayom this week: “Even then, in our personal conversation, she revealed hostility toward the very idea of a Jewish state in the Land of Israel, in which she saw an exact reflection of South Africa’s apartheid regime.”
He called this year’s peace prize “evidence of the deep anti-Israel politicization that has spread through international institutions… The anti-Israel stamp of approval has become a springboard to the biggest prize of them all.”
Elbashan also noted that Pillay “is now leading the push to redefine the legal definition of ‘genocide’ so that it fits and encompasses Israel’s actions in Gaza. She is doing so as an ad hoc judge… in Gambia’s case against Myanmar at the International Court of Justice in The Hague.
“She isn’t crafting this new legal test for the Rohingya people. She is crafting it to convict Israel.”
With winners like Pillay, world peace and justice are the losers.

Eighty years after Nuremberg, October 7 shows why evidence still matters - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:21:41 UTC
20:21:41 KST

On October 16, 1946, 80 years ago, 10 Nazi war criminals were executed following the Nuremberg trials. Atrocities were investigated. Evidence was gathered. Witnesses testified, and criminals were judged and sentenced.
Three years after the atrocities of October 7, 2023, we confront a different reality. Hamas terrorists launched a brutal assault on Israeli lives.
Today, a second assault is underway – not over territory or sovereignty, but over truth itself: whose testimony is believed, whose suffering is acknowledged, and what future generations will know about what happened that day.
I recently had the opportunity to meet Dr. Cochav Elkayam-Levy, chair of the Civil Commission on October Crimes by Hamas Against Women and Children.
She helped lead a two-year investigation resulting in Silenced No More, a nearly 300-page report documenting the sexual and gender-based violence committed during the Hamas attacks and against hostages in captivity.
Drawing on survivor and witness testimony, photographs, videos, interviews, and official records, the commission concluded that sexual violence was not incidental to the attacks. It was widespread, systematic, and integral to them.
The report is harrowing. Women, children, and men were assaulted and violated in ways that defy comprehension. At the Nova music festival. In kibbutzim. Along the roads of southern Israel. During October 7 itself and through hundreds of days of captivity.
Paradoxically, the report’s power lies in its dispassionate character. No rhetorical embellishment. Testimony corroborated. Evidence cataloged. Patterns identified. Conclusions carefully drawn.
The language is forensic, almost clinical, set against atrocities that strain the limits of human understanding. The unspeakable given language.
Reading the report, I found myself asking a question that initially seemed inappropriate: What, practically speaking, is all this documentation meant to accomplish?
At Nuremberg, the answer was clear: there were defendants to prosecute, verdicts to render, sentences to carry out. The perpetrators of October 7, by contrast, may never face anything resembling judicial accountability.
Many are already dead. Others may never be identified, much less brought before a court. No verdict will restore the murdered. No prison sentence will erase the trauma of survivors.
So why such painstaking attention to testimony, corroboration, photographs, dates, locations, and legal categories? Why document crimes that may never be prosecuted?
An answer comes, unexpectedly, from the opening chapters of the Bible. When Cain murders his brother Abel, God confronts him: “What have you done? The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to me from the ground.”
The original Hebrew presents a grammatical curiosity. The word translated as “blood” is actually plural: d’mei achicha. Literally, “your brother’s bloods.”
For centuries, Jewish commentators have debated the significance of that plural. One explanation is that Cain murdered not only Abel but also the generations of descendants who might have followed him. Another suggests that the plural evokes the many wounds inflicted on Abel’s body.
Documentation matters
October 7 suggests another interpretation. The first blood cries out for justice for the lives taken. The second cries for fidelity to the truth of what occurred.
The first demands that perpetrators be held accountable. The second demands that we, the living, bear witness, safeguard the evidence, tell the stories, preserve the names, and ensure that those murdered are not victimized a second time through the erasure or distortion of their suffering.
The first demand may never be fully answered. The second remains within our power, urgently so.
Consider the grotesque inversion surrounding the response to October 7’s sexual atrocities. Ordinarily, perpetrators seek to conceal their crimes, while human rights organizations seek to expose them and stand with victims.
On October 7, the perpetrators recorded, broadcast, and celebrated their brutality.
Yet so deeply entrenched is the hostility toward Israel, so toxic the epistemic antisemitism, that even in the face of overwhelming evidence, many institutions dedicated to defending victims of sexual violence responded not with solidarity but with skepticism, equivocation, silence, and even outright denial.
The dangers of historical revision abound, such as the moral perversity of New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s October 7 social media post offering only passing acknowledgment of Hamas’s atrocities before pivoting to Israel’s conduct in Gaza.
Or the choices made by those who award the Nobel Peace Prize.
We see it on university campuses, where the reality of October 7 continues to be contested. We see it on social media, where lies travel faster than facts and documented atrocities are already subjected to denial, distortion, and revisionism.
Nothing about investigating the crimes of October 7 requires minimizing Palestinian suffering or excusing Israel’s conduct in its prosecution of the war. The suffering of one people does not negate the suffering of another.
We can, and must, hold more than one truth at a time.
In our post-truth, AI-driven age, memory is no longer merely inherited. It is constructed, searched, summarized, and increasingly mediated by algorithms. What future generations know about October 7 will depend on the archives we preserve, the education we provide, and the technologies we harness today.
This is why documentation matters even when prosecution appears unlikely. Testimony is not merely preparation for a courtroom. It is an obligation to history.
On October 7, innocent blood was spilled. We cannot undo the horrors. We cannot restore the lives taken. But we can ensure that the truth of what happened is not buried alongside the victims.
That is the second blood crying out from the Earth. And it is ours to answer.
The writer is rabbi of Park Avenue Synagogue and author of For Such a Time as This: On Being Jewish Today (HarperCollins).

Middle Israel: From Caesar to Netanyahu, Israel prepares to enter a post-charisma era - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:21:11 UTC
20:21:11 KST

Theodor Mommsen was infatuated.
Julius Caesar, wrote a future Nobel laureate in The History of Rome, was “a statesman genius,” one so “perfect” that such a figure emerged only “once in a thousand years,” like the “consummate beauty” that even the most gifted painter “can only be silent” in its face.
Written in 1856, it was the kind of partiality that historians are expected to avoid, reflecting a German nationalist’s thirst for a charismatic leader who would unite his politically splintered people. That great leader would be far wiser, bolder, and more visionary than ordinary people. Charisma, the gift of natural leadership, would make that superhero deliver what no one else could achieve.
A similar attitude inspired Zionist historian Joseph Klausner’s depiction of the Messiah as “Judaism’s Ubermensch,” a superhero “far greater and stronger than the multitude, a personality to which all willingly submit.”
Inspired by Mommsen’s portrait of Caesar, Klausner painted Hasmonean King Alexander Janneus not as the Judean despot that rabbinical memory recalled, but as “a great king… dedicated to his country’s expansion and the spread of its faith.”
WWII produced fascist nightmares that tainted the charismatic leader
Such thinking was legitimate, even common, among German-educated intellectuals for generations – until World War II. The fascist nightmare produced a new breed of historians who realized that charisma is not necessarily a gift, and in fact can become a curse.
Writing in his acclaimed Caesar: A Biography, historian Christian Meier shrank Mommsen’s superhero into an opportunistic politician who had no coherent vision of Rome’s future, and thus did not shape the great events in which he played a central role. Instead, Caesar was now portrayed as a shrewd tactician who responded to events that were shaped by forces larger than himself.
For Jewish graduates of the 20th century, suspicion of charisma goes without saying, even though charisma also did us good, most memorably when David Ben-Gurion used it to win war, and when Menachem Begin used it to deliver peace. Now, however, the Jewish state is in the process of shifting from an era of charisma to an era of anti-charisma.
How long this transition will last is anyone’s guess, but for an Israel crushed by Benjamin Netanyahu’s overbearing charisma, the post-charismatic era’s emergence will not be one day too early.
Israel has already had two post-charismatic eras, and their results were surprisingly good.
The current age of charisma began in 1996, when Netanyahu first became prime minister. Though there were other prime ministers during the subsequent decades, Netanyahu shaped the era. And Netanyahu, even his rivals agree, led by charisma.
Netanyahu was more handsome, eloquent, and brash than any of his opponents. None could work a crowd, manage a press interview, phrase a political slogan, engineer a journalistic photo, or deliver a televised speech more effectively than he could.
In turn for all of this, and as has so often happened with charisma, these merits came coupled with a soloist’s failure to consult, or even just tolerate the presence of, other able people. The charismatic leader thus gradually became not merely the government’s leader, but the government itself.
How will Israel fill Netanyahu's big shoes?
That is why people now wonder, after surveying his potential successors: how will they get into his big shoes? It is the same question people asked in 1963, when David Ben-Gurion stepped down after leading Israel’s creation, and that is what people asked in 1983, when Menachem Begin stepped down six years after unseating Ben-Gurion’s successors.
In both cases, the question was even harsher than it is now, not only because Ben-Gurion and Begin were so much larger than Netanyahu, but because their successors were even less charismatic than the men who may soon replace Netanyahu at the State of Israel’s helm.
Levi Eshkol was an unassuming, bespectacled, balding, and grandfatherly man who loved to tell Yiddish jokes and looked like a tailor who had just emerged from a Lower East Side sweatshop. Whether in his intellectual curiosity, literary diet, historical insight, political vision, or rhetorical ability – he was no David Ben-Gurion.
Similarly, Yitzhak Shamir was no Menachem Begin. Begin spent decades in the public limelight, delivering fiery, eloquent, and unwritten speeches in mass rallies, and heading the opposition for nearly 30 years. Shamir spent most of the same years in the opaque labyrinths of the Mossad. Short, stocky, bushy-eyebrowed, introverted, and ineloquent, he was charisma’s antithesis.
Even so, this pair of antiheroes did incredible things.
Eshkol built the army that struck the greatest military victory in Jewish history. Before that, as finance minister in the 1950s, he built an economy that was the fastest-growing in the world, alongside Korea and Japan. And as prime minister, he inspired national reconciliation, first by ordering an official funeral for his party’s historic nemesis, Ze’ev Jabotinsky; then by canceling Israel’s military rule over its Arab towns; and finally, by bringing Menachem Begin into the government that won the 1967 Six-Day War.
Similarly, the uncharismatic Shamir led four million Israelis’ successful absorption of one million immigrants from the fallen Soviet Union. While at it, he airlifted Ethiopian Jewry. In the interim, he managed, with great poise, Israel’s precarious situation during the First Gulf War. And before all that, he and his arch-rival, Labor’s Shimon Peres, jointly saved a hyper-inflationary economy from collapse.
Shamir and Eshkol registered all these achievements not despite, but because of their lack of charisma. Their grayness only made them positively humble, focusing on the issues rather than on themselves, harnessing rather than fearing talent, and inspiring business-minded teamwork instead of spending their days thinking of the next photo op, soundbite or speech.
Now, as the post-Netanyahu era steadily approaches, this is what Gadi Eisenkot and Naftali Bennett offer, and what a traumatized Israel demands.
www.MiddleIsrael.net The writer, a Hartman Institute fellow, is the author of the bestseller, The Jewish March of Folly (Yedioth Books 2026), now available in English on Amazon.

The Trump administration has reopened an investigation into US Rep. Ilhan Omar’s citizenship, seven years after federal officials examined similar allegations and found insufficient evidence of wrongdoing, The Washington Post reported Thursday.
Federal agents searched the Minnesota Democrat’s Washington, DC, home on Monday as part of a renewed inquiry into whether Omar or her late father provided false information on immigration paperwork, according to the report.
The current investigation focuses on documents submitted after Omar and her family arrived in the US as Somali refugees decades ago, including paperwork used to obtain legal status and eventual citizenship. Omar and her family were granted asylum when they came to the US in 1995, when she was 12 years old, and she became a citizen when she was 17.
During Trump’s first term, Homeland Security officials reviewed Omar’s immigration history after a political appointee sought evidence of possible fraud, the Post reported, citing former immigration officials.
Investigators examined her family’s refugee history, questions about her birthdate and her father's past military service in Somalia, along with longstanding allegations about her marriage.
The review concluded there was “insufficient evidence of wrongdoing,” one former official told the newspaper.
The renewed inquiry could lead to criminal charges or an attempt to challenge Omar’s citizenship if investigators obtain evidence of fraud, according to officials cited by the Post.
 
Omar’s team claims ‘abuse of power’

“Trump has spread lie after lie about the Congresswoman in a desperate attempt to justify his extraordinary abuse of power,” her spokesperson said Thursday.

One former official familiar with the earlier review questioned the basis for reviving the case.
“I think her citizenship is solid and there wasn’t any fraud there,” the official told the Post.
Asked about Omar this week, Trump denied directing the investigation.
“I think she’s a terrible person,” he told reporters. “But that’s really up to the DOJ (Justice Department). I have nothing to do with it.”
Under standard policy, the Justice Department avoids taking any action that might be seen as influencing an election within 60 days of that election.

A senior official of an Armenian church foundation in southeastern Türkiye’s Diyarbakir province has welcomed the ongoing normalisation process between Ankara and Yerevan, saying increased contact could deepen friendship between the two countries.
“We view the ongoing rapprochement between Armenia and Türkiye very positively,” Ohannes Gafur Ohanyan, vice president of the Surp Giragos Armenian Church Foundation, told Anadolu.
Ohanyan spoke during a visit by seven Turkish and seven Armenian journalists to Surp Giragos Armenian Church in Diyarbakir’s historic Sur district. The visit was part of an EU-funded media tour supporting normalisation between the two countries.
“We believe that as these kinds of visits and events increase, the friendship between the two countries will grow even stronger,” he said. “Hopefully, the borders will open soon too.”
Türkiye and Armenia have no diplomatic relations, and their land border has been closed since 1993. The two countries launched a normalisation initiative in late 2021, appointing retired Turkish Ambassador Serdar Kilic and Armenian parliament Deputy Speaker Ruben Rubinyan as special envoys.
Türkiye’s Foreign Ministry said in May that technical and bureaucratic work to reopen the border was ongoing, although preparations for direct trade had been completed.
In early May, Turkish Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz visited Armenia, where officials signed a memorandum on the joint restoration of the historic Ani Bridge, a medieval structure spanning the border.
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan also discussed advancing normalisation, strengthening trade and economic ties, and improving regional transport links during a meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York last month.
Church draws Armenians from around the world
Diyarbakir’s Armenian community numbers around 60 to 65 people, according to Ohanyan. Despite its small size, the community maintains an active religious and social life centred on the church.
“Because we do not have a permanent resident clergyman here, we hold around eight to 10 services a year during important religious holidays,” he said.
Ohanyan described Surp Giragos as an 800-year-old church and the largest Armenian church in the Middle East, attracting visitors from Armenia and the diaspora in Europe and the United States.
After decades of disuse, the church underwent extensive restoration led by the local foundation, with subsequent support from Turkish state institutions, including the Culture and Tourism Ministry, before reopening for worship.
The church was later damaged during clashes in Sur in 2015 involving the terrorist group PKK. It was restored with funding from Türkiye’s Minister of Environment, Urbanisation and Climate Change, under the coordination of the General Directorate of Foundations, and reopened for worship after seven years.
Restoration continues at second historic church
The foundation’s second church, the roughly 500-year-old Surp Sarkis in the Alipasa neighbourhood, fell into disrepair over time because it had no congregation. It was further damaged by the February 2023 earthquakes centred in Kahramanmaras.
Restoration began in 2024 with a grant from the Ministry of Culture and Tourism.
“Surp Sarkis has been in ruins for nearly a century,” Ohanyan said. “We have made considerable progress and have largely completed the structural work on the main building.”
He called on businesspeople, philanthropists and the wider public to provide further support.
“A major church is being saved,” he added.

How Chinese Mesh Modems Ended Up in Russian Drones Striking Deep Into Ukraine

How Chinese Mesh Modems Ended Up in Russian Drones Striking Deep Into Ukraine
Chinese technology company Shenzhen Xingkai Technology has reportedly agreed to supply mesh communication modems to a Russian drone manufacturing facility, despite being informed that the equipment would be used for military purposes, according to an investigation by The Insider on October 14.
The investigation revealed that the Chinese manufacturer was willing to provide communication systems to a drone production facility in Alabuga, Russia, where the equipment could be used to support long-range drone operations against Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
A journalist from The Insider examined a Xingkai Tech mesh modem recovered from a Russian Gerbera drone in Ukraine before contacting the manufacturer while posing as a Russian military equipment supplier.
During the exchange, the investigator obtained evidence that the company was prepared to supply the equipment to the Alabuga facility, despite being explicitly informed of its intended military application.
When the journalists requested a quotation for 500 devices to be delivered to Alabuga, the manufacturer issued an invoice totaling 19.5 million yuan (approximately $2.87 million)
According to the investigation, Shenzhen Xingkai Technology continued discussing the potential transaction even after the prospective buyers disclosed that the modems were intended for military use.
The company also reportedly proposed processing payments through accounts at DBS Bank, Ping An Bank, and China Merchants Bank.
The Insider estimates that Shenzhen Xingkai Technology accounts for approximately half of the market for high-powered mesh modems used in Russian Geran and Gerbera drones, making its supplies particularly important to Russian military equipment manufacturers.
The investigation also highlighted the role of mesh communication technology in enabling Russian drones to operate at extended distances over Ukrainian territory.
Unlike conventional communication systems that rely on a direct connection between an operator and a drone, mesh networks allow multiple devices to transmit data through interconnected nodes. Under this system, individual drones can function as signal relays, maintaining communication with other aircraft operating beyond the direct range of their operators.
This capability allows Russian drones to receive commands and be manually controlled during flights deep into Ukrainian territory, enabling operators to exploit gaps in Ukraine's air defense coverage.
The findings come amid broader scrutiny of Chinese companies’ alleged involvement in supporting Russia’s military activities, even as the European Union and Beijing negotiate trade arrangements involving other Chinese firms.
The European Union is considering lifting trade restrictions on an unidentified Chinese company accused of supporting Russia’s war against Ukraine as part of a proposed agreement with Beijing aimed at protecting a key supplier to ASML Holding NV.
Under the proposed arrangement, China would remove restrictions on Sindlhauser Materials GmbH, a small German company that supplies components within ASML’s semiconductor manufacturing supply chain.

According to the monitoring channel Exilenova+, a series of explosions was reported in the Moscow region, where local residents also reported a fire following the attacks.
Amid the drone activity, Russia’s Federal Air Transport Agency, Rosaviatsiya, temporarily suspended operations at all four Moscow airports—Vnukovo, Domodedovo, Zhukovsky, and Sheremetyevo. More than 20 aircraft were diverted to alternative airports.
Accordong to Astra, Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin claimed that Russian air defenses intercepted 94 Ukrainian drones heading toward the capital between 11 p.m. on October 15 and 8 a.m. on October 16.
The overnight attacks also extended to Vladimir, where residents reported multiple explosions. Reports circulating on social media suggested that a data center operated by Russian technology company Yandex may have been targeted again. However, there was no confirmation that the facility had been struck.
Meanwhile, in Russia’s Rostov region, Governor Yury Slyusar confirmed that falling drone debris damaged production and warehouse facilities, sparking a fire. Emergency services were dispatched to the scene.
Slyusar also reported that a man was injured in the Aksay district during the attack and was receiving medical assistance. According to the governor, the Aksay and Chertkovo districts, as well as the city of Bataysk, were among the areas affected by the overnight drone activity.
The strikes on Russian territory followed an intensified wave of Russian drone attacks against Ukraine, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy reporting that Moscow had launched more than 850 Shahed-type drones between the beginning of October 14 and 9 a.m. on October 15.
In an October 15 statement, Zelenskyy said Russian drones had entered Ukrainian airspace in successive waves, maintaining an almost uninterrupted aerial threat throughout the reporting period.
“The drones kept coming in waves, and there was not a single hour when our skies were clear of them. From midnight yesterday through 9 a.m. today, there had already been more than 850 ‘shaheds.’ We managed to shoot down some of the ‘shaheds.’ But unfortunately, there were also dozens of hits,” he said.

France Opens Its Arsenal to Ukraine—Aster 30, Hammer and SCALP Production Licenses Are Now in Kyiv’s Hands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:17:51 UTC
20:17:51 KST

- Category
- World
France Opens Its Arsenal to Ukraine—Aster 30, Hammer and SCALP Production Licenses Are Now in Kyiv’s Hands
Ukraine has received all of the weapons-production licenses previously promised by France, clearing the way for Ukrainian industry to manufacture systems including Aster 30 air-defense missiles, AASM Hammer precision-guided bombs, and SCALP long-range cruise missiles, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on October 15.
French President Emmanuel Macron announced the planned transfer of the licenses in July following a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing in Paris.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The package covers three weapon families that already play important roles in Ukraine’s air defense and long-range strike capabilities.
The Aster 30 is used by the Franco-Italian SAMP/T air-defense system, several of which have already been supplied to Ukraine.
The modern Aster 30 Block 1 can engage aircraft, cruise missiles, and drones at ranges of up to approximately 120 kilometers and altitudes of up to 25 kilometers. It also has an anti-ballistic capability, allowing it to intercept some short-range ballistic missiles at distances of roughly 30 kilometers.
Domestic production would be particularly significant for Ukraine as demand for high-end air-defense interceptors continues to rise amid sustained Russian ballistic missile, cruise missile, and drone strikes.
Expanding production beyond existing European lines could help increase the number of missiles available to Ukrainian SAMP/T batteries over the longer term.
The AASM Hammer represents a different part of the equation. Rather than being a complete bomb produced from scratch, Hammer is a guidance and propulsion kit that converts conventional Western aerial bombs into precision-guided weapons.
Unlike the US-made JDAM family, Hammer incorporates its own rocket motor, extending its reach substantially. Depending on the release profile, the weapon can strike targets at roughly 15 kilometers when launched from low altitude and up to around 70 kilometers from higher altitude.
Current variants include the Hammer-250 for the 500-pound-class Mk.82 bomb and the significantly heavier Hammer-1000 for the roughly 2,000-pound Mk.84. Different guidance packages are available depending on the intended target and mission.
The third weapon covered by the French licensing package is the SCALP EG, the French version of the Franco-British Storm Shadow long-range air-launched cruise missile.
SCALP measures about 5.1 meters in length, weighs roughly 1,300 kilograms, and carries a 450-kilogram warhead designed to penetrate and destroy hardened fixed targets. The missile has been in French and British service since 2003 and is currently produced by MBDA.
The French SCALP EG and British Storm Shadow are fundamentally the same weapon, differing mainly in software and integration requirements for their respective carrier aircraft. Ukraine has already used the missile extensively for long-range strikes against high-value Russian military targets.
Earlier, a Ukrainian Mirage 2000-5F fighter jet supplied by France reportedly scored a first, shooting down a Russian S8000 Banderol cruise missile not with an air-to-air missile, but with bursts from its built-in 30mm cannons.
