The Yemen trap: Why Saudi Arabia should reject Israel’s help
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:16:21 UTC
20:16:21 KST

If reports are true that Benjamin Netanyahu tried to offer Israeli involvement on Saudi Arabia’s side in the war in Yemen, this should not be read as help. It should be read as a political and strategic trap.
Israel does not want to save Saudi Arabia from Yemeni missiles. It wants to insert itself into the heart of Gulf security, connect this role to normalization, and open a new door for political and military pressure. This is exactly what Saudi Arabia should reject.
The idea is simple. If Israel enters the Yemen war under the title of “helping Saudi Arabia”, it does not give Riyadh extra strength. It gives Saudi Arabia’s opponents a golden narrative: Saudi Arabia is no longer fighting alone; it is fighting as part of an American-Israeli front. This would damage Saudi Arabia’s political legitimacy, strengthen the Houthi narrative, and open the door to wider escalation.
The problem is that Israel has not been able to protect itself from the Yemen front. When Yemeni missiles and drones targeted Israel, Tel Aviv did not stop them. It struck Hodeidah port, but the attacks continued, the Red Sea remained unstable, and Eilat port entered a deep crisis. If Israel cannot protect itself from this front, how can it claim that it can protect Saudi Arabia?
This is why the Israeli “gift” is not a gift. It is a burden.
Saudi Arabia does not need Israeli aircraft to solve its problem with Yemen. It needs to close this file politically and security-wise. Continuing the war threatens the basic idea behind Saudi Arabia’s new project: security, investment, energy, and stability.
The Gulf sells a clear image to the world: we are a safe and stable region, able to guarantee energy, attract investment, and build a post-oil economy. But this image cannot survive under missile fire. You cannot invite investors to Riyadh while airports and vital infrastructure are under threat. You cannot build Vision 2030 in the shadow of an open war. You cannot become a global center for tourism, energy, technology, and services while your capital itself may be targeted.
Security is not a detail in the Gulf. Security is the core of the Gulf model.
This is why the war in Yemen is not only a military problem. It is a direct economic and political threat to Saudi Arabia’s future.
Every additional day of war weakens the image of Saudi Arabia as a stable country. Every missile strike, even if it does not cause major military damage, creates a serious psychological and investment cost.
This is where Israel’s game becomes clear.
Israel lives on regional chaos. The more Arab states are busy with internal and regional wars, the more Israel advances: in Gaza, the West Bank, southern Lebanon, and Syria. It wants to tell Arabs: your enemy is Iran, your enemy is the Houthis, your enemy is this group or that group. Then it uses this division to present itself as a security partner, as if it is not the same power destroying Gaza, turning southern Lebanon into burned land, and pushing toward annexation and displacement in Palestine.
The first strategic question in any regional policy is this: who is the main threat?
If the answer is wrong, everything built on it will also be wrong. If Saudi Arabia sees Yemen alone as its existential problem, it will enter a long war of exhaustion. If it sees Iran as the only enemy, it will remain trapped in a framework imposed for years by Washington and Tel Aviv. But if it sees the full picture, it will understand that the biggest danger is the fragmentation of the region itself and its transformation into permanent battlefields.
This does not mean the Houthis are innocent. It does not mean Iran has no project, influence, or interference. And it does not mean Saudi Arabia should not worry about its security. Saudi Arabia has every right to protect its borders, cities, infrastructure, and people. But protecting security does not mean staying in an endless war. And it does not mean opening the door for Israel to enter the Yemen file in the name of “help”.
The solution is not to import Israel into the Gulf. The solution is to redefine Gulf security.
Real Gulf security is not built on expensive Israeli defence systems, changing American promises, or turning Yemen into a permanent war of attrition. Real security begins with closing the Yemen front, opening serious negotiations, establishing a non-aggression arrangement, securing borders, protecting navigation, and stopping Yemen from being used as a card by regional and international powers.
Oman can play a role here. Iran can also play a role in mediation if it has influence. Wider regional arrangements are possible, not based on humiliating anyone, but on stopping the bleeding. The alternative is clear: the longer the bombing continues, the more blood is spilled. And the more blood is spilled, the harder it becomes for anyone to step back.
Long wars do not create political courage. They create memories of revenge.
That is why the most dangerous scenario today would be turning the Saudi-Yemeni war into a Saudi-Israeli war against Yemen. In that case, Saudi Arabia would not gain military support. It would lose its narrative, open a new door to escalation, and give Israel a place inside the Gulf security equation.
Netanyahu does not want peace in Yemen. He wants a longer war. He wants Saudi Arabia to remain in need of weapons and protection. He wants Yemen to remain a pressure card. He wants to appear before Washington and the world as part of the region’s “security solution”, while in reality he is part of the problem.
Saudi Arabia was right to reject this path. But rejection alone is not enough. What is needed now is a brave political initiative to close the Yemen file before it becomes a black hole swallowing security, investment, and regional standing.
The difficult path is not always the wrong path. Sometimes the hardest decision is the smartest one: stop the war, open negotiations, and prevent the Gulf from becoming another arena for Israel’s wars.
Saudi Arabia does not need Israel to be safe. It needs a regional policy that reduces enemies, closes fronts, protects its home front, and prevents Netanyahu from dragging it into a war that serves only his project.
The Yemen war should never have started. Today, what matters most is that it should not continue.
The views expressed in this article belong to the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial policy of Middle East Monitor.

Lake Mead barrel murder victim identified after 40 years, with mob links suspected
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:16:07 UTC
20:16:07 KST

The remains of an American man who was shot in the head and placed inside a rusty barrel were identified Thursday as those of Edward Jackson of Arkansas. Jackson was murdered in the 1980s, and the barrel containing his remains was discovered on the shore of Lake Mead after water levels dropped.
Jackson was believed to have been in his mid-50s when he was killed. Despite the identification, the murder remains unsolved, and authorities have appealed to the public for information that could help solve the case. Police said they had found no evidence directly linking the killing to organized crime in nearby Las Vegas, despite longstanding speculation. However, they have not ruled out that possibility. An expert on the city's mob history said the case bears the "hallmarks" of a Mafia hit, although many questions remain unanswered.
The victim was identified using a bone sample submitted for genealogical DNA profiling, along with three views of a facial reconstruction and a description of the clothing he was wearing when he died. The discovery of the barrel by boaters in May 2022 revived memories of Las Vegas' mob era, which stretched from the 1940s to the mid-1980s. Organized crime played a role in the city's development, and placing a body inside a barrel was considered a hallmark of a Mafia killing.
Jackson, who investigators believe lived in Hot Springs, Arkansas, had a brief criminal history in Salt Lake City, Utah, in the early 1980s. His record included one charge of aggravated arson and conspiracy to commit fraud. His family told investigators that he enjoyed traveling, and detectives found records placing him in California, where he lived with his wife in the early 1970s. It remains unclear why he was in Las Vegas.
Family members said they last saw Jackson in Arkansas in the early 1980s. They never reported him missing. Authorities said he had been shot and believe he was murdered in the early 1980s. Robert Price of the Las Vegas Police Department's homicide unit said investigators would continue working to determine what happened to him. "It's an unsolved case. It will never be closed until we solve it," he said.
Geoff Schumacher of the Mob Museum in Las Vegas said the discovery of Jackson's remains in a barrel recalled a 1976 case in which Italian mobster John Roselli was murdered, placed inside a barrel and dumped in a bay off Miami Beach.
Las Vegas historian Michael Green said whoever committed the crime probably believed the body would "never come near the surface." He noted that Lake Mead's water level was extremely high in the early 1980s, whereas today it is at historic lows following years of excessive water use, prolonged drought and rising temperatures.
The falling water levels have already exposed other human remains. In 2022, authorities identified a person who had drowned 20 years earlier, a Las Vegas resident who disappeared in 1988 and a man who drowned in 1974. Additional human remains were discovered in August this year.
Lake Mead and Lake Powell are the two largest artificial reservoirs in the United States. They are part of a system that supplies Colorado River water to communities across the southwestern United States and Mexico.
In 2022, Lake Mead's declining water level exposed Las Vegas' uppermost drinking-water intake. That forced authorities to switch to a deeper intake to maintain the water supply for the city's 2.4 million residents.

Ben-Gvir and Katz among a dozen placed under investigation
ROME,
16 October 2026, 13:15
ANSA English Desk

- ALL RIGHTS RESERVED
Two Israeli ministers are among those placed under investigation by Rome prosecutors Friday in a probe into the Israeli assault on the Global Sumud Flotilla for Gaza in May, judicial sources said. The Rome Public Prosecutor's Office has placed about a dozen individuals under investigation in connection with the mission of the "Global Sumud Flotilla," they said. The proceedings target members of the Israeli chain of command. In addition to National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, Defence Minister Israel Katz has also been named in the investigation. The actions of Ben Gvir in particular spurred outrage in Italy and led to Rome summoning the Israeli ambassador to protest about them. The minister was shown in a video posted from the port of Ashdod taunting Italian activists detained from the Global Sumud Flotilla for Gaza who had been handcuffed, blindfolded and forced to kneel in front of him with their faces to the ground, an incident in which the Israeli minister had reached the "lowest" level, President Sergio Mattarella said.
The investigation targets Israel’s entire chain of command, including the two government ministers, with charges ranging from torture to kidnapping.
They are accused of naval boarding operations carried out in violation of international law, poor detention conditions, degrading treatment, and a failure to uphold basic rights and the right to a legal defence.
The probe regards another mission as well as the May one.

Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen accused Madrid of doing “almost the exact opposite” of that adopted by other EU countries, intensifying tensions with her fellow Socialist, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez.
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen called on the European Commission to scrutinise Spain’s plan to legalise the status of 600,000 irregular migrants, directly challenging Madrid’s migration policy during the EU leaders’ summit.
“I have asked the European Commission to examine what happens when a country does almost the exact opposite of what the rest of us are doing,” Frederiksen said on Friday at the start of the summit’s second day.
Her comments put her at odds with Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, despite both leaders belonging to the same broad Socialist political family, which has traditionally taken a more liberal stance on migration.
Spain approved a decree in January last year to regularise the status of around 500,000 undocumented migrants, in a move to uphold what Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez described at the time as a migration model “based on human rights, integration, coexistence and compatible with economic growth and social cohesion”.
“I believe this runs counter to the migration policy supported by a large majority in Europe today,” Frederiksen said, criticising Spain’s move.
EU leaders are expected to face a heated debate on migration over lunch on Friday.
The latest draft makes no mention of Spain’s plan, which Denmark views as a potential “pull factor” that could attract more irregular migrants to Europe.
“Denmark tried to introduce outlandish amendments to the summit conclusions,” a diplomat from another EU country told Euronews.
This is not the first migration-related clash between Sánchez and Frederiksen. The Danish prime minister has long advocated a tough approach to migration.
At the previous EU summit in June, the two leaders reportedly exchanged heated words, with Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni backing Frederiksen, according to a diplomat.
Frederiksen and Meloni are now part of a group of countries pushing for tougher measures to curb irregular arrivals.
Denmark is also working with Germany, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands to establish the first return hub outside the EU for rejected asylum seekers.

Zelenskyy holds first one-on-one meeting with Hungary's PM
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has held his first official meeting with Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar.
Source: European Pravda, citing informed sources
Details: The meeting took place on the sidelines of the EU summit in Brussels and was held one-on-one.
According to one of the sources, the conversation lasted about 30 minutes, which significantly exceeded the plans announced by Hungary. Magyar had publicly predicted that he would speak for 10-15 minutes. However, the Ukrainian side had anticipated the duration that ultimately took place.
Notably, at the request of the Hungarian side, neither the Ukrainian nor the Hungarian press was allowed even into the protocol part of the meeting, several independent sources claim. It was also the Hungarian side that insisted the meeting be held entirely one-on-one, without assistants or delegation members, which is quite unusual for negotiations between leaders.
The meeting in Brussels took place following months of negotiations regarding the time and venue. Kyiv viewed this meeting as an opportunity to turn the recent diplomatic thaw into concrete progress in relations between the two countries.
Background:
- Ihor Zhovkva, Deputy Head of the Office of the President of Ukraine, reported that Volodymyr Zelenskyy had been invited to attend events marking the 70th anniversary of the Hungarian Revolution in Budapest. They are scheduled for 23 October.
- Zelenskyy and Magyar met after the Verkhovna Rada (the Ukrainian parliament) approved amendments to the law on education on Monday 12 October. These changes were necessary for Hungary to agree to the opening of clusters 2 and 3 in the negotiations on Ukraine's accession to the EU.
- The following day, the EU opened negotiations with Ukraine on the two clusters after Hungary lifted its objections.

Zelensky, Hungary's Magyar hold first 'one-on-one' talks at EU summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:12:56 UTC
20:12:56 KST

Editor's note: The story has been updated with the latest details.
President Volodymyr Zelensky and Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar met for their first bilateral talks in Brussels on Oct. 16, as their countries seek to open a "new chapter" in relations.
Both leaders are in Brussels for a two-day EU summit, where Kyiv seeks to drum up European support amid deteriorating ties with the U.S.
The meeting comes the same week Zelensky signed a law on the educational rights of Ukraine's national minorities, a step Hungary had demanded before allowing Kyiv's EU accession talks to proceed.
"We see the Ukrainian parliament's adoption of the minority education law and the immediate start of its implementation as a first step towards rebuilding mutual trust," Magyar said on X after the meeting.
The Hungarian prime minister also said that both countries would continue talks at the ministerial level, focusing on the situation of national minorities.
Magyar underscored that both countries agreed on the need "to build a new foundation for our political and economic relations" and expressed solidarity with Ukraine in the face of "Russia's brutal aggression."
After Ukraine passed the minorities bill, Hungary lifted its veto on the opening of two more negotiation clusters for Ukraine, allowing their official launch on Oct. 13.
The law gives Ukraine's Hungarian-speaking minority and other EU-language minorities more room to use their native language in education.
Ukrainian officials have said it would formalize existing education rights for national minorities rather than bring major practical changes.
Roughly 80,000 ethnic Hungarians live in Ukraine's westernmost Zakarpattia Oblast.
Zelensky said the meeting focused on Ukraine's EU accession efforts, as well as opportunities for bilateral cooperation, trade, and agricultural issues.
"We also discussed diplomacy and efforts to end Russia's war," the president said, adding that the leaders agreed to exchange visits.
"We're moving on our relationship with Hungary; we had a very good meeting," Zelensky said later at a press conference in Brussels. He did not rule out traveling to Budapest.
"I hope that we will get to the point where a new chapter opens (in Hungarian-Ukrainian relations)," Magyar said about his meeting with Zelensky a day prior, saying the two could then meet again in Berehove, a Zakarpattia Oblast town considered the heart of the Hungarian-speaking community in Ukraine.
Magyar has floated a meeting in Berehove since the spring, but no firm date has been set so far. The two held brief conversations in June in Brussels, and then again in July at the NATO summit in Ankara.

Swiss postal revamp plan faces fire during consultation
A revision of legislation governing the Swiss postal service has drawn criticism from both the left and the right of the political spectrum during a consultation process., which concluded on Thursday.
Swiss Post said it welcomed the government’s proposed changes as the consultation period ended on Thursday.
By putting its draft proposal out for consultation in June, the government was responding to the decline in demand for traditional postal services and to Swiss Post’s expansion of commercial activities beyond its core remit.
Business circles have criticised the insufficient opening up of the market and the overly lax restrictions on corporate takeovers.
Left-wing parties and the regions, for their part, have condemned the planned reduction in services from 2030 onwards, fearing a less dense postal network and a reduction in the number of delivery days.
Swiss Post has welcomed the planned changes, describing them as “dynamic regulation”. It has emphasised the importance of having room for manoeuvre.

UNDP local governance project to cover five regions of Kazakhstan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:11:16 UTC
20:11:16 KST

UNDP local governance project to cover five regions of Kazakhstan
Five regions of Kazakhstan will join a new UNDP-backed initiative aimed at strengthening local self-government, officials said at the 11th meeting of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) Coordination Council chaired by Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Economy Serik Zhumangarin, Qazinform News Agency reports.
The meeting brought together UN representatives, heads of central government agencies, and regional administrations.
Zhumangarin said Kazakhstan remains strongly committed to the global sustainable development agenda and has established itself as a regional leader in Central Asia, enhancing its positions at the international arena.
“As President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has repeatedly emphasized, the implementation of the SDGs is directly linked to our national priorities. Speaking at the 80th session of the UN General Assembly, the President noted that Kazakhstan had integrated sustainable development goals into state planning and budgeting processes. We attach particular importance to cooperation with international organizations in achieving these objectives,” he said.
UN Resident Coordinator in Kazakhstan Sarangoo Radnaaragchaa highlighted the importance of preparing an annual national SDG report, aligning budget planning with sustainable development goals, and strengthening regional cooperation. She also emphasized joint efforts between Kazakhstan and the United Nations on climate change and water resource management.
UNDP Resident Representative in Kazakhstan Katarzyna Wawiernia underscored the country’s progress in integrating the SDGs into the national planning system. She said the next key step would be adapting national priorities to the specific needs of each region, expanding local self-government, and unlocking territorial economic potential.
With support from the European Union, a three-year initiative to advance local self-government reform has been launched. The project will be implemented jointly with the Ministry of National Economy and local executive authorities in five regions: Abai, Zhetysu, Turkistan, Mangystau, and Kostanay. The initiative aims to stimulate local economies, strengthen regional capacity, expand employment opportunities, and increase household incomes.
Participants reviewed interim SDG implementation indicators and discussed future priorities. Among the achievements highlighted was progress in the SDG indicator measuring population coverage by the social protection system. The number of beneficiary families declined from 54,400 in 2025 to 41,300 currently.
In Kyzylorda кegion, 99.3% of schools have created conditions for inclusive education, while issues related to three-shift and dilapidated schools have been fully resolved.
In Zhetysu region, 110 settlements have been gasified, up from just five in 2022. Regional gasification has reached 67.2%, covering 467,000 people. Authorities plan to gasify another 16 settlements this year, increasing coverage to 72%.
Participants identified the development of a comprehensive national system for regular monitoring and evaluation of SDG implementation as a key priority, with efforts to localize SDG indicators set to continue at the regional level.
Earlier, it was reported that the Kazakh Energy Ministry together with the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) proceeded to developing a project initiative on digital intelligent power grids.

German lawmakers back monthly state pension contributions for children, with families able to add more
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:11:00 UTC
20:11:00 KST

Germany news: Parliament approves pension plan for children
Published October 16, 2026last updated October 16, 2026
What you need to know
- Germany's Bundestag backs a plan to give money toward private retirement savings to children aged six to 18
- Critics warn the scheme could widen inequality because wealthier families can afford to make much larger contributions
- Jewish student representatives say they have received death threats after blocking a far-right lawmaker from a synagogue commemoration
- The students defended their protest at an event marking seven years since an antisemitic attack on a synagogue in Halle
Here is a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on Monday, August 10, 2026:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.
Germany, France agree deal to support European car industry
Germany and France have reached a deal to protect Europe's automotive industry, the countries said in a statement Friday.
The plan aims to cut CO2 emissions and support the development and construction of electric cars in Europe, the statement added.
Read more about the story here.
German central bank chief sees scope for lasting growth
Joachim Nagel, president of Germany's central bank, the Bundesbank, says the country's economic recovery could last into 2028, while warning that further interest rate increases may be needed to curb inflation.
Speaking at the International Monetary Fund's annual meeting in Bangkok, Nagel rejected the suggestion that Germany's improving growth outlook was a flash in the pan. The IMF recently raised its German growth forecast for 2026 to 1.3%.
The recovery could continue next year and potentially into 2028, he said. Government reforms and a boost from artificial intelligence could help build momentum, with room for growth forecasts to improve further.
Nagel said the European Central Bank (ECB) would do whatever was necessary to bring inflation back to its 2% target over the medium term.
"We have raised key interest rates twice recently. If the situation remains as it is, I cannot rule out that we may have to act again," he said.
Eurozone inflation rose to 3.8% in September. Nagel said volatile market conditions justified deciding interest rates at each meeting based on the latest data.
Jewish students report death threats after protest against far-right AfD
Representatives of Germany's Jewish Student Union (JSUD) say they have received death threats after blocking an Alternative for Germany (AfD) lawmaker from attending a synagogue commemoration in Halle.
"We have faced significantly more hostility and significantly more hate — including death threats," JSUD chairman Ron Dekel told the RND media group.
The students blocked Hans-Thomas Tillschneider at an event marking seven years since the antisemitic attack on the synagogue. Dekel defended the action, saying right-wing extremists had no place at a synagogue, particularly when survivors and victims' relatives were mourning.
The far-right AfD is classified as extremist in Saxony-Anhalt, where Halle is located and where the party won September's state election. Tillschneider, a deputy speaker of the state parliament, criticized the students and said he had never opposed Jewish life.
Dekel also accused parts of Berlin's socialist Left Party of antisemitism, urging its prospective coalition partners, the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) and environmentalist Greens, to take this into account.
German lawmakers approve pension savings for children
Germany's parliament has approved a scheme giving children aged six to 18 a monthly state payment of €10 ($11) toward private retirement savings. The legislation still needs approval from the Bundesrat, which represents Germany's states.
Lawmakers from the governing conservatives and center-left Social Democrats (SPD) hailed the decision as historic. Michael Thews of the SPD said it would help many people build adequate retirement savings.
Fritz Güntzler, finance spokesperson for the center-right Christian Democratic Union and Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU), said the scheme would also introduce young people to the opportunities offered by capital markets.
Opposition lawmakers argued that it would deepen inequality because parents and grandparents can contribute up to €6,840 ($7,500) a year.
Stefan Schmidt of the environmentalist Greens called it a two-tier system, saying children who won the "parent lottery" could gain far more than a modest start to retirement saving.
The scheme is part of the government's broader pension reform agenda as Germany's aging population puts pressure on the state retirement system.

UN: civilian casualty toll in Ukraine remains at record high
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
14:10:34 EEST
20:10:34 KST

Intensified attacks by Russia across Ukraine in September continued the trend of 2026, where the number of civilian casualties significantly exceeds figures recorded in previous years, having devastating consequences for the civilian population, the United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine (HRMMU) reported, releasing its monthly update on civilian harm in Ukraine.
As noted by the HRMMU, repeated attacks on energy infrastructure threaten to further exacerbate these sufferings.
The HRMMU verified that at least 328 civilians were killed and 2,105 injured in September, bringing the total number of killed and injured 85 percent higher than in September 2025 (249 killed and 1,068 injured).
Civilians were killed or injured in 22 regions of Ukraine and Kyiv, with particularly high casualty numbers recorded in the capital, Kherson, Kharkiv, Sumy, and Zaporizhia. In Kyiv alone, civilian casualties were recorded on 22 out of 30 days – more frequently than in any previous month since the start of the full-scale invasion.
In October, the number of civilian casualties also remained high, the HRMMU reported. For example, on the night of October 6–7, the Russian armed forces carried out an attack using cruise missiles and drones across several Ukrainian regions, including Chernihiv region, where 22 civilians were killed and 45 injured in Pryluky. The HRMMU documented other mass-casualty attacks on civilians, including in Kramatorsk on October 8, Zaporizhia on October 10, and Lutsk on October 14.
"The first two weeks of October were among the deadliest for civilians in recent years. In just a few days, attacks by the Russian armed forces resulted in mass casualty incidents in Kharkiv, Zaporizhia, Kramatorsk, and Kyiv," said Head of the HRMMU Danielle Bell.
Verified data for September includes 18 killed and 44 injured civilians in Russian-occupied territory of Ukraine. The actual figure is likely significantly higher, as a lack of access and independent sources of information complicates the verification of many incidents.
The high number of civilian casualties in September and October occurred against the backdrop of the Russian armed forces resuming systematic attacks on energy infrastructure across Ukraine. On August 30, the Ministry of Defense of Russia announced that it had begun preparations for delivering "massive strikes on Ukraine's energy facilities." On September 30, an attack damaged generation, distribution, and transmission facilities in three regions and Kyiv, causing emergency power outages.
Attacks on Ukraine's electrical and thermal infrastructure continued in October. During a recent attack on October 13–14, the Russian armed forces struck a number of energy facilities across Ukraine, including three main power plants in Kyiv. According to Ukrainian authorities, the attack temporarily left 600,000 people in Kyiv without electricity.
In a report on attacks on energy infrastructure during the 2025–2026 winter, the OHCHR documented the consequences of such attacks for civilians and concluded that these attacks likely violated foundational principles of international humanitarian law.

20:10:11 KST

Human Rights Watch (HRW) has warned that at least 50 detainees face imminent execution at Gernada military prison in eastern Libya, after forces led by Khalifa Haftar reportedly executed at least 31 people following military trials that the organisation described as seriously unfair.
In a statement dated 14th October, the rights organization said the Libyan Arab Armed Forces had carried out the executions since late August 2026, raising concerns about further death sentences being implemented.
According to HRW, the executions were the first known instances of capital punishment in Libya since 2010, ending a de facto moratorium on executions that had lasted approximately 15 years.
The organisation called on authorities in eastern Libya to immediately suspend the implementation of death sentences and establish a comprehensive moratorium on executions.
HRW reported that a military prosecutor affiliated with Haftar’s forces announced on 23rd August that ten individuals had been executed by firing squad following convictions for murder and terrorism-related offenses.
Human rights organisations subsequently documented at least 31 executions by 10th September, according to HRW.
The organisation warned that additional detainees remained at risk of execution, particularly those held at Gernada military prison, and raised concerns about the fairness of the military judicial proceedings that resulted in the death sentences.

EU summit: Zelensky brings begging bowl to Brussels under Trump cloud
Vladimir Zelensky has put the pressure on his European backers by joining the second day of an EU summit in Brussels, in the week he chose to lash out at US President Donald Trump, and as European leaders grapple with soaring energy bills and the prospect of a difficult winter.
The gathered EU leaders will unlikely welcome having been effectively cornered into backing Zelensky’s “forever war” policy while attempting to secure ongoing US support in a week that protests and national strikes over pay and public services intensified across the continent.
The falling-out began last week when Trump announced a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to release additional Russian diesel onto global markets and ease sanctions in an attempt to bring down fuel prices. He also pressed Kiev to stop attacking Russian energy infrastructure.
- Zelensky rejected the arrangement, saying he felt “betrayed” by Trump and called the US president’s decision “weak.”
- Trump then called for Ukraine to get a “new president,” and questioned Zelensky’s willingness to reach a settlement with Moscow.
- Zelensky announced continued refinery attacks and complained of restrictions on American intelligence support and Starlink services.

- Trump called the attacks a “disgrace” and accused Zelensky of “driving up fuel prices for everyone.”

He also alleged that US missiles supplied to Kiev had been sold on the “open market.”
- Washington also announced it would prioritize its own munitions stocks over others. “Once we are really stocked, we will start letting our allies buy them from us,” Trump said.
EU leaders are likely to try to bridge the deep divide on stealing Russian sovereign assets held in Belgium. German Chancellor Friederich Merz, despite no popularity at home, is seeking to force Belgium’s Bart de Wever into a move. Merz outright dismissed a US proposal to integrate the billions in sovereign Russian assets into a peace formula.

In the same breath, however, he acknowledged that the restrictions had also disrupted medium-range strikes. He denied using the network for attacks deep inside Russia, but complained that lower speed limits had deprived Kiev of other strike capabilities. Musk has said Starlink should serve civilian and defensive purposes, describing offensive operations as “inappropriate for a commercial company.” Zelensky said partners had promised to restore the capabilities, although the previous speed limits had not yet been fully reinstated.
- 11:32 GMT EU has call for more pressure on Russia, no sanctions relief, and continued funding for Ukraine. Von der Leyen also accused Russia of failing to respect Trump’s proposed energy ceasefire. However, Kiev’s attack on a refinery in Russia’s Ryazan Region on Thursday went unmentioned. BRUSSELS, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- European Union (EU) leaders vowed Friday to continue financial and military support for Ukraine, and reaffirmed their commitment to advancing its EU accession process, as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky joined the second day of an EU summit here.

EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas also called for stronger support for Ukraine ahead of winter, while acknowledging Europe's dependence on U.S. military technology.
"Starlink is really necessary for Ukraine, and unfortunately, in the short term Europe can't replace this capability," Kallas told reporters ahead of the summit.
She also acknowledged difficulties in coordinating with Washington over the conflict, saying the EU was trying to persuade its American partners to increase pressure on Russia.
Costa and von der Leyen reaffirmed their support for Ukraine's EU accession, welcoming the opening of two additional negotiating clusters. Von der Leyen said the goal was to open the final two clusters by the end of the year, while Zelensky pledged to continue implementing necessary reforms. ■

U.S. companies to top CIIE exhibition area for eighth straight year
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
19:08:19 CST
20:08:19 KST

The State Council Information Office (SCIO) holds a press conference on preparations for the 9th China International Import Expo, in Beijing, capital of China, Oct. 16, 2026. (Xinhua/Pan Xu)
BEIJING, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- U.S. companies will top the exhibition area at the ninth China International Import Expo (CIIE) for the eighth time, with their area up 1,500 square meters from last year, an official said on Friday.
The ninth CIIE will be held in Shanghai from Nov. 5 to 10. Launched in 2018 as the world's first national-level expo dedicated to imports, the CIIE was designed to expand China's opening up and turn its vast market into a shared opportunity for the world.
Preparations for the ninth CIIE are basically complete. A total of 162 countries, regions and international organizations will take part, with 4,142 overseas companies exhibiting, China's Vice Minister of Commerce Yan Dong told a press conference.
The overall exhibition area will exceed 440,000 square meters for the first time. In the enterprise exhibition, companies from the United States, Germany, Britain and France will lead the pack in terms of exhibition space.
For the first time, the number of Fortune Global 500 companies and industry leaders attending the event will surpass 300. Additionally, over 2,000 companies will be exhibiting at the CIIE for the first time.
This year's CIIE will feature over 200 representative global debuts and first-time exhibits. A variety of cutting-edge innovations that empower industries and enhance people's lives will be showcased together, including endoscopic surgical robots and cochlear implants.
Ahead of this year's CIIE, matchmaking sessions themed under "export to China" were held in countries including Egypt, Germany and Britain, bringing procurement talks to the doorstep of trading partners.
The CIIE is a prominent example of China's efforts to expand imports and provide more channels for quality products from around the world to enter the Chinese market. This commitment has remained high on China's agenda, and the results are tangible.
According to the General Administration of Customs, China's imports reached 16.7 trillion yuan (about 2.48 trillion U.S. dollars) in the first nine months of this year, up 22.3 percent, the fastest growth since 2021.
Minister of Commerce Wang Wentao said earlier this year that China's market holds huge potential, adding that the country will bring in more agricultural goods, quality consumer products, advanced technology equipment and key components. Meanwhile, platforms like the CIIE will be fully used to expand import channels, he said.
"Exports and imports are like two wheels of a vehicle. The more balanced they are, the smoother and farther it goes," Wang said. ■

The idea was to allow residents to express their views on whether or not they agreed "that the Lisbon City Council" should cease "to authorise the operation of electric scooter-sharing schemes in the municipal public domain once the current licences have expired."
In an interview with the Now outlet on Thursday, the mayor indicated that he would present the proposal at a council meeting, expressing hope that the Socialist Party, which also voted in favour of a similar suspension in Braga, would support the decision, so that an "immediate suspension of shared scooters" in the city could be implemented.
The issue is set to be discussed at a council meeting on 21 October.

====================================================================================================

T-beam installation completed on 2nd China-Mongolia cross-border railway
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
19:08:11 CST
20:08:11 KST

ULAN BATOR, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- The installation of all T-beams on the Gantsmod-Gashuunsukhait railway, the second cross-border railway link between China and Mongolia, was completed on Friday following the placement of the final prefabricated beam.
Measuring 32.6 meters in length and weighing approximately 134 tonnes, the final T-beam was installed by China Railway Construction Bridge Engineering Bureau Group Co., Ltd. The milestone lays a solid foundation for subsequent construction work.
The Gantsmod-Gashuunsukhait railway is the second cross-border railway link between China and Mongolia, nearly 70 years after the Erenhot-Zamiin-Uud railway opened in 1956. The project is expected to become a new link in infrastructure connectivity between the two countries.
The railway is being jointly developed by China and Mongolia under the principle of "unified design, independent construction and integrated commissioning." The line crosses the border at the Gantsmod port in China and the Gashuunsukhait port in Mongolia before connecting to Gashuunsukhait station in Mongolia's Umnugovi Province.
Construction of the cross-border railway project began in May 2025. The route is 9.91 kilometers long, including a 6.08-kilometer cross-border bridge section that requires the installation of 760 T-beams. The heaviest individual beam weighs 149.5 tonnes.
Handling and installing such heavy structural components requires a high level of technical expertise, rigorous safety management and precise equipment operation. Construction has also been complicated by the route's desert environment. Having overcome numerous challenges, the project team completed all work to high standards and quality.
The Gantsmod-Gashuunsukhait railway marks a significant step forward in strengthening strategic alignment and practical cooperation between China and Mongolia.
Once operational, the railway is expected to transport 30 million tonnes of cargo annually, linking the Gantsmod Railway with Mongolia's southbound railway network. The project is expected to expand bilateral trade, improve transport and logistics connectivity, and stimulate economic activity along the route. It could also support the development of cross-border logistics services, industrial parks and border trade facilities in both countries.
The railway is expected to play an important role in deepening China-Mongolia economic cooperation and advancing high-quality cooperation under the Belt and Road Initiative. ■

Chinese FM meets Israeli president
China

2026-10-16

Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, meets with Israeli President Isaac Herzog on the sidelines of the Seventh Summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (CICA) in Baku, Azerbaijan, Oct. 15, 2026. (Xinhua/Chen Junfeng)
BAKU, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi met with Israeli President Isaac Herzog at the latter's request on the sidelines of the Seventh Summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia here on Thursday.
Herzog said the Jewish and Chinese peoples have a long history of exchanges. The two peoples helped each other during the World Anti-Fascist War, forging a friendship that has become a memorable chapter in history.
Israel firmly adheres to the one-China policy and is committed to advancing friendly relations with China, he said. Israel is willing to take the 35th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations between the two countries next year as an opportunity to expand exchanges and cooperation in areas such as science and technology, investment and people-to-people exchanges.
Herzog briefed Wang on Israel's views and position on the situation in the Middle East, saying that Israel seeks peace, not war, but faces threats and challenges to its national security that require a strong response.
China has always been an important constructive force in promoting peace in the world and the region, Herzog said. Israel attaches importance to the relevant initiatives and proposals put forward by China, appreciates China's efforts to promote regional peace and stability, and stands ready to maintain communication with China, he added.
Wang, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, said that during World War II, both the Chinese and Israeli peoples suffered greatly from the ravages of war and extended a helping hand to each other in times of hardship, giving rise to many moving stories.
Since the establishment of diplomatic relations more than 30 years ago, bilateral relations have developed steadily and practical cooperation has yielded positive results, Wang said, adding that the key lies in upholding mutual respect, treating each other as equals and pursuing mutually beneficial cooperation.
Next year will mark the 35th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations between China and Israel and the 10th anniversary of the establishment of their innovative comprehensive partnership. China stands ready to work with Israel to take the anniversaries as an opportunity to review experience, advance cooperation and consolidate the foundation of public support for bilateral relations, Wang said.
Wang said promoting peace and reconciliation in the region is the cornerstone of China's Middle East policy. China has consistently maintained that the Palestinian question is the greatest historical injustice of this century and that the two-state solution is the right way to resolve the question.
The situation in the region remains tense, while peace and tranquility are still on a long way to go, Wang said, the current top priority is to open full access to the Gaza Strip. The 2 million civilians there must not be left struggling on the brink of survival, nor should the humanitarian catastrophe be allowed to continue spreading; Israel should halt and reverse the forced establishment of settlements in the West Bank, he added.
Wang stressed that since the beginning of this year, President Xi Jinping has put forward a series of initiatives and proposals to promote peace and security in the Middle East, which are public goods that China has provided to the Middle East and the world.
China stands ready to work with the international community to uphold and practice the vision of common, comprehensive, cooperative and sustainable security, encourage all parties to return to the track of dialogue and consultation as soon as possible, and seek political solutions to conflicts, Wang said.
Wang said Herzog's father, former Israeli President Chaim Herzog, promoted the establishment of diplomatic ties between China and Israel during his presidency and was the first Israeli president to visit China.
The elder Herzog wrote in his memoir that compromises and negotiations do not always result in losing something, but often bring about important gains and long-term trust. These words remain relevant and instructive under the current circumstances, Wang said.
The Palestinian question is the root cause of the Middle East issue, Wang noted, adding that both the Jewish and Palestinian peoples have the right to live in peace and establish independent states.
China believes that as long as all parties remain committed to and maintain their resolve to pursue peace, seek a path to peace by moving toward each other, and stay on the right course of the two-state solution, the peace that people have long yearned for will eventually come, Wang said. ■

Explainer: Will Washington pull the trigger on Houthis?

WASHINGTON, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- U.S. President Donald Trump on Tuesday accused Yemen's Houthi group of resuming attacks on Saudi Arabia and deliberately seeking to drive up oil prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.
"The Houthis are behaving very badly," Trump wrote on Truth Social, warning that he would "never forget" the attacks.
Following a series of Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, including strikes on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport, speculation is mounting over whether the United States will enter the fray militarily.
ALLY BUT NOT WAR PARTNER
The Trump administration has so far stopped short of joining Saudi Arabia's direct military campaign against the Houthis, despite Riyadh's calls for greater U.S. involvement. Multiple U.S. media outlets reported in September that Saudi Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohammed bin Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud urged Trump to order U.S. strikes against the Houthis, but Trump declined, opting instead for intelligence sharing and targeting assistance.
The exchanges reflect the limits of the U.S.-Saudi security alignment. Although Washington has a longstanding interest in Saudi security, it does not automatically share Riyadh's military objectives in Yemen. For the United States, protecting its ally and safeguarding regional shipping routes do not necessarily require directly taking part in Saudi offensive operations.
Ali Bin Hadi, an Aden-based military observer, told Xinhua that he saw "little appetite in Washington for another confrontation with the Houthis" after previously seeking to disengage from that front. "Washington may help contain the fire, but it is unlikely to step into it," he said.
Jarrah Mutlaq Al-Qazaa, media adviser at the Kuwait Journalists Association, said that continued escalation could alter Washington's calculation. He said the likelihood of direct U.S. military involvement would depend largely on whether Houthi attacks continue to cause heavy casualties, the extent to which Riyadh seeks U.S. participation, and whether Washington sees scope for limited strikes capable of restoring deterrence without drawing it into a prolonged war.
Trump's remarks on Tuesday offered a further indication of his approach. He told reporters he might ask Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan to intervene in support of Saudi interests. "President Erdogan, I think, would do as I ask," Trump said. The comment reflects Washington's apparent preference for greater involvement from regional partners rather than committing U.S. forces directly.
DEPLETED MUNITIONS LIMIT OPTIONS
One reason Washington may be reluctant to launch military strikes against the Houthis is its depleted weapons stockpiles after months of operations against Iran, during which it has used substantial numbers of missile interceptors to defend its bases and allies. This depletion has not only left Gulf partners, Saudi Arabia in particular, increasingly vulnerable, but also constrained its options in pondering any direct military intervention against the Houthis.
The Congressional Research Service, in a report updated on Oct. 5, noted concerns over the stockpiles and availability of U.S. munitions, including missiles and interceptors, following the U.S.-Israeli military operations against Iran that began in late February. The report warned that depleted stockpiles could narrow Washington's options for sustaining operations and supporting its allies.
Citing a Congressional Budget Office estimate, the report said the United States had "probably used between one-half and two-thirds" of its inventory of certain missile interceptors. Such weapons are critical to protecting U.S. forces and regional allies against missile attacks, while replenishing stocks could take considerable time.
Farzan Sabet, a Middle East expert at the Geneva Graduate Institute, was quoted by Reuters as saying that Saudi Arabia's air defense capabilities and integrated defense network remained less advanced than those of Israel or Ukraine. He added that Saudi Arabia's sheer size makes defense against air attacks harder than defending Israel or any single U.S. base.
The challenge is also compounded by the Houthis' evolving military capabilities. The group has developed greater capacity to assemble and deploy drones and missiles, while years of fighting have given it experience in adapting its tactics.
OIL PRICES RAISE POLITICAL STAKES
The conflict also carries domestic political risks for Trump as the United States approaches its Nov. 3 midterm elections.
On Tuesday, Trump accused the Houthis of "purposefully trying to drive up Oil Prices, probably prior to the U.S. Elections." He warned: "I'll be there after the Elections, and I will never forget!"
His remarks linked the security crisis to a domestic concern that could weigh on voter views of his administration.
The economic pressure is already evident. U.S. Consumer Price Index rose 3.7 percent in September compared with a year ago, while gas prices jumped 9.1 percent from the previous month, according to data released Wednesday by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.
And rising fuel costs driven by the conflict in Iran have piled pressure on Americans ahead of the midterm elections.
A Pew Research Center survey released Oct. 8 found that 74 percent of Americans were "very concerned" about gasoline and energy prices, up from 60 percent in July. Separately, 84 percent of registered voters said the economy was "very important" to their vote in the Nov. 3 mid-term elections. The findings suggest that any further rise in fuel prices could add to voters' economic concerns as they assess the administration's performance.
Against this backdrop, energy prices have become an increasingly prominent concern for the Trump administration. ■

Disaster Risk Reduction Week: building resilience starts at home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:08:04 UTC
20:08:04 KST

Disaster Risk Reduction Week: building resilience starts at home
TEHRAN – Iran is marking Disaster Risk Reduction Week from October 13 to 19, focusing on the importance of improving the health of individuals, families, and the safety of homes, raising public awareness, and strengthening family economic resilience before the disaster strikes.
The beginning of the week coincided with the International Disaster Risk Reduction Day, IRNA reported.
 
The days of the week highlight the following topics:
 
Tuesday, October 13, ‘healthy individual, the cornerstone of societal resilience’
 
Wednesday, October 14, ‘family mental health, the first step towards resilience’
 
Thursday, October 15, ‘a safe and resilient home for everyone’
 
Friday, October 16, ‘raising social children, a resilient generation’
 
Saturday, October 17, ‘a resilient home, simple steps to take from now on’
 
Sunday, October 18, ‘resilience culture, training everyone’
 
Monday, October 19, ‘family economy, a resilient family’
The International Day for Disaster Risk Reduction was started in 1989, after a call by the United Nations General Assembly for a day to promote a global culture of risk-awareness and disaster reduction. Held every 13 October, the day celebrates how people and communities around the world are reducing their exposure to disasters and raising awareness about the importance of reining in the risks that they face.
Themed ‘Resilience Starts at Home’, this year the day highlights that everyone deserves a home that is safe, affordable and able to withstand the hazards around it. There’s no place like home. It is where we seek comfort, safety and shelter. But when floods rise, extreme heat takes hold or other hazards strike, the place meant to protect us can become the frontline of disaster.
Making that possible takes more than individual preparedness. Governments need safer planning and building standards; businesses must put long-term safety before short-term gains; and communities need information, resources, and a voice in decisions about where and how they live.
Around the world, solutions are already taking shape — from families moving to safer homes in the Philippines to centuries-old earthen building techniques keeping homes cooler across West Africa.
 
Because resilience is not only about rebuilding after disaster. It starts before disaster strikes, and it starts at home.
UNESCO chair inaugurated
In September, Minister of Science, Research, and Technology Hossein Simaei-Sarraf, and the Secretary-General of Iran’s National Commission for UNESCO, Hassan Fartousi, inaugurated the UNESCO Chair in Disaster Risk Reduction and Resilience Engineering at Kharazmi University.
The chair is established on a synergistic approach aligned with the Sendai Global Framework for Risk Reduction, the Sustainable Development Goals, and UNESCO’s approaches to expanding education, science, technology, knowledge exchange, climate considerations, and the development of sustainable communities, msrt.ir reported.
According to Kharazmi University, the establishment of the chair represents a scientific and strategic imperative, given the current national and regional conditions in the country, such as climate change, the growing complexity of hazards, the expansion of human settlements, technological and human-induced risks, and the cascading effects of disasters.
This UNESCO Chair develops effective methods to assess and mitigate risks from natural hazards to existing and new school infrastructure, contributing to improved equitable access to safe learning environments for children in vulnerable communities, ensuring continuity of education services, and reducing life losses. The Chair has created a community for resilience engineering exceeding 3,000 members from more than 100 countries, instrumental in sharing knowledge to support disaster risk reduction initiatives.

Japan weather agency apologizes for mistakenly issuing "9.9-magnitude" earthquake warning
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
19:08:00 CST
20:08:00 KST

TOKYO, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- Japan's weather agency on Friday apologized for mistakenly issuing an early warning of a megaquake and strong seismic shaking around midday. The warning was canceled minutes later but temporarily disrupted train services in parts of the country.
The Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) said the error was caused by its system misidentifying the epicenter and overestimating the temblor's magnitude as a catastrophic 9.9.
The agency said it is investigating the cause of the erroneous projection.
At around 12:40 p.m. local time, the JMA issued the alert for a wide area stretching from northern to central Japan, warning that strong shaking could occur in those parts. However, eight minutes later, it issued a follow-up notice canceling the warning.
The agency later confirmed that a 6.9-magnitude earthquake had struck Russia's Kamchatka Peninsula at a depth of about 160 km at around 12:38 p.m.
The early warning had forecast shaking of up to 7, the highest level on Japan's seismic intensity scale, but the strongest shaking actually recorded was an intensity of just 1, in Hakodate City, Hokkaido Prefecture, according to the JMA.
Public broadcaster NHK reported that the JMA's earthquake early warning system detects the faint tremors in the initial moments of an earthquake and automatically estimates its focus, magnitude, and seismic intensity using waveform data observed by seismographs near the epicenter.
When the system forecasts strong shaking of lower 5 or above on Japan's seismic intensity scale, it issues an earthquake early warning. ■

A second essential condition is the provision of financing assurances from partners, stated Mateusz Szczurek, Director of the IMF’s European Department.
"We plan to conduct the second and third reviews of the program by the end of this year. Naturally, this depends on the resumption of reforms, as well as on the provision of financing assurances by partners," he said during a press conference held on the sidelines of the IMF and World Bank Group Annual Meetings in Bangkok on Friday, according to an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent.
Szczurek emphasized the critical importance of adopting legislation and implementing other measures related to revenue mobilization and public administration, as these are vital for securing further donor financing, starting as early as 2026.
Regarding new assumptions and the potential need to revise the EFF program, the IMF European Department Director pointed to the Ukrainian government’s draft state budget for 2027, currently submitted to parliament, which is based on the assumption that the war will continue for a longer period.
"This, of course, increases the financing requirement for 2027 (...) As for the structuring aspects, that is a topic for discussion during the combined second and third reviews of the program, so we will provide details once they are made public," noted Szczurek.
During this year’s IMF Annual Meetings, held from October 12–18, the Ukrainian delegation is discussing with the Fund the implementation of the new four-year Extended Fund Facility (EFF) program, valued at $8.1 billion, which was approved at the end of February this year. This program is part of a broader $136.5 billion external financing package for the 2026–2029 period, based on the baseline scenario.
In July, the IMF completed the first review of the program and disbursed a second tranche of approximately $690 million, bringing the total funding received under the new program to $2.2 billion. At the same time, it was noted that some of the program’s structural benchmarks had not been met by their respective deadlines. Following the first review, the EFF program was updated to include eight additional structural benchmarks, seven of which are fiscal in nature.
Discussions are currently underway to combine the second and third program reviews, with the aim of presenting the matter to the Executive Board before the end of this year. This would coincide with the approval of a combined third and fourth tranche disbursement, totaling approximately $1.65 billion.
"Bringing this to the Board depends on receiving sufficient and credible financing assurances to cover the projected funding gap, on terms that are consistent with maintaining Ukraine’s debt sustainability," IMF spokesperson Julie Kozack stated in early October.
Finance Minister Marchenko noted that, ahead of the expected IMF mission visit in November, it would be desirable to secure confirmation for all sources of the $52.6 billion in external financing required for the 2027 state budget; currently, about $32.6 billion of that total still awaits confirmation.
According to Marchenko, Kyiv expects the European Union to fulfill its commitment to cover two-thirds of Ukraine’s external financing needs for next year as well—a move that would increase confirmed funding by approximately $17.5 billion. As for the remaining balance of roughly $15 billion, the minister explained that there are several potential sources to cover it, including bilateral financing, guarantees, and programs with international financial institutions.

Pezeshkian urges ‘peace diplomacy’ to protect biodiversity, condemns ecocide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:05:55 UTC
20:05:55 KST

Pezeshkian urges ‘peace diplomacy’ to protect biodiversity, condemns ecocide
TEHRAN – President Masoud Pezeshkian has called for “peace diplomacy” to protect biodiversity, condemning the devastating environmental impact of wars of aggression as ecocide and urging the international community to establish effective, transparent and enforceable mechanisms to safeguard natural heritage during wartime.
Speaking on Friday, October 16, at the summit of heads of state and government held as part of the 17th Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17) in Yerevan, Pezeshkian said war is not only a threat to people and infrastructure but also a direct driver of environmental destruction. “War burns forests, destroys wetlands, contaminates soil and water, and displaces wildlife,” he said.
Pezeshkian described environmental cooperation as a bridge between nations, stressing that biodiversity conservation could serve as an important pillar of “peace diplomacy.”
“In a region facing security crises stemming from the illegal and expansionist presence of powers, as well as climate change, water scarcity and ecosystem degradation, environmental cooperation can build bridges between nations,” he said.
Such cooperation, he added, can pave the way for peace and security for all, peace with nature, and a future in which human life is aligned and in harmony with the natural world.
“Today, we stand at a pivotal moment in history when biodiversity is no longer merely a scientific or environmental concern. It is also an issue of peace and security, human health, food and water security, and intergenerational justice for all the inhabitants of our planet,” Pezeshkian stressed.
“The Islamic Republic of Iran was among the first countries to recognize the legal and international significance of this issue and become a party to the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD). However, Iran’s relationship with biodiversity goes far beyond its membership in an international convention.
With an ancient tradition of living in harmony with nature and an extraordinary diversity of ecosystems, species and genetic resources, Iran is the custodian of an invaluable and irreplaceable natural wealth. This heritage is the result of millions of years of evolution, natural dynamism and adaptation, and is reflected in the culture, customs, livelihoods, indigenous knowledge and historical identity of the people of this land.
Owing to its exceptional geographical location, Iran lies at the intersection of several biogeographical regions. From the Hyrcanian and Arasbaran forests to the Zagros Mountains, and from arid and desert landscapes to the coasts of the Persian Gulf, the Sea of Oman and the Caspian Sea, Iran is home to thousands of plant and animal species, as well as valuable genetic resources. These natural assets underpin the country’s ecological stability and sustainability, provide a vital foundation for water and food security and human health, strengthen resilience to natural hazards, and serve as a cornerstone of sustainable development.
In Iran, biodiversity, together with climatic and geographical diversity, is deeply intertwined with human history and civilization. Friendship with, respect for and protection of nature are integral to the cultural, religious and ritual identity of Iranians. Nature has long been regarded as an inseparable part of human life and a trust to be preserved for future generations. Many traditional ways of life, agricultural and livestock-raising practices, the use of medicinal plants, and the indigenous knowledge of Iranian communities have evolved over time through an understanding of and adaptation to nature, reflecting thousands of years of interaction between humans and the natural world.
For Iran, therefore, biodiversity conservation means far more than protecting species and their habitats. It means safeguarding a natural, cultural and civilizational heritage.
In my country, drawing on a long-standing culture of respect for nature and in line with national and international goals and commitments, the National Biodiversity Strategies and Action Plan has been developed and approved. The Department of Environment has been designated as the national coordinating authority, while a mechanism for non-governmental participation, with priority given to local communities, has also received government approval.”
He highlighted that protecting threatened species and restoring vulnerable populations are among the key priorities. These efforts include expanding protected areas and monitoring flagship wildlife species.
“War does not target only human lives and economic infrastructure. It also damages nature: burning forests, destroying wetlands, contaminating soil, threatening water resources, destroying habitats, displacing wildlife, and introducing chemicals and heavy metals into natural cycles. The environmental consequences of war can persist for years after hostilities have ended.
The international community now recognizes that environmental destruction during armed conflicts is not a minor or incidental consequence of war. Such damage is directly linked to the security and well-being of future generations.
In our region, including Iran, the environmental consequences of military conflicts must receive greater attention from the international community. The war of aggression launched by the United States and the Israeli regime in our region has threatened natural ecosystems and damaged environmental protection infrastructure built over years of efforts to conserve biodiversity. Attacks on industrial and energy facilities, fires, pollutant emissions, and soil and water contamination have all contributed to these threats.
This is not merely a domestic issue or one confined within a country's political borders. Nature recognizes no political boundaries, and the spread of water, soil, and air pollution does not stop at national frontiers. The environmental damage caused by war is therefore global in nature and requires international solutions.”
The effects of war on ecosystems can persist for years or even generations, affecting areas hundreds or thousands of kilometers away. One stark example is the scale of destruction in Gaza, where, according to experts, parts of the territory's soil may remain incapable of supporting natural life, vegetation, and ecological cycles for hundreds of years. The destruction caused by wars of aggression in our region amounts to what is known as “ecocide,” or environmental genocide, and must be condemned, Pezeshkian underlined.
“The international community is expected to establish effective, transparent, and enforceable mechanisms to protect natural heritage and biodiversity. No country should be allowed to treat nature as a silent and defenseless victim of war.
The Islamic Republic of Iran is committed to implementing the Convention on Biological Diversity and advancing global goals for nature conservation. In Iran, we pursue the protection of natural areas, wetlands, forests, rangelands, wildlife habitats, and genetic resources alongside sustainable development.
However, we must be realistic and fair. A country facing the mounting pressures of climate change, drought, water scarcity, desertification, and dwindling natural resources, while also grappling with the effects of economic sanctions and restricted access to technology and financial resources, needs genuine international cooperation to implement its environmental programs and repair the damage it has sustained. This is particularly true when the country has been targeted in two consecutive years by what it describes as criminal wars involving the extensive use of destructive and prohibited weapons, with attacks in many cases allegedly intended to cause environmental damage, including strikes on fuel storage facilities in the capital.”
He emphasized that biodiversity conservation will remain confined to negotiations, resolutions, and the setting of targets unless it is backed by adequate financial resources, equitable access to knowledge and technology, and capacity-building.
“If developing countries are expected to protect their forests, wetlands, species, and genetic resources, they must also be provided with the means to fulfill that responsibility. This is the true meaning of environmental justice.
We therefore call on United Nations agencies, international financial institutions, and relevant organizations and bodies working in environmental protection and sustainable development to strengthen mechanisms for mobilizing financial resources, assessing environmental damage, restoring damaged ecosystems, and supporting affected countries in addressing the environmental consequences of armed conflicts.”
In conclusion, Pezeshkian said that the Islamic Republic of Iran stands ready to cooperate constructively with the international community in this joint effort by sharing its scientific and academic capacities and experience with other countries. “We believe that biodiversity conservation can serve as an important pillar of “peace diplomacy.”
In a region grappling with security crises stemming from the unlawful and expansionist presence of powers, climate change, water scarcity, and ecosystem degradation, environmental cooperation can build bridges between nations. These bridges can pave the way toward peace and security for all, peace with nature, and a future in which human life is aligned with and harmonious with the natural world.
 
It is a future free from war, bloodshed, and destruction, in which biodiversity serves as a shared foundation for the well-being and prosperity of present and future generations.”
