AI-Generated Hot Girls Are Ripping Off Comedians to Boost Their Horny Content
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

Last week, the stand-up comedian Julia Jasunas was on Instagram when she got a DM from a fellow comic. Did she know, her friend wrote, that a random Instagram influencer had ripped off a joke from her stand-up act?
Initially, Jasunas was mad but not overly shocked. Plagiarism is not uncommon in the stand-up comedy world, and comics are “really sensitive about it, because there's not a ton of protection against it,” she tells WIRED. “So we all look out for each other.” Then she clicked on the link.
The video was of a purported stand-up comic named Aylen Skye, a buxom blond with leonine cheekbones and 250,000 Instagram followers. In the clip, Skye, wearing a crop top and Daisy Dukes, tells a joke about renting out a room in her two-bedroom apartment to a cute guy. To Jasunas’ shock, it was, verbatim, her joke, down to the “ums” and “ahs.”
Whoever Skye was, she didn’t appear to be a comic; the website she advertised in her video, AylenTV.com, redirected to NSFW content on Fanvue, a subscription-based OnlyFans competitor that markets itself as the “No1 AI monetisation platform for creators.” And not only did she appear to not be a comic, she also didn’t seem to be real. After looking at Skye’s comments section, Jasunas was fairly convinced she was AI.
“You look at any female comic’s comments section and you’ll see all these men berating her, objectifying her body, saying she’s not funny or the joke is bad,” she says. But with Skye, all of the comments were positive. “That’s how I knew she was fake,” she deadpans.
For Jasunas, being ripped off by a sexy AI-generated comedian was “violating on so many different levels.” “It’s one thing to have your jokes stolen,” she says. “It’s another to funnel your work into something so sexualized, for someone else’s profit.” She immediately reported the video to Meta for impersonation, but says Meta told her it did not violate community guidelines because Skye wasn’t pretending to be Jasunas; it was just passing off her joke as its own. “They just didn’t seem to care,” Jasunas says. (The majority of Skye’s posts are now flagged as AI content, though the account itself is not.)
Jasunas is far from the only stand-up comic to have been targeted by Skye. Nor does Skye appear to be the only AI-generated hot girl account targeting comics. WIRED has identified eight comics whose videos have been replicated by scantily clad, AI-generated women, many of whom follow each other on social media. All of the videos are copies of already-successful viral stand-up clips, except the AI-generated counterparts are playing to bigger audiences, with better lighting, better sound, and more skintight outfits—essentially, all the elements required to ensure virality. The accounts also post flirty, clearly AI-generated late-night TV show interviews with hosts like Conan O’Brien and Jimmy Kimmel, as well as the occasional “edgy” racist or transphobic joke catering to the MAGA crowd.
Though Instagram’s community guidelines prohibit impersonation, such policies don’t extend to copying someone else’s content, particularly if that content isn’t copyrighted. The platform also does not have any prohibitions against AI content, so long as it is appropriately labeled as such. Some of the accounts are labeled as AI-generated—but others are not, or their videos are inconsistently labeled. (Skye did not respond to a request for comment, though it has commented on many stand-up comics’ videos calling it out: “if you focused on putting out content instead of making whinny [sic] posts like this, you’d be as successful as me,” it wrote on one comic’s Instagram post.)
Particularly grating to the comics being ripped off is that some of the AI-generated videos perform better than the originals, spawning calls for increased protections for original content on Instagram. “AI is evolving very fast, and we need rules to protect creators before this becomes a bigger issue,” says Mandy Martino, who also had one of her jokes lifted by Skye. “It’s not just about a joke being stolen—it’s about this being a change that we need to get ahead of. And Instagram saying this isn’t a problem is the scariest part.”
Comics have been complaining about AI accounts stealing their content since June, with the stand-up Steph Clark regularly documenting such “weird pick-me AI slop” on her Instagram. In one early video, the AI stand-up in question is a leggy redhead sitting on a stool, awkwardly delivering a nonsensical punch line comparing faking orgasms to being a bad cook, a vacant expression on its face.
In the following months, however, the technology for such clone videos has improved exponentially, to the degree that it’s difficult to tell whether or not the women in the videos are actually real people. One such example is Tiffany Sloane, which identifies itself as an actress in its bio on Instagram, where it has more than 375,000 followers. A pear-shaped 19-year-old bombshell with a septum piercing and a BBL, Sloane does crowd work and jokes about quarter-zips and Jimmy Buffett songs on its Instagram page—which, similar to Skye, also includes a Highlights link to its OnlyFans profile.
Since starting the Instagram account in August, Sloane amassed a robust following and is also on TikTok and Facebook, where it has built out a “super horny AI-generated short-form video content farm,” as the writer Ryan Broderick puts it. On October 3, the comedian George Brett Olson posted a viral video captioned “AI stole my joke!!!” showing a side-by-side comparison of his stand-up bit—a joke about how Republicans ignore the risks of AI in favor of manufacturing panic over illegal immigration—next to Sloane’s near-identical one. In both clips, the comics are standing in front of identical backdrops and wearing similar salmon shirts and khaki shorts. Only the punch line, which features an expletive in Olson’s version, is different.
“I was kind of in shock,” Olson tells WIRED of seeing Sloane’s video for the first time. “I just thought it was so weird to see people openly stealing in real time.” He says his followers told him they reported it to Meta, and according to them, Meta responded by saying Sloane’s video did not violate any community guidelines. “I couldn’t believe it,” he says. “This is my intellectual property. I created it. And not only did this person or whatever steal it, they stole my likeness too.”
After Olson made his video calling out Sloane, he was flooded with comments from fellow stand-ups and fans supporting him and vowing to report Sloane’s account to Instagram. Even Sloane weighed in, leaving a comment on Olson’s page saying, “sorry, won’t happen again” before deleting its video, as well as many other Reels on its page. (Sloane didn’t immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment.)
Ultimately, however, Olson was dispirited by the inaction on Meta’s end. After tagging Instagram head Adam Mosseri, Mosseri responded by saying that while he did not think it was “practical for us to try and ban AI content” from Meta, the platform was “very invested in trying to drive more traffic to original content creators, and if an AI creator is ripping off content wholesale, it would be good for us to work out what we can do about that.”
Responding to WIRED, Francis Brennan, a spokesperson for Meta, declined to comment further, saying, “Our policies are pretty clear around this stuff, and Adam’s comment speaks for itself.” All of the AI-generated accounts flagged by WIRED are still on the platform.
As of now, there’s very little that comedians can do about AI creators “ripping off content wholesale.” Legally, jokes have historically enjoyed very little copyright protection, in part due to the ephemeral nature of stand-up and the fact that many setups and punch lines have been used in the industry, with slightly different variations, for years. There’s also the matter of the financial stakes being relatively low, according to Aaron Perzanowski, now a law professor at the University of Michigan, who told NPR in 2017, “when you're talking about accusations of infringement dealing with fairly low-dollar-value creative work, we don't see a lot of litigation." (Olson says this sentiment was echoed by an intellectual property lawyer he consulted with, who he claims told him that unless Sloane was making millions of dollars on OnlyFans, threatening a lawsuit was probably more trouble than it was worth.)
The negative sentiment against these AI-generated creators does not appear to be shared by some in the tech industry, such as Andreessen Horowitz partner Justine Moore, who publicly praised Sloane in an X post, referring to her online presence as “a genius marketing hack.”
Olson is not overly optimistic that AI evangelists will rush to the defense of the creatives whose labor is being exploited. Nor, for that matter, does he believe that the “lizard-brained” commenters rushing to post horny comments on Sloane’s and Skye’s pages particularly care whether they’re real, or who actually crafted the jokes they’re telling in their viral clips.
“To me, we're asking the essential question, does the artist matter?” he says. “And to those 350,000 people that follow Tiffany Sloane, the answer is clearly no. And that’s really demoralizing.”

The officials in Brussels vowed to maintain support for Ukraine and urged the US to put pressure on Russian President Vladimir Putin.
September civilian casualties 85% higher than last year
Russia is blitzing not just Ukraine's power grid but also apartment buildings, public transport, cargo ships, data centres and food stores.
Ukrainian civilians are paying a high price for the escalating Russian attacks, the United Nations human rights office in Kyiv said in a monthly report published on Friday.
At least 328 civilians were killed and 2,105 wounded last month, a total 85% higher than in September last year, the report said, noting that intensifying Russian attacks in October already have killed dozens of civilians, including children.
“The first two weeks of October were among the deadliest periods for civilians in years,” said Danielle Bell, the head of the UN office.
Trump and Zelenskyy barbs raise questions about US support
Tension and uncertainty are gripping Ukraine and Europe after Zelenskyy and Trump publicly made cutting remarks about each other.
On Thursday, Zelenskyy said he felt betrayed by the American president and Trump openly declared his dislike of the Ukrainian leader.
Arriving at the EU summit in Belgium, Zelenskyy thanked the 27-nation bloc for its support from what he said were “real leaders.”
“We want to end this war as (quickly) as possible,” Zelenskyy told reporters. “We don’t see now signals from (the) Russian side that they are ready for this, to end this war. That’s why we have to prepare for the winter.”
The public spat between Trump and Zelenskyy raised the spectre of further reductions in US support for Ukraine’s war effort.
Ukraine is desperately short of the US-made Patriot missiles it needs to protect against Russia’s devastating ballistic missile attacks, despite Zelenskyy’s pleading for Washington to send more.
Zelenskyy complained about a breakdown in Western intelligence sharing and sudden restrictions on the use of Starshield, US company SpaceX’s military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet service that is the backbone of Ukraine’s drone operations and military communications.
He also slammed Trump’s diesel deal with Russia, which came despite an international effort to sanction Russia and diplomatically isolate Putin over his invasion.
Trump promised to swiftly end the war, but Ukrainian officials have complained he is trying to bulldoze Zelenskyy into surrendering land to Russia.

INTERVIEW – Armenian church official sees Türkiye-Armenia normalization as path to ‘stronger friendships’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:57:32 UTC
19:57:32 KST

INTERVIEW – Armenian church official sees Türkiye-Armenia normalization as path to ‘stronger friendships’
Vice president of Surp Giragos Armenian Church Foundation welcomes efforts to improve bilateral ties, expresses hope that land border will soon reopen
Beril Canakci
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
DIYARBAKIR, Türkiye
A senior official of the Armenian church foundation in southeastern Türkiye’s Diyarbakir province has voiced support for the ongoing normalization process between Ankara and Yerevan, saying growing contact between the two sides will deepen friendship.
“We view the ongoing rapprochement between Armenia and Türkiye very positively,” Ohannes Gafur Ohanyan, vice president of the Surp Giragos Armenian Church Foundation, told Anadolu.
Ohanyan spoke during a visit by 7 Turkish and 7 Armenian journalists to Surp Giragos Armenian Church in Diyarbakir’s historic Sur district as part of an EU-funded media tour aimed at supporting normalization between Türkiye and Armenia.
“We believe that as these kinds of visits and events increase, the friendship between the two countries will grow even stronger,” he said. “Hopefully, the borders will open soon too.”
Türkiye and Armenia do not have diplomatic relations, and their land border has been closed since 1993. The two countries launched a normalization initiative in late 2021, appointing retired Turkish Ambassador Serdar Kilic and Armenian parliament Deputy Speaker Ruben Rubinyan as special envoys.
Türkiye’s Foreign Ministry said in May that technical and bureaucratic work to reopen the shared border with Armenia was still ongoing, although preparations for direct trade had been completed.
In early May, Turkish Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz visited Armenia, where officials signed a memorandum on the joint restoration of the historic Ani Bridge, a medieval structure spanning the border between the two countries.
During a meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York last month, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan also discussed advancing normalization, strengthening trade and economic ties, and improving regional transport links.
Center of attraction for Armenians worldwide
The local Armenian community in Diyarbakir comprises roughly 60 to 65 people, according to Ohanyan. Despite its compact size, social and community life surrounding the church remains active, with regular religious services organized around major holidays.
"Because we do not have a permanent resident clergyman here, we hold around 8 to 10 services a year during important religious holidays," Ohanyan said.
Describing Surp Giragos as an 800-year-old church and the largest Armenian church in the Middle East, he said it draws Armenians from Armenia as well as from the diaspora in Europe and the US.
Following decades of disuse, comprehensive restoration initiatives spearheaded by the local foundation and supported in subsequent years by Turkish state institutions including the Culture and Tourism Ministry, allowed the site to formally reopen for worship.
The church was later damaged during 2015 clashes in Sur involving the terrorist group PKK. It was restored with funding from Türkiye’s Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change Ministry, under the coordination of the General Directorate of Foundations, and reopened for worship after seven years.
The foundation’s second church, the roughly 500-year-old Surp Sarkis in the Alipasa neighborhood, fell into disrepair over time because it had no congregation and was further damaged in the February 2023 earthquakes centered in Kahramanmaras. Restoration work began in 2024 with a grant from the Culture and Tourism Ministry.
"Surp Sarkis has been in ruins for nearly a century," Ohanyan noted. "We have made considerable progress and have largely completed the structural work on the main building."
Ohanyan also called on businesspeople, philanthropists and the wider public for further support.

Ukrainian children abroad will be able to receive a school-leaving certificate without repeating their studies: the government explained the mechanism
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:56:53 EEST
19:56:53 KST

Ukrainian children abroad will be able to receive a school-leaving certificate without repeating their studies: the government explained the mechanism
Kyiv • UNN
Ukrainian children abroad will be able to receive a school-leaving certificate through recognition of their foreign education and a Ukrainian studies component. The program can be completed in person or remotely.
Ukrainian schoolchildren who are abroad because of the full-scale war can obtain a Ukrainian certificate of completion of secondary education without having to repeat the full educational program. Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said this during his speech in parliament on October 16, UNN reports.
To this end, the state has provided for the possibility of recognizing the results of education at foreign schools in combination with the study of Ukrainian studies subjects.
Details
The issue of providing education to Ukrainian children abroad was raised by Deputy Speaker of the Verkhovna Rada Olena Kondratiuk. According to her, based on estimates cited in a report by the Ministry of Education and Science of Ukraine and the Accounting Chamber for September 2026, between 320,000 and 400,000 Ukrainian children are currently studying outside Ukraine. Kondratiuk emphasized that one of the state's key tasks remains preserving these children's connection with the Ukrainian education system, as well as creating conditions for their return after the war ends.
In particular, she asked how effectively the mechanisms for reintegrating schoolchildren, simplifying the recognition of education documents, and providing opportunities to study the Ukrainian language at educational institutions in other countries are working.
Answering the question, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi emphasized that Ukrainian children abroad remain one of the priorities of the state's education policy.
Our children abroad are our children; they are Ukrainian children. And we must do everything so that, once the danger of war has ended, they return to Ukraine and support and develop the Ukrainian economy
According to the head of government, education is one of the most important tools for preserving the younger generation's connection with Ukraine. At the same time, he acknowledged that children who are already studying at schools in their host countries often do not have the opportunity to fully master the Ukrainian educational program in parallel because of the excessive workload.
How Ukrainian schoolchildren abroad can obtain a certificate
To solve this problem, the state proposed a Ukrainian studies component that makes it possible to combine education at a foreign school with the study of subjects necessary to preserve ties with Ukrainian education. According to the head of government, the relevant program can be completed either directly at educational centers abroad or remotely through Ukrainian schools.
It (the program, — ed.) can be completed at verified centers operating in other countries—there are already more than 120 of them that have been verified by the Ministry of Education. It can also be done remotely through Ukrainian schools operating in a remote-learning format
The program provides that, in their free time outside their main studies, Ukrainian children study the Ukrainian language, the history of Ukraine, the geography of Ukraine, cultural studies, as well as individual subjects of their choice. In other words, schoolchildren do not need to repeat the entire program they are already studying at educational institutions in their host countries.
As the head of government explained, under the agreements reached, the Ukrainian side may recognize the results of education obtained abroad. After completing the Ukrainian studies component, the child will also be able to receive a Ukrainian document certifying completion of secondary education. This, in particular, opens the possibility of admission to Ukrainian universities and allows schoolchildren to remain part of the Ukrainian educational and cultural environment.
In addition, the government is cooperating with Ukrainian communities abroad, including religious communities, to support the activities of educational centers and provide them with educational literature.
Ukrainian as a second foreign language in European schools
Particular attention during the discussion was devoted to the possibility of studying Ukrainian as a second foreign language in schools in European countries.
Olena Kondratiuk noted that the relevant practice already exists in a number of countries that have taken in Ukrainian refugees. According to her, approximately 45 Polish schools are already working in this direction. Similar approaches are being applied in certain educational institutions in the United Kingdom and Austria. The lawmaker also noted France's active involvement. In her view, expanding such opportunities will allow Ukrainian children to take relevant exams in their host countries while maintaining their knowledge of their native language.
Kondratiuk also emphasized that introducing Ukrainian as a second foreign language could become an alternative to studying Russian in European schools. She urged the Ukrainian authorities to intensify cooperation with the education ministries of European Union states to expand this practice.
Some Ukrainian children abroad may remain outside the education system
Another problem highlighted by the Deputy Chairperson of the Verkhovna Rada was the absence of some Ukrainian children from education institution registration systems.
Kondratiuk emphasized that meetings with the education ministers of European countries revealed that some Ukrainian children are studying neither in local schools nor remotely at Ukrainian educational institutions. She called this a serious gap requiring the attention of the Ukrainian authorities and the education agencies of the host countries.
In Kondratiuk's view, Ukraine should maintain regular contact with such children, ensure their access to education, and create conditions enabling them to remain part of the Ukrainian educational space even during an extended stay abroad.
Previously
Earlier, UNN reported that due to the war and the search for prospects, female graduates are leaving Ukraine en masse to study abroad.

Iran ships some LPG, jet fuel despite US blockade, data shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:55:27 UTC
19:55:27 KST

Iran ships some LPG, jet fuel despite US blockade, data shows
DAMASCUS/LONDON, Oct 16 - Iran has managed to export some liquefied petroleum gas and jet fuel since July, despite a US naval blockade, shipping intelligence showed and people involved in security said.
Tehran has in recent weeks been concealing such cargoes among a growing volume of ship-to-ship transfers by other Gulf producers off Oman, four people in maritime security who track Gulf oil movements told Reuters.
The Iranian exports and methodology are reported for the first time here. While a fraction of its former energy exports, the cargoes are rare evidence of petroleum products getting through a blockade that has halted Iran's crude exports.
Analysis by US advocacy group United Against Nuclear Iran (UANI), which monitors Iran-related tanker traffic using ship and satellite tracking, shows at least eight gas tankers carrying Iranian LPG have left the Gulf of Oman since mid-July.
Another tanker carrying Iranian jet fuel reached Myanmar in September, additional satellite imagery and analysis by maritime intelligence group SynMax show.
The US imposed targeted sanctions in 2023 on Myanmar's jet-fuel industry, citing military airstrikes on civilians that the United Nations says have killed thousands of people. Myanmar's military government has repeatedly denied targeting civilians, saying its operations are directed against armed groups.
Six of the eight gas tankers and the jet fuel tanker are under US sanctions for transporting Iranian petroleum and petrochemical products, a Reuters analysis of the vessels and sanctions imposed on ships by the US Treasury showed.
"What we have seen passing is a handful of tankers carrying Iranian LPG, but the overwhelming majority of tankers laden with Iranian products have been redirected by US forces," said Jemima Shelley, senior research analyst with UANI.
Shelley said some Iranian LPG tankers transferred cargoes near the Omani coastal towns of Shinas and Sohar, while others waited in the Gulf of Oman before heading past the US blockade, which US Central Command has said sits across the Gulf of Oman near the Iran-Pakistan border.
The total amount of these LPG cargoes was estimated at 4.1 million barrels, Shelley said.
Shelley said the shipments were driven "more by opportunism" than showing a new trend of Iran trying to export its oil and petrochemicals by using smaller ships.
Most of the cargoes sailed to Malaysia's Eastern Outer Port Limits to conduct further STS transfers for likely destinations in China, Shelley said, based on UANI's analysis.
The Iranian government did not respond to a request for comment. Myanmar's military-backed government did not respond to a request for comment on whether the country had received Iranian jet fuel.
US MILITARY SAYS BLOCKADE 'IRONCLAD'
The US military's Centcom said its naval blockade, which was first imposed on Iran-related oil exports on April 13, is "ironclad". The blockade was lifted in June after the US reached a draft understanding with Iran, but it was reimposed on July 14 following the collapse of the agreement.
A US military official told Reuters that the passage of a vessel does not necessarily mean it had evaded the blockade. Every ship was assessed individually, including through a review of its papers, and some vessels could be allowed through for humanitarian reasons, the official added.
The official said the appearance of a vessel on US sanctions lists is not the only factor to make it subject to the blockade, adding that US forces are also closely monitoring some ships without taking action against them for operational reasons.
Centcom said in an update on October 13 that during the three months of the latest blockade, four commercial vessels had been disabled and 135 ships had been turned around by US forces.
The US military has turned around ships from Asia and also seized some tankers, previous Centcom statements said.
Washington has coupled its blockade with a sanctions campaign aimed at severing Iran's remaining financial links and depriving it of revenue. Last week, it imposed fresh sanctions on 17 vessels involved in transporting Iranian crude, petrochemicals and petroleum products.
A US Treasury spokesperson questioned shipping data suggesting vessels had evaded the blockade, saying ships could spoof their locations or use false identities when loading.
Such data "should be taken with a grain of salt", the spokesperson said.
The Treasury spokesperson said Operation Economic Outcast, together with the blockade, was "suffocating the Iranian regime".
Torbjorn Soltvedt, principal Middle East analyst at risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft, said although there was no sign of Washington easing its blockade, worsening economic conditions in Iran could push Tehran to take greater risks.
"If Iran can move product tankers through, even in small numbers, jet fuel may be a good option. Iran's aviation industry is under increasing pressure from US sanctions, with a growing number of planes grounded, and a potential surplus of jet fuel at Iranian refineries," Soltvedt added.
Iranian crude exports fell to zero in September, according to Kpler, the first month without a shipment since the analytics firm began tracking the producer in 2013.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has said the blockade prevented most Chinese purchases of Iranian oil and left Iran unable to deliver crude to customers. REUTERS

Romanian Institutions Bought Banned Russian Cybersecurity Software
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:54:00 UTC
19:54:00 KST

Reported by
More than 80 Romanian public institutions continued to purchase cybersecurity software from a Russian-founded company after the government explicitly banned its use over national security concerns, a review of public procurement records reveals.
Following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Romania passed a 2022 law prohibiting public entities from acquiring cybersecurity software originating fromRussian individuals or entities. In March 2023, a government order officially blacklisted a broad range of products from Kaspersky, a Russian cybersecurity firm.
However, procurement data shows that between March 2023 and September 2026, 83 public institutions and authorities made 131 purchases of prohibited software.
In an emailed statement, Kaspersky said it “does not have any inappropriate ties to any government.”
“Kaspersky has maintained that the claims about alleged security risks that the company’s products might have and related restrictions are based on the current geopolitical climate rather than a technical analysis of Kaspersky software security,” the company said.
“To date, no party has presented any public evidence that the company’s products might pose a threat to corporate or private users,” Kaspersky added.
The Romanian buyers of Kaspersky software included hospitals, municipal governments, schools, and other public institutions.
Notably, less than two months after the blacklist was published, the National Institute for Laser, Plasma and Radiation Physics bought two-year Kaspersky antivirus licenses for three devices. According to its annual reports, the research institute generates classified information and works under contracts with the Ministry of National Defense, the "Ferdinand I" Military Technical Academy, and NATO.
“We would like to clarify that the purchased product has never been installed or actually used on any computer, server, or other IT system belonging to the institute,” the institute said in an emailed response to questions.
Sebastian Burduja, who headed Romania's Ministry of Research, Innovation and Digitalization when the rules were introduced, attributed the continued purchases to a lack of enforcement staff.
"On the other hand, as we all suspect, we likely have a pro-Russian strain within Romanian state institutions," said Burduja said, who is now a deputy in the country’s parliament.
Kaspersky is named after its founder, Eugene Kaspersky, a former software engineer for the Soviet Union Defense Ministry who studied mathematics at a school sponsored by state authorities like the KGB, the secret police and intelligence agency. From its founding in 1997, Kaspersky grew into one of the world's largest cybersecurity providers. But the company’s business has been hampered by international restrictions, including a 2024 action by several countries.
The U.S. prohibited the sale of many Kaspersky products, citing risks to national security. The company rejected the allegations, claiming the ban was based on the "geopolitical climate and theoretical concerns" rather than product integrity.
Germany, Lithuania, and Italy have also issued formal warnings or implemented measures to phase out the software from critical infrastructure.
Under Romanian law, violating the ban on Kaspersky products is an administrative offense carrying fines between 50,000 and 200,000 lei (between $10,500 and $42,000).

3D-printed brick phone brings back the art of simply answering calls
designer kevin noki recreates the 1980s brick phone as a 3D-printed bluetooth handset with 19 physical keys, allowing users to answer iphone calls without the usual smartphone distractions.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
ADHD ONE REVISITS THE 1980S BRICK PHONE
As smartphones become increasingly difficult to put down, Cologne-based designer and maker Kevin Noki has taken a rather unconventional approach to digital detox: building a handset that looks straight out of the 1980s. Named ADHD ONE, short for Anti Distraction Handset Device, the project revisits the oversized brick phones of early mobile communication, complete with a physical keypad, compact display, and unmistakably chunky silhouette. Unlike most contemporary devices, however, its purpose is to offer fewer features rather than more.
The concept is relatively straightforward. Instead of replacing a smartphone, ADHD ONE connects to an iPhone via Bluetooth, allowing users to receive and answer calls while keeping the original device out of sight. By configuring the iPhone’s Do Not Disturb settings to permit calls from selected contacts, Noki creates a more controlled communication experience. The handset has no independent cellular connection and relies on the paired smartphone to function. In practice, it preserves one of the phone’s most basic purposes without inviting its owner into another endless round of scrolling.
BLUETOOTH TECHNOLOGY MEETS 3D-PRINTED RETRO DESIGN
Despite its deliberately outdated appearance, ADHD ONE relies on contemporary electronics. At its core is an FSC-BT1026C Bluetooth module based on Qualcomm’s QCC3024 chip, which uses the Hands-Free Profile (HFP) to transmit call audio between the handset and the connected iPhone. A Raspberry Pi Pico development board manages the device’s functions, while additional components include an OLED display, a microphone, a speaker, a rechargeable lithium battery, and a charging controller. A custom printed circuit board brings the electronics together inside the compact housing.
Kevin Noki designed the enclosure in Autodesk Fusion before producing its components through 3D printing. The housing draws heavily on the visual language of early mobile phones, with substantial proportions, a prominent antenna, and tactile buttons replacing the smooth surfaces of contemporary smartphones. The design incorporates a 19-key keypad and offers several possibilities for customization, including three speaker grille styles (Classic, Holes, and Stripes) and three antenna designs (Retro, Slim, and Screw). An alternative housing even eliminates the antenna entirely, although that arguably takes away some of the brick phone’s charm.
KEVIN NOKI RELEASES DIY FILES FOR HIS RETRO HANDSET
For those interested in building their own version, Noki has made the digital construction files available through his website. The downloadable package includes 3D-printable STL files for the housing, back panels, internal mounting frame, display cover, battery holder, and keypad, alongside ready-to-flash firmware in UF2 format. Gerber and drill files allow users to order the custom PCB from a manufacturer, while a bill of materials and quick start guide provide the necessary references for sourcing components and assembling the device. The package does not include physical parts, editable CAD or PCB files, or the firmware’s source code, and is licensed for personal use only. A separate physical DIY kit is listed on the website but is not yet available.
Ultimately, ADHD ONE occupies an interesting position between nostalgia, experimental product design, and the growing desire for simpler digital experiences. It does not eliminate the smartphone, which must remain within Bluetooth range, nor does it attempt to recreate the independence of an actual 1980s mobile phone. Instead, it rethinks how people physically interact with technology they already own, turning a familiar communication function into a deliberately limited experience. There is a certain irony in designing, printing, and assembling an entirely new electronic device just to avoid using another one. Then again, perhaps that is precisely the point.
project info:
 name: ADHD ONE – Retro Brick Handset
designer: Kevin Noki | @kevinnoki
location: Cologne, Germany

Student protests sweep Europe amid anger over costs of living
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:53:00 UTC
19:53:00 KST

Student protests that began with high school blockades in France have spread across Europe, drawing young people into the streets over deteriorating school conditions, teacher shortages, rising education costs and a housing crisis that is making it harder to study.
From France and Belgium to Albania, Greece, Spain and Italy, demonstrations have included school occupations, mass marches and protest camps, with some escalating into clashes with police.
Though national grievances differ, the unrest reflects growing frustration among young people who say governments are failing to provide the resources and opportunities they need to build their futures.
The protests began in mid-to-late September, when students in the Paris region, particularly around Creteil, blockaded school entrances with trash bins and makeshift barriers.
They cited missing teachers, overcrowded classrooms and deteriorating facilities, including mold, broken toilets and classrooms reaching 40 degrees Celsius (104 degrees Fahrenheit) during heat waves.
Students have also criticized demanding schedules and Parcoursup, France's university admissions platform, which they say adds stress and uncertainty to the transition to higher education.
The demonstrations quickly spread nationwide, disrupting hundreds of schools. At the peak, more than 200 high schools were reportedly fully closed, while others faced partial closures or interruptions to classes. University students have also joined the movement.
Turnout estimates have varied widely. On Oct. 13, the Interior Ministry counted at least 161,500 demonstrators, while unions estimated participation at nearly 480,000. Other major protest days earlier in October also drew large crowds.
Climate activist Greta Thunberg joined demonstrators at a blockaded school in Saint-Denis, north of Paris, on Oct. 13, arguing that young people were being denied a meaningful role in decisions affecting their futures.
Police conduct has become another flashpoint. A teenager lost a hand in Lens, prompting authorities to suspend the use of stun grenades. Other reported injuries included eye damage and dental trauma, while complaints alleging police brutality were under investigation.
Justice Ministry figures cited in reports put the number of people taken into custody at roughly 6,800 to 8,000, with about 85% to 86% of those detained being minors.
Students, school staff and officers were among those reported injured. Although most marches remained largely peaceful, some ended in clashes involving tear gas, police charges and property damage.
Student unions are demanding an emergency school renovation program, large-scale teacher recruitment, improved schedules and greater student representation. They also want major changes to Parcoursup or its repeal, alongside more nurses, psychologists and career advisers.
Education Minister Edouard Geffray announced plans to deploy about 3,000 substitute teachers to the hardest-hit schools. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu promised a broader plan by the end of October, including consultations and adjustments to the 2027 budget, while citing financial constraints.
President Emmanuel Macron has called for patience and dialogue, but student leaders have dismissed the initial measures as insufficient and vowed to continue demonstrating.
In Belgium, students began demonstrating in early October against tuition reforms, overcrowded classrooms and funding cuts. Some categories of students face fees of up to 1,194 euros for the 2026-27 academic year. Protests spread from Liège to Brussels and other cities, with arrests reported during disorderly demonstrations.
Students also joined a nationwide union-led strike on Oct. 9 against austerity measures. The action drew tens of thousands of participants, while isolated clashes near Brussels Central Station involved water cannon, tear gas and fires.
In Albania, student grievances over university conditions, education costs and limited job prospects have merged with wider protests against corruption and inequality.
Demonstrations have overlapped with the months-long Flamingo Revolution, which opposes a luxury coastal resort project linked to Jared Kushner.
Protests in Tirana escalated into violence, with demonstrators attacking government buildings, banks and infrastructure. Police responded with tear gas, water cannon and batons. Reports described more than 100 arrests at peak points, injuries and significant property damage.
Prime Minister Edi Rama has refused to resign, pledging to address legitimate education concerns while condemning violence and defending his government's push for European Union membership.
In Greece, students set up tents in Athens' Syntagma Square opposite Parliament around Oct. 13 to protest soaring rents and inadequate public housing. Small apartments can cost 500 to 600 euros a month or more, putting accommodation beyond many students' budgets.
Demonstrators are demanding rent controls, more student housing, increased subsidies and better education funding. School sit-ins have also increased over teacher shortages and poor conditions.
In Spain, an indefinite teachers' strike began in the Madrid region on Oct. 14, bringing together educators, students and families under the Marea Verde, or Green Tide, movement. Protesters want increased public funding, smaller classes, higher salaries, reduced teaching hours and more specialized staff. Critics also accuse the regional government of encouraging privatization at the expense of public schools.
In Italy, students have occupied high schools in Turin and Rome, adopting slogans inspired by France as they protest underfunding, deteriorating buildings and rising living costs. Smaller demonstrations elsewhere reflect similar concerns.
Across Europe, the protests expose mounting pressure on public education systems after years of financial constraints, teacher recruitment difficulties and aging infrastructure. Rising rents, energy bills and everyday expenses have compounded those problems, making education increasingly difficult to afford.
Young people also express frustration over their future prospects, arguing that governments are failing to address barriers to education, employment and housing.
France's demonstrations have drawn comparisons with the student unrest of May 1968, although today's movement focuses largely on practical demands involving school conditions, staffing and access to education.
Governments have offered targeted concessions and promised dialogue while emphasizing budget limitations. Yet allegations of police excess, mass arrests and injuries have intensified scrutiny of how authorities respond to youth-led dissent.

nightswimming: giovanna silva on discotheques, light, and nightlife

nightswimming: giovanna silva on discotheques, light, and nightlife
the italian photographer reflects on the changing spaces of club culture, from italian discotheques to the improvised dance floors of contemporary nightlife.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
The following text is reproduced from NIGHTSWIMMING: Discotheques from the 1960s to the Present, a book by photographer Giovanna Silva, and shared with designboom courtesy of the author. 
NIGHTSWIMMING – Giovanna Silva
I started photographing discotheques when Monditalia commissioned a project from me on the architecture of Italian nightlife for the 2014 Venice Architecture Biennale. I must admit this was a completely unknown subject to me, which I am just beginning to get familiar with now, when the exhibition in Venice has closed and our project has become a book. My unfamiliarity with the topic surely gave me an unconventional and detached eye, but required an extra effort and the restraint of all my compulsiveness.
We started by collecting the books already published on the subject: on the one hand, we needed to gather all the possible information, on the other, discotheques are buildings that change their appearance rather frequently – having to adjust to fashion, to the music, and to the progress in lighting and sound technology – therefore books were the main way of seeing images of most of the discotheques we were finding out about. These books brought actual people into the project: critics, architects, DJs, art directors, club owners… the night swimmers.
After examining Italy, we realized it was important to analyze the state of the art in four big European cities: Berlin, London, Paris and Barcelona. Choosing the locations in each of these cities has not been an easy task. The research we presented at the Biennale had to be exhaustive, but here we had to be selective. We aimed at listing the clubs that are (or sometimes were) both socially and musically important, and at the same time architectonically interesting. I photographed those discotheques that today outline a specific perception of the night: increasingly, every day, places not designed to be discos are occupied and transformed into party locations, a sort of legalization of the 1990s concept of the rave. The photographs depict these places sometimes empty and sometimes full, pointing out – among other things – how the people erase the very concept of space.
When entering a club, the first thing to hit me was always the smell, maybe because I photographed the majority of these places out of hours, during the day. It is some sort of madeleine, everywhere a constant. I am still trying to figure out whether it is the smell of the cleaning or if this is simply the smell of the night, a mixture of human beings, smoke and detergent. The second thing you immerse yourself in are the lights. Lights are everything.
We have been told discotheques are like old ladies: they shouldn’t be seen without their make-up. And I completely agree with this, light does an important part of the trick here, it changes the space at the touch of a switch. Some of the photos have been shot with white light, a light that makes everything look flat and clinical. It is funny how something that began in such a detached way has become more and more familiar every day. For this I would like to thank all those who had the patience to explain to me what the night is.
Giovanna Silva (b. 1980) lives and works in Milan. Between 2005 and 2007 she was a regular contributor to the magazine Domus, and from 2007 to 2011, served as photo editor of the magazine Abitare. Her books include Days without Number, Napoli*, Black Coffee No Sugar. Genova, Milan. City, I listen to your heart, Islamabad Today, Imeldific, Tehran, 17 April 1975: a Cambodian Journey, Afghanistan: 0 Rh-, Syria: A Travel Guide to Disappearance, Foxtrot Gate – Cyprus, Libya: Inch by Inch, House by House, Alley by Alley, Baghdad: Red Zone, Green Zone, Babylon (Mousse Publishing); Saudiscapes, Never walk on crowded street – Rome (Nero Editions);UN, CH (bruno); Niemeyer4ever, Palmyrah (Art Paper Editions); Walk like an Egyptian, Good Boy 0372, Motto Books and Mr. Bawa, I Presume (Hatje Cantz). In 2014, she participated in the Venice Architectural Biennale with the project Nightswimming, Discotheques in Italy from the 1960s until now. She has participated in exhibitions at MACRO in Rome, Fondazione Bevilacqua la Masa in Venice, at the Triennale, Milan and at the American Academy, Rome. She is the founder of Humboldt Books and San Rocco Magazine. She teaches at NABA Milan and ISIA Urbino.

Catholics in Africa outnumber those in Europe, Vatican says
VATICAN CITY, Oct 16 - There are now more Catholics in Africa than in Europe, the Vatican said on Friday, releasing the latest Catholic Church statistics compiled by its news agency Fides.
The total number of Catholics in the world stood at 1.422 billion at the end of June 2024, representing 17.8% of the global population, and up 0.1% year on year.
Some 20.3% of Catholics live in Africa and 20.2% in Europe, with the Americas accounting for 47.7%, Asia 11% and Oceania 0.8%.
In last year's statistics, relating to the end of June 2023, there were 1.405 billion Catholics globally, with about 20% of them living in Africa and 20.4% living in Europe.
Fides also counted 5,525 bishops around the world and 407,421 priests, noting that the number of priests, up by 425, had increased for the first time in five years. REUTERS

Are we addicted to our phones? Why you can’t stop scrolling
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:49:23 UTC
19:49:23 KST

Rachel Feltman: For Scientific American’s Science Quickly, I’m Rachel Feltman.
How much time did you spend on your phone this week? It’s okay; you don’t actually have to tell me. But chances are good, like really good, that the number is higher than you’d like it to be: according to a recent survey by Pew Research Center, more than half of U.S. adults say they spend too much time on their phones. Folks under 50 are especially dissatisfied with their device usage: 64 percent of adults aged 30 to 49 think their screen use is out of hand, and 70 percent of adults aged 18 to 29 say the same.
Setting aside the survey data and just speaking personally, I think that these days, you’re either someone who actively avoids using screened devices, someone who knows they use screened devices too much or someone who’s currently in deep denial.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
There are now apps, physical phone accessories and even pared-down smartphones designed to help us curb our reflexive swiping and scrolling. But some people are taking things a step further by treating screen addiction with the same kind of programming traditionally reserved for substance abuse.
Scientific American associate editor Allison Parshall explored the new frontier of screen addiction in a feature for the latest issue of the magazine. She’s here to tell us what she’s learned about our dependence on technology—and what we can do to take back control.
Allison, thanks so much for coming on to chat. It’s always great to have you.
Allison Parshall: Thank you for having me.
Feltman: So I’d love to start by asking how you, you know, first got interested in writing this piece.
Parshall: I don’t know if you saw there were a lot of court cases to do with social media addiction earlier this year. They’re still ongoing, but, like, some of the biggest headlines were hitting. Basically Meta and Google were on trial from plaintiffs who said that their products were addictive and that they’d addicted kids, and the jury actually held them liable for that, which was a big first. So that got me interested in understanding, kind of, what’s behind these social media addiction claims because the companies claim it’s not an official addiction because there’s no diagnosis, and then, on the other side, you know, clinicians are like, “No, we’re seeing a problem.” So I kinda wanted to understand and get to the bottom of that tension.
But there was also a more personal motivation, which was that I just kept getting those, like, Sunday weekly screen time recaps, and they were always, like, way higher than I could possibly ever have fathomed. Like, I think I pushed up to seven hours a day, and that’s outside of work. So I’m doing the math, going like, “Am I on my phone literally every waking moment? That doesn’t seem possible.”
Feltman: Eight hours for work, eight hours for sleep, eight hours for what you will—is all we will phone. [Laughs.]
Parshall: All I will is phone. And then I, like, run through justifications, right? It was the winter. I was actually talking with friends most of the time; I’ve got a lot of really close long-distance friendships. A lot of it was, like, engaging creatively in things that I was very passionate about.
And then a lot of it was frankly just TikTok scrolling. So, I basically have just been kind of at war with myself and noticing a lot of my friends at war with themselves over these screen times and, like, wondering, “At what point do I say this is actually a problem? At what point does this helplessness and ambiguity I feel, like, resemble something closer to the experience of people who experience addiction to substances or to gambling and other behaviors?”
So that’s kind of where I started, with a little bit of a personal mission to figure out if I thought this was a problem or not. I can’t say I landed on a really satisfying place.
Feltman: [Laughs.] Well, it is, as you know, like, such a complex question. You know, even just speaking personally and, you know, based on the experiences of other people I know personally, because so much of it is very contextual, like you said. Like, there isn’t a distinction between online life and real life anymore. We live a lot of our lives through the channeling of these devices, so it’s like, there are many, like, good, prosocial, beneficial things one can and maybe even should do that involve staring at a screen. And then there’s the stuff that we know is just scrolling through TikTok.
I’m curious, you know, I have some familiarity with the whole, you know, “Is it an addiction?” question, not just for screens and social media specifically but really anything that’s behavioral. And I think it feels especially complicated when it’s behavioral and involves a relatively new technology. So I’d love to hear, sort of, you know, what you’ve learned and, and what your takeaways are in terms of that whole “Is it an addiction?” question.
Parshall: I think, [the] “Is it an addiction?” question is one that I am just going to have to say: I think we’re just gonna have to live in the nuance of this forever. I don’t think we’re ever gonna have a super satisfying answer because the more you look into the history of our concept of addiction, the muddier it gets.
I think a lot of people have an understanding of, like, okay, drugs are straightforwardly addictive because they can hook your brain in a chemical way. Then when we start getting into behaviors, things get a little more squishy. Gambling, we’re like, “That’s really an addiction because it does something very specific to your brain, almost like a drug.” So, you know, that—you could put it there. Well, then you get into love and sex addiction, food addiction, and it all gets quite complicated.
But I think the thing that I realized in talking to researchers was, like, even when you go back into the history of drug addiction, we’ve had to push this line to get cocaine accepted as an addictive drug. So there’s, like, all of [these] questions of: “At what point are we going to broaden it enough?” And there’s a lot of concern among various pockets of addiction researchers and clinicians that if we make it too broad, the word loses meaning. It’s, like, a serious concern, but at the same time, you do have to let it be broad enough to encompass the problems that people are experiencing, and people are experiencing this problem of tech addiction.
Feltman: Yeah. There is so much nuance, and the focus on whether screen addiction is a real addiction or not can kind of miss the point. I mean, what do we know about why screens are so compelling to us and, so often, you know, leave us feeling worse or to make worse choices in our lives?
Parshall: Well, I mean, I think it would be helpful to start with, kind of, threading the needle on where we do want to demarcate the line of addiction, not around specific behaviors and what can and can’t be addictive but around, like, what we actually see with people that we say, “Okay, that’s where it becomes an addiction. That’s where it’s not. Hanging out with your friend for eight hours on video games, that’s where it actually becomes a problem.”
One of the researchers I talked to is Mark Griffiths, and he’s one of the people who helped develop this framework. And he was saying, you know, video game addiction, you can have someone who plays video games for seven or eight hours a day, and they are not addicted to video games. Excessive use and the length of time you spend doing something is not the marker of it. It can really dovetail with it, but it’s not the marker.
So there’s six characteristics of addiction, according to this framework, that a lot of researchers use. It needs to involve a salient behavior or a drug, so something that, kind of, is grabby to you, that causes mood modification effects, which you develop tolerance to over time, which leads to this cycle of increasing use and then withdrawal when you can’t use enough. Then those withdrawals induce craving, which induces a relapse, and that can cause conflict in your life. So those six factors are salience, mood modification, tolerance, withdrawal, relapse and conflict.
And it’s not like every single researcher agrees that you need all of these in order for things to be addictive. There’s a lot of questions specifically around withdrawals and their importance because that, kind of, comes from the drug framework and not necessarily the behavioral one. But it’s really, like, this cycle of amplification where things are getting worse and your life is deteriorating that I think is what leads people to seek help in the first place from doctors or from 12-step programs, and that leads doctors to point to that and say, “Okay, we can count that as addiction.”
And for tech addiction, specifically, or social media addiction or Internet addiction or whatever grab bag of technologies you wanna use, there’s not really any great data showing the prevalence of it. Like, it seems like it’s in the low single digits, but it really depends on how wide of a net you wanna cast. People will overestimate their own addiction to technology if you give them the opportunity. People are more ready to say, “I’m addicted to this technology” and then you give them little screening tools, and they’re actually not really that addicted. Part of that is because we use this word very casually, colloquially.
Just to, like, set the groundwork here, there’s a lot of people probably who are clinically addicted to social media and technology. Whether you want to call what I’m experiencing, which is, like, periodic loss of my ability to stop scrolling TikTok even though I know it’s not good for me, and maybe, like, I’m not taking full advantage of the in-person opportunities of my life because of it, that’s a very different thing.
Feltman: So moving from this idea of “Is it addicting?” “Are people addicted?” You know, we know that the reality is, like you said, separate from people who do have clinically significant addictions to this behavior. Many of us, myself included, again, feel this compulsion to be using screens, be on social media, be on the Internet more than we know actually makes us feel good. And I feel like it’s important to stop and reflect on the fact that that is what they are designed to do. So can we talk a little bit about tech culpability here?
Parshall: Yeah. I mean, I talked to, like, 30 people for this story. Everyone I talked to would stop in the middle of saying—whether or not they were saying, “Social media addiction’s overblown. We should just call it problematic social media use,” whether they were saying, you know, “The tech companies are driving us into the ground”—um, basically everyone stopped in the middle to say, “This is how these products are designed.” And there’s a concern with putting a lot of focus on the individual: How do they deal with social media? What are their habits? What is their, I don’t know, family genetic history of addiction and predisposition to find this really hooking?
There’s a concern that you’re, kind of, looking in the wrong place for the problem. And I’m very sympathetic to that. Like, I think part of the reason I can’t put this down, even though I wouldn’t say I have a lot of tendencies toward addictive things, is because it’s, like, kind of uniquely designed to hook me, and I will scroll forever. You know, you know that thing where you go back to see a video you just saw, and you scroll back up to it, and it’s, like, actually 10 videos ago? That’s what these cases are kind of resting around. These cases are really more about showing what social media companies knew based off of internal documents about the potential of their products to hook people, especially kids, and how they proceeded, kind of, regardless of those concerns.
So there’s a lot of papers that came out both in the Facebook files—I know that The Social Reckoning movie will be out by the time listeners hear this—and through these court cases with discovery, there are cases of people internal at Meta saying explicitly, “Instagram is a drug. We’re basically pushers.” What the plaintiffs argue is a company that knew what its product could do and could have harms and didn’t do anything about it. So the company argues that, like, you know, social media addiction is not an official diagnosis, which means that it’s not something we should be resting these court cases on.
It was interesting how hard it was to find legal experts to analyze these cases on the terms of social media addiction. It’s kind of like the word we use to talk about it, but it’s actually not the main character of these trials. The main [characters] of these trials are, like, the kids who are bringing these personal liability cases and the state’s [attorneys] general that are saying, you know, “You defrauded our consumers,” or, um, “You’ve [misled] our consumers.”
Feltman: Well, so getting back to individual action, in this idea of addiction or at least, you know, excessive, unhappy social media use. You talk to folks who are really treating this in themselves as an addiction, including with 12-step programs. Could you tell us a little bit about how this seems to be similar to, you know, treating drug or alcohol addiction and how it seems to be different?
Parshall: I talked to one woman who I met through this Internet and Technology Addicts Anonymous. And she had her own struggles with alcoholism, and she has been clean and sober for 30 years now, and from alcohol specifically.
And then, you know, when Facebook came out, she kind of realized that she was getting sucked in. And sometime in the last, I believe it was five years, she managed to start attending these basically AA meetings but for technology and get sober from that. She says that it feels like the same thing to her. Like, internally, this, like, loss of control, this [is] doing things that she doesn’t want to do and looking around at the people in her life that she feels like she’s constantly letting down and are increasingly learning to expect very little of her as, like, kind of the same kind of heartbreak.
It seems from talking to these people who go to these 12-step programs that, for certain people, they can be really beneficial in the same way that they’re really beneficial for people who are struggling with other addictions. I mean, just from the outside looking in, it seems like a lot of that is down to community support and dedication. You get involved in these programs, and you can just go to meetings. There’s, like, a saying, “Meeting makers make it.” But also a lot of the people I talked to said, like, getting involved, volunteering, helping run the meetings, everything like that really helped pull them out.
And I think some of that is, like, it’s something to fill your life with purpose, becoming a sponsor for other people. You know, some of the addiction researchers I talked to pointed out that there’s a reason that you’re smoking all the time, or there’s a reason that you are filling all your time with TikTok. I mean, I feel that way, like, at times of life when I feel that TikTok is hardest to resist is when everything else feels like a monumental effort, and scrolling is the only thing that can, kind of, turn my brain off. The things that 12-step programs and then other forms of treatment that are more clinically evidence-based, like, you know, seeing psychologists or therapists, many of which do use 12 steps but—can help you, kind of, fill that gap or fill that hole or however you wanna think about what it is that the vice is coming into your life to replace or to fill.
And so, yeah, I think that could be done through 12-step programs. For some people, those don’t work very well ’cause they have such a heavy focus on sobriety. You can get trapped in a cycle of shame of, like, getting sober and then breaking it and then hating yourself and coming back crawling, and for some people, that just doesn’t work well. Addiction treatment in general is kind of trying to move away from the sobriety approach to a more evidence-based harm reduction. Like, okay, we’re not going to say you have to be 100 percent sober from this thing. You see this with sex and porn addiction a lot where, like, that can be a really harmful cycle.
And so the point of therapy might not necessarily be: we’re gonna cut out social media entirely. It might be: we’re going to build these guardrails around it, or we’re gonna make sure that you find a way to only stick to just a little bit. For some people, that’s also not possible, and that’s why they go for the whole sobriety thing. The researchers and clinicians and people who have been through these 12-step programs, they all kind of stress that, like, you need to have compassion with yourself and find something that works for you.
Feltman: Yeah, I know that, for me personally, relative to how much I was on social media until this point, for the last couple of years, I’ve been, like, functionally not on social media. And it’s really interesting because, every once in a while, I start to feel, you know, disconnected enough that I really want to, like, be spending some time on Instagram on my phone, and I redownload it. And the first couple times this happened, it was a real shame cycle because I was like, “Wow, I can’t do it in moderation.”
And now I’ve really, I think, successfully reframed it as less of trying to be sober from social media and more like detoxing, where it’s like, you know, I know what it feels like when it doesn’t feel good anymore. And, like, when I really miss it in a way that feels kind of holistic and healthy and that, like, I just sort of want to be enjoying the Internet again, I redownload it. And then when I get to the point where I’m like, “Oh, no, now, now it’s poisoned my brain again,” then I get rid of it for a while.
And I think it does, for me at least, seem to work in terms of, like, recalibrating me to stop, the decreased sensitivity to it where you’re just, like, totally desensitized and spending more and more time on there and not actually using it for the things that, like, again, are prosocial and actually feel good, like reaching out to friends and seeing cool art they’re making and stuff. But, yeah, I feel like it—what that looks like is [so] personal and context dependent that it feels really tough and unfair that, like, everybody has to figure out what that looks like for them.
Parshall: And it’s constantly changing, too. That’s the thing that gets me. Like, I feel like I’ve navigated, I’ve, like, negotiated a good relationship, and then it changes. It’s kind of like the slippery slope doesn’t stop.
Feltman: Yeah, the algorithm changes; what’s going on in your life changes.
Parshall: I think part of that is, like, the way they’re designed to, like, kind of keep it as a slow slope. So, like, even if you start it with a good relationship, it is pretty easy to stop, and then you look up and you go, “Where am I?” And then you delete the app because you’re like, “I don’t like that I’m here.” I think your point about reframing is a really good one and one that I wanna stress that, like, if the addiction framing to you feels like it is unhelpful, it is really not necessary that you think of it as addiction.
There’s a lot of other ways to think about it. Some researchers really like just thinking about it as a habit. And the differences between those things are a little bit hard to literally pin down. You know, a habit is like biting your nails. We don’t really say people are addicted to biting their nails, but it’s like there’s a particular cue: “I’m bored; I’m anxious.” With your phone it might be “It’s bedtime,” and you develop these habits.
And, like, you know the thing where, like, you literally can open Instagram through muscle memory or any other app that you use and start scrolling and realize you didn’t even realize that you’d chosen to do it? So, like, the researchers I talk to stress that, like, we do know how to get people to change their habits. I mean, we have more research than we do maybe on, like, tech addiction. You can shuffle around the way the apps are on the home screen. You can delete them entirely. Something I do with TikTok is: on the iPhone, it lets you remove it from your home screen but not from your phone entirely, so every time I want it, I have to search for TikTok. That doesn’t always work. Um, but it stops, it stops me from having a literal rote muscle memory on it. I might need to do that with Instagram soon, honestly. So yeah, there’s little tweaks that you can do to try to resist this thing that is probably, profit-motive-wise, going to continue to exist to want to pull you in.
And you don’t have to think of it like addiction if you don’t want to. That can be a really stigmatizing framework, and it can be one that, you know, I mean, especially with alcoholism, like, the, kind of, the way that people who are alcoholics talk about it often is like, “I am an alcoholic,” and for the rest of your life, you frame yourself as an alcoholic. You’re just, like, in recovery. People I talk to in 12-step programs, some of them did have that framing for tech addiction. But I would say their experience is, like, more extreme than a lot of the people that I know who use technology—in, subjectively, in their experience—too much.
Feltman: We’ve brushed against this, but I would love to hear where you actually have landed in terms of managing your own screen use and social media use?
Parshall: Yeah, I would love to say that I cut down my screen time drastically. When I first started this story, I was like, “How great of an arc would it be if, at the end, I can say that I managed to cut it down to three hours a day, and here’s what I did?” I did not do that. My screen time last week was higher than ever, but I was sick, in my defense.
And I think what I’ve noticed through observing these Sunday screen time notifications every week is: it really depends on the type of week I had. And there isn’t some terrible trend line for me where it’s getting worse and worse and worse and worse. It looks like this more than anything. And I think taking the advice of the researchers I talked to who said to give yourself grace ’cause you’re in kind of a screwed-up system, I’ve been trying to do that.
I’ve also been trying to listen to myself when I have that little voice in my head that’s saying, like, “You’re doing this to numb yourself,” and the things that are worth living about life in the physical world are things that take time to build. Like, you’re gonna have to go through going to, like, a deeply unpleasant social situation for a little while in order to meet the friends, to meet the friends, to meet the friends, instead of just focusing on the vicious cycle of screen time, thinking of the virtuous cycle of doing things that you’re passionate about and that can be on a screen. Trying to not have this bifurcation in my head of, like, screen time—bad. Like, noticing when I have had seven hours of screen time, being like, “Oh, actually four of those was ’cause I was reading a book I really liked, and that’s okay.” So yeah, I, I haven’t fixed myself. But I do think I’ve started to pay more attention in a way that is healthier. I would say I hope other people can, too, but I know that I’m not leading the charge on this. I’m in the muck with every single person in my life, trying to figure out what works for them. So I hope you’re able to, to make it work better for you, too.
Feltman: Thank you so much for that. And, thank you for coming on to talk about your story with us.
Parshall: Thank you for having me.
Feltman: That’s all for today’s episode. You can check out Allison’s feature article online or in the latest issue of Scientific American, on newsstands now. We’ll be back on Monday with our weekly science news roundup.

LONDON — Police are conducting a criminal investigation into a dispute connected to the founding of Your Party, a left-wing political party that was established last year.
A spokesperson for London’s Metropolitan Police said it had launched an investigation following a report in September 2025 “relating to the alleged unauthorised access of a political party’s database.”
Officers recently arrested a man in his 20s on suspicion of an offence under the 1990 Computer Misuse Act, the spokesperson said. He was released pending further enquiries and has not been charged.
Advertisement
Officers also previously interviewed a woman in her 30s under caution in connection with the same investigation. The spokesperson added: “The investigation continues.”
Scotland Yard did not name any political party in its statement, and the spokesperson did not confirm which political party its investigation related to.
However, three other people with knowledge of the circumstances, all of whom were granted anonymity to discuss an ongoing case, said the investigation relates to a long-running dispute connected to the establishment of Your Party.
The left-wing party was co-founded in summer 2025 by the former Labour Leader Jeremy Corbyn and the former Labour MP Zarah Sultana, both of whom now sit as Your Party MPs in the House of Commons.
The two MPs clashed publicly over a September 2025 email that was sent to around 800,000 people on the new party’s mailing list, encouraging them to sign up as paying members. Sultana had promoted the membership portal while Corbyn described its launch as “unauthorised.” Sultana later said her sole aim had been to “safeguard the grassroots involvement that is essential to building this party.”
Neither the man arrested, nor the woman interviewed by police, are MPs and neither have been charged with an offence. Neither Corbyn nor Sultana are accused of wrongdoing.

A Your Party spokesperson said: “It would not be appropriate to comment any further about ongoing police investigations.”
They also said: “We can reassure our members and supporters that our systems are secure and that this was an isolated incident.”
