ETS splits EU leaders and tests bloc's climate goals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:47:04 UTC
19:47:04 KST

EU leaders are trying to counter soaring energy prices, with some arguing that carbon pricing is hurting the bloc's competitiveness.
The European Union's carbon market emerged as one of the most contested topics at a summit of EU leaders in Brussels on Thursday and Friday – just days after high-level political talks between EU environment ministers revealed deep splits on the issue.
In lengthy debates that dragged late into the night on Thursday, the leaders of the three Nordic members faced off against the four-nation Visegrad group – Hungary, Slovakia, the Czech Republic and Poland –over the future of the bloc's Emissions Trading System (ETS).
Italy and Greece also backed the Visegrad four as the bloc's carbon market has emerged as a core friction point, with several capitals linking the immediate energy price crisis to the bloc's carbon costs.
The ETS makes companies pay for their pollution, with the dual aim of reducing emissions and encouraging industry to invest in more sustainable alternatives. Since its onset in 2005, emissions covering affected industries have dropped by 51%, according to the European Commission.
In Europe, the ETS currently covers heavy industries, power plants, as well as airlines and shipping. Additional sectors such as international aviation, landfills and incinerators are set to be included in the summer review tabled by the Commission.
Finland, Denmark and Sweden warned EU leaders on Thursday that watering down the ETS would undermine investment in clean technologies and those who have already invested.
"Any weakening of the ETS would undermine the predictability on which investment decisions depend and risk slowing the pace of industrial decarbonisation," reads a letter penned by the three EU countries and seen by Euronews.
But Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis sharply attacked the ETS and carbon taxes, blaming carbon market speculators for destroying Europe's competitiveness.
“Someone is making billions at the expense of the European industry, which is in decline and which of course has major problems,” Babis told reporters on Thursday.
Babis said EU climate policies are "ideological stuff" that ignore economic realities. He added that carbon allowance prices skyrocketed far past original forecasts, arguing that the system rewards financial gamblers while punishing traditional manufacturing and regular citizens.
Babis and his Italian counterpart Giorgia Meloni recently urged Brussels to provide immediate economic oxygen to struggling European factories.
EU countries are using the current geopolitical shock as leverage to recalibrate carbon market rules, depending on their national energy mixes. Fossil-heavy nations are pushing for lower carbon price pressures, while green-forward nations demand steadfast transition timelines.
The Nordics argue that cutting ambition would also "shift the burden of emission reductions to other sectors of the economy" where mitigation options are often more difficult and politically difficult.
"This is not a new issue, but the current situation gives renewed urgency to the debate. Leaders shared their expectations in the context of ongoing legislative negotiations," one EU diplomat said.
ETS encourages decarbonisation
The countries backing the ETS see it as an enabler of decarbonisation, both because of its raised revenues and because it encourages heavy-industry sectors to invest in green technologies to avoid higher carbon costs.
"(The ETS) has played an important role in decarbonisation. We must now maintain the price signal and ensure the scheme continues to function by implementing corrective measures," a second EU diplomat told Euronews.
"We must preserve the structural mechanisms whilst providing short-term flexibility for the member states most affected," the diplomat added.
EU leaders invited the Commission to examine further short-term interventions and urged EU lawmakers to accelerate work on the Market Stability Reserve, the mechanism governing the supply of allowances in the ETS with the aim of limiting carbon-market price volatility — and ultimately carbon pricing.
Battle for ETS2
However, a plan by the four Visegrad countries — backed by Italy and Greece — to delay the new version of the Emissions Trading System (ETS2) until 2030 has hit a wall late on Thursday.
The four countries argued that households and small businesses will inevitably face higher costs. They said that "price differences between the EU regions and EU countries are enormous", particularly in Eastern Europe.
The ETS2 is the new carbon market set to cover fuels used in road transport and buildings as of 2029.
The climate tool was already delayed once over concerns about its social impact on the most vulnerable, as the mechanism will inevitably increase energy bills further, despite the bloc's attempts to regulate price spikes.
Despite the concerns raised by the six countries, one EU diplomat told Euronews that the proposed amendments "would never get the required unanimity".
"There is little support for it and they know it. That's why they try it at the European Council instead of the Environment Council because there's no majority there for this," another EU diplomat said.
Nonetheless, the six countries succeeded in requesting an impact assessment to determine its design and safeguards, which the Commission will handle, according to the Council conclusions.

European Central Bank clears UniCredit to raise Commerzbank stake above 30%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:45:54 UTC
19:45:54 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
The European Central Bank (ECB) has authorized Italy’s UniCredit to raise its stake in Germany’s Commerzbank above 30%, clearing a key hurdle in its bid to take control of the German lender.
UniCredit said Thursday that the approval allows it to cross the 30% ownership threshold and "increase its stake further without upper limits."
The bank expects to secure the remaining regulatory approvals and meet the offer conditions around year-end, giving it approximately 50% of Commerzbank’s voting rights and enabling it to take control of the bank.
UniCredit described the decision as a significant milestone in the acquisition, saying it reflected the ECB's positive assessment of the transaction and confidence in UniCredit's financial foundations and position within Europe's banking sector.
The transaction comes as the ECB advocates cross-border banking mergers as a way to strengthen the European Union's single market.
 
Berlin seeks guarantees
The takeover has faced resistance from the German government and Commerzbank’s management, but Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil on Friday described talks with UniCredit as constructive.
Speaking on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund’s annual meeting in Bangkok, Klingbeil said discussions between the two sides’ teams were continuing after a “very constructive start” to his talks with UniCredit Chief Executive Andrea Orcel, German news agency dpa reported.
Berlin wants to protect jobs, preserve Commerzbank’s Frankfurt headquarters and stock market listing and maintain its lending to small and midsize businesses.
“I have not seen any hardened positions, but rather believe that all these issues can be addressed constructively together,” Klingbeil said.
The German government, which rescued Commerzbank with billions of euros in taxpayer money during the financial crisis, still holds a 13.3% stake in the bank.
Commerzbank's management, led by Chief Executive Bettina Orlopp, has long resisted the takeover effort while seeking a negotiated solution with UniCredit.

Britain studies US autonomous warfare command for lessons
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:45:41 BST
19:45:41 KST

Britain will engage closely with the United States as it establishes an Autonomous Warfare Command and will see what lessons apply here, while continuing to assess the most effective organisational arrangements of its own, according to a written answer in the House of Lords.
Lord Sarfraz, the Conservative peer, asked what assessment the government has made of the American decision and what consideration has been given to establishing an equivalent integrated capability within British defence.
Lord Coaker, the Minister of State for Defence, said: “Given the importance of autonomous systems to the future of warfare, we will continue to engage closely with our US counterparts as they establish an Autonomous Warfare Command and see what lessons apply to the UK Defence system.
“The UK’s approach reflects our own operating model and structure. Defence is developing an integrated approach to optimise the balance between crewed, uncrewed and autonomous systems across the Armed Forces. This includes the establishment of the Uncrewed Systems Centre as a Defence centre of excellence alongside Defence’s Rapid AI Delivery (RAID) taskforce, to accelerate the development, integration and adoption of these capabilities. This is backed by a defence investment plan commitment of over £5 billion by 2030 in autonomous systems across the Integrated Force. This investment will support capabilities including the Hybrid Navy, uncrewed ground vehicles and Collaborative Combat Aircraft, increasing the mass, lethality and readiness of the Armed Forces while retaining appropriate human responsibility and accountability. We will continue to assess the most effective organisational arrangements for delivering these capabilities.”
The Pentagon announced the new command at the start of October, putting a four-star officer in charge of artificial intelligence and uncrewed systems across the American services and consolidating work that had been spread between the individual branches and a set of separate offices. Standing up a command of that weight around autonomy goes further than anything Britain has done, and Coaker’s answer stops short of promising an equivalent while keeping the possibility in play.
Britain has instead built the Uncrewed Systems Centre as its centre of excellence, with the Rapid AI Delivery taskforce working alongside it. Neither carries command authority over operational units in the way an American combatant command does, and both are designed to coordinate and accelerate work that is still owned by the services. The Army conceded at Apex Europe this month that its a number of its own drones cannot talk to each other, which is precisely the fragmentation the centre was created to address.

Netanyahu made the remarks at a conference in the northern Israeli city of Acre, according to the Hebrew-language newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth, triggering a public dispute over the distribution of cabinet portfolios ahead of the Knesset elections scheduled for 27th October.
Ben-Gvir, leader of the Otzma Yehudit (Jewish Power) party, has said during his election campaign that he intends to seek the National Security portfolio. He has also called for the Justice Ministry to be assigned to Tally Gotliv, the second candidate on his party’s electoral list.
Responding to Netanyahu’s remarks, Otzma Yehudit accused the prime minister of preparing to exclude the party from a future governing coalition.
“What was hidden has now come to light,” the party said in a statement.
The party argued that Netanyahu’s intention to retain the Interior, National Security and Justice ministries for Likud suggested a plan to exclude Ben-Gvir and Otzma Yehudit from the coalition while bringing in former Israeli military chief Gadi Eisenkot.
It further alleged that Netanyahu intended to transfer key ministerial portfolios to parties on the political left.
The dispute follows criticism by Ben-Gvir two days earlier, when he accused Netanyahu of attempting to draw votes away from Otzma Yehudit rather than expanding support beyond the right-wing electorate.
Speaking at a conference organised by Yedioth Ahronoth and Ynet, Ben-Gvir addressed Netanyahu directly, saying: “Instead of taking seats away from me, go and take them from Eisenkot.”
Ben-Gvir also accused Netanyahu of considering a unity government with Eisenkot and warned against such an arrangement.
“Do not make this mistake; the camp must remain entirely right-wing,” he said.
The exchange highlights growing tensions between Likud and Otzma Yehudit over the composition of a potential future coalition and control of key government ministries.

Indonesia tests dry ice technology to disperse toxic haze from forest fires
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:45:03 UTC
19:45:03 KST

Faisal Mahmud
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
Indonesia has begun testing dry ice technology to disperse toxic haze from forest and peatland fires, with officials reporting improved visibility near an airport in South Sumatra.
The National Disaster Management Agency said Thursday that the trials use atmospheric modification techniques to disperse smoke without requiring rain clouds, according to state news agency Antara.
Berton S.P. Panjaitan, acting head of the agency's data, information and communication center, said the method targets dense smoke directly, unlike conventional cloud seeding, which uses salt particles to stimulate rainfall.
He explained that forest fires create atmospheric inversion layers that trap hazardous smoke close to the ground.
Response teams release 3-millimeter dry ice granules at minus 75C (minus 103F) to disrupt these layers and help smoke disperse.
A Cessna Caravan aircraft flew two flights Thursday at an altitude of 4,500 feet, releasing 1,600 kilograms (3,527 pounds) of dry ice over Palembang's Sultan Mahmud Badaruddin II International Airport.
The disaster agency said that following the operation, visibility jumped from 650 meters (2,133 feet) to 2,800 meters (9,186 feet).
The trials are set to continue through Sunday before authorities assess possible expansion to other affected provinces.

RABAT, OCT. 16 — Leonardo’s grandfather’s journey to Morocco is the focal point of the book presentation for “Genia da Vinci,” which will take place in the Garibaldi Hall of the Italian Consulate in Casablanca on October 20 at 6:00 p.m. The meeting with the authors, Alessandro Vezzosi and Agnese Sabato, is part of the events for the 26th Week of the Italian Language in the World, scheduled for October 19–25. And just as today, in 1402 as well, Leonardo’s grandfather was welcomed with great friendship and hospitality.”

The Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO) and the National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) have completed the pre-trial investigation in the case of former Deputy Prime Minister for European and Euro-Atlantic Integration – Minister of Justice of Ukraine Olha Stefanishyna concerning illicit enrichment amounting to UAH 13.9 million.
"On October 15, 2026, the SAPO prosecutor decided to complete the pre-trial investigation in the case against the former Deputy Prime Minister – Minister of Justice of Ukraine. The individual is suspected of illicit enrichment totaling over UAH 13.9 million and submission of inaccurate declarations (Articles 368-5 and Part 2 of Article 366-2 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine)," SAPO reported in a Telegram post on Friday.
According to the pre-trial investigation, in 2024–2025, the individual acquired two apartments in the Faina Town residential complex valued at UAH 6.9 million, registering them in the name of a close female friend, as well as UAH 7 million in cash, part of which was spent on renovating these properties.
"It also transpired that she was negotiating the purchase of a house near Kyiv with an estimated value of $550,000, intending to pay with cash ($250,000) and the two aforementioned apartments. However, she later abandoned the deal, presumably due to her appointment to a diplomatic position abroad," the statement notes.
According to SAPO, an analysis of income and expenses confirmed that despite an official income of about UAH 3.7 million (recorded from early 2024 to mid-2025), approximately UAH 4.2 million was spent solely from bank accounts.
Furthermore, the anti-corruption prosecution emphasized that the individual failed to declare information regarding the use, at various times, of assets registered in third parties' names.
This concerns an apartment in the capital's business-class residential complex Lvivska Ploshcha (registered in her mother's name) and a "MERCEDES-BENZ GLC 220D" vehicle (registered in the name of a subordinate).
"Currently, upon the prosecutor's instruction, NABU detectives have disclosed the case materials to the defense counsel for review," SAPO informed.

The prosecutor's office had requested a bail of UAH 13.3 million. She is suspected of illicit enrichment and false declaration. According to the investigation, she failed to declare two apartments in Kyiv, renovation expenses, housing rental costs, the use of a Mercedes-Benz, as well as payments for plane tickets and her mother's medical treatment.
Stefanishyna stated that she did not have the funds for the bail set by HACC but would look for them, and that she would consult with lawyers regarding a possible appeal. On August 13, the "Ilyashev & Partners" law firm posted the designated bail for Stefanishyna.
On August 20, the HACC Appeals Chamber upheld the preventive measure for Stefanishyna. Since the bail was paid, procedural obligations were imposed on the suspect, including reporting to detectives, prosecutors, and the court upon summons, notifying them of any change of residence, and refraining from communicating with a specified circle of persons.
On June 4, Ukrayinska Pravda published an investigation stating that the Asset Recovery and Management Agency (ARMA) had selected a management company for the Trade Unions House in Kyiv that may be linked to Stefanishyna's family, specifically her former husband. According to the investigation, this is already the fourth valuable asset acquired by the same company.

Merz und Macron bestätigen Einigung zum Verbrenner-Aus und „Made in Europe“
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:41:40 UTC
19:41:40 KST

Der französische Präsident Emmanuel Macron und Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz haben sich zu „Made in Europe“ für Autos geeinigt. Zudem soll das Verbrenner-Aus aufgeweicht werden. | Ludovic Marin/AFP via Getty Images
BERLIN – Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz und der französische Präsident Emmanuel Macron haben sich auf ein gemeinsames Vorgehen zum Auflockern des Verbrenner-Aus und zu „Made in Europe“ für Autos geeinigt, teilten beide Regierungen in einer gemeinsamen Erklärung mit.
„Unser Kurs bleibt unverändert: Wir streben eine deutliche Senkung der CO2-Emissionen an und stärken zugleich Europas Kapazitäten für die Entwicklung und Fertigung der nächsten Generation von Elektrofahrzeugen“, heißt es in der Erklärung.
Die beiden Regierungen wollen „mit ihren europäischen Partnern zügig auf eine Einigung hinarbeiten“. Das Paket verbinde „einen ehrgeizigen europäischen Dekarbonisierungspfad mit der nötigen regulatorischen Flexibilität, um unterschiedlichen Marktgegebenheiten und Technologieoffenheit Rechnung zu tragen“.
Umweltminister Carsten Schneider hatte die Einigung jedoch zunächst mit einem Brief an Kanzler Friedrich Merz am Mittwoch aufgehalten. Darin verlangte der SPD-Minister mehr Konditionierung für grünen Stahl, erzählten mehrere Beteiligte POLITICO. Am Freitagmorgen gab es Gespräche der SPD-Minister über das weitere Vorgehen. Im Anschluss daran gab Schneider seinen Widerstand schließlich auf. Aus Kreisen des Umweltministeriums hieß es, die Beschaffung von grünem und recyceltem Stahl könne man auch national regeln.
„Mir war wichtig, dass wir bei dieser Gelegenheit auch klima- und industriepolitische Fortschritte für die Stahlindustrie erreichen“, sagte Schneider in einer Mitteilung. „Es soll Anreize geben, damit Autos künftig mit klimafreundlichem grünem Stahl gebaut werden.“
Laut dem Abkommen würde Deutschland strengere „Made in Europe“-Kriterien für den Automobilsektor im „Industrial Accelerator Act“ akzeptieren, auf die Frankreich gedrängt hat, im Gegenzug wird das Verbrennerverbot weiter aufgeweicht, eine der langen Forderungen Berlins.
„Wir wollen nicht, dass in Deutschland nur noch Komponenten aus Asien zusammengeschraubt werden, sondern dass entscheidende Komponenten hier entwickelt und hier produziert werden“, sagte Vizekanzler und Finanzminister Lars Klingbeil in einer Mitteilung. „Dazu gehört auch die Batteriezellfertigung und alles, was wir für deutsche E-Autos brauchen. Er verspricht der Autoindustrie „mehr ‚made in Germany’ und ‚made in Europe’“. Nun seien die Automobilhersteller in der Verantwortung, „in die Zukunft der deutschen Standorte zu investieren und Arbeitsplätze zu sichern“, so Klingbeil.
Derzeit sieht das Ziel der EU vor, dass Unternehmen die Emissionen von Verbrennungsmotoren bis 2035 um 100 Prozent gegenüber dem Niveau von 2021 senken, wobei sie die Möglichkeit haben, sich durch Initiativen wie Ausgleichsmaßnahmen und Investitionen einen Spielraum von 10 Prozent bei den Emissionen zu „erwerben“.
Im Rahmen des vorgeschlagenen Abkommens wollen Frankreich und Deutschland das Ziel für 2035 auf 90 Prozent absenken und im Gegenzug für Investitionen in alternative Kraftstoffe einen zusätzlichen Spielraum von 10 Prozent einräumen (was insgesamt 80 Prozent ergibt).
Jordyn Dahl und Georgio Leali haben zu diesem Artikel beigetragen.

How prepared is Kenya for an Ebola outbreak?
October 16, 2026
Kenyais rushing to contain Ebola linked to the deadliest outbreak on record in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) . The East African nation has reported two cases and one death, while the DRC has reported over 9,000 cases and 4,400 deaths.
Kenya's first Ebola patient died at Nairobi hospital on October 5. The 40-year-old Kenyan had traveled by road from the DRC to Uganda before boarding a flight to Nairobi in Entebbe on October 3.
One of his relatives is now confirmed to have contracted the virus. The 39-year-old was under quarantine when he developed symptoms on October 13. "Both cases are linked, and there is no evidence of spread in the wider community," Kenya's health ministry said.
Contact tracing has been ongoing since officials first detected the case. Of the 128 people who came into contact with the first Ebola patient, 113 have been identified, according to the health ministry. All, except five—who are in unspecified countries abroad—have been quarantined.
Should Kenyans worry about Ebola spreading?
Public anxiety is rising, with fears of lockdowns and economic disruption and skepticism about government readiness.
"It's a very dangerous disease, so it's very shocking," a Nairobi resident told DW. Another citizen said he was disappointed: "The government has been caught unaware. It appears to me that the government was not prepared, especially at the entry point of this particular person who was found to be suffering from Ebola."
One woman said she felt there was a lack of public information on the disease. "The government should do more in educating and sensitizing about it, and raising awareness," she said.
Kenya's Health Ministry, through its Cabinet Secretary, Aden Duale, has been seeking to allay fears, urging Kenyans to remain vigilant and encouraging anyone who develops symptoms to report to the nearest medical facility. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), symptoms can develop between 2 and 21 days after infection.
Early symptoms include: fever, fatigue, malaise, muscle pain, headache and sore throat. Later, a patient may suffer from vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, and kidney and liver infection.
However, these symptoms might be similar to other illnesses such as malaria or typhoid, and only an Ebola test can confirm if one has been exposed to the virus.
Criticism and calls to improve screening
Several prominent figures, medical unions and opposition politicians have criticized Kenya's response to its first Ebola cases. Former Chief Justice David Maraga, who has declared interest in running for the presidency in the 2027 election, questioned how a man carrying the Ebola virus could pass through screening at Jomo Kenyatta International Airport, Nairobi.
"We don't know how many have been infected. We must demand appropriate action be taken so that we don't have deaths arising from that disease," Maraga told The Standard.
Kalonzo Musyoka, Kenya's vice president from 2008 to 2013, meanwhile noted that doctors at Nairobi Hospital, not border systems, detected the danger.
Dr. Dennis Miskellah of the Kenya Medical Practitioners, Pharmacists and Dentists Union believes that the Ebola cases show that Kenya's health system is not pandemic-ready. "This system is not yet resilient. This system did not learn from the COVID pandemic that we had a few years ago," he said.
"Since May, we've had this outbreak in the region. Uganda, our immediate neighbor, had almost 20 cases. So, we had ample time to prepare adequately. But it seems like somebody dropped the ball."
Kenya went on high alert after the DRC declared the Ebola outbreak in May. The government designated several hospitals as isolation centers.
It also enhanced screening at airports and border points, deploying mobile labs. Flights from several African countries were ordered to land in designated airport wings for screening.
Where are the gaps in Kenya's health system?
"Top of it all is that there's has been a serious lapse of leadership in governance of healthcare this country," said Miskellah. "All those broken pillars, there's no clear responsibility or chain of command, whether its the Ministry of Health or the 47 county governments who are semi-automous."
Capacity at some isolation centers is limited. Rural facilities lack resources such as the protective gear available at major hospitals, according to Miskellah. And there's also a shortage of health workers due to a freeze on public service workers.
Meanwhile, healthcare workers, many of whom have no healthcare cover, are reportedly wary of putting their lives at risk. Dozens of Kenyan nurses and doctors lost their lives during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Kenya's agreements on Ebola with its neighbors are being called into question since the first case was recorded in Kenya, which has one of the strongest healthcare systems in the region.
Experts are questioning the state of regional cooperation on Ebola, where borders have largely remained open despite the surge in cases and deaths. "Before we trust these agreements and cooperation, then we have have to audit them and question them so that we don't just blindly believe that Kenya is doing the right thing, or that the DRC is doing the right thing," said Miskellah.
Then, there's the question of individual responsibility. Kenya requires travelers arriving from Congo, Uganda, Tanzania, Ethiopia, Angola, Zambia, Rwanda, Burundi, Central African Republic and South Sudan to complete a health declaration form — truthfully.

BNN IN FOCUS | Political scientist’s view: Real action to weaken Russia is needed, not politicised slogans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:40:41 UTC
19:40:41 KST

This week, Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs suddenly appeared to realise that grain transported in transit from Russia and Belarus does not belong to Russian companies but to major international traders from the United States and other countries. Moreover, grain transit through the European Union has never been prohibited. The Ministry of Transport also finally released calculations showing that banning grain transit through Latvia would cost the country 290 million euros annually and could increase domestic rail freight costs by up to three times. Since the government had already been aware of these figures in early September, it appears that ministers first familiarised themselves with the consequences, then announced their determined fight against Russian grain transit, and only afterwards explained to the public why that fight could not be won.
What was really behind this sequence of events? BNN asked political scientist Filips Rajevskis, co-owner of the company Mediju tilts.
“I think all these issues related to grain and sanctions have become excessively politicised in Latvia,” the political scientist said. “Instead of pursuing sensible policies genuinely aimed at taking effective action to weaken Russia and help Ukraine, we have turned the issue into shouting politicised slogans while concealing and withholding the true situation. And that is much worse than simply addressing the problem rationally.”
“Who tried to introduce a voice of reason by asking whether we are doing everything possible, and whether we are doing the right things, to restrict Russia and inflict maximum damage on it?” Rajevskis asked rhetorically, adding that this was precisely the problem.
Asked by BNN whether the prime minister genuinely had no knowledge of EU regulations governing grain transit until this week, Rajevskis replied: 
“I am absolutely convinced that he knew. But he had to play by the rules established during the election campaign.
 If he had told the truth then, what he is saying now, all the politically aligned media would most likely have attacked Kulbergs, creating problems for him during the election campaign. It is clear that policy in this area will not change at the European level either.”
Asked whether public controversies such as the “Russian grain affair” and the “timber industry scandal” could be regarded as instruments of domestic political competition, Rajevskis agreed. “For example, the entire grain and sanctions issue was important to New Unity, while the timber industry affair was important to the Progressives. This correlates very directly with the ministries controlled by these parties and the ministries that distribute funding to the media.”
What should be done to put an end to such practices?
According to Rajevskis, the first fundamental question that needs to be reconsidered is whether such substantial amounts of public money should be allocated to the media.
 “We can see that the more money the media receive nowadays, the more their audiences decline. Instead of informing society, they engage in ‘conditioning’ people, as we remember very well, spreading certain ideas and propaganda. This is actually very dangerous. As a result, alternative information environments emerge, beyond the state’s reach, where the real dialogue with society takes place. These environments remain invisible, and consequently all sorts of unusual individuals get elected to parliament, leaving everyone asking: how did they get there?“The answer is that they are capable of establishing their own dialogue with society.”
BNN pointed out that Latvia’s parliament currently includes a rather unusual political party whose leader is facing legal proceedings and has fled the country.
Rajevskis responded that this party was among those attempting to establish alternative channels of communication. “Until its leader started making obscene gestures from the Saeima rostrum and speaking Russian, he was actually doing quite well at it.”
Could all the controversy surrounding Russian grain, the timber industry affair, the proposed buyout of shares in Swedish-owned Tet and LMT, and other major economic issues ultimately lead to a split within the United List?
Rajevskis is convinced that attempts to create such a division will occur.
 “To create a split, or at least the impression of one, they will use media outlets controlled through funding and people placed in key positions. There will certainly be pressure. The important thing is that the United List should understand the need to use more modern tools, including sociological research, to determine what society actually thinks. If your only understanding of public opinion comes from the media and social networks, you cannot build successful policies,” Rajevskis said.
He added that studies have shown people support pragmatic policymaking. “The question is what people mean by that, how they understand it, and how to respond to this demand for both change and pragmatic policies that would benefit the country and society.”

Ukrainian military tests new SkyFall drone for aerial evacuation of wounded soldiers – AP
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:38:00 EEST
19:38:00 KST

Ukrainian military tests new SkyFall drone for aerial evacuation of wounded soldiers – AP
Ukrainian company SkyFall has developed the StarGate drone for aerial evacuation of wounded soldiers and handed it over to the military this week for frontline testing.
Source: Associated Press
Details: A SkyFall spokesperson said the idea emerged after a request from the military.
Quote from AP: "Last year, Flint, commander of the 475th Separate Assault Regiment, known as Code 9.2, approached SkyFall's founder about developing a safer way to evacuate wounded soldiers from hard-to-reach positions."
Details: In some parts of the front line, the so-called kill zone – an area constantly exposed to drone and artillery fire – extends 10-15 km (6-9 miles) or more. StarGate can fly up to 15 km one way, potentially reaching critically wounded troops stranded deep within this dangerous zone.
According to a unit commander with the alias "KVN", ground robots usually take two to three hours to reach a position.
"Covering 10 km in minutes would be a drastic change on the front line," he said.
StarGate has a maximum payload capacity of 150 kg (330 pounds), the manufacturer says, enough to transport a wounded soldier in body armour with their combat gear.
The drone has a cruising speed of 65 km/h (40 mph) and a maximum speed of 105 km/h (65 mph). Preparing it for flight takes about 10 minutes.
The StarGate has two communication channels: Starlink and its own L-Link system. The drone is operated remotely, while AI features help it function without GPS and in conditions of electronic warfare interference. According to the developers, if communication is completely lost, the drone can independently plot a route to a safe area.
During a field demonstration, a StarGate took off carrying a stretcher loaded with equipment simulating a wounded soldier wearing body armour. The test range also simulated an FPV drone attack and activated electronic warfare systems. When one of the drones approached, StarGate fired a net that entangled it and knocked it off course.
SkyFall estimates that one system will cost at least US$50,000, depending on its configuration. The company plans to ramp up production to as many as 1,000 units per month by the end of 2026.
The military is currently testing the StarGate in frontline conditions. KVN said at least a month of use will be needed to assess the drone's effectiveness.
SkyFall is a Ukrainian manufacturer of heavy Vampire drones, known as Baba Yaga, and Shrike FPV drones. The company has also developed the P1-SUN interceptor drone.
Background: In March, Ukrainian company Gurzuf Defence unveiled the Ayudag-6 heavy drone, capable of carrying up to 90 kg of cargo. The multicopter is also being considered for evacuating wounded soldiers from the battlefield.

Arab-led parties could emerge as kingmakers in Israel’s Oct. 27 election, despite Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his main rivals ruling out coalition agreements with them, as the country’s Palestinian minority faces growing discrimination, rising crime and restrictions on freedom of expression.
Mansour Abbas, leader of the Islamist Ra’am party, broke a longstanding taboo in 2021 by bringing an Arab party into an Israeli coalition government.
He condemned Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023, attack and has focused on local issues, including crime, rather than the war in Gaza and Israel’s occupation of the West Bank. Critics accuse him of sidelining the broader Israeli-Palestinian conflict to gain political influence.
Palestinian citizens and their descendants make up about 20 percent of Israel’s population. Although they hold citizenship and voting rights, activists say they face discrimination and inadequate protection from violent crime.
The homicide rate among Palestinian citizens is more than 22 times higher than among Jewish Israelis. The Abraham Initiatives, an Israeli organization advocating equal rights, has recorded 184 crime-related killings in Arab communities so far this year, with only 12% of cases reported in the first half of 2026 solved.
Authorities have also restricted anti-war protests, displays of Palestinian flags and online expression, according to the rights group Adalah.
The Israeli government maintains that minorities have equal rights and says restrictions are rooted in security concerns.

Zelensky rallies EU support as Trump says Ukraine leader 'more difficult to deal with than Putin'
- Published
US President Donald Trump has renewed his sharp criticism of Volodymyr Zelensky, saying the Ukrainian leader is "more difficult to deal with than [Russian President Vladimir] Putin".
Trump, who recently made a controversial deal with Moscow to import its diesel to the American market, called Ukraine's fresh wave of strikes on Russian oil refineries a "disgrace".
Zelensky had paused the attacks for three days at Trump's request for a ceasefire on energy targets, but said on Thursday they would resume because Moscow had never stopped.
Tensions between Washington and Kyiv have escalated recently over the US-Russia diesel deal and restrictions on Ukraine's satellite communications on the battlefield.
Zelensky has not commented on Trump's latest criticism, however thanked "real leaders" for their support as he arrived at an EU summit in Brussels on Friday.
He was flanked by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa.
"Of course we supported President Trump's energy ceasefire but we've seen that Russia did not respect it, not a single minute," Von der Leyen told reporters, adding that sanctions on Russia "have to increase".
Moscow said it had never agreed to the energy ceasefire that Trump suddenly announced last week.
Costa did not mention the US, but said that "this is no time to withdraw support" to the country and "no time to relieve Russian sanctions", as the US has done in agreeing to the deal with Russia to import 300,000 tonnes of its diesel.
The summit's agenda focuses on funding for Ukraine and helping it get through another cold winter - the fifth since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
"Russia is trying everything to destroy the energy and water infrastructure," Von der Leyen told Zelensky before the summit began, "but we stand by your side, we support you as we did in the other winters."
Zelensky said his country wants the war to end "as quick as possible", but added that Russia is not showing signs that it wants the same thing.
"That's why we have to prepare for the winter. A winter package is not only energy, it's also defence and funding," he said.
Deadly attacks on Ukraine continued overnight, with several people killed in a Russian drone strike in the north-eastern city of Kharkiv, while some 270,000 households were without power after strikes in the western Volyn region, the local governors said.
Trump's comments about Zelensky, during an interview with US outlet Newsmax on Thursday evening, reflect the deteriorating relationship between the US and Ukraine.
The US president said he is "not a big fan of Zelensky" and that he is "not a good guy for us to deal with.
"He doesn't want to settle. He says he wants to settle, but he doesn't," Trump said.
"As you know, Putin hates Zelensky, and Zelensky hates Putin," he added. "And when you have that kind of hatred, it's very hard to get something settled."
When asked about Ukraine's renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries, Trump said it was "a disgrace".
"All he's doing is making the world oil price higher... There are a lot of targets that you can hit."
Trump is frustrated at Ukraine's continued targeting of Russian oil refineries because it affects Moscow's ability to export its diesel to America, as per the deal the US recently made with Russia, in an effort to bring down fuel prices.
Since the war with Iran started in February, US fuel and especially diesel prices have skyrocketed, souring Trump standing with the American public - something he wants to fix before next month's mid-term elections.
The diesel deal infuriated Zelensky, who called it a gift to Putin and an "investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged."
His anger was further heightened earlier this week, when restrictions were placed on the US-owned Starlink internet network, which is critical for Kyiv's military abilities to defend itself.
On Tuesday night, when the communications network was limited, there were several deadly Russian strikes on Ukraine, with residents and the government saying there was no prior warning of the incoming attack.
The Trump administration had previously warned that it could withhold intelligence sharing - which is crucial for Ukraine's defences - if Kyiv does not stop hitting Russia's oil refineries.

Italy cuts air traffic in half amid data transmission issue
October 16, 2026
Air travelers across Italy faced delays and cancellations on Friday because of a problem with the country's air traffic control systems.
The ENAV air traffic control authority ruled out foul play such as a cyberattack, and said it was forced to introduce temporary restrictions of the volume of flights after identifying a data transmission problem.
Major airports in cities like Rome and Milan warned of likely disruptions and advised passengers to check with their airlines.
What did authorities say about the problem?
ENAV said it first identified the issue overnight. It was forced to restrict the volume of flights at around 6 a.m. (0400 GMT/UTC) as the number of scheduled services increased.
"We would like to inform you that this morning we guaranteed the greatest possible number of departures, including intercontinental flights," ENAV said.
Shorter-distance services were more likely to be interrupted.
"Despite the anomalies encountered on the data transmission network, we are deploying all available resources to minimize disruption and restore full operations as soon as possible," ENAV said. "We confirm an operational capacity of 50% of total air traffic, ensuring maximum safety at all times, which remains the Company's top priority."
ENAV said it had ruled out the possibility of the disturbance being caused by "malicious acts."
Rome airports operator ADR warned passengers that "flight delays and cancellations may occur" and advised passengers to contact their airline if uncertain. Milan airports company SEA issued a similar notice.

Major hurricane Trudy keeps strengthening as it nears Mexico's Pacific coast
Oct 16 - Hurricane Trudy rapidly intensified into a major hurricane on Friday morning, carrying maximum sustained winds near 120 mph (195 kph) and higher gusts, as it moves closer to Mexico's Pacific coast.
Additional strengthening is still forecast before Trudy is expected to approach the Mexican coast on Saturday as a life-threatening major hurricane, the US-based National Hurricane Center said.
"Trudy has the potential to even reach Category 4 or 5 intensity," said Alex DaSilva, a hurricane meteorologist at private forecaster AccuWeather.
Mexico's civil protection agency asked residents to start preparations for the storm's arrival by securing doors and windows, and removing objects that could be thrown around by the strong winds.
The hurricane will strike Mexico's Pacific coast, a region that has already been battered in recent weeks by storms that left several dead and caused severe flooding.
Located about 250 miles (400 km) south-southwest of resort city Acapulco, the storm is expected to produce up to 12 inches (30 cm) of rain in the states of Michoacan, Colima and Jalisco, increasing the risk of life-threatening flooding and landslides, according to the NHC.

American attack helicopters open fire in Korea
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:35:07 BST
19:35:07 KST

American Apache crews carried out aerial gunnery at the Rodriguez Live Fire Complex in South Korea at the end of September, validating weapons employment, target engagement and crew coordination under live-fire conditions, according to the unit.
The crews came from 4th Battalion, 2nd Aviation Regiment, part of 2nd Combat Aviation Brigade in the 2nd Infantry Division and Republic of Korea and United States Combined Division. The division said the training strengthens combat readiness and proficiency, and the imagery released shows AH-64 Apaches engaging simulated targets at low level over wooded ridgelines, with rocket motor flashes beneath the fuselage and impact smoke rising from the hillsides.
Rodriguez Live Fire Complex sits near Pocheon in Gyeonggi Province, around twenty-five kilometres from the Demilitarised Zone, and it is the principal range on the peninsula where American and South Korean units can shoot and manoeuvre together with live ammunition. Its proximity to the border has made it a politically sensitive site, with noise and safety complaints from nearby villages a recurring issue.
2nd Combat Aviation Brigade is the only permanently forward-stationed combat aviation brigade in the United States Army, and the “Fight Tonight” tag the division attaches to its material reflects what the formation exists to do, which is to be ready for combat without a deployment timeline. The brigade operates from Camp Humphreys, the largest American overseas base, and its Apache battalions are among the few American attack aviation units held at that readiness state permanently.
The British Army flies the AH-64E Apache from Wattisham Flying Station under 1 Aviation Brigade Combat Team, having completed the transition from the Westland-built Mk1 fleet, and the American and British fleets now operate the same baseline aircraft. British crews train in similar gunnery cycles at ranges including Castlemartin and Otterburn, and have exercised alongside American attack aviation in Europe and the United States.

The Guardian newspaper reported that Lange said a Switzerland plus deal could be negotiated within months of any decision to strengthen relations with Brussels and that he would "love to see the UK back."
Switzerland is not a member of the EU but has a number of bilateral agreements with the bloc that allows the country access to parts of the single market and ensures what it calls "smooth relations" across areas including trade, security, transport, and education. Switzerland pays a financial contribution to the EU's economic and social cohesion fund in return for its partial integration into the single market. The arrangement also includes free movement of people.
Brexit debate reopens
Lange's comments come as the Brexit debate has once again reignited across the UK after British Prime Minister Andy Burnham called for the country to readdress its relationship with Brussels.
Burnham told MPs earlier this week that "sticking with the current status quo is not good enough for Britain" and that a conversation over future relations must be had "if we are serious about promoting growth, controlling immigration, upholding our values and security."
Burnham, who recently said Brexit had "done more harm than good," has repeatedly signalled his intention to move the UK closer to the EU and said re-entering the bloc was one of a number of potential options for the country.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has accused the prime minister of "unpicking" the Brexit withdrawal agreement with the EU and warned he would not get a better deal.

Digested week: No Nobel again for Trump but he looks a cert to retain Fifa peace prize | John Crace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:34:15 UTC
19:34:15 KST

Monday
It might have been more, shall we say, diplomatic if Donald Trump had taken some deep breaths after finding out he had been overlooked for the Nobel peace prize for the second year running before virtually declaring war on Norway. But maybe we should just be grateful he refrained from rubbishing the South African human rights activist Navi Pillay, who picked up the award, and shelved his plans to livestream the execution of the Norwegian prize committee. There again, you can understand his frustration. It’s hard to think of someone who has done more to make the world a safer place. Where would we be had not The Donald started a war with Iran which he shows no sign of knowing how to finish and which has forced up the price of global energy? And it was so good to see him intervening so positively in Russia’s war with Ukraine by appearing to side with the aggressor. These are just the things everyone is looking for in a Nobel peace laureate. The president is also put out that no one has noticed he has personally ended eight global conflicts; though it would be helpful if he could let us know which ones. Are they ones he has personally started – Trump appears disappointed that Argentina hasn’t invaded the Falklands again – or ones that only he knows about. During a press conference at Chequers in 2025, he claimed to have brought about a lasting peace between Albania and Azerbaijan. Maybe there are other wars going on we just don’t know about. Perhaps Australia and New Zealand have been bombing each other for years with neither side noticing. And perhaps the border between France and Italy has been a no-go zone ever since the fight between Zinedine Zidane and Marco Materazzi in the 2006 World Cup final. Still, Trump looks a cert to retain Gianni Infantino’s Fifa peace prize – if only because it seems likely to be scrapped, making him the only winner.
Tuesday
We may be facing higher levels of global threat and energy costs, but the political outlook isn’t all bleak. You’d need to have a major sense of humour failure not to be enjoying Reform sliding in the polls and falling out with one another. Things seemed to start going wrong when the Guardian exposed Nigel Farage’s £5m bung from the Thai-based crypto-billionaire Christopher Harborne. Nige has still not come up with a convincing explanation of how the money would be spent. Other than maintaining an expensive lifestyle. Then there was the Channel 4 sting when two of Farage’s closest political allies were caught allegedly trying to take an illegal overseas donation. Nige’s excuse? He wasn’t listening to his conversation with the donor. Who hasn’t dozed off when there’s £500,000 at stake? Since then everyone in Reform appears hell-bent on being the worst versions of themselves as the party loses support by tacking ever further to the right. On Monday, Robert Jenrick declared he would personally be happy to give the order for the Royal Navy to blow every small boat crossing the Channel out of the water. This was too much for Zia Yusuf. Zia is widely loathed within the Reform elite but no one has found a way of saying no to his money, so he gets to call himself the bogus title of shadow home secretary. His main objection to Honest Bob’s plan is that he wasn’t the one to think of it first. Meanwhile, Nige just sits back and pockets the money. Seemingly unable to stop his party collapsing around him.
Wednesday
After several years of consultation, the Bank of England has announced the four animals, insects and birds that will appear on the new banknotes. What goes on what denomination has yet to be decided, but the ones chosen are the European hedgehog, the barn owl, the buff-tailed bumblebee and the Atlantic puffin. And while I’d have quite liked to have seen my much-missed dog Herbie, who died last year, on one of the notes, they all seem reasonable choices to me. I guess the last thing the Bank wanted was to start a war between cat and dog lovers. But not everyone is happy. Partly because they are mad but mostly because they don’t apparently understand how the selection process worked. It was the public who got to choose both the theme of the banknotes and the actual creatures. Needless to say, leading the charge against the new notes are Kemi Badenoch and Nigel Farage, who see the hedgehog and the puffin as some kind of woke symbols. A country going to the barn owls and the bumblebees. They have moaned, what was wrong with having Winston Churchill? Are we now ashamed of our past? No, you halfwits. You don’t have to plaster Churchill’s face on everything to prove you are British. Most of us are secure enough in our identity not to need countless flags and symbols as a reminder. It’s just nice to have a change from time to time. And how many people used to see Churchill’s face on a £5 note and feel a well of pride every time you wanted to buy a sandwich? For that matter, how many people even use cash these days? Mind you, once AI has mined all our data from our emails and bank accounts we could be back to a cash and letter-writing society.
Thursday
In one of his last conversations with a close friend, Jeffrey Archer was asked if he had any regrets. While he admitted to having some flaws, Archer went on to say that there was nothing he would change. I find that remarkable. I’m not expecting him to apologise for having invented so much of his life – a fantasist is going to fantasise – and he had every right to be proud of his book sales. But not to feel a tiny bit of regret about having lied on oath and being sent to prison. Or feel guilty for the lives he ruined as a result of his lies. That feels borderline sociopathic. Isn’t it human to wish you had done some things differently? I’ve been thinking about this now I’ve turned 70. There’s a lot about my life that I love – family, friends, job – but I have a lasting sadness and guilt about my 20s that I find hard to forgive. The waste, the self-destruction, the damage I did to myself and others. Many of those who knew me had doubts I would even live to 30. I had those doubts, too. And sometimes didn’t much care either way. So yes, I have a whole decade I would love to have done differently. The repair job has been a lifetime’s work and it’s still ongoing. It will probably always be thus.
Friday
The Celebrity Traitors continues to be addictive television. A class above the civilian version, partly because we all know something about the celebs, but mainly because the game is different. The civilians are playing for money, the celebs are playing for screen time. That’s why Amol Rajan was gutted to be banished inside 24 hours. The one exception was Richard E Grant, who didn’t care one way or the other. Since his wife died he’s become more disinhibited. The worst has already happened to him. Halfway in, Maya Jama and James Acaster are making great traitors. Maya because she’s so hard to read as her face doesn’t move, James because he genuinely believes he’s too nice to be a traitor while stabbing his friends in the back. I’m amazed Jerry Hall is still in. Not because she’s particularly suspicious but more because she’s incredibly annoying. And why has no one asked her what it was like being married to Rupert Murdoch? The faithful who is playing a blinder is Sharon Rooney. So far she has said and done nothing to attract the film crew, which means she’s likely to be around for a while yet. Being boring is not a bad strategy. I’d like to see a version of The Traitors for politicians, and in my forthcoming shows (Birmingham MAC on 31 October, Huntingdon theatre in Worcester on 26 November) I will be inviting the audience to offer suggestions for possible contestants. So please come along and let’s see if we can make it happen.

Putin Hands Control of 5 Western Firms to Ukraine War Veteran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:33:30 UTC
19:33:30 KST

President Vladimir Putin signed a decree Thursday placing the Russian assets of five major Western manufacturing companies under the temporary management of a little-known firm owned by an ex-official who fought in Ukraine.
The targeted European and U.S. assets include French flooring giant Tarkett, Belgian hygiene manufacturer Ontex Ru, German plastic packager Menshen, corrugated producer Kappa Rus and metal packaging producer Eviosys, a subsidiary of the U.S. Sonoco Products Company.
Their combined 2025 revenue exceeds 53 billion rubles ($633.2 million), with Tarkett accounting for 19.3 billion rubles, Kappa Rus 16.5 billion rubles, Ontex Ru 10.3 billion rubles, and Eviosys and Menshen 6.1 billion rubles and 1.4 billion rubles, respectively.
Putin’s decree hands management rights to Tsentr Kapital Management Company, a Moscow entity established in February 2026, according to corporate registry data cited by RBC.
Tsentr Kapital is owned by 47-year-old Marat Mirkhaidarov, the former deputy governor and chief of staff of Far East Russia’s Zabaikalsky region.
Mirkhaidarov volunteered to serve in Ukraine with Chechnya’s Akhmat unit in early 2024, according to exiled media reports.
“I’m a patriot, I served in the special military operation [in Ukraine]. I have combat awards,” Mirkhaidarov told the Agentstvo outlet on Friday, expressing caution about his and his family’s safety over the news.
Mirkhaidarov stepped down from his regional administration post in March 2025, citing the need for medical rehabilitation after sustaining injuries during a delivery mission near the frontline.
Putin signed an order in 2023 granting the state the authority to place foreign assets under its temporary management. The regime strips foreign owners of operational control over their Russian subsidiaries while preserving nominal legal title.
Moscow has described the asset seizures as a response to “hostile actions” taken by “unfriendly” foreign governments.
On Friday, the Kremlin said the latest transfers represent a continued policy “trend” targeting countries that froze more than 210 billion euros in Russian reserves in Europe.
“Their origin was one of the factors taken into account when making the decision,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters during a daily briefing.
“We’re talking about those countries that take part in illegally holding Russian money, Russian assets. These are countries that take part in the illegal expropriation of Russian companies’ property,” Peskov said.
Reuters contributed reporting.

The new multiannual financial framework (MFF): A future vision for the EU
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:32:30 UTC
19:32:30 KST

The EU's new multiannual financial framework for 2028-2034 should channel funds more efficiently to bolster the bloc's competitiveness and future resilience, argues Markus Töns, the SPD parliamentary group's spokesperson on European affairs, in an opinion piece for Euronews.
Currently, negotiations are under way on the European Union's new Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) for 2028 to 2034.
The Commission's proposal one year ago charted a new course. In the wake of the Draghi and Letta reports on boosting the EU's competitiveness and future viability, the MFF has been realigned in order to use funds more efficiently.
Overall, the proposed new structure is welcome, as it opens up future prospects and offers the chance to respond more flexibly to crises and challenges.
But this restructuring brings not only opportunities; it also entails major cuts.
Many social projects in Germany are funded solely by the EU
Social, cohesion and agricultural support programmes such as the European Social Fund Plus (ESF+) and the European Regional Development Fund (ERDF) are to be grouped together in the so-called first pillar.
Because funds are no longer firmly earmarked for individual programmes, a battle over distribution is looming.
The detailed allocation will then lie with the member states under their National and Regional Partnership Plans (NRPP).
Although the Commission has already proposed a quota of 14% for the social field, this is where most is at stake. Many, particularly social, projects in Germany are financed exclusively by the EU.
The German budget cannot plug this gap if EU funding is not continued. Once such structures have been dismantled, they will not easily be rebuilt. That is why we are calling for a minimum quota of 20% for social projects.
If this cannot be agreed at European level, our goal is at least to enshrine it for the German NRPP in a federal-state ordinance.
Fortunately, Germany has already reached agreement that tried-and-tested federal allocation structures will be maintained and that the EU's preference for centralised national allocation will not be followed.
Future industries: Using funding to narrow the global gap
The biggest innovation lies in the second pillar with the Competitiveness Fund.
Its purpose is to support innovation and investment in the single market. It should not be overlooked that the EU, and Germany in particular, remain key industrial locations.
In future industries and artificial intelligence, however, we are currently lagging far behind on the global stage.
Targeted funding now gives us the chance to reduce this deficit. If we want to strengthen our European resilience and drive forward the transformation of the economy, we must now be bold and take a major step forward.
New MFF: Sanctions mechanisms as an additional tool
Europe's responsibility in the world is reflected in the third pillar. This will place a stronger focus on the common foreign and security policy, but also on European development cooperation.
Both within Europe and in our relations with international partners, the new MFF offers the chance to set the course.
Not only through innovation guidelines, but also through sanctions mechanisms when countries turn away from the rule of law.
A clearer distinction from extremist and terrorist organisations when allocating development aid would also be welcome as a supplementary guideline.
The best-known EU programmes are Horizon and Erasmus, in which non-member states can also participate. Joint research and education programmes are a European strength, because they build networks and encourage people to look beyond their own horizons.
By placing them in the second pillar, there is an opportunity to give them even greater weight and to promote their links with the economy in a meaningful way.
This enables Europe's innovative power to unfold across the board through targeted cooperation between young people, new ideas and investment.
That is precisely what we must keep bringing to the fore in times of ever-growing challenges and economic as well as geopolitical pressure: this is about Europe's future.
A Europe in peace and prosperity, offering diverse opportunities and bringing its citizens ever closer together. An EU that also continually reaches out to its neighbours.
If no MFF is adopted by 2028, funding will expire
It is therefore wrong to regard the EU budget from a national perspective as a necessary evil.
Recently, however, Germany has joined the "Frugals" (Editor's note in German: "die Sparsamen" meaning Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Sweden, Denmark and Finland) in calling for cuts of around €200 billion.
In its proposal, the Irish Council presidency likewise spoke of €141 billion. The single market and European cooperation are our greatest assets. Every euro paid to Brussels returns many times over.
Despite all the tensions surrounding the German budget, paying in less would restrict Germany's options.
Chancellor Merz has already threatened a European shutdown (in German: "Haushaltsperre", that is, a budget freeze) if the member states cannot agree on radical cuts. Unlike a national budget that has not been adopted, the MFF does not move into provisional budget management.
If no new MFF is agreed by 2028, funding simply comes to an end.
Cutting agricultural subsidies is not 'sacrosanct'
If cuts do ultimately prove unavoidable, it is essential that they are applied horizontally, contrary to the proposal from the Irish Council presidency.
That means reductions are made evenly across all areas. Agricultural subsidies under the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) are still often treated as sacrosanct, even though that is no longer appropriate.
Twenty-first century funding programmes must adapt to the realities of the time. The CAP cannot be exempt. Modern agricultural support must be targeted, not sprayed everywhere like water from a watering can, simply to avoid slurry being dumped in front of the European Parliament.
Here too a perspective could be created, namely that of sustainable, climate-friendly farming which guarantees Europe's food security. This would again create opportunities for research, innovation and cooperation.
There is no question that rural areas will continue to receive support through the LEADER programme (Editor's note: EU funding instrument for the autonomous and sustainable development of rural areas), but this too must no longer be distributed blindly on the basis of land area; it has to be awarded with a focus on innovation.
Only in this way can we address the real problems on the ground and increase the attractiveness of rural regions.
A digital tax would send a signal to the USA
Another challenge is repaying the Next Generation EU Covid support instrument and the interest arising from the borrowing, which comes on top of the new MFF.
To repay it, the EU wanted to introduce new own resources. That has still not happened.
Yet only own resources can act as an effective lever for stable financing, because there can be no fresh borrowing.
On NextGenerationEU (Editor's note: NGEU is the EU's temporary recovery instrument to tackle the economic and social impact of the COVID-19 pandemic) Germany's Federal Constitutional Court has taken a clear position, stating that it is a one-off.
New own resources would also offer a dual opportunity, as they could serve as instruments of political steering.
For example, a digital tax would send a clear signal to the USA. Without agreement among EU finance ministers on new own resources, or a willingness on the part of the member states to channel more money from their national budgets to Brussels, European funds will remain scarce.

Germany, France agree deal to support European car industry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:32:00 UTC
19:32:00 KST

Germany, France agree deal to support Europe's struggling car industry
Published October 16, 2026last updated October 16, 2026
Germany and France have reached a deal to protect Europe's automotive industry, the countries said in a statement Friday.
The plan aims to cut CO2 emissions and support the development and construction of electric cars in Europe, the statement added.
"Our shared ambition is clear: to successfully transform our automotive industry while maintaining our climate ambition and ensuring that the cars of the future are produced in Europe," the countries said.
The pact also includes incentives for investment, research and production.
Leaders welcome agreement
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz welcomed the agreement, describing it as a "good day for car drivers and for jobs in Germany, France and Europe."
"This is an investment signal to industry," he posted on his X account.
French President Emmanuel Macron, for his part, said the agreement shows a "clear ambition to successfully transform" the European automotive industry while upholding Europe's climate goals.
"We hope that this Franco-German dynamic can swiftly lead to an agreement with our partners, for our jobs and our industry," Macron wrote.
According to a Handelsblatt report, the two leaders have also agreed in principle to require automakers to cut exhaust emissions from new cars by 90% from 2035, without having to offset the remaining 10%, revising the bloc's proposed target.
The pact will need backing from other EU states and the European Parliament to become law.
Europe's automotive industry faces tough competition from China
European car makers have been struggling to compete with their Chinese counterparts in the electric vehicle market, resulting in cost-cutting measures.
Lower Saxony Premier Olaf Lies hailed the agreement as a "strong signal" in support of Europe's car industry that protects jobs in the sector.
Lower Saxony is where German automotive giant Volkswagen's headquarters are located, in the city of Wolfsburg. Lies is also part of VW's supervisory board.
Germany's auto industry faces a deep structural crisis due to intense pressure from Chinese rivals, the transition to electric vehicles (EVs), higher production costs and other challenges.
As Europe's biggest carmaker by volume, VW has the heaviest exposure to overcapacity in its German plants, high fixed costs and its reliance on China.

Türkiye targets stronger laws against capital market crimes by early 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:31:31 UTC
19:31:31 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
Türkiye plans to complete legal changes to strengthen its fight against capital market crimes by the beginning of 2027, Treasury and Finance Minister Mehmet Simsek said Friday.
The planned measures will also address coordinated transactions by funds, Simsek said in a statement on Turkish social media platform NSosyal, outlining steps to improve market transparency and bolster investor confidence.
Relevant institutions are implementing significant regulations, taking into account assessments by international index providers, he said.
Regulations introduced by the Capital Markets Board have strengthened the flow of information and made ultimate share ownership more transparent, Simsek added.
A fund guide announced at the end of August enabled weekly disclosure of hedge fund portfolios, alongside announcements when funds traded on the Turkish Electronic Fund Trading Platform, known as TEFAS, cross specified shareholding thresholds.
The measures also introduced concentration limits for funds and required borrowing transactions to take place on organized markets on a collateralized basis.
Simsek said authorities would closely monitor the results and take any additional steps without delay in consultation with stakeholders.
“Our priority is to complete the liquidation of problematic funds and protect investors' rights,” he said.
Sanctions will be applied resolutely against those who disrupt the fair and competitive functioning of markets, he added.
“Our goal is to establish a transparent, reliable, and efficient capital market where investor rights are protected,” Simsek said.

Ukraine Gets Two-Thirds of Its Allied Intelligence From Europe, France Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:31:30 UTC
19:31:30 KST

- Category
- World
Ukraine Gets Two-Thirds of Its Allied Intelligence From Europe, France Says
European countries now provide roughly two-thirds of the intelligence Ukraine receives from its international partners, with France among the major contributors, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said on France Inter on October 15.
“Two-thirds of the intelligence provided to Ukraine today comes from Europeans, including France,” Barrot said.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
His comments come as Kyiv faces uncertainty over US intelligence support following tensions surrounding Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries. The figures suggest that Europe has already assumed a much larger role in supplying the battlefield and strategic intelligence Ukraine needs than it had earlier in Russia’s full-scale war.
According to Militarnyi, European assistance covers a broad range of intelligence capabilities, including optical and radar satellite imagery, signals intelligence, information on Russian force movements, and warnings about ballistic missile threats. The latter have become especially important because ballistic weapons leave Ukrainian civilians and air defense units very little time to react after launch.
European countries can detect some ballistic threats using ground-based electronic intelligence systems and long-range radars capable of tracking missiles once they rise beyond the radar horizon. France is also investing heavily in expanding those capabilities.
Paris recently announced a major modernization of its Nostradamus strategic radar in the Eure-et-Loir department. The over-the-horizon system is capable of detecting activity thousands of kilometers away, covering an area stretching from the North Sea toward the Ural Mountains without mechanically rotating its antennas.
Developed by France’s ONERA aerospace research agency in the 1990s, Nostradamus spent years largely mothballed. France is now bringing the system back into a more active role amid growing threats from Russia and Iran, investing more than €50 million in its modernization.
Unlike conventional radar, Nostradamus uses high-frequency radio waves reflected by the ionosphere, allowing it to detect objects far beyond the normal line of sight. Its antennas are arranged across roughly 12 hectares in a star-shaped configuration and can monitor an enormous volume of airspace extending from ground level to an altitude of around 250 kilometers.
Earlier, Russian leader Vladimir Putin stated that Moscow will consider using all available weapons, including its nuclear arsenal, if Kaliningrad or any other Russian territory faces a direct attack or blockade.

ARMA prepares for sale of seized Russian dry-cargo vessel EMMAKRIS III, currently in Chornomorsk port
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

19:30:34 KST

The Asset Recovery and Management Agency (ARMA) is preparing for the sale of the seized dry-cargo vessel EMMAKRIS III, which is owned by a company based in Rostov-on-Don (Russian Federation).
According to the agency’s website, the vessel is currently located within the waters of the Chornomorsk seaport in Odesa region.
Built in Japan in 2000, the vessel measures 225 meters in length and 32.26 meters in width, with a deadweight of 73,280 tonnes, a draft of 6.8 meters, and seven cargo holds. An appraiser has concluded that the asset is in satisfactory condition and could be utilized as a floating grain storage facility for the storage and transshipment of dry cargo.
In April 2023, Pechersky District Court of Kyiv issued a ruling to transfer the seized vessel—owned by a Russian entity—to the management of ARMA.
The agency added that the current preparations for the sale are intended to ensure a transparent process and to secure the transfer of proceeds from the asset's disposal into the state budget.

Spaces by Manah signposts Chennai community centre with barrel-vaulted roof
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:30:32 UTC
19:30:32 KST

Spaces by Manah signposts Chennai community centre with barrel-vaulted roof
Local architecture studio Spaces by Manah has completed The Soil & Sea community centre in Chennai, India, with a brick barrel-vaulted roof that serves as a "visible landmark" on the site.
The 4,330-square-metre building was designed to provide learning space for a local education centre, as well as to house community workshops and events.
Spaces by Manah designed its single-storey masonry structure to appear as though it were "growing out of the existing landscape", creating a series of outdoor and open-air spaces that overlook its lush surroundings.
"The project sits within a lush, tree-lined parcel of land with the design growing out of the existing landscape," the studio told Dezeen.
"The building is positioned to retain its connection with the trees and outdoor spaces through a sequence of shaded, open and enclosed spaces, while the dominant barrel vault rises above the canopy to create a visible landmark within the site," it added.
Raised on a rubble stone foundation, the centre is organised around a flat-roofed volume, flanked on two sides by an L-shaped verandah that was conceived by the studio as an "intermediate, informal zone" between the building and landscape.
Steps and a ramp at the building's front lead up to the verandah, which is sheltered by the barrel-vaulted roof on one side to form a main gathering space for the community.
Meanwhile, its other edge is topped with a sloping, tiled roof. A series of granite stone pillars frame the space, along with built-in seating.
"The architecture responds to this idea through a strong central gathering space, expressed by the barrel vault, with more intimate and informal spaces arranged around it," the studio said.
"An L-shaped veranda acts as an intermediate, informal zone between the enclosed spaces and the landscape, with built-in seating and ramps supporting movement, accessibility and interaction throughout the building."
The bricks used for the structure's load-bearing walls were left exposed throughout the space. To complement the brick design, the studio sourced doors, windows and Mangalore floor tiles locally and repurposed them throughout the building.
This materiality extends to the building's interior, where exposed brick walls and roof elements are set off by glossy tiles.
"The material palette was intentionally kept natural, tactile and largely raw, allowing the building to sit comfortably within its landscape," the studio said.
Also on the site is a separate toilet block, which is similarly perched atop a stone foundation, and complete with load-bearing brick walls and a tiled canopy roof.
Elsewhere in Chennai, Ekarth Studio has used bamboo to form a sculptural venue for the Maestro Ilaiyaraaja Centre for Music Learning and Research, while Habitat Collaborative has threaded a curved school through a tree-filled site in Vadodara.
The photography is by Sreenag Pictures.
