Dad fined after son, 2, died in Cyprus hotel fall
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:28:56 BST
19:28:56 KST

Dad fined after son, 2, died in Cyprus hotel fall
- Published
A father whose two-year-old boy fell from a fourth floor window at a hotel in Cyprus has been fined €3,000 (£2,500) for causing his death.
Joshua Foster thought the window was closed when he placed his son on a sill to show him the view of a waterpark and "lost control" of him, Paphos District Court previously heard.
The toddler fell nearly 40ft (12.1m) at the five-star King Evelthon Beach Hotel and Resort on 12 July, the first day of the family's holiday in Chlorakas.
Foster, 37, from Essex, admitted causing death through a reckless, rash or dangerous act and was sentenced on Friday morning.
He told reporters afterwards: "Thank you for the support. I'm looking forward to going home and being with my wife and daughter."
Foster, an auditor, arrived in Cyprus hours before the incident with his wife, two children and in-laws.
They enjoyed various activities and swimming, before getting ready for dinner in the evening.
At about 18:00, Foster, his father-in-law and son walked towards an elevator. As they approached the lift, the boy noticed a waterpark outside.
Foster pushed the lift button, placed the child on the windowsill and the "inconceivable" unfolded before he could react.
The court heard the window was 2.85m (9.3ft) wide and 1.2m (3.9ft) high.
The boy was taken to Paphos General Hospital and later pronounced dead.
"The window did not appear to carry markings that would necessarily have alerted the defendant to the fact that one section was open," said District Judge Froso Christodoulidou.
His "failure to establish that the window was closed before lifting his son towards it... led to the tragic result.
"It was a momentary error which created a dangerous situation with fatal consequences."
The judge said there was "no evidence that the defendant deliberately exposed the child to danger", according to a translation of proceedings.
She added no sentence could outweigh the "personal consequences of the loss of his child".
In a voluntary statement to police, Foster said when he placed his son on the windowsill, the boy "fell before he had a chance to grab him".
While Foster had alcohol in his system, it did not form a significant part of the case against him - and his lawyer said there was no testimony he was drunk.
After the sentencing, Foster's lawyer, Alexandros Alexandrou, told reporters the case should have "never gone to court".
He said Foster was held in custody for eight days immediately after the incident and had to call his daughter from custody to explain what had happened.
"Within this three months, there was a lost opportunity for this man to grieve as he wanted to, to be with his family," he said.
He described his client as an "incredible father".
"[He is] an exemplary family man with a beautiful family behind him, that support him, that embraces him, that has always been by his side."

A senior official from the Justice and Development Party (AKP) said disputes between Türkiye and Azerbaijan should be resolved “within the family” amid recent controversies.
“There may be differences in the way our states proceed,” AKP deputy chair Kürşad Zorlu said at an event in Ankara marking Kyrgyzstan’s Independence Day.
He said the two countries respected each other’s decisions and sovereignty despite possible differences in their approaches.
“We also know how to discuss our problems within our family council, in a manner befitting us,” he added.
Relations between Ankara and Baku have been tested over differing approaches to ties with Israel and a regulatory change in Azerbaijan that has raised concerns about restrictions on students wearing headscarves in schools.
The new rules covering primary, middle and high schools prohibit additional clothing items that “disrupt the uniformity of school uniforms and are incompatible with the principle of secularism in education.”
Oktay Saral, a chief adviser to President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, criticized the measure in a social media post on Oct. 13.
“Preventing the right to education of students wearing headscarves in Azerbaijan is unacceptable!” Saral wrote. “Such an approach must never be allowed in this day and age!”
Erdoğan has not publicly commented on the issue yet.
Azerbaijan’s parliamentary working group on interparliamentary relations with Türkiye said it felt “serious concern and sadness” over criticism of Baku by some Turkish media outlets and political circles.
AKP spokesperson Ömer Çelik later said groups protesting against Azerbaijan in Türkiye had no affiliation with the ruling party or government.
Zorlu directed attention to Erdoğan and Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan for Ankara’s position on the issues.
“Our President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan’s love for Azerbaijan comes from the heart, from the soul and encompasses a vision that will continue to move resolutely into the future,” Zorlu said.
Erdoğan is likely to meet Azerbaijani President İlham Aliyev on the sidelines of a summit in Türkiye later this month.

Türkiye targets 4.2% growth in 2027 as government unveils budget proposal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:27:45 UTC
19:27:45 KST

Türkiye expects economic growth to accelerate to 4.2% in 2027 from a projected 3.3% this year, supported by an improving global outlook and a recovery in external demand, Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz said Friday with next year's proposed budget in hand.
Presenting the government's 2027 budget proposal at the presidential complex in Ankara, Yilmaz said stronger growth among Türkiye's trading partners would create opportunities for exports and support balanced economic expansion.
The Turkish economy grew 3.7% in 2025, he said, adding that investment outpacing private consumption had strengthened production capacity and improved the composition of growth.
“In 2027, we expect our growth to rise to 4.2%, supported by the anticipated improvement in the global outlook and the recovery in external demand,” Yilmaz said.
The government aims to gradually accelerate growth to 5% by the end of its medium-term program through policies focused on productivity, technological transformation, and innovation, he said.
Employment is expected to increase by 657,000 people next year, with labor force participation reaching 53.4% and unemployment declining to 8%, from a projected 8.1% in 2026.
 
Inflation forecast to decline to 21%
Yilmaz said annual inflation, which fell below 30% in September, was expected to reach 28.4% by the end of this year before declining to 21% by the end of 2027.
“Price stability is the fundamental priority of our program,” he said.
Fiscal discipline and incomes policies will continue to support monetary policy, while supply-side measures, particularly in social housing and food, will reinforce disinflation.
Despite fluctuations stemming from energy and commodity prices, the underlying inflation trend continues to improve, Yilmaz said, reiterating the government's medium-term goal of achieving lasting single-digit inflation.
He said the current account deficit was expected to fall below 2% of gross domestic product next year from a projected 2.6% in 2026.
Türkiye will continue policies to boost exports, strengthen energy supply security, and reduce dependence on energy imports, he added.
Goods exports this January-September rose 5.2% year-on-year to $211 billion, bringing the rolling annual total to a record $283.7 billion, Yilmaz said.
The share of medium-high- and high-technology products in exports reached 44%, compared with around 28% in the early 2000s, he added.
 
Budget spending projected at $551.2B
The 2027 budget proposal projects expenditures of 27.276 trillion Turkish liras and revenues of 23.408 trillion liras ($551.2 billion), with national income expected to reach $2.24 trillion.
The figures imply a budget shortfall of $78.1 billion, equivalent to a projected 3.5% of GDP. Excluding earthquake-related expenditure, the deficit is forecast at 2.8% of GDP.
Yilmaz said the proposal would be submitted to parliament with President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's signature, calling it a budget of “resilience, prosperity and transformation.”
Interest expenditures are projected at $80.2 billion, personnel spending at $143.7 billion, and current transfers at $206.7 billion. The budget is expected to maintain a primary surplus next year.
For 2026, the government forecasts a deficit of 3.1% of GDP, below the initial 3.5% projection, despite spending pressures from higher energy and commodity prices.
Urban transformation funding will rise 176% to $5.57 billion in 2027, Yilmaz said, with disaster resilience remaining a priority alongside expanded social and rental housing provision.
Earthquake reconstruction spending over 2023-2026 totaled $109 billion at current prices, equivalent to $104 billion, he said, with 455,357 independent units completed and delivered.
Türkiye's EU-defined general government debt declined to 22.3% of GDP in the second quarter from 23.1% in the first, Yilmaz added, describing low public indebtedness as an important advantage amid global uncertainty.

NCP parliamentary group proposes tightening Finland's asylum rules
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:27:07 EEST
19:27:07 KST

The National Coalition Party's (NCP) parliamentary group wants Finland to move towards a policy of selective immigration, in an aim to give the country more control over who can enter and remain in Finland.
The group published its new immigration policy guidelines on Friday, with proposals prepared under the leadership of MP Atte Kaleva (NCP), who has led the work since January.
They have proposed moving asylum processing outside the EU and tightening the conditions for family reunification and access to social security.
"This means that Finland must be able to decide under all circumstances who is allowed to enter the country and under what conditions, as well as who is allowed to remain here," Kaleva said.
The proposals include linking immigrants' eligibility for unemployment benefits to their employment history in Finland and tightening the conditions for receiving the national pension and guarantee pension.
Asylum processing outside the EU
The parliamentary group proposes transferring asylum processing entirely to reception and return centres outside the EU.
It also wants to restrict repeated asylum applications deemed unfounded and make returns more efficient.
"Asylum has been misused as a channel for mass migration, which it was never intended to be. We are returning to protecting individual people who are in need of protection. This also removes the market for people smuggling," he said.
The group further proposes that serious or repeated criminal offences could lead to the revocation of a person's residence permit and their deportation.
Regarding quota refugees, the group proposes that authorities also take into account their prospects for integrating into Finnish society and culture.
"We have certain fundamental values in Finland that we cannot compromise on: democracy, individual freedoms, equality, the equality of women and girls, and minority rights," Kaleva said.
"If a person is unable to adapt to these values, then of course they cannot be accepted into Finland," he added.
Unemployment benefits linked to work in Finland
Under the proposals, immigrants' eligibility for unemployment benefits would depend on the work they had done in Finland. The level of support would vary according to the length of their employment.
The group also proposes tightening family reunification rules by requiring the person bringing family members to Finland to be able to support them through employment or business activities.
Kaleva said the party wanted to encourage work-based immigration, but opposed the creation of a low-wage labour market in Finland.
"We cannot create a cheap labour market in Finland, where people come here to work for companies that do not pay a sufficient salary," he said.
Kaleva said responsibility for integration should lie primarily with immigrants themselves, but also with their employers.
The parliamentary group's proposals were outlined in its new immigration policy programme, titled 'Towards Selective Immigration' (Kohti valikoivaa maahanmuuttoa), included in their press release (in Finnish).

Ukraine makes its anti-drone road nets a national standard in a new strategy for defensive lines through 2028. It has already strung over more than 1,000 kilometers of road
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:26:04 UTC
19:26:04 KST

Ukraine’s government has approved a Strategy for the Engineering Equipment of Defensive Lines through 2028. It makes strengthening anti-drone protection of logistics routes one of its priorities, the Defense Ministry says.
Russian FPV drones hunt almost anything that moves within 15 to 30 kilometers of the front, which has forced Ukraine to drape its logistics roads in overhead netting, wire-mesh canopies and reinforced barriers that catch an attacking drone before it reaches a vehicle. Ukraine had already built more than 1,066 kilometers of such protection by mid-July and aims for 4,000 kilometers by the end of 2026.
The new strategy turns that scramble into a single national standard, setting deadlines, assigning responsibility, and building control mechanisms, the ministry explained.
“Solutions that have proven effective we will scale. But we will also account for new challenges, threats and changes in Russian tactics. The main goal is the protection of our service members and civilians,” the Defense Ministry says.
One digital map for every trench and net
The plan puts the entire defensive network onto a screen. To track and monitor the state of defensive lines, Ukraine will introduce a single digital geographic information platform, built on and expanding existing systems, including the DELTA situational-awareness system.
The database will hold object passports, photographs, and data on each structure’s location and condition, helping officials verify that work is done, identify repair needs, and distribute resources on evidence rather than guesswork.
From trenches to supply roads, one cycle
The strategy covers the full span of military engineering. Its main lines of work are building and maintaining fortifications, laying engineering obstacles, strengthening anti-drone protection of logistics routes, using modern designs, materials and camouflage, creating a reserve of construction materials, and maintaining digital records of the work.
Developed on the Defense Ministry’s initiative based on combat experience, the document spans the entire cycle from planning and construction to accounting, upkeep, and restoration, the ministry noted. Financing will come from the state and local budgets for the relevant year and from other sources not prohibited by law.

The update said: “Over the course of one week, Russia suffered three tactical and strategic aircraft losses. These airframes have been involved in strike campaigns against Ukraine.
“On 29 September 2026 Russia’s Long Range Aviation fleet lost one of its workhorse Tu-95MS BEAR H on a training flight shortly after take-off in eastern Russia. The BEAR H suffered multiple engine failures before crashing. These aircraft have been used extensively to strike Ukraine over the course of the conflict, almost certainly creating a significant maintenance burden on the fleet.
“On 04 October 2026, a Ukrainian one-way attack uncrewed aerial vehicle strike destroyed a Su-35S FLANKER M multi-role fighter and Su-34 FULLBACK fighter-bomber and a munitions depot at Khanskaya airbase, Russia, 500km from Ukraine.
“FULLBACK aircraft are used on daily operations to launch glide munitions into Ukraine. Analysis of commercial satellite imagery dated 04 October 2026 identified the attack had destroyed two fighter aircraft, cratered the parking apron and the taxiway, destroyed one building and destroyed and damaged two munitions’ depots.
“Russia has lost more than 100 fighter aircraft in the Ukraine conflict since February 2022.”
Russia will find the Bear the harder of the two losses to absorb, because production of the Tu-95MS ended in the early nineteen nineties. They fly the Kh-101 cruise missile strikes that have hit Ukrainian cities through the war, launching from well inside Russian airspace and turning for home without entering contested air.
Khanskaya sits in the Republic of Adygea in southern Russia, well outside the range at which Russian commanders had been willing to disperse aircraft earlier in the war. Ukraine’s long-range one-way attack drones have steadily pushed that calculation back, and airfields that were treated as rear areas have had to adopt the revetments, decoys and dispersal that frontline bases adopted years ago.

OpenAI tries to solve mathematician backlash problem by pledging $5 million to math foundation

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:25:55 UTC
19:25:55 KST

“Mathematicians did not ask for this work to be done,” said the Association for Human Mathematics.
After causing an uproar among mathematicians, ChatGPT maker OpenAI is donating millions of dollars to a maths foundation.
The move comes days after the Association for Human Mathematics (AHM) slammed the artificial intelligence company and alleged plagiarism for solving a decades-old math problem.
In September, OpenAI said an unreleased AI model had cracked a major result on the Navier-Stokes equations, which apply Newton’s second law of motion to fluids, a problem that has stumped mathematicians for almost a century.
But, according to TechCrunch, two human mathematicians say they were close to a similar result, and they question whether OpenAI’s work drew on theirs. OpenAI denies seeing their work. One of the mathematicians, Levent Alpöge, works at Anthropic and was collaborating in a private capacity.
The Sam Altman-led company said on October 6 the model had published more than 700 manuscripts and produced almost 400 other mathematical results, which aimed to tackle some of the most complex questions in maths and computer science, according to OpenAI.
AHM said “Mathematicians did not ask for this work to be done,” adding that OpenAI had a “total disregard for the norms of scientific research”.
On Thursday, OpenAI announced on social media site X that it would make a $5 million donation to the maths-focused Simons Foundation, intended to “help mathematicians examine, understand, and build on results produced by AI”.
“We want to support the mathematics community in turning progress in AI into deeper human understanding and new discoveries,” OpenAI said in a post on X.
“To support that goal, we are contributing $5 million (€4.5mn) to a new Simons Foundation initiative to help mathematicians examine, understand, and build on results produced by AI, including the results we recently published.”
The money will pay for “workshops, conferences, and special programs,” OpenAI said. “We will also provide access to our models and computing resources to Simons Foundation-supported researchers.”
The initiative totals $15 million in combined funding and resources from the Simons Foundation, Anthropic and OpenAI.

Turkish foreign minister to attend Muslim bloc OIC meeting in Baghdad
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:22:43 UTC
19:22:43 KST

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan will attend a meeting of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), scheduled to take place in Baghdad on Saturday and Sunday.
According to Turkish Foreign Ministry sources, Türkiye will hand over the OIC chairmanship to Iraq at the meeting, which will be held under the theme, Dialogue and Solidarity: Two Essential Pillars for Promoting Peace and Sustainable Development.
Türkiye has held the rotating chairmanship since June 2025.
The meeting is expected to address Israel's ongoing genocidal policies in Gaza, its occupation and annexation activities across Palestine, developments in other conflict zones across the Islamic world, counterterrorism, UN reform, Islamophobia and the situation of Muslim communities in non-OIC member states.
The meeting is expected to conclude with the adoption of the "Baghdad Declaration."
Fidan is scheduled to address the meeting and hold bilateral talks with his counterparts on the sidelines of the visit.
 
Unity on Palestine
In his address, Fidan is expected to stress that Israel's aggression and expansionist policies remain the greatest security threat in the Middle East.
He is also expected to emphasize the need for OIC member states to demonstrate a united stance in response to Israel's actions and coordinate their efforts with responsible international actors.
Fidan is expected to call for decisive measures against countries that relocate their embassies to Jerusalem and efforts to prevent further initiatives of this kind, stressing the importance of preserving the city's status.
He is also expected to reiterate that implementing a Palestinian state based on a two-state solution is the only path to a just and lasting peace, and underline the vital importance of ensuring that humanitarian aid reaches those in need in Gaza fully and without interruption.
 
Regional security and minority rights
He is further expected to highlight the importance of demonstrating strong solidarity with Turkish Cypriots and supporting efforts to end the unjust isolation they face.
Fidan is also expected to stress the importance of OIC-led efforts to protect the fundamental rights and freedoms of the Muslim Turkish minority in Western Thrace and the Muslim Turkish population living in the Dodecanese Islands.
On Syria, he is expected to call for continued joint efforts to preserve the country's territorial integrity and unity, revive its economy and help it achieve a prosperous future.
Regarding Lebanon, he is expected to underline the importance of safeguarding the country's sovereignty and territorial integrity for regional stability and stress that Israel must withdraw completely from southern Lebanon.
Addressing tensions in the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz, Fidan is expected to highlight their adverse consequences, particularly for Gulf countries, and describe attacks against these states as unacceptable.
He is also expected to emphasize that ensuring freedom and security of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait is essential for regional stability and global trade.
Fidan is further expected to strongly condemn Houthi attacks targeting civilians and critical infrastructure and reaffirm Türkiye's solidarity with Saudi Arabia.
 
Organization of Islamic Cooperation
The OIC, formerly known as the Organization of the Islamic Conference, was established on Sept. 25, 1969, at a summit in Rabat, Morocco, in response to the arson attack on Al-Aqsa Mosque in occupied East Jerusalem.
With 57 member states, the OIC is the world's second-largest intergovernmental political organization after the United Nations and the only official body representing Muslims worldwide.
The Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC), Russia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Thailand and the Central African Republic hold observer status at the OIC.
Ismail Ould Cheikh Ahmed of Mauritania was elected the organization's new secretary-general at the 23rd Extraordinary Session of the OIC Council of Foreign Ministers, held in August this year.
 
Türkiye and the OIC
Türkiye is one of the OIC's 25 founding members. Its Permanent Mission to the organization began operations in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, on July 24, 2015.
Türkiye assumed the OIC chairmanship for its 51st session at the Council of Foreign Ministers meeting held in Istanbul on June 21-22, 2025. It has previously hosted Council of Foreign Ministers meetings three times, in 1976, 1991, and 2004.
Türkiye hosts the second-largest number of OIC-affiliated institutions after Saudi Arabia.
Several OIC-affiliated bodies are based in Türkiye, including the Statistical, Economic and Social Research and Training Centre for Islamic Countries (SESRIC), the Research Centre for Islamic History, Art and Culture (IRCICA), and the Standing Committee for Economic and Commercial Cooperation of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (COMCEC), one of the OIC's four standing committees.
Other affiliated institutions, including the Islamic Cooperation Youth Forum (ICYF), also operate from Türkiye.

This will reduce the back-office burden, improve productivity and release capacity for front-line activity while maintaining effective support to all personnel.”
July 2028 gives the department a little under two years from now to hit the target.

====================================================================================================

Trump rules out using a nuclear bomb on Iran: Why that matters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:21:12 UTC
19:21:12 KST

Trump rules out using a nuclear bomb on Iran: Why that matters
It is the first time the president has definitively addressed nuclear weapons, but he did not deny US could use ‘mother of all bombs’.
United States President Donald Trump has for the first time explicitly ruled out the use of a nuclear weapon against Iran, but has not denied US media reports that his administration is considering deploying the US’s most lethal non-nuclear munition, nicknamed the “mother of all bombs” in the near future.
In an interview published on Thursday by right-wing American news site Newsmax, Trump suggested he does not plan to use nuclear weapons, but also clarified that the devastating aerial weapon, the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb (MOAB – ‘mother of all bombs ) “is not nuclear”.
“I wouldn’t use nuclear. We don’t have to. We’re the greatest nuclear power in the world,” he told Newsmax.
The comments marked Trump’s first definitive statement on the nuclear topic following speculation about a possible atomic conflict earlier in the US and Israel’s war on Iran. They also appeared to confirm speculation that another phase of the war is imminent, likely after the US midterm elections on November 3.
Here’s what we know:
What did Trump say?
Trump told Newsmax that the US might indeed launch another strike on Iran’s nuclear sites, particularly on Pickaxe Mountain, where Tehran is believed to be hiding a nuclear facility deep under layers of granite.
He ruled out using a nuclear weapon or a tactical nuclear weapon.
“I wouldn’t use nuclear. We don’t have to. We’re the greatest nuclear power in the world,” he said.
He also clarified that the MOAB, which CNN reported the US government is considering using, “is not nuclear”.
Responding to a question about whether the MOAB is “tactical nuclear” – meaning smaller nuclear munitions – Trump reiterated that it is not.
“Well, the mother of all bombs is not nuclear,” Trump said. “It’s not nuclear at all. This is just an extremely large bomb.”
Trump declined to say whether he had authorised its use in Iran.
Trump also suggested renewed attacks are likely in the near future. The US cannot end the war now because it has to ensure Iran cannot produce a nuclear weapon, he argued, saying he believes that “if they had it, they would use it, in my opinion, instantaneously”.
Trump also reiterated that the war would end “very soon” whether by force or diplomacy and that oil prices would then drop.
When asked if he would put “troops on the ground”, Trump said: “No, I don’t see that, I don’t see it.” Earlier in the war, Trump had made comments regarding sending in troops, a move analysts said would be devastating for US soldiers because of Iran’s mountainous territory.
What is the ‘mother of all bombs’?
The MOAB carries a massive payload of about 8,500kg (18,000 pounds or 8.5 tonnes) of high explosives. It weighs 9,800kg (21,605 pounds or nearly 10 tonnes) – about the same as four cars – and is just over nine metres (about 30 feet) long. Stealth bombers are too small to carry it, so it has to be deployed by larger, Lockheed C-130 Hercules transporters.
It is designed to explode a few metres above the ground, sending out intense fireballs that can blast buildings and other hard-surface structures within a 1km radius, experts have told Al Jazeera. It is so powerful that a mushroom cloud from its blast has been seen 32km (20 miles) away in tests, the US Air Force has said.
“Its large explosive charge can produce devastating blast effects against exposed personnel, equipment and vulnerable structures,” Brussels-based military and weapons analyst Elijah Magnier said. “Its purpose is to generate an exceptionally powerful blast across a surface area.”
However, Magnier said there is doubt about whether using the massive surface explosive would be effective against deeply buried nuclear installations in Iran. He added that the terrain in Iran could be difficult for larger cargo aircraft to access.
What has Trump previously said about nuclear weapons?
Trump has never explicitly mentioned using a nuclear weapon, but he has also never ruled it out.
Speculation regarding whether Washington might use nuclear weapons was rife in the early days of the conflict, largely because of the extreme nature of Trump’s numerous threats against Tehran.
In April, for example, as Iran enforced a blockade on ships in the Strait of Hormuz, Trump posted on his Truth Social site that “…a whole civilisation will die tonight, never to be brought back again”, if Iran did not agree to a peace deal and reopen the strait.
He also threatened to destroy Iran’s infrastructure, saying a bombing campaign “will be Power Plant Day and Bridge Day, all wrapped up in one”, in Iran.
Experts widely interpreted his statements as a threat of nuclear destruction, but one that still failed to force Iran to the table.
Although Trump largely moved away from his sabre-rattling rhetoric in the following weeks, he reiterated at the United Nations General Assembly in New York last month that he could “annihilate” Iran. He also told the assembly that he believed a deal would emerge after the midterms.
What is a ‘tactical’ nuclear weapon?
“Tactical” nuclear weapons (TNW) are smaller nuclear munitions designed for the battlefield as opposed to strategic nuclear munitions designed for mass destruction.
Some perceive TNWs as having a lesser impact than an atomic bomb, but experts warn that their names are misleading and they can nevertheless be devastating. Their explosive yield, between 0.3 and 50 kilotons, can impact areas within a 500-600km radius.
The US dropped a 15-kiloton nuclear bomb on Hiroshima, meaning that weapon would today be considered a TNW. The US, North Korea and Russia have TNWs in their arsenals, although no country has ever used them. TNWs are not subject to any international treaties and are largely unregulated.
What might another US attack on Iran look like?
With Trump failing to rule out dropping the MOAB, analysts speculate that the US might launch another – perhaps final – intensive bombing campaign targeting Iran’s nuclear and defence sites, particularly Pickaxe Mountain.
The US could also continue its naval blockade on Iranian ports, while providing escorts for commercial ships through the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran has vowed to respond to escalatory strikes by targeting oil and digital infrastructure in neighbouring Gulf states.
Senior defence officials have also warned that Iran will invade its neighbours if the US launches a ground operation, although Trump appears to have ruled that out.
Earlier in the war, he hinted at the possibility of sending ground forces to retrieve some 400kg of highly enriched uranium that Washington and Israel claim Tehran has hidden underground.
Trump’s phone calls in March to Kurdish militia groups fighting Iran provoked speculation that Washington could coordinate with them for an invasion, although that did not happen.

Expert: Trump does not have the power to force Ukraine to capitulate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:21:00 UTC

Expert: Trump does not have the power to force Ukraine to capitulate
While Donald Trump's unpredictable behavior and disruptions to Starlink are complicating the situation in Ukraine, the U.S. president does not have the power to force Ukraine to surrender, security expert Ilmar Raag finds.
Security expert Ilmar Raag shared his view on social media that U.S. President Donald Trump is not Estonia's ally. Raag explained on ETV's "Ringvaade" that Trump and the United States should not be equated.
"We have American allied troops here in Estonia and when our military personnel interact with them, they are doing their own jobs. I also hear about what is happening in Washington. Following Trump's latest statements, there are senators in the Republican camp who say they disagree with him. I have to say that if there are Americans anywhere whom I consider my Americans, they are the Republicans who are currently standing up to Trump."
Trump, who has recently been pressuring Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to make peace, signed a diesel fuel deal with Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin last week in an attempt to regain popularity in the United States ahead of the midterm elections. In recent days, he has also threatened to stop sharing U.S. intelligence with Ukraine and has partially restricted the war-torn country's access to the Starlink satellite communications system. During a visit to the United Kingdom, Zelenskyy told journalist Piers Morgan on his show that he felt betrayed by Trump.
"First of all, we can say that no major catastrophe is going to happen immediately, for two reasons. First, although American intelligence is very important, it does not do everything. When we talk about Starlink, it serves many different functions in drone warfare, but not all of them. For example, units can still communicate with one another via Starlink and headquarters can communicate with teams on the front line operating these drones. That accounts for half of what Starlink does. The problem is that the most effective drones the Ukrainians have will naturally be affected if Starlink's more important functions — those provided by Starshield — are not working," Raag said.
According to Raag, it is impossible to say for certain whether the Starlink disruptions were accidental or deliberate, but the coincidences are significant enough to suggest that something else may be behind them.
"It appears to be some kind of unilateral action by a smaller group. You can see that Ukrainians are receiving warnings about incoming missiles too late after Starlink actually stops working for them. The Americans are not speaking with one voice, saying they made a decision and acted accordingly. Some are saying one thing, while Trump is already saying it never happened. This shows that the head does not know what the tail is doing, or vice versa. That brings us to the second argument that describes the current situation: Trump, being as unpredictable as he is, could change his mind yet again," Raag explained, adding that this was a sign that Europe needed to take responsibility for its own affairs.
European leaders have responded to Trump's statements and decisions. While many have condemned the U.S. president's rhetoric, others believe Trump should be approached more calmly to avoid provoking him further.
"It is true that Trump is a very emotional man and in some ways he thrives on conflict — he can always escalate things further. In that respect, European leaders have already realized that if they keep their heads down and wait a little, perhaps the midterm elections will come around and Trump will lose much of the power he currently holds. That is what many are hoping for," the security expert said.
According to Raag, surveys conducted in the United States show that most Americans consider Putin the aggressor and support Ukraine, raising hopes that if Trump suffers a defeat in the midterm elections, Congress may adopt a more supportive position toward Ukraine.
"Ukraine cannot afford a situation in which people are losing their lives while Trump is allowed to play games, shifting back and forth. People are dying in the meantime. In that respect, Trump is influenced most by his approval ratings in the United States, fuel prices and, ultimately, European leaders as well. He has now demonstrated several times that when Europe says a very clear 'no,' Trump returns to his previous positions," Raag said in response to the host's question about whether diplomatic exchanges had become too heated.
There are also concerns that if Trump stops receiving praise from Europe and Ukraine, he may become more interested in holding talks and making deals with Putin.
"But what can he really agree on? Trump can conclude various economic agreements with the Russians and do business with them. But Trump does not actually have the power to force Ukraine to capitulate. That is not going to happen and Trump has realized that as well. Perhaps that is also one of the sources of his frustration — that he simply cannot do it, just as he cannot impose on the Iranians the peace terms he has been announcing for quite some time," Raag said.
According to Raag, the war has escalated since August, but the Ukrainians are holding out and have already learned how to deal with the challenges they face.
"The escalation began in August when it became clear that the Ukrainians currently lack sufficiently effective air defenses against ballistic missiles and therefore face a very difficult winter. However, they have spent several years learning and the Ukrainians themselves say that although they curse Trump and Putin, they will survive this," Raag said.

Putin seizes five more European firms, continuing Russia's hostile asset crackdown
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:18:40 UTC
19:18:40 KST

The decree covers a flooring manufacturer, a paper packaging firm, a hygiene products maker, and two metal- and plastic-packaging companies, all of which continued operating in Russia after the all-out invasion of Ukraine in early 2022.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has signed a decree ordering the compulsory seizure of Russian assets belonging to French flooring manufacturer Tarkett and four other European companies, whose combined annual revenue exceeds 50 billion roubles (€532 million).
The assets have been placed under the interim control of a management company called Centre Capital, registered in February 2026.
Its chief executive is listed as Marat Mirkhaydarov, former head of the administration of the regional governor of Zabaykalsky, who stood down in 2025 following an injury sustained in Russia's ongoing war in Ukraine.
The decree also covers paper packaging producer Kappa Rus, formerly part of Ireland's Smurfit Kappa, hygiene product maker Ontex RU, part of the Belgian Ontex group, metal packaging manufacturer Eviosys Packaging Kuban, part of US-based Sonoco Products Company, and Menshen Packaging CIS, owned by German plastics producer Menshen.
All five companies continued operating in Russia after the country's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Tarkett, which ranks third globally by floor covering sales and leads the market in vinyl flooring according to its 2024 annual report, kept two plants in Russia out of its 34 production sites worldwide and continued paying taxes to the Russian budget.
The latest seizures follow a series of similar moves in September, when Putin placed the Russian assets of Swiss food giant Nestlé, German hypermarket chain Metro, French retailer Auchan and home improvement chain Leroy Merlin under temporary administration.
Those assets were transferred to a company called LEV Management, established shortly before the decision and reported by Russian media to have links to the country's security services. A manufacturer of plastic dispensing systems owned by French holding Aptar Europe Holding was also placed under temporary administration shortly afterwards.
A presidential decree signed in April 2023 established the mechanism for such seizures, authorising the imposition of temporary administration over certain Russian assets of foreign companies.
Western governments and international legal experts have described the move as unlawful expropriation. Companies whose assets are seized can, in principle, pursue compensation through international arbitration under bilateral investment treaties Russia has signed with EU member states, although enforcing judgments against the Kremlin and its entities is nearly impossible.
The first targets under that decree were Danish brewer Carlsberg and French dairy group Danone.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov directly linked the transfer of Nestlé's and Auchan's assets to the fact that they are companies from what Moscow terms "unfriendly countries".
“Unfriendly countries” is an official Russian government designation applied to all EU member states, the US, the UK and other states that imposed sanctions following the 2022 full-scale invasion, in an attempt to dissuade them from aiding Kyiv.
Russia has framed the asset seizures in part as a response to the EU’s decision to freeze approximately €300 billion in Russian sovereign assets following the all-out invasion.

Türkiye expects economic growth to accelerate to 4.2 percent in 2027 from a projected 3.3 percent this year, supported by an improving global outlook and a recovery in external demand, Vice President Cevdet Yılmaz said on Oct. 16 with next year’s proposed budget in hand.
Presenting the government’s 2027 budget proposal at the presidential complex in Ankara, Yılmaz said stronger growth among Türkiye’s trading partners would create opportunities for exports and support balanced economic expansion.
The Turkish economy grew 3.7 percent in 2025, he said, adding that investment outpacing private consumption had strengthened production capacity and improved the composition of growth.
“In 2027, we expect our growth to rise to 4.2 percent, supported by the anticipated improvement in the global outlook and the recovery in external demand,” Yılmaz said.
The government aims to gradually accelerate growth to 5 percent by the end of its medium-term program through policies focused on productivity, technological transformation and innovation, he said.
Yılmaz said annual inflation, which fell below 30 percent in September, was expected to reach 28.4 percent by the end of this year before declining to 21 percent by the end of 2027.
“Price stability is the fundamental priority of our program,” he said.
Fiscal discipline and incomes policies will continue to support monetary policy, while supply-side measures, particularly in social housing and food, will reinforce disinflation.
Despite fluctuations stemming from energy and commodity prices, the underlying inflation trend continues to improve, Yılmaz said, reiterating the government’s medium-term goal of achieving lasting single-digit inflation.
He said the current account deficit was expected to fall below 2 percent of gross domestic product next year from a projected 2.6 percent in 2026.
Türkiye will continue policies to boost exports, strengthen energy supply security and reduce dependence on energy imports, he added.
The 2027 budget proposal projects expenditures of 27.28 trillion Turkish liras and revenues of 23.41 trillion liras ($551.2 billion), with national income expected to reach $2.24 trillion.
The figures imply a budget shortfall of $78.1 billion, equivalent to a projected 3.5 percent of GDP. Excluding earthquake-related expenditure, the deficit is forecast at 2.8 percent of GDP.
Yılmaz said the proposal would be submitted to parliament with President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan’s signature, calling it a budget of “resilience, prosperity and transformation.”
Interest expenditures are projected at $80.2 billion. The budget is expected to maintain a primary surplus next year.
For 2026, the government forecasts a deficit of 3.1 percent of GDP, below the initial 3.5 percent projection, despite spending pressures from higher energy and commodity prices.
Urban transformation funding will rise 176 percent to $5.57 billion in 2027, Yilmaz said, with disaster resilience remaining a priority alongside expanded social and rental housing provision.
Earthquake reconstruction spending over 2023-2026 totaled $109 billion at current prices, equivalent to $104 billion, he said, with 455,357 independent units completed and delivered.

&quot;We can no longer do this&quot;: Le Pen opposes further financial support for Ukraine

"We can no longer do this": Le Pen opposes further financial support for Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
Marine Le Pen said that after winning in 2027, she would end financial aid to Ukraine within six months. She is also opposed to Ukraine joining the EU.
French far-right politician and representative of the National Rally party Marine Le Pen said that Europe, and France in particular, can no longer increase its financial support for Ukraine. UNN reports this, citing Financial Times and French media.
Details
If she wins the 2027 presidential election, she plans to stop direct financial aid to Kyiv six months after taking office. The politician also opposes Ukraine's membership in the European Union and any further increase in European countries' financial commitments.
In an interview with the Financial Times published on October 14, Marine Le Pen said that European states had already undertaken significant financial commitments to support Ukraine and that the possibilities for further increasing aid were limited. According to the French politician, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy needs to be openly told about the financial constraints faced by European partners.
To deal honestly with Mr. Zelenskyy is to tell him, in fact to warn him: listen, we cannot do more. We have already provided loans totaling €90 billion, of which €18 billion falls to France. That is a truly large sum
She emphasized that France could no longer afford to support Ukraine at previous levels because of the difficult situation with its public finances. In addition, Le Pen questioned the rationale for further financing Kyiv through the European Union if this would result in an additional financial burden on the French budget.
The politician also called for a significant reduction in the EU budget and a limitation of the powers of European institutions.
Le Pen promised to stop funding Ukraine six months after winning the election
On October 14, while in Brussels, Marine Le Pen clarified her position in an interview with the Belgian television channel VRT News. She said that if elected president of France, she would not stop financial support for Ukraine immediately after taking power. Instead, she envisages a six-month transition period.
From the moment of my election, for six months we will maintain aid so as not to leave anyone in an impossible situation. But after that, we will stop financial aid to Ukraine, because we no longer have the ability to provide it
At the same time, she did not rule out maintaining certain forms of military cooperation, including operational support and the training of Ukrainian service members.
Le Pen opposed Ukraine joining the EU
The politician separately criticized the prospect of Ukraine's membership in the European Union. According to her, Ukraine's accession to the EU could lead to significant economic losses for France, particularly in the agricultural sector. Le Pen claims that Ukrainian agricultural products would create additional competition for French farmers and that the distribution of European subsidies would change to France's disadvantage.
In her conversation with the Financial Times, she called Ukraine's possible accession to the European Union a "harakiri" for France, linking it to threats to national sovereignty and significant economic losses.
What Volodymyr Zelenskyy replied to Le Pen
On October 15, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy commented on the French politician's statements in an interview with the Financial Times. The head of state emphasized that Ukraine's cooperation with France and other Western partners is not limited to financial support. According to him, European states are gaining valuable experience from the Ukrainian military that can be used to develop their own defense technologies and improve the combat readiness of their armies.
In particular, the president mentioned the Franco-Italian SAMP/T air defense systems, which were improved based on experience from combat use, as well as SCALP/Storm Shadow cruise missiles. Zelenskyy emphasized that Ukraine's experience of modern warfare has practical value for European defense companies.
We also give something in return
In his view, French industry could benefit from the joint production of weapons, technological cooperation, and the use of Ukrainian military expertise.
The president also expressed the conviction that Le Pen does not fully take into account certain aspects of defense cooperation between the countries.
What is known about financial support for Ukraine from the EU
Despite Le Pen's statements, the European Union continues to provide Ukraine with military, economic, and budgetary assistance. In particular, the EU approved a €90 billion loan program for 2026–2027. It provides funding for Ukraine's defense needs and support for the state budget. However, funds under this program are disbursed gradually, and their allocation depends on the agreed conditions and Ukraine's implementation of the necessary reforms.
In addition, European institutions are considering mechanisms for further financing Ukraine in view of the country's significant needs amid the continuation of the full-scale war with Russia.
Context
Marine Le Pen is one of the leading representatives of France's far-right forces and has consistently advocated reducing France's financial contributions to the European Union budget. She has repeatedly criticized European sanctions against Russia while stating that she condemns Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Against the backdrop of preparations for the 2027 presidential election, Le Pen has stepped up statements regarding the need to review France's foreign policy and budgetary priorities.

There are fears that unrest could spread beyond Ethiopia’s borders in the fragile Horn of Africa region where other powers vie for influence.

ICC serves Europe’s ‘colonialist interests’ – analyst (VIDEO)

ICC serves Europe’s ‘colonialist interests’ – analyst (VIDEO)
The International Criminal Court (ICC) has become a tool of Western influence that selectively targets countries of the Global South while shielding European interests and ignoring crimes in Ukraine, international legal analyst and academic Alexandre Guerreiro has said. He accused the tribunal of applying double standards rather than delivering universal justice.
Criticism of the ICC has intensified in recent months amid growing accusations of political bias and selective justice. Venezuela, Chad, Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger have moved to withdraw, accusing the court of serving Western interests and engaging in “neocolonial repression.”
In an interview with RT on Thursday, Guerreiro argued that the court had abandoned its original purpose as an independent institution capable of holding perpetrators accountable regardless of nationality, and has become increasingly politicized and dominated by European powers.
“In practice, what we have is a court that serves European interests, colonialist interests,” he said, arguing that the tribunal is used to pressure Global South nations while avoiding similar scrutiny of European countries.
Guerreiro pointed to the court’s handling of cases involving Afghanistan, Iraq and Kenya, arguing that political interference had repeatedly undermined the principles of impartial justice.
He also accused the ICC of ignoring alleged crimes in Ukraine, including the deadly May 2014 Odessa clashes between Ukrainian nationalists and opponents of the Western-backed coup in Kiev, as well as the sniper shootings during the preceding Maidan unrest.
“This is not justice,” he said, arguing that the court only pursues cases that serve the interests of the current Ukrainian authorities and the Western bloc as a whole.
The remarks come days after Washington imposed sweeping new sanctions on the ICC, accusing it of overstepping its jurisdiction in cases involving American and Israeli nationals. The court issued arrest warrants in 2024 for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.
Meanwhile, the ICC’s investigation into alleged war crimes by American forces in Afghanistan has produced no criminal charges against US personnel.

Europe Has No Starlink Replacement as Ukraine Faces Satellite Disruptions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:14:27 UTC
19:14:27 KST

Europe cannot replace Starlink anytime soon, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas warned Friday, as disruptions to Elon Musk’s satellite network raised concerns over Ukraine’s battlefield communications.
“Starlink is really necessary for Ukraine and unfortunately in the short term Europe can’t replace this capability,” Kallas told reporters ahead of an EU summit attended by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Ukraine relies on Starlink and its military-grade counterpart, Starshield, for battlefield communications, mid-range strikes on Russian-occupied territory and interceptor drones used to shoot down Russian attack drones.
Starlink’s satellite network is unmatched in scale, while its business model and portable, affordable terminals give it a major advantage over competitors that rely on bulkier, more expensive equipment.
Kyiv reported restrictions on military Starlink connections this week, with Ukrainian officials reporting slower speeds on some terminals on Wednesday. Musk said any disruption was the responsibility of the US government, not his SpaceX company.
Europe scrambles for alternatives
Kallas said the European Defence Agency had mapped the critical military capabilities Europe lacks and must develop.
“We need to fill these gaps as soon as possible,” she said.
Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs acknowledged that Europe was not yet equipped to provide a full alternative.
Le Pen Looms Large as Macron Enters Final Months on EU Stage
“Starlink is the key for Ukraine actually to fight or fight back,” he told reporters on Friday, according to AFP. Europe has some comparable capabilities, but not enough to meet Ukraine’s needs.
Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten told AFP he had discussed the issue with French President Emmanuel Macron on Thursday, focusing on how European countries could provide more satellite communications services in the near future.
EU eyes satellite backup
The European Commission is negotiating Ukraine’s participation in GOVSATCOM, an EU program that pools satellite resources to provide secure communications for government users.
“We are currently in talks with Ukraine to fully associate Ukraine to GOVSATCOM,” Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier said Wednesday.
The system could give Kyiv another way to maintain secure communications during Russian attacks on infrastructure and disruptions to conventional networks. But Brussels has yet to confirm whether it can match Starlink’s capabilities for combat operations.
The EU could add commercial satellite services as early as 2027, potentially helping meet military needs, Regnier said. Its longer-term plan, the IRIS² constellation of more than 300 satellites, is expected to become fully operational in 2029.
Until then, Ukraine remains heavily reliant on Starlink – and Europe has no immediate replacement for a system critical to its war effort.
Why Ukraine needs another option
The European discussions have gained urgency after restrictions detected overnight on Oct. 13–14 disrupted Ukrainian drone operations.
Ukrainian Defense Ministry sources said units received no advance warning and reported connections dropping at different movement speeds, approximately 72 to 161 kilometers per hour.
The ministry contacted the United States, SpaceX and NATO partners while checking backup communications channels.
The disruption affected interceptor and medium-range strike drones, alongside reconnaissance, logistics and communications relay missions.
The reported speed limits concern how fast a terminal is moving, rather than its internet download speed.
Former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov said on Wednesday evening that connectivity at speeds of up to 160 kilometers per hour was being restored, while calling for Starshield’s speed restriction to be removed entirely.
That partial restoration does not resolve every operational requirement. Two Ukrainian officials told RFE/RL that connections had improved below the threshold, but restrictions continued to complicate interception of Russia’s jet-powered drones.
One Ukrainian source said operating speeds needed to reach at least 450 kilometers per hour.
President Volodymyr Zelensky has accused those responsible of deliberately restricting the service during Russian attacks, saying the disruption weakened Ukraine’s defenses and endangered civilians. Who authorized the restrictions remains disputed.
Musk said Starshield systems are controlled by the US government and that their operational limits are determined by the US military and ultimately the president. A senior White House official, however, told Axios that the Trump administration was not involved.
Why switching networks will take time
According to Reuters, Europe has no ready-made replacement that Ukrainian troops can immediately attach to their drones.
Eutelsat already provides connectivity in Ukraine through its low Earth orbit and geostationary networks.
But independent satellite consultant Christian Freiherr von der Ropp told Reuters that OneWeb faces capacity and performance constraints, while terminal cost, weight, size and power consumption limit frontline suitability.
Switching would also require replacing thousands of terminals: Starlink equipment uses proprietary technology and cannot simply connect to OneWeb.
European political pressure to develop alternatives is growing. In a statement on Thursday, Oct. 15, Renew Europe President Valérie Hayer urged EU leaders to strengthen support for Ukraine and address dependence on American satellite services.
“Recent days have also shown the urgent need for a European alternative to Starlink,” she said.
Russia races to build its own Starlink
Russia could deploy an alternative to Starlink across the front line within a year, Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces commander Robert “Madyar” Brovdi warned in May.
Russia’s main project is Rassvet, developed by Russian company Bureau 1440. The company launched 16 spacecraft in March 2026, while six Rassvet satellites were in orbit at the time, according to Russian media outlet Kommersant.
Despite the limited constellation, Ukrainian defense outlet Militarnyi reported that the satellites’ regular passes over Ukraine could provide usable coverage for some frontline applications. However, Rassvet remains far behind Starlink in scale and established operational capability.
Russian troops have also relied on alternative equipment, including terminals referred to as “Gazprom.” In an intercepted conversation published by Kyiv Post in February, a Russian serviceman dismissed one such terminal as “f**king shit.”
Starlink operates more than 7,800 satellites, while Russia is still building its network. Moscow’s ability to expand Rassvet and improve its terminals could nevertheless become a growing concern for Ukraine, particularly as both sides depend increasingly on satellite connectivity to control drones and coordinate battlefield operations.

Turkish exports to BRICS nations top $18.2 bln in January-September
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:14:21 UTC
19:14:21 KST

Türkiye’s exports to the 10 member states of the BRICS grouping totaled $18.2 billion in the first nine months of the year, according to the Turkish Exporters’ Assembly (TİM).
While Türkiye’s total global exports this January-September grew 5.2 percent to $210.9 billion, Russia was the largest destination among other BRICS member states, receiving $4.1 billion in exports despite a 2.5 percent annual decline.
BRICS includes longtime members Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa, plus recent additions Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, and the United Arab Emirates.
The UAE followed Russia as the second-largest destination for Turkish exports to BRICS, accounting for $3.3 billion even after a 4.12 percent contraction in export volume.
Egypt followed with a rise of 28.6 percent to $3.1 billion, China with a surge of 40.8 percent to $3 billion, and Iran with $1.8 billion, making the country the fifth-largest BRICS destination for Turkish goods.
Turkish exports increased in eight of the 10 BRICS member states, with shipments in Ethiopia surging the most by 79.6 percent.
The chemicals and chemical products sector accounted for most of these exports to the bloc, generating $3.5 billion in the first nine months of the year, the data showed.
Mining exports grew 33.5 percent to $2.1 billion, a net gain of roughly $539 million, followed by the jewelry sector, whose exports fell 45 percent to $1.3 billion.
The textiles and raw material exports climbed 8.7 percent to $1.2 billion at the same time.

Indian police warn 'Cockroach' movement founder against holding protest
Police warned the founder of India's 'Cockroach' movement against going ahead with a protest on Friday, local media reported, setting the stage for a possible confrontation with the group that is demanding the resignation of the election chief.
The youth-led 'Cockroach Janta Party' (CJP), opposition groups, and student organisations have held almost daily protests this month demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation over a revision of voter lists that critics say favours Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
More than 130 million voters were deleted during the revision but the Election Commission has denied favouring any party and said wrongly deleted voters can re-enrol. The BJP has accused rivals of trying to undermine democracy by wrongly questioning legitimate electoral processes.
CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke called Friday's protest in support of two CJP leaders detained and sent to jail this week for five days for demonstrating at a protest site in violation of a ban.
The group and left-wing student organisations have urged supporters to gather at the Central Park in New Delhi's busy Connaught Place shopping and food district on Friday evening to wave and hoist the national flag.
Dipke said police visited him and served a notice saying the group was engaging in "unlawful activities and inciting people".
"Don't we even have the freedom to hoist our own tricolour in our own nation?" he said in a statement.
The notice said that prohibitory orders were in effect in Connaught Place and no permission had been given for a rally, news agency ANI reported, citing police sources.
The notice also said that legal action would be taken if Dipke went to the location, ANI said.
Delhi Police did not respond to a Reuters request for comment.
'Don't join', Police warn
Security was stepped up in the city and police urged people not to join "such assemblies", saying it can instead facilitate a group of select people to carry the national flag and sing the national anthem at a "suitable place".
The civic authority said the park itself would be closed for two days "due to administrative reasons".
Traders in the area petitioned the Supreme Court to prevent the protest, which they say "would cause severe loss", and demanded compensation for losses suffered during a similar rally planned over the weekend that was foiled by a security crackdown.
The cockroach movement has emerged as one of the biggest political challenges faced by Modi and his BJP in his 12 years in power.
A weeks-long sit-in by its supporters earlier this year forced Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation over exam paper leaks.
The latest demonstrations erupted after The Indian Express newspaper reported that Kumar's two deputies raised concerns internally about voter list changes, registration procedures and digital systems.
Defence Minister Rajnath Singh said the demonstrations were main opposition Congress party's attempt to "seize power".
"Instead of channelling the energy of the youth toward nation-building, they are being used as pawns in the politics of anarchy," he said at a media briefing on Friday.

Russia is pushing its drone war westward, into a Ukrainian region that borders NATO. Russian drones attacked Volyn Oblast through the night of 16 October, hitting civilian and critical infrastructure and leaving 370,000 subscribers without power, regional administration head Roman Romaniuk says. Volyn borders Poland, a NATO member, and Belarus, a Russian ally.
Russia’s jet-powered drones keep flying farther west, and now the strikes reach deeper into the center and the EU-facing frontier too. Moscow launched more than 850 Shahed drones at Ukraine in about a day and a half, including a record roughly 360 on the central Kirovohrad Oblast, precisely as a speed cap on Starlink degraded the interceptor drones Ukraine’s air defense relies on.
Moscow escalates its attacks after winning sanctions relief from the diesel deal of US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin and sensing pressure on Ukraine, exploiting the moment its defenses were artificially restricted.
“Russia takes advantage of every such moment and must be held accountable for what it does,” Zelenskyy says, noting the skies had not been clear for a single hour.
A night that turned deadly in the west
In Volyn Oblast, the damage was concrete and lethal. Debris fell on a power line in the central Lutsk community, cutting electricity and disrupting water supply, and the city lost power entirely with public transport halted, Lutsk council secretary Andrii Razumovskyi says.
The heaviest toll came in Manevychi, where a drone hit the private enterprise Agrofrukt LTD, killing one person and injuring eight. By 10:46 AM, the fire there was contained, and residents were asked to seal windows, doors, and vents due to the risk of an ammonia release from a damaged facility.
A capital-to-border map of the same assault
Throughout the day, Russia has struck Kyiv and its region, and the Dnipropetrovsk, Odesa, Rivne, Kharkiv and Donetsk regions, along with Zaporizhzhia, Kherson, Mykolaiv, Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Khmelnytskyi, Poltava and Ivano-Frankivsk.
By reaching western border regions at once, Russia is widening the pressure on civilians across the country and edging closer to the EU.

19:11:53 KST

Türkiye plans to complete legal changes to strengthen its fight against capital market crimes by the beginning of 2027, Treasury and Finance Minister Mehmet Şimşek said on Oct. 16.
The planned measures will also address coordinated transactions by funds, Şimşek said in a statement on Turkish social media platform NSosyal, outlining steps to improve market transparency and bolster investor confidence.
Relevant institutions are implementing significant regulations, taking into account assessments by international index providers, he said.
Regulations introduced by the Capital Markets Board have strengthened the flow of information and made ultimate share ownership more transparent, Şimşek added.
A fund guide announced at the end of August enabled weekly disclosure of hedge fund portfolios, alongside announcements when funds traded on the Turkish Electronic Fund Trading Platform, known as TEFAS, cross specified shareholding thresholds.
The measures also introduced concentration limits for funds and required borrowing transactions to take place on organized markets on a collateralized basis.
Şimşek said authorities would closely monitor the results and take any additional steps without delay in consultation with stakeholders.
“Our priority is to complete the liquidation of problematic funds and protect investors’ rights,” he said.
Sanctions will be applied resolutely against those who disrupt the fair and competitive functioning of markets, he added.
“Our goal is to establish a transparent, reliable and efficient capital market where investor rights are protected,” Şimşek said.

Detainees at a third U.S. immigration detention center go on hunger strike, including Russian nationals
More than 30 people have gone on hunger strike at the El Valle immigration detention facility in Texas, the mother of one of the protesters told Vot Tak.
She said 15 women began the hunger strike October 11, and 20 men, including Russians, joined them later. The protesters say they face poor detention conditions and a lack of medical care, and are demanding that their rights be upheld.
The husband of one of the hunger strikers told journalists that, contrary to the rules, prison administrators are not monitoring the health of those refusing food: “The administration tells them straight out that there’s only one way out of this detention — deportation. They say, if you want, go ahead and sit there, starve. If you croak, we’ll take you away and bury you.”
El Valle Detention Facility has become the third immigration detention center where detainees have declared a hunger strike. In early October, asylum seekers at the D. Ray James immigration detention facility in Georgia filed a collective complaint about detention conditions and announced plans to begin a hunger strike. Museum releases historical photos of island where Amelia Earhart may have crashed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:09:14 UTC
19:09:14 KST

A New Zealand museum has released nearly 50 photos from a 1938 aerial survey of the island where Amelia Earhart is believed to have crash-landed, offering amateur sleuths new evidence to scour for traces of the pioneering aviator and her plane.
The black-and-white images were published by the Air Force Museum of New Zealand after renewed interest in one of the biggest mysteries of the 20th century, spurred by a US expedition to the Pacific atoll of Nikumaroro in search of new clues.
While some low-resolution copies have been uploaded on blogs, the Air Force Museum of New Zealand said it had received several requests for the photos and had released the full set of 47 images in digital high-resolution format on its website.
The negatives were found more than a decade ago by Matthew O’Sullivan, the keeper of photographs at the museum in Christchurch.
Earhart’s most prominent investigator, Ric Gillespie, described the images as a “goldmine” in his blog, saying they were a complete set of aerial photos taken on 1 December 1938 by an amphibious biplane during a New Zealand survey of Pacific islands that was looking for suitable airbase locations.
What happened to Earhart and her navigator Fred Noonan when they disappeared on 2 July 1937 during an attempt to circumnavigate the globe at the equator has been a stop-and-start search over eight decades, filled with false leads.
A leading theory is that the aviator, who broke several records including becoming the first woman to fly a nonstop solo trip across the Atlantic, ran out of fuel and was marooned on Nikumaroro, then known as Gardner Island.
The hypothesis is that she survived for a while, drinking rainwater and eating fish and turtles, based on signs of a castaway’s campsite and artefacts, including glass from a jar that is thought to have contained cosmetic cream.
This week, archaeologists and scientists from Earhart’s former benefactor, Purdue University in Indianapolis, are searching a part of the island for the “Taraia Object”, an elongated shape in a lagoon named after the part of the island where it was first noticed in a 2020 satellite image. Other longtime Earhart explorers, including Gillespie, are not convinced, saying it is probably a fallen tree and not the wreckage of her Lockheed Model 10-E Electra. The small atoll has been visited dozens of times.
In their latest update on Nikumaroro, which is part of the archipelago country of Kiribati, the expedition said severe weather had hampered their metal-detecting but that they would release an update within 48 hours.
“Despite Thursday’s weather delay, the expedition remains on schedule, with two more days of field operations planned – and an update on the identification of the Taraia Object expected,” Purdue University said.
Rick Pettigrew, the expedition lead and executive director of the Archaeological Legacy Institute, said: “We understand the tremendous interest in what we’re doing at Nikumaroro, and we appreciate everyone’s patience. This is a complex scientific process. You don’t simply arrive at a site and immediately identify what’s there. We have to carefully collect the data, analyse it and reach sound conclusions.”
The New Zealand military images are some of the earliest photographic evidence of the island. There is no immediate sign of an object in the Taraia area.
