Israel cannot afford another election: Why Netanyahu, Eisenkot must consider unity - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:08:30 UTC
19:08:30 KST

In the summer of 2019, Yuli Edelstein, then speaker of the Knesset, came to meet with us at The Jerusalem Post.
Israel had held an election in April that failed to produce a government and was forced back to the polls in September. It was the first time in the country’s history that one election had led almost immediately to another, and Edelstein, then a senior figure in Likud, had a clear message: This would not happen again. Whatever the personal differences between the political camps, the country would find a way to form a government.
Sadly, he was wrong, as were many of us who believed that Israel’s politicians would eventually come to their senses. Instead, the country went to the polls five times in three-and-a-half years, until the current government was established following the election at the end of 2022.
When people think about October 7, they understandably focus on the intelligence failures, the IDF’s failure to defend the border, and the questions surrounding the warnings that did or did not reach Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Some go further back to the year before the attack, when the government’s judicial overhaul tore Israeli society apart. Rarely, though, do we go back further than that.
The truth is that Israel arrived at October 7 battered, divided, and polarized in ways we have yet to fully process. The judicial overhaul was devastating, but it did not come out of nowhere. It followed five elections marked by relentless political fighting, personal rivalries, and the growing belief that defeating the other side mattered more than governing the country. The overhaul deepened those divisions, eroded trust in institutions, and made the country weak and vulnerable.
Hamas saw an opening in this division and took it on October 7. The fact that we have yet to establish a commission of inquiry into the events that led to the attack is a gamble with Israel’s future.
This history matters as we approach the October 27 election, because the polls suggest that another stalemate is a real possibility. Neither bloc appears to have the 61 seats needed for a conventional majority government, and neither seems capable of persuading enough politicians from the other side to join it. Much can change before election day, particularly with undecided voters and parties hovering around the electoral threshold. But we need to ask now what outcome is actually in the country’s interest.
The opposition’s criticism of Netanyahu is legitimate. He has been in office for too long, the failures have piled up, and it is time for change. His decision to govern with the far Right has caused Israel immense damage, internally and internationally. But Netanyahu is also right that the opposition’s boycott of him has contributed to the prospect of deadlock. This is what happens when personality politics overwhelms almost everything else.
Three possibilities to avoid another election
ANOTHER ELECTION, in my mind, would be catastrophic. Israel is militarily stronger today because its enemies are weaker, but military superiority does not remove the danger of political paralysis. With so many challenges still unresolved, returning to the cycle of election after election would put us back on the same destructive path that preceded October 7.
If avoiding that outcome is the objective, there are essentially three possibilities.
The first is that one side wins 61 seats, as hard as that is to imagine based on current polling. It could be Netanyahu and it could be the opposition. This would be the clearest outcome – one side would win, and while the other would be angry and disappointed, the voters will have spoken. Even if one side does not get 61 in its current form, we cannot rule out defections – parties switching alliances – something that has happened repeatedly in the past.
The second possibility is that neither side reaches 61 seats and the opposition tries to establish a minority government. The most plausible version would bring together Gadi Eisenkot, Naftali Bennett, Avigdor Liberman, and Yair Golan. They would not need the Arab parties to vote in favor of the government, but they would need enough Arab MKs to not vote against it.
Such a government could remove Netanyahu from office and establish a state commission of inquiry into October 7, a lofty objective that should have been done a long time ago. Beyond that, however, it will not be able to function, and the minority government would be established simply to take the country straight back to another election.
As tempting as this might be, there is a danger in this that the opposition should not underestimate. Firstly, the path leads anyhow to another election, no different than the deadlock option. Second, there is a chance that Netanyahu would return even stronger after the next election, arguing that he had warned voters Eisenkot and Bennett would govern with the support of Arab parties and that they had proved him right.
The third possibility is what is often referred to as a unity government. I know how unrealistic this sounds today, but it deserves consideration if the alternative is yet another election. In many respects, this would not even be unity across an enormous ideological divide. The principal obstacle between Netanyahu, Eisenkot, Bennett, Liberman, and Golan is not necessarily their view of Israel’s central security challenges but their view of one another.
Set aside judicial reform for a moment and consider the major issues. Is there really such a vast difference between them on confronting Iran, rebuilding support in the United States, the future of the Palestinian conflict, or maintaining far stronger defenses along the borders with Gaza and Lebanon?
There are meaningful disagreements on the rule of law, the West Bank, and responsibility for October 7, and they cannot be wished away. But there is also more than enough common ground to at least explore whether a stable government could be formed.
THE OBVIOUS objection is that Netanyahu cannot be trusted. He has broken political promises in the past, manipulated coalition partners, and brought down governments when it served his interests. All of that is true, and anyone considering joining him would have to enter such an arrangement with eyes wide open and an incredible amount of suspicion.
But politics is not about choosing between a good option and a bad one. Often, it is about deciding which of the bad options will do the least damage. If the alternative to exploring a unity government is another election, followed perhaps by another stalemate, which course would be worse for the country?
Netanyahu has been a central figure in Israeli politics for more than 30 years, since first becoming prime minister in 1996. He is a political chameleon who knows how to move left, shift right, settle in the center, and adapt his alliances based on political survival. If staying in office requires him to govern with different partners, and to accept different constraints, he usually knows how to do so.
None of this means that Netanyahu can suddenly be trusted politically, and we have no way of knowing whether he has changed. Is survival in office the only objective for him today, or is there still something within him that will put the country first even if it means restraints and policies that for the last four years he has avoided, like a commission of inquiry?
It is true that such a government might prove impossible, and that even if formed it will quickly collapse. But surely we owe it to ourselves to test the possibility rather than dismiss it outright.
Edelstein’s warning in 2019 was that Israel could not afford to become a country incapable of forming a government. We ignored that warning and allowed years of political division to become normal. October 7 should have taught us that national security depends not only on military strength but also on social cohesion and leadership capable of putting the country ahead of personal rivalries.
Hopefully, October 27 will produce a clear winner. If it does not, Israel’s political leaders will have to decide whether their refusal to sit together matters more than the country they are supposed to serve. After everything Israel has endured, another round of elections cannot be treated as an acceptable outcome.
The writer is a co-founder of the MEAD policy forum, a senior fellow at JPPI, and a former editor-in-chief of The Jerusalem Post. His newest book is While Israel Slept.

UK expands sanction powers, enabling action against companies supporting West Bank settlements
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:08:06 UTC
19:08:06 KST

Britain brought new regulations into force on Thursday, significantly expanding its sanctions powers in a move that could enable action against construction companies, developers, and financial institutions supporting settlement expansion in the West Bank.
The measures took effect four days before the deadline for submitting bids for construction in the E1 area between Jerusalem and Ma'aleh Adumim, amid a diplomatic dispute between Israel and Britain over the closure of the British consulate in east Jerusalem.
The new regulations expand Britain's sanctions framework concerning human rights and international humanitarian law. They allow sanctions against individuals and entities directly involved in activities classified as serious violations of international law, as well as those financing, facilitating, or promoting such activities, subject to specified legal conditions.
Possible measures include asset freezes, financial restrictions, travel bans, and disqualification from serving as company directors. The regulations could also allow sanctions against entities involved in settlement-related activities if they meet the established criteria, but do not impose blanket restrictions on all companies operating in the area.
UK sanctions expansion comes ahead of E1 settlement construction deadline
The timing is particularly significant as Israel advances construction plans in the E1 area. The deadline for submitting bids for 1,234 housing units, part of a broader plan involving approximately 3,400 units, is scheduled for October 19, while consideration of the bids by the tender committee has been postponed until after November 19.
Britain opposes the project, arguing that construction in the area would undermine the territorial continuity required for a future Palestinian state. Israeli officials view the development as part of settlement expansion and efforts to strengthen continuity between Jerusalem and Ma'aleh Adumim, rejecting the argument that international opposition should prevent the project from proceeding.
The tender is expected to close in the coming days despite the postponement of the committee's review. Companies seeking to participate must therefore submit their bids before it becomes clear whether Britain intends to exercise its new sanctions powers against entities connected to the project.
British advocates of expanded sanctions are seeking to deter companies and financial institutions from participating at the bidding stage, before contractors are selected and construction begins.
British lawmakers warn banks over financing E1 construction
Political figures and organizations in Britain opposed to settlement construction have also been working to increase pressure on businesses that could participate in the project.
Last month, members of Parliament contacted banks and financial institutions, warning of the risks associated with financing construction in E1. This week, the Britain Palestine Project, an organization supporting measures against settlements, warned that companies and contractors participating in the development could jeopardize their international business relationships.
In letters sent to financial institutions, lawmakers called on banks to assess their potential exposure to the E1 project and raise the issue at board level, including the legal, economic, and reputational risks involved.
Although the letters represent requests from lawmakers rather than binding government directives, they are intended to increase pressure on banks and other institutions providing financing and guarantees, encouraging them to avoid involvement in the project.
Concerns over possible future sanctions could influence commercial decisions even before Britain announces restrictions against specific companies.
Peace Now warns British sanctions could affect broader Israeli economy
The Israeli settlement watchdog Peace Now responded sharply to the regulations taking effect on Thursday, warning that their consequences could extend beyond companies directly involved in settlement construction.
"This is a real alarm. Today, it is already clear that settlements are not only an obstacle to peace and a danger to security, but also an economic threat to the country's future," the organization said.
Peace Now accused Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich of advancing construction in E1 and warned that the consequences of sanctions could eventually affect the broader Israeli public.
"The price of this messianic adventure could be paid not only by settlers, but by millions of law-abiding Israeli citizens," the organization said. "Today, these are sanctions on settlements. Tomorrow, they will reach every household in Israel."
Concerns about broader economic consequences were also raised last month. According to concerns expressed within the Israeli government, foreign importers and financial institutions could struggle to distinguish between companies operating in settlements and other Israeli businesses, potentially imposing stricter commercial conditions on companies that are not themselves subject to sanctions.
For now, these remain assessments of possible consequences, and the scale of any economic damage, if it occurs, remains unknown.
New sanctions rules could increase scrutiny of Israeli companies and banks
The regulations could also have further implications for the financial sector.
If sanctions are imposed on a particular company or entity, financial institutions subject to British law would be required to comply with the applicable restrictions, including asset freezes and prohibitions on making funds or economic resources available.
Companies not included on sanctions lists could also face additional information requests and more stringent reviews by banks and business partners, as part of compliance and risk-management procedures intended to ensure that transactions do not violate the restrictions.
However, business ties with the West Bank do not, in themselves, automatically constitute grounds for sanctions against a company or bank.
UK expands global human rights sanctions and introduces fast-track mechanism
The new regulations also cover matters unrelated to settlements. Britain will be able to impose sanctions for obstructing humanitarian assistance and for serious violations of the right to liberty and personal security, including unlawful detention.
The regulations also introduce a mechanism allowing London to temporarily adopt sanctions already imposed by partner countries for up to 112 days while considering whether to introduce independent British sanctions.
The mechanism will allow the British government to apply restrictions through an accelerated procedure based on decisions already taken by other countries.
Britain advances separate restrictions on settlement trade and imports
The British move forms part of a broader plan presented by Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband on September 8, which also includes a proposed ban on imports from settlements and restrictions on related commercial activities.
Separate legislation introducing the import ban has not yet been completed. In recent months, Britain has also coordinated with other countries in taking action against individuals and entities accused of involvement in settler violence and its financing.
According to London's plan, the separate trade legislation also includes restrictions on advertising and marketing settlement real estate in Britain.
In September, 12 European and Western countries, including Britain, France, and Canada, announced support for advancing trade restrictions concerning settlements, each in accordance with its domestic procedures. In some countries, the measures remain in the drafting and legislative stages.
British opposition raises concerns over Palestinian workers
The sanctions have also generated debate within Britain.
The opposition Conservative Party has previously warned that economic restrictions could harm Palestinian workers and businesses not involved in the activities targeted by the government.
Conversely, Emily Thornberry, chair of Parliament's Foreign Affairs Committee, has supported measures against settlements while criticizing the time required to complete the legislation.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham clarified in Parliament this week that security and intelligence cooperation with Israel continues despite the political disagreements.
The potential impact on Palestinian workers was also raised in a parliamentary question submitted to the British government.
In a response issued earlier this month, the government emphasized that its measures target settlement activity it considers illegal, as well as violence and extremism, while Palestinian businesses will continue to benefit from existing preferential trade arrangements.
However, the response did not include an estimate of the number of Palestinian workers who could be affected by restrictions on economic activity in settlements.
The British government has not yet presented data that would allow an assessment of the potential impact on those workers.
UK-Israel diplomatic tensions continue over east Jerusalem consulate
The regulations took effect one week after understandings were reached between Israel and Britain concerning the British consulate in east Jerusalem.
Israel reduced Britain's diplomatic presence and halted additional activities in response to London's measures, but Britain has not reversed its sanctions policy.
Although the new regulations are now in force, no new sanctions have been announced under them against companies, developers, or financial institutions involved in E1 construction.
British Foreign Office clarifies sanctions are global, not Israel-specific
A spokesperson for the British Foreign Office clarified that the updated regulations represent a change in global sanctions policy rather than a measure specifically targeting Israel or settlements.
According to the spokesperson, the existing framework had allowed Britain to impose sanctions on individuals and entities involved in serious human rights violations or breaches of international humanitarian law worldwide.
The updated policy expands the range of serious violations that could trigger sanctions, regardless of where they occur.
The spokesperson stressed that the regulations are separate from the legislative process and sanctions measures concerning settlements considered illegal under international law, and do not introduce any trade-related restrictions.
The Foreign Office also emphasized that the updated policy does not target any specific country.
Rather, it is intended to allow Britain to respond more quickly to individuals and organizations involved in serious human rights violations or breaches of international humanitarian law anywhere in the world.

The battle for Israel: As Netanyahu rallies the Right, Eisenkot makes his move for power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:07:56 UTC
19:07:56 KST

As the election nears, Netanyahu targets right-wing alternatives, while Eisenkot seeks the commanding lead that would make him the opposition’s undisputed PM candidate
Think of Israel as one big cruise liner. Considering the country’s hyper-stressed reality, that may require some imagination, but bear with it for a moment.
On the starboard side of the ship, the right side, are all the voters in the pro-Netanyahu camp, split into different halls and ballrooms.
The Likud occupies the biggest hall, with smaller rooms for Shas, United Torah Judaism, Otzma Yehudit, and the Religious Zionist Party.
On the port side, separated from starboard by a hallway with doors leading to both sides, are the rooms of the anti-Netanyahu camp.
Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar has the biggest room there, followed by Naftali Bennett’s B’Yachad, with smaller rooms for the Democrats and Avigdor Liberman’s Yisrael Beytenu.
In the hallway itself stand Ofer Winter’s People of Israel party and Yoaz Hendel and Yaron Zelekha’s reservist-economist party. Behind the ship, in a separate tugboat, sail the two Arab parties.
As the cruise liner steams toward its destination, Election Day, just 11 days away, representatives of the two sides shout the expected accusations across the hallway.
From one side: “You are responsible for the worst disaster in Israel’s history and are leading the country toward catastrophe.” From the other: “You will join forces with those in the tugboat and establish a Palestinian state.”
But the more consequential action is taking place on each side of the ship.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu looks down the hallway, trying to persuade Winter’s and Hendel’s voters to abandon them and come to his side of the ship. Over on the port side, Eisenkot is trying to expand his already large ballroom at the expense of the rooms occupied by those sharing his side of the liner.
Netanyahu intensifies campaign to consolidate right-wing voters
Those two maneuvers are dominating the final stretch of the voyage to Election Day. And what is a sure sign the campaign has entered that final stretch? Netanyahu’s sudden ubiquity on the airwaves.
After months when the prime minister’s interviews were largely reserved for foreign media, ABC, CBS, Fox News, and various podcasts, he showed up in Israeli studios this week, and not only on Channel 14.
Granted, on Tuesday he was, again, on Channel 14, where a “home crowd” greeted him rapturously. But the next day he was on Channel 11, and in between he appeared on Army Radio.
His message had two parts: the election is perilously close, and right-wing voters cannot afford to gamble.
The first is familiar. Netanyahu has sounded the same alarm in numerous campaigns, warning his voters that victory is slipping away. On Channel 14, he anticipated the obvious response: people would dismiss this as his traditional gevalt campaign. This time, he insisted, he really is worried. The race is tied, he said.
And where, precisely, did he see right-wing voters gambling?
Once you cut through the familiar warnings about Eisenkot joining forces with Ahmad Tibi and the election determining whether a Palestinian state will be established, a much smaller target comes into view: Winter’s party.
Netanyahu’s relentless attacks on the retired brigadier-general stand out in this final stretch. At a time when he might be expected to concentrate his fire on Eisenkot and Bennett, he is devoting considerable energy to a small party standing in the hallway.
Netanyahu said he had tried to persuade Winter to join the Likud and, when that failed, to team up with another small right-wing party. That, too, failed, so now he is going after him mercilessly.
In one of the anti-Winter messages he put out this week, Netanyahu charged that Winter would take right-wing votes and carry them over to Liberman on the port side of the ship.
“It’s no coincidence that a senior figure on Liberman’s list, Yulia Malinovsky, says that ultimately Winter will join a government with Liberman. That’s what will happen. That’s the plan,” Netanyahu said.
Then came a blistering comparison with Bennett, who formed a government in 2021 with Yair Lapid’s Yesh Atid and Mansour Abbas’s Ra’am.
“If he walks like Bennett and talks like Bennett, he’s Bennett. Vote Likud, vote Right. Winter is not right-wing. Winter is Bennett 2. We mustn’t squander the Right’s votes. Don’t vote for Winter.”
Winter's coalition conditions complicate Netanyahu's election strategy
Netanyahu’s concern is twofold.
First, Winter’s party will fail to cross the 3.25% electoral threshold, sending votes cast by people on the Right down the drain. Of the 19 major polls taken since October 1, the party crossed the threshold in 11, including four of the seven taken in the last week.
That is enough to keep Winter in the race, but hardly enough to reassure Netanyahu that the votes will count.
The second concern is that Winter will cross the threshold, then peddle his seats elsewhere.
Winter and others in his party say they will recommend Netanyahu to the president as prime minister. But they also say they will not join a government in which the haredi parties hold the balance of power unless those parties agree to a widespread haredi conscription law.
But what if Netanyahu does not accept those conditions? Asked precisely that in a Channel 12 interview on Saturday night, Winter replied, rather inelegantly, that Netanyahu could essentially “go take a hike.”
Nobody owns me, he declared
Winter did not explicitly rule out joining an Eisenkot or Liberman government. He did, however, rule out sitting with Yair Golan, because “he smears Israel abroad.”
For Netanyahu’s campaign, that left an opening wide enough to drive a campaign bus through.
A recommendation is one thing; a commitment to join a government is another. Winter is offering the former, with conditions attached to the latter. Netanyahu wants right-wing voters to hear that distinction and draw the conclusion he is supplying: Winter could be Bennett all over again.
The pressure has extended to billboards and signs in areas where candidates on Winter’s list live. Davidi Ben-Zion, eighth on the list, withdrew, reportedly telling colleagues that pressure on his family, including negative posters strategically placed near the bus stops his children use, had become too much.
Netanyahu’s concerns also extend to the other party in the hallway: Hendel and Zelekha’s.
In the Channel 14 interview, Netanyahu went after Zelekha, whom Netanyahu – as finance minister – appointed accountant-general in 2003. Despite the party’s appeal to right-wing voters, Netanyahu charged that Zelekha had voted for Meretz in the past and participated enthusiastically in anti-government protests on Balfour Street in Jerusalem and Kaplan Street in Tel Aviv.
He also attacked Zelekha on his home turf, the economy, challenging his credentials as a free-market champion.
Hendel and Zelekha’s party crossed the threshold in all seven major polls taken this week. But unlike Winter, they have not pledged to recommend Netanyahu. Hendel says the party will use its leverage to establish a broad Zionist government without the Arab and haredi parties.
Given the coalition arithmetic, how that government would come together remains an enigma. Like Winter, Hendel is clearer about his conditions than about how he would assemble a government that meets them.
But Netanyahu doesn’t need their coalition plans fully worked out to worry about them. He needs the voters attracted to those parties back in his camp.
Eisenkot seeks commanding lead to establish opposition leadership
Across the ship’s hallway, Eisenkot has a different calculation.
His campaign to make Yashar the largest party is aimed, in part, at voters already on his side of the boat. He wants them to leave the other rooms and enter his ballroom.
For Netanyahu, the immediate task is to consolidate the camp. For Eisenkot, it is also to establish who commands it.
That is why the leaders of the other parties in his bloc are less than enthusiastic about his strategy. A voter moving from Bennett, Liberman, or Golan to Eisenkot does not enlarge the bloc. It enlarges Eisenkot.
The bigger Yashar is, and the wider its lead over the Likud, the stronger his claim to form the next government – even if his bloc falls short of 61 seats.
Eisenkot repeated one phrase this week: Netanyahu must not be allowed to win by losing. By that, he means Netanyahu must not remain caretaker prime minister through another cycle of inconclusive elections simply because no one else can form a coalition.
In a Yediot Aharonot interview this week, Eisenkot said, “If you [Netanyahu] think you will do to me what you did to others in the past – meaning, remain in office at the head of a caretaker government – that will not happen.” When Israel held five elections in under four years, from April 2019 to November 2022, Netanyahu served 19 months as caretaker prime minister over two stretches.
Eisenkot considers minority government to prevent Netanyahu remaining in office
One route Eisenkot envisages to prevent a repeat of that scenario is to bring a minority government to the Knesset for approval and secure the support of a majority of those voting.
A government does not need 61 members to win such a vote; it only needs a majority of those in the plenum casting a vote. This scenario would be made possible, for instance, if the Arab parties simply don’t vote.
Once this minority government is approved, Eisenkot can then attract defectors from the other side of the ship. A substantial lead over the Likud would give that effort greater public legitimacy.
There are other considerations, too.
First, in the unlikely event that a rotation agreement with the Likud became a serious possibility, a decisive lead in seats would bolster his claim to go first as prime minister.
More immediately, the larger Yashar becomes, the harder it would be for Bennett or Liberman to argue that someone else should lead the bloc.
The four parties in the “change bloc” have yet to agree on a mechanism to determine their prime ministerial candidate after the election.
Eisenkot has said, logically enough, that the leader of the party that wins the most votes should be the bloc’s candidate. Since Yashar currently leads the bloc by a considerable margin, that formula would obviously favor him.
It remains unclear, however, whether the others are prepared to accept this. But the wider the gap, the harder it would be to explain why the leader of a much smaller party should get the top job.
Eisenkot is campaigning both against Netanyahu and for an outcome within his own bloc that would make his leadership hard to challenge.
Both Netanyahu’s and Eisenkot’s maneuvers make sense.
Netanyahu wants to prevent right-wing votes from being lost or carried into another government. Eisenkot wants to ensure that, if there is an opportunity to replace Netanyahu, he will be the one to seize it.
But both maneuvers have their limits. For Netanyahu, keeping his passengers together does not guarantee enough support to retain command. And for Eisenkot, having the biggest ballroom on one side of the ship does not guarantee enough support to become captain of the whole vessel.

Somporn Yamyong, 62, travelled from rice-rich central Suphan Buri province to draw attention to years of debt and meagre earnings.
The rice farmer said she wanted Thai leaders and the IMF and World Bank to hear about the "hardships facing farmers" like her.
Thailand received an IMF loan three decades ago but paid this off in 2003. It has some projects with the World Bank.
Coconut farmer Sombat Chuekrod, 51, from Prachuap Khiri Khan province, south-west of Bangkok, added: "Thai people are already poor. Please don't make us any poorer."
There were some non-Thai protesters in the crowd, including Harry May, a 59-year-old South African activist and researcher, who said global lenders were "bankrupting our countries, especially developing countries".

On Thursday, there were brief scuffles when police blocked protesters as they tried to hang a banner from a footbridge in the Thai capital, but there was no sign of trouble on Friday morning.

Social media favourites, Pompeii's cats star in new photo book
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:06:50 UTC
19:06:50 KST

Photographed by thousands of visitors every year, the cats of Pompeii’s Archaeological Park now star in a new book. Around 50 live among the ruins.
After charming thousands of visitors and turning into genuine social media celebrities, the cats that live inside the archaeological area of Pompeii have now become the stars of a photographic book dedicated to them.
The book, entitled Cats of Pompeii, is published by Giunti Editore in collaboration with the Pompeii Archaeological Park. Richly illustrated, it tells the stories of the everyday life of the feline colony that inhabits the UNESCO World Heritage site.
The volume grew out of photographs donated to the Park by archaeologist and photographer Silvia Vacca and offers a journey into the most unusual and captivating side of the ancient city. The shots capture the cats as they roam among domus, gardens and Roman streets, providing an original perspective on a presence that has long since become an integral part of the Pompeian landscape.
The Park’s feline colony numbers between forty and fifty animals, and their presence is constantly monitored through a management and protection system that makes it possible to combine animal welfare with the conservation of the archaeological heritage and the safety of visitors. The Park has also introduced a video surveillance system to prevent animals being abandoned.
Thanks to cooperation with the charity Archeogatti Onlus, chaired by Antonella Carotenuto, the Archaeological Park also ensures sterilisation campaigns, health checks, measures to prevent abandonment, and the management of feeding the colony and arranging adoptions for some of the "archaeologist" cats.
Cats in ancient Pompeii
The presence of cats in Pompeii is a symbolic feature of life at the site. Ongoing archaeological research sheds light on the relationship between humans and felines in the ancient world, while today these animals remain a familiar sight and are much appreciated by visitors from all over the globe.
The camera lens reveals intimate, evocative images taken during the Park’s quietest moments, when the streets of the ancient city fall silent once more. Out of this comes a portrait of a different Pompeii, where safeguarding cultural heritage goes hand in hand with protecting the animals that have inhabited its spaces for years.
"Cats of Pompeii" is available at sales points in the Pompeii Archaeological Park and through Giunti’s distribution channels.

A British man has been handed a €3,000 (£2,500) fine after his two-year-old son fell nearly 12 metres (40ft) to his death from the fourth floor window of a hotel in Cyprus.
Joshua Foster thought the window was closed when he placed the boy on a sill to show him the view of a waterpark and “lost control” of him, the court previously heard.
The 37-year-old appeared at Paphos district court on Friday for sentencing having pleaded guilty to a charge of causing death through a reckless, rash or dangerous act.
Foster, an auditor, held back tears as his sentence was read out by the district judge Froso Christodoulidou.
After the 25-minute hearing, Foster hugged his lawyer before embracing his parents.
The boy fell from the fourth floor of the five-star King Evelthon Beach Hotel and Resort in Chlorakas on 12 July, the first day of the family’s holiday.
The court previously heard that Foster, his wife, two children and in-laws had arrived in Cyprus in the early hours of the morning on the date of the incident.
After various activities, including visiting the pool, the family returned to their rooms to get ready to go out for dinner.
At about 6pm, Foster, his father-in-law and son walked towards the lift, and his lawyer Alexandros Alexandrou told the court that the defendant was in a “good mood” and was playing with his son.
The court was told that as they approached the lift, the boy noticed a waterpark outside.
It was said that Foster pushed the lift button, placed the child on the windowsill, the boy looked out, and the “inconceivable” unfolded before Foster had a chance to react.
Alexandrou told the hearing, which took place on 6 October, that Foster’s life “changed for ever” from that moment.
It was heard that Foster had not realised that the section of the window was open, and that he thought there was protective glass.
Prosecutor Chryso Pergandi said that at around 6.40pm, police received reports that a child had fallen from the fourth floor of the beachfront hotel under unknown circumstances.
The boy was taken to Paphos general hospital where, despite efforts to resuscitate him, he was pronounced dead.
In a voluntary statement to police, Foster said that when he placed his son on the windowsill, the boy “fell before he had a chance to grab him”.
After the incident, Foster was taken to Paphos general hospital and a blood sample to detect drugs and alcohol was taken.
Tests showed that the alcohol concentration in his blood was an estimated 124mg.
Alcohol consumption did not form a significant part of the case against Foster, and his lawyer said there was no testimony that he was drunk.
The lawyer told the court that Foster had no previous convictions and his remorse “is clear”.
He said he was held in custody for eight days immediately after the incident, adding that while grieving for his child he had to call his daughter from custody to explain what had happened.
The court heard the window was 2.85 metres wide and 1.2 metres high.

Hegseth's TV instincts backfire as Trump rejects execution livestream

But Hegseth's TV instincts, while perhaps one of the tools he relies on most in his Pentagon role, appear to have failed him on Thursday when President Donald Trump pulled the plug on his plans, announced last week, to livestream the Army's firing-squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan.
Trump had been unaware of Hegseth's unprecedented plan to broadcast the execution, said a White House official who spoke on condition of anonymity. Many fellow Republicans, along with religious leaders and international observers, raised objections to the plan, and defense officials who spoke to Reuters on Thursday expressed relief that the livestreaming would not go forward.
Defense secretaries often cycle out after a couple of years in the job and speculation in Washington has mounted whether Trump might see value in bringing new management to the Pentagon after November's midterm elections.
But Republican strategists said it was too soon to say whether Trump's decision to overrule Hegseth would affect their relationship, which has remained strong despite mounting public opposition to the war in Iran.
"They've been kind of very closely knit and I don't know whether it means anything at all," Republican strategist Douglas Heye said. Charlie Black, a veteran Republican strategist, said it would likely blow over.
"It's a wild thing but nobody will remember it next week," Black said, adding Trump "did the right thing."
The Pentagon sought to downplay the first major public split between Trump and Hegseth, saying the two spoke before the US president posted his decision on Truth Social.
"The Secretary supports the President's decision, and they are completely aligned," said Sean Parnell, the Pentagon's chief spokesperson.

Trump regularly extols Hegseth publicly, and has given the former Army National Guard soldier significant leeway as he seeks to reshape the Pentagon, including by firing its most senior officers.

While Representative Thomas Massie's measure is not expected to succeed, Democrats could look to move forward with impeachment proceedings if they win control of the House in the upcoming elections in November.
At times, the conflict between Hegseth and members of Congress has become personal. Kelly on Thursday introduced a bill that would prohibit livestreamed executions.
"Livestreaming an execution is un-American and dangerous. It is the kind of thing we see with regimes like Iran and the Taliban in Afghanistan," Kelly said in a statement.
The event would have been extraordinary, even for a country that has long employed capital punishment. A government execution has never been broadcast or livestreamed, according to death penalty experts, and the US military has not executed anyone by firing squad since 1945.
Hasan was convicted of premeditated murder for shooting dead 13 people and wounding 32 others in a medical facility at the vast Fort Hood base in 2009. Now 56, he requires a wheelchair, having been shot by police during his arrest.
Hegseth had argued that making the event public would help show "there's serious consequences for these types of things."
Trump appeared to accept Hegseth's argument, saying on Thursday livestreaming it "might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan."
But Trump, who is himself a former reality television star, ultimately decided a public show went too far.
"Many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device. He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed," Trump wrote. REUTERS

Brazil's incoming right-wing Congress takes aim at judge who jailed Bolsonaro

Brazil's incoming right-wing Congress takes aim at judge who jailed Bolsonaro
BRASILIA, Oct 16 - Brazil's next Congress is spoiling for a fight with the Supreme Court, including plans for an unprecedented impeachment of one of its justices that could dramatically expand the reach of a right-wing agenda, more than a dozen experts and officials at both the Senate and court told Reuters.
Driving the effort are allies of far-right former President Jair Bolsonaro who dominated legislative elections this month and plan to take aim at Alexandre de Moraes, the Supreme Court justice responsible for the ex-president's arrest and conviction on coup-plotting charges.
That would represent a major escalation by the legislative branch in a years-long power struggle with an empowered Brazilian judiciary, reasserting the influence of Congress and potentially pushing the court to the right for years to come.
If Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the former president's son, beats leftist incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in an October 25 runoff as polls now suggest, a defanged judiciary would also reduce one of the main checks on his power.
BLOCKING RIGHT-WING POLICIES
Brazil's Supreme Court was the main obstacle to his father's agenda during his 2019-2023 presidency, blocking efforts to weaken environmental protections, ease pandemic restrictions and facilitate gun purchases, for example.
The top court continues to hold back some of the most strident right-wing legislation, effectively defining policy on matters from Indigenous rights to regulating the internet.
This month's election could prove pivotal, as the next president could name at least 4 of the court's 11 justices, including an already vacant seat and replacements for 3 justices who will reach the mandatory retirement age of 75 before the president's term ends.
After former President Bolsonaro named two justices to the court, a victory by his son could spell a majority of the court appointed by the Bolsonaro family by the time he would leave office in 2031.
Impeaching Moraes, 57, would hasten that majority's arrival.
"Should Flavio win, the next administration and the Senate can reshape the majority of the 11-member bench, which means defining, literally, the balance of power in Brazilian democracy for a generation," said Bruna Santos, director of the Brazil Program at the Inter-American Dialogue.
SCORNED BY TRUMP, MUSK
Ex-President Bolsonaro has been in jail since November for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election to Lula. Moraes, who oversaw the case, became one of Brazil's most polarizing figures, drawing even the ire of US President Donald Trump, who described the case as a "witch hunt" and briefly sanctioned the judge in 2025.
Moraes also drew criticism when he ordered X suspended in Brazil in 2024, after the platform defied court orders. Its owner Elon Musk accused him of censorship and authoritarianism.
Bolsonaro supporters have rallied to remove the judge after a federal police report revealed communications between Moraes and a jailed banker accused of the country's biggest-ever banking fraud. Bolsonaro, who himself is being investigated for ties to the same banker, has also called for Moraes' removal.
"Defending the Judiciary means confronting this problem — opening an impeachment process and giving him the right to a defense, concluding it and turning this page," Senator-elect Domingos Savio, from Bolsonaro's Liberal Party (PL), told Reuters.
Lula has publicly supported unsealing the investigation, calling for transparency, disclosure, and an impartial investigation into all allegations of corruption.
Neither Moraes nor the Supreme Court responded to questions from Reuters. He and the wider court have defended their actions as necessary to uphold Brazilian law and protect democratic institutions. He has referred to the probes as politically and electorally motivated as revenge for the conviction of former President Bolsonaro, and requested his own investigation into another justice who released the reports.
LEGISLATIVE FIREPOWER
Senator Bolsonaro's running mate, lawmaker Alfredo Gaspar, told Reuters there is "a need to review what is happening today in the relationship between the Supreme Court and the other branches of government, and that involves examining whether justices have committed impeachable offenses."
Brazil's constitution allows the Senate to try Supreme Court justices for infractions that violate the constitution or risk public security. Votes from two-thirds of the 81-member Senate — 54 senators — are needed to convict and remove a justice.
Senator Bolsonaro's allies may already be close when the next Senate takes office in February. His party won a record 28 seats, and the senator has already secured backing from five other parties that together hold another 22 seats.
That would bring the conservative coalition to 50 senators. The remaining four votes could come from the 15 senators with non-aligned parties.
Since 2023, there have been 48 unsuccessful requests to impeach Moraes within the Senate, which never made it to trial because the Senate president must choose to advance a complaint against a justice.
That could change, as Senator Bolsonaro's campaign manager Rogerio Marinho is likely to become the next Senate president.
Marinho has in recent days told several Supreme Court justices that Brazil's upper house will not seek opportunities for revenge, he said to journalists, though adding that the current Senate is "failing to act" to hold justices accountable.
"If impeachable offenses are committed, they must be investigated. No one is above the law," Marinho said. REUTERS

Reservations under the new system: why the government’s assurances failed to allay the concerns of business and parliament
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:05:31 EEST
19:05:31 KST

Reservations under the new system: why the government’s assurances failed to allay the concerns of business and parliament
Kyiv • UNN
The Cabinet of Ministers is finalizing amendments to the rules for reserving employees of critical enterprises, despite warnings from businesses and members of parliament about risks to defense capabilities and the economy. At the same time, the National Agency for the Prevention of Corruption identified a number of corruption risks in the government initiative.
The government resolution on reducing reservation quotas for critical enterprises has sparked a wave of outrage among business representatives, the public, and parliament. Today it became known that the Cabinet of Ministers has not yet made a final decision, but the debate around the proposed changes is gaining momentum. Despite assurances from Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi that there would be no radical changes for the defense industry and energy sector, business representatives and members of parliament continue to insist that the initiative be canceled and that consultations be held with business representatives, reports UNN.
Government decision to restrict reservations
On October 13, the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine considered amendments to Resolution No. 76, which regulates the procedure for reserving military-liable employees. According to media reports, during the meeting the government did not make a final decision on reducing reservation quotas for critically important enterprises.
The draft resolution proposed reducing the percentage quotas for reservations for enterprises in the defense-industrial complex and energy sector—from 100% to 85%, and for the municipal sector—from 75% to 60%. The relevant changes are to be revised within 5 days.
The document removed the provision excluding employees who have a deferment (students, parents of many children, and others) from the calculation.
The government decided to establish a Coordination Center involving the Security Service of Ukraine, the Defence Intelligence of Ukraine, the Foreign Intelligence Service, and the National Police, with the relevant decision to be further revised.
At the same time, business representatives pointed out that the proposed changes had not been discussed with them and that business had not received any official clarifications regarding the decisions made. Business associations sharply criticized the government initiative, noting that such a decision would deepen the personnel shortage in critical sectors and cause economic losses for the state.
The details will be provided when they are made public
Commenting on the issue of reducing reservation quotas for critical enterprises, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi confirmed that the government had not discussed this initiative with business.
This resolution is currently being worked on; it will definitely be revised, adopted, and published. There is no betrayal here. All the details will be provided exactly when they are published and all the relevant decisions are made. So the skepticism currently being discussed in society has no basis. There are no official decisions, so there is nothing to criticize at this point
At the same time, Koretskyi added that the mobilization process needs improvement.
There is no need for critical enterprises that are genuinely critical for both the defense complex and the energy complex to worry. I can say with great confidence that there will be no radical changes for these people, these enterprises, or these production facilities
At the same time, Koretskyi did not mention other critically important sectors that had already expressed concern about changes to the reservation rules and reductions in quotas.
According to the Prime Minister, 100% reservations create opportunities for manipulation, and enterprises with critical status can endlessly expand their workforce and reserve employees regardless of their qualifications.
Unfortunately, this system has already grown to a considerable scale. Therefore, this is the only reason why we are considering the 100% threshold—whether to modify it or nevertheless leave it as it is, because, unfortunately, there are many abuses
Koretskyi said that he considers enterprises that support defense capability and life-sustaining services to be critical. At the same time, the Prime Minister did not mention enterprises in related sectors that also help provide for the army or fulfill government contracts.
As an example, he cited a company that carries out work for "Ukrenergo", where all personnel are reserved. According to him, only some of the employees work under contracts for the energy company, while the rest are engaged in business.
At the same time, Koretskyi is evidently deliberately ignoring the fact that, in order to be able to operate, private companies also need to have funds to maintain their personnel.
Parliament plans to cancel the government's decision
Just now, Resolution No. 16160 was registered in parliament, authored by me and 62 other MPs from all factions and groups. (…) I will not put the adoption of this resolution to a vote because I understand that it needs to be prepared, but I have an appeal and a request to the Prime Minister and the members of the Cabinet of Ministers. This is not only the position of members of parliament; it is the position of business, think tanks, local government and, most importantly, energy workers and the defense-industrial complex — stop this decision, hold consultations, and only after that adopt the final document
Iryna Friz, a member of the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine Committee on National Security, Defense and Intelligence, said that the committee had considered the issue of changes to the reservation system announced by the government.
According to the report by representatives of the Ministry of Economy and the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine, as of now, there is still no final text of the Cabinet of Ministers' Resolution. It is still being coordinated, revised and awaiting a political decision….
According to her, during the discussion, parliamentarians pointed out that government officials had not substantiated the need to reduce reservation percentages for critical enterprises in certain sectors, nor provided methodological calculations or modeling of the consequences of such a decision.
She recalled that the Ministry of Defense had opposed reducing the reservation limits in the defense-industrial complex from 100% to 85%. In addition, according to her, committee members did not receive exhaustive arguments from government officials regarding the expediency of creating a Coordination Center, its functions and powers. The committee's decision points to the lack of justification and the risks of reducing quotas for the defense-industrial complex.
I must emphasize that the government's proposed reduction of reservation quotas to 85% for defense and energy enterprises and to 60% for heat and water supply enterprises and other utility services creates risks for the stable operation of both defense-industry enterprises and critical infrastructure
She added that the state's mobilization needs and the capabilities of the defense industry and critical infrastructure must be balanced.
The government must finally understand that without the people who produce weapons, restore the energy system and ensure the country's vital functions, it is impossible to guarantee the state's resilience during wartime. That is why changes must be developed and adopted exclusively on the basis of sectoral audits, an analysis of compliance with criticality criteria, and accountability and the inevitability of punishment for corrupt schemes involving personnel reservations
NACP warns: the government's decision carries corruption risks
The UNN editorial office has a decision by the National Agency on Corruption Prevention at its disposal, which contains comments on the government resolution.
In particular, the NACP recommended removing the provision under which the government proposed excluding employees with deferments from the calculations of the quotas, which significantly reduced the calculation base. In this regard, the Cabinet of Ministers took the comments into account and, as already mentioned, the provision was removed.
In addition, the Agency pointed out that the creation of a Coordination Center in the version proposed by the Cabinet of Ministers — without specifying the rules of operation, the deadlines for granting enterprises critical-importance status, and the grounds for refusal — "creates preconditions for corrupt practices".
According to the government resolution, the Coordination Center will provide recommendations, while the final decision on critical status will be made by the ministry. The NACP also has comments on this provision; the Agency believes that under such conditions, the recommendations should be mandatory in order to eliminate opportunities for abuse.
Thus, despite the government's assurances that there will be no radical changes for critically important enterprises, the proposed amendments to the reservation rules continue to raise a number of questions. The lack of economic calculations, proper consultations with businesses, and the NACP's comments regarding corruption risks indicate that the document requires further work. The government has not modeled the consequences of the changes either for the defense industry and energy sectors or for related critically important industries. Clearly, combating abuse in the reservation system is necessary, but it should not create new risks for enterprises on which the state's resilience during the war depends.

A complaint has been filed against former orthodox Protestant SGP MP Roelof Bisschop, who said publicly that he had bought wine in protest against the Dutch ban on goods from illegal Israeli settlements, public broadcaster NOS reported.
Pro-Palestinian group BDS Netherlands (Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions) filed the criminal complaint with the public prosecution service (OM). Activists had earlier reported Bisschop to the fiscal investigation service FIOD.
Bisschop bought two bottles on September 23, the day after the ban took effect, and posted a photo of them on social media. Two days later he told Christian television channel Family7 that the purchase was a “statement” against the ban.
Since September 22, the Netherlands has banned imports of goods from illegal settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories and the Golan Heights. The rules also ban buying and selling such goods, intermediary trade and any form of circumvention.
In its complaint, BDS Netherlands said Bisschop had deliberately acted against the sanctions policy and promoted this on several platforms.
“Anyone who, as a former MP, publicly announces they are deliberately testing the law can expect the OM to look at whether that is a criminal offence,” the group said in the complaint.
It is not yet clear whether the wine is covered by the ban. The producer, Teperberg Winery, has vineyards in the occupied West Bank and is on a UN list of companies active in settlements. However, it says these wines are made just inside Israel. Bisschop told NOS he did not know exactly where the bottles came from.
The OM said it is aware of the complaint and will assess whether there are grounds to open an investigation.

Türkiye's Fidan to attend OIC foreign ministers' meeting in Baghdad
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:01:07 UTC
19:01:07 KST

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan will attend the 52nd session of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation’s (OIC) Council of Foreign Ministers in Baghdad on October 17-18, Türkiye’s Foreign Ministry has said.
Held under the theme “Dialogue and Solidarity: Two Essential Pillars for Promoting Peace and Sustainable Development”, the meeting will see Türkiye transfer the organisation’s rotating presidency to Iraq, which it has held since June 2025.
Discussions are expected to cover Israel’s actions in Gaza and across the occupied Palestinian territories, other conflicts in the Muslim world, counterterrorism, United Nations reform, Islamophobia and the situation of Muslim communities in non-member countries.
The meeting is expected to conclude with the adoption of the Baghdad Declaration.
Fidan to call for coordinated action on Palestine
In his address, Fidan is expected to describe Israel’s aggressive and expansionist policies as the biggest security threat to the Middle East and urge OIC members to coordinate their response with responsible international actors.
He is also expected to call for steps to protect Jerusalem’s status, oppose further moves by countries to relocate their embassies there, and reaffirm that a two-state solution leading to an independent Palestinian state is the only path to a just and lasting peace.
Fidan is expected to stress the need to ensure uninterrupted humanitarian aid reaches people in Gaza.
Regional security and freedom of navigation
The Turkish foreign minister is also expected to address rising tensions in the Gulf and around the Strait of Hormuz.
He is expected to emphasise the importance of ensuring safe and free navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al Mandab for regional stability and global trade, while condemning Houthi militia attacks on civilians and critical infrastructure and reaffirming Türkiye’s solidarity with Saudi Arabia.
Fidan is also expected to call for the protection of Syria’s and Lebanon’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, including a complete Israeli withdrawal from southern Lebanon.
OIC to discuss rights of Muslim communities
The meeting is also expected to address the rights of Turkish Cypriots, who face what Ankara describes as unjust isolation, as well as the fundamental rights and freedoms of the Muslim Turkish minority in Western Thrace and Muslim Turkish communities in the Dodecanese islands.
The OIC, established in 1969, has 57 member states and is the world’s second-largest intergovernmental organisation after the United Nations.
Türkiye is one of its 25 founding members and took over the rotating presidency at the previous Council of Foreign Ministers meeting in Istanbul in June 2025.
Fidan is also expected to hold bilateral meetings with counterparts on the sidelines of the Baghdad gathering.

Some adults’ brains look older than their age, and gut biology may be part of the picture
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:00:55 UTC
19:00:55 KST

Some young and middle-aged adults have brain activity patterns that look “older” than their actual age, and new research suggests these differences are linked to thinking skills, mood, and the gut. Adults with older-looking brain patterns tended to score somewhat lower on tests of working memory and executive function, report more depressive symptoms, and have modestly different gut bacteria and stool chemicals. The findings were published in eBioMedicine.
A central concept in this research is the brain aging index. Researchers train a computer model to estimate a person’s age from brain scans alone, and the index is the gap between that estimate and the person’s actual age. A positive score means the brain looks older than expected, while a negative score means it looks younger. The authors of a 2017 review argued that such estimates could serve as a marker of brain health, pointing to evidence that an older-appearing brain is linked to poorer cognitive and physical aging and a higher risk of death.
Most of this research has focused on older adults who are already at risk for cognitive decline. However, the authors of a 2024 review argued that middle age may mark a turning point, with biological changes during this period shaping a person’s later brain health.
At the same time, evidence has grown linking the digestive system to brain health. A 2025 study comparing people with Alzheimer’s disease, people with mild cognitive impairment, and healthy adults found that gut bacteria and stool chemicals shifted step by step across these groups, and these shifts were tied to brain shrinkage and poorer thinking skills. A study covered by PsyPost in 2024 similarly found that depressed adults tend to have an imbalance of gut bacteria that relates to altered brain connectivity.
This progression of research led Kanhao Zhao, who conducted the study during his postdoctoral training under Arpana Church at the Church Lab at the University of California, Los Angeles, to test whether gut biology relates to early brain aging in young and middle-aged adults. The work was supported by National Institutes of Health grants awarded to Church.
“Most brain-age research has focused on older adults or people who already have neurological disease,” Zhao, who is now a postdoctoral scholar in the Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences at Stanford University School of Medicine, told PsyPost. “We therefore wanted to ask whether meaningful differences in brain aging could already be detected in young and mid-life adults, and whether these differences were linked not only to cognition and mental health, but also to gut microbial and metabolic features.”
To investigate this, the research team analyzed brain imaging and biological data from healthy adults aged 18 to 65. They divided the data into three separate groups to ensure their results were consistent across different samples: a discovery group of 674 people, a replication group of 444 people, and an independent group of 344 people.
The participants underwent resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging. This technique measures changes in blood oxygen levels, which rise and fall with brain activity, while a person lies still and rests. By tracking which regions rise and fall together, a pattern known as functional connectivity, scientists can see how different brain regions communicate.
Participants also completed various tests to measure their cognitive and emotional health. These included assessments of intelligence, working memory, executive function, and self-reported questionnaires for depressive symptoms.
In the independent group of participants, the researchers collected stool samples. They analyzed these samples using metagenomics, which sequences the genetic material of the bacteria living in the gut, and metabolomics, which identifies specific metabolites. Metabolites are the small chemical molecules left over from cellular processes, digestion, and bacterial activity.
Across all three groups, the model’s age estimates tracked participants’ actual ages reasonably well, though imperfectly: its predictions were off by about 6 to 9 years on average. People whose brains looked older than expected showed a consistent pattern. A higher index score was associated with stronger connections involving the default mode network, a set of regions most active during inward-focused thought such as daydreaming and recalling memories, and the frontoparietal network, which helps control goal-directed thinking. The strongest links involved the precuneus and posterior cingulate cortex, regions along the brain’s midline that are involved in internal thought and memory retrieval.
At the same time, people with older-appearing brains showed weaker connections in the ventral attention network, a brain system that helps humans orient themselves to sudden changes in their environment. This network imbalance was linked to worse performance on cognitive tests. Individuals with a higher brain aging index scored lower on performance IQ, working memory, and executive function tasks, while also reporting more symptoms of depression.
These associations were modest. Correlations between brain-age scores and individual test results ranged from about 0.12 to 0.38, meaning brain-age scores accounted for at most about 14 percent of the variation in any single measure, and usually much less. Not every measure lined up: verbal IQ showed no reliable link in either group where it was tested, and several test scores were linked in one group but not another. In the first group, the links held after accounting for participants’ actual ages.
“The effects should be viewed as meaningful population-level associations rather than as a diagnostic test for an individual person,” Zhao noted. “An important strength of the study is that the brain-age pattern was examined across multiple independent cohorts, but the associations with cognition, mood, and gut biology were generally modest. At this stage, the brain aging index is better understood as a research marker of individual variability in brain health than as something that could tell a person how quickly their brain is aging in a clinical setting.”
The gut findings were similarly small. In the 182 participants with complete data, a combined profile of gut bacteria and stool chemicals accounted for only about 2 percent of the differences in brain-age scores, though this was more than would be expected by chance. The bacteria most strongly tied to older-looking brains in this profile included species of Clostridium and Collinsella, and the stool chemicals included ceramides and 24-hydroxycholesterol, fat-related molecules involved in inflammation, cellular stress, and cholesterol processing.
Some of these bacteria have been tied to inflammation in other research, but the authors note that in these healthy adults they appeared alongside bacteria typically associated with a healthy gut. People with younger-looking brains, by contrast, had higher levels of stool chemicals related to neurotransmitter function and amino acid processing. One of the molecules most strongly tied to a younger-looking brain was estetrol, a form of estrogen, which the authors suggest could hint at a protective role for reproductive hormone pathways.
“What I found particularly interesting was that the signal was not confined to the brain,” Zhao said. “We observed coordinated associations involving functional brain networks, cognition and mood, and gut-derived biological features, including microbial and metabolic signatures related to lipid metabolism, immune and vascular processes, synaptic function, and mitochondrial pathways. This convergence across very different biological levels suggests that understanding brain aging may ultimately require looking beyond the brain alone.”
Notably, the cognitive and mood measures were tied to the brain network patterns rather than directly to any specific gut bacteria or stool chemicals.
“One important message is that people of the same chronological age can show meaningful differences in how their brain networks resemble patterns associated with aging,” Zhao explained. “We also found that these brain-age differences were linked to patterns in gut microbes and metabolites, suggesting that brain aging may be related to broader biological processes across the brain-gut system rather than occurring in isolation.”
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. “The most important caveat is that this was a cross-sectional observational study, so our findings do not establish causality,” Zhao emphasized. “We cannot conclude that particular gut microbes or metabolites cause the brain to age faster, nor that changing the microbiome would necessarily make the brain ‘younger.'”
Because everything was measured at a single point in time, it is also possible that brain changes influence the gut, or that other factors, such as diet, shape both. Zhao also noted that the brain-age measure is a “statistical index derived from functional connectivity, rather than a literal measurement of the biological age of a person’s brain.”
Additionally, the gut microbiome analysis was conducted on 182 participants, mostly women, and the cohorts drew on datasets from the U.S. and Japan. The researchers note that larger, more balanced studies will be necessary to verify the exact bacterial and metabolic signatures identified in this group. The genetic sequencing used in the study also identifies broad bacterial species but cannot pinpoint specific bacterial strains, which might have differing effects on human health.
“The next step is to move from cross-sectional associations toward longitudinal and prospective studies,” Zhao said. “We would like to determine whether these brain-body signatures can predict future cognitive trajectories and whether they change in response to modifiable factors or interventions. More broadly, we are interested in expanding beyond the brain-gut axis toward a more integrated view of brain-body aging. Emerging research suggests that brain function is also closely related to cardiovascular physiology and other organ systems.”
“In future studies, we hope to combine brain imaging with cardiac imaging, physiological signals such as ECG and PPG, and molecular measurements to better understand how aging processes across different organ systems interact,” he added. “Ultimately, our goal is to identify multimodal biomarkers that explain why individuals age differently and may eventually help guide personalized strategies for maintaining brain health.”
An ECG records the heart’s electrical activity, while PPG uses light sensors, like those in many smartwatches, to track pulse and blood flow.
Studying these processes over time could help scientists develop interventions to maintain brain health during middle age. “I think an important broader message is that brain aging is unlikely to be a process that begins suddenly in old age,” Zhao concluded. “Individual differences in brain network organization and their relationships with cognition and peripheral biology can already be observed much earlier in adulthood. Understanding these earlier differences may eventually help us shift the focus from treating late-stage decline toward identifying trajectories of brain health before substantial impairment develops.”
The study, “Brain-gut crosstalk associated with brain ageing in young and mid-life adults: a multicohort cross-sectional study,” was authored by Kanhao Zhao, Gabriel A. Vignolle, Jennifer S. Labus, Emeran A. Mayer, Allison Vaughan, Marika Dy, Priten Vora, Ming W. Hung, Keith Vossel, Chris Gill, Daniele Del Rio, Catherine Stanton, R. Paul Ross, John F. Cryan, Rima Kaddurah-Daouk, Yu Zhang, and Arpana Church.

Leonardo DRS wins place on US counter drone contract
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:00:20 BST
19:00:20 KST

Leonardo DRS has been awarded an indefinite delivery, indefinite quantity contract with a ceiling of 500 million dollars and a three-year period of performance by Joint Interagency Task Force 401, giving it the right to compete for orders to field counter drone sensing equipment to American forces, according to the company.
The arrangement covers the rapid delivery of integrated counter uncrewed aircraft system sensing capabilities supporting force protection and low altitude air defence, with task orders competed over the life of the contract.
John Baylouny, president and chief executive officer of Leonardo DRS, said: “Today’s threat environment is evolving faster than ever, and our customers need proven capabilities delivered at operational speed. This JIATF IDIQ positions DRS to accelerate the delivery of integrated C-UAS sensing technologies through rapid fielding of operationally relevant capabilities that help protect forces and strengthen low-altitude air defense as new threats emerge.”
Max Cohen, senior vice president and general manager at the Leonardo DRS RADA Technologies business unit, said: “Our counter UAS and air defense radars have demonstrated proven detection, tracking, and force protection performance in operational environments. We design, manufacture, and deliver combat-proven sensing systems at speed, and we’re ready now to support JIATF with mission-ready expeditionary radar capability that can be fielded rapidly as operational needs for C-UAS evolve.”
The award is one of ten made under an effort the American side calls Domestic Shield, aimed at protecting prioritised military facilities and assets inside the United States from drones. Combined ceilings across the ten run to roughly 4.15 billion dollars. Seven firms, including RADA Technologies, hold awards at the 500 million dollar level, alongside Allen Control Systems, Digital Force Technologies, DroneShield, Napatree Technology, SRC and L3Harris WESCAM. Echodyne and PVP Advanced EO Systems hold 250 million dollar awards and SmartShooter 150 million.
The task force is directed by Brigadier General Matt Ross. Brent Ingraham, Assistant Secretary of the Army for Acquisition, Logistics and Technology, said the multi-vendor marketplace enforces strict open architecture standards, which is the mechanism intended to let new sensors and effectors be swapped in as the threat changes.
Orders under the arrangement have already started moving. SRC received a first delivery order worth 10.24 million dollars for one Gryphon R1440 and two R1540 radars with integration, installation, support and training.
RADA came to Leonardo DRS through the merger with the Israeli radar maker RADA Electronic Industries in 2021, and its compact active electronically scanned array radars are widely used for short range air defence and counter rocket, artillery and mortar work, including on American vehicle-mounted systems. Leonardo DRS is the American arm of the Italian group Leonardo and trades on Nasdaq.
