Human Judgement Is the Most Powerful Technology in the AI Age
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:00:03 UTC
19:00:03 KST

In Ukraine, a Russian drone guided by artificial intelligence killed three civilians at a gas station, including a 19-year-old university student. In Gaza, an AI-assisted intelligence tool helped Israeli forces locate a Hamas commander. The subsequent airstrike killed him and, according to independent estimates, at least 125 other people.
Different wars. Different circumstances. But a deeply troubling question: As machines become more involved in decisions of life and death, are we losing sight of the human beings whose lives hang in the balance?
That question brought me back this month to a small white house in Reykjavík, Iceland.
Forty years ago, Ronald Reagan and Mikhail Gorbachev met at Höfði House, representing rival nuclear superpowers divided by decades of distrust. They left without an agreement. Yet their willingness to talk, listen, and imagine what had seemed impossible helped lay the groundwork for historic nuclear arms reductions.
I remember that moment vividly. I was a young Icelandic exchange student living in the United States, watching two world leaders meet in my small home country. I could never have imagined that 40 years later, as President of Iceland, I would return to that same house to ask a new generation of leaders to find the courage to talk.
The enduring lesson of Reykjavík is not simply about nuclear weapons or diplomacy. It is about the extraordinary power of human connection and dialogue. And we urgently need to remember it.
Never have we possessed more sophisticated tools to communicate, yet our ability to understand one another seems increasingly fragile. We are connected across continents in milliseconds, but too often separated by fear, anger, and mistrust.
Our technologies can transform medicine, education, and human prosperity. Yet they can also accelerate conflict, undermine democracy, and challenge human control.
Crucial questions for the AI age
Thanks to new technologies like AI, our power has grown exponentially. But has our wisdom kept pace?
Over the past week, Iceland has explored that question not only through another conventional summit, but through a journey from remembrance to dialogue, and from dialogue to responsibility.
We began with a traveling exhibition from the Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum and the testimony of a survivor of the atomic bombing. More than 80 years later, she still vividly recalls what she describes as the sudden appearance of a thousand suns, followed by unimaginable destruction, decades of devastating illness, and the stigma endured by survivors. No discussion of nuclear deterrence should ever lose sight of the human lives behind those words.
We then confronted the promises and dangers of artificial intelligence with technology experts, including Tristan Harris and Aza Raskin. The central question was not simply what AI can do, but what we should allow it to do—and who gets to decide.
Perhaps the most important conversations, however, happened far from the conference halls.
Across Iceland, young people invited fellow citizens to put down their phones and sit together to discuss the future they want to create. Students, parents, grandparents, teachers, and neighbors talked about education, belonging, technology, nature, and peace.
The young people were not asking adults to arrive with all the answers. They wanted to be heard. To be taken seriously. To have a voice in decisions that will shape their lives long after today's leaders have left office.
They understood something we too often forget: decisions made far from the people they affect are rarely wise ones.
I found that both humbling and hopeful.
Because dialogue is more than exchanging opinions. At its best, it is an act of recognition: I see you. Your experience matters. Your future matters. Even when we disagree, we share responsibility for what comes next.
The demands of dialogue
The purpose of dialogue is not always consensus. It is connection. And connection is where trust begins. Without trust, even the most brilliant solutions struggle to take root.
We carried that spirit back to Höfði House, where leaders from politics, technology, science, business, and civil society gathered to ask what responsible leadership demands of us today.
The result was A Call from Reykjavík, signed by three women presidents and open to others who wish to join. It calls for meaningful human control over powerful technologies, insists that decisions about war and nuclear weapons remain firmly in human hands, and places peace and responsibility to future generations at the heart of leadership.
The following day, in a public conversation moderated by renowned journalist Christiane Amanpour, President Nataša Pirc Musar of Slovenia, former Irish President Mary Robinson and I reflected on the choices before humanity.
Forty years after two powerful men met in Reykjavík, three women—indeed, three world leaders—came together to continue the conversation. Not because women have all the answers. We do not. But because progress requires more voices, more perspectives, and a willingness to listen across differences. And because the future must never belong only to those who currently hold power.
I do not believe dialogue is a soft alternative to leadership. I believe it is one of its most demanding forms.
It takes courage to listen to someone with whom we profoundly disagree. Humility to acknowledge what we do not know. And strength to resist reducing complex human challenges to slogans, enemies, or simple answers.
Dialogue does not mean abandoning our values, excusing aggression, or accepting injustice. Nor is it a substitute for action. It is how we begin to build the trust and understanding that make lasting action possible.
AI-assisted warfare
The wars in Ukraine and Gaza remind us of the devastating human cost of conflict. AI-assisted warfare adds another dimension: the danger of placing ever greater distance between those making decisions and those living with their consequences.
We must not surrender human judgment, accountability, or conscience to machines.
But technology alone is not the problem, and technology alone cannot provide the answer. We also need stronger human infrastructure: relationships, institutions, shared values, and habits of cooperation that allow us to respond collectively to danger.
We must equip the next generation not only with technical skills, but with the deeply human capacities to shape our future: listening, critical thinking, empathy, courage, and collaboration. In an age of intelligent machines, these may be our most essential skills.
Iceland is a small nation. We cannot dictate the course of global affairs. But perhaps our size reminds us of something larger nations sometimes forget: no one can build a peaceful future alone.
Forty years ago, Reykjavík showed that even the deepest divisions need not determine our destiny. Today, we need a new Reykjavík moment. Not one confined to a single house, summit, or handful of world leaders.
We need it in parliaments and boardrooms, classrooms and communities, across generations and between nations in conflict. Wherever fear has replaced curiosity, wherever people have stopped listening, wherever power has outrun wisdom.
The world does not lack intelligence, information, or ambition. What we too often lack is the courage to truly connect.
Of course, dialogue alone will not save us. But without it, I struggle to see how we can save ourselves.
The future will not be shaped only by the power of our technology or our weapons, but by the quality of our conversations—and the courage of the choices that follow.
Fortunately, we still have time. And we still have each other.

Factory in Bangladesh that "redefines manufacturing architecture" wins RIBA International Prize

Factory in Bangladesh that "redefines manufacturing architecture" wins RIBA International Prize
A rug factory in Rangpur, Bangladesh, designed by Dhaka-based studio Nakshabid Architects to dismantle workplace hierarchies, has won the RIBA International Prize for 2026.
Named Green Field Factory, the project is the fifth winner of the biennial award, presented by the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA) to the world's best new building outside the UK.
Nakshabid Architects was praised by the RIBA jury for designing a factory that incorporates passive design principles and prioritises the wellbeing of its 5,000 employees.
"Green Field Factory redefines manufacturing architecture in South Asia and beyond," said RIBA president Christ Williamson.
"By putting people, wellbeing and their everyday experiences at its core and actively supporting its female workforce, it proves that thoughtful design can dismantle traditional hierarchies to create profound social and environmental change."
It was announced as the RIBA International Prize winner at the Stirling Prize ceremony in London last night. This year's prestigious Stirling Prize was given to Mary Duggan Architects and Ruff Architects for the Lion Green Road housing development in London.
Commissioned by rug manufacturer Karupannya Rangpur Limited, Green Field Factory is a seven-storey building surrounded by fields and small settlements.
Nakshabid Architects based the design on the traditional Bengali home, incorporating natural ventilation and biophilic design principles.
Courtyards, verandas, gardens and a monumental green facade were designed to let natural light and airflow into the building, minimising the need for mechanical systems.
Green Field Factory has one main entrance with two grand staircases for all workers, intended to challenge hierarchies in the workplace. This responds to other factories in the area that have separate entrances for factory workers and people in management roles.
Shared spaces in the factory provide areas for workers to take breaks and socialise. Other areas are designated to support workers' families and the wider community during the day and outside of working hours, including a rooftop daycare centre, on-site medical practice, grocery shop and prayer room.
A connection to nature is provided through low-maintenance planting throughout, which also supports insects and birds, while artwork and sculptures celebrate the role of women in the workplace, family and community.
"The project demonstrates the dissolution of architecture as a topological space, with a single-pointed focus on dismantling civilisational oppression and hierarchy, for woman and man alike," said grand jury chair Bijoy Jain.
"Through the simple gesture of two grand stairs as an equanimous shared portal, it transforms a space and symbol once reserved exclusively for the king of the region, as landlord and ruling class, and for the colonial power that pervaded the length and breadth of the country," he continued.
"The architect and owner shared how the women and men working in the factory would bring their families with pride to show them where they worked, and the women empowered in their self-reliance to take life and familial decisions on their own."
The RIBA International Prize is awarded biennially to a building that "demonstrates visionary, innovative thinking, and design excellence whilst making a distinct contribution for its users and within its physical context".
Green Field Factory was selected ahead of BRAC University in Bangladesh by WOHA, Z33 art museum in Belgium by Francesca Torzo Architetto and the renovation of Royale Belge in Belgium by Caruso St John Architects, Bovenbouw Architectuur and DDS+.
Alongside the International Prize, RIBA awarded this year's International Emerging Architect Award to Maker Architecten for its YIMBY residential project in Kortrijk, Belgium.
The project revamped 18 plots across a 1920's garden city neighbourhood, utilising reclaimed materials for new facades and creating communal green space.
In 2024, Peris + Toral Arquitectes won the RIBA International Prize for an "inclusive and sustainable" social housing project in Barcelona.

India’s mass voter purge is hollowing out democracy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:00:01 UTC
19:00:01 KST

India’s mass voter purge is hollowing out democracy
The SIR is disenfranchising marginalised communities and advancing the Hindu nationalist project.
Over the weekend, thousands of protesters demanding the resignation of India’s chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, faced mass detentions and a heavy police crackdown in New Delhi. The demonstrations, which have brought together youth activists and opposition parties, centre on the removal of more than 130 million names from India’s electoral rolls, raising profound questions about the state of Indian democracy.
The deletions are the result of the controversial Special Intensive Revision (SIR) undertaken by the Election Commission of India (ECI). The ECI periodically revises electoral rolls to add new voters and remove the names of those who have died or permanently moved away. The last intensive revision was completed in 2003-2004. What makes the current SIR unprecedented, however, is its scale, the arbitrariness and overreach of its procedures, and the mass disenfranchisement that has followed. The exercise has disproportionately affected Muslims, women, migrants and other marginalised communities while also raising questions about the legitimacy of the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party’s (BJP’s) electoral victories in Bihar and West Bengal.
Both the ECI and the ruling party have defended the exercise by using the language of “purification”. In a caste society, that rhetoric is deeply troubling but also revealing. The bureaucratic procedures and technological infrastructure underpinning the exercise barely mask its intention to create two classes of citizenship in India, one endowed with political voice through the right to vote and the other reduced to what the philosopher Giorgio Agamben calls “bare life”.
The SIR’s intent, procedures and outcomes reveal a sinister design: to maximise voter exclusions rather than enhance voter participation. This subverts the promise of universal adult suffrage, a cornerstone of India’s constitutional democracy. The ECI initially excluded the government-issued Aadhaar card from the list of documents accepted for voter verification during the SIR, supposedly because it was considered “overinclusive”. If that did not expose the exercise’s exclusionary intent, the ECI’s invention of the category “logical discrepancy” during the West Bengal SIR certainly did. This pseudo-legal innovation accounted for 2.7 million of the nearly 9 million names removed from electoral rolls in Bengal. The demand for educational certificates, land records, legacy documents and family trees as evidence also places a heavy burden on poor and marginalised voters, especially in regions still reeling under mass poverty, landlessness and rampant illiteracy. With the “burden of proof” shifted to ordinary voters, the SIR aims to achieve precisely what it set out to do: mass deletions and consequent disenfranchisement.
Customised apps and online forms, digitised electoral rolls and the requirement to upload scanned documents in prescribed formats are all presented as evidence of the SIR’s efficiency and objectivity. But this approach ignores the digital divide in a deeply unequal society. Technology does not operate outside relations of power. In fact, it often serves as a mechanism of control. The category of “logical discrepancy” relies on an AI-enabled application, ERONET (Electoral Roll Officers’ Network), which compares voters’ details with older electoral rolls and flags discrepancies in names and family relationships. The use of such centralised systems has also raised questions about who controls electoral data and how these discrepancies are assessed. Women are particularly vulnerable to these procedures. Many change their names or addresses after marriage and may lack the documents needed to establish links with older electoral records. The excessive exclusion of women demonstrates how ostensibly neutral technological procedures can reinforce existing inequalities and weaken people’s political voice.
The SIR’s purported neutrality is at odds with its effects, which fall heavily on the weak and the marginalised. Among religious minorities, Muslims across the country bear a particularly heavy burden of deletions. In Bengal, Muslims reportedly accounted for about 65 percent of the 2.7 million people removed from electoral rolls on grounds of “logical discrepancy”. With only 19 specially constituted tribunals to handle more than 3.8 million appeals, the corrective process in effect has remained inaccessible to many excluded voters. In Hyderabad, 1.94 million names were marked for deletion under the “absent, shifted, dead and duplicate” (ASDD) category. An estimated 40.7 percent of those entries appeared to belong to Muslim voters, compared with Muslims’ 30 percent share of the city’s population. In some constituencies in Hyderabad’s Old City, Muslims accounted for as much as 80 percent of the names marked for deletion. The pattern is repeated in the National Capital Region, Delhi, where nearly one-third of the existing electorate was missing from the draft SIR roll. Studies flag especially high rates of exclusion in areas with large minority and migrant populations and among residents of informal and unauthorised settlements. The disproportionate exclusion of Muslims suggests an ideological alignment between the SIR’s ostensibly impersonal bureaucracy and the social and political programme of the Hindu right.
As a political and ideological instrument, the exercise has proved to be doubly potent. Through mass deletion of voters from targeted social categories, such as Muslims, it has contributed to shrinking the electoral base of the BJP’s principal rivals. The elections in Bihar and Bengal after the SIR suggest a discernible pattern. In the 2020 Bihar Assembly elections, the Rashtriya Janata Dal (RJD)-led alliance lost to the BJP-led alliance by just 0.03 percentage points in vote share. In contrast, in the 2025 elections after the removal of 6.8 million names from the existing rolls and the addition of 2.1 million new voters, the BJP alliance’s lead increased to nearly 9 percentage points. Analysis of the 2026 Bengal Assembly elections also points to the decisive role SIR deletions played in the electoral outcome. The exercise disproportionately affected Muslim, migrant and poorer voters in districts where the BJP had historically struggled to gain support. In many constituencies won by the BJP, the number of deleted or disputed voters exceeded the party’s margin of victory.
Furthermore, the bureaucratic exercise reinforces the larger ideological project of a “pure Hindu” nation. It has also legitimised calls for the expulsion of “Rohingyas”, “infiltrators” and “Bangladeshis”, terms used as dog whistles for Muslims, helping to polarise elections along communal lines. Although Bengali Hindus and others also found their names removed from electoral rolls, the political messaging around the SIR in a communally charged election campaign cast Muslims as a suspect community, imperilling their civil and social rights. Predictably, the newly elected BJP governments in Bihar and Bengal moved to deny Public Distribution System benefits to those who found their names expunged from the electoral rolls.
The SIR is thus fuelled by the imagined spectre of a vile and illicit intruder who must be expelled to preserve the existing order. It follows the Supreme Court-supervised National Register of Citizens (NRC) in Assam, which left 1.9 million of the state’s residents, mostly Bengali speakers, essentially stateless. It also resembles the Citizenship Amendment Act of 2019, which introduced religiously differentiated access to citizenship, an affront to the republic’s secular structure. The recently established High-Level Committee on Demographic Change, mandated to assess demographic changes occurring across India due to “illegal infiltration” and “abnormal” population changes among “religious and social communities”, is cut from the same cloth. Ultimately, the SIR is one of several instruments at play to criminalise, disenfranchise and denationalise social groups and communities considered inimical to the Hindutva vision of an ethnic state.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

Jabra Enhance Select M3 Review (2026): A Big Price for Small Wins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Outstanding quality. Great noise control at lower volumes. Autofocus improvements are noticeable, if short of life-changing.
TIRED
The massive case desperately needs a redesign. Still very expensive. Poor streaming quality.
This fall, hearing-aid manufacturers have been busily rolling out new and improved devices en masse, including Jabra, a leading maker of direct-to-consumer, over-the-counter devices. The brand has replaced its entire product lineup with all-new gear, swiftly retiring the Jabra Enhance Select 700, 500, 300, and 50R, all of which were only a year or two old. Three new models replace them: Enhance Select M3, M2, and M1. Each of the M-series hearing aids looks and works about the same as the models from last year and the year before that. Most of the updates here happen under the hood—but even those changes are hardly extreme, as I learned with the M3 pair I tested.
Historically, a more expensive device has meant a slightly smaller chassis—not so with Jabra's new hearing aids. Each of the three new models weighs the same: 2.12 grams, give or take a few hundredths of a gram, depending on the ear tip you choose. While the M2 and M1 share an identical form factor, the M3 is a bit squatter in design, measuring a few millimeters shorter than its siblings. Even so, all three are virtually indistinguishable unless you look at the fine print. That is, unless you select the red model; it's an M3 giveaway, as the M1 and M2 aren't available in that color.
Jabra M1 on left, M3 on right
Photograph: Christopher Null
Taking the traditional form of behind-the-ear teardrops, the M3 aids feature a single button on the back. Various presses and holds let you use these buttons for power, volume adjustments, and environmental mode changes that work to varying degrees of usefulness. Even so, the device is among the best available right now.
Within Earshot
Photograph: Christopher Null
Jabra calls its audio enhancement system SoundScape, which launched last year and claims to reduce noise and improve overall speech clarity. SoundScape features are variably available across the three devices in the M line, and two new capabilities are exclusive to the M3. These include a revamped autofocus tool that “locks onto” speech in complex, noisy environments, like restaurants, which I found to be moderately effective. I experienced clean dialog, even when a conversation partner walked fully around me in a circle.
INSERT GROUP ASSET: IMG_3735 and IMG_3734
ScreenshotSoundScape app via Christopher Null
ScreenshotSoundScape app via Christopher Null
The other new SoundScape feature for the M3 is an advanced adaptive listening mode that's responsive to a given environment (whether a restaurant, outdoors, or several other options) in real time to optimize noise reduction. The environmental modes weren’t very useful; keeping the hearing aids in “all around” mode, then tweaking levels manually (especially noise reduction) was the best way to improve the hearing experience.
I tested the M3 hearing aids in a variety of settings and am pleased to report that they work just as well as previous Jabra generations. Clarity in quiet environments (like having a one-on-one conversation or watching television) was just about perfect. Keeping the volume at 30 percent maximized hearing improvement while minimizing hiss, which grows geometrically louder with each upward tick of volume level.
Bluetooth streaming quality has never been Jabra’s strong suit, and while these new devices support Auracast—which lets various audio sources broadcast directly to the hearing aid—I don't expect I’d use any of the streaming modes much. Overall streaming audio quality on the M3 offers a slight improvement from previous generations, but music and movie audio are both too washed out at any level below the highest volume. And any amount of ambient noise still kills the experience completely.
Programming on Demand
Photograph: Christopher Null
The app and other features in the new lineup remain remarkably similar to previous Jabra models. Jabra has a history of offering great customer service: All purchases include three years of access to on-staff audiologists who can make tuning adjustments live over video chat and train new users on their hearing aids. Jabra’s built-in self-test system also remains top-notch, allowing you to create an audiogram from scratch in just a few minutes.
Its massive case unfortunately hasn’t changed, providing three recharges of your spent hearing aids before it also needs to be plugged in. A fully charged pair of hearing aids still lasts for 24 hours, as specified. In fact, I got closer to 26 hours in my testing before I needed to power up.
Notably, pricing also remains consistent, with the M3 starting at $1,995—the same launch price as the Jabra 700 last year. If history is any guide, a few months of patience are likely to reward you with a $200 price cut, and Jabra coupons are available fairly regularly. It's still a big ask for a nonprescription product. But to be fair, you’d likely pay twice as much for a prescription aid that can match the quality of these latest M3s.
My bottom-line recommendation? If you can afford the two grand for the Jabra M3 hearing aids, you'll get the most advanced over-the-counter devices available. That said, those with more modest means will do nearly as well with the $1,695 M2 or $1,195 M1 hearing aids—or one of the even more affordable options featured in my Best Hearing Aids buying guide.

The New Fan’s Guide to the Unreal World of Nathan Fielder
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

There has been no shortage of coverage on Elizabeth Holmes, the Silicon Valley fraudster whose biotech startup Theranos reached a peak valuation of $9 billion in 2014 before its supposedly groundbreaking blood test machine was revealed to be vaporware. Books, magazine articles, documentaries, TV dramatizations—the exposés have piled up high.
So, you might ask yourself, why the hype for the forthcoming You Can See Everything, yet another documentary about Holmes, and one that spans three hours?
The excitement is thanks to Nathan Fielder, one of the film’s directors. (Fielder codirected the documentary with Lance Oppenheim). Fielder is a cult-favorite television auteur whose devotees have awaited his showdown with Holmes ever since rumors about him visiting her in prison surfaced last year.
Now that Fielder appears poised to break the containment of an obsessed fan base and conquer the cineplex, it behooves you to get caught up. This will not be a typical documentary: Fielder has made a career of heightened unreality, sowing confusion wherever he goes. To give you some notion of what to expect from his analysis of Holmes, here’s a rundown of his unusual and captivating style.
Business Bona Fides
One reason Fielder makes sense as an interlocutor for big tech’s most notorious con woman is his own history of corporate chicanery. In his breakout TV series Nathan for You (2013–2017), he contrived and implemented bizarre publicity stunts for struggling small businesses. (While he jokes that he “graduated from one of Canada's top business schools with really good grades,” the fact remains he did graduate, unlike Holmes, a Stanford University dropout.)
Andrew Bricker, an associate professor of English at the University of Ghent and academic coordinator for the research project Democratic Literacy and Humour, writes in an email that it’s important to recognize that, throughout his career, Fielder has always played the same altered version of himself, leaving us unsure just who he really is.
Fielder “has made the borderlands of persona and person so ambiguous, so indeterminable, so indefinable, that none of us is entirely in on the joke,” Bricker says.
Nathan for You and Fielder’s subsequent HBO series The Rehearsal, Bricker explains, cast him as “a kind of outlandish problem-solver, someone possessed of what I sometimes call the engineer’s brain, which sees the world strictly through the radically simplified framework of problems and solutions, even if the solutions themselves, ouroboros-style, always lead to new problems.”
Indeed, in his fixer role on Nathan for You, Fielder seeks out overcomplicated loopholes and goes to great lengths to carry out any particular scheme once he sets his mind to it. To help an international exporter avoid high shipping costs on smoke alarms, for example, he comes up with a plan to market them as musical instruments. Then he creates an instructional DVD on how to play one, forms a band that records an original track that includes the device’s shrill beeping, and gets the song featured on the local news, all to legitimize the tariff dodge.
Fielder’s Nathan for You promotions involved careful readings of pertinent laws in order to skirt liability—he went viral by opening a coffee shop called Dumb Starbucks—as well as clever hoaxes and media manipulation. He staged a video of a pig saving a goat from drowning in a pond at a petting zoo, successfully tricking social media users and news stations into thinking it was real, and founded Summit Ice, a nonprofit winter apparel brand that stands against Holocaust denial, which earned it mainstream exposure.
Holmes, of course, played investors and the press for years with savvy PR, styling herself as the next coming of Steve Jobs in order to hype a bogus advance in medical science. If there’s anyone who can grasp the scope and scale of duplicity it took to make the world believe in a nonexistent product, it’s Fielder.
Awkward, Maybe Neurodivergent … and Mean?
Early in his career, Fielder tackled the business world with a recurring spot on the satirical CBC Television news show This Hour Has 22 Minutes. His segment, “Nathan on Your Side,” was a send-up of local consumer advocacy investigations and an early showcase for Fielder’s deadpan humor, as seen in a 2008 report where he role-plays as a customer at an electronics store and invites a salesman to pitch him on an MP3 player but continually dismisses these efforts because he is “just browsing.”
Throughout Nathan for You and The Rehearsal, Fielder has relied on this discomfiting affect to maximize the awkwardness of his conversations with everyone he encounters. Although polite and unassuming—many of his fellow Canadians relate—he lets heavy silences linger, maintains uncomfortable eye contact, and never quite breaks, no matter how funny a situation may be. Fielder also has a knack for flatly echoing what someone else has told him in a way that underscores its absurdity.
With these tics, Bricker says, Fielder often catches his interview subjects off guard, spurring them to blurt out surprising confessions.
Holmes is an ideal target for this poker-faced approach. Kate Rennebohm, a professor of film at Lawrence University, has written about the ethics and artifice of HBO’s The Rehearsal, which follows Fielder as he constructs elaborate simulations of pivotal life events in order to better understand human behavior. Rennebohm writes in an email that Holmes the fraudster represents something like an ultimate test of Fielder’s methods.
Holmes is, according to Rennebohm, “a woman whose infamy rests solely on her apparent ability to totally disregard reality.” For this reason, Rennebohm expects Fielder’s skills as a performer and instigator “will get perhaps their most strenuous exercise yet in this match.”
Bricker says that “we are about to witness a bizarro-land Frost/Nixon, where both interviewer and subject have almost exclusively inhabited semi-fictional personae in public”—Fielder as a mad social scientist, Holmes as an inventor ahead of her time.
But while Holmes may be deserving of invasive scrutiny, some critics are unable to stomach how Fielder incorporates unwitting, ordinary people into his satirical plots, occasionally allowing them to look somewhat foolish or flustered while he remains unflappable. Just as your appetite for “cringe” comedy will determine whether you laugh at the scenarios Fielder orchestrates, the shows have turned into litmus tests on questions of conscience and empathy. Does he take advantage of the working-class folks and background performers drawn into his elaborate web of control, or is he merely reflecting a dysfunctional society back to us?
This tension, along with Fielder’s preoccupations and overall demeanor, have occasioned plenty of speculation around whether he has ever been diagnosed with a mental condition. The Rehearsal has led to viewers theorizing that Fielder is on the autism spectrum or otherwise neurodivergent. Fielder acknowledged this discourse in the second season of the show and underwent an fMRI brain scan that could have pointed toward such a diagnosis, though he did not divulge the results.
Others have thrown the word “sociopath” around when discussing Fielder’s work, but not always in a negative sense. As one X user recently noted in a post anticipating You Can See Everything: “Nathan Fielder doing a movie about how Elizabeth Holmes is a deceptive sociopath feels exactly like when Dexter takes down a worse serial killer.”
Unpredictable Anthropology
Even starting from the simplest premise, Fielder ventures into strange territory. In a Nathan for You episode in which he counsels a realtor to employ a psychic medium to ensure that the homes she’s selling aren’t haunted, she drops the bombshell that she was once choked by a ghost in Switzerland. In another, Fielder has a gas station owner advertise impossibly cheap prices, attainable only through a hilariously inconvenient rebate process. Yet the memorable part of the segment is when the business owner reveals that he drinks his grandson’s urine when he feels scared.
Fielder often follows up on peculiar discoveries, allowing people’s eccentricities and the unintended consequences of his own meddling to dictate where he goes next. As such, there’s an investigative element to his process that is certainly appropriate when dealing with an enigma like Holmes, a convicted criminal who continues to proclaim her innocence with a cheery warmth that comes off like utter self-delusion.
In 2023, Fielder and Oppenheim, the codirectors of You Can See Everything, moved into the Del Mar, California, house shared by Holmes and her partner, Billy Evans. The group lived together in the house for over a month, right up until the day Holmes reported to prison for her 11-year sentence. They weren’t sure if what they were shooting could be turned into a movie, but as Fielder said at the New York Film Festival last month, a sense of deepening mystery compelled them to move forward.
“Lance and I would talk about what we thought happened there, and we’d completely disagree on … what we thought was happening,” he explained. “And we were like, ‘Oh, this is really interesting, if we can’t agree on what’s happening, there’s something here.’”
Fielder has “a remarkable talent” for using those frictions to twist and expand his narrative, Rennebohm says. She cites The Rehearsal's second season, which is inspired by Fielder’s theory about how the breakdown in communication between airline pilots and copilots can lead to deadly accidents. In order to act out his model of cockpit cooperation, he spends two years earning a commercial license for himself, ultimately flying a Boeing 737 full of actors (all of whom have scripted roles to perform while aboard) from San Bernardino, California, to the Nevada border and back.
When it comes to Fielder following a thread as far as he can, Rennebohm says, “I expect this document of his time with Holmes to be no different.”
The Search for Reality
What has emerged in Fielder’s most recent output might be described as anxiety over the nature of truth.
The Rehearsal (2022–present) is, on its face, a setup to explore the way we conduct ourselves under destabilizing circumstances. In the first season, Fielder concocts a scene where a man can practice confessing to his bar trivia team that he lied about having a master’s degree. For the rest of the season, Fielder is consumed by an elaborate, multi-episode experiment in which a woman evaluates what life would be like as a mother, aided by child actors (and Fielder serving as her platonic coparent).
Yet there are countless moments when Fielder is more concerned with the authenticity of these staged interactions—and their ongoing failure to fully match reality—than their potential outcomes. The actual subject of the show, we learn, is his fanatical mode of observation.
Fielder is often shown walking around with a laptop attached to his torso with a harness so he can take notes on the move. He catches the smallest inaccuracies and oversights, and he tweaks the next reproduction accordingly. He intuits the psychological dissonance of pretending to do something instead of really doing it, and he has frank interviews with his cast and consultants in hopes of closing those gaps.
The Rehearsal, according to Rennebohm, “offers the fictionalized Nathan the chance to substitute manufactured, seemingly controllable realities for the reality of his actual life, though often even these fabricated scenarios ultimately resist Nathan's totalitarian drives.”
Bricker points out that the fundamental “paradox” of Fielder’s “supposed revelations of truth” is that he only arrives at his conclusions through his constructed persona and meticulous simulations. “Even if these are true moments of authentic self-disclosure, how would we even know, given the artificial framework of their disclosure?” he asks.
But that, too, makes You Can See Everything a fascinating proposition. Bricker notes that Fielder and Oppenheim are in a position to play with the “mushy boundaries between reality and fiction” through dramatic reconstruction, stylization, and careful editing.
Rennebohm says that Holmes also serves as an avatar of a tech industry with ambitions of exceeding or dispensing human reality itself. In this and so many other ways, a face-off between Fielder and the disgraced startup founder is the collision of an unstoppable force and an immovable object. All you can do is brace for impact.

Why is France Burning?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

The French like to take to the streets, and they do it often.
On Sept. 17, students at Lycée Saint-Exupéry, a rather underprivileged high school in the Paris suburb of Créteil, erupted in protest over the abysmal conditions of their institution: chronic shortfall of teachers, poor facilities, long declining quality of education. Two weeks later, a wave of protests had swept cities across France. Students from hundreds of schools and scores of universities joined the protests, backed by their parents, teachers, and trade unions. More than 160,000 students and trade unionists protested across France on Tuesday in the third week of demonstrations.
France has never seen so many violent incidents in a movement made up largely of high school students. So far, over 200 students, 85 school staff, and 700 police officers have been injured in clashes across the country. Protesters have broken into schools and, in some cases, set fire to occupied or blockaded buildings. On Oct. 5, a 15-year-old boy had his hand blown off by a police grenade during a protest in Lens in northern France, an incident that crystallized the heavy-handed response authorities had adopted from the earliest days of the protest. More than 6,000 protesters have been arrested, most of them minors, and later released without charge.
The protests erupted after nearly a decade of Macronisme, the right-of-center, top-down governing style that President Emmanuel Macron of France incarnates. And they express a broader discontent: anger over disparities in school quality, university admissions decisions, and latent racial discrimination, and a sense among young people that those in power were not listening to them, that the country offered them little hope for the future.
The protests are also occurring amid a wider crisis of political confidence in the country. France is holding its presidential elections in April 2027, and the far-right and far-left are leading the opinion polls. The frontrunner is Marine Le Pen, who has worked for years to make her far-right party, the National Rally, more electable while campaigning on immigration, crime, and denunciation of an out-of-touch political class. Her party is already the largest opposition party in parliament, and a snap legislative election following the presidential vote could entrench it further.
On the other side is Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the leader of France Unbowed, a far-left party, who is promising a sweeping redistribution of power and resources toward the working class. Both have built much of their appeal on opposition to the political establishment, the promise to wish away budget constraints, and deep hostility toward the European Union.
If France today feels like it is at a crossroads, it is because it is. The postwar model of a large welfare and regulatory state, run by a class of civil servants charged with modernizing the economy, tempering market forces and defining the common good, has run its course.
The collapse of postwar France
France now runs one of Europe’s largest budget deficits: its public debt stands at 119.3 % of GDP and is expected to rise next year. Fears of a crippling financial crisis are growing. Borrowing costs have risen so high that France is drawing comparisons with Greece, whose debt crisis in 2010 threatened the survival of the Eurozone. And with economic growth stagnating, there is no easy way out.
If anything, France would need to spend more: on defense, as Russia grows more threatening, the war in Ukraine continues, and the United States retreats from its traditional role as Europe’s security guarantor; on new technologies, as the country that once produced Concorde and high-speed trains now trails in high-tech innovation and AI; on strained public services, from schools to hospitals to neglected neighborhoods; and on infrastructure capable of withstanding the growing effects of climate change.
Successive French governments have promised to turn things around and allow for these badly needed investments in the country’s future, but none has succeeded.
The French malaise goes deeper. Inequality has been one of the students’ central grievances. They are not wrong. As in many countries, economic inequalities in France have widened over the past two decades under the combined effects of globalization, industrial decline, and the growing concentration of inherited wealth.
In Capital in the Twenty-First Century, the French economist Thomas Piketty showed how wealth perpetuates across generations and widens the divide between those who own capital and everyone else. This concentration of wealth and power remains deeply resented: for many, President Macron’s original sin is still his brief stint at the Rothschild investment bank before entering politics.
But the most injurious form of inequality lies elsewhere: in the power of France’s national meritocratic myth, which holds that people broadly owe their social position largely to their academic performance. At the top of that system sit the highly competitive grandes écoles, the elite institutions of higher education that have produced leaders in politics, culture, and business.
What makes the myth so corrosive is not that academic achievement goes unrewarded but that it remains a pretty reliable path to better jobs, higher status, and positions of power. In such a system, students from underfunded public schools face a profound disadvantage compared with peers who attend better-resourced schools and whose better-educated parents know how to navigate the system.
Private schools offer another route, but are still frowned upon as a way to buy an advantage. It is no surprise that the protests broke out in Créteil, a working-class suburb just outside Paris, where schools are chronically under-resourced.
We shall always have Paris
Racial and geographic discrimination also contribute to the crisis of France. The collection of ethno-racial statistics is prohibited by French law; it is a laudable restriction in principle but problematic in practice. Visible minorities remain vastly underrepresented among France’s political and business elites.
Families with immigrant backgrounds, many with roots in African and Asian countries once colonized by France, are disproportionately concentrated on urban peripheries, where jobs are scarce and residents often face discrimination from employers elsewhere.
Islamophobia has also grown over the last decade amid conflicts in the Middle East and a string of Islamist-inspired terrorist attacks. Rhetoric once largely confined to the far right has seeped into the mainstream right, where calls for “order” and “security” often carry an anti-immigrant charge. Macron’s references to the “decivilization” of some young people and former Interior Minister Bruno Retailleau’s description of immigrants’ participation in the protests that followed the police killing of a teenager in 2023 as a “regression towards ethnic origins” are emblematic of that shift.
There is another problem with France’s meritocratic ideal: Paris. Political power, economic opportunity, cultural prestige, and elite education remain extraordinarily concentrated in the capital. The result is a deep economic divide between Paris and the rest of the country and an elite that lives largely among its own, surrounded by people with similar educations, careers, and assumptions, and cut off from much of the country.
The Yellow Vest revolt of 2018 to 2019 was an earlier social explosion of precisely that resentment. It is hardly surprising that students are denouncing the unequal distribution of resources between Paris and the rest of the country, or that the protests began in Créteil, close enough to the capital for the contrast to be impossible to miss.
When students from my own former school, the elite Lycée Henri-IV, where I was a rather poor student, joined the movement in its third week, I noticed how carefully they described themselves as protesting “in solidarity” with less privileged schools. They knew which side of the divide they were on. So much for meritocracy.
Racing to the Elysée
Where does this leave France? With the presidential elections approaching next April, political parties are scrambling to position themselves in relation to a protest movement that has shown no sign of abating. On Oct. 6, more than a quarter-million people took to the streets as high school students were joined by university students, teachers, parents and trade unions. An even wider “national day of protest” is planned for Oct. 17.
Both familiar and new dynamics will shape the election. The familiar one is the runoff dilemma: voters may once again be asked to support a candidate from the opposite political camp simply to prevent Le Pen from reaching the Élysée. Le Pen made the runoff in both 2017 and 2022 and is leading the polls by a large margin. This time, however, the field trailing her is unusually fragmented. Two former prime ministers under Macron, Édouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal, are in the race; Philippe is competing with Mélenchon for second place, while Attal trails both.
Whatever the outcome, the presidential vote may resolve little. A president from the far-right National Rally could find herself governing without a stable parliamentary majority or broad support among the public or within the civil service. A compromise candidate from the center or left could face the same fractured parliament that has bedeviled the final years of Macron’s presidency, during which France has had five prime ministers in two years.
What is new is the extent to which France is being reshaped by forces now familiar across the globe: a crisis of confidence in democracy, conservative billionaires building media empires and financing ideological movements, polarizing social media, foreign interference in elections, and growing voter distrust of supranational institutions, including the European Union.
France, unlike the United States, places strict limits on campaign spending, but money still shapes the broader political ecosystem. Pierre-Édouard Stérin, a self-described “conservative libertarian,” has committed substantial resources to organizations seeking to advance right-wing and far-right agendas. The industrialist Vincent Bolloré has assembled a vast media empire that includes CNews, a Fox News-style channel that has become an important platform for the nationalist right.
Europe on the line
Whatever the result of the Presidential elections, the outlook is troubling for Europe. A Le Pen or Mélenchon presidency would test European cohesion on everything from Ukraine and relations with Russia to migration, budgets, and the authority of the European Union. But even a more centrist president would likely lack a strong enough coalition to govern effectively, mirroring the current situation in Germany, where Chancellor Friedrich Merz is hobbled by unpopularity and a surge in support for the far-right Alternative for Deutschland.
With France and Germany together accounting for roughly 40% of the E.U. economy, political weakness in both capitals would deprive Europe of its traditional engine at a particularly dangerous moment. Europe faces mounting pressure on three fronts: China’s industrial onslaught, reflected in an annual trade deficit of roughly €360 billion; Russia’s war against Ukraine and escalating “gray warfare” operations; and the American turn against the postwar international order on which Europe has long depended. All this comes as Europe must also prepare for the profound disruptions of climate change and AI.
The remedy laid out by Mario Draghi, famed for rescuing the euro during his tenure as president of the European Central Bank, calls for greater integration of the single market, more investment and industrial consolidation, and a greater capacity to act collectively. France is indispensable to any such reforms. A politically paralyzed France would leave Europe weaker at precisely the moment when it can least afford it.
The revolution still to come
At the heart of the French Revolution of 1789 was the abolition of the privileges of the aristocracy and clergy. Close to two and a half centuries later, privilege remains deeply embedded in French society, dispersed across an array of almost caste-like social and professional groups, from journalists, lawyers, and intellectuals to civil servants and unionized workers, each with its own advantages, protections, pension arrangements, and claims on state resources. The result is a politics in which almost everyone agrees that reform is urgently needed, provided someone else pays, and their own group’s advantages remain untouched.
If this sounds like an overreading of 1789, consider Macron’s own choice of title for the book that launched his presidential bid: Révolution. His presidency may not have proved entirely revolutionary, yet many of his larger prescriptions have aged well: governments around the world have embraced state-led industrial policy, greater strategic autonomy, and reduced dependence on fossil fuels, while distrust of American hegemony and calls for deeper European integration have gained traction as the postwar order fragments.
Macron can also claim some credit for preserving, and in places renewing, France’s traditional strengths: an electricity system powered largely by nuclear energy, global leadership in luxury goods, tourism and hospitality, and a deep reservoir of scientific talent, now exemplified by Mistral, Europe’s closest thing to a world-class AI contender.
A skilled diplomat and relentless advocate for the multilateral system, Macron has also taken principled stands on Ukraine, Gaza, Lebanon, debt relief for the world’s poorest countries, and climate change, while carefully navigating France’s relationships with America and China. France’s permanent seat on the U.N. Security Council gives it diplomatic weight far beyond the country’s economic size, a status French diplomats ironically describe as “flying first class on an economy ticket.”
Yet neither these prescriptions nor these assets have been enough to reverse France’s decline over the past two decades. Perhaps what has been missing is a revolution not so much in policy as in political culture: a new social compact in which the sacrifices required to adjust to France’s reduced means and diminished relative power are accepted because the burdens are seen to be shared fairly. If such a revolution is to come, it is less likely to start in the Élysée or the ministries than among the students in the streets demanding to be heard.

Press review: Russian asset grab back on EU agenda and Starlink or no, Ukraine to fight on

MOSCOW, October 16. /TASS/. This week's EU summit returns to the idea of seizing Russian assets; facing threats of being cut off from Starlink, Ukraine makes other plans; and what is the future of the US Green Card Lottery. These stories topped Friday's newspaper headlines in Russia.
Izvestia: EU revisits idea of confiscating Russian assets at summit
The EU opened a two-day summit in Brussels on October 15. For the first time since the special military operation began, the Europeans postponed discussions on Ukraine to the second day of the event as they decided to discuss the European Union’s new budget for 2028-2034 first. Earlier, the European Commission (EC) proposed a bloated budget of €1.76 trillion.
Meanwhile, European auditors are ringing alarm bells about the growing debt, which could climb to €1 trillion by 2027 and cause a "hole" in the current budget. Moreover, all EU economies are struggling amid the energy crisis around the situation in the Strait of Hormuz.
The problem is also aggravated by Kiev's growing demands. According to the draft budget, the EC proposed allocations of up to €88.8 billion for 2028-2034.
However, there is no extra money, and the EU is now coming back to the idea of using frozen Russian assets by transferring them to a special European structure to finance Ukraine further down the road. "This idea is being considered and revisited," French member of the European Parliament Thierry Mariani told Izvestia. "Belgium, which holds the bulk of these funds, dissuaded its partners from putting that idea into practice in December, and the EU eventually agreed a €90 billion loan. Today, Kiev insists that this issue be reconsidered," he noted. "As regards Belgium, it considers this idea crazy as Moscow could immobilize European assets in response," Mariani warned.
Today, the likelihood of using these assets for a loan to Ukraine is extremely low. Such a step would require absolute unanimity within the European Union, Mikhail Vedernikov, a senior researcher at the Institute of Europe of the Russian Academy of Sciences, explained to Izvestia. However, some leaders, including Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico, have openly opposed this initiative and promised to block it. Nevertheless, Slovakia will hold an early election in 2027, with Fico’s positions assessed as quite weak. If left-liberal politicians who support the policy course pursued by Brussels come to power in Bratislava, a decision on assets may well be made in a year, the expert concluded.
Apart from Russia’s assets, European bureaucrats will discuss additional restrictions on Moscow. According to Politico, the EU is planning to call for more restrictions on Russian oil exports in the summit communique. Earlier, Brussels approved a 22nd sanctions package, blacklisting hundreds of new Russian individuals, lenders and oil tankers. However, the EU’s sanctions policy cannot affect Russia’s policy on Ukraine, Mariani argued. "This shows that this sanctions policy does not work and only leads to impoverishing the population," the politician maintained.
Nezavisimaya Gazeta: Ukraine ready to push ahead amid potential Starlink cutoff
Tensions between Kiev and Washington will seemingly escalate after Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky said that the Ukrainian armed forces will continue to target Russian oil refineries. Earlier, according to media reports, the Americans warned Kiev that the United States would in that case "immediately" cancel intelligence sharing, cut off the Starlink satellite internet system, and halt military aid.
Even as this has not happened yet, the possibility remains, observers say. Therefore, the Zelensky regime is apparently preparing to wage combat against Russia without support from the United States, relying on NATO’s European allies and the EU instead. This slightly increases Russia’s chances of achieving the objectives of its special military operation and defeating the enemy faster. Whether things progress that way - only time will tell.
A recent remark from SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has been making the rounds in the media and with pundits, after the billionaire called on Zelensky to resign, otherwise "the slaughter" would continue. The call came after almost identical statements from US President Donald Trump.
"It is Musk who owns the rights to Starlink, therefore he can de facto influence Ukraine’s defensive capabilities," retired Lieutenant-General Yury Netkachev, a military expert, told Nezavisimaya Gazeta. According to him, with the diesel deal and ambitions to ease sanctions on Russia, Trump has provided Moscow with an opportunity not only to improve its economic situation but also buttress its position in negotiations to end the conflict.
However, Netkachev warned, one should not be lulled into a false sense of security by this "friendly" position of the current US administration, for Trump’s foreign policy options could be significantly curtailed following the Congressional election, and the US political elite may return to supporting Ukraine.
Meanwhile, Kiev's intelligence situation isn't all lost without the US. "Two-thirds of the intelligence received by Ukraine come from European countries, primarily France," French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot told France Inter. According to him, among other things, European countries share satellite images that Kiev uses to detect targets. His remark came amid reports that the US has threatened to limit information sharing because of strikes on Russian oil refineries. Barrot also said the Europeans provide the bulk of support for Ukraine. The EU has recently transferred €6 billion to Kiev, he added.
Vedomosti: Odds US brings back Green Card Lottery
The US State Department was ordered to reopen the Green Card Lottery by October 18 and publicly announce the registration dates on its official platforms. The order came from a US federal judge in California, according to the court’s database updated on Wednesday night. Registration will remain open for 30 days, in line with the court order. In other words, anyone who wants to can enter the 2027 drawing.
The issue reverberated after the Trump administration formally refused to open registration citing delays, even as back in November 2025 the US Department of State shared plans to reopen registration for the 2027 fiscal year running from October 1, 2026 on its website.
It is worth noting that the Green Card Lottery is a mandatory process, as Congress authorizes the allocation of up to 55,000 such documents annually to foreign citizens. However, only a portion of all available Green Cards are distributed through the lottery, not all of them. According to the US Department of State’s website, 20.8 million people applied for the 2026 program, from which 129,516 individuals were selected. Among Africans registered for the DV-2026 Diversity Visa Program, the bulk was from Algeria (5,457 applicants), Afghanistan led all Asian countries with 4,200, the Bahamas - North America with 23, 599 Australians led the way for Oceania, and 1,596 Peruvians from South America. Russia led all European countries with 5,510 registered and selected applicants, followed by Ukraine with 5,283.
Even as the DV-2026 program was mandated by federal law enacted by Congress, the Trump administration effectively delayed the start of the registration process, Marina Chernykh, a research fellow at the Institute for US and Canadian Studies of the Russian Academy of Sciences, explained to Vedomosti. According to her, the California court ruled that the US State Department provide an opportunity for applications to be submitted, whereas the federal government insisted that it is no longer possible to carry out the program as originally intended now that the established deadlines have passed. The Trump administration has the right to appeal the ruling at the US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit. Filing an appeal would not automatically nullify the court ruling as a separate court decision will be required for that. The case could eventually be taken to the US Supreme Court, the expert noted.
"And the US Supreme Court is highly likely to rule in Trump’s favor as the majority of judges there are conservative. At the same time, it cannot be assumed that the administration can simply ignore the ruling as it was handed down by a court of first instance," the expert concluded.
Rossiyskaya Gazeta: Archaic Russia-EU partnership agreement clashes with present-day antagonism
The agreement on partnership and cooperation concluded between Russia and the European Union signed more than three decades ago makes little practical sense after Brussels openly declared Russia its opponent and adversary, said participants in a round table discussion at the Federation Council on Thursday.
The EU has essentially transformed into an anti-Russian military bloc, Rossiyskaya Gazeta quoted Grigory Karasin, chairman of the upper chamber’s Committee on International Affairs, as saying. There have been statements from European politicians, including Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski or European Commissioner for Defense Andrius Kubilius, about preparations for war with Russia in 2029-2030.
The matter is not limited to rhetoric only as Sweden and Finland have joined NATO, EU countries are sharply increasing their defense expenditure, military construction has been expedited, and exercises to simulate scenarios of a blockade of the Kaliningrad Region and Russia’s Baltic seaports are held near national borders.
Karasin also pointed to the EU’s expansion plans at the expense of Moldova, Ukraine and Armenia. At that, the senator emphasized, Russia is not threatening European countries nor is it planning to do so, while the European people seem to agree, as evidenced by the rising popularity of opposition parties in Germany and France.
The EU has undergone a major evolution, Federation Council Deputy Speaker Konstantin Kosachev argued. Originally a purely economic association, the EU is increasingly mulling militarization, including its own army. "Never before has there been a single international organization built on regional economic integration that set establishing an army as its goal. This is a first," Kosachev noted. "The idea of militarization has completely consumed the minds of European politicians, who have also embraced extreme Russophobic rhetoric," he added.
Kosachev commented on the Partnership and Cooperation Agreement, which was signed in 1994 and entered into force in 1997. He singled out Article 55 as the most objectionable part of the document which envisaged the unilateral harmonization of Russian laws with European ones. "Thank God, this article--along with all the other provisions of the agreement--has been frozen," he said. The agreement’s initial ten-year term expired in 2007 and it has been automatically renewed on an annual basis ever since until one of the parties provides written notice to the contrary. "It has lost any practical meaning. The EU has openly declared us its adversary and enemy, while the agreement envisages partnership and cooperation," Kosachev maintained.
Vedomosti: Russia could step in to meet Africa's growing electricity needs
African countries are facing electricity shortages even as they have enough oil and gas and capabilities to generate power from renewables. Key obstacles include a lack of capital and grid weaknesses. Russian technology could be in demand in the fields of nuclear-and natural gas-based power generation, hydropower and energy-related engineering, but prospects here depend on project economics and the specific needs of certain countries. Russian and African experts told Vedomosti which areas of partnership can yield a long-term effect and what has prevented a transformation from individual supplies to complex projects.
Today, African countries need to supply electricity to a growing population, their industries, transport, and digital economy, Alexey Maslov, a professor and director of the Institute of Asian and African Studies at Lomonosov Moscow State University, noted. While many of these countries possess gas, oil, and coal reserves, along with potential for hydropower, solar, and wind energy generation, the mere availability of such resources does not guarantee a stable supply, he argued.
According to Nikita Panin, an expert at the analytical department at the HSE Centre for African Studies, countries with a developed industrial base need large-scale power generation. Meanwhile, the need for localized power generation is already reflected in projects currently under discussion between Russian companies and their African partners. There is no universal solution for the continent as the specifics of each country require an individual approach, he explained.
As African partners view it, technology transfer should be accompanied with the development of local competences, Anna Abaho, a senior lecturer in international relations and security research at Nkumba University in Uganda, told Vedomosti. She linked Russian-Ugandan cooperation to industrial electrification, food production, irrigation and refrigeration of agricultural products. The country needs engineers and technical specialists capable of maintaining the equipment for that, she said.
A transition to purer energy does not mean Africa will abandon traditional sources in the next few years. The continent is expanding access to electricity amid the rising demand from industries, transport, and cities. For this reason, a variety of technologies, ranging from gas and hydropower to solar generation, energy storage, and nuclear projects, will be needed in the energy mix, Maslov argued.
