China-North Korea border bridge may do little to spur trade, experts say
Sanctions and a North Korean leadership that prioritises security dim prospects for economic cooperation, analysts say.
As China and North Korea cut the ribbon on New Yalu River Bridge this week, officials described the new border crossing in momentous terms.
Chinese Premier Li Qiang said the 3km (1.9-mile) bridge, which links China’s Dandong and North Korea’s Sinuiju, would “vigorously promote” trade and “strengthen emotional bonds”.
North Korean Premier Pak Thae-song expressed his belief that the crossing would “accelerate the advance for the prosperity of the two countries” and “add fresh vigour” to their economic cooperation.
Analysts on China-North Korea ties are much more circumspect.
While the bridge is a concrete symbol of China and North Korea’s efforts to revitalise relations that have waned from their Cold War-era peak, the prospects for trade are hindered by obstacles ranging from international sanctions to a North Korean leadership that prioritises security above all else, experts say.
“It reflects China’s renewed effort to strengthen its relationship with North Korea at a time of changing regional alignments,” Phillip Park, a professor at the University of North Korean Studies in Seoul, South Korea, told Al Jazeera.
“But whether this leads to substantially deeper economic integration, greater North Korean dependence, or a significant shift in Pyongyang’s strategic orientation remains an open question.
“The bridge could facilitate trade and logistics, but it does not remove international sanctions,” Park added.
China, whose troops fought alongside Pyongyang in the 1950-53 Korean War, has long been North Korea’s most crucial economic benefactor.
China accounts for as much as 95 percent of official trade with the secretive country, which is among the world’s most diplomatically and economically isolated states.
Before the four-lane New Yalu River Bridge officially opened on Thursday, road and rail freight between Dandong and Sinuiju, the main route for China-North Korea trade, travelled exclusively via the ageing Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge.
Opened in 1943, the bridge, which has a single-lane road and a rail track, can only carry vehicles weighing a maximum of 20 tonnes.
Jae-woo Joo, a professor of Chinese foreign policy at Kyung Hee University in Seoul, said the new bridge could “tremendously” boost trade between the sides, including the transfer of components banned under sanctions against Pyongyang’s nuclear and missile programmes.
“It is therefore really significant to open this bridge with China,” Joo told Al Jazeera.
After coming under strain from North Korea’s nuclear weapons tests in the mid-2000s, Beijing-Pyongyang ties have warmed under Chinese President Xi Jinping and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.
At Xi and Kim’s most recent meeting in June, their seventh summit since 2018, the leaders pledged to enhance cooperation in areas spanning trade, defence, agriculture, law, science and technology.
Analysts have, in part, cast Beijing’s deepening engagement with Pyongyang as a response to the latter’s growing ties with Moscow, which have included the deployment of thousands of North Korean troops to the front lines of Russia’s war in Ukraine.
Last month, North Korean and Russian officials opened the first road bridge linking their countries across the Tumen River.
North Korea and China’s two-way trade grew 25 percent in 2025 to reach $2.74bn, according to figures from China’s General Administration of Customs.
Bilateral trade has continued to grow in 2026, jumping nearly 20 percent to reach $1.5bn in the first half of the year, putting it on track to reach its highest volumes since the COVID-19 pandemic.
But while growing, trade remains relatively minuscule in the context of global commerce.
With China’s overall trade hitting $6.36 trillion in 2025, North Korea’s contribution to the total was a little more than 0.04 percent.
Official trade between the neighbours also remains substantially below its 2010s heyday.
Trade hovered around $5-6bn throughout much of the decade, peaking at $6.45bn in 2013.
Economists have offered explanations for the slowdown that range from tightened sanctions to China’s waning reliance on imports amid its efforts to boost economic self-reliance.
Christopher Green, a senior consultant for the Korean Peninsula at International Crisis Group, said the new border crossing’s significance should not be overstated, considering that China-North Korea trade “is fundamentally driven by politics”.
“Lack of cross-border transit routes is not the main obstacle,” Green told Al Jazeera.
“If the bridge opening signifies a political desire on both sides to give political cover to rising trade volumes, then a boost to trade should follow,” Green said, describing ties up until now as “steady-as-she-goes” economic engagement.
“Time will tell. But the key is the politics of national security, not economics.”
As much as officials have hailed the New Yalu River Bridge as a reflection of Chinese-North Korean cooperation, the project had a long and torturous road to completion.
Construction began in 2011 and was finished on the Chinese side in 2014.
But North Korean authorities only completed roads and customs facilities on their side of the river this year following repeated pauses in construction amid tensions with Beijing.
“The 12-year delay certainly suggests that economic cooperation is more conditional than the language of friendship might imply,” Marco Mari, a PhD researcher at Bocconi University in Italy who studies China-North Korea economic ties, told Al Jazeera.
“The bridge can facilitate supplies and economic activity, while Russian support gives North Korea alternatives that diminish Beijing’s leverage,” Mari added.
“This does not necessarily imply broader economic reform or a comparable improvement in ordinary people’s lives.”
Weiqi Zhang, an associate professor at Suffolk University who studies relations between North Korea and China, said the history of China-North Korea economic ties is littered with abortive projects, such as the Hwanggumpyong Special Economic Zone, a North Korean-Chinese development near Dandong.
“There were cases, like the Hwanggumpyong Special Economic Zone – established by China and North Korea – where China built infrastructure on its side, but North Korea didn’t even pave the road on their side,” Zhang told Al Jazeera.
“One reason is that, unlike its neighbours, North Korean government doesn’t really pay much attention to trade for economic development,” Zhang said.
“International trade is used by North Korea more like a foreign policy tool.”
With China wishing to demonstrate its “indispensability” as a trade partner and North Korea eager to strengthen their economic ties, trade is likely to grow, said Edward Howell, a lecturer in international Relations at the University of Oxford.
Even so, economic engagement will be subject to political considerations, Howell said.
“North Korea will obviously want to avoid facing any Chinese influence to change its economic model, but Pyongyang will want to reap the economic benefits of trade with its principal economic benefactor,” Howell told Al Jazeera.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — KMT New Taipei mayoral candidate Lee Shu-chuan (李四川) is seeking his first elected office after more than 40 years in government.
CNA reported that Lee unveiled policies for immigrants during a campaign visit to Xizhi on Wednesday. His proposals include better interpretation services, multilingual public information, financial support for immigrant-owned businesses, and care for older immigrants.
Existing interpretation services are spread across different city agencies, Lee said, making them difficult to access. He proposed a shared database of interpreters and more multilingual information on public transport, in hospitals, and during emergencies.
Lee is running against DPP Legislator Su Chiao-hui (蘇巧慧) in the Nov. 28 local elections. He hopes to succeed KMT Mayor Hou Yu-ih (侯友宜), who is term-limited and cannot run again.
Born into a fishing family on Xiaoliuqiu, an island off Pingtung County, Lee grew up in modest circumstances, according to Mirror News. He studied electrical engineering at what is now National Taipei University of Technology and later earned a master's degree there, per Mirror Media.
Lee began his public service career in engineering and later became public works chief and deputy magistrate of Taipei County, which became New Taipei in 2010. He oversaw infrastructure projects and flood prevention work, per UDN.
Lee later served as Cabinet secretary-general and deputy mayor of New Taipei, Kaohsiung, and Taipei. His senior positions brought him experience in city administration under several KMT leaders.
Lee served as Kaohsiung deputy mayor under former Mayor Han Kuo-yu (韓國瑜), who was removed from office in a 2020 recall vote. He later joined Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an's (蔣萬安) administration, where he helped oversee major development projects.
In Taipei, Lee helped resolve fire safety issues at the Taipei Dome before the stadium opened in 2023. He also played a key role in negotiations over Nvidia's planned Taiwan headquarters, helping move the project through land and planning approvals, per CTS News.
Despite his long government career, Lee has never won elected office and has spent most of his career in appointed positions. His mayoral campaign marks his first election bid, shifting him from administrator to candidate.
Transport and development are central to Lee's campaign, with proposals for new rail connections and better roads. He has also called for closer cooperation between New Taipei and neighboring cities to reduce commuting times, per Newtalk.
Lee has promised to continue major projects begun under Hou's administration, including plans for a new indoor stadium in Shulin. He also wants to develop an AI technology hub in Tamsui to attract investment and create jobs.
Housing is another campaign priority, with Lee proposing more affordable homes for workers, young families, and older residents. He has also pledged to expand support for young entrepreneurs through easier access to loans and business advice, per UDN.

U.S. Army’s Europe Typhon battery fires its first Tomahawk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:20:57 UTC
18:20:57 KST

- A U.S. Army Typhon battery assigned to Multi-Domain Command Europe fired its first Tomahawk at China Lake, California, on Sept. 28, 2026.
- It was the third Typhon launch in the continental United States, after soldiers completed five weeks of training with the U.S. Navy and Lockheed Martin.
A newly fielded U.S. Army Typhon missile battery assigned to Europe has fired its first Tomahawk cruise missile, launching it during a live-fire at Naval Air Weapons Station China Lake, California, on Sept. 28, 2026, in what the service said was the third Typhon launch within the continental United States.
The Mid-Range Capability Battery of 3rd Battalion, 12th Field Artillery Regiment, a long-range fires battalion under Multi-Domain Command Europe, carried out the launch. Typhon, built by Lockheed Martin, is a truck-mounted launcher that fires the Tomahawk Land Attack Missile and the SM-6, missiles originally developed for U.S. Navy warships, and it fills the gap between the U.S. Army’s shorter-range rocket and missile launchers and its long-range hypersonic weapon, letting ground commanders hit targets more than 1,600 km (1,000 miles) away with Tomahawk.
“We get that range for that combatant commander to give them options and capabilities where they really haven’t had it before from the land force,” said Lt. Col. Derek Bartlett, commander of 3-12 Field Artillery.
Bartlett said strikes at that range would previously have been requested from the joint force, typically from the U.S. Navy, and that “the Army now has that capability.” Before the launch, soldiers in the battery went through a five-week training program run by the U.S. Navy and Lockheed Martin field service representatives to learn how to operate and maintain the system.
“They’re incredibly good at what they do now,” said Bartlett. “I’m very comfortable deploying them forward after these five weeks.”
The 3-12 battery is one of four Mid-Range Capability batteries the U.S. Army has created and falls under Multi-Domain Command Europe, which brings together the service’s land, air, sea, space and cyber capabilities to strike targets. According to the U.S. Army, the first battery was activated in January 2024, while the 3-12 battery was activated in November 2025.
“It requires all domains to work in unison for a kinetic strike to happen,” said Command Sgt. Maj. John Hespe, the battalion’s senior enlisted advisor.
“Rockets in the field artillery community are going to continue to evolve,” said Hespe. “It’s going to provide better options for commanders to choose to fire from land based emplacement in any country at any time.”
Typhon has already deployed outside the United States: a battery went to the Philippines in April 2024 for exercises, and the system was shown in Japan in 2025, moves that drew protests from China. In Europe, Washington and Berlin announced in July 2024 that the United States would begin episodic deployments of long-range fires to Germany in 2026, including Tomahawk and SM-6 missiles, which puts a Europe-based Typhon unit in line with those plans.

Amsterdam police have seized a server belonging to Autistici/Inventati (A/I), a dissolved hacker network that provided online services and support to left-wing political groups. The US says this included Antifa, which the Trump administration has designated a terror organisation.
The server, located at the Science Park in the east of the city, was taken without any public announcement by local police. A spokesperson told NRC that an image of the server would go “straight to America”.
Trade association Dutch Cloud Community has demanded clarity over why the police agreed to the US’ demand. The public prosecution department has also made no official statement about the incident.

Similar fears have arisen over the potential acquisition of Solvinity, the cloud provider that hosts Dutch government services like DigiD, by an American company.

Taiwan's Yentity explores personal identity in SS27 collection
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:20:54 UTC
18:20:54 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwanese fashion brand Yentity explores the different sides of personal identity in its Spring/Summer 2027 collection.
Titled “A Slice of Self,” the designs look at how seemingly opposite qualities can coexist, from strength and softness to structure and fluidity. Rather than settling on a single look, Yentity combines contrasting shapes and textures, leaving room for individual interpretation, according to a Taipei Fashion Week press release.
Loose, voluminous silhouettes sit alongside fitted designs, while crisp fabrics contrast with softer, draped materials. Details that conceal or reveal parts of the body add another dimension to the designs, bringing together different elements without adhering to a uniform aesthetic.
A key feature of the collection is its use of Taiwan-made functional fabrics, materials more commonly associated with outdoor gear and sportswear, into contemporary clothing. Their emphasis on comfort and ease of movement is paired with Yentity’s understated approach to design.
The SS27 collection also continues Yentity’s exploration of photography as part of garment design. Images are cut, transferred and layered onto garments through rubber printing and transparent treatments. Fragmented, overlapping and blurred effects turn the photographs into part of each garment’s visual composition rather than conventional prints.
The title reflects the idea that no single perspective can fully capture a person. Through its mix of silhouettes, materials and photographic details, the collection approaches identity as something with multiple facets rather than a single, fixed definition.

Marine Le Pen ready to 'debate' Zelenskyy after vow to end French aid to Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:20:40 UTC
18:20:40 KST

Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused the National Rally's presidential candidate of ignoring key details of military cooperation between Paris and Kyiv.
French aid to Ukraine has become an issue in the 2027 presidential campaign. Marine Le Pen, who says she will end it if she reaches the Élysée Palace, has said she is ready to debate the question directly with Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Speaking on CNews on Thursday, Marine Le Pen said she was prepared to travel to Ukraine to discuss the issue with the Ukrainian president: "We could perfectly well debate this issue whenever he wishes," she said. "
If Mr Zelenskyy would like us to talk, I will gladly come to Ukraine. But what I want to tell him is that we no longer have the financial means to provide assistance," she added.
"I have nothing, personally, against Zelenskyy," she added.
Earlier, on Wednesday, speaking to Flemish television VRT News, the far-right candidate condemned the cost of French support for Ukraine, which she puts at €6 billion a year.
That figure roughly corresponds to the average annual level of French aid to Ukraine since February 2022, including bilateral support and contributions to European mechanisms.
"From my election, for six months we will maintain the aid...so as not to force anyone's hand. But afterwards we will stop financial assistance to Ukraine because we no longer have the means to do so," she said.
The Ukrainian president responded to her comments, saying that "Madame Le Pen does not fully grasp certain details" of Franco-Ukrainian military cooperation.
Zelenskyy: Ukraine also contributes to France's defence
In an interview with the Financial Times published on Thursday, Zelenskyy defended the benefits of military cooperation between France and Ukraine, particularly in the field of weapons technology.
France "can only gain" from this partnership, he insisted. "We give something back," he stressed.
Zelenskyy notably pointed out that the experience gained by his army on the battlefield allows France to test and improve its equipment in real combat conditions.
He cited the Franco-Italian SAMP/T air-defence systems, which have been modified several times to adapt to realities on the ground, as well as the Franco-British Scalp/Storm Shadow missiles. A "win-win" partnership, according to the Ukrainian leader.
Emmanuel Macron reiterates France's support
Incumbent President Emmanuel Macron reiterated France's support for Ukraine on Thursday, after talks with Zelenskyy in Brussels.
In the face of intensifying Russian attacks, the French president said it was "vital" to provide Kyiv with "all the means necessary" to defend itself and protect its population and infrastructure, stressing that "France will continue to shoulder its responsibilities".
French foreign minister Jean-Noël Barrot also responded to Marine Le Pen's statements, arguing that ending French aid to Ukraine would be "the surest way of bringing the war closer to our borders."
Outcry from Marine Le Pen's opponents
Gabriel Attal, the Renaissance candidate for the presidency, also criticised Le Pen's position on Franceinfo, accusing her of wanting to "let Ukrainians be butchered."
"Supporting Ukraine is not a humanitarian operation to make ourselves feel good, it is our own defence," the former prime minister insisted.
MEP Raphaël Glucksmann, winner of the social-democratic primary, likewise denounced a "capitulation" and "submission" to Vladimir Putin.
"If we cut aid to Ukraine, that means subjecting the whole of Europe to Vladimir Putin," the centre-left presidential candidate said on France 5, arguing that Le Pen should "absolutely not take power."
Horizons candidate Édouard Philippe described Marine Le Pen's comments as a "betrayal" in a message on X.
"To say that France will stop helping Ukraine at the end of 2027 is to weaken it even further at a time when, more than ever, we need to close ranks around it," he wrote.
Marine Le Pen's comments have also stirred reactions beyond her rivals in the race for the Élysée.
Liberal lawyer Charles Consigny, a commentator on RMC's Les Grandes Gueules and former Les Républicains candidate in the 2022 legislative elections, believes Le Pen's position serves Vladimir Putin's interests.
"Putin is eagerly awaiting Marine Le Pen's victory," he argued in a post on X.
Within the National Rally camp, MP Laure Lavalette has defended ending French financial support for Kyiv.
"We can no longer help Ukraine. The coffers are empty," she said on RMC, before admitting that she did not know the amount of France's contribution.
Germany, Europe's leading contributor to aid for Ukraine
According to figures from the German research centre, the Kiel Institute, France has committed a total of €27 billion to supporting Ukraine since the start of the Russian invasion, including €7.9 billion in bilateral aid and €19 billion via European mechanisms.
In absolute terms, Germany remains Europe's biggest contributor to aid for Ukraine, with more than €50 billion pledged since February 2022, ahead of France, Italy and the Netherlands.
Relative to GDP, however, bilateral aid is highest in Denmark and Estonia.

Ma said the stock market’s roughly 70% rise this year has created a wealth effect that supports domestic demand, while the divide associated with a K-shaped economy has eased, though disparities remain.

Koretsky: 100% reservation provides opportunities for major manipulations
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:20:09 EEST
18:20:09 KST

Prime Minister of Ukraine Serhiy Koretsky states that 100% reservation for enterprises creates opportunities for significant manipulation, a problem that has grown to a large scale.
"100% reservation provides opportunities for major manipulations. If you have 100%, it means you can endlessly expand your staff and reserve people: and it doesn't matter whether a person is a repair worker or not, an energy worker or not. And this system has already reached a large scale, unfortunately. Therefore, this is the only reason why we are looking at the 100% barrier – to modify it or leave it as it is. Because, unfortunately, there are many abuses," Koretsky said during the "Question Time with the Government" in the Verkhovna Rada on Friday.
The Prime Minister noted that additional reservations continue to be granted by the tens of thousands monthly at such enterprises.
"It is necessary to separate criticality and the economic block. Because wages and the absence of tax debt do not always mean that an enterprise is critical. Criticality is the defense capability and life support of the state," he added.
To substantiate his words, Koretsky gave an example of a contractor performing work for an energy company, where only 20 out of 100 employees actually carry out the subcontract for that company, yet all 100 are reserved.
Earlier, the Prime Minister stated that when modifying the reservation system, there will be no radical changes for critical enterprises in the defense and energy sectors.
"The resolution is being processed, it will definitely be finalized, adopted, and published. There is no betrayal there. All details will follow once they are made public and all relevant decisions are made," he said.
As reported, on October 13, the Cabinet of Ministers adopted the resolution On certain issues of organizing the reservation of persons subject to military service during mobilization and in wartime, introducing changes to the reservation system. As of today, the resolution has not been published.
Earlier, MP Yaroslav Zheleznyak published a draft government resolution providing for the reduction of reservation limits for the defense-industrial complex and energy sector from 100% to 85%, for municipal enterprises from 75% to 60%, as well as changing the calculation base for the 50% quota and creating a Coordination Center under the Cabinet of Ministers. According to his data, the Coordination Center was proposed to be established with 17 members, including representatives of the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU), the Main Directorate of Intelligence (GUR), the Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine (SZRU), and the National Police. Without a positive recommendation from this body, enterprises would not be able to obtain the status of critically important or a reservation quota exceeding 50%, with the center also having the authority to recommend revoking such status, while clear deadlines, criteria, and appeal mechanisms were absent in the document.
A group of MPs from all parliamentary factions appealed to Prime Minister Serhiy Koretsky demanding the cancellation of plans to create a Coordination Center for Organizing Reservation.
Chairman of the Subcommittee on Cybersecurity, MP Oleksandr Fediyenko, emphasized that the creation of a new agency risks causing delays in reservation procedures for enterprises in the defense-industrial complex, energy, and critical infrastructure, threatening the non-fulfillment of state contracts.

Indian police launch New Delhi clampdown for Cockroach Party rally

Indian police launch New Delhi clampdown for Cockroach Party rally
Cockroach Janta Party standoff with government extended as youth-led movement calls protest over jailing of activists.
Authorities have tightened security in New Delhi after the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) called for a new protest over the jailing of two of its activists.
Thousands of additional police officers were deployed in the Indian capital on Friday as the Indian government appeared to prepare for further confrontations. The youth-led CJP movement has held a series of protests in recent weeks to demand India’s election chief resign. Its demonstrations have been met with a tough crackdown.
CJP supporters have been called to gather in New Delhi’s Central Park at 5pm (11:30am GMT). The rally was called after two of the movement’s leaders were jailed for five days this week for allegedly trespassing at a protest site.
Authorities have closed the park, citing “administrative reasons”, and set up metal barricades at key intersections.
CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke suggested police may try to arrest him before the protest but declared he and his supporters are “not afraid” and are “ready” to go to jail.
In a social media post, Dipke accused the government of hypocrisy and denounced police crackdowns against the movement.
Members of the government may never have come to power had they experienced similar protest restrictions, he asserted.
“The very party that is in power today spent decades organising protests, taking to the streets and questioning the governments of the day when it was in opposition,” Dipke said.
“Had the same restrictions, intimidation and police crackdowns been used against them, many of those who occupy positions of power today might never have reached where they are.”
The rally is just the latest facing a crackdown by the authorities.
The CJP has held almost daily demonstrations this month demanding electoral reforms and the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
The commissioner oversaw the removal of more than 130 million names from the electoral roll and is accused by the CJP of voter fraud. Election authorities said the changes were made to remove duplicate, deceased and fraudulent entries.
The CJP was founded in May amid anger over the leaking of exam papers and the poor prospects facing India’s youth.
The movement swiftly became a conduit for India’s Gen Z, many of whom feel disenfranchised during an unemployment crisis under Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s right-wing government. The movement has since forced the resignation of the education minister.
With the political opposition quick to support the protests, Modi has come under intense pressure with some analysts saying he is now facing the worst crisis since he came to office in 2014.

Yisrael Beytenu chairman Avigdor Liberman on Friday accused Yashar party leader and former IDF chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot of planning to join forces with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and the Likud party when forming a government after the upcoming elections.
"The campaign being run by Eisenkot is not intended to shift a single vote from the 'draft dodgers' bloc to the 'those who serve' bloc," Liberman said, referring to the issue of haredi (ultra-Orthodox) Israelis refusing to serve in the IDF as other citizens are made to serve months of reserve duty.
"This stands in complete contradiction with the agreements reached by the bloc's leaders during their last meeting, undermines unity, and raises one simple question: What lies behind this move?" Liberman asked.
Liberman said Eisenkot's strategy is to siphon votes from the parties that seek to enforce enlistment, then negotiate with Netanyahu to form a government once he has more mandates than Likud. To that end, on Thursday, Israeli journalist Ben Caspit reported that Eisenkot's Yashar party has recently decided to launch a campaign to draw votes from other parties in the opposition bloc, overtake Likud, and become the largest party in the Knesset. "The race to become the largest party is close. We must be the largest party and overtake Likud. "From Yigael Yadin and Ehud Barak to Benny Gantz, military rank and experience are no substitute for political experience. Even Yitzhak Rabin, following his first term as prime minister, needed many years to return, gain experience, and get re-elected."
'Ignore the spin...for the good of the State of Israel,' Eisenkot says

"We are 11 days away from the [most] fateful elections since the founding of the state," Eisenkot wrote. "At this historic moment, we must keep a cool head and focus on the goal."

UK government courted UBS over London HQ move
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:16:30 UTC
18:16:30 KST

UK government courted UBS over London HQ move
Former UK Chancellor of the Exchequer Rachel Reeves pitched the City of London as an alternative home for the Swiss bank, which is weighing its options amid new capital proposals.
Britain’s Labour government sought to persuade UBS to shift its headquarters and stock market listing to London in the event of the bank relocating out of Switzerland because of strict new capital rules.
Rachel Reeves pitched London as a potential new home for UBS in discussions with the bank’s chair Colm Kelleher during her time as chancellor, according to people briefed on the talks.
The pair discussed the possibility of UBS moving its legal headquarters and listing to the UK if it were to redomicile, the people added, with the most recent meeting taking place earlier this year.
The discussions illustrate how foreign governments have attempted to court Switzerland’s biggest bank while it is mired in a protracted political battle over regulatory reforms in its home market.
UBS relocating to London would represent a major coup for the UK, with its valuation of CHF129 billion ($157 billion) making it the fourth-largest company in the FTSE 100, behind only HSBC, Shell and AstraZeneca.
UBS already has a significant presence in the UK, where it employs about 8,000 people across investment banking, wealth management and asset management.
The bank suffered a setback last month when Swiss lawmakers pressed ahead with strict new rules that the lender said would require it to hold about $16 billion of additional capital, rejecting a compromise proposal.
>> How new Swiss capital requirement rules have sparked debates about a possible UBS move:
More
‘Switzerland has spoken’. Will UBS leave?
While UBS has said that its goal is to continue operating out of Switzerland, Kelleher publicly acknowledged last month that the lender could reconsider its Swiss base if the regulatory clampdown proved too onerous.
Two major shareholders have also called on the board to consider moving its headquarters, with US asset manager Artisan Partners saying in recent weeks that Switzerland was “no longer an attractive or desirable location” for UBS.
UBS’s board has examined contingency plans in response to the capital reforms, including redomiciling, the FT previously reported. However, there is no indication that the bank is actively planning to relocate to the UK or any other jurisdiction at present.
Many industry observers view the US as the most likely alternative for the Swiss lender given its lighter regulatory regime and UBS’s ambitions to compete in wealth management with Wall Street rivals such as Morgan Stanley.
Senior executives at the bank last year held talks with Donald Trump’s administration officials about a potential relocation to the US.
However, some analysts have questioned the feasibility of a move, citing legal complexities and the possibility of Switzerland imposing a hefty exit tax on the bank. Others believe a merger with a large US or European bank could be a more likely alternative.
The discussions between Reeves and Kelleher also underline how Labour has sought to court international businesses since assuming power in 2024.
Reeves won praise from banking executives after sparing the sector from tax rises in last year’s Budget following an intense lobbying campaign.
However, there is concern among executives that her successor, John Healey, could target the industry for tax increases in his first Budget this month.
UBS and Reeves declined to comment.
The Treasury did not respond to a request for comment.

EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas called on the US to step up pressure on Russia, saying Moscow must be squeezed into negotiations to end the war in Ukraine.
Speaking to reporters ahead of the second day of the EU leaders' summit in Brussels on Friday, Kallas said there were no indications that Russia was willing to end the war or engage in a truce or peace process.
"We are working on the new sanctions package to put pressure on Russia. And, we, of course, hope that we do this with all our partners around the world," she said.
"We are trying to convince also our American partners that if we want to end this war, then we have to squeeze the aggressor because it's not only to end this war, but to make sure that there are no no more wars started by by Russia," Kallas added.
Together with EU foreign ministers, she said she had prepared a list of European security concerns and demands that should be presented to Russia in any negotiations.
"We should also present to Russia" these concerns and avoid granting Moscow everything it wants without securing concessions in return, she said.
"But of course, you can see that with our American allies, it's very difficult at the time," Kallas added.
On Ukraine's reliance on Starlink, Kallas said the satellite communication system remained essential for Kyiv and that Europe could not replace its capabilities in the short term.
She said EU leaders would also discuss European defense readiness, noting that the European Defense Agency had identified critical capabilities and industrial capacity gaps that Europe needed to address.
"The question is the implementation of this, and we need to do this as soon as possible, because we need the capabilities ourselves," Kallas noted.

U.S. Marine Corps stands up first missile battalion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:13:53 UTC
18:13:53 KST

- The U.S. Marine Corps re-designated 1st Battalion, 10th Marines as its first medium-range missile battalion on Oct. 9, 2026, at Camp Lejeune.
- The battalion will operate NMESIS, which carries two Naval Strike Missiles with a range of more than 130 nautical miles.
The U.S. Marine Corps has turned a 2nd Marine Division artillery battalion at Camp Lejeune, North Carolina, into its first medium-range missile battalion, built around a launcher that fires Naval Strike Missiles at enemy ships from land.
1st Battalion, 10th Marine Regiment was formally re-designated on Oct. 9, 2026, under the service’s Force Design 2030 modernization plan, the 2nd Marine Division said. The battalion will operate the Navy-Marine Expeditionary Ship Interdiction System, or NMESIS.
“The Medium-Range Missile Battalion employs the NMESIS,” said Lt. Col. Joseph Mozzi, commanding officer of 1st Battalion, 10th Marines. “[The NMESIS] is the Marine Corps’ emerging ground based anti-ship missile capability, and it will also be a ground based long-range precision fires platform.”
NMESIS pairs a launcher carrying two Naval Strike Missiles with an uncrewed, remotely operated vehicle known as the ROGUE-Fires carrier, built on a Joint Light Tactical Vehicle chassis. Without a driver or crew aboard, the launcher can be positioned along a coastline while Marines control it from a distance. The Naval Strike Missile, developed by Norway’s Kongsberg and produced in partnership with Raytheon, has a range of more than 130 nautical miles (240 km) and can hit ships at sea as well as fixed targets on land, according to the Marine Corps.
“The requirement for the Marine Corps to have a land-based capability to conduct sea denial was identified as a crucial step to facilitate the maritime component commanders to fight for sea control,” said Mozzi.
The system first went to the 3rd Marine Littoral Regiment in Hawaii in 2024. The Marine Corps tested it during Large Scale Exercise 2021, firing a Naval Strike Missile off the coast of Hawaii at a target ship, and Marines have since deployed NMESIS to the Philippines during Balikatan exercises near the Luzon Strait.
The battalion at Camp Lejeune is the first of the service’s artillery battalions to convert to missiles, giving an East Coast unit a capability that until now sat with the Marine Littoral Regiments focused on the Pacific. As part of the service-retained force, the battalion is available to the commanding general of II Marine Expeditionary Force and the wider Marine Corps for crisis response.
The change does not end the regiment’s cannon artillery. 10th Marines will keep M777 lightweight howitzers in another battalion, and Col. William Soucie, the regiment’s commander, called NMESIS a complement to cannon artillery.
“Projecting combat power ashore from the sea is historically what [Marines] do,” said Soucie. “What we will be able to do with [the NMESIS] is shoot in support of not only maneuver that’s already ashore, we will also be able to shoot in support of maneuver at sea.”
Soucie said the Marines and sailors in the battalion are the same people who served in it as an artillery unit.
“While the transition of the weapons platform is interesting, what makes the story compelling is that the Marines and Sailors in that formation are not changing,” said Soucie.
The 2nd Marine Division described the re-designation as the start of a broader modernization of artillery battalions across the Marine Corps, with 1st Battalion, 10th Marines now the first unit to carry the medium-range missile battalion title.

"We see that Zelenskyy now has only one ally, and that is essentially the Europeans," Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs said in an interview with Bloomberg TV in Brussels.
"The Western alliance is now in a weaker position than it was a few days ago," Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen told reporters as she arrived for talks in the Belgian capital on Thursday. "If you do not support Ukraine, then you are putting Europe as a whole, and therefore NATO as a whole, in a much, much more dangerous situation."
"Of course, Trump and Zelenskyy have been in this situation before and have always found a way to mend relations," the publication notes.
At the same time, the publication notes that "their latest disagreement comes at a particularly inopportune moment. Winter is approaching, and Ukraine lacks the American Patriot interceptor missiles needed to shoot down Russian missiles. Kyiv's military spending is also creating a hole in its budget that Europe is trying to fill. Meanwhile, Russia is striking a greater number of civilian targets, periodically leaving Kyiv facing disruptions to its electricity and water supplies," the publication says.
Next month, Kremlin chief Vladimir Putin will have an opportunity to meet Trump at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China, which neither Zelenskyy nor the Europeans will attend.
"Trump, for his part, is several weeks away from the midterm elections, in which his Republican Party is expected to suffer major losses, forcing him to seek quick ways to lower fuel prices. This fixation is shaping Trump's desire to buy Russian diesel fuel despite the sanctions, as well as his calls for Ukraine to stop attacks on oil refineries, even though experts say that the U.S. war against Iran is the biggest reason for high fuel prices," the publication notes.
"The most important thing we will discuss today is what he needs for this winter. Everything depends on this winter," the Latvian prime minister told Bloomberg. "We must also understand that the United States is now approaching the midterm elections. This is election time," Kulbergs said. "It is a different atmosphere."
For now, most Europeans are advising Zelenskyy to soften his criticism of Trump, given that there is no alternative to cooperation with the United States, sources say
It adds that the United States "continues to sell weapons to Ukraine and share intelligence vital to Kyiv's defense."
"If that intelligence disappeared, Europe would not have a good solution," one official said.
That is presumably why EU leaders were careful not to voice excessive public criticism of Trump when they arrived in Brussels on Thursday for the summit. However, behind closed doors, some did express shock at the US president’s recent behavior, sources said
An Élysée Palace official said that France’s priority was for Europe to continue supporting Ukraine. A spokesperson for the office of the German chancellor did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
As the publication notes, "Europe is standing its ground, supporting sanctions and insisting that Ukraine must not surrender territory as part of a peace settlement," especially after the Defense Forces retook some of the territories lost in the Donbas, which Putin wants to control.
"US influence over Ukraine has also declined over the past few months. Although intelligence remains an important factor, the money to support Kyiv and purchase American weapons is coming primarily from Europe. Ukraine is also finally receiving ammunition for F-16 fighter jets to shoot down threatening Russian jet-powered drones," the publication said.
Meanwhile, the publication writes, "Washington’s efforts to establish the peace Trump promised to bring shortly after taking office last week have not made significant progress." "The latest meetings in Florida last weekend, which the Ukrainian delegation walked out of after Trump’s deal with Russia on diesel fuel, were largely focused on discussing the same set of points that the president’s envoys—Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner—developed several months ago," according to people familiar with the matter.
"During Monday’s meeting, EU foreign ministers privately agreed that Europe’s policy toward Ukraine must remain unchanged, regardless of fluctuations in Washington," according to people familiar with the discussions. They "decided to engage with the US whenever possible and maintain their support for Kyiv when that is not possible."
"We definitely have a different approach to this war," EU chief diplomat Kaja Kallas told reporters in Brussels on Thursday. "We see that we need to put pressure on the aggressor to stop the war, not on the victim to surrender. Putting pressure on Ukraine is the wrong approach," she stressed.

The Italian Embassy in Israel participated in the Holocaust Memorial—Yad Vashem in Jerusalem—at the commemoration of the 83rd anniversary of the deportation of Rome’s Jews on October 16, 1943, organized by the association Hevrat Yehudè Italia Be-Israel.
                                    
The ceremony began at the Tent of Remembrance, where the Italian Ambassador to Israel, Luca Ferrari, lit the commemorative flame in memory of the victims of the deportation. This was followed by remarks from Vito Anav, president of Hevrat Yehudè Italia Be-Israel; Ambassador Ferrari; and Samuele Rocca, a member of the association’s Executive Committee. The evening also featured testimonies from several representatives of the Italian community in Israel. In his remarks, Ambassador Ferrari emphasized the profound significance of the commemoration, stating that gathering at Yad Vashem to remember October 16, 1943, means “not merely repeating a ritual formula,” but “rediscovering the profound meaning of being a community.”
“On October 16, 1943, in Rome, over a thousand Jews were torn from their homes and deported to Auschwitz. They were Italian citizens; they were Romans; they were an integral part of our society. Almost none of them ever returned,” the ambassador recalled, highlighting the tragedy of that day and the resulting duty of responsibility for democratic Italy and for Europe. Eighty-three years after that “Black Saturday,” Ferrari continued, “looking through the lens of memory” means understanding the present, recognizing the dangers, and remaining vigilant. The incidents of antisemitism that continue to occur in Europe and Italy—from attacks on people of Jewish identity to acts of vandalism against memorial sites—demonstrate how necessary it is to combat all forms of hatred and discrimination.
                                    
A few days before the third anniversary of the October 7 massacre, the Ambassador also emphasized that that day represents “an abyss, a deep wound in the history and soul of Israel and the Jewish people.” He then reiterated the importance of acknowledging the reality of what happened and preserving an accurate record of the facts, protecting it from any attempt at distortion, even in the international public debate. Ferrari also dedicated a passage to the role of the Italian community in Israel, describing it as a “living bridge” between the two countries: a community that knows both nations intimately and bears witness to the fact that “human bonds are not broken, even in the darkest moments.” “If there is one certainty we must reaffirm with courage, it is that violence and terror will not prevail,” he stated. Referring to the legacy of Yad Vashem and the example of the Righteous Among the Nations, the ambassador recalled how many, during the Holocaust, chose to risk everything to save the lives of others. An example that, through the testimony of men and women who refused to look the other way, continues to point the way toward individual and collective responsibility in the face of injustice. “A just world is not a world free of dangers and misunderstandings. It is a world in which a community knows it is not alone, knows that its institutions and its homeland will never leave it alone,” Ferrari stated, reaffirming the commitment of Italy and its institutions to combating antisemitism and safeguarding the security of schools, synagogues, and gathering places of the Italian Jewish community.

Turkish exports to BRICS group countries top $18.2B in January-September
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:07:22 UTC
18:07:22 KST

Yunus Turk and Emir Yildirim
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
Türkiye’s exports to the 10 member states of the BRICS grouping totaled $18.2 billion in the first nine months of the year, according to the Turkish Exporters’ Assembly (TIM).
While Türkiye’s total global exports this January-September grew 5.2% to $210.9 billion, Russia was the largest destination among other BRICS member states, receiving $4.1 billion in exports despite a 2.5% annual decline.
BRICS includes longtime members Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa, plus recent additions Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, and the United Arab Emirates.
The UAE followed Russia as the second-largest destination for Turkish exports to BRICS, accounting for $3.3 billion even after a 4.12% contraction in export volume.
Egypt followed with a rise of 28.6% to $3.1 billion, China with a surge of 40.8% to $3 billion, and Iran with $1.8 billion, making the country the fifth-largest BRICS destination for Turkish goods.
Turkish exports increased in eight of the 10 BRICS member states, with shipments in Ethiopia surging the most by 79.6%.
The chemicals and chemical products sector accounted for most of these exports to the bloc, generating $3.5 billion in the first nine months of the year, the data showed.
Mining exports grew 33.5% to $2.1 billion, a net gain of roughly $539 million, followed by the jewelry sector, whose exports fell 45% to $1.3 billion.
The textiles and raw material exports climbed 8.7% to $1.2 billion at the same time.
Türkiye’s top five exporter provinces -- Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Kocaeli, and Bursa -- accounted for a combined $12.5 billion of all Turkish exports to BRICS.
Istanbul was the largest source of these exports, making up $8.2 billion of the output, followed by Ankara with $1.9 billion, Izmir with $1 billion, Kocaeli with $703 million, and Bursa with $658 million.

Europe promotes sovereign, trusted AI as it struggles to catch US and China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:07:00 UTC
18:07:00 KST

Europe pushes homegrown AI agenda as US, China retain lead
October 16, 2026
If supremacy in artificial intelligence (AI) was an Olympic discipline, there would only be two serious contenders for gold on current trajectories: the US and China. Europe, as has been the case in many areas of cutting-edge technology in recent times, is barely in the conversation.
Former president of the European Central Bank Mario Draghi, whose 2024 report highlighted the EU's desperate need to be more innovative to become more competitive, said recently that AI is "perhaps the most promising" route Europe has to raise growth today. However, he decried the fact that the EU controls little of the value chain.
"Being cut off from AI, once the economy runs on it, would be more like being cut off from the US financial system," he wrote in an opinion piece for the Financial Times. "The effects would be catastrophic."
Draghi's spirit was on full display in Dublin on Wednesday at an international AI summit the Irish government convened as part of its 6-month stint hosting the rotating EU presidency.
The summit's motto, "Harnessing AI to Revolutionize Europe's Competitiveness," might as well have been dreamed up by the Italian former prime minister.
AI safety concerns shadow growth agenda
Harnessing AI has become a lot more complicated. A slew of controversies around AI agents going rogue, from the Hugging Face attack in June when 1,200 agents hacked an online platform, to an Anthropic-designed agent sending a fake tip to US police over an unsolved murder, have caused alarm.
Many from within the tech industry, including Microsoft founder Bill Gates and the leading AI frontier labs themselves, have called for a development pausein order for safety measures to catch up.
Yet positivity was largely the name of the game at the summit, with tech and AI industry leaders joining Irish and EU politicians to declare AI's transformative economic and societal potential — while also emphasizing the need for strong regulation and safety standards.
Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin made it clear that Ireland was all in on AI. He echoed European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen's recent assertion that the technology represented a "tipping point." He also repeatedly highlighted what he sees as the bloc's commitment to safety.
"We are determined to capture the dividend by mitigating the risks," Martin told the event. "In Europe, we have charted our path ... balancing innovation and opportunity with a trustworthy, human-centered approach to AI."
AI critics say key concerns overlooked
Meanwhile, Henna Virkkunen, the European Commission executive vice-president for tech sovereignty, security and democracy, revealed at the event that the EU had begun its first enforcement actions under its new AI Act, requesting information around security and safety from advanced AI model providers.
However, other topics that concern AI's many critics, from those fearing the massive environmental impact of data centers to others warning about possible AI-related job losses, were largely absent from the discussions.
Outside the venue, a group of protesters led by People Before Profit, a left-wing Irish political party, criticized the summit for not focusing on these issues.
"There is a deliberate blurring of the line here with the type of AI that is being promoted," Alexandra Day, one of the protest organizers, told DW.
"It is really being pushed on workers with very little consent. There's no right for workers to opt out of using AI now that it's coming into the workplace."
Europe faces a widening AI gap
A sense of urgency was palpable from the speakers inside the summit. Executives from some of the world's biggest AI and tech firms talked up Europe's potential. Yet the EU evidently has plenty of ground to catch up on in terms of AI development.
Despite ramping up its data center capacity, it still lags far behind the US and China. It hosts 5% of the world's AI computing capacity compared to around 75% for the US.
The EU is conspicuously absent from lists of the leading AI frontier labs, with only French company Mistral coming close to rivaling the top labs. Its production of leading-edge chips is also nowhere near that of the top US or Taiwanese producers.
As part of its plan to make ground on the US and China, the Irish government, in its role as EU presidency host, presented a policy document at the event.
The so-called "Dublin Declaration" outlines political commitments to strengthen Europe's AI capabilities, including infrastructure investment and financial backing for European AI companies.
In keeping with Draghi's calls for Europe to develop its own AI sovereignty, particularly in supply chains and infrastructure, the declaration suggests that European firms reliant on non-EU cloud and computing services may face additional compliance pressures.
Can Europe balance innovation and regulation?
However, not everyone is convinced by the EU's capacity to either ramp up AI capacity or develop effective regulation.
Eddie Wilson, CEO of European airline Ryanair, said he doubted Brussels could regulate AI well without stifling innovation.
"The last thing you want is people regulating this industry who don't know anything about it," he told DW. "That's generally what happens in Brussels."
Ryanair recently made a major deal with Google to use its cloud data system and its AI platform Gemini Enterprise. It's precisely the kind of collaboration with US AI supply chains that the EU says it wants companies to move away from.
"I worry for Europe because these tech companies need to move at speed," said Wilson. He believes the environment in the US is more amenable to innovation.
"If they're not going to do it here, they're going to do it elsewhere. They're going to do it in China and they're going to do it in the US."

We are teaching children maths they will never use. Isn’t it better to help them speak fluently? | Simon Jenkins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:00:57 UTC
18:00:57 KST

At last the fourth R is born. Articulation – speaking – is to join reading, writing and arithmetic in the education canon. What has become the mighty struggle against the dictatorship of the screen can begin in earnest. The spoken word, human-to-human communication, must finally be recognised by the gods of reactionary schooling. The pundits call it oracy.
On Thursday, the education secretary, Lucy Powell, called the academics’ bluff. She wants a radical reform of the national curriculum in England to reduce “desktop” working in favour of verbal fluency and practical skills. This will take courage. For decades, education’s senior leaders have been ramming easily forgotten “subjects”, such as maths and French, into children’s brains so they can be judged and measured in league tables. These tables have grown ever more dominant as ministers seek to climb “global rankings”.
After the second world war, an “academic” secondary education was shaped by the increased demand for a university-educated workforce. Higher education was expanded, but Britain’s technical and vocational schools and colleges were relegated out of sight. Teaching became enslaved to exam quantification and lost contact with the real world.
But the act of excluding communication skills from this academic orthodoxy has come home to roost. Artificial intelligence and mobile phones are progressively distancing young people from adults and each other. I notice gatherings of young people who used to chatter, laugh and banter. They now stand gazing at their screens or they just shout at each other. Conversation – sharing, informing, discussing, sympathising – seems on the way out.
Speaking itself is going out of fashion. Research suggests that in the past two decades the number of words people say each day has shrunk by nearly a third. They prefer texting. A quarter of young people now say they never even answer the phone unless pre-arranged. They fear a phone call means bad news.
Powell’s promotion of oracy means teaching young people once again to use the spoken word to their advantage. It is about conveying what one means clearly; listening, debating and handling disagreement. Speaking well means using eye contact and appropriately adjusting your tone of voice. It means politeness and tolerance. Above all, it enables young people to present themselves to others effectively, whether in work, play, argument or friendship.
To the Greeks and Romans, oracy was the towering skill of rhetoric. It was central to citizenship. The New Education movement of Steiner and Montessori in early 20th-century Europe stressed building on the qualities of the individual child rather than imposing rote learning from above. It is significant that the movement has seen a revival in the Waldorf schools now favoured by California’s AI executives in Silicon Valley.
That such ideals of progressive education have long been drummed out of the English curriculum is outrageous. The aversion to the spoken word has corresponded with the increasing prominence of maths in the curriculum, its skills beyond foundational arithmetic irrelevant to all but a tiny minority of adults. Children need to master elementary maths in primary school. But after that they only need to know how to use a calculator. I wonder how many readers remember being able to answer this question from last year’s GCSE paper: “The volume of a sphere is 4/3πr³ where r is the radius. Work out the volume of a sphere with diameter 20cm in terms of π.”
It is extraordinary that passing this exam is still required for most apprenticeships. Yet while he was prime minister, Rishi Sunak wanted maths to be compulsory until the age of 18. Small wonder it has long headed the list of “most hated” school subjects.
Quite how the teaching profession will react to Powell is not clear. The hyper-centralisation of British government has meant ever more school time spent on exams. This has led to cutting back on individualised learning and creativity, which typically flourishes in teaching of the arts. Teachers are pressed to “teach to the test”, at peril of damnation from Ofsted. These days, only the private sector dares resist. Winchester college devotes an hour a day to its form of oracy: “div” and “forum” sessions, when pupils discuss contemporary topics not covered by the examination syllabus: scientific ideas, philosophy, politics, music, critical thinking and the acceptance of others’ opinions.
Such speech-centred concepts as group learning and peer tutoring are being pursued in some universities, and the cause was taken forward in the 2024 oracy commission report. But the catch is always resources. The essence of teaching people how to speak must lie in personal contact. It is in the human relationship of tutor and pupil, which was once the essence of teaching as a profession, not a mechanical skill.
One key might lie in killing maths. Leave it to its enthusiasts. For the rest, school should be about the world outside, a world of other human beings. It is about how to go about handling them that young people have most to learn.
- Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnist

‘A direct cultural threat’: your questions on the rise of the right across Europe answered
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:00:56 UTC
18:00:56 KST

Support for far-right parties has been growing across Europe, with radical right, populist parties in coalition governments in Croatia, Czechia, Italy and Finland, and leading in the polls in Austria, Belgium, France and Germany.
The Guardian reported this year that nearly a quarter of voters in Europe voted for far-right parties in their most recent national elections, a fivefold increase since 1995.
In Germany, Alternative für Deutschland recently booked a historic state election victory in Saxony-Anhalt. Elsewhere, though – in the Netherlands, in Hungary and in Sweden, where the Sweden Democrats lost vote share – far-right parties have suffered defeats. But their ideas – and their influence on mainstream politics – are today clearly visible across the continent, notably on policies around immigration and law-and-order.
The coming months will see further crucial elections, beginning in Spain in November and continuing in France, Estonia, Finland, Greece, Slovakia, Poland and Italy next year.
How might these elections shape the political future of Europe? What is the impact of their policies – and what might prevent their continuing rise?
The Guardian’s Europe correspondent Jon Henley has reported for the Guardian from 23 of the EU’s 27 member states, while Europe community affairs correspondent Ashifa Kassam was on the ground in Sweden and Germany’s Saxony-Anhalt state to speak with people ahead of the elections.
Jon and Ashifa answered questions about their reporting and experiences. Read the Q&A below.
One user asked: It’s no secret in Europe that Donald Trump and his allies are funding far-right parties all over the continent. Trump is unpopular enough in Europe that even the majority of people planning to vote for the AfD et al despise him. So how can so many Europeans who hate Trump still vote for the far right?
Jon Henley: You’re absolutely right about the Trump administration’s efforts to promote far right parties in Europe. That was made very plain in the US National Security Strategy policy document last year – I wrote about that here.
But while there may be an ideological affinity between European far right and nationalist voters on issues like anti-immigration, hostility toward the EU, and softer stances on Russia, Trump’s “America First” policies (demands re Greenland, tariff threats, etc.) and constant unpredictability pose major problems for far-right leaders trying to look credible in Europe, because they scare all European voters – including far-right voters.
Leaders including Giorgia Meloni in Italy and Marine Le Pen in France have openly criticised Trump and distanced themselves from his more erratic pronouncements, conspiracy claims and hostility toward European security.
European far-right voters’ support for Trump varies from country to country but is broadly low – clearly peace and security in Europe matter more than anti-immigration sentiment. Ultimately, nation-first means putting your nation first, and Trump has made clear that the US’s interests are not Europe’s interests.
The evidence would seem to suggest that many of Europe’s far-right voters think their own far-right parties will be more responsible as regards (many of) those issues – though whether they actually will be or not is moot, of course.
00000000000000000000 asked: How do you measure when a grassroots movement represents a genuine structural shift versus an isolated vocal minority?
Ashifa Kassam: Our jobs involve covering a wide range of community actions, whether it’s people fighting back against datacentres, protests against tourism, or the vandalisation of mobile phone masts by people who seemingly linked them to the coronavirus pandemic.
Oftentimes the reporting starts small and local. For example, perhaps it’s focused tightly on a protest against tourists in Barcelona or a push to restrict cruise ship dockings in Dubrovnik. From there, myself and the editors often continue to watch these movements and their reach; are politicians responding in any way? Are others joining in? Will the movements lead to policy changes? These are the kinds of questions that I tend to consider when deciding how much to make of the grassroots movements and how much coverage to give them.
At times it’s been incredible to see just where these movements will go, whether it’s the housing protests in Spain that led to snap general elections or the opposition movement that coalesced around Péter Magyar in Hungary in 2024 and which, more than a year later, saw him oust Viktor Orbán from power.
Gramoun-kal asked: Can the EU survive the rise of the extreme right? What if AfD and RN get into power at the same time?
Jon Henley: One of the very few upsides of Brexit is that hardly any European far right parties now want their countries to leave the EU. Instead, they want to “transform it from within”, turning it more into a looser “Europe of nations”.
But that’s not to say the EU would not be considerably weakened by, say, a President Le Pen, who could paralyse decision-making, challenge the supremacy of EU law and push a “France First” agenda undermining the single market and Schengen free-travel zone and opposing EU expansion, climate action, etc.
I’m not sure there’s any imminent risk of the AfD coming to national power in Germany (and if Le Pen wins France’s presidential election, which isn’t certain but looks highly plausible, she is also unlikely to have a parliamentary majority, which will limit her room for manoeuvre).
Plus, the AfD is too extreme even for the RN – Le Pen’s outfit (which kicked the AfD out of its European parliament grouping a while ago over various issues including comments to the effect that not all Nazis were bad), has repeatedly made it clear it is not an ally of the German party and does not share its views on eg. “remigration” – the mass deportation of immigrants.
But for sure – if Spain, Italy, France and Poland all see far-right parties in government after elections due over the next 12 months or so, the EU will face some major challenges. I don’t think it will collapse, but it will certainly find it even harder to reach agreement on many major issues than it already does, and so move (even) more slowly. Natalie Tocci wrote a great comment piece about this.
OrangeSpaceMan5 asked: Do you see Nato and the EU disintegrating if we see Far-Right victories across Britain, Germany and France?
Jon Henley: No, I don’t see the EU and Nato disintegrating, just becoming a lot more complicated/difficult to run … The EU could be “eroded from within” above all by far right-led governments using their veto (as Orbán did with Hungary) in major decisions like the EU budget, EU enlargement, the green deal, etc. They may well also simply ignore EU law, as Orbán also did. And for Nato, see previous answer – it would survive but become more paralysed in terms of longer term decision making.
Ashifa Kassam: I think we saw a glimpse of how complicated things can become in the European parliament after an EU vote earlier this year aimed at increasing deportations. The immediate aftermath laid bare just how deeply polarised the EU has already become, as right-wing MEPs chanted “send them back” and centre-left and left-wing MEPs shot back with “Shame on you.”
ElendX asked: Why and how have the left and centre parties failed to respond to the concerns of the electorate? How do they now need to respond?
Ashifa Kassam: What comes to mind immediately is the housing crisis in Spain and beyond. It’s been just over two weeks now since the Spanish protests and encampments over the housing crisis burst into public view, laying bare the long-simmering anger over soaring housing costs.
I think it’s an issue that has long been overlooked by many left and centre parties across Europe, even as vulnerable people and minorities have been disproportionately affected, and analysts warn that the crisis could drive voters into the arms of the far right. Last year I spoke to Jaume Collboni, the Socialist mayor of Barcelona, who (along with 21 mayors across Europe) are urging the EU to treat the surging housing costs as a “new pandemic” by unleashing billions in funding to boost affordable housing and give mayors a seat at the table to ensure measures capable of tackling housing speculation. Speaking to me, Collboni warned: “We cannot remain stuck in the rhetoric of defending democracy, inclusive societies and equal opportunities if people’s standard of living is getting worse.”
I also think left and centre parties have done little to address the precariousness of the labour market, ie. the rise of gig jobs and, in many cases, the deterioration of public services. If you keep an eye on the Eurobarometer, the cost of living constantly ranks among the top concerns for people across Europe, hinting at the idea that this could be fertile territory for politicians to focus on. Immigration, in contrast, was in 7th place in the most recent survey.
Jon Henley: I think broadly speaking mainstream parties have failed to adequately address people’s concerns about the cost of living, declining public services (healthcare, education, transport), economic/job security, etc. – as I said above, fear of/anger at some kind of “loss of status” is one of the key drivers of the far right vote. (I’m not suggesting that’s easy – it clearly isn’t, economies are struggling.)
I’d also add that far-right parties are clearly extremely effective at exploiting voters’ concerns politically, including by pointing the finger at the group they think are most to blame and promising to fix things by getting rid of them.
And I’d also note that mainstream parties really have not helped themselves by adopting far-right parties’ framing on several issues in hopes of hanging on to disillusioned voters – electoral evidence shows that almost never works, mainly because, as Marine Le Pen’s father Jean-Marie put it, people tend to prefer the original to the copy.
Dc740 asked: Did you measure any change in online activity for extremist parties like Vox in Spain after the Yandex datacentre was targeted by Ukraine?
Ashifa Kassam: Funny you should ask – earlier this week, I sent out queries on this to several research groups, so it’s something we’re looking into. It’s a really interesting question. Last week, in an interview with news site Eldiario.es, the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez was asked whether he was worried about foreign interference in the elections given his high profile opposition to Israel’s war on Gaza and the US-Israeli attack on Iran. His answer: “Yes, and not only by nations, but also by non-state actors.”
Capitao_barbosa asked: How much foreign funding, especially from Russia and America, is being funnelled to these parties? And can we value how much indirect support (bots, disinformation by state actors, algorithm meddling on X, etc.) they are receiving?
Jon Henley: Our data team looked at this question a couple of years ago, before the last European parliament elections. They concluded a quarter of all private money donated to political parties in the EU was going to far-right, far-left and populist movements – aided by the fact that only a quarter of EU countries require parties to identify private donors – with €97m (about one in every seven private donation euros across the EU) going to far-right parties.
A European parliament report from 2023 estimated that about $1.18bn in funding towards organisations targeting LGBTQ+ rights and promoting traditional family policies flowed into Europe from 2019 to 2023, and a 2022 declassified US intelligence assessment found the Russian government had covertly funnelled at least $300m to foreign political parties, often in Europe, from 2014.
Ashifa Kassam: We’ve also had some recent reporting on the flow of funds from the US. In July, the Guardian reported that Donald Trump’s state department intended to allocate $12m to organisations in the UK founded by prominent conservatives. Of these funds, $7m was to go to 878, a thinktank that describes itself as being devoted to “the rediscovery of our ancient culture” and “ending mass migration.”
In July, the state department issued a notice of funding, offering grants for organisations and institutions interested in promoting what it described as “civilisational self-confidence in Europe”.
While research out of Europe, such as the Munich-based Ifo Institute, has found “no correlation” between migration and higher crime rates, the US state department notice suggested it was hoping the grants would lead to outcomes including reports on the impact of mass migration on local safety and tools to analyse impact of mass migration on democratic institutions.
One user asked: How serious would you describe the threat these far-right parties pose to democracy? And to what extent do you think there is a collaboration between them and powerful social media personalities or state sponsored online social media propaganda?
Jon Henley: Some far right parties definitely pose more of a threat to democracy than others. Political scientists divide far-right parties into those that essentially operate within basic democratic norms (“radical right” parties), and those that seek to overturn the system, to the extent even of condoning violence (“extreme right” parties).
If we take one example, AfD in Germany could be described as extreme right in some respects (and some local branches are indeed classified as such by German domestic intelligence). Some of its positions are in clear contradiction with liberal democracy: it is openly racist, homophobic, misogynistic. It believes citizens should be ranked by its own warped criteria, including ethnicity, gender and religious belief. It flirts continually with Nazi rhetoric, imagery and symbolism.
On this question I recommend this column by Cas Mudde, a top scholar of populism and the far right, after AfD won in the recent state elections in Saxony-Anhalt. He argues that mainstream parties have to wake up to the fact that they are not in a battle that’s about vote share and elections, it’s about democracy itself.
Ashifa Kassam: I would add that we’ve seen some fairly high-profile examples of collaboration, from Elon Musk’s repeated endorsements of the AfD on X to his 2025 X talk with the party’s co-leader, Alice Weidel. The Guardian has also regularly explored the interplay between the far right and social media, such as a 2025 investigation that looked at how a network of far-right Facebook groups had become an “engine of radicalisation” by exposing hundreds of thousands of people in Britain to racist and extremist disinformation.
KilmaSelth asked: Do you think the hard right parties tend to moderate as they approach power, or do they maintain their radicalism?
Jon Henley: Based on Meloni and Le Pen, I would for a long time have said yes – Meloni basically struck a bargain to get elected in which she promised to be responsible on the economy, in the EU and as regards foreign policy, as long as she could do her culture-wars stuff domestically. Le Pen has spent years “detoxifying” the National Rally and kicking out over-radical undesirables. But if you look at AfD, they haven’t moderated their language at all – if anything, they’ve hardened it – and it manifestly is not doing them any harm. And as Meloni and Le Pen have moderated their positions, we’ve started to see them being outflanked on their right, by the likes of Roberto Vannacci and his National Future in Italy and Eric Zemmour’s Reconquête in France. So I think we may be heading into a period where the former far right is effectively now part of the political landscape, like “regular” parties that will sometimes win and sometimes lose elections, and will be increasingly challenged on their right by more extreme elements.
Ashifa Kassam: Vox offers another way to look at this question, as the party was founded in 2013 by disgruntled members of the conservative People’s party (PP). Its leader, Santiago Abascal, is a career politician who was among those who saw an opportunity to push further on the right flank of Spanish politics when it came to Catalan separatism, immigration, abortion and LGBTQ+ rights. It was a hardline stance that was often (but not always) diluted when Abascal was part of the PP; now as a separate party, they’ve seized on their electoral momentum in some regions to push the party to heed their agenda.

Bulgaria seeks NATO anti-drone systems, says defence minister

Bulgaria seeks NATO anti-drone systems, says defence minister
SOFIA, Oct 16 - Bulgaria has formally asked NATO to deploy combat aircraft and anti-drone systems to bolster its defences after a series of drone attacks on commercial shipping in the Black Sea, Defence Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said on Friday.
Drones hit two ships which caught fire off Romania's Black Sea coast this week. On Tuesday, a commercial vessel sank off Bulgaria's Black Sea coast following a drone attack, prompting Sofia to summon Russia's ambassador.
The attacks have highlighted the growing threat that drone warfare linked to the Russia-Ukraine conflict poses to commercial shipping near NATO's southeastern flank, prompting Bulgaria to push for stronger alliance defences in the Black Sea.
"We have sent letters and a request to the NATO Secretary General and the Supreme Allied Commander, urging them to strengthen our capabilities, which also means deploying additional forces on our territory. We are awaiting their decision," Stoyanov said.
NATO did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Stoyanov said he planned to meet his Romanian and Turkish counterparts soon to discuss coordinating action and a common approach to the situation in the Black Sea.
Bulgaria, which has proposed a moratorium on attacks on civilian ships in the Black Sea, also expects to join a NATO anti-drone initiative by the end of October. REUTERS
