Taiwan buys three years of support for MQ-9B drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:45:13 UTC
17:45:13 KST

- Taiwan is paying General Atomics $38.8 million for MQ-9B contractor logistics support through August 2029 under a sole-source Foreign Military Sales contract.
- Taiwan has ordered four MQ-9Bs, with the first two handed over in March 2026 and the remaining two due in 2027.
Taiwan is paying General Atomics Aeronautical Systems $38.8 million to keep its new MQ-9B SkyGuardian drones flying, under a contractor logistics support deal that runs through August 2029, the U.S. Department of War said.
The award, announced on Oct. 15 in the Pentagon’s daily contract list and signed on Oct. 1, covers sustainment services and contractor logistics support for Taiwan’s MQ-9B fleet. Contractor logistics support means the manufacturer handles much of the maintenance, spare parts supply and technical support for the aircraft instead of relying entirely on the operator’s own maintenance system.
Taiwan is covering the full cost through the Foreign Military Sales program, and all of the money was obligated at signing. The U.S. Air Force Life Cycle Management Center at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio, which manages the sale for Taipei, awarded the contract to General Atomics on a sole-source basis, with the work to be performed at the company’s facility in Poway, California.
Taiwan has ordered four MQ-9Bs, a medium-altitude, long-endurance drone developed from the Reaper that can stay airborne for more than 40 hours. The State Department approved the sale in 2020. The U.S. government then signed a $217.6 million contract for the first two aircraft in May 2023 and a $250 million contract for the final two in March 2024, with two ground control stations included across the deals, Defense News reported.
The first two drones were handed over to the Republic of China Air Force at a ceremony in the United States on March 17, 2026, attended by Taiwanese Vice Defense Minister Hsu Szu-chien. The aircraft were to stay in the U.S. for several months of testing, and Taiwan’s air force chief of staff said they were scheduled to arrive on the island in the third quarter of 2026. The remaining two are due in 2027.
Taipei plans to use the drones for long-range surveillance and reconnaissance around the island, where Chinese military aircraft and ships operate almost daily. Analysts have said the MQ-9Bs could take over some patrol missions now flown by Taiwan’s fighter jets and its aging P-3 maritime patrol aircraft, and help locate targets for Taiwan’s anti-ship missiles.
The drones will join a fast-growing Taiwanese unmanned fleet. The Ministry of National Defense announced plans in July 2025 to buy nearly 49,000 drones of five types for about NT$50 billion ($1.56 billion), alongside locally developed systems from the state-run National Chung-Shan Institute of Science and Technology.
Under the new contract, General Atomics will support Taiwan’s MQ-9B operations through Aug. 31, 2029.

Ukrainian Composer’s Opera on Abducted Children Premieres in Warsaw
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:44:22 UTC
17:44:22 KST

Warsaw, Oct. 16 – The Polish National Opera at Teatr Wielki presents the fully staged world premiere of “The Mothers of Kherson,” an opera by Ukrainian composer Maxim Kolomiiets with a libretto by acclaimed American playwright George Brant. Commissioned by New York’s Metropolitan Opera, the work brings Russia’s abduction of Ukrainian children to the international stage.
Conducted by Canadian-American maestro Keri-Lynn Wilson and directed by Barbara Wysocka, the production combines artistic achievement with a call for international attention to the fate of Ukraine’s children.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“One of history’s most sinister war crimes”
Ahead of the premiere, Wilson dedicated her message to Ukrainian families still waiting for their children to return.
“As we have our final dress rehearsal this evening in Warsaw for ‘The Mothers of Kherson,’ my heart is with my beloved sisters and brothers in Ukraine who are waiting and hoping for the more than 20,000 children who are still missing – innocent victims of Russia’s brutal child kidnapping program,” Wilson said.
“Our world premiere Friday night is the true story of the mothers who embark on the heroic journey to rescue their children,” adding that “we hope the world will join us in bearing witness to one of history’s most sinister war crimes.”
Wilson conducted the opera’s concert premiere in Kyiv in early June at the National Opera of Ukraine. The Warsaw production marks its first fully staged performance.
22 US Lawmakers Press Trump to Enforce Russia Sanctions Ahead of Oct. 18 Deadline
                                                                                                                                                                         Photo via Kinga Karpati & Daniel Zarewicz                             
According to Ukraine’s “Children of War” platform, 20,651 children had been registered as deported or forcibly displaced since Russia’s full-scale invasion began. Of these, 2,689 had been returned, according to the figures provided for this article.
Three women, one mission
The opera follows three women from southern Ukraine: Kateryna (Izabela Matuła), Dasha (Kamila Dutkowska), and grandmother Olha (Małgorzata Walewska). They undertake an exhausting journey to recover children taken to Russian-controlled territory.
                                                                                                                                                                         The final dress rehearsal. Photo via Krzysztof Bielinski.                             
Based on real events, the work explores maternal love, solidarity, and the trauma of families torn apart by war. It opens with a lullaby combining an authentic Ukrainian folk melody with a newly composed section by Kolomiiets – a musical reminder of the protection every child deserves.
Ukrainian baritone Andrii Bondarenko plays Vitaly, a Ukrainian Armed Forces serviceman and Kateryna’s husband, whose story connects the opera to the liberation of Kherson from Russian occupation on Nov. 11, 2022.
An international commission for Ukrainian music
The production marks a significant milestone for Ukrainian contemporary opera, bringing Kolomiiets’s work to two leading international institutions and ensuring that the stories of Ukrainian families reach audiences beyond the country.
In an interview with Kyiv Post, Kolomiiets discussed creating the opera and bringing Ukraine’s wartime experience to the international stage.
Metropolitan Opera General Manager Peter Gelb has also spoken about the institution’s commitment to Ukraine and the role of culture in bearing witness to the war. “This war is now longer than World War II, I think… It’s good for Ukrainian citizens to understand that there are efforts being made. I mean, even if the US government has stopped helping Ukraine, the fact that its premier arts institution has never given up in supporting Ukraine, and that we’re bringing this story to the world… I think by doing it here, first [it] shows the Ukrainian people that the world has not forgotten them” Gelb said.
Since 2022, Gelb and Wilson have become the prominent international advocates for Ukrainian music. Wilson conducted concerts in Ukraine and abroad, while also supporting Ukrainian musicians through the Ukrainian Freedom Orchestra.
The opera’s US premiere at the Metropolitan Opera in New York is scheduled for the 2027-28 season.

"Now, if you tell me that Zelenskyy is again shooting at refineries, all he's doing is making the world oil price higher. Well, I think that's a disgrace... there are many other targets to hit," Trump said.
According to the head of the White House, strikes on refineries producing diesel fuel harm the global energy market. Trump seeks to reduce energy prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections on November 3, 2026, including through an agreement with Putin regarding the purchase of Russian diesel. Assessing the prospects of ending the war by the end of his term, the U.S. President expressed confidence that hostilities should end soon, but questioned the Ukrainian leader's readiness for compromises. According to Trump, negotiating with Zelenskyy is harder than with Putin, while mutual personal hostility between the two leaders presents an additional obstacle to a settlement.
Furthermore, the American president spoke in favor of holding elections in Ukraine, questioning the level of public support for the current government amid ongoing missile strikes on residential buildings. He also criticized his predecessor Joe Biden for providing Kyiv with multi-billion-dollar military aid and stated that the current administration is replenishing its own stockpiles of Patriot anti-aircraft missile systems and Tomahawk cruise missiles at record speed, after which Washington will permit allies to purchase these arms.
Separately, Trump reported that his administration is holding talks with Russia and China regarding the reduction of nuclear arsenals. According to his assessment, the U.S. ranks first in the world in nuclear capability, Russia second, while Beijing is currently less inclined toward denuclearization due to a lag that it could close within five to six years. The American president did not specify a timeframe for these negotiations.
On Thursday, Ukraine resumed strikes on Russian oil infrastructure following a three-day pause that Kyiv agreed to after Trump announced an energy ceasefire on Sunday. A senior Ukrainian official confirmed a drone attack on an oil refinery in Russia's Ryazan region, located approximately 290 km southeast of Moscow, where a fire broke out.
Previously, Ukraine fully agreed to U.S. President Donald Trump's proposal for an energy truce and did not attack any energy facilities in Russia in response to their strikes.

At least 12 dead after migrant boat sinks off Gambia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:43:01 UTC
17:43:01 KST

The IOM says increased controls in traditional departure spots in Morocco, Mauritania, and Senegal have pushed some migrants seeking to reach Europe further south, towards countries such as The Gambia.
At least 12 people died after a boat carrying migrants sank off the coast of Gambia, the Red Cross said.
The incident occurred off of Jinack Kajata in the country's North Bank region, the Gambia Red Cross Society (GRCS) said on Thursday. The migrants were reportedly heading towards Europe via the West African Atlantic Route.
"The number of people missing remains uncertain, and further updates are expected as response efforts continue," the GRCS said in a statement, adding that it was "working closely with relevant authorities and response partners as the situation unfolds."
According to Gambian media, the village of Jinack Kajata on Jinack Island has become an increasingly popular launch site for migrants looking to make the journey to Spain's Canary Islands in the Atlantic Ocean.
The United Nations' International Organization for Migration (IOM) says the West African Atlantic Route is a key pathway for West African migrants travelling to Europe, despite it becoming increasingly dangerous.
"Data from the West African Atlantic Route show that while arrivals to the Canary Islands fell considerably since the 2024 peak (62 per cent decrease from 2024 to 2025), recorded deaths and disappearances remained broadly unchanged, falling 4 per cent from 2024 to 2025 (1,215 to 1,172), highlighting how the route has become much more dangerous for migrants," the IOM said earlier this week.
It added that increased controls in traditional departure spots in Morocco, Mauritania, and Senegal have pushed some migrants seeking to reach Europe further south, towards countries such as The Gambia.
"These alternative departure points can add up to 750 kilometres to the crossing, extending some journeys to approximately 2,200 kilometres and exposing people to longer periods at sea, more remote and less monitored coastlines, and greater risks of shipwreck, dehydration and disappearance," the IOM said.
In July, dozens of migrants were reportedly dead or missing after a vessel travelling from The Gambia was shipwrecked off the coast of Mauritania.

- EU leaders say they will keep sanctions and aid in place, press the US when possible, and avoid forcing Ukraine to give up land.

BRUSSELS – European leaders know they can’t stop courting Donald Trump. But as the US president menaces Ukraine and offers Russia an economic lifeline, they are preparing for a world where he effectively sides with Moscow.
In the span of a week, Trump has trashed years of energy sanctions on the Kremlin, pressured Kyiv to quit bombing Russian oil refineries and suggested Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelensky was an illegitimate president – echoing Moscow’s propaganda.
At one point, Ukraine also lost full access to the Elon Musk-owned Starlink system, leaving it hobbled on the battlefield.
In response, Zelensky let rip. He felt betrayed, he said. He called out Trump in public.
It was a dismaying moment for the Europeans, according to people familiar with the conversations at a leaders’ summit in Brussels this week.
For many, it exposed a painful reality they’ve been avoiding for months: Trump’s instinct is to bash Kyiv and boost Russia.
And that’s unlikely to change, several European Union leaders, including those of France and Germany, said during their private conversations.
Zelensky himself will address the meeting on Oct 16.
“We see that Zelensky has only one ally now, it’s actually the Europeans,” Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs told Bloomberg TV in Brussels.
Trump and Zelensky have been here before, of course, and always found a way to patch things up.
Their first meeting in the Oval Office in 2025 descended into a shouting match and prompted the US to briefly curb intelligence sharing.
Later, the US tried to convince Kyiv to accept a 28-point peace plan that overwhelmingly favoured Russia, prompting Zelensky to warn his country risked losing its key partner.
By this summer, European leaders had managed to persuade Trump to show a degree of sympathy for Ukraine’s long fight against the Russian invasion.
At the Group of Seven (G-7) summit in France, President Emmanuel Macron engineered a brief meeting with Trump at which Zelensky showed him pictures of a cathedral in Kyiv decimated by Russian missiles.
“The western alliance is in a weaker position now than it was a few days ago,” Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen told reporters as she arrived for talks in the Belgian capital on Oct 15.
“If you do not support Ukraine, then you put Europe as a whole, and in my view therefore also NATO as a whole, in a much, much more dangerous situation.”
Their latest falling-out is happening at a particularly inopportune moment.
Winter is setting in and Ukraine has a shortage of the US-made Patriot interceptors needed to shoot down Russian missiles.
Kyiv’s military costs are also blowing a hole in its budget that Europe is struggling to fill.
Meanwhile, Russia is striking more civilian targets, leaving Kyiv experiencing intermittent power and water supply cuts.
In November, Russian President Vladimir Putin will have a chance to meet with Trump at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China – where neither Zelensky nor the Europeans will be present.
Trump, for his part, is weeks away from a midterm election where his Republican party is expected to suffer heavy losses – sending him searching for quick ways to lower gas prices.
That fixation is informing Trump’s push to buy Russian diesel despite sanctions, and his calls for Ukraine to halt attacks on oil refineries, even if experts say the US war on Iran is the largest culprit behind high fuel costs.
“The most important thing that we’re going to discuss today is what he needs for this winter. It’s all about this winter,” Kulberg told Bloomberg.
“We also have to understand that the United States is now running into the midterms. It’s election time,” Kulbergs said. “That’s a different vibe.”
For now, most Europeans are recommending that Zelensky temper his criticism of Trump, given there is no alternative to working with the US, the people said.
The country continues to sell Ukraine weapons and share intelligence vital to Kyiv’s defence.
If that intelligence disappeared, Europe would not have a good solution, one official said.
That’s likely why EU leaders were careful not to be too publicly critical of Trump as they arrived on Oct 15 for their summit in Brussels.
Behind closed doors, however, several still expressed shock at the US president’s recent behaviour, the people said.
An Elysee official said France’s priority is for Europe to continue supporting Ukraine.
A German chancellery spokesperson didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment.
Europe is sticking to its guns by upholding sanctions and insisting that Ukraine shouldn’t cede territory in a peace settlement, especially after Kyiv’s forces regained some lost ground in the eastern region of Donbas Putin wants to control.
US leverage over Ukraine has also diminished over the last few months.
While intelligence remains an important factor, the money to support Kyiv and buy US weapons comes primarily from Europe.
Ukraine is also finally receiving ammunition for F-16 fighter jets to shoot down Russia’s menacing jet-powered drones.
Meanwhile, Washington’s efforts to deliver peace, which Trump promised to bring shortly after taking officein 2025, haven’t made much headway.
The latest meetings in Florida over the weekend, which the Ukrainian delegation cut short following Trump’s Russia diesel deal, largely focused on going over the same set of points that the president’s envoys – Steven Witkoff and Jared Kushner – drew up months ago, according to people familiar with the matter.
During a meeting on Oct 12, EU foreign ministers privately agreed that Europe’s policy on Ukraine must remain constant, regardless of the gyrations in Washington, according to people briefed on the discussions.
They resolved to engage the US when it’s possible, and maintain their support for Kyiv when it’s not.
“We definitely have a different approach to this war,” EU top diplomat Kaja Kallas told reporters in Brussels on Oct 15. “We see that we have to pressure the aggressor to stop the war, not the victim to surrender. Squeezing Ukraine is not the right approach.” BLOOMBERG

Cambodia fully restores centuries-old West Mebon Temple in famed Angkor park
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:39:41 CST
17:39:41 KST

This photo taken on Oct. 15, 2026 shows part of the restored West Mebon Temple in Siem Reap province, Cambodia. Archaeologists have successfully restored the centuries-old West Mebon Temple within Cambodia's UNESCO-listed Angkor Archaeological Park, according to an APSARA National Authority (ANA) news release on Friday. (ANA/Handout via Xinhua)
PHNOM PENH, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- Archaeologists have successfully restored the centuries-old West Mebon Temple within Cambodia's UNESCO-listed Angkor Archaeological Park, according to an APSARA National Authority (ANA) news release on Friday.
Situated on an island in the middle of the West Baray -- the Angkor area's largest reservoir -- the temple is surrounded by vast expanses of water, creating a distinctive and captivating landscape.
While the ANA prepares the site for its official opening in November by cleaning the area, organizing the surroundings, and enhancing the environment, eager tourists have already begun visiting the temple to take photographs and admire its remarkable architecture.
Through a joint effort between the ANA and the French government, the temple underwent extensive restoration to recover its former appearance after suffering significant structural damage and stone loss over the centuries.
"The completion of this work marks an important achievement in the ongoing efforts to preserve and restore Angkor's cultural heritage," the news release said.
Built in the middle of the 11th century as a Hindu sanctuary, the West Mebon Temple was constructed using laterite and sandstone. A short boat trip takes visitors to the monument, which marks the exact center of the massive 8 km by 2.2 km reservoir, the ANA said, adding that the site offers a uniquely serene atmosphere, especially at sunset.
The West Mebon Temple stands as one of the major cultural monuments within the Angkor Archaeological Park, Cambodia's most popular tourist destination, located in northwestern Siem Reap province. ■

S. Korea's interbank forex trading volume grows in Q3
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:39:38 CST
17:39:38 KST

SEOUL, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's interbank foreign exchange trading volume grew in the third quarter due to a substantial rise in foreign exchange (FX) swap transactions, central bank data showed Friday.
The daily average transaction of foreign currencies and derivatives in the domestic interbank market increased 2.25 billion U.S. dollars from three months earlier to 55.65 billion dollars in the July-September quarter, according to the Bank of Korea.
FX swaps served as the main driver of growth, mounting 1.80 billion dollars from the previous quarter to hit a daily average trading of 25.92 billion dollars in the third quarter.
Spot exchange volume ticked up 0.07 billion dollars to 23.48 billion dollars, and forward contracts trading added 0.20 billion dollars to 2.60 billion dollars.
The transaction of other derivatives, including currency swaps and options, was up 0.18 billion dollars to 3.66 billion dollars.
The daily average volatility in the South Korean won versus U.S. dollar exchange rate advanced to 0.52 percent in September from 0.31 percent in August.
The won versus dollar exchange rate slightly dipped to 1,352.8 won per dollar at the end of September from 1,368.6 won tallied a month earlier.
Premium on credit default swap, which gauges credit risk for five-year government bonds, averaged 22 basis points in September, unchanged from the previous month. ■

MOSCOW, October 15. /TASS/. Moscow and its partners in Central Asia are taking every measure possible to counter threats posed by arms and drug trafficking from Afghanistan, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said.
"Attempts continue to smuggle weapons and drugs from Afghanistan into Central Asia and onward to Russia. Russia and its partners in the region need to give an appropriate comprehensive response to these challenges, and this is what we are doing," he pointed out, addressing a conference on security issues in Central Asia and Afghanistan involving the Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO), the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS), and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO).

"At the political level, we focus our efforts on consolidating external support for the Kabul authorities and the areas of their activities that serve the interests of regional security. Russia fully shares the vision that Afghanistan should be an independent, united and peaceful country, free of war and drugs," the Russian foreign minister concluded.

Mystery foreign buyer pays for its own custom F-35
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:38:38 UTC
17:38:38 KST

- An unnamed foreign customer is paying Lockheed Martin $18.8 million for development and integration work on an F-35 variant tailored to its requirements.
- The award continues a contract that funded similar work in 2022 and 2025, with the new effort running through December 2030.
An unnamed foreign government is paying Lockheed Martin another $18.8 million to develop and integrate a version of the F-35 fighter jet built to its own specifications, the U.S. Department of War said on Oct. 15.
The Pentagon’s daily contract announcement said the modification to an existing contract with Lockheed Martin Aeronautics in Fort Worth, Texas, adds scope for system development, demonstration and integration work on an F-35 variant tailored to the requirements of an unspecified Foreign Military Sales customer. The customer is covering the full $18.8 million, which was obligated when the contract was signed.
Foreign Military Sales is the government-to-government route Washington uses to sell weapons abroad, and Pentagon contract notices sometimes leave the buyer unnamed when the customer’s identity is considered sensitive.
About 80% of the work will take place in Fort Worth, where Lockheed builds the F-35, and the remaining 20% at undisclosed locations in the continental United States. The work is scheduled to run through December 2030, and Naval Air Systems Command at Patuxent River, Maryland, which handles F-35 contracting, awarded the sole-source deal.
The award is the latest step in a long-running effort on the same contract. The U.S. Navy awarded Lockheed a $53.4 million modification in August 2022 for continued engineering on the design and development of a Joint Strike Fighter variant tailored for an unspecified FMS customer, followed by a $12.9 million modification in August 2025, according to federal contracting records. The new action, numbered P00011, now combines cost-plus-incentive-fee and firm-fixed-price terms.
The F-35 comes in three versions: the conventional-takeoff F-35A, the short-takeoff and vertical-landing F-35B, and the carrier-based F-35C. Lockheed has delivered jets to more than a dozen foreign air forces, and some customers integrate national weapons, communications or electronic warfare gear on their aircraft. Israel’s F-35I Adir is the best-known example of a country-specific version, carrying Israeli-developed systems on the F-35A airframe.
When a similar tailored-variant contract surfaced in 2021, aviation analysts speculated about which country was behind it, with Key Aero pointing to customers such as Singapore that were then taking first deliveries. The Pentagon has never publicly named the customer under this contract.
The latest award comes as F-35 production remains near record levels. Lockheed delivered 191 F-35s in 2025, and recent long-lead contracts for Lots 20 and 21 cover nearly 200 more jets for U.S. services, partner nations and foreign buyers.
Work on the tailored variant under the new modification is set to continue for more than four years, through December 2030.

No, this oil tanker didn’t carry Russian diesel to the United States
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:36:46 UTC
17:36:46 KST

No, this oil tanker didn’t carry Russian diesel to the United States
Following US President Donald Trump's October 9 announcement of an agreement signed with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel into the United States, a number of pro-Russian social media accounts began claiming that a Russian oil tanker was already carrying thousands of barrels of diesel to the United States. The ship was actually carrying fertiliser.
US President Donald Trump announced on Friday, October 9, that he had reached an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import millions of tons of Russian diesel.
“Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter. Additionally, based on the condition of their Diesel Refineries, Russia will then deliver, within a short period of time, 3,000,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel,” Trump wrote on his platform Truth Social.
The next day, the pro-Russian X account Russian Market (which uses the handle @runews) posted that Russian diesel was already being delivered to the United States, scarcely a day after the deal.
The account claimed that the Minerva Zen, an oil and chemical tanker, was carrying close to 280,000 barrels of diesel from Russia… and was bound for the United States. The post even featured a map of the route it was taking, starting with when the cargo was supposedly loaded on September 22 in Saint Petersburg, Russia.
The fake news spread quickly, appearing in different posts and garnering more than 570,000 views on X. It was also picked up by media outlets in Nigeria.
A ship carrying fertiliser, according to Tanker Trackers
This claim, however, is wrong. The Minerva Zen was not carrying diesel from Russia.
It is true that the Minerva Zen, an oil and chemical tanker (which means it is equipped to carry chemical products as well as petrol products), did leave the port in Saint Petersburg on September 23. You can see this on the site Global Fishing Watch, a site that makes it possible to follow marine traffic.
MarineTraffic, another site that tracks ships across the globe, shows that the Minerva Zen docked in Wilmington, North Carolina on the night of October 11 to 12.
The FRANCE 24 Observers team spoke to Tankertrackers.com, a company specialised in tracking oil tankers in particular, who said that the Minerva Zen wasn’t carrying diesel but fertiliser, specifically urea ammonium nitrate (UAN). This information was confirmed by the economic intelligence company Vortexa.
“When the US imposed sanctions on Russia back in February/March 2022, they banned the import of hydrocarbons such as crude oil, fuel oil, LNG, etc., but they allowed fertiliser,” Tanker Trackers said.
As you can see on a site that records imports, Russian fertiliser was also imported into Wilmington back in June. The June cargo was delivered to a company called Eurochem North America, which specialises in fertiliser production. According to Tankertrackers, the October 12 delivery was also bound for Eurochem North America.
Cargo not unloaded in the port’s petrol terminal
Another supporting the information that the Minerva Zen was not carrying diesel is that the tanker was not unloaded in the port’s "Apex Oil Co Wilmington" petrol terminal, which is located to the south of Wilmington port.
According to the data gathered by MarineTraffic, the tanker was unloaded in the “NSCPA” Terminal located to the north of the port. This terminal is where agricultural and chemical products as well as containers are unloaded.
Finally, Minerva Marine, the company that owns the Minerva Zen, told US local TV station Wwaytv3 that the tanker was carrying urea ammonium nitrate, not diesel.
This article has been translated from the original in French by Brenna Daldorph.

Norway wealth fund urged to ease nuclear arms ban after Gaza investment row
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:36:13 UTC
17:36:13 KST

Norway wealth fund urged to ease nuclear arms ban after Gaza investment row
Review prompted by Gaza action calls for Norway’s sovereign wealth fund to lift ethical risk limitations on its investments.
A government-appointed committee has called for Norway’s sovereign wealth fund to lift limitations on its investments based on ethical risks, including those regarding nuclear weapons and Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.
In a report released on Thursday, the committee said the world’s largest sovereign wealth fund, which controls assets totalling nearly $2.3 trillion, should be allowed to invest in companies that produce nuclear weapons. With reference to Gaza, it also called for the fund to refrain from involvement in “diplomatic” issues.
Led by former Central Bank Governor Svein Gjedrem, the committee recommended easing the fund’s investment conditions as part of a broader overhaul that would give its manager, the Central Bank, greater discretion over how it addresses ethical risks.
The review was prompted in part by controversy over the fund’s disinvestment last year from United States construction giant Caterpillar. The fund said the move was prompted by Caterpillar’s purported involvement in rights violations perpetrated by Israel amid its genocidal war on Gaza and in the occupied West Bank. Washington has since pressured Oslo over the move.
“Parts of the rationale for the appointment of the Committee was the Fund’s management related to the war in Gaza,” the committee commissioned by the government said. In the report, it argued that decisions regarding “another state’s conduct” should not be made by the fund but “reserved for the ordinary diplomatic channels of the Norwegian authorities”.
The unanimous recommendations of the committee in the report, which was submitted to the Ministry of Finance, also called for a review of the fund’s exclusion of investment in companies involved in the production of nuclear weapons.
Citing Norway’s reliance on NATO’s nuclear deterrent and a worsening security environment, the report suggested that investments in companies based in the US, United Kingdom and France that are involved in the production of nuclear weapons should be allowed.
The proposals also extended to reshaping the role of the fund’s independent ethics watchdog, allowing a number of assessments of potential investments to remain confidential.
‘Pandora’s box’
The report has already provoked a backlash in Norway, with opposition politicians slamming the potential changes. Meanwhile, analysts suggested that weakening ethics considerations could have a wide impact.
“If the Norwegian sovereign wealth fund – often considered a global gold standard – changes its posture towards nuclear weapons, it will open Pandora’s box for many global investors to follow suit,” Lawrence Loh, director of the Centre for Governance and Sustainability at the National University of Singapore Business School, told Al Jazeera.
The committee framed the proposed change as an obligation to protect Norway’s national security, citing the country’s dependence on its allies’ nuclear umbrella.
“The global security situation has changed. Norway is building up its defence capabilities, and the protection provided by NATO’s nuclear umbrella has become increasingly important. The companies that would be reincluded produce weapons that Norway needs for its own defence”, the report argued.
Gareth Evans, former Australian foreign minister, told Al Jazeera the report was “an encouraging initiative in a world that has become alarmingly complacent about the risks of nuclear war, with every major nuclear arms control agreement dead, dying or on life support, and the longstanding taboo against threat or use eroding”.
Amid US President Donald Trump’s shake-up of NATO, European countries are increasingly looking to join France’s nuclear deterrent umbrella.
Trump said on Thursday that Washington is holding talks with Russia and China aimed at denuclearising the countries with the biggest stockpiles of nuclear weapons.
However, Loh warned that shifting the Norwegian fund’s investment conditions could encourage investment by others in nuclear companies “in scenarios different from the Norwegians’ condition of the invested companies being based in allied, nuclear-armed NATO countries”.

Economists warn Lithuania’s 2027 budget risks rising debt and deficit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:35:00 UTC
17:35:00 KST

Lithuania’s proposed 2027 budget will further widen the government deficit and increase public debt, while ambitious revenue targets could prove difficult to meet, economists warned Friday after the government approved the draft budget.
The spending plan reflects continued fiscal expansion, with expenditure growing faster than nominal gross domestic product, even when the impact of European Union structural funding is excluded, said Indrė Genytė-Pikčienė, an economist at Artea Bank.
“Next year will be another year of generous fiscal expansion,” she told BNS, adding that declining EU structural support and fewer one-off economic tailwinds would make the outlook more challenging.
Tadas Povilauskas, an economist at SEB Bank, said fiscal policy would again stimulate the economy through borrowing. But rising deficits and public acceptance of persistent overspending could make it more difficult to consolidate public finances in the future without slowing economic growth.
The budget deficit is set to grow mainly because of higher social benefits and public-sector wages, much of which is linked to automatic indexation of pensions, benefits and salaries, Povilauskas said.
He questioned the need for an additional 150 million euros earmarked for a proposed family support package, arguing that some spending increases went beyond what indexation required. He also criticised the lack of emphasis on improving public administration efficiency.
However, he said higher social spending could support domestic businesses by boosting consumption among lower-income households.
Revenue targets under scrutiny
Genytė-Pikčienė questioned whether the government would collect all the revenue projected in the budget. Lithuania’s economy benefited this year from increased consumption following a reform of the second-pillar pension system, but that boost is expected to fade next year.
Povilauskas also described several revenue forecasts as ambitious.
Excise tax revenue is projected to rise by 11%, while value-added tax revenue is expected to increase by about 7.2%. He questioned whether the VAT target was realistic, particularly because 158 million euros of the expected increase is attributed to improved tax administration.
Household consumption is expected to grow more slowly next year as the effect of withdrawals from second-pillar pension funds fades, he said.
He also urged caution over the plan to collect 2.1 billion euros in corporate income tax, noting that the target for this year is expected to be missed.
Debt costs and EU deficit rules
Genytė-Pikčienė said the projected deficit was significant enough to raise the possibility of an infringement procedure by the European Commission because it would exceed the EU’s Maastricht deficit limit of 3% of GDP. She noted, however, that Lithuania was not the only country exceeding the threshold.
She warned that relying on borrowing to finance public spending could create serious long-term problems as debt servicing costs rise and leave less room for future policy decisions.
Povilauskas said interest payments would increase by 370 million euros next year, adding the equivalent of 0.3 percentage points of GDP to budget expenditure.
Public debt is expected to rise by another 6.5 billion euros in 2027, following an increase of 6.8 billion euros this year, reaching 48.2% of GDP by the end of next year.
The government is financing much of the increase in defence spending – from 2% to 5% of GDP over several years – through borrowing, while also increasing other expenditure, Povilauskas said. The Finance Ministry has acknowledged the risk that public debt could approach 60% of GDP by the end of the medium-term planning period.
Genytė-Pikčienė said lawmakers should carefully scrutinise any additional spending proposals during the budget process to prevent the deficit from growing further. She stressed that national defence and security must remain priorities because they are essential to economic prosperity, attracting foreign investment and supporting business stability.
Social spending and inflation
The draft budget maintains a strong focus on social spending and raising incomes, Genytė-Pikčienė said.
The average old-age pension is set to increase at a double-digit rate, while pensions for people with the required length of service are expected to rise by 11%. Salaries for teachers, statutory officers and cultural workers are planned to increase by 7.5%, with pay for judicial assistants rising by nearly 6%.
The government is seeking to offset pressure on household purchasing power from imported inflation, including higher fuel prices and heating costs, by increasing incomes, she said.
Lithuania has refrained from introducing broad measures to counter energy price increases, unlike some neighbouring countries, instead relying more heavily on income growth to cushion the impact on households.
Economist Romas Lazutka criticised the proposed 150 million-euro family package, saying its measures were universal rather than specifically targeted at people in the greatest need.
He said much of the budget deficit was effectively predetermined by legislation and existing commitments, including social benefits, education spending and public-sector collective agreements.
Reducing the deficit would likely require cuts to social spending, a politically unpopular step that would be difficult to implement, he said.
Lazutka also pointed to what he described as a structural imbalance between the state budget and the Sodra social insurance fund. Sodra regularly records a surplus and builds up reserves, while the central government runs a large deficit and borrows at interest rates higher than the returns earned on those reserves.
The arrangement means the government is paying more to borrow than it earns by investing money accumulated in the social insurance system, he said.

Foreign ministers from Türkiye and 18 other countries have strongly condemned Colombia’s opening of an embassy in West Jerusalem, describing the move as contrary to relevant United Nations Security Council resolutions and an obstacle to international efforts to achieve a just and lasting peace based on a two-state solution.
In a joint statement dated October 16 2026, the ministers from Türkiye, Algeria, Djibouti, Indonesia, Palestine, Qatar, Kuwait, Lebanon, Libya, Malaysia, Egypt, Pakistan, Somalia, Sudan, Syria, Saudi Arabia, Oman, Jordan and Yemen said they firmly rejected the opening of the Colombian embassy in the city.

They cited relevant UN Security Council and General Assembly resolutions, particularly Resolutions 476 and 478, both adopted in 1980. These resolutions reject attempts to change Jerusalem’s character or status and call on states to withdraw their diplomatic missions to Israel from the city, which forms part of the Palestinian territories occupied in 1967.
The statement called on the Colombian government to reconsider and reverse its decision, comply with its obligations under international law and refrain from measures that undermine the legitimate rights of the Palestinian people.
These rights, the ministers stressed, include the right to an independent and sovereign Palestinian state, with East Jerusalem as its capital.

‘Clean air is not a favour’: Indonesia’s neighbours fed up with acrid haze as Singapore threatens to prosecute
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:34:01 UTC
17:34:01 KST

Singapore is threatening to prosecute companies responsible for some of the worst fires in years in neighbouring Indonesia, as the region grows increasingly frustrated with a persistent, acrid haze that could result in diplomatic relations fraying.
Lawrence Wong, the Singaporean prime minister, said his government was distributing masks to vulnerable citizens and working with countries in the region to deal with the smoke. “At the same time, we are looking into which companies may be responsible for the fires,” he said in a Facebook post on Thursday, adding that he was exploring the idea of “joint action with other countries”.
Singapore has no plantations or forests of its own, but several companies with concessions in Indonesia are reportedly based in the city-state.
Haze is a persistent problem in Indonesia, but drier-than-usual conditions mean the thick smoke has been drifting into nearby Singapore, Malaysia, Brunei and Timor-Leste, and as far afield as the Philippines and Vietnam. Millions are affected, with school closures, respiratory illness spiking and air pollution indexes reaching unhealthy levels.
Malaysians and Singaporeans have been sharing images online of their cities, with skyscrapers disappearing into the smog, and frustration with the region’s most populous country is boiling over.
“Year after year, the haze comes back. It affects our health, closes schools, hurts businesses, and costs us billions,” a veteran Malaysian social activist and former politician wrote in a public letter this week. Lee Lam Thye said that real enforcement and “not just polite words” were needed. “Those responsible must be named, investigated, and punished. Clean air is not a favour. It is a basic right.”
While Indonesia regularly battles wildfires in the dry season, these blazes are the most intense in more than a decade and exacerbated by slash-and-burn practices to clear land for agriculture, including palm oil, of which Indonesia is the world’s largest producer.
Regional diplomats have offered to help Indonesia, but their offers have not always been immediately accepted. On Monday, an Indonesian official said the country was “still capable of handling it”. By the end of the week, Jakarta said it would accept assistance
Such delicate diplomacy is routine among the region’s Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean), which is built on quiet engagement and non-interference. A meeting of regional foreign ministers in the Philippines is due next month, but that might be too late.
Nerves are fraying. In remarks that went viral on social media, Syahganda Nainggolan, the head of Indonesia’s government communication agency, hit back at the criticism on Saturday. “We don’t only send haze,” he said, “the oxygen in Singapore and Malaysia comes from our forests.”
Rare strong words came earlier this month from Anwar Ibrahim, the Malaysian prime minister. He said he had been in contact with Indonesia’s president, Prabowo Subianto, “who agreed to take the necessary steps, and this commitment must be followed by immediate and effective action from the Indonesian side to tackle the root causes of the haze”.
At the same time, pressure is growing on Jakarta to declare a national disaster, first from civil society groups but now also from Indonesian politicians and neighbours.
According to the Jakarta Post, Indonesian students have been holding protests across Kalimantan and Sumatra, demanding accountability and government action. In one video posted online, a child in a mask stands outside under a dark orange sky and calls on the local and national government to help. He holds a sign that says: “Save our little lungs”.
The country has dispatched firefighters and announced a crackdown on arsonists, but declaring a disaster would unlock funds and help thousands with medical expenses.
On Friday, the Indonesian forestry ministry said four firefighters were killed in a national park in Java.
Longtime onlookers say the issue is not just firefighting, but targeting the companies involved. In recent years, several attempts to take legal action against the companies exacerbating “transboundary haze” have failed, both locally and internationally, and posed a diplomatic minefield.
Haze is complex for Singapore and Malaysia, as they host companies working in Indonesia. A Greenpeace report published this month identified businesses based in Singapore and Malaysia that it claimed were linked to burning land in Indonesia.
Ultimately, Indonesians bear the brunt of the blazes. The health ministry has reported nearly 280,000 people in the country with respiratory infections linked to the fires, with children under five accounting for more than 60,000.
Michelle Dyonisius, a campaigner at Amnesty International Indonesia, said rights groups and civil society organisations were ramping up pressure on the government to declare a national disaster emergency. “It has been going on for months, affecting millions and millions of people, including abroad,” she said.
“I think there is a refusal to acknowledge the gravity of the issue at hand and also the belief that it is under control. But considering the gravity of the issue and all of the people affected, it seems quite naive to remain in that position.”

KMT's Ko Chih-en makes second bid for Kaohsiung mayor

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — KMT Kaohsiung mayoral candidate Ko Chih-en (柯志恩) is seeking to lead the southern city with a campaign focused on jobs, affordable housing, and infrastructure.
Speaking at a youth forum at National Sun Yat-sen University on Wednesday, Ko said Kaohsiung needs better job opportunities to keep young people from leaving. The former professor said her 26 years of teaching had made her particularly concerned about graduates struggling to find work outside science and engineering, CNA reported.
Ko is making her second bid for mayor after losing to incumbent DPP Mayor Chen Chi-mai (陳其邁) in 2022. She is running against DPP Legislator Lai Jui-lung (賴瑞隆) in the Nov. 28 local elections, hoping to regain the city for the KMT, per UDN.
Born in Pingtung, Ko studied education at National Chengchi University before earning a master's degree from Michigan State University. She later received a doctorate in educational psychology from the University of Southern California, per Legislative Yuan.
Before entering politics, Ko taught at Tamkang University for more than two decades and served as dean of student affairs. Her academic career helped establish her reputation as an education specialist.
Ko was first elected to the Legislative Yuan in 2016, representing a district in New Taipei. She lost her re-election bid in 2020 but returned in 2024 as a KMT legislator elected through the party-list system, per Yahoo News.
Ko has also held senior KMT positions, including deputy secretary-general and head of the party's women's department. She previously led the National Policy Foundation, a KMT-affiliated think tank that develops policy proposals.
In 2022, Ko challenged Chen in Kaohsiung, a longtime DPP stronghold. She received 529,607 votes, or 40.16%, against Chen's 766,147 votes, or 58.1%, per Business Today.
Ko has remained active in Kaohsiung politics since her defeat while serving in the legislature. Her latest campaign emphasizes economic development, better public services, and more investment in areas outside the city center, per UDN.
At Wednesday's forum, Ko said Kaohsiung's young workforce had declined by about 100,000 in recent years. She called for higher wages, stronger local industries, and more job opportunities beyond the technology sector.
Ko has also proposed affordable housing for working families who cannot afford homes at market prices. She wants the city's growing concert and tourism industries to create more lasting jobs for local businesses and workers.

Strong winds fuel fires near Los Angeles as the region recovers from last year's deadly blazes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:33:00 UTC
17:33:00 KST

California wildfires force evacuations near Malibu
October 16, 2026
Several brush fires burned across southern California on Friday, forcing evacuations near Malibu as hot, dry winds fueled the flames.
The rapidly spreading Bryson Fire grew to about 81 hectares (200 acres) and threatened a Los Angeles County juvenile detention and rehabilitation facility, which was evacuated Thursday night.
What is happening near Malibu?
Authorities ordered residents to leave the Encinal Canyon area near Malibu, a coastal town west of Los Angeles. Surrounding parts of the Santa Monica Mountains were placed under evacuation warnings.
The National Weather Service forecast stronger gusts overnight that could intensify the fires.
The Bryson Fire was first reported around 5 p.m. local time Thursday (0000 GMT Friday), north of Malibu. A large plume of dark smoke rose above the hills and could be seen from miles away.
Los Angeles County officials urged residents to follow emergency instructions and check on neighbors who might need help, if safe to do so.
"If you feel unsafe due to a fire nearby ... do not wait for an official alert to leave," officials said.
The blaze was burning about 32 kilometers (20 miles) west of the area devastated by the Palisades Fire in January 2025.
Where else are firefighters battling blazes?
In Azusa, north of Los Angeles, about 200 firefighters tackled a wind-driven fire that burned more than 16 hectares (40 acres).
Crews stopped its forward spread by mid-afternoon, and evacuation orders for a neighborhood in the foothills of the San Gabriel Mountains were downgraded to warnings.
Further south, a fire at Camp Pendleton, a military base near San Diego, burned more than 3.8 square kilometers (1.5 square miles), threatening buildings and infrastructure.
Power companies cut supplies to about 127,000 customers across California to reduce the risk of electrical equipment sparking further fires.
The Palisades and Eaton fires killed 31 people in the Los Angeles area in January 2025. Forecasters said the current winds were not expected to reach the strength recorded during those disasters.
Edited by: Natalie Muller

Prices have risen again: which products became more expensive in Ukraine in just three days
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:32:45 EEST
17:32:45 KST

Prices have risen again: which products became more expensive in Ukraine in just three days
Kyiv • UNN
From October 12 to 15, 2026, prices increased for tomatoes, chicken, bananas, grains, and oil. A basket of seven items became 1.94% more expensive.
In Ukrainian supermarkets, average prices for a number of popular food products increased between October 12 and 15, 2026. Pink tomatoes, chicken and bananas became notably more expensive. The price increase also affected grains and sunflower oil. Although in most cases the difference amounts to just a few hryvnias, even such short-term fluctuations gradually increase Ukrainian families’ expenses on everyday shopping.
Which products Ukrainians already have to pay more for, how much the cost of a typical grocery basket has changed, and what factors may affect price tags in supermarkets were examined by UNN.
Tomatoes lead in price growth: how much they cost in October 2026
Pink tomatoes saw the largest price increase since the beginning of the current week. If a kilogram cost an average of UAH 112.33 on October 12, by October 15 its price had risen to UAH 115.67. In just three days, tomatoes became UAH 3.34, or 2.97%, more expensive. A similar trend can be observed in the plum tomato segment. Their average price increased from UAH 99.33 to UAH 100.79 per kilogram. Thus, the increase amounted to UAH 1.46, or 1.47%.
Both varieties of tomatoes have now exceeded the mark of UAH 100 per kilogram. At the same time, pink tomatoes remain almost UAH 15 more expensive than plum tomatoes. Experts analyzing the fruit and vegetable market explain that one possible reason for the increase in tomato prices is the seasonal decline in supply. In autumn, the amount of vegetables grown in open fields on the Ukrainian market gradually decreases. Meanwhile, greenhouse produce accounts for an increasingly larger share, and its cost depends on expenses for heating, electricity and maintaining the necessary growing conditions.
In addition, at the beginning of October, EastFruit analysts reported a reduction in tomato supply at trading platforms and an increase in wholesale prices. This may have created conditions for a further increase in vegetable prices in retail chains.
At the same time, it is important to take into account that the retail price depends on a number of components that may not be immediately obvious: logistics costs, the trade markup and the promotional policy of a particular supermarket. Therefore, an increase in the average price over three days does not mean that tomatoes became more expensive by the same amount in all stores across Ukraine.
Chicken and bananas increased in price by almost 3%
Among meat products, chicken carcasses showed a noticeable price increase. The average cost of one kilogram rose from UAH 114.25 on October 12 to UAH 117.50 on October 15. The price difference was UAH 3.25, or 2.84%. In terms of the absolute price increase, chicken almost matched pink tomatoes.
It should be noted that for buyers purchasing a whole carcass weighing more than one kilogram, the actual increase in the cost of the purchase will be higher. For example, a two-kilogram carcass at the average price on October 15 would cost UAH 235. Just three days earlier, on October 12, the same purchase would have cost UAH 228.50.
Chicken prices may be affected by producers’ expenses on feed, electricity, veterinary services, transportation and product storage.
Bananas ranked third in terms of the rate of price growth. Over three days, the average price per kilogram increased from UAH 76.33 to UAH 78.13. The tropical fruit became UAH 1.80, or 2.36%, more expensive. This happened because, unlike local seasonal vegetables, bananas come to Ukraine mainly from abroad. Accordingly, their price depends on the terms of import purchases, international logistics, transportation within the country and the exchange rate. In particular, changes in the value of foreign currencies may affect the purchase prices of imported products, since settlements with suppliers are made primarily in currencies other than the hryvnia.
Groceries are also becoming more expensive: how much buckwheat, rice and oil cost now
The price increase also affected long-shelf-life products that Ukrainians traditionally buy in reserve.
In the grains segment, buckwheat rose in price the most. The average cost of one kilogram increased from UAH 82.57 to UAH 84.10. The difference was UAH 1.53, or 1.85%. At first glance, this is an insignificant increase. However, for families that regularly consume buckwheat, the price increase will result in additional expenses. Thus, five kilograms of the grain would cost UAH 420.50 at prices on October 15, compared with UAH 412.85 three days earlier. According to experts, the increase in buckwheat prices may be related to the volume of the harvest, offers from processing enterprises, and the cost of storage and delivery to retail chains.
The price of long-grain parboiled rice changed somewhat less. While a kilogram cost an average of UAH 61.37 on October 12, by October 15 it already cost UAH 62.20.
Among the popular products that Ukrainians buy daily for their tables, the price of refined sunflower oil "Oliyna" increased the least. A bottle with a volume of 850 ml cost an average of UAH 107.20 on October 12, while on October 15 its price was UAH 107.67. In other words, the price increased by 47 kopecks, or 0.44%. For now, such a fluctuation does not provide grounds to speak of a significant increase in the price of sunflower oil overall. To assess the market situation, it is necessary to take into account price dynamics over a longer period, as well as the cost of products from other manufacturers.
In addition, supermarket promotional policies affect the prices of grocery products. The end of temporary discounts or changes in the product range may affect the average cost of goods even without a corresponding increase in manufacturers' selling prices.
How much the Ukrainian consumer's grocery basket rose in price over three days
To assess the impact of the price increase on daily expenses, one can compare the cost of a hypothetical grocery basket made up of all seven analyzed items.
It includes one kilogram each of pink tomatoes, plum tomatoes, a chicken carcass, bananas, buckwheat, and rice, as well as one 850 ml bottle of sunflower oil. As of October 12, the total cost of such a set was UAH 653.38. By October 15, the same list of products would have cost UAH 666.06. In three days, the hypothetical grocery basket had increased in price by UAH 12.68, or approximately 1.94%.
The largest contribution to the increase in total expenses came from the higher prices of pink tomatoes and chicken. Together, these two items added UAH 6.59 to the cost of the basket, accounting for more than half of the total increase.
Should we expect food prices to continue rising
The price increases recorded between October 12 and 15 indicate a short-term rise in the cost of certain everyday products. However, economists emphasize that it is incorrect to draw conclusions about an overall acceleration of food inflation based solely on seven product items. They explain that a comprehensive assessment of the price situation requires taking into account a much broader range of products, changes in prices over several weeks or months, as well as official state statistics.
According to forecasts from fruit and vegetable market analysts, the prices of vegetables may soon be affected by a seasonal reduction in the supply of open-field produce. For imported fruit, purchase prices and logistics will remain important, while for meat and grains, production costs and the balance of supply and demand will be key.
Possible disruptions to energy supplies remain an additional risk factor for the food market, as refrigeration equipment, warehouses, processing enterprises, and retail chains depend on stable access to electricity.
Recall
Earlier, UNN reported that young potatoes had tripled in price in a week. The price rose from UAH 20 to UAH 60 per kilogram. Meanwhile, old potatoes cost several times less.

Mapping sanctions against Israel: 121 measures across 61 countries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:32:44 UTC
17:32:44 KST

The Jewish People Policy Institute (JPPI) has launched a new database mapping sanctions and restrictive measures imposed on Israel by countries around the world. The database identifies 121 measures across 62 countries, including 93 currently in effect, 19 classified as historical and nine proposed or planned measures.
The Foreign Ministry said the figures presented in the report do not accurately reflect the sanctions situation. Diplomatic officials added: "Ultimately, there are no substantial sanctions against Israel. Will that continue? There's no guarantee it will last forever. It's possible that, at some point, the outcome will be different."
The database allows users to examine measures by country, category and status, and to view their geographic distribution on a world map. The findings indicate that pressure on Israel is not confined to a single sector. Financial measures account for the largest category, with 40 measures, about one-third of the total. Defense and security and trade follow, with 24 measures each. The database also records 14 diplomatic measures and 12 legal measures.
According to JPPI Director General Dr. Shuki Friedman, the findings should be assessed not only by the number of sanctions but, more importantly, by their potential cumulative impact on Israel's economy and its ability to maintain international trade relationships, investment flows and supply chains.
"Anyone who thinks sanctions against ministers, individuals in the West Bank or products from the area will stop at the Green Line is mistaken," Friedman said. "Sanctions have a ripple effect. When they accumulate, they can affect banks, companies, investors and trading partners that have no connection whatsoever to the person or entity being sanctioned. The real danger is the transition from targeted sanctions to damage to the systems on which Israel's economy and security depend."
The database also identifies the countries where the highest number of measures have been recorded. Spain leads with 10 measures, followed by the United States with eight, all currently limited to the academic sphere, along with two "historical measures" and five proposals to prevent supplies of various types of weapons. Britain follows with seven measures, while Belgium and Turkey have five each.
However, the number of measures does not necessarily indicate their severity or potential impact. A single measure may be far more consequential than several others. The map is therefore intended primarily to illustrate the scope of the phenomenon and its geographic spread. Alongside European countries, where a substantial share of the measures is concentrated, the database includes measures from North America, Latin America, Asia, Africa and Oceania.
"The figure of 121 is only the starting point," Friedman said. "The important question is what will happen if this trend continues. A single sanction may be limited in scope. But 121 measures across 62 countries already warrant a systemic assessment. Israel needs to examine this risk as it would any other strategic threat: map it, prepare for it and act to prevent further deterioration.
"A national mechanism is needed to address the risk, one that examines the implications of these measures for the financial system, trade, investment, supply chains and the defense industry. The response cannot be limited to dealing with each sanction separately. It requires a comprehensive approach."
Diplomatic officials said the map contains distortions, noting, for example, that European Union sanctions are also counted at the individual country level. They also argued that entry bans imposed on certain individuals should not be equated with sanctions against Israel itself.
"Ultimately, there are no substantial sanctions against the State of Israel, and that was not a foregone conclusion," the officials said. "There was a realistic possibility of a different outcome, in which we would have ended 2026 facing EU sanctions against Israel. A great deal of the Foreign Ministry's energy was devoted to thwarting those measures."
They added: "There were sanctions that were prevented. The major threat was thwarted. If the EU had decided to undermine the trade agreement, every Israeli citizen would have felt the impact. The economic consequences would have been dramatic, but that was prevented. That diplomatic Iron Dome continued to hold.
"When you're inside an Iron Dome and a lot of missiles are fired at you, some get through. But the warhead carrying a ton of diplomatic and economic explosives did not penetrate. Ultimately, we succeed because we have friendly countries we can mobilize, such as Germany, Italy and the Czech Republic. It's not just Hungary. Hungary has changed, and the diplomatic Iron Dome remains intact."
The officials continued: "It's true that Smotrich and Ben-Gvir cannot enter the EU and that there are sanctions against settlers. But ultimately, people shopping at supermarkets in Ramat Gan and Tel Aviv are not feeling the impact of the biggest weapon, which is the trade agreement. The Horizon agreements and the Open Skies agreement have also been preserved."
However, they warned that the situation could change. "Will this continue? There's no guarantee it will last forever. It's possible that, if the trends continue in the same direction, the outcome will be different in the future."
According to the officials, "The Netherlands, Spain and Ireland are frustrated that they cannot achieve the outcome they want in Brussels. At the last meeting of European foreign ministers, there was frustration that it wasn't working. So, with no other choice, they are pursuing other channels, such as the Dutch sanctions.
"We are managing to preserve the core interests, and we have also reversed negative measures in countries such as Slovenia and Colombia. It's painstaking, thankless work because nobody sees what we have managed to prevent."
The officials nevertheless acknowledged that measures introduced by Spain, Ireland and Britain concerning trade with Israeli settlements "are not positive," adding that a concerning consequence is the shift toward action by individual countries.
The Foreign Ministry said in response: "The figures presented in the report do not accurately reflect the sanctions situation, whether political or economic. The Foreign Ministry is continuously engaged in this effort and is investing enormous resources in the fight against sanctions targeting Israel.
"For example, through a sustained effort lasting a year and a half, we prevented sanctions against Israel in the European Union and numerous other countries. We are also investing considerable efforts in reversing sanctions imposed by hostile governments following changes in leadership. We have done so with considerable success in Colombia, Slovenia and elsewhere.
"Countries that promote or impose sanctions against Israel undermine their own standing and influence in the region. As we have demonstrated in our dealings with various countries, most recently the Netherlands and Britain, Israel will respond firmly and forcefully to any country that takes such measures against it."

08:32:23 UTC
17:32:23 KST

Geraldine Achiah had been married for barely two months when she died in September, leaving behind an 18-year-old son who is struggling to come to terms with her death and demanding justice for what relatives allege was a fatal beating by her husband.
Achiah, an elementary school teacher in her 30s, had encouraged her only child, Courage Abombi, to pursue his dream of becoming a mechanical engineer. He sat for a university entrance exam just one day after her burial.
“My mom died an unexpected and painful death,” Abombi said.
Her death has become part of a growing crisis of femicide in Cameroon, where nearly 70 women have been killed this year in gender-related killings, according to the Ministry of Women's Affairs. The figure exceeds government estimates of at least 50 cases in 2023 and 67 in 2024.
The rising toll has prompted protests in major cities, including Douala and Yaounde, with demonstrators demanding stronger legal protections, more effective investigations and accountability for perpetrators. Many cases remain unresolved, while others go unreported.
Manfred Amambua, Achiah's husband, has denied killing her, police said. He has been charged with murder and is being held in jail awaiting trial. His lawyer was unavailable for comment.
Hospital records obtained by The Associated Press (AP) documented “several bruises on her face and lips” before her death. Ndzana Bienvenu, an officer involved in the investigation, said police had also collected phone footage showing Achiah and her husband after the alleged beating, along with a blood-stained bedsheet.
Her relatives say they want justice not only for Achiah but also for other women who have died in similar circumstances.
“We want justice for our daughter who died a violent death. This was a teacher who imparted knowledge on thousands of young Cameroonians,” said Regina Ngukum, Achiah's cousin.
Activists say femicide in Cameroon is fueled by economic dependence, unequal control over family property and inadequate legal protections in a society where men traditionally hold greater authority within households.
Financial hardship can make it difficult for women to leave abusive relationships, particularly when they have children to support. Some endure violence in the hope that their partners will change, activists say, while stigma and limited resources can make seeking help even harder.
“The current economic situation in the country is not helping matters. With limited resources, many women tend to endure violence in their marriages, hoping that their men will change, which is not usually the case,” Women's Affairs Minister Marie-Thérèse Abena Ondoa recently told the state broadcaster.
Ondoa described femicide cases in Cameroon as having reached a “cruel” and “alarming” proportion and pledged further government action.
The crisis mirrors a wider global pattern. About 50,000 women and girls were killed by intimate partners or other family members in 2024, according to United Nations data.
Activists argue that Cameroon needs stronger laws and a more effective judicial system to prevent gender-related killings and ensure perpetrators face meaningful punishment.
The country's Penal Code criminalizes offenses including rape but does not explicitly define femicide as a separate crime. Cases are therefore handled under broader provisions governing homicide and other violent acts.
Similar approaches are used in many African countries, where killings motivated by gender are generally prosecuted under existing homicide laws, although some governments have taken legal or policy steps specifically addressing femicide.
Cameroon's government is preparing a bill that would establish femicide as a standalone criminal offense while strengthening broader protections against gender-based violence. The proposed legislation is expected to be submitted to parliament for consideration in November.
Activists caution, however, that changing the law alone will not resolve the problems that allow cases to stall or perpetrators to escape accountability.
Carole Grace Mbarga, a Cameroonian activist based in the United States, said investigations and court proceedings can be undermined by intimidation, corruption and procedural errors that may lead to reduced charges or acquittals.
“When investigations drag on, evidence deteriorates, witnesses lose confidence, and families become discouraged,” she said.
Even when convictions are secured, the penalties can fall short of victims' families' expectations. In 2025, a man who pleaded guilty to killing his wife received a suspended five-year sentence and a fine of 52,000 CFA francs, equivalent to about $90.
For activists, such outcomes reinforce concerns that the justice system does not adequately deter violence against women.
Family members and friends gathered in Yaounde for Achiah's burial following her death just two months after her wedding in July.
Her relatives are now waiting for the legal process to take its course while joining a broader movement demanding action against femicide. Thousands of people have taken part in protests in Douala and Yaounde, calling on authorities to strengthen protections for women and ensure that cases are properly investigated and prosecuted.
Laura Sen, one of the protest organizers, said the proposed legislation must be accompanied by efforts to address systemic barriers and improve support for victims of domestic violence.
For women facing abuse, leaving a relationship can be especially difficult when they depend financially on their partners or fear social stigma. Those raising children may face additional obstacles.
Achiah's death has left her son grieving the woman who supported his ambitions and helped him imagine a future beyond their loss.
Abombi said he continues to pray that the legal process will deliver justice for his mother.
“I pray that justice will follow its due course and that her killer will face the law,” he said.
He also described dreams in which his mother returns to comfort him.
“She keeps appearing to me in a dream, consoling me not to despair and that she is still with me,” he said.

Estonia gets €32m EU funding for 'free world's first line of defense' surveillance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:31:00 UTC
17:31:00 KST

Estonia gets €32m EU funding for 'free world's first line of defense' surveillance
The European Commission has given preliminary approval for nearly €32 million toward Estonia's eastern border drone surveillance system, a project already partly built.
The funding is the latest installment in a program announced in March, with the first fixed systems installed on the south-eastern border in May and the full system due by the end of 2029.
The Police and Border Guard Board (PPA) will continue building the multi-layered integrated drone detection and air surveillance system on the EU's external border in cooperation with the Estonian Defense Forces (EDF).
"In cooperation with the Defense Forces, we can buy and install radars and cameras, equipment needed for drone detection, and the IT system supporting them, for a shared situational picture," said Interior Minister Igor Taro (Eesti 200).
"This will improve our ability to detect and assess potential threats so we can respond quickly. Our aim is to prevent threats before they reach the point of affecting the security of Estonian people," the minister went on.
Taro said Estonia's eastern border is currently the free world's first line of defense. "The European Union's support for strengthening drone surveillance here says that we have done good work so far, have been on the right path, and shows trust in our skills and capability to protect the EU's external border."
Veiko Kommusaar, deputy director general of the PPA for border management, said the Commission's decision was a clear sign of trust in Estonia and confirmed that the EU sees strengthening the external border as a shared security question.
"With this support, we can, over the next three years together with the Defense Forces, take air and land surveillance on the eastern border to the next level, create a more complete situational picture and improve our ability to detect and assess potential threats on land, on the Narva River and in the airspace," Kommusaar said.
He added that the investment's greatest value is not its individual radars or drones, but the ability to see what is happening on the eastern border as a whole, and to be able to respond to potential threats faster and more precisely than ever before.
The funding comes through the EU's border management and visa policy fund, with 10 percent national co-financing.
The system was announced by Prime Minister Kristen Michal in March, with over €200 million earmarked for drone defense and around €214 million for drone surveillance and countermeasures over four years. The first fixed counter-drone systems were installed on three sections of the south-eastern land border in May, and the PPA says full coverage of the Russian border should follow. The first phase — the external border and Estonia's four largest cities — is due by the end of 2027, with the full system complete by the end of 2029.

The families of children killed in a roof collapse at a school in northwest Pakistan called for "justice" on Friday, a day after more than 30 pupils and a teacher were crushed to death.
