From Hormuz to Bab el-Mandeb: Saudi Arabia’s difficult choices
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:29:20 UTC
17:29:20 KST

Developments in Yemen today cannot be separated from the repercussions of the war waged by the United States and Israel against Iran. The prolonged nature of this war, and the fact that it remains unresolved, arguably compel the countries of the region to reassess their strategic realities from a perspective different from the traditional approach that has shaped their thinking for decades. The US-Israeli war against Iran has brought about significant shifts in the region’s military, economic and political calculations, confronting Tehran with serious challenges and looming threats to its security, economy and future regional standing. For its part, Iran has drawn on a range of strategic assets at its disposal across the region to mitigate these threats by raising the costs borne by its Gulf neighbours. This Iranian strategy has exposed serious challenges facing the Gulf states, particularly Saudi Arabia, the most influential among them, with direct implications for their security and economies. Examining the escalating confrontation between Yemen and Saudi Arabia offers a means of analysing the challenges confronting the Kingdom today within a broader, emerging strategic perspective on the region and its future.
Saudi Arabia is facing a renewed wave of Houthi missile and drone attacks targeting its airports and oil facilities, alongside threats to Saudi shipping in the Red Sea. These targets are not new. The Kingdom faced similar attacks during the earlier years of the war in Yemen, before the de-escalation that followed the 2022 truce. That period of relative calm began to unravel on 13 July 2026, when the coalition targeted the runway at Sanaa airport to prevent an Iranian aircraft from landing. The Yemeni government claimed responsibility for the operation, while the Houthis attributed it to Saudi Arabia. Following this, the Houthis announced that they had targeted Abha airport, before declaring a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia on 20 July. Within Yemen, the escalation has shifted from exchanges of strikes to battles aimed at changing territorial control, particularly along the western coast. Last month, Houthi forces advanced towards Mokha and areas bordering the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Saudi-backed government forces then launched a counter-offensive at the beginning of this month, announcing that they had recaptured Mokha, Dhubab and positions overlooking the strait. Fighting between the warring parties continues.
Since the outbreak of the US-Israeli war against Iran, Saudi Arabia has faced mounting pressure on the routes through which it exports oil, the mainstay of its economy. Its eastern oil export route through the Strait of Hormuz has been hit by the turmoil in shipping arising from US-Iranian confrontations in the strait. As the Kingdom became increasingly reliant on transporting oil overland through the East-West Pipeline to Yanbu on the Red Sea, this alternative route was also interrupted, having assumed greater importance following the damage to its eastern maritime outlet. The East-West Pipeline was targeted in a drone attack last month, for which Riyadh held Iraqi groups close to Iran responsible, before operations resumed. The blockade declared by the Houthis against Saudi Arabia’s western maritime outlet and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait added a further, compounding burden, particularly on the passage of Saudi oil tankers through the strait. Houthi attacks on Saudi oil tankers were not confined to the waters around the strait, but extended as far as the waters off Yanbu.
These developments explain the shift in Saudi Arabia’s stance towards the Houthis. After years of seeking to consolidate the de-escalation and negotiate a political settlement, Riyadh has once again turned towards military confrontation.
Recapturing coastal positions near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait has become an objective linked to protecting its economic interests and exports, particularly amid the disruption of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. In 2023, Defence Minister Khalid bin Salman affirmed Saudi Arabia’s support for dialogue aimed at reaching a comprehensive political settlement under United Nations auspices. By contrast, Reuters reported at the beginning of this month, citing informed sources, that Riyadh was preparing a ground offensive to be carried out by Yemeni forces with Saudi air support. The agency also quoted Western diplomats and Gulf officials as saying that Riyadh could not enter into new peace negotiations while the Houthis remained in control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. This shift has been reflected in Saudi air support for the latest offensive launched by Yemeni government forces against the Houthis.
Nevertheless, a return to war offers Saudi Arabia no guarantee of a decisive outcome. The previous war, which began in 2015 and involved a Saudi-led coalition with the participation of the United Arab Emirates, failed to achieve its objective of defeating the Houthis. Nor did it restore the government that the Houthis had driven out of Sanaa, leaving the capital and most of northern Yemen under their control. Similarly, the US air campaign against the Houthis in 2025 failed to eliminate their power in Yemen, despite costing more than $1 billion, destroying weapons and facilities, and killing Houthi field commanders. The campaign ended with an agreement to halt reciprocal attacks between the United States and the Houthis, an arrangement that did not extend to Israel.
Nor will the recent Mecca Alliance between Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey help the Kingdom in its fight in Yemen beyond defensive and technical support, particularly while the alliance remains in its early stages.
It is also difficult to rely on the United States, given Washington’s refusal to meet a Saudi request to participate in air strikes, limiting its involvement to providing advice, intelligence and targeting data. US strategy in the region is based on expanding the role of regional partners in defending themselves, the region and US interests within it. This explains Trump’s request to Turkey a few days ago to intervene in support of Saudi Arabia.
These developments compel the countries of the region to reassess their security calculus and strategic balances, recognising that Iran and its allies are part of the regional reality and that lasting stability cannot be built by disregarding them. Relations based on cooperation and mutual interests remain an essential foundation for such stability, alongside the need to establish a balance between the instruments of power available to the Gulf states and those possessed by Iran. Throughout the current war against it, Iran has demonstrated that it possesses significant strategic assets that have inflicted heavy costs on the countries of the region, exposing an imbalance in their ability to impose comparable costs in return. If the Gulf states possessed instruments of power that made harming their security and interests costly for Iran, the costs of escalation would become mutual, potentially encouraging the parties to seek balanced political solutions that support cooperation and future stability.
The views expressed in this article belong to the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial policy of Middle East Monitor.

Editor's note: The story has been expanded with additional comments made by Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis.
BRUSSELS, Belgium — Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis expressed his disdain for EU plans to earmark billions of euros of support for Ukraine in its next seven-year budget, in comments made to journalists at the Oct. 16 summit of EU leaders in Brussels.
The EU operates on a seven-year budget cycle that needs to be unanimously agreed upon, and leaders hope to reach consensus on the 2028-2034 budget before the end of the year, as 2027 will be a bumper year for elections across the bloc.
While consensus on the budget as a whole remains out of reach, support for Ukraine seemed like a consensus issue until Babis' latest comments.
"I don't like that there are 100 billion euros ($112 billion) from the European budget for Ukraine, that this money should be borrowed," Babis said.
"It should not be in the multi-year financial framework, where member states don't have enough money," he added.
The 100 billion euros figure is already outdated, reflecting the amount initially proposed for the budget by the European Commission earlier in the year.
That figure was reduced to 89 billion euros ($100 billion) in June as part of a first compromise proposal, and it remained unchanged in the second and latest compromise, published Oct. 10.
"In any case, Czechia will not guarantee for it," Babis added.
Surprising in the other direction was Babis' criticism of U.S. President Donald Trump, after portraying himself as aligned with Trump for several years.
"Trump effectively betrayed us by concluding the business deal with Putin, and we have to do something," Babis said, echoing President Volodymyr Zelensky's take on a set of recent pro-Russian moves made by the U.S. against Ukraine.
Babis said the day before that Europe needs to agree on how to proceed with issues such as peace talks, given that at the moment, "we are completely out."
His turn on Trump brings Babis closer to the European mainstream, with many EU leaders not holding back in condemning the U.S. president for his latest overtures towards Moscow.

Government agrees 60 million euro fuel-price relief package, rejects Finns Party proposal
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:24:02 EEST
17:24:02 KST

The government has reached an agreement on a 60 million euro package aimed at easing the impact of rising fuel prices.
Environment and Climate Minister Sari Multala (NCP) confirmed to reporters in Parliament on Thursday that a deal had been agreed, noting that all governing parties support the package as a whole.
The measures include a reduction in vehicle tax, an increase in the maximum commuting expense deduction, and fuel subsidies for the transport, agriculture and forestry sectors.
The government has also agreed to introduce flexibilities in the fuel distribution obligation, which sets requirements for the share of renewable fuels blended into transport fuels. The limits on cross-fulfilment and over-compliance will both rise from 30 percent to 100 percent, allowing companies to meet their obligations more cost-effectively, the government said.
However, the government has not adopted the broader reduction in the distribution obligation advocated by the Finns Party.
The package consists of: 30 million euros for fuel subsidies for businesses in the transport, agriculture and forestry sectors, 20 million euros to reduce vehicle tax, up from the previously agreed 10 million euros, and 10 million euros to raise the maximum commuting expense deduction from 7,000 euros to 7,800 euros in 2027.
Multala acknowledged that the measures would have only a limited impact on consumers’ fuel costs.
"We cannot afford to make tax cuts worth hundreds of millions, for example," she said.
According to a press release, published by the ministry on Friday, the 60 million euro package will be funded from within the government's spending limits.
Of the total, 40 million euros will be redirected from funding for biogenic carbon capture capacity that will go unused this year, with the remaining 20 million euros coming from the cutting of funding for basic transport infrastructure management.
Finns Party says measures are insufficient
The Finns Party has criticised the agreement, arguing that the package should have gone further in easing the fuel distribution obligation to bring down prices at the pump.
Jani Mäkelä, chair of the Finns Party parliamentary group, said his party had accepted the agreement because "some solution had to be found".
"The government seemed to be quite incapable of acting in this matter, and the prime minister also had to save face," Mäkelä said.
Mäkelä further argued that easing the distribution obligation, as proposed by his party, could have reduced fuel prices at the pump by a significant amount.
He said the fact that the government had agreed on the package was not sufficient reason to rule out that option.
"If the distribution obligation cannot be compromised in a situation where the price of fuel is so high, it reflects a certain mindset," Mäkelä said.
Multala was asked whether the Finns Party could have been persuaded to accept the agreement if the funding had come from money allocated to climate action. She replied that the question should be put to the party itself.
Orpo defends government’s decision
Speaking in Brussels on the sidelines of an EU meeting, Prime Minister Petteri Orpo (NCP) said that easing the distribution obligation would not have brought down fuel prices quickly.
"Being in the government means that when we are making decisions together, sometimes it is difficult to defend them, even if we have made the decision ourselves," Orpo said.
He stressed that the government had little room for manoeuvre during the negotiations, but noted he was pleased that the money had been directed towards commuters and professional transport.
Fuel prices are also on the agenda at the EU summit. Orpo said high prices at the pump were linked to the situation in the Strait of Hormuz and Russia’s war of aggression in Ukraine.
Relief measures will not lower pump prices directly
Hanna Kalenoja, a leading transport expert at the Central Chamber of Commerce, said the measures would not directly affect petrol and diesel prices.
Instead, they would ease costs for some motorists and businesses, but not all, she noted.
The vehicle tax reduction will be reflected in the tax bills of eligible car and van owners, rather than at the petrol station.
For example, a household whose vehicle tax period began in July would not see the reduction until its next tax period in July next year, Kalenoja said.
She estimated that the vehicle tax cut would save eligible motorists around 12 euros per year. The reduction applies to older cars and vans.
The increase in the maximum commuting expense deduction, meanwhile, could benefit people with high travel costs.
The government also plans to raise the maximum deduction, with Kalenoja estimating that the change would benefit people who commute more than 60 kilometres.
The deduction can be adjusted through a revised tax card, although eligibility depends on the circumstances of the commute. In some cases, expenses can be deducted based on the use of a private car if public transport is not reasonably accessible.
The fuel subsidies are aimed at businesses in the transport, agriculture and forestry sectors. A similar subsidy was made available retrospectively through the State Treasury in 2022.
Experts welcome decision to retain distribution obligation
Kalenoja said she was largely relieved by the government's decision, particularly because it did not ease the distribution obligation.
The requirement sets the minimum share of renewable fuels that must be included in transport fuels. Reducing it would lower the share of low-emission biofuels.
According to experts, easing the obligation would not necessarily have an immediate impact on pump prices. Kalenoja also warned that it could undermine planned investments in the biogas sector.
"It is a big relief that the decision not to lower the distribution obligation was made now," she said.
The Confederation of Finnish Industries (EK) also welcomed the decision in a statement on Thursday.
However, Kalenoja said it was disappointing that the government had not included a reduction in diesel excise duty in the package.

Russia’s Digital Development Ministry has proposed using artificial intelligence to analyze VPN services’ characteristics, aiming to detect and block them more effectively.
The proposal appears in one draft version of a national plan for implementing AI technologies through 2030, the Russian business daily Kommersant reported.
The plan’s drafters said AI could achieve 95% effectiveness in blocking VPN services.
The Digital Development Ministry told Kommersant that “the current version of the draft national plan for implementing AI technologies contains no such information.”
A source who spoke to the outlet, familiar with discussions around the initiative, said algorithms for intelligent traffic analysis are already in use, though these do not constitute AI.
“AI tools make it possible to find VPN servers relatively quickly based on indirect signs: how a node behaves, what hosting it uses, what neighboring addresses look like. And most importantly, this makes it possible to respond more quickly to changes in network activity,” a source in the industry told Kommersant.
However, several sources told the outlet that the use of AI, “especially during the initial stages of training,” would likely result in the erroneous blocking of “legitimate traffic.”
Demand for VPNs has surged in Russia amid blocks on popular social networks, services, and messaging apps. Russian authorities have responded by stepping up efforts to combat circumvention of these blocks. Russia’s budget for the next three years earmarked a record 60 billion rubles for traffic filtering. Reports have repeatedly said the Digital Development Ministry wants to charge higher rates for international traffic (operators treat VPN traffic as international).

Egypt has indefinitely suspended the passage of trucks bound for Sudan through the Qustul land port after two Egyptian drivers were killed and a third was injured in a shooting at a market south of the Sudanese capital, Khartoum.
The management of Egypt’s Qustul port, which operates under the General Authority for Land and Dry Ports at the Ministry of Transport, has ordered all trucks heading to the port to stop. Trucks will not be allowed to cross by ferry into Sudan until further instructions, citing “security developments in Sudan’s Northern State”.
The suspension does not apply to passenger traffic. Buses, private cars, minibuses and individual travellers are still allowed to cross, while the restrictions apply only to trucks.
An earlier decision by Egypt’s Land and International Transport Regulatory Authority banned Egyptian trucks from entering conflict zones in Sudan. It limited commercial transport to Wadi Halfa, Argeen and the city of Dongola in Sudan, as part of measures to protect drivers from security risks.
The authority stressed that truck drivers must comply with regulations governing transport within Sudan, exercise the utmost caution and avoid entering designated areas under any circumstances.
The instructions are based on directives issued by Egypt’s Ministry of Transport on 11th May 2025, requiring drivers to avoid conflict zones and unload goods only in safe areas of Sudan’s Northern State.
The suspension comes amid security risks affecting road transport between Egypt and Sudan as a result of the armed conflict. Two Egyptian drivers were killed and a third was injured in a shooting at a market south of Khartoum.

Türkiye’s year-end inflation expectations hold steady at 29.6 percent: Survey

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:17:08 UTC
17:17:08 KST

Market participants’ expectations for inflation at the end of 2026 remained broadly unchanged in October, while forecasts for inflation over the next 12 months edged higher, according to the Central Bank’s latest Survey of Market Participants.
The survey, which monitors the expectations of decision-makers and experts in the financial and real sectors regarding key economic indicators, showed that year-end consumer price inflation (CPI) expectations rose marginally to 29.63 percent from 29.61 percent in the previous survey period.
The 12-month-ahead inflation expectation increased to 23.89 percent from 23.70 percent, while the 24-month-ahead inflation forecast declined to 17.94 percent from 18.32 percent.
According to the survey, the Central Bank is expected to set its policy rate at 36 percent at the upcoming October Monetary Policy Committee meeting.
The survey showed little change in expectations for the Turkish Lira at the end of the year. The year-end exchange rate forecast for the U.S. dollar stood at 51.55 lira, compared with 51.57 lira in the previous survey.
However, the 12-month-ahead exchange rate expectation increased to 59.26 lira per dollar from 58.60 lira in the previous survey.
Participants forecast Türkiye’s gross domestic product (GDP) to expand by 2.9 percent in 2026, down from a previous estimate of 3 percent.
The GDP growth forecast for 2027 remained unchanged at 3.9 percent, according to the survey.

ABN Amro caught in crossfire amid ICC sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:17:07 UTC
17:17:07 KST

ABN Amro caught in crossfire amid ICC sanctions
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Dutch bank ABN Amro, which handles the finances of the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague, could face heavy US penalties if it keeps doing so once American sanctions take effect next April, RTL has reported.
The US government announced sanctions against the ICC last week, a significant escalation after it had already sanctioned 13 of the court’s judges and officials. The US says the court threatens American service personnel, and has attacked its decision to issue arrest warrants for Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former defence minister Yoav Gallant.
The sanctions will freeze any ICC assets in the US and bar Americans from providing funds, goods or services to the court. The measures have been delayed for 180 days to allow time for diplomatic talks, and are due to take full effect on April 7, 2027.
ABN Amro is exposed through ABN Amro Clearing, the division that settles share trades for clients and has a large US business. RTL reported that this gives Washington the leverage to fine the bank, bring criminal charges or, in the worst case, put ABN Amro itself on the sanctions list.
The Financieele Dagblad reported that the clearing division made a net profit of €298 million in 2025. The Dutch state is ABN Amro’s largest shareholder.
It is not clear how real the risk is. “The legislation is not at all clearly worded,” Cedric Ryngaert, professor of international public law at Utrecht University, told RTL. He said the uncertainty creates a “chilling effect”, because companies cannot tell whether they are covered.
The cabinet has condemned the sanctions. Prime minister Rob Jetten called them “deeply regrettable” but said dialogue with Washington was still important.
Legal experts and campaign groups want the European Commission to activate the EU’s blocking statute, which would bar European companies from complying with the US measures.
The cabinet previously told MPs it would push for activation if new sanctions were expected to seriously hamper the court’s work.
If that happened, ABN Amro could be forced to choose between breaking EU rules and breaking US ones, RTL said.

Ofgem could force energy suppliers to pay rivals if they lure customers with cheaper deals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:14:53 UTC
17:14:53 KST

Energy suppliers could be forced to pay a charge to rivals if they lure customers with cheaper deals, as the industry regulator for Great Britain attempts to prevent suppliers going bust this winter.
Ofgem has published a consultation on a proposal to reintroduce the market stabilisation charge (MSC), which aims to prevent suppliers failing if there is customer exodus, as it frets over the impact of sharp swings in energy prices linked to the conflict in the Middle East.
The charge was last activated between April 2022 and March 2024, when Russia’s invasion of Ukraine sparked soaring wholesale prices that caused more than 30 energy companies to go bust.
“We’re preparing for what is likely to be a difficult winter for many households,” said Neil Kenward, the interim director general of markets at Ofgem. “While the energy market is stronger than it was during the energy crisis, volatility remains and the market stabilisation charge helps to protect consumers from that volatility.
“In volatile market conditions, it’s important that suppliers can continue to secure the energy their customers need without taking unsustainable risks.”
Under the mechanism, the MSC would be triggered if wholesale prices fall more than 10%. At that point, suppliers who win customers by being able to then offer cheap deals would have to compensate rivals 85% of the drop in wholesale rates.
“When wholesale prices fall sharply, suppliers that have bought energy in advance for customers on default tariffs can face losses if large numbers of customers switch to cheaper fixed deals,” Ofgem said.
When Ofgem last activated the MSC in 2022 Martin Lewis, the founder of the consumer advice site MoneySavingExpert, swore at the regulator on a press call and said the mechanism sold consumers “down the river” because it would deter competition. He later posted an apology for his “emotional rant” on the social media platform X.
Reacting to Ofgem’s consultation, Lewis said on Friday that consumers’ will not get as good deals if wholesale prices drop because the mechanism acts as a “switching penalty”.
He added: “The new supplier can’t pass a chunk of the saving from lower wholesale rates on to you, because it has to hand much of it to your old supplier. The cheap fixes and switcher deals offered will be a lot more expensive, in order to protect energy firms’ profits. It ain’t good for consumers.”
He questioned the need to reintroduce the mechanism, pointing out that many energy companies have made significant profits since last time it was triggered.
“The supplier market is pretty stable, and I doubt we are at the domino risk of suppliers going bust in the way they did in the early 20s,” he said. “Protecting them over winter by effectively dampening competition … feels raw. I don’t like it.”
Ofgem said that reactivating the MSC would not “automatically create charges or increase customer bills”.
The consultation is seeking views on how the mechanism should operate, including trigger levels, notice periods and deactivation arrangements.
“The MSC supports responsible energy purchasing and helps reduce the risk of instability in the market during periods of significant price volatility,” Kenward said. “By acting now, we can help maintain a stable and resilient energy market and protect consumers from the costs and disruption that can arise when markets become unstable.”
Households are facing the highest energy charges in three years this winter after rising market wholesale prices pushed up the government’s price cap from this month.
 
About 22m homes are paying the equivalent of £1,723 a year for typical gas and electricity usage between October and December, up from £1,663 for the July to September period.
 
Ofgem’s quarterly energy price cap is forecast to climb by the equivalent of a further £149 a year in January, according to energy consultants at Cornwall Insight, which would put the average annual bill at £1,872.
The chancellor, John Healey, is planning a major intervention to cut energy bills for poorer households in this month’s budget.

Indonesian stocks plunge 11% as MSCI proposes emerging market downgrade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:13:31 UTC
17:13:31 KST

The index provider is weighing reclassifying the country from emerging market to standalone status, potentially forcing funds tracking MSCI's emerging market indexes to sell their Indonesian holdings.
Indonesian shares lost about 11% on Friday. This was the largest single-day fall in 28 years, as the country's stock market status came under scrutiny from one of the world's largest stock market index providers, threatening outflows from global investment funds.
MSCI said that following investors' concerns, Indonesia's continued emerging-market status was "no longer appropriate". The index provider is launching a consultation on a proposal to classify Indonesia as a "Standalone Market", which would leave the country outside MSCI’s main global market groupings.
MSCI classifies markets as developed, emerging, frontier or standalone.
The proposed reclassification would move Southeast Asia's biggest economy out of the emerging market category, bypassing frontier market status, and put it in the same category as Jamaica, Panama and Palestine.
This could result in global funds tracking MSCI's emerging market index having to sell their Indonesian holdings.
The index provider said in a statement that "market participants had raised significant concerns regarding the investability of the Indonesian equity market". These include a lack of clarity in shareholding structures and suspected coordinated trading.
The index provider had already raised the possibility of downgrading the country's status in January. Following that, authorities in Jakarta said in April they had completed reforms, hoping to avoid the downgrade.
MSCI noted that although Indonesian authorities have announced reforms, sufficient progress has not been made and "significant concerns remain around market dysfunction".
"MSCI expects to proceed with the proposed reclassification unless the consultation identifies clear evidence of material improvements in market governance and functioning to warrant reconsideration."
MSCI will announce its final decision by the end of June 2027.
According to Bloomberg, this comes as a hit to investors' confidence at a time when global funds have already pulled a net $4.9bn from the country's stock market so far this year – leaving the country on track for the worst year ever. Jakarta's benchmark index has fallen approximately 39% since January, dragging down the local currency; the rupiah has lost about 8%. That’s even as Bank Indonesia reiterated its commitment to maintaining rupiah stability.

"The Committee's decision points out the groundlessness and risks of lowering quotas for the MIC. She believes that the government's proposed reduction of reservation quotas to 85% for defense and energy enterprises and to 60% for heat and water supply enterprises and other public utilities creates risks for the stable operation of both the defense industry and critical infrastructure.

Wildfire kills 4 firefighters in Indonesia's Mount Bromo national park
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:11:00 UTC
17:11:00 KST

Blaze kills 4 firefighters in Indonesia's Mount Bromo national park
October 16, 2026
At least four people have died and two others suffered severe burns while battling wildfires in a national park on Indonesia's main island, officials said on Friday.
They were trapped by thick smoke and fast-spreading flames in the Bromo Tengger Semeru National Park in East Java, a Forestry Ministry statement said, as the country's worst wildfires in a decade swept through the area.
The southeast Asian country has been battling a months-long crisis of blazes and toxic smoke, forcing schools to shut down and causing a surge in respiratory complaints in the region.
The victims were part of a 12-member firefighting team consisting of national park personnel, members of the community fire brigade, and local volunteers, said East Java police spokesperson Jules Abraham Abast.
"This incident serves as a reminder that forest and land fire extinguishing is a high-risk operation," the ministry statement said, adding there had been a jump in hotspots detected by satellites as areas of unusually high temperatures. Not all hotspots necessarily translate into individual fires.
By Thursday evening, the number of hotspots in Indonesia stood at 799 , up from 372 a day earlier. The forest and land fires have worsened this year as weather phenomenon El Nino prolonged the dry season.
Toxic haze spreads across southeast Asia
The smoke from Indonesia's wildfires are causing a health crisis in neighboring southeast Asian countries such as Singapore, Malaysia and the Philippines.
Malaysia on Friday ordered hundreds of schools to close down due to deteriorating air quality.
Singapore, meanwhile, topped IQAir's live ranking of the world's most polluted major cities, with Kuala Lumpur second and Jakarta sixth.
Malaysian Foreign Minister Mohamad Hasan rejected calls from some lawmakers to seek compensation from Indonesia, saying the crisis should be addressed through diplomatic engagement and established mechanisms.
He said Malaysia was coordinating assistance for Indonesia and would push for stronger regional cooperation on haze management.
Singapore probing companies linked to fires
Singapore also called for closer cooperation. Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said authorities were investigating companies allegedly linked to Indonesian forest and land fires that have worsened the haze.
"Where warranted, we will take action under Singapore's Transboundary Haze Pollution Act, and also explore joint action with other countries," he said.
Singapore enacted the Transboundary Haze Pollution Act in 2014 after a bout of severe pollution.
The law allows authorities to target companies whose activities overseas cause or contribute to unhealthy haze levels in Singapore. That said, legal experts cautioned that pursuing companies under the law will be challenging.

"We try to remain realistic and thus realize that it will take a long time to overcome the unfortunate legacy left by the United States and other NATO countries following two decades of their inglorious occupation of Afghanistan," Lavrov concluded.

Russian drones violated Moldovan airspace five times overnight
Several Russian UAVs violated Moldovan airspace on the night of 15-16 October and on the morning of 16 October.
Source: European Pravda, citing TV8
Details: The drones crossed the border amid large-scale Russian attacks on Ukraine. The incidents were recorded in northern and south-eastern Moldova. No crashes or explosions were reported.
The first violation was recorded at 23:02. An object crossed the border from the direction of Tymkove in Ukraine's Odesa Oblast and headed towards the village of Ivanovca. Eighteen minutes later, it left Moldovan airspace and headed towards the Ukrainian settlement of Bronit.
The second incident was recorded at 03:37. A drone flew from the direction of the Ukrainian village of Starokozache in Odesa Oblast towards the village of Tudora in Ștefan Vodă District. One minute later, it returned to Ukrainian territory along the same route.
At 03:46, another drone crossed the border in the north from the direction of Mohyliv-Podilskyi, heading towards the town of Otaci. Two minutes later, it left Moldovan airspace near the village of Hădărăuți in Ocnița District.
The fourth violation was recorded at 05:59. A drone entered the country's airspace from the direction of Starokozache and headed towards the village of Căplani in Ștefan Vodă District. One minute later, the drone left Moldovan territory near the village of Olănești.
At 06:09, the same drone crossed the border again near the village of Purcari in Ștefan Vodă District. One minute later, it left the country's airspace via the Dnestrovsc area in the Transnistrian region, heading towards the Ukrainian settlement of Hradenytsi.
In less than seven hours, Moldova's Defence Ministry recorded five unauthorised incursions by aircraft into the country's airspace.
Background:
- On the night of 14-15 October, a drone once again violated Moldovan airspace during a Russian attack on Ukraine. Moldova's defence minister said the drone was "definitely" Russian.
- On the morning of 30 September, a drone flew through Moldovan airspace before crashing outside the village of Hîrbovăț in Anenii Noi District and exploding.

AI generated
PARIS – UN chief Antonio Guterres on Oct 16 urged governments to stop subsidising the production of fossil fuels that are “boiling our planet and are the scourge of biodiversity”.
Addressing leaders in Armenia ahead of next week’s UN biodiversity summit, Guterres said governments were still “spending money on the wrong things” and singled out incentives for fossil fuels.
“Subsidising fossil fuels is subsidising suicide,” Guterres said at an event in Yerevan.
“They are boiling our planet and are the scourge of biodiversity. I urge governments everywhere to end these handouts once and for all, and to use the savings for people and planet instead.”
Nations have made little headway since pledging in 2022 to reduce public spending on activities that harm nature such as mining, fossil fuel extraction and intensive farming.
The United Nations says that for every dollar invested in protecting or restoring nature, about US$30 (S$38) still goes into activities that degrade it.
This includes an estimated US$2.6 trillion a year in public subsidies that negatively impact nature and the climate.
Nearly 200 nations are participating in the UN biodiversity negotiations in Yerevan starting on Oct 19, where a lack of finance for nature will be a core focus.
Guterres launched a report on Oct 16 showing that the world was off track to achieving the 2030 biodiversity targets enshrined in a landmark pact for nature. AFP

Saab, FMV and the Swedish Armed Forces launch uncrewed underwater vehicle
Less than one year after contract award, Saab, the Swedish Defence Materiel Administration (FMV) and the Swedish Armed Forces have successfully developed, built and launched a demonstrator for a Large Uncrewed Underwater Vehicle (LUUV).
Developed at pace and according to plan, the demonstrator has progressed from concept to a fully functional vehicle. Following successful sea trials, the first phase of the project has been completed. The next phase is expected to focus on developing more advanced capabilities. The results will support the continued development of software, sensors and autonomous functions, while also contributing to future product development.
The vehicle illustrates how close collaboration between industry and government authorities can significantly reduce the time from identifying an operational need to testing a new capability.
“This project demonstrates how new technologies can be rapidly translated into practical operational value. The uncrewed underwater vehicle can contribute to increased endurance, enhanced situational awareness and strengthened underwater capabilities. The fact that we have also been able to develop and test the system in such a short timeframe demonstrates the strength of the collaboration between the Swedish Armed Forces, FMV and Saab,” says Mats Wicksell, head of Saab’s business area Naval.
The demonstrator has been developed to support the development and evaluation of future underwater capabilities and to enable operations alongside existing naval platforms, such as submarines.
The rapid development has been enabled by Saab’s software-centric approach and the integration of Autonomous Ocean Core, Saab’s autonomous control system that provides surface and subsurface vehicles with autonomous capabilities. Combined with Swedish expertise in submarine design and sensor integration, this has made it possible to take the project swiftly from concept to sea trials.
The LUUV project builds on Saab’s earlier investments and work in autonomous underwater systems and is now led by FMV in cooperation with the Swedish Armed Forces and Saab. The project provides a basis for Swedish authorities’ decisions regarding the future acquisition and operational use of autonomous underwater systems.

Robert Jenrick has sought to defend Reform UK against fresh allegations that it hosts extremists by claiming that Nigel Farage has “probably done more than almost anybody to stand against racism and the far right”.
The remarks came after Farage was berated by a Reform official for “protecting” a mayoral candidate who was accused of making racist remarks about the former Labour deputy prime minister David Lammy.
The exchange emerged in an undercover investigation by ITV Exposure, which has also shown councillors and election candidates for Reform making threats of extreme violence and expressing racist, Islamophobic and misogynistic views.
In the latest footage released by ITV, a senior Reform official is seen warning Farage that he was “protecting” a high-profile mayoral candidate accused of making racist comments about Lammy.
Sarah Pochin, one of two female MPs for Reform, is also seen complaining that other party officials “are so fucking chauvinistic” and that “they just exclude you if you are a woman”.
Jenrick, the party’s Treasury spokesperson and MP for Newark, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme on Friday: “[Farage] is the most heavily scrutinised figure in British politics, and he’s someone who’s probably done more than almost anybody else to stand against racism and the far right, and to protect our politics from that over the course of my lifetime.
“And this documentary failed to besmirch his character, which presumably was the ultimate objective.”
Farage has made repeated promises over the last two years to rid Reform of “extremists” and “bigots” and introduce vetting. The party says it carries out vetting checks on everyone who wants to stand for election.
However, the first clips from ITV’s year-long undercover investigation showed Alan Feeney, a Reform councillor and deputy mayor of Solihull, calling Asian homeowners “parasites”, and stating that “no more than 1% of [the] British population can be non-white”.
Further footage released on Thursday shows Farage discussing the case of Chris Parry, a retired rear admiral picked to contest the Hampshire and the Solent mayoral election for the party.
The party stood by Parry for months after it emerged he had said the former foreign secretary should “go home to the Caribbean” last year, and suggested that at least eight other politicians from minority ethnic backgrounds did not have a primary loyalty to the UK.
Reform eventually suspended him in March after the Guardian revealed other remarks by Parry, but clips from the ITV documentary show Farage pushing back against senior advisers who said the candidate had to be sacked. They included Ed Sumner, Reform’s head of communications, who had told another press officer in an earlier discussion that Parry was “clearly a racist”.
In a conversation between Farage and Sumner, which was recorded by the undercover reporter, the Reform leader said Parry “must apologise to Lammy” and was told that a text had been written for the candidate.
“He must do it and move on … Tell him that from me,” Farage said, to which Sumner said: “You’re protecting him.”
To laughter, Farage replied: “It’s showing a bit of … bit of sorrow. Look, ‘I’m sorry’ is probably a good thing to hear. Just take the fucking deal. Trouble is he’s a rear admiral. That’s the problem.”
Jenrick defended Reform’s vetting policy. “In my experience, all political parties have bad apples. I mean, you can see that’s plain to see from the conduct of other political parties. In fact, Councillor Feeney, the one that you presented before I came online, was for a short time a Reform councillor, but for a much greater time a Conservative councillor.”
He added: “We actually have very strong vetting, and we invest a huge amount in it, and it’s improving all the time. I don’t know what the vetting is like in every other political party. I can say in the Conservative party, because it was my former party, there is absolutely no vetting whatsoever by the central party for local councillors.”

UK and Germany strengthen defence ties in London talks

UK and Germany strengthen defence ties in London talks
UK and Germany deepen defence-industrial cooperation at Lancaster House talks, building on the Trinity House Agreement and Kensington Treaty.
- UK and Germany strengthened defence-industrial cooperation at the latest talks at Lancaster House.
- The talks build on the Trinity House Agreement and Kensington Treaty, reinforcing cooperation between the two nations across air, land, sea and space.
- Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry Luke Pollard and German counterpart State Secretary Jens Plötner joined industry leaders to discuss industrial priorities for collaboration.
UK-German work on key industrial collaboration and new technology was advanced yesterday as Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry Luke Pollard hosted his German counterpart, State Secretary for Armament and Innovation Jens Plötner, at Lancaster House in London.
The latest UK-Germany Ministerial Group on Equipment and Capability Cooperation (MECC) meeting brought together senior officials and military leaders from both nations to review progress on joint defence capability programmes and to deepen the industrial partnership between the UK and Germany, two of NATO’s leading defence powers.
Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry Luke Pollard MP said:
  Germany is one of our closest and most valued defence partners, and today’s talks demonstrate our determination to turn that ambition into real capability for our armed forces and real opportunity for our defence industries.
As threats to our shared security evolve, the UK and Germany are standing together, strengthening our forces, our industrial bases and our resilience in lockstep.
Discussions built on the Trinity House Agreement, signed in October 2024, which set out an ambitious programme of bilateral cooperation across air, land, maritime, cyber and space domains. The agreement sits under the wider Kensington Treaty, signed in July 2025, which provides the strategic framework for the UK-Germany relationship.
Among the flagship programmes on the agenda was Deep Precision Strike, a joint UK-Germany initiative to develop long-range strike capability, reflecting the shared ambition of both nations to address critical capability gaps and strengthen NATO’s deterrence.
The talks follow the Prime Minister’s visit to Berlin on 8 October, during which the UK and Germany agreed to deepen cooperation on space and to establish a new UK-Germany Counter-Hybrid Partnership, strengthening joint resilience against grey-zone threats.
Following the MECC meeting, Minister Pollard joined State Secretary Plötner at the German Embassy in London for a panel discussion which saw senior policymakers and industry leaders take stock of defence-industrial progress and identify practical priorities for deepening cooperation.
Minister Pollard was joined on the panel by State Secretary Plötner, Dr Philipp Kerth, co-founder and chief executive of German defence technology company Hypersonica, and Alex Zino, Director Business Development & Future Programmes at Rolls-Royce.
The MECC forms part of a wider programme of UK-German engagement in the lead-up to the EU-UK summit. The UK-Germany defence relationship continues to grow as both nations work towards a more resilient Euro-Atlantic security architecture, underpinned by a modern, innovative and competitive defence industrial base at the heart of NATO’s deterrence and readiness.

EU leaders rally around Zelenskiy as Trump calls Ukrainian strikes on Russia a 'disgrace'
BRUSSELS/KYIV, Oct 16 - European Union leaders rallied around President Volodymyr Zelenskiy at a summit on Friday as US President Donald Trump fired another salvo at Ukraine, calling its strikes on Russian refineries a "disgrace".
The EU is hosting Zelenskiy in Brussels at one of the most difficult moments for Ukraine, with missiles and drones raining down on Ukrainian cities and fears that the US could pull back intelligence sharing and weapons support from Kyiv.
Trump blindsided Zelenskiy last weekend by announcing that Ukraine and Russia had agreed not to target each other's energy facilities. Facing US midterm elections in November, Trump has blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries for pushing up energy prices that could cost him at the ballot box.
The US has also struck a diesel deal with Russia, angering Ukraine and European allies.
"We want to end this war as quick as possible. We don't see now signals from the Russian side that they are ready for this, to end this war. That's why we have to prepare for the winter," Zelenskiy said as he arrived at the summit, hugging many of the leaders as he met them.
"The winter package is not only energy, it's also air defence and funding," Zelenskiy said.
In the latest attacks, Russian drone strikes on the city of Kharkiv killed three people, while strikes elsewhere left hundreds of thousands of people without power.
In an interview, Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal told Reuters that the EU would probably have to provide a new loan to Ukraine to help cover its budget gap for next year.
“Last winter was already hell, this one will be once again like hell,” Michal said.
"We have a lot of gaps to fill, and this is a European mission to fill the gaps that Ukraine needs. Because always, at the start (and) at the end of every conversation, people need to be reminded that we are sitting in a warm room, lights are on, heating is on, the coffee is warm, and we cannot get tired of the war in Ukraine, because they are fighting ... for us."
NO READY-MADE EUROPEAN ALTERNATIVE TO STARLINK
Ukraine's leadership has been alarmed by disruptions to the SpaceX Starshield satellite system used by Kyiv for battlefield communications and drone operations. A source in Ukraine's defence ministry said on Thursday that Starshield receptors were only working at speeds of up to 100 miles per hour (160 kph), complicating their use for military missions.
A US official has denied that Trump ordered a deliberate slowdown of Starshield, which is the military-grade version of the Starlink service operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX, and Trump said this week intelligence sharing with Ukraine continued.
Europe does not have a ready-made alternative to Starlink, although European governments and companies are working on long-term options.
"Starlink is really necessary for Ukraine. And unfortunately, in short term, Europe can't replace this capability," said the EU's foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas.
"We are working on the new sanctions package to put the pressure on Russia, and we of course hope that we do this with all our partners around the world," she added.
Ukraine struck a Russian oil refinery after Zelenskiy declared that Kyiv was abandoning the energy ceasefire that Trump had announced.
"All he's doing is making the world oil price higher. Well, I think that's a disgrace," Trump said in an interview with the Newsmax news outlet.
While EU leaders hit out at the US deal to buy Russian diesel, they are also grappling with how to tackle energy prices that have soared since the Iran war, exposing divisions between member states on day one of the summit on Thursday.
Zelenskiy told Reuters earlier this month that Ukraine had agreed a plan with European partners that would allow it to close a $27 billion deficit in its military spending for this year, allowing it to order the drones needed to continue fighting at the start of 2027.
However, Finance Minister Sergii Marchenko said recently Ukraine still faced an unfunded budget gap for next year of $32.6 billion – and that does not include an estimated $40 billion in direct military supplies from allies.
"I am unhappy with the number of countries that have been willing to pledge new financial support to Ukraine," said Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten.
Sounding a more sceptical note, Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker urged caution in the debate over making new, far-reaching financial commitments to Ukraine.
"There are so many figures being bandied about that we now need to put them into context, explain them and make it clear where this shortfall is coming from. I’m surprised too," he said. REUTERS

Tatarstan and India exploring data center cooperation – minister

Tatarstan and India exploring data center cooperation – minister
India and Russia’s Republic of Tatarstan are exploring joint data center and digital infrastructure projects, with Indian cloud provider Bharat AI Cloud planning to sign a cooperation agreement with the region’s IT Park. 
The plans emerged at the second Russia-India TIME Business Forum in Kazan on Thursday. A technology hub in India’s southern Telangana state has expressed interest in jointly developing infrastructure in Tatarstan, the Russian region’s deputy minister of digital development, Bulat Gabdrakhmanov, said. 
The proposed partnership could allow both sides to exchange cloud technologies and expertise. Bharat AI Cloud, which earlier announced plans to open an office in Kazan, is also looking to enter the Russian market. 
Russia has established data infrastructure providers, while India’s large domestic market offers opportunities for expanding digital services, director of the Chamber for Indo-Russian Technology Collaboration (CIRTC), Subham Sarkar, said at the forum. 
The discussions build on earlier cooperation between the two sides. At last year’s TIME forum, Tatarstan’s IT Park signed a three-year agreement with CIRTC to promote technology partnerships, investment, and market access. 
Officials also explored building an artificial intelligence data center with Indian operator CtrlS in October last year. The proposed project remains under consideration, with its progress dependent on electricity costs, market demand, and opportunities to expand in Russia, according to Tatarstan’s Digital Development Ministry.
The latest talks have also brought up the possibility of establishing a so-called data embassy, which would involve hosting data infrastructure abroad under special arrangements intended to protect data sovereignty. 
Sarkar compared the proposed arrangement to the protections afforded to diplomatic missions. He said the project was technically feasible, although questions of sovereignty and regulation would take time to resolve.
India has explored similar arrangements with other countries. In January, New Delhi and the United Arab Emirates agreed to examine the possibility of establishing digital embassies under mutually recognized sovereignty arrangements. The two countries also discussed cooperation on data centers.
The India-Tatarstan discussions extend beyond data infrastructure to healthcare, AI, cybersecurity, and digital public services.
Russia could offer Indian partners domestically developed operating systems, office software, email platforms, and messaging services, the Tatarstan Information Technology Center’s deputy director general, Kamil Gazizov, said at the Kazan forum. He also highlighted opportunities for both sides to work together against cybersecurity threats.

Ensuring security of transport corridors benefits all regional countries: Iranian minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:57:06 UTC
16:57:06 KST

Ensuring security of transport corridors benefits all regional countries: Iranian minister
TEHRAN- Iran’s Minister of Transport and Urban Development, emphasizing the necessity of protecting civilian infrastructure and guaranteeing the continuity of transport and transit flows in the region, presented proposals and called for the formulation of operational and time-bound plans to remove border obstacles, develop rail cooperation, and strengthen the resilience of regional corridors.
According to an IRNA report from the Ministry of Transport and Urban Development, Farzaneh Sadegh, at the 14th Meeting of Ministers of Transport of the Economic Cooperation Organization (ECO) member states in Kazakhstan, expressed appreciation for that country’s hosting and stated: Due to its privileged geographical location, the ECO region has the capacity to become an integrated network of road, rail, and sea routes—a network that can strengthen connectivity among Central Asia, West Asia, the Caucasus, and open waters.
Referring to the approvals of the 13th ECO Meeting of Ministers of Transport in Tehran, she emphasized the necessity of assessing the extent of implementation of past agreements, identifying obstacles, and determining operational priorities, and said: This meeting must lead to specific, time-bound, and measurable decisions for developing regional cooperation.
The Minister of Transport and Urban Development, referring to the damage inflicted on Iran’s transport infrastructure during the attacks by the United States and the Israeli regime, said: Disruption in any part of the region’s transport network, regardless of where it occurs, can increase the time and cost of moving goods and also affect the security of supply chains of other countries.
Sadegh emphasized: Protecting civilian infrastructure, ensuring the security of communication routes, and continuing the flow of transport and transit are common interests for all ECO member states.
She asked the organization’s secretariat to examine the effects of security disruptions on regional corridors and present practical solutions for increasing the resilience of the transport network.
Sadegh further considered facilitating the movement of the road fleet and border crossings among the priorities of regional cooperation and emphasized reducing truck dwell time, simplifying customs procedures, harmonizing transport documents, and exchanging information among border authorities.
The Minister of Transport and Urban Development, referring to the revival of the ECO train and its successful operation on the Turkey, Iran, and Turkmenistan route, considered this experience a basis for expanding rail cooperation among member states.
Noting that the damaged bridges on the aforementioned rail route were repaired by Iranian engineers within 72 hours and the route was reopened, she emphasized the importance of technical readiness and maintaining the continuity of regional rail connections.
Sadegh also considered the Almaty–Tehran–Istanbul rail connection an opportunity for developing regional trade and proposed that tariff, customs, technical, and operational obstacles on rail routes be examined and a clear mechanism be created for coordinating train movements and developing regular and competitive services.
The Minister of Transport and Urban Development listed access of landlocked countries to open waters as one of the priorities of cooperation in ECO and said: Achieving this goal requires the integrated linking of ports, rail lines, roads, and logistics services.
Referring to the capacity of Chabahar Port and other southern ports of Iran, she considered the connection of Chabahar to the country’s rail network an effective factor in strengthening the link between land and sea transport, diversifying trade routes, and reducing transport costs.
The Minister of Transport and Urban Development, further emphasizing the necessity of determining the responsibilities of countries and the secretariat in following up on approvals and presenting a progress report at the next meeting, noted: Developing transport and transit in the ECO region, in addition to increasing trade and economic growth, helps strengthen regional ties and enhance the economic resilience of member states.
Sadegh proposed that the ECO secretariat, in cooperation with member states, prepare a comprehensive report on the extent of implementation of previous approvals and remaining obstacles, formulate a time-bound plan for facilitating road transport, border and customs coordination, and developing rail and multimodal services, and place on its agenda solutions for protecting civilian infrastructure and increasing the resilience of corridors.

At least 4 killed while fighting wildfire in East Java, Indonesia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:55:32 UTC
16:55:32 KST

Saadet Gokce
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
At least four people were killed while battling a wildfire in Mount Bromo in Indonesia's East Java province.
The death toll rose to four on Thursday after another person died while being transferred to a hospital, the state-run news agency Antara reported.
The victims included two officers from Bromo Tengger Semeru National Park and two hotel staffers.
Two other people suffered serious burns while fighting the fire and were hospitalized for treatment.
Probolinggo District Head Muhammad Haris said wildfires had occurred in the national park almost every year, but had not previously caused fatalities.
Twelve people initially joined efforts to contain the current fire under standard operating procedures, but the blaze spread and the team split up, leaving six people trapped as winds shifted rapidly, Haris said.
Indonesia faces an unusually prolonged dry season, with El Nino contributing to conditions favorable for wildfires.

Ukrainian Tencore signs memo with Canadian Dominion Dynamics for joint production of TerMIT unmanned ground vehicles in Canada
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:55:18 EEST
16:55:18 KST

Ukrainian defense company Tencore and Canadian defense-technology firm Dominion Dynamics have announced the signing of a memorandum of understanding, which provides for the production of TerMIT unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) in Canada, as well as the integration of the AuraNet technology suite into these systems.
According to a press release from Dominion Dynamics, the agreement was signed during the AUSA 2026 defense conference in Washington.
Dominion Dynamics reportedly plans to establish production of the TerMIT system at its Canadian facilities, with manufacturing slated to begin in 2027.
Meanwhile, experts from Tencore will oversee the technology transfer process and train Canadian personnel in the assembly of these unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs).
Furthermore, Dominion Dynamics will integrate the AuraNet system—designed for autonomous control and coordination across diverse operational environments—into the TerMIT platform. The company also intends to develop a version of the TerMIT platform specifically adapted for Arctic conditions.
“Battlefield requirements change in weeks, so production, operational feedback and engineering have to run as a loop: build, deploy, learn, change, scale. Canada gives us the manufacturing base, suppliers and reliable power to run that loop alongside allies who need these vehicles," Tencore co-founder Roman Tkachenko is quoted in the press release as saying.
It is noted that the signing of this agreement follows a joint declaration on defense cooperation, which was concluded in September between Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
At that time, the parties committed to producing thousands of combat-tested drones and unmanned systems over the next two years, with one-third of these to be allocated for Ukraine’s defense needs, the company stated.
“This agreement is how two companies start turning that commitment into vehicles, and we intend to move fast,” said Eliot Pence, founder and CEO of Dominion Dynamics.
Dominion Dynamics is an Ottawa, Canada-based defense technology company specializing in the development of autonomy, sensor monitoring, and control systems.
Tencore is a Ukrainian defense technology company that specializes in the development, serial production, and integration of unmanned ground robotic systems (UGRS) for the Defense Forces of Ukraine.

New house sales in Türkiye rise 3.9% in September
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:54:31 UTC
16:54:31 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
New house sales in Türkiye rose 3.9% year-on-year to 51,519 in September, according to official data released Friday.
New homes accounted for 36.2% of total housing transactions during the month, data from the Turkish Statistical Institute (TurkStat) showed.
Overall house sales fell 9.3% from a year earlier to 142,390, as existing home sales dropped 15.3% to 90,871.
Adjusted for calendar effects, new house sales increased 3.8% annually. On a seasonally and calendar-adjusted basis, they rose 5.5% from August, while existing home sales remained unchanged.
Mortgaged house sales climbed 5.1% year-on-year to 23,397, accounting for 16.4% of total transactions.
Sales to foreign buyers increased 9.9% to 2,167, representing 1.5% of the total. Russian citizens purchased the most homes with 388, followed by Iraqis with 166 and Germans with 162.
In January-September, new house sales edged down 0.6% from the same period last year to 359,913, while total housing transactions declined 7.2% to 1.09 million.

Russia attacked energy infrastructure in Kyiv and four regions, leaving some residents without electricity - Ministry of Energy
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:50:36 EEST
16:50:36 KST

Russia attacked energy infrastructure in Kyiv and four regions, leaving some residents without electricity - Ministry of Energy
Kyiv • UNN
Russian drones attacked energy facilities in Kyiv and the regions, causing new power outages. Schedules for power cuts are in effect in some regions.
Russia attacked energy infrastructure in four regions and Kyiv overnight and in the morning of October 16, leaving some residents without electricity. Overall, new power outages have been reported in at least eight regions and the capital. UNN reports this, citing data from the Ministry of Energy and NPC Ukrenergo.
Enemy attack on energy infrastructure
"Overnight and in the morning, Russia attacked a number of energy facilities in Kyiv, as well as the Kyiv, Volyn, Odesa and Rivne regions. As a result, some consumers were left without electricity," the Ministry of Energy reported.
According to the Ministry of Energy, "due to shelling and hostilities, there are new power outages in the Dnipropetrovsk, Zaporizhzhia, Sumy, Kharkiv, Khmelnytskyi and Chernihiv regions as of this morning."
Ukrenergo confirmed that "overnight and in the morning, the enemy launched a massive drone attack on energy facilities in several regions." "As a result, as of this morning there are new power outages in the city of Kyiv, as well as the Kyiv, Volyn, Odesa, Zaporizhzhia, Dnipropetrovsk, Kharkiv, Sumy and Chernihiv regions," Ukrenergo's data show.
Energy workers are working to restore the damaged equipment and return electricity to consumers. Repair work is continuing wherever the security situation allows; however, due to continuous air-raid alerts, crews are forced to interrupt their work, the Ministry of Energy said.
Severe weather
As a result of the severe weather, 12 settlements in the Poltava and Sumy regions remain without electricity.
Repair crews are working to restore the power supply.
Schedules
"Due to grid restrictions caused by Russian attacks, hourly outage schedules and capacity restriction schedules for industry and business are in effect in some regions today. These are necessary measures to stabilize the operation of the power system and prevent larger-scale accidents," the Ministry of Energy reported.
"To avoid overloading equipment damaged by previous Russian shelling, capacity restriction schedules for industry and hourly outage schedules (up to two queues) for all categories of consumers will necessarily be applied in some regions today until the end of the day," Ukrenergo clarified.
Consumers were urged to use electricity sparingly while the restriction measures are in effect.
Consumption
According to Ukrenergo, electricity consumption is in line with seasonal levels. Today, October 16, as of 09:30, it was at the same level as the previous day—Thursday.
Yesterday, October 15, the daily consumption peak was recorded in the evening. It was 3.9% higher than the peak of the previous day—Wednesday, October 14. This was caused by a drop in air temperatures in most regions of Ukraine, prompting consumers to use electric heaters during the evening hours.
"Given the consequences of Russian shelling and the weather conditions, please limit the use of high-powered electrical appliances from 16:00 to 22:00," Ukrenergo emphasized.
It also noted that due to Russian attacks on energy infrastructure, the situation in the power system may change.

====================================================================================================

AI threatens democracy. But we are not powerless: here’s how to fight back | Carine Fouteau
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:49:45 UTC
16:49:45 KST

Big tech companies pose an immeasurable threat: socially, politically, militarily and ecologically. They are also causing a profound crisis of information. The tools they design now serve as weapons of mass destruction against democracy. There is so much at stake that an urgent and broad mobilisation is required.
From the harvesting of personal data and the weaponisation of public opinion, to the destruction of jobs, the infringement of civil liberties and environmental damage, ordinary citizens are the main victims of this predatory economy – an economy with an agenda that aligns with the interests of the planet’s most authoritarian and reactionary states.
The threats facing the information landscape affect us all. Journalists of my generation have witnessed four major digital revolutions: the internet, social media, smartphones, and now, artificial intelligence. What fundamentally changes with AI is our relationship with the truth. For big tech companies, the boundary between truth and falsehood has vanished. This makes it essential to reaffirm the role of public-interest journalism. Our mission is to publish information that is in the public interest by seeking the factual truth, standing against “fake news” and propaganda. Our mission is to help create a democratic public sphere that serves citizens.
Yet AI companies are completely reshaping this space to their own advantage; their mission is not the public interest, but generating profits. Their methods include plundering news outlets without authorisation or compensation. By disseminating so-called summaries of our reporting, they siphon off our audiences and revenue, serving the private interests of a select few at the expense of the common good.
The difference between AI-generated content and a real news article is journalism. AI-generated responses are not information. They are merely a logical assembly of words that all too often produces falsehoods, distorts facts and misinterprets information. A real news article is something else entirely. Quality journalism is the product of expertise guided by ethical standards: persuading sources to speak, painstakingly gathering eye-witness testimonies, cross-referencing, verifying and establishing facts. This process relies on reporting or investigative work – in other words, human effort in the field.
Good journalism organises and prioritises information, providing context and nuance; AI, by contrast, levels everything down to the lowest common denominator and breeds confusion. Journalism uncovers facts that certain parties – particularly economic and political powers – would prefer to see hidden, ignored, or suppressed. Generative AI uncovers nothing, it merely regurgitates and condenses existing material.
Quality journalism comes at a high price. Some of the costs can’t even be quantified. Journalists who report from war zones for example, risk their lives. Mediapart’s recent investigation into Jordan Bardella, the head of Marine Le Pen’s far-right party, has resulted in anonymous cyber-harassment and death threats against our editorial team.
Ultimately, media outlets are accountable for the information they publish. They answer to the courts and to their readers. AI companies appear answerable only to their shareholders. They refuse to vouch for the reliability of their conversational agents to evade legal liability. If nothing is done to stop it, this pillaging will result in the destruction of journalism. This is dangerous not just for news publishers, but for all of us, because it signifies the demise of a public sphere defined by free, pluralistic and democratic discourse.
Do we want a public sphere that guarantees access to reliable, independent information, or one governed by algorithms that amplify fake news, deepfakes and propaganda – fuelling fear, anger and division?
Fortunately, the tech companies have sown the seeds of their own downfall. Since they are bleeding dry the very sources of information from which they derive their profits, they are courting their own failure; without quality information, they will produce nothing but AI slop.
This is precisely where we find leverage. OpenAI has admitted that it would be impossible to train today’s leading AI models without using copyrighted material. A Microsoft vice-president acknowledged that training models on quality content significantly improves the quality of output.
The priority is to act collectively, pressuring these platforms by every available means – including legal action – to uphold the rights of the press and the public. Some newspapers, such as the New York Times, have taken legal action. Its publisher, AG Sulzberger, recently cited a figure of $20m spent on litigation. Legal proceedings are also under way in France – notably through the organisation responsible for collecting press-related neighbouring rights.
Beyond pressuring lawmakers at national and European level, we must broaden our fightback to include the entire research and knowledge community – stakeholders who, like us, are committed to the public interest and factual truth.
It falls to us, as journalists, to convince the public that our work is an essential part of democracy. We have to demonstrate that our reporting – aimed at holding power to account – has real impact and drives change; that it makes sense of a rapidly shifting world and serves as a powerful catalyst for civic action.
- Carine Fouteau is president and publishing director of the French investigative news outlet Mediapart
- Mediapart is hosting Hacking Big Tech, a public event about technology, AI and democracy in partnership with the Guardian, in Paris on Saturday 17 October 2026. The conference will be live-streamed free on Mediapart’s website, app and YouTube channel and can be accessed here from 1pm CEST on 17 October
