Co-op memorandum signed: Iran, Eurasia take new step for free trade, integration
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:49:23 UTC
16:49:23 KST

Co-op memorandum signed: Iran, Eurasia take new step for free trade, integration
TEHRAN- The Minister of Industry, Mining and Trade stressed, at the signing of a cooperation memorandum with the member states of Eurasia, the full implementation of the free trade agreement, the removal of trade barriers, and the expansion of transit cooperation.
According to IRNA from the Ministry of Industry, Mining and Trade, Seyyed Mohammad Atabak, on Wednesday evening, at the signing of the memorandum with the member states of the Eurasian Economic Union during the second meeting of the Joint Committee for the Implementation of the Free Trade Agreement between Iran and this union, called for operational follow-up of the agreements, the removal of trade barriers, and maximum use of the capacities of this agreement to develop economic exchanges.
The Minister of Industry, Mining and Trade described transparency in import regulations, timely exchange of statistical information, and the removal of tariff and non-tariff barriers as requirements for fully benefiting from free trade.
He emphasized the necessity of following up on issues related to vehicle recycling fees, access of Iranian cement products to the markets of the union’s member states, and requirements for importing food products, and declared Iran’s readiness to cooperate in examining and removing these barriers.
The Minister of Industry, Mining and Trade further called for turning agreements into specific executive plans with a clear timetable and determining the responsibilities of each party.
He proposed that the secretariats of both sides, by creating a mechanism for continuous monitoring of the implementation of the approvals, present a progress report on measures at the next meeting of the Joint Committee.
The Minister of Industry, Mining and Trade stated: The negotiations held will be constructive and result-oriented, and the summary of the negotiations and approvals in specialized committees should be the basis for regular follow-up of commitments.
He expressed hope that the implementation of the agreements, while facilitating the activity of traders and increasing trade exchanges, would lead to strengthening economic cooperation between Iran and the Eurasian Economic Union and enhancing the position of the parties in regional and international relations.
The second meeting of the Joint Committee for the Implementation of the Free Trade Agreement between Iran and the Eurasian Economic Union was held, hosted by the Ministry of Industry, Mining and Trade, with the presentation of solutions for trade facilitation, the development of economic cooperation, and the removal of existing barriers.
In this committee, the minister responsible for trade of the Eurasian Economic Union, officials of the Economic Commission, ambassadors, deputy ministers of the Ministry of Industry, Mining and Trade, representatives of the Iran Trade Promotion Organization, the Customs of the Islamic Republic of Iran, the Iran Chamber of Commerce, Industries, Mines and Agriculture, the Ministries Transport and Urban Development and Agriculture, and the National Standards Organization of Iran and the Iran Veterinary Organization were present.
Accelerating the establishment of the electronic system for verification of origin, developing transit cooperation within the framework of the International North–South Corridor, and strengthening technical and health cooperation related to trade were among the most important axes of this meeting.
Also, the signing of the cooperation memorandum of understanding between the Business Council of the Eurasian Economic Union and the Iran Chamber of Commerce, Industries, Mines and Agriculture was assessed as a step toward strengthening communication among private sector actors and expanding trade cooperation between the two sides.
Awarding highest honorary badge of Eurasian Economic Union to industry, mining and trade minister
The highest honorary badge of the Eurasian Economic Union was awarded to Seyyed Mohammad Atabak, Minister of Industry, Mining and Trade of the Islamic Republic of Iran, in appreciation of his effective efforts in developing and deepening Iran’s economic relations with this union, by Andrey Slepnev, Minister of Trade of the Eurasian Economic Commission.
According to an IRNA from the Ministry of Industry, Mining and Trade, this honorary badge was awarded in appreciation of the measures and efforts of the Minister of Industry, Mining and Trade to expand economic cooperation, strengthen trade interactions, and develop the relations of the Islamic Republic of Iran with the member states of the Eurasian Economic Union; cooperation that is pursued with the aim of utilizing mutual capacities, facilitating trade, and expanding economic ties between the parties.
Andrey Slepnev, Minister of Trade of the Eurasian Economic Union, arrived in Tehran on Wednesday to participate in the second meeting of the Joint Committee for the Implementation of the Free Trade Agreement between Iran and the Eurasian Economic Union, and in a meeting attended by Seyyed Mohammad Atabak, Minister of Industry, Mining and Trade, and other ambassadors of member states, they addressed the presentation of solutions for trade facilitation, the development of economic cooperation, and the removal of existing barriers.
On October 1, the Head of Iran’s Trade Promotion Organization (TPO), in a meeting with the Trade Minister of the Eurasian Economic Union, referring to the upward trend of trade between Iran and the member states of the union, emphasized the Islamic Republic of Iran’s determination to expand and deepen trade relations and strengthen ties between the private sectors of the two sides.
According to a report by the Public Relations of Iran’s Trade Promotion Organization, Mohammad Ali Dehghan Dehnavi, in a meeting with Slepnev, referring to the course of trade between the Islamic Republic of Iran and the member states of the Eurasian Economic Union, said: “Despite all challenges and problems, trade statistics between Iran and the Eurasian Economic Union have taken an upward trend, and this promises bright prospects for the development of trade relations in the future.”
The Deputy Minister of Industry, Mining and Trade, emphasizing the will and determination of the Islamic Republic of Iran to expand trade relations with the member states of the Eurasian Economic Union, added: “Iran has regular cooperation and trade relations with Russia and other member states of the union, and we are striving to make these ties deeper than before.”

It is worth noting that Dehghan Dehnavi traveled to Minsk to participate in the 19th meeting of the Joint Economic Cooperation Commission of the Islamic Republic of Iran and the Republic of Belarus.
Also, in mid-September, Iran’s Minister of Economic Affairs and Finance, offering a positive assessment of the results of his Tuesday meetings with officials of the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), announced the proposal of initiatives such as setting a base currency to accelerate transactions and appointing special representatives to resolve obstacles facing bilateral trade.
According to IRNA, Seyyed Ali Madanizadeh, speaking to reporters after separate meetings and talks with the Chairman of the Executive Board and the Minister of Trade of the Eurasian Economic Commission at the union's headquarters in Moscow, added: "We held very good sessions."
He stated: "On Iran's behalf, we expressed our interest and readiness to expand relations and fully implement the free trade agreement with the Eurasian Economic Union, and that we are prepared to cooperate with this union in various fields; the union's officials, in turn, expressed their willingness and interest in expanding ties with our country."
The Minister of Economic Affairs and Finance, referring to the efforts of the enemies of the Iranian nation to fuel economic warfare and block trade and financial channels, said: "What is evident is that, thanks to God, these countries support Iran and our economy, and that Iran has managed to maintain production and trade relations with countries under the toughest conditions." He added: "The member states of the Eurasian Economic Union are equally committed and eager to develop these relations."
Continuing his Moscow visit agenda for multilateral consultations, the Minister of Economic Affairs and Finance attended the Eurasian Economic Union's headquarters and met with the Chairman of the Executive Board and the Minister of Trade to discuss accelerating bilateral trade.
Seyyed Ali Madanizadeh, and Bakytzhan Sagintayev, Chairman of the Board of the Eurasian Economic Commission, emphasized their shared determination to expand cooperation during this meeting.
Prior to this meeting, the Minister of Economic Affairs and Finance held a separate session with Andrey Slepnev, Minister in charge of Trade of the Eurasian Economic Commission, and a group of union officials to review the progress of cooperation following the implementation of the free trade agreement. Slepnev, noting that the second meeting of the Iran-EAEU working group would be hosted by Tehran in the coming months, expressed hope that the upward trend in bilateral trade would continue.
Iran's Ambassador to Russia, Kazem Jalali, and Mehdi Heydari, Deputy Minister of Economy and head of Iran's Organization for Investment, Economic and Technical Assistance, accompanied Madanizadeh during these meetings.
The free trade agreement between Iran and the Eurasian Economic Union came into force in May 2025 after completing legal procedures in the signatory countries, subsequently eliminating customs duties on 87% of goods in bilateral trade.
Within this cooperation framework, the path has been smoothed for Iranian goods to enter the market of over 180 million people in the union's member states, and reciprocally, this opportunity is available for traders from the five signatory countries in commerce with Iran.
Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and Armenia are members of the Eurasian Economic Union, and Iran holds observer status in the union.
The Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) is a regional economic integration bloc in the post-Soviet space, established by a treaty signed in 2014 and launched on January 1, 2015. Its five member states are Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and Armenia, with Iran, Cuba, Moldova, and Uzbekistan holding observer status.
Modelled in part on the European Union, the EAEU aims to create a single internal market with the free movement of goods, services, capital, and labour. Its core objectives include improving living standards, ensuring sustainable economic development, and boosting the global competitiveness of member economies.
The bloc is driven by institutions such as the Supreme Eurasian Economic Council and the Eurasian Economic Commission. While the EAEU has expanded external ties—notably through a free trade agreement with Iran—internal integration remains uneven, with Russia dominating trade flows in a "hub and spoke" model. The bloc has set a long-term vision to become a self-sufficient and attractive macro-region by 2045.

University's satellite collects data on space radiation at various heights above Arctic
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:46:24 UTC
16:46:24 KST

ARKHANGELSK, October 16. /TASS/. The ArcticSat-1 spacecraft of the Northern Arctic Federal University (NArFU) collected data on space radiation at different heights above the Arctic. Researchers obtained data from 500 to 200 km, and there is practically no information about radiation at low levels in the circumpolar regions, leader of the university's Space Monitoring Center Roman Alyoshko told TASS.
"The main data that we were collecting is data on space radiation," he said. "This is an urgent task exactly for the polar regions. During the spacecraft's mission, we collected data on space radiation, starting from altitudes of about 500 km when it was launched into orbit, and then it was gradually decreasing over about a year and a half, to 200 km when it already began burning up. And it is even more relevant data when it was in low orbits of about 200 kilometers. There are practically no spacecraft in such orbits, and therefore data on space radiation at these heights is very valuable."
ArcticSat-1 belongs to a group of satellites that fly in low orbits, at an altitude of 400-600 km. Strictly speaking, there is no space vacuum there, and therefore the satellite constantly touches the atmosphere molecules and gradually loses speed. It does not have an engine to compensate for this, so the satellite is slowly descending. The lower is the satellite, the denser is the air and the faster is the deceleration. The Sun also affects the descent rate: with high solar activity, the atmosphere heats up and "swells", increasing the braking effect at the orbit altitude.
ArcticSat-1's orbit is polar, with an inclination of about 97 degrees. In such an orbit, the spacecraft passes over high latitudes, where the geomagnetic field does not protect well from space particles. This coincides with the project's main topic: the impact of space weather on small spacecraft in the polar regions.
"We have focused on how this affects satellites. We were receiving data on space radiation and at the same time we were receiving information about the satellite. Our goal is to make recommendations for operators of such satellites on what to do in a certain situation. In case of a very strong surge of space radiation, it may be reasonable to put the satellite into the sleep mode, that is, not to interact with it - not to cause breakdowns," the scientist said, adding it was important to find how to "prolong the life" of such satellites.
An octopus in space
On board the satellite was an art object, an octopus, - Octo-Pax by artist Nastya Miro. This is a figurine of about ten by ten centimeters, made of a domestic metal powder composition. It was in a separate cube chamber inside the satellite. Inside the chamber was also a camera facing the art object.
The octopus, according to calculations, burned down along with the satellite. The art object ended the journey the way the artist had intended it to happen: it did not stay in orbit. Entering the atmosphere, the figure traveled the same path as the spacecraft. "This fate fits deeply the project's idea. Octo-Pax was holding in its tentacles debris that is common for the orbit, and symbolized the space's cleanup from debris. The art object did not become part of this debris, as it dissolved into the atmosphere, without leaving anything behind over there - outside the Earth," the university said.
The ArcticSat-1 satellite burned down in dense layers of the atmosphere. It had worked in orbit for about a year and a half. Scientists will be processing the data obtained by it for about a year.

porsche mission S reinterprets the sports car with cues from its racing heritage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:45:21 UTC
16:45:21 KST

porsche mission S reinterprets the sports car with cues from its racing heritage
drawing on the 550 spyder, 911, and GT1, the vision model proposes a future for porsche that looks to its motorsport heritage, questioning the growing dominance of screens inside the car.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
a new sports car shaped by Porsche’s historic models
Porsche unveils the Mission S, a mid-engined super sports car vision model that reinterprets its design identity by drawing on historic racing automobiles while featuring a deliberately restrained digital interior. Developed by Style Porsche under Vice President Tobias Sühlmann, the concept forms part of the brand’s Sportwagenschmiede ‘35 strategic realignment and offers an early indication of the design direction Porsche intends to carry into future models. The project places particular emphasis on the relationship between driver and machine, retaining physical controls and familiar instruments. The Mission S points toward a potential expansion of Porsche’s sports car range. According to Chairman of the Executive Board Dr. Michael Leiters, the company is considering a permanent mid-engined super sports car positioned above the 911.
mission S points to a new chapter
The Mission S makes its connection to Porsche’s past through its proportions and individual design details. Its mid-engined architecture creates a low front end, prominent fenders, and the characteristic roofline that Porsche describes as a ‘flyline’. These elements establish the silhouette of the car, while a continuous line connecting the front and rear lighting gives the exterior a more unified appearance. The round headlights and pronounced fenders recall the 911, while the treatment of the bodywork’s shut lines references the G-model generation. The low front takes cues from the GT1, and the roofline extending toward the rear wing evokes the 959. At the back, a ‘car-in-car’ concept also draws on the GT1, translating an earlier racing design into a contemporary form.
The wheels reinterpret the dial-like pattern associated with the 928, with a new design intended to emphasize lightweight construction. Other functional details include a cooling solution inspired by the Porsche 917’s radiator fan and an integrated active rear wing. Together, these features present the Mission S as an exercise in adapting recognizable design references to a new vehicle architecture. Porsche describes the forms as ‘floating volumes’, with surfaces that appear to sit above the car’s underlying technical structure. A main horizontal line separates the more sculptural upper bodywork from the lower sections, where functional elements become more visible. This division gives the concept a visual language that balances muscular proportions with a relatively clean exterior.
the interior puts physical interaction back in focus
Porsche draws on the interiors of the 550 Spyder and 356, using two defining lines that extend across the dashboard and doors to establish a continuous visual relationship between the cabin and exterior. The instrument cluster combines five circular gauges with digital information. At its center, a rev counter uses an analogue needle with a display behind it. Depending on the selected driving mode, the arrangement of the instruments changes, with their housings positioned alongside one another or staggered to adjust the driver’s view. The concept also incorporates a reworked Sport Chrono element and push-pull controls for selected comfort and driving functions.
Instead of a built-in central screen or a passenger display, the Mission S has a retractable smartphone holder compatible with MagSafe. The phone can be used for navigation and other information, while the My Porsche App gives access to the car’s functions and different designs for the digital instruments. The setup keeps the dashboard simple, combining digital features with physical controls and a focus on driving.
a historical reference point for a future design identity
Porsche unveiled the Mission S on a pier in Queens, New York, the same location where photographs of the mid-engined 550 Spyder were taken in 1953. The setting connects the new concept to the company’s history and its early sports cars. The car’s white, gray, and red color scheme also references Porsche’s racing heritage. Special finishes, including Firn White Metallic and Light Red Metallic, are combined with Black Chrome and Special Black details. Porsche describes its future design direction through three principles: ‘authentic, consequent and timeless’. The Mission S brings together design elements from historic models with a new approach to the car’s proportions and interior.
For now, the Mission S remains a vision model, with no confirmed production plans. It offers an early look at how Porsche intends to develop its sports cars while retaining the design features and driving experience associated with the brand.

manufacturer: Porsche AG | @porsche
design: Style Porsche, Tobias Sühlmann, Vice President Style Porsche

26 years apart, two old friends raise a trophy together in Rome
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
15:44:42 CST
16:44:42 KST

by Xinhua writers Gao Jingyan, Diao Ze, Ren Yaoting
ROME, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- Scanning the crowd at the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) headquarters, Yin Yuzhen pointed to her American friend Ronald Sakolsky. Sakolsky was then invited onto the stage, and the two embraced tightly as a wave of applause reverberated across the plenary hall.
Just moments earlier, Yin was awarded a crystal trophy honoring her as one of the FAO's 100 Women Heroes in Agrifood Systems and Rural Development. Standing right by her side, Sakolsky clasped his hands together, clearly moved, before they both lifted the award to face the applauding assembly.
Their friendship began 27 years ago, when Sakolsky, then in China on a teaching exchange, raised 5,000 U.S. dollars to support Yin's tree-planting efforts. Neither could have imagined the emotional reunion that awaited them decades later.
Yin was the final honoree announced at Thursday's ceremony. The Chinese farmer has spent more than four decades combating desertification in the Maowusu Sandy Land in north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, helping transform the once-barren landscape into a green expanse.
A short video played on the large screen, showing Yin planting trees, as well as footage of the two friends when they were young, and their reunion in China in August. As the images unfolded, both were moved to tears.
Taking the microphone on stage, Sakolsky struggled to speak, his voice faltering several times with emotion.
"She planted many seeds, and only a few lived at first. She didn't quit. She planted more seeds, and a few more lived," he recalled Yin's determination in the early years of her work.
Wiping his eyes, he added, "Today, our story planted a seed for everyone here."
When it was Yin's turn to speak, she was just as moved, struggling to choke back tears as she addressed the crowd.
"Sakolsky, whom I regard as an elder brother, and we had not seen each other for 26 years. I never thought that just over two months later, we would meet again here," she said, thanking Sakolsky for helping her green the desert.
Earlier in the morning, the two friends had visited the rooftop garden of FAO headquarters. Beneath an olive tree, Yin bent down to pick up several fallen black olives and examined them carefully in her palm. A reflection of her four decades of afforestation work, her observant eye naturally gravitated toward the surrounding greenery wherever she traveled.
Three crape myrtles were planted in the garden that morning, including one by Yin, who carefully wrote her name and the date on its trunk.
"This honor belongs not only to me, but also to the many kind-hearted people who have helped me in the Maowusu Sandy Land, and to countless others," Yin said. ■

16:44:23 KST

CAIRO, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- Serbia's Aleksandra Stojadinovic won the women's 10m air rifle gold medal at the ISSF World Cup Rifle/Pistol here on Thursday, edging compatriot Andelija Stevanovic by just 0.3 points for a Serbian one-two finish.
Stojadinovic finished with 250.6 points, ahead of Stevanovic's 250.3, while Japan's Nobata Misaki claimed bronze with 229.2.
China's Fan Xinyi placed fourth with 208.6 points, eliminated after the 20th shot and missing the podium by 0.4 points.
The Serbian pair was level at 229.5 after 22 shots and remained tied at 239.9 after 23. On the final shot, Stojadinovic fired a 10.7 to Stevanovic's 10.4 to secure the gold.
Stojadinovic, 22, claimed her first senior World Cup medal in her fifth World Cup final appearance after qualifying eighth for Thursday's final.
Tearful after winning her first World Cup gold, Stojadinovic told Xinhua, "I am so happy. I feel I'm going to cry," adding that she had trained hard for the competition.
Looking ahead to next month's World Championships in Doha, Qatar, where the first shooting quota places for the Los Angeles 2028 Olympic Games will be awarded, Stojadinovic said the Cairo victory was an important step in her preparations.
"I think this World Cup is very good preparation because I have so much self-confidence right now," she said.
Stojadinovic credited her coach Goran Stojadinovic with helping her achieve the victory.
"We intensify training three or four weeks before competitions. As the event gets closer, we switch to lighter training," her coach told Xinhua.
The Serbian coach described the Cairo World Cup as the team's final preparation for the World Championships in Doha. "Securing Olympic quota places will be very hard, but we hope we will make it," he said.
Earlier in the day, France's Lucas Kryzs snatched gold in the men's 50m rifle three positions final, overtaking Norway's Jon-Hermann Hegg with the final shot to win by just 0.5 points.
Kryzs entered the decisive 35th shot trailing Hegg by 0.6 points, but scored 10.1 to Hegg's 9.0, finishing with 360.1 points to Hegg's 359.6.
Czechia's Jiri Privratsky claimed bronze with 348.6 points after overtaking compatriot Filip Nepejchal in the closing stages. Nepejchal finished fourth with 338.0.
The result reversed their meeting in Munich in late May, when Hegg beat Kryzs for gold.
"It's incredible. For me, it was very difficult because I finished with silver medals twice, in Granada and Munich," Kryzs told Xinhua. "So today, to take this step and win the gold medal, it's very special."
"Maybe it's experience. I've been on the podium twice, so I think that experience, along with hard work, made the difference," he said, adding that he hoped to win another gold medal at the World Championships in Doha.
Hegg said he was pleased with his silver medal despite narrowly missing out on gold.
"I'm pretty happy. It's been a challenging day, especially in standing," Hegg told Xinhua. "Even though I had a really good start in prone and kneeling, I knew I had to do my very best to be at the top, and I managed to do it, almost."
On his hopes for Doha, Hegg said, "Of course, I know I'm capable of securing a quota place, but there are so many other people who are also capable. So I will work hard, do my best, and we will see."
Thursday marked the end of competition at the ISSF World Cup Rifle/Pistol, which brought together hundreds of shooters from 51 countries and regions at Egypt International Olympic City in the New Administrative Capital, east of Cairo.
France topped the medal standings with two golds, one silver and two bronzes, followed by Germany with one gold, two silvers and two bronzes, while Czechia finished third with one gold, one silver and one bronze. ■

Thawing rate of glaciers depends on climate as well as on their shape, scientists say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:44:03 UTC
16:44:03 KST

ST. PETERSBURG, October 16. /TASS/. Scientists of the Arctic and Antarctic Research Institute (AARI, St. Petersburg) found that the rate of glacier melting depends not only on climatic factors, but also on the ice mass' shape, the institute's press service said.
"The rate of glaciers' melting depends not only on climate warming, but also on the glaciers' shape and size," the press service said. "Without adjusting assessments to the "geometry" factor, the climate estimates, based on temperature changes data, risk being inaccurate."
The scientists came to this conclusion based on results of years-long glaciological monitoring of two mountain-valley glaciers - the Aldegonda and the West Grenfjord - on the Spitsbergen Archipelago. Between 2013 and 2025, the glaciers lost about 18-20 meters of water equivalent mass, they said.
The scientists used two ways to calculate the mass balance - based on the annual changes in the glacier's surface shape, and based on the geometry relative to that recorded in 2008. The specialists found that as a result of the glaciers' shifting to lower, warmer altitude zones, they are losing annually additional 1-2% of ice on the Aldegonde and 0.5-1% on the Western Grenfjord in addition to what may be attributed to the climate. According to the scientists, over recent two decades, this addition is still not big and does not distort the overall climate assessment. However, the longer the series of observations, and the faster the glacier is melting, the more noticeable this "addition" becomes.
"The glacier is a living, constantly changing object," the institute's senior researcher Anton Terekhov explained. "As it is melting, its surface is sinking lower and lower, and down there, the air is warmer - and as a result, the ice starts melting even faster, even if the weather has not changed by a single degree. Right now, this effect is not big, but if it is not taken into account when analyzing longer series of observations, we risk mistaking part of that "geometric" history of a glacier for a climate signal that does not actually exist."
The institute's experts suggest applying this research method to other glaciers in the world. They are confident that thanks to satellite digital terrain models covering the entire Arctic and Antarctic, such calculations could be made for almost any glaciation center.
"This way we will be able to separate more accurately the real consequences of global warming from the "internal processes" of the glaciers and, accordingly, to predict more accurately their future," the press service said in conclusion.

====================================================================================================

Germany set to hike tobacco tax: Cigarette packs could reach close to €12 by 2030
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:44:01 UTC
16:44:01 KST

With the planned tax increase, the German government is aiming to raise an additional €12 billion over four years.
In Germany, an average pack of 20 cigarettes would currently set you back around €8.05, but that could be about to change after the Bundestag voted to gradually increase tobacco taxes.
Based on the calculations behind the proposed legislation, prices for a standard pack of cigarettes are expected to rise to €8.77 from 2027, €9.56 from 2028, €10.42 from 2029, and €11.36 from 2030.
Some premium brand cigarettes could cost as much as €14, whilst hand-rolling tobacco is also set to become significantly more expensive.
Germany's cigarette prices are therefore gradually catching up with those in other European countries, but they are still expected to remain below prices in some of the continent's most expensive markets, including Ireland, France, and the Netherlands.
Government hopes to boost tax revenue
With the planned increase, the German government aims to raise an additional €12 billion over four years.
Additional revenue of around €1.5 billion is expected for 2027, rising to €4.5 billion by 2030. Last year, the government generated €17.6 billion in revenue from tobacco duty.
The tobacco industry, however, doubts that the government will actually raise as much revenue as it hopes, with industry representatives warning that higher taxes could also drive smokers increasingly towards the black market or towards cheaper cigarettes from other EU countries. Legal tobacco retailers could be among those hit hardest.
CDU MP Carsten Brodesser has called for more moderate tax increases, arguing that steeper hikes could risk both lower tax revenues and adverse effects on the legal tobacco trade. However, he was unable to get his proposal adopted.
During a debate in the Bundestag, SPD MP Ingo Vogel acknowledged that reform was partly intended to help balance the budget but that it also had a public health objective - making nicotine less attractive.
Vogel welcomed news that taxes on cigars and cigarillos would not rise as sharply as had previously been planned. Taxes on e-cigarette liquids, however, were increased slightly more than had been expected.
"Inexpensive products, in particular, should not become an easy gateway to nicotine consumption, which is why we are raising the price threshold in this area," Vogel said, adding that concerns raised by customs officials and their union about a possible rise in the black market were being taken "very, very seriously."
Should demand shift to illegal channels, then "we will not only lose out financially, but we will also have to deal more with criminal networks," he said.
AfD, Die Linke, and Greens criticise hikes
The far-right AfD party has criticised the increase, with MP Christian Douglas pointing to what he sees as a contradiction in the government's approach: it justifies higher tobacco taxes on public health grounds whilst also expecting tax revenues to increase, suggesting the coalition does not actually expect tobacco consumption to fall.
The Greens, on the other hand, support a higher tobacco tax in principle but consider the planned increases to be too small.
Die Linke, like the AfD, voted against the reform.
According to the 2025 microcensus, around 19% of people aged 15 and over in Germany smoke. Some 14% regularly and 5% occasionally.
The German Cancer Research Centre said around 131,000 people died from tobacco-related illnesses in 2023. Health experts regard higher prices as an effective means of encouraging people to give up smoking.
On Friday, the Bundesrat will vote on the amendment to the tobacco tax law. With no objections currently anticipated, the tax increase is expected to be approved.

OTTAWA, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney warned Thursday night that external forces are attempting to "divide and own" Canada, calling on voters in Alberta to choose to stay in Canada in an upcoming referendum.
Carney made the remarks while addressing thousands of attendees at a "Forever Canadian" rally in Calgary, Alberta.
Alberta is holding a nonbinding referendum on Monday to decide whether to remain part of Canada or hold a second, legally binding referendum on separation.
Pointing to a more dangerous and divided global landscape, Carney said, "Some outside our borders are working to break us so they can own us."

"Careful: they might think that is election interference," Carney quipped.
Carney is scheduled to attend another "Forever Canadian" rally in Edmonton, the capital of Alberta, on Friday. ■

S. Korea's job growth stays in 100,000 range for 3rd month in September
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
15:43:48 CST
16:43:48 KST

SEOUL, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's job growth stayed in the 100,000 range for a third straight month, driven by a turnaround in the manufacturing industry in over two years, statistical ministry data showed Friday.
The number of employed people aged 15 and older gained 113,000, or 0.4 percent, from a year earlier to 29,266,000 in September, according to the Ministry of Data and Statistics.
After hitting a decrease of 40,000 jobs in May, employment rebounded in June with an increase of 63,000 before surpassing the 100,000 threshold in July, August and September.
The overall employment rate for those aged 15 and older slipped 0.2 percentage points year on year to 63.5 percent in September, but the OECD-standard hiring rate for those aged 15-64 rose 0.2 percentage points to 70.6 percent.
Employment among manufacturers mounted 16,000 in September on a yearly basis, marking the first rebound since June 2024.
Jobs lost in the construction industry reached 48,000 last month, extending the losing streak to 29 months.
The accommodation and food services sector, a key indicator of domestic consumption, saw a drop of 97,000 jobs, keeping a downward trajectory for two consecutive months.
The losses were offset by strong hiring in the health and social welfare service, the transport and warehousing, and the finance and insurance industries, which recorded job increases of 207,000, 54,000 and 32,000 each.
The cold spell for youth labor was prolonged. The number of employed people aged 15-29 plummeted 147,000 in September from a year earlier, continuing to go down for 47 straight months.
The youth employment rate tumbled 1.1 percentage points to 44 percent, falling for 29 months in a row.
The elderly population compensated for the slack in youth hiring. The number of jobs for those aged 60 and older surged 172,000, while the figures for those in their 30s and 50s swelled 81,000 and 48,000 each.
The number of unemployed people totaled 600,000 in September, down 34,000 from a year earlier. The unemployment rate dipped 0.1 percentage points to 2 percent.
The expanded jobless rate, called the labor underutilization indicator, shrank 0.6 percentage points to 7.3 percent, while the corresponding rate for those aged 15-29 added 0.5 percentage points to 15.6 percent.
The economically inactive population, who had no willingness to seek a job and remained unemployed, rose 179,000 from a year earlier to 16,188,000 in September.
The reading for discouraged jobseekers dwindled 1,000 to 368,000 last month.
The number of the "take-a-rest" group, who replied that they took a rest during a job survey period, reduced 25,000 to 2,497,000 in the cited month. ■

Australian gov't to establish first dedicated commissioner for Indigenous aged care
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
15:43:48 CST
16:43:48 KST

CANBERRA, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- The Australian government will permanently establish a dedicated commissioner to oversee aged care for the Indigenous population under new laws.
Minister for Aged Care and Seniors Sam Rae said in a statement on Friday that Australia will establish its first Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Aged Care Commissioner from July 2027, after legislation passed the federal parliament with bipartisan support on Thursday.
Rae said the new commissioner will work directly with regulatory systems that oversee the aged care sector to communicate feedback and priorities from Indigenous elders and inform government decisions.
"Every older Australian deserves care that sees them, knows them and treats them with respect," he said.
"The establishment of Australia's first permanent Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Aged Care Commissioner will give an independent voice to First Nations peoples and deliver better outcomes for them and their communities."
The federal government's landmark Royal Commission into Aged Care Quality and Safety, which handed down its final report in 2021, found that the system failed to provide culturally safe care for Indigenous Australians and made several recommendations for reform, including a dedicated commissioner.
Rae said that the commissioner will be appointed following consultation with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander organizations and advocates. ■

Syria's 2013 Baniyas massacres: What happened and who was Ali Kayali?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:42:31 UTC
16:42:31 KST

The arrest on Thursday of Ali Kayali, better known as Mihrac Ural, has renewed attention to the 2013 massacres in the village of al-Bayda and the Ras al-Nabaa neighbourhood of Baniyas, both in Syria’s western Tartus Governorate.
They involved mass killings and summary executions of hundreds of civilians, including women and children, during the tenure of ousted Syrian regime leader Bashar al Assad, who led the country from 2000 until late 2024.
The Syrian Arab News Agency (SANA) said the General Intelligence Directorate had arrested Kayali while he was attempting to flee across the border, describing him as the “main suspect” in the Baniyas massacres.
Videos circulated online showed mosques in Al-Bayda broadcasting chants of “Allahu Akbar,” with those sharing the footage saying residents were celebrating news of his arrest.
The massacres took place on May 2 and 3 2013, when Assad regime forces and allied armed groups carried out military operations in Al-Bayda and the Ras al-Nabaa neighbourhood of Baniyas that included summary executions and mass killings of civilians.
The massacres
According to an August 2013 report by the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Syria, regime forces surrounded Al-Bayda on May 2, closed access routes and shelled the town before entering alongside members of the National Defence Forces.
The commission documented arrests and summary executions of civilians as well as dozens of bodies found inside homes and in the streets. Some had been burned, while others bore signs of having been beaten with blunt objects.
The following day, the operation extended to Ras al-Nabaa, where attacking forces surrounded the area, prevented residents from leaving through the main roads, shelled the neighbourhood and then entered it. Families, including children, were among those executed.
The UN commission found that the two operations were linked and said there was no indication of armed opposition activity in either area during the killings.
It estimated that between 150 and 250 civilians were killed in Al-Bayda and between 150 and 200 in Ras al-Nabaa.
The UN investigation concluded that Assad regime forces and allied armed groups, including the National Defence Forces, were responsible for killings amounting to war crimes.
Kayali’s role
During the Syrian uprising, Kayali led an armed group known as the Syrian Resistance, which fought alongside Assad regime forces and took part in military operations in several parts of the country.
Syrian authorities linked Kayali and his group to the Al-Bayda and Ras al-Nabaa massacres and announced his arrest more than 13 years after the killings.
On October 4, Syria’s Interior Ministry announced the arrest of Jamal Trabelsi, Kayali’s deputy.
The ministry said Trabelsi had participated in combat operations in support of the former regime, including the Al-Bayda and Ras al-Nabaa massacres, as well as fighting in the countryside of Hama, Idlib and Aleppo.
Kayali’s arrest came 11 days after his deputy was detained, marking a new development in efforts to pursue those accused of violations committed during the former regime’s rule.
In May, residents of Baniyas and its countryside marked the anniversary of the massacres, demanding accountability for those responsible and answers about the fate of missing people.

Addressing the 17th Summit of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (COP 17), held in the Armenian capital of Yerevan on Friday, Pezeshkian emphasized that US and Israel waged an unprovoked war of aggression against the Iranian nation which produced adverse effects on the ecosystem of the regional countries.
Condemning the destructive impact of wars of aggression on nature, Iranian President Pezeshkian termed it "ecocide," or environmental genocide, stating that preserving biodiversity can be important arenas for peace diplomacy.
Iranian president called for stronger international mechanisms to assess and repair environmental damage caused by armed conflict, warning that war threatens biodiversity far beyond national borders.
Turning to the Israeli massacre of Palestinians in the Gaza Strip, he stressed, “Gaza stands as a stark testament to ecocide, with devastation whose horrific impacts will endure for generations.”
President Pezeshkian warned that war caused lasting environmental devastation, citing that Gaza's contaminated soil as proof that ecological damage crosses borders and requires international intervention.
Nations subjected to illegal sanctions and foreign-imposed wars must not be forced to pay the heavy toll of these crises, Pezeshkian warned.
Protecting biodiversity can be an important arena for peace diplomacy, he said, stressing, “Not only war is merely a threat to humans and infrastructure, but also as a direct cause of the destruction of nature.”
War burns forests, destroys wetlands, pollutes soil and water, and displaces animal species, he underlined.
“We believe that biodiversity conservation can serve as a significant arena for "peace diplomacy." In a region grappling with security crises stemming from the illegal and expansionist presence of powers, as well as climate change, water scarcity, and ecosystem degradation, environmental cooperation can build bridges between nations, the bridges that pave the way for peace and security for all, peace with nature, and a future lived in harmony with the natural world.”
Pezeshkian described the environmental devastation caused by the wars in the region, including in Gaza, as “ecocide” that must be condemned, adding that pollution and ecological damage transcend national borders.
He then called on the international community to ensure that nature is not treated as a “silent and defenseless victim” of war. He said international agencies and relevant institutions should strengthen mechanisms for assessing environmental damage, mobilizing financial resources, restoring damaged ecosystems and supporting countries affected by the environmental consequences of armed conflicts.
Highlighting Iran’s biodiversity, which spans the Hyrcanian and Arasbaran forests, the Zagros Mountains, deserts and the coasts of the Persian Gulf, Sea of Oman and Caspian Sea, Pezeshkian said nature conservation is part of the country’s cultural and civilizational heritage. He noted that Iran has adopted a national biodiversity strategy and action plan, designated its Department of Environment as the national coordinating body, and prioritized the protection of endangered species and the expansion of protected areas.
The president also stressed that developing countries need fair access to financial resources, modern technologies, scientific knowledge and capacity-building opportunities to meet their environmental commitments.
He said countries facing economic sanctions or military aggression should not be left to bear alone the environmental costs of sanctions or wars they did not initiate. Without adequate funding and equitable technology transfer, he warned, global biodiversity targets would remain little more than declarations and negotiations.
“What has happened in our region as a result of wars of aggression is ‘ecocide or environmental genocide,’ which must be condemned,” he said.
Pezeshkian also pointed to the combined effects of climate change, drought, water scarcity, desertification, economic sanctions and restricted access to technology and financial resources on Iran’s environmental protection efforts.
He said Iran has been targeted by criminal wars for two consecutive years, involving the extensive use of destructive and prohibited weapons, with attacks in many cases deliberately aimed at damaging the environment, including strikes on fuel storage facilities in the capital.
The president called for genuine international cooperation to help Iran implement environmental programs and compensate for the damage inflicted.
He said Iran’s diverse ecosystems, species and genetic resources formed a natural and cultural heritage shaped by millions of years of evolution over time. From the Hyrcanian and Arasbaran forests to the Zagros Mountains, deserts and the coasts of the Persian Gulf, Gulf of Oman and Caspian Sea, these resources underpin the country’s resilience and sustainable development, he said.
President Pezeshkian said Iran had adopted a national biodiversity strategy and action plan and designated the Department of Environment as its national coordinator. Priorities include expanding protected areas to 28 percent, monitoring key species, developing wildlife rehabilitation centers and implementing action plans for 25 vertebrate species. National task forces have been established for species including the Asiatic cheetah and Persian fallow deer, he said.
Turning to armed conflict, President Pezeshkian said war burns forests, damages wetlands, contaminates soil and water, destroys habitats and introduces pollutants and heavy metals into natural systems. Such harm can persist for years after fighting ends and affect the security and well-being of future generations.
He said the United States and the Israeli regime are causing environmental damage through military operations in the region, citing damage to industrial and energy facilities, fires, pollution and harm to protective infrastructure. He said environmental impacts crossed political borders and required solutions.
Referring to Gaza, he warned that damage to soil and ecological systems could endure for generations and described the destruction as ecocide, which he emphasized should be condemned.
President Pezeshkian also highlighted the challenges facing countries dealing with climate change, drought, water scarcity and desertification while facing economic sanctions and limited access to finance and technology. Biodiversity commitments, he said, would remain on paper without adequate funding, fair access to technology and capacity-building.
He called on United Nations agencies, international financial institutions and environmental and sustainable-development bodies to strengthen funding mechanisms, assess environmental damage, restore affected ecosystems and support countries dealing with the consequences of armed conflict. Countries under sanctions or subjected to military aggression should not be left to bear these costs alone, he said.
Pezeshkian said Iran’s commitment to biodiversity protection is rooted not only in its international obligations but also in its longstanding cultural and civilizational heritage.
He noted that Iran is a country with an ancient tradition of living in harmony with nature and has a remarkable diversity of ecosystems, species and genetic resources.
From the Hyrcanian and Arasbaran forests to the Zagros Mountains, deserts and the coasts of the Persian Gulf, the Sea of Oman and the Caspian Sea, Iran’s natural wealth provides a foundation for water and food security, public health, resilience to natural hazards and sustainable development, he said.
Respect for nature, Pezeshkian added, has long been part of Iranian cultural, religious and ritual identity. Traditional agriculture, animal husbandry, the use of medicinal plants and indigenous knowledge have also developed through centuries of interaction with the natural environment.
Protecting biodiversity, he added, could become an important arena for peace diplomacy, with environmental cooperation serving as a bridge between nations and helping advance peace with nature and a safer future for coming generations.
Pezeshkian reaffirmed Iran’s readiness to share its scientific expertise, academic capabilities and experience with other countries, describing biodiversity conservation as an important avenue for “peace diplomacy.”
Cooperation could help bridge divides between nations and contribute to peace and security, coexistence with nature, and the well-being of present and future generations, he concluded.

Chicken satay brings the flavors of Malaysian street food to the buffet. The grilled skewers are served with cucumber, red onion, and peanut sauce, pairing lightly smoky chicken with a creamy dip.
For a different take on coconut-rich flavors, Malaysian curry noodles are served in a fragrant, coconut milk-based broth with a rich blend of spices and a hint of heat from sambal. Topped with chicken breast, fish balls, and fried potatoes, the dish is finished with calamansi juice for a refreshing citrus kick.
The dessert station offers a distinctly Malaysian treat with colorful layers of shaved ice, red beans, attap seeds, grass jelly, and creamed corn. Malaysian brand D Masking’s Musang King durian ice cream adds a rich, fragrant finish to the refreshing combination.
Iced Milo brings another familiar taste of Malaysia. Diners can also add Milo powder and ice cream at the dessert station to create local-style variations.

Carnival Cruises axes half of Australian fleet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:38:12 UTC
16:38:12 KST

In short:
Carnival Cruises will drop two of the four cruise ships in its Australian fleet.
All other major cruise lines have pulled their full-time Australian ships.
Australia is a hard market for cruises to stay profitable, according to an industry expert.
Carnival Cruises has announced it will remove two of its four Australian cruise ships from March 2028, despite more than 1.4 million Australians going on a cruise last year.
Carnival, which is the only major cruise company operating full-time in Australia, announced it was pulling the Carnival Adventure and the Carnival Luminosa.
Other major cruise operators such as Disney and Royal Caribbean no longer operate full-time in Australia.
Carnival said ship schedules were considered years in advance and it was considering "long-term certainty and globally competitive operating conditions to support itinerary planning and investment".
The decision was an economic one, according to Chris Frame, a maritime historian.
"Australia is an end-of-the-line destination, and it's a huge investment."
Mr Frame said higher levels of regulation, such as tough biosecurity rules, and little cruise infrastructure made it hard for cruises to stay profitable in Australia.
"Berthing fees are higher than other markets, refuelling is higher and provisioning the ship with food is higher, as you just don't have the economies of scale."
He said that for the company, the ships were assets and "they can always be redeployed somewhere else more profitable".
New changes to cruise laws
The moves comes after a decades-old temporary exemption, allowing cruise ships to circumvent Australian labour laws, was extended earlier this month, but with new protections added for workers for the first time.
Earlier this year, an ABC News investigation revealed that workers had accused the company of 12-hour work days for seven days a week, medical neglect, not providing safe drinking water and wages less than $3 an hour. Carnival denied the allegations.
Carnival's country manager Peter Little said in a statement the company had "greater exposure to changes in local market and operating conditions" than other cruise lines. Carnival did not respond to requests for comment.
However, Jake Field of the Maritime Union of Australia claimed this was the third time Carnival had threatened to withdraw from Australia, and that it was a negotiating tactic.
"There are 80 cruise vessels that are scheduled to come to Australia, only four of them don't have collective agreements with their crews, and those are the four Carnival ships," he said.
"We'll still be surrounded by water, and be an international cruise destination. Those 80 other cruise ships will still be coming here."

The Cheonghae Unit has operated in the Gulf of Aden off Somalia since 2009, escorting South Korean vessels and protecting them from piracy.

The Strait of Hormuz is a crucial energy corridor for South Korea, while the conflict involving Iran and increased activity by Yemen’s Houthi group around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait have raised concerns over shipping and crude supplies.

Threatening him with a pistol, the attackers forced the man to transfer cryptocurrency worth $51,000 to a prepared wallet. After that, he was supposed to call his mother and demand that she hand over all the family's savings. Fearing for her son's life, the woman gave them more than $17,000.
After taking the money, the suspects threatened to kill the man if he contacted the police or a hospital. According to the investigation, they divided the money among themselves

US missile defence shortages could last until 2030, ousted general warned: report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:36:45 UTC
16:36:45 KST

Ousted US Army Chief of Staff General Randy George warned months before the US-Israeli war against Iran that American missile defence stockpiles were critically low and could take until 2030 to recover, CBS News reported on Thursday, citing US officials familiar with his assessment.
George raised the warning in late December, two months before the conflict began. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth removed him from his post in April as the war was under way.
The assessment, included in the Pentagon’s fiscal 2027 force allocation planning, identified shortages of Terminal High Altitude Area Defence (THAAD) interceptors and Patriot missiles, with supplies expected to remain at strategically low levels until 2030.
Officials attributed the shortfall to weapons transfers to Ukraine, US military support for Israel and limited defence industry production capacity, according to the report.
War further strains supplies
The conflict with Iran has added pressure on US stockpiles. A Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimate found that US forces entered 2026 with about 2,300 Patriot interceptors and used between 1,050 and 1,430 of them during the conflict.
The US had about 355 THAAD interceptors before the war, of which an estimated 190 to 290 were expended, according to the estimates.
Mark Cancian, a retired Marine colonel and senior adviser at CSIS, told CBS News that the systems would be crucial in a potential conflict with China.
“Air defence, missile defence, that will be huge,” he said, explaining that a major confrontation with Beijing would require substantial interceptor supplies.
Replenishing the stockpiles could take years. CSIS estimates that new THAAD interceptor contracts take more than four years to fulfil, while Patriot PAC-3 orders take an average of three and a half years.
Pentagon denies shortage
The Pentagon rejected claims that US forces face a shortage of munitions.
“Claims of US munitions shortages are false,” chief spokesperson Sean Parnell told CBS News.
He added that Washington retained “everything required to strike at the time and place of the President’s choosing”.

Scale of attacks
- On-duty air defenses intercepted and destroyed 644 Ukrainian fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles over Russian regions from 8:00 p.m. Moscow time on October 15 to 8:00 a.m. Moscow time on October 16 (5:00 p.m. - 5:00 a.m. GMT), the Defense Ministry said.
- According to the ministry, the drones were shot down over the Bryansk, Vologda, Volgograd, Voronezh, Vladimir, Kaluga, Kursk, Lipetsk, Nizhny Novgorod, Novgorod, Orenburg, Oryol, Pskov, Rostov, Ryazan, Samara, Saratov, Smolensk, Tambov, Tver, Tula, Ulyanovsk, Moscow, Leningrad, Krasnodar and Tatarstan regions, as well as Crimea and the Black Sea.
- Air defenses downed another 15 drones heading for Moscow, Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said on the Max social media platform.
- Earlier, Sobyanin said that 37 drones had been shot down shortly before midnight.
- A total of 57 drones flying toward Moscow have been shot down since midnight, according to TASS calculations based on data from Sobyanin.
- About 50 UAVs and projectiles were destroyed in Russia’s southern Rostov Region overnight, Governor Yury Slyusar said.
- According to him the city of Bataisk and nine districts came under attack.
- Air defenses shot down 27 Ukrainian drones over the central Kaluga Region, Governor Vladislav Shapsha wrote on Max.
- Another 15 Ukrainian drones were downed over the central Tula Region, Governor Dmitry Milyayev said.
- Earlier, he said that ten UAVs had been destroyed.
- Air defenses downed 12 Ukrainian drones over the western Smolensk Region last night, Governor Vasily Anokhin said.
- Ten Ukrainian UAVs were destroyed over the Voronezh Region in southwestern Russia, Governor Alexander Gusev wrote on Max.
- Eight drones were shot down over the central Yaroslavl Region, Governor Mikhail Yevrayev said on Max.
- An attack involving three drones was repelled in the northwestern Novgorod Region, Governor Alexander Dronov said.
Consequences
- A man was injured in a drone strike in the Aksaisky District of the Rostov Region, Governor Slyusar said.
- The man has been taken to the hospital.
- Falling drone debris damaged production and storage facilities in the Aksaisky District.
- A fire broke out but it has now been extinguished.
- The windows of two private houses were damaged in the Kuibyshevsky District.
- There were no casualties.
- Falling drone fragments damaged several windows and balconies in an apartment building, as well as a car, in a municipality in the Voronezh Region, Governor Gusev said.

Deutsch-Französische Einigung zu „Made in Europe“ und Autoabgasen verzögert sich – SPD erhebt Einwände
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:35:00 UTC
16:35:00 KST

Deutsch-Französische Einigung zu „Made in Europe“ und Autoabgasen verzögert sich – SPD erhebt Einwände
Der Vertragsentwurf sieht strengere Zulassungsbedingungen für Nicht-EU-Länder hinsichtlich der Teilnahme an öffentlichen Ausschreibungen und der Inanspruchnahme öffentlicher Fördermittel vor und mildert das Verbot von Verbrennungsmotoren ab dem Jahr 2035 ab.
Der französische Präsident Emmanuel Macron auf dem internationalen Pariser Autosalon an der Porte de Versailles in Paris am 12. Oktober 2026. | Poolfoto von Thibault Camus/AFP via Getty Images
BRÜSSEL — Frankreich und Deutschland konnten sich am Donnerstag nicht auf einen gemeinsamen Standpunkt zum Geltungsbereich der künftigen „Made in Europe“-Vorschriften der Union sowie zu größerer Flexibilität bei der Reduzierung der CO2-Emissionen und zum Verbot von Verbrennungsmotoren ab 2035 einigen.
Der Entwurf des Gegenseitigkeitsabkommens, über den POLITICO erstmals im Juli berichtet hatte, stellt eine bedeutende Annäherung zwischen den beiden Ländern dar und sollte eigentlich in Kürze unterzeichnet werden. Am Donnerstagabend geriet das Abkommen jedoch ins Stocken, da der Koalitionspartner SPD Einwände erhob. Befürchtet wurde, dass wichtige Umweltziele gestrichen worden seien.
„Eine endgültige Einigung steht noch aus“, erklärte ein Sprecher der deutschen Bundesregierung.
Advertisement
Anfang dieser Woche hatte der französische Präsident Emmanuel Macron angedeutet, dass nun Deutschland am Zug sei. „Auf der anderen Seite des Rheins gibt es politische Zwänge, und ich respektiere die Koalitionsgespräche voll und ganz“, sagte Macron am Montag am Rande des Pariser Autosalons.
Gemäß den Bedingungen des vorgeschlagenen Abkommens würde Deutschland strengere „Made in Europe“-Kriterien für den Automobilsektor im „Industrial Accelerator Act“ akzeptieren, auf die Frankreich gedrängt hat, im Gegenzug für eine Abschwächung des Verbots von Verbrennungsmotoren, einer der langfristigen Forderungen Berlins.
„Angesichts der erheblichen technologischen, wirtschaftlichen und geopolitischen Veränderungen seit der Einführung des bestehenden Rechtsrahmens sollte das Automobilpaket ein besseres Gleichgewicht zwischen Klimazielen, industrieller Wettbewerbsfähigkeit, technologischer Entwicklung und der Stärkung der europäischen Wertschöpfung herstellen“, schrieben die beiden Länder in einem POLITICO vorliegenden Vertragsentwurf.
„Auf der Grundlage der deutsch-französischen Ministerräte in den Jahren 2025 und 2026 schlagen Deutschland und Frankreich daher ein ausgewogenes Verhandlungspaket vor, das ehrgeizige CO2-Reduktionsziele mit zusätzlicher Flexibilität und gezielten Anreizen für die europäische Wertschöpfung verbindet“, heißt es in der Vereinbarung weiter.
Derzeit sieht das Ziel der EU vor, dass Unternehmen die Emissionen von Verbrennungsmotoren bis 2035 um 100 Prozent gegenüber dem Niveau von 2021 senken, wobei sie die Möglichkeit haben, sich durch Initiativen wie Ausgleichsmaßnahmen und Investitionen einen Spielraum von 10 Prozent bei den Emissionen zu „erwerben“.
Im Rahmen des vorgeschlagenen Abkommens wollen Frankreich und Deutschland das Ziel für 2035 auf 90 Prozent absenken und im Gegenzug für Investitionen in alternative Kraftstoffe einen zusätzlichen Spielraum von 10 Prozent einräumen (was insgesamt 80 Prozent ergibt).
Advertisement
Entscheidend für die Stahlhersteller und die linke SPD in Deutschland wäre, dass das deutsch-französische Abkommen die Investitionspflicht für „grünen Stahl“ abschaffen und damit einen wichtigen Anreiz beseitigen würde.
„Das zerstört den Leitmarkt für die Stahlindustrie“, erklärte ein Lobbyist der Branche gegenüber POLITICO unter der Bedingung der Anonymität, um über dieses heikle Thema sprechen zu können. Da der Vertragsentwurf keinen Druck auf die Automobilhersteller ausübe, „grünen Stahl“ zu beziehen, werde dieser dadurch zu einem „nice-to-have“-Extra, erklärte die Person.
Als Zugeständnis an Berlin wird im Vertragsentwurf betont, dass der sogenannte „Utility-Faktor“ – mit dem die Emissionen von Plug-in-Hybridfahrzeugen anhand des Verhältnisses zwischen der Nutzungshäufigkeit des Elektromotors und des Verbrennungsmotors berechnet wird – auf der Grundlage von Laborergebnissen und nicht, wie von der Kommission gefordert, anhand von Daten aus dem realen Fahrbetrieb ermittelt werden sollte. Diese Änderung wird den Automobilherstellern helfen, mehr Plug-in-Hybride zu verkaufen und gleichzeitig die übergeordneten Emissionsziele zu erreichen.
Als Gegenleistung für diese Emissionszugeständnisse schloss sich Deutschland der Forderung Frankreichs an, den Geltungsbereich der „Made in Europe“-Regelungen im Rahmen des „Industrial Accelerator Act“ der EU in Bezug auf den Automobilsektor einzuschränken.
Der Text gilt nur für die 27 EU-Mitgliedstaaten und wird unter bestimmten Voraussetzungen auf das Vereinigte Königreich ausgeweitet.
Der EU-Industriekommissar Stéphane Séjourné erklärte am Dienstag gegenüber POLITICO, er unterstütze das Abkommen als Weg aus der Sackgasse, und fügte hinzu, dass das Vereinigte Königreich derzeit die Voraussetzungen für das Label „Made in Europe“ erfülle.
Advertisement
Die Vereinbarung könnte den Stillstand sowohl bei der CO₂-Verordnung als auch beim IAA beenden, bei denen Frankreich und Deutschland bisher auf gegensätzlichen Seiten standen. „Die Bestandteile dieses Gesamtpakets sollten so schnell wie möglich und gleichzeitig verabschiedet werden“, schrieben die beiden Länder.
Die britische Regierung begrüßte die mögliche Einbeziehung des Vereinigten Königreichs in die „Made in Europe“-Vorschriften für Kraftfahrzeuge.
„Dies ist ein deutsch-französischer Vorschlag, und es muss noch ein europäischer Prozess durchlaufen werden, aber sollte er bestätigt werden, begrüßen wir das Ziel, das Vereinigte Königreich in den ‚Industrial Accelerator Act‘ einzubeziehen – das wäre eine gute Nachricht für die britische Automobilindustrie sowie für die Arbeitsplätze und Investitionen, die sie im gesamten Vereinigten Königreich sichert“, erklärte ein Sprecher von Downing Street Nr. 10 in einer Stellungnahme.
Sollte der deutsch-französische Deal unterschrieben werden, muss es noch von den anderen EU-Mitgliedstaaten und vom Europäischen Parlament gebilligt werden, die derzeit über das „Industrial Accelerator Act“ und das Automobilpaket, einschließlich der Emissionsziele für Automobilhersteller, beraten.
Carlo Martuscelli, Francesca Micheletti und Graham Lanktree haben zu diesem Bericht beigetragen.

Rugby League World Cup : Australia defeats Fetu Samoa 40-0
Australia's quest for a fourth consecutive Women's Rugby League World Cup has started with a bang courtesy of a 40-0 victory over Fetu Samoa.
Unbackable favourites leading into the tournament opener, the Jillaroos overcame an ill-disciplined opening 10 minutes to shut out Samoa in the seven-try rout.
Things were far from easy for Australia in the second half, but the damage was already done by half-time, with five-eighth Jocelyn Kelleher and reigning Dally M medallist Tamika Upton leading the way with two try assists apiece.
Kelleher, making her Jillaroos debut, was named player of the match, where she was dangerous in attack and her kicking game troubled Samoa.
Speaking to ABC Sport, Kelleher said she had been waiting a long time for her chance to play for the Jillaroos.
"It's a dream come true," she said.
"Was in the squad last year, but got my debut jersey this year. So excited and so happy to be here."
Despite the 40-point win, it was far from a perfect performance from the reigning world champions.
"We still have a lot of things to fix from today. It wasn't perfect out there," Kelleher said.
Samoa, in their first World Cup since 2008, had several chances early but lacked the class to capitalise against their much-fancied opponents.
Gold Coast Titans star Jaime Chapman ended her three-year Jillaroos exodus by scoring Australia's first try in the 11th minute, beating opposite winger Freedom Crichton Ropati out wide.
Australia's greatest ever try-scorer, Julia Robinson, lived up to her reputation seven minutes later when she beat three would-be defenders for her 23rd Jillaroos try in 14 appearances.
Tries to back-rower Shaylee Bent and hooker Keeley Nizza followed in quick succession before lock Olivia Kernick crossed moments before halftime to seal a 28-0 lead at the break.
Kernick turned playmaker in the opening five minutes of the second period when she handed the ball off for Keilee Joseph to extend the Jillaroos' lead.
Brave defence might have turned the tide for Samoa, who ground their way to more opportunities at the Jillaroos end over the final 25 minutes.
Prop Laikha Clarke went the closest to securing some consolation points for Samoa, but was ruled to have dropped the ball over the line.
Of further concern for Samoa was a suspected knee injury in the dying stages to centre Sarina Masaga.
A try in the final two minutes from Australian centre Jessica Sergis capped the Jillaroos' victory and extended their almost three-year unbeaten run.
Samoa's men thrashed France in the opening match of the day, putting on a record score to win 78-4.

REPORT: Samoa 78 def. France 4
— reporting by AAP
Samoa have opened their World Cup campaign by crushing France in a 78-4 win that gives an early boost to the Pacific nation's hopes of reaching the knockout stages.
In a 14-try-to-one victory in which centre Stephen Crichton kicked 11 goals and Melbourne flyer Sua Fa'alogo crossed four times, the Samoans barely worked up a sweat at Western Sydney Stadium in Sydney on Friday.
Taking on a French side mostly made up of Super League players, the star-studded Samoan team raced out to a 28-0 lead inside 20 minutes.
The only blemish for coach Ben Gardiner was the sight of Brisbane winger Deine Mariner going off in the first half with a suspected injury.
And while they had lapses of discipline and concentration with the result sewn up — France scored their sole try through winger Guillermo Aispuro-Bichet — the heavy win will increase Samoa's points differential and their hopes of making it to the semi-finals.
One of Samoa, England or Tonga will miss the knockout stages as a result of the new tournament format, in which the top two teams from across group B and group C make it to the last four.
Samoa face Papua New Guinea in Port Moresby next week before concluding their pool games in an all-Pacific match-up for the ages against the Tongans.
The Kumuls on home soil and Tonga in Sydney will provide a much sterner test than the French, who were left for dead in a blistering opening quarter.
Mariner scored the opening try for the Toa in the third minute soon after his father Lapi had sung the country's national anthem that brought stars including Jarome Luai and Spencer Leniu to tears.
Benaiah Ioelu, Jermaine McEwen, Fa'alogo, and Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow all crossed in the next 15 minutes as the French defence was cut to shreds.
Aispuro-Bichet briefly stemmed the bleeding before Fa'alogo went in again just before halftime to make it 34-4 at the break.
The French had little resistance in the second period, with Fa'alogo adding two more while Crichton, Chanel Harris-Tavita, Shawn Blore, Izack Tago, Francis Molo and Ioelu all went over.

Syria arrests 'Butcher of Baniyas' accused of 2013 coastal massacres
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:33:01 UTC
16:33:01 KST

Ali Kayali, 70, known as Mihrac Ural, commanded al-Assad-affiliated militia forces that carried out summary executions of more than 450 civilians in Bayda and Baniyas in May 2013.
Syria's General Intelligence Directorate has arrested Ali Kayali, the al-Assad era militia commander linked to the 2013 Bayda and Baniyas massacres, as he attempted to flee the country, state-run SANA news agency reported.
Known by his alias Mihrac Ural, Kayali is accused of commanding armed groups that carried out killings alongside forces of ousted dictator Bashar al-Assad, including in the coastal province of Tartus, and in rural areas of Latakia, Aleppo and Idlib.
The Syrian Observatory for Human Rights cited unnamed sources who said Kayali was taken from his home in the Mansourieh area of Lebanon, not at a Syrian border crossing.
According to those sources, armed men with Lebanese accents entered the property, apprehended Kayali's wife and brother-in-law, and removed him from the premises. Lebanese authorities have not commented on this report.
Kayali, 70, has been linked to the killings in Bayda and Baniyas in May 2013, when regime forces and allied militias stormed residential areas in Tartus province and carried out summary executions of civilians.
The Syrian Network for Human Rights documented 264 deaths in Bayda, including 36 children and 28 women, and 195 in Ras al-Nabeh, including 56 children and 43 women.
A Human Rights Watch report published in September 2013 documented at least 248 deaths across the two locations, noting the real figure was likely higher.
Witness accounts described bodies left in streets, shops and basements, executions carried out with firearms and bladed weapons, and homes set alight alongside the dead.
Who is Ali Kayali?
Born in the Turkish city of Antakya in 1956, Kayali was active in armed organisations including the Popular Salvation Front in Turkey and the Front for the Liberation of the Iskenderun Brigade, both designated terrorist organisations by Ankara.
He fled to Syria in 1982, obtained Syrian citizenship and changed his name. He reportedly cultivated close ties to the al-Assad family through his wife.
When the Syrian civil war began in 2011, he took command of the Popular Front for the Liberation of the Iskenderun Brigade, which fought alongside regime forces, primarily along Syria's coast.
Kayali's detention follows that of Jamal Trabelsi, described in reports as his deputy, who was arrested by Syria's Internal Security Forces on 4 October.
Turkish authorities announced the separate arrest of Omar al-Khatib earlier this month as he attempted to reach Europe by sea. Media reports describe him as one of the planners of the Reyhanli bombing and say he coordinated with members of al-Assad-era intelligence services.
Syria's Interior Ministry has said it is continuing to pursue individuals accused of involvement in abuses under the former regime as part of efforts to achieve transitional justice.
Damascus has stepped up efforts to restore trust in Syria's government and its services following a 13-year-long war in the country that resulted in the deaths of hundreds of thousands and saw millions displaced and seeking refuge outside the country.
Trust in authorities in neighbouring Lebanon is among the lowest in the world, with 56% of Lebanese citizens believing the government does not care about them at all, about double the global figure (29%), according to the latest research by Gallup for Lloyd's Register Foundation's World Risk Poll.

Lithuania extends military support for patrolling Kaliningrad border

Lithuania has extended military assistance to patrol its border with Russia’s Kaliningrad region until mid-November, Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said.
“Assessing the potential flows of residents fleeing the Kaliningrad region and related incidents of illegal border crossings, we are extending enhanced border protection until mid-November for preventive purposes,” Kaunas said.
The Defence Ministry said the decision was made at the request of Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas. Military resources will be coordinated with the needs of the State Border Guard Service.
About 100 troops are currently deployed to assist border guards.
Military intelligence has reported no significant changes in military activity in the Kaliningrad region, and the threat level along Lithuania’s border has not increased.
The deployment is linked to public reports of a planned mobilisation in Russia following parliamentary elections. Katelynas has said he expects people might try to seek asylum in Lithuania to avoid military service.
Military personnel and State Border Guard Service officers patrol areas around border checkpoints. Mobile patrols, mobile observation posts and military police units can also be deployed as needed.

Ralf Tribuntsov takes third at World Cup,sets Estonian record
Swimmer Ralf Tribuntsov set a new domestic record in the 100-meter backstroke at the World Cup stage in Astana, Kazakhstan, finishing third in 49.88 seconds.
It was the second time in his career he has swum under 50 seconds, improving last year's record by 0.04. Pieter Coetze won in 48.40, with Pavel Samusenko second in 49.29.
Tribuntsov qualified fifth from the morning heats in 50.70, then set the national record in the final.
The 32-year-old said he was especially pleased with the second half of the race, usually his weaker suit.
"[Estonian swimmer] Daniel [Zaitsev] and [coach] Toni [Meijel] are my lucky charms! As soon as they arrived, I got a medal! I'm incredibly happy, especially that I managed to swim the second half of the race faster, which is usually my weaker side. Today I managed to beat the other men precisely with the second half of the race," Tribuntsov said after the event.
"In the last 25 meters, when I came up from under the water, I already understood that there was still strength left, that I could fight and that this would be a decent swim. I managed to do exactly what I wanted, and that doesn't happen often in sport! The feeling in the water is quite good, so I'm expecting good results in other events too," he added.
Coach Meijel said a different competition schedule played a part too. At the previous two stages the 100m backstroke was on the third day, but in Astana, Tribuntsov could start his primary event on day one.
"A very decent swim! This time the 100m backstroke was on the schedule on the first day, and the Estonian record came fresh as well!" was Meijel's evaluation of his charge's performance.
Meijel said there is still room for improvement, noting some errors but highlighting Tribuntsov's strong final 25 meters.
Tribuntsov has improved his 100m backstroke time at every World Cup stage this year: Fifth in Baku in 50.12, fourth in Tashkent in 50.05, and third in Astana in 49.88. The final World Cup stage continues on Friday and Saturday, with Tribuntsov and Zaitsev down to swim the 50m freestyle on Friday.
