Russia Builds Massive Jet Drone Launch Base Near Ukraine in Just Six Weeks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:31:09 UTC
16:31:09 KST

Russia has nearly completed a massive new launch base for jet-powered attack drones in its southwestern Rostov region in just six weeks, satellite imagery analyzed by Reuters shows, as Moscow ramps up attacks that are increasingly difficult for Ukraine to intercept.
The facility near Millerovo, roughly 3.5 kilometers (2.2 miles) from a Russian air base, has grown from an empty field into a complex covering about 0.9 square kilometers (0.3 square miles) – roughly the size of 126 soccer pitches – between Aug. 31 and Oct. 14.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Defense experts say the site is designed to launch Russia’s latest jet-powered drones, the Geran-4 and Geran-5, which can reach speeds of up to 600 kilometers per hour (373 miles per hour).
Mike Monnik, founder and CEO of private intelligence company DroneSec, identified eight launch platforms along the facility’s western edge. Two already had launch rails installed, according to Reuters’ analysis of satellite imagery.
The base could be operational within weeks, if not sooner, Monnik said.
“The speed of construction ... demonstrates the ease with which Russia can bring now-established offensive capabilities to bear rapidly,” he said.
Russia ramps up faster drone attacks
The construction comes as Russia sharply increases its use of jet-powered drones against Ukraine, with Kyiv and the surrounding region among the hardest-hit areas.
Russian use of the faster drones increased roughly sixfold over three months this summer, according to Ukrainian military data.
White House Ordered Restrictions on Ukraine’s Starshield, Disrupting Drone Defense – Reuters
Unlike slower, piston-powered drones, jet-powered models are harder to stop with relatively inexpensive interceptor drones that Ukraine has increasingly relied on to counter Russian attacks.
With the full-scale war in its fifth year, Ukraine expects Russia to intensify drone and missile strikes this winter, putting additional pressure on its air defenses.
The new facility could potentially launch 100 or more jet-powered drones in 24 hours, depending on available supplies and operational requirements, Monnik said. Russia typically launches its drones in smaller waves throughout the day.
New base could be harder for Ukraine to hit
The new site is located close to Millerovo air base, home to Russia’s 31st Guards Fighter Aviation Regiment.
DroneSec assessed that the launch facility likely falls within the air-defense coverage of the military air base, potentially making it more difficult for Ukraine to strike.
The rapid expansion of Russia’s drone-launch infrastructure also poses a potential challenge for NATO countries, which face growing concerns over Russian sabotage, cyberattacks and drone incursions.

Transforming Barcelona's Waterfront: A Story of Urban Renewal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:30:00 UTC
16:30:00 KST

As one walks along the beachfront of Barcelona, the shoreline feels like it has always been there: sand, palm trees, a long promenade, restaurants, shops and modern hotels, when the reality is that it has not always been this way. Until the 1980s, Barcelona's seafront was a working barrier of railway lines, factories and informal housing, and wastewater ran straight into the Mediterranean. Starting in 1987, Barcelona has continuously created large promenades and passages between the city and the sea, creating an environment that today many might read as previously empty space, but is actually the result of decades of infrastructure and social complexity, along with a municipal effort to transform the city's territory and its relationship to the water. Following that transformation raises three questions that frame this article: who was displaced to open the waterfront, who governs it today, and who keeps it standing?
The first attempt to create a relationship with the water dates back to the late 1980s, in preparation for the 1992 Olympics, according to a 2025 review on the topic by N. Benach and N. Font-Casaseca. For decades prior, a railway line had separated Barcelona's industrial fabric from the sea, and shanty towns existed along the city's coastline, on beaches like Somorrostro. The same review places the concrete start of these efforts in 1987, with the Spatial Plan of Port Vell and the Moll de la Fusta. According to J. Henrich i Monrás, this plan grew out of a broader urban study published by the City of Barcelona, Àrees de Nova Centralitat, and aimed to replace port and storage functions with leisure, hotels and commercial uses.
The Olympic works then gave that vision its physical form. Benach and Font-Casaseca also describe how the rail line was buried and how wastewater, previously discharged directly into the Mediterranean, began to be treated. At the same time, the city created and stabilised new beaches, improved access along the coast, and delivered the Vila Olímpica and a marina on former industrial land in Poblenou. Yet they also point out that the waterfront was never empty to begin with. It was full of industrial sites, housing and, as mentioned, shanty towns. In that light, they note that opening the city to the sea meant clearing an area that, by the mid-twentieth century, hosted around 15,000 people.
This history makes the central question of the topic hard to avoid: who claims land when a city reclaims its waterfront, and is the result an integrating effort or economic speculation? Montesinos i Curió et al. frame two possible outcomes. Either the space becomes accessible and welcoming to all locals, or it becomes an attraction for a specific group, in this case tourists. In their reading, after the worldwide success of the 1992 Games the city continued using its new spaces to promote its own image and reputation, which points to the second outcome as the better fit.
That tourism-driven logic is visible today at the port, where the question of who claims the waterfront has become one of institutional ownership. According to a 2025 article from the Port of Barcelona, a new protocol between the city and the port plans to demolish three old cruise terminals, build a new modern terminal and incorporate new technologies in the port. The article presents this public-private investment as a commitment to the sustainable development of cruise activity. It adds that, for the city, maritime tourism is an economic sector of significant weight, but one that requires planning and management measures to achieve a more orderly and efficient model that respects Barcelona's urban and environmental setting. The waterfront is thus being claimed by two institutions with different incentives, and its future depends more on negotiation than on design alone.
Regardless of who governs the shore, a third problem still remains: keeping it in place. Many of the beaches that resulted from the late twentieth-century plans were entirely or partially man-made, which creates an ongoing issue of maintenance and sustainability. According to the City, Barcelona's beaches lose approximately 30,000 m³ of sand per year, and other sources point to climate change as a further factor, as intensifying storms and sea-level rise erode the coastline. The usual response has been to bring in more sand, sometimes sourced locally from nearby construction sites. Yet this is not enough, and sand is sometimes brought from elsewhere in Spain or from abroad. The beach that was meant to reconnect the city with the sea now depends on a continuous supply of material from somewhere else.
Barcelona did not expand buildable land by filling the sea. Its reclamation was subtler: it took land back from industry and the port, and built beaches with imported sand. Even so, this soft form of reclamation created a permanent obligation, because a shore built in a couple of years has to be kept for decades. In that sense, Barcelona suggests that a city's relationship with its waterfront is ultimately a compromise among actors with different interests, and that the water's edge deserves the same attention as roads and housing: planning, funding and care over time, as it reminds us that the solutions of one era eventually become the maintenance bill of the next.
This article is part of the ArchDaily Topic: The Architecture of Water: Territories, Tensions & Transformations. Every month we explore a topic in-depth through articles, interviews, news, and architecture projects. We invite you to learn more about our ArchDaily Topics. And, as always, at ArchDaily we welcome the contributions of our readers; if you want to submit an article or project, contact us.

G7 nations to provide EUR 260 mln for urgent repairs to Chornobyl NPP containment structure following Russian drone attack
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:28:25 EEST
16:28:25 KST

The G7 nations will provide EUR 260 million to fund urgent repairs to the New Safe Confinement structure at the Chornobyl Nuclear Power Plant (NPP) in Ukraine, which sustained significant damage following a Russian drone strike in February 2025, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) announced on Thursday.
“The EBRD is grateful to the G7 nations for their continued leadership and commitment to nuclear safety at Chornobyl. We join the G7 in calling on the wider international community to contribute to these efforts at a donor conference we are convening in Paris on 9 November 2026, co-chaired by France, Ukraine and the EBRD,” EBRD President Odile Renaud-Basso said.
According to a press release, the decision was announced following a meeting of G7 finance ministers held during the autumn meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank in Bangkok. The G7 nations expressed deep concern regarding risks to nuclear safety resulting from the Russian attack, pledged to mobilize funds for the restoration of the containment structure, and called on other international partners to help cover the remaining financial requirements.
Preliminary assessments indicate that at least EUR 500 million will be needed to repair the damage and restore the structure to full functionality. The work needs to be completed by 2030 to limit the risk of corrosion of the steel arch and safeguard the structure’s 100-year design life.
Chornobyl’s New Safe Confinement was severely damaged by a Russian drone strike on 14 February 2025. The attack breached the structure’s inner and outer cladding, damaged critical systems and severely compromised its two primary functions: containing radioactive material and enabling the safe dismantling of the unstable original sarcophagus over Reactor Four.
The EBRD has led global efforts to stabilise and manage risks at Chornobyl since 1995, mobilising over EUR 2.5 billion in international contributions – much of it from the G7 nations – and providing more than EUR 700 million of its own resources to fund nuclear safety and decommissioning projects linked to the site. The Bank is now leading international efforts to restore the full functionality of the New Safe Confinement and to mobilise the remaining funding needed for urgent repairs.

SC declines urgent plea against Central Park closure ahead of ’s Tiranga march
NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Friday declined an urgent hearing on a plea challenging the New Delhi Municipal Council's decision to shut Central Park in Connaught Place ahead of the Cockroach Janta Party's (CJP) proposed ‘Lehra do Tiranga’ protest, saying it hoped “better sense will prevail” among all concerned.A bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justice Joymalya Bagchi said it was conscious of the difficulties that a closure could cause to small shopkeepers and their families, while observing that the right to protest, the need to maintain law and order and the livelihood of traders were interconnected issues.
“We hope better sense will prevail on everyone. Small shopkeepers earn their livelihood during these days. We know the hardship and difficulty entire families will face,” the bench said.Justice Bagchi said the court could intervene if the restrictions resulted in business losses, adding that it would consider exercising its constitutional jurisdiction if required."If there's loss of business, we will exercise our powers under Constitutional jurisdiction. Let's cross that bridge when it comes," Justice Bagchi said.
During the hearing, the petitioner's lawyer submitted that the NDMC had issued directions late Thursday night to close Central Park, effectively preventing businesses from operating in the area. The civic body had announced that the park would remain closed to the public on October 16 and 17 for administrative reasons.The bench indicated that the plea could be listed on October 26 or 27.
CJP says protest will go ahead
CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke has called on citizens to gather at Central Park with the national flag at 5 pm on Friday, alleging that party members Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka were jailed for unfurling the Tricolour. The party has said it will proceed with the march despite the closure of the park and security restrictions.In a post on X, Dipke defended the party's protests, rejected allegations that it was promoting anarchy and accused the government of restricting democratic rights.
"Businesses do not suffer because of peaceful protests. They suffer when the govt decides to shut down an entire city, suspend internet services and restrict the movement of its own citizens and turn the city into a war-zone.""Since its inception, the Cockroach Janta Party has maintained that we will always follow Mahatma Gandhi’s path of peace and non-violence, and we have stood by that commitment. We have organised protests in Mumbai, Pune, Jaipur, Lucknow, Bengaluru and Nagpur, and every single one of them has been peaceful. I was personally assaulted in Jaipur, but even then, I chose not to retaliate because responding to violence with violence goes against everything we believe in. We would rather exercise the rights guaranteed to us by the Constitution, drafted under the leadership of Dr. BR Ambedkar, than resort to physical force. Our strength comes from our commitment to constitutional values, and no amount of provocation will make us abandon them.""Despite this, there are constant attempts to portray us as anarchists simply because we refuse to remain silent. But demanding answers from the govt is not anarchy, protesting against injustice on the streets is not anarchy, and questioning those who hold public office is certainly not anarchy. These are the most fundamental expressions of democracy. The very party that is in power today spent decades organising protests, taking to the streets and questioning the governments of the day when it was in opposition. Had the same restrictions, intimidation and police crackdowns been used against them, many of those who occupy positions of power today might never have reached where they are. It is deeply hypocritical to celebrate protests as a democratic right when you are in opposition and treat the same act as a threat to public order when you come to power."ALSO READ: ‘No one called Mahatma Gandhi African’: Sanjay Raut slams order against actor Imran Khan"We are not asking for privileges or special treatment. We are simply asking to exercise the rights that belong to every citizen of this Republic, irrespective of which party is in power. So let us fulfil our duty as citizens of this country by questioning those we elect, demanding accountability and speaking up whenever we witness injustice.""A govt that has been elected by the people is bound to listen to the people, not silence them. Democracy does not end once the votes have been counted."
Security tightened ahead of ‘Lehra do Tiranga’ march
The proposed demonstration comes amid a standoff between the CJP and Delhi Police over protests against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.The CJP had announced the march after Das and Ranka were arrested for allegedly entering Jantar Mantar, which had been denotified as a designated protest site, and raising slogans demanding Kumar's resignation. If the right to vote is not saved, democracy will not be saved," Dipke said at a press conference on Thursday.He also questioned the scale of voter deletions during the SIR exercise and alleged that the revisions could affect electoral outcomes."The margin of victory in 2024 was just 2 per cent. Over 13 crore voters deleted -- around 14 percent," he said."Where 2 per cent is deciding the election, you are deleting 13 crore votes. What is this if not a setting?" he added.The CJP has alleged that the government is shielding Kumar from scrutiny. These allegations have not been established by the court.

Protesters can hold demonstrations at Ramlila Maidan, Burari Ground or CBD Ground after obtaining the requisite permission," a senior police officer said.Security has been tightened around Connaught Place and Jantar Mantar, with several companies of paramilitary personnel stationed in the national capital. Police are deploying personnel at strategic locations, erecting barricades and regulating the movement of protesters and commuters to prevent any untoward incident.The NDMC issued its closure notice on Thursday, stating that Central Park would remain shut on October 16 and 17 for administrative reasons. The decision came a day after the CJP announced its proposed march at the park, located in the centre of Connaught Place's inner circle.The party's agitation began in Mumbai on October 2 and subsequently moved to Delhi. On October 10, a planned demonstration at Jantar Mantar was met with a police crackdown, with Dipke, Das and Ranka detained at the airport after arriving from Mumbai. Opposition leaders, activists and students were also detained during protests in the capital.

Opposition leaders later met President Droupadi Murmu on October 9 to raise their concerns.The CJP has since framed its proposed Connaught Place march as a campaign for voting rights and the constitutional right to protest, setting up another confrontation over the restrictions imposed on demonstrations in central Delhi.

Southern California wildfire prompts evacuations as Bryson Fire grows to 200 acres

Berk Kutay Gokmen
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
ISTANBUL
A wildfire burning in the hills of Malibu in Southern California grew to about 200 acres (809 decares) by nightfall, prompting evacuation warnings and orders across a wide area as officials warned of heightened fire danger due to strong winds.
The Bryson Fire broke out in the state’s Encinal Canyon area, near the Camp Kilpatrick juvenile detention facility, according to CBS News on Thursday.
Los Angeles County issued evacuation warnings and orders covering areas stretching toward Leo Carrillo State Park, Pepperdine University, and the Pacific coast.
Pepperdine said the blaze was burning about eight miles northwest of its Malibu campus, adding that winds were blowing southwest, away from the university.
“The fire does not currently pose a threat to Pepperdine’s Malibu campus,” the university said on US social media company X.
Camp Kilpatrick evacuated 38 young people from its detention facility, transferring them to Barry J. Nidorf Juvenile Hall in Sylmar.
“We understand that an evacuation can be stressful for youth and their families,” the Los Angeles County Probation Department said, adding that staff were providing support and parents and legal guardians were being notified.
Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass said city officials were closely monitoring developments, although the fire remained outside city limits.
The Los Angeles Fire Department “is prepared to respond to any fire threat that could emerge,” Bass said.
She added that resources had been positioned across several areas, including the San Fernando Valley, Santa Monica Mountains, and West Los Angeles.
Meanwhile, Southern California Edison initiated a public safety power shutoff affecting more than 60,000 residents.
The National Weather Service issued a Red Flag Warning, citing an expected moderate-to-strong Santa Ana wind event that could increase critical fire danger through Saturday.

Europe's answer to Starlink: Who is building IRIS² and what is Germany's role
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:18:59 UTC
16:18:59 KST

Who controls the satellites on which armies rely? Reports of Starlink limits in Ukraine highlight the question. The EU is building IRIS², a 348-satellite network with a Bremen manufacturer.
This week, the Ukrainian army reported restrictions to the Starlink satellite service. The connection drops as soon as the receivers are travelling at more than 160 kilometres per hour, as is the case with drones.
The service was initially partially restored, but an upper limit remained in place. It is unclear who ordered the restriction.
SpaceX boss Elon Musk rejected responsibility that the company ordered the shutdown. Starshield is under the direct control of the US government, he wrote on X.
It is important to distinguish between the two systems: Starlink and Starshield are both developed by SpaceX but aimed at different customers. Starlink is the service for private and business users, Starshield is designed for governments and the military.
Polish foreign minister Radosław Sikorski reacted sharply on X, writing: "Hey, Elon Musk, you big man, are you once again playing politics with your products? As your European customers we are keeping a close eye on you."
Poland has paid for a large share of the Ukrainian terminals. This has once again raised the question of how dependent armed forces are on satellite links. Europe has therefore been working for some time on its own solution.
The European answer: IRIS²
The EU has been developing IRIS², its own satellite network, for around six years. The acronym stands for "Infrastructure for Resilience, Interconnectivity and Security by Satellite".
In German this roughly means infrastructure for resilience, connectivity and security via satellites. The system is intended to provide secure connections for governments, companies and citizens and to close mobile coverage gaps in Europe and Africa.
For encryption it will rely on quantum technology via the European quantum communication infrastructure EuroQCI.
In early August, the European Commission and the SpaceRISE consortium agree on the implementation. The network will grow to 348 satellites, 330 in low Earth orbit and 18 in medium Earth orbit.
A further 66 additional satellites are intended specifically to strengthen defence, security and emergency services. According to the Commission’s calculations, this will increase secured capacity for public-sector users by 60 percent in the EU and by 54 percent worldwide.
The focus is on states, the military and critical services; later on, private individuals are also to be able to use the network. The first satellites are scheduled to launch in 2029. Initial services are to be introduced gradually from 2029 or 2030.
Germany's role
Germany is represented by the Bremen-based space company Orbitale Hochtechnologie Bremen (OHB).
On 31 August it signed a contract worth just under €1 billion with satellite operator SES for 18 satellites in medium Earth orbit for IRIS².
A single satellite weighs around 2.6 tonnes at launch. OHB chief executive Marco Fuchs sees the programme as an important step towards greater European independence.
Germany’s share of the project sparked disputes early on.
In December 2023, the Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs sent a strongly worded letter to the companies involved demanding urgent clarification of the German industry’s participation and its share in value creation, as reported by the Frankfurter Rundschau daily.
Bundeswehr: Its own satellite network?
Independently of IRIS², the Bundeswehr is planning its own satellite network. It is a national project financed by the federal government.
Major General Armin Fleischmann, the Bundeswehr’s space commissioner in the Cyber and Information Domain, told regional public broadcaster MDR that the plan is for a constellation similar to Starlink, only smaller.
He told the Handelsblatt business newspaper they wanted to have "flying Fritzboxes" in space. The network is initially to cover NATO’s eastern flank, under national control. Individual components will come from Western partners, including the United States.
As early as September 2025, defence minister Boris Pistorius announced at the space congress of the Federation of German Industries in Berlin that a total of €35 billion would be invested in military space projects by 2030. In July he visited OHB in Bremen to inspect satellite programmes and ongoing production.
The project is called SATCOMBw 4, short for satellite communication of the Bundeswehr. In its final expansion stage, according to the Bundeswehr, it is to comprise a three-digit number of satellites in low Earth orbit and cost between eight and ten billion euros. An initial partial constellation with up to 40 satellites is scheduled to be operational as early as 2029, with full operations planned from 2030.
The joint venture "OHB Rheinmetall Space Networks", based in Bremen, is bidding for the contract According to company information, OHB would be responsible for the satellites, Rheinmetall for the ground stations and end devices. No decision has yet been taken.
Industry reports suggest that the contract award could come around the turn of the year, though insiders consider early 2027 possible as well. OHB would then be involved in both major projects: in IRIS² as satellite manufacturer and in the Bundeswehr network as part of the joint venture.
Up to now, the Bundeswehr has been using two of its own satellites in geostationary orbit at around 36,000 kilometres altitude, COMSATBw-1 and COMSATBw-2, launched in 2009 and 2010.
Their successors are being built by Airbus and are scheduled to be handed over in orbit in 2029. The first of the three German radar satellites SARah was launched in 2022 on a Falcon 9 rocket from SpaceX.
Young Belgian company helping to build Europe’s satellite network
The satellites for IRIS² are being built by several companies. The largest share will not be supplied by an established group but by a young company:
Aerospacelab, founded in 2018 and based in Charleroi in Belgium, is building 264 satellites for low Earth orbit.
The order volume amounts to €2.4 billion, according to the company. The satellites are to be delivered by 2030. They will be produced in a new factory in Charleroi, where up to 500 satellites per year are to be built from 2027.
Airbus is building at least 66 satellites in the first layer for military communication, which are due to be ready in 2029. This means the entire low-orbit segment with 330 satellites has been allocated.
Together with the 18 OHB satellites for medium orbit, the network will comprise 348 satellites.
How realistic is 2029?
Whether the timetable can be met remains an open question. The first satellites are scheduled to launch in 2029; according to media reports, the original plan was for them to go up two years earlier.
Experts view rocket launches as the bottleneck. Even the best satellites cannot reach space without rockets and those unable to launch them themselves remain dependent on others.
Europe is relying on the Ariane 6 launch vehicle, which has been lifting off into space since 2024. Andreas Knopp of the Bundeswehr University Munich points out in the weekly paper Das Parlament that the number of launches is limited, while political scientist Antje Nötzold of TU Chemnitz speaks in MDR of a "launcher problem."
So far this year, Ariane 6 has launched four times, three of those flights carrying satellites for Amazon Leo into orbit, the US company’s satellite internet service that is also intended to compete with Starlink.
Amazon has booked at least 18 Ariane 6 launches. In early August, the Commission named the procurement of launch services for IRIS² as one of the next steps.

Italy data network glitch hits airports: Flights delayed and cancellations

A problem affecting Italy's airport data network caused delays and flight cancellations on Friday morning. Enav says it was not a cyber attack or sabotage.
Disruptions and cancelled flights were reported on Friday morning at many Italian airports due to faults in the data transmission network that supports air traffic control services, the national air navigation service provider Enav has announced.
"From 6:00, in view of the steady increase in air traffic and the persistence of the faults, in order to continue guaranteeing the highest level of operational safety, flow management measures have been introduced, which mean a temporary reduction in the capacity to handle aircraft in Italian airspace", reads the statement issued in the morning, which also rules out any link between the faults and hacker attacks or sabotage.
Enav also said that, although the faults were detected during the night between Thursday and Friday, "normal management of air traffic, without any reduction in operating capacity" was ensured until 6:00 on Friday morning.
The authority explained that the source of the faults has been identified in the data transmission network and that it is working to determine the causes and restore full system operations.
Delays and cancellations in Rome, Milan and Naples
Italian airports are nevertheless experiencing disruption because of the network problem. At least four flights have been cancelled at Rome Fiumicino airport, to Milan Linate, Riyadh, Tirana and Trieste, while other services are reporting delays of up to 60 minutes. There are also delays and cancellations at Milan Linate, Milan Malpensa and Naples Capodichino airports.
Airport operators are urging passengers to check the status of their flight with their airline.

Group of forensic experts served suspicion notice for falsifying evidence in interests of SBU official – NABU
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:15:02 EEST
16:15:02 KST

The National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine and the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office have served notices of suspicion to forensic experts of the Kyiv Research Institute of Forensic Expertise (KRIFE) of the Ministry of Justice of Ukraine who drew up deliberately false conclusions regarding the value of elite real estate belonging to the wife of a high-ranking Security Service of Ukraine official.
"In December 2023, the wife of the high-ranking official purchased an apartment for UAH 21.6 million. At the same time, according to the contract, its value was intentionally understated to UAH 12.8 million. In April 2024, a lawyer acting in the interests of the couple initiated a forensic construction and technical examination at KRIFE. Already in May, a commission of experts issued a conclusion stating that the market value of this apartment is UAH 12.3 million, which is UAH 9.3 million lower than the actual price. To achieve this result, the experts intentionally used non-relevant real estate objects for comparison. Subsequently, this document was used by the defense as evidence in the NACP, NABU, and court," the NABU press service reported on its Telegram channel.
In the same month, NABU detectives, investigating criminal proceedings into the apartment's purchase, ordered a commission examination, which was recalled on November 11, 2024, with a request to return the materials without execution.
"However, the experts ignored the investigative demand and continued their research. They agreed on limiting the value of comparison objects to no higher than $2,500–2,600 per square meter (instead of the market $3,000) and consciously chose the cheapest offers starting from $1,550, while ignoring other available analogues. In early December 2024, the experts signed the conclusion but backdated it to November 8, 2024 (i.e., prior to the recall by the NABU detective). Significantly, detectives received a copy of the conclusion not from KRIFE, but from the lawyer of the suspected high-ranking official," the report notes.
NABU emphasizes that such manipulations of evidence would be impossible if an independent expert institution operated under the Bureau.
"The Bureau's leadership has for several years emphasized the critical need to create an independent expert institution. This would eliminate corruption risks, prevent external pressure on experts, and significantly increase the efficiency of pre-trial investigations in top corruption cases," NABU summarized.

"If I were prime minister, and I discovered during normal times, not during a war, that one of my advisers was working as a lobbyist for the Italian government, which was paying him to promote its interests, I would throw him out in disgrace. Because you are an adviser to the prime minister of Israel. Only Israel's interests should be before your eyes.
"But this is not Italy. This is an enemy state, Qatar, the financiers of the Nukhba terrorists, and this is not during normal times, it is during a war. And you are not just an adviser; you are actively promoting it. For me, this story has long since stopped being about Urich. It is about Netanyahu. And there is one question that I have also heard quite a few Likud voters ask me, one thing he must do before the elections: Netanyahu must explain what is going on between him and Qatar. What is happening there? Why doesn't he throw Urich out of the Prime Minister's Office? Why doesn't he designate Qatar as an enemy?"
'We'll take it from here'
When Levin asked why he believed Netanyahu continued to support Urich, Bennett said he had never previously suspected the prime minister of compromising Israel's security for financial gain.
"I have never attributed to him an action against Israel's security for financial gain. For example, in the submarine affair, I did not believe he was capable of it, and to this day I do not know.
"But the question right now is: You are embracing a traitor, a traitor, a traitor. What is wrong with you? And I don't know. This is the first time I have said to myself: Wait a minute, what is going on here?" Bennett added.
"And I have a son who is a combat soldier in a commando unit. It is terrifying. And people ask me: You don't trust Netanyahu on security matters? I don't trust him at all. I have lost every shred of trust. Who is he working for? The State of Israel and the people of Israel, or other interests? I don't know. It is shocking, and that is why he simply has to go home already."
Bennett ended the interview with a direct call for Netanyahu to step down.
"Go home, let go. We'll take it from here, and we're better, too."

Houthi attack on Aden presidential palace kills five

07:07:58 UTC
16:07:58 KST

A Houthi missile attack on the presidential palace in Yemen’s interim capital Aden killed five people and wounded 16 on Oct. 15, Health Minister Qasim Buhaibeh said.
The casualties included guards and civilian employees. Prime Minister Shaya al-Zindani was at the Al-Maashiq compound but was unharmed, a government minister speaking on condition of anonymity said.
The unnamed minister said five missiles hit command centers used by Yemeni government forces and the Saudi-led coalition. He reported Yemeni and Saudi casualties but gave no breakdown.
Houthi-affiliated media said the group had targeted a military operations headquarters led by Saudi officers and weapons depots at the palace.
Zindani condemned the attack, accusing the Houthis of repeatedly striking civilians and civilian sites.
It was the first attack on the compound since fighting resumed in July after a years-long truce.
The Iran-backed Houthis have seized territory along Yemen’s Red Sea coast in recent weeks despite a Saudi-backed government counteroffensive.
Saudi Arabia has led a military coalition supporting Yemen’s internationally recognized government since 2015.
Rayed Krimly, the Saudi Foreign Ministry’s deputy minister for public diplomacy, accused Iran of continuing to arm and train the Houthis.
“We think that the escalation by the Houthis at this latest stage of the conflict is encouraged by Iran,” he said.
Krimly said Riyadh remained in contact with Tehran. He also said the Houthis had refused an invitation to meet in Muscat, which the ministry later clarified was made in July.
The coalition said it intercepted Houthi drones directed at Saudi Arabia’s south, including Khamis Mushait. Yemeni government forces also reported ballistic missile attacks on Marib.
Riyadh’s international airport has been targeted 20 times this month, according to the coalition.
An attack there on Oct. 10 killed 13 people and wounded about 300.

Fonds publics détournés : pourquoi la Cour des comptes européenne pourrait avoir plus de mal à les repérer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:07:57 UTC
16:07:57 KST

La volonté de la Commission européenne de rendre les milliards de l'UE plus réactifs aux crises à venir pourrait aussi les rendre plus exposés aux risques d'abus, avertit la Cour des comptes européenne.
Son président Tony Murphy alerte que les principaux piliers de la réforme du budget à long terme de l'UE, élaborée par la Commission, risquent de brouiller la vision des agents chargés de veiller à ce que les fonds publics soient dépensés comme prévu.
"Il nous est plus difficile de suivre l'argent", a-t-il souligné. "On dit à l'Etat membre : 'Voici une somme considérable, et vous faites en sorte que tout est en ordre.' C'est en quelque sorte d'autocontrôle."
Advertisement
Cet avertissement intervient alors que l'épineux débat du montant du budget 2028-2034 de l'UE est au menu du sommet des dirigeants européens à Bruxelles cette semaine, et que la Cour a constaté une augmentation des irrégularités dans l'utilisation des fonds publics.
Outre le montant total des moyens, se pose la question de leur répartition. Après un cycle budgétaire marqué par la pandémie, les guerres et les conséquences du changement climatique, la Commission souhaite rendre le prochain budget plus agile. Pour ce faire, elle prévoit d'en affecter environ la moitié — soit près de 1 000 milliards d’euros sur sept ans — à une enveloppe unique dans laquelle les pays pourront puiser pour remplir leurs objectifs dans des domaines comme l'immigration, l’agriculture ou le développement régional.
Ces fonds destinés à l'agriculture et au développement régional — souvent octroyés sous forme de subventions aux exploitations agricoles et aux projets locaux — sont depuis longtemps exposés à la fraude et aux détournements.
Selon Tony Murphy, accorder aux gouvernements nationaux une plus grande marge de manœuvre pour réorienter leurs dépenses rendrait le suivi de ces dernières encore plus difficile.
"Il y aura une certaine flexibilité, mais à quel prix ?", a-t-il soulevé lors d'une interview. Une grande partie du contrôle dépendra des mesures de surveillance que chaque pays a déjà mises en place.
D'autant que les irrégularités dans l'utilisation des fonds du budget de l'UE sont en hausse. Les erreurs de versement se sont élevées à 5 milliards d'euros l'année dernière, selon le dernier rapport de la Cour des comptes européenne.
Advertisement
Dans le prochain budget de l'UE, il pourrait même s'avérer impossible d'estimer ce chiffre, a prévenu Tony Murphy, car les auditeurs de chaque pays ont des rôles et des méthodes de travail différents. "Année après année, nous avons constaté que le travail de ces autorités d'audit n'est pas entièrement fiable", a renchéri son chef de cabinet, Wolfgang Stolz, lors de l'entretien.
Dans un communiqué, la Commission a défendu sa proposition, soulignant que les "principes fondamentaux" du système de contrôle actuel resteraient en vigueur. Les autorités nationales "fonctionnent bien", a-t-elle affirmé, tout en précisant qu'elle se réservait le droit de demander aux Etats membres de "modifier le plan ou de mettre en place des mécanismes de correction si nécessaire".
Des fonds mélangés aux budgets nationaux
L'une des innovations proposées par la Commission consiste à intégrer la politique agricole commune (PAC) — qui constituait jusqu'à présent une ligne budgétaire à part entière — dans un fonds gigantesque appelé plan de partenariat national et régional.
Tony Murphy a souligné qu'il ne prônait pas un modèle plutôt qu'un autre. Mais à mesure que les fonds européens s'intègrent de plus en plus aux budgets nationaux, il sera plus difficile pour Bruxelles de contrôler où va réellement son argent. La PAC est plus facile à contrôler lorsqu’“elle n'est pas mélangée à ce méli-mélo”, a estimé le président de la Cour des comptes européenne.
Les articles de presse sur des subventions agricoles versées pour de faux pâturages en Grèce ou sur des fonds destinés à soutenir le tourisme rural en Slovaquie qui financent de luxueuses villas pour les riches illustrent de manière frappante la difficulté de contrôler ces versements dans le cadre du système actuel.
Et le modèle sur lequel repose le nouveau système de dépenses — le fonds de relance post-Covid de l'UE — n'est pas de bon augure, a pointé Tony Murphy. Si les pays ont désormais plus de facilité à affecter les fonds là où ils sont nécessaires, les dépenses sont également devenues plus opaques. Les nouveaux plans nationaux ont été élaborés selon le même modèle.
Advertisement
Dans le cadre du système budgétaire actuel, la Cour des comptes européenne peut se rendre physiquement sur place dans une exploitation agricole bénéficiant de fonds européens. En revanche, dans le cadre du fonds de relance post-Covid, l'UE ne publie chaque année que la liste des 100 principaux bénéficiaires.
"Ce n’est pas très transparent. Je veux dire, où va réellement l'argent de l’UE ? C’est ça qui compte", a insisté Tony Murphy. "On a un fonds qui regroupe différentes politiques publiques, avec des objectifs et des échéances complètement différents, des mécanismes de mise en œuvre différents et moins de prévisibilité."
Cet article a d’abord été publié par POLITICO en anglais, puis a été édité en français par Jean-Christophe Catalon.

Museums fear research funding shuffle threatens key projects
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:06:00 UTC
16:06:00 KST

Museums fear research funding shuffle threatens key projects
Museums are concerned that the loss of research funding will jeopardize their projects and hope the decision will be reversed.
Under a government decision, the Ministry of Culture's research and development funding, totaling approximately €900,000, will be transferred to the Ministry of Education and Research's budget starting in 2028.
The transfer means that, starting in 2028, the Ministry of Culture will no longer hold funding rounds for creative research, nor will it have research and development funding in its budget to support museum research projects.
The decision stems from a proposal by Minister of Education and Research Kristina Kallas (Eesti 200) to channel ministries' research and development funding through the Ministry of Education and Research's strategic research program.
The explanatory memorandum accompanying the regulation indicates that although the funding will formally pass through the Ministry of Education and Research's budget, the Ministry of Culture will retain its own "quota" and decision-making authority to support strategic objectives and research projects within its area of responsibility, including museums. Nevertheless, the transfer of research funding to the Ministry of Education and Research has sparked discontent, particularly among Estonian museums, which have been among the main beneficiaries of these funds.
"This is incredibly bad news and the wording is utterly hopeless. This research funding has been absolutely vital to the Art Museum of Estonia in recent years, supporting virtually all the more substantial parts of our exhibition and publication programs. Now we're supposed to maneuver our way back under the umbrella of universities and convince them that exhibitions and creative research also count as research," Kumu Director Kadi Polli wrote on social media.
Mariann Raisma, director of the University of Tartu Museum, is also unhappy with the plan but remains hopeful that an exception will be made for the Ministry of Culture's area of responsibility when research funding is allocated.
"I still very much hope that this decision is not final. We have a regular meeting of the Museum Council coming up at the end of the month where we will meet with the minister of culture and I sincerely hope that there is still some way to reverse this decision," Raisma told ERR.
According to Raisma, the regulation's entry into force would be very bad news for Estonian museums, which fear that this much-needed funding will effectively disappear for them in the future. One major concern is that the new funding scheme sets a relatively high minimum grant of €150,000 per year for projects lasting two to four years, while museums need grants roughly one-tenth that size.
"Another thing I would highlight about this funding, which was particularly good, is that the amounts awarded were not very large. We weren't distributing hundreds of thousands of euros; instead, the grants made it possible to carry out smaller projects. That suits museums particularly well. Of course, the total amount of funding wasn't very large either, but it has certainly been extremely important for museums," Raisma told ERR.
"We carried out several very important research projects that enabled museums and research institutions to work together on topics for which funding would otherwise not have been available," Raisma said.
Ministry adviser: We'll lose flexibility and some projects will be discontinued
Viivian Jõemets, research adviser at the Ministry of Culture, is also concerned about several aspects of the new funding allocation system. She likewise noted that the program requires projects that are too large for the cultural sector's current capacity.
"The annual budget of €150,000 per project required under the new rules — amounting to at least €300,000 over two years — is unreasonably large for a museum. Current projects at our museums with nationwide responsibilities and research obligations, as well as the National Library, range from €40,000 to €70,000, depending on whether it is a large or small museum," Jõemets said.
According to Jõemets, building research capacity on this scale takes time and cannot be accomplished in a single year. "In the cultural sector, it is simply not possible to immediately develop projects with budgets this large in several important research areas," she added.
"Another concern is that the Ministry of Culture's total sector-specific research funding amounts to approximately €800,000. If we distribute it among smaller groups, each museum can develop something — activities take place and progress is made. But if we allocate very large sums to just three projects across our entire area of responsibility, what happens to all the other important areas of research?" Jõemets asked.
"What will happen to the research areas we have developed so far, such as efforts to advance research at the Art Museum of Estonia and the study of musical heritage? Under the strategic research regulation, it is unclear how we can continue developing our fields in these circumstances," she added.
Jõemets noted that other questions also remain unanswered. For example, if no applications are submitted for a particular research area simply because there are no potential applicants, it is unclear what will happen to that funding within the Ministry of Education and Research's budget.
"But if those funds remained in the Ministry of Culture's budget, we could flexibly reallocate them to other important activities," she added.
Jõemets emphasized that the government's decision to channel sector-specific research funding through the strategic research program affects all ministries and that the Ministry of Culture was granted a one-year extension compared with the others.
"I hope that in the near future there will be an assessment of the successes and shortcomings of the reform of sector-specific research funding, weighing its advantages and disadvantages. Perhaps a new government will want to revisit this decision. For now, however, transferring sector-specific research funding from the Ministry of Culture's budget to that of the Ministry of Education and Research remains the current government's decision," Jõemets said.
Jõemets does not have to worry about losing her position.
"My position at the Ministry of Culture will not be eliminated as part of this reform. Even now, funding rounds for the Ministry of Culture's research programs are administered by the Estonian Research Council under regulations issued by the minister of culture and there will be no significant change in that regard. The only change concerns where and how flexibly we can allocate sector-specific research funding and we will have to operate under a regulation issued by the minister of education and research," she said.
"Not all of the Ministry of Culture's current research activities will be able to continue under this regulation," Jõemets concluded.
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski

WA Greens kept crisis comms document about Jordon Steele-John
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:05:58 UTC

WA Greens kept crisis communications document about Jordon Steele-John
In short:
The WA Greens maintained a crisis communications document for years in the event that complaints against Jordon Steele-John were made public.
Senator Steele-John has rejected concerns raised against him in a letter by Greens members to leader David Shoebridge. The letter did not contain any specific allegations.
What's next?
Senator Shoebridge says an independent investigation will be conducted.
Members of the WA Greens maintained a crisis communications document on how to respond if concerns about senator Jordon Steele-John were made public.
The Sydney Morning Herald has reported that since 2016 WA Greens staff kept a 47-page document with methods to manage media coverage of any allegations made about Senator Steele-John, and instructed staff to monitor social media discussions by party members.
Greens leader David Shoebridge denied any previous knowledge of the document, saying he understood it be "from some seven years ago".
"I was not aware of the document and I was not aware of the allegations," he told the ABC.
Yesterday the same outlet reported that a number of current and former Greens members had written to Senator Shoebridge asking him to investigate concerns regarding Senator Steele-John's behaviour towards women.
The letter said women had been warned "not to be alone" with the senator and alleged there were "multiple" concerns about his behaviour "in the presence of women" spanning his career in parliament.
No specific allegation has been made against Senator Steele-John, who has said "utterly" rejects "this characterisation of me".
Senator Shoebridge said none of the authors of the letter "asserted to any direct knowledge of the matters involved".
"And of course that creates some additional complexity in dealing with it, but the matters concerned are taken seriously," he told ABC News Breakfast.
"The best way of dealing with this is a fair, an independent and a timely process commissioned by the WA Greens."
In a statement, the co-convenors of the WA Greens said it "responded to allegations about Jordon Steele-John in 2016".
"The allegations were not substantiated and the named persons have never lodged a formal complaint."
"Reference has been made to an internal document that has been provided to the media. The document outlines the management of communications about this matter."
Leader's office denies knowledge
The ABC has confirmed the existence of the crisis communications document, which names several federal Greens members, including senior staff in the leader's office.
The Greens leader's office has denied previously seeing the document and says it has no record of ever receiving it.
"This is not a document made by, used by or seen by the leader's office," a spokesperson for the office said.
"The office is committed to having the matters comprehensively investigated with a fair, independent and timely process.
"Everyone deserves a safe workplace, and all complaints should be considered in a fair and robust process."
A senior staffer named in the document confirmed they had searched their record and found no record of the document ever being sent, shared or accessed by them.
Party members say it is not unusual for a document to identify individuals in the federal party as points of contact.
It is also standard for Greens senators to receive media training from the leader's office, as Senator Steele-John did when he entered parliament.
Senator Steele-John has taken a leave of absence and will not attend parliament while the investigation is underway.
"I utterly reject this characterisation of me, which tries to assert I am someone I am not," he said in a statement on Thursday.
"These claims are made without specifics, any allegation of this nature is extremely serious and must be treated accordingly. If someone has made an allegation, I am prepared to address it."
Senator Shoebridge said he did not know of the complaints until two weeks ago.
"I knew absolutely nothing until assuming this position as leader, and then when I received the correspondence I acted with what I think is timely and appropriate urgency," he said.

Hackers steal data from Swiss magazine Republik
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:04:11 UTC
16:04:11 KST

Hackers steal data from Swiss magazine Republik
Swiss online magazine Republik has fallen victim to a cyberattack. The magazine says user data was compromised, but no credit card details were leaked.
Unknown individuals exploited a security vulnerability in an analytics tool.
On Wednesday morning, one of the analysis tools had stopped working, according to a statement on the Republik website. It marked the end of an unauthorised access incident that had been ongoing since August.
“The security vulnerability had been known since August 6, but we failed to take the necessary countermeasures in good time,” the statement reads.
Republik does not know who was behind the attack. There is much to suggest it was a broad, automated wave of attacks. The attackers are said to have first searched for what was contained in every Metabase installation – the tool with the security vulnerability – such as login details and keys for AI services that could be resold.
So far, there is no indication that anyone specifically targeted Republik. However, the data has been leaked. The attackers certainly accessed the details of active publishers, subscribers, newsletter recipients and all former users.
The data records included email addresses, names and, where provided, telephone numbers, year of birth and gender. This means that people who never had a subscription but merely subscribed to a newsletter were also affected.
When the Metabase was taken offline, the attackers also lost their access, Republik added. On Thursday, following the completion of the initial damage assessment, the magazine reported the incident to the Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner.

He said the government is rolling out measures to boost the yacht economy, including steps to make visits by such vessels easier, and will host the Festival of Connoisseurs from November 4 to 6.
Wong added that four new marina projects – at the airport, Lamma Island, Aberdeen and Hung Hom – are moving ahead. Together they will provide more than 1,100 berths, a 30 percent increase from the existing total, he said. 
"Whether it's Hong Kong yachts heading north or Guangdong yachts heading south, the essence is mutual benefit – a win-win-win," Wong said. 
"We believe the travel scheme can open up a brand-new maritime channel for residents and visitors on both sides, jointly driving economic development in both places," he said.
He also thanked the central government and relevant units in Guangdong and Hong Kong for their support in implementing the travel scheme.

Revealed: VW, Ford and Tesla batteries linked to destructive deforestation of indigenous lands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:00:56 UTC
16:00:56 KST

Volkswagen, Ford and Tesla are among the electric carmakers whose batteries may contain nickel mined in indigenous woodlands plagued by deforestation, an analysis has found, highlighting the struggle to make vehicles that are free from environmental destruction.
Corporate disclosures and trade flows from the last two years show mines in the battery supply chains of automotive giants are linked to the loss of trees in Sulawesi, a wildlife hotspot in Indonesia that houses the world’s largest nickel deposits. The metal is widely used in cathodes in car batteries because it boosts energy density and increases range.
Ore from the Cahaya and Hengjaya mines was traced through regional smelters and Chinese processing plants run by Zhejiang Huayou Cobalt, a cathode manufacturer that supplies CATL, the world’s largest battery maker. Huayou’s corporate reports list US and European carmakers as end-users, while additional corporate files and trade data show a separate route from Huayou to LG, a South Korean group that also supplies battery products to leading carmakers, via Poland.
Satellite analysis shows the mines have led to widespread deforestation of primary rainforest in nickel-rich lands inhabited by the indigenous Tolaki people.
“We used to ask the forest for protection in return for our offerings,” said Wadimula, a Tolaki elder whose home sits on the edge of the 21,000-hectare Cahaya mining concession. “Destroying it means destroying our own life.”
Electric vehicles are less environmentally harmful than fossil fuel-burning engines, which spew gases that foul the air and heat the planet, but western carmakers have struggled to clean up supply chains for batteries built with critical minerals from Africa, Asia and South America. Environmental groups warn that a failure to curb the boom of material-hungry SUVs is exacerbating the destruction by increasing the quantity mined.
Ore from the two mining concessions is sent to a nickel smelter in an industrial complex in Morowali, on Indonesia’s eastern coast, operated by Huayou’s local subsidiary, where limonite is refined into mixed hydroxide precipitate, the primary raw material used to make battery cathodes.
In 2024, $606m worth of mixed hydroxide precipitate was shipped from the Morowali plant to ports in China, followed by further shipments worth $470m in 2025. The processed ore was transported overland to Huayou cathode manufacturing sites in Quzhou, near Shanghai, and Yulin, near the border with Vietnam.
Public filings do not disclose specific volumes or timings of sales from Huayou to CATL, which would be needed to directly connect specific ore shipments to car batteries, but Huayou confirmed group-level supplies to CATL in response to a regulatory inquiry by the Shanghai Stock Exchange in 2024. Chengdu B&M, a downstream subsidiary of Huayou, has also confirmed the supply of “large quantities” to CATL.
The investigation, published in partnership with Voxeurop and other European media partners, traced shipments from mines and refineries in Sulawesi to China, and then again from Huayou cathode and CATL battery factories to the assembly lines of carmakers in the US and Europe. Volkswagen’s facility in Braunschweig, for instance, received a shipment in October 2024 of 24 tonnes of cell modules worth about $390,000, according to data from Volza, a trade platform.
The shift to a carbon-free economy is pushing up demand for critical minerals in countries with weak environmental safeguards, though experts have argued the mining boom can be tempered without slowing the shift away from dirty fuels. In 2023, a report found lithium demand in the US transport sector could be reduced by 18% to 66% compared with a business-as-usual scenario, by improving public transport, walking and cycling more, and buying smaller cars. Better recycling could bring demand reductions as high as 92%, the report found.
Global demand for nickel is set to double to 5.5m tonnes by 2040, according to the International Energy Agency, much of it mined in Indonesia and then refined in China. The loss of trees in mining concessions means the carbon footprint of nickel from the worst mines may be up to 500 times greater than previously reported, a study in Nature Communications found last year.
The Cahaya and Hengjaya mines are located in woodlands designated as “production forest”, which are intended for forestry rather than industrial activities. However, successive Indonesian governments have weakened safeguards and carved out exemptions for miners as demand for nickel has soared.
Nickel mining may be responsible for two-thirds of the forest loss recorded since 2001 within the area encompassed by the Cahaya concession, and over half of the loss in the Hengjaya concession, spatial analysis conducted by geospatial firm The TreeMap suggests.
Sulawesi Cahaya Mineral (SCM), the company that operates the Cahaya mine, contributed to clearing an additional 330 hectares of forest in 2024, according to an analysis by Auriga, an Indonesian nonprofit. The same year, it delivered 11m tonnes of limonite ore – almost all of its production – to Huayou’s smelter. Deliveries increased to nearly 12.5m tonnes throughout 2025. The plant also continued to receive ore from the Hengjaya mine by road, local lorry drivers said.
SCM received two administrative sanctions last year for illegally clearing more than 450 hectares of forest beyond the boundaries of its permitted clearing area. The company is a subsidiary of Merdeka Battery Materials, part of a group whose shareholders include Huayou and CATL.
The carmakers identified as end-users of Huayou cathodes or recipients of shipments from CATL include Volkswagen, Volvo, Ford, General Motors, Tesla, BMW, Stellantis and Hyundai. Mercedes-Benz was separately linked to Huayou.
Many of the companies said they did not source nickel directly, they assessed and mitigated adverse impacts, and they required suppliers to comply with responsible sourcing standards. They declined to share the results of on-site audits.
Volkswagen, Europe’s leading manufacturer, which powered one-quarter of its vehicles with CATL systems in 2024, said it could not rule out that the companies may fall within its supply chain.
Volkswagen said: “We take potential risks in our supply chain very seriously. However, due to contractual obligations with our business partners, we cannot disclose specific details on our supplier relationships or their supply chain.”
Ford said: “We are committed to protecting human rights and the environment. We are reviewing the allegations and will determine any appropriate next steps based on that review.”
Mercedes-Benz said: “We take reports of environmental and social harm in raw material supply chains – including nickel from Indonesia – seriously and assess them as part of our risk-based due diligence.”
Renault Group said: “We have identified a nickel mining site in Sulawesi, Indonesia, as being a tier-n supplier (eg. indirect) in our battery supply chain. We have engaged with the relevant business partners to verify some ESG information concerning Sulawesi Cahaya Mineral.”
Volvo Cars said: “During 2025, we conducted […] onsite audits […] on suppliers [who are] part of our battery supply chains, two of them located in Indonesia […] with further battery supply chain partners during 2026 and onward.”
General Motors said: “We are aware that nickel mining in Indonesia presents significant environmental, human-rights and community-related risks.”
Stellantis said: “We are aware of the environmental and social challenges associated with nickel production in Indonesia, including risks related to deforestation, biodiversity loss and ecosystem degradation.”
Hyundai said: “We recognise the importance of protecting forests, biodiversity and local communities. We regularly monitor and assess our suppliers, including mineral suppliers, to ensure compliance.”
CATL, Huayou, SCM and Tesla did not respond to requests for comment. Tsingshan, the main shareholder of Nickel Industries, which operates Hengjaya mine, did not respond to a request for comment.
This investigation was supported by Journalismfund Europe and The Pulitzer Center. Lorenzo Di Stasi and James Jackson contributed reporting.

UK could quickly re-enter EU with ‘Switzerland plus’ deal, senior MEP says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:00:55 UTC
16:00:55 KST

The UK could re-enter the EU in a “Switzerland plus” package that could be negotiated within months of any decision to deepen ties with the bloc, the head of a European parliament committee has said.
Bernd Lange, who was heavily involved in Brexit negotiations, said: “I would love to see the UK back.” He said the EU missed the UK in decision-making because of its strong history of promoting open markets and democracy.
A Swiss style arrangement is often considered a halfway house to full membership of the bloc but involves free movement and regulatory alignment.
Switzerland is not a member of the EU but it struck a deal last year cementing its “frictionless access” to the single market across more than 100 agreements with a new framework deal.
This gives it access to the EU’s electricity market, space programmes, Erasmus and the Digital Europe research programme, and participation in the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control.
In exchange, Switzerland agreed to the free movement of people and to pay €375m (£326m) a year into the EU’s economic and cohesion funds.
Lange, a German MEP who has an important role in the European legislative process as chair of the European parliament’s trade committee, said the Switzerland framework could be a model for the UK, but it was a “passive” agreement that would not involve the country in EU decision-making.
“As a step by step [process], of course, there are a lot of possibilities, but I would love to have the UK come back also in the political decision-making process and politically be engaged. So we have the model of Switzerland … Switzerland plus, I would say, as that has some kinds of engagement but not the full membership.”
He said the decision about what relationship the UK wanted with the EU was entirely “in the hands of the UK”, but if it opted for something like Switzerland plus, an agreement could be achieved quickly, notwithstanding political hiccups.
He was speaking in London, where his schedule includes a meeting with the trade minister, Anas Sarwar, who is part of a team working on the UK’s new position on EU relations.
Lange also threw his weight behind Andy Burnham’s call for the EU not to lock the UK out of Made in Europe legislation that would restrict UK suppliers from inclusion in public procurement tenders as well as some corporate contracts such as car fleets.
French and German leaders were reportedly close on Thursday to agreeing a proposal that the UK could be included, provided it aligned with the EU’s 2024 tariffs on imports of Chinese electric vehicles.
This week the boss of Mercedes said the EU would be making a “deliberate choice” to harm the EU car industry if it did not allow the UK into the Made in Europe package.
Burnham has backing from the Netherlands, Germany and Italy. France, which came up with the legislative proposals, was opposed, saying it needed to get the legislation on the books urgently to guard against cheap competition from China, and that allowing the UK and other allied countries in could hold up the lawmaking.
Lange said the UK should “of course” be included because it was already aligned with the EU on environmental standards and employment laws.
He said France’s position was “not rational” and “also so emotional” but could be born from the desire to be seen as putting France first before next April’s presidential elections, in which Marine Le Pen, who is opposed to globalism, could take power.
Locking the UK out of Made in Europe could also cause a legal dispute over the trade and cooperation agreement that allows UK goods to be sold in the single market without barriers as long as they the meet the bloc’s standards.
The Made in Europe package, or the Industrial Accelerator Act, is expected to get political approval by the end of the year or early 2027, meaning Burnham does not have much time to get clauses inserted designating the UK as European for the purposes of the legislation.
But Lange said there could be time after that, given the processes of the European parliament, where three committees have scrutinising powers.
“There are 5,100 amendments,” he said, referring to the protracted process ahead, including one on UK inclusion.

Britain is addicted to prisons. Our crumbling probation service proves they don’t work | Polly Toynbee
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:00:54 UTC
16:00:54 KST

Public services need more investment across the board. Every day, another wretched story. Look at the Institute for Government’s (IFG) Public Services Performance Tracker for a plain assessment of A&E corridor care, councils struggling to meet the demands of social care and the Send system, the courts backlog, GP caseloads or families lost in temporary accommodation. A chancellor approaching a budget is besieged by need. It’s easy for us journalists to pick out shock stories and claim each one is an absolute priority, but how should a chancellor choose?
Today it’s the probation officers, whose conference in Newcastle is launching a ballot for industrial action. Their caseloads overflowed long ago, but now thousands of prisoners released early – 2,000 this month – have been thrust upon them. The responsibility is overwhelming, with officers blamed for crimes their clients commit.
The probation story is told in scores of reports: the National Audit Office found the service running on half the staff needed to cover released prisoners. It also reported failures in electronic tagging, echoed by the IFG reporting only 55% of tags were fitted in time. Napo, the probation officers’ union, blames the problems on awarding contracts to the lowest bidders at prices that mean the job isn’t done properly.
The number of offenders charged with serious further offences while on probation has increased, with the public accounts committee blaming staff shortages. Vacancies leave probation services 25%-30% below target levels. The government is training another 1,300, but that’s not enough, says Napo, considering the high dropout rate once recruits discover the abuse, threats and stress of the work, alongside the fact that the most common cause of staff sickness is mental ill health.
The sheer impossibility of their caseloads caused the government to abandon any attempt to say what their caseload should be, so the “workload measurement tool” was abruptly ditched in September just before the October raft of new prisoner releases. There is no point in stating an official workload standard that can’t be met.
Eleven hostels and seven halfway houses, places that help probation officers supervise released prisoners, have just closed for repairs and because of a lack of staff. Drug addiction and mental health problems untreated in prisons, coupled with cuts to education, training and rehabilitation, make prisoners even less prepared for release.
The probation system was broken by a disastrous privatisation when Chris Grayling (who banned the sending of books to prisoners) split it apart into 21 private companies, with the workforce organisationally divided in two. Private companies only handled offenders judged low to medium risk, while the most serious offenders remained under the control of the state. Companies under-invested, experienced staff left, and none of the innovation promised was delivered. After this ideological privatisation was abandoned in 2021, the probation service never recovered.
The lord chancellor is set to address the probation officer’s conference. “But please,” says Napo chair Ben Cockburn, “no bullshit. Don’t tell us how well we do an exceptionally difficult job. We know that.”. Napo rejected a 5% pay offer on the grounds it falls far behind equivalent offers to workers in local government, police and social work. Under planned industrial action, Cockburn says probation officers will work to contract and refuse unpaid overtime. That, he says, will cause collapse.
What probation officers need immediately is reduced workloads, pruned to the riskiest cases, leaving less serious cases unallocated. “Put the service into special measures,” Cockburn says. He also wants the courts to stop piling on more cases until there are enough staff to cope. “We are firefighting from one emergency to another,” he says – or called away to someone in a police cell, or to a paedophile found dating a woman with a child, or a domestic violence case.
Cutting workloads for probation officers is only a short-term solution, one that avoids the real question. Why is there an ever-rising prison population, despite the sustained, multi-decade fall in crime rates?
“We are addicted to prison,” Cockburn says. In his view, probation works when officers have time for long-term working relationships with offenders. “It’s the best job in the world,” he says, recalling the journey of one prisoner who had committed a terrible crime as a young man. “I saw him in prison, knew him for 15 years, with time for therapeutic work.” But, these days, that’s so rare. “Someone now might see eight different officers, retelling their story over and over, creating no trust.”
Why build more prison cells? An inspection of a brand new private prison, HMP Millsike in East Yorkshire, found it unsafe due to a lack of experienced staff, as well as chronic staff shortages. Even at its opening, it was “chaotic”, lacking basic processes for important things like locking doors and counting prisoners. Hundreds of cells are still empty because of a lack of officers.
Public pressure to lock up more prisoners and supervise them when released will never be matched by a willingness to pay the taxes needed to cover the cost of attracting people to work in this sector. That’s the truth Cockburn wants politicians to be brave enough to tell. This country is not alone in wrongly believing crime is ever-rising when all across Europe it has fallen for decades. But no one believes it. A news and drama fixation on horrific crime stirs primal fears that belie these facts. Politicians everywhere score points with a frightened public by clamouring for more punishment.
When I last visited a hard-pressed prison, I asked the governor what she most needed, and was astonished when she said she wouldn’t invest here, but “right at the start, before the damage is done, in early years”.
Asking where every pound spent does most good is the kind of mega-question budgets don’t answer. But a brave chancellor would cut prison funding down to housing only the most dangerous, and spending better on what works, such as well-funded probation officers.
Keep telling this fact: all crime is horrible – sex crime is at last reported more often – but the overall drop in neighbourhood-level crime in England and Wales has been about 80% since its peak in 1995. Meanwhile, prison numbers have risen significantly. In his upcoming speech at the probation officer’s conference, it would take unprecedented political bravery for the lord chancellor to dare end the pretence that prison works.
- Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist
