Is washing your face with water after outages dangerous? An immunologist explained what to watch out for
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:37:44 EEST
15:37:44 KST

Is washing your face with water after outages dangerous? An immunologist explained what to watch out for
Kyiv • UNN
After prolonged outages, it is recommended to let the water run because of possible rust and sediment. Boiling destroys microorganisms but not heavy metals.
After prolonged water supply outages, tap water may change color and acquire an unpleasant odor due to having remained in the pipes for a long time. At the same time, transparency and the absence of an odor do not guarantee that it is safe. UNN journalist was told in greater detail by immunologist Borys Donskyi why, after water service is restored, it is advisable to let the water run, whether boiling it is sufficient, and whether its quality can be determined independently.
Why water may become dirtier after outages
According to the doctor, water quality depends on the amount of impurities that may enter it at the water intake stage or while it is passing through pipes. In particular, after remaining in the water supply system for a long time, its condition may deteriorate.
There are certain standards governing what substances water may contain, and exceeding the permissible levels of these substances is already considered hazardous to health. As you understand, this is a quantitative issue: the cleaner the water, the better it will be. Certain impurities are added to this water: it picks them up while passing through the water supply system
The immunologist noted that after outages, water may come into contact with rust and other deposits in the pipes, which is why it sometimes has a characteristic color and odor when supply initially resumes. Therefore, after water service is restored, it is worth paying attention to its appearance and not using water with obvious signs of contamination.
Have you often observed the following after a water outage, even one lasting several hours: you turn on the tap, and rusty water flows out? This happens because a pocket of air has passed through the pipes, the water has stood in them and picked up rust, so it should be drained at first. If it remains in the pipes for even longer, it may become less clean and more contaminated
Can you wash your face with such water, and will boiling help?
In Borys Donskyi’s opinion, the risk of infection through intact skin should not be equated with the risk of consuming contaminated water. However, during hygiene procedures, water can still get into the mouth, eyes, or onto mucous membranes. Therefore, according to the doctor, if contamination is suspected, it is better not to use it for brushing your teeth or for other procedures during which water could enter the body.
I do not think it can be so contaminated that it would pose a risk through the skin. But if water remains in risers and pipes for a week, it is possible that it will contain more dangerous microorganisms and be more heavily contaminated
At the same time, according to the immunologist, boiling does help disinfect water, in particular by destroying many pathogenic microorganisms; however, it should be noted that it does not eliminate all possible contaminants.
Boiling disinfects water. But if it is also rusty and contains high levels of heavy metals, boil it or do not boil it—it will remain dirty. Therefore, it should at least be passed through household filters
At the same time, it is impossible to determine water quality solely by its color, odor, and taste, because even clear water may contain substances that cannot be detected without special testing.
You can independently determine that it is unfit for use. But you should not independently determine that it is definitely safe and can be consumed, because you do not have that capability. There are services that do this; they are supposed to regularly check water quality. And we hope they do so
Borys Donskyi also separately cautioned against trying to independently determine the cause of deteriorating health after contact with potentially contaminated water, because poisoning symptoms depend on the type of contamination: microorganisms, in particular, can cause intestinal infections, while chemical substances can cause other disorders.
Self-diagnosis is not advisable. Any deterioration in your health may indicate that something has entered your body. If the water is saturated with microorganisms, this will result in intestinal infections. If it contains heavy metals, the symptoms will be completely different
Moreover, according to the immunologist, some toxic effects may not appear immediately but as certain substances accumulate in the body, so the safety of water should not be assessed solely based on how you feel. If unusual symptoms occur after contact with suspicious water, it is advisable to consult a doctor directly.
ATTENTION! This material is for informational purposes only. If you are concerned about your health, consult a doctor.

Flying cars: Tesla's new Roadster uses SpaceX thrusters to turn in the air, can drive upside down

06:35:50 UTC
15:35:50 KST

Tesla unveiled a redesigned Roadster powered with rocket-style thrusters on Thursday and said it would start production in 2028, more than a decade after it first showed a next-generation version of its electric sports car.
The white two-seater vehicle, developed in collaboration with CEO Elon Musk's rocket company SpaceX, drove upside down on a ramp using a suction system, turned in the air and landed using built-in thrusters. Later in the event it used the thrusters to jump over a truck and other vehicles, twisting in the air during the maneuver.
Some watchers saw the collaboration as Musk drumming up interest in a merger of the two big companies he controls, an idea he has explored by discussing their overlap.
The reveal gives Tesla a showpiece car after years of missed Roadster deadlines, but it comes as the company shifts its focus to self-driving technology and robotics, and days before third-quarter results that analysts say matter more to investors.
"It was an engineering flex with no commercial value beyond embarrassing traditional car makers," Gene Munster, managing partner at Tesla investor Deepwater Asset Management, said on social media platform X/Twitter.
"The Roadster event is the latest example of why Elon can't wait to bring (Tesla) and (SpaceX) together," Munster said.
Car carries symbolic weight for Tesla
Musk has played down the car's importance to Tesla's finances, describing it in 2023 as a "small potato situation" that would not "move the needle in a major way financially."
But the car still carries symbolic weight.
"Tesla does not currently have a halo car, or high-performance luxury vehicle designed to showcase an automaker's best engineering and technology. The Roadster will be Tesla's new halo car," Morningstar analyst Seth Goldstein said in a note last month.
Viewers and witnesses gushed over the spectacle of the launch.
"That was the most insane product demo I've ever seen," Tesla fan and investor Sawyer Merritt posted on X. "I just saw this in person, and I'm still asking how this wasn't AI."
Musk and other executives did not specify any target prices at Thursday's event, although Tesla nearly a decade ago quoted a base price of $200,000 for the vehicle.
Tesla's reservation page for the Roadster after Thursday's event showed a "Performance" version of the vehicle requiring a $50,000 deposit and a "Thrust" version with "acceleration thrusters" requiring a $250,000 deposit. A "Rocket" variant, which Tesla says is "invite only," is described as a single-seat model with a "full flight system."
'Halfway to the speed of sound'
The event at a SpaceX test site in McGregor, Texas, had all the elements of a classic Musk product reveal: dramatic music, smoke, mechanical hissing sounds and a launch countdown.
"This is the culmination of incredible work by Tesla and SpaceX engineers working closely together to make something that you haven't seen in any movie," Musk, wearing a silver Western-style belt buckle emblazoned with the Tesla logo, told a cheering crowd of enthusiasts and investors.
The Roadster can accelerate from zero to 60 mph in less than one second and can hit a top speed of over 230 mph, Tesla vehicle engineering chief Lars Moravy said.
"Definitely much faster than that," an excited Musk said. "I think you've got to crack halfway to the speed of sound."
The Roadster can also travel over 300 miles on a single charge. That is less than half of what Musk promised in 2017, when Tesla first revealed a prototype of the second-generation Roadster and said that deliveries would begin in 2020.
Roadster comes as Tesla shifts focus to self-driving tech, robotics
The original Roadster, released in 2008 and on sale until 2012, was Tesla's first-ever electric vehicle and used a Lotus Elise chassis. It helped change the world's view of what an EV could be. The company has since been known for its Model Y and Model X SUVs and Model S and Model 3 sedans.
The reveal of the second-generation Roadster comes amid a sharp shift in Tesla's focus to artificial intelligence-led self-driving tech and robotics, from manufacturing cars for human drivers.
This year, Tesla stopped selling Model S and X vehicles to make space for production of its Optimus humanoid robots. It also launched Cybercab - a two-seater robotaxi that comes without manual controls such as a steering wheel, pedals and mirrors.
Tesla is set to report third-quarter results on October 21.
Sales of Tesla's aging lineup of EVs have declined over the past two years, although high gas prices helped boost deliveries in the third quarter.
"The margin and cash flow numbers will carry far more weight with investors than anything they saw at the reveal," said Josh Gilbert, lead analyst for Asia-Pacific at trading platform eToro.

Which countries waste the most food, and how to reduce waste at home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
06:31:57 UTC
15:31:57 KST

Which countries waste the most food, and how to reduce waste at home
This World Food Day, 645 million people are going hungry, yet more than a billion tonnes of food is wasted annually.
For every five plates of food served around the world, roughly one ends up in the bin. That adds up to more than a billion tonnes of food a year.
Meanwhile, 645 million people, about one in 13 of the world’s population, went hungry in 2025, according to the UN.
That gap is the focus of World Food Day on October 16, the annual UN observance marking the founding of the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) in 1945. This year’s theme, “Innovate today, nourish tomorrow”, calls for food systems that feed more people and waste less.
In this visual explainer, Al Jazeera looks at global hunger, which countries waste the most food and simple ways to waste less at home.
Hunger is falling, slowly
Global hunger has fallen for a third year in a row, but it remains above levels seen before the COVID-19 pandemic.
According to the UN’s annual State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World report, an estimated 645 million people, or 7.8 percent of the world’s population, faced hunger in 2025. That is down from 8.1 percent in 2024 and a peak of 8.6 percent in 2022, but still about 61 million more people than in 2019.
Where are people the most hungry?
Africa has more hungry people than any other region.
In 2025, an estimated 309 million people in Africa were undernourished. That is one in five people on the continent and almost half of the world’s hungry people.
By comparison, 292 million people in Asia (6 percent of the population) and 32 million in Latin America and the Caribbean (4.8 percent) were undernourished.
The 2026 Global Hunger Index shows a similar pattern at the country level. The index scores countries out of 100, combining undernourishment with child stunting, child wasting and child mortality. Scores of 35 or more are considered “alarming”.
Hunger is classed as alarming in eight countries, seven of them in Africa. Somalia has the worst score of the 122 countries ranked, followed by the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Chad and Madagascar.
Sudan, South Sudan, Burundi and Yemen were also classed as alarming, but conflict and data gaps meant the index could not calculate their scores.
At the same time, a large share of the food the world grows never reaches a plate.
How much food is wasted every year?
Food is lost and wasted at every stage of its journey from farm to table.
According to the FAO, about 13 percent of the food produced globally is lost after harvest and before it reaches shops, spoiling in storage, during transport or in processing. Fruits and vegetables suffer the highest losses.
Food lost before it reaches shops is worth more than $400bn a year, according to the FAO.
Shops, restaurants and households then throw away almost a fifth of the food available to consumers, about 1.05 billion tonnes in 2022, according to the UN Environment Programme (UNEP). That is equivalent to 52.5 million trucks, each carrying 20 tonnes.
Households account for the most, 60 percent, followed by restaurants and other food services at 28 percent and shops at 12 percent.
How to reduce food waste at home
Most food waste happens at home, which means households can make a real difference. Here are some simple steps recommended by food waste campaigners and UN agencies:
- Plan before you shop: Check what you already have, plan meals for the week and shop with a list to avoid buying more than you need.
- Understand date labels: “Use by” dates are about safety, but “best before” dates are about quality. Food is often still safe to eat after its “best before” date.
- Store food properly: Keep your fridge at 5C (41F) or below, and store fruit and vegetables where they last longest. Bananas, for example, speed up the ripening of other fruit nearby.
- Use the freezer: Bread, cooked meals, meat and many fruits and vegetables can be frozen before they go off.
- Cook the right amount: Measuring portions, especially for rice and pasta, cuts down on leftovers that get thrown away.
- Eat the oldest food first: Move older items to the front of the fridge and cupboard so they get used before newer ones.
- Use leftovers and scraps: Turn leftovers into new meals, and use vegetable peels and stalks in soups and stocks.
- Compost what you can’t eat: Composting inedible parts such as peels and eggshells keeps them out of landfills, where rotting food releases methane.
Which country wastes the most?
On average, every person in the world wastes about 132kg (291 pounds) of food a year, roughly the weight of two adults. Of that, 79kg (174 pounds) was thrown away at home.
But the amount varies widely. Hotter countries tend to waste more at home, UNEP says, possibly because of more fresh produce and less refrigeration.
The Maldives wastes the most food, with each person throwing away about 260kg (573 pounds) a year, about twice the global average. Syria, the Dominican Republic, Seychelles, Mexico and Tunisia follow, each wasting more than 210kg (463 pounds) per person, according to UN estimates.
Spain recorded some of the lowest levels, at around 39kg (86 pounds) or less per person.
What does food waste cost?
Food loss and waste costs the global economy more than $1 trillion a year, according to the UN.
To put that in perspective, what else could $1 trillion buy?
Use the + buttons to add items to your cart and see how the money would be spent across 35 categories.
Throwing food away also wastes the money, land and energy used to produce it.
About 1.4 billion hectares (3.5 billion acres) of land, or 28 percent of the world’s agricultural land, is used to grow food that is never eaten. That is an area larger than Canada.
Food loss and waste also generate an estimated 8 to 10 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions, including methane released as food rots in landfills.

The Insider’s correspondent in Ukraine examined an Xingkai Tech mesh modem recovered from a Russian Gerbera drone. The investigation identified the Chinese manufacturer as a major supplier of communications equipment used in Russia’s Geran and Gerbera drones.
How mesh modems help Russian drones
Mesh modems allow drones to pass signals between one another, effectively creating a communications network in the air.
In simple terms, one drone can relay commands to another, helping it stay connected to its operator even when the direct signal is weak or unavailable. The technology can extend the range over which Russian forces control drones and allow them to operate farther into Ukrainian territory.
White House Ordered Restrictions on Ukraine’s Starshield, Disrupting Drone Defense – Reuters
Unlike drones that rely solely on a direct connection with an operator, UAVs using mesh networks can transmit information through intermediate drones acting as signal relays.
According to The Insider, Shenzhen Xingkai Technology accounts for around half of the market for high-performance mesh modems used in Russian Geran and Gerbera drones. The equipment is therefore a significant component of Russia’s drone communications supply chain.
The technology also allows Russian forces to maintain control of drones during flight and potentially exploit gaps in Ukrainian air defenses, the investigation reported.
Ukrainian military personnel warned in April that mesh modems used to control Shahed-type and Gerbera drones were allowing Russian forces to conduct reconnaissance deeper into Ukraine and expand their area of control.

Türkiye’s textile sector exported goods worth $7.16 billion in the January-September period of 2026, according to data from the Southeastern Anatolia Exporters’ Associations.
During the first nine months of the year, textile producers shipped 1.84 million tons of products to 201 countries and free zones, generating export revenues of $7.16 billion.
The European Union remained the sector’s largest export market, accounting for $2.69 billion in sales. Exports to African countries rose 7.8 percent year-on-year to $1.17 billion.
On a country basis, Italy remained the leading destination for Turkish textile exports, with purchases totaling $563 million. It was followed by Egypt, where exports increased 13 percent to $464 million, and the United States, where exports rose 18.2 percent to $452 million.
By product group, fabrics accounted for the largest share of exports at $4.35 billion, followed by yarn with $1.87 billion and fiber with $943 million.
Among Turkish provinces, Istanbul recorded the highest textile exports at $2.75 billion. It was followed by Gaziantep with $1.23 billion, Bursa with $927.6 million, and Kahramanmaraş with $570 million.
Türkiye Exporters Assembly (TİM) Vice Chairman and Textile and Raw Materials Sector Representative Ahmet Öksüz said while strengthening its position in Europe, the sector should make more effective use of opportunities in alternative markets, particularly the United States.
He said he believes exports could gain strong momentum if global demand gradually recovers and inflationary pressures ease in strategic markets during the remainder of the year and in 2027.
According to Öksüz, the sector’s main goal is not only to increase export volumes but to increase the value-added content of its exports, thereby strengthening its international competitiveness on a lasting basis.

Unknown Publisher

New Zealand's High Court has rejected a bid to stop the incoming PNG NRL team from using the Chiefs identity.
New Zealand Rugby's application for a final injunction is still before the court and legal action in Australia is possible.
What's next?
The PNG Chiefs are set to reveal their jersey and logo on Wednesday.
New Zealand's High Court has knocked back an application for an interim injunction on the PNG Chiefs NRL franchise using its name in the country.
New Zealand Rugby (NZR) had rushed to court before the PNG team's logo and jersey reveal in Port Moresby next week.
The organisation claimed use of the Chiefs name, which is also the name of the long-standing Super Rugby Pacific outfit, would cause confusion and damage to the brand.
But a judge at today's two-hour Wellington hearing turned down the application after hearing an injunction could harm the NRL expansion outfit's efforts to attract players ahead of a 2028 debut.
"The PNG Chiefs welcome today's decision in the New Zealand High Court and look forward to the launch of our inaugural logo and supporter jersey in Port Moresby on Wednesday,," PNG Chiefs CEO Lorna McPherson said.
"As the matter remains before the court, no further comment on this matter will be provided at this time."
The dispute continues, with an application for a final injunction still before the court and legal action in Australia under consideration.
ARLC executive chairman Peter V'landys last week labelled NZR's action one of "mind-blowing hypocrisy", using the example of the Auckland Blues' arrival decades after NSW "had been the Blues".
"Today's decision is not a judgment on the strength of our case and the matter will still be heard in full," NZR boss Steve Lancaster said.
"As the trademark holder, our responsibility to protect the Chiefs brand hasn't changed. We remain open to working with the ARLC on a solution."
NZR's lawyer Earl Gray argued today that the PNG Chiefs' use of "PNG Chiefs" and "Chiefs" interchangeably created confusion for fans of both codes and that, with no clear distinction between the two, it would strip the rugby Chiefs of brand exclusivity.
He said NZR had trademark protections for the Chiefs in New Zealand that the NRL had not acknowledged.
ARLC lawyer Clive Elliot argued that the request for an urgent injunction, about a year after NZR became aware of the PNG Chiefs name, was not appropriate.
He said an injunction now would cloud the franchise's reputation ahead of a recruitment blitz once free agency opened next month.

MSCI freezes certain Türkiye index changes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
06:28:37 UTC
15:28:37 KST

MSCI announced that it will apply a freeze on certain index related changes for Turkish equity securities resulting from Index Reviews or corporate events, effective immediately and until further notice.
As part of the MSCI 2026 Market Classification Review, MSCI highlighted concerns raised by institutional investors about possible coordinated trading through fund holdings closely affiliated with certain smaller listed companies, which undermines the reliability of free float estimates and market integrity.
MSCI noted that it would look for tangible and credible progress, including granular and timely disclosure of beneficial ownership, robust surveillance and enforcement against coordinated trading behavior, and a transparent rules-based framework for identifying and treating securities with structurally distorted free float.
Institutional investors will need to see credible and sustained enforcement against coordinated trading, and disclosure standards that enable independent verification of the free float of Turkish securities, MSCI said.
MSCI said it will not implement increases to Foreign Inclusion Factors (FIF) or Number of Shares (NOS), additions to the MSCI Türkiye Investable Market Index (IMI) or upward migrations across size-segments indexes.
Should sufficient progress not be evident by June 2027, MSCI sai it will consider additional measures, including a consultation on a potential reclassification of the MSCI Türkiye Indexes from Emerging Market to Frontier or Standalone Market status.

Houthis’ diverse arsenal fuels renewed attacks on Saudi Arabia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
06:26:10 UTC
15:26:10 KST

Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis have built a diverse missile and drone arsenal that allows them to sustain attacks against Saudi Arabia and strategic maritime targets, raising concerns about the duration and intensity of the renewed conflict.
Since early September, the group has struck key oil infrastructure and airports across Saudi Arabia, including Riyadh’s airport, which has been targeted 20 times, according to the supplied account. It has also attempted, unsuccessfully, to strike the holy cities of Mecca and Medina.
The renewed hostilities followed a Saudi bombardment of Sanaa’s airport in July aimed at preventing a Houthi delegation from landing in the Yemeni capital, ending a four-year truce.
April Longley Alley, a Yemen specialist at the Washington Institute think tank, described the subsequent exchanges as a strategy of reciprocal escalation.
“The Houthis framed this campaign as blockade for blockade, airport for airport, escalation for escalation,” she said.
The Houthis possess ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and aerial and maritime drones, giving them multiple options for attacking infrastructure and threatening shipping near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a strategic passage linking the Gulf of Aden with the Red Sea.
Their weapons come partly from military stockpiles seized when they captured Sanaa in 2014. Others have been smuggled into Yemen as complete systems or assembled locally from imported components, primarily brought in through the Arabian Sea, said Niranjan BS, a strategic weapons analyst at Jane’s.
According to the International Institute for Strategic Studies’ Military Balance database, the group operates several medium-range ballistic missiles, including systems derived from Iranian designs such as the Kheibar Shekan.
Its shorter-range weapons include the Asef anti-ship missile, derived from Iran’s Khalij Fars missile family, according to the Wilson Center think tank.
The Houthis also possess cruise missiles from Iran’s Quds family. The Quds-4 variant is believed to have a range of about 2,000 kilometers (1,200 miles), the Wilson Center said.
Their drone arsenal includes the Waeid-1 and Waeid-2, local copies of Iran’s Shahed-131 and Shahed-136 one-way attack drones, respectively, Niranjan said.
This combination allows the group to vary its attacks and threaten targets at different distances, complicating efforts to neutralize its capabilities.
Iran has provided critical military assistance to the Houthis, particularly through missile and drone technology, according to the Middle East Institute.
In a report, the institute said components manufactured in Iran are smuggled into Yemen by small boats, container ships or across the border with Oman before being assembled locally.
However, analysts caution against portraying the Houthis as a force that simply follows Tehran’s orders.
Danny Citrinowicz, an Israeli analyst specializing in Iran, said the Houthis viewed themselves as partners of Iran rather than proxies.
Iranian personnel linked to the Quds Force, the foreign operations arm of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, maintain a presence in Yemen and advise the group, Citrinowicz said at a recent conference in Paris. But he said they do not decide Houthi military operations.
In June 2024, the U.S. Treasury Department sanctioned a man in China suspected of links to the Houthis, accusing him of playing “a key role in procuring materials that enable Houthi forces to manufacture advanced conventional weapons inside Yemen.”
The Houthis have survived years of conflict and sustained air campaigns by Saudi Arabia, the United States and Israel, leaving them experienced in operating under military pressure.
Longley Alley said their ability to withstand previous bombardments suggested that further strikes might not quickly end the confrontation.
“We need to remember with the Houthis that they have withstood punishing air campaigns before, from the Saudis, from the Americans, and from the Israelis,” she said.
“This is a battle-hardened group, and they have much less to lose than the Saudis.”
She added that the Houthis likely believed they could sustain the conflict longer because they were accustomed to absorbing attacks.

Ousted US general warned before Iran war of missile defense shortages lasting until 2030: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
06:26:05 UTC
15:26:05 KST

Berk Kutay Gokmen
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
Ousted US Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George warned months before the US-Israeli war against Iran that American missile defense stockpiles were critically low and could take until 2030 to recover, CBS News reported Thursday.
George raised the warning in late December, two months before the conflict began, according to US officials familiar with his assessment. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth removed him from his post in April as the war was underway.
The general’s assessment, included in the Pentagon’s fiscal 2027 force allocation planning, identified shortages of Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) interceptors and Patriot missiles, with supplies expected to remain at strategically low levels until 2030.
The officials reportedly attributed the shortfall to weapons transfers to Ukraine, US military support for Israel, and limited defense industry production capacity.
The war with Iran has further strained supplies, according to the report. A Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimate found that US forces entered 2026 with approximately 2,300 Patriot interceptors and used between 1,050 and 1,430 during the conflict.
The country’s prewar THAAD inventory stood at around 355 interceptors, of which an estimated 190 to 290 were expended.
Mark Cancian, a retired Marine colonel and senior adviser at CSIS, told CBS News that these systems would be crucial in a potential conflict with China.
“Air defense — missile defense — that will be huge,” he said, explaining that a major confrontation with Beijing would demand substantial interceptor supplies.
Replenishing the stockpiles remains a lengthy process, the report said. The CSIS estimates that new THAAD interceptor contracts take over four years to fulfill, while Patriot PAC-3 orders take an average of 3 1/2 years.
The Pentagon rejected claims of a shortage. Chief spokesman Sean Parnell told CBS News: “Claims of U.S. munitions shortages are false.”
He added that Washington retains “everything required to strike at the time and place of the President’s choosing.”

The number includes 1,790 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report, Russia has also lost 12,414 tanks, 25,552 armored combat vehicles, 163,554 vehicles and fuel tanks, 51,242 artillery systems, 2,217 multiple-launch rocket systems, 1,708 air defense systems, 449 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 2,958 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.

A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action.
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action.
The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

Lithuania’s 2027 budget: 5% for defence, growing government deficit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
06:24:00 UTC
15:24:00 KST

Lithuania’s draft budget for 2027 allocates more than 4.8 billion euros to defence, equivalent to 5% of projected GDP, the Finance Ministry said Thursday. The government approved the proposal on Friday morning and will present the budget bill to the parliament, Seimas.
The proposed allocation would increase defence spending by nearly 35 million euros from this year. It includes funding for the Defence Ministry and the State Defence Fund, which is set to receive more than 896 million euros.
Although defence spending was lower in monetary terms this year, it accounted for a larger share of the economy, at 5.38% of GDP.
Early last year, Lithuania’s State Defence Council, which includes the country’s political leadership and representatives of its national defence system, agreed to allocate 5% to 6% of GDP to defence annually from 2026 through 2030. The increased spending is intended to help develop an army division and prepare Lithuania to host a German brigade.
The Finance Ministry on Thursday registered draft budgets for the state, municipalities and social funds for next year, projecting a general government deficit of 3.8% of GDP.
State budget revenue is expected to reach nearly 22.2 billion euros, including European Union funds, while expenditure is projected at 27.9 billion euros.
The projected deficit exceeds the European Union’s Maastricht criterion, which generally limits government deficits to 3% of GDP. Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said in an earlier interview that most spending beyond revenue was linked to the goal of allocating 5% of GDP to defence and to increases in benefits that are indexed.
The government is also proposing pay increases for statutory officers and cultural workers in 2027. Additional funding has been earmarked for a proposed package of measures to encourage families to have children.
Revenue for the Sodra state social insurance fund is projected at nearly 7 billion euros next year, with expenditure expected to exceed 5.5 billion euros.
The average pension is set to rise by 10.4% to 825 euros a month, increasing to 895 euros for people who meet the required length-of-service criteria. The budget allocates 715 million euros for the pension increases.
The Compulsory Health Insurance Fund is expected to collect nearly 3.3 billion euros in revenue in 2027 and spend almost 3.2 billion euros.
General government debt is projected to reach 48.2% of GDP next year.
Sinkevičius said Lithuania would continue to devote one of Europe’s largest shares of GDP to defence.
Finance Minister Taurimas Valys said the budget sought to balance stronger national security with income growth above inflation and the economy’s long-term growth potential.

Lisbon airport taxis: Fixed fares aim to end 'tourist trap'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
06:17:23 UTC
15:17:23 KST

Since Thursday, passengers landing at Lisbon airport who want to take a taxi can now rely on a fixed price for their trip.
Over the past few years, there have been many reports from tourists about excessive prices, scams and even drivers refusing to take passengers from Lisbon airport.
Faced with problems affecting both foreign visitors and locals, a protocol was signed last September to set fixed fares for taxi journeys.
Several complaints on social media describe allegedly tampered taximeters, mileage being diverted and cases in which taxi drivers will only accept cash payments.
Back in August, Josien Nation, a Dutch citizen living in Portugal, described the situation as a "tourist trap". In a video posted on the Facebook page Nations Without Borders, she said that "not all taxi drivers are 'crooks'", but that some try to negotiate the fare before setting off and then make the trip with the meter switched off, a practice expressly banned in Portugal.
In another account, posted in a Reddit group, a passenger says that on a journey from Lisbon airport to Rossio he was charged 18.50 euros, even though the meter showed 13 euros. According to the post, the driver justified the difference with an additional luggage fee. He also refused to let the passenger pay by card.
Most of these accounts come from tourists or foreign nationals living in Portugal who are allegedly treated as tourists. However, there are also testimonies from residents who use the service, such as a Portuguese man who shared his experience on the same platform.
"The last time I arrived in Lisbon, after a trip, I got into a taxi and immediately got back out again," he began. "The driver said he didn't take card payments. I asked him how much the journey from the airport to my home might cost, as I had some cash with me, but he replied that the price depended on a series of factors, such as traffic and how long the journey would take, among other nonsense."
Other users also say that some taxi drivers take less direct routes to reach their destination, in an attempt to make the journey longer and thus justify overcharging.
To prevent many of these situations, a fixed-fare mechanism came into force on Thursday, under which everyone will pay the same for trips to certain areas. Anyone travelling to areas within the so‑called "zone 1" (see image below) will pay 16 euros during the daytime, from 7:00 to 22:00, and 20 euros at night, from 22:00 to 7:00.
For trips to "zone 2", a daytime journey costs 19 euros and rises to 23 euros at night. These fares also apply at weekends and on public holidays.
Destinations not covered by the scheme will continue to be charged using the meter.
The fares include luggage, removing the additional fee of 1.60 euros that used to be charged for bags exceeding 55x35x20 centimetres.
Carlos Silva, president of the Portuguese Taxi Federation (FPT), explained in comments to Portuguese news agency Lusa that the system will only be fully operational from November and that a price still needs to be set for areas outside the capital, such as Moscavide, Sacavém and Prior Velho.
He believes "it is not fair for someone to pay 16 euros to Parque das Nações and, if the destination is a little further on but already in another municipality, Loures, and so close to the airport, for the service then to be paid according to the meter".
'Tourist prices'
Reactions to the new price list were quick to appear on social media, with many people branding the fares far too high and pointing to short journeys, such as trips from the airport to the parish of Alvalade or to Parque das Nações, both little more than two kilometres away.
An Instagram user says she usually takes a taxi to Oriente station, in Parque das Nações, and used to pay between 7.50 and 10 euros. "And now a fixed fare at such a high rate, why?", she asks. Among the comments, some argue that alternative transport platforms, such as TVDE services, will be the main beneficiaries of the new fares.
Some accuse the authorities of setting "tourist prices" or "rubber-stamping" the high fares and practices of many taxi drivers. "They are going to legalise what some have already been doing for years: turning off the meter," reads one comment.
Others, meanwhile, recognise the need for fixed prices in the name of transparency. "Having already seen this system in other countries, having the fares per destination set in advance without depending on the meter is actually useful," writes one user on Reddit.
The possibility of using public transport, such as the metro and the bus, is also mentioned in the comments, although users point to obstacles such as "large, heavy suitcases" or "travelling with children".
Protocol goes beyond fares
The new fares, which came into force on Thursday, will cover all taxi drivers in this first phase, even those not yet accredited to operate at the airport taxi rank. "Accreditation will also start to be carried out on Thursday," the official explained.
Carlos Silva also believes that these new rules could attract more drivers and ensure more taxis are available at the airport rank. "We know that many do not stop at the airport for various reasons, but that they are considering doing so if there are rules, because at the moment they do not feel comfortable. Fixed prices may be more advantageous, offsetting the time they might have to wait", he said.
If you arrive at Lisbon airport today, you can already expect these prices on taxi services. However, information panels are still missing in the arrivals area and outside, displaying this information so that it is visible to everyone. Transparency is one of the pillars of this new regulation, along with "improving the quality of the service and protecting users".
The protocol on fixed-price journeys, signed in September by Lisbon City Council, ANA - Aeroportos de Portugal, the Lisbon Tourism Association (ATL), the FPT (Portuguese Taxi Federation) and ANTRAL - National Association of Road Transport in Light Vehicles, also lays down other rules, such as the "non-refusal of services" by taxi drivers.
Taxi drivers are also obliged to accept vouchers and electronic payments, meaning the payment terminal must be operational.
PSP inspections confirmed need for regulation
The tightening of measures, even though they will only be fully implemented at the start of next month, also follows a major inspection operation by the Public Security Police (PSP) at the arrivals area of Humberto Delgado Airport in Lisbon at the end of August, during which 67 offences related to taxi activity were detected.
In a statement, Lisbon Metropolitan Command (COMETLIS) said that around 100 taxis were inspected at the site, resulting in 32 offences for "incorrect positioning of the taximeter", out of a total of 67.
Among the offences detected, eight related to lack of a CMT (Taxi Driver Certificate), six to lack of mandatory documents, six to fire extinguishers past their expiry date, three to lack of vehicle inspection and three to "lack of Group 2 on the taxi driver's licence" (the mandatory driving licence certification for taxi drivers).
Two offences were also recorded for a taximeter past its validity period, two for taxis in poor condition, one for failure to use restraint systems, one for lack of insurance, one for driving under the influence of alcohol and one for parking in a private car park.
The PSP also issued two warnings to present documents and complied with two requests for external action that were pending against one of the drivers.
Joana Mourão Carvalho contributed to the writing of this article.

SCALP, AASM Hammer, and Aster 30: France Has Granted Ukraine All the Promised Licenses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
06:16:29 UTC
15:16:29 KST

Ukraine has received all the licenses France promised for the domestic production of three types of weapons: Aster 30 air defense missiles, AASMHammer guided bombs, and SCALP cruise missiles.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced the development.
In July, French President Emmanuel Macron announced the licensing agreement following a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing in Paris. The agreement allows Ukraine to produce these weapons domestically under French licenses.
Ukrainian forces have been successfully employing Aster 30 missiles for an extended period as part of the SAMP/T surface-to-air missile systems supplied by France and Italy.
The modern Aster 30 Block 1 variant can engage aerodynamic targets, including aircraft, cruise missiles, and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), at ranges of up to 120 km and altitudes of up to 25 km.
In addition, the system can intercept tactical ballistic missiles at ranges of up to 30 km.
The French AASM Hammer is a guidance kit that converts conventional unguided Western-designed bombs into precision-guided munitions.
Unlike the American JDAM, AASM Hammer kits are equipped with an integrated rocket motor, enabling them to engage targets at ranges of up to 15 km when released from low altitudes and up to 70 km when released from high altitudes.
Currently, two versions are available: the Hammer 250, designed for 227 kg Mk 82 bombs, and the Hammer 1000, designed for 908 kg Mk 84 bombs. Both are available with different guidance systems.
The Franco-British SCALP EG / Storm Shadow is an air-launched cruise missile measuring 5.1 metres in length, weighing 1,300 kg, and equipped with a 450 kg warhead designed to destroy hardened, fixed targets.
The missile was developed by Matra and British Aerospace beginning in the late 1990s. It has been in service with France and the United Kingdom since 2003 and is manufactured by the MBDA consortium.
The French SCALP-EG and British Storm Shadow variants are essentially identical in design, differing primarily in their software and the specifics of their integration with carrier aircraft.

HOLLOWED BRAZILIAN QUARTZITE HOUSES HIDDEN LIGHTING ELEMENTS
The CONCAV collection, designed by Ignacio Martínez Todeschini and Ignacio Noel and produced in Argentina, explores geometric forms and lighting through Brazilian quartzite and galvanized steel. The central element of the series is a hollowed, curved quartzite module created through CNC milling and hand-finishing. This process houses the light source within the stone, creating a backlit linear element that contrasts the material’s inherent density. The piece pairs an L-shaped support and a mobile C-element connected by hidden magnets to turn a functional bookend into an interactive luminary gesture.
MAGNETIC light SWITCHING pairs WITH ADJUSTABLE BOOK SUPPORT
The inaugural release, CONCAV Book, functions as a hybrid bookend and luminaire. The design by Ignacio Martínez Todeschini and Ignacio Noel – Imto Deschini Studio comprises two distinct components: a fixed L-shaped steel base that houses the light source and acts as the main support, and a mobile C-shaped element. Hidden magnets regulate the internal circuitry, activating the light source when the two components are connected and turning it off when separated. This magnetic connection allows the user to adjust the configuration based on the arrangement and volume of books.

UK bookstores scramble as Sally Rooney's novels are pulled over Palestine Action support

UK bookstores scramble as Sally Rooney's novels pulled over Palestine Action support
Critically acclaimed Irish novelist Sally Rooney's announcement that her books could no longer be sold in the UK due to her support for proscribed group Palestine Action has left British booksellers rushing to stock up on her works before distributors run out. The British government's ban on the group, which practiced non-violent direct action and sabotage against UK military assets believed to be working with the Israeli government, makes support for Palestine Action punishable by up to 14 years in prison.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
British booksellers are have been left scrambling after Irish novelist Sally Rooney said her books can no longer be sold in the UK because she financially supports the banned group Palestine Action.
The announcement by Rooney’s British publisher that it will no longer distribute her books has reignited debate over the UK government’s decision last year to outlaw the direct-action protest group as a terrorist organisation. The ban makes membership in – or, crucially, support for – Palestine Action a crime punishable by up to 14 years in prison.
Rooney, 35, is the critically praised author of four novels: “Conversations with Friends”, “Normal People”, “Beautiful World, Where are You” and “Intermezzo”. Her books have sold millions of copies, and both “Conversations with Friends” and “Normal People” were adapted for television by the BBC.
She supports the Palestinian-led Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement, which calls for boycotts of Israeli businesses, universities and cultural institutions over Israel’s treatment of the Palestinians.
Read moreWhat is Palestine Action, the protest movement banned under UK terror act?
After the UK banned Palestine Action in July 2025, Rooney said she would use proceeds from her books and their TV adaptations to support the group. On Wednesday her UK publisher, Faber, said that paying her royalties could violate the terror ban and it had “taken the decision that we can no longer supply her works in the UK in any format”.
"To sell a writer's work and not be able to pass on earnings is an unconscionable situation for a publisher," Faber said in a statement.
The publisher stressed the decision had been made with Rooney's agreement.
“I have made every effort to be honest with the public about my beliefs and intentions, and I am wholly prepared to accept the consequences,” the writer said in a statement.
Faber’s announcement left British bookstores scrambling to understand whether they were breaking the law by selling Rooney’s books.
The Booksellers Association later said it had “confirmed with Faber that whilst those titles are no longer available to UK bookshops to order, they can continue to sell their existing stock within the UK market”.
Some stores rushed to stock up on Rooney’s novels, but found distributors had already run out.
“We were thinking, we’ll just get a whole bunch before we stop being able to,” said Lucy Burke, a bookseller at London’s Camden Town Bookshop. “Because she’s a hugely popular seller here, and quite evergreen. But now it seems like what we have is all we’re going to have.”
Burke described the situation as “absolutely ridiculous” and said it amounted to censorship of “one of our most prominent writers”.
Palestine Action, founded in 2020, aims to stop UK military support for Israel, which it says is committing genocide against the Palestinians – a claim Israel strongly denies. An independent UN committee found in September 2025 that Israel was carrying out a genocide in the besieged Gaza Strip.
The group says it aims to stop genocide by disrupting “corporate enablers of the Israeli military-industrial complex".
In 2024 its activists broke into a factory owned by Israeli weapons manufacturer Elbit Systems UK, smashing equipment with sledgehammers and crowbars. The next year, activists broke into a Royal Air Force base in June 2025, sprayed red paint into the engines of two tanker planes and caused further damage with crowbars.
The group says it does not advocate violence against people, but a police officer suffered a fractured spine when she was hit with a sledgehammer as police tried to arrest members of the group during the factory break-in.
The British government says Palestine Action has “carried out acts of terrorism, celebrated those who took part in them and promoted the use of violence".
“The proscription of Palestine Action does not affect lawful protest in support of the Palestinian cause, which remains a fundamental democratic right,” the Home Office said in a statement.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Civil liberties groups say the ban unjustifiably restricts the rights to protest and free speech. In response to the government’s decision, thousands of people have tested the law by silently holding signs reading “I support Palestine Action.”
More than 3,000 people have been arrested, and more than 1,200 have been charged under the Terrorism Act, though no one has yet been convicted.
The scale of the arrests, and the profile of those detained – including retirees in their 80s and 90s – has put Britain’s Labour Party government under pressure.
The centre-left government has tried to rebuild bridges with pro-Palestinian supporters since Prime Minister Andy Burnham replaced Keir Starmer in July.
Last month the UK formally recognised a Palestinian state and banned goods from Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, which are illegal under international law. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said his message to people “moved and outraged by the plight of the Palestinian people” is: “We hear you. You were right.”
But the government has not lifted the ban on Palestine Action, and the group continues to challenge its proscription in court.
The High Court ruled in February that classing Palestine Action as a terror group alongside the likes of al Qaeda and Hamas was disproportionate and unlawful. The Court of Appeal overturned that decision in June, saying outlawing the group was “justified and proportionate”.
Next month the group’s lawyers will ask the country’s top court, the UK Supreme Court, to quash the ban.
John Clegg, a bookseller at the London Review Bookshop, told the Guardian that Rooney’s stance could help in changing the law.
“Good on her for taking a stand, it seems a ridiculous law. If this thing convinces the Home Office to move faster to get rid of it, I’m all for it.”
(FRANCE 24 with AP)

Beyond legal advice: Hong Kong charity helps bridge the gap in access to justice
Spirit of Hong Kong Awards finalist Pro Bono HK links people in need with lawyers, social workers and community groups, while promoting legal education
Pro Bono HK is known for helping people in need access justice in Hong Kong, but its work extends beyond legal advice to connecting clients with social workers and community groups for further support and promoting legal education.
Founded in 2014, the organisation helps people who may not qualify for legal aid or cannot afford private representation. Its work ranges from tenancy and family disputes to inheritance matters and emergency legal support.
Pro Bono HK and its volunteers are finalists for the Spirit of Teamwork Award in this year’s Spirit of Hong Kong Awards, co-organised by Sino Group and the South China Morning Post.
CEO Vincent Yeung said founder Davyd Wong established the organisation to improve access to justice for people unable to obtain help through either private legal services or Hong Kong’s legal aid system.

China protests Estonian politicians attending a Taiwanese event in Tallinn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
06:15:00 UTC
15:15:00 KST

China protests Estonian politicians attending a Taiwanese event in Tallinn
The Embassy of the People's Republic of China in Estonia submitted a formal diplomatic note to the Riigikogu over lawmakers' attendance at an event celebrating Taiwan's National Day in Tallinn.
In the note, the embassy expressed concern that Riigikogu members Marko Mihkelson (Reform), Peeter Tali (Eesti 200), Kristo Enn Vaga (Reform), Kalle Laanet (Reform), Jüri Jaanson (Reform), Riina Sikkut (SDE), Anti Poolamets (EKRE) and Evelin Poolamets (EKRE) attended a reception marking the National Day of the Republic of China (Taiwan) in Tallinn on September 29, organized by the Taipei Representative Office in Latvia.
The embassy recalled that Estonia has made a clear commitment to recognize the government of the People's Republic of China as the sole legitimate government of China and Taiwan as an inalienable part of Chinese territory.
"The government of the Republic of Estonia has undertaken not to establish formal or official relations with Taiwan in any form," the Chinese Embassy said.
"Members of the Riigikogu are officials of an Estonian state institution. The attendance of the aforementioned Riigikogu members at the 'reception' can be regarded as a form of official interaction with Taiwan, which violates the commitments made and undermines China's sovereignty and territorial integrity," the note said.
The embassy called on the Riigikogu members in question to adhere to the one-China principle and exercise caution in their words and actions concerning Taiwan to avoid further damage to bilateral relations.
The Chinese Embassy has also sent diplomatic notes in previous years over Riigikogu members' contacts with Taiwan. The most recent such note was sent last summer, following a visit to Taiwan by the Riigikogu's Estonia-Taiwan Parliamentary Friendship Group.
The parliamentary group plans to continue attending events
According to Kristo Enn Vaga, chairman of the Riigikogu Estonia-Taiwan Parliamentary Friendship Group, it has become something of a tradition for the Chinese Embassy to send diplomatic notes whenever the group attends Taiwan-related events.
"When communist China writes that I or other Riigikogu members are doing something wrong, I take it as a compliment because it must mean I'm doing something right," Vaga said.
He noted that although Estonia has diplomatic relations with China, no foreign country can dictate what members of the Riigikogu may or may not do.
"Estonia does not recognize Taiwan as a state and there are no plans to change that. But from a pragmatic perspective, we see Taiwan, with the world's fastest-growing economy, as a potential partner," Vaga said.
Vaga emphasized that Estonia and Taiwan have cooperated on several projects. For example, the Taiwanese government has made financial contributions in cooperation with Estonia to support Ukraine.
"Thanks to these donations, a family home was opened in Zhytomyr Oblast at the end of the summer. It was built entirely with funding from the Taiwanese government and the project was carried out by ESTDEV, the Estonian government agency responsible for humanitarian aid."
According to Vaga, economic cooperation with China is being scaled back.
"This has also been highlighted in the Estonian Foreign Intelligence Service's annual reports, which say that reducing dependence on China would be advisable, particularly in the technology sector, as it could become a security threat. Even now, the use of Chinese technology in certain critical sectors may pose a security threat to Estonia," Vaga said.
The Estonia-Taiwan Parliamentary Friendship Group has no intention of yielding to Chinese criticism.
"I personally, along with many of my colleagues, intend to continue engaging with Taiwan just as actively as we have in the past and Chinese criticism or diplomatic notes certainly won't change that," Vaga said.

====================================================================================================

Prices of soviet-era apartments in Riga remain at 2006 levels, while wages have increased 4.5 times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
06:08:09 UTC
15:08:09 KST

Apartments in Soviet-era residential buildings still account for nearly half of all housing transactions in Riga, with 3,626 transactions registered in the city by October this year. Although transaction prices in some neighbourhoods have increased by 5–7% since the beginning of the year, the current price per square metre in these apartment buildings is comparable to levels recorded back in 2006. At the same time, today’s buyers are in a very different financial position: average wages have increased 4.5 times, while monthly mortgage payments have remained almost unchanged.
Real estate agency Latio has observed that, alongside the basic need for housing, strong demand for apartments in Soviet-era buildings is also driven by investment interest and rising property prices in neighbouring countries, a trend that could eventually affect Latvia as well.
“If we look at the Vilnius market, where property prices, including apartments in Soviet-era residential buildings, have at least doubled, buying a home in Riga seems like a logical decision. We will not escape rising property prices in the coming years either,” says Ksenija Ijevleva.
Low Mortgage Payments Also Encourage Purchases
Despite the growing market for newly built residential developments and buyers’ preference for modern, high-quality renovated homes, apartments in Soviet-era buildings remain the most affordable option for many households.
Looking at housing prices over a longer period, Latio concludes that an apartment in a Soviet-era residential building in Riga’s neighbourhoods costs approximately the same as it did 20 years ago — an average of just under EUR 1,200 per square metre.
However, this does not mean prices have remained static. The market has experienced periods of growth, a sharp decline following the financial crisis, and a prolonged recovery. Even today, price growth for apartments in Soviet-era buildings remains moderate.
For example, in the third quarter of this year, the average price per square metre of internal apartment space in neighbourhoods on the left bank of the Daugava River increased by just under 7% compared with the beginning of the year. In neighbourhoods on the right bank, prices rose by approximately 4%, while apartments in Soviet-era buildings in the city centre recorded an increase of around 2%.
Much more significant changes have occurred in average net wages, which have increased more than 4.5 times since 2006 — from EUR 308 to EUR 1,400.
Twenty years ago, a mortgage payment would have accounted for approximately 90% of an average monthly salary. Today, the equivalent figure is less than 20%.
For example, the estimated monthly mortgage payment for a 55-square-metre apartment in a Riga neighbourhood, financed with an 85% mortgage over 30 years, would have been EUR 285 in 2006, compared with EUR 270 in 2026.
According to Ijevleva, buyers planning to purchase property with a mortgage primarily assess their ability to cover the monthly repayments. Apartments in Soviet-era buildings offer some of the most manageable mortgage payments, making affordability one of the main drivers of demand.
“Buyers first want to understand how much they will have to pay the bank each month. For someone earning EUR 1,500 net per month, a longer mortgage term with a monthly payment of EUR 300 is a more affordable option, while an apartment in a new development may exceed their financial means.
“If their income continues to grow over time, they become more confident in their ability to maintain these payments in the long term. This is precisely why practical considerations determine the choice of an apartment in a Soviet-era building — above all, the opportunity to buy a home now,” Ijevleva explains.
She adds that high prices in new residential developments are redirecting some demand towards older apartment buildings, particularly among buyers willing to compromise on the building’s condition, location, and overall housing quality to stay within their budgets.
At the same time, the supply of apartments available for sale is gradually declining, creating conditions for further price increases.
Buyers Expect Prices to Move Closer to Neighbouring Countries
Another motivation for purchasing apartments in Soviet-era residential buildings is the desire to protect savings against inflation.
For many buyers, a small apartment in a Lithuanian-type prefabricated building or a Khrushchev-era apartment block represents a straightforward investment. Such properties can be rented out to generate regular income, potentially covering monthly mortgage payments, and sold at a later date.
This gives buyers the prospect of both rental income and long-term capital appreciation.
The largest share of apartments currently available for sale in Soviet-era buildings consists of so-called Lithuanian-type residential projects, both older and newer versions, which account for more than 20% of the market.
Approximately 17% of available properties are located in brick and prefabricated concrete-panel Khrushchev-era buildings, while a similar share consists of apartments in Series 602 buildings.
Apartments in Series 103 and Series 119 buildings, as well as Czech-type residential projects, appear considerably less frequently in property listings.
Although many buyers are concerned about the remaining service life of Soviet-era residential buildings, Ijevleva emphasises that purchasing an apartment also means investing in its location and the opportunities to use the property for different purposes.
“As long as there is demand for rental housing in a particular neighbourhood and apartments in new developments remain too expensive, the market for Soviet-era apartments will remain active.
“The logic is simple: buy while prices still seem low, rent out the property, and wait until selling prices rise.”
Examples can be found just across the border.
In Vilnius’s most sought-after residential districts, transaction prices for two-room apartments in Soviet-era buildings have increased by 18% over the past year.
Furthermore, the price gap between Vilnius and Riga is substantial.
For example, a two-room apartment in a Lithuanian-type residential building in the densely populated and popular Žirmūnai district of Vilnius is advertised at EUR 3,200 per square metre.
By comparison, an apartment of similar size and condition in Riga’s nearby Purvciems neighbourhood can be purchased for approximately EUR 1,200 per square metre.
“When you see how much an almost identical property costs in Vilnius, it is easy to feel that real estate in Riga is still relatively inexpensive. Taking inflation into account, this encourages buyers not to postpone their purchases.
“However, higher property prices in neighbouring countries do not automatically mean that prices will rise in Latvia at the same pace.
“Prices will certainly increase, but the question is whether this will happen in three, five, or ten years.
“Vilnius and Tallinn have different economic conditions and investment dynamics, which also contribute to property price growth.
“An apartment in a Soviet-era residential building can certainly be a good investment in Riga as well, but investors need to be patient,” Ijevleva concludes.

Doomsday Glacier will keep melting even if oceans cool. Here’s why cutting emissions still matters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
06:02:15 UTC
15:02:15 KST

The total collapse of Thwaites Glacier, known as the Doomsday Glacier, would contribute an estimated 65cm to global sea level rise.
Thwaites Glacier, aka the ‘Doomsday Glacier’, will keep melting even if our turbocharged oceans cool down, scientists have warned.
The world’s oceans reached their highest daily temperature on record this summer, with sea surfaces outside the polar regions averaging 21.1°C on 22 August. With El Niño still intensifying in the Pacific, it is unlikely temperatures will drop dramatically in the near future.
But even under the “most extreme ocean cooling conditions imagined”, new research led by British Antarctic Survey (BAS) has found that the Doomsday Glacier, located in West Antarctica, will continue losing ice for at least the next 150 years.
The total collapse of the ice sheet would contribute an estimated 65cm to global sea level rise. To put that into perspective, for every centimetre of sea level rise around an additional six million people on the planet are exposed to coastal flooding.
‘Unavoidable future ice loss’ for Doomsday Glacier
Researchers ran a modelling experiment for Thwaites Glacier and its neighbour Pine Island Glacier, which are currently the largest contributors to ice loss from this area of Antarctica.
They completely switched off the melting effects of the ocean – driven by climate change – beneath both glaciers in three independent computer models.
Published in the science journal Geophysical Research Letters, the study revealed a “striking difference” between how the two glaciers fared over a 150-year period.
Pine Island Glacier responded as scientists might have expected. Under the modelling, the ice sheet stopped melting and began thickening – advancing back towards the position it held in the first half of the 20th century.
However, Thwaites Glacier continued to lose ice, even without any ocean melting. The rate of ice loss slowed down over time as the glacier thinned.
“These results show that past changes in ocean-driven melting have now committed us to unavoidable future ice loss from Thwaites Glacier,” says Dr Rosie Williams, a glaciologist at BAS and lead author of the paper.
“This ice loss cannot be undone or prevented by simply cooling the ocean.”
Can we stop the Doomsday Glacier melting?
A zero-melting scenario would never occur in the real world, as the presence of seawater below glacier ice alone is enough to cause some level of melting.
BAS ocean modeller and co-author of the report Professor Paul Holland explains that the Thwaites Glacier started to retreat in the 1940s, with the warming of our oceans becoming a “major factor” driving ice loss.
While the simulations show that historical melting of Thwaites Glacier has “committed future generations to the challenges of sea level rise”, the ice loss will be further exacerbated if the world does not reduce and ideally reverse the emissions of greenhouse gases.
“We don’t yet know if Antarctica’s other major glaciers are moving into a state of committed change,” Holland says.
“We urgently need to take action to modify the human activities that are driving changes in ocean melting of these glaciers.”

The number of foreign residents in Japan reached a record 4.28 million at the close of June 2026, accounting for 3.4% of the country's total population, according to data released by the Immigration Services Agency, Qazinform News Agency cites Kyodo.
The figure increased by approximately 155,000 compared with the end of 2025.
Despite the growth in the foreign resident population, tighter immigration regulations have affected some visa categories. Widespread service disruptions

The company offered fee relief to eligible cloud and Yandex 360 customers and worked with alternative providers, including Selectel, VK Cloud and K2 Cloud, to migrate affected corporate clients’ data and services.
The outages also affected Yandex applications in neighbouring Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan, where users reported problems with taxi bookings and food delivery.
AI infrastructure under pressure
The targeted Yandex facilities housed two of the company’s three supercomputers used to train its YandexGPT model, as well as infrastructure supporting business cloud services. The extent of damage to the AI hardware remains unclear.
Separately, Sberbank First Deputy Chairman Alexander Vedyakhin said a drone struck the bank’s data centre in Balakovo, in Russia’s Saratov region, on Wednesday. He said no employees were injured and the bank’s systems continued operating normally.
Regional Governor Roman Busargin said the attack also damaged residential buildings and killed one person.
Moscow reviews data centre security
Russia’s Digital Development Minister Maksut Shadayev told a State Duma committee that his ministry was working with the Defence Ministry on measures to protect data centres against drone attacks.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said the government was discussing the disruptions, adding that it was too early to assess potential financial losses or determine whether compensation would be provided.
Russian data centre operators are also reportedly seeking additional protective equipment and upgrading defences around critical facilities.
The attacks follow Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries, fuel depots and logistics infrastructure.
Since mid-July, drone attacks have also hit warehouses operated by e-commerce companies Wildberries and Ozon, forcing changes to distribution and delivery operations.

UK ‘an outlier in Europe’ for letting Farage and other politicians present TV shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
06:00:54 UTC
15:00:54 KST

The UK has been confirmed as an outlier in Europe for allowing Nigel Farage and other serving politicians to present TV shows covering current affairs, according to an unprecedented analysis of broadcasting rules.
Farage is one of a series of Reform UK figures who are permitted to present shows on the rightwing network GB News. The Reform MP Lee Anderson and former candidate Matt Goodwin also have regular slots on the channel.
Their status as presenters has led to repeated concerns about the enforcement of Britain’s rules on impartial broadcasting.
Last month, Farage used his first GB News show for six months to defend his party’s decision to accept two record £36m donations from the crypto billionaires Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo.
However, an international study has confirmed that the UK’s decision to allow politicians to present such shows is highly unusual across Europe. In 35 of the 37 European nations studied, regulators found no recent examples of serving politicians presenting news or current affairs programmes. Only Iceland, which has a population of about 400,000 people, and Malta bucked the trend.
In Malta, political parties are even permitted to own television channels. There have been instances where MPs have presented interview programmes, although according to its regulator these are not the norm.
Eight countries – including France, Georgia and Norway – expressly ban politicians from presenting news or current affairs programmes, either through broadcasting legislation or other restrictions.
The practice is constrained indirectly in 26 countries via rules covering impartiality, transparency or independence from government.
Three countries – Armenia, Finland and Malta – had no specific legislation or regulation covering the issue. However, regulators in Armenia and Finland reported no examples of it occurring.
The study, by an academic from the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism for the Demos thinktank, will be used as evidence by critics who believe that Ofcom, Britain’s media regulator, has failed to protect impartiality by allowing the politician-led shows.
Ofcom has said that such shows are within broadcasting rules because they are classed as “current affairs” shows by the watchdog, rather than news programmes – a distinction that has been challenged by critics, given the politicians regularly discuss some of the biggest news stories of the day.
The analysis, by the research associate Dr James Painter, found the issue had only caused a serious debate in the UK. “This demonstrates the extent to which the UK is an outlier in Europe with regards to the practice of political presenting news and/or current affairs programmes and the regulatory framework that surrounds it,” the analysis concluded.
Lisa Nandy, the culture secretary, has previously raised concerns about allowing serving politicians to present TV shows and has said she was “exploring action in this space”. However, it remains unclear whether she is considering a change in the law.
GB News has always said Reform politicians are allowed to present current affairs programmes under Ofcom’s rules – a point it has proved in court. Angelos Frangopoulos, its chief executive, has also said its coverage includes a range of political perspectives.
An Ofcom spokesperson said: “Ofcom’s broadcasting code … is clear that no politician may be used as a newsreader, interviewer or reporter in any news programmes unless, exceptionally, it is editorially justified.
“While politicians are permitted to present non-news programmes – provided they are not standing in an election taking place – such programmes must still comply with the other due impartiality rules in the code.
“The code contains rules which Ofcom considers best secure the standards objectives set by parliament – including the special protection afforded to news over non-news content. Changes to the standards objectives are rightly a matter for government and parliament.”

Speaking to the Guardian’s editor-in-chief, Katharine Viner, at NAZA’s UK premiere in London on Thursday night, Glazer, who is an executive producer on the film, said he was “shocked into silence” the first time he watched NAZA, which is produced by the Guardian and details Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza.
He noted that it was “clearly in dialogue” with and “deals with very similar themes” to The Zone of Interest, the 2023 historical drama he directed and that depicted the mundane daily lives of Nazi officers overseeing the extermination of Jews at Auschwitz.
“Both films deal with dehumanisation,” Glazer said. “And how we get to where we do as a species by othering and dehumanising, and what that then leads to.”
The Israeli government has promoted an online film project that mimics the style of NAZA in an attempt to counter the film’s findings. When asked whether he was surprised by the intense reaction of the Israeli government to NAZA, Glazer said some of it was expected but that, “in my point of view, it was much more venal” than anticipated.
Abraham said the film allows viewers to look at the “mechanisms that allow human beings to do this to other human beings”, and Szor said the idea to shoot footage looking inside Tel Aviv citizens’ apartments was to focus on the “ritual” of people gathering around the TV to watch the “news and to see the absence or justification” of the devastation happening in Gaza.
NAZA is in UK cinemas and will be shown in more than 50 countries. As well as its global cinema releases, NAZA will be available free on the Guardian’s website from late November. When the film opened in Italy last month, it surpassed the Marvel movie Avengers Endgame: Encore to open at No 1.
The film contains 24 interviews with Israeli military insiders who detail how an AI-assisted apparatus of mass surveillance was activated during the Gaza war, revealing the systems that were used to target Hamas operatives in the knowledge that large numbers of Palestinian civilians would also die.
Various bodies, including the UN, Amnesty International, B’Tselem and Physicians for Human Rights, the latter two of which are Israeli-based, have said Israel is committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.
The film premiered at the Venice film festival, where it was met with a 25-minute standing ovation – a festival record. The documentary went on to win the special jury prize.
Israeli government officials have attempted to discredit NAZA’s content, while far-right activists have threatened to hunt down the directors.
The Israel Defense Forces’ chief of staff, Eyal Zamir, has said they will use “every tool at our disposal” against the film, while the military has issued a 10-page response to NAZA, which was based on interviews with more than 100 sources with knowledge of the military systems used in the war.
Demonstrators have gathered outside the home of Szor’s parents, demanding that she face the death penalty, and a mural depicting the film-makers through the sights of a gun appeared in the Israeli city of Ashdod.
Szor and Abraham addressed the backlash to their documentary at a Q&A after its New York premiere. “Our country is doing so much to hide these systems,” Szor told the audience. “It’s not a world that is open even to the Israeli public.”
The Zone of Interest won the Oscar for best international film in 2024. Accepting the award, Glazer said he refuted his “Jewishness and the Holocaust being hijacked by an occupation which has led to conflict for so many innocent people” in Gaza and Israel, comments that led to backlash and an outpouring of support.
He went on to say: “All our choices were made to reflect and confront us in the present, not to say look what they did then, but rather look what we do now. Our film shows where dehumanisation leads at its worst. It’s shaped all of our past and present.”
