Ülle Madise on 51-aastane ja pärit Tartust. Aastatel 2015–2026 töötas Madise õiguskantslerina. Esimesed ametlikud visiidid presidendina tegi Madise Lätti ja Soome.
Ukraina rünnakute järel vähenes Yandexi liiklus Eesti veebilehtedele ligi 100 protsenti
Venemaa Yandexi võrgust Eesti veebilehtedele tulev liiklus vähenes pärast Ukraina rünnakuid ettevõtte andmekeskustele peaaegu nullini.
Riigi infosüsteemi ameti (RIA) teatel langes 13. oktoobriks Yandexi päringute arv septembri keskmisega võrreldes 420 korda. Kokku vähenes päringute arv 99,8 protsenti.
Ukraina ründas eelmisel nädalal kolme Yandexi andmekeskust, mis asuvad Moskva lähedal, Sasovos ja Kalugas.
RIA sõnul on veel vara öelda, kas see mõjutab Venemaa küberrünnakuid Eesti vastu. Rünnakuteks kasutatakse Yandexist sõltumatuid süsteeme.
Politsei pidas Tallinnas Nõmmel kinni kümme ebaseaduslikult riigis viibinud inimest
Politsei pidas pühapäeva õhtul Tallinnas Nõmme linnaosas kinni kümme ebaseaduslikult Eestis viibinud inimest. Neist üheksa viidi kinnipidamiskeskusesse ja üks haiglasse.
Kella 19.30 paiku sai politsei teate kahest mehest, kes seisid Valdeku tänaval ühe maja juures ja paistsid olevat eksinud. Politsei pidas mõlemad mehed kinni. Tegemist oli Sudaani kodanikega, kes viibisid Eestis ebaseaduslikult.
Mehed rääkisid politseile, et läheduses varjavad end veel teisedki. Politsei asus piirkonda läbi otsima, kasutades droone, maastikusõidukeid ja koeri. Otsingutel aitas ka päästeamet.
Droon märkas metsas liikuvaid inimesi ning politsei leidis sealt veel kaheksa meest. Üks meestest kukkus põgenedes ja vigastas kätt.
Kõik kümme meest viibisid Eestis ebaseaduslikult ning isikut tõendav dokument oli neist vaid ühel.
Hiiumaal ei saa naised enam sünnitada
Alates juulist ei saa Hiiumaa naised enam kodusaarel sünnitada. Endiselt pole selge, kuidas korraldada sünnitajate transport mandrile ja tagasi ning kes selle eest maksab.
Kärdlas elav Kärolyn Kivistik ootab oma viiendat last, kelle sünnitähtaeg on 8. novembril. Haiglakott on tal juba pakitud. Kuna ta ei soovi sünnituse ajal reisida, läheb ta tõenäoliselt nädal varem Tallinna. Pere hinnangul kaasneb sellega ligi 1000 eurot lisakulusid.
Hiiumaa haiglas on sünnitusabi osutamiseks vajalikud ruumid ja seadmed, kuid puuduvad töötajad. Lastearst läks juulist pensionile ning septembris puudus neljal päeval ka naistearst.
Haigla juhi Riina Tamme sõnul esitati esmaspäeval haigla nõukogule tegevuskava, kuid sünnitajate mandrile ja sealt tagasi toomise küsimus on endiselt lahendamata.
Tamme hinnangul on tegemist regionaalpoliitilise probleemiga, mis ei puuduta ainult Hiiumaad.
Eesti esimene selge keele standard aitab tekste arusaadavamaks muuta
Oktoobri alguses jõustus Eesti esimene selge keele standard, mis annab soovitusi avaliku teabe arusaadavamaks kirjutamiseks.
Standardi koostanud komisjoni juhtinud Kristel Ressi sõnul tuleb teksti kirjutades kõigepealt mõelda sellele, kes seda lugema hakkab. Näiteks külmas paadis telefonist juhiste lugemine erineb kodus teksti lugemisest.
Ressi sõnul on standard abivahend, mitte rangete reeglite kogum. Ta sedastas, et esimest korda on kõik need soovitused koondatud ühte lühikesse juhendisse.
ERR-i keeletoimetaja Ester Põldma sõnul on soovitustest kasu kõigile, kes kirjutavad veebitekste. "Lugeja peaks juba esimesel lugemisel aru saama, mida lausega öelda tahetakse," ütles Põldma.

US sanctions leave Iranians facing flight cancellations and soaring costs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
05:51:40 UTC
14:51:40 KST

US sanctions leave Iranians facing flight cancellations and soaring costs
New US aviation sanctions force Iranians to take longer, costlier journeys as international flight routes disappear.
In late September, travellers could still fly directly from Tehran to Dubai in less than three hours, with a ticket costing between $100 and $200.
Less than a month later, it can take up to 18 hours to make the same journey and cost more than $1,000.
The change is the result of a new round of United States sanctions targeting Iranian airlines and foreign companies providing them with services. The restrictions intensified after a September 23 deadline for companies to stop servicing Iranian carriers, leading to the suspension of direct flights between Iran and the United Arab Emirates, as well as a number of other countries.
The United States has sought to block routes into and out of Iran and, more broadly, restrict access to the country. In August, the US announced Operation Economic Outcast as a means of increasing pressure on Iran, targeting the few remaining sectors of the Iranian economy still connected to the global economy.
As part of the campaign, the US sanctioned 27 airlines operating in Iran. Airports, fuel suppliers, ground-handling service providers and other foreign companies working with Iranian airlines were threatened with secondary sanctions, potentially cutting them off from the US financial system.
The first sign of the impact of the new sanctions came on September 24, when an Iranian flight travelling from Tehran to Dushanbe was forced to turn back mid-journey and return to Tehran after it was denied permission to enter Turkmenistan’s airspace.
The UAE, Azerbaijan, and Georgia also suspended services for Iranian flights. Flights between Iran and Muscat and Baghdad were halted, while a number of flights from Iran to neighbouring Turkiye were cancelled. Flights from Iran to the popular Shia pilgrimage destination of Najaf in Iraq were also briefly disrupted in late September.
All this was happening against the backdrop of the US-Israeli war on Iran, which had already caused widespread disruption to the country’s international air links. The vast majority of international airlines have yet to resume their services to Iran.
Flights to countries including China and Russia have continued despite the latest US measures, but restoring suspended routes will require negotiations with other governments.
Mass disruption
More than three weeks after the new aviation sanctions came into effect, routes to destinations including Moscow, Najaf, Istanbul, Yerevan and Guangzhou in China have continued operating. But Iran’s international flight network remains severely restricted.
The situation has created major disruption for both people travelling to Iran and those leaving the country.
Amir, 43, who lives in the US state of Illinois, described the challenges his ailing mother faced in attempting to travel to Iran.
“My mother lives in the United States, but her medical records are in Iran,” he said. “For months, her medical appointments have been delayed because of the war and the conditions it has created.
“A few weeks ago, we decided to take advantage of the relative calm and make a trip to Iran so she could receive medical care. But then the new sanctions were announced, effectively disrupting flights to Iran.
“Now, to get to Iran, we have to fly to Istanbul and wait there for several hours or even several days, depending on when a flight to Iran is available,” Amir said, adding that it was also difficult to purchase Iranian airline tickets from outside the country as a result of international sanctions.
“Making such a journey is extremely stressful for a woman travelling alone who is also ill. It is completely unfair.”
The sanctions have also had a significant impact on Iran’s domestic travel.
Majid Hosseini-Nejad, the founder of Alibaba Travel Group, one of the country’s largest online platforms for booking travel tickets and accommodation, told Al Jazeera that the new sanctions had affected ticket sales.
“As a result of the recent sanctions, around 20 percent of the flights operating from Iran to international destinations have been suspended,” Hosseini-Nejad said. “This has reduced revenues for airline ticket-booking services. Airlines’ revenues have also fallen significantly because of the sanctions.”
On October 11, Iran’s Foreign Ministry announced that its Department of Economic Affairs was continuing efforts to facilitate Iranian flights to destinations in other countries.
Flights to and from Iran continue to face lengthy delays, last-minute cancellations and, in some cases, even diversions back to their point of departure.
For now, Iranian travellers have little clarity about when the situation might change.
Another traveller named Amir, an Iranian national who flies regularly between Iran and Oman for work, said, “Beyond the other financial losses caused by the sanctions, flight cancellations have added another layer of difficulty to our lives. Every trip between Muscat and Tehran now takes several times longer and costs several times more than before.
“It is unclear when the situation will change, or whether it will improve at all.”

Russia takes control of more European corporate assets ahead of Zelenskiy's appearance at EU summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
05:50:24 UTC
14:50:24 KST

Russia takes over more EU companies' assets over Ukraine support
MOSCOW, Oct 16 - Russia has seized control of the local assets of four companies from France, Germany, Sweden and Belgium, according to a decree by President Vladimir Putin, in retaliation for Europe's wartime support for Ukraine.
Thursday's decree listed assets belonging to French flooring maker Tarkett, German packaging maker Menshen, Swedish packaging maker Sverige International Holdings and Belgian hygiene product company Ontex.
The decree also listed Russian assets of former European metal-packaging business Eviosys acquired by US packaging group Sonoco in December 2024. The decree listed the assets as owned by Sonoco's Dutch unit.
EU leaders rallied around President Volodymyr Zelenskiy at a summit on Friday at one of the most difficult moments for Ukraine amid fears that the US could pull back intelligence sharing and weapons support from Kyiv.
The Kremlin said that the assets' takeover continued a trend after a similar move last month against food giant Nestle and retailers Auchan and Metro.
"Their country of origin was one of the factors taken into account in making the decision," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said, adding that these countries were involved in "illegal expropriations of Russian property."
Temporary administration of the European companies' properties was handed to Russian companies that had been largely unknown.
PUTIN NOTES 'DOWNSIDES'
Ontex, which employs 350 people in Russia and operates a factory outside Moscow, said it has been informed about the decree and will "consider appropriate actions to safeguard its assets and the continuity of Ontex Russia’s operations."
Sonoco said in its 2025 report that it had finalised its own exit from Russia in 2022 but acquired more assets, making up 0.5% of the company's total, as part of the Eviosys deal.
Tarkett said it was "losing effective control over its operations in Russia" and was assessing the situation.
The Kremlin said the measures responded to EU nations' involvement in "direct battlefield hostilities" but were also "reversible."
Speaking to Russian businessmen just before the decree was published on Thursday, Putin acknowledged that taking Western assets had "certain downsides" without giving more details.
He urged the Russian businesses taking over the assets to seek domestic financing sources instead.
Putin cited the 2008 global financial crisis, which had a profound impact on the Russian economy, as an example of the risks of excessive exposure to global markets. He said foreign countries pursued their own interests through investment.
There have been some reports that the US could seek control of some Russian assets frozen in Europe as part of efforts to provide incentives for Russia to negotiate with Ukraine.
Russia criticises the EU for freezing about €210 billion ($238 billion) of its sovereign assets in response to the war and for targeting assets belonging to Russian companies in Europe and other Western countries. REUTERS

14:50:07 KST

Istanbul Airport ranked as Europe’s busiest airport during the week of Oct. 5-11, averaging 1,530 arriving and departing flights a day, according to EUROCONTROL.
Amsterdam Schiphol followed with 1,386 daily flights, ahead of Paris Charles de Gaulle with 1,361, Frankfurt with 1,358 and Madrid Barajas with 1,305.
Antalya Airport ranked 10th with an average of 909 flights a day.
Türkiye placed sixth among European countries for arrivals and departures, averaging 3,837 daily flights, down 2 percent from the previous week.
The United Kingdom led with 6,067 daily flights, followed by Spain with 5,961, Germany with 5,585, Italy with 4,625 and France with 4,343.
The report also said traffic between Europe and the Middle East, excluding overflights, remained 14 percent below 2025 levels so far this year. EUROCONTROL put the decline from pre-crisis levels in January and February at 20 percent.
Flight levels at Emirates, Etihad Airways and Qatar Airways remained 23 percent below pre-crisis levels, compared with around 82 percent for European carriers.
Israeli airlines were operating 56 percent above pre-crisis levels.
Across the European network, arrival punctuality stood at 74.1 percent and departure punctuality at 69.8 percent, both lower than in the same week of 2025.
Air traffic flow management delays averaged 2.5 minutes per flight.
Jet fuel prices reached $4.82 per gallon on Oct. 9, up 2 percent over the preceding two weeks.
The October average to date was $4.74 per gallon, 2.5 percent above September’s average of $4.63.

To live better I need to live differently. It might seem obvious that I can only change my life by changing what I do, but I often want to avoid this fact. I might occasionally admit that some kind of change is needed, but the actual action of change does not follow.
My failure to act is evidence of a profound attachment, one that pervades my entire life. It is an attachment to all of the behaviours and habits to which I have become accustomed. Because I am attached to this way of living, I believe that no genuine alternative to it exists. But it is precisely here that change is most needed.
It is my existing pattern of life that keeps me from seeing what I must do to live more joyfully. To expect things to improve without making changes to this pattern would be foolish. For the improvement I desperately need is not a minor shift towards slightly less stress or slightly more happiness but the total transformation of suffering into joy.

India's Reliance Industries rejected on Friday suggestions it was blocking Elon Musk's Starlink satellite internet service in the country, saying it welcomed competition and had "never feared" rivals.
The statement came days after the tech billionaire accused "oligarchs" of preventing Starlink's rollout in India to protect their monopolies, reigniting a long-running debate over access to the country's lucrative telecommunications market.
"We see it as the truest test of who serves the customer best," Reliance said in a statement. "We welcome competition in satellite communications, including Starlink."
The conglomerate, owned by billionaire Mukesh Ambani, said it was responding to recent remarks about Reliance and the Indian market but did not directly name Musk.
The potential launch of Starlink, which provides high-speed internet access to remote locations by low Earth orbit satellites, has seen fierce debate in India over issues ranging from pricing to spectrum allocation.
In March 2025, telecom operator Jio Platforms, Reliance's digital arm, signed an agreement with Musk's SpaceX to offer Starlink services to its customers.
However, Starlink has yet to launch, with Jio's own satellite service still awaiting regulatory clearance.
Earlier this month, Musk wrote on X that Starlink was being "blocked" in India.
"Unfortunately, we are being blocked by certain oligarchs in order to maintain their monopolistic chokehold on the Indian people," Musk said.
"You can guess who they are... This is a crime against the people of India!"
In a subsequent post, Musk addressed Ambani directly, calling him "prime minister" in an apparent jibe at his perceived closeness with Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
Soon after, India's communications ministry, without mentioning Musk, said the government maintained a "fair and non-discriminatory authorisation framework" for all telecom services.
Reliance said on Friday that every operator, including Jio, "must serve the people of India and abide by the laws and policies of the land".
The dispute comes as Reliance pushes deeper into telecommunications and digital services, key pillars of Ambani's drive to diversify the conglomerate beyond its oil refining and petrochemicals roots.
The comments also follow Jio's announcement this week that it plans to raise $3.2 billion in what would be India's largest initial public offering, after unveiling pricing details ahead of next week's share sale.

Small investors first in fund repayment plan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
05:42:05 UTC
14:42:05 KST

Small investors would receive priority in interim payments of up to 1 million Turkish Liras per investor under a fund liquidation bill, one of its sponsors has said.
“Our main principle is to make payments starting with the smallest investors,” ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) lawmaker Ersan Aksu told parliament’s Plan and Budget Committee on Oct. 14.
The committee approved the bill, which still requires approval by parliament’s general assembly.
Explaining how payments would depend on available cash, Aksu gave the example of a fund holding 1.5 million liras. Investors with net investments of 200,000 liras and 800,000 liras would receive those amounts in full.
An investor owed 2 million liras would receive the remaining 500,000 liras, while another with 10 million liras would receive no payment in that round.
Aksu said further interim payments would follow as assets were converted into cash and money was recovered. The process would involve the Savings Deposit Insurance Fund (TMSF) and extend to the personal assets of portfolio company owners, founders and managers held liable for losses.
Deputy Treasury and Finance Minister İlhan Hatipoğlu said authorities had made 48 requests to 29 countries for information on the assets of 278 individuals and legal entities.
Hasan Kaymak, head of the Financial Crimes Investigation Board (MASAK), said some transactions were not recorded, complicating asset tracing.
He said the agency had repeatedly contacted foreign-based cryptocurrency service providers to ask whether relevant transfers had taken place.
In an interview with daily Milliyet published on Oct. 16, Parliament Speaker Numan Kurtulmuş described the alleged diversion of investors’ savings as “immoral and dishonorable.”
He called for everyone responsible to be identified and held accountable, saying the public expected accountability in the courts.
Asked about statements by conservative civil society groups, Kurtulmuş said wrongdoing should be investigated regardless of the religious identity of those involved.

Estonia's €50m planned island e-ferry passes first model tests with flying colors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
05:40:00 UTC
14:40:00 KST

Estonia's €50m planned island e-ferry passes first model tests with flying colors
A scale model of Estonia's planned €49.93 million electric ferry has passed its first tests in Germany, reaching 14 knots where the contract requires 12.
The boat, once built, will be the fifth ferry in the fleet serving Saaremaa, Muhu and Hiiumaa, and is planned for the Virtsu–Kuivastu route. It will be Estonia's first shore-charged electric ferry.
The week-long tests at the Schiffbau-Versuchsanstalt Potsdam center evaluated the vessel's seagoing and hydrodynamic properties and checked energy efficiency and propulsion solutions, the State Fleet said. Ice model tests follow in Finland in late November.
Model testing allows planned solutions to be checked and improved before construction begins. The tests used an 8.2-meter scale model of the hull matches the planned vessel's shape and proportions exactly, fitted with accurate scale copies of its drives and propellers.
Eero Avi, a shipbuilding engineer and chief specialist with the State Fleet's (Riigilaevastik) ferry project, attended the tests and said they showed good work had been done on the hull design. Energy consumption is low for the vessel's size and remains within contract limits, with some margin.
"The tests showed that although the construction contract sets the vessel's maximum speed at 12 knots, the model was able to reach 14 knots, with some power reserve still remaining," Avi added.
Ice model testing takes place at the end of November at Railotech's ice model basin in Helsinki, checking the hull and propulsion system's performance in level ice of varying thickness and in brash ice, meaning an accumulation of floating sea ice or river ice made up of small fragments not more than 2 meters across.
The project is co-financed by the EU Modernization Fund, whose terms require the new vessel to be significantly more energy-efficient than existing ones.
The full-sized ferry will have a 3 MWh battery, allowing fully electric operation in normal conditions on the route. Biodiesel generators will keep service running in heavier seas and emergencies, and its range without refuelling is at least 1,000 nautical miles.
The actual ship when build will be close to 100 meters in length and able to accommodate up to 380 passengers and up to 110 passenger vehicles, or eight trucks.
The vessel will be built by Polish shipyard CRIST S.A. and designed by subcontractor LMG Marin France, which also designed the ferries now operating the route. The contract is worth €49.93 million, with €28 million from the EU Modernisation Fund and the rest from Estonia's national CO₂ quota sale funds.
The Virtsu–Kuivastu route links the mainland with Muhu and, via a causeway, Saaremaa, and is one of Estonia's busiest ferry crossings. The fifth ferry is part of a wider fleet renewal and is due to enter service at the end of 2028.
A cold spell at the start of this year led to thick sea ice and falling sea levels and caused problems with island ferry connections, with cancellations and some of the smaller islands cut off from the mainland.

A 23-Year-Old Kazakh Owns Two New State-Backed Universities. He’s the President’s Great-Nephew.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
05:30:00 UTC
14:30:00 KST

A 23-Year-Old Kazakh Owns Two New State-Backed Universities. He’s the President’s Great-Nephew.
A young Kazakh man founded two major educational ventures that went on to receive significant state support. Reporters found that he is the grand-nephew of Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev.
Banner:
Press Service of the Government of the Republic of Kazakhstan
|
Nurassyl Medeu (in sunglasses), the founder of the Kazakh National University of Sports, shows a model of the university to Kazakh Prime Minister Oljas Bektenov in July 2026 in Astana. Medeu started the university when he was just 18 years old, and a university student himself.
Reported by
Radio Azattyq
October 16, 2026
|
7 min read
Share Article
×
Aa Text Settings
×
Text Size
SmallMediumLarge
Line Spacing
CompactNormalSpacious
Declaring 2026 the “year of artificial intelligence,” Kazakhstan’s president is in the midst of an ambitious drive to transform the Central Asian nation into a “digital state,” with AI at the center of the effort.
Two weeks after creating a Ministry of Artificial Intelligence in September 2025, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev announced the next prong of his government’s agenda: setting up an AI research university, which would be granted “special status.”
That initiative is now in full swing. And the company tapped to spearhead the project was founded by Tokayev’s 23-year-old great-nephew, before a state institution acquired shares in the venture, an investigation by Radio Azattyq has found.
Qazaq AI Research University, which opened its doors to students last month, is one of two universities that were founded by Nurassyl Medeu, the grandson of Tokayev’s sister, and now have significant state support, company filings and open-source records show.
An entrance to the Qazaq AI Research University campus in Astana.
The rapid rise of Medeu — and the allocation of state property and technology resources to his private ventures — raises questions about potential conflicts of interest and presidential favor in Kazakhstan, which Tokayev has governed since succeeding long-ruling strongman Nursultan Nazarbayev in 2019.
Medeu is the grandson of Tokayev’s younger sister, Karlyga Izbastina. She maintains a low public profile, but was named among the country's 25 most influential women in 2024 by Forbes magazine, which cited her presidential ties and reported corporate holdings. Her daughter and Medeu’s mother, Dana Medeuova, recently secured a seat in parliament representing Adilet, the pro-Tokayev ruling party.
Founded by Medeu in April of this year, Qazaq AI Research University — which touts itself as “Central Asia’s first AI-enabled university” — quickly received an operating license from the Ministry of Science and Higher Education.
That same month, a state-owned company, QazExpoCongress, acquired a 5-percent stake in the institution and relocated it to a striking, eight-story spherical building in the Kazakh capital, Astana, that was originally built as the centerpiece of the country’s EXPO 2017.
QazExpoCongress now operates the exhibition site and is transforming it into an AI hub called the “Exponential Cluster.”
Credit: Yasin Baturhan Ergin/Anadolu/Anadolu via AFP
A view of Astana.
Meanwhile, a for-profit sports academy that Medeu founded when he was 18 years old was rebranded into a university this year, and moved into a $250-million state-owned facility. The government has also acquired a minority stake in the firm behind the sports school, reporters found.
Medeu did not respond to requests for comment, but he did give an interview to the state-run Qazsport television station this month to address questions about his family relationship with President Tokayev.
He said he wanted to quell rumors on social media that the connection had given him “special privileges.”
“I do not know where such assertions come from,” he said. “If you wish, you can also open a university and obtain a license. There is nothing extraordinary about it.”
The presidential administration referred questions on the universities to the Kazakh Ministry of Science and Higher Education.
The ministry told reporters that it bases its licensing decisions on educational criteria, not ownership structure. It did not respond directly to questions about the state’s stakes in Medeu's companies or their operations on state premises.
A Sporting Chance
The new AI university wasn’t Medeu’s first foray into higher education — or his first business partnership with the Kazakh state.
In 2021 — while he was still an 18-year-old undergraduate at Boston University, according to his LinkedIn profile — Medeu founded the Academy of Physical Education and Mass Sports as a private company in Astana.
An archived version of the academy’s website shows it was intended to become “a leading national center for training personnel for the sports sector.”
Company records show that Medeu was its sole owner for several years. Then, in August 2025, KazSportInvest — a state-owned entity established to develop the country’s sporting industry — took a 5-percent stake in the academy, according to the Tourism and Sport Ministry.
At some point early this year, it was rebranded into the Kazakh National University of Sports. In April it was relocated to a $250-million sports complex built by the Tourism and Sports Ministry, with 220,000 square meters of buildings and sports facilities spread across a 20.6-hectare site. It now describes itself as “one of the largest educational projects” in Central Asia.
Credit: Press Service of the Government of the Republic of Kazakhstan
The Kazakh National University of Sports in Astana, Kazakhstan.
In response to questions on the sports complex, the Tourism and Sport Ministry told reporters that Medeu’s university operates the facility under a “trust management agreement.”
Sports School Won Millions in Government Contracts
Medeu’s Kazakh National University of Sports has won government contracts worth over $4.2 million since it was set up in 2021, according to data from the Kazakh government’s official procurement portal.
These contracts have primarily focused on training specialists and providing higher-education services. The largest of them, worth more than $2.5 million, was awarded in March 2026 by the Financial Center, an entity under the Kazakh Finance Ministry, for training students and personnel.
The Tourism and Sports Ministry also said in a statement to reporters that 250 state educational grants had been allocated to the university for the 2025-2026 academic year under a program to train physical-education teachers. It did not disclose the specific amount of funding.
The Kazakh National University of Sport has not released financial statements, making it impossible to determine its income. However, according to the tax registry, the university has paid nearly $800,000 in taxes since 2022, the year after it was founded.
Medeu did not respond to multiple requests for comment, but after receiving reporters’ questions he did give a public interview about the university’s ownership structure, saying that he wanted to address “misconceptions” in the media.
“KNUS is a private university that I established in 2021,” he told the online news outlet EU Reporter. “However, the campus itself is not owned by KNUS or by its founders. The property is state-owned and is used by the university for educational purposes under a contractual agreement. The terms of that agreement explicitly prohibit privatization, disposition, or any transfer of the property into private ownership.”
Speaking at the university’s inauguration in Astana in July, Medeu boasted that the project had “become a major center where the pursuit of knowledge, talent, and hard work converge.”
“Today, we can proudly say that we have laid a solid foundation. I am confident that even greater achievements, international recognition, and new victories in science and sports lie ahead," he said.
Nurassyl Medeu (second from left) at the inauguration of the Kazakh National University of Sports in Astana, Kazakhstan.
A 'Special Role' for AI University
Medeu’s second educational venture, Qazaq AI Research University, known as QAIRU, was established as a private company in April.
Eleven days later, the Kazakh state-owned company QazExpoCongress became a co-owner, corporate records show. Although the size of its stake is not clear from publicly available information, QazExpoCongress told reporters that it was 5 percent.
The company said the AI university was a key part of the Exponential Center, a new “integrated innovation and technology ecosystem” located inside the former EXPO site, and this was why it had been headquartered there.
“QAIRU’s location within the EXPO business complex is attributable to its direct integration into this ecosystem and its alignment with the strategic development priorities of the Exponential Cluster,” it said.
Tokayev soon made a personal visit to the “AI hub” inside the spherical building where Qazaq AI Research University was headquartered. He was given a tour of the space and viewed a presentation about the plans for the school.
Photographs of the event published on the presidential administration’s website show Medeu sitting next to Deputy Prime Minister Zhaslan Madiyev, who also serves as Kazakhstan’s minister of artificial intelligence and digital development.
Credit: Press Service of the Government of the Republic of Kazakhstan
Kazakh president Kassym-Jomart Tokayev (center) and Deputy Prime Minister Zhaslan Madiyev (right) at Qazaq AI Research University.
Credit: Press Service of the Government of the Republic of Kazakhstan
Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev (center) and Deputy Prime Minister Zhaslan Madiyev (left) at Qazaq AI Research University.
Credit: Press Service of the Government of the Republic of Kazakhstan
From right to left, Nurassyl Medeu, Deputy Prime Minister Zhaslan Madiyev, and Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev at Qazaq AI Research University.
Later that day, Tokayev publicly praised the up-and-coming educational institution, saying that when it opened its doors, it would be “an important event for the field of science.”
In June, the school started accepting students for admission, inviting them to come “build the future together.” Last month, classes began for an inaugural group of 400 undergraduate and 100 master’s degree students, local media reported.
Meanwhile, the president has singled out the new university for public accolades at least twice — most recently on October 2, when he spoke about it at a technology conference in Astana.
“[W]e must establish a national scientific and engineering school capable of training educated, highly qualified, and innovation-minded professionals,” he said at the event. “In this regard, a special role is assigned to the recently opened Qazaq AI Research University."

World Monuments Watch 2027 Nominations Point to Government Austerity, Climate Impact and Skills Shortages as Main Threats to Heritage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
05:30:00 UTC
14:30:00 KST

The World Monuments Fund (WMF), an independent nonprofit organization dedicated to the preservation of historic architecture and cultural heritage since 1965, receives nominations through the World Monuments Watch, a flagship advocacy and conservation program. Every two years, the Watch selects 25 sites from the nominations received from individuals and community-based organizations worldwide. Nominations for the 2027 World Monuments Watch closed on March 20, 2026, with a total of 372 public nominations from 84 countries and territories. Before announcing the selected sites in early 2027, the WMF offers an analysis of the nominations. Global data shows three main causes of heritage endangerment worldwide: government austerity, intensifying climate impact, and lack of access to specialized skills and expertise. At a time when political priorities tend to stray from history, the call is to recognize heritage sites as an area of shared opportunity rather than a burden.
Inadequate public funding was the most common driver of heritage endangerment across geographic regions. Among all nominators, 86% cited funding shortages and economic development as a primary issue, up from 80% in the 2025 cycle. In the nominations for the 2027 Watch, 65% cited "insufficient funding and resources" as the most important cause. The three main resource problems were inadequate public funding (22%), local economic constraints (17%), and rising costs for specialized materials and labor (10%). The preservation of world heritage is affected by current political and economic instability and cultural transformations on a global scale, with shrinking public budgets as the leading cause. However, 63% of the nominations identified opportunities to leverage heritage to support local economies through sustainable tourism, job creation and urban regeneration. In a virtuous cycle, built heritage can be viewed not simply as an economic burden but as a source of resources and employment.
Intensifying climate hazards were listed as the second most important cause, highlighted in 66% of the nominations. They were the primary challenge in 54% of the cases, up from 6% in the 2025 selection process. The problem is tangible, as 30% of the sites have been directly threatened by extreme weather events such as flooding, storms, drought, and wildfires. The WMF has two specific programs supporting stewards of historic landscapes and coastal heritage: Cultivating Resilience and Coastal Connections. The first focuses on strengthening the ability of historic gardens and cultural landscapes to adapt to the growing impacts of climate change, while the second gathers a global network of coastal heritage sites to share knowledge and practical solutions for addressing coastal impacts. The programs have documented environmental impacts worldwide, registering damage from severe storms, disrupted agricultural calendars, drought, and subsequent erosion leading to ground destabilization.
From a practical standpoint, and as a window of opportunity for action, the institution identified a growing need for technical expertise in historic preservation. Among all nominators, 44% highlighted access to specialized skills and expertise as a critical issue, a 10% increase from the last cycle. Within this category, the lack of local preservation knowledge or the availability of specialists was noted in 35% of the nominations. This reality adds to global movements calling to revive traditional crafts and pass that knowledge to future generations, not only to preserve heritage but also to create more resilient and sustainable architecture. Historic sites are not only places to remember but also places to study. WMF project sites offer conservation work that is used to train new specialists. Municipal staff, local conservation professionals, and university students gain hands-on experience, as working with monuments requires passing specialized building skills to local stewards.
 For three decades, the World Monuments Watch has given us a direct view of what communities are facing on the ground. This year's nominations show that the pressures on heritage are intensifying while the resources to protect it are not keeping pace. According to findings in the UNESCO Global Report on Cultural Policies, only one in four countries has the means to safeguard its heritage. Communities are being asked to do more with less as climate change accelerates and the skills needed to care for these places grow scarce. These findings are a call to action, and they will help guide where our work is needed most. ― Bénédicte de Montlaur from the World Monuments Fund
The nominations undergo internal and external evaluation based on cultural significance, threat urgency, and the feasibility of community-driven solutions. The final selection for the 2027 World Monuments Watch is being deliberated by a panel of international heritage practitioners and experts chaired by Brinda Somaya, founder and principal of Somaya Sompat. The panel also includes Victoria Herrmann, founder and executive director of Preserving Legacies; Rohit Jigyasu, program manager at SEAMEO-SPAFA; Ishanlosen Odiaua, senior social development specialist at the World Bank and member of ICOMOS Nigeria; John Schofield, professor and director of studies for cultural heritage management at the University of York; Roger Valencia, minister of foreign trade and tourism and former minister of culture of Peru; and Patiphol Yodsurang, associate professor in the Faculty of Architecture at Kasetsart University. The complete 2027 World Monuments Watch list will be officially announced in February 2027.
ArchDaily and World Monuments Fund have partnered to support conservation work at modernist heritage sites around the globe, focusing on protecting the past while informing and inspiring the future of architecture. Through interviews and feature articles, we publish stories about buildings that reflect moments in local and international history, such as Amancio and Delfina Williams' modernist house Casa sobre el Arroyo in Argentina; Angola's Namibe Cinema-Studio; and, among India's earliest experiments in modernist public architecture, the Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel Stadium. Recently announced WMF initiatives include a new list of ten heritage places representing the history of the United States on the occasion of the 250th anniversary of its Declaration of Independence; official support for 21 heritage preservation projects launched this year; and the 2026 World Monuments Fund/Knoll Modernism Prize, awarded to Australia-based architecture firm Architectus for the conservation of the United Nations' Africa Hall in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia.

Rubio presses Lebanon on confiscation of weapons from Hezbollah
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16

Rubio presses Lebanon on confiscation of weapons from Hezbollah
Lebanon’s president reaffirms the commitment to bring all arms under state control.
Lebanon’s President Joseph Aoun has discussed the confiscation of explosives intended for use against Israel during a telephone call with United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio, the Lebanese Presidential Palace has announced.
Aoun received the call on Thursday, assuring Rubio that Lebanese security forces are fully carrying out their duties in confiscating illicit arms across the country.
Last week, an explosive-laden truck carrying 780kg (1,720lb) of explosives was intercepted on a highway between Beirut and the eastern Bekaa Valley.
On Thursday, Hezbollah lawmaker Hassan Fadlallah acknowledged the group’s connection to the shipment, stating that the materials were intended for operations against Israel.
Speaking to reporters at the Lebanese parliament, Fadlallah said Hezbollah had immediately contacted security agencies to clarify ownership of the vehicle and cargo, demanding the materials be returned and detained personnel released.
Rubio urged Aoun to hold accountable those who ordered, financed, and directed the shipment, warning that “returning explosives to [Hezbollah] should be out of the question,” a State Department official told US media.
The official added that Rubio also advocated for direct military-to-military communication between Lebanese and Israeli forces “for deconfliction”.
In response, the Presidential Palace reported that Aoun asked Rubio to press Israel to halt its attacks and destruction in southern Lebanon.
Separately on Thursday, Rubio spoke with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu regarding Iran, according to Israeli media reports.
The explosives-laden truck
On Monday, Prime Minister Nawaf Salam confirmed that Lebanon would conduct an investigation to track down members of Hezbollah linked to the incident.
Judicial officials told The Associated Press news agency that the truck was carrying 780kg (1,720lb) of explosives, including 250kg (550lb) of TNT and 550lb of C4 plastic explosives.
Salam described the transport as a “criminal operation” and praised security forces for intercepting the vehicle along the strategic highway linking Beirut with the Bekaa Valley.
For years, Hezbollah moved weapons freely across parts of the country. However, in March, the Lebanese government declared all military activities by the group illegal. Despite the government’s pledge to bring all weaponry under state control, the group has stated its intention to continue transporting arms in its confrontation with Israel.
Earlier this spring, Lebanese and Israeli envoys met in Washington under the auspices of US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, marking the first direct diplomatic contact between the two nations in decades.
Despite that diplomatic push from Washington, Israel has repeatedly violated the November 2024 ceasefire deal between it and Hezbollah, with Lebanon frequently reporting civilian casualties.
The renewed diplomatic friction comes as heavy Israeli attacks continue across southern Lebanon, where dozens of villages have been systematically demolished and large areas remain under Israeli military occupation, despite a framework agreement signed in June.

Amazon has unveiled new AI gadgets - what they can do and how much they cost
Kyiv • UNN

On October 15, Amazon unveiled two new listening devices from Bee, including a wearable device and a credit card-sized recorder, marking the company's latest move into the artificial intelligence gadget market. CNBC reports, writes UNN.
Details
Bee Frontier is an upgraded version of Amazon's existing device, which can be worn on the wrist or attached to clothing. Like previous generations, Bee Frontier offers up to seven days of battery life, but it is also more expensive—$75 compared with $50 for its predecessor.
In July 2025, Amazon acquired Bee, a San Francisco startup known for its wristbands that constantly listen in on conversations, for an undisclosed sum. Bee's wristbands are equipped with artificial intelligence and microphones that can record, transcribe, and analyze conversations.
The two microphones on Bee Frontier have improved noise filtering, "so it can capture what matters and ignore what doesn't, even in noisy environments, such as a crowded restaurant or an open office," Amazon said in a blog post.
Amazon also unveiled the $100 Bee Eclipse, which works like other Bee devices, but instead of being worn, the credit card-sized gadget attaches magnetically to the back of a smartphone.
Bee Frontier was set to go on sale on October 15, while Bee Eclipse "will be available soon," the company said.
Amazon is updating its Bee lineup as technology companies prepare for the holiday season with a range of new artificial intelligence devices. Amazon has dropped its budget Fire tablet lineup in favor of three new Alexa tablets with AI support, while Microsoft unveiled a Windows-based laptop with an Nvidia processor, and Apple introduced its HomeView smart home hub with Siri AI.
Bee gadgets will compete with other AI-enabled wearables already on the market.
When turned on, Bee devices constantly record conversations. Amazon says this enables key features such as conversation summaries and the ability to review memories from the past few days to recall what you discussed. The device can also track "recurring patterns or themes" to set personalized goals or assign tasks.
A subscription to Bee Pro, which costs $12 a month, gives users unlimited brief conversation overviews and daily memories, as well as integration with Amazon's online store, the Alexa+ voice assistant, and third-party applications. For example, if a user mentions that they need to buy dish soap, they may see a recommended product on Amazon's homepage or in Bee's mobile and desktop apps.
The company said Bee devices are designed so that no one, including Amazon, can access your data. Users can delete their transcripts and brief overviews at any time, and "audio is never stored," Amazon said.
An LED indicator signals that Bee devices are recording, Amazon said.
Addition
Earlier in October Amazon unveiled a set of new, more expensive Alexa tablets and said it was discontinuing its budget Fire lineup, signaling a significant shift in the e-commerce giant's device strategy. The company introduced 8-inch, 11-inch, and 12-inch models, priced from $230 to $550 for the version equipped with Amazon's "Nanomatte" display technology, developed in partnership with Corning to "significantly reduce screen glare."
Amazon's voice-controlled Echo smart speaker enabled users to become accustomed to interacting with the Alexa AI assistant, but the devices were designed to begin listening only when activated by a so-called wake word.

Over the weekend, an anticyclone will bring drier weather and frost
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
05:23:33 UTC
14:23:33 KST

While the weather earlier this week was largely influenced by cyclones—bringing rain to many areas—the influence of an anticyclone will strengthen towards the weekend. According to the Latvian Environment, Geology and Meteorology Centre, although precipitation will decrease, fog may still form at night in some places, and in parts of the country, temperatures could drop below 0°C on certain nights.
As the week draws to a close, atmospheric pressure will gradually rise, and the sky will see varying cloud cover. On Saturday, rain is expected during the day in the western and central regions; by the night into Sunday, light rain will be confined to the central regions, while the day itself will bring dry and predominantly sunny weather.
During this period, fog may form at night—primarily in the eastern and central regions—and in some places, it may persist into the morning or even the forenoon.
Meanwhile, a light to moderate southerly wind will blow, shifting to a northerly direction by Saturday afternoon.
At night, temperatures will generally cool to between +3°C and +8°C, though in some eastern areas, frost is possible, with temperatures dropping to between 0°C and -2°C. During the day, maximum temperatures will range from +8°C to +13°C, with Friday being a couple of degrees warmer. At the beginning of next week, the center of an anticyclone will approach Latvia, bringing pleasant, dry weather with frequent sunshine. Daytime temperatures will reach +7…+12°C, while at night, slight frost may still occur in some places.

Ukraine Plans More Powerful Drone Campaign to Paralyze Russian Airports – The Atlantic
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
05:21:03 UTC
14:21:03 KST

Ukraine is preparing to escalate its campaign to disrupt Russian airports, deploying AI-guided drones capable of evading air defenses and striking aviation infrastructure directly.
The operation, codenamed “M&Ms,” was developed under former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov and envisioned using small, low-cost drones capable of navigating and identifying targets without human operators, according to two sources familiar with the plan.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The drones would carry detailed maps and images of designated targets, allowing their onboard computers to compare live camera footage with stored data. Once a target was identified, a drone would dive into it and detonate without requiring further confirmation from an operator, the report said.
The upcoming operation is expected to be significantly more aggressive, with drones that do not depend on US intelligence and could soon enter mass production, Ukrainian officials told The Atlantic.
The Ukrainian official also said a drone prototype had already been used in combat in the Donbas, although development is ongoing. The drones have not yet been deployed against Russian airports.
The current campaign has already disrupted air travel across Moscow. Between Oct. 3 and 9, Russian airports canceled 345 flights and delayed nearly 4,000, with some passengers facing waits of 10 hours or more.
On Oct. 10, another 692 flights were delayed and 93 canceled. On Oct. 14, 238 flights were delayed and 124 canceled. Moscow’s airport network was shut down for an average of around three hours daily, according to the report.
22 US Lawmakers Press Trump to Enforce Russia Sanctions Ahead of Oct. 18 Deadline
Even Russian President Vladimir Putin’s plane was reportedly unable to land in Moscow on Oct. 9 while returning from Turkmenistan, as two of the capital’s four airports were closed for seven hours during a drone attack.
Prolonged airport shutdowns could force international carriers, including Turkish Airlines and Emirates, to reconsider flights to the Russian capital, disrupting a key connection between Russia’s political elite and the outside world.
The plan was reportedly presented to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in early 2026. Although he raised concerns about risks to civilian aircraft, passengers and airport workers, he allowed preparations to continue, according to The Atlantic’s earlier report.
Trump’s energy ceasefire fails to stop Russian attacks
The planned escalation comes amid growing tensions between Kyiv and Washington over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil infrastructure.
Last week, on Oct. 9, Trump announced an agreement for Russia to supply diesel to US and global markets, drawing criticism from US lawmakers and European allies.
Zelensky described the deal as a “simple victory” for the Kremlin in an interview with British broadcaster Piers Morgan on Wednesday.
“It’s a pity that we are losing a strong partner,” Zelensky said.
He also accused Trump of taking Russia’s side in the war, arguing that Washington should remain neutral rather than favor Moscow.
“This is our country, our body, our home, our children,” Zelensky said. “That’s why it’s painful when Trump chooses one side.”
Trump called for a halt to attacks on energy infrastructure and announced what he called a mutual energy ceasefire.
However, Russia continued striking Ukrainian cities and energy facilities, with missile and drone attacks leaving hundreds of thousands of people without electricity.
Ukraine had temporarily suspended strikes on Russian refineries at Washington’s request. Kyiv argued that any energy truce must apply to both sides, rather than restrict Ukraine’s ability to retaliate while Moscow continues attacking its power grid.
On Oct. 14, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told the Financial Times that Kyiv would no longer observe the pause in refinery strikes.
“The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We’re done,” Zelensky said.
Ukraine struck an oil refinery in Russia’s Ryazan Oblast early on Oct. 15, triggering a fire at the facility about 300 kilometers (186 miles) southeast of Moscow.
Later that day, Trump called Ukraine’s decision to resume refinery strikes a “disgrace,” accusing Kyiv of driving up global energy prices in an interview with Newsmax.
“Well, I think that’s a disgrace,” Trump said when asked about the renewed attacks.
Energy analysts, however, say Trump’s deal to resume Russian diesel exports is unlikely to significantly lower fuel prices.
The main driver of the global price surge has been the US-Israel war with Iran, which has disrupted oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz.
Trump also portrayed Zelensky as a greater obstacle to ending Russia’s war against Ukraine than Putin.
“It should end soon. I think they actually both would like to see it end,” Trump said. “But I think I find Zelensky to be more difficult to deal with than Putin.”
Zelensky met NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte in Brussels on Oct. 15 and held talks with European leaders ahead of the EU summit, seeking continued military and political support for Ukraine.
“Don’t attack us. Don’t kill our children. We will stop attacking your diesel,” Zelensky said in an Oct. 11 interview with ABC News, outlining Kyiv’s position on a reciprocal energy ceasefire.
Kyiv prepares to escalate airport campaign
Trump, however, has not publicly objected to Ukrainian attacks on Russian airports or data centers, which Ukrainian forces targeted last week, The Atlantic reported.
When Trump first called Zelensky last month, he reportedly suggested that Kyiv could strike targets other than oil refineries.
“There are many other targets,” Trump said.
According to The Atlantic, Trump is becoming less interested in mediating between Moscow and Kyiv and increasingly appears to be pursuing a deal on the Kremlin’s behalf.

The European Union is coming to terms with the fact that its multibillion-euro support for Ukraine won't be enough next year as Russia launches an all-out campaign to devastate the local economy.
Railways, warehouses, data centres, power stations and water facilities have all come under attack in recent months. For next year, Brussels intends to disburse €45 billion under the support loan, in addition to residual funding under the Ukraine Facility and the European Peace Facility. The European Commission hasn't yet validated the number but admits the hole will be substantial. The problem is that there aren't easy solutions to plug it: joint debt is difficult amid rising borrowing costs, the Russian assets remain highly divisive and bilateral contributions risk leaving the burden on a few wealthy member states.
EU leaders won't address the issue in depth today, but everyone knows that, sooner or later, a serious debate will need to happen.

Four killed as Indonesia battles worst forest fires in more than a decade
The deaths come as Jakarta says it will accept foreign help to tackle its worst forest fires in more than a decade.
Four people tackling a wildfire in a national park on Indonesia’s island of Java have been killed, the Forestry Ministry said, as the country battles its worst forest fires in more than a decade.
The victims were caught in the flames on Thursday in Bromo Tengger Semeru National Park in East Java, the ministry said on Friday.
Two others suffered serious burns and are receiving medical treatment. The forest fires have extended beyond Indonesia’s borders, blanketing neighbouring countries in haze, Reuters reported.
The ministry did not identify the victims. In a statement, it expressed “deep condolences” and paid tribute to the “courage and dedication” of the officers, volunteers and residents working on the fire lines.
The deaths, it said, were “a reminder that extinguishing forest and land fires is a high-risk operation”, adding that safety “must be the main concern”, including tracking how the fire is spreading and the wind direction, keeping evacuation routes ready and assessing conditions before and during operations.
The islands of Sumatra and Borneo, close to Singapore and Malaysia, are the worst affected.
Hotspots increase
The ministry said satellite monitoring detected 799 high-confidence hotspots nationwide as of Thursday night, up 427 from the day before. The ministry cautioned that hotspots are not the same as fires, as one blaze can register as several.
Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto has approved accepting help from neighbouring countries, Foreign Minister Arrmanatha Nasir said, according to Reuters.
Malaysia offered last month to send three helicopters, an aircraft and 52 personnel, but there has been no follow-up, Reuters reported. Singapore has also said it is ready to help.
Indonesia has faced heavy criticism over the fires, which have caused respiratory problems for hundreds of thousands of people and forced school closures in Malaysia and East Timor, according to Reuters.

Finland to introduce mobile phone emergency alert system in November
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:13:54 EEST
14:13:54 KST

Emergency warnings will be sent directly to mobile phones in Finland under a new system called FI-Alert, according to the Ministry of Interior in a press release.
The system will complement Finland's existing emergency warnings by enabling authorities to send alerts almost instantly to phones in specific affected areas.
Currently, emergency warnings are available through the 112 Suomi and Yle apps, radio and television broadcasts, teletext page 112, and the 112.fi and yle.fi websites. Authorities can also use public warning sirens.
The new system is being introduced as authorities seek to improve their ability to reach the public quickly during emergencies, amid a changing security situation.
No app or personal information required
FI-Alert is based on Cell Broadcast technology and the EU Alert concept.
Such technology allows mobile phones to receive alerts without users having to share personal information, such as their phone number or location data.
The only requirements are that the phone is switched on and configured to receive Cell Broadcast messages. No app needs to be installed in advance, and users do not need to subscribe to the service.
The technology uses a distinctive sound to draw attention to alerts, even when a phone is set to silent. Messages appear on the phone screen automatically and remain there until the user acknowledges them.
The ministry has previously stated that the system is suited to emergency situations because it does not place the same strain on mobile networks as mass text-message distribution.
Similar systems are already in use or being developed in several European countries, and the Ministry of the Interior says the technology is becoming the most common way of using mobile phones to warn the public.
In August, the government proposed amending the law on emergency warnings to allow alerts to be sent using Cell Broadcast technology. President Alexander Stubb is expected to approve this legislation on Friday and bring it into force at the beginning of November.

Youth-led protests are mounting pressure on Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi as frustration over unemployment, alleged electoral manipulation and unfulfilled promises fuels demonstrations across the country.
Despite the deployment of tens of thousands of security personnel, young protesters scaled barricades, chanted anti-government slogans and clashed with police during demonstrations in New Delhi and elsewhere last week.
“Long live the revolution,” one protester shouted before police bundled him into a bus.
The independent Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (ACLED) says street protests in India this year are on course to reach their highest level in a decade. Analysts say the unrest, coupled with renewed opposition activity, represents Modi’s most serious political challenge since he took office in 2014.
“The nation has suddenly found its voice,” said activist Yogendra Yadav, who has played a leading role in the demonstrations. “I would not say this is the beginning of the end of the Modi regime, but this definitely is the beginning of a downward spiral.”
Modi’s government and his Bharatiya Janata Party declined to comment.
The latest demonstrations have centered on demands for the resignation of Election Commission chief Gyanesh Kumar over a voter-roll revision that opposition parties and activists allege favors the BJP and has helped it win recent state elections.
The government, the BJP and the Election Commission deny the accusations, with the ruling party attributing its electoral success to Modi’s popularity and economic growth.
But the protests reflect broader dissatisfaction with the government, including frustration over unemployment, examination paper leaks, crimes against women and the influence of wealthy businessmen alleged to have close ties to Modi.
Many young Indians also accuse the government of prioritizing Hindu nationalist politics over jobs and economic opportunities, while raising concerns about violence against religious minorities, particularly Muslims.
“The fear in us is gone,” said Ananya Raturi, a 21-year-old Delhi University student who joined protests in the capital.
Raturi said demonstrators were no longer deterred by the prospect of detention or police violence. Police have denied beating protesters and said officers followed established procedures.
The demonstrations have been energized by the Cockroach Janta Party, a youth-led movement that grew from online satire into a nationwide campaign in June after India's chief justice likened unemployed people to “cockroaches.”
Activists have used mobile phones and independent YouTube news channels to circulate footage of the protests, gaining audiences despite what critics describe as limited coverage by India's largely pro-government mainstream media.
CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke and left-wing activist Neha Bora have emerged as prominent online voices, while Congress Party leader Rahul Gandhi has joined demonstrations alongside tens of thousands of supporters.
The unrest has drawn comparisons with youth-led protests in neighboring Bangladesh and Nepal that brought down governments. However, analysts caution that India's political landscape and Modi's continuing support make direct comparisons difficult.
Employment remains a major source of anger among young people who grew up during Modi's rise to power and expected greater economic opportunity.
Although India has recorded strong economic growth, government figures put overall unemployment slightly above 5%. Unemployment among Indians aged 15 to 29 reached 9.9% in 2025, according to government data.
Azim Premji University's State of Working India 2026 report found that nearly 40% of graduates aged 15 to 25 were unemployed, while about one in five graduates aged 25 to 29 remained jobless.
Repeated examination paper leaks have added to the frustration. In May, protests erupted after the government invalidated examinations for admission to national medical colleges following leaked test papers.
Rubby Singh, a 30-year-old social activist in New Delhi, said the scandals had deepened young people's distrust of a system they believe is denying them opportunities despite years of study.
“This generation has been facing the brunt of not having proper education, which leads to not being able to get good opportunities,” she said.
The government, meanwhile, says the economy generated 168.3 million new jobs in the six years through 2024. Modi has repeatedly rejected allegations of religious bias, saying his administration serves all Indians.
India's next general election is not due until 2029, but elections in Uttar Pradesh, the country's most populous state, early next year could offer an indication of whether the growing discontent is weakening the BJP's electoral support.
Analysts caution that street protests do not necessarily translate into votes, and the ruling party retains considerable political strength.
“The BJP may not be as strong as it was a few months ago,” said Rahul Verma, a fellow at the Centre for Policy Research in New Delhi. “But whether there are going to be electoral implications, it is too early to say.”

Interview: Thai official hopes for closer vocational cooperation with China to prepare skilled workforce for future

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:08:57 CST
14:08:57 KST

BANGKOK, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- A Thai Education Ministry official has expressed hope that closer vocational education cooperation with China will help prepare a skilled workforce for future-oriented industries.
Sanga Taechersai, deputy secretary-general of the ministry's Office of the Vocational Education Commission, said he looks forward to further expanding Thailand-China "Order Class" programs and other joint training programs leading to dual diplomas.
He also voiced hope that the two sides will broaden the range of relevant programs to serve future-oriented industries such as clean energy, semiconductor and AI and robotics, jointly training skilled workforce for the future.
Thailand and China have maintained close, fruitful cooperation in vocational education, Sanga said in an interview with Xinhua ahead of the 2026 World Vocational and Technical Education Development Conference, which runs from Thursday to Saturday in Tianjin, China.
Under an agreement with the Chinese Education Ministry's Center for Language Education and Cooperation, and within the framework of the Belt and Road Initiative, the two sides have established the China-Thailand Institute of Chinese Language and Technical and Vocational Education and Training as a platform for cooperation.
Through various programs, Thai students have improved their Chinese language proficiency and obtained vocational competency certificates based on Chinese standards in areas including electrical engineering, electric vehicle (EV) technology, mechatronics, electronics and digital business technology, Sanga said.
The two sides have also carried out "Order Class" programs under a tripartite cooperation model involving Thai vocational institutions, Chinese educational institutions and Chinese enterprises operating in Thailand.
According to Sanga, these programs provide full financial support through study and guarantee employment upon graduation in target fields such as mechanical and electrical engineering, information technology and advanced manufacturing.
Sanga believes that the key challenge now facing vocational education is whether it can adapt quickly enough to meet industry demand, particularly amid advances in AI, the EV industry and advanced manufacturing technologies.
"No country can, on its own, develop a workforce capable of meeting the needs of every technology," he said.
International exchanges involving curricula, technology, personnel and occupational standards can help shorten workforce development cycles and build a strong regional workforce ecosystem capable of supporting cross-border investment, he added.
On China's vocational education development, Sanga said China has long been at the forefront of the field, particularly in connecting vocational colleges with high-tech industrial supply chains and promoting Chinese vocational education standards internationally.
The Thai official expressed hope that Thailand and China will continue to deepen mutual learning in vocational education and jointly train a more skilled workforce.
Sanga depicted the Tianjin conference as a platform to exchange views on vocational education policies and visions among policymakers, representatives of relevant institutions, experts and scholars from around the world, and learn from global best practices in improving vocational education.
He said that training a skilled workforce for the future is a shared goal of Thailand-China vocational education cooperation, and that the Tianjin conference will serve as a new starting point for achieving the goal with tangible outcomes. ■

Font size
The Aviation Museum near Bulgaria's second-biggest city Plovdiv will mark 16 October - Bulgarian Aviation and Air Force Day - with a special programme. The commemorative date is associated with the first combat reconnaissance flight, carried out on 16 October 1912 during the Balkan War. The flight was made by Lieutenants Radul Milkov and Prodan Tarakchiev in an Albatros L.2 aircraft in the area of Edirne.
Visitors will be able to explore an exhibition tracing the development of Bulgarian aviation and step inside the cockpits of two aircraft: an Mi-24 helicopter and a MiG-21 fighter jet. Aviation enthusiasts will also have the opportunity to see the ASH-62IR engine in operation. It was used to power the An-2 aircraft.
The youngest visitors can take part in the educational game Pilot - Explorer, which will challenge them to discover fascinating details about the design of the aeroplanes and helicopters on display in the museum’s outdoor exhibition.
