LRT English Newsletter: Migration, algorithms, and diesel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

LRT English Newsletter – October 16, 2026.
Lithuania is planning to change the laws surrounding platform work. The changes aim to make the conditions better for the growing workforce who are named as “partners”, but have few – if any – possibilities to negotiate rates or even challenge automatic decisions taken by algorithms. Around 141,000 people worked for platforms like Wolt and Bolt in the country, according to data from 2024. The number is expected to rise to 157,000 by 2028.
Many of them are migrants or students, often from non-EU countries. They have also been at the centre of political efforts to point at the (allegedly) runaway migration taking place in the country. Amid a flurry of anti-migration rhetoric, the interior minister proposed limiting the right of foreign, non-EU students to work on a self-employed basis.
But who are the people that make up the immigrant community? Probably unsurprisingly, Belarusians and Ukrainians remain the two biggest nationalities. Meanwhile, Lithuania is at risk of increasing out-migration of its own citizens due to war fears and economic pressures.
DIESEL AND YANDEX
Donald Trump’s diesel-sucking deal with Russia received a bitter response even in Lithuania that normally backs Washington’s endeavours, with Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius saying the decision of the country’s strategic partner was “shameful and dishonourable”. The foreign minister, Kęstutis Budrys, tried to play it down, saying “this latest episode is not the worst we have seen in nearly two years”.
Speaking at the Warsaw Forum earlier this week, Sinkevičius also said Ukraine should strike more data centres, wink wink.
US TROOPS, BALTIC BORDERS
And speaking of America, the first US troops arrived in the country earlier this week. Up to 100 US troops are now here as part of a returning rotation, with the rest of the 1,000-strong force expected by mid-November.
Despite the returning Americans, the Baltic borders remain on edge. Last week, there was an armed incident on Latvia’s border with Belarus; the previously unknown “Black Russian” group claimed responsibility. But the whole announcement looked sus, with experts saying the group could be a front for security services. Or, this whole “group” could be a psyop product in the first place, seeing how Europe is bracing itself for “escalation” on Baltic borders. In any case, read more here.
In other defence updates, Lithuania is investing over 33 million euros into military fuel infrastructure. And if you’re feeling lost about all the different initiatives taking place in Lithuania to prepare for a potential conflict, we've got you covered.
SHOOTING IN VILNIUS
But it was an armed incident closer to home that proved deadly, when a former policeman shot a former kickboxing champion after an altercation outside an apartment block. In related news, a man escaped from a court hearing by pushing aside a police officer and making a run for it. Predictably, he was arrested a few hours later.

They fled Russia, but the West sent them back
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
05:57:28 BST
13:57:28 KST

They fled Russia, but the West sent them back
- Published
Russian security services were waiting when the flight landed in Moscow in December. On board were Russians the US had deported, including activists denied political asylum.
"It was unbelievably frightening. My knees were shaking with fear," says Katya, one of the deportees. We have changed her name to protect her identity, as she remains in Russia.
Katya had left Russia and claimed asylum in the US two years earlier.
When Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, many countries publicly welcomed fleeing Russians. But more than four years later, attitudes have hardened. The numbers of anti-war Russians forcibly returned from Western countries is rising, and Katya's experience highlights the potential risks they face.
US authorities rejected her application for asylum, after she said she had provided evidence that she had taken part in protests and was a member of an opposition movement.
In Moscow, Katya says officers from the FSB security service handed all the male deportees military papers, requiring them to register with the local enlistment office, from where men are often sent to the war in Ukraine. Another passenger on the flight and an activist confirmed her account.
The officers interrogated her, and many others, for several hours.
"At one point, they found incriminating information on my phone," says Katya, "Their faces changed in a second. I was very afraid that they would simply bundle me off somewhere."
Katya was eventually released and allowed to stay with relatives. But she says police continue to call her and visit her at home.
"I feel as if I'm in a cage, like in a zoo," she says, "Whenever I see a police car, I feel terrified and start thinking, "What if they're coming for me?"
Katya showed the BBC documents and photographs confirming her story, which matches accounts from other deportees.
Removals from the US rose from 222 in 2023 to more than 1,200 in 2025, amid a wider increase in deportations under President Donald Trump's second term. Activists say Russian deportees included dissidents and Russian army deserters, some of whom were imprisoned or sent to war after returning to Russia.
One such case is Leonid Melekhin, an anti-war activist who sought asylum in the US after being arrested at protests in Russia. He had posted photographs of Russian President Vladimir Putin online with the message "Putin: murderer, fascist, usurper". After being deported back home last year, Melekhin was charged with "justifying terrorism" and sentenced to six years in prison.
"We have several examples of people who got eight years in prison when they crossed the [Russian] border," says Andrei Pivovarov, from Russia's exiled opposition Anti-War Committee.
And deportations are taking place from Europe too. His organisation has changed its advice to dissidents escaping Russia: the EU is no longer safe, it is better to seek refuge elsewhere.
Germany has sharply increased the number of Russian nationals it deports. Seven were sent back in 2023, rising to more than 110 in 2025, according to German government figures. More than 21,000 Russians sought asylum in Germany between 2022 and 2025, but the proportion of positive decisions fell from 29% in 2023 to just 6.8% in the first eleven months of 2025.
"Protection is only granted if there is an actual, well-founded fear of persecution," Germany's migration and asylum agency, BAMF, told the BBC.
Last year, Berlin suspended its humanitarian visa programme for Russians, and across the EU, the proportion of Russian applicants granted some form of asylum protection fell from 23% in 2024 to around 17% in the first nine months of 2025, according to EU data.
Russian opposition activists fleeing repression have become caught up in a wider crackdown on immigration, as governments across Europe and the US toughen rules amid political pressure over high numbers of irregular migrants and asylum applications, as well as over security concerns.
Western governments are "focused on limiting humanitarian programmes and asylum seekers", says lawyer Anastasia Burakova, founder of rights group Kovcheg (Ark), which helps anti-war Russians leave the country. The clampdown is "in response to public concerns and rising support for right-wing populist parties", she adds.
Following a negative asylum decision, Russian nationals are often given the chance to leave independently, but a rising number are being forcibly returned to Russia, usually escorted via third countries.
Several Russian activists in exile told the BBC that immigration officials had told them they faced "no danger" in Russia, and that officials often lacked an adequate understanding of the risks that activists face.
"I tried to explain that if they sent me back, I would be put in prison, or sent to war where I'd be killed," explains former soldier Artyom, who deserted from the Russian Army in 2022 after officers threatened to send him to Ukraine. "They just didn't believe me."
He says he provided US authorities with proof that a criminal investigation had been opened against him back in Russia for desertion. But he was put on a deportation flight back to Moscow via Egypt.
"I was preparing for death," says the former soldier, "I was thinking, 'how can I die without it being painful?'".
Back in Moscow, Artyom was held in a military detention facility but managed to escape. He is now in hiding abroad.
"Another country could investigate me better and give me asylum. Why didn't they give me that chance? Instead they deported me specifically to Russia," says the deserter. "It ruined my life."
The US Department of Homeland Security told the BBC: "All illegal aliens receive due process. If a judge finds an illegal alien has no right to be in this country, we are going to remove them."
The asylum clampdown comes as repression inside Russia has reached "an unprecedented level", according to Nobel Prize-winning Russian human rights group Memorial. Their list of political prisoners grew from 803 to 1,265 during 2025, a record increase.
The Russian Embassy in London did not respond to a request for comment.
Anti-war activist Mikhail says he and his wife Dasha are awaiting deportation from Finland "any day". Their names have been changed to protect their identity, as Mikhail fears for relatives back home.
Russian authorities blocked his social media accounts over anti-war posts, and police visited his mother and accused him of spreading "fake information".
Dasha is a Jehovah's Witness, an organisation banned as "extremist" in Russia. The couple provided Finnish authorities with evidence, seen by the BBC, including a video of Russian police telling his mother that more than 300 posts had violated Russian law. A single post can result in a long prison sentence.
The Finnish Immigration Service has rejected their asylum request five times, deciding there is "no reasonable basis to believe" the couple would face serious rights violations if returned.
"We're sitting here and someone could knock on our door at any moment, take us to the Russian border and simply hand us over to Russian officers," says Mikhail. "We fear for our lives!"
"We came to Finland for help, and they're refusing us," he adds. "My wife cries constantly."
Amnesty International, which is supporting the couple, says they could face a "real risk" of detention, prosecution, imprisonment and torture if returned.
The Finnish Immigration Service said all asylum decisions were based on international refugee law standards, and the share of Russian citizens receiving asylum was in line with EU averages.
For Mikhail and Dasha, the threat of deportation comes as more Russians may be considering leaving.
There are rumours that Vladimir Putin may announce a new wave of mobilisation to boost the ranks of his army in Ukraine, which the Kremlin denies. The last mobilisation in 2022 prompted hundreds of thousands of Russians to flee, many to ex-Soviet states such as Armenia and Georgia.
Anastasia Burakova's organisation says requests for help from Russians wanting to leave rose tenfold in August compared with May. For those now looking to escape, the question is whether the West will offer them refuge — or send them back.

Children bear brunt as Ethiopia fighting fuels fears of wider war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
04:55:00 UTC
13:55:00 KST

Ten-year-old Iyerusalem lies in a hospital bed in northern Ethiopia, her amputated legs propped up by rolled blankets as she struggles with pain and the loss of her older brother, who was killed alongside their horse when fighting struck their home.
“I was in our compound with my older brother and our horse when we were hit. My brother and the horse died,” she told Agence France-Presse (AFP) from Ayder Comprehensive Specialised Hospital in Mekelle, the capital of the northern Tigray region.
Iyerusalem is among dozens of civilians wounded since fighting erupted between the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and Ethiopian federal forces on Sept. 23, reviving a conflict in a region still scarred by the devastating 2020-22 war.
Federal forces repelled the TPLF offensive and took control of Mekelle without resistance on Oct. 3 after rebel leaders and fighters abandoned the city.
The fighting has nevertheless left civilians, including children, with severe injuries and families mourning relatives killed in bombardments.
Many wounded people come from remote villages in southern Tigray, hours from medical care along difficult roads affected by fighting and shelling.
Iyerusalem, from Qarsole village in Alamata district, said her amputated legs were causing severe pain.
“If I get medical treatment and can walk again, I want to go back to school,” she said, as her father, Hiluf, watched anxiously.
Nearby, 12-year-old Hana was recovering from severe facial injuries and a broken leg. The explosion that wounded her killed her mother and brother.
“First I heard a loud explosion, and the whole house shook. I was scared and did not even know what had happened. I could not open my eyes or my mouth,” she said.
“The sound of the explosion keeps coming back in my head.”
In another room, Betelhem, 10, was being treated for a broken leg, while her 6-year-old sister, Melet, had suffered a neck injury. Their pregnant mother was killed when heavy artillery struck their home.
“The bomb hit our house directly, all these people have died, but no one is being held responsible. There is no government,” said their father, Haftom, a 39-year-old shopkeeper.
Birhanu Hailemariam, the emergency coordinator at Ayder hospital, said 34 people wounded by heavy artillery, drones, gunfire and explosives had arrived in recent days. Twenty-three were children, and one patient had died.
Medical staff lacked basic equipment and medicines, including anesthesia, he said.
“But we are doing our best to treat everyone,” he said.
Although the latest fighting had not reached the scale of the previous Tigray war, which the African Union (AU) estimates killed about 600,000 people, fear remained pervasive among patients and medical workers.
“Both are hurting people,” another doctor said of the TPLF and federal forces, asking not to be identified.
Families were reluctant to assign blame for attacks. Hiluf said he did not know who had bombarded his village and feared reprisals if he accused either side.
“I do not want to fight with anyone,” he said. “Let there be peace for us.”
Farther north, residents of the border town of Zalambessa say they are caught between Ethiopian and Eritrean troops as the risk of a broader conflict grows.
Eritrea has deployed thousands of troops to northern Tigray to support forces opposing Ethiopia's central government, according to a security source.
“Ethiopian troops are on one side, and Eritrean troops are on the other,” said Selam, 33, whose first name was changed for security reasons.
Eritrean soldiers initially advanced south before drone strikes forced them to retreat into the surrounding mountains, she said. Although the area was no longer seeing active fighting, her home and small shop had been without electricity or water for a week.
“We are caught in the middle and living in deep anxiety,” she said.
Conflict monitor ACLED reported that Ethiopian federal forces had moved heavy weapons toward Zalambessa in recent days. Eyewitnesses reported seeing a substantial convoy of tanks and other heavy weaponry advancing from the south, though AFP could not independently verify the reports.
Residents described deserted streets, closed businesses and growing shortages as blocked roads disrupted supplies.
“Most people only go out to attend church and pray,” said Hadush, 45, who also requested anonymity.
“Now there is no bread,” he said, describing the worsening hardship.
Selam said federal soldiers were preventing residents from traveling to Adigrat, about 30 kilometers (18 miles) south, making it difficult to visit relatives or obtain essential supplies.
Eritrean Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel did not respond to AFP questions about the reported presence of Eritrean troops.
The military buildup has raised international concern that the fighting in Tigray could draw the neighboring countries into another war.
On Wednesday, the United States urged Ethiopia and Eritrea to pursue “de-escalation,” calling on all countries to respect their neighbors' sovereignty and territorial integrity and avoid cross-border incursions.
Eritrea gained independence from Ethiopia in 1993. The countries fought a deadly border war from 1998 to 2000 before relations improved in 2018, when Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed took office and pursued closer ties with Asmara.
Relations have since deteriorated, with the two countries severing ties this month amid the renewed Tigray conflict.
Ethiopia accuses Eritrea of backing the TPLF, which launched its offensive on Sept. 23. Eritrea alleges that Ethiopia intends to exploit the fighting to invade its territory and seize Assab port on the Red Sea.
The TPLF initially made gains in the Afar region but has since retreated ahead of advancing federal forces, abandoning towns for the surrounding hills.
Federal troops took Mekelle without resistance on Oct. 3 and subsequently seized several other towns without encountering opposition. The latest reported advance brought government forces to Rama, about 7 kilometers (4 miles) from the Eritrean border, according to two residents.

PETROPAVLOVSK-KAMCHATSKY, October 16. /TASS/. A perceptible earthquake with an intensity of up to four magnitude points has been registered in Kamchatka, the Kamchatka branch of the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Geophysical Service said.

Reserve Bank governor paid $1.2 million as RBA workers fight real wage cuts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
04:50:02 UTC
13:50:02 KST

Reserve Bank governor paid $1.2 million as RBA workers fight real wage cuts
In short:
RBA governor Michele Bullock received total remuneration of $1.22 million in 2025-26.
RBA workers are demanding an 11 per cent pay increase over three years, but the RBA is offering 9.5 per cent.
What's next?
The latest data show Australia's unemployment rate is 4.7 per cent, but economists say the RBA may not have finished lifting rates.
The Reserve Bank's senior officials are among the highest paid people in Australia.
RBA governor Michele Bullock received total remuneration of $1.22 million in 2025-26, with a base salary of $1.01 million.
Deputy governor Andrew Hauser received total remuneration of $955,033, with a base salary of $903,217.
The RBA's four assistant governors received total remuneration between $743,000 and $868,000 each, and its chief operating officer received total remuneration of $905,543.
The figures can be found in the RBA's 2026 annual report, which was released on Thursday afternoon.
The median annual earnings for all employees in Australia is $74,672.
In March this year, Ms Bullock received unwanted media attention when she and her husband bought a $2 million home in Yamba, in northern NSW, on the same day that the RBA lifted interest rates on February 3.
It was her third investment property.
Her property purchase was recorded in her declaration of material personal interests on the RBA's website.
The RBA governor's pay is slightly above most federal departmental or agency heads, which are mostly clustered around $900,000-$1,000,000.
However, the chief executives of some publicly owned corporations are paid far more.
Ellie Sweeney, the NBN Co chief executive, received $3.4 million in total remuneration in 2025-26, up from $1.9 million a year earlier, making her Australia's highest-paid public servant.
Paul Graham, the chief executive of Australia Post, received $3.3 million in 2024-25. Dennis Barns, the chief executive of Snowy Hydro Limited, received $2.1 million in 2024-25.
RBA workers don't want a real wage cut
The RBA is currently arguing with junior RBA staff about pay and conditions.
Lower-ranked RBA staff have been asking for a pay increase of 11 per cent over three years and an inflation-protection mechanism that triggers additional pay rises if inflation outpaces wages, to avoid real wage cuts in coming years.
But last month, hours after the RBA lifted rates for the fourth time this year, Ms Bullock emailed RBA staff and asked them to vote for a pay offer of 9.5 per cent over three years.
A majority of RBA staff had rejected a similar proposal in July.
The Finance Sector Union says enterprise agreement negotiations have been dragging on since late last year and the RBA has refused to move on its original pay offer.
The latest round of voting for the RBA's proposed enterprise agreement will close on Monday at 5pm.
After lifting interest rates last month, Ms Bullock said she sympathised with the plight of Australian workers.
But she said the only way workers could keep receiving sustainable increases in real wages was from productivity growth, and Australia's economy was struggling to deliver it.
"People are feeling, quite rightly, very annoyed and very upset about the fact that the costs of everything are rising, that their wages are not keeping pace with that, they’re seeing real wage cuts," she said.
"If we don't get productivity growth, there's not going to be real wage rises coming down the pipeline."
According to the RBA's annual report, the bank has 2,201 employees, equating to 2,082 full-time equivalent employees.
It has 76 senior executives, and another 222 highly paid staff.
The RBA's workforce has increased by 8 per cent over the past 12 months. The RBA says that reflects the additional resources it needs to implement its transformation and change agendas.
The additional staff are concentrated in technology and corporate support functions.
Higher unemployment will help to control inflation
Australia's unemployment rate is 4.7 per cent, in seasonally adjusted terms.
It is higher than the RBA forecast for this point in its rate-hiking cycle.
At a fireside chat last month, Ms Bullock said Australia may need an unemployment rate of 5 per cent to get inflation completely under control.
"[W]hat level of unemployment eases the pressure on the supply side of the economy?" she asked.
"I think between 4.5 and 5 will probably take enough heat out of the labour market that it'll ease pressure on inflation,"
she said.
On Thursday, Bureau of Statistics data showed that Australia's unemployment rate has risen 0.6 percentage points (from 4.1 per cent to 4.7 per cent) since the RBA started lifting interest rates in February this year.
Tom Kennedy from JP Morgan said outside of the COVID-19-related volatility, it was the largest nine-month increase in unemployment in more than a decade.
"The deterioration is also more pronounced than the RBA had forecast back in August," he said.
"Importantly, it's too early to see any effect from the RBA's September rate hike, which we think will weigh on both GDP growth and labour demand in coming quarters."
RBA records $11.3 billion negative equity position
The RBA's annual report shows the bank had a "negative equity" position of $11.3 billion at the end of June (compared with a negative equity position of $5.3 billion in June 2025).
The deterioration in its net equity position reflected a large "accounting loss" in 2025/26, which was partially offset by valuation gains on its gold holdings.
The RBA's Governance Board says negative equity does not affect the RBA's ability to operate effectively or perform its functions, but it is important that the equity position is restored over time.
"This can be achieved by retaining future year profits," the RBA says in its annual report.
"Based on market expectations for the cash rate as at 30 June 2026 and market prices and exchange rates at this time, negative equity is expected to diminish over the next few years.
"However, a return to target for the Reserve Bank Reserve Fund probably remains more than a decade away."

VW prepares recall in Germany
With recalls already under way in the US and the UK, VW is planning and rolling out recall campaigns in Germany and other markets.
Some battery cells in Volkswagen electric cars are defective. Internal quality checks have revealed the problem, according to Handelsblatt. A Volkswagen spokesperson told the outlet that several thousand vehicles are affected.
VW cited production faults at suppliers as the cause of the faulty battery cells. The issue is limited to a specific production period.
Because of the defect, the batteries may be exposed to increased thermal stress, according to the information available. In extreme cases, a fire in these electric vehicles cannot be ruled out, VW said.
According to Handelsblatt, the VW ID.3, ID.4, ID.7, ID Buzz and Cupra Born models produced between 2023 and 2025 are among those affected. The company has not yet confirmed this list of models.
The recall is being prepared in close coordination with the relevant authorities, the spokesperson said. It has not yet appeared in the databases of Germany’s Federal Motor Transport Authority (KBA).
VW sets out immediate measures
To prevent possible damage and incidents, the group is now recommending that potentially affected cars be charged only to a maximum of 80%. The manufacturer plans to recall some of the vehicles to service centres to check the batteries. Once the batteries have been inspected, the charging limit will be lifted for cars in which no fault is found.
If a defective battery is identified, the high-voltage battery module would not necessarily have to be replaced and could potentially be brought up to date with a software upgrade.
Customers whose vehicles are affected will be contacted by the company, according to the report. Owners will receive a letter informing them of the next steps.
A damaged screw led to a recall of around 2.86 million VW and Audi vehicles worldwide in September. The component could have caused the steering to fail, the KBA warned.
20% of VW deliveries are electric
VW’s electric-car business is strongest in Europe compared with the rest of the world.
The share of battery electric vehicles in Volkswagen Group’s European deliveries rose to 20% in the first three quarters of 2026, meaning one in five vehicles delivered was fully electric.
Overall, the group is grappling with falling demand worldwide, with business in China in particular slumping. In Germany, VW continues to dominate both the market for new electric car registrations and the used EV market.

Income after rent: How much is left across European cities?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
04:45:20 UTC
13:45:20 KST

One salary is not enough to afford a three-bedroom flat in many European city centres. Euronews Business takes a closer look at how much a working couple has left after paying the rent.
Many European countries face a housing crisis, with a shortage of homes and rising prices. Rents also continue to increase, and city centres are particularly expensive. A single salary is no longer enough to cover the rent for a family-sized flat in the heart of a major city for many European households.
But what if a couple both work and share the rent? Is that enough? How much money would they have left each month after paying rent? And how do European cities compare globally?
The Mapping the World’s Prices 2026 report, published by Deutsche Bank Research Institute, sheds some light on the topic. It looks at two people earning a local net salary and deducts the rent on a three-bedroom apartment in the given city centre. What remains is the household’s disposable income after rent.
Among 28 European cities, the disposable income after rent ranges from €253 in Lisbon to €9,140 in Zurich.
Swiss cities lead the ranking
Zurich has the most expensive rent (€5,502) among the 28 cities. But it also has the highest net salary (€7,321). As a result, a couple in Zurich has the most money left after rent (€9,140).
In addition to Zurich, Geneva is far ahead of the rest. In Geneva, a couple has €8,783 left each month after rent. This is thanks to the second-highest net salary (€6,516).
Luxembourg is third with €5,890. It has the third-highest net salary (€4,548). Its rent is also high (€3,206), but lower than in cities such as London, Dublin and Amsterdam. This leaves couples with more money at the end of the month.
Birmingham follows with €5,238, just ahead of Copenhagen with €5,233.
Birmingham vs London: Rent makes the difference
A couple in Birmingham has €5,238 left each month after rent. In London, the figure is €3,148. That means couples in Birmingham have €2,090 more each month.
Salaries are lower in Birmingham, but rent is much cheaper. A city-centre flat costs €1,949 in Birmingham, compared with €4,362 in London.
Couples also have more than €4,000 left after rent in Oslo (€4,936), Frankfurt (€4,786), Munich (€4,575) and Amsterdam (€4,431).
Amsterdam’s rent is among the five highest (€3,542), but a high net salary (€3,986) makes up for it.
Vienna (€3,709) and Stockholm (€3,674) are very close to this level.
Berlin beats Paris thanks to lower rent
Salaries in Paris are higher than in Berlin (€3,171 compared with €2,946). Yet couples in Berlin have more left after rent (€3,554 compared with €3,336). The reason is rent. A city-centre flat costs €3,005 in Paris but €2,339 in Berlin.
Dublin has a higher net salary (€3,455) than Paris, Berlin, Vienna and Stockholm. But couples there have less left after rent than in all of these cities (€3,038). Rent in Dublin is the fourth-highest in Europe (€3,873), and it is higher than one net salary.
Southern Europe is at the bottom
Cities in southern Europe have the lowest income after rent. Lisbon and Milan are the hardest cities for couples. In Lisbon, just €253 is left after rent. The net salary there is €1,408, but the rent is €2,561.
In Milan, only €697 is left. In Madrid, a couple has €1,905 left each month. In Barcelona, they have €1,832. The figure falls to €1,265 in Rome and €1,148 in Athens. In Athens, the rent (€1,164) is slightly higher than one net salary (€1,156).
Istanbul follows Lisbon at the bottom of the European list with €353. The net salary there is €1,027, but the rent is €1,701.
Central and Eastern Europe do better than the south
Some cities in Central and Eastern Europe perform better than those in Southern Europe. In Prague, a couple has €2,054 left after rent. In Warsaw, they have €1,985, and in Budapest €1,548. All three are above Rome and Athens.
It is important to note that rent is the only cost included. Couples still need to pay for food, bills and transport.
Is one salary enough to pay the rent?
The answer is no in many cities. In 11 cities, rent is higher than one net salary. These are Athens, Barcelona, Budapest, Dublin, Istanbul, Lisbon, London, Madrid, Milan, Prague and Rome.
Lisbon has the biggest gap. The net salary is €1,408, while rent costs €2,561, which is 82% more than one salary. In Milan, a net salary is €1,940, compared with rent of €3,184.
In Prague and Budapest, rent and one net salary are almost the same.
How does Europe compare with the rest of the world?
Europe performs well in the global ranking. Zurich (€9,140) and Geneva (€8,783) top the list of 69 cities, ahead of San Francisco (€7,992). Seven of the top 10 are in Europe.
No European city is in the bottom 10. All of them are in Latin America, Asia and Africa. In six, rent costs more than two net salaries. Manila (-€882) and Bangkok (-€759) are at the bottom.
In Moscow, a couple has €313 left after rent. The net salary is €1,570, but the rent is €2,827.
Several European cities also do better than New York (€1,921).
Younger generations in Europe have lower homeownership rates than earlier generations. In 2026, house prices and rents continue to rise across Europe, outpacing inflation in many countries.

NEW DELHI: Seven research centres across leading Indian institutions have been selected by the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) to develop priority medical devices and diagnostic technologies, with projects spanning portable screening for primary healthcare, biomaterials and technologies for eye and vascular diseases.The selected institutions are the Indian Institutes of Technology (IITs) at Kharagpur, Delhi, Bombay, Kanpur and Madras, the Indian Institute of Science (IISc), Bengaluru, and Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham, Coimbatore.Among the selected projects, IIT Bombay's centre, led by Dr Abhijit Majumder, will focus on portable screening, monitoring and point-of-care medical technologies for primary healthcare. Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham's centre, led by Prof Gopal S Pillai, will work on developing, validating and translating healthcare technologies for ophthalmic and vascular diseases, while IISc Bengaluru will focus on biomaterials and translational medical devices.IIT Kharagpur's PRAGATICAR, led by Prof Suman Chakraborty, will focus on frugal diagnostics, regenerative and personalised healthcare, artificial intelligence, digital health and advanced therapeutics. IIT Delhi's CAR-PATH, led by Prof Vivekanandan Perumal, will work on priority applied technologies for healthcare.At IIT Kanpur, Prof Amitabha Bandyopadhyay will lead a multidisciplinary proposal to develop 10 priority healthcare products.
IIT Madras will host TARaNGaM, a translational hub for next-generation medical technology, devices and diagnostics, led by Prof Mohanasankar Sivaprakasam.The initiative aims to accelerate the development of affordable, accessible and indigenous healthcare technologies addressing unmet clinical needs. To identify these needs, ICMR undertook an exercise involving clinicians from different healthcare settings, including tier-1, tier-2 and tier-3 cities, and drew up a curated list of around 100 priority medical device and diagnostic technologies.Under the original call for proposals, applicants were required to propose the development of at least eight to 10 technologies from this list, covering a mix of low-risk and high-risk products. The scheme provides for funding of up to Rs 15 crore per centre over five years, with an emphasis on regulatory-compliant product development and eventual commercialisation.
The call prioritised institutions with a track record in research, prototyping, technology transfer and commercialisation. It also required centres to leverage existing infrastructure, build a trained medical technology research workforce and continue functioning beyond the funding period, with host institutions expected to sustain them as permanent activities.The key challenge will be translating research into validated products that can address clinical needs and reach patients. The results list does not specify the individual devices to be developed by most of the selected centres, their development timelines or when the technologies could become available for clinical use.

What We Know So Far About the Elementary School Shooting in Bend, Oregon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
04:45:05 UTC
13:45:05 KST

A 16-year-old opened fire at an elementary school in Bend, Oregon, on Thursday, killing three children and a teacher before being shot dead by a community member, police said.
Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said in a press conference that the children killed at Silver Rail Elementary School were aged 5, 8, and 11. Also, a 7-year-old and a 54-year-old teacher were transported to St. Charles Bend hospital with critical injuries.
Krantz said the suspect, a male city resident who has not yet been publicly identified, was spotted entering the school by a community member, who eventually pursued him into the school and shot him. The chief said the suspect forced his way into the school by firing at locked doors.
Police did not speculate on the shooter’s motive and said they did not know whether the suspect knew anybody in the school or if he had attended.
FBI Director Kash Patel posted on social media that the agency’s Portland field office is assisting in the investigation. “We will make every resource they need available,” he added.
A vigil was held Thursday evening in the wake of the shooting.
“A school should be a safe place where children can learn and feel secure,” Bend Mayor Melanie Kebler said at the same press conference the police chief spoke at. “What happened today should never happen.”
Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek said at the same conference that her heart was “absolutely broken” over the incident: “No parent should have to have this kind of day, and no community should have to live through this kind of day.” She also thanked the community member who pursued the shooter.
CNN’s analysis of incidents reported by the Gun Violence Archive, Education Week and Everytown for Gun Safety shows that the shooting at Silver Rail Elementary marks the 36th one on K-12 school grounds this year. It is the 52nd school shooting in the country this year.
What happened?
Krantz said that at 12:59 p.m., police received a 911 call from a person in a vehicle who reported being shot at multiple times by someone “with a long gun.”
Multiple calls followed, reporting that a shooter had entered Silver Rail Elementary School, which is about 120 mi. southeast of Portland. The school enrolls more than 400 students from kindergarten to 5th grade.
Krantz said police directed the school to go into lockdown at 1:01 p.m. and first responding officers arrived a minute later. Upon entering the school building, Krantz said, officers confirmed that the suspect was dead and found the four other people who died from their injuries, and their families have been notified.
Krantz did not speak on the weapon used in the shooting. But an unidentified law enforcement official briefed on the shooting told the Associated Press that it was a pump-action shotgun purchased by the suspect’s mother.
How are politicians reacting?
Oregon’s Republican candidate for governor, state senator Christine Drazan, posted on social media that her heart was with the affected families, students, and teaching staff. “We have to commit to protecting our kids,” she added. “We have to put a complete stop to shootings at our schools. This has to end.”
Rep. Janelle Bynum, a Democrat who represents the district that includes Bend, said in a statement: “Our babies are supposed to do arts and crafts at school, not use their desks as cover from gunfire. They’re supposed to make friends, not mourn them.”
U.S. Senator Ron Wyden (D, Ore.) lamented in a statement that the victims in Silver Rail Elementary School and their loved ones faced the “awful consequences” of another school shooting in the country. He added that the “best way to honor” them is to “at long last pass common-sense gun laws that reduce the risks of more children, parents, teachers and staff forced to live in fear of similar nightmares for their schools.”

Australians were getting this vaccine for free. Now they could pay up to $180
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
04:42:03 UTC
13:42:03 KST

IN BRIEF:
- There is no national set price for private COVID-19 vaccines, with prices varying across pharmacies.
- Experts have said that, while costs could deter some, at-risk populations should be the priority.
Australians could now pay anywhere up to $180 for a COVID-19 vaccination, depending on which pharmacy they attend, with one retailer telling SBS News it was unlikely to stock it at all.
On 1 October, the COVID-19 vaccine was moved into the routine National Immunisation Program (NIP) schedule, replacing the standalone National COVID-19 Vaccine Program established during the pandemic that offered free jabs.
While the NIP will continue to cover the cost of COVID-19 vaccinations for at-risk cohorts, such as older Australians and severely immunocompromised people, those who are ineligible will have to pay an out-of-pocket cost to get the jab.
With no nationally set price, vaccination providers have discretion to set costs for those ineligible under the NIP.
SBS News identified significant price differences across Australian pharmacies, with one TerryWhite Chemmart outlet charging $120 while consumers were paying $179.99 at Chemist Warehouse stores Australia-wide.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
A spokesperson from Priceline Pharmacies told SBS News that, as each of its outlets was independently owned and operated, the decision to offer COVID-19 vaccinations and set their prices was made on a store-by-store basis.
One Priceline store in Sydney's CBD quoted the private cost of the vaccine at $130.
Another in the Melbourne CBD said that, while they weren't currently offering the vaccine for people not covered by the NIP, they were expecting to charge a price similar to Chemist Warehouse's $179.99.
Another nearby Priceline store said that, due to the wholesale cost, it was unlikely to stock the private vaccine.
A spokesperson for Terry White Chemmart wasn't available to comment, but SBS News identified that prices for the shot across the chain's locations ranged from $120 in Melbourne CBD to $170 in central Adelaide.
No national set price or requirement to stock
Anna Theophilos, who owns a TerryWhite Chemmart pharmacy, told SBS News that the high wholesale price for the private vaccine meant pharmacists would make "business decisions" based on demand, including whether to stock the vaccine.
Theophilos, who is also the inaugural national vaccination ambassador at the Pharmaceutical Society of Australia, said minimum order requirements and the expiration date of current stock were key issues.
"The current vaccine has a short expiry date of February, which is contributing to the hesitation," she told SBS News.
"Usually we have a longer expiry date and pharmacists have agreements with wholesalers to ensure suppliers can buy back expired stock."
She said an agreement between wholesalers and pharmacies regarding expired stock would be the "final piece that comes into play".
Australia 'can't provide every vaccine free'
Under the NIP, the COVID-19 vaccination is available for free to adults aged 75 and over every six months, and adults aged 65 to 74 every 12 months.
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people aged 50 to 74 also remain eligible for an annual dose, as do adults aged 18 and over who are severely immunocompromised.
University of New South Wales School of Population Health professor Holly Seale said that, while the price of a private COVID-19 vaccine might deter some Australians, the decision to move it onto the NIP was the right one.
She said it would align Australia with other countries and ensure people who most needed the vaccine received it as part of a broader package of adult vaccinations.
"The government has to assess who is most at risk and where vaccines will have the greatest impact," she told SBS News.
"We can't provide every vaccine free of charge, nor do we need to."
Seale said the decision prioritised those more likely to be hospitalised, and was based on available evidence and international data.
New vaccines are in development that could see two vaccines combined, for example COVID-19 and flu, that could mean the cost of an individual vaccine is reduced, she said.
"We are in a transition phase, but I think there are lots of new developments happening around the COVID vaccine that we just have to wait for, and see what happens."
The latest respiratory surveillance report shows that only 8 per cent of Australians received a COVID-19 vaccination in the past year, compared with the influenza vaccine at 30.5 per cent.
Cost was reported as a barrier by about a quarter of people who experienced difficulty getting a flu vaccine, according to Australia's National Vaccine Insights Survey.
Theophilos said it "would be naïve to say the price won't deter some people".
"Of course it will. But I think it will ultimately come down to people understanding their individual risk and whether vaccination is recommended for them."
Australians 'lagging' behind new vaccines
Earlier reporting from SBS News revealed that the latest COVID-19 vaccine tailored for new variants remained unavailable in Australia.
Pfizer and BioNTech's latest COVID-19 vaccine, adapted to target the XFG subvariant, was approved in the United States for the 2026-27 season, following international guidance to more closely match vaccines with contemporary circulating variants.
While Australia does not yet have that formulation registered, Seale said it wouldn't be the main factor affecting vaccine uptake, adding that Australia had managed similar strain updates with influenza vaccines for many years.
"There are a lot of factors involved in vaccine procurement and supply. Just because an updated vaccine becomes available internationally doesn't mean it's immediately possible to secure enough doses locally," she said.
Pfizer and BioNTech's LP.8.1-adapted COVID-19 vaccine was registered on the Australian Register of Therapeutic Goods in late 2025 and became available in Australia in December.
Moderna's LP.8.1 formulation has also been registered in Australia.
A 'positive step'
While the private COVID-19 vaccine rollout was still in its early stages, Theophilos said she was pleased to hear reports of customers undeterred by the new price.
"Australians place a lot of value on their health, and sometimes we underestimate that. People who are proactive about staying up to date with recommended vaccinations may still choose to receive the vaccine despite the cost," she said.
"It's something we'll need to assess once people actually have the opportunity to purchase it."
Seale said it was important to recognise that moving the vaccine onto the NIP was a "positive step" that ensured coverage was targeted toward those who needed it most.
"If people do feel they're at risk, or if there's an increase in cases in their community, they still have the option to purchase the vaccine privately."

Stent safety concerns reach Centre after reports of complications with Indian-made devices in Sri Lanka
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
04:34:02 UTC
13:34:02 KST

Rajya Sabha MP Ajeet Madhavrao Gopchade has urged a review of coronary stent safety standards after reports of complications involving Indian-made devices in Sri Lanka
NEW DELHI: The Cabinet Secretariat has taken up concerns over the safety and quality of coronary stents with the Union health ministry after a Rajya Sabha MP sought intervention following reports of complications involving Indian-made devices in Sri Lanka.In an October 5 letter, Cabinet Secretary T V Somanathan acknowledged a representation from Rajya Sabha MP Dr Ajeet Madhavrao Gopchade, a medical doctor, said it had been forwarded to the department of health and family welfare for appropriate action and a reply.Gopchade’s September 28 representation cited media reports that Sri Lanka’s regulator had directed the withdrawal of three models of Indian-manufactured drug-eluting stents over concerns including improper positioning, stent dislodgement, acute stent thrombosis and failure to expand properly. The reported issues were identified during an investigation by Sri Lanka’s Medical Device Evaluation Committee, according to the letter.
The MP cautioned that the reported concerns might not all ultimately be substantiated, but said they warranted scrutiny of existing safeguards for device performance, clinical appropriateness and the detection of complications after implantation.The representation calls for more stringent pre-market testing of stents and delivery systems, including assessments of durability, deployment, expansion and dislodgement.
It also seeks stronger clinical documentation to ensure stenting is performed only when medically indicated and alternatives are considered where appropriate.A key recommendation is end-to-end traceability through batch and serial numbers for every implanted stent, allowing affected devices and patients to be identified quickly if a safety alert emerges. The MP has also sought stronger adverse-event reporting, particularly for stent thrombosis, migration, incomplete expansion, deformation and delivery-system complications.The representation further calls for a mechanism to swiftly review safety alerts, recalls and withdrawals issued by foreign regulators when the same or similar devices are marketed in India. Better patient follow-up and long-term safety data collection have also been proposed to detect emerging risks early.
Citing regulatory guidance from the US, the UK and Canada, Gopchade highlighted the importance of engineering and durability testing, clinical evidence, traceability and timely regulatory action when safety signals emerge. He urged the health ministry and the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) to examine the issues with cardiology experts and other stakeholders.The Cabinet Secretariat’s communication does not establish that the government has accepted the allegations, ordered a formal investigation or approved new regulatory measures. NEW DELHI: The Cabinet Secretariat has taken up concerns over the safety and quality of coronary stents with the Union health ministry after a Rajya Sabha MP sought intervention following reports of complications involving Indian-made devices in Sri Lanka.In an October 5 letter, Cabinet Secretary T V Somanathan acknowledged a representation from Rajya Sabha MP Dr Ajeet Madhavrao Gopchade, a medical doctor, said it had been forwarded to the Department of Health and Family Welfare for appropriate action and a reply.Gopchade’s September 28 representation cited media reports that Sri Lanka’s regulator had directed the withdrawal of three models of Indian-manufactured drug-eluting stents over concerns including improper positioning, stent dislodgement, acute stent thrombosis and failure to expand properly. The reported issues were identified during an investigation by Sri Lanka’s Medical Device Evaluation Committee, according to the letter.The MP cautioned that the reported concerns might not all ultimately be substantiated, but said they warranted scrutiny of existing safeguards for device performance, clinical appropriateness and the detection of complications after implantation.The representation calls for more stringent pre-market testing of stents and delivery systems, including assessments of durability, deployment, expansion and dislodgement.
It also seeks stronger clinical documentation to ensure stenting is performed only when medically indicated and alternatives are considered where appropriate.A key recommendation is end-to-end traceability through batch and serial numbers for every implanted stent, allowing affected devices and patients to be identified quickly if a safety alert emerges. The MP has also sought stronger adverse-event reporting, particularly for stent thrombosis, migration, incomplete expansion, deformation and delivery-system complications.The representation further calls for a mechanism to swiftly review safety alerts, recalls and withdrawals issued by foreign regulators when the same or similar devices are marketed in India. Better patient follow-up and long-term safety data collection have also been proposed to detect emerging risks early.
Citing regulatory guidance from the US, the UK and Canada, Gopchade highlighted the importance of engineering and durability testing, clinical evidence, traceability and timely regulatory action when safety signals emerge. He urged the health ministry and the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) to examine the issues with cardiology experts and other stakeholders.The Cabinet Secretariat’s communication does not establish that the government has accepted the allegations, ordered a formal investigation or approved new regulatory measures. The reported concerns also do not, by themselves, establish that similar complications have occurred in India.

WASHINGTON – European Union leaders rallied around President Volodymyr Zelensky at a summit on Oct 16 as US President Donald Trump fired another salvo at Ukraine, calling its strikes on Russian refineries a “disgrace”.
The EU is hosting Zelensky in Brussels at one of the most difficult moments for Ukraine, with missiles and drones raining down on Ukrainian cities and fears that the US could pull back intelligence sharing and weapons support from Kyiv.
Trump blindsided Zelensky last weekend by announcing that Ukraine and Russia had agreed not to target each other’s energy facilities.
Facing US midterm elections in November, Trump has blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries for pushing up energy prices that could cost him at the ballot box.
The US has also struck a diesel deal with Russia, angering Ukraine and European allies.
“We want to end this war as quick as possible. We don’t see now signals from the Russian side that they are ready for this, to end this war. That’s why we have to prepare for the winter,” Zelensky said as he arrived at the summit, hugging many of the leaders as he met them.

In the latest attacks, Russian drone strikes on the city of Kharkiv killed three people, while strikes elsewhere left hundreds of thousands of people without power.

“Last winter was already hell, this one will be once again like hell,” Michal said.

“Because always, at the start (and) at the end of every conversation, people need to be reminded that we are sitting in a warm room, lights are on, heating is on, the coffee is warm, and we cannot get tired of the war in Ukraine, because they are fighting... for us.”
No ready-made European alternative to Starlink
Ukraine’s leadership has been alarmed by disruptions to the SpaceX Starshield satellite system used by Kyiv for battlefield communications and drone operations.
A source in Ukraine’s defence ministry said on Oct 15 that Starshield receptors were only working at speeds of up to 160kmh, complicating their use for military missions.
A US official has denied that Trump ordered a deliberate slowdown of Starshield, which is the military-grade version of the Starlink service operated by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, and Trump said this week intelligence sharing with Ukraine continued.
Europe does not have a ready-made alternative to Starlink, although European governments and companies are working on long-term options.
“Starlink is really necessary for Ukraine. And unfortunately, in short term, Europe can’t replace this capability,” said the EU’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas.
“We are working on the new sanctions package to put the pressure on Russia, and we of course hope that we do this with all our partners around the world.”
Ukraine struck a Russian oil refinery after Zelensky declared that Kyiv was abandoning the energy ceasefire that Trump had announced.
“All he’s doing is making the world oil price higher. Well, I think that’s a disgrace,” Trump said in an interview with the Newsmax news outlet.
While EU leaders hit out at the US deal to buy Russian diesel, they are also grappling with how to tackle energy prices that have soared since the Iran war, exposing divisions between member states on day one of the summit on Oct 15.
Zelensky told Reuters earlier in October that Ukraine had agreed a plan with European partners that would allow it to close a US$27 billion (S$34.5 billion) deficit in its military spending for 2026, allowing it to order the drones needed to continue fighting at the start of 2027.
However, Finance Minister Sergii Marchenko said recently Ukraine still faced an unfunded budget gap for 2027 of US$32.6 billion – and that does not include an estimated US$40 billion in direct military supplies from allies.
“I am unhappy with the number of countries that have been willing to pledge new financial support to Ukraine,” said Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten.
Sounding a more sceptical note, Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker urged caution in the debate over making new, far-reaching financial commitments to Ukraine.

Country diary: A three-day perambulation around my own parish | Simon Lockett
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
04:30:50 UTC
13:30:50 KST

I was sitting at my desk again, with the dull hum and the blue glow of the screen. It seems that every occupation traps people at their desk, and being a vicar is no different. But I wanted to resist, and it happened to be the 800th anniversary of Saint Francis of Assisi’s death. With Jesus of Galilee as inspiration, Saint Francis was known for his vow of simplicity, his love of the Earth and his critique of the wealth accumulated by the religious elite at the expense of the poor. He was also horrified by the Fifth Crusade, so he travelled to Egypt, hoping to make peace.
Francis also walked the walk, as it were, sleeping in caves in the Umbrian hills, taking nothing with him. No sitting at the desk for Francis. So I decided to do the same, spending three days walking the bridleways, holloways, footpaths and country lanes of the Golden Valley, speaking to people along the way. My sanctuary for the night was one of my parish churches – Madley, Tyberton, then Peterchurch, with its very welcome underfloor heating.
The conversations were rich. People love Saint Francis because of his love of animals. Some found his actions, such as disrobing before a bishop – a sign of his rejection of church corruption – “extreme”. Thomas, a young farmer, challenged me when I said Francis’s rejection of wealth inspired me. Thomas spoke of the importance of “the posture of the heart” towards wealth – that riches can be used for good. The children in the primary school loved the story of Francis taming a wolf.
But the conversation that stayed with me most took place looking over the valley, with Bill, a businessman out walking his dog. We chatted about Saint Francis, and he bemoaned the culture that was taking hold in his business. His wish was for a Franciscan simplicity. Instead of a company that cherished belonging, community and purpose, one that was relational and people-oriented, it had become full of policies, programmes and technique. Simplicity had given way to complexity.
I walked on through an oak wood, buzzards mewing overhead, a complexity of relationships that had led to simplicity. Ecology and Saint Francis have much to teach us.

Russia’s nighttime strikes on Ukrainian regions — where explosions were heard and the consequences
Kyiv • UNN
Russia attacked Ukraine with drones: there are casualties in Cherkasy and Sumy regions, fires in Khmelnytskyi region, and power outages in Kyiv and the surrounding region.
During the night of October 16, Russian forces attacked a number of regions of Ukraine with attack drones and other means of destruction. Casualties were reported in Cherkasy and Sumy regions, fires broke out in Khmelnytskyi region, and widespread power outages occurred in Kyiv and the surrounding region. This was reported by regional military administrations, police and energy companies, UNN writes.
Details
In the city of Uman, Cherkasy region, a high-rise building caught fire as a result of a Russian drone crashing. A guardhouse was also destroyed, and a man was rescued from beneath the rubble. According to Ihor Taburets, head of the Cherkasy Regional Military Administration, five people were injured, three of whom were hospitalized. In addition, fires broke out at commercial warehouses and on the premises of a private enterprise.
Russian drones attacked Khmelnytskyi region repeatedly. According to Serhii Tiurin, head of the regional military administration, air defense forces shot down enemy targets; however, a fire broke out at an oil depot in Shepetivka district. Relevant services were involved in dealing with the aftermath.
Strikes on energy infrastructure and shelling of frontline regions
In Kyiv and Kyiv region, a Russian strike on a critical energy infrastructure facility caused widespread power outages in certain districts. Energy workers reported that damage assessment and emergency repair work would begin after the air raid alert ended.
In Sumy region, Russians carried out 85 strikes on 31 settlements over the past day. According to the police, eight people were injured. Five people were injured in the Sumy community, and two more men in the Seredyna-Buda community.
Zaporizhzhia region was also subjected to intense shelling. Over the course of the day, the occupiers carried out 669 strikes on 48 settlements, including 29 airstrikes.
In addition, explosions were reported overnight in Lutsk, Khmelnytskyi, Zviahel, Korets and other cities in western Ukraine. Information about the consequences of the attacks in these settlements is being уточнено.

Organisers say cockroaches symbolises filth and dirt in home and society
NEW DELHI: A 30-foot-tall cockroach effigy will be burnt alongside those of Ravan, Kumbhkaran and Meghnad during Dussehra celebrations in the national capital this year, with organisers saying the insect will symbolise filth and unhygienic conditions as part of their cleanliness message.The Shri Keshav Ramlila Committee, which organises the Ramlila in Pitampura, said the initiative aims to highlight the need to eliminate filth from homes, neighbourhoods and society at large, in keeping with the Swachh Bharat and Swachh Delhi campaigns.Ashok Goel Devaraha, president of the committee and Model Town BJP MLA, said the decision was intended to reinforce the message of the triumph of good over evil and was not politically motivated.Speaking to ANI, Devaraha said Vijayadashami symbolises the victory of truth over falsehood and righteousness over unrighteousness. He added that the committee had previously burnt effigies representing issues affecting the country, including Naxalism and terrorism.“Keeping these principles in mind, we have also, in the past, burned effigies representing various afflictions plaguing our nation, such as Naxalism or terrorism.
This year, our committee has decided to burn an effigy of a cockroach, a symbol of filth,” he said.
The effigy will be set alight at the committee grounds in Pitampura. Devaraha described it as a 30-foot-tall structure shaped like a cockroach, adding that the aim was to draw attention to the need to rid homes, neighbourhoods and society of dirt and unhygienic conditions.How did ‘cockroach’ become a political name?The choice of the insect comes amid protests by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) and opposition parties in Delhi, which had been campaigning against former Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan and is now demanding the resignation of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.The group staged protests against Pradhan in June and July, including a demonstration at Jantar Mantar and a march towards Parliament on July 20. Pradhan subsequently resigned as education minister in July, while Pralhad Joshi took over the portfolio.
The CJP has since returned to the streets over its allegations concerning the electoral roll revision process, joining opposition parties and student organisations in demonstrations. Several activists, students and journalists were detained during protests in the capital.The committee president, however, has denied that the cockroach effigy is politically motivated, maintaining that it is intended to convey a message about cleanliness.Also read: 6,000 cops, 200 CAPF companies: As CJP pushes ahead with Tiranga march, Delhi prepares for a high-security fridayOn May 15, while hearing a case in the Supreme Court, CJI Surya Kant had compared certain individuals with fraudulent degrees to “cockroaches” who become social media or RTI activists to attack the system. The remarks triggered widespread backlash among young people and inspired the satirical “Cockroach Janta Party” (CJP) movement.He later clarified that his oral remarks during a Supreme Court hearing were “misquoted” and later used with “malicious intent” to mislead the country’s youth.

Carney says US trying to break Canada amid vote for Alberta independence referendum
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
04:24:00 UTC
13:24:00 KST

Carney implies US trying to 'break' Canada as Alberta vote looms
October 16, 2026
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney warned the people of oil-rich Alberta against looming threats, suggesting that the United States was trying to "break" Canada so it could "own us."
Carney was speaking at a pro-Canada rally in Calgary, ahead of a vote which will decide if the disgruntled western province will begin a legal process toward separation from Canada.
"The world has become more dangerous and divided. Some outside our borders are working to break us so they can own us," he said, without naming the US or its president, Donald Trump.
This is not the first time Carney has made such a claim. His warning comes as Washington and Ottawa are in the middle of a trade war and Trump has threatened to make Canada the 51st US state.
Meanwhile, Carney's push toward making Canada less dependent on the US has irked Trump.
What is Alberta voting for?
Monday's vote in Alberta is not a direct referendum on independence. Rather, the province, which has the world's fourth-largest proven oil reserves, will vote to decide whether to remain a province or instruct the government to begin the legal process toward a referendum on separation.
Polling indicates less than a quarter of Alberta's roughly five million people want to break away from Canada.
Albertans have long held grievances with liberal governments in Ottawa, from concerns about immigration and federal power to oil industry management. While Carney, who grew up in Alberta, has attempted to address frustrations, a lot stands to be resolved.
"The frustrations that many Albertans have felt are real," Carney said, adding that Ottawa had made Albertans feel "like our resources weren't our own."
However, he urged the public there to not use the vote as a "message" to the federal government.
"Don't be fooled by the idea you can 'send a message' with your vote," Carney said. "This is not poker. A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep division and great uncertainty."
Mitch Sylvestre, who heads the Alberta Prosperity Project, a prominent separatist organization, told AFP that US interests "don't play a role" in Alberta "until we win and become a government." At that point, he would ensure free-flowing trade.
"There is no animosity toward America here," he said, adding that he didn't see a reason to stop trading with the world's largest economy.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has called Alberta a "natural partner" for the United States, and Alberta Prosperity Project leaders have held several meetings at the State Department.
Edited by: Natalie Muller

"I want to come back, but ... obviously I have to think about it," Hasselbaink added.

And thereafter, we have explained how the contempt is not made out,” he said.“It is with reference to compliance of that law that in every affidavit, this is the first paragraph. Now, in media and social media, things are going on that govt has apologised and they want to say nothing,” he complained.CJI Kant said, “We have not read those media reports, nor are we taking cognisance of any such report.” Justice Bagchi added, “We are neither taking cognisance of the media reports nor your unqualified apology. An order to implement speed restrictions on Starlink systems for the Ukrainian military came from within the White House, Reuters reported on Oct. 15, citing U.S. and Western officials.
Starlink, implemented speed restrictions on Oct. 14 without warning, limiting speed to 100 miles per hour (160 kilometers per hour). The unexpected restriction disrupted active military operations, including the use of mid-range strike and interceptor drones.
Ukraine relies on Starlink for several military applications including operating its "middle strike" campaign in Russian-occupied Ukraine, as well as interceptor drones that defend against Russia's new jet-powered attack drones. It is restricted from using it inside Russia itself.
Pentagon officials received notice from within the White House that the Starshield service — Starlink's military package — needed to be slowed down, two U.S. officials, and another Western official, told Reuters on the condition of anonymity. Officials did not state who was responsible for issuing the order.
The speed restrictions were accompanied by signal disruptions and instability, even at lower speeds. Military personnel from multiple units reported serious issues with Starlink throughout the day.
Presidential adviser Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov said that "several" military missions severely disrupting amid the restrictions.

====================================================================================================

Wind Sled, Spanish invention to cross Antarctica without emissions: 'Unique in the world'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
04:01:50 UTC
13:01:50 KST

Explorer Ramón Larramendi will lead an 80-day, 3,400 km South Pole expedition in a kite-powered vehicle that can travel up to 80kph.
Spanish polar explorer Ramón Larramendi will lead a scientific expedition that will travel around 3,400 kilometres across the interior of Antarctica over roughly 80 days, without using fossil fuels for transport.
The Antarctic Wind Sled 2026-2027 project will carry equipment to conduct 16 research projects in some of the most inaccessible regions on the planet, with the aim of expanding knowledge of ice, climate change and polar ecosystems.
"The wind sled is something completely unique in the world," Larramendi tells Euronews during an interview in Madrid's central Plaza de España. The explorer believes that the vehicle he has designed is an exceptional combination of traditional techniques and advanced technology, conceived to cover long distances without combustion engines or air drops.
The expedition will leave Spain on 18 October and is due to return in early February. The route will start near Russia's Novolazarevskaya base, in Queen Maud Land, and end at the French-Italian Concordia station at Dome C, after crossing the Pole of Inaccessibility and passing close to the Pole of Cold.
A wind-powered vehicle to cross Antarctica with zero emissions
The Wind Sled is a polar exploration platform that uses kites to harness the power of the wind and solar energy to fuel scientific equipment. Its design, inspired by Inuit culture, as Larramendi explains, is the result of some 25 years of development and experimentation, during which the explorer has travelled more than 28,000 kilometres over ice on different expeditions.
"This sled combines Inuit techniques, which can look like old-fashioned and slightly strange bits of technology. That makes it a very, very unusual mix, but hugely efficient," says the explorer, who sees sustainability as one of the fundamental pillars of the project.
The vehicle consists of four modules and is 15 metres long. It can carry up to 2,100 kg of cargo, although on this occasion it will initially transport around 250 kg of scientific instruments.
The crew will have 20 kites, with sail areas ranging from five to 150 square metres, which they will deploy according to the weather conditions. In favourable conditions, the sled can reach 80 kilometres per hour, with an average speed of around 25 kilometres per hour.
The absence of fossil fuels reduces both the environmental impact and the logistical needs of the expedition. By way of comparison, the 2011-2012 Scientific Transantarctic Expedition covered a similar distance using tracked trucks, snowmobiles and sleds, consuming around 170,000 litres of fuel in two months.
Larramendi hopes this campaign will showcase the vehicle's potential as a scientific platform for future crossings. "Other systems powered by renewable energy may emerge to cross Antarctica, but none will be more sustainable and have a lower impact than the Wind Sled," he argues.
Sixteen projects to study ice, pollutants and microbial life
The expedition will carry out 16 scientific projects selected through a call coordinated by the Spanish Polar Committee. The research, involving CSIC, CIEMAT, INTA, six Spanish universities and international bodies, will provide direct measurements in areas where data is scarce, complementing information gathered by satellites and permanent stations.
Among the projects is a study by NASA's Ames Research Center, led by Spaniard Alfonso Dávila, which will examine whether conditions favourable to microbial life can exist inside salt rocks exposed to Antarctica's extreme cold. Sensors will measure temperature, relative humidity and electrical conductivity to determine whether liquid water may have formed inside them, despite the low temperatures and the arid environment.
Another project, called Dinglac and led by glaciologist Francisco Navarro of the Polytechnic University of Madrid, will use ground-penetrating radar to analyse the top 10 metres of snow. The measurements will help to understand how snow layers accumulate and move and to improve estimates of how Antarctic ice mass is evolving in the context of climate change.
The campaign will also study the presence of microplastics, persistent pollutants and possible microorganisms and viruses, as well as investigating the Earth's magnetism and the performance of the European Galileo navigation systems. Some of the experiments will use instrumentation linked to space exploration.
For Larramendi, the value of this work also lies in the fact that it will be carried out in territory that is virtually unknown from a scientific point of view. "It is taking place in an area for which there are practically no data," he explains. The system makes it possible to venture into regions where the difficulties and costs of conventional operations mean research campaigns are especially complex.
Four people isolated for 85 days: An experiment for future space missions
The expedition will be made up of four Antarctic veterans: Larramendi himself; Hilo Moreno, polar guide and mountain technician; Mariusz Potocki, a researcher at the University of Maine in the United States; and Javier Selva, photographer, documentary-maker and head of technical image direction. Selva already accompanied Larramendi on an Antarctic expedition between 2011 and 2012.
As well as taking part in fieldwork, the four explorers will themselves be study subjects. The WindSled Mind project, led by Gabriel G. de la Torre from the University of Cádiz, will analyse the effects of prolonged isolation on the crew's psychological responses, sleep and social interaction. "We are part of the research project and yes, we do feel a bit like guinea pigs, but we are happy," Larramendi says with a smile.
The study aims to generate knowledge applicable to future long-duration space missions, in which astronauts will have to face conditions of confinement, danger and extreme remoteness from Earth. Antarctica is one of the most suitable environments on the planet for studying these factors and testing instruments intended for future planetary exploration.
"We are the experiment ourselves. Four people isolated for 85 days in the interior of the Antarctic continent," Larramendi notes. The explorer explains that there are two projects in which the members of the expedition themselves are the object of research.
Self-sufficiency will be one of the keys to the journey. The team will carry the supplies and equipment needed to remain for weeks without external support, although they have an evacuation plan in place in case of a medical emergency or any other extraordinary situation.
An unprecedented route with an eye on future expeditions
The crossing, which can be followed live on the Trineo de Viento website, is the culmination of decades of development of the Wind Sled and will test its ability to carry a scientific payload unprecedented in Larramendi's Antarctic expeditions. The four members will set up five scientific stations along the route, with extended stops to collect samples, carry out experiments and take measurements.
On arrival at Concordia, the explorers will leave the continent by air, while the scientific material will return to Spain with French support. The sled will remain dismantled at the base, ready for a possible future journey in the opposite direction.
The aim is for expeditions to be repeated so that data gathered in different campaigns can be compared, something essential for identifying changes in ice and climate. "Repeated data collection is absolutely key to tracking variations," Larramendi stresses.
The journey, integrated into the XL Antarctic Research Campaign, which marks the 40th anniversary of the Spanish polar expedition, thus aims to consolidate a low environmental impact route for scientific exploration into the interior of the continent. It offers an alternative that combines research in one of the most extreme regions on Earth with the development of technologies that could contribute to future space missions.
