They [the terrorists] will spray gasoline or diesel fuel from a special tanker, then burn the place, and broadcast the pictures," the terror leader wrote.
The documents also show how Sinwar tricked Israel's political, defense, and intelligence establishments, and tricked them into believing he was leaning towards a political settlement with Israel.
Sinwar also wrote what could happen in the event that other terrorist organizations from the West Bank and the Iran-led "Axis of Resistance" would join in the massacre.
"There may be indications of the enemy's collapse from the very beginning, and it is possible that the movements of our people in the 'interior,' in Jerusalem and the West Bank, as well as Hezbollah's intervention, will encourage this," he wrote.
"Therefore, we must be prepared to expand the attack to its maximum. The core of the plan should include control of the centers of power and command and control of our central forces. Forces of the Palestinian factions can be sent to population centers, but our forces must be concentrated on important defined objectives and key positions," he added.
What happened during Sinwar's assassination?
Combat teams from the Nahal and 828th Brigades, respectively, were conducting operations in the Tel Sultan neighborhood of Rafah based on intelligence indicating potential high-value Hamas targets in the area, when they spotted terrorists leaving a building.
A firefight ensued; the terrorists scattered, and unbeknownst to the soldiers at the time, Sinwar remained alone, abandoned in a building.
He was killed in a firefight shortly thereafter.
Detailing the combat encounter
Several weeks before Sinwar was killed, the IDF's Gaza Division assumed responsibility for the Rafah sector of the Gaza Strip.
On the day of the engagement in which Sinwar was killed, lookouts spotted three armed terrorists moving through a damaged, IDF-controlled area roughly 300 meters from an ongoing engineering operation, the military said on Friday.
Two of the terror operatives carried a blanket, and the third wore a tactical vest, the military added.
A battalion commander spotted them, opened fire, and wounded one in the arm. This wounded operative was later confirmed to be Sinwar.
Soldiers encircled the area using tanks and drones. One soldier was severely wounded and evacuated during a firefight.
Sinwar, wounded from the aforementioned shooting, fled, entering a separate building from the other two terror operatives.
An IDF Paratrooper Brigade company entered to search the building that Sinwar had entered. A platoon commander noticed a pool of blood, indicating a wounded terrorist nearby. Moments afterward, two grenades were thrown at the soldiers, one of which detonated, the military said.
Soldiers applied heavy fire on the structure, including tank shells, machine gun fire, and small arms fire. That evening, an IDF drone entered the structure and located the remains of a body. Soldiers waited until the next morning to complete searches due to operational risks, the military noted.
When search teams entered the structure, they were able to positively identify Sinwar and confirm his death.

Editor's Notes: A break with Israel would hurt American Jews, too - comment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
03:18:44 UTC
12:18:44 KST

During a visit to the US a few months ago, I met a woman born in postwar Europe to Holocaust survivors. She told me she felt another Holocaust was coming. Zohran Mamdani had been elected mayor of New York, and she was frightened.
She usually voted Democratic. She and others I spoke with were frustrated and unsure whom to support. Trump offended much of what they believed in. They were trying to work out how to vote without ignoring either their fears or their values.
I listened. I live in Israel, where a Jewish vote for a politician hostile to Israel can be hard to understand. An American Jew may feel just as strongly about Israelis voting for National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir.
Reconsidering a political allegiance is reasonable. So is taking the consequences of a change seriously. American Jews have to live with the government they elect, including its decisions about their safety and their economic future.
What if frustration with politics leads some Jews to withdraw from Israel altogether?
My greater concern is that frustration with politics will lead some Jews to withdraw from Israel altogether. That would hurt Israel, and it could also leave American Jewish life poorer. For many families, Israel helps give being Jewish a place in everyday life. Losing that connection would affect what they pass on to their children.
This week, CNN’s Harry Enten presented Siena polling averages showing that Democrats’ lead among Jewish voters in New York on the congressional ballot had fallen from 49 percentage points in 2022 to 13 this year.
A national Mellman Group survey of 800 Jewish registered voters for the Jewish Electorate Institute, conducted in late August and early September, found Democrats ahead by 71% to 23%, essentially unchanged since March. Thirty-five percent of Jewish Democrats said the rise of anti-Israel candidates made it harder to identify with their party. Many still intended to vote Democratic.
British Jews have already been through several such reassessments. JPR, the Institute for Jewish Policy Research, put Labour’s share of the reported Jewish vote at 12% in 2019 under Jeremy Corbyn, when concerns about antisemitism drove many traditional supporters away. Labour recovered to 44% under Keir Starmer in the 2024 election. By mid-2025, its share of Jewish voting intention was down to 30%. Both major parties were losing support to the Greens and Reform UK.
Israel has to keep working with people, despite political changes
Those figures show how much a party’s standing can change. Voters are entitled to ask whether a familiar party still represents them. Its response to antisemitism and its treatment of Israel belong in that assessment, along with personal safety, livelihoods, and other deeply held beliefs. Conduct that would be unacceptable in a rival party deserves scrutiny at home.
Israel has to keep working with people through these changes. Waiting for frustrated Jewish Democrats to become Republicans assumes they will resolve their disagreements in the way most convenient to us. Some will, and others will reach a different conclusion.
The same JEI survey found that 86% of Jewish voters described themselves as pro-Israel, including 65% who criticized some or many Israeli government policies. There is considerable attachment to Israel among people who object to the way it is governed. That distinction should be familiar to anyone who follows Israeli politics.
Natan Sharansky has argued for years that a connection to Israel helps Jews remain Jewish. In The Jerusalem Post in 2022, he identified “only two factors that can slow down the assimilation: tradition and Zionism.” He warned that the grandchildren of Jews connected to neither would probably no longer be Jewish.
I take Sharansky seriously because, for families with little religious practice, Israel can account for much of their involvement in Jewish life. It might be the place where relatives live, where someone studied or volunteered, or where a family’s history becomes easier to understand. A relationship like that takes years to develop. Children learn its importance partly from the attention their parents give it.
The link between religion and Israel also appears in the wider American polling. Gallup has long found that people who attend religious services frequently are more likely to sympathize with Israelis. Its historical research found that association within both major parties.
Pew’s April 2026 survey found favorable views of Israel among 65% of white evangelical Protestants, 64% of Jewish Americans and 35% of Catholics, compared with 22% of the religiously unaffiliated. The pattern varies by religion: Only 4% of Muslim Americans viewed Israel favorably.
For Christian Zionists, support for Israel can be a religious obligation. Christians United for Israel grounds its mission in God’s promise to Abraham in Genesis 12:3: “I will bless those who bless you.” Its supporters understand that commitment as part of their own faith.
Religion has become less important in many Americans’ lives. Gallup’s March 2026 report found that 47% considered it very important in 2025, down from 58% in 2012, although the figure had stabilized in recent years. Gallup’s Frank Newport argued in a 2024 analysis that declining religious involvement was weakening a longstanding source of support for Israel.
We should account for that when deciding where Israel puts its effort. The religious and family connections that made Israel important to many Americans will carry different weight for their children. A sympathetic older generation gives us an opportunity to reach younger people; it provides little assurance that they will share their parents’ views.
Israel’s own politics matter as well. We need a broad unity government to help repair the country internally and improve our standing abroad. I would want Likud, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s party, to build it with Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar, former prime minister Naftali Bennett, Avigdor Liberman, Yoaz Hendel, and Ofer Winter. Ben-Gvir, left-wing leader Yair Golan – and the haredi, or ultra-Orthodox, parties would remain outside.
Its ministers should hear Jewish Democrats explain why Trump troubles them with the seriousness they expect when explaining Israel’s security concerns. Work inside the Democratic Party should be a priority. Our diplomats and political leaders need regular contact with Democrats who care about Israel, including when those Democrats have difficult questions.
American supporters of Israel should stand behind leaders prepared to defend the relationship within their own party. Israel has an interest in their success, whatever happens to the Jewish vote in November.
Israel should help families afford Jewish education and give young Jews more opportunities to study, volunteer, and spend time here. They need time outside an organized itinerary to meet Israelis, hear the arguments we have among ourselves, and form their own opinions.
When the parties negotiate Israel’s next government, I want this work to have ministers responsible for it and money assigned in the budget. Ministers should be able to explain which Democratic relationships they are working to repair, which Jewish education programs they are supporting, and how they are helping more young Jews spend time here. We will soon be electing the Israelis responsible for those decisions. Their plans deserve at least some of the scrutiny we devote to the voting intentions of Jews in America.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Tainan’s railway history and modern transformation come together on a limited-edition iPass featuring the city’s century-old train station.
The card commemorates the first phase of a railway project to move the city’s tracks underground, with the new section set to begin operations on Saturday. Priced at NT$150 (US$5) each, the cards are limited to 1,000 copies, according to TaiSounds.
The design captures Tainan Station’s transformation while retaining the character of its historic architecture. The front features minimalist champagne-pink lines tracing the modernized station’s outline, while the back showcases its historic design.

Taiwan Railway said Tainan Station has served generations of travelers. The first phase of the underground railway project will move an 8.23-kilometer section of tracks below ground, easing traffic congestion while preserving the station’s historic architecture, according to CNA.
A farewell event is scheduled at 9 p.m. Friday at the station, ahead of the last southbound Tze-Chiang Limited Express train departing from its ground-level platform at 10:29 p.m. The driver will sound the horn three times, marking the end of an era for the city’s above-ground railway operations and ushering in the beginning of a new chapter, according to UDN.

A Tesla Flying Car? I Don’t Know, Man
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
03:18:30 UTC
12:18:30 KST

Where is my flying car? The enduring question sort of, kind of, might have an answer: In McGregor, Texas.
On Thursday, Tesla showed off a version of its new Roadster 2 sports car in a demonstration at SpaceX’s rocket development testing facility. And in its own way, with an awkward jerking maneuver, the Roadster flew a few dozen feet. The vehicle, which doesn’t yet have a price but is likely to be very expensive, is slated to go into production in 2028. The vehicle didn’t have a human occupant during the demo “to make sure we don’t kill anyone,” Tesla CEO Elon Musk said at the event.
Tesla’s Roadster “sort of, kind of, might” be an actual flying car because aviation experts say legally catching air in the vehicle will likely involve plenty of government permissions and red tape.
“The [Federal Aviation Administration] has jurisdiction over any machine that leaves the surface of the earth,” says Scott Miller, an airline pilot and a lecturer in the Aviation and Technology program at San José State University. The vehicle “is going to introduce a whole set of regulatory issues.”
At the event Thursday, Musk acknowledged as much. “I’m not sure it’s necessarily legal in all jurisdictions," he said. “This is not necessarily a safety-optimized car.”
The FAA did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Any flying vehicle that weighs more than 250 or so pounds would need to go through an FAA approval process and require clearance to operate in the national airspace, says Michael McCormick, a former FAA official who now heads the Air Traffic Management program at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University. Getting that certification, he predicts, could take “at least a year.” Your standard drivers license, meanwhile, wouldn’t cut it. Any Tesla owner piloting such a vehicle would likely have to obtain a recreational aviation license.
Actually taking off and landing the Roadster 2 would likely present its own set of issues. Most states require aircraft to take off from airports or designated helipads. Launching from the road to the air would fall under state or local rules, says Miller, and many places do not look kindly on the concept of sudden aircraft intrusions on their streets and highways. That’s the reason “it’s pretty rare to be able to jump in a helicopter and land at your favorite steakhouse to have a steak,” he says. Drivers might only be able to truly operate the vehicle on a large, private piece of land.
The FAA today is working on rules, regulations, and pilot projects around another sort of “flying car,” or what’s more commonly known as an electric vertical take-off and landing (eVTOL) vehicle. These aircraft use several smaller electric motors and propellers to carry up to four passengers between 20 and 150 miles, sometimes autonomously. The companies building the technology envision them taking off from small, local “vertipads,” allowing riders to skip urban traffic by floating above the fray.
The Trump administration this year launched a limited, three-year pilot project using the aircraft, where companies are able to test the tech in several states. It has taken years for the companies to receive certifications from the federal government.
When it comes to the Roadster 2, there are practical questions, too. True flying cars have struggled to take off because of the physics-led contradiction at the heart of the idea. What makes a car safe and durable enough to operate on roads is weight. But “weight is the enemy of an airplane,” says Miller. “Flying cars haven’t been able to find that balance of power versus weight.”
Still, Miller found himself impressed by Thursday’s demo. “If this does make it into production, that is a truly impressive engineering and production feat,” he says.

Taiwan’s former Army chief of staff punished over M1A2T procurement irregularities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
03:18:24 UTC
12:18:24 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Army Command Headquarters confirmed Thursday that seven military officials involved in the M1A2T main battle tank procurement project had been disciplined for what it described as “administrative oversight.”
KMT Legislator Ma Wen-chun (馬文君) pointed out in May that the budget for the M1A2T procurement project, which runs from 2019 through 2027, had unexpectedly increased by NT$4.8 billion (US$148 million) to NT$45.3 billion in the 2026 budget, per Storm Media. Defense Minister Wellington Koo (顧立雄) acknowledged the error at the time and said the officials responsible would be disciplined.
DPP Legislator Wang Ting-yu (王定宇) stressed that whether the Army had overlooked the issue or failed to inform the legislature, spending unauthorized funds was illegal. He called on the Ministry of National Defense to take responsibility for the violation.
Department of Strategic Planning Director-General Lieutenant General Huang Wen-chi (黃文啟) explained how the discrepancy arose. During the budgeting process, the Army removed certain items from its proposed procurement package to keep the project within the NT$40.5 billion budget.
However, Huang said the Army ultimately signed the A3 version of the letter of offer and acceptance which reinstated previously cut items, including six M1070 heavy equipment transporters and 14 M88A2 recovery vehicles.
Huang said the Army initially expected exchange rate fluctuations between 2019 and 2023 to help offset the additional costs. However, the strengthening of the US dollar since 2024 undermined the plan.
Ma criticized the Army’s handling, saying it should have requested additional funding if the existing budget was insufficient, per UDN. She argued that raising the cost issue after the US had delivered all the equipment effectively put the legislature under pressure to approve the additional funding.
Asked about the disciplinary action, Army Deputy Chief of Staff Major General Wu Sung-ling (吳松齡) said Thursday that the officials involved, including then-Army Chief of Staff Lieutenant General Chang Yuan-hsun (章元勳), had been disciplined in accordance with Army regulations, per Tai Sounds.
Retired Colonel Chou Yu-ping (周宇平), former head of the Air Force Surveillance Warning Center, said the case reflected the military’s long-standing failure to maintain a sufficient pool of qualified administrative specialists, compounded by overly restrictive procurement rules, per CMedia. He said the military’s practice of rotating personnel among service branches and positions prevented procurement officials from passing on expertise in negotiations, finance and project management.
Regarding procurement regulations, Chou proposed relaxing restrictions to give officials greater flexibility to negotiate time-sensitive deals while providing legal backing for them to seek better terms from the US. He also warned against relying on exchange rate fluctuations to cover budget shortfalls, calling for a more comprehensive exchange rate monitoring and hedging mechanism given that such projects often involve billions of Taiwan dollars.

Ursula von der Leyen suggests creating EU strategic gas reserves — Politico
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
03:12:01 UTC
12:12:01 KST

BRUSSELS, October 16. /TASS/. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has invited European leaders to consider creating the bloc-wide strategic gas reserves, three diplomats and two EU officials have told Politico.
The initiative was put forward amid concerns that the EU may face fuel shortages this winter.
The report says that the existing European gas storage facilities, normally refilled throughout the year by commercial actors, are running at record lows amid high summer prices, linked to the conflict in the Middle East.
The report says that the bloc was left "unprepared for winter."
It wasn't immediately clear to diplomatic officials what form the reserve idea would take, Politico wrote.
Earlier TASS reported that Europe risks starting the heating season with record-low gas stocks. By the traditional start of the autumn-winter period, EU countries may fill their storage facilities to only 70-75% capacity, marking an all-time low for the beginning of the heating season.
Under European Commission requirements, EU nations must ensure their gas storage facilities are 90% full between October 1 and December 1 each year. A 10% margin of flexibility is permitted in the event of challenging filling conditions. Consequently, net injections into European storage facilities must total at least 68 bcm by the start of the 2026-2027 autumn-winter season to meet the filling target. However, anticipating a very mild winter, the European Commission is prepared to lower this threshold to 80% for the current year.

US lifts some sanctions restrictions on overseas assets of Russia's Lukoil
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
06:03:00 EEST
12:03:00 KST

US lifts some sanctions restrictions on overseas assets of Russia's Lukoil
The US Department of the Treasury has extended until 24 April 2027 the validity of general licences authorising transactions involving some of the overseas assets of sanctioned Russian oil company Lukoil.
Source: a notice from the US Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC)
Details: According to the department, the licences cover Lukoil's petrol stations outside Russia and four Bulgarian entities, including an oil refinery in the city of Burgas.
The first licence governs the activities of Lukoil International GmbH, which holds the Russian oil giant's overseas assets. The authorisation also covers entities in which it holds a direct or indirect stake of 50% or more, including its US subsidiaries Lukoil North America and Lukoil Americas Corporation.
The licence allows customers to buy fuel and related goods at Lukoil petrol stations outside Russia. It also permits the provision of maintenance, measures to keep the stations operating or their gradual closure. OFAC said this move is intended to protect retail consumers from the adverse effects of sanctions. Permitted transactions include payments to suppliers, rent, insurance premiums and staff wages.
However, Washington has strictly prohibited the transfer of any funds to individuals or organisations in Russia or to accounts held with Russian banks. The licence also excludes any transactions involving the Central Bank of Russia, the Russian Finance Ministry or the National Wealth Fund.
The second general licence allows transactions involving four of the company's Bulgarian subsidiaries: the Lukoil Neftohim Burgas oil refinery as well as Lukoil Bulgaria, Lukoil Aviation Bulgaria and Lukoil Bulgaria Bunker. The exemptions also cover subsidiaries in which these entities hold a stake of at least 50%, but do not extend to other sanctioned assets belonging to the group.
According to Reuters estimates, the easing of restrictions covers a network of around 2,000 petrol stations across Europe, Central Asia, the Middle East and North America. These include around 200 stations in the US states of New York, New Jersey and Pennsylvania, 600 in Türkiye and more than 300 in Romania. Lukoil also holds leading positions in the retail fuel markets of Moldova and Bulgaria.
Background:
- On 22 October 2025, the US Department of the Treasury added Rosneft, Lukoil and 34 of their subsidiaries to its sanctions list. Washington said the decision reflected Moscow's unwillingness to take meaningful steps towards ending the war in Ukraine.
- In late October 2025, the Russian oil group announced plans to sell its foreign assets and agreed to sell Lukoil International to commodities trader Gunvor. However, the deal fell through after the US regulator refused to approve the transaction.
- On 10 December 2025, OFAC introduced a special licence allowing Lukoil's overseas assets to be sold to companies not subject to sanctions.
- On 14 April 2026, the US extended the licences allowing the company's foreign petrol station network and Bulgarian businesses to operate until 29 October 2026.
- In early October 2026, The New York Times posted a report saying that negotiations between Donald Trump's administration and the Kremlin had expanded to include discussions about a multi-billion-dollar deal involving Lukoil's international assets. According to sources, a group of investors with links to White House special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner is seeking to acquire the portfolio of oil fields, refineries and petrol stations.

China tells Israel to stop ‘forced establishment’ of West Bank settlements
“The Palestinian question is the greatest historical injustice of this century,” China’s foreign minister said.
China’s Foreign Minister Wang Yi has told Israeli President Isaac Herzog during a meeting in Azerbaijan that Israel should stop and reverse its “forced establishment” of West Bank settlements, China’s foreign ministry said in a statement.
Wang told Herzog that China has consistently viewed the Palestinian question as the greatest historical injustice of this century, the ministry said in the statement on Friday.
Wang emphasised that the “two-state solution” is the right path to a resolution and said the immediate priority is to fully open access to the Gaza Strip so a humanitarian “catastrophe” is not allowed to spread.
Wang added that China is willing to work with the international community to push all parties to return to dialogue as soon as possible and seek a political settlement.
Wang is attending the Seventh Summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence-Building Measures in Asia, held in Baku, Azerbaijan, as the special representative of President Xi Jinping, China’s state news agency Xinhua reported.
China urges new Middle East framework
In September, Chinese President Xi Jinping visited Cairo for the first time in a decade and called on Middle East countries to oppose external influence and consider reshaping the region’s security order.
Xi’s rare visit arrived as Beijing seeks to expand its influence in the region amid the US-Israel war on Iran.
The talks covered the US-Israel war on Iran, with both presidents urging “diplomatic solutions” to reach a “comprehensive agreement to end the war”, according to a statement from Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi’s spokesperson.
In March, China criticised the US and Israeli attacks on Iran, with Beijing demanding an immediate halt to the joint attacks. Wang told his Israeli counterpart, Gideon Saar, that the attack on Iran came as negotiations between Washington and Tehran had “made significant progress, including addressing Israel’s security concerns”, China’s foreign ministry said in a statement following the start of the war.
China was Iran’s largest trading partner, buying up to 90 percent of its oil, according to the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission. In 2021, Beijing signed a 25-year “comprehensive strategic partnership agreement” with Tehran.
At the same time, Beijing has spent the past decade cultivating closer ties with Gulf countries, including Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, and remains a top trade partner of both the US and Israel.

At least 35 people, including 34 students and a teacher, were killed and more than 45 others were injured when the roof of a private school collapsed in Peshawar, northwestern Pakistan, on Thursday, Qazinform News Agency cites Al Jazeera.

22 US Lawmakers Press Trump to Enforce Russia Sanctions Ahead of Oct. 18 Deadline

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
02:40:17 UTC
11:40:17 KST

A bipartisan group of 22 US lawmakers urged President Donald Trump on Thursday, Oct. 15, to fully enforce sweeping sanctions against Russia ahead of an Oct. 18 deadline, warning that continued Russian energy revenues are financing President Vladimir Putin’s war against Ukraine.
In a letter to the White House, Republicans and Democrats called for the full implementation of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, including penalties against Russian officials, financial institutions and foreign companies helping Moscow circumvent Western restrictions.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The appeal comes amid growing bipartisan opposition to Trump’s decision to ease restrictions on Russian diesel exports, which lawmakers fear could provide the Kremlin with additional revenue while Russian forces continue attacking Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure.
“As Russia prepares to wage a fifth winter campaign against Ukraine, the United States has an opportunity to reinvigorate peace efforts by placing maximum pressure on Vladimir Putin and the governments and networks that finance his war,” the lawmakers wrote.
They argued that sanctions enforcement was essential to compelling Moscow to engage seriously in negotiations.
“Utilizing the tools for economic pressure in this law will be decisive in forcing Putin to take peace talks seriously.”
The letter was led by Democratic Rep. Jim Costa and senior members of the Congressional Ukraine Caucus, including Mike Quigley, Marcy Kaptur, Republican Brian Fitzpatrick and Republican Joe Wilson. Republican Michael McCaul, a former House Foreign Affairs Committee chairman, also signed the appeal.
Russia Strikes Kyiv, Hits Apartment Building in Uman, Injures Five in Overnight Drone Attacks
Lawmakers demand sanctions against Russia’s energy network
The lawmakers urged the administration to target not only Russian officials and state enterprises but also the international financial and commercial networks sustaining Moscow’s war economy.
Their demands include mandatory sanctions on Russian oligarchs, banks and state-owned companies, alongside penalties targeting foreign financial institutions and intermediaries facilitating Russian transactions.
They also called for secondary tariffs on major purchasers of Russian oil and gas, measures against vessels operating in Moscow’s shadow fleet, and restrictions on companies helping Russia evade existing sanctions.
The letter emphasizes that foreign governments and financial institutions facilitating Russian energy trade should not be allowed to shield Moscow from the economic consequences of its invasion.
At the same time, lawmakers urged the White House to protect US allies that are actively reducing their dependence on Russian energy, using exemptions and tariff adjustments permitted under the legislation.
The group requested detailed information on which sanctions and tariffs the administration intends to implement by Oct. 18, whether any provisions will be delayed or waived, and how their effectiveness will be measured.
Trump’s Russian diesel deal draws fresh criticism
The letter specifically challenges the Treasury Department’s Oct. 9 decision to issue General License 135, authorizing certain transactions involving Russian-origin diesel.
Lawmakers warned that relaxing energy restrictions risks restoring revenues to the Kremlin at a time when Washington should be increasing economic pressure on Moscow.
They asked Trump to reverse the authorization and explain how the license complies with existing US restrictions on Russian energy imports.
The controversy follows a separate bipartisan appeal from 12 US senators earlier this week, who criticized the diesel agreement as financially beneficial to Moscow and unlikely to deliver meaningful relief to American consumers.
The senators argued that the volume of Russian diesel expected to enter global markets would have little effect on prices, which have risen sharply amid disruptions linked to the war with Iran.
Trump has defended the agreement as a measure to lower fuel costs, while also blaming Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries for rising energy prices.
Congress demands answers by Oct. 18
The lawmakers outlined five questions requiring clarification ahead of the sanctions law’s first implementation deadline, including which Russian officials, banks and companies would face restrictions and which countries would be subject to secondary tariffs.
They also demanded measurable benchmarks showing whether the measures are reducing Russian energy revenues and discouraging third countries from purchasing Moscow’s oil and gas.
Any presidential waiver, they argued, should be narrowly defined, temporary and linked to verifiable reductions in support for Russia’s war.
The letter further requested congressional briefings and regular updates on enforcement, including reviews of sanctions effectiveness every 180 days.
“Putin has repeatedly shown that he responds to pressure, not goodwill,” the lawmakers wrote.
They concluded that fully enforcing the legislation would demonstrate bipartisan American resolve and increase the economic costs of continuing Russia’s invasion until Moscow agrees to meaningful peace negotiations.
“We remain committed to Ukraine’s defense and to a just and lasting peace,” the letter said.

====================================================================================================

Economic Watch: Chinese firms bring homegrown expertise, innovation to fuel Dubai's growth
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:37:36 CST
11:37:36 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- A growing number of Chinese companies are expanding their business activities in Dubai, the United Arab Emirates (UAE), translating their experience in China into more localized business practices that benefit the host community.
From trade to investment, China's economic ties with the UAE are gaining momentum, with Dubai emerging as a magnet for Chinese businesses looking to expand overseas.
In 2025, bilateral trade between the UAE and China reached 108 billion U.S. dollars, making the UAE China's largest export market and second-largest trading partner in the Middle East. Chinese exports totaled 72.88 billion dollars, while imports from the UAE amounted to 35.12 billion dollars. China's direct investment in the UAE reached 2.6 billion dollars last year, official statistics show.
The growing business presence of Chinese firms is increasingly visible in Dubai. The number of active Chinese member companies registered with Dubai Chambers has more than doubled since 2016, reaching 6,650 by the end of September.
CHINESE EXPERIENCE, LOCAL BENEFITS
In Dubai, hot meals now arrive faster and at lower prices.
Since Keeta, the international brand of Chinese food delivery giant Meituan, entered the market in September 2025, the company has brought its homegrown delivery model to the UAE, reshaping the experience for both customers and riders.
At the heart of its service is an "on-time promise" that has made punctual delivery a selling point. For local consumers, the appeal means more competitive prices and meals that arrive hot and on schedule.
Behind each delivery is a logistics algorithm designed to make better use of riders' time. By helping them complete more orders per hour, the system can boost their earning potential, creating an incentive for more people to join the industry.
The ripple effects are reaching beyond the food delivery sector, extending even to driving schools as more job seekers look to obtain the licenses needed to work as riders.
"The entry of new platforms like Keeta is fueling strong competition for riders. This has led to improved pay scales and structured benefits, encouraging more job seekers to invest in a license," explained Suzanne Accetta, CEO of Dubai's First Driving Centre.
Chinese companies are not only improving local consumer services, but also actively aligning their operations with the emirate's long-term development vision.
In 2023, Dubai launched the ambitious Dubai Economic Agenda (D33), a comprehensive 10-year strategy aimed at building the emirate into one of the world's top five logistics hubs.
The plan has opened up opportunities for firms such as Chinese express delivery company J&T Express, which views Dubai as a strategic gateway connecting the company's operations across the Middle East. J&T has now invested in a large automated warehouse and sorting center in Dubai Industrial City, adding capacity to the emirate's logistics infrastructure while advancing its own regional expansion.
EMPOWERING LOCAL INNOVATION, DEVELOPMENT
On Dubai's roads, the arrival of driverless taxis is offering a glimpse of how Chinese technology is helping shape the emirate's next phase of development.
In April 2026, Chinese internet company Baidu, in partnership with Dubai Taxi Company (DTC), launched Apollo Go, a commercial driverless ride-hailing service in the emirate, bringing autonomous driving technology into everyday urban mobility.
"Baidu Apollo reflects the integration of autonomous mobility systems into an emerging global framework for applied AI deployment," Yang Nan, vice president of Baidu and general manager of the overseas business unit, intelligent driving group, said at the Dubai Business Forum China held by Dubai Chambers in south China's Shenzhen on Wednesday.
This launch has highlighted the importance of local regulatory support. In March 2025, Dubai's Roads and Transport Authority signed a memorandum of understanding with Apollo Go to test 100 autonomous taxis. In November 2025, Dubai introduced a comprehensive regulatory framework for autonomous vehicles, setting out safety standards and operational guidelines to support their deployment.
The arrival of driverless taxis in Dubai is setting off changes that extend well beyond the roads, prompting advances in regulation, financial services and the wider innovation ecosystem.
In September, the UAE approved new federal rules covering the inspection, registration, licensing and testing of self-driving vehicles, establishing a common national framework for regulating the technology.
In May, Dubai Insurance launched a specialized coverage framework tailored to DTC's self-driving fleet. By encouraging regulatory and financial services to innovate, the Chinese company is contributing to the broader foundation for Dubai's smart city development.
Building such an innovation-driven economy, however, requires more than advanced technology. It also depends on a steady supply of skilled local talent. Chinese technology company Huawei, for instance, has integrated its ICT Academy into the core curriculum at the College of Technological Innovation at Zayed University in Dubai, bringing courses in cutting-edge artificial intelligence and cloud computing into official degree courses.
Speaking at the forum in Shenzhen on Wednesday, Sultan bin Saeed Al Mansoori, chairman of Dubai Chambers, said China-Dubai ties were entering a new phase, marked by a shift toward the "co-creation of industries, capital flows and innovation platforms." ■

Tesla reveals next-generation Roadster after almost a decade of delays
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
02:36:37 UTC
11:36:37 KST

Tesla showed off its long-delayed next-generation Roadster on Thursday, almost a decade after Elon Musk's company started taking deposits for the electric sports car.
The event was livestreamed from a SpaceX test site in McGregor, Texas, near Waco, starting at 7:55 p.m. local time, or 8:55 p.m. ET. In attendance along with Musk were design leader Franz von Holzhausen and Lars Moravy, vice president of vehicle engineering.
"You're going to see some crazy stuff tonight," Musk said. "You're going to see the results of what happens when you have a collaboration with the world's best car company and the world's best rocket company."
Tesla's original Roadster, designed and engineered by a team led by founding CEO Martin Eberhard, was based on a Lotus Elise chassis and was first delivered in 2008, selling for roughly $100,000 in small volumes until 2012.
The next-generation Roadster is expected to be a high-end, low-volume model that relies on SpaceX technology to enable it to hover. While Musk fanatics expressed their excitement on social media, the Roadster isn't likely to have any material financial impact on the company.
At the event, Musk and his team showcased a white sports car that raced up a curved ramp, then clung to it upside down and vaulted off it, flipping in mid-air and hovering slowly before landing on the ground.
The two-seater can go from zero to 60 miles per hour in under a second, according to Tesla's timer, a feat Moravy demonstrated for the live audience.
Musk said the next-generation Roadster would enter production in 2028. The price wasn't announced, and the company didn't disclose specifications about other performance-level variants of the new Roadster.
Tesla reopened reservations for the refreshed Roadster in recent weeks, accepting $50,000 deposits from prospective buyers in the U.S., Canada and China.
Musk first promoted the refreshed Roadster concept at an event in November 2017, and the following June in a series of tweets. He wrote at that time, "SpaceX option package for new Tesla Roadster will include ~10 small rocket thrusters arranged seamlessly around car." The engines would improve speed and braking, and may "even allow a Tesla to fly."
The prototype Tesla showed on Thursday is built to be as lightweight as possible with a steer-by-wire system, steering yoke, and an array of technologies developed by SpaceX, including thrusters, carbon overlay pressure vessels and diffusers, and powerful fans that enable the car to do some gymnastics.
One feature Tesla left out of its forthcoming Roadster is the company's "FSD" or automated driving system. Musk said the new Roadster will be the last vehicle the company produces that's intended to be controlled by a human driver.
Tesla started taking $50,000 deposits for the revamped Roadster in 2017, but has since missed every targeted delivery date. As recently as last October, Musk was hyping a Roadster demo that he hoped would happen before the end of 2025. That didn't take place either.
Musk's former friend and OpenAI co-founder Sam Altman mocked the Tesla CEO in posts on X last year over the extreme delays, showing screenshots of his reservation and refund requests.
"I really was excited for the car! And I understand delays," Altman wrote. "But 7.5 years has felt like a long time to wait."
Altman got his refund, and the two ended up in court earlier this year over a separate matter related to OpenAI's governance and ownership structure.
Others have kept their reservations.
Lawrence O'Connor, founder and CEO of Other World Computing in Austin, Texas, told CNBC ahead of the event that he reserved a Founder's Edition of the new Roadster in November 2017, effectively giving the company what he called an "interest-free loan" of $250,000.
O'Connor wrote in a message that he would be attending the show and was "excited to see what has been 9 years in the making." After the event, O'Connor said what he saw was "off the charts."
Tesla is scheduled to report third-quarter results after the bell on Wednesday.

UN chief urges nations to end ‘war on nature’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
02:30:00 UTC
11:30:00 KST

UN chief urges nations to end ‘war on nature’
- UN chief Antonio Guterres said the “war on nature has not yet ended” as a report showed countries are off track on biodiversity goals.
- Nearly 200 nations are failing to meet the 2030 targets, including protecting 30% of land and oceans, cutting pollution, and reducing harmful subsidies.
- Guterres urged governments to fund nature properly and act faster before COP17 in Armenia, while experts warned species are disappearing and ecosystems are collapsing.
AI generated
PARIS -– UN chief Antonio Guterres said on Oct 15 that the “war on nature has not yet ended” as he launched a report showing the world was falling short of its biodiversity commitments.
Nations will assess progress and pitfalls toward a 2030 goal to stop the destruction of nature when they meet in Armenia next week for the UN biodiversity negotiations.
Nearly 200 countries joined the landmark Paris Agreement For Nature four years ago but have been slow to act on its objectives.
The pact laid out 23 targets for halting and reversing nature loss by 2030, including reducing pollution, protecting threatened species and conserving 30% of the world’s land and oceans.
But many of these targets are off track, said Guterres as he launched a global report spotlighting the gaps between ambition and action.
“It’s not all bad news... There is progress, but not enough. We are far from what is necessary,” he told reporters in the Armenian capital Yerevan where the COP17 talks start on Oct 19.
“The report shows that many of the critical elements of progress... are still missing in action”.
This meant the “war on nature has not yet ended”, he added.
The report showed that government policies were insufficient to meet the centrepiece biodiversity goal to protect 30% of Earth’s land and waters by 2030.
Other targets were lagging further behind.
Guterres said countries must honour their financial pledges to developing countries and spoke to a lack of headway in tackling government spending that harms nature.
Countries have vowed to reduce harmful subsidies by US$500 billion (S$641.24 billion) a year by 2030 – state incentives for industries like fossil fuel production, mining and agriculture – but little progress has been made.
For every dollar invested in protecting or restoring nature, about US$30 still goes into activities that degrade it, according to UN figures.
“Nature won’t thrive on good intentions,” Guterres said.
He pointed to the “very strong influence” of some sectors that had “too much power” over government including industrial fishing, fossil fuels and logging operations.
The lack of finance has been identified as a particular barrier to achieving the biodiversity goals.
Governments are not expected to make major new pledges at COP17 but will be under pressure to correct course.
“Biodiversity is in crisis. Species are disappearing and ecosystems are collapsing,” said Sue Lieberman from the Wildlife Conservation Society.
“Governments and all stakeholders must see that investing in nature is not a luxury, it is the very key to our survival.” AFP

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — FIC Global Inc. is expanding its optical communications business, with its subsidiary opening a second plant in Malaysia on Thursday.
The company plans to invest NT$1.6 billion (US$50 million) to expand production capacity in Malaysia. Its subsidiary Pro3C began gradually ramping up production at its first plant in Johor in the first quarter of this year, according to CTEE.
The expansion follows strong demand from US optical communications company Coherent, which has already filled the planned capacity of Pro3C's first Johor plant. Efforts to diversify production outside China are also contributing to the company's growth plans.
Optical communications uses light-based signals to transmit data, offering higher speeds and greater capacity than traditional copper cables. As AI infrastructure drives demand for faster data transmission, copper-based systems face growing challenges from signal loss, heat generation, and rising power consumption, according to Business Weekly.
These challenges become more pronounced as transmission speeds increase from 800 gigabits per second to 1.6 terabits per second. Pro3C's first Johor plant already produces 800G optical transceivers, which convert electrical signals into optical signals for data transmission and convert them back at the receiving end.
As cloud data centers upgrade from 400G to 800G transmission speeds, demand for 1.6T optical transceiver modules designed for AI supercomputing systems is also emerging. FIC plans to expand production to include 1.6T and 3.2T flip-chip optical transceiver modules, as well as products related to co-packaged optics and silicon photonics. Production of the new products will be introduced according to customer schedules.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News)— Sukiyaki Kappou Hiyama, the famed Tokyo sukiyaki institution with a history spanning over a century, is marking its one-year anniversary in Taiwan with a newly introduced full-beef tasting menu showcasing Yamagata Wagyu.

The brand expanded to Taipei last year (2025), introducing its traditional Kanto-style sukiyaki and beef selection techniques to the Taiwanese market.
To celebrate its first anniversary, the Taipei location has launched the “Top-Tier Yamagata Wagyu Full-Beef Feast.”
Sourced from Yamagata Prefecture, known for its extreme seasonal temperature variations that foster finely marbled and tender beef, the meat is selected by Hiyama’s expert appraisers.
Due to limited imports, only about 60 kilograms of this specific Wagyu are allocated to Taiwan each month.
The new eight-course seasonal menu, priced at NT$5,880 (US$182) per person, features various cuts of Yamagata beef prepared in traditional kaiseki style.
Courses range from Wagyu sashimi utilizing rare cuts to steamed beef, Hoba leaf-grilled Wagyu, and thick-cut ribeye cooked in Hiyama’s signature sukiyaki sauce.
The meal concludes with a seasoned Wagyu and wild mushroom rice dish, clear beef broth with abalone, and a traditional seasonal dessert.
As part of the anniversary promotion running from Oct. 13 to Nov. 12, diners ordering the full-beef feast receive complimentary handmade udon noodles.
The restaurant is also offering a 10 percent discount on all set menus on calendar dates containing the number "1."

Russia's finance minister attended a Group of 20 meeting in Bangkok on Thursday, his second in-person appearance at the event since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, testing how far Washington's rapprochement with Moscow will strain ties with Europe.
Anton Siluanov and Bank of Russia Deputy Governor Elizaveta Danilova were listed as Russia's delegates at the finance ministers and central bank governors' meetings on the sidelines of the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Thailand, according to a seating plan seen by CNBC. Siluanov was in the meeting, according to a person familiar with the matter.
According to the layout document, Russian delegates were seated between attendees from South Korea and the United Arab Emirates.
German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil was also listed as an attendee. At the August G20 finance meeting in Asheville, North Carolina, he told Siluanov that Moscow must end the war and declined to pose in a group photo with him. The traditional group photo was ultimately taken without the Russian delegation after European officials protested.
Klingbeil has pushed back on the U.S. efforts to bring Russia back on to the international stage, reportedly saying after the Thursday meeting that "there will be no pretending that Russia is now returning as a normal member of the G20 and simply taking its seat at the table again — not with me, and not with the other Europeans."
Russia's seat at the table tests how far Washington can ease pressure on Moscow without breaking with its European allies. The U.S., which took over the G20 presidency this year, welcomed Russia's finance minister back to the finance talks after years of isolation over the invasion of Ukraine.
The Trump administration also introduced a deal to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian diesel imports until April, drawing criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and European allies. Dombrovskis told CNBC on Wednesday that "now it's not a time to ease sanctions on Russia."
In a statement issued after the Thursday meetings, Australian Treasurer Jim Chalmers said Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz and attacks on commercial vessels "must end." Those impacts "are exacerbated by Russia's unprovoked and unjustifiable war in Ukraine," he said, adding that Australia calls for Russia to end the war and respect Ukraine's sovereignty.
The finance chiefs ended the meeting without a joint communique, underscoring persistent divisions among members over the Middle East conflict, trade imbalances, and Russia's war with Ukraine. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who would normally chair the talks, skipped the meetings to stay in Washington.
The Asheville meeting also ended without a communique, after China objected to language on several issues, including efforts to rectify excessive global trade surpluses. The U.S. instead issued a chair's statement backed by every member present except China, with Bessent calling China "the dissenter."
Delegates started the day with a plated breakfast of baked goat cheese, spinach and egg soufflé with chutney made from locally grown Bijin tomatoes, according to a menu card at the venue. The bread basket came with "Nam Dok Mai" mango jam. Every card carried the U.S. presidency's stars-and-stripes G20 logo and its "Freedom 250" tagline, marking America's 250th anniversary.
The finance ministers' meeting Thursday could have helped lay the groundwork for improved coordination on a raft of global challenges, including energy problems stemming from the Middle East conflict and concerns about record public debt in advanced economies. Leaders are expected to convene at the next G20 summit in Miami in December.

Ukraine has run out of missiles for Patriot air defence systems – WP
Ukraine has completely exhausted its stock of interceptor missiles for the US-made Patriot air defence systems.
Source: The Washington Post, citing two Ukrainian officials and a NATO representative
Details: According to one source, Ukraine had only 10 Patriot missiles left as of 7 October.
"These were used up during the attacks. Currently, there are only a couple remaining," a Ukrainian official said.
Quote: "A second person familiar with Ukraine's deteriorating air defence situation said the country is out of the sophisticated weapons, which are critical to shooting down incoming Russian ballistic missiles."
Details: A Ukrainian official stressed that "the situation is extremely tense".
CNN reported earlier that Ukraine had run out of Patriot missiles. According to its source, the shortage of ammunition was the reason Ukrainian air defences had been unable to intercept Russian ballistic targets during the latest large-scale attack.
Global missile stocks have been rapidly depleted by the war in the Middle East, launched by US President Donald Trump. In the first month of the war with Iran alone, the US used more than 1,000 Patriot and THAAD interceptors.
Washington has made accelerating production a priority, but manufacturing a single missile can take up to 36 months.
Until now, missiles for Ukraine have been supplied through the PURL programme The Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) programme allows NATO allies to finance purchases of US-made weapons for Ukraine , under which European countries pay for US-made weapons.
A senior NATO official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the programme remained operational and that "air defence munitions like Patriot interceptors continue to flow".
However, a Ukrainian official raised concerns about the nature of the deliveries.
"Since May, supplies have been irregular, and right now no one can say with any certainty or guarantee that a delivery will actually arrive," the official said.
Background:
- Throughout the summer and autumn of 2026, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has repeatedly urged Ukraine's partners to urgently increase supplies of missiles for Patriot air defence systems. In August, he stressed that Ukraine needed between 300 and 360 Patriot missiles to get through the winter safely. Meanwhile, Western deliveries had fallen sharply, from 675 missiles in 2023 to 364 in 2025, with only 264 planned for 2026.
- Meanwhile, according to reports in the media, the governments of Greece and Spain would rather keep Patriot missiles nearing the end of their service lives in storage than transfer them to Ukraine.

About 200 people—including politicians, academics, journalists, representatives of international organizations, diplomats, and college students—participated today at Rafael Landívar University in Guatemala City in a roundtable discussion marking the 30th anniversary of the peace accords that ended the civil war in Guatemala (1960–1996). The event, titled “Peace Remains Our Task: Memory, Reconciliation, and Commitment Thirty Years After the Peace Accords,” was organized in collaboration with the Italian Embassy in Guatemala and the Community of Sant’Egidio.
                                    
Among the participants were Raquel Zelaya, a well-known economist, former member of the government negotiating commission, and signatory to the agreements; retired General Julio Balconi, who served as Minister of Defense at the time; and Sandino Asturias, a political scientist and son of the negotiator for the armed guerrilla group (URNG).
                                    
The Italian Ambassador to Guatemala, Gabriele Meucci, opened the proceedings alongside the university’s Secretary General, Andrade-Abularach, emphasizing the importance of the Italian Constitution’s rejection of war.
                                    
The highlight of the day was the speech by Roberto Bonini, who, on behalf of the Community of Sant’Egidio, participated directly in the most confidential phase of the negotiations that led to the signing of the peace agreements between the military government and the armed guerrilla group. His personal experience inspired the book *Dare una mano alla pace* (*Lending a Hand to Peace*), in which Bonini recounts the Community of Sant’Egidio’s role in facilitating direct dialogue between the warring parties through secret meetings, the first of which took place in Rome at a convent.

Argentine students protest on campus over Milei’s austerity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
02:11:33 UTC
11:11:33 KST

Argentine students protest on campus over Milei’s austerity
Judge fines government for failing to fund universities as protests over Milei’s cuts turn violent.
“This cannot go on!” students shout during an assembly in the middle of the central hall of the University of Buenos Aires Exact and Natural Sciences building.
It is part of Argentina’s prestigious public university system.
The faculty’s central hall is covered with dozens of banners protesting President Javier Milei’s spending cuts. Students have called an assembly to announce the occupation of the university, a traditional form of protest in Argentina meant to raise public awareness and pressure the government.
They say they will take over the building for a day. Many students and professors here are concerned about the impact of Milei’s austerity policies on public universities and say the future of free higher education is at risk.
“Our best professors are leaving en masse. With salaries that cannot cover their basic needs, they are leaving for private universities,” Emiliano Gato, a physics student who is part of the group, told Al Jazeera.
“I dream of doing research and teaching at the public University of Buenos Aires. It’s a prestigious school. But now, with this austerity plan, I don’t know what will happen.”
Public universities in Argentina have become a major battleground of Milei’s austerity plan. Students and professors are protesting the lack of funding and the erosion of salaries, which they say is a major threat to the country’s public education.
Milei is implementing one of the harshest austerity plans in Argentina’s history.
Since taking office in 2023, he has laid off thousands of state employees, shut down ministries, reduced subsidies and cut government-funded programmes. The measures were meant to fight high inflation, which was a major problem in Argentina. Almost three years later, inflation has fallen to around 2 percent a month. Milei says his plan is going well.
“Argentina is growing at a remarkable pace. We have now recorded 27 consecutive months of sustained growth, and today the country is expanding at four times its historical rate. This growth is being felt across almost every sector of the economy,” said Milei during a recent visit to Washington.
Ripple effects
But not everyone agrees. His plan is also having a profound impact on public education, welfare plans for people with disabilities, pensioners and others who depend on state support. The opposition has tried to block many of Milei’s reforms.
Last year, Congress overturned presidential vetoes and approved two laws, one increasing funding for public universities and another declaring a disability emergency. But Milei’s government has refused to implement them, arguing that Congress failed to identify how they would be financed.
A federal judge has now begun fining the government 100,000 pesos (around $70) a day for failing to implement parts of the financing law, which requires Milei’s government to restore university salaries and student scholarships lost to inflation, regularly update budgets and provide funding for research, hospitals and infrastructure.
And that’s why thousands of people took to the streets on Thursday to demand that the government implement it. All around Buenos Aires, long columns of people blocked the centre of the city as they called for a general strike. Although the protest was meant to be peaceful, it soon turned violent. Police fired tear gas and rubber bullets as protesters threw rocks.
The plaza in front of Congress resembled a battleground. At least 25 people were detained, and several others were injured, including members of the security forces.
Maria Teresa de Jesus is a professor in the University of Buenos Aires chemistry department. She says she makes around $700 a month and it has become difficult to make ends meet. “I have come to this protest as a last resort. I am professor. I love teaching, doing research. I shouldn’t be here,” she told Al Jazeera. “Public education is crucial in this country, to make education accessible to all. And the government is ignoring it.”
Many in Argentina continue to support Milei’s economic plan. They are hoping the government’s plan to exploit the country’s vast natural resources will pay off and translate into more jobs, higher wages and improved living standards.
But many others have stopped believing and are prepared to raise the stakes. They accuse Milei’s government of protecting the interests of a privileged few while asking the rest of the country to bear the cost of his economic plan.

thessaloniki’s layered historic center weaves into expandable pedestrian network

thessaloniki’s layered historic center weaves into expandable pedestrian network
linked by a neutral urban skin, apostolopoulos tasoulis’ masterplan establishes an expandable urban network designed to unify over seventy monuments and archaeological sites across thessaloniki, greece.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
EXPANDABLE city NETWORK UNIFIES THESSALONIKI’S HISTORICAL layers
The Armosi (Άρμοση) masterplan, designed by Apostolopoulos Tasoulis, establishes an expandable urban network to unify over seventy monuments and archaeological sites across Thessaloniki, Greece. Structured along the historic Egnatia Street axis and its intersection with Aristotelous Street, the design framework integrates Roman, Byzantine, Ottoman, Jewish, and modern historical layers into a cohesive public landscape informed by UNESCO’s Historic Urban Landscape approach.
NEUTRAL MATERIAL TOOLKIT REDEFINES SITE BOUNDARIES AND URBAN AXES
To improve urban legibility without adding visual complexity, the proposal by Apostolopoulos Tasoulis architectural studio applies a unified design toolkit. A continuous, light-colored paved surface creates a neutral backdrop, supported by standardized lighting, signage, and discreet street furniture. Site boundaries are reconfigured through subterranean facilities, new public access points, and light enclosures, with targeted interventions restoring the historic imperial axis at the Rotunda and Galerian Complex and introducing a new axial entry at the Roman Forum.
GREEN PEDESTRIAN CORRIDORS LINK ARCHAEOLOGY WITH PUBLIC TRANSIT
Pedestrian movement and climate resilience dictate the ground plane. Existing vegetation is expanded into continuous green corridors connected to the city’s metro network and public transport system, establishing traffic-calmed routes that allow Thessaloniki’s historical stratification to operate as an active part of daily urban mobility.

Tesla launches flying Roadster concept car
Unknown

Tesla launches flying Roadster concept car
Electric car company Tesla has unveiled its flying Roadster vehicle with a demonstration in which the car drove upside down, flipped off a ramp and briefly flew, using compressed-air thrusters that Tesla claims will make it the world's quickest production car.
During a live event in Texas, the two-seat Roadster model drove up a half-pipe ramp and launched off the top, remaining in the air for a few seconds before landing
It also became airborne after building up speed on flat ground, launching over a row of parked vehicles. It then lifted off from a stationary position.
A series of thrusters in the bottom and back propelled the car into the air and cushioned the landings.
It was designed by Tesla and SpaceX, both companies led by businessman Elon Musk, who called the second-generation Roadster "a collaboration with the world's best car company and the world's best rocket company".
The thrusters can also fire rearward to boost acceleration. Tesla demonstrated the car reaching 60 miles per hour in a claimed 0.81 seconds, and said it would be the "quickest" production vehicle to 60 miles per hour.
On the half-pipe ramp, the vehicle was able to remain upside down due to a fan suction system. The air tanks in the vehicle are rechargeable and can be recompressed without fuel, according to Tesla.
Long term, Musk said the car will be the "only manual" vehicle in its lineup, referencing plans for driverless vehicles. Though the demonstration used a pre-programmed sequence with no driver.
Tesla chief designer Franz von Holzhausen said the car was designed with an "aerospace aesthetic". It has an angular supercar exterior with scissor doors and a deployable spoiler, and is a coupe with a hard top.
The seats are moulded directly to the chassis, and it features wire steering, which replaces the mechanical link between the steering wheel and wheels with electronic controls.
Musk referenced the uncertainty of street legality for the flying capabilities and said that "success is not guaranteed" before the test.
Production on the vehicle is set for 2028, according to Tesla. The company first unveiled a second-generation Roadster in 2017, with deliveries planned for 2020.
Tesla's last major launch was the Cybertruck, unveiled in 2019.
Other recent concept cars include Alef's concept vehicle.
The imagery is courtesy of Tesla.

“Where is the cash that we gave to Ukraine? Where is all the equipment? Biden was giving them missiles, and they were being sold on the open market,” Trump said.

According to a report by Small Arms Survey, the Ukrainian authorities intercepted a vehicle carrying 18 US-made Javelin anti-tank missiles and other hardware in Kiev-controlled part of Russia’s Donetsk People’s Republic in 2024. The driver lacked the proper paperwork to transport the weapons, which suggested that they could have been intended for sale, it said.
Ukraine has also been rocked by numerous corruption scandals in military procurement involving officials close to Zelensky. In August, the country’s National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) reported losses of 254 million hryvnias ($6 million) as a result of an alleged embezzlement scheme which revolved around purchases of drones for Ukrainian forces.

Former Ukrainian Defense Minister Rustem Umerov has been questioned as a witness in the case.

Trump has repeatedly criticized Biden for providing Ukraine with weapons and funds without preconditions and proper oversight. During Thursday’s interview, the US president compared Zelensky to P.T. Barnum, a 19th-century American showman and traveling circus-owner, known for publicity stunts and sensational attractions.
“Zelensky is not a good guy for us to deal with. Biden gave him billions and billions of dollars,” he said.
Trump also questioned the Ukrainian leader’s willingness to reach a diplomatic resolution to the conflict with Moscow.
“He says he wants to settle but he [doesn’t],” he said, adding: “No, I’m not a big fan of Zelensky. They’ve destroyed that country.”
The remarks followed Zelensky’s criticism of Trump’s decision last week to ease sanctions on Russian diesel exports in order to contain surging energy prices ahead of the November 3 US midterm elections. The Ukrainian leader said he felt betrayed by Washington’s move and defied Trump’s demand to halt attacks on Russian oil refineries.
The US president, meanwhile, made clear that Washington would prioritize rebuilding its own depleted weapons inventories rather than continuing to supply Kiev.
“Once we are really stocked, we will start letting our allies buy them [the arms] from us,” he said.

Democrats go into November’s midterms hoping to regain the US House and Senate. Polls suggest the Democrats are currently ahead, but is this because of Trump’s historically low approval ratings rather than the popularity of the Democratic Party itself?
And after losing to Donald Trump in both 2016 and 2024, what lessons have the Democrats learned for the future direction of the party, and how much of a litmus test is the topic of Israel for future candidates?
Mehdi Hasan goes Head to Head with Neera Tanden, who held senior roles in the Clinton, Obama and Biden administrations and worked on Hillary Clinton’s Senate and presidential campaigns. She is CEO and president of the Center for American Progress think tank.

Sharing care for my son is hard. But I'm learning
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
02:01:03 UTC
11:01:03 KST

perspective
How I'm learning to share the invisible load of being a carer
At 27, Dimity's son Stu moved into his own home.
Stu, who is autistic and requires substantial levels of support, has been living in the purpose-built house with 24/7 care for almost two years.
The transition has been an opportunity for independence that Stu craved, and a shift in responsibilities for mum Dimity.
But like for many carers, there is an invisible caring load that remains.
Dimity still recruits and trains support workers, meets regularly with a team leader, oversees Stu's support program, advocates for him and acts as his nominee.
"It's the hardest thing to do, to share that load. Even with other people in your family," 67-year-old Dimity says.
"To trust another person to take on that responsibility."
But Dimity is learning to share Stu's care with others.
These are her words.
A determined young man
Stuart is my fourth child. I always say it was as if I had three children and then I got 10, because of the energy that he had.
He's an individual. There can be a tendency to think all autistic people are the same. And that is not true.
He has his own temperament and personality.
He is a very determined person. He is very perfectionistic, very focused. He loves cooking, crafting and creating things.
He micromanages; he observes. He has learned to knit simply by watching me knit.
On top of that, he struggles with issues of his autism: being non-verbal, illiterate, issues with emotional regulation, a need for predictable routines and rituals, problems with sensory overload, minimal social awareness, and intellectual disability.
Planning for the future
When Stu lived with us, it became apparent that, like all young men, he wanted more independence. He wanted to "divorce" his mother, as most sons eventually do.
It's the goal of every parent for children to reach independence; it was no different from my other sons.
He became resentful of my interference in his life.
We started to consider the process of creating a life for him where he had more control, more of a sense of agency over his own life.
Of course, in the background I still manage it, but it's not in his face.
Sign up to the ABC Lifestyle newsletter
In the couple of months prior to him actually moving, it was frenetic because I had a million ducks in a row.
I kept worrying that the degree to which this was working depended on me.
What would happen if his support workers weren't there? All sorts of worries started encroaching.
I actually had a medical event related to the stress, and from that time forward I started planning for a future of becoming somewhat redundant in his life.
I needed to work out how he was going to be supported when I'm not here. In a positive way.
Articulating my invisible load
Now I negotiate a lot with the disability support agency we work with, working to expand their responsibilities and what they are willing to share. Also forward planning for Stuart’s future, including other people in his circle of support, like siblings and extended family, for them to share caring responsibilities.
I'm developing a working document that explains in detail everything I do as Stu's mother and advocate and manager.
When he lived at home, I was definitely like the boss.
Now I look to his care team to guide me, too. It's not just me teaching, guiding and managing; I'm part of the team, and we're learning together the best ways to support Stu.
I look after grandchildren for three half-days a week, on top of what I do with Stu.
It's busy.
As his mother, my job is to look after him. No-one else is ever going to love him like I do.
And while being a carer is a lot of work and most of my life has been devoted to caring for my children and now my grandchildren, that's OK. That's my job.
What I'm trying to work on by working with a circle of support, creating the working document, is the space for people in that circle to then volunteer to take on that responsibility.
The running joke is "If I end up under a bus, would you be willing to take on this role?"
While I cover it all now, there will come a time when multiple people need to cover it.
Our relationship has improved
I remember one night talking to my husband and deeply realising and feeling the loss of Stuart from my home. And really having a big cry about it.
That was hard.
However, my relationship with Stuart has improved vastly since he moved into his own home.
When home life is challenging, often overwhelming, it's easy over a period to start to diminish the degree you feel or engage in affection for someone.
To have relieved both of us of that has been such a gift.
Now when he visits, he sits next to me and holds my hand. He puts his head on my shoulder. He touches my cheek. He cuddles me.
I've always been devoted to him.

Ministry will not break down Boxer deliveries by variant
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
03:00:40 BST
11:00:40 KST

The Ministry of Defence has declined to say how many of each Boxer variant have been delivered to the Army, calling the information commercially and operationally sensitive, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked for a breakdown by variant of the contractually delivered Boxer fleet to date, following an answer of 8 September.
Luke Pollard, the Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, said: “I refer the hon. Member to the answer I gave him on 18 December 2025 to Question 100025, which sets out the total number of Boxer vehicles contracted for by variant. It is not possible to provide a breakdown by variant of the Boxer vehicles delivered to date, as this information is commercially and operationally sensitive.”
The department has therefore published what it has ordered by variant while withholding what it has received by variant, which leaves the balance between infantry carriers, command vehicles, ambulances and specialist versions in the delivered fleet unknown.
In a separate answer the same day, Mr Pollard was asked when the review of programme performance for the Armour Main Battle Tank Programme would be complete. He said: “The review of programme performance for the Armour Main Battle Tank Programme forms part of the programme’s ongoing reapproval process. Under current plans, the outcome of this process is expected during Financial Year 2026-27.”
A reapproval outcome inside the current financial year gives a window closing at the end of March, and no narrower date was offered.
Britain rejoined the Boxer programme in 2018 after leaving it in 2003, and the vehicle is built under licence by Rheinmetall BAE Systems Land at Telford and WFEL at Stockport. Orders now run to more than six hundred vehicles across infantry carrier, specialist carrier, command and ambulance variants, the four base types from which the Army’s mechanised infantry brigades are being equipped.
The Armour Main Battle Tank Programme covers Challenger 3, the rebuild of 148 Challenger 2 hulls around a new turret and a 120mm smoothbore gun, also being carried out by Rheinmetall BAE Systems Land at Telford.

Tesla unveils long-awaited next generation Roadster sports EV after years of delay
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
02:00:01 UTC
11:00:01 KST

Tesla has unveiled a redesigned Roadster equipped with thrusters, nearly nine years after it first showed a next-generation version of its electric sports car and said it would start production in 2028.
Tesla demonstrated on Thursday the two-seater vehicle, developed in collaboration with CEO Elon Musk's rocket company SpaceX, showing it driving upside down on a ramp using a suction system and turning in the air and landing using in-built thrusters. The use and legality of such features on public roads were not immediately clear.
The Roadster can accelerate from zero to 96 kilometres per hour in less than one second and can hit a top speed of over 370 kph, Musk said at a SpaceX test site in McGregor, Texas.
Tesla revealed a prototype of the car in 2017 and said then that deliveries would begin in 2020.
Musk has played down the car's importance to Tesla's finances, describing it in 2023 as a "small potato situation" that would not "move the needle in a major way financially."
Optimus humanoid robots
But the car still carries symbolic weight.
"Tesla does not currently have a halo car, or high-performance luxury vehicle designed to showcase an automaker's best engineering and technology. The Roadster will be Tesla's new halo car," Morningstar analyst Seth Goldstein said in a note last month.
Musk had set expectations in 2017, saying a four-seat Roadster would travel 1,000 km on a single charge.
Goldstein expects Tesla to sell around 2,000 Roadsters a year — a fraction of the 1.6 million vehicles Tesla sold last year.
The original Roadster, released in 2008 and on sale until 2012, was Tesla's first-ever EV and used a Lotus Elise chassis.
It helped change the world's view of what an electric vehicle could be. The company has since been known for its Model Y and Model X SUVs and Model S and Model 3 sedans.
The reveal of the second-generation Roadster also comes amid a sharp shift in Tesla's focus to artificial intelligence-led self-driving tech and robotics, from manufacturing cars for human drivers.
This year, Tesla stopped selling Model S and X vehicles to make space for production of its Optimus humanoid robots. It also launched Cybercab - a two-seater robotaxi that comes without manual controls such as a steering wheel, pedals and mirrors.
