In Europe, the Trump shock factor is wearing off
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

U.S. President Donald Trump looks on as he speaks to the media on the tarmac before boarding Air Force One at Missoula Montana Airport on October 14, 2026. | Alex Wong/Getty Images
Jamie Dettmer is associate editor and a foreign affairs columnist for POLITICO.
Cast your mind back to last year, when European leaders scrambled back and forth across the Atlantic, seeking to patch up tattered relations between U.S. President Donald Trump and Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
After the Oval Office brawl where a scolded Zelenskyy pushed back against Trump and his vice president before being ejected from the White House, then-U.K. Prime Minister Keir Starmer and French President Emmanuel Macron led the effort to engineer a call between the pair, during which the Ukrainian president expressed regret about the meeting — but fell short of apologizing.
But this time, after Trump unveiled a controversial diesel deal with Russia and called — once again — for Zelenskyy to step down, the European reaction has been less febrile. Of course, they have offered Kyiv strong rhetorical support and unveiled more Russia sanctions, but there has been no frantic, panicky outreach effort to Trump to mediate a speedy repair.
Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy looks on during a bilateral meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York, on September 22, 2026. | Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images
Why not?
Because the Trump shock factor is wearing off, hazards Ukraine’s former Foreign Minister Dmytro Kuleba. “The primary answer is that they have got used to him,” he told POLITICO. “They have all had an immunity shot, and they don’t feel as scared as they did last year.”
“Another reason is they’re drowning in their own problems,” he added. “And I think that first they feel they have to try to figure out how what Trump is doing will impact them — how big their bill will become as a result.”
European leaders are not scrambling like they did last year because Trump is “losing his leverage,” said Lia Quartapelle, an Italian lawmaker from the opposition Democratic Party who is vice chair of the parliament’s Foreign and European Affairs Committee. “We realize he cannot be trusted and we are on our own,” so there’s little point lobbying him.
Advertisement
According to the Financial Times, EU officials plan to urge Zelenskyy to tone down his increasingly sharp remarks about Trump, fearing they are only inflaming the situation. Starmer’s successor, Andy Burnham, is positioning himself as someone who can “lay the ground” for a reconciliation, he explained to the House of Commons Wednesday.
Nonetheless, the calmer reaction to Trump’s maneuvers stands out, acknowledges Daniel Fried, a former senior U.S. diplomat who served as assistant secretary of state for European and Eurasian Affairs under U.S. President George W. Bush.
“The Europeans seem to have taken Trump’s measure,” Fried told POLITICO. “They want to avoid the worst. They want to mitigate the damage over the next two years while Trump is in office. They do work with people in the Trump administration with whom they can work. And there are such people.”
Speaking from Warsaw, fresh from attending a recent security conference in the Polish capital, he said the Europeans understand now that much of what Trump does is performative and has a short life span — like the Russian diesel deal, which has a shelf life of two or three days, he said. “I’m not sure it’s going anywhere as it is utterly impractical and legally questionable, and it isn’t clear the Russians actually can supply the diesel,” he said. In other words, why get worked up about it?
Daniel Fried, Atlantic Council speaks at The 2017 Concordia Annual Summit at Grand Hyatt New York on September 19, 2017 in New York City. | Paul Morigi/Getty Images for Concordia Summit
Fried said in his conversations with European leaders and officials, he has detected increasing exasperation with the overall inconsistency of the American position: “Trump wants Europe to do more militarily, but it must buy American,” he said. “But we can’t sell to the Europeans because of our needs, so they will have to wait even though they can’t build it themselves. Nonetheless, they have to carry the load in Ukraine without us. That’s utterly inconsistent, and they are exasperated by it.”
And they’re just tired of having Trump jerk them around, Fried added. “One thing they are trying to avoid is having Trump snap his fingers and they come flying. Because then it looks like they are at Trump’s beck and call and are his supplicants, and they don’t want to do that. Besides, if they fly out and talk him into something, how long will what he agreed to last?”
Of course, the Europeans can also console themselves with the high chance of Trump reversing himself. “There is a pattern,” said Kuleba. “He launches a cavalry attack … and then retreats. That’s what we saw in February last year. That’s what we saw in November 2025. And that’s what we will see this time too.”

Marine Le Pen’s EU dream is a nightmare for Brussels
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

The year is 2030 and French President Marine Le Pen’s sweeping overhaul of both her own country and the EU shows no sign of slowing down.
The Berlaymont, or the European Commission’s HQ, has been repurposed as the Ministry of National Sovereignty, except for the 13th floor —the current work base and living quarters of Commission President Ursula von der Leyen — which is now a cat cafe.
Advertisement
Other buildings in the EU Quarter of Brussels (or, as it’s now known, the 21st arrondissement) have not been so lucky. Most have been razed to the ground. Some have been occupied by disgruntled former EU staff, who are refusing to leave and have set up a working group to discuss a future roadmap that will feed into a discussion on how to bring back a European Union that Le Pen has largely destroyed.
Largely, but not completely. There is still an official EU office; the corner table in the branch of sandwich shop Exki near the Schuman roundabout (ironically, Le Pen used some of the money saved from dismantling the EU to finish the roundabout as planned). It is staffed 24/7 by Maroš Šefčovič, and he has a plentiful supply of leaflets.
Le Pen had more in store for the EU after her crushing 2027 presidential election win over Kylian Mbappé (who won a primary against Raphaël Glucksmann to be the unity centrist candidate, which was decided by who could do the most keepie-uppies).
The phrases “non-paper,” “stakeholder” and “trilogue” have been consigned to la poubelle de l’histoire. The European Committee of the Regions and the European Economic and Social Committee were closed down within weeks of Le Pen taking office, which shocked millions of Europeans who had no idea they ever existed. The European Parliament building is still there but is now occupied by a strange breed of zombie-like creatures wandering aimlessly through the corridors in search of something to do. No one can tell the difference.
Von der Leyen was, as Le Pen promised would happen, sent back to Germany where — in a somewhat unexpected move — she has become chancellor, succeeding Angela Merkel, who herself came out of retirement and orchestrated a coup to bring down current Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
Anyway, back to 2026 and an EU reeling from a Le Pen speech in which she pledged to turn the Commission into a “secretariat” in the service of its member countries, and scrap some institutions altogether.
Advertisement
Le Pen gave her speech in Brussels on Wednesday and caught the train from Paris to Gare du Midi — if you haven’t been, imagine what the train station in Hell would look like, but with paninis. According to POLITICO’s railways correspondent, Miles Trackman, Le Pen was close to running into Michel Barnier, a former French prime minister (and who among us hasn’t been French prime minister?) and fervent Europhile who was spotted at the Paris station at the same time.
The question being asked in Brussels circles (and everything in Brussels goes around in circles) is: “Will Le Pen do a Meloni?” — as in, will she soften her stance if elected? The future of the Schuman roundabout may depend on it.

Britain’s Lib Dems are having a mini-meltdown. Here’s what’s going on.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Britain’s Lib Dems are having a mini-meltdown. Here’s what’s going on.
A surprise resignation followed by an extremely long show of unity: Britain’s centrist force — a potential key player in a future coalition — doesn’t seem ready to topple its leader just yet.
LONDON — The Liberal Democrats used to watch their rivals indulge in messy factional squabbles with glee. Now they are scrambling to project an image of unity.
Britain’s third-largest Westminster group could hold significant power after the next election if no party wins a majority of MPs and Prime Minister Andy Burnham is casting around for a deal.
But for now, the focus is on weathering an internal storm in the centrist outfit. MPs rallied around their leader Ed Davey this week at a marathon four-hour meeting — held days after one of his frontbenchers resigned in an ill-fated attempt to oust the party chief.
Advertisement
The botched coup comes as the Liberal Democrats try to answer a more existential question: what are they actually for and how do they make an impact in Britain’s fragmented political landscape?
POLITICO’s Poll of Polls shows the Lib Dems coasting along. After getting 12.2% in the 2024 general election — and bagging a record 72 members of parliament as a result — the party has slipped down, polling between 9% and 11% since Andy Burnham became prime minister.
POLITICO explains why Lib Dems are now openly discussing Davey’s future; how much danger he is in; and exactly how the man known for a cheery demeanor and eye-catching paddle-board stunts could be capsized.
1) Why is Davey’s future in the headlines?
The surprise resignation of the Lib Dems’ Treasury spokesperson Charlie Maynard a week ago triggered the latest round of soul-searching about the leader’s future — but the grumbling goes back a bit further.
Maynard’s resignation followed costly tax-cutting pledges from Davey at the party’s conference in September and came hot on the heels of sharp responses — including from 2024-intake Lib Dem MPs Tom Gordon and Vikki Slade — to the way Davey defended an existing guarantee on state pensions. Some MPs believe the party isn’t adequately representing younger voters by opposing changes to the so-called triple lock, now targeted for reform by Burnham.
The immediate threat looks to have receded. Maynard’s resignation has gone down badly among a host of colleagues.
Advertisement
One Lib Dem frontbencher — granted anonymity to speak about internal matters like others in this piece — said the “vast majority of us think it’s beyond ridiculous and are really angry.” A second frontbencher said it was “bang out of order” for colleagues to brief internal policy discussions to the press.
2) So he’s safe?
Not quite — fizzled plots like this have a habit of still bringing grumbling to the surface (just ask Theresa May)
There remains frustration among some MPs over Davey’s perceived failure to exploit a gap in British politics opened up by voters’ deep dislike of Keir Starmer’s Labour government after the 2024 general election.
YouGov’s Anthony Wells explains that the party was stagnant “during a period where the Starmer government came in, became extremely unpopular [and] lost a huge amount of support” that “didn’t go to them.”
He contrasted this with how the Lib Dems gained traction in the 2000s when the Labour government was in big trouble. The Lib Dems are normally good at grabbing “the low-hanging fruit of unpopular left-of-center governments.”
“They haven’t nailed their colors really firmly to any mast,” says Wells. “They have been something to all men — and it means they may have suffered in comparison to people like the Greens under [leader] Zack Polanski, who’ve been much clearer about what they stand for.”
Advertisement
Removing a Lib Dem leader remains reasonably easy — though a crunch meeting of the parliamentary party on Tuesday suggests there currently aren’t enough MPs to actually trigger a ballot of no confidence, let alone win one.
Eighteen MPs (25% of the parliamentary party) would need to push for a vote of no confidence to be held. An absolute majority — 36 MPs — would then have to vote no confidence in Davey for a leadership election to be triggered.
Davey could stand in that leadership election if he could secure nominations from 10% of Lib Dem MPs and 200 members from at least 20 different local parties.
Unlike in the Conservatives, where a leader cannot be challenged again for a year after they win a no-confidence vote, Davey would be given no such grace period if he survived — meaning another ballot could take place just months after he saw off a coup attempt.
3) What’s the view from Davey world?
The arguments in the leader’s favor appear to have won out — for now.
For one, he has a record of winning. Davey can point to having taken the party to its largest number of constituencies in its modern form by focusing on a fight-by-fight, seats-first strategy. The 2024 campaign prioritized targeted campaigning in specific areas, rather than seeking a higher national vote share that doesn’t translate to a high number of MPs.
Advertisement

SpaceX Dragon docks with ISS, delivering new cargo
The spacecraft docked at 10:27 a.m. EDT with the space-facing port of the station’s Harmony module. The mission marks SpaceX’s 35th commercial resupply mission to the ISS for NASA.
The cargo includes the final set of International Space Station Roll-Out Solar Arrays (IROSAs), scheduled for installation later this fall. It also carries equipment for experiments aimed at advancing medical research and materials science.
Researchers will work on manufacturing artificial retinas in microgravity to help restore vision, developing 3D heart tissue models for large-scale drug testing, and studying how a new type of glass forms in space. The mission also carries brain organoids that could help identify targets for treatments for neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s and multiple sclerosis.
The Dragon spacecraft is scheduled to remain at the station until mid-November before returning to Earth with time-critical research and cargo. It is expected to splash down off the coast of California.
The mission launched on Oct. 13 aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida.

Majority of Israelis back Haredi draft law, October 7 inquiry, IDI survey finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
01:52:55 UTC
10:52:55 KST

A majority of Jewish Israelis supported requiring haredi (ultra-Orthodox) men to enlist in the IDF and establishing a state commission of inquiry into the October 7, 2023, Hamas massacre, while Arab Israelis expressed the strongest support for exploring negotiations with the Palestinians.
The Viterbi Family Center for Public Opinion and Policy Research at the Israel Democracy Institute conducted the survey between October 5 and 8, surveying 602 Jewish Israelis and 149 Arab Israelis aged 18 and above, and published its findings on Wednesday.
According to the findings, 72% of Jewish respondents supported passing a law requiring young ultra-Orthodox men to enlist in the IDF, while 71% supported establishing a state commission of inquiry into the October 7 massacre, according to the survey.
Support for conscription legislation and a state commission of inquiry was highest on the Left (93.5%) and in the Center (89%), while respondents on the Right expressed lower levels of support (62%).
One quarter of Jews in Israel support negotiations with Palestinians
Only a quarter of Jewish respondents supported exploring the possibility of negotiations with the Palestinians, while the IDI said this proposal received its highest level of support among Arab Israelis, with 58% of those surveyed favoring it.
The findings also showed differences between Jewish and Arab-Israelis over the government's settlement policy in the West Bank. Overall, 55% of respondents said the policy of allowing and encouraging settlements was the correct course of action, while 32% disapproved of current Jewish settlement policies.
Over two-thirds of Jewish respondents viewed the Jewish settlement in the West Bank favorably, compared with half of Arab-Israeli respondents, who said it was incorrect. The IDI noted that the share of Jewish respondents supporting the policy had increased by about 10 percentage points since a similar question was asked in May 2017.
Israeli attitudes toward European sanctions on Israeli settlements
The United Kingdom, along with Canada and France, announced sanctions on goods originating from Israeli settlements in the West Bank. In response to the trade ban, Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar announced that the UK's consulate in east Jerusalem would be shut down.
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband defended the sanctions as a response to what he believes is an attempt by Israel to bury the two-state solution by illegally expanding its occupation of Palestinian land.
The survey examined attitudes toward the European sanctions on imports from West Bank settlements. Some 63% of respondents supported a strong Israeli response and equal treatment for settlement products and products made elsewhere in Israel.
Around 70% of Jewish respondents supported demanding equal treatment for products from Israeli settlements, while approximately half of Arab respondents supported recognizing other countries' right to restrict imports.
The survey also examined public perceptions of reports that Netanyahu had received warnings from senior Arab figures in the weeks before October 7 about a planned Hamas attack.
Respondents were divided over the credibility of the reports, with 46% of the overall sample saying they were not credible and 43% saying they were credible.
However, 63% of respondents believed the reports were published in recent weeks to influence the upcoming election results, while 27% believed the information had only recently come to light. The majority view that the timing was intended to influence the election was shared by both Jewish and Arab respondents.
The survey recorded a rise in optimism about the future of democratic rule, national security, the economy and social cohesion compared with the previous month. The largest increase was in optimism about democratic rule, which rose by 9.5 percentage points, followed by an eight-point increase in optimism about national security.

Small-scale desalination offers water security solution for remote Australia
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:48:21 CST
10:48:21 KST

SYDNEY, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- A small-scale desalination unit is helping secure water supplies for a remote Aboriginal boarding school in the state of Western Australia, demonstrating its potential to address rural water scarcity.
Developed by researchers at Australia's Murdoch University in collaboration with state government agencies, Water Corporation and industry partners, the off-grid unit turns salty groundwater into freshwater at Wongutha Christian Aboriginal Parent-Directed School, located more than 700 km from the state capital, Perth, according to a university statement released on Thursday.
The school, which cannot connect to the state's water grid, had relied on a nearby farm for water, but the supply's quality and quantity had steadily declined.
The unit, housed in a shipping container and powered by solar panels and batteries, also pumps rejected saline water to a nearby field of saltbush, a drought-resistant native plant used for livestock feed, the statement said.
Wongutha facilities manager Kris Nostrini said the unit had supplied more than 7.5 megaliters of water to the site, improving water quality and reliability for residents and students.
Although desalination technology has been commercially available since the late 1980s, research has largely focused on large-scale systems, prompting researchers to develop lower-cost, decentralized and off-grid solutions for rural communities and agriculture, it said.
The project is part of the state government's WaterSmart Farms initiative, which is evaluating more than 50 on-farm desalination units to assess the potential of local water and renewable energy to support farms and remote communities, according to Murdoch University. ■

====================================================================================================

Extreme warmth drives plant extinctions, diversity booms: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:48:07 CST
10:48:07 KST

MELBOURNE, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- Extreme global warmth drove both mass extinctions and explosions in plant diversity during two periods over the past 140 million years, offering new insights into how flowering plants became dominant on Earth, a new study has found.
The study examined fossilized pollen and spores to show that the mid-Cretaceous and early Cenozoic periods of extreme global warmth were central to plant evolution, both for flowering plants and the other main types on Earth, according to a statement released Thursday by Australia's University of Tasmania (UTAS).
Researchers said that land plants sustain almost all terrestrial animals, fungi and bacteria, while flowering plants are the most productive and diverse group, with about 400,000 species worldwide.
The team examined more than 60,000 fossil occurrences and applied methods that overcome the major biases in the fossil record, generating revised estimates of fossil pollen and spore diversity over the past 130 million years, according to the study published in Nature Plants.
Both plant extinctions and the emergence of new but evolutionarily related plant groups occurred mostly during the two periods of extreme global warmth, said the study's co-author, UTAS Professor Greg Jordan.
Each interval lasted several million years, with warming simultaneously destroying and promoting plant diversity "over million-year timescales," Jordan said. In contrast, cooler periods were marked by little change in plant diversity.
However, the researchers warned that human-driven warming is likely to cause plant extinctions much faster than past extreme warming events. ■

BEIJING, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- Brazil's Rafael Camara will make his Formula 1 debut with Haas in 2027 after signing a multi-year contract with the American team, replacing the outgoing Esteban Ocon.
The 21-year-old Ferrari academy driver, who currently leads the Formula 2 championship, was selected following an evaluation process involving four candidates, including reigning F2 champion Leonardo Fornaroli and Haas reserve drivers Jack Doohan and Ryo Hirakawa.
Camara impressed Haas during a test at Portugal's Portimao circuit in August, driving the team's 2025 F1 car. Team principal Ayao Komatsu said the Brazilian's pace had been the decisive factor in securing the seat.
"I always said we would choose a driver by performance. He showed incredible speed. That was the fully overriding factor above everything else," Komatsu said.
"In Portimao, he was just simply outstanding. We really wanted to go for someone who had that natural speed."
Camara joined Ferrari's driver academy in 2021 and has established himself as one of the most promising talents in junior single-seater racing.
He won the Formula Regional European Championship in 2024 before claiming the Formula 3 title in his rookie season in 2025.
The Brazilian has continued his rapid progress in Formula 2 this year, winning three races and holding a seven-point championship lead over Red Bull junior Nikola Tsolov with two scheduled rounds remaining in Qatar and Abu Dhabi.
Should Camara secure the F2 crown, he would become the first driver since Oscar Piastri to win consecutive titles in Formula Regional, F3 and F2.
Komatsu praised Camara's ability to adapt quickly to F1 machinery despite his limited experience.
"He showed that he could handle himself very well with not a huge amount of time to learn the car. He showed us more than just raw speed," Komatsu said.
Camara expressed his gratitude to Haas and Ferrari, while acknowledging the challenges awaiting him in his debut season.
"It's an important step in my career and I want to thank [team founder] Gene Haas and Ayao Komatsu for the trust they have placed in me," he said.
"Now my focus is on preparing myself in the best possible way for this new challenge. There will be a lot to learn, and I'm looking forward to working closely with the team, understanding the car and continuing to develop as a driver."
Camara will replace Ocon, whose departure was confirmed last month after two seasons with Haas. The Frenchman has struggled to match the performances of teammate Oliver Bearman during his time with the team.
Haas has yet to formally confirm its second driver for 2027, although Bearman is widely expected to remain for a third season, potentially giving the team an all-Ferrari academy lineup.
"It is our intention to continue with Ollie. It is just a matter of timing and finalising certain details," Komatsu said.
Camara is the first rookie confirmed for the 2027 F1 grid. His promotion also ensures Brazil will have at least two representatives in the championship next season for the first time since 2016, with Gabriel Bortoleto set to continue at Audi. ■

Why has "China Haul" become new buzzword on social media worldwide?
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:47:47 CST
10:47:47 KST

Foreign tourists buy handheld camera equipment at a flagship store of DJI in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province, June 24, 2026. (Xinhua/Liang Xu)
By Liu He
More and more foreign visitors are arriving in China with empty suitcases and returning home with bags full of Chinese goods. What is behind this trend? British YouTuber Elliot Page offered a glimpse of the appeal with a shopping vlog filmed in Guangzhou, south China's Guangdong Province. Exploring Chinese sportswear brands such as Li-Ning and Anta, Page was impressed not only by their affordability, but also by their design and quality.
Sportswear is just the tip of the iceberg. As "China Haul" gains traction on social media worldwide, an increasing number of international visitors are traveling to China not only to explore its attractions, but also to discover and shop for products that catch their eye.
In the first seven months of 2026, people from overseas spent 263.6 billion yuan (about 39 billion U.S. dollars) in China, an increase of 27.8 percent year on year, according to the Ministry of Commerce.
What is drawing international consumers to Chinese goods?
The growing appeal of homegrown Chinese brands is giving international consumers more reasons to take notice. "Chinese products, like clothes, accessories and daily necessities, are not only competitively priced, but also feature trendy designs that are hard to find in stores in my home country," said Carlos Alvarado, an international student from Guatemala, now a seasoned shopper in China.
An increasingly visitor-friendly shopping environment is making it easier for international tourists to spend in China. Visa-free entry arrangements and expanded departure tax refund services have further enhanced the country's appeal as a shopping destination.
From sprawling shopping malls and efficient delivery services to delivery robots that bring orders right to hotel doors, China offers a seamless shopping experience that lowers the barriers for foreign visitors. "Foreign tourists now account for 30 percent of our daily customer flow," said Zhou Man, manager of a Xiaomi store in Chengdu, southwest China's Sichuan Province.
Chinese cultural products are broadening the appeal of shopping in China, giving visitors more opportunities to connect purchases with the stories and creativity behind them.
From globally popular designer toys such as Labubu to the animated blockbuster Ne Zha 2, Chinese cultural products are capturing international attention. As international audiences become more familiar with Chinese cultural creations, shopping in China can offer another way to discover the country's contemporary culture and everyday life.
China Haul, at its core, reflects a simple shift: foreign visitors are discovering China's global appeal firsthand, exploring its products and brands for themselves rather than relying on secondhand impressions. By sharing their shopping finds online, they are introducing the world to a more diverse and appealing side of China.

At a press conference on Thursday, Clark county coroner Melanie Rouse shared his name publicly for the first time: Edward Lelburian Jackson.

An initial autopsy revealed the man had been killed by a single shot to the head. Investigators determined he was likely killed in the mid-1970s to early 1980s – an era when organized crime ran rampant in Las Vegas – due to the style of his clothing.
In the years since he was found, authorities revealed he had been wearing a button-down short-sleeve shirt, light blue jeans, a silver wristwatch and blue-and-white tennis shoes. They also released composite renderings of what he may have looked like, in the hopes that someone might come forward with information.
Behind the scenes though, they searched for his DNA in crime databases, uploaded his description into a national missing persons database, and sent bone samples to a lab to obtain a genealogy profile.
A break in the case didn’t come until this year, when a forensics team at Oklahoma State University, which had partnered with investigators, received a strong lead. With a DNA sample from Jackson and his believed family member, “we were able to confirm that the remains were, in fact, Mr. Jackson,” Rouse said.
Jackson was from Arkansas, Las Vegas Metropolitan police department Lt Robert Price said, adding that detectives have not yet found a single thing that would tie him to the Las Vegas area. His family last saw him in the early 80s and there are records of him in California, where he briefly lived with his wife, and in Utah, where he was charged with aggravated arson and a conspiracy fraud case.
“There has been speculation in the past that the homicide had ties to an organized criminal group,” Price said. “At this point of our investigation, we don’t have any information to support those theories.”
Now that he has been identified, Price added, the investigation into what happened – and who was responsible – for Jackson’s murder can continue.
Jackson’s remains weren’t the only ones uncovered from Lake Mead in recent years, as its water levels reached historic lows due to years of overuse, longstanding drought and increasing temperatures. The water level of the 90-year-old reservoir has continually dropped, exposing areas that were previously underwater and leading historians to predict more bodies will be found.
A few days after the barrel was discovered, a second barrel was found by a KLAS-TV news crew, not far from the first. It was empty. Shortly after that, paddleboarders discovered human remains on a newly surfaced sand bar, but officials found no evidence of foul play.
In August, more human remains were discovered and police again determined there was no evidence of foul play.
Lake Mead and the upstream Lake Powell are the largest human-made reservoirs in the US, part of a system that provides Colorado River water to more than 40 million people, tribes, agriculture and industry in Arizona, California, Colorado, Nevada, New Mexico, Utah, Wyoming and across the southern border in Mexico.
The Associated Press and Uwa Ede-Osifo contributed reporting

Myanmar’s coup leader-turned-president wins back neighbours despite war

2026-10-16

Myanmar’s coup leader-turned-president wins back neighbours despite war
From Thailand to Malaysia, ASEAN leaders are embracing Min Aung Hlaing, but critics warn it emboldens a military that is still bombing civilians.
Rohingya activist says it’s unfair to send refugees back to Myanmar
Yangon, Myanmar – When Malaysia invited Myanmar’s coup leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing for a visit in September, it insisted the trip did not amount to recognition. The purpose, an official said, was to address the “longstanding issue” of refugees and migrants from Myanmar in Malaysia.
But when Min Aung Hlaing arrived in Kuala Lumpur last week, the former general – whose power grab in 2021 triggered a devastating civil war – received a red carpet welcome, complete with an honour guard.
After an official luncheon on Thursday, Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said Myanmar was prepared to take its nationals back at its own cost, a message with appeal in a country where anti-refugee sentiment is growing. Malaysia hosts about 193,000 Myanmar nationals, most of them from the persecuted Rohingya Muslim minority.
“Because the weather is favourable, I will dispatch Navy ships to repatriate them,” Min Aung Hlaing said.
For his part, Anwar pledged to help reintegrate Myanmar into the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), the 11-member regional bloc that has barred Min Aung Hlaing from its high-level meetings for refusing to carry out its peace plan. Malaysia was a vocal supporter of the plan, which is known as the Five Point Consensus and calls for an end to violence and “constructive dialogue” between the warring parties.
The civil war in Myanmar is now in its fifth year and has killed as many as 100,000 people and displaced at least 3.5 million, according to monitoring groups.
“Malaysia will do whatever is possible to make sure that we … ultimately, take Myanmar as part of our community of nations, without prejudice, and particularly in the context of ASEAN,” Anwar told reporters.
Malaysia is the fifth ASEAN nation to host Min Aung Hlaing since he became president in April, after an election held in December and January, which major opposition parties were barred from participating in. In recent months, he has visited Thailand, Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos.
Following his return from Malaysia, his spokesperson said Indonesia and Brunei could be next.
“Malaysia’s reversal on Min Aung Hlaing has broken a dam of opposition to the junta,” said Bridget Welsh, an honorary research associate at the University of Nottingham’s Asia Research Institute in Kuala Lumpur. She said regional leaders who have welcomed Min Aung Hlaing, despite accusations that he has committed crimes against humanity, were putting pragmatism ahead of human rights.
“It is a step back for ASEAN as an organisation, and for Myanmar,” she said. “It does not offer any concrete path to the resolution of the Myanmar crisis, and in fact, arguably worsens it by giving the military legitimacy internationally, a legitimacy it does not have in Myanmar itself.”
‘Convenience plays a part’
Min Aung Hlaing’s rehabilitation extends beyond Southeast Asia.
Since April, the former general has also visited India, China, Russia and Belarus. At each stop, he has tried to present his government as stable and “on the path to democracy”, while pitching trade and infrastructure deals.
Even the United States appears to have opened the door.
Washington has begun direct talks with Min Aung Hlaing’s government, the Reuters news agency reported last week, despite sanctions on him over human rights abuses. These include the 2017 crackdown on the Rohingya, which sent more than 700,000 people fleeing into Bangladesh and which the US has called a genocide.
Reuters said the latest talks have focused on shutting down scam centres operating from Myanmar that have defrauded Americans of billions of dollars.
Khin Zaw Win, director of the Tampadipa Institute in Yangon, said Min Aung Hlaing’s quest for international legitimacy has been aided by a coordinated push from China, India and Thailand, all of which share borders with Myanmar. The three neighbours have experienced spillover from the war, such as fighting near their borders, disrupted trade and influxes of refugees.
Khin Zaw Win said the three countries “have the biggest stakes in how Myanmar pans out” and want the military-installed government recognised. Russia and Belarus, meanwhile, are both major arms suppliers to Myanmar, and Naypyidaw has backed Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
“Convenience plays a part for all of them,” he said.
The growing diplomatic recognition, however, has done little to resolve the conflict.
While Min Aung Hlaing has invited all armed groups to peace talks, fighting continues to rage across much of the country. His forces have launched offensives to retake territory lost to opposition armed rebels and ethnic armed groups in Rakhine, Chin, Kachin and Karen states and the Sagaing region. They have been aided by an intensified air campaign and a recruitment drive that has added tens of thousands to their ranks. China, too, has helped by brokering ceasefires between the military and powerful ethnic armed groups on its border.
Still, Laetitia van den Assum, a former Dutch diplomat, said the military is unlikely to regain control of the whole country.
“That would require a huge occupation army and not – as now – a garrison army that controls a particular location,” she said. “That is why Min Aung Hlaing… bets on an increasing number of temporary ceasefires in some parts of the country so that troops can be directed to areas where he wants to continue fighting”.
Van den Assum said she found it “quite surprising” that ASEAN nations are seeking Rohingya repatriation from the very man accused of orchestrating crimes against them.
Myanmar has long denied the Rohingya citizenship, so it is unclear whether it would accept them as nationals. And with much of Rakhine State – their homeland – now held by the ethnic Arakan Army, it is far from clear where they would go.
“It is the blind speaking to the blind,” she said.
‘Low-cost, high optics’
Min Aung Hlaing has made other gestures.
Shortly before his trip to Thailand in August, he allowed the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) to see Aung San Suu Kyi, the civilian leader he deposed in 2021. The 81-year-old Nobel laureate has been held incommunicado since the coup, and the ICRC visit on August 3 produced her first photographs in years.
Sai Kyi Zin Soe, a research fellow at the University of Sydney, called the move a “low-cost, high-optics gesture rather than a real political opening”. The visit confirmed only that Aung San Suu Kyi is alive, “nothing more”, he said.
He noted that the military’s air raids have continued unabated even as ASEAN leaders roll out the red carpet, including a September 28 strike on a market in Rakhine State that killed an estimated 50 people.
The continuing attacks, he said, were the “strongest evidence that soft diplomacy hasn’t produced any deterrent effect”.
Sai Kyi Zin Soe also warned that the legitimacy conferred by the foreign visits would embolden the military further.
“Given the near-total absence of deterrence, no meaningful sanctions enforcement, an ASEAN pivoting toward re-engagement, and continued arms and fuel access via China and Russia, the military has every structural incentive to keep escalating, particularly in contested zones like Sagaing and Rakhine, where its grip is weakest,” he said.
Much now depends on the Philippines and Singapore, ASEAN’s current and incoming chairs.
Phil Robertson, director of Asia Human Rights and Labor Advocates, said the two countries must set an agenda that pushes back hard on entreaties from others in the region to allow “Myanmar fully back into the fold” and keep pressing the bloc’s five-point peace plan.
He also urged the US, the United Kingdom, Canada, Australia and the European Union to adopt targeted sanctions, such as an aviation fuel ban, rather than leaving “the whole Myanmar conundrum” to the regional bloc.
“International accountability is now more urgent than ever, whether that comes through additional universal jurisdiction cases or some sort of breakthrough to refer Myanmar’s generals to the International Criminal Court,” he added.
Zaheena Rasheed reported and wrote from Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia.

Trump's comments come months after the Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty expired earlier this year.
The New START treaty, signed in 2010, allowed one single extension, which was agreed to by former president Joe Biden and Russian President Vladimir Putin for five years. Any new extension would require an executive decision to voluntarily extend the limits of the treaty.

A hidden device was found on an Australian Navy ship. Fallout is being felt across the fleet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
01:28:18 UTC
10:28:18 KST

In brief
- A hidden video recording device was discovered in a women's bathroom on a Navy vessel.
- The Australian Defence Force says a service member has been identified as a person of interest.
The discovery of a video recording device hidden in the women's shower block of an Australian Navy ship has been described as a "despicable betrayal of trust" and prompted calls for cultural change in the military.
A defence spokesperson confirmed on Thursday that an Australian Defence Force (ADF) member had been identified as a person of interest after a video recording device was found on the HMAS Leeuwin in Cairns in far north Queensland.
"This person is now assisting the Joint Military Police Unit with its inquiries," the spokesperson said, adding that "Navy's focus and priority is providing support to those who are impacted by this incident."
The department earlier said it's taking the incident "extremely seriously" and there was no tolerance for such behaviour.
Here's what we know so far.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
What happened?
On Wednesday morning, federal senator Jacqui Lambie alleged in parliament that a camera had been found hidden in a women's shower on the vessel while it was docked in Cairns.
That afternoon, the Department of Defence released a statement confirming a device had been found in a cabin three days earlier and an investigation was underway.
Chief of Navy Vice Admiral Matt Buckley later said the incident was being taken seriously and bathrooms across the entire fleet were being checked.
"This act is the most despicable betrayal of trust and is fundamentally misaligned with our values," he said in a statement.
"We will not, however, be defined by acts of this nature. Our Navy is one where highly professional warfighters must rely day in, day out on their shipmates. Anything that undermines the trust and respect we need for one another will not be tolerated.
"You have my assurance and commitment that we will tackle this act of sexual violence with all of our energy.
"Any perpetrator will be held to account. Further, you should all know that eradicating sexual violence in our workplace is fundamental to the fighting efficiency of our Navy. I invite all of you to make this your priority."
What has the reaction been?
Before the ADF publicly confirmed the incident, Lambie — a former Army member and defence advocate — told the Senate she'd been tipped off by a former Navy member.
"I was also told this had occurred recently and prevented the vessel from sailing while investigations were ongoing," she said.
"Even more disturbing are claims that footage from these cameras may have been uploaded online before the cameras were discovered.
"How many of our female sailors have unknowingly been recorded in their most private moments? How much footage has been distributed online so far, retained or uploaded without knowledge or consent?
"These are the questions I ask the Navy today."
Lambie later said she was unhappy with defence's response and called for an independent body to be set up to investigate.
"This is a culture that, unfortunately, defence has not been able to clean up, and it hasn't even come close," she told ABC TV on Thursday.
"The only way to fix this problem is to take the legal system outside of defence's hands.
"Their job is to fight in a war ... and they don't deal with this very well when it comes to the legal system."
She said others had come forward alleging similar incidents in recent months.
What happens next?
No charges have been laid yet, but the incident has already prompted calls for cultural change within the military.
Defence Industry Minister Pat Conroy said one in five ADF personnel were women and they needed to be treated with respect and dignity.
"The culture has to change to accommodate that," he said, noting it was a key finding from the Royal Commission into Defence and Veteran Suicide.
The commission's 2024 final report found systemic bullying, abuse, sexual violence and an entrenched "code of silence" were linked to high rates of suicide within the ADF.
Communications Minister Anika Wells said women had a right to feel safe at work.
"I really feel for all of the people who are on that ship who are learning this and the people that may have been victims of this act," she told ABC TV on Thursday.
"You deserve to be safe in your workplace, and the rise of tech-facilitated abuse, particularly upon women, is horrific."
Greens leader David Shoebridge described the incident as "incredibly concerning".
"We know many women aren't feeling safe inside defence spaces, and again we say to Labor: You've got to restore faith with defence personnel, you’ve got to make women and other people feel safe in defence spaces."

Defence Member and Family Helpline: 1800 624 608

The Tesla Roadster 2 Is Here—and It Flies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
01:22:51 UTC
10:22:51 KST

On Thursday night, Tesla and CEO Elon Musk unveiled what’s been billed as the company’s last human-driven car. Maybe human-piloted is a more accurate way to say it.
At a demonstration event in McGregor, Texas—at SpaceX’s rocket development and testing facility—the new car did what Musk has long promised. With a herky-jerky burst of steam, it flew into the air. At one point, the car appeared to flip over the automaker’s entire line-up, floating several feet over its electric semi-truck. Tesla executives said the vehicle could accelerate from 0 to 60 mph in one second.
“This is not necessarily a safety-optimized car,” Musk said. (It’s also likely to raise the eyebrows of federal regulators.)
Tesla says it will begin production on the Roadster 2 in 2028. Fans have waited a long time for the vehicle. The Roadster 2—the successor to Tesla’s first vehicle, the Roadster—was first announced in 2017, and at the time Tesla said the new sports car would be the fastest production vehicle in the world.
The “flying” technology is enabled by four thrusters, Tesla vehicle engineering head Lars Moravy said. He said the production version would “hopefully” travel up to 230 miles per hour, though Musk said he hoped to “crack halfway to the speed of sound”—around 385 mph. Modern Formula 1 vehicles usually top out around 220 mph. The company said the vehicle would travel more than 300 miles on one charge, middling for a mainstream EV and lower than most luxury vehicles. Tesla’s own Model 3 can travel up to 360 miles on a charge.
Tesla said the thrusters are powered by onboard compressed gas. Musk said that the same technology that allows the vehicle to fly will also create downward force that allows the vehicle to turn corners very quickly. “It’s going to crush every track record that has ever existed,” he said.
The company initially promised the Roadster 2 would ship in 2020. On Thursday, the Tesla team did mention the new timeline, but did not mention what the new car will cost. Musk has a long history of not following through on his loftiest product ambitions, and timelines for many Tesla releases have repeatedly missed targets.
The company posted on X that the Roadster 2 would come in three variants: a two-seater “Performance” road-ready version that lacks the thrusters Tesla showed off on Thursday; a “race ready” Thrust variant; and an “air ready” Rocket variant that has only one seat. The Tesla website lists the Rocket as “invite only” and the Thrust as “limited.” You can currently only place reservations for the Performance and Thrust versions.
When it was first announced, enthusiasts put down $50,000 deposits for what was advertised as a $200,000 car. (That deposit is worth more than $68,000 in 2026 dollars.) Some got sick of waiting. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman complained on X last year that he had trouble canceling his reservation. Musk posted that Altman received a refund in 24 hours.
A reservation page posted on Tesla’s site now charges a $5,000 reservation fee for the Performance variant, with an additional $45,000 due within 10 days. The Thrust is available for an initial $5,000 fee, with $245,000 due within 10 days.
Musk has said that Tesla should no longer be regarded as a carmaker and that the company is focused on building autonomous vehicle technology and robots.
The unveiling event comes at a weird time for electric vehicles. Sales of EVs have stalled in the US after the GOP-led Congress nixed federal support. Meanwhile, the global energy crisis has EV sales booming elsewhere. Electric luxury hypercars—the class to which the Roadster 2 belongs—are in an especially tricky spot. Several luxury automakers have said that wealthy buyers are now looking for the sound and power of a typical gas-powered vehicle. Lamborghini shelved its plans to make an EV earlier this year.

New York’s Plaza Hotel to shut for four-year clean-up of its celebrated facade

Unknown Publisher

New York’s Plaza Hotel to shut for four-year clean-up of its celebrated facade
Andy Newman
- The Plaza Hotel in New York will close in January for a four-year facade restoration, announced by Fairmont Hotels & Resorts.
- The 119-year-old landmark has a rich history, with luxury rooms, condos, and famous guests, but needs major upkeep to protect its heritage.
- Fairmont gave no cost or work details. Hotel staff can return at the same pay when it reopens, and the union will seek other jobs in the meantime.
AI generated
NEW YORK – One of New York City’s most iconic hotels is closing for four years for a face-lift.
The 119-year-old Plaza Hotel will shut its gilded doors in January for a restoration of the 18-storey building’s landmark facade, the hotel’s operators, Fairmont Hotels & Resorts, announced on Oct 14.
Since the hotel’s opening day in 1907, when a Vanderbilt scion signed the guest register with a flourish, the Plaza, at the corner of Central Park South and Fifth Avenue, has been synonymous with a particular New York brand of opulence.
But maintaining that elegance requires periodic upkeep. The hotel, which has had at least half a dozen owners over the years – including US President Donald Trump, who took it into bankruptcy in the 1990s – has undergone several rounds of renovation.
It was partly converted into condominiums in the early 2000s and now has 282 hotel rooms and 181 condo units.
The fortress-like Plaza was created by architect Henry Janeway Hardenbergh, who also designed the Dakota on Central Park West.
New York Times architecture critic Paul Goldberger wrote in 1982 that the hotel had been “designed in a style that is generally described as French Renaissance but is essentially New York eclectic – a French chateau blown up to the size of a small skyscraper and embellished with myriad classical details”.
He called the Plaza “the only hotel in the city that is as crucial a part of New York’s architectural heritage as are such public buildings as Grand Central Terminal and the New York Public Library”.
Fairmont did not offer details on what exactly the work would consist of or how much it would cost, but said that the restoration plan “reflects the complexity of maintaining a property of such architectural and historical significance, with careful consideration given to preservation requirements and the building’s long-term care”.
The company added that “the scope and complexity of the facade works require detailed planning and coordination with relevant stakeholders”.
Fairmont also declined to say whether the residents of the condo would be displaced during the restoration. Receptionists at the hotel’s event rooms and the Palm Court restaurant said that those venues would also close in January.
Andrew Dolkart, a professor of historic preservation at Columbia University, said that the building’s facade had been redone when part of the hotel was converted to luxury housing, and that he was surprised to hear that it required another extensive round of renovation.
He said that even if the work was only on the exterior, it made sense to close the hotel. “It’s going to be noisy, and they must figure they can’t charge luxury prices for a hotel when there’s construction work going on outside your window,” he said.
As for the fate of the Plaza’s staff, a spokesperson for the Hotel & Gaming Trades Council, which represents hotel workers, said that the 378 members who worked at the Plaza would have the right to resume their jobs at the same pay when the hotel reopened. In the meantime, the union will try to find them other jobs.
The Plaza’s customers over the years have included F. Scott Fitzgerald, Truman Capote, the Beatles and the children’s book heroine Eloise. Her all-pink quarters can be reserved for more than US$4,000 (S$5,100) a night.
A room with a king-size bed was listed for US$1,421 on booking.com. The Grand Penthouse, a two-bedroom terrace suite, goes for US$36,140 – plus US$5,329 in tax.
- This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

Fees for professional courses can be hiked midstream only in exceptional cases: SC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
01:14:20 UTC
10:14:20 KST

SC quashed a 37% fee hike for BTech courses for the 2023- 27 cohort at Dr BC Roy Engineering College in West Bengal.
NEW DELHI: In a relief to students pursuing professional courses like engineering and medicine in private colleges who have to face a fee hike midstream, Supreme Court has held that any change in fee structure after admission can be allowed only in exceptional circumstances.While appreciating the contribution of self-financing institutions to the education sector, a bench of Justices P S Narasimha and Alok Aradhe said there should be certainty regarding fees, and students must not be forced to pay more than that prescribed at the time of admission."For the overwhelming majority of households, the fee payable for a professional course constitutes a substantial part of the family's income and savings; it is not a matter of incidental expenditure. The parents make provisions for the fees... with the aspiration that their children will acquire better qualifications, secure better opportunities and build a future that may be better than their own. Many students and families also depend on educational loans to finance professional higher education," SC said, noting fees charged in professional courses are reported to be 711% higher than in general courses.
The court said it was a matter of good governance for the state and its regulatory bodies to create an ecosystem in which there was certainty about the financial obligation that students and their families need to undertake to acquire professional qualifications.
"Adverse variations in financial commitment, and the insecurities that it may create, will impact the student and the family, and, in the long run, have an adverse effect on the quality and character of the professionals in the making. We are of the opinion that it is not difficult to formulate a scheme through which such uncertainties can be avoided," it said.SC quashed a 37% fee hike for BTech courses for the 2023-27 cohort at Dr BC Roy Engineering College in West Bengal. The college had also imposed a new development fee.Passing an order in favour of students who had challenged the fee hike, the bench said, "The regulatory regime for fixation of fees, as contemplated in the decisions of this court, AICTE regulations, National Education Policy 2020 coupled with principles of certainty, necessitates the relevant authorities to notify fee payable for the entire course before a student takes admission... Variation is permissible only in exceptional instances such as unforeseen increase in the expenditure."

Can Zimbabwe’s ZiG win trust and replace the US dollar?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
01:12:26 UTC
10:12:26 KST

Can Zimbabwe’s ZiG win trust and replace the US dollar?
After repeated currency crises, Zimbabweans remain wary of the ZiG.
Harare, Zimbabwe – The government is trying to persuade citizens to use its own currency more widely, with the longer-term aim of reducing reliance on the US dollar. But after years of currency instability, many remain reluctant to trust the latest attempt.
The Zimbabwe Gold (ZiG), introduced in April 2024, is a government effort to restore confidence in the local currency. The Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe (RBZ) says the currency is backed by foreign currency and precious metal reserves, including gold.
Yet the challenge extends beyond introducing a new currency or strengthening its reserves. Zimbabweans who have watched their savings lose value and their wages shrink through successive currency crises remain cautious about holding money in a currency whose purchasing power they fear could deteriorate.
Zimbabwe abandoned its local currency in 2009 after a period of hyperinflation and adopted a multicurrency system dominated by the US dollar. A domestic currency returned in 2018, but repeated instability has made rebuilding public confidence difficult.
The cost of lost confidence
For primary school teacher Charles Mbwandarikwa, the experience of earlier currency crises remains a warning.
He receives about a third of his salary in ZiG and says he exchanges it quickly rather than holding on to it. His caution stems from the losses he suffered when Zimbabwe’s previous currency collapsed.
He lost his pension savings during the 2009 crisis. When the local currency was reintroduced in 2018, he says, the value of his salary fell from the equivalent of $540 to $40 by the end of that year.
Such experiences help explain why official assurances about the ZiG have not necessarily translated into confidence among earners.
The RBZ has sought to strengthen the currency’s credibility. On April 7 , the bank introduced an upgraded series of ZiG banknotes with revised designs and security features.
According to the RBZ, annual ZiG inflation stood at 3.7 percent last month. But relatively low inflation alone does not guarantee that people will choose to save in the currency or use it for everyday transactions.
Economist Cornelius Dube says demand for the ZiG remains weak.
“ZiG has to be available in a ratio relative to its demand. Demand for ZiG is currently very subdued,” he says.
A currency few customers use
For businesses, the currency’s acceptance by customers is a practical test of whether it can gain a larger role in the economy.
Sesedzai Chigumira, a clothing retailer, says she has made only a handful of sales in ZiG. Her experience reflects the difficulty in encouraging wider use of a currency when customers and businesses remain more comfortable transacting in US dollars.
The government’s push to reduce dollar dependence also faces a broader challenge: the existence of gold and other mineral resources does not, by itself, guarantee confidence in a currency. People must believe that it will retain its value and remain useful for paying for goods, meeting expenses and saving for the future.
Where businesses expect customers to prefer dollars, they may be reluctant to price goods or accept payments in ZiG. Consumers, in turn, have little incentive to hold the local currency if they fear that its value could fall.
That creates a cycle that policy measures alone may struggle to break.
What it will take to win trust
The RBZ has moved away from its previous target of adopting a single currency by 2030, instead outlining a gradual, market-led transition towards greater use of the ZiG. The approach depends on sustained macroeconomic stability and conditions that encourage businesses and consumers to use the currency voluntarily.
The central bank has also sought to expand the ZiG’s role in domestic transactions, including through its use in tax payments and public-sector transactions, alongside measures affecting the foreign exchange and national payments systems.
But wider use in payments is not the same as confidence in a currency as a store of value. People may use ZiG when required or when circumstances leave them little choice without being willing to keep their savings in it.
For Mbwandarikwa, the memory of losing his pension savings remains part of the calculation. For Chigumira, the limited number of customers paying in ZiG shows how far the currency still has to go to become a routine part of business.
Dube says de-dollarisation is possible, but it cannot be achieved overnight. “History shows that it is possible to de-dollarise, though it’s not easy. It takes time,” he says.
For Zimbabweans who have lived through repeated currency crises, the test will be whether the ZiG can preserve their earnings and savings over time. Expanding its use through policy may be possible, but persuading people to trust it will require sustained stability and confidence in the currency.
“Policy should not try to force a conversion but should create the necessary incentives which will eventually see both businesses and consumers being indifferent to holding ZiG or US dollars,” Dube says.

Budget showdown slips to November as Costa pushes for quick deal

2026-10-16

European Council President António Costa with Commission President Ursula von der Leyen at the EU headquarters in Brussels, on Oct. 15, 2026. | Ludovic Marin/AFP via Getty Images
BRUSSELS — EU leaders will go back to the drawing board in November as they race to finalize a deal on the bloc's next seven-year budget by the end of the year.
During the first day of a two-day summit in Brussels on Thursday, European Council President António Costa announced he was convening an additional gathering on Nov. 26 in a bid to overcome disagreements and lay the ground for a final deal in December. To bring the sides closer to an agreement, he will present new budget figures before the meeting, according to an EU official, who was granted anonymity to discuss the confidential planning.
Costa is pressing leaders to finalize negotiations by the end of the year — before elections in France, Italy and Poland in 2027 threaten to derail the talks.
Advertisement
In a speech to the leaders, Costa warned that going past the end-of-year deadline will delay EU payments to farmers and researchers past Jan. 1, 2028, when the new budget is scheduled to come into force.
If leaders fail to reach a deal in December, the electoral calendar might push an agreement to May or even October 2027, Costa warned leaders in his concluding remarks, according to two EU diplomats briefed on the discussions.
Pressure on governments
Costa's plan received a major boost on Thursday from French President Emmanuel Macron, who told fellow leaders that he won’t have a political mandate to sign a deal close to the French presidential elections in April 2027.
European Council President António Costa, Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever and French President Emmanuel Macron pictured at the European Council Summit on Oct. 15, 2026. | Nicolas Maeterlinck/Belga/AFP via Getty Images
This is a major reversal for France, which has previously been unwilling to commit to the end-of-year deadline.
Macron’s words put more pressure on governments to advance the talks over the coming weeks — although some cast doubt on his good intentions.
“There are so many elections next year. [French far-right leader Marine] Le Pen herself [said] it's undemocratic if we were now to agree,” said one EU diplomat.
Advertisement
Just hours before the leaders’ gathering, Le Pen renewed calls to halve France’s contributions to the EU budget if she wins the presidential elections next year.
She said that rushing the budget agreement before the French elections would be "a democratic scandal."
The new frugal
Costa is stuck between messy domestic politics across Europe and hardening stances among the EU’s 27 leaders.
The so-called frugal EU countries pushing for major budget cuts — Germany, Netherlands, Austria, Sweden, Denmark and Finland — have publicly said that an Irish proposal envisioning €159 billion cuts doesn’t go far enough.
On Thursday, the six hardliners were joined by Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever, who joked in a press conference after the summit that “I’m married to a Dutch person so I’m very frugal also in my personal life.”
However, behind closed doors the budget hardliners employed a more conciliatory tone.
Advertisement
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz — the unofficial leader of the frugal camp — said that the Irish proposal has achieved progress despite reductions still being needed, said two EU diplomats briefed on the discussions.
He pointed to EU payouts to poorer regions, as opposed to farmer's subsidies, as an avenue for cuts.
On the other side of the spectrum, Spanish Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez — who will try to cling on to power in an election on Nov. 29 — insisted that the budget is way too small.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez addresses journalists upon arriving at the European Council Summit on Oct. 15, 2026. | Nicolas Tucat/AFP via Getty Images
“It is a distribution of misery,” he told fellow leaders during the discussions, according to the diplomats. He was joined by Italy’s right-wing Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni — an ideological foe on most issues, but an ally of sorts in the budget battle. She insisted that no further cuts to the budget will be accepted.
To bring sides together closer to a deal, Costa promised to advance progress on EU-wide taxes, or own resources, to finance the next seven-year budget and reduce national contributions.
He will explore the European Parliament’s proposed taxes on crypto firms, online gambling and tech giants as well as a Greek idea to funnel future national sales of 6G mobile spectrum to the EU budget.
But given the level of opposition, getting EU countries to agree to any of these options will be no mean feat.
“It is time to be realistic and work on what is plausible and reasonable, instead of wishful thinking,” said another EU diplomat.

'Righteousness of Arms': Ben-Gvir plans to change IDF Code of Ethics if named defense minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
00:55:07 UTC
09:55:07 KST

National Security Minister and chairman of the far-right Otzma Yehudit party, Itamar Ben-Gvir, unveiled a plan to change the IDF’s Code of Ethics if he is named the new defense minister.
The proposed changes, presented as part of Ben-Gvir's plan for the Defense Ministry in a Thursday statement, would significantly revise the IDF's ethical framework, known as "The Spirit of the IDF," with the stated goal of strengthening the military's Jewish identity and emphasizing victory in battle.
This would include replacing the principle of "Purity of Arms" with "Righteousness of Arms" and placing greater emphasis on Jewish values, military victory, and the defeat of Israel's enemies.
Under the proposal, the IDF's main objective would be defined as achieving victory and decisively defeating the enemies of the State of Israel and the Jewish people, alongside maintaining national security.
The proposal would also expand the sources from which the IDF derives its values, placing greater emphasis on Jewish moral values rooted in the Bible, Jewish ethics, Jewish law, and the traditions of the Jewish people.
It would further define Israel as the Jewish people's national home and the IDF as a "Jewish, state-run army."
'Purity of Arms' to be replaced with 'Righteousness of Arms'
One of the proposed changes concerns the principle of "Purity of Arms," which Ben-Gvir seeks to remove from the IDF Code of Ethics and replace with "Righteousness of Arms."
The revised code would explicitly establish the principle "If someone comes to kill you, rise early and kill him first" as a fundamental moral guideline for soldiers carrying out their missions.
At the same time, the proposal removes language in the existing code requiring soldiers to use force "only to the extent necessary."
It also removes explicit provisions prohibiting harm to "non-combatants" and prisoners of war.
In addition, all references to "universal moral values" which appeared in the existing version would be removed from the new code.
Revised framework of core IDF values
The proposal sets out a revised framework of core IDF values, beginning with the military's purpose and continuing with its commitment to the Jewish people, human dignity, and its role as a state institution.
"The purpose of the IDF is to achieve victory and decisively defeat the enemies of the State of Israel and the Jewish people, while safeguarding the security of the state, its citizens, and its residents," the proposal states as the IDF's mission.
It continued, stating that "service in the IDF is founded on love for the Jewish people and the homeland, as well as commitment and dedication to the State of Israel, a Jewish state that serves as the democratic national home of the Jewish people, and to its citizens and residents."
The revised ethics code included that "the IDF and its soldiers are committed to preserving human dignity. Every person possesses inherent worth, regardless of origin, religion, nationality, gender, status, or position."
Lastly, the proposal emphasized that the IDF is "the people's army, a Jewish and state-oriented military subject to the authority of the law and the government."
Under this principle, IDF soldiers are expected to place their mission, the military's values, and the security of the state above all other considerations while carrying out their duties with integrity, professionalism, and conduct appropriate to their role as representatives of the IDF.

Minibus crashes into train at French Channel Tunnel entrance, injuring 19
Nineteen people were injured Thursday when a minibus carrying truck drivers crashed into a vehicle shuttle train at the French entrance to the Channel Tunnel near Calais, forcing a 90-minute suspension of shuttle services. Two people were hospitalised with serious but non-life-threatening injuries, French authorities said.
A minibus carrying truck drivers crashed into a train transporting vehicles through the busy Channel Tunnel between France and England on Thursday, injuring 19 people and briefly disrupting cross-Channel traffic, French authorities said.
The minibus was heading towards the tunnel entrance when it veered off course and struck the side of the shuttle train, the regional administration, or prefecture, said in a statement.
Two people were hospitalised with serious but non-life-threatening injuries, while 17 others sustained minor injuries. The minibus driver was among those hurt.
About 200 emergency responders and other personnel rushed to the scene. Vehicle shuttle services through the tunnel were suspended for 90 minutes before gradually resuming by late evening, authorities said. Eurostar passenger trains and freight services were unaffected.
Read moreFrench police suspect Normandy train derailment was result of sabotage
The injured victims were of multiple nationalities, and the relevant consulates had been notified, local official Agathe Cury told reporters. She did not specify which countries.
All those injured had been aboard the minibus, and all are men, Cury said.
The reason for the crash is unclear and an investigation is under way, she added.
In remarks shown on French media, Cury said it was the first time a crash had occurred at the loading area for the trains that shuttle vehicles under the Channel. The crash happened at the entrance to the tunnel in the town of Coquelles near Calais.
The tunnel, which opened in 1994, carried 3.4 million vehicles last year, along with millions of Eurostar passengers.
