Trump and Putin’s ‘terrible’ alliance threatens to strain EU’s resolve on Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
00:39:32 UTC
09:39:32 KST

Traditional matryoshka dolls depicting Russian President Vladimir Putin and U.S. President Donald Trump pictured in a tourist shop in downtown Moscow on Oct. 21, 2025. | Olesya Kurpyayeva/AFP via Getty Images
BRUSSELS — Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy will make a direct pitch to European leaders for more help on Friday, amid a crisis of faith among allies over Donald Trump’s latest steps favoring Russia.
At the second day of an EU summit in Brussels, Zelenskyy joins European prime ministers and presidents as they discuss Ukraine’s need for more weapons and cash, with concern growing that Kyiv faces a shortfall of billions of euros next year.
The reality of the threat to European security from the four-year-long war penetrated the summit bubble after air drones hit two ships in or near Romanian waters, prompting emergency talks with NATO.
Advertisement
“We all in Europe want this war to end,” Zelenskyy said on social media as he arrived in the Belgian capital on Thursday. “And for that, signals of strength are needed — more real pressure on Russia and more defense support for Ukraine.”
It is especially important, Zelenskyy said, to “act together to protect lives.” But unity among European leaders is in short supply at a meeting already riddled with tensions.
EU governments are pitted against each other in their own fraught negotiations over how much money to commit to the 27-country bloc’s budget. With populists surging, discontent raging and elections scheduled in major power centers across the continent, under-pressure leaders are a long way from approaching a deal.
Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on the sidelines of the EU summit in Brussels on October 15, 2026. | Nicolas Tucat/Pool/AFP via Getty Images
That’s the combustible mix of financial discussions the U.S. president waded into.
Trump’s decision to open up American markets to previously banned Russian diesel — intended to ease price pressures in the U.S. — risks tilting the balance of an expensive war in Russia’s favor, three European officials warned. Putin’s war chest can now swell from additional fossil fuel exports, while Ukraine struggles for cash.
As they arrived for the first day of the marathon two-day gathering on Thursday, EU national leaders began informally discussing options for how to help redress the balance. That discussion should to be picked up again around the summit table on Friday.
Advertisement
Russian assets
One idea rapidly rising back up the agenda is the fraught question of whether, or how, to make use of some hundreds of billions of euros of frozen Russian financial assets held in European banks.
The bulk of these rest with the Euroclear depository in Brussels. A previous attempt to grab the funds and send them directly to Kyiv was blocked by the Belgian government ― and other countries less prominently ― over concerns it would be exposed to legal action.
But Sweden, Finland and Germany want to take another look at the assets. The European Commission is to come up with a new detailed assessment of Ukraine’s funding needs and an options paper on how to help, including the use of assets, according to officials from these countries.
As the summit began, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said he had been urging his counterparts to “do everything we can to help Ukraine get through the winter and continue to support it next year as well.”
“We will also have to increase funding once again in order to provide Ukraine with truly long-term assistance,” he said. “I remain firmly convinced that we are not only defending Ukraine’s territorial integrity, but also the political order of Europe, which is truly under pressure from Russia in every respect.”
A German official earlier suggested that of the available options to help Ukraine, including a loan and direct grants from national governments, using the assets was the most viable way forward and should be “discussed.”
Advertisement
A U.S. proposal to unfreeze some of the Russian assets and transfer them to a U.S.-controlled entity so Washington could use them as leverage in peace talks with Moscow also attracted strong criticism.
Merz told reporters that the assets had been frozen in Europe and “should remain frozen in Europe … That is our business, and we will decide on it.”
‘Try again’
Finland’s Prime Minister Petteri Orpo told POLITICO as the summit began: “The best solution would be that we will have a solution on how to use frozen assets … We have to try again.”
Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo speaks to journalists at the European Arctic Summit in Rovaniemi, Finland, on Sept. 14, 2026. | Jouni Porsanger/AFP via Getty Images
Sweden is also backing the move to re-examine options on using the assets to help Ukraine’s future funding needs. “Doing nothing is not an option,” Swedish EU Affairs Minister Jessica Rosencrantz told POLITICO. “The Commission is looking into different financial options, and we need to get them on the table quite soon,” she said.
Leaders at this week’s summit should “be really honest that Ukraine needs increased financing” and that the EU “must really step up,” she added.
Zelenskyy met Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever, the main opponent to a deal on assets, for talks on Thursday and thanked him for his country’s support so far.
Speaking to reporters after the first day of the summit, De Wever said the assets should be looked at as part of a future peace agreement. “Are there people on this planet who maybe dream of doing it differently this time and operationalizing those assets earlier for certain purposes? The answer to that question is: Yes there are,” he said. “Are they in this building? They are. Are there outside this building? Yes there are. Do I want to talk about it? No, I don’t.”
Advertisement
For Finland’s Orpo, Trump’s “terrible deal” with Putin on diesel, and the apparent U.S.-imposed limits on Starlink technology to help Ukraine counter Russian attacks, are hard to understand.
“My message to [Trump] is that we are allies,” Orpo said in an interview. “We are in NATO. And what is the biggest threat against NATO? It’s Russia — and that is why there is no logic. I don’t have answers. I have many questions.” He said Trump may be focusing on winning votes ahead of next month’s midterm elections in the U.S. but he should remember that his real allies lie in Europe and he should not “trust” Putin.
Election anxiety
Finland holds its election next year at the same time as what could be a seismic contest in France. Far-right leader Marine Le Pen is leading the polls for the French presidency and wants to cut aid to Ukraine and slash the EU’s budget.
French President Emmanuel Macron, who is constitutionally barred from standing next year, warned EU leaders that they must get a deal on the bloc’s next budget by December, otherwise it will be too late.
But the 27 leaders remain split and show no signs of bridging the gap between “frugal” countries like Germany, Sweden and the Netherlands, who want to limit the settlement, and others such as Italy and Romania, who are on the side of bigger pots of cash for regional development and farming.
European Council President António Costa also sees the urgency. He believes a deal before the end of the year is not only necessary but achievable, according to two EU officials.
Advertisement
Costa, who is taking over the negotiations from Ireland in its role at the helm of the rotating presidency of the Council of the EU, believes failing to secure a deal by December would push the entire budget negotiating process beyond the electoral cycle. That would potentially delay a deal until October next year — perilously close to the new EU budget taking effect in January 2028.
In an effort to make progress on the budget talks, EU leaders will return to Brussels for an extra summit next month.
Camille Gijs, Hanne Cokelaere and Gregorio Sorgi contributed reporting.

Meta releases Muse Spark Open, a new ‘open-weight’ AI model
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
00:34:28 UTC
09:34:28 KST

Meta on Thursday launched a new open-weight AI model which it claims rivals, and in some cases outperforms, similar products from leading Chinese developers.
Muse Spark Open “is the most capable US open-weight model to date,” Meta’s chief of AI Alexandr Wang wrote on X.
Unlike so-called closed models – such as Anthropic’s Claude or OpenAI’s ChatGPT – developers can download the parameters, known as weights and biases, of an open-weight model and modify them.
Chinese developers have emerged as dominant players in the open-weight market for AI models over the past couple of years.
Alibaba’s Qwen, Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 and Z.ai’s GLM models have been considered open-weight frontrunners globally, but Meta claims its new open model now competes on a similar level.
“Built for coding and agentic work,” Muse Spark Open “excels at long-horizon tasks, complex software engineering, and multi-step reasoning,” Meta said in a blogpost, adding that “strong safeguards” have been integrated into the new model.
Muse Spark Open is also “optimized” to run on Apple’s advanced M5 Ultra chips, Meta said, signaling an unusual partnership between the two tech companies.
Muse Spark Open requires significant computing power. Users can run the model on two Mac Studios with M5 Ultra chips to create a “supercomputer” on their own desktop, Meta said.
The launch comes just days after Meta announced its newest closed model, which it said rivalled the most advanced versions of ChatGPT and Claude.
Meta’s AI efforts were initially focused on open models, but more recently Zuckerberg has pushed the company to compete with OpenAI and Anthropic.

Iraq parliament approves al-Zaidi’s cabinet amid growing economic concerns
Iraq’s parliament has completed the formation of Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s government after lawmakers approved previously vacant cabinet posts and three deputy prime ministers, including one who is under US sanctions.
Lawmakers voted on Thursday, approving 11 portfolios, including Nayef al-Shammari as defence minister, Yasir al-Maliki as interior minister, a planning minister, a culture minister and a minister of higher education and scientific research.
Lawmakers postponed a vote on the nominee for migration and displacement minister due to disagreement among parties.
Lawmakers also approved three deputy prime ministers, including Laith al-Khazali, a senior leader of the Iran-backed Asaib Ahl al-Haq movement and brother of the group’s leader, Qais al-Khazali.
The US designated Asaib Ahl al-Haq as a foreign terrorist organisation in 2020 and named both brothers as “specially designated global terrorists”, citing attacks including a 2007 assault that killed five US soldiers. The Treasury Department had sanctioned the brothers in 2019 over the killing of protesters in Iraq.
In a statement following the cabinet approval, al-Zaidi thanked parliament and called upon his fellow deputy prime ministers and ministers to “fulfil their responsibilities with the highest levels of commitment, competence and integrity”. He said the government was embarking on a phase of accelerated, diligent work to address exceptional economic and security challenges imposed by the US-Israel war on Iran, which began on February 28.
Challenges facing Iraq
Iraq is facing severe liquidity shortages stemming from the ongoing conflict. Before the war, Iraq exported roughly 3.5 million barrels of oil per day through the Strait of Hormuz, generating 90 percent of government revenue. Al-Zaidi said the war “has imposed, and continues to impose, extraordinary economic challenges on Iraq.”
To cover essential public spending and government salaries, al-Zaidi, a former banker, devalued the dinar by almost 15 percent against the US dollar.
He said his government inherited public debt exceeding 208 trillion Iraqi dinars ($139bn at the new exchange rate) when it took office in May, raising questions about former Prime Minister Mohammed Shia al-Sudani’s administration. Al-Zaidi added that the state needs about 10 trillion dinars ($6.7bn) monthly to cover salaries and critical spending.
Al-Zaidi vowed to fight corruption, disarm non-state armed groups and strengthen sovereignty by completing the withdrawal of US forces from the country.

The investigation appears to centre on whether the Somali-born Omar, who has represented a Minnesota district since 2019, or her relatives gave false information upon entering the US as refugees in the mid-1990s or during the process of becoming American citizens.
The sealed warrant for the search on Oct 12 listed conspiracy, false statements on immigration paperwork and immigration fraud as potential crimes being investigated, one of the sources familiar with the matter said.
Like the others, they spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss an ongoing investigation.
One of the sources familiar with the probe told Reuters that one potential aim could be to strip Omar of her US citizenship and deport her, ideas that both US President Donald Trump and his Homeland Security chief have floated.
The targeting of a left-wing member of Congress whom Trump has long attacked in personal and bigoted terms has renewed concerns that his administration is using federal law enforcement to punish his political opponents, especially three weeks before an election when Omar is running to retain her seat.
Omar has denied wrongdoing, characterising the raid as an act of “political intimidation”.
The Department of Homeland Security, which oversees the immigration enforcement agency, referred questions to the Justice Department (DOJ).
A DOJ spokesperson declined to comment on the Omar investigation.
But in a statement, the spokesperson said that US citizenship “must be obtained lawfully and honestly” and the Trump administration would investigate any case where the facts support denaturalisation, the legal process of revoking citizenship that was acquired after birth.
A spokesperson for Omar had no immediate comment.
A rare step
Former immigration officials said denaturalisation investigations have historically been rare, and it is extremely unusual for them to involve search warrants, as the government should already have the relevant immigration records.
“Most of the denaturalisation cases that we engaged in related either to very serious international human rights violations, or very serious crimes, such as Nazi war criminals,” said Kerry Doyle, a former deputy general counsel in the Department of Homeland Security during the Biden administration.
Agents with Homeland Security Investigations, a branch of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, seized Omar’s personal cell phone during the search, according to two of the sources.
Federal prosecutors also issued more than a dozen subpoenas, including to at least one of Omar’s relatives, the two sources said.
One of the sources said a sister of Omar spoke voluntarily with federal agents.
It was unclear what evidence prosecutors presented to the federal magistrate judge who approved the raid.
A coalition of 14 news organisations, including Reuters, asked a federal judge on Oct 15 to unseal records related to the search.
Protections for Congress
The DOJ has traditionally refrained from investigative acts against political figures that are likely to become public within 60 days of an election, particularly if the evidence can be collected after votes are cast.
Omar’s status as a sitting member of Congress made the timing all the more unusual, and the probe potentially more fraught.
Courts have ruled that the federal authorities cannot review material related to the legislative acts of a member of Congress, which is protected under the US Constitution.
Before approving the search, US Magistrate Judge Matthew Sharbaugh ordered screening procedures to prevent such a review, according to three sources familiar with the matter.
Under the terms of the warrant, prosecutors were supposed to inform Omar’s lawyers about the protocol for protecting legislative records, but that has not happened, one of the sources said.
Denaturalisation
Omar was 12 when her family arrived in the United States in 1995 after fleeing civil war in Somalia and spending years at a refugee camp in Kenya. She became a naturalised citizen in 2000.
Omar’s background has been central to her political rise – and a consistent target of her right-wing critics.
Trump has repeatedly attacked her heritage, her Muslim faith and the Somali community in Minnesota.
Asked by the New York Times in January if he thought Omar should lose her US citizenship, Trump replied: “Oh, absolutely.”
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told a conservative podcaster in September there may have been “some illegal activity for them (Omar’s family) to come to the United States to begin with” and suggested deportation as a possibility.
A naturalised US citizen can lose citizenship if a judge finds it was obtained illegally or through the concealment or wilful misrepresentation of material facts.
The DOJ has filed at least 164 denaturalisation cases in Trump’s second term. Between 1990 and 2017, just 11 denaturalisation cases were opened on average each year, according to the Immigrant Legal Resource Center. REUTERS

Torah MiTzion marks 30 years of strengthening ties between Israel, Diaspora Jewry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
00:24:16 UTC
09:24:16 KST

Three decades after it began sending Israeli educators to Jewish communities around the world, Torah MiTzion marked its 30th anniversary on Tuesday with a celebration in Jerusalem attended by hundreds of former emissaries, community leaders, immigrants, and supporters.
The gathering at the International Convention Center brought together generations of Israelis who had served in Jewish communities abroad through the religious-Zionist organization, which was founded in 1996 to strengthen Jewish identity, Torah education, and ties between Israel and Diaspora Jewry.
Over the past 30 years, Torah MiTzion has established a network of religious study centers and community programs in more than 20 countries. According to the organization, approximately 1,700 emissaries have participated in its overseas activities, including married Torah scholars, yeshiva students, and young women undertaking national service.
Reflecting on careers dedicated to the Jewish diaspora
The anniversary celebration, held under the theme “Past, Present, and Future,” offered an opportunity for former emissaries to reconnect with one another and reflect on their experiences living and working in Jewish communities overseas.
“Over three decades, we have succeeded in building a living, human, and enduring bridge between us and Jewish communities in the Diaspora,” said Torah MiTzion founder and executive director Zeev Schwartz.
Schwartz credited the organization’s achievements to cooperation among Jewish communities, donors, educational institutions, and the emissaries themselves.
“The Jerusalem Prize and this 30-year milestone reflect an extraordinary collective effort by community leaders, philanthropists, educational institutions, and above all, our remarkable emissaries, who answered the call and worked with tremendous dedication for our brothers and sisters overseas,” he said.
Remembering a fallen emissary
Among the participants was Rachel Goldberg, whose husband, Rabbi Avi Goldberg, was killed while serving as an IDF reserve officer in southern Lebanon in October 2024.
The couple had previously served as Torah MiTzion emissaries in Memphis, Tennessee. Rabbi Goldberg later became a teacher at Jerusalem’s Himmelfarb High School, where he taught Hersh Goldberg-Polin, who was subsequently murdered in Hamas captivity in Gaza.
The anniversary program included Rachel Goldberg’s participation and a tribute featuring a recording of her late husband speaking about the meaning of serving Jewish communities abroad, as well as musical performances by members of the Goldberg family.
The tribute connected the organization’s history of educational work overseas with the personal losses experienced by its extended community during Israel’s wars.
Jerusalem Mayor Moshe Lion also attended the event and praised the organization’s contribution to strengthening connections between Israel and Jews worldwide.
“For out of Zion shall go forth the Torah, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem,” Lion said, quoting the biblical verse from which the organization takes its name.
From Jewish education to public service
Government Cabinet Secretary Yossi Fuchs, himself a former Torah MiTzion emissary, reflected on the influence his overseas experience had on his subsequent career.
“I would never have reached my current mission as cabinet secretary without the mission I undertook with Torah MiTzion,” Fuchs said. “It simply changes the course of your life.”
Fuchs, who previously served as an emissary in Memphis, said the experience helped him develop a broader sense of responsibility toward the Jewish people.
“Instead of focusing on building your own home and life, you suddenly realize that you need to act on behalf of the people, the nation, the Jewish people in the Diaspora and in Israel,” he said. “And that has stayed with me to this day.”
The evening was hosted by journalist Sarah Beck, a former Torah MiTzion emissary, and included accounts from participants about their experiences abroad and the relationships they maintained with Jewish communities long after returning to Israel.
The organization’s leadership also presented plans to expand its network of emissaries and establish new partnerships with Jewish communities worldwide.
The celebration concluded with participants gathering for a group photograph commemorating the organization’s three decades of activity, bringing together emissaries and alumni from different generations.
Torah MiTzion received the Jerusalem Prize in 2016 in recognition of its efforts to strengthen Jewish identity and connections with Israel. Its leadership said the anniversary would serve as an opportunity to expand its educational work in the coming years.

James Talarico, Texas’ Democratic nominee for the US Senate, said he holds Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, rather than the Israeli people, responsible for civilian devastation in Gaza.
Talarico, a Texas state representative, is running neck and neck against Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton, in a race whose results could affect which party controls the Senate this November. Israel has been one of many sources of disagreement among the candidates, who have sparred on issues ranging from affordability to immigration to reproductive rights.
“I believe that Israel, like any nation, has a right to defend its people,” the candidate said while fielding questions on Wednesday at a CNN town hall. “But I don’t believe that Benjamin Netanyahu has a right to wage war against civilians or use collective punishment or restrict aid to civilians.”
Polls show Paxton trailing Talarico by three points
A Texas Politics Project poll, issued by the University of Texas this week, showed Paxton trailing Talarico by 3 percentage points, with 47% to the Democrat’s 50% and a margin of error of 3.34 percentage points.
Talarico said in August that he supported stopping arms sales to the Netanyahu government and conditioning military aid “on ending the death and the destruction in Gaza and the West Bank.” He declined to call the crisis “genocide,” noting that the term is being litigated in the International Court of Justice. But he said he’d “use every bit of our nation’s diplomatic and financial leverage to protect the lives of Palestinians.”
When he was pressed further by Rabbi Holly Levin Cohn of Congregation Beth El Binah in Dallas during the town hall, Talarico stressed the importance of directing his criticisms “toward Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and not the Israeli people.”
Addressing Israelis’ trauma, Talarico acknowledged that the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack on Israel “was the deadliest day for the Jewish people since the Holocaust.”
Talarico advocates for a two-state solution
Cohn pushed back on his comments regarding aid restrictions, noting Israeli support of humanitarian efforts and arguing that there’s much more going on in the country than the media may be projecting.
Talarico told the rabbi he recognized that his “words carry weight” and gave her his word that he’s “going to continue to listen to all sides of this conflict.” He also expressed hope that “we can all come together to fight for a two-state solution where we have security for Israel, and we have freedom and self-determination for Palestinians.”
Talarico also gave a “shoutout” to a local rabbi, Neil Blumofe at Congregation Agudas Achim in Austin. “I spent my first year of my seminary studies learning the Hebrew scriptures from a local rabbi,” he said. “Shout out Rabbi Neil Blumofe!” Cohn grinned.

How Brandeis University is reimagining the liberal arts for a new generation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
00:23:34 UTC
09:23:34 KST

Brandeis University, known for its proud past, is reimagining itself for the future.
Located in a Boston suburb, Brandeis opened in 1948 at a time when Jews and other minorities faced open discrimination at many American universities. Named for Justice Louis Brandeis, the first Jewish member of the US Supreme Court, the university’s founders pioneered a nonsectarian, research-oriented institution focused on undergraduate education and grounded in Jewish values.
Nearly 80 years later, Brandeis builds on its founding ideals with a bold new vision to prepare students for our increasingly global and digitally connected world. Last year, the university launched the Brandeis Plan to Reinvent the Liberal Arts, an initiative to combine the university’s renowned academic rigor with an unprecedented emphasis on career readiness.
“The liberal arts have historically been most effective when connected to the world beyond the classroom,” said Arthur Levine, the president of Brandeis. They “were only successful when they had one foot in the library, the accumulated knowledge of humanity, and one foot in the street, the real world.”
Brandeis is focusing on the connection between academic learning and post-graduation achievement, emphasizing internships, job shadowing, and “micro-credentials” skills such as computer program mastery or project management proficiency that can be learned in a short time. These credentials will be part of a secondary transcript that Brandeis students will receive.
Brandeis has also opened a Center for Careers and Applied Liberal Arts that focuses on the connections between academic learning and career preparation.
At the same time, Brandeis has joined a growing number of colleges and universities offering increased financial aid, including free tuition for children of families making $75,000 or less and half scholarships for children of families making between $75,000 and $200,000. They’re also emphasizing cost transparency: In May, Brandeis launched Faye, an interactive cost calculator that provides prospective students a personalized net price based on their financial and academic information.
“Today’s students need more than knowledge; they need the skills, experiences, and confidence to lead in a world we cannot yet predict,” Levine said. “We are advancing a new model. We need reinvention. And that’s exactly what Brandeis is establishing.”
As these three profiles of current students show, Brandeis undergraduates are taking advantage of the myriad opportunities on campus to challenge themselves academically, engage with Jewish ideas and prepare for career success.
The Israel advocate and future lawyer
For Matthew Pfeffer, Brandeis turned out to be a case of mother knows best. When Pfeffer’s older sister and their mom visited the school when she was looking at colleges, his mother thought Brandeis would be a great choice for Matthew.
At the time, Pfeffer was in eighth grade. But just a few years later, it turned out his mother was right: As a university that offers a warm Jewish community, rigorous but not cutthroat academics and solid preparation for the job market, Brandeis checked all of Pfeffer’s boxes.
After visiting campus three times, he applied early decision to the school and was overjoyed when he was accepted.
Now a senior, Pfeffer is just as happy with his decision. Indeed, if Brandeis had an official school cheerleader, Pfeffer might be that person.
“The amount of support here is incredible, from professors to administrators,” he said. “I love it here.”
Pfeffer is double-majoring in economics and art history and minoring in French and Judaic studies. A Long Island native, he’s also been involved in Brandeis’ Hillel, where he serves as the organization’s Israel engagement coordinator, spearheading Israel advocacy and cultural and dialogue-building events. He also helped plan last year’s Israel Fest, which was held on campus for Israel Independence Day.
In addition to spending a semester in Paris, Pfeffer has done three summer internships in the New York City area while at Brandeis. At one of them, he interned at UJA-Federation of New York, where he worked in development and fundraising and learned about planned giving, endowment trusts, and estates. He also worked at a law firm in New York City, where he was supervised by a Brandeis alum.
These experiences have helped lay the foundation for his career path: He plans to work for two years in the client services, legal, or Jewish nonprofit industries before going to law school.
“I wanted to be set up for career success,” Pfeffer said. “Brandeis wants you to succeed.”
The Southerner who’s exploring her Jewish identity
After growing up in a small Jewish community in Jackson, Mississippi, Lauren Balfour found the smorgasbord of Jewish experiences available at Brandeis to be eye-opening.
“I was like a kid in a candy store,” Balfour said.
She dove right into Jewish life on campus. As a first-year student, she was involved in the Reform Jewish group, where she served on the board and planned social events.
Today, as a junior, Balfour is the vice president of Masorti, the Conservative egalitarian group on campus. She is also a lifeguard at a local JCC and works at a local Sunday school teaching third-graders.
To prepare for her role as a Sunday school teacher, participated in the Mandel Undergraduate Teaching Fellowship Program, a Brandeis program that offers professional learning, mentorship and a stipend to undergraduates working in supplemental Jewish education.
The program “helped me catch up on my Jewish education and fill in the gaps,” she said.
And despite moving hundreds of miles away, studying at Brandeis helped Balfour connect with her Southern roots. The summer before her sophomore year, she interned at the Institute for Southern Jewish Life, headquartered in her hometown. During the internship, for which she received a stipend from Brandeis’ World of Work fellowship, she did archival research on Jewish involvement in the civil rights movement to help create a curriculum for Hebrew schools.
Balfour’s classes also shaped her identity. One of her favorite classes she took at Brandeis is called “Religious Education in America.” Taught by Professor Ziva Hassenfeld, the course helped her understand her Jewish upbringing in the South and the historic complexities and pain of the Jewish experience there.
Jewish life and learning aren’t the only things keeping Balfour busy on campus. A biology major, she’s a teaching assistant for a biology lab course. She’s also on Brandeis’ swimming and diving team, which means she’s at the pool early in the morning six days a week.
As for the future, Balfour is considering medical school or another medicine-related career. She’s gained experience in the medical field while at Brandeis; she shadowed doctors at Boston’s Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and is getting certified to be an EMT.
“Brandeis creates an environment where I’m able to do it all,” Balfour said.
The entrepreneur who’s also a film major
Allison Fuller is the epitome of an undergraduate student focused on career readiness, even if she’s not yet sure what path she wants to take. After graduation, she hopes to move to New York to work in the film and TV industry, either in production management or marketing.
Before enrolling at Brandeis, the Long Island native spent a gap year studying at a yeshiva in Jerusalem. While there, Fuller, now a junior, also did freelance work for FEED, a New Jersey-based video production company.
The summer after her first year at Brandeis, Fuller worked in digital marketing for the ROC Nation management company. This past summer, she worked as a management intern for Zero Gravity Media, an emerging film and TV production company, and she’s also been a social media manager for Here I Am, Israeli activist Shai Davidai’s podcast.
For Fuller, who is double-majoring in business (with a concentration in marketing) and film/TV/media, part of Brandeis’ attraction was being able to study “what I love while also doing a practical thing,” she said.
“If you only do one major here, you’re out of the ordinary,” Fuller added. “Brandeis makes it easy to do that.”
In addition to her work experiences, Fuller is a teaching assistant for a financial accounting class, and she said that her classes are giving her practical skills, too. For example, a marketing class taught her how to pitch ideas to potential clients and how to design a marketing plan.
“I’ve used those skills in real life,” she said.
Fuller also has an entrepreneurial streak; she and a friend are working on an app called Bento that is focused on helping students who eat at college dining halls make the best choices for their nutrition goals. They launched the app at Brandeis and hope to expand to other schools soon.
A Long Island native, Fuller is also part of Brandeis’ Orthodox minyan, one of many options at a university with a large Jewish student population. “You don’t have to be friends with the only five Jews on campus,” Fuller said.
Brandeis gave Fuller and other university students career-related experience last winter when, over the February break, they visited Bloomingdale’s and Horizon Media in New York City as part of a Brandeis-sponsored networking event.
“That’s something out of the box that they thought of,” she said.
These kinds of ideas make her feel happy about her college choice. "Brandeis cares about my future,” Fuller said. “It’s nice to feel that my school is supporting that.”

White House ordered restrictions on Starshield in Ukraine – Reuters
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
03:17:00 EEST
09:17:00 KST

White House ordered restrictions on Starshield in Ukraine – Reuters
The order to restrict Starshield, a satellite system Ukraine uses for battlefield communications and to control interceptor drones, came directly from the White House.
Source: Reuters, citing two US officials and one senior Western official
Details: The sources, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said Pentagon officials had received instructions from the White House to slow down the Starshield system for the Ukrainian military.
They did not specify who had made the decision or who was responsible for implementing the order.
The decision to temporarily restrict this communications system, which is vital to Ukraine, came after US President Donald Trump began demanding that President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stop attacks on Russian oil refineries.
When asked to comment on the order restricting Starshield, a senior US official denied that Trump was involved.
"No such request was ever made by the president," the official said.
The White House, however, declined to answer questions about whether the request could have come from other administration officials.
After Starshield's operations were unexpectedly restricted on 13 and 14 October, senior Ukrainian officials called the White House, the State Department and the Pentagon. According to one Ukrainian official, Washington told Kyiv that the decision had been made by the White House.
Ukrainian officials and military personnel said the restrictions had significantly hampered strike missions against Russian forces and logistics operations in temporarily occupied territories. They have also limited the use of interceptor drones to shoot down Russian Shaheds.
Starshield was developed by SpaceX using its Starlink satellite network specifically for government clients and national security agencies, including the Pentagon.
Elon Musk, the CEO of SpaceX, said on X (Twitter) that Starshield belongs to and is controlled by the US government, meaning that any restrictions on its speed or use are determined by the Pentagon or Trump.
Background:
- On the night of 12-13 October 2026, Ukrainian military personnel detected a sudden speed restriction affecting Starlink and Starshield satellite terminals. The system began shutting down when a drone's speed exceeded 160 km/h and, in some cases, 80 km/h. This made intercepting Russian drones almost impossible.
- President Volodymyr Zelenskyy publicly described the communications restrictions as a mistake that would lead to casualties and destruction.
- Axios previously reported that Trump's administration supposedly had nothing to do with the incident. Washington attempted to shift responsibility to SpaceX, saying the White House does not control the company's actions.
- On 15 October, Zelenskyy rejected suggestions that technical problems had caused the Starlink restrictions in Ukraine.

Foreign Minister Wang Yi called for more cooperation among members of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (Cica) as he attended the group's summit in Baku on Thursday.

The foreign minister also said Beijing encourages the United States and Iran to return to the political and diplomatic track to resolve their disputes, and calls on the parties involved in the Yemen issue to exercise restraint.
The sovereignty and security of countries in the region should be respected, the stability of international industrial and supply chains should be ensured, and important shipping routes such as the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea should remain open, Wang said.
Wang also voiced support for Palestinians, saying the Palestinian question should be brought back onto the right track of the two-state solution as soon as possible.
On global governance, Wang said efforts should be made to reinvigorate the authority and role of the United Nations, uphold the basic norms governing international relations established by the UN Charter, strengthen capacities in digital governance, disaster prevention and mitigation, and public health, and jointly build a more efficient, inclusive and resilient governance system in Asia.

FBI, US Postal Service investigate suspicious mailings to election officials, lawmakers

- Several letters were intercepted in states such as Pennsylvania, Ohio and Idaho, while officials like Alex Padilla said the threats show the “very real dangers” facing election workers.
- USPS said it is “absolutely ready” for millions of ballots and plans extra measures, after a Supreme Court setback for a rule tied to mail-in ballots and Donald Trump’s push to tighten voting by mail.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – The FBI and US Postal Service’s law enforcement arm said on Oct 15 they were investigating suspicious mailings, including some sent to state election officials and lawmakers’ offices ahead of the Nov 3 midterm elections.
The FBI said some of the letters contained an unknown substance.
The investigation come less than three weeks before the midterms, which will determine control of the US Congress, as the Postal Service prepares to handle millions of mailed ballots.
Spokespeople for Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, Alex Padilla, a California Democrat, and Chris Murphy, a Connecticut Democrat, all said the US Postal Service intercepted letters containing a suspicious substance mailed to their offices.
“This incident is a stark reminder of the very real dangers facing those who serve the public and who help administer our elections,” Padilla said in a statement.
The US House of Representatives sergeant at arms, the House’s chief law enforcement officer, told staff in an e-mail seen by Reuters that some public officials had received letters containing suspicious white powder substances.
Brendan Donahue, a deputy chief inspector with the US Postal Inspection Service, said some suspicious letters had been intercepted and that an investigation was ongoing.
“We are committed to protecting our nation’s election officials from threatening and dangerous mail. Any threat or attack on an election official is unacceptable,” Donahue told reporters.
The National Association of Secretaries of State and the National Association of State Election Directors said late on Oct 14 that a series of suspicious letters was sent to state election offices.
Letters bound for several state election offices were intercepted before they were delivered, including in Pennsylvania, Ohio and Idaho.
The Wisconsin Elections Commission said on Oct 15 it received a suspicious letter with an unidentified powdery substance that was deemed not hazardous.
“Let this be very clear: this incident will not shake us,” said Meagan Wolfe, the state’s chief election official.
An email to Senate staff said suspicious letters could have postmarks that do not match the return address and included an image of an envelope with a return address labelled “DSA” and a New York City address.
Postal service plans new measures
Earlier on Oct 15, US Postmaster General David Steiner said USPS was “absolutely ready” to handle millions of ballots for the midterm elections.
USPS said in October it would take “extraordinary measures” for the 2026 election, including extending hours at some retail locations and expediting handling, extra deliveries and special pickups of ballots.
On Sept 14, the US Supreme Court declined to let USPS enforce a rule targeting mail-in ballots, dealing a setback to President Donald Trump’s effort to restrict voting by mail. USPS said it would not enforce the rule under the order.
The agency adopted the measure after Trump issued a March executive order aimed at tightening rules governing mail voting.
In 2024, USPS delivered 99.2 million ballots to and from voters in the presidential election. About 30% of votes were cast by mail in the November 2024 presidential election, down from 46% in 2020.
Trump’s fellow Republicans are locked in a tight battle to retain control of Congress in the midterms. Democratic voters disproportionately use mail-in ballots, according to various surveys, so restricting them could benefit Republicans.
Under the rule that was blocked, states would have had to provide lists of mail-ballot recipients to USPS and use agency-approved outbound and return ballot mail envelopes outfitted with unique barcodes.
The Postal Service could then have refused to send out ballots that did not comply or were associated with voters not appearing on the lists. REUTERS

BoP's Mladenov: Suspension of private sector goods into Gaza is 'unacceptable'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
00:07:02 UTC
09:07:02 KST

Nickolay Mladenov, director-general of the Board of Peace, said on Thursday that he had received a letter from the Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories (COGAT) informing him of the suspension of coordination for private-sector goods entering Gaza following reports of threats and coercion by Hamas.
In a post on X/Twitter, Mladenov condemned the reported intimidation of merchants and interference with commercial supply chains.
“As I have warned repeatedly, such practices are unacceptable and must end immediately. The intimidation of merchants and interference in the supply chain only deepen the suffering of Gaza's civilians,” Mladenov posted.
He stressed the urgent need to establish new governance and security arrangements in the Gaza Strip.
“These developments demonstrate why the rapid deployment of the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG) supported by the International Stabilization Force (ISF), is urgently needed,” he wrote.
“Civilian supplies, humanitarian assistance and commercial activity must be protected from coercion, exploitation and interference,” Mladenov added.
He called on all parties to work with the Board of Peace to implement US President Donald Trump's comprehensive peace plan for Gaza, endorsed by the UN Security Council in Resolution 2803, without delay.
Mladenov emphasized the need to move forward with the arrangements required for NCAG and ISF operations in Gaza.
“This includes the decommissioning of weapons, the transition to legitimate transitional governance and the protection of humanitarian and commercial supply chains,” he concluded.
Commercial goods banned from entering Gaza over tax dispute between local merchants and Hamas
Israel said commercial goods were no longer entering Gaza over what it said was a dispute over taxes between local merchants and Hamas, shutting off a vital source of food and other goods in the territory where the population is dependent on aid.
COGAT, which oversees humanitarian affairs in Gaza, made the announcement in a statement on Wednesday, citing what it said was a decision by Gazan merchants to stop coordinating with COGAT on the entry of commercial goods.
It said the Gazan merchants had told COGAT that they had made the decision in response to a NIS 10,000 ($3,220) fee imposed by Hamas on each truck entering Gaza and a demand for 30% of all of their sales in Gaza to be carried out in cash.
Hamas later claimed that the NIS 10,000 fee was a voluntary payment by wealthy Gazans to a national fund that seeks to provide for those in need, such as widows and orphans. It also said that cash payments were encouraged due to what it described as an acute cash shortage in the war-torn territory.
Nahed Shhaibar, the head of the private transport union in Gaza, claimed that not a single truck carrying commercial products from Israel entered Gaza on Thursday. However, he said trucks carrying humanitarian aid had entered, as had trucks carrying commercial goods from Egypt via an Israeli-controlled crossing.
COGAT said the decision by Gazan merchants would cut the total number of trucks, which carry both humanitarian and commercial goods, entering Gaza each day to around 300, or half.
Diplomats say that far fewer than 600 trucks normally enter Gaza each day. Shhaibar claimed the figure was closer to 300, with two-thirds carrying commercial goods.
Israel is obliged under a US-mediated agreement to allow a minimum of 600 trucks carrying humanitarian aid to enter Gaza each day. However, it says it is required to allow only 600 trucks and that commercial goods are needed to supplement aid supplies.

Costa angers EU leaders as splits mar summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
00:03:30 UTC
09:03:30 KST

European Council President António Costa and France's President Emmanuel Macron speak together ahead of a round table in Brussels, on Oct. 15, 2026. | Ludovic Marin/AFP via Getty Images
BRUSSELS ― António Costa is supposed to be the dealmaker who brings European leaders together. Increasingly, his efforts are going unrewarded.
At a summit of the bloc’s national leaders on Thursday, Costa — who, unlike most of the EU’s current big beasts, is a Socialist — suffered his most stinging criticism since taking the role of European Council president nearly two years ago. The ire centered on his handling of unrelated negotiations over curbing energy prices and the EU’s next seven-year budget.
Governments were looking for both debates to show signs of progress at the two-day gathering, which was scheduled to continue on Friday. What they got was, at best, stalemate ― at worst, mounting division. And a day of talking that dragged on for 14 hours with little to show for it.
Advertisement
The longer budget negotiations last, the “more difficulties we will have,” Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo told POLITICO. “So we have to work to find a solution this year. I understand very well that it is difficult. A huge challenge.”
The stakes could barely be higher. The EU is desperate to ease the cost of living crisis and get a deal on the budget before national elections next year make finding an agreement much tougher. Disunity between the bloc’s 27 members looks even starker when Donald Trump makes moves to take Russia’s side in the Ukraine war, the economy is struggling to match the might of China and anti-EU nationalists get closer to power in Europe’s biggest capitals.
All 16 diplomats and officials who POLITICO spoke to for this article were granted anonymity to allow them to speak on a sensitive issue. They were all either in the summit room on Thursday or were immediately briefed by leaders who were. While most were critical of Costa, others spoke more positively.
Costa’s spokesperson declined to comment.
European Council President António Costa, Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever, Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten and French President Emmanuel Macron in conversation at the European Council Summit on Oct. 15, 2026. | Nicolas Maeterlinck/Belga Mag/AFP via Getty Images
Bogged down
Costa, a former Portuguese prime minister, is appointed by leaders to chair their summits and corral them into agreement. As Brussels Playbook reported on Thursday, EU officials judge he’s entering a defining period of his presidency, racing against time to overcome huge divisions on the budget. He is widely expected to push for reappointment for a second two-and-a-half-year term next year, officials said.
Thursday’s summit was dominated by discussions unraveling on the second phase of the bloc’s carbon pricing regime, known as ETS2.
Advertisement
The showdown over the Emissions Trading System — both the current one, and the second iteration which is already legislated and will put a carbon price on heating and transport from 2028 — became so bogged down it forced Costa to cancel the summit’s planned press conference and delay further talks until after dinner, because they had become a “mess,” three EU diplomats told POLITICO.
With German Chancellor Friedrich Merz incensed by what Berlin saw as his Italian counterpart Giorgia Meloni’s intransigence, fiery negotiations pitted a coalition made up of Germany, Spain, France, Portugal, the Nordics and the Netherlands against a stubborn bloc of Italy with Hungary, Czechia, Slovakia and Poland (known as the Visegrád Four). Rome and the V4 group wanted the EU to postpone ETS2 because of the burden it would place on energy bills, according to five diplomats.
Leaders were fuming at Costa for allowing talks to go off the rails, two EU diplomats from different member countries said. While the pre-summit conclusions didn’t point to any rethink of ETS2, the countries tried to unpick the legislation in the summit room, leaving Costa flustered, one of them said.
Costa “wants to have conclusions ready from [pre-summit meetings of ambassadors] and not to open them during EUCO,” the diplomat said. “He is not a fan of drafting on the spot.”
Another said there was “huge frustration,” calling the tug-of-war over the wording of the energy policy “insane chaos.”
“They just went on with Italian drafts and disregarded texts that were handed in before by others, seemingly not understanding the political nuances of the whole ETS discussion,” they added.
Another accused Costa of “losing control of the room,” saying he had failed to keep track of proposed amendments and present them to EU leaders in time for the discussions. As a result, leaders were left debating without them, contributing to negotiations going on past midnight.
One diplomat and one EU official separately compared Costa with his immediate predecessors, Charles Michel ― who governments frequently criticized for a lack of dealmaking know-how ― and Donald Tusk, who enjoyed broad support throughout his term in office.
Advertisement
Costa performed “worse than Charles Michel” on Thursday, the diplomat said. The official said “there is frustration that things are not being dealt with a bit more Tusk-style.”
Honest broker
The annoyance went beyond the energy debate. While governments weren’t expecting a breakthrough on the EU budget on Thursday, they have started raising questions about Costa’s handling of that topic too.
High Representative Kaja Kallas addresses the press on Oct. 15, 2026. | Nicolas Maeterlincl/Belga/AFP via Getty Images
Costa is determined to secure an agreement by the end of the year. In his job, the Council president must act as a honest broker and facilitate a deal among 27 governments.
Northern EU countries are worried he’s favoring southern countries, according to a further four EU diplomats.
One EU diplomat accused Costa of being two-faced and not acting as an honest broker in the budget negotiations.
Another diplomat, from a country that wants the budget to be smaller, said: “Costa personally and politically belongs to the other camp.”
Advertisement
“There is some skepticism on how he will take the process further from here,” they said. The so-called frugal countries are calling on Costa to propose further cuts ahead of a special EU summit on the budget that was confirmed Thursday for Nov. 26.
‘Superb deal maker’
Many governments still believe Costa may succeed over the long term. Even those who acknowledge that his honeymoon is over ― a period when he was roundly praised for being a safe pair of hands and avoiding diplomatic faux-pas ― retain faith in him.
Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever defended Costa as “capable” and “shrewd” after the first day of the summit — praising the Council president for largely avoiding drafting on the day, unlike Michel.
Costa “avoids negotiation about the wording on the table which happened all the time under his predecessor and which annoyed the hell out of everybody because then you are here until three o’clock to discuss about syllables, commas and words that the next morning you cannot see the difference anymore,” De Wever said. “You don’t even know anymore what you are negotiating about.”
Other diplomats said the disarray wasn’t Costa’s fault, and blamed the leaders who tried to unpick the energy legislation, notably Meloni. “He did not want to reopen the conclusions, it was the V4 and Italy who did so,” one said. “I don’t see what he could have done differently.”
Another EU official defended the sheer difficulty of the task faced by the Council president. “Discussing drafting at leaders’ level is not the most straightforward thing in general.” On energy, the official said leaders wanted to have “proper consideration” of the different proposals by countries, which had “opposing interests.”
One of the diplomats more critical of his political leanings on the budget said Costa was “impeccable” in his behavior. “He’s a superb deal maker.”
The next few weeks will show how true that turns out to be.
Hanne Cokelaere, Camille Gijs, Sebastian Starcevic, Gerardo Fortuna and Hans von der Burchard contributed to this article.

France and Germany agree to ease EU car emissions rules in new deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
23:48:57 UTC
08:48:57 KST

France and Germany agree to ease EU car emissions rules in new deal
Paris and Berlin on Friday confirmed their deal aimed at protecting Europe's struggling automotive sector, having reached agreements on the flashpoint issues of EU car emissions and "made in Europe" components. A draft deal reviewed Thursday showed the two countries backing looser EU emissions rules for carmakers.
France and Germany said in a joint statement they agreed on a common approach to secure the future of the European automotive industry, aiming to cut CO2 emissions while ensuring next-generation electric vehicles are developed and built in Europe.
The plan sets out a European decarbonisation pathway with regulatory flexibility and incentives for investment, research, production and resilient supply chains, the statement said.
"Our shared ambition is clear: to successfully transform our automotive industry while maintaining our climate ambition and ensuring that the cars of the future are produced in Europe," the two countries said.
Diplomatic sources confirmed to AFP Thursday that Paris and Berlin had backed a further scaling down of EU emission rules for cars as part of the long-negotiated deal.
Europe's two economic powerhouses also agreed to include Britain in the definition of what vehicles would count as "made in Europe" under EU measures aiming to bolster the bloc's industries, according to a draft document outlining the pact.
Watch more2026 Paris Motor Show: Western carmakers face steep competition from Chinese rivals
Paris and Berlin had long been at loggerheads on the course Europe should take as it seeks to revive its struggling auto industry and the accord is likely to shape the continent's policy going forward.
Germany wanted less stringent carbon emission targets for carmakers and a broad interpretation of "made in Europe" to include key non-EU trade partners.
France on the other hand had pushed to preserve the bloc's climate ambitions and to keep the "made in Europe" public procurement scheme the purview of EU nations.
Berlin won the first argument while Paris carried the day on the latter, the draft showed.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
The European Commission had proposed that the bloc's ban on sales of new petrol and diesel vehicles in 2035 be scrapped in favour of a requirement for manufacturers to cut new vehicle exhaust emissions by 90 percent.
The remaining 10 percent would have had to be compensated for through various credits obtained among other things by using low-carbon steel.
The Franco-German deal scraps the latter requirement, according to the draft, stating that residual emissions should not have to be compensated by manufacturers.
It also opens the door for cars running on renewable fuels to count as "zero-emission" and makes it much easier for automakers to reach CO2 targets.
So-called "super credits" the commission had suggested carmakers would benefit from for small "affordable" electric cars are extended to all vehicles "irrespective of their size or length".
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
'Good news' for Britain
The agreement on "made in Europe" restricts its application regarding cars to the EU's 27 countries, with an opt-in for a handful of others, notably Britain and Norway under certain conditions.
That is a narrower definition than the one proposed by the commission in March.
London hailed the move. If confirmed, it "would be good news for the British automotive industry and the jobs and investment it supports across the UK", the office of Prime Minister Andy Burnham said.
The EU executive had unveiled plans to tie companies' access to public money to minimum thresholds for EU-made parts in their products – to ensure that public and foreign investments support manufacturing inside the bloc.
But under Brussels' proposal, dozens of partner countries that have deals with the EU allowing European companies to access public money on a par with local firms could have been brought into the fold.
European carmakers had asked for Britain to be included, citing deeply integrated supply chains.
The pact will need backing from other EU states and the European Parliament to become law, but carries weight given the economic heft of the two signatories.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP and Reuters)

Google boosts news and link visibility in AI mode
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
23:47:00 UTC
08:47:00 KST

Google boosts news and link visibility in AI mode
- Google will show website and article links more prominently in AI search results. It will push links higher, expand its carousel, and use preferred sources, social posts and forums.
- The change follows concern from brands and publishers about falling traffic. AI Overviews now has more than two billion monthly users, but studies say summaries cut link clicks.
- Chartbeat reported a 40% drop in Google traffic for news sites between July 2025 and July 2026. In France, Apig told the Competition Authority AI summaries broke 2022 agreements with publishers.
AI generated
NEW YORK – Google announced on Oct 15 it will start displaying links to websites and articles more prominently and higher up in search results powered by artificial intelligence (AI), as brands and news publishers warn of a sharp decline in their traffic.
The Alphabet subsidiary began integrating more AI features in its search results over two years ago.
In May 2024 it launched AI Overviews, where Google generates summarised answers to search queries, rather than only showing links as it historically did.
Then in March 2025 Google added AI Mode which opens in a separate window and provides a more comprehensive answer and more links than AI Overviews.
Now, contextual links will be featured more “more frequently” and higher up in AI-generated search content.
Google will also expand worldwide its link “carousel”, which are cards displayed directly below AI Overviews that show headlines with images for relevant articles.
The algorithm will prioritise articles from sites a user has previously identified as “preferred sources”, and it will also be able to pull in content from relevant social media posts and other forums.
Google will also make links displayed at the end of AI-generated summaries “more engaging and prominent” for users who want to “dig deeper”.
During its second quarter 2025 results, Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai said that AI Overviews had more than two billion monthly users in over 200 countries.
Several studies have shown that replacing traditional search with AI summaries significantly reduces the rate at which users open the suggested links.
According to a report by consultancy Chartbeat, news website publishers saw a 40% drop in traffic coming from Google between July 2025 and July 2026.
In August, Apig, a group representing daily newspapers in France, alerted the Competition Authority that AI summaries were in breach of agreements reached with news publishers in 2022. AFP

What is celebrated on October 16 in Ukraine and around the world
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
02:38:01 EEST
08:38:01 KST

What is celebrated on October 16 in Ukraine and around the world
Kyiv • UNN
October 16 marks World Food Day, Anesthesiologists' Day, World Bread Day, and Healthy Eating Day. The faithful honor Saint Longinus.
On October 16, the world, under the auspices of the UN, marks World Food Day and World Anaesthesia Day. According to the new-style church calendar, Saint Longinus the Centurion, who stood at the Lord’s Cross, is commemorated, while according to the old style, Saint Dionysius the Areopagite, Bishop of Athens, is remembered, UNN writes.
World Food Day
An official UN date proclaimed in 1979 at a conference of the UN Food and Agriculture Organization. The date was chosen to commemorate the founding of the FAO on October 16, 1945. The main goal of the day is to draw the global community’s attention to the problems of hunger and malnutrition, ensuring food security, developing sustainable agrifood systems, and overcoming poverty in developing countries.
World Anaesthesia Day
A professional observance for anesthesiologists, resuscitation specialists, and intensive-care physicians around the world. The date commemorates a historic event: on October 16, 1846, at Massachusetts General Hospital, American dentist William Thomas Green Morton publicly performed the first successful operation under ether anesthesia in history, ushering in modern anesthesiology and painless surgery.
World Bread Day
Established in 2006 at the initiative of the International Union of Bakers and Confectioners. The event is dedicated to one of the most popular and important foods in human history; it highlights the importance of the work of farmers and bakers, promotes breadmaking traditions, and draws attention to the rational use of food resources.
World Healthy Eating Day
A global observance that echoes World Food Day and calls on humanity to reconsider its daily diet. The event emphasizes the importance of consuming high-quality, natural, and balanced foods, and reducing the intake of sugar, salt, and ultra-processed foods to prevent obesity, cardiovascular disease, and cancer.
World Restart a Heart Day
Established by the European Resuscitation Council with the support of the WHO and the International Liaison Committee on Resuscitation. The event aims to teach as many people as possible first-aid skills, cardiopulmonary resuscitation, and the use of automated external defibrillators to save people experiencing sudden cardiac arrest.
World Spine Day
A global medical initiative under the auspices of the World Federation of Chiropractic, aimed at promoting an active lifestyle, maintaining musculoskeletal health, preventing osteochondrosis and posture disorders, and reducing the risk of chronic back pain through ergonomics and physical exercise.
International Boss’s Day
Established in the United States in 1958 by Patricia Haroski, who worked as a secretary and registered the observance in honor of her manager father’s birthday. The observance is intended to strengthen positive relations between managers and subordinates and express gratitude to top managers for honest leadership, fairness, the organization of work processes, and support for the team.
World Raw Foodists’ Day
An unofficial observance dedicated to promoting raw foodism as a dietary approach involving the consumption of uncooked plant-based foods in order to preserve the maximum amount of vitamins and enzymes.
Memorial Day of Saint Martyr Longinus
According to the new calendar, Orthodox and Greek Catholic believers commemorate Saint Longinus the Centurion, who stood at the Lord’s Cross. According to the Gospel and church tradition, the Roman centurion Longinus commanded the soldiers at the crucifixion of Jesus Christ and, having witnessed the miraculous signs and the Savior’s death, recognized Him as the Son of God. After Christ’s Resurrection, Longinus refused a bribe from the Jewish elders, left military service, was baptized, and set out to preach in Cappadocia, where he later suffered martyrdom by beheading on the orders of Pontius Pilate.
According to the old calendar, the faithful commemorate Saint Hieromartyr Dionysius the Areopagite, Bishop of Athens—a disciple of the Apostle Paul, who was a member of the highest Athenian court, embraced Christianity after the apostle's sermon, and became the first Bishop of Athens, later suffering a martyr's death in Lutetia.

Kiev out of Patriot interceptors – CNN
Ukraine has exhausted its remaining US-made Patriot interceptor missiles used to defend against Russian strikes, CNN reported on Thursday, citing a person familiar with the matter.
The reported shortage comes amid a public feud between US President Donald Trump and Vladimir Zelensky over Trump’s diesel deal with Moscow and Ukraine’s attacks on Russian oil refineries.
According to CNN, the Ukrainian Air Force said it had intercepted four Russian ballistic missiles, apparently using the last of its remaining Patriot interceptors.
“Almost all the ballistic missiles from the last strike were not intercepted due to lack of the (interceptor) missiles,” a source told the network.
Zelensky said he felt betrayed after Trump lifted sanctions on Russian diesel exports earlier this month in the hopes of lowering energy prices ahead of the US midterm elections in November. Trump defended the move as beneficial to consumers and consistent with his “America First” agenda.
When asked about Zelensky’s criticism of the diesel deal, Trump suggested that it was “time for Ukraine to get a new president.” Zelensky, whose five-year presidential term expired in 2024, has refused to call new elections, citing martial law and the need for a months-long ceasefire with Russia. The Kremlin has argued that Ukraine would use a prolonged truce to replenish its armed forces and said it was only prepared to suspend strikes on election day.
Earlier this week, Zelensky said he would defy Trump’s demands to halt strikes on Russian energy facilities, which the US president blamed for high energy prices. Zelensky said Ukraine would agree to an energy truce only if Russia did the same. Moscow, however, said it was seeking a comprehensive peace deal on its terms rather than an unconditional ceasefire, which it argued Ukraine would exploit to its advantage.
The Trump-Zelensky rift deepened further this week after Ukraine reported sudden disruptions to Starlink and Starshield, satellite services provided by SpaceX that Kiev uses for drone strikes.
Ukrainian officials also said they had received no advance warning from their Western partners of Russian missile strikes on Kiev on two consecutive nights, Monday and Tuesday.
According to US media reports, American officials attributed the failure to detect the missile launches to bad weather, an explanation their Ukrainian counterparts reportedly found difficult to believe.
Zelensky renewed his plea for additional Patriot interceptors on Wednesday, urging the US and other partners “not to turn a blind eye to reality” and “to respond forcefully.”
The US, however, depleted much of its interceptor missile stockpile during the war with Iran, as widely reported by American media and confirmed in a Pentagon inspector general’s report last month. Trump has downplayed the shortages, claiming that US stockpiles were virtually unlimited.

Two Syrian pipelines damaged amid spate of attacks on energy infrastructure
Fuel theft cited in Baniyas-Homs leak as gas export line in Hasakah catches fire.
Two pipelines carrying gas and oil products were damaged in separate incidents in Syria, state media reported, the latest disruptions to the country’s energy infrastructure following a series of suspected sabotage attacks.
The state-owned Syrian Petroleum Company announced the damage on Thursday, according to the Syrian Arab News Agency (SANA). The incidents add to a number of attacks on Syria’s oil and gas network in recent months, as the government tries to revive its energy sector.
An explosion struck the Jbessa gas pipeline in southern Hasakah province in the late afternoon, hours after damage to a pipeline transporting oil products from the coastal city of Baniyas to Homs caused a fuel leak.
The company said the gas pipeline had been targeted in a “sabotage attack”, according to SANA.
Neither SANA nor the company named a suspect or group responsible for the attacks.
Repairs under way
Oday al-Satouf, head of the company’s media office, told SANA that a hole was found in the Baniyas-Homs pipeline in the Hadida area, west of Homs. Crews isolated the affected stretch and secured the surrounding area, he said, closing valves on either side of the damaged section. Repairs have begun, while other teams monitor the area for safety. State media said the leak was believed to be linked to an attempted fuel theft.
Al-Satouf said gas would continue to reach power stations through alternative arrangements, and that domestic gas supplies were unaffected, according to SANA.
A string of incidents
More than a week ago, the company said an oil pipeline near Tal Hamis in the northeastern province of Hasakah was damaged in a sabotage attack. It added that authorities had arrested those responsible.
In late September, a fire broke out on a gas pipeline between al-Shoula and Deir Az Zor in the east, halting gas flows from the Jbessa plant to power stations, SANA reported. Hisham al-Saleh, a gas sector official at the company, said gas pressure in the area fell as crews worked to extinguish the blaze.
Syria has been working to restore its energy infrastructure and increase domestic oil production. That includes resuming operations at oil fields in Hasakah to supply refineries in Homs and Baniyas. In January, the petroleum company announced plans to transport crude from recently recovered fields to the two refineries as part of efforts to revive the sector.

WASHINGTON – Top Pentagon officials have expressed their intention to hold off on releasing an internal report into the attack on a school in southern Iran until after the US midterm elections at the earliest, according to sources familiar with the matter.
Advisers to Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth have communicated these plans to some Pentagon personnel, said the sources, who requested anonymity as they are not authorised to speak publicly on private deliberations.
The move comes amid growing political pressure over the months-long investigation into the attack on the school in Minab, Iran and a series of civilian-casualty incidents that followed in recent months.
On the first day of the war, US air strikes on Shajarah Tayyebeh Elementary School killed more than 150 people, including at least 123 children. In terms of child casualties, it was the deadliest American military targeting error of the 21st century.
Pentagon investigators discovered that flawed intelligence, outdated imagery and an over-reliance on artificial intelligence contributed to the attack, according to a Bloomberg News investigation. A report on the full US probe, which began in March, has not been released – though officials said it has been all-but-complete for several months.
No final decisions have been made on the precise timeline for disclosing any details from the Minab report.
In response to questions, a Pentagon official said the investigation is ongoing and that there were “no updates to announce at this time”.
The delayed report raises broader questions about government transparency, military accountability and the public’s access to information about civilian casualties during operations that are funded by American taxpayers.
Senator Kirsten Gillibrand, a New York Democrat who serves on the Senate armed services panel, cited Bloomberg’s reporting on Oct 15 in a news release that called delays in the report on Minab “disgraceful”.
“We have waited months – release the report,” Gillibrand said. “Congress and the American people deserve full transparency and accountability around this attack, and I will not rest until we have it.”
US Central Command, which conducted the Minab attack, declined to comment on Gillibrand’s remarks.
“Transparency is important – obviously for those affected but for us as well – for the nature of our government, which is supposed to be open and transparent,” Mark Esper, who served as US Defence Secretary during the first Trump administration, said in an interview. “We should acknowledge our mistakes and fix it to make sure it doesn’t happen again.”
The House Armed Services Committee defense policy Bill for the fiscal year that began Oct 1 contains a provision that would require the Pentagon to submit to the panel the final report on the attack not later than 30 days after completion.
That measure was introduced by committee member Representative Sara Jacobs, a California Democrat.
The Senate’s draft Bill contains language that also would seek to compel the release of the report on Minab and other civilian-harm investigations. Congressional negotiators are working on a final measure.
Centcom is hosting a symposium this week at its headquarters in Tampa to discuss civilian-harm mitigation strategies with technical experts and some foreign allies in attendance.
Earlier in 2026, Admiral Brad Cooper, who heads Centcom, testified to Congress that the command is focusing on enhancing civilian harm mitigation – and the symposium reflects that objective, according to a Centcom spokesman.
“Centcom’s culture entails periodically convening experts to discuss procedures and best practices for minimising civilian harm,” Captain Tim Hawkins, the command’s public affairs director, said on Oct 14.
On Oct 8, more than 70 Democratic lawmakers sent a letter to Hegseth, pressing him to answer questions on civilian casualties in Iran, including at the Minab school.
“We are deeply alarmed by the continued pattern of civilian casualties resulting from US operations in the war in Iran, and the apparent lack of action and accountability from the Department,” the lawmakers wrote. BLOOMBERG
