Indonesian President Replaces Head of Disaster Management Agency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
23:35:00 UTC
08:35:00 KST

Indonesia’s President Prabowo Subianto yesterday replaced the head of the country’s disaster management agency in a bid to restore confidence in the government’s ability to bring intensifying land and forest fires under control.
Lt.-Gen. Kristomei Sianturi, 50, was sworn in as the chief of the National Disaster Management Agency (BNPB) at the State Palace in Jakarta, replacing Lt.-Gen. Suharyanto. Speaking after the ceremony, the two-star army general said that Prabowo had given him orders to move as quickly as possible to bring the fires under control.
“The directive is clear: keep pushing forward and start your duties promptly,” he said, according to Kompas. “The target is as soon as possible, because the people are already affected.”
Kristomei said that he would review the BNPB’s response procedures to ensure faster action during disasters and prevent avoidable deaths.
“Responsiveness must be measured in minutes, not hours. That is what we will evaluate going forward, so there are no more unnecessary casualties,” he said.
No official reason was given for Suharyanto’s replacement, but the change came a day after the outgoing BNPB chief’s younger brother was arrested over alleged corruption involving emergency relief funds, the Straits Times reported. The Corruption Eradication Commission said that the investigation centers on BNPB’s ready-to-use emergency funds, which are used to meet urgent needs during disasters, but did not say whether money intended to fight the forest fires was misappropriated.
Kristomei’s appointment – the second major change to Prabowo’s cabinet since the appointment of a new foreign minister on October 1 – is also likely intended to reassure Indonesia’s neighbors that it remains committed to fighting the wildfires that are currently raging on the islands of Borneo and Sumatra. The forest and peatland fires have created a thick toxic haze that has darkened the skies above Indonesia, Singapore, Malaysia, Timor-Leste, Brunei, and parts of the Philippines, forcing school closures and impacting the health of tens of millions of people.
As the haze has persisted, Jakarta has become the focus of increasing criticism for its failure to contain – or prevent – the fires, many of which Indonesian officials admit were lit deliberately to clear agricultural land. As I noted yesterday, Social media users in Malaysia, Singapore, and Indonesia have become increasingly angry at Jakarta’s response to the fires, with some Indonesian netizens even urging Singapore and Malaysia to impose sanctions on their own government.
Meanwhile, politicians in Malaysia have called for Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s government to lodge formal diplomatic complaints with Jakarta, and the country’s foreign minister said that he plans to raise the issue at an upcoming meeting of his ASEAN counterparts.
Yesterday, after air quality readings in some parts of Singapore reached the worst levels in more than a decade, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said that the government was looking into which companies may be responsible for the fires in Indonesia.
“Where warranted, we will take action under Singapore’s Transboundary Haze Pollution Act, and explore joint action with other countries,” he said on social media.
Under the Transboundary Haze Pollution Act, passed in 2014, Singaporean authorities can take legal action against companies responsible for causing or contributing to haze pollution in Singapore, even if their activities take place overseas. History suggests that Singapore will refrain from confronting Indonesia directly over the haze issue, but the fact that Wong raised the prospect of investigations is a sign of the government’s growing frustration with its large neighbor.
Indonesia has announced a number of other measures designed to combat the fires. Prabowo yesterday approved foreign assistance for its fire-fighting efforts, Foreign Minister Arrmanatha Nasir said yesterday. “The president has also given his approval, and discussions are now underway at the technical level. In this case, the technical discussions are being handled by BNPB,” he said at a closed-door meeting.
“What we need to emphasize is that this is a matter of great seriousness and is receiving the President’s direct attention,” Arrmanatha said, although he did not specify which countries had offered assistance or what form the assistance would take.
Also yesterday, the BBC reported that aircraft were deployed to scatter pellets of dry ice (solid carbon dioxide) in the air above South Sumatra province, one of the regions most affected by the haze. Indonesian police have also named more than 200 people and nine companies as suspects in forest and land fire investigations across the country.
Wasisto Raharjo Jati, a political analyst at the National Research and Innovation Agency, told the Straits Times that the fires had “damaged the government’s image” within ASEAN, and that the reappointment of the BNPB head was “certainly part of efforts to restore the government’s image domestically and internationally.”
One way or another, the current fires will come to an end. Whether Indonesia succeeds in winning back the confidence of its neighbors will also depend on whether it puts in place policies and structures that can prevent a recurrence of a similar crisis in future.

Are student protests being manipulated ahead of France's presidential election?
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
00:25:06 BST
08:25:06 KST

Are student protests being manipulated ahead of France's presidential election?
- Published
The French passion for protest is legendary in Europe.
Over the last few years, we have regularly witnessed farmers angry about costly regulations lobbing manure at local mayoral offices, while masked youths periodically hurl homemade grenades at riot police in disadvantaged city suburbs.
For over three weeks now, thousands of students have barricaded entry to high schools and taken their grievances to the streets.
This Saturday, hundreds of new demonstrations have been announced across France.
Students are expected to be joined by workers' unions and key figures from the so-called "yellow vest" movement.
France's Prime Minister, Sébastien Lecornu, suggested this week that student anger was being manipulated as politics heats up ahead of next year's presidential election.
The gilets jaunes (yellow vests) demonstrated against cost-of-living hikes for over a year from 2018 - becoming one of the longest-lived protest movements in French history.
Jérôme Rodrigues, a prominent gilets jaunes activist, has used Instagram to encourage people to join Saturday's demonstrations.
The protests should give a voice to those who "want to be able to live decently, no longer have to count every cent, and no longer have to choose between eating and driving", he said in a video.
"Anger has no political party. An empty fridge has no political party," he added.
So what is going on in the EU's second largest economy?
Social unrest, government borrowing costs at eye-watering highs, a deeply divided French parliament and an apparent revolving door of exasperated French prime ministers - six prime ministers over the last five years - all claiming to want to reduce their country's public debt.
Is France at breaking-point - and what does this all mean for the eurozone currency the French are such a huge part of?
"You can't compare France to the Greece debt crisis of 2012 or Argentina in 2001. And the financial markets know it," economist Anne-Laure Delatte told me.
She is a CNRS Tenured Researcher at the Economics Department of Paris Dauphine University; a well-known face in debates on French media on the parlous state of the country's public debt.
"The markets recognised already in 2024 that we would have a budgetary problem after [snap] elections left parliament deeply divided between three [opposing political] blocs but they also realise France is a big country with the ability to raise taxes if necessary."
"Our situation is more like the UK in 2023 with Liz Truss," suggests Delatte, referring to the then UK prime minister's so-called mini budget, which triggered a sharp drop in the pound, a spike in government bond yields and soaring mortgage rates.
"The crisis was relatively short-lived because the markets recognised the UK had the financial tools to right itself."
"Here in France it would be painful, but a 4% increase in VAT would raise the 120bn euros needed to plug government debt. Investors know that," she concludes.
Maybe, in theory. And, as Delatte also points out, the European Central Bank would likely intervene if France's finances nosedived to the point where other European economies would be affected.
But with so many French citizens already visibly unhappy with the status quo, imagine the reaction if taxes were to increase, or welfare and education budgets decrease, further.
France's national motto is liberté, égalité, fraternité (freedom, equality and fraternity), but that is certainly not the sense you get on seething streets and in viral social media posts.
I met 17-year-olds Maxime, Madeleine and Elodie this week, perched on big green dustbins that have been used to block the entrance to their high school as part of the weeks' long protest.
They told me things were bad enough here, in the 3rd district of Paris, with holes in classroom walls, swelling class sizes and a dearth of teaching staff, but the teenagers were more than aware, they said, that the situation was far worse in their capital city's disadvantaged suburbs.
"France likes to speak of égalité," they told me "but the reality is the poor here are prejudiced against, while the rich benefit."
None of them will be old enough to vote in the presidential election in France next spring but they questioned whether the changing face of politicians in power made all that much difference anyway.
The three young women told me large-scale protests seemed the only way to get heard by French authorities.
- France's school protests: What lies behind the anger 
  - Published8 October
They are part of a defiant French tradition.
Cultural icon Victor Hugo, the 19th-Century author of French Revolution classic Les Misérables, also an activist for the French Republic, proclaimed: "Si vous n'êtes pas contents, manifestez, criez, hurlez, mais ne subissez pas."
("If you are not happy, protest, shout, scream but do not give up and give in.")
Amongst crowds of protesting students walking through Paris on Thursday, I came across a number of mums, with placards around their necks, reading: "Mums in solidarity."
Were they there to protest or to protect their kids, I asked? "Both!" was the emphatic response.
Gwen, 37, said she and other mothers were taking it in turns every morning to co-ordinate between students and police at their local school lock-in.
This came after mounting accusations of police brutality, denied by France's interior ministry, during protests earlier this month in which hundreds were injured and a 15-year-old boy in the town of Lens lost a hand.
France's interior minister has since suspended the use of stun grenades by police at high school demonstrations.
Gwen told me she did not mind that her son was missing weeks of school as a result of the lock-ins. "It's a far better education for him to wake up to his civic duty and to fight for what is just in society," she said.
At Thursday's demo I also came across 17-year-old Lola and her mother, Sandrine, sharing a placard that said revolution was the most beautiful expression of humanity.
"My mum took to the streets in '68," Lola said proudly. "Now it's my turn. No point in waiting for the presidential election in France. We want change now."
Student protests in Paris in May 1968 are the stuff of legend in France. Demands for better education inspired workers to join the marches which turned into the biggest general strike in French history. It set the standard for revolutionary upheaval for a generation and is credited with creating new opportunities for the French left.
Now, though, with six months to go before an already fraught presidential election in France, there are accusations that the hard left, under presidential hopeful Jean-Luc Mélenchon, is weaponising student frustration.
"Members of [Mélenchon's] France Insoumise (LFI) are instrumentalising the high school movement for their electoral advantage," said Sébastien Lecornu on Wednesday. He accused them of encouraging protests, then going through the motions of condemning any violence.
"This hypocrisy damages France," said Lecornu.
But "Mélenchon for President!" is a chant you often hear amongst the students in the streets.
Supporters applaud his desire for a wealth tax in France, for lowering the voting age to 16 and for being the only presidential candidate to turn up to French schools to examine the state of them, several demonstrators told me.
For Marine Le Pen, the nationalist anti-immigration favourite in France's presidential race, the solution is cutting the country's €11bn contribution to the EU's budget.
There is, though, reason to doubt that any new French president, from the left or the right, will be able to break the impasse over France's finances.
France is far from alone in Europe right now faced with an ageing population, a generous welfare state to run and a national economy squeezed by outside pressures such as US President Donald Trump's trade tariffs and the war in the Gulf.
Whether in France, Germany, Sweden or Italy, there is an inherent tension between politicians who hesitate to tell voters the truth about shrinking public finances, the defence establishment's demand for higher defence spending and citizens' insistence on improved public services.
In France, that pressure is particularly acute. French public expenditure, at about 57% GDP, is one of the steepest amongst wealthy nations worldwide.
Social spending, particularly on pensions, is exceptionally large, while French citizens pay one of the highest overall tax and social contribution burdens in Europe. Simply put, they expect a welfare and public service bang for their buck.
But economist Anne-Laure Delatte does not believe having a new president will ease her country's financial migraine.
"We need constitutional change. A new system. A new Republic," she told me.
"Our Fifth Republic is centred around a powerful president. Parliament is there to block him or her rather than to find consensus or to make new laws."
For France to progress, she says, that has to change.
The French parliamentary election that follows the 2027 presidential vote is likely to be as divided as ever, she believes: "We need a system where MPs have more power and should learn consensus and coalition-building from our European neighbours."
In her opinion, education had to be protected and funds better distributed. It was an investment in France's financial future, she told me.
"Our current system of inequality in schooling and low wages for teachers means we lose out from benefiting from the best and brightest across French society. That is not only unfair on individuals but our economy ultimately loses out on innovation and productivity."
Re-writing France's constitution is not on the cards, at the moment. So, what about the here and now, I asked centrist politician Anne-Catherine Loisier.
She's a senator for the Centrist Union in France's upper house of parliament and vice president of the parliamentary group for sciences and technology.
Loisier, along with pretty much every leading French politician across the political spectrum, says the protesting students "must feel heard".
"Our budgets are limited," she admitted, "but you don't necessarily need more money. You can make improvements by redistributing funding better. Education is a regional competence in France. Every region should take a look at local needs and address priorities accordingly. That action can be taken immediately."
I asked Loisier if she agreed with UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, the former mayor of Greater Manchester, that regions should be given greater powers. "Absolutely," she replied. "France has traditionally been very Paris-centric but so much could be improved by decentralising the country."
"My France isn't broken. I don't recognise that image you see portrayed in the media. My country is made up of lots of Frances. Paris, the regions; northern and southern France. We need to give power back to the people. Local governments can look people in the eye directly, so voters feel they have power over their own future, rather than politicians handing them their fate from up high in Paris."
"That way I hope we can restore voters' - and students' - faith in politics."
It's a promise you hear from politicians - right and left - ahead of France's huge elections next year.
But opinion polls here, as across most of Europe, indicate public faith in the political class is in dwindling supply.

A Neanderthal was killed with a spear 75,000 years ago: scientists found traces of ancient violence
Kyiv • UNN
Traces of a fatal injury to a Neanderthal caused by a sharp weapon were found in Shanidar Cave. A year before his death, he had also suffered a facial injury.
Scientists from the University of Cambridge examined the remains of a Neanderthal who lived about 75,000 years ago. Analysis of the bones showed that he likely died from a blow from a sharp weapon to the chest. Haaretz reports this, citing a study in Scientific Reports, UNN writes.
Details
The remains of the man, known as Shanidar A, were found in Shanidar Cave in Iraqi Kurdistan. He was approximately 45 years old at the time of his death.
Researchers led by Emma Pomeroy discovered a hole in his left shoulder blade. A sharpened stick likely penetrated his chest, passed through his lung, and damaged the bone. Similar marks have previously been found on animal remains.
What else the scientists discovered
Approximately one year before his death, the Neanderthal also sustained facial injuries and lost a front tooth.
Earlier, researchers examined the remains of another Neanderthal in the cave, Shanidar 3, who lived about 50,000 years ago. He had a rib injury and a foot disease that required long-term care.
According to Pomeroy, these findings demonstrate the complexity of ancient human behavior.

Order to limit Starshield for Ukraine came from inside White House, sources say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Order to limit Starshield for Ukraine came from inside White House, sources say
NEW YORK/WASHINGTON – The order to limit a satellite system used by Ukraine for battlefield communications and drone operations came from inside the White House, according to two US officials and a Western official briefed on the matter.
The officials said leaders at the Defense Department received a message that the SpaceX Starshield service for the Ukrainian military needed to be slowed.
The officials, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, did not specify who in the White House made the decision or who was responsible for implementing the order. 
The Pentagon is the biggest customer of Starshield, which is the military-grade version of the Starlink service.
Ukrainian officials said this week that military-grade Starlink receptors stopped working in Ukraine when mounted on fast-moving objects, interfering with the performance of Ukrainian drones that rely on them for onboard guidance systems over Ukrainian territory.
A person in Ukraine’s Defence Ministry said on Oct 15 that the receptors were now working when in motion, but only at speeds of up to 160kmh.
US pressures Ukraine over refinery attacks
The move to temporarily restrict the vital communications system came as US President Donald Trump has pressured Kyiv to stop its attacks on Russian refineries, which he has blamed for the soaring energy prices that are denting his Republican Party’s prospects in the November midterm elections.
But experts say that surge in energy costs is mainly the result of the US-Israeli war with Iran, which brought Iranian attacks on energy facilities and has largely shut the vital Strait of Hormuz.
In response to a request for comment about the order to limit Starshield, a senior US official said: “No such request was ever made by the president.”
The White House did not respond to questions about whether other administration officials might have made the request.
Starshield was developed by SpaceX specifically for government and national-security customers, particularly the US Department of Defense. Starshield uses the Starlink constellation as its backbone.
Ukrainian officials said the restrictions complicated strike missions against Russian forces and logistics in occupied territory and slowed interceptor drones used to shoot down incoming Russian Shahed drones.
Elon Musk, the chief executive of SpaceX, said on X on Oct 15 that because Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government, any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military or the president.
SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment.
The Department of Defense and the Ukrainian embassy in Washington also did not respond to requests for comment.
Decline in relations
Relations between Kyiv and Washington have deteriorated in recent days following a meeting in Miami on Oct 9 that convened representatives from both countries as well as Europe and the World Bank.
Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, the Trump administration’s Middle East envoy, struck a tough tone with Ukraine in the meeting, according to a separate person familiar with the matter. 
They told Ukrainian officials that the US was frustrated with Kyiv’s continued strikes on Russian refineries despite repeated requests from Washington to stop.
The US delegation also explained Washington’s decision to strike a diesel deal with Russia, saying the White House hoped it would soften Moscow’s stance on peace talks.
That deal, under which Russia will supply more than 2.25 million barrels of diesel to US and global markets, has triggered a backlash from some US lawmakers, who say it will give Moscow cash to pursue its war without forcing Russian President Vladimir Putin to make concessions to end the conflict.
In the days that followed, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and Trump criticised each other, with Zelensky calling the US decision on the Russian diesel deal “weak”.
Trump called for elections in Ukraine and Zelensky’s ouster.
Behind the scenes, American officials threatened to stop providing intelligence to Kyiv about Russian missile launches that Ukraine uses to thwart attacks, as Reuters previously reported. On Oct 14, Trump said Washington was still sharing intelligence with Ukraine.
Following the move to restrict Ukraine’s access to Starshield, the Ukrainians made calls on Oct 14-15 to find answers from senior officials at the White House, State Department and Pentagon, a senior Ukrainian official said, adding that Kyiv was told it was a White House decision.
The Pentagon has spent billions of dollars on the Starlink and Starshield services.  
It has also bought dedicated Starshield satellites, including communications spacecraft for missile-warning missions and a spy constellation for the National Reconnaissance Office, Reuters reported in 2024. REUTERS

RIYADH/ADEN, Yemen, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- Five people were killed and 16 others wounded in an attack launched by the Houthi group on the presidential palace compound in the southern Yemeni port city of Aden, Yemen's government said Thursday, as Houthis claimed Saudi military officers were killed or wounded in the attack.
Minister of Public Health and Population Qassem Buhaibeh said in a statement that those killed and wounded included security guards and civilian employees working at the Al-Ma'ashiq Presidential Palace compound, the temporary seat of the internationally recognized Yemeni government.
Earlier on Thursday, a local security official told Xinhua that five missiles struck the presidential palace compound, while another attack targeted the headquarters of the Saudi-led coalition forces in Aden's Al Buraiqa district.
Loud explosions rocked Aden during the strikes, with smoke rising from the vicinity of the presidential palace, according to a Xinhua reporter on the ground.
Local sources told Xinhua that "high-level meetings" had recently been held at the compound to prepare Saudi-backed government forces for fighting the Houthis.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Sarea said the group targeted the "Saudi military operations headquarters" in Aden, without specifying its exact location.
Houthi-run al-Masirah TV, citing a Houthi military leader, later said Saudi military officers were killed or wounded in an attack targeting a "military operations headquarters run by Saudi officers" inside the presidential palace compound in Aden.
There was no immediate comment from Saudi Arabia or the Saudi-led coalition on the claim.
The attack marked a further escalation in the confrontation between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia, with the two sides trading intensified strikes in recent days.
The Saudi-led coalition said Thursday that Houthi attacks on King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh have killed 17 people and injured more than 330 others since Oct. 1, with the airport coming under 20 attacks during the two-week period.
Meanwhile, the Houthis said Saudi warplanes conducted 65 air and missile strikes on Houthi-held areas in Yemen during the past 24 hours.
The UN Security Council on Thursday strongly condemned escalating Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia, including attacks affecting civilian aviation and energy infrastructure.
Saudi Deputy Minister for Public Diplomacy Rayed Krimly told reporters Thursday that the Houthis rejected Riyadh's call for a meeting in Oman "to resolve outstanding differences" at the beginning of this escalation in July, media reports said.
Yemen has been mired in conflict since late 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and much of northern Yemen, forcing the government out of the capital. ■

NEW YORK, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- U.S. stocks recovered on Thursday as falling Treasury yields provided relief to equity markets, helping technology and semiconductor shares stabilize amid debt-financing worries.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 556.21 points, or 1.08 percent, to 52,177.69. The S&P 500 added 25.12 points, or 0.33 percent, to 7,744.06. The Nasdaq Composite Index increased by 20.16 points, or 0.08 percent, to 26,713.03.
Eight of the 11 primary S&P 500 sectors ended in the green, with health and materials leading the gainers by going up 1.84 percent and 1.71 percent, respectively. Meanwhile, energy and technology led the laggards by losing 1.55 percent and 0.54 percent, respectively.
Market sentiment found footing as benchmark borrowing costs retreated, allowing heavily pressured tech equities to pare steep losses.
In the AI infrastructure sector, cloud compute provider CoreWeave gained nearly 6 percent, reversing a portion of Wednesday's more than 15 percent drop triggered by concerns over excessive debt accumulation to finance its hardware expansion. Memory manufacturer Micron Technology also recovered most of its intraday decline, closing 1.87 percent higher.
Concerns across the AI ecosystem were compounded by a CNBC report that Anthropic's quarterly revenue reached 16.8 billion U.S. dollars in the third quarter. While representing massive growth, the pace raised questions among some market participants about whether revenue expansion remains swift enough to sustain lofty valuations across underlying chipmakers.
Despite the broader equity recovery, inflation pressures remained pronounced. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Thursday that the producer price index (PPI) for final demand jumped 1.3 percent in September, lifting the annualized wholesale rate to 6.3 percent, its fastest pace since 2022.
The sharp acceleration followed Wednesday's hotter-than-expected consumer price index (CPI) reading, further complicating the Federal Reserve's policy trajectory as officials weigh persistent price spikes ahead of their upcoming interest rate decision.
"Today's PPI report, after Wednesday's CPI, confirms inflation is getting worse as energy prices stay high," said David Russell, global head of market strategy at TradeStation. "Election or no election, prices are rising and the Fed might be forced to act."
According to CME FedWatch, traders now see a 29 percent likelihood the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates at its meeting in two weeks, and an 88 percent likelihood the central bank will lift rates at least a quarter-percentage point at its December meeting.
Broader market gains were underpinned by defensive and consumer-oriented sectors outside of technology. Walmart advanced 1.47 percent, after Deutsche Bank upgraded the stock to "buy" from "hold," citing a positive outlook for 2027. The bank expects incremental margins to improve and noted current inflation levels could help the company attract consumers.
Nike jumped more than 5 percent, leading consumer discretionary gainers. Apple, which on Wednesday joined Nvidia as the only companies ever to close with a market capitalization above 5 trillion dollars, ended 0.28 percent lower. ■

Ukrainian Neptune missiles struck six Su-34 fighter-bombers at the Russian Borisoglebsk airfield during the attack on the night of October 15. This is more than Russia has reportedly received in new aircraft of this type since the beginning of 2026. Defense Express reported this, citing data from the Ukrainian Navy, according to UNN.
Details
The Su-34 is one of the main aircraft used by the Russian army to launch guided aerial bombs at Ukrainian positions and frontline settlements.
According to military analysts' estimates, Russian aviation received no more than 4–5 new Su-34s during 2026. In other words, a single Ukrainian strike may have put more aircraft out of action than Russian factories delivered in more than nine months.
How serious Russia's aviation losses have become
In 2025, Russia reported the delivery of 18 Su-34 bombers in seven batches. This year, the pace of replenishing the aircraft fleet has, according to open-source data, proved significantly lower.
Six Su-34Ms destroyed by Neptune strike at Russian airfield - Navy15.10.26, 11:00 • 32676 views
Before the strike on the Borisoglebsk airfield, open sources had already recorded three Su-34s destroyed or damaged during 2026.
Thus, taking the latest attack into account, the total number of affected aircraft of this type may reach at least nine since the beginning of the year.
At the same time, reports that six aircraft were hit do not mean that all of them were completely destroyed. The extent of the damage to each Su-34 has not yet been specified.

Norway will build a factory near Ukraine to produce weapons against drones
Kyiv • UNN
Norway's Kongsberg plans to launch a counter-drone systems factory in Poland by 2028. The investment will amount to approximately €45 million.
Norwegian defense company Kongsberg plans to open a plant in Poland to manufacture systems for combating unmanned aerial vehicles. The new facility will boost production of Polish SAN air defense systems designed to protect against drones. Defense Express reports this, citing a company statement, according to UNN.
Details
The contract for the construction of the plant is planned to be signed by the end of 2026, after which work will begin. The total investment will amount to 200 million zlotys, or approximately 45 million euros.
The facility is expected to begin operations as early as 2028. It will manufacture counter-drone systems that will allow Poland to reduce its dependence on the supply of foreign components for its own air defense.
Which air defense system will be strengthened by Norwegian developments
The reference is to the Polish SAN anti-aircraft system, which includes Kongsberg PROTECTOR combat modules with 30 mm cannons. They are designed to destroy drones without using expensive anti-aircraft missiles.
In addition to cannons, the SAN system will be equipped with 12.7 mm machine guns, SA-35 self-propelled 35 mm anti-aircraft guns, electronic warfare systems, APKWS missiles, and Merops interceptor drones.
Poland has already ordered 18 batteries of these systems, which will include 18 command platoons and 52 firing platoons. The weapons will be mounted on Legwan off-road vehicles and Jelcz trucks.
According to Defense Express, cannon and machine-gun systems make it possible to intercept drones at significantly lower cost compared with using anti-aircraft missiles. At the same time, they have limitations in terms of engagement range and altitude.
In addition to Poland, Slovakia had previously expressed interest in SAN systems.

Meta unveils new ‘open’ AI model to rival Chinese competition
- Meta launched Muse Spark Open, an open-weight AI model it says rivals leading Chinese systems and is its most capable US open-weight model to date.
- The model is built for coding and agentic work, with strong safeguards, and it can run on Apple’s M5 Ultra chips, showing a rare Meta-Apple link.
- The launch follows Meta’s new closed models Wonder and Wonder Full, as Zuckerberg shifts the firm to compete more directly with OpenAI and Anthropic.
AI generated
SAN FRANCISCO – Meta on Oct 15 launched a new open-weight AI model which it claims rivals, and in some cases outperforms, similar products from leading Chinese developers.
Muse Spark Open “is the most capable US open-weight model to date”, Meta’s chief of AI Alexandr Wang wrote on X.
Unlike with so-called closed models – such as Anthropic’s Claude or OpenAI’s ChatGPT – developers can download the parameters, or weights, of an open-weight model and then customise it.
Chinese developers have emerged as dominant players in the open-weight market for AI models over the past couple of years.
Alibaba’s Qwen, Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 and Z.ai’s GLM models have been considered open-weight frontrunners globally, but Meta claims its new open model now competes on a similar level.
“Built for coding and agentic work”, Muse Spark Open “excels at long-horizon tasks, complex software engineering, and multi-step reasoning”, Meta said in a blog post, adding that “strong safeguards” have been integrated into the new model.
Muse Spark Open is also “optimised” to run on Apple’s advanced M5 Ultra chips, Meta said, signalling an unusual partnership between the two tech giants.
Meta boss Mark Zuckerberg wrote on X that the new model “runs great on new Mac Studios thanks to work” with Apple and its new chief executive John Ternus.
Ternus, who took over as Apple’s chief from Tim Cook in September, responded that it is “amazing to run a model of Muse Spark Open’s calibre and scale this efficiently, right from your desk. Mac Studio keeps pushing the boundaries of on-device AI!”
Muse Spark Open still requires significant computing power, though.
Users can run the model on two Mac Studios with M5 Ultra chips to create a “supercomputer” on their own desktop, Meta said.
The launch comes just days after Meta announced its newest closed model.
On Oct 12, the company unveiled two new “frontier” models called Wonder and Wonder Full, which the company claimed rival the most advanced versions of ChatGPT and Claude.
Meta’s AI efforts were initially focused on open models, but more recently Zuckerberg has pushed the company to compete with OpenAI and Anthropic.
Meta launched its Spark model in April, marking a departure from its open-source model known as Llama, which lagged behind the rest of the industry. AFP

Episode 4: A7A5: Russia's Stablecoin Lifeline
How a rouble-backed stablecoin, Tether’s USDT and an alternative payments network are testing the reach of Western sanctions.
Russia's search for alternatives to the Western financial system is increasingly moving into crypto.
One experiment in particular has attracted attention: A7A5, a rouble-backed stablecoin linked to the wider A7 payments network and designed to facilitate cross-border payments outside conventional banking channels.
In this episode of the Suspicious Transaction Report, host Tom Keatinge speaks with Dr Tom Robinson, Chief Scientist and Founder of blockchain analytics company Elliptic, about what A7A5 reveals about the evolution of sanctions evasion.
They explore the relationship between A7A5, Ilan Shor, Russian state-owned bank PSB and Kyrgyzstan; why the token itself is only part of a much wider financial infrastructure; and how A7A5 can act as a bridge from roubles into the globally liquid dollar-backed stablecoin USDT.
The conversation also considers whether sanctions are working. Blockchain data shows how enforcement can restrict liquidity and disrupt crypto infrastructure — but also how rapidly networks adapt.
Ultimately, the episode asks where policymakers should focus next: on individual tokens, or on the exchanges, liquidity providers and exit points that make alternative payment systems usable.

Berlin plans to acquire 400 Tomahawks and three Typhon batteries, supplementing them with cheaper “Bars” missiles. Ukraine has already used the missiles against targets in Moscow Oblast.
Germany plans to supplement American Tomahawk cruise missiles with cheaper long-range strike capabilities, including the Ukrainian Bars missile-drones currently under consideration. The Bundeswehr wants to receive the new weapons as early as 2027 in order to be able to launch massive strikes over long distances. Defense Express reports this, citing the German publication hartpunkt, according to UNN.
Details
According to Christian Freuding, a representative of the Bundeswehr leadership, Germany seeks to create ground-based means of striking targets at distances of up to 1,500 km. According to journalists, the Ukrainian Bars and the American Anthem missile are among the promising options under consideration.
At the same time, Berlin plans to purchase 400 Tomahawk missiles and three batteries of Typhon launchers. Combining expensive cruise missiles with cheaper systems will make it possible to increase the number of simultaneous strikes and complicate the work of the enemy's air defense.
Where Ukraine has already used the Bars
Although Germany is only preparing to receive the Ukrainian missile-drones, Ukraine's Defense Forces are already using them against Russian military facilities.
In particular, on May 17, 2026, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported the use of the RS-1 Bars together with other Ukrainian drones to strike targets in Moscow Oblast. Earlier, the use of jet-powered Bars during attacks on Russian military enterprises was also reported.
The Ukrainian system belongs to the class of relatively inexpensive long-range strike capabilities. It is precisely the possibility of their mass use that makes such missiles attractive to the Bundeswehr.
In July, Ukraine and Germany signed an agreement on the joint production of Bars missiles. It will allow the German side to manufacture these missiles for its own needs.
At the same time, no final decision has yet been made on adopting the Bars into Bundeswehr service. Before any possible purchases, the Ukrainian missiles must undergo the necessary inspections.

At least 4, including 3 children, killed in US elementary school shooting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
22:51:56 UTC
07:51:56 KST

Three children, one teacher killed in Oregon school shooting
The police chief in Bend, Oregon, identified the shooter as a 16-year-old who was killed by a bystander at the school.
At least four people have been killed in a shooting at an elementary school in Oregon, part of the northwestern United States, according to local law enforcement.
The shooting on Thursday took place at Silver Rail Elementary School in the city of Bend, about 160 kilometres (100 miles) southeast of Portland.
Three children were among the dead: they were aged five, eight and 11, according to Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz. A teacher was also killed.
In addition, a seven-year-old child and a 54-year-old teacher were transported to St Charles Medical Center in Bend with critical injuries.
In an afternoon news conference, Krantz identified the alleged shooter as a 16-year-old Bend resident, who was killed at the scene. The suspect has yet to be named.
“What the initial investigation is showing is that the shooter had forced their way into the school by shooting at locked doors,” Krantz said. He added that investigators were still determining whether the suspect had attended the school at any point.
Emergency services began receiving calls for help around 12:59pm local time (19:59 GMT), with “dozens” of additional calls in the ensuing minutes.
The first call, Krantz explained, came from “a person in a vehicle who reported being shot at multiple times by a person with a long gun”. The elementary school went into lockdown at 1:01pm (20:01 GMT), and officers arrived on the scene shortly thereafter.
“Moments later, an officer reported that a suspect had been shot by a community member who had seen the suspect enter the school and pursued him into the school and engaged him,” Krantz said.
“Our officers entered the building and confirmed the suspect was dead. They cleared the school to ensure there were no additional threats and then rendered emergency aid to the victims.”
He emphasised that the police investigation was ongoing and further information would be released to the public in the coming days.
The families of the victims have been notified of the attack. Police evacuated each room in the school, and students and staff were transported by bus to a nearby church where they could be reunited with their loved ones.
“This is the kind of thing we never want to see happen in Bend. It’s devastating,” said Sheila Miller, the communications manager for the Bend Police Department, on Thursday.
Kash Patel, the director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), said in a post on social media that the agency was on the scene assisting local law enforcement in the investigation.
“We will make every resource they need available,” he wrote.
Oregon Governor Tina Kotek called on Oregonians to come together to support each other through their grief.
“All Oregonians mourn this loss today. This is a horrible day. No parent should have to have this kind of day, and no community should have to live through this kind of day,” Kotek said.
She also addressed the unnamed bystander who confronted the shooter. “To the community member who heroically intervened to stop further loss of life, your actions carry a heavy emotional burden, and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well.”
Jeff Merkley, who represents Oregon in the US Senate, was among the political leaders to offer condolences in the wake of the shooting.
“My heart is with the Bend community and all of the students and families affected. No one should have to fear violence at school,” he wrote in a post on the social media platform X.
The Gun Violence Archive, which tracks shootings across the US, has documented 369 mass shootings in 2026 so far, defined as incidents where there were four or more victims injured or killed, not including the suspect.
The violence prevention group Everytown for Gun Safety has counted at least 100 incidents of gunfire on school grounds in the US this year. Thirty-four people have died as a result.

A 16-year-old shooter opened fire on Thursday at an elementary school in Bend, Oregon, killing four people, including three children, before being killed by an armed member of the community who had pursued the assailant into the school, police said.
The shooter entered Silver Rail Elementary School by firing through locked doors, police said, without offering any details beyond the suspect's age.

School shootings have become a recurring feature of American life, including high-profile attacks such as those at Columbine High School in 1999, Sandy Hook Elementary School in 2012, Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in 2018, and Robb Elementary School in Uvalde, Texas, in 2022.
Each shooting revives debates over gun laws in a country where gun rights are protected under the Constitution's Second Amendment. Gun rights advocates have argued for arming teachers as a means of defense.
Police trained for a mass shooting, Oregon governor says
Krantz said every Bend police officer went through a full day of active shooter training in August.
"Unfortunately, this is something we train for on a regular basis, and we must," Krantz said. "This is going to be a long investigation."
Thursday's shooting took place in Bend, a city of about 100,000 people in rural central Oregon, 175 miles (280 km.) southeast of Portland, in the Oregon high desert adjacent to the Deschutes National Forest.
Silver Rail Elementary School serves kindergarten through fifth grade, roughly ages 5 to 11, and has about 450 students and 40 staff members, officials said.
Gun control advocate Gabrielle Giffords, a former congresswoman who survived a mass shooting in 2011, said in a statement she was "heartbroken" by the shooting in Bend.
"This cannot continue to be a reality in our country. Leaders at every level must step up and act,” Giffords said.
Emergency responders received a call at 12:59 p.m. from a person in a vehicle who reported being shot at multiple times by someone with a long gun, Krantz said.
In the minutes afterward, dozens of calls were received saying the shooter had entered the school, Krantz said. Law enforcement immediately directed the school to go into lockdown, he said.
Officers arrived at 1:02 p.m., and moments later an officer reported the suspect had been shot, Krantz said. Police entered and confirmed the suspect was dead, he said.

Holocaust memory compels us to reject false genocide claims and face Gaza’s agony - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
22:43:38 UTC
07:43:38 KST

There is a rising and troubling consensus that the Jewish state may be guilty of the very crime that led in part to its establishment: “genocide,” a term and concept originally introduced in 1944 to describe the industrial-scale murder of the European Jews at the hands of the Nazis.
The explosive allegation achieved a significant victory last week, with the awarding of the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize to the South African jurist Navi Pillay, the head of a United Nations commission that concluded in a 2025 report that Israel has committed a genocide in Gaza.
The trouble with the 2026 Peace Nobel is not that Pillay is sharply critical of Israel’s conduct of the Gaza war; it is that the UN report in question, which shockingly failed even to address, let alone condemn, the Hamas atrocities of Oct. 7, is rooted in such an extreme anti-Israel bias as to render her an apologist for Hamas’s terrorism and disqualify her as an honest broker.
Pillay’s award puts her in line with multiple human rights organizations and genocide scholars that have reached the same conclusion, and the allegation has significant traction in public opinion. About three in 10 American voters now believe that Israel has committed a genocide in Gaza, as does about half of the British public, according to recent polls.
The fierce battle over the term “genocide” is far more than a fight over the specific nature of alleged war crimes in a particular military campaign. It is nothing less than a fight for the memory of the Holocaust itself - to whom that memory most belongs, what its apparent lessons are or should be, and who is entitled to arbitrate its uses.
Israel's conduct does not meet criteria of genocide, but pain must not be ignored
We write as two Jews who have long been deeply invested in this question, personally and professionally. One of us, Menachem Rosensaft, teaches the law of genocide at two Ivy League law schools and served on the United States Holocaust Memorial Council for 20 years.
The other, James McCauley, interned at the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum in Washington early in his career before writing books on various aspects of Holocaust memory. We come from different generations and different backgrounds, but we write with the same profound heartbreak.
We do not believe that Israel’s fierce, potentially disproportionate conduct in Gaza meets the legal criteria of genocide. Under the Genocide Convention, the crime requires the “intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group as such.” Moreover, such a goal must be the dolus specialis, or the specific purpose, for any finding of genocide rather than a tangential side effect or byproduct.
Israel waged its war against Hamas in Gaza after the ravages of Oct. 7 to remove that terrorist organization as an existential security threat after the most devastating attack in its history. Moreover, it is clear that the Israeli government did not intend to eliminate the Palestinian presence in Gaza, even if the reckless rhetoric of some extremist ministers suggested otherwise. There were some two million Palestinians living in Gaza prior to Oct. 7, and there remain just about the same number after the ceasefire went into effect in October 2025.
But whatever position one takes on the issue, the nature of Holocaust memory is in crisis. To some, the horrors of the Holocaust are the ultimate justification for Jewish security and self-defense by any means necessary, an ostensible justification for Israel to pursue its enemies however and as long as it sees fit. For others, the true lesson of the Holocaust is the moral imperative of human rights and human dignity for all, Jews and non-Jews alike. One “lesson,” as it were, is Judeocentric, the other universal.
Without question, many are all too eager to accuse the Jewish state of the very crime that led to its establishment; they are seemingly intent on delegitimizing its standing in the global arena by 6 if not altogether, delegitimizing the memory of the slaughtered Jews of Europe. But rejecting the charge of “genocide” against Israel - and saying nothing more in its place - far too often serves as a convenient semantic shield that avoids any confrontation with the inescapable reality that Gaza is indeed a humanitarian catastrophe. Merely because it may not qualify as a genocide or does not compare to the Holocaust does not mean it can or should be ignored.
Israel shouldn't use Holocaust memory to justify failure to confront violence
Israel and its supporters should not use Holocaust memory as a justification for failing to confront military excesses on its part or the brutal violence of Israeli settlers against Palestinian civilians in the West Bank. At the same time, Israel’s enemies should not use the Jewish catastrophe as a cudgel to delegitimize the very existence of the Jewish state.
On Kol Nidre, Rabbi Elliot Cosgrove of New York City’s Park Avenue Synagogue urged his congregation, and Jews worldwide, to avoid what he called “the fantasy of innocence,” and instead to claim agency in their lives as individuals and as a people. “We Jews, historically the targets of indiscriminate blame, can ourselves, at times, fall prey to the temptation to leverage our own hurt as a shield against moral accountability,” he said.
Religious leaders and elected officials often speak of the “lessons” of the Holocaust as if there was ever a consensus about what, exactly, these are. In fact, there was never such a consensus in the immediate aftermath of the war, and there is no such consensus today. But a lesson that we may not ignore is that we must decry injustice regardless of who its victims are, just as we must hold any and all perpetrators of such injustice accountable.
Whether or not there has been a genocide in Gaza, the horrific plight of Palestinian civilians there is undeniable, and we, whether as an international society or as Jews, have a collective obligation to recognize and alleviate their anguish and agony.
“We must remember the suffering of my people,” Auschwitz survivor Elie Wiesel said in his lecture when he won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1986, “as we must remember that of the Ethiopians, the Cambodians, the boat people, Palestinians, the Mesquite Indians, the Argentinian ‘desaparecidos.” He continued: “There may be times when we are powerless to prevent injustice, but there must never be a time when we fail to protest.”
Our challenge to our fellow Jews and anyone else outraged by the term “genocide” with respect to Gaza is to follow Wiesel’s lead. If one particular word is unacceptable to you, find others that aren’t. Doing so does not mean turning your back on Israel - quite the contrary. It shows a deep love for Israel, and a belief in the Jewish state living up to its own vaunted values.
Nuance matters, but silence is not an option.
The views and opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the views of JTA or its parent company, 70 Faces Media.

Rotting meat smell sparks protest at Mexico's screwworm sterile-fly plant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Rotting meat smell sparks protest at Mexico's screwworm sterile-fly plant
METAPA DE DOMINGUEZ, Mexico, Oct 15 - A rotten smell hanging over a town in Mexico's southern Chiapas state drove residents into the streets on Thursday to demand the removal of a sterile-fly plant at the center of the US-Mexican fight against the flesh-eating New World screwworm parasite.
Residents in Metapa de Dominguez compared the odor to rotting meat and spoiled food, describing it as “pungent in your nose and mouth” and causing nausea. The smell, once concentrated around the plant, could now be detected farther away, particularly when winds carried it across the town, protesters said. The odor had reached schools near the plant and disrupted classes.
"We don't care about the investment they made. What we want is for this plant to leave here, because the smell coming over the town is too much," said truck driver Mercedes Becerra de la Cruz.
The complaints come less than four months after Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum and US Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins inaugurated the facility on June 27. The US Department of Agriculture invested $21 million toward the $51 million facility, part of a broader effort to halt a screwworm outbreak that disrupted the cross-border cattle trade.
Sterile flies are the main defense against screwworm, a parasite whose larvae burrow into the living flesh of cattle and other warm-blooded animals and can kill them if untreated.
Eradicated from the US decades ago, the pest has surged north from Central America through Mexico, prompting Washington to impose a more than year-long ban on Mexican cattle imports. The Metapa plant is expected eventually to produce 100 million sterile flies a week.
Mexico has recorded nearly 48,000 cases of screwworm in the current outbreak and the United States 53.
Inside the Metapa plant, millions of flies are bred each week, their larvae fed a carefully formulated mixture of egg, milk and powdered hemoglobin that mimics the nutrient-rich conditions of a wound. The flies are sterilized before being released by the millions to mate with wild females without producing offspring, gradually suppressing the population.
Outside its walls, residents said daily life has increasingly been shaped by an overpowering odor that drifts into surrounding neighborhoods and schools.
"We need the federal government to respond and have the plant relocated. It is far too close, right in the middle of the town," said 49-year-old homemaker Rosalba Merida Herrera. "For the sake of our children and our elderly, we are asking them to look at the situation, as this issue is now affecting the entire town."
A spokesperson for Mexico's Agriculture Ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment. REUTERS

Army Building Up New Space Operations Branch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
22:37:27 UTC
07:37:27 KST

The Army has long been dependent on space capabilities to navigate terrain, communicate in hard-to-reach areas, and identify and strike targets. Now, the service wants to deepen its space operations expertise and is making plans to expand its own cadre of operators in the coming years.
In June, the service established its a Space Operations Branch, consolidating space-related career paths and created to train Soldiers to operate and deploy space systems.
This week, during the annual Association of the U.S. Army Annual Meeting in Washington, after transverring 600 enlisted Soldiers into the branch Oct. 1, Army officials predicted the Space Operations Branch will eventually include thousands of officers and troops.
The 600 transfers were reclassified as 40D Tactical Space Operations Specialists, the Army’s Military Occupational Specialty code for space troops—uniting them with 40A Space Operations Officers. The enlisted Soldiers had previously been temporarily reassigned to space-related units from Air Defense Artillery, Signal, and Military Intelligence fields.
Speaking with reporters Oct. 14 during the conference, Col. Joseph Mroszczyk, director of the Army’s Transformation Integration Directorate for Space Superiority and High Altitude, said the service’s space operations cadre has almost doubled since 2012, and he expects that to continue within the new Space Operations Branch.
“When we talk about the branch and the targets, having a couple thousand dedicated folks within the branch, between the enlisted and the officer side, is a significant contribution across the service,” Mroszczyk said when asked if the Army has a target level of growth for the branch. He didn’t offer more specifics on how long it might take the service to get there.
After the Space Force was created in 2019, space operators and units transferred from the Air Force, Navy, and Army, with the bulk of Space Force operators coming from the Air Force. Army officials have continued to make the case that they need to have their own space-focused Soldiers. While critics charge that this risks duplicating effort and blurring roles and missions, the Army says the difference is that while the Space Force is focused on maintaining space superiority in orbit, its role is integrating space capability and effects into tactical multidomain operations from the ground.
Lt. Gen. John Rafferty, commander of the Army’s Space and Missile Defense Command, told Air & Space Forces Magazine in an Oct. 13 interview that as demand for these capabilities grows, the Army needs to provide the same professional pathways and training for space operators that it does for other specializations, like artillery, infantry, and aviation.
“Training, education, experience, and talent management is how you create great leaders, and that’s how you build great units with great leaders,” Rafferty said. “It became apparent to the Army that in order to capitalize on the momentum, the gains that we’ve made in Army space-delivered capabilities, we need to professionalize the branch and do it fast.”
Rafferty highlighted a few areas where the Army expects to need more space personnel and effects in the coming years.
The service on Oct. 8 activated its a new Multi-Domain Task Force at Fort Carson, Colo., one of four elements stationed around the world and designed to integrate air, land, sea, space, and cyber operations in theater. A fifth is slated for activation in 2028. Each task force incorporates space effects, and Rafferty said that as the service adds more MDTFs, it will naturally need more space personnel and systems.
He also pointed to the creation of a new Theater Strike Effects Group at U.S. Army Pacific, which will require space support. The service also wants to expand the focus of its 1st Space Brigade—headquartered at Fort Carson, but distributed across six countries—beyond GPS, theater missile warning, and satellite communications into new capability areas. He did not provide details.
As for space systems, the Army hasn’t revealed plans to field its own satellites, but Rafferty and others said the service has an interest in building out an architecture of stratospheric platforms in the “near-space” region—between 60,000 and 100,000 feet in altitude.
“That’s a—no pun intended—space that is just ripe with potential, and the opportunities for various payloads to be on those is remarkable right now,” Rafferty said. “It’s affordable and scalable, and we’ve just got to really pursue that as part of the space branch growth.”
Mroszczyk described the region as a sort of transition point between the air and space domains where platforms could host a variety of payloads supporting missions like sensing and communications, and even serve as platforms for “launched effects”—the Army’s term for small, air- or ground-launched autonomous systems.
As an example, Mroszczyk said high-altitude platforms could form a “complementary” layer for some of the Space Force’s data transport efforts, like the Space Development Agency’s Proliferated Warfighter Space Architecture or the Space Data Network. Systems in that layer could help distribute data during a conflict and provide resiliency should space systems be targeted.
He told reporters the Army is looking at a range of systems—from smaller platforms to larger balloons—and is planning multiple experiments in the coming year.
“That operational space allows some persistence and broad coverage in an area where you can deliver space-like capabilities in terms of payloads, but then also take advantage of the deep access that you get from a stratospheric balloon,” he said.

UN warns of food shortages if Hormuz fertiliser crisis continues
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
22:22:23 UTC
07:22:23 KST

Breadcrumb
UN warns of food shortages if Hormuz fertiliser crisis continues
A failure by the United States and Iran to agree within weeks on a UN-backed plan for moving fertiliser through the Strait of Hormuz could cause a food security crisis in parts of Asia and Africa, an official overseeing the proposed scheme said on Wednesday.
The United Nations set up a taskforce in March to facilitate passage of fertilisers through the strait. It is yet to implement the mechanism it drew up, but United Nations Under-Secretary-General Jorge Moreira da Silva said this could be activated within 7-10 days of an agreement between Washington and Tehran.
"It's absolutely crucial to get the deal in the next few weeks. Otherwise, we will miss the planting season," he said in an interview in Bangkok, on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank annual meetings.
In response to questions from Reuters, a US State Department spokesman said the US military has assisted thousands of commercial vessels with transiting the strait.
"The United States will continue to take decisive action against Iran's attempts to disrupt freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and hold the global economy hostage," he said.
The White House and Iran's Embassy in Bangkok did not immediately reply to a request for comment.
Iran has sought to tighten its grip on the Strait of Hormuz since US and Israeli strikes on 28 February, using the chokepoint to pressure Washington, which has been pressing its own naval blockade of Iranian ports.
Before the war, the waterway handled roughly a third of globally traded urea - the world's most widely used fertiliser - and nearly half of seaborne sulphur, a key input. It is also a major conduit for global oil supplies.
Fertiliser shipments out of the Gulf region remained largely halted more than six months after the start of the conflict, the Washington-based International Food Policy Research Institute said in a note last month. Fertiliser products accounted for a "very negligible" share of the resumption of some shipping during a ceasefire between mid-June and mid-July, it said.
Five vessels a day
If the Hormuz disruption continues, commodity prices could rise by up to 81% for cereals, 66% for oil crops and 30% for animal products, according to an August report by the International Chamber of Commerce.
"If we miss that planting season, the productivity of agriculture would significantly drop and the impact on prices will significantly increase," said Moreira da Silva, who is also the executive director of the United Nations Office for Project Services.
The proposed operation would use a coordination centre in Oman to register vessels and coordinate safe passage, with UN monitors working alongside local authorities at Gulf ports to verify cargo loading.
The passage of only five vessels per day through Hormuz could keep fertiliser supplies flowing to countries in critical need, Moreira da Silva said.
Ships would be tracked during transit, and additional inspections could be carried out if countries raised concerns about a vessel or its cargo, he added.
Multiple shipping chokepoints
Iran and the United States have exchanged proposals through intermediaries since a June interim ceasefire collapsed, but efforts to reopen the Strait of Hormuz have stalled over Tehran's conditions and Washington's insistence on addressing Iran's nuclear programme from the outset.
The proposed UN mechanism could operate alongside negotiations on a comprehensive deal aimed at securing lasting peace and freedom of navigation, Moreira da Silva said.
"What we are telling them is, while you continue your discussions towards a comprehensive deal, let us work, let us do our job," he said, declining to specify the exact bottlenecks to a deal as discussions continue with both sides.
Beyond the Hormuz crisis, a deteriorating situation in the Black Sea region, where cargo vessels have come under attack, and an offensive by Iran-backed Houthi militants along a key Red Sea shipping route are compounding the threat to global food security.
"What we are witnessing now is a concentration of factors," Moreira da Silva said. "Climate crisis, simultaneous disruption of maritime chokepoints on the Black Sea, on the Red Sea and on Hormuz."
(Reuters)

Putin orders seizure of Tarkett and four other European companies' Russian assets
Russian leader Vladimir Putin has signed a decree ordering the takeover of Russian assets owned by French flooring manufacturer Tarkett and four other European companies, which together generate more than RUB 50 billion (about US$596 million) in annual revenue.
Source: Russia's official legal information portal; The Moscow Times, an independent Amsterdam-based news outlet
Details: Under Putin's decree, assets belonging to French flooring manufacturer Tarkett have been transferred to the temporary management of Centre Capital Management Company.
According to the document, European owners have been forcibly stripped of 187,500 ordinary shares and 500,000 preference shares in Tarkett. The shares belonged to Tarkett's Serbian subsidiary in Bačka Palanka as well as an equivalent block of shares in Tarkett's parent company.
In addition, 100 ordinary shares in Tarkett RU and 100% of the ownership interests in Tarkett Sommer, both owned by Russian company Tarkett, have been transferred to Centre Capital.
Under the same decree, Putin ordered the seizure of assets belonging to four other European companies that had continued operating in Russia for years. The assets placed under Russian control include 12,565 shares in paper packaging manufacturer Kappa RU and the entire stakes in hygiene products maker Ontex RU, metal packaging producer Eviosys Packaging Kuban and packaging manufacturer Menshen Packaging CIS.
Tarkett is an international flooring manufacturer serving the residential, commercial, industrial and sports sectors. In its 2024 report, the company said it was the world's third-largest flooring seller and the global leader in vinyl flooring. Despite Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, it continued operating two factories in Russia, out of 34 production sites worldwide, and paying taxes to the Russian state.
According to sources in the Russian government and business community who spoke to Reuters, major European companies that chose to remain in Russia have become a tool for the Kremlin to put pressure on the EU in response to sanctions and its support for Ukraine.
"The time has come for asymmetric measures. Let them think about what measures they are taking and what sanctions they are introducing," a senior Russian government official familiar with the situation told Reuters on condition of anonymity.
Commenting on potential targets, including the Russian subsidiaries of the Italian banking group UniCredit and the Austrian banking group Raiffeisen, the Russian official openly threatened foreign investors: "Let them be scared."
Background:
- On 25 April 2023, Putin signed Decree No. 302, On the temporary management of certain assets. The document justified the forced seizure of businesses as "retaliatory measures" in response to the "confiscation" of Russian property in the US and countries that had joined it. The first companies affected were the Russian subsidiaries of energy groups Uniper and Fortum.
- In July 2023, the Kremlin used the same mechanism to seize the Russian assets of French food producer Danone and Danish brewing group Carlsberg. The businesses were subsequently transferred to entities linked to the Russian authorities.
- In September 2026, the Kremlin launched a new large-scale wave of takeovers targeting European businesses. On 17 September, Putin transferred the Russian assets of Swiss food manufacturer Nestlé, French retail chain Auchan, logistics operator FM Logistics and DIY superstore chain Lemana PRO (the new brand name for the chain formerly known in Russia as Leroy Merlin). to the temporary management of an obscure company called LEV Management.
- On 21 September, a manufacturer of plastic packaging and dispensing systems owned by French holding company Aptar Europe Holding was placed under temporary management in Russia.
- On 28 September, Putin signed a decree transferring the Russian assets of German hypermarket chain Metro to the management of UK Torg Rus, a company registered just three weeks earlier with a share capital of RUB 10,000 (about US$119).

Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, as Special Representative of Chinese President Xi Jinping, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, attends the Seventh Summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (CICA) and delivers a speech in Baku, Azerbaijan, Oct. 15, 2026. (Xinhua/Chen Junfeng)
BAKU, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, as Special Representative of Chinese President Xi Jinping, attended the Seventh Summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (CICA) here on Thursday and delivered a speech.
Wang, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, said that CICA is a platform for dialogue and cooperation initiated and jointly built by Asian countries.
Since its establishment, CICA has actively championed the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence, systematically advanced cooperation on confidence building measures, consistently practiced multilateralism, and worked tirelessly to strengthen the foundation of trust for peace and security in Asia.
China highly appreciates Azerbaijan's efforts during its CICA chairmanship to advance CICA cooperation, and stands ready to continue its strong support for and active participation in the CICA process, Wang said.
Amid accelerating changes unseen in a century, only by fostering a sense of community with a shared future, standing on the right side of history, and upholding solidarity and cooperation can Asian countries stand at the forefront of the times, turn crises into opportunities and jointly create a better future, he said.
Wang put forward four proposals:
First, jointly safeguard peace and stability. Asia does not need a Cold War mentality and does not welcome bloc confrontation. Asia's problems should ultimately be addressed by the people of Asia through solidarity and cooperation, and Asia's security should be ensured by upholding the vision of common, comprehensive, cooperative and sustainable security.
Second, jointly promote prosperity and revitalization. Development is the master key to solving all problems. Efforts should be made to better align high-quality Belt and Road cooperation with the development initiatives of various countries, safeguard an open environment for cooperation, advance trade and investment liberalization and facilitation, ensure the stable and efficient operation of international transport corridors, and strengthen supply security for critical raw materials, energy resources and food, so that Asian countries can work together to accelerate their progress toward modernization.
Third, jointly promote exchanges and mutual learning among civilizations. Asia is the continent with the greatest diversity of civilizations. Efforts should be made to firmly promote the Asian values of peace, cooperation, openness and inclusiveness, respect countries' independent choices of development paths and governance models, deepen exchanges and cooperation in culture, tourism and health, as well as among women's and youth groups, media organizations and think tanks, and promote people-to-people exchanges and closer bonds between peoples, so that diverse civilizations can learn from one another and flourish together.
Fourth, jointly improve global governance. Efforts should be made to reinvigorate the authority and role of the United Nations, uphold the basic norms governing international relations established by the UN Charter, strengthen capacities in digital governance, disaster prevention and mitigation, and public health, and jointly build a more efficient, inclusive and resilient governance system in Asia.
Wang stressed that China will remain firmly committed to the path of peaceful development, bring greater stability to the international landscape through its own high-quality development, and provide stronger impetus for global growth.
China stands ready to work with all parties to build consensus, deepen cooperation and jointly build a peaceful, stable, prosperous, open and inclusive Asian community with a shared future, making greater Asian contribution to world peace and development, Wang said.
Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev briefed on the work undertaken by Azerbaijan during its two-year CICA chairmanship and put forward proposals for cooperation.
Participants exchanged views on the security and development situation in the CICA region and the implementation of confidence building measures. They agreed that CICA member states should practice multilateralism, strengthen solidarity and cooperation, address common challenges, safeguard the common interests of the Global South, and promote peace and development in Asia.
The summit adopted and issued the Baku Declaration of the Seventh CICA Summit.
On the sidelines of the summit, Wang also met separately with Israeli President Isaac Herzog, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov, Bahraini Foreign Minister Abdullatif bin Rashid Al Zayani, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan and Palestinian Foreign Minister Varsen Aghabekian Shahin, and had friendly exchanges with dignitaries from various countries. ■

UN report warns global biodiversity action off track, urges implementation
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
06:18:48 CST
07:18:48 KST

YEREVAN, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on Thursday launched the first global assessment report on the implementation of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, warning that global efforts remain off track to meet the 2030 targets despite widespread national commitments.
The State of Biodiversity Action report, released in the Armenian capital of Yerevan ahead of the 17th meeting of the Conference of the Parties (COP17) to the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD), evaluates collective progress under the landmark framework adopted in December 2022, which sets out 23 targets to halt and reverse biodiversity loss by 2030 and four long-term goals for 2050.
According to the report, nearly 90 percent of the CBD's 196 Parties have established national biodiversity targets, close to 60 percent have developed national biodiversity strategies and action plans, and over 70 percent have submitted national reports. Indigenous peoples and local communities, subnational governments, businesses and civil society organizations have also registered around 5,000 commitments.
However, such widespread engagement has not yet translated into sufficient progress. None of the 23 global targets presents a fully positive picture, and fewer than half of the national targets assessed by Parties are currently on track, the report found.
While national targets address an average of 22 of the 23 global targets, many fail to cover their full scope. For instance, far fewer countries have committed to reducing harmful subsidies under Target 18 than promoting positive incentives, and current national pledges under Target 3 fall well short of the goal to conserve 30 percent of land and sea by 2030.
The report identified gaps in financing and other means of implementation, whole-of-government and whole-of-society action, as well as data and knowledge needed to track progress. Targets requiring action beyond environment ministries -- including business action, sustainable consumption, harmful incentives and finance -- are among those lagging furthest behind.
"The report shows that many of the critical elements of progress, including finance, capacity, cooperation and data, are still missing in action," Guterres said. "Nature won't thrive on good intentions."
The UN chief called for greater financial and technical support, particularly for developing countries, the reform of harmful subsidies, nature-positive investment, and stronger integration of biodiversity across public policies and budgets.
"The very biodiversity we depend on needs tangible progress, not more promises," Inger Andersen, executive director of the UN Environment Programme, said in the report's foreword, urging immediate action to overcome implementation challenges.
The report will inform the first global review of collective progress under the framework at COP17, scheduled for Oct. 19 through 30 in Yerevan. ■
