5 killed in Yemen palace strike as Houthis claim hit on Saudi jet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
21:07:00 UTC
06:07:00 KST

At least five people were killed and 16 wounded Thursday when Yemen's Houthi forces struck the presidential palace complex in the southern city of Aden, as the group also claimed to have hit a Saudi fighter jet amid escalating hostilities with the Saudi-led coalition.
The missile and drone attack targeted Al-Maashiq palace, the headquarters of Yemen's internationally recognized, Saudi-backed government, marking the first such strike on the complex in the latest round of fighting.
Yemeni Health Minister Qasim Buhaibeh said the casualties included security guards and civilian employees, while Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani confirmed that the prime minister and Cabinet members were unharmed.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree claimed responsibility for the attack, saying the group had targeted what it described as a Saudi military operations headquarters in Aden.
The Houthi-run SABA news agency alleged that Saudi officers operated the facility and that it housed weapons depots, claims that could not be independently verified.
Meanwhile, the Houthis released footage purportedly showing a missile striking a Royal Saudi Air Force Eurofighter Typhoon over Yemen's northern Saada province late Wednesday.
Saree claimed the fighter jet, which reportedly departed from Saudi Arabia's Taif Air Base, had been directly hit and was at risk of crashing.
However, the infrared footage appeared to show a missile detonating near the aircraft rather than striking it directly, with the pilot apparently maneuvering away from the explosion.
A visible trail from the aircraft's left wing raised speculation about possible damage from missile fragments, although neither the extent of any damage nor the authenticity of the footage could be independently confirmed.
Saudi authorities have not confirmed the incident, and there have been no verified reports of a fighter jet being shot down.
The missile involved was believed by some observers to be a Barq surface-to-air missile, a weapon associated with Houthi air defense systems and reportedly linked to Iranian missile technology.
The alleged engagement came as Saudi Arabia accused the Houthis of intensifying missile and drone attacks against airports, ports and energy infrastructure across the kingdom.
Saudi-led coalition spokesperson Turki al-Maliki said Thursday that Houthi forces had launched 20 attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh this month, killing 17 people and injuring 333 others.
Separate attacks on Abha airport in southwestern Saudi Arabia killed three people and wounded 28, according to the coalition.
Maliki accused the Houthis of acquiring advanced weapons, including ballistic missiles, drones and explosive-laden boats, with assistance from regional actors.
He also said coalition forces had destroyed 127 weapons storage facilities and launch platforms in Yemen.
The coalition separately announced that it had intercepted and destroyed drones over Khamis Mushait and another area in southern Saudi Arabia.
Following the developments, the Houthis warned airlines that Saudi airspace and airports were unsafe, excluding the airspace above the holy cities of Mecca and Medina.
The renewed violence follows the collapse of a prolonged lull in Yemen's civil war, which began in 2014 when the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa, prompting a Saudi-led military intervention the following year.
Fighting resumed last month amid a broader regional conflict that erupted following U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran in February.
Yemeni government forces have since launched operations to recapture Houthi-held territory, including areas near the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a vital route for international shipping.
Humanitarian organizations have warned that the renewed fighting risks worsening Yemen's already severe humanitarian crisis.

KFC to switch to Coca-Cola beverages in U.S. restaurants for the first time in decades
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
21:03:50 UTC
06:03:50 KST

KFC's U.S. restaurants will ditch PepsiCo and switch to Coca-Cola beverages next year, marking the first time in decades that the Yum Brands chain has changed its drink supplier, the restaurant company said Thursday.
Some of KFC's international markets serve Coke products, but the chain's U.S. restaurants have stuck with PepsiCo drinks ever since Pepsi bought KFC in 1986. At the time of the acquisition, KFC was Coke's second-largest fountain account, trailing only McDonald's. Pepsi later spun off KFC, along with sister chains Pizza Hut and Taco Bell — but even as the combined Yum Brands, the company stayed loyal to its previous owner. Without Pepsi, Taco Bell would not serve its iconic Mountain Dew Baja Blast.
The change comes as KFC aims to win back U.S. diners, who have ditched the fried chicken chain for rivals such as Chick-fil-A or Popeyes.
"This decision is a critical step in the Kentucky Fried Comeback," KFC U.S. President Catherine Tan-Gillespie wrote in a memo to franchisees and employees obtained by CNBC. "A new beverage offering, with a new partner in Coca-Cola, gives us a platform to innovate, meet changing tastes and give customers more reasons to choose us."
For many fast-food chains, beverages have become a critical way to attract consumers. A number of restaurants, including McDonald's and Taco Bell, have broadened their drink offerings with options such as refreshers or "dirty soda." For its part, KFC recently unveiled new drinks, including iced coffees and shakes, at Open House, its innovation restaurant in McKinney, Texas.
Coke told CNBC earlier this year that the company has helped many of its restaurant partners create new drinks.
KFC expects to be pouring Coke beverages in all of its U.S. restaurants by the end of the first quarter of 2027, Tan-Gillespie said.
Tan-Gillespie also said that Pepsi remains an important partner for KFC's parent company and the chain's international markets.
For decades, Coke and Pepsi have tussled over important restaurant partners, which represent both a sales opportunity and the chance to grow the visibility of their beverage brands.
It is unusual for large restaurant chains to switch beverage providers, but not unprecedented. In 2024, Pepsi poached Subway, the largest U.S. restaurant chain by number of locations, from Coke. Besides KFC, Coke has wooed away a number of notable Pepsi customers in recent years, including Culver's, Arby's and Panda Express.

ICE tactics spark debate before pivotal US midterm elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
21:02:31 UTC
06:02:31 KST

ICE tactics spark debate before pivotal US midterm elections
Polls have found that Trump’s hardline immigration enforcement effort has divided voters before the 2026 midterm race.
United States President Donald Trump’s mandate for aggressive immigration enforcement has fractured public support in advance of next month’s critical midterm elections.
In the lead-up to the November 3 vote, Fox News released a poll that found 53 percent of registered voters felt the immigration crackdown had “gone too far”.
That rate was even higher among demographics that may be key to the Republican Party’s prospects in November.
The poll, conducted in September, found that 60 percent of independent voters agreed with the idea that Trump’s immigration efforts have overreached. Two-thirds of Hispanic participants also agreed with the campaign having “gone too far”.
Experts say the political debate about immigration in the US has shifted since the last major election in 2024. At the time, the focus was largely on border security. But increasingly, attention has fallen on how enforcement operations are being conducted.
Cynthia Penaloza is among those questioning the Trump administration’s tactics.
In August, her sister, 23-year-old Joceline Penaloza Magana, was arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in Houston, Texas, during a traffic stop. Joceline remains in custody to this day.
“We’re always afraid. We’re uncertain of what’s going to happen, if she’s going to be sent back to Mexico, if we’re ever going to be together again or how this is going to change our lives forever,” Cynthia told Al Jazeera correspondent Phil Lavelle.
She rejects Trump’s assertion that his administration’s immigration enforcement operations have targeted “the worst of the worst”.
Joceline, according to the Penaloza family, was an honour roll student who does not have a criminal record. She was brought to the US as a young child, about five years old.
“She’s always been a good girl,” Cynthia told Lavelle.
A focus on ‘criminals’
Still, the Trump administration has tied its campaign of mass deportation to efforts to control crime.
In a statement earlier this year, the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees immigration enforcement, credited Trump’s policies with having “unleashed ICE to target the worst of the worst criminal illegal aliens, including pedophiles, murderers, gang members, terrorists, and rapists”.
Immigration arrests have been on the rise under Trump. In September, ICE announced it had tallied two consecutive months with more than 50,000 immigration arrests, beating a record set in June, when 43,900 people were detained.
Homeland Security has argued that approximately 70 percent of its immigration detainees are criminals, if pending charges are factored in.
But critics have questioned that statistic, given that the legal system in the US gives suspects the presumption of innocence until they are proven guilty in a court of law.
In other words, many of the accused could be acquitted or see their charges dropped. A large portion of those with criminal charges may also be accused of non-violent crimes.
Analysts have found that a majority of people currently in immigration custody are not considered criminals under the law. According to the Deportation Data Project, which analyses government data sets, some 70 percent of those held in ICE detention have no criminal record.
The Trump administration has nevertheless pushed to increase detentions.
“We need more. We need more arrests, and we need more deportations,” Tom Homan, the White House “border czar”, said in an interview in July.
Pushback on the campaign trail
The aggressive arrest tactics may have repercussions on the Republican campaign for the midterms, though.
Republicans are hoping to defend their majorities in both chambers of Congress, as well as in key state and local elections.
Trump made significant gains in the 2024 elections with Hispanic voters. During his re-election bid, he received nearly 48 percent support among Latinos, according to an exit poll from the Pew Research Center — up 12 percentage points from the 2020 election.
But Pew found that his gains may be eroding. Among the Hispanic voters who supported him in 2024, his approval rating has steadily declined, from a high of 93 percent at the start of 2025 to a low of 57 percent as of last week.
Some Republicans running in the midterm election, including Congress member Maria Elvira Salazar of Florida, have even openly criticised the president’s hardline immigration policies.
“Mr President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far,” Salazar said in an advertisement campaign launched in September. She cited the large number of immigrants who were arrested without a criminal record.
Other Republicans, however, blame previous presidencies for creating the conflict over immigration enforcement.
“A mess was created, and now cleaning it up is dirty business,” Jeremy Price, a Republican in Texas, told Al Jazeera. “You’re having to find people, arrest them against their will and remove them from the country because they don’t want to leave.”
Democrats, meanwhile, hope to convert that outrage over immigration enforcement tactics into votes, come November.
“I would hope they’d abolish ICE,” Richard Gonzales, the chair of the Hidalgo County Democratic Party in Texas, said in an interview with Al Jazeera’s Lavelle.
“I mean, in my perspective, I think that they’ve, the agency has just lost its identity, and there’s no way to rehabilitate that.”

AI Hacks Leave a Mess That AI Companies Aren’t Paying For
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
21:00:28 UTC
06:00:28 KST

When Philadelphia police criticized Anthropic last week for submitting a false tip about an unsolved murder, I thought it might become one of the first cases where an AI company faced legal consequences for misconduct by their agents.
The incident occurred on July 18, when Anthropic said it was testing its Claude Haiku 4.5 model’s ability to perform “example tasks on randomly selected webpages.” The model was instructed not to “submit anything destructive,” and yet, Claude filed a tip to police looking for information about an ongoing murder investigation. “I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area … during that time period,” Claude wrote. The submission, which didn’t include a name or contact information, landed in a spam folder, and officers didn’t review it until Anthropic discovered the gaffe on September 28 and notified the department October 7.
Knowingly providing fictitious information about a crime to police is a misdemeanor in Pennsylvania, but so far, authorities have not pressed charges against Anthropic, and it's unclear if they ever will. Solomon Leach, a spokesperson for the Philadelphia district attorney, says the office “does not comment on whether something is being actively investigated.”
Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Despite all the attention paid to OpenAI’s hack of Hugging Face and many other examples of AI agent misbehavior that have come to light in recent months, only one major known lawsuit has been filed seeking to hold model makers liable. That case was brought by an advocacy group, rather than a direct hacking victim.
AI agents have interfered with hobbyist forums, government websites, and various software tools. The victims have shouldered some costs, including for extra strain on their servers and the time they have expended plugging latent security vulnerabilities.
Government regulators, including the European Union, the US Federal Trade Commission, and some US states, are reportedly still investigating OpenAI and Anthropic over the incidents. But a deference across continents toward promoting innovation could enable companies to escape any immediate penalties.
When Rick Elrod, a software engineer living in Germany, noticed a URL shortener he helps maintain behaving oddly recently, he called up two security researchers he was friendly with to see if they could diagnose the issue. The researchers found agents from Anthropic and other providers using the service, known as da.gd, to get around rules the AI labs put in place to control their behavior, Elrod says. (For instance, Anthropic says it limits the length of website addresses Claude can visit to prevent it from taking malicious actions by stuffing data onto the end of the URLs.)
Da.gd’s investigation and ongoing efforts to prevent further abuse of its tool have taken “a fair bit of time,” says Joe Needleman, one of the security researchers providing pro bono assistance. But he and the others supporting da.gd view the situation as a valuable learning opportunity.
“This was eye-opening,” Needleman says, adding that da.gd has “no means and no plans” to seek compensation from Anthropic for the cleanup, since “we saw many agents doing similar activities, not all was attributable to autonomous agents,” and “not all of it was Anthropic alone.”
Sellers of cybersecurity tools are eager to pass the buck to the victims. At an event this week hosted by the bug-hunting software developer Snyk, panelists from the startup, one of its investors, OpenAI, and Google all encouraged organizations to use AI agents to shore up their defenses against, well, other AI agents. “We've got to reinvent everything to match machine scale with machine scale,” said Ed Sim, a general partner at Boldstart Ventures. He and others expressed little interest in regulating AI labs.
Manoj Nair, chief technology and innovation officer at Snyk, said large businesses patch an average of one bug for every eight they find because of limited human resources. But he said it was imperative for people to hand over some of the bug hunting, fixing, and monitoring to AI agents. “You got to get to a point where you can fix everything, because in the age of agentic hacking, “those 10 things are gonna become 100 things before you know it.” He later added that AI “is not an adversity if you flip it to a strength.”
Some companies are responding to the call to arm up. Bank of America announced this week it had hired 1,000 contractors to remediate bugs discovered by AI. Nair said just last week he heard from major corporations who were willing to temporarily shut down their systems to prioritize plugging security holes.
Anthropic and OpenAI have said they expect to continue reporting concerning incidents from their own testing. But the companies’ revenues continue to surge, whether it be from attackers or defenders, as consequences prove elusive.

Three children and one teacher have been killed in a shooting at an elementary school in the northwestern US state of Oregon, police said, in which the shooter was also killed.
"The deceased at the scene include three children, ages five, eight, and 11, and one teacher," Mike Krantz, Chief of Police at the Bend Police Department, told reporters on Thursday hours after the shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School.
"We have identified the suspect as a 16-year-old Bend resident," Krantz said, adding that "the suspect had been shot by a community member who had seen the suspect enter the school and pursued him into the school and engaged him."
Officials said they were alerted to respond to a critical scene at 1:00 pm local time, and that police were on the scene approximately two minutes later.

Bend-La Pine Schools Superintendent Steven Cook said they are "stunned and heartbroken by this senseless tragedy."
Cook extended his deepest sympathy to the families and to everyone affected by "the violence."
"No words can adequately express the grief our community is experiencing. Our immediate priorities are caring for our students and staff and assisting law enforcement and emergency responders," he said.
World's most heavily armed society
The United States, where firearms are readily available, is a frequent scene of gun violence, with thousands of people killed every year.
It has the highest rate of gun-related deaths among all developed nations.
The deadliest school shooting in US history took place at Virginia Tech on April 16, 2007, when South Korean student Seung-Hui Cho killed 32 people and wounded 17 others before taking his own life.
There have been more than 360 mass shootings in the United States so far this year, according to the Gun Violence Archive, which defines a mass shooting as four or more people shot.
Persistent mass shootings in the US have repeatedly heightened public calls for stricter federal gun control measures.
Despite repeated calls over the years, the US Congress has yet to enact such restrictions.
The United States holds the highest rate of civilian firearm ownership globally, making it the world's most heavily armed society.

Zelensky rallies European allies as Trump ties slump
Unknown

Zelensky rallies European allies as Trump ties slump
BRUSSELS – Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky sought to rally European allies on Oct 15 after saying Kyiv would no longer abide by US President Donald Trump’s demands not to strike Russian oil refineries.
Relations between Kyiv and Washington have soured since last week, when Trump eased sanctions on Russia in exchange for Moscow releasing large amounts of diesel onto global markets.
Anger in Ukraine has been further heightened by outages to a critical US-provided satellite system that have hampered its military’s ability to counter Russia’s intense bombardments.
Zelensky had told the Financial Times that the pause in strikes against Russian refineries was “done”, as Moscow was not abiding by the ceasefire on hitting energy infrastructure that had been announced by Trump.
In response, Trump called the renewed Ukrainian attacks a “disgrace” and said Kyiv was driving up global energy prices. “I think I find Zelensky to be more difficult to deal with than Putin,” the US leader said in an interview with Newsmax published on Oct 15.
European leaders, in contrast, have broadly thrown their support behind Zelensky, as they look to weather the latest storm in Trump’s volatile relations with Kyiv.
French President Emmanuel Macron on Oct 15 said it was “crucial” that Ukraine receive “all the means necessary to protect itself”, after meeting Zelensky.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk posted online: “I can reassure you, dear Ukrainian friends and President Zelensky: You are not alone.”
The Ukrainian President met NATO chief Mark Rutte in Brussels on Oct 15 and held a string of bilateral meetings with European leaders, and will join an EU summit on Oct 16.
“All of us in Europe want this war to end. And for that to happen, strong signals are needed – more real pressure on Russia and more defence support for Ukraine,” Zelensky wrote online.
“It is especially important now to act together to protect lives.”
‘Maximum destruction’
As he met Macron in Brussels, Zelensky said that the Kremlin had “launched yet another vile drone strike on Ukrainian energy infrastructure” in the city of Lutsk, causing blackouts.
“Russia has demonstratively disregarded the American President’s proposal for an energy ceasefire. And now it is taking advantage of problems with Starlink operations to cause maximum destruction to everything that sustains everyday life,” he wrote online.
The Kremlin, meanwhile, accused Ukraine of derailing US peace efforts by resuming its strikes on refineries, with the Russian authorities reporting a drone attack on an oil refinery south of Moscow that caused a fire.
Kyiv “continues to launch strikes against these facilities”, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters. “It is coming into serious conflict with the peace efforts of the United States and American negotiators, who are making vigorous efforts to initiate the peace process,” he added.
In Kyiv, residents told AFP they sensed a change in Washington’s attitude towards Ukraine.
“Let them live here for two to three days,” said Alyona Nikitina, 30. “All these night-time attacks, what people here are going through – blackouts, no electricity. And then maybe (Trump) will see all this differently.”
Russia has intensified its bombardment of Ukraine and its capital in recent months, leading to mounting civilian casualties and disrupting daily life for citizens.
Satellite row
Much of the outrage in Ukraine this week has been over restrictions to the Starshield satellite communications system that its military relies upon to detect incoming Russian attacks and to coordinate its front-line response.
Defence officials confirmed that the US had threatened to withdraw intelligence-sharing if Ukraine continued long-range strikes on Russian oil refineries.
But tech billionaire Elon Musk, who has also called for Zelensky to be replaced as leader, said his SpaceX company was not behind any disruption to the Starshield system.
“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government,” he said.
“Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” he added, referring to Trump.
Ukraine uses the Starshield system from Musk’s SpaceX for battlefield communications, mid-range strikes on Russian-occupied territory and interceptor drones.
It is separate from the parallel Starlink civilian satellite system, which Ukraine also uses but not for offensive operations.
Speeds were slower on Oct 14, affecting connectivity, officials said. AFP

Defence writes off millions owed since the seventies
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
21:51:53 BST
05:51:53 KST

A write-off of almost £3.7m recorded in the Ministry of Defence’s accounts relates to money owed to the department by a foreign nation between 1971 and 2006, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked why the International Military Services outstanding claim write-off appeared in the annual report and accounts for 2024 to 2025, published on 4 November last year.
Luke Pollard, the Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, said: “The write off was due to a historical debt balance relating to monies owed to MOD between 1971 and 2006 by a foreign nation.”
International Military Services was the Ministry of Defence’s own arms sales company, set up to handle government-to-government defence exports and wound down from the mid-1980s. It has been in members’ voluntary liquidation for decades and exists now mainly to deal with the legal and financial tail of contracts signed half a century ago. Balances dating back to 1971 are therefore still passing through departmental accounts in 2026.
The best known of those tails is the long dispute with Iran over tanks ordered by the Shah before the 1979 revolution and never delivered. That case ran through the English courts and international arbitration for more than forty years and ended with a settlement, reported at around £400 million, paid in 2022 at the same time as the release of Nazanin Zaghari-Ratcliffe and Anoosheh Ashoori. The write-off described here is a separate and far smaller item, and the department has not identified the country involved.
Losses and special payments of this kind are reported each year in a department’s accounts under Treasury rules, with any individual item above a threshold disclosed and explained. A debt that has sat on the books for decades is eventually written off when there is no realistic prospect of recovery, which is an accounting decision and not a forgiveness of the obligation.

Houthis launch deadly attack on Yemen presidential palace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
20:51:32 UTC
05:51:32 KST

Breadcrumb
Houthis launch deadly attack on presidential palace in Yemen's Aden
The Houthis launched a deadly missile attack Thursday on the presidential palace in the Yemeni government's interim capital of Aden, as Saudi Arabia blamed Iran for the recent dramatic escalation in the long-running war.
The attack hit command centres located inside the presidential compound used by government forces and the Saudi-led military coalition that supports them, a Yemeni minister said on condition of anonymity.
Saudi Arabia and the internationally recognised Yemeni government it backs have come under sustained Houthi attack of late, shifting the focus of the wider Middle East war that erupted with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in February.
The Iran-backed Houthis have seized swathes of territory along Yemen's Red Sea coastline in recent weeks, and a government counteroffensive with Saudi air support has so far failed to reverse the gains.
Government military sources in Yemen said at least four people were killed and 10 wounded in Thursday's strikes on Aden's Al-Maashiq palace in the divided country's south.
An AFP journalist saw smoke rising and residents of the city reported hearing explosions during the attack, the first on the complex since Yemen's civil war flared back to life in July.
A government minister said on condition of anonymity that Prime Minister Shaya al-Zindani had been present at the time, but "was not harmed in any way".
The minister said the Houthis hit a command centre for Yemeni government forces with three missiles, and another for Saudi-led coalition forces at the complex with two missiles, adding that there were Yemeni and Saudi casualties, without providing a specific toll.
Media affiliated with the Houthis said they had targeted "the headquarters of military operations, led by Saudi officers, at the Al-Maashiq Palace in Aden, as well as weapons depots belonging to them".
Yemen's civil war - in which Saudi Arabia has led a military coalition supporting the government since 2015 - reignited after the collapse of a years-long truce, with the Houthis going on to launch their lightning offensive in September.
Riyadh on Thursday accused Iran of encouraging the escalation, saying it continued to arm and train the group.
Saudi Arabia's deputy minister for public diplomacy at the foreign ministry said Riyadh was still in touch with Iran, but that Tehran did not appear ready to make concessions.
"We think that the escalation by the Houthis at this latest stage of the conflict is encouraged by Iran," said Dr. Rayed Krimly.
The Saudi-led coalition said drones fired by the Houthis at the kingdom's southern region and the city of Khamis Mushait were intercepted.
Yemeni government forces said the Houthis had also fired "several ballistic missiles" at the central city of Marib, which sits in a strategic oil-rich region.
Oman meeting refused
In 2023, regional rivals Iran and Saudi Arabia reached a deal mediated by China to thaw a longstanding freeze in ties, but the latest violence might threaten to upend the entente.
The Saudi ministry official went on to accuse the Houthis of refusing to meet as fighting ramped up between the two sides.
"At the beginning of this escalation, we asked them to meet in Muscat, Oman and they refused," he added.
The ministry later said that the exchange took place in July.
Saudi Arabia suffered its deadliest attack in more than a decade on Saturday when a strike on Riyadh's international airport killed 13 people and wounded around 300 others.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said the group had attacked Riyadh's airport 20 times this month.
Coalition spokesman Turki Al-Malki said "the Houthis must immediately cease all terrorist operations targeting civilians and civilian facilities, including airports, ports, oil facilities, and infrastructure".
He added the group had "worked to obtain advanced technologies with the help of regional actors", saying they now had "ballistic missiles, attack and suicide drones, and fast explosive-laden boats".
The attacks on Saudi Arabia have tested the country's infrastructure and resilience, the energy minister acknowledged earlier this week.
Riyadh usually hosts a packed calendar of events this time of year, including its flagship investment conference drawing foreign leaders and business titans.
In Yemen, the conflict has caused what the United Nations calls one of the world's worst humanitarian crises, leaving most of the nation's population dependent on aid.
(AFP)

Ukraine Accuses Captured Russian Soldier of Executing Five Unarmed Troops, Killing Civilian
Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU) has charged a captured Russian soldier with killing five unarmed Ukrainian servicemen and a civilian, according to the Security Service of Ukraine on October 15.
The suspect was identified as 36-year-old St. Petersburg resident Leonid Ryzhikov, call sign “Yula.” He served in the 2nd Battalion of Russia’s 1009th Motorized Rifle Regiment, part of the 68th Motorized Rifle Division.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The SBU stated that Ryzhikov fled Russian positions near Starytsia in the Kharkiv region after coming under Ukrainian fire on October 5-6. Armed with an AK-74, he moved toward Kharkiv on foot and stole civilian clothing from an abandoned house.
Investigators allege that on October 13, Ryzhikov shot and killed a 60-year-old civilian fishing near Mykhailivka before pushing his body into the water. Later that day, he allegedly entered a house in Momotove and killed five Ukrainian servicemen who were unarmed and wearing civilian clothes. Some were asleep at the time.
The SBU noted that the five servicemen were not participating in hostilities at the time and were protected under the Geneva Convention. Ryzhikov allegedly hid his rifle near a gardening community and continued toward Kharkiv while concealing himself in forest belts.
The SBU, National Police, and National Guard detained Ryzhikov in Kharkiv’s Saltivskyi district on October 14 and recovered his AK-74. He was charged under Article 438 of Ukraine’s Criminal Code for war crimes resulting in deaths and faces life imprisonment.
Violence by Russian servicemen in the Kharkiv region has also turned inward.
On October 25, 2025, Alexey Korolev, a soldier recruited from prison after seven criminal convictions, allegedly shot dead six fellow troops and wounded two others near Lyman Pershyi during Russia's offensive around Kupiansk.
Among the dead was a specialist from the FSB's highly classified 16th Center, a unit focused on signals intelligence and cyber espionage. Korolev now faces murder and extortion charges in a closed-door military court in temporarily occupied Donetsk.

Europe Provides Two-Thirds of Intelligence to Ukraine, French Foreign Minister Reveals

What Is Starshield, SpaceX's Military Version of Starlink, and Why Is It So Important to Ukraine?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
20:44:33 UTC
05:44:33 KST

Ukrainian forces said Wednesday its battlefield efforts had been hampered overnight after losing some access to SpaceX’s military-grade satellite Internet service, which has become a lifeline as Kyiv weathers Moscow's attacks.
Starlink offers Internet connectivity from satellites in low-Earth orbit. Its sister service Starshield, a military version developed for the Pentagon, relies on the Starlink network and has recently been used by Ukrainian forces to strengthen its far-reaching drone strike missions and air defenses.
Serhiy Beskrestnov, a military technology expert who advises Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, said speed restrictions had been imposed on the "military package" of Starshield services, leading to the “failure” of several military missions. “Our defense forces have not received any warnings about this restriction,” he said. Beskrestnov claimed the restrictions, which he said applied to devices traveling over 100 miles per hour and using Starshield, were “related to the current political situation.” He did not offer further details.
Tensions are high between the U.S. and Ukraine, as Zelensky has been vocal in his disapproval of U.S. President Donald Trump’s plan to import diesel from Russia, despite previous sanctions prohibiting it. The move has also caused a split in Trump’s own party, with several Republican lawmakers urging him to reverse course. After making the deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin last week, Trump announced an “energy cease-fire” between Russia and Ukraine—but Zelensky swiftly accused Moscow of violating any such agreement and Ukraine has, in turn, resumed strikes on Russian oil refineries, despite pressure from Washington. Trump called Ukraine's fresh wave of strikes on Russian refineries a "disgrace" in an interview that aired Thursday.
Speaking from the U.K., Zelensky said Wednesday it was a “pity” Ukrainian forces had experienced “difficulties” with Starlink services and intelligence, adding that he was surprised by the developments in Ukraine’s partnership with the U.S. In an interview on Piers Morgan Uncensored, Zelensky suggested he believed Starlink had been slowed down to damage him, and warned “people will die, if attacks will continue and if Starlink will not work … it’s not helpful.” He said he hoped the restriction was only a “mistake,” suggesting it was perhaps "a huge technical problem” at SpaceX.
However, in another interview, Zelensky said: "It was not a technical problem, it was the will.”
SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk addressed the matter, insisting that Starlink and Starshield are different. He cited the U.S. authorities as being in control of the latter’s usage determinations.
“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military and ultimately POTUS,” he said on X. “Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company.”
When approached for comment, a senior U.S. official told TIME: “No such request was ever made by the President.”
Reuters, citing three U.S. officials, later reported that the decision came from inside the White House.
TIME has reached out to the White House for further comment.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian national news agency Ukrinform reported Thursday, citing sources within the Ministry of Defense, that the Starshield service had resumed. TIME has reached out to Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense for comment.
The discourse has raised questions about what Starshield is and how uniquely important it has become on the Ukrainian battlefield.
What is Starshield?
Starshield is a program developed by Musk’s SpaceX that draws on the satellite and launch capability behind Starlink, its commercial satellite Internet network, to support national security operations.
According to SpaceX, Starshield is designed for government use, with an initial focus on three areas: Earth observation, communications, and hosted payloads.
“Starlink is basic interconnectivity, it's like the Internet. Starshield essentially grows out of the experience of Starlink,” Mark Hilborne, a senior lecturer in defense studies at King’s College London, tells TIME.
But the military value of that connectivity extends far beyond access to the Internet, Hilborne adds.
“In and of itself, satellite communications are not military technology, but it enables the military to communicate and amass a real-time, multi-domain picture of the battlefield, which some argue nobody else actually has at this stage,” he says.
Both systems also offer high-speed connectivity because of the satellite technology underpinning them.
“Starlink and Starshield are low on the Earth’s orbit, and they have a very high bandwidth, so lots of information can pass through those satellites, with virtually no delay on the signal,” Hilborne says.
There are more than 10,000 satellites in the Starlink network, while Hilborne says Starshield uses “a much smaller number of satellites.” However, the exact number of satellites associated with Starshield remains unknown, with experts telling TIME that such details are closely guarded due to national security considerations.
“They keep the contracting details on these things classified,” says Todd Harrison, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute.
SpaceX, on its website, says Starshield is “designed to support U.S. National Defense use cases for the Department of Defense and other government partners.”
How is Starshield different from Starlink?
While both systems rely on closely related satellite technology, they differ in the services they provide and how they are intended to be used.
“Starshield refers to military services that actually operate through Starlink,” Harrison explains, comparing the services to “two different brands of a cell phone provider, even though your phone calls are going through the same towers.”
Starshield offers additional capabilities designed for military operations, including more advanced encryption and satellite imaging, experts tell TIME.
“It's got another extra set of capabilities over and above Starlink,” Hilborne says. “They use some of the same technologies, but it would be highly encrypted, and they have different sensors that allow them to image what they call ‘Earth observation.’ That can give a radar imaging of the Earth [which] has advantages over optical pictures.”
Yet experts say the distinction between the two systems is not always clear, particularly given how closely their underlying technology and operations are connected.
How important is Starshield for Ukraine?
Starshield and the satellite communications technology underpinning it have become vital to Ukraine’s military operations against Russia.
Hilborne describes the technology as “highly critical” to Ukraine, explaining that any restrictions could cut communications with military equipment traveling above that speed, leaving operators without the information needed to guide their missions, as once that speed threshold is exceeded, the connection “suddenly cuts off and it's flying blind,” he says.
The consequences are particularly serious for Ukrainian drone operations, which rely on communications for both strikes against Russian targets and defensive missions against incoming attacks.
“It's really critical for drones, both the offensive medium range strikes, but also affects Ukraine's ability to fly defensive drones against the incoming Russian drones,” says Hilborne.
Beyond its role in drone missions, experts say satellite communications also offer important advantages over other forms of battlefield connectivity.
Harrison notes that “the big benefit of using satellite-based communications is that you can communicate over longer distances in a variety of terrain, and it does have some jam-resistant features to overcome electronic forms of attack.”

NATO is considering deploying additional counter-drone capabilities to the Black Sea region following a series of attacks on civilian shipping.
Romanian President Nicușor Dan told Politico about this.
According to the publication, Bulgaria, Romania, and Turkey raised this issue with NATO and asked the Alliance to pay more attention to the region’s security and provide joint support.
On October 15, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte discussed security in the Black Sea and the recent attacks on merchant ships with Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev and Romanian President Nicușor Dan.
After the meeting, Rutte stated that the Alliance has already strengthened its eastern flank defenses, in particular, by enhancing its capabilities to counter drones, and will continue to adapt its defensive posture in line with the situation.
On October 12, Bulgaria appealed to the European Union and NATO for technical assistance in investigating drone attacks on merchant ships in its exclusive economic zone.
Bulgaria also agreed with Romania to intensify trilateral cooperation with Turkey to protect shipping in the Black Sea.
Tighter security measures are being discussed following a series of attacks on merchant ships near Bulgaria and Romania. On October 6, aerial and maritime drones attacked the vessels ALFA WATAN and ABLE in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone.
The ALFA WATAN sustained critical damage and sank, while a fire broke out on the ABLE.
The Bulgarian government officially confirmed the attack on the two merchant ships by aerial and maritime drones. Following an exchange of information between Ukrainian and Bulgarian officials, Ukraine stated that this was a combined Russian attack.
On October 13, drones attacked two more merchant ships near the Bulgarian coast. One of them was the Chelsea 3, owned by a Ukrainian company. The Bulgarian government reported conducting a rescue operation following the attack.
Attacks have also been reported near Romania. On October 14, an unidentified drone struck the tanker YARA J near Sulina in the country’s territorial waters.

Trump addresses Michigan synagogue as antisemitism event sparks Jewish community backlash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
20:41:56 UTC
05:41:56 KST

President Donald Trump addressed a Michigan synagogue by video Wednesday evening as part of an event orchestrated by Leo Terrell, chair of the administration’s task force for combating antisemitism, and the Zionist Organization of America.
Trump’s greeting, which was prerecorded, was met with applause from the estimated 500 Jews who had come to Congregation Shaarey Zedek in the Detroit suburbs amid a pivotal Senate election in the state that has prompted deep anxieties among its Jewish population.
The president told the crowd that Terrell “speaks for our country” and “speaks for a lot of people, a lot of people that love Israel but really, more than anything else, they don’t want to see false and inaccurate statements made about this horrible subject of antisemitism.”
The event was billed as the first stop on Terrell’s “American Tour Against Hate” and was staged by the US Justice Department, while also serving as a fundraiser and booster for ZOA. Attendees were handed donation forms for ZOA’s Michigan chapter. The organization’s national director, Mort Klein, is close with Terrell and said he intends to participate in all future stops on the tour.
Several other Trump officials, including Terrell and US Attorney General Todd Blanche, would address the crowd over the course of the night to emphasize the administration’s efforts to combat antisemitism.
(L-r) Leo Terrell, chair of the Trump administration’s Task Force to Combat Antisemitism, with US Department of Labor official Kenneth Wolfe at an event to combat antisemitism at Congregation Shaarey Zedek in Southfield, Michigan, on Oct. 14, 2026. (Andrew Lapin/JTA)
Michigan Jewish leaders accuse Trump administration of politicizing antisemitism
A group of progressive-leaning Michigan Jewish leaders denounced the event Wednesday, saying in a statement that it “risks fueling antisemitism and dividing the Jewish community.”
The statement accused the administration of trying to “distract” from its own “authoritarian policies,” called ZOA “a far-right radical group” and criticized the Trump administration for its campus antisemitism policies, including freezing university funding and “kidnap[ping] university students.”
The Trump administration has been criticized for its handling of some anti-Israel campus protesters, including Tufts University student Rumeysa Ozturk, who was grabbed and detained by masked federal agents last year after co-authoring an op-ed calling to boycott Israel. A judge later ordered Ozturk’s release.
“Trump’s cynical use of antisemitism as a tool for stifling his opponents puts all Jews in danger, ” Rabbi Josh Whinston, of Temple Beth Emeth in Ann Arbor, said in the statement. “We should all be uniting to fight the real issues of antisemitism rather than using it to score political points and stifle dissent.”
Michigan Democratic state Rep. Samantha Steckloff, who represents Shaarey Zedek’s district, said in the same release that the administration was taking advantage of “an extremely challenging time for the Metro Detroit Jewish community.”
“We must continue building bridges with our neighbors to create safer communities, not put up walls,” Steckloff said. “This administration has continued to espouse divisive rhetoric that pits communities against one another and deepens the challenges we face. All of us deserve to feel safe.”
Kobi Erez, director of ZOA’s Michigan chapter, told the Jewish Telegraphic Agency after the event that the evening was designed to be “nonpartisan.”
“It’s a tour against hate, and we can’t choose one side,” Erez said. “We have to fight antisemitism and hate for all.”
He argued that the event was not a ZOA fundraiser in his view, saying that it was free to attend and that the organization was asking for donations mainly to cover security costs.
He also said that the organization had been in touch with the head rabbi of Shaarey Zedek, Aaron Star, to address any concerns about the nature of the event so close to Election Day. “We had to promise Rabbi Starr that we were going to make a disclaimer that Shaarey Zedek doesn’t necessarily represent all the views of the speakers.”
Terrell did make that disclaimer, midway through the two-hour event.
Starr told JTA that there had been a back-and-forth with ZOA over the Trump video due to “a string of miscommunications and some last minute changes over the course of the day.”
Michigan Senate race deepens divisions among Jewish voters
Polls have shown that a majority of Jews nationwide have opposed Trump and his policies since his entry on the political scene. Yet recent fears about growing antisemitism and anti-Israel sentiment on the left have also alienated many Jews from the Democratic Party.
Some Michigan Jews are preparing to vote for a Republican for the first time over their objections to the Democratic Senate candidate, Abdul El-Sayed, a harsh critic of Israel whose prior remarks on Jewish safety have also upset many in the community.
Starr and Whinston, the rabbi who signed the letter denouncing the entire Trump event, are the co-organizers of Nonnegotiable Michigan, a petition urging El-Sayed to agree with a series of statements affirming Jews and Israel.
El-Sayed’s name was not uttered from the stage Wednesday, but the Trump officials on hand took many opportunities to praise their boss’s work on Jewish issues.
“This administration, unlike any other administration, is committed 24/7 to fighting antisemitism,” Terrell told the crowd.
An estimated 500 Michigan Jews applaud Trump administration officials during an event held to address antisemitism at Congregation Shaarey Zedek in Southfield, Michigan, Oct. 14, 2026. (Andrew Lapin/JTA)
Justice Department, Zionist Organization of America defend antisemitism event
The Conservative synagogue was billed online as a “co-sponsor” of the event along with Frankel Jewish Academy, a local Jewish day school. But Starr told JTA, “It wasn’t our event.”
Midway through the program, Terrell stated that Shaarey Zedek “is not sponsoring this event,” adding, “The words of the speakers, mine and others, are theirs alone and are not a representation of this great religious institution.”
Terrell stated that DOJ and ZOA were the sponsors — itself an unusual arrangement between a federal agency and an activist group. Klein told JTA following the event that Terrell had contacted his organization to help organize the tour, and that ZOA “really did all the work.”
US Attorney General Todd Blanche, who has been criticized for appearing at campaign events and who recently penned a memo loosening restrictions on political activism for senior federal officials, also addressed the crowd in a prerecorded video.
“In recent years, we have seen a disturbing rise in antisemitic rhetoric and acts of hatred against fellow citizens,” Blanche said. “Hate has no place in America, and this Department of Justice remains committed to confronting it wherever it appears.”
Initially billed as a conversation between Terrell and Klein, the event functioned more as an informational session for Jews to learn how their government is responding to antisemitism.
Flyers from the FBI instructed attendees on how to respond to various categories of threat. A roundtable of local and federal law enforcement officials, led by the FBI Detroit office field director who had responded to the terror attack on Temple Israel in the state in March, sought to assure the Jews in attendance that they had their backs.
Terrell also unveiled a just-launched “American Tour Against Hate” app that, he said, would enable its users to take a pledge to fight antisemitism and “report” antisemitic incidents. It wasn’t immediately clear where the reports would be filed to. The Combat Antisemitism Movement, another activist group, was credited for the app on its download page.
Trump administration official Leo Terrell addresses Congregation Shaarey Zedek in Southfield, Michigan, on the first stop of his “American Tour Against Hate,” Oct. 14, 2026. (Andrew Lapin/JTA)
Trump officials highlight antisemitism efforts amid political tensions
Still, politics seeped in, and much of the crowd seemed happy about it. Klein attacked another anti-Zionist politician, New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani, by name in his remarks. He also drew enthusiastic cheers for calling to “fight the open-border policies that we had in the past, which allows unvetted people from countries whose governments and populations overwhelmingly hate Jews.”
Other Jewish speakers alluded to El-Sayed — particularly his initial reaction to the Temple Israel attack, which many Jews believed was equating the attack with Israel’s war in Lebanon. The candidate has since apologized for his initial remarks.
“No conflict overseas can ever justify trying to murder innocent people here at home, and no political candidate should ever excuse terror and hate,” Erez told the crowd.
Later, during an interfaith roundtable, Rabbi Shneur Silberberg of the Bais Chabad Torah Center in West Bloomfield leveled a more direct accusation.
“If you respond differently to a terror attack against a group of Jewish schoolchildren, and your response is any different than it would be to any other group of children, then that’s antisemitism,” Silberberg told the crowd.
During the program, Terrell inveighed against antisemitism with a showman’s flair, often to the delight of the audience, some of whom shouted his name. “News flash: I’m not Jewish. Who cares?” Terrell asked the crowd early on, to laughter and applause. He donned a red hat in the style of Trump’s “Make America Great Again” merchandise, with the lettering instead spelling, “American Tour Against Hate.”
He went after college campuses and K-12 teachers he said were “indoctrinated,” and repeatedly denounced what he called “the Jewish tax,” which he defined as the high security costs the community bears in order to safeguard its houses of worship and other institutions.
Flyers from the Federal Bureau of Investigation laid out on a table during the “American Tour Against Hate,” an event staged by the Trump administration at Congregation Shaarey Zedek in Southfield, Michigan, Oct. 14, 2026. (Andrew Lapin/JTA)
“For you to enjoy your right to walk down the street, to enjoy your synagogue, to go to a Jewish community center, to have your kids walk through their school, you have to pay extra security, millions of dollars,” Terrell said. “That’s going to stop.”
Terrell and Klein plan to meet with the head of Detroit’s Jewish federation as well as with rabbis at Temple Israel during their stay in town, Klein told JTA.
Erez said that Terrell’s visit to Michigan also included meetings with the mother of a Temple Israel preschooler who had been in the building during the March attack, as well as with Jewish college students who had experienced antisemitism. Terrell also met with leaders of Frankel Jewish Academy, one of the event’s co-sponsors, as well as the local Jewish Community Center, he said.
A longtime supporter of Trump, Klein said he believed the event demonstrated that more Jews were warming to the president as concerns about antisemitism have grown.
“I think more Jews certainly are more supportive of Trump than they were before, because they see what he’s done,” he said.
Sharon Matlen, a resident of nearby Farmington Hills who grew up in Skokie, Illinois, during the infamous neo-Nazi march of the 1970s, told JTA she had come to the event because “I’m very interested in antisemitism.”
“I really got a lot out of it,” Matlen said, of the talk. She spoke highly of Terrell: “I think he has our back. I’m glad that he’s there for us.”
Of El-Sayed, she said, “I pray he does not get in.”

Ousted general warned of missile defense shortage before Iran war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
20:39:03 UTC
05:39:03 KST

Ousted general warned of years-long missile defense shortage before Iran war
Washington — In late December, two months before the U.S. war with Iran began, Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George warned that his service was critically short on missile defense munitions and that the shortage would last another five years, according to multiple U.S. officials familiar with the matter. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth ousted George in April, as the Iran war was underway.
George's risk analysis appeared in the Pentagon's Global Force Management Allocation Plan, a defense secretary-approved annual order determining where troops and weapons will be allocated across the globe, according to the U.S. officials who spoke to CBS News.
He warned that the stockpile of Terminal High Altitude Area Defense batteries and Patriot missiles would continue to be strategically low until 2030. His assessment was written for the Defense Department's plan for fiscal year 2027 and before the outbreak of the U.S.-Israel-led war with Iran, now in its seventh month.
U.S. officials who spoke to CBS News under condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly said his assessment stemmed from the transfer of Patriots to Ukraine after Russia's invasion in 2022, the expenditure of munitions to defend Israel, and the reduced capacity of the defense industrial base.
CBS News is withholding the exact percentage figures conveyed by U.S. officials because of security concerns, and George declined to comment. U.S. officials say that while the U.S. possesses a significant stockpile of some offensive munitions, like the Joint Direct Attack Munition and Small Diameter Bombs, missile defense munitions used in Terminal High Altitude Area Defense, or THAAD, batteries, and Patriot missile systems are at low strategic-risk levels.
The THAAD system is one of the U.S. military's most advanced missile defense systems, designed to intercept and destroy incoming ballistic missiles during the final phase of their flight, either inside or just outside Earth's atmosphere. The Army has eight THAAD batteries. Each battery consists of 90 soldiers who operate six truck-mounted launchers, with each truck possessing eight launchers. A full battery controls 48 interceptors, according to a 2025 report from the nonpartisan Congressional Research Service.
The Patriot air-defense system is designed to protect military installations, troops and other critical infrastructure from incoming ballistic and cruise missiles, as well as hostile aircraft. It can engage a broader range of aerial threats at lower altitudes than a THAAD battery, but when used together, they provide even more effective overlapping layers of defense against missile attacks.
The Patriot munition at a critical low is the Patriot Advanced Capability-3, or PAC-3, a high-velocity surface-to-air interceptor designed to destroy incoming tactical ballistic missiles and cruise missiles by ramming into them. PAC-3s can also bring down enemy aircraft, according to U.S. officials who spoke to CBS News.
"Those are the two Army munitions that would be most heavily used in a conflict with China," said Mark Cancian, a retired Marine colonel and CSIS Defense and Security senior adviser. "You're not gonna use that many Javelins, for example, because the amount of ground combat is going to be relatively limited, even artillery will be limited, but air defense — missile defense — that will be huge."
An April estimate from the Center for Strategic and International Studies showed that it currently takes defense contractors four years and five months to complete delivery of new THAAD interceptor contracts. Patriot PAC-3 interceptor orders have an average delivery time of three and a half years.
CSIS' estimate said that before the Iran war, the U.S. entered 2026 with roughly 2,300 or so Patriot interceptors and expended between 1,050 and 1,430 during the conflict, potentially consuming as much as 61% of its prewar inventory. Fewer than 500 replenishment munitions were expected to be delivered in fiscal year 2026.
The stockpile for THAAD systems prior to the Iran war sat at around 355 interceptors, with the Iran war using between 190 to 290, or about 82% of its prewar inventory, according to CSIS. There were no expected deliveries for replenishment in fiscal year 2026. In the current fiscal year — 2027 — the U.S. has requested more than 800 THAADs.
Two of the nation's largest defense contractors — Lockheed Martin and RTX, through its Raytheon business — are involved in manufacturing these systems and their key components. They've recently signed agreements aimed at accelerating production.
In January, Lockheed Martin announced a plan to quadruple the production capacity of THAADs from 96 to 400 interceptors per year.
While the war with Iran has caused missile defense munitions to be depleted at a much higher rate, decades of Pentagon spending decisions, a shrinking defense industrial base and successive military operations that consume weapons faster than manufacturers can replace them have contributed to the current shortages.
One U.S. official told CBS News that even if the United States could avoid expending additional THAAD or Patriot munitions in Iran or in other conflicts, it would take until the midterm elections of the next presidential administration — 2030 — to replenish the stockpile to the already-low December 2025 levels.
Contacted by CBS News, Pentagon chief spokesman Sean Parnell said, "Claims of U.S. munitions shortages are false. When the Fake News media irresponsibly amplifies these lies, the real-world consequences is clear: our enemies are emboldened to provide — or attack — American troops."
He added that the U.S. still has "everything required to strike at the time and place of the President's choosing."
"Across multiple combatant commands," Parnell said, "we have already executed successful operations while maintaining a deep, ready arsenal to defend our people and our interests."
How munitions are used around the world
The U.S. military is divided into 11 unified combatant commands, each responsible for either a region of the world or specialized military mission. For operations against Iran, U.S. Central Command, led by Navy Adm. Brad Cooper, is in charge.
Each combatant command needs a certain number of troops and weapons. The Pentagon uses a framework known as Global Force Management to decide where American troops, their units and some of the military's most sought-after weapons are sent around the world.
The Global Force Management Allocation Plan, or GFMAP, is at the center of the process, laying out which forces will be provided to combatant commanders, for what missions and for how long.
The plan is typically organized around the federal fiscal year. Generally, the Pentagon enters a new fiscal year with an existing plan for many of the forces expected to deploy or remain deployed during the coming 12 to 24 months, rather than deciding from scratch each time a commander asks for troops or weapons.
But the plan is not set in stone. Wars erupt, crises develop, missions end and commanders are faced with unanticipated events to address.
For instance, the commander of U.S. European Command might want more Patriots in Poland at the same time that U.S. Central Command wants those same resources in Kuwait, while U.S. Indo-Pacific Command may also need the systems for contingencies involving China.
There's a constant shuffling of troops and assets from one region to another — in one instance in April 2025, Adm. Samuel Paparo, the commander of U.S. Indo-Pacific Command, told the Senate Armed Services Committee that the Army had transferred a Patriot battalion from his region to U.S. Central Command amid ongoing fighting with the Iranian-back Houthi rebels in Yemen.
What led to the current weapons systems shortage?
After the collapse of the Soviet Union, American military planners abandoned the assumption that the U.S. might need to fight a prolonged war against another superpower, explained Cancian.
"After the Cold War, we planned on fighting short regional conflicts against countries like Iraq or North Korea. And for those countries we didn't need the large inventories that we had needed during the Cold War," Cancian said. "We needed much smaller inventories."
He added: "We shrank the industrial base. There was the famous 'Last Supper' which was literally a dinner that the deputy defense secretary put on for the heads of the defense industry, and he told them there's not enough money to keep you all in business, so you're going to have to consolidate or move out of the business, which they did."
The resulting mergers reduced the number of major aerospace and defense contractors from 51 to five, according to the CSIS analysis.
Also, historically, the Pentagon's procurement decisions have reduced spending on ammunition and missiles to free up money for fighter jets, tanks and warships, even while acknowledging that those weapons are essential to war fighting.
Cancian told CBS News that the consolidation of the defense industrial base shaped an industry that produces efficiently during peacetime but is not designed to surge production.
"We squeezed all the surge out because it was seen as unnecessary. So, that's where we end up when the war in Ukraine begins," said Cancian. "And after six months or so, we realized that we just don't have enough munitions and equipment for a protracted conflict."
Under the Biden administration, there was a renewed interest in building surge capabilities back into the defense industrial base but that would take time. As the war between Russia and Ukraine began in full, the U.S. transferred roughly 600 Patriot interceptor missiles to Ukraine. However, not all of those weapons came from American military stockpiles; some were manufactured through the Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative or provided by European countries.
Additionally, both Biden and Trump administrations used Patriot and THAAD missile interceptors to defend Israel against Iranian strikes. Six months before Gen. George's warning assessment, U.S. forces fired roughly 150 THAAD interceptors and almost 80 Patriot interceptors during the Twelve Day War.
Cancian noted that the five-year timeline to bring Patriot and THAAD stockpiles just to the low pre-Iran war levels is based on the assumption that the production schedule stays on track — and that additional military operations do not further deplete the inventory.

concert design, art spaces, and the mechanics of audience with DuckUnit

concert design, art spaces, and the mechanics of audience with DuckUnit
founded in 2005, the bangkok-based design studio combines creative disciplines to build stage environments and installations shaped by light and movement.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
setting the stage with DuckUnit
Based in Bangkok, Thailand, the design and production studio DuckUnit uses light, mechanical movement, and the possibilities of the stage as its tools for creating spectacular events that range from concerts to contemporary art installations to performance. Founded in 2005 by Wit Pimkanchanapong, the group starts by working on concerts and other works of art. Now, the group is led by Rueangrith Suntisuk and Pornpan Arayaveerasid, alongside a team of creatives who work together to bring creative spectacles to life.
In the midst of a project in Paris, Rueangrith Suntisuk chats with designboom about the studio’s current technical explorations and its work between the worlds of music and art.
Rueangrith Suntisuk in conversation with designboom
The group recently wrapped a large-scale installation at the international performing arts festival in Brussels, Kunstenfestivaldesarts. It was called A Flower of Forgetfulness and was a collaborative effort between DuckUnit, Thai filmmaker Apichatpong Weerasethakul, and sound engineers and composers Akritchalerm Kalayanamitr and Koichi Shimizu. Inside an old chapel, projected videos, sound, light, and movement were put into dialogue to create a profound performance. In the days leading up to and surrounding the work, the many members of DuckUnit were busy perfecting the mechanical elements of the show, documenting their work, and making sure the timing was perfectly in tune with the rest of the installation’s elements.
Looking back on the many hands and varied talents that the installation required, the group recalls a busy flock, which is how they came up with the name. Suntisuk shares, ‘We started as a design collective working across many fields, from concerts and theatre to art. We combine the different disciplines we’ve learned and understood to make our work. The name DuckUnit comes from our curiosity in many directions, and from constantly trying to do things we don’t yet know how to do.’
From concert halls to art spaces
‘When we work on concert stages or films, we usually try to make the audience take in the same story from the same point of view,’ remarks Suntisuk on the more traditional performances they work on, where the audience and the spectacle are two discrete things. The group recently worked on the show FLURE LIFE for the Thai alt-rock band. In the show, giant watercolor illustrations of eyeballs, slithering snakes, and sleeping faces rise and fall to tell a kind of fable behind the band’s concert.
‘In our recent art works, we try to think the opposite way.’ DuckUnit has created a multitude of installations, including the silent disco Embargo of Silence and the outdoor installation Two Who Remember the Sea, made with Weerasethakul and Guo-Liang Tan. ‘We open up space for variety among the audience and the work, so that the audience dissolves into the space and becomes part of the work itself. We’ve found that this opens up possibilities for both the audience and ourselves to understand the piece, with different kinds of beauty that we could never have predicted from the start.’
timelapse of the FLURE LIFE concert, 2026
Working with an audience’s expectations
A silent disco, where the audience gets the music via headphones rather than speakers, is just the beginning of the particular environments DuckUnit has designed. Consider Love after Death by artist Korakrit Arunanondchai, remade for exposition at Bangkok CityCity Gallery. For this piece, the studio suspended a semitransparent panel that caught a projection and bent light that oozed out into a space behind the screen. ‘In a concert, audience satisfaction usually starts at 100, and people hope for even more.’ Suntisuk goes on to contrast this with the other world the studio works in: ‘In art, the audience’s attention and focus sometime start at 0. Understanding these different states of the audience has strongly shaped our newer work, and moving between these different demands shapes how we make our work.’
Developing new technical abilities
One thing evident in the studio’s work, regardless of genre, is its constant experimentation with how light and movement can add an element to visual storytelling. To refine its approach to scenography, the studio revisits its scenographic techniques. ‘In many recent works we’ve used fabric, smoke, motors, projection, light, and objects we can’t fully control. The new things that happen usually come from trying to control these elements and then letting them go. They tend to appear at the moment when these elements meet. Right now we’re learning how they coexist and what effect they have on each other.’
project info:
studio: DuckUnit | @duckunit_
location: Bangkok, Thailand
studio leads: Rueangrith Suntisuk and Pornpan Arayaveerasid

19 injured as train hits minibus at France's Channel Tunnel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
20:35:00 UTC
05:35:00 KST

At least 19 people were injured, five seriously, when a minibus carrying truck drivers collided with a train on the French side of the Channel Tunnel on Thursday evening, authorities said, adding that no deaths were reported and none of the injuries were life-threatening.
The minibus was transporting truck drivers preparing to board a Le Shuttle train for a journey through the tunnel linking France and Britain.
The driver was among those injured, but none of the injuries were considered life-threatening, according to a statement from the local prefecture.
Emergency crews, including a helicopter-based medical response team and border police, were dispatched to the scene as rescue operations continued.
The incident also disrupted rail services, with two Eurostar trains operating between France and England listed as canceled Thursday evening.
The local deputy prefect was expected to hold a news conference at Eurotunnel's nearby headquarters at 10:30 p.m. local time (8:30 p.m. GMT) to provide further details on the accident.

"Welcoming and inclusive" London housing wins RIBA Stirling Prize 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
20:30:53 UTC
05:30:53 KST

"Welcoming and inclusive" London housing wins RIBA Stirling Prize 2026
The Lion Green Road housing in south London, designed by local studios Mary Duggan Architects with Ruff Architects, has won this year's RIBA Stirling Prize for the UK's best new building.
Located in Coulsdon, the high-density development commissioned by Croydon Council provides 157 homes across five blocks, which are stitched together by a series of shared green spaces.
The Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA) named the project as winner of the prestigious prize at a ceremony in London this evening.
It is the fourth housing scheme to win the prize since its inception 30 years ago, following Accordia in Cambridge in 2008, Goldsmith Street in Norwich in 2019 and Appleby Blue Almshouse in London in 2025.
The jury hailed Mary Duggan Architects and Ruff Architects for "addressing the pressing need for national housing" and providing environmentally considerate homes with ample access to light, nature and community.
"More than a housing development, the scheme has created a welcoming and inclusive place where people can connect with one another, and with nature," read the citation.
Lion Green Road comprises five blocks with a mix of private and socially rented homes. They are staggered across its steeply sloped site – a topographically challenging plot previously used as a car park.
The blocks have faceted, star-shaped plans, which are rotated to offer unique views across the landscape and ensure each home is dual-aspect, maximising natural light.
A trio of complementary brick types clad the buildings, helping to visually unify them while giving each its own unique aesthetic.
Shared outdoor spaces that weave through the blocks enhance this unification, giving residents opportunities to meet and engage with each other.
RIBA president Chris Williamson said the scheme demonstrates how high-density housing "can be achieved without compromising the quality of the places we create".
"Through a consistent specification, with subtle variation in height and orientation, it offers housing at scale without uniformity," he reflected.
"The architects have created a new kind of garden neighbourhood that balances privacy and generous views with a strong connection to nature – it's a living landscape," Williamson continued.
"This is thoughtful, resourceful architecture that proves that even the most challenging of sites can be transformed into truly distinctive places for people to call home."
The RIBA Stirling Prize has been awarded annually to the UK's best new building since 1996. Lion Green Road was chosen from a six-strong shortlist, revealed in July.
It was announced as this year's winner at a ceremony at Old Billingsgate this evening, where RIBA also revealed the recipients of its five Special Awards.
This included the RIBA Neave Brown Award for Housing, which was won by Satish Jassal Architects for Rowan Court, a cluster of brick-clad social housing blocks in Seven Sisters.
Collaborators Samuel Chisholm Studio and Takero Shimazaki took home the RIBA Reinvention Award for Oru Sutton, a co-working space in an old department store, while Tonkin Liu Architects won the RIBA Client of the Year Award in recognition of the York Minster Centre of Excellence.
Finally, the RIBA Conservation Award was given to Architectural Thread for The Buttermarket, an arts-focused community hub in Cornwall, which also won the RIBA Stephen Lawrence Prize for emerging architectural talent.
Previous winners of the Stirling Prize include London's Elizabeth Line in 2024, The New Library at Magdalene College in 2022 and a seaside pier in Hastings in 2017.
Last year's award, which was won by the "hopeful and imaginative" Appleby Blue Almshouse social housing, sparked concerns about London bias, with four of the six shortlisted buildings located in the capital city.
Earlier this year, the shortlist for the 2026 Stirling Prize was a topic of conversation in our Dezeen Weekly podcast, with our journalists pondering if architecture has become too boring.
The photography is by Lorenzo Zandri unless stated otherwise.
