Car insurance premiums jump by almost 60 per cent in four years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
20:30:28 UTC
05:30:28 KST

Car insurance premiums increase almost by almost 60 per cent in four years
In short:
Comprehensive car insurance premiums have jumped another 10 per cent after similar hikes last year.
It follows an ASIC review that called for more transparency behind insurer calculations.
What's next:
The federal government has called on insurers to step up with fairer pricing and greater transparency.
Car insurance premiums continue to increase well beyond inflation as customers who have already endured exponential hikes since 2020 are slugged with another 10 per cent.
Comprehensive car insurance for this journalist's station wagon, for example, has just gone up 10 per cent (after a similar increase last year), representing a 57 per cent hike since 2023 when it cost $703.
Recently billed $1,110 to insure it for another year, the same car under the same conditions cost just $566 in 2020 — an astonishing 96 per cent increase since the start of the decade that would have been higher without a change of insurer.
It follows an ASIC report released in August that found premiums had surged by more than 42 per cent from 2019 to 2024, and a further 8 per cent in the 12 months to July 2025.
It also found insurers were not detailing how their premiums were being calculated, and 73 per cent were only giving generic reasons for rate increases.
Federal Assistant Treasurer and Minister for Financial Services Daniel Mulino said the government had committed $2.4 million to reforms to improve insurer transparency.
"While this work is targeted at home and contents insurance at this stage, the government is considering the issue of premium transparency in the motor insurance market,"
he said.
"I have also called on the industry to step up with fairer pricing, greater transparency, and better value for Australians."
Higher repair costs blamed
An Insurance Council of Australia spokesperson blamed the insurance premiums on the cost of paying claims, which had risen "sharply".
She said the average motor claim had increased 32 per cent to $6,266 over the four years to 2026 due to higher vehicle replacement, parts and labour costs, and longer repair times.
She said this was "caused by national parts and skills shortages, and the specialised equipment and expertise modern vehicles require".
"The most effective way to ease pressure on premiums is to tackle the costs driving them,"
the spokesperson said.
"The Insurance Council has called on governments to regulate the credit hire industry, address repair workforce shortages and require manufacturers to make spare parts available in Australia."
The government said it was strengthening skills and training for Australians, having legislated to make its Free TAFE program permanent and deliver at least 100,000 fee-free places annually from 2027.
Free TAFE enrolments have already surpassed 850,000 people since the program was launched in 2023.
But the Motor Trades Association of Australia last month said the vacancy fill rate for automotive workers was just 48 per cent, and average applicant numbers per job had fallen from 8.2 in 2024 to just three in 2026.
It estimated there was a 38,000-person shortfall in automotive trade professionals and technicians.
It called for automotive trades to be recognised alongside other "priority occupations" in the wake of Federal Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke's skilled migration changes announced last month.
'Misleading pricing practices'
An ASIC spokesperson said "misleading pricing practices that affected the cost of living for Australians were an ASIC enforcement priority" this year.
It said its 2026 review found that car insurance premiums had increased significantly and most consumers were being given only vague or incomplete information about why.
"ASIC's aim through the review was to achieve compliance outcomes across the motor insurance industry by lifting the standard of disclosures and information provided to consumers," the spokesperson said.
The ASIC review called on insurers to explain the key factors behind their premiums, why they had changed, and how factors like excess and payment methods affected price.
"ASIC will continue to monitor industry practices and consider further regulatory action where appropriate,"
the ASIC spokesperson said.
Using 'up-to-date' information
An AAMI spokesperson said premiums were recalculated each year using the most "up-to-date information available at the time of renewal, rather than using or carrying forward the previous year's premium".
Loading...
"Even if nothing has changed on your end, your premium can increase because of changes in the cost and frequency of claims across similar policies, updated assessments of risk in comparable locations and broader cost pressures such as repair and replacement expenses," she said.
She advised people to check what value their car was insured for, ensure the kilometres selected reflected how many kilometres they drove yearly, consider increasing the excess to pay more if there was an accident, and to remove anyone listed on the policy if they were not driving.
The ABC reported in 2024 that while premiums may reflect the rising cost of repairs, profitability in the Australian car insurance market still rose by $1 billion the previous year.
Insurers increased profitability through long-term customers who did not shop around when they received increased bills, nor try to have their premiums discounted or reduced before accepting them.

Porsche reveals Mission S concept car that previews new design identity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
20:30:01 UTC
05:30:01 KST

Porsche on Thursday revealed a concept car called Mission S that signals a new design direction and flagship model for the famed German sports carmaker.
The debut of the sleek midengine vehicle is part of a turnaround plan revealed last week by the Volkswagen-controlled brand that includes efforts to boost profits through higher-end products and lower vehicle sales.
Porsche described Mission S as "a first glimpse of the brand's evolved design identity" that also represents a "super sports car platform" that will be positioned above its iconic 911 sports car.
The vehicle's design is recognizably Porsche but with more aggressive styling compared with its current models, including new hood vents and a roof scoop. Its rear features more differentiated flair in which the vehicle's spoiler flows into its rear panels.
"A Porsche must be recognisable as a Porsche at first glance," Porsche Chairman Michael Leiters said in a release. "The Mission S provides a glimpse of the ideas and design features that will shape Porsche in the coming years."
Automakers routinely use concept vehicles to gauge customer interest, showcase future technologies and signal the direction of a vehicle or brand.
The company did not release expected pricing or performance specifications for such future models. Starting prices for its current 911 models range from roughly $135,500 for an entry-level Carrera to more than $203,000 for a Carrera 4 GTS convertible.
During Porsche's capital markets day on Oct. 7, the company outlined its "Sportwagenschmiede '35" turnaround plan, which focuses on emphasizing high-end sports cars and luxury SUVs to get the carmaker back on track.
Porsche's operating margin last year was only 1.1%, compared with 14.1% in 2024, as the company deals with increased costs, U.S. tariffs and declining sales in China.
The turnaround plan includes a long-term target for a group operating margin of 15% and a midterm breakeven point of 200,000 units or below annually. That compares with sales of 279,449 in 2025.

The Australian Taxation Office (ATO) is warning Australians to stop claiming private expenses on their tax returns, with some attempting to claim baby expenses, personal gifts and meal deliveries as work-related.

US Fed's Warsh says AI path will be 'very bumpy'
US Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh says the AI road will be "very bumpy," and its near-term effect on jobs and the real economy is unknown.
Warsh spoke at a fireside chat with the International Monetary Fund's managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, as part of the weeklong IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok on Friday.
He said its was the most "consequential change to the US economy" in his lifetime, and "a big deal for central banks".
While he's optimistic that artificial intelligence will make economies that use it more productive and wealthier, the path "is likely to be a very bumpy one".
Warsh declined to say what he will do at the Fed's upcoming October 27-28 meeting.
The central bank raised rates to a range of 3.75 per cent to 4 per cent last month, its first hike since 2023.
"I don't prejudge meetings. I don't believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year," he told the meeting.
He said the global economy was showing resilience that he could not have predicted 12 months ago and that, “I believe optimistically, you might think naively, at least in the US, we’re going to come out of this stronger with a more durable economy, more capable of leading the world on economic growth".

Analysts forecast gold prices will likely rise in 2027
ANZ's Soni Kumari and Daniel Hynes forecast that the gold price will remain capped in the short-term before rising through 2027, and that silver will likely follow.
"Gold has shown resilience in the face of rising yields and a stronger US dollar," they write.
"US 10 year real yields have risen nearly 50 basis points since September to around 3 per cent, yet gold has declined by less than 5 per cent, with prices staying above USD4,100/oz."
"A stronger USD is typically a drag on gold, but the impact has been less pronounced this time as investors appear more willing to accommodate a firmer currency.
"We believe that if US yields remain elevated and the USD stays firm, risks to the gold price will remain on the downside through to the end of this year."
But a retreat in yields and the US dollar would pave the way for gold to resume its rise above USD5,000/oz in 2027.
Silver will likely follow gold, but they were "cautious due to subdued interest from investors, exchange inventory rebuilding and emerging industrial demand headwind".

Key Event
David Chau's chart of the day: Economic misery at its highest since 2023
Happy Friday everyone! Every afternoon, I'll give you a sneak peek at what I'll be discussing on tonight's 7pm News finance segment.
Today's chart is anything but happy I have to say. See for yourself!
It shows economic misery in Australia has risen to a three-year high — back towards its post-COVID highs. And collectively, we're likely to stay miserable until (at least) the end of 2028.
That's according to the latest "misery index" from the Committee for Economic Development of Australia (CEDA).
How do you measure 'misery'?
To work out how much economic strain people are feeling, CEDA has added up Australia's unemployment rate, inflation and the Reserve Bank's cash rate target.
Generally, when it's harder to find work, consumer prices are rising rapidly and the RBA is lifting interest rates, that's the perfect recipe for unhappiness.
The misery index was created by US economist Arthur Okun back in the 1960s.
CEDA adapted his idea and made an Australian version in 2007.
Looking ahead, inflation is expected to fall (which is good news), but interest rates are forecast to remain around their current levels and unemployment is likely to keep rising, based on the RBA's assumptions in its August statement on monetary policy.
That's why the Melbourne-based economic think tank reckons our "misery levels" will go down, but still remain quite high for at least the next couple of years. Now that's a sobering thought.
Key Event
Auction clearance rates face 'weakest run since 2011'
Tom Kennedy from JP Morgan notes that Australia's national housing auction clearance rates have now averaged below 50 per cent since June, the weakest run since 2011.
"Auction clearance rates and annual house price growth are correlated through time, with the former a seemingly reliable leading indicator," he writes.
So far, Cotality's median price metric is 4 per cent below its peak, while hedonic prices, which take into account dwelling-specific characteristics, are down closer to 5 per cent, he said.
"Taking this relationship at face value implies the remaining price adjustment will be less significant from here, in our view, culminating in a peak to trough decline in the mid/high single digits," he said.
He said there are two main uncertainties around this view.
"First, it's too early for the RBA's September rate hike to be fully accounted for in the data," Mr Kennedy said.
Secondly, the federal government's changes to negative gearing and capital gains tax would also have an impact.
"These changes make housing a less attractive asset class for speculators, evident in investor credit growth and loan demand shifting lower," he said.
This, he argues, creates two-sided uncertainty.
"The housing market could simply be weaker across the board than historical relationships would imply. Or, more of the adjustment may play out in volumes, relative to prices," he noted.
"We have argued the latter, as the bar for current property investors to sell is higher, given negative gearing benefits are grandfathered.
"This is another reason not to focus as much on prices, as turnover/sales are more relevant anyway for credit growth, and consumption."
He says that that's all added to the general pessimism around the housing price outlook. It has weighed on total auction volumes, which are down 30 per cent compared to last year, and are approaching levels last reported during the 2022/23 hiking cycle.

Northern Ireland ex-DUP leader Donaldson sentenced to 15 years for child sex crimes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
20:12:27 UTC
05:12:27 KST

Northern Ireland ex-DUP leader Donaldson sentenced to 15 years for child sex crimes
Judge says Jeffrey Donaldson never apologised to victims as politician seeks to appeal his convictions.
The former leader of Northern Ireland’s largest unionist party has been sentenced to 15 years in jail for child sex offences.
Jeffrey Donaldson, who led the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP), stared straight ahead as Judge Paul Ramsey handed down the 63-year-old’s sentence on Thursday.
Ramsey described the case as “disturbing and disquieting”, assessing Donaldson as having a medium chance of reoffending. He described the politician’s fall as “a catastrophic descent into disgrace”.
Donaldson has been in prison awaiting sentence since June after he was convicted of one count of rape, 13 counts of indecent assault and four counts of gross indecency against two girls between 1985 and 2008.
He denied all the charges and is seeking to appeal against his convictions.
The case is one of the highest-profile cases in the British-run region in recent times.
Donaldson was one of Northern Ireland’s best-known politicians and its longest-serving lawmaker in the British Parliament when he was arrested and charged in March 2024.
He immediately resigned as the leader of the DUP after he was charged with what he called “allegations of an historic nature”.
‘Worst moment’ of victim’s life
Prosecutor Rosemary Walsh told a pre-sentencing hearing last month that one of the victims described the abuse as “the worst moment of her life”.
The other victim said her childhood had been stolen and that she had carried around feelings of “shame” ever since. The victims, neither of whom can be identified for legal reasons, gave evidence during the trial.
Judge Ramsey said Donaldson had doubled down on his denials and not offered one word of an apology or expressed shame.
Donaldson will likely spend seven-and-a-half years in prison as he qualifies for an automatic remission of his sentence, the Lady Chief Justice’s Office of Northern Ireland said. This is because the offences were committed before a change in the law allowing a judge to choose what portion of a sentence is spent in custody.
In 2021, Donaldson became leader of the DUP, the party founded by Protestant cleric Ian Paisley at the height of three decades of sectarian bloodshed, which ended after a 1998 peace deal.
Donaldson was central to the negotiation of a crucial post-Brexit trade deal with the United Kingdom government two months before his arrest.
It enabled the end of the DUP’s two-year boycott of the devolved power-sharing assembly at Stormont and had also been expected to lead his party into the next UK general election.
Donaldson was knighted by the late Queen Elizabeth for his political services in 2016.
He asked for his knighthood to be renounced two days after his conviction.
The jury also found that Donaldson’s wife, Eleanor, aided and abetted her husband. She has also denied the charges.
The court ruled her unfit to stand trial last month due to mental health issues, meaning she could not face criminal conviction.

Poll shows Bolsonaro with slight lead over Lula ahead of Brazilian run-off

Poll shows Bolsonaro with slight lead over Lula ahead of Brazilian run-off
Poll shows right-wing candidate with two percent advantage over Lula going into second round of voting on October 25.
A new poll has found that right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro maintains a slight lead over President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva as the two candidates seek an edge ahead of Brazil’s tense October 25 runoff vote.
A Quaest poll released on Thursday found that Bolsonaro, son of former far-right President Jair Bolsonaro, has received 46 percent support among respondents, compared to Lula’s 44 percent.
But that difference still falls within the two-percent margin of error, with many experts considering the runoff too close to call.
Bolsonaro outperformed expectations during the first round of voting on October 4, beating Lula by less than two points despite most polls suggesting that the leftist president was on track for a marginal first-round win. Neither candidate secured the majority necessary to avoid a run-off.
The poll, the first released by Quaest since the initial round of voting, shows that Bolsonaro has held onto his lead and remains the favourite heading into the second round.
A separate Datafolha poll released on Thursday also found that Bolsonaro leading Lula. But it determined that his advantage has shrunk over the last week from four points to two points.
While Bolsonaro had 49 percent support last week, in Thursday’s poll had his advantage narrowing to 47 percent, compared with 45 percent for Lula.
Lula has sought to rally his supporters after the October 4 loss, holding large rallies that have drawn millions of people onto the street.
While Bolsonaro has remained ahead in the polls, analysts have pointed out that he has not benefitted as much from the elimination of several conservative candidates, whose supporters would presumably prefer him to Lula, as might have been expected after the first round.
Bolsonaro has nevertheless made progress securing endorsements from right and centre-right parties,as he seeks to consolidate support from conservatives and build a coalition friendly to business interests and investors.
Lula, meanwhile, has been touting his platform for social reform in the final weeks before the runoff election.
Brazil’s Senate approved a constitutional amendment on Wednesday reducing the country’s maximum workweek from 44 to 40 hours per week without a reduction in pay.
That change was a key policy priority for Lula, as the president presses his case to an electorate that is anxious about cost-of-living issues.
“Today is a day to celebrate a historic achievement for millions of workers,” Lula said in a statement. “This means having more time to live, rest, be with family, watch your children grow up, take care of yourself, and enjoy life. Those who work so hard to build Brazil also deserve to have time to live.”
The president also recently banned sports betting, which had caused an explosion of gambling addiction and contributed to surging household debt across the country.
On Thursday, he indicated that he would submit a constitutional amendment to Congress guaranteeing free public transportation in all Brazilian cities on weekends, in another gesture to lowering costs for working-class households.

Somalia says it will hold elections in 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
20:04:02 UTC
05:04:02 KST

Somalia says it will hold elections in 2027
Critics say unilateral decision to call polls is a recipe for more conflict.
Somalia’s election commission has announced that parliamentary and presidential elections will be held in the country next year.
Abdikarim Ahmed Hassan, chief of the Independent National Elections and Boundaries Commission (INEBC), made the announcement on the state broadcaster on Thursday, saying that elections for members of parliament for both the lower and upper chambers are planned for April 15, 2027, followed by a presidential vote scheduled for May 15.
A statement by the electoral body said the vote to elect a president was in accordance with a rule “which stipulates that the president’s term of office is five years, beginning on the date the president is sworn into office”.
President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud’s second term – starting in 2022 – ended earlier this year, but his government declared a “transition period” through a constitutional amendment in May, despite an agreement with the opposition to hold elections.
Opposition parties boycotted that vote to amend the constitution and have rejected the changes since.
Mohamud is pushing to hold party-based elections to replace a system of electing established clan elders, but his attempts have been opposed by critics, who call his move a power grab.
Former President Mohamed Abdullahi Farmaajo called the decision to hold elections a “dangerous threat to Somalia’s statehood and future” in a post on X, and urged an agreement with all factions before a decision can be made on the polls.
Sheikh Sharif Sheikh Ahmed, another former president, who was previously a leader of the opposition, warned that a “contested [electoral] process could lead to parallel elections” and even “civil conflict”, according to the AFP.
Meanwhile, the government welcomed the polling date announcements as an “important stage … towards reinforcing the country’s democratic system” and called on all parties to engage with the process, peacefully “in good faith”.
“There’s no political agreement to hold those elections,” analyst Samira Gaid told the AFP news agency.
“All the processes that the government is starting are leading to further fragmentation,” she said, adding that the government was essentially made up of Mogadishu and “two or three allied member states”.
Elections, Gaid said, would lead to “conflict and more confrontation within the remaining federal member states”.
There was also scepticism in the capital Mogadishu, with some residents calling the announcement “one-sided”.
“Announcing an election schedule through a process driven by one side, and rejected by the opposition, is effectively declaring a new conflict,” Omar Said, a resident of the capital, told AFP.
Security challenges
Speaking to Al Jazeera earlier this month, President Mohamud said the country still faced significant security challenges, despite the al-Shabab group having no presence in the major cities, and despite there being little possibility of the group taking control in Somalia.
Al-Shabab is a Somali armed group that emerged from the Islamic Courts Union in the mid-2000s and pledged allegiance to al-Qaeda in 2012. It has fought Somalia’s federal government for years, holds territory in parts of southern and central Somalia, and has carried out deadly attacks, including in Mogadishu and in neighbouring Kenya.
Mohamud said the United States remained Somalia’s strongest partner in the fight against “terrorism”.
He also spoke on Somalia’s relations with neighbouring Ethiopia, describing ties as good, highlighting that Mogadishu does not object to landlocked Addis Ababa gaining access to the sea through a joint agreement to use Somali ports for its economic interests.
In January 2024, Addis Ababa signed a memorandum of understanding with Somaliland on sea access, which Somalia condemned as a violation of its sovereignty. Somalia and Ethiopia later agreed to ease tensions.

Britain to fit its own kit to Ukraine donated weapons
United Kingdom

21:01:04 BST
05:01:04 KST

Britain will retrofit British capability onto equipment given to Ukraine by other partners, the Prime Minister told President Zelensky at Downing Street, alongside a fresh package of Lightweight Multirole Missiles and talks on accelerating long range support before winter, according to the government.
Andy Burnham welcomed Volodymyr Zelensky to Downing Street on Wednesday afternoon, and the two began by reflecting on their call the previous Saturday and on what the government described as Russia’s blatant indiscriminate attacks on civilians and energy infrastructure since President Trump called for an energy ceasefire. It was clear Russia had no interest in peace, the leaders underlined.
On how Ukraine’s allies could step up, particularly against Russia’s barrage of jet-powered drones, the Prime Minister set out the latest British package of Lightweight Multirole Missiles. He added that Britain would continue to develop innovative military solutions for use on the battlefield in Ukraine, including retrofitting British capability onto equipment gifted from other partners.
On long range missiles, the leaders discussed how Britain could accelerate defensive support ahead of the winter, and the Prime Minister said Britain would continue diplomatic efforts to support international supplies of defensive equipment.
Donated equipment arrives in Ukraine from more than fifty countries in a bewildering variety of types and standards, much of it Soviet-era, some of it decades old, and a great deal of it without the sensors, communications or guidance that would let it work inside a modern targeting chain. Fitting British seekers, fuzes, datalinks or electronic warfare packages onto someone else’s donated hardware turns a stock problem into an integration problem, and the British defence industry is better placed to solve the second than the first.
Britain has already done something along those lines at a smaller scale. Stone Cloak, the tablet-sized jammer designed by the government to stop Russian air defences tracking the drones it is fitted to, is manufactured under a British contract and its intellectual property has been handed to Ukraine so that Ukrainian industry can mass-produce it.
Jet-powered drones are the specific threat behind the latest missile package. The Geran-3, a jet version of the Shahed-136 design, flies considerably faster than the propeller-driven type Ukraine has been shooting down since 2022, which compresses the time available to detect, track and engage and pushes targets out of reach of the machine guns and small arms that handle the slower ones. Lightweight Multirole Missiles are one of the few interceptors cheap enough to use against them in quantity.
Thales builds those missiles in Belfast, where production now runs at four times its 2022 rate with £100 million committed to expanding further. The company says the work sustains 1,100 direct jobs in Northern Ireland and around 700 more across its British supply chain.

====================================================================================================

Your job says little about what you want in a partner, study suggests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
20:00:25 UTC
05:00:25 KST

The kind of industry a person works in appears to say very little about what they look for in a romantic partner, according to new research published in Personality and Individual Differences. Across seven countries, a person’s sex and whether they were imagining a short-term or long-term relationship were far more strongly linked to partner preferences than whether they worked in a people-focused, things-focused, or ideas-focused sector.
Vocational interests refer to the broad preferences that guide people toward certain types of work. Psychologists often map these interests along a spectrum that contrasts working with people, like nursing or teaching, with working with objects or systems, like engineering or logistics. A second dimension contrasts working with data and working with ideas, as in technology or finance; the researchers combined these into an “abstract” category. Interest theory treats these career interests as expressions of personality rather than just a taste for specific daily tasks.
If career interests reflect deep parts of personality, they might shape other major life choices, such as picking a partner. Men and women also differ markedly along the people-versus-things dimension: a 2009 meta-analysis found that men generally lean toward working with things and women toward working with people. This divide appears across cultures, as noted in a study covered by PsyPost in 2022 showing a global trend of women preferring people-oriented jobs and men preferring things-oriented occupations.
At the same time, relationship research has established that partner preferences differ by biological sex and relationship goals. The authors of a 1993 paper proposing sexual strategies theory argued, with supporting evidence, that what people prioritize in a partner changes dramatically depending on whether they are looking for a short-term fling or a long-term commitment. The new research brings these two lines of work together to test whether the dispositions that draw people to certain kinds of work also shape their romantic preferences.
The research was led by Peter K. Jonason of Vizja University and Dritjon Gruda, an invited associate professor of organizational behavior at Católica Porto Business School, Universidade Católica Portuguesa, and lecturer at Maynooth University School of Business.
“Vocational psychologists treat whether you are drawn to people or to things as a deep part of personality, more stable over time than the Big Five and very different between men and women,” Gruda told PsyPost. “If that holds, a pediatric nurse and a structural engineer should want different things in a partner, and nobody had checked whether they do.”
The Big Five refers to the five broad traits psychologists commonly use to describe personality, such as extraversion and conscientiousness.
To answer this question, the researchers recruited 1,974 adults (968 men and 982 women) through Prolific from seven countries, including the United States, Germany, and South Africa. The participants completed an online survey about their current employment and their romantic preferences. The researchers grouped participants into three occupational orientations based on their current industry: people-oriented (746 workers), things-oriented (289 workers), and abstract-oriented (710 workers).
To measure mate preferences, the team used a forced-choice task. In each of ten pairings, participants picked which of two traits mattered more from a set of five qualities: physicality (attractiveness and fitness), compassion (warmth and kindness), competence (intelligence and capability), compatibility (shared values and lifestyle), and character (honesty and moral values).
Participants completed this task twice, once imagining a short-term relationship and once imagining a long-term partnership, with the order varied across participants. Because each person made 10 choices per scenario, a trait chosen at an average rate would score 2. Choosing one trait meant passing on another, allowing the researchers to measure the relative priority of each quality on a scale from zero to four.
The results showed that occupational orientation had almost no association with partner preferences. The researchers used equivalence tests, which check whether a difference is small enough to count as negligible rather than simply failing to find one. By this standard, people-oriented and things-oriented workers made practically identical choices for competence and compatibility in both scenarios, and for character in the long-term scenario. Abstract-oriented workers, whom the researchers expected to favor character and compatibility, also chose these traits at rates equivalent to everyone else.
“Your job says very little about what you want in a partner,” Gruda explained. “Among 1,974 adults in seven countries, the sector people worked in had almost no bearing on how often they picked looks, compassion, competence, compatibility, or character. Their sex, and whether they were imagining a fling or a long-term relationship, mattered far more.”
Because things-oriented jobs were held mostly by men (68 percent) and people-oriented jobs mostly by women (63 percent), the researchers analyzed occupation and sex together. Things-oriented workers did choose physical attractiveness somewhat more often than people-oriented workers, but accounting for sex removed about two-thirds of that gap, leaving only a small difference.
The association the authors highlight involved compassion. In the long-term scenario, men in people-oriented jobs chose compassion more often than men in things-oriented jobs (an average of 2.21 versus 1.76 choices out of four), while women chose it at nearly identical rates regardless of sector. Because the researchers tested many outcomes, they applied a stricter threshold to guard against chance findings, and this link did not meet it; it also vanished when things-oriented workers were left out, so the authors treat it as exploratory.
The persistence of the sex difference within the same kinds of jobs stood out to the researchers. “Men in people-focused work like teaching and care, where most colleagues are women, still picked compassion less often than the women next to them,” Gruda noted. “The one occupational link we found, with people-oriented men valuing compassion more in a long-term partner, was small and did not survive correction for multiple tests.”
Sex and relationship context, by contrast, were consistently linked to partner preferences. In both long-term and short-term scenarios, men chose physical attractiveness more often than women did, while women chose compassion and competence more often than men did. For example, in long-term relationships, men chose physicality at an average rate of 1.13 choices compared to 0.60 choices for women, while women chose compassion 2.51 times versus 2.08 times for men. Men and women did not differ in how often they chose compatibility, and differed only slightly on character.
Relationship context reorganized priorities far more heavily than occupation did. When considering a short-term relationship rather than a long-term one, participants selected physicality nearly three times as often, jumping from an average of 0.85 choices to 2.33 choices. To accommodate this focus on looks, choices for compatibility, compassion, and character each fell by roughly half a choice, while competence dipped only slightly.
“Occupation explained extremely little in how often people picked any one trait,” Gruda pointed out. “Relationship context mattered far more.”
The pattern of choices was broadly similar across the seven countries, though some differences emerged, such as fewer compassion choices in Germany and Poland. Country accounted for about five times as much of the variation in compassion choices as occupation did, which the authors take as evidence that the task could detect group differences where they existed.
The authors interpret the weak role of occupation as support for the view that partner preferences are shaped by psychological mechanisms specialized for mating, rather than by the broad dispositions that steer people toward particular kinds of work. Because sex differences in career interests emerge early in life, they suggest sex may shape both the jobs people hold and what they want in a partner, though the study’s single-snapshot design cannot confirm this.
“For me, the main finding is that knowing the industry where somebody works tells us rather little about their partner preferences, once sex is taken into account,” said Toivo Aavik, an associate professor of individual and social psychology at the University of Tartu in Estonia, who has expertise in sexology and mate preferences and was not involved in the research. “Whether the person is thinking about a short-term or a long-term relationship makes a much larger difference. The results concerning sex and relationship context are broadly in line with previous research. The more novel part is the weak association with industry.”
“But here I see the main limitation: the study measured current industry, not vocational interests themselves,” Aavik continued. “These are related, but they are not the same thing. A nurse and a data analyst may both work in healthcare, while having quite different interests and daily tasks. Therefore, I would not yet conclude that vocational interests have little relevance for partner preferences.”
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these findings. The study used the participants’ current employment industry as a stand-in for their actual vocational interests. People work where they do for practical reasons such as income, availability, or location, meaning a person’s current field may not reflect their underlying interests.
Gruda acknowledged the limitation while also cautioning against oversimplifying the findings. “We measured the industry people work in, not their vocational interests, and people take jobs for all sorts of reasons,” he said. “That noise would hide a real effect rather than create a false one, yet the same task picked up country differences several times larger than anything occupational. The results also do not mean men want only looks and women only kindness, because for a long-term partner both sexes picked character and compatibility most often.”
Measuring vocational interests directly with specialized assessments, rather than relying on current industry, could provide a more direct test in future investigations. The noise introduced by using industry as a proxy might make subtle associations harder to detect.
“I have reasonable confidence in the narrower result,” Aavik said. “The sample is relatively large, includes seven countries, and the authors used equivalence tests. This is a strength, because finding no statistically significant difference is not sufficient evidence that a difference is small. But still, a large sample cannot fully compensate for an indirect measure of the central concept.”
The forced-choice task also asked participants to choose between broad, abstract traits. While this approach reveals which general qualities people prioritize, real-world dating involves weighing complex combinations of these traits in actual people.
“Participants chose between desirable qualities in hypothetical relationship contexts,” Aavik observed. “Choosing attractiveness more often necessarily leaves fewer choices for other qualities. It does not mean that kindness or honesty is no longer valued. Also, these are average differences between groups; they tell us much less about a particular man or woman.”
The researchers also excluded participants who identified as non-binary or reported a sexual orientation other than heterosexual because those groups were too small to analyze separately. In addition, all seven countries in the sample were Western, industrialized nations, which leaves open the question of whether similar patterns would appear in other cultural settings.
Looking ahead, the researchers hope to build on this line of inquiry. “We would like to measure vocational interests directly instead of inferring them from industry, and to test samples beyond our seven Western countries,” Gruda stated.
Aavik similarly outlined key priorities for future investigations. “What I would most like to see next is a study measuring vocational interests directly and following actual romantic choices,” he told PsyPost. “From a sexology perspective, I would also want sexual compatibility to be assessed explicitly and sufficient representation of people (maybe) with different sexual orientations and/or gender identities.”
The study, “Sex, love, and work: What you do is not whom you want,” was authored by Peter K. Jonason and Dritjon Gruda.

Brazil candidates focus fiscal plans on voter-friendly measures before runoff
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
19:56:09 UTC
04:56:09 KST

Brazil candidates focus fiscal plans on voter-friendly measures before runoff
BRASILIA, Oct 15 - As Brazil's presidential runoff campaign enters its final stretch, both candidates are focusing plans for fiscal adjustments on politically palatable measures, reinforcing economists' views that strategies to curb the country's rising debt burden will only come to light after the election.
The country's gross debt has risen more than 10 percentage points during President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's current term, reaching 82.9% of gross domestic product (GDP), as the leftist incumbent seeks reelection after unexpectedly trailing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro in the first round earlier this month.
Right-wing Bolsonaro entered the race promising a faster fiscal adjustment, targeting a 1.5% of GDP improvement in the primary balance within 18 months to trigger a confidence shock and lower borrowing costs.
Long-term interest rates have fallen sharply since Bolsonaro's first-round victory, reflecting investor optimism about a potential change in government, although his campaign has yet to explain how such an adjustment would be delivered.
Lula's campaign has also pledged fiscal consolidation, albeit at a slower pace, while saying that spending cuts should not fall on lower-income Brazilians, a message that has defined the president's economic agenda.
With polls showing Bolsonaro ahead by a narrow margin, both campaigns have stuck to politically safe fiscal proposals, sidestepping measures that would tackle the structural causes of Brazil's worsening fiscal outlook, analysts say.
Economists broadly agree that the main challenge lies in the rapid growth of mandatory spending and an increasingly rigid budget. The federal government's discretionary spending accounted for only about 7.6% of total expenditures last year, versus 14.2% in 2000, when Brazil's Federal Budget Panel series began.
Bolsonaro's economic adviser Daniella Marques rejected suggestions that a future administration would reduce social benefits, saying pensions and welfare programs would be untouched.
"You can make the government work by cutting its own excesses," Marques told broadcaster Band on Wednesday, pointing to things like cuts in political appointments and ministries, among other measures.
Lula's running mate Geraldo Alckmin has argued fiscal consolidation should focus on tackling campaign funding and outsized salaries earned by some public-sector workers.
Neither campaign has confronted the deeper reforms required to stabilize debt, said Rafaela Vitoria, chief economist at Brazilian lender Inter.
"There is no short-term magic solution," she said. "The debate on structural measures is extremely difficult during an election campaign because they are unpopular."
Gradual adjustment remains feasible, Vitoria said, adding that discussions over benefit indexation rules, mandatory spending and overlapping social programs will likely have to wait until after the election. REUTERS

All suspects in the 2013 bomb attacks in Reyhanli, a district of Türkiye’s Hatay province, have been apprehended in operations coordinated by the National Intelligence Organization (MIT).
The process of apprehending those responsible for the attacks began with the capture of terrorist Yusuf Nazik in 2018. It continued with the 2025 arrests of Muhammed Dib Korali and Temir Dukanci, followed by the 2026 arrest of Omar al-Khatib.
Authorities brought all four to Türkiye in various operations.
Most recently, terrorist Mihrac Ural, who was on the “red category” of Türkiye’s wanted terrorists list, was captured near the Syrian border while attempting to flee abroad in an operation conducted by MIT and Syria’s General Intelligence Service, according to security sources.
Details of captures
Yusuf Nazik, one of the organisers of the Reyhanli attacks, was captured in an MIT operation in Latakia, Syria, on September 12, 2018, and brought to Türkiye.
About six years after Nazik’s capture, Muhammed Dib Korali, who was among the planners of the attacks, was also apprehended in an MIT operation.
Korali, who was reportedly involved in supplying the bombs, was brought to Türkiye following an operation in Syria on January 14, 2025.
Temir Dukanci, who was listed in the “orange category” of Türkiye’s wanted terrorists list, was captured in an operation along the Syria-Lebanon border.
Omar al-Khatib was the latest target in the operations against those responsible for the attacks.
Al-Khatib, who was wanted under a “red notice,” was captured by MIT on Oct. 1, while attempting to flee to Europe by sea.
On May 11, 2013, 53 people were killed, and many civilians were wounded in two separate bomb attacks in the Reyhanli district of southern Hatay Province.

- Getlink’s passenger shuttles stopped for one hour, then normal traffic resumed. Eurostar said its services were not affected and “All Eurostar trains will run as scheduled.”
AI generated
PARIS – A minibus collided with a stationary train in a Channel Tunnel vehicle boarding area in France on the evening of Oct 15, injuring the driver and 18 passengers, the authorities said.
Five people were severely injured though no one’s life appeared to be in danger, the local prefect said in a statement.
The minibus was carrying truck drivers of various nationalities who were heading to travel on a LeShuttle train, which carries vehicles and their passengers through the tunnel.
The area around the tunnel entrance was sealed off on the evening of Oct 15, AFP correspondents at the scene reported, with a helicopter and several emergency vehicles present.
An investigation has been opened on suspicion of unintentional injury, the local prosecutors’ office in Boulogne-sur-Mer told AFP.
Calais deputy prefect Agathe Cury told a news conference that freight traffic was not disrupted but Getlink passenger shuttles were suspended for an hour while emergency services took care of the victims.
Speaking at 8.30pm GMT, she said normal traffic had resumed.
Passenger train service Eurostar said its services were not affected.
At 50km in length, the Channel Tunnel is the longest infrastructure of its kind in the world.
It has linked Coquelles in northern France and Folkestone in England since 1994.
Operated by Getlink, it is used by several hundred trains every day.
Getlink runs Le Shuttle, trains carrying vehicles between France and the United Kingdom, as well as a rail freight service.
According to its website, the company handles around 2.2 million car crossings a year and carries eight million passengers.
Separately, Eurostar, which has held a monopoly on cross-Channel passenger rail services for decades, said it carried 11.8 million passengers in 2025.
However, the Oct 15 evening’s accident involved “no Eurostar train and has no impact on Eurostar services to and from London”, the company said in a statement.
“All Eurostar trains will run as scheduled.” AFP

UK Sends More Storm Shadow Missiles to Ukraine to Disrupt Russian Attacks Before Winter
The United Kingdom is sending Ukraine additional long-range Storm Shadow cruise missiles to disrupt Russian military operations targeting civilian infrastructure ahead of winter, according to Bloomberg on October 15.
The additional deliveries were discussed during Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s visit to London on October 14, when he met British Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
Bloomberg cited people familiar with the matter who requested anonymity because the weapons shipment has not been publicly announced.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The UK has not disclosed how many missiles are being transferred or when they will arrive. British officials consider Ukrainian strikes against Russian military facilities involved in attacks on civilians and critical infrastructure to be defensive operations, the sources noted.
The sources also indicated that London opposes restricting Ukraine’s strikes inside Russia while Moscow continues attacking Ukrainian territory. The position contrasts with Washington’s reported pressure on Kyiv to suspend drone strikes against Russian oil refineries, the outlet added.
The UK government declined to comment on the reported shipment. Britain has not disclosed the total number of Storm Shadow missiles supplied to Ukraine since 2023 and does not routinely announce individual deliveries, Bloomberg noted.
Manufactured by European defense company MBDA, Storm Shadow missiles have a range exceeding 250 kilometers and use terrain-hugging flight profiles to penetrate enemy air defenses. Ukraine first deployed the British-supplied missiles against military targets inside Russia in November 2024.
Alongside the long-range strike capability, Britain is also strengthening Ukraine's air defenses ahead of winter. London has committed $2.12 billion to supply more than 5,000 Lightweight Multirole Missiles over four years, a weapon effective against the jet-powered drones Russia increasingly uses in deep strikes.
A further $59.7 million in surface-to-air missile deliveries was announced alongside Zelenskyy's visit, with $13.3 million accelerated to meet Ukraine's most urgent winter air-defense needs. Britain is also pressing partners to tighten sanctions and adopt a ban on maritime services for Russian liquefied natural gas exports.

Hadassah Medical Center inaugurated a medical center in Limassol, Cyprus, on Thursday evening and announced plans for a hospital near the island’s capital, Nicosia, expanding the Jerusalem-based institution’s services overseas.
The Limassol facility had begun treating patients ahead of the formal inauguration. Hadassah said the center would bring together Cypriot doctors and healthcare professionals with specialists from its Jerusalem medical teams.
Services included MRI and CT scans, cardiology, neurology, laboratory testing, specialist clinics, rehabilitation and preventive medicine. The center would draw on Hadassah’s clinical expertise and maintain ongoing professional cooperation with its staff in Israel, the institution said.
President Isaac Herzog welcomed the initiative in a message for the inauguration, describing it as a new chapter in relations between Israel and Cyprus.
“The opening of the center symbolizes a bridge between our peoples and between dedicated professionals committed to improving human life,” Herzog said.
Hadassah presented the project as a further area of cooperation between the two countries, alongside their ties in energy, security, trade, research and tourism.
Hospital planned near Nicosia
The planned hospital near Nicosia would include inpatient wards, research activities and partnerships in medical education and training, Hadassah said. It was intended to broaden the range of care the institution could offer in Cyprus.
Hadassah did not provide a construction timetable or cost estimate for the hospital in its announcement.
Prof. Yoram Weiss, Hadassah’s director-general, said the Cyprus expansion reflected the institution’s commitment to making its medical expertise available beyond its existing hospitals.
“The boundaries of medicine should extend far beyond the walls of our hospitals,” Weiss said. “We should make medical care accessible wherever we can help, heal, save lives and teach.”
He said Cypriot medical professionals would work alongside Hadassah specialists to serve patients from Cyprus and the wider region.
Dalia Itzik, chairwoman of Hadassah’s board and a former speaker of the Knesset, Israel’s parliament, said the initiative would create opportunities for closer cooperation between the two countries’ medical communities.
“I am particularly proud that this initiative contributes to strengthening the longstanding friendship between Cyprus and Israel,” she said.
Carol Ann Schwartz, national president of Hadassah, the Women’s Zionist Organization of America, said the partnership would extend the reach of the institution’s medical work.
“The cooperation in Cyprus reflects Hadassah Medical Center’s commitment to bringing to the world the medical breakthroughs it has led in Israel, improving people’s lives across national borders, and strengthens our belief that medicine can serve as a bridge to peace,” Schwartz said.
Hadassah expands medical services across Israel and abroad
The Cyprus project followed Hadassah’s expansion of services within Israel through medical centers in Beit Shemesh, west of Jerusalem; Ramat Gan, near Tel Aviv; and Netivot, in the south.
The Netivot center opened in February to serve residents of the western Negev. Hadassah said its expansion strategy combined the development of services closer to patients’ homes in Israel with new medical partnerships abroad.

Nepal Should Not Shoulder the Himalayan Climate Crisis Alone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
19:36:00 UTC
04:36:00 KST

Have you wondered why the current global order expects frontline geographies to absorb the astronomical shocks of climate disasters entirely on their own, especially when those very states face the unprecedented brunt of a crisis born from a total failure of global collective action? Who funds the recovery when the baseline geography of a nation is structurally altered overnight, especially when the crisis is entirely outside of their own making?
Of course, Nepal’s civilizational history has been a long, adaptive iteration to deal with an unforgiving topography and the sheer gravity of terrains that constantly pull everything down. But the scale of what we saw on August 26, 2026 was entirely unprecedented. The staggering images of landscapes dissolving that looked like a terrifying sci-fi reel made rounds among global audiences,
The Unprecedented Shock
Seven weeks have passed since a massive rockslide detached from a high mountain face in northern Nepal’s Langtang Lirung massif, slamming into the glacial lake below and triggering a catastrophic debris torrent along the Rasuwa-Trishuli corridor. The mud remains heavy, unyielding, and thick with the wreckage of a singular, devastating event. Ever since that unimaginable disaster, Nepal has grappled with the heartbreaking loss of close to 1,500 lives. Thousands remain missing. And thousands more are desperately trying to rebuild their shattered lives from scratch.
The loss is vast. And that stretches far beyond human lives and the statistical tallies of washed-away bridges and infrastructural damages. Or of erased roads or buried houses.
Take the sudden megawatt loss of hydropower assets clustered along this single corridor, projects that were either already online delivering power or actively under construction. Cumulatively, this single cascading hazard knocked over 400 megawatts of clean energy offline in a single afternoon. This is a fundamental blow to a country that has courageously looked toward a future of 30,000 megawatts of clean energy capacity by the next decade. Crucially, much of that power was not meant for domestic consumption alone but was strategically destined to flow southward across the border to anchor the green transitions of our neighbors too. The disaster wiped out roughly 10 percent of Nepal’s total installed electrical capacity in a single afternoon; that does more than disrupt domestic energy equations.
The damage also includes the immediate destruction of the primary cross-border trade artery to our northern neighbor, China, the vital and the nearest entry point for the electric vehicles driving Nepal’s national green transition. Against all conventional global assumptions, Nepal has emerged as a global leader in green mobility, with new passenger EV adoption skyrocketing past 75 percent as the nation aggressively pursues the goal of becoming a fully electric economy. These efforts have now been paralyzed.
Even more devastating is what this corridor represents to the human spirit, and to our resilient high mountain communities. The tragedy impacted the sacred artery for international pilgrims journeying toward the ancient Kailash-Mansarovar sanctuary, a landscape deeply revered across Hindu and Buddhist civilizations, and a legendary frontier of adventure for global explorers. Tragically, many of those currently dead or missing under the mud include these very pilgrims and tourists.
By flattening connecting bridges, stranding cross-border travelers, and decimating localized ecotourism infrastructure, these disasters have dismantled the historic human and economic ties and spiritual sanctuary of the region that bind South Asian nations together, directly threatening the collective dream of an interconnected green grid.
Then came September. Then came October. And both months bought multi-front disasters that defied everything we thought we could predict.
In September, extreme late-monsoon saturation triggered massive landslides across multiple districts simultaneously, repeatedly snapping grid transmission lines and fracturing vital economic corridors just as fast as recovery teams could repair them.
October stripped away any remaining illusion of predictability. On October 11, a morning landslide and the subsequent breach of the natural dam along the steep Budhigandaki River corridor in central Nepal, west of Kathmandu, did more than wash away roads. The landslide slammed directly into the construction site of the 341 MW plant down the valley, specifically engineered to run off the river’s natural flow and step in during our hours of highest electricity demand. While the major structure was not entirely wiped away, the impact leaves us with fundamental questions about systemic safety, early warning capabilities, and the steep costs of re-engineering our infrastructure for a volatile future.
Ultimately, if these vulnerabilities are left unaddressed, the cascading risks will not stop at our borders; they will inevitably strip the entire region of the very clean energy opportunities needed to power our collective green transition.
Nepal, of course, has a lot of serious reflection to do regarding its own development thinking; we are by no means oblivious to that. But the broader crisis remains clear, because no matter how much we reform our internal engineering, a frontline nation simply cannot manage the shocks of a global systemic failure alone.
This gives immediate, painful validation to the warning delivered by Prime Minister Balendra Shah at the United Nations General Assembly in New York. Addressing the international community, the prime minister laid bare a grim economic reality, warning that physical recovery from these escalating disasters could consume up to 10 percent of Nepal’s national GDP. For a nation that contributes less than 0.1 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions, isn’t this far more than a localized setback? Is it not a crushing, completely unjust financial penalty imposed by an unequal global architecture?
Why should a frontline nation independently underwrite the immense physical and financial risks of cross-border infrastructure that the entire subcontinent’s survival depends on? Rather than pointing fingers among ourselves, isn’t this a definitive wake-up call for all of us in the region to come together, align our strategies, and act as a unified front? If our collective green future is at stake, is this massive burden truly for Nepal to shoulder alone, or is it the ultimate test of shared regional solidarity and global accountability?
As we prepare to gather next month at the U.N. Climate Change Conference in Antalya, Nepal will undoubtedly be discussed as a definitive case study. But what will the optics of that discussion be? Will we once again be treated as a passive, flat statistic on a ledger, or as a living warning of what happens when climate shocks freeze a real-world green transition?
The current global climate financing architecture remains stubbornly blind to the high-velocity crises of the Himalayas. If a nation that did everything right, pioneering citizen-funded hydro-infrastructure and skyrocketing its EV adoption, can have its clean energy core paralyzed in a single afternoon, who is it that truly needs to change? Is it Nepal that must reshape its ambitions, or is it a broken global financial system that must finally overhaul its slow-moving bureaucracy before the millions who revere and depend on these ecosystems downstream pay the ultimate price?

Albanian PM condemns 'chaos' as violent unrest spreads
Violent protests spread from Albania's capital to smaller cities on Thursday, as student-led demonstrators demand prime minister Edi Rama's resignation for a third straight day.
Protesters again clashed with police in Albania's capital in hours-long confrontations, with crowds targeting government buildings, banks and shopfronts.
Demonstrators, who had earlier gathered in the thousands, are demanding that Rama step down and that the government offer more support for students, citing poor university conditions and high tuition fees.
On Thursday, protests spread to several smaller cities, as more students joined university boycotts.
In Shkodra, in Albania's northwest, protesters smashed city hall windows and pelted the ruling Socialist Party and opposition Democratic Party headquarters with stones, local media reported.
Broadcast images also showed protesters confronting police in southern coastal cities, with reports of Korce students smashing school windows and blocking streets.
In Tirana, AFP journalists saw repeated clashes with police across the city, with police using water cannons and tear gas as protesters lobbed stones, barricaded roads and set fire to trash.
Streets remained shrouded in smoke and tear gas into the early evening, littered with debris and shattered glass from smashed shopfronts.
The escalation comes after months of anti-government demonstrations in the country originally sparked by a controversial resort development linked to US President Donald Trump's family.
"We demand real change, not empty promises. We want a government that works for its people, not against them," journalism student Teftalia Papa told AFP.
She said the people had many issues accessing basic services, but students were being particularly "crushed by rising costs".
Protesters in Tirana on Tuesday and Wednesday smashed their way into several government buildings and set at least one ablaze.
Rama earlier posted a video on his Facebook page of him touring the burnt-out remains of an office at a college campus in Tirana.
"Until yesterday, this was the office of the College of Europe, the school of a united Europe," he said in the video - his first public comments since the protests began.
"Today this is the ruin left by hands that are not, and can never be, the hands of students," Rama said, blaming opposition figures for the violence at the demonstrations.
"Everyone who has had a hand in this chaos will certainly pay."
'Ruin' and 'chaos'
Meanwhile, protest groups circulated an "ultimatum" demanding the prime minister's resignation by 1:00 pm (1100 GMT).
Rama's office did not respond to AFP's request for comment on the protests and the calls for his resignation.
For more than four months, anti-government protests in Albania have routinely drawn crowds in the thousands.
They were triggered by a luxury hotel project linked to Trump's daughter, Ivanka, and son-in-law, Jared Kushner, that became a symbol of alleged corruption and inequality in the country.
Protester and media analyst Altin Tufa said several factors fueled the demonstrations, but the alleged clearing of land for the project in a protected coastal area was the "last straw, unleashing people's discontent and anger".
"It is the indifference, arrogance and failure of the entire political class to listen to people's concerns about economic, political, social and healthcare issues," Tufa said as he marched with protesters.
The European Union's delegation in Tirana strongly condemned Thursday's "violent escalation".
"We call on protesters to exercise restraint and to refrain from any acts of violence," it said in a statement.
The EU had also previously urged prompt investigation into allegations of excessive police force.
Police said 65 people were arrested during Wednesday's protests, suspected of "attacking police officers, institutions, public and private property".
A total of 71 police officers had been injured in the unrest, some seriously, police chief Skender Hita told reporters on Thursday.
He urged the demonstrators to "immediately distance themselves from masked and violent individuals", pledging that police will not back down.
The health ministry said that hospitals in Tirana treated 89 people on Wednesday, including 61 police officers.
Four officers and two protesters remained hospitalised, with one officer in intensive care, according to the authorities.

Three dead as Istanbul sees heaviest rainfall in 80 years

The rain began lashing Turkey's largest city in earnest on Wednesday morning and intensified throughout the day, causing chaos and flash flooding, with footage showing cars being dragged away by the fast-flowing waters.
"We are talking here about the highest level of precipitation in Istanbul since records began in 1942," Istanbul governor Davut Gul said.

The storm also claimed the life of a 14-year-old boy who was electrocuted when he stepped into a puddle in the Balat area. He was rushed to hospital but medical personnel were unable to save him, officials said.

There was no immediate official confirmation of his death.
Dramatic images
Istanbul municipal teams and firefighters were carrying out cleanup operations at schools, football pitches, garages and other sites on Thursday, pumping water out of flooded areas and clearing mud, an AFP photographer reported.
On Wednesday evening, the governor said schools would be shut across Istanbul until Monday, urging people to stay home "unless absolutely necessary" and advising those living in basement properties "to spend the night on safer, higher floors".
Dramatic footage posted online late Wednesday and collated by DHA showed a line of parked cars in the northern Sariyer district being pushed into the torrent of muddy water, where they were swept away.
Another showed people being hauled from the raging waters to safety through a first-floor window, while elsewhere two people with umbrellas were seen stepping into the shovel of a large mechanical digger, which took them away.
Power and water cuts have also hit areas of the city, notably in Sariyer where shopkeepers could be seen trying to salvage their goods from the mud, an AFP journalist said.
Floods in other cities
Heavy rainfall in the nearby province of Sakarya caused a two-storey villa on the banks of a stream to collapse in Sapanca neighbourhood. As the house had been evacuated earlier, no one was killed or injured.
And in the neighbouring Kocaeli province, a stream overflowed in Gebze district, sweeping away a driver who was later rescued by emergency workers with ropes. In another district, Basiskele, one man was missing after being carried away by floodwaters, reports said.
Forty-three flights bound for Istanbul Airport had to be diverted Wednesday, as did three flights heading for Sabiha Gokcen on the Asian side, which temporarily suspended take-offs due to strong winds, the transport ministry said.
Turkey's AFAD disaster agency has set up a crisis desk to manage incidents caused by the heavy rainfall, which by nightfall Wednesday had risen to 1,277 flooding incidents, 15 landslides, 47 people stranded and two roofs blown off.
The heavy rains are expected to continue over the weekend.
(AFP)

Russia has resumed the process of mothballing and deploying new and refurbished armored vehicles at its storage bases.
This was reported by OSINT researcher Jompy.
Back in June, the researcher noted that at the 349th storage base, the return of refurbished tanks and infantry fighting vehicles was recorded.
This confirms that Russia is actively repairing, modernizing, and manufacturing a significant number of armored vehicles.
In particular, the 22nd storage base is being replenished with T-90M tanks, BTR-82A armored personnel carriers, BMP-3M infantry fighting vehicles, and armored recovery and evacuation vehicles.
This facility is just one of several identified arsenals where a systematic buildup of heavy weapons has been documented.
A similar process is taking place at Storage Base No. 80, which specializes primarily in 2S19 Msta-S self-propelled artillery systems.
At the 374th base near the Finnish border, the accumulation of new 2S43 Malva and 2S44 Hyacinth-K self-propelled artillery systems has been documented since 2025.
Active deliveries are also being tracked at the 6018th base, where BMP-3M infantry fighting vehicles and BMD-4M airborne combat vehicles are being deployed.
The appearance of BMP-2s and T-72B3Ms at the 349th base may indicate either the delivery of refurbished equipment from factories or the routine redeployment of existing resources from other arsenals.
The researcher emphasizes that we are currently talking specifically about long-term storage bases, not bases of active combat units, which also receive equipment.
The observed trends indicate a replenishment of Russia’s strategic reserves.

UN envoy slams calls for Palestinians to prove 'commitment to peace' amid mass killings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
19:23:19 UTC
04:23:19 KST

Palestine's deputy UN envoy told the Security Council that Palestinians are being asked to prove their commitment to peace while enduring mass killing, displacement and annexation, declaring that "occupation must end".
Speaking at a council meeting on Palestine on Thursday, Majed Bamya noted the aftermath of the 7 October events, saying he remembered condemnations for the attacks and demands for the release of hostages, as well as claims by some colleagues that Israel had to defend itself.
He said he searched his memory for any occasion when Palestinians were told, after a massacre, that they had the right to do whatever is necessary.
"Never. Not once before October 7, not once since, not when 10,000 Palestinians were killed, not when 20,000, not when 50,000, not when 70,000 Palestinians were killed," he said.
Bamya said Palestinians warned of the massacres to come, as well as forced displacement and annexation, and responded by seeking diplomacy.
"We sought protection, not justification of violence, whether legitimate or illegitimate. We sought justice, not vengeance," he said. "Yet, we are the ones asked to prove our commitment to peace."
He said "entire multi-generational" families had been wiped out in Gaza, while others were forced to keep running for their lives with no time to mourn, and that "92% of homes in Gaza have been destroyed or damaged".
Bamya said more than 1,000 Palestinians have been attacked in the occupied West Bank, including in the occupied East Jerusalem, in three years.
"Approximately 6,000 settler attacks have occurred since the beginning of this year," he said.
Bamya said Palestinians supported the ceasefire plan and the Security Council resolution endorsing it because they embodied principles including "no bloodshed, no occupation, no annexation, no forcible displacement".
"Yet Israel opposes every one of them," he said.
Noting that the Palestinian Authority has been undermined, with most of its employees unpaid for 15 months, Bamya asked council members which of their countries would still have a standing government under those conditions.
He said Israel "demands reforms while obstructing them, disarmament while its occupation forces continue killing, and while it continues arming settlers, security while denying ours".
"This is not peace; it is permanent subjugation," he said.
Rejecting security as a justification for annexation, he said, "Annexation cannot be justified by the need for security, not in Palestine, not in Lebanon, not in Syria, not anywhere, or borders would be meaningless, and wars would be permanent."
"We are either sovereign states, equal in rights and duties, sharing security and prosperity, or warring parties forever," he said. "Occupation must end."

Government urged to do more over Australian's arrest in Vietnam
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
19:19:33 UTC
04:19:33 KST

Human rights groups want more pressure on Vietnam over Australian's arrest
In short:
Human rights groups have called Vietnam's arrest of Australian pro-democracy campaigner Hiep Tran "outrageous and unacceptable" and urged the federal government to be "quite bold" in pushing for his release.
Mr Tran's supporters allege he was likely abducted by Vietnamese authorities while in Cambodia and bundled across the border.
The Vietnamese government denies the allegations and says Mr Tran was caught trying to illegally enter Vietnam to engage in "terrorist and sabotage activities".
Human rights groups are urging the federal government to ratchet up pressure on Vietnam over the fate of an Australian pro-democracy campaigner who is languishing in jail after disappearing in Cambodia last month.
Melbourne man Hiep Tran vanished after travelling to the region in September to meet Vietnamese human rights groups in Cambodia.
More than a week later, Vietnam's Ministry of Public Security said it had caught Mr Tran and another human rights activist, Norwegian citizen Duc Thuan Nguyen, trying to illegally enter Vietnam to engage in "terrorist and sabotage activities".
But that has been furiously denied by Hiep Tran's supporters, who say the two men had no plan to enter Vietnam, and who allege they were likely abducted by Vietnamese authorities and bundled across the border.
Human rights groups have also pointed out that the two men missed other scheduled appointments in Cambodia and left their luggage and personal items in their hotel rooms in Cambodia — suggesting they had no plans to leave the country.
The two men are members of Viet Tan, an overseas Vietnamese opposition group that the country's ruling party has labelled a terrorist organisation.
Most scholars say that while Viet Tan has roots in armed anti-Communist groups that emerged in the aftermath of the Vietnam War, it relaunched in the 2000s as a political party committed to peaceful change.
Arrest 'outrageous and unacceptable'
Human rights advocate Phil Robertson told the ABC that Hiep Tran's arrest was "outrageous and unacceptable" and another sign that Vietnamese authorities were increasingly determined to target political opponents overseas under its powerful president, former security chief To Lam.
"To Lam has made a point of going after vocal critics whenever he can, and that has included abductions in Thailand, abductions in Germany, abductions now in Cambodia," he said.
Oslo-based lawyers for Duc Thuan Nguyen called his disappearance a "textbook case of enforced disappearance, within a framework of Vietnamese transnational repression".
Cambodia has denied handing over the men to Vietnam, saying they were intercepted at the border crossing.
Vietnam's government has denied targeting critics overseas, saying those allegedly abducted in Thailand were trying to cross illegally back into Vietnam, while the Vietnamese citizen who disappeared in Germany actually returned home voluntarily.
Government making representations
Last week, Foreign Minister Penny Wong told the ABC she would deal with the matter carefully in public.
"I can confirm I'm aware of this case and that Australian officials are aware," she said.
"I can confirm that we have made representations, including from me, in relation to this matter.
"But I'm not in the position, because of privacy considerations, to give you any more information than that."
Mr Tran's supporters say he is currently being detained in the notorious B34 detention centre in Ho Chi Minh City, where political prisoners are often held before trial.
Australian officials had not yet been granted consular access to him as of Monday this week — although it was not clear if that has changed in recent days.
His wife, Chloe Dang, said she was "heartbroken" to be separated from her husband, and has pleaded with Vietnam to set him free.
Hiep Tran is not the first Australian member of Viet Tan to be targeted by authorities in Vietnam — Sydney man Chau Van Kham was released in 2023 after Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and other Australian government ministers lobbied the government to free him.
Mr Robertson said Australia should be "quite bold" and "be prepared to really push hard, both privately and publicly, for Hiep Tran's release".
"Otherwise, we're going to have him facing, you know, a kangaroo court trial and a long prison sentence, that is going to cause major problems for his family and for Vietnamese Australian relations," he said.
'I've been crying a lot'
The case has also stirred debate in the Vietnamese community in Australia, which includes both government supporters and opponents of the communist ruling party.
Brisbane-based community activist My Linh Do, who is a prominent pro-democracy advocate and critic of Vietnam's ruling party, said Hiep Tran's experience reminded her of her own confrontation with Vietnamese authorities almost 15 years ago.
"Since Hiep Tran's incident last week, I got very scared, and I have been losing sleep," she told the ABC.
"I haven't been able to eat. I've been crying a lot."
My Linh told the ABC she was detained in 2012 at the Vietnamese border and interrogated for five days before being released.
She said authorities intimidated her, tried to access her Queensland state government email account and even tried to recruit her to provide intelligence back to the Vietnamese government.
"They didn't use the term 'work as a spy', but they said they want me to report any suspicious activity by a Vietnamese in Australia who is involved in anything," she told the ABC.
DFAT officials 'continue to engage'
A spokesperson for the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT) did not say if they had been granted consular access to Mr Tran.
"Australian officials in Vietnam continue to engage with the Vietnamese government," they said.
DFAT's official travel advice for Vietnam warns that people can be detained for "perceived involvement with non-state-sanctioned political organisations or groups perceived by the Government of Vietnam to be associated with dissident groups".
Allegations 'unfounded and misleading'
Vietnam's embassy in Canberra told the ABC that the allegations of forced abduction were "unfounded and misleading."
"In Viet Nam, arrests and prosecutions are carried out in accordance with the law, as in other countries," a spokesperson said in a statement.
The spokesperson also denied that Vietnamese Australians were treated inappropriately when travelling to the country.
"The steady growth in Australian visitors to Viet Nam, reaching a record half a million last year — including thousands of Australians of Vietnamese origin — reflects Viet Nam's appeal as a travel destination and the growing people-to-people ties between our two countries," they told the ABC.
Cambodia's embassy in Canberra did not respond to the ABC's questions.
