More Than the Sum of Its Parts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
18:42:38 UTC
03:42:38 KST

Maya Valencia Goodall, Amelia Larson, and Miguel Cardona explain why structure, language, and literacy belong together
A midsized urban district serving many Multilingual Learners did something unique: looked hard at their data before the pandemic hit, not after. It would have been easy to let COVID take the blame for what they found, and that’s the story most people assume, but they didn’t reach for that explanation. Their scores had already started slipping in the years leading up to 2020, well before remote learning became a reality. When they pulled the numbers, without disaggregating by language or by school, one figure was impossible to look past: only about a third of their students were reading at or above proficiency. The other two-thirds were being let down by the approach itself, not by circumstance, and the district knew it.
They had spent years in balanced literacy, and between what the data was telling them and a new state law requiring evidence-based reading instruction, the direction was clear. What wasn’t easy was the timing. They rolled out new professional learning in structured literacy in the middle of COVID, over the same laptops their teachers were already using to hold remote classrooms together, because the data wasn’t going to wait for an easier moment.
That district’s experience wasn’t unique, even though the timeline was. Over 40 states now have some version of a reading law on the books (Schwartz, 2022/2026), and many of those laws landed on districts still sorting through years of what was often labeled the reading wars—the public debate that sometimes mistakenly framed evidence-based foundational instruction and multilingual or bilingual education as opposing positions. Instead, they need to inform one another: children need explicit instruction in how print works and opportunities to develop language, knowledge, comprehension, and literacy across the languages they use.
This is exactly the space the three of us set out to create together: a place where the distance between what the research already knows and what students actually experience stops being something districts manage around and starts being the actual work of implementation, turning what the research knows into what a classroom does, one lesson plan at a time. For a district, that means explicit, systematic instruction in the written code sitting in the same plan as oral language, comprehension, writing, and knowledge building, all of it drawing on the languages and experiences Multilingual Learners already bring, visible in the same lesson rather than scattered across separate initiatives.
Where the Research Has Already Converged
We know a great deal about how people learn to read, and for Multilingual Learners, that foundation does not change. What continues to develop is the nuance of implementation, how those same universal processes play out for a learner building literacy and language in two languages at once. The conversations continue because Multilingual Learners deserve instruction built around the full complexity of what they bring, not a simplified version designed for someone else and adjusted afterward. The components long treated as universal to reading, decoding, comprehension, and oral language are realized differently, and more richly, for a bilingual brain drawing on more than one language system. That means more oral language—more real speaking practice—has to be part of instruction from the start, not added once the other pieces are considered secure.
The Distance Between Legislation, Research, and Practice
Recently, we sat in on a panel conversation with state lawmakers and district leaders who shared their commitment to getting every student, including Multilingual Learners, the reading instruction the new laws are asking for. Across the conversation, the same thing came through clearly: the barriers are real, but so is the effort behind trying to solve them. Everyone at the table took the time to work through the nuances rather than reach for the easy answer, weighing what came next with real care. Funding is tight in places, and some state laws set timelines that assume a pace no district can actually move at. Others don’t name Multilingual Learners at all, leaving districts to figure out on their own what the law’s intent means for the students who need it most. Yet despite those barriers, we watched leaders turn them into opportunities, staying committed to making sure every student gets the instruction they’re owed.
None of that is a reason to stop, and none of the people in that room treated it as one. Every barrier named clearly is a barrier that’s closer to being solved, and what came through, over and over, was a field choosing to treat its barriers as design problems rather than dead ends.
From Convergence to Classroom Practice
At the classroom level, language and literacy don’t develop on separate timelines. They develop together, simultaneously and mutually reinforcing, not one paving the way for the other. Students should encounter worthwhile ideas through discussion, read-alouds, reading, and writing while they receive explicit instruction in the sound–spelling patterns they need. Their home languages, knowledge, and ways of expressing ideas are resources in that work. No student should have to demonstrate complete oral English proficiency before gaining access to substantive texts or writing about what they know.
In practice, a lesson can include explicit phonics instruction and purposeful discussion of content. When a student encounters an unfamiliar written word, the teacher directs attention to the letters and spelling patterns. Meaning can then help the student check a plausible pronunciation or understand a correctly decoded word. If the word is unfamiliar in English, a brief explanation, visual, discussion, or connection to a language the student knows can build understanding without asking the student to guess from context. Reading, speaking, listening, and writing reinforce one another throughout the lesson.
Integration over Isolation
The last piece of this is resisting the pull to let any single component of literacy carry the whole house on its own. Students need accurate word reading and opportunities to make meaning from text. Oral language, vocabulary, content knowledge, discussion, and writing develop alongside foundational skills. Teachers can examine whether a difficulty lies in decoding, unfamiliar English vocabulary, pronunciation variation, or comprehension, then respond with the support the student actually needs.
We use structured language and literacy to describe this intentional design: explicit, systematic instruction in the written code integrated with language development, knowledge building, meaningful reading, writing, and oracy. It is a way to plan and examine instruction, not a claim to have invented a new research framework or program.
Multilingual Learners are central to that design. They bring linguistic and cultural resources, and their literacy may develop across more than one language. Instruction can draw on cognates, morphology, cross-language comparisons, and students’ existing knowledge while teaching the English patterns they need. Their accents or developing English vocabulary should not automatically be mistaken for decoding problems. It is long overdue to consider the needs and strengths of Multilingual Learners as we plan core curricular and instructional design, not as an intervention post-core instruction.
That same principle extends beyond the classroom. Families carry language, knowledge, stories, culture, and literacy practices that schools can build on rather than work around. Strong literacy systems don’t ask families to set aside the language they know best so a child can learn English. They help families use that language to strengthen conversation, knowledge, and reading at home, which reinforces rather than competes with what’s happening at school.
Building a Cohesive Structure
Now we’ve established that the Science of Reading is broad enough to encompass methodologies that work for all students, including Multilingual Learners, we need to ensure that all educators have the tools, training, and support to give students the most appropriate instruction every day. Teachers across the curriculum should have the structure to be able to work cohesively using research-based instruction to achieve literacy goals.
The forward-thinking district we described earlier is still doing this work and its success at boosting literacy rates, including those of Multilingual Learners, still needs to be assessed. However, the decision to examine the data, strengthen foundational instruction, and plan language development alongside literacy offers a direction well worth studying in our pursuit of providing instruction that helps more children learn to read accurately in multiple languages, with depth of comprehension, while using their varied linguistic resources.
References
Schwartz, S. (2022; updated 2026). “Which States Have Passed ‘Science of Reading’ Laws? What’s in Them?” Education Week. www.edweek.org/teaching-learning/which-states-have-passed-science-of-reading-laws-whats-in-them/2022/07
Maya Valencia Goodall is chief impact officer at CORE Learning.
Amelia Larson is chief academic officer at Summit K12.
Dr. Miguel Cardona is president of Cardona Solutions and was the twelfth US secretary of education.

Fuel crisis compo clause could leave one state's taxpayers facing $80bn bill

IN BRIEF
- Victoria considered overhauling decades-old fuel emergency laws amid fears of substantial legal liability.
- Proposed changes were never introduced, leaving any overhaul to the next parliament.
Victorian taxpayers could be on the hook for tens of billions of dollars in the event of a major fuel crisis under legislation that allows payment for those suffering economic loss.
The prospect of a budget black hole of up to $80 billion had forced the state government to consider updating its 1970s-era fuel emergency laws, which allow the preservation and allocation of fuel supplies during declared fuel emergencies.
The rethink came in June amid higher fuel costs due to the war in the Middle East and as the federal government extended fuel excise relief.
But the legislative amendments were ultimately not introduced before the end of the parliamentary sitting year, meaning any changes would now have to wait until the next parliament, with the state election due in late November.
Federal, state and territory governments can declare fuel emergencies, with the Victorian government initially appearing concerned over what liability it could be exposed to in the event it used powers under its laws.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Such declarations are made if any kind of fuel is likely to become unavailable, allowing compensation to be paid to those who suffer financial losses as a result of being forced to comply with ministerial directions.
The broad powers allow the minister to control, direct, restrict or prohibit the production, supply, distribution, sale, use or consumption of the fuel; or direct at what times and places services may be used.
The laws also allow people to be compensated for complying with the directions if they suffer losses or damages.
"Any sums required to be paid or provided for the purposes of this Act shall be paid out of the Consolidated Fund," the law states, referring to the state's primary financial account into which all revenue is paid.
Declaring a state of emergency under the Fuel Emergency Act is rare. A 2020 parliamentary library research paper found the most recent declaration was in 2004, after a factory fire triggered a briquette shortage. The state government invoked the powers and secured the remaining briquette supply to keep hospital boilers running.
At the time, and still today, there was no indication of any immediate threat to Australia's or the state's liquid fuel supply.
Prices, however, have risen across the country following the end of temporary fuel excise relief, and against the backdrop of continued conflict in the Middle East and volatility in global oil markets.
The war has also sparked questions over Australia's energy security and how the nation might be impacted if there were severe disruptions or shortages.
In the case of Victoria, if it were to expose itself to compensation claims through the use of emergency powers, the state government could face a legal burden of up to $80 billion that would ultimately fall to taxpayers, according to a June draft government proposal seen by SBS News.
The potentially heavy cost was a key driver for the changes, the proposal states, as well as the inordinate amount of time and money it would take to manage claims and potential lawsuits.
The state government believed the current laws were out of step with other jurisdictions, where some fuel emergency regimes provide explicit immunity from certain legal claims, while compensation may be unavailable or subject to tighter thresholds.
A Victorian government spokesperson had previously told SBS News the Fuel Emergency Act would be updated to align it with other states and territories, ensuring a "consistent, modern approach" to managing fuel supply disruptions.
Asked last week why the government had not gone ahead with the amendments and whether it still believed the laws would expose it to substantial financial liability in the event of a state-declared fuel emergency, a spokesperson did not answer directly.
"The review of Victoria's Fuel Emergency Act was part of national contingency planning in response to global fuel supply risks," the spokesperson said.
"Victoria is now better prepared to respond to any fuel emergency, with stronger national coordination, better visibility of fuel supplies and clear arrangements to manage disruptions."
The spokesperson said the state's fuel supply "remains strong" and that the government was working with the federal government and industry to "prepare for any potential disruption".
The spokesperson did not address how the potential liability of up to $80 billion was calculated.
Earlier this year, Australia was gripped by concerns over fuel supply sparked by global oil shortages due to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz — the vital waterway through which about a fifth of the world's oil supply flows.
The head of the International Energy Agency warned the global economy was facing a "major threat" to supply, describing the situation as worse than the two oil crises of the 1970s combined, as well as the crisis caused by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Political figures such as One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce had called for federal fuel rationing measures in the cities to mitigate the impact of shortages in the regions, calling on the federal government to enact a state of emergency over the situation.
The federal government had reportedly crisis-planned in the event of a national shortage, with measures including fuel rationing and limits on fuel purchase per vehicle, according to a report by Guardian Australia in May.

====================================================================================================

Google’s quantum Willow chip may be able to grow ‘magic states’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
18:39:34 UTC
03:39:34 KST

Quantum computers promise exponential computational power by processing many possibilities simultaneously. But the machines we have today are still far from this ideal. For one, their bits, called qubits, are prone to frequent errors, and as a result, quantum computers are limited for now. To overcome errors, the machines need to tap into so-called magic states—and scientists at Google Research think their quantum chip could help get them there. In a new study published today in Science, the researchers show how to supply magic states more cheaply using a gardening-inspired technique called cultivation.
Traditional computers build every calculation from a few simple logic gates, such as AND, OR and NOT. By contrast, “quantum computers have their own analogy of these operations called the Clifford gates,” explains Emma Rosenfeld, a researcher at Google Quantum AI and the study’s lead author. Clifford gates, however, can be imitated by a normal computer. “But there is one particular gate that unlocks the quantum computer’s power,” Rosenfeld says. “Physicists call it a non-Clifford gate, most often a T gate.” This extra gate is produced using a magic state.
A quibit in a magic state is prepared in a very specific blend of the states 0 and 1 (occupying a mixture of states is a specialty of quantum computers). Fed into a calculation, it is used up to perform the extra gate, and any flaw in the state becomes a flaw in the gate. “It has to be made very, very precisely,” Rosenfeld says.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The standard recipe to make magic states is called distillation, and it creates fewer, more accurate quantum states from many imperfect ones. “You can have up to 95 percent of your quantum computer being spent just generating these high-fidelity magic states,” Rosenfeld says. To bypass this bottleneck, in 2024 her colleagues at Google Research proposed an alternative technique called cultivation, which works on a single state.
Using Google’s Willow chip, Rosenfeld’s team encoded a rough magic state in a few qubits and then measured it. Measuring a quantum state typically collapses it, forcing it into one of two possible answers. So instead of asking the question, “Are you 0 or 1?” which collapses the quantum state to either of those two options, the team asked, “Are you the right magic state: yes or no?”
States that pass this test are then spread across more qubits for stronger protection, hence the gardening name: the state starts small, gets checked and then grows. Without cultivation, about four attempts in 1,000 produced a faulty state. With it, errors fell by roughly 40-fold. The experiment used 54 physical qubits out of Willow’s 105.
“The Google experiment shows that cultivation works in practice,” says Kenneth Brown, director of the Duke Quantum Center at Duke University, who was not involved in the study. He notes, however, that the technique relies on a quality assurance step that rejects low-quality states, discarding 92 percent of attempts.
The result is still far from what practical applications demand. For example, using a quantum computer to break the current RSA-2048 encryption employed in website security, banking and electronic ID cards would require magic states that would fail only once in 10 billion tries. To simulate molecules, a use Rosenfeld says is more attainable, we would need such states with only one error in a million to one in 100 million. Right now the team stands at roughly one error in 10,000 attempts. Still, the new work represents a step in the right direction, she says.
“We’re more galvanized than ever to get to these near-term scientific applications,” Rosenfeld says.

WATCH: Israel ‘very close’ to creating conditions for regime change in Iran, Netanyahu adviser says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
18:38:30 UTC
03:38:30 KST

Israel was “very close” to creating conditions for regime change in Iran, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s foreign policy adviser Ophir Falk told The Jerusalem Post in a studio interview, while stressing that the Iranian people would have to determine their country’s future.
“I think we’re very close to creating those conditions,” Falk said when asked how close pressure on Tehran had brought the prospect of regime change. “Those conditions are being created as we speak right now.”
Speaking with Post Editor-in-Chief Zvika Klein and diplomatic correspondent Amichai Stein, Falk said Israel’s actions were creating conditions that would allow Iranians to challenge their rulers.
“Regime change in Iran is up to the Iranian people,” he said.
Falk described the US-led economic blockade as successful, while noting that economic pressure needed time to produce results. He argued that Iran and its regional proxies had been severely weakened by the war, citing strikes on senior figures, nuclear scientists, missiles, launchers and production capabilities.
Stein asked whether Israel and the US had done enough to provide the Iranian people with the means to challenge their rulers. Falk described Operations Rising Lion and Roaring Lion as “two of the most successful military operations in recent history,” saying their achievements had been “incredible” while acknowledging that no military operation could be perfect.
He also acknowledged the danger facing Iranians who took to the streets, citing the regime’s violent repression of protesters.
“I can appreciate the concerns of people,” he said when the discussion turned to their fear of demonstrating.
Falk did not offer a timetable for political change in Tehran or detail what further assistance might be provided to Iranians seeking it.
Gaza disarmament and the proposed two-week pause
Turning to Gaza, Falk said Hamas could disarm “in an afternoon” if it wanted to, and that Israel would not redeploy before the terrorist group was fully disarmed. Reconstruction, he said, would have to wait for demilitarization.
“If Hamas wanted to disarm, they could do that in an afternoon,” he said. “And that’s what we expect.”
Falk outlined three requirements for Gaza: disarming Hamas, demilitarizing the territory and deradicalizing its population. He presented those goals as consistent with US President Donald Trump’s 20-point plan.
“That means zero weapons,” he said of demilitarization.
The Trump-led Board of Peace was established to oversee implementation of the plan, including Gaza’s reconstruction and transition to a new governing framework.
Stein pressed Falk on why Israel would not agree to a two-week pause in targeted killings and other military activity to allow an attempt at securing Hamas’s disarmament. The question followed Klein’s description of frustration among figures in the Trump administration over Israel’s approach to the board’s work.
Falk said he was unfamiliar with the 14-day proposal. He reiterated that Hamas and all other terrorist organizations in Gaza had to disarm, and that Israel would not redeploy before Hamas was fully disarmed throughout the territory.
“We’re not going to settle for anything less,” he said.
When Klein pointed out that changing attitudes among Gaza’s population could not be accomplished in an afternoon, Falk agreed that deradicalization would take time. He reiterated that Hamas could disarm in an afternoon if it wanted to.
‘We have not been as successful’ in information warfare
Falk’s assessment of Israel’s diplomatic position was consistently upbeat. He pointed to relations with the US, India, South American countries and European partners as evidence that Israel’s military strength had reinforced its international standing.
Klein challenged that assessment, asking about hostility toward Israel among Democrats and signs of erosion within the Republican Party. Stein raised statements marking October 7 in which US political figures devoted substantial attention to Palestinian suffering and criticism of Israel.
Falk acknowledged a problem in the public arena.
“We’ve been fighting a seven-front war, and on the eighth front, the information warfare, we have not been as successful as we have been on the battlefield,” he said. “And we will need to address that as well.”
He nevertheless maintained that the strategic relationship with Washington remained exceptionally close, citing joint military activity, planning and frequent conversations between Netanyahu and Trump.
Asked how many times the two leaders had spoken over the preceding week or two, Falk said they spoke often but could not recall the precise timing.
“I haven’t seen daylight between the president and the prime minister on the big issues,” he said when asked about differences over Iran.
Pressed on whether American requests had constrained Israeli military decisions, Falk said Netanyahu’s approach was to agree when possible and refuse when Israel’s security required it. He added that Netanyahu had said no on a number of occasions.
‘We’re going to get them all out’: Falk on the hostage negotiations
Falk said Netanyahu rejected an early working assumption held by some that Hamas would kill all the hostages and insisted that bringing every hostage home become a formal war objective.
“The prime minister did not accept that,” Falk said. “He said we’re going to get them all out, and we’re going to put it as a war objective to get them all out.”
Falk maintained that military pressure, diplomatic pressure and a united Israeli-American position were the combination that produced hostage releases. He said perceived differences between Jerusalem and Washington encouraged Hamas to retreat from negotiations.
Falk also credited Netanyahu with pressing then-president Joe Biden to increase pressure on Qatar to secure additional releases during the first agreement in November 2023.
One of the most pointed exchanges concerned whether Israel could have secured an additional hostage agreement between the November 2023 releases and the January 2025 deal.
Stein asked whether any agreement had been possible during that period, distinguishing between the availability of a deal and whether it would have been a good deal for Israel.
“No, there was no deal on the table,” Falk initially replied.
When pressed, he defined that answer in terms of the government’s war objectives: dismantling Hamas’s military and governing capabilities, freeing all the hostages and ensuring Gaza could no longer threaten Israel.
“There was no deal that could enable Israel to achieve its war objectives,” he said.
Falk argued that an arrangement requiring Israel to release large numbers of Palestinian prisoners, withdraw and leave the prewar threat intact would have contradicted the goals approved by the cabinet. He cited an Israeli proposal that then-US secretary of state Antony Blinken described in April 2024 as “extraordinarily generous,” saying Hamas had rejected it.
His account addressed a dispute that has resurfaced around former White House Middle East coordinator Brett McGurk’s book, Brink: Inside the Race to Free the October 7th Hostages, and McGurk’s recent interview with the Post.
In a separate interview on Dan Senor’s Call Me Back podcast, McGurk called the suggestion that Hamas had been ready to release all the hostages in the days after October 7 “complete bullshit.” He said Hamas had demanded the release of all Palestinian prisoners, continued Hamas rule and a return to the prewar status quo.
Phil Gordon, who served as national security adviser to then-vice president Kamala Harris, challenged claims that McGurk’s account vindicated Netanyahu. Gordon alleged that Netanyahu introduced additional conditions in July 2024 after Hamas accepted the basic framework, delaying an agreement by six months.
Asked about McGurk’s impression that members of Israel’s negotiating team had sometimes gone beyond Netanyahu’s position, Falk declined to dispute the former US official’s personal assessment.
“I don’t want to argue with Brett’s feelings,” he said. He added that Netanyahu and the cabinet would not approve an agreement that jeopardized Israel or its war objectives.
Falk praised Trump’s approach, while declining to speculate about whether Israel would have reached the same position had Kamala Harris won the 2024 presidential election or Biden served another term.
He accused the Biden administration of imposing a “de facto embargo” on some weapons Israel needed before the Rafah operation. The Biden administration paused a shipment of heavy bombs in May 2024 over concerns about civilian casualties, while other US weapons continued to flow to Israel.
October 7: ‘It’s going to be a long war’
Falk also described his own morning on October 7, 2023, saying he was asleep when the attack began and was called shortly afterward to the Kirya, Israel’s military headquarters in Tel Aviv.
Before leaving, he woke his children, who were serving in the military, and told them to report to their units.
He described Netanyahu as focused while receiving updates on the unfolding attack.
“He told me it’s going to be a long war,” Falk recalled, saying the remark came on the way to an initial briefing from the security chiefs.
According to Falk, Netanyahu’s immediate instructions included reinforcing the northern front to deter Hezbollah from joining the fighting, enabling the military to concentrate on the south, preventing the terrorists who had entered Israel from returning to Gaza and calling up as many reservists as needed.
Falk said that, to the best of his recollection, French President Emmanuel Macron was the first foreign leader to call Netanyahu that day. He recalled Macron offering to mediate on the day of the massacre and Netanyahu rejecting the approach.
According to Falk, Netanyahu compared Hamas to ISIS and warned that Macron would face the group in Paris if Israel did not dismantle it in Gaza. Falk said Netanyahu also told Macron not to convey messages on his behalf, adding that Hamas would soon receive a message from Israel.
He also denied reports raised by Klein that UAE President Sheikh Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan had telephoned Netanyahu before October 7 to warn him of an impending attack.
“There was no such call,” Falk said.
Klein distinguished that allegation from possible communications between the countries’ intelligence agencies. Falk said he was unaware of any warning or caution, while reiterating his denial of a warning call between the leaders.
Abraham Accords and Saudi Arabia
On regional diplomacy, Falk praised the United Arab Emirates and said economic relations under the Abraham Accords, the US-brokered normalization agreements launched in 2020, had continued to develop through the war.
Asked why the UAE had publicly acknowledged Netanyahu’s visit, Falk said doing so served both countries’ national interests. He described the visit as “fantastic.”
He expressed support for normalization with Saudi Arabia but gave no details of negotiations or conditions for an agreement.
The discussion also touched on the flydubai passengers diverted to Saudi Arabia. Asked about the refusal to allow an Israeli civilian aircraft to collect them, Falk emphasized reports that they had been treated well and had reached Israel safely. He said a joint investigation into the incident was underway.
On the Houthis, the Iranian-backed movement in Yemen, Falk condemned attacks on civilians and said Israel would act to defend its security and national interests. He did not specify whether Israel was assisting Saudi Arabia against the group.
Asked what needed to happen for additional countries to establish relations with Israel, Falk initially said Israel had to win the war and then secure peace. When pressed on whether normalization would therefore have to wait, he said agreements could come whenever prospective partners were ready.
“I think that can happen and will happen much quicker than you think,” he said.

Syrian gas pipeline targeted in another sabotage attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
18:35:00 UTC
03:35:00 KST

A gas pipeline in Syria's northeast was damaged in a "sabotage attack, " the state-owned petroleum company said Thursday, the latest such incident against an energy conduit in recent weeks.
The explosion followed a separate incident on Thursday morning in which a pipeline transporting oil products from the coastal city of Baniyas to the central province of Homs was damaged in what the Syrian Petroleum Company described as sabotage aimed at stealing fuel.
Years of civil war before the fall of longtime dictator Bashar Assad in late 2024 devastated Syria's oil, gas and electricity sectors, with the country becoming heavily reliant on imports to meet its needs.
"The Al-Jabsa production gas pipeline was targeted" in Hasakah province, causing a fire, the Syrian Petroleum Company said, according to official news agency SANA.
The company said that the 16-inch pipeline exploded at 5:15 p.m. in an area about 60 km from the city of Al-Shaddadi.
Technical teams isolated the damaged section by closing valves at the plant and the Deir ez-Zor gas station in the al-Bughailiya area, while firefighting and safety crews headed to the site to secure the area, the statement said.
"Relevant authorities are monitoring the situation. The area has been cordoned off, the isolation valves on either side of the targeted section have been closed, and the surrounding area has been secured," the company said.
That incident at the Baniyas-Homs oil products pipeline caused a gasoline leak, the company said, adding that work was continuing to repair the damage and restore the line to service.
The state petroleum company said last week that an oil pipeline in the country's northeast was also damaged in a sabotage attack.
On Sept. 29, sabotage targeting a gas pipeline in eastern Syria caused an explosion, according to SANA.
And in early October, an explosion at a gas pipeline near the capital Damascus took three power stations offline.
The incidents come after demonstrations last month over rising fuel prices, which authorities linked to price hikes caused by the Middle East war.

Top German court orders Cabinet minister to delete video accusing Left Party of antisemitism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:44:36 UTC
21:44:36 KST

Ayhan Simsek
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
Germany’s top court has ordered Economy Minister Katherina Reiche to remove an Instagram video from her ministry’s official account in which she accused the Left Party of openly embracing antisemitism.
The Federal Constitutional Court said in an interim order published on Thursday that sharing such claims from an official government account may violate the socialist Left Party’s right to equal participation in political competition.
“This is particularly relevant given the ongoing discussions regarding the formation of a government in the city-state of Berlin,” the court said, referring to exploratory talks after the Left Party’s election victory in the German capital on Sept. 20.
“The continued circulation of the statements in question is capable of severely discrediting the applicant in the public eye. This could also make it more difficult for potential coalition partners to enter into a coalition agreement with it,” the court said.
“Consequently, political realities could be created that extend far beyond the negative characterizations directed at the applicant,” it added.
 
Video to remain offline until final decision
The judges ruled 6-2 that the video must remain offline until a final decision on the Left Party’s complaint, for no longer than six months.
The court did not rule on whether Reiche’s remarks were unconstitutional and stressed that she remains free to express her views on the topic as a politician or as a private citizen.
The Left Party took the case to the Karlsruhe-based court after the ministry refused its demand to delete the video by Sept. 29, arguing that a federal ministry must not use state resources and official authority to campaign against a political party.
Reiche, a conservative politician from Chancellor Merz’s center-right CDU, argued through her lawyers that the remarks were constitutionally sound and did not violate the government’s duty of political neutrality.
In the clip, posted on Sept. 24 and taken from a speech she gave a day earlier at a business event, Reiche warned against a possible Berlin government involving the Left Party, criticizing its long-standing plans to expropriate large private housing companies as a response to soaring rents.
She also attacked it as a party “that openly embraces antisemitism, that makes Jews in this city afraid.”
Left Party politicians have repeatedly criticized their opponents for using antisemitism allegations to silence criticism of Israeli government policies and of what they describe as crimes committed by the Netanyahu government in Gaza.
The Left Party’s lead candidate in Berlin, Elif Eralp, has repeatedly dismissed claims of antisemitism against her and the party.
She said party leaders had distanced themselves from a small number of isolated incidents at some campaign events.
She added that the Left Party opposes all forms of racism and noted that during her career she has been involved in projects combating antisemitism.
Eralp’s Left Party won Berlin’s city-state election on Sept. 20 with 25.7% of the vote, more than doubling its share from three years ago. The party is currently holding talks with the center-left SPD and the environmentalist Greens on forming a potential coalition government.

EXPLAINER – Israel elections: What do main parties say about Palestinians?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:39:57 UTC
21:39:57 KST

Growing international recognition of Palestinian statehood and a UN inquiry’s finding that Israel committed genocide in Gaza have not stopped leading candidates in Israel’s Oct. 27 election from campaigning against Palestinian independence and promising further military action.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his far-right coalition pledge to double down on their policies in Gaza and the occupied West Bank. However, key opposition figures also reject Palestinian statehood, criticizing Netanyahu more for failing to dismantle Hamas than for the devastation of Gaza.
The parties differ over annexation, settlement expansion and who should govern parts of Palestinian territory. But their positions suggest that replacing Netanyahu would not necessarily break with policies that have prolonged the occupation and denied Palestinians sovereignty.
Here is where the main parties stand on Gaza, settlements and Palestinian self-government. All seat projections come from an Oct. 14 Madad poll, which put the four coordinating opposition lists at 50 seats and Netanyahu’s existing coalition parties at 47 – both short of a 61-seat majority.
Netanyahu’s Likud leads the government that took office in December 2022 and oversaw the military campaign that devastated Gaza and killed nearly 75,000 people.
Netanyahu faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity, including starvation as a method of warfare.
Still his party is polling second, with 18 projected seats.
On Gaza, he insists Hamas must fully disarm before Israeli forces end their occupation.
Likud portrays Palestinian statehood as a security threat, accusing opposition leaders of enabling it even when they explicitly reject it.
Its government has accelerated settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank, with ministers presenting construction as a means of preventing Palestinian independence. Occupier violence against Palestinians has also increased.
At his September UN General Assembly speech, Netanyahu dismissed reports of record Israeli occupier violence against Palestinians in the West Bank as a “handful of young juvenile delinquents.”
Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionism, a far-right coalition partner, received six projected seats and could again help Netanyahu govern.
Speaking on a Ynet podcast in September, Smotrich called for dismantling the Palestinian Authority and extending Israel’s genocidal war to the West Bank: “do there what we did in Gaza.”
He also demanded annexation of territory Israel occupies in Gaza.
His West Bank agenda includes annexing approximately 82% of the territory, under a proposal presented in September 2025. That would leave Palestinians in fragmented areas rather than a territorially connected state.
Under this strategy, the primary stated goal is to permanently eliminate the possibility of an independent Palestinian state.
National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Jewish Power, another far-right coalition partner, received eight projected seats.
At a September campaign news conference, Ben-Gvir presented a plan to displace 1.86 million Palestinians from Gaza over seven years under what he calls “voluntary emigration.”
Ben-Gvir advocates restoring Israeli settlements in Gaza rather than Palestinian self-government.
He has also defended extreme measures such as reducing food for Palestinian detainees.
In August 2026, he called for Israeli forces to kill “30 to 40” people in Gaza every night, while declaring that “all of Gaza” belonged to Israel.
Former military chief Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar led the poll with 20 projected seats, making him a leading contender to head an opposition government.
Speaking near Gaza on Thursday, Eisenkot pledged to end Hamas’s rule within 18 months of becoming prime minister, either through US President Donald Trump’s framework or military action, leaving open the prospect of further Israeli military operations in the enclave.
Eisenkot told a Channel 7 podcast on Oct. 11 that “the principle of two states for two peoples is a mistake,” rejecting the two-state solution.
He also opposes incorporating millions of Palestinians into Israel, saying he wants to preserve a strong Jewish majority.
Former prime ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid’s Together alliance received 12 projected seats and could emerge as a key partner in an opposition coalition. Despite differences over Gaza’s future, both have opposed Palestinian statehood in the near term.
Bennett rejects Palestinian statehood and has called for continued Israeli military operation in Gaza until Hamas is disarmed.
Although Lapid has expressed support for a two-state solution in the longer term and occupier settler violence, he has not committed to reversing settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank.
Bennett, meanwhile, supports settlement expansion, which further entrenches Israeli control over Palestinian land and undermines prospects for an independent Palestinian state.
Avigdor Lieberman’s secular nationalist Yisrael Beytenu received nine projected seats and joined the opposition campaign pact.
Lieberman proposes dismantling the Palestinian Authority and canceling the Oslo agreements, replacing Palestinian self-rule in Areas A and B of the occupied West Bank with Jordanian administration while Israel retains control over Area C, which accounts for around 60% of the territory.
He openly presents the proposal as a way to prevent an internationally recognized Palestinian state, denying Palestinians a sovereign future while preserving Israeli control over much of the occupied territory.
For Gaza, Lieberman has advocated cutting off water, electricity and fuel supplies while backing continued Israeli military operations.
Ofer Winter’s new Amcha Israel received four projected seats. It opposes Palestinian statehood and promotes Palestinian displacement from Gaza. A potential Netanyahu partner, it also supports ultra-Orthodox enlistment, creating possible friction with his religious allies.
Those allies, United Torah Judaism and Shas, received eight and seven seats respectively. Their priorities center on religious institutions and military-service exemptions.
Shas supports dismantling Hamas and demilitarizing Gaza while opposing indefinite Israeli control. United Torah Judaism has no comparably detailed independent Gaza policy, according to the Jerusalem Post.
The poll also gives four seats to the separate Reservists list led by Yoaz Hendel and Yaron Zelekha, adding another potential factor in coalition negotiations.
The Joint List received nine projected seats and Ra’am six. Their votes could be decisive, but Netanyahu and leading opposition figures reject governing partnerships with Arab-led parties.
Ra’am leader Mansour Abbas has called for recognition of an independent Palestinian state and an end to occupation. His party previously joined the Bennett-Lapid government in 2021.
Joint List leader Yousef Jabareen has made progress toward Palestinian statehood a condition for negotiating support for a new government.
Their demands also challenge continued Israeli control of Palestinian territory. In its July 2024 advisory opinion, the International Court of Justice found Israel’s continued presence unlawful and said it must end new settlement activity and evacuate settlers.

Frank Lloyd Wright's only planetarium restored in Florida
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
18:25:37 UTC
03:25:37 KST

Frank Lloyd Wright's only planetarium restored in Florida
Campus architects at Florida Southern College have updated the only planetarium designed by American architect Frank Lloyd Wright as part of a decades-long restoration project at the school, which was masterplanned by Wright.
The restoration included interior and exterior updates of the building, known simply as the Planetarium. The structure, which sits at one end of the Polk County Science Building, has been largely closed since 2004, when the projection system stopped working.
The renovation was guided by Jeff Baker, resident campus architect and a principal at MCWB Architects. Baker has worked on Wright projects at Florida Southern College (FSC) for twenty years and said the Planetarium has long been a goal.
"Since the outset of these overall restoration efforts, the college was always looking for an opportunity to restore the Planetarium, knowing full well its potential to excite and inspire audiences of all ages as they get a glimpse into the heavens and the great genius of Frank Lloyd Wright," Baker told Dezeen.
Work on the exterior began in 2021. The team replaced the roof, flashings, failed stucco on upper portions of the facade and replaced over 280 hand-cast "textile" tiles that line the building's perimeter.
The team then moved inside starting in 2023, where "decades of interventions since Wright's death had dramatically altered the room", according to Baker.
The team updated the Planetarium's technology and audio, repainting the walls from a deep blue, and paring down or removing insertions such as a computer closet built in the 1980s.
It also included working with local craftsmen to restore the original Wright-designed seating made of plywood and colored vinyl upholstery, and repositioning it to its rightful orientation.
"The removal of the old computer closet retrieved the space as it was designed," said Baker. "This removal allowed us to restore and reinstate all the seating in its original circular form, which we learned is a very rare survival in planetariums throughout the country."
Other updates included reinstating the original paint and plaster, and restoring the floor in a "Cherokee Red" finish.
It is one of thirteen Wright buildings built between 1938 and 1958, which the university has been updating since 2007.
Previous restoration work included updating the Waterdome, Wright's largest built fountain, the Esplanades, monolithic covered walkways that traverse the campus and the towering Annie Pfieffer Chapel.
Baker said, like working on other buildings on campus, Wright's "elemental" architecture proved to be the most challenging aspect of the project, as there are "no 'poche' spaces to hide modern building systems".
"Frank Lloyd Wright spent his life conceiving architecture as a synthesis of art and structure," he said.
"At Florida Southern College, this is manifested in buildings that are elemental – the concrete floors are the ceilings for the rooms below, the concrete ceiling is also the roof above."
"We believe we were able to devise methods to insert these systems in sensitive ways that meet the needs of the college yet allowed us to retrieve Wright's vision for the space."
The team completed the ongoing work through grants from institutions such as the J Paul Getty Foundation, which supported the preparation of the original Campus Heritage Plan in 2007.
The college has used the plan as a guide to update Wright's buildings.
It is the only college Wright master-planned. FSC president Ludd Spivey commissioned the architect in 1938 and, deemed a National Historic Landmark in 2012, it is the largest single-site collection of Frank Lloyd Wright architecture in the world.
The Planetarium is now open to the campus and public for tours and screenings.
Dezeen recently rounded up six other Frank Lloyd Wright preservation projects across the US, including recent updates to the famed Falling Water house in Pennsylvania.
The photography is courtesy of Florida Southern College.

Trade between Brazil and China reached a record US$143 billion in the first nine months of the year, driven by Brazilian oil sales that surged after the war on Iran disrupted Gulf supply, according to a report by the Brazil-China Business Council.

Cornell faculty pressure president ahead of no-confidence vote
NEW YORK – Cornell University president Michael Kotlikoff is facing mounting pressure over the school’s handling of sexual assault allegations, after faculty peppered him with questions ahead of a no-confidence vote against the university’s leadership.
On Oct 14, members of the Cornell Faculty Senate questioned Kotlikoff over the safety of Greek life, the organisational structure of university leadership and how the Ivy League school has responded to the allegations.
Kotlikoff, who became interim president in 2024 and was named president the following year, also addressed concerns from current and former staff about how the sexual assault case has shaken trust in the school’s leaders.
“If this university feels that they will solve this problem by replacing a president, that, itself, is not good for Cornell’s reputation because I don’t think it’s the right way you address situations like this,” Kotlikoff responded to one question.
The meeting was closed to the media and accessible only to those with a school ID or log-in information, according to Cornell’s faculty dean.
A Cornell spokesperson declined to comment about the meeting.
The meeting comes as the faculty senate prepares to begin voting in October on a resolution expressing “no confidence in the ability of the central administration to effectively address the ongoing crisis of sexual assault”. The body does not have the power to remove the president, but the resolution could be a barometer of support for Kotlikoff’s leadership.
Since September, protests have roiled the school in response to a former student’s allegations that she was drugged and raped at a fraternity house in 2024. The case has drawn scrutiny beyond Cornell’s upstate New York campus over how the university and local authorities handled her allegations – which were laid out in a civil lawsuit – and why an earlier probe into the matter did not result in criminal charges.
During the meeting, several members of the faculty advocated reforms or the outright removal of Greek life. Andrew Moisey, an associate professor of art history and visual studies, said Cornell has been in an “abusive relationship with fraternities” dating back to a hazing death in 1873.
Fraternities “tell task forces that they’ll never do it again”, Moisey said. “A therapist or a good friend would advise us to say thanks for the memories, but it’s time to break up.”
Kotlikoff said the university should determine the overall safety of Greek life through data and study, not act on emotion.
“I just came from a town hall of alums who made the other point – that they felt that their sorority experience and fraternity experience was a very important part of their life at Cornell,” the president said. “We have to all take a step and carefully study this issue.”
Kotlikoff also said he was looking into whether Cornell’s public safety chief should continue to report to its top finance officer, an arrangement he described as “awkward”. Former faculty dean Charles Van Loan said the relationship could fuel suspicion that donor concerns influence prosecutions.
“I think you make an excellent point,” Kotlikoff told Van Loan.
At several points during the meeting, Kotlikoff said the university needed more data on sexual violence on campus. As is, the president said the university had a survey of students with a “very low participation rate”. “We do not have great data on this situation,” Kotlikoff said. “We need better data.”
Critics of the university’s handling of the case have grown to include New York Governor Kathy Hochul, an ex-officio Cornell trustee who said on Oct 13 that the university “failed that young woman”. But Kotlikoff said he was committed to making Cornell a leader in sexual violence response.
Throughout the meeting, faculty members suggested the university has responded to the former student’s allegations too late. Darlene Evans, a former lecturer, further questioned why Cornell would allow social gatherings at the fraternity on the night of the alleged assault after university police pursued a drug arrest at the location hours earlier.
After the alleged assault, the university conducted a Title IX investigation, assembled a task force on sexual assault, barred the fraternity from campus and sought punishments for the students involved. There have been no criminal charges in relation to the incident.
“This has been an issue on our campus and every college campus. It’s something I know people would like a president or provost to be able to immediately eliminate,” Kotlikoff said. “It’s something that we all have to work very hard to try and address.” BLOOMBERG

Ahead of US midterms, voters are frustrated with Trump, want change: Poll

Unknown Publisher

Ahead of US midterms, voters are frustrated with Trump, want change: Poll
Widespread voter disillusionment and pocketbook anxieties set a volatile stage for the GOP weeks before election night.
Voter sentiment across the United States is increasingly negative towards US President Donald Trump’s domestic and foreign policies, according to a new Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll.
In the closing weeks before the November 3 US congressional midterm elections, 80 percent of Americans polled said the country needs substantial change or “complete and total upheaval” in how it is run, according to the survey of over 1,100 US adults released on Thursday.
Democrats and independents are much more likely than Republicans to want a total overhaul of the country’s direction, the survey found, but even Republican voters are still looking for some change. Slightly fewer than half, 45 percent, want substantial change, while 13 percent are seeking upheaval.
The results point to a pervasive appetite for legislative realignment that poses a risk to the Republican Party’s power as it looks to keep control of both houses of the US Congress.
Fuelled by soaring living costs, everyday economics is driving a majority of the electorate, with 85 percent of respondents saying the economy is one of the most significant issues in weighing their vote in the upcoming election. About eight in 10 registered voters disapprove of how Trump is handling the cost of living, and about three-quarters disapprove of his performance on the economy.
Only about one-third of registered voters overall have a “very” or “somewhat” favourable view of the Republican president, and a similar share approve of his performance as president.
More voters want Democrats to win control of Congress and have a more negative view of Republicans.
Immigration and crime rates are also top concerns for some voters, according to the survey results, with 45 percent of voters identifying them as top priorities, though the two issues are prioritised disproportionately by Republican voters who reference them more frequently than Democrats. Conversely, Democratic voters are more prone to name healthcare as their top priority.
Emerging cultural and technological concerns drew less immediate alarm across the board: 35 percent of voters ranked artificial intelligence as a substantial issue, while transgender issues sit significantly lower at 12 percent.
Healthcare is also considered a top issue for 69 percent of voters, while 64 percent cite the war on Iran as top-of-mind.
Despite their grievances, a majority of voters across both major American parties still value civic engagement.
About two-thirds of registered voters in the survey say it’s “extremely” important to vote in the upcoming election, while about two in 10 say it’s “very” important. Seventy-five percent of Democratic voters view it as “extremely” important, compared to roughly 60 percent of Republican respondents.

Why Data Centers Have Become Military Targets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
18:17:04 UTC
03:17:04 KST

When the U.S. and Israel launched attacks against Iran earlier this year, Tehran responded by striking energy infrastructure across the Gulf. The result was a severe shock to global energy markets that continues to this day. Less publicized at the time were its strikes on another kind of infrastructure: data centers.
Similar attacks have since taken place in Russia and Ukraine, where both sides have been trading tit-for-tat strikes on data centers.
Experts say these attacks represent a new front in warfare, in which facilities powering the technology behind many critical industries have become military targets.
The AI boom has led to a surge in demand for computing power, data storage and cloud services, making the data centers that provide them a crucial part of modern infrastructure. A mass of data center construction is currently underway in the U.S., and tech companies are investing hundreds of billions of dollars a year to meet AI demand. Telecommunications companies, banks, hospitals and energy suppliers all rely on them.
“Data centers are now on the critical path for modern digital infrastructure,” Kirk Cameron, founding director of the Institute for Advanced Computing at Virginia Tech, tells TIME. “The loss of key data centers could collapse economies, disrupt public and private transportation with loss of GPS, and affect government essential services for health, emergency dispatch, and power grids.”
Military use of AI for targeting and information processing has made data centers crucial to fighting a war. Ukraine uses AI for an array of battlefield functions such as drone targeting, battle planning, and missile analyzing Russian missile attacks. U.S. tech companies such as Palantir now work closely with Ukraine’s military to develop new AI-powered weaponry, taking advantage of the ability to immediately test their technology on the battlefield. The U.S. military also uses Palantir’s Maven system to help identify targets for strikes.
“Data centers are competitive advantages in warfare,” Cameron says. “Knocking out capabilities means potentially crippling combat operations for an adversary. It’s also a form of economic warfare and could lead to longer-term competitive challenges for the target.”
Where have data centers been attacked?
The first wave of attacks on data centers was carried out in March this year by Iran, when it launched strikes on two Amazon facilities in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and another in Bahrain was damaged by a nearby drone strike.
Those facilities have been mostly offline ever since; Amazon said on Sept. 15 that it had been “unable to restore access to the resources and data” hosted in those two regions.
Russian attacks on Ukrainian data centers in late September disrupted television broadcasts and internet access. Russia’s Defense Ministry said it was striking data centers because they “process and transmit intelligence data for the Ukrainian Armed Forces.”
Ukraine’s response began on Oct. 8, and it has since carried out drone strikes on three data centers belonging to tech giant Yandex, often called Russia’s version of Google. The first site hit, in Sasovo, houses two of the three supercomputers Yandex uses to develop its AI models, Meduza reported, and the outage disrupted several companies relying on Yandex’s cloud services, including Russian Railways, MegaFon, T-Bank, and several media outlets.
Following the first strike, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky defended the retaliation: "We always respond in kind. You all know that they are hitting and hitting our data centers; we responded to them.”
How have tech companies responded?
The spate of attacks over the last year has already caused tech companies to rethink how and where they build data centers.
The United Arab Emirates is reportedly revising plans for a 5-gigawatt AI data center project following the Iranian strikes. The original plan envisioned a 10-square-mile campus in Abu Dhabi, to be built in partnership with American tech companies like Oracle, Nvidia, and Cisco. Now the data centers will likely be spread out across the UAE, according to officials who spoke to Reuters.
Emily Harding, director of the Intelligence, National Security, and Technology Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, believes that data centers have become a new frontline in warfare—and that may require new strategies.
“If you’re Russia and you attack a Microsoft data center, is that an attack on Ukraine? Is that an attack on Microsoft? Is that an attack on a U.S. company and, by extension, the U.S.?” she asks.
The U.S. has largely followed a policy that attacks on American companies do not constitute an attack on the United States, but Harding says the government may need to decide on a new approach “that creates deterrence not just to protect life and health, but also data.”
And while the threat to data centers in the U.S. may be relatively low compared to the Gulf and Ukraine or Russia, tech companies will also have to think more about the security of their facilities when building, while trying to keep pace with massive demand.
“The knock-on effect is that the companies that own the data centers are realizing they can't protect them, and that kind of calls into question the cloud model in general,” Harding says. “They're having to make big adjustments. You could see a time in the future where Amazon starts losing business to Microsoft because Microsoft does a better job of hiding where their data centers are.”

Clean Energy Must Avoid the Mistake of Overdependence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
18:17:00 UTC
03:17:00 KST

For decades, energy security has meant oil. Countries worried about their dependence on the Middle East and Russia, the security of shipping lanes, and the geopolitical consequences of relying on a small number of producers for the oil that powered global economies. The transition to renewable energy was supposed to rebalance that equation. Yet in doing so, we may be creating a potentially greater vulnerability, since the clean energy supply chain is dominated by China.
Take Europe as an example. The year before Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Russia supplied 45 percent of the EU’s natural gas imports. The war has forced European countries to scramble for new energy sources.
The war in the Middle East showed again how quickly concentrated energy supplies can become an economic liability. Roughly one-fifth of global oil consumption passes through the Strait of Hormuz – or did, before the strait was effectively closed by the conflict.
Clean energy can reduce exposure to these specific chokepoints, but the world must diversify its energy dependence without simply relocating it.
China leads in the industries powering the next phase of the global economy. It is the world’s largest supplier and exporter of green technology. In July 2026, China’s green energy exports rose 51 percent year-on-year, with new energy vehicles rising an astonishing 90 percent.
China dominates the clean energy value chain. Today, the country provides roughly 85 percent of global solar production capacity and 80 percent of lithium-ion batteries. This is essentially a monopoly. In electric vehicles, China accounted for almost three-quarters of global production in 2025.
Its control also extends upstream. China holds critical positions in processing and refining the minerals essential to new energy technologies, from batteries to electric motors and wind turbines. It also possesses much of the manufacturing expertise – and increasingly the equipment – needed to turn those materials into finished products.
Therefore, clean energy dependence extends across an entire industrial ecosystem – from processing through technology, components and manufacturing equipment to the finished product. A disruption at any point in the supply chain could reverberate through the entire system.
The International Energy Agency (IEA) estimated that each month of a halt in Chinese battery supply chain exports could reduce output from EV factories elsewhere by some $17 billion, with more than half of those losses occurring in Europe.
The risk is not hypothetical. China’s use of export controls on rare earths and other critical materials has demonstrated how concentrated supply chains translate into strategic leverage. China mines roughly 60 percent of the world’s rare earths but produces about 90 percent of its rare earth permanent magnets, leaving downstream manufacturers with few immediate alternatives.
Oil reserves are fixed by geology, while China’s dominance in clean technology is the product of industrial policy, capital investment, and accumulated manufacturing expertise. That should, in theory, make clean energy dependence more reversible. In practice, however, diversification is difficult.
A critical part of China’s advantage is manufacturing efficiency. The IEA attributed more than 40 percent of China’s battery cost edge over Europe to automation and efficiency. In critical mineral mining and refining, China’s position also rests on decades of accumulated processing capacity and a willingness to bear environmental costs that many other countries have been reluctant to accept. None of this can be replicated quickly.
China’s enormous investment and innovation in clean technology has helped drive down costs and accelerate deployment. Attempting to exclude China entirely would make the energy transition slower and more expensive. Interdependence is not the problem, and energy security has never required producing everything at home. It requires enough diversity that no single supplier can disrupt the system.
As with trade, the answer is not decoupling but diversification.
Countries should identify where domestic capacity is strategically necessary, build alternative sources of supply with allies and emerging markets, and continue trading and investing with China where it makes economic sense.
It can be done, but it takes time, capital, and political will. Las Vegas-based MP Materials operates North America’s only rare earth mine of scale, producing more than 10 percent of global rare earth supply. The company is building heavy rare earth processing capacity and investing more than $1.25 billion in a magnet manufacturing campus. Importantly, its strategy is becoming international: in 2025, MP Materials, the U.S. government, and Saudi Arabia’s Maaden agreed to develop a Saudi rare earth refinery to supply rare earth oxides to U.S., Saudi, and allied manufacturers.
This one refinery is not, on its own, a solution, but it points to the kind of allied, government-supported investment in processing that rebalancing requires.
While the world will remain dependent upon fossil fuels for the foreseeable future, the diversification to clean energy will continue, and the stakes will rise as demand grows. The world should not spend decades reducing its dependence on Middle Eastern and Russian hydrocarbons only to discover that it has exchanged one form of strategic dependence for another – this time on China.

Details: Welcoming the Ukrainian president, Tusk emphasised that Ukraine can count on Polish assistance.

He also stated that Ukraine had received non-public aid from Warsaw to help defend Kyiv against Russian attacks.
Quote from Zelenskyy: "What you have done... Okay, sometimes it should stay between the two of us."
"But we are grateful because it is very difficult to defend our country and the capital from massive attacks. And we are grateful for this, as well as for the 20-mm ammunition [used for air defence – ed.] and other things. This is exactly what we are now asking various countries, and all of Europe, for," Zelenskyy stated.
Details: The president did not specify exactly what he meant, but it is known that Ukraine is currently asking all states to provide interceptors capable of repelling ballistic attacks.
Background:
- Poland previously reported that it is increasing its troop presence in the Lublin Voivodeship, which borders Ukraine.
- On 1 October, Poland changed its response rules for air defence amid Russian attacks on Ukraine.

Germany’s Far-Right AfD Calls Trump’s Russian Diesel Deal “Pragmatic” and Pushes for Its Own
Alice Weidel, co-leader of Germany’s far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, has called for Germany to pursue its own diesel deal with Russia, ariva.de reported on October 15.
She presented US President Donald Trump’s recent agreement with Moscow as a model.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“We also want a diesel deal for Germans, for our country, for Germany. And for that we have to sit down at the table,” Weidel told journalists in Berlin, according to ariva.de.
Ahead of Germany’s 2027 state elections AfD has repeatedly taken positions favorable to Moscow, including opposing military support for Ukraine and sanctions on Russia. German officials have also raised concerns that AfD lawmakers sought sensitive information on critical infrastructure that could potentially benefit Russia.
Weidel described Trump’s approach to Russian energy supplies as “the right path” and “very pragmatic.”
“He has pulled out, he is concluding diesel deals for his consumers, for American consumers, while we are being left behind here,” she stated.
Ariva.de reported that Weidel also described Germany’s policy toward Ukraine as having failed.
Germany will hold five state elections in 2027: Schleswig-Holstein and Saarland on April 18, North Rhine-Westphalia on April 25, Bremen on May 30, and Lower Saxony on September 26, Germany’s Federal Returning Officer reported.
The AfD is entering that election cycle with strong national polling numbers, reaching 30% in an INSA survey published on October 13, while other recent polls have placed the party between 26% and 30%, according to Wahlrecht.de.
Her comments followed Trump’s announcement after a conversation with the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin, that more than 300,000 tonnes of Russian diesel would be made available “immediately” for the US and global markets.
The agreement has drawn criticism from the EU, ariva.de noted.
The outlet also reported that Trump called for a new Ukrainian president and claimed that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had repeatedly passed up opportunities to end the war.
However, Russia recently rejected Zelenskyy’s proposal for a 60-day ceasefire that would allow Ukraine to hold presidential elections. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov stated that Moscow was not interested in a temporary pause in fighting.
