Trump ramps up third-country US deportations despite global rights outcry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
17:54:26 UTC
02:54:26 KST

Trump ramps up third-country US deportations despite global rights outcry
Official data shows tens of thousands of migrants and asylum seekers have been sent to countries they have no ties to.
United States immigration authorities have dramatically stepped up detentions and deportations since January 2025, when Donald Trump became president.
Trump campaigned on a pledge to implement the “largest deportation operation in American history”. Officers with the Department of Homeland Security, the agency tasked with the crackdown, now make thousands of arrests a day across the country.
That includes people who are seeking asylum in the US, who are supposed to be given a chance to explain dangers they might face in their home country. And US law and international treaties, like the United Nations Convention Against Torture, prohibit authorities from deporting someone to any country in which they will be persecuted or tortured.
Many of those being detained in the US immigration crackdown say they are at risk of being hurt or killed if they return to their native countries, so the Trump administration has looked for alternative places to deport them, including places someone might have no cultural or legal ties to.
Third-country deportations, as the practice is known, have been criticised by the US as well as global rights groups like Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch, as well as the UN.
Critics of the practice say some of the countries taking in the deportees have a record of human rights abuses themselves, or are so dangerous that the US government tells its own citizens not to travel there. They also say there is little to ensure these third countries will give deportees a fair hearing on their cases for asylum, and in the end might send them back to their native countries to face persecution there.
Third-country deportations are not new, but rights groups say they were extremely rare before the Trump administration, and have never been used by the US at the scale they are now. Those being sent to other countries, rights groups say, would not have been deported without their consent. Some US courts have said the practice is illegal, but the US Supreme Court has allowed it to continue, including in a ruling in September.
Experts at the UN have said the practice was leading to a “cascade of human rights violations” across the globe, threatening to undo norms around how refugees and asylum seekers are treated.
A closer look at the third-country deportations
Rights groups have tried to tally forcible third-country deportations, and according to the nonprofits Refugees International and Human Rights First, more than 25,000 people have been subject to forcible third-country deportations so far, based on media reports and information from attorneys.
The Department of Homeland Security’s own data includes more than 16,000 cases of third-country deportations since Trump came into office in January 2025 and August 2026, the latest month for which data is available. The data, provided to the Deportation Data Project based at the University of California, Berkeley and the University of California, Los Angeles and analysed by Al Jazeera, is likely an undercount.
Deportations to these countries need the approval of authorities there, so the Trump administration has sought to make agreements, or reach informal understandings on how to send deportees to a growing list of countries.
Some countries have agreed to keep deportees in prisons, like El Salvador and Eswatini.
Others have agreed to hold deportees temporarily, with some signing Asylum Cooperative Agreements with the US, or “Safe Third Country Agreements”, which allow deportees to pursue asylum claims in a third country that has agreed to host them.
According to rights groups Refugees International and Human Rights First, many of those deported have no idea where they are being sent, and end up finding themselves in countries where they do not speak the language and have little cultural understanding. Some don’t even have any documents like passports or identification cards, making it difficult to live there.
The list of countries people are being deported to has grown as the US offers financial aid, or business or visa concessions, in exchange for countries taking in third-country nationals the Trump administration wants to remove.
Liberia has agreed to take up to 1,200 deportees, for instance. The Trump administration at one point said it would extend the validity of certain visas for Liberians from 12 to 36 months, and has committed $124m for the country’s health services.
In Cameroon, which agreed to take third-country nationals from the US in December 2025, the Trump administration has pledged to give $30m for the UN’s refugee work there, and $400m over the coming years for the country’s health services.

President Donald Trump said Thursday that the planned execution by firing squad of convicted Fort Hood mass killer Nidal Hasan would not be livestreamed, canceling the Pentagon's plans to do so.

Hasan, who during his 2013 court-martial said he was motivated to defend the "leadership of the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan, the Taliban," could seek to delay the execution with a new legal challenge.
"Nidal Malik Hasan, a former U.S. Army Major turned traitor, is a very bad and evil man," Trump said Thursday in a Truth Social post. The president noted Hasan had killed 13 people — one of whom was pregnant — and injured 32 others in the Nov. 5, 2009, shooting spree.
"With all of that being said, I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan but, many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device," Trump wrote.
"He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed."
"That said, the execution may be viewed in person by the immediate families of the victims, if they so choose," Trump wrote. "They deserve to witness JUSTICE!"
Hours before Trump's announcement, a Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll was released and showed that 80% of Americans said the execution should not be streamed live, versus just 18% who supported the idea.
About 53% of Americans support Hasan's execution by firing squad, according to the poll of 2,545 U.S. adults, which had a margin of error of plus or minus two percentage points.
Pentagon Spokesman Sean Parnell, in a statement to CNBC after Trump's announcement, said, "President Trump and Secretary Hegseth spoke about the decision to not livestream Hasan's execution ahead of the Truth Social announcement."
"The Secretary supports the President's decision, and they are completely aligned," Parnell said.
On Monday, Archbishop Timothy Broglio, who leads the Catholic Archdiocese for the Military Services, USA, said in a statement that any Catholics assigned to the firing squad should "request to be excused from this action contrary to the teaching of the Church."
The Pentagon on Oct. 5 said Trump had approved a recommendation by Hegseth to have Hasan, 56, executed by an Army firing squad.
Presidential approval is required for military executions under the Uniform Code of Military Justice.
Hasan would be the first member of the U.S. military executed by firing squad since World War II. The execution also would be the first carried out by the U.S. military since 1961, when Army Pvt. John Bennett was hanged at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas, for the rape and attempted murder of a girl in Austria.
Hegseth on Oct. 8 said the execution would be at Fort Hood and, "He's going to get a firing squad of soldiers, as it should be."
"And we'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public, because people need to understand that ... there's serious consequences for these types of things," Hegseth said.
The Pentagon later said it would be livestreamed.
Before Trump's announcement Thursday that the livestream would not happen, it was unclear which major video-streaming platforms, if any, would have aired the execution.
The Verge reported last week that YouTube, Twitch, Meta and X did not respond when asked if they would allow the execution on their sites, while TikTok pointed to the company's policies barring "shocking and graphic content."
Vice President JD Vance raised doubts last week about whether the livestream is "actually going to happen," saying he would not watch it if it did.
"So whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don't forget that this is the guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people," Vance said. "Now, that said, if it's ultimately livestreamed, I'm not going to be watching it."
Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., last week said in a post on X that the idea of livestreaming the execution was "beyond disgusting."
"Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do," Tillis posted. "It should not be happening in America."
Former Army Sgt. Alonzo Lunsford, whom Hasan shot seven times during the attack, said he opposed the execution being livestreamed even as he said he planned to attend it in person.
"I want to be in the room where I can see him, and he can see me," Lunsford said last week, according to CBS News. "People have to be held accountable for their sins, but I don't want this to be some pay-per-view event, like some John Wick movie."
"As a country, we're better than that."
Archbishop Paul Coakley, president of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops, condemned the plan to show the execution publicly.
"Our God is the God of life. In no way can [Hasan's] actions be condoned but this decision is a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered. The word of God exhorts us: 'do not repay anyone evil for evil,'" Coakley said, quoting St. Paul's Letter to the Romans.
"The public execution even of one who has done grave harm will only further undermine the moral fabric of our nation and be a blight on the conscience of its people," Coakley said.
CNBC has reached out to the Pentagon for comment on Trump's post.
Nader Hasan, a cousin of Nidal who had spoken out after the Fort Hood shooting, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
University of Notre Dame Law School Professor Richard Garnett said, "The president's decision to abandon the livestreaming plan will, among other things, head off legal challenges that would likely have delayed the scheduled execution."
"As a wide range of officials and citizens have noted, a livestreamed execution would have more likely resulted in brutalization of viewers and coarsening of culture than in deterrence," Garnett said.

Apple and Meta team up to make Muse AI model run on Mac computers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
17:52:01 UTC
02:52:01 KST

Tim Cook and Mark Zuckerberg have clashed for years, but with John Ternus taking the reins at Apple, the rivals are finding common ground in artificial intelligence.
Meta and Apple revealed a new collaboration Thursday that will enable developers to easily run Meta's new open-weight AI model on Apple's high-end desktop computers.
The collaboration centers on Muse Spark Open, the most capable open-weight model released under a license that allows for limited commercial use, according to Meta. It's an 816-billion-parameter model using a so-called mixture-of-experts architecture. As an open-weight model, developers can download the technology's parameters, or weights, from the internet and run the model on a wide range of hardware.
Customers will be able to pair between two and four Mac Studio PCs to use Muse Spark to code, analyze video or do other agentic work. The model runs locally, instead of in the cloud, adding a layer of security and saving users money, the companies said.
Thursday's announcement, following months of collaboration, is a sign that the AI boom has shifted historical alliances in Silicon Valley. For years, Apple and Meta regarded each other warily and avoided public partnerships, and the relationship hit rock bottom after Apple introduced privacy changes in 2021 that limited the targeting capabilities of digital ad companies. Meta estimated in early 2022 that the change would cut its revenue that year by $10 billion.
Representatives from Apple and Meta declined to say if the Muse Spark Open collaboration was the start of a deeper relationship.
Zuckerberg posted a picture on X showing the Meta agent working on a Mac computer. He wrote, "Muse Spark Open -- weights releasing today -- runs great on new Mac Studios thanks to work with @johnternus and Apple."
Ternus responded, "Congrats to the team! Amazing to run a model of Muse Spark Open's caliber and scale this efficiently, right from your desk. Mac Studio keeps pushing the boundaries of on-device AI!"
Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang said in an interview that many powerful open-weight models are too big to be run on the majority of personal computers, but Apple's Mac Studios make enough memory available to users so that it's practical to run Muse Spark Open.
The move represents an important show of confidence in Meta's rebooted AI efforts and could pose a challenge to OpenAI and Anthropic. It could also signal Apple's growing strength in AI chips, a market that Nvidia has dominated so far due to their prevalence in large data centers.
"We worked with Apple to bring leading Agent capabilities to your desktop for the first time on the Apple M5 Ultra Mac Studios, so you know we're really excited about this," Wang said. Developers can download a version of the AI model from websites like Hugging Face without extra configuration for Apple's silicon. Muse Spark Open has also been tuned to run faster on Apple's hardware, and the iPhone maker revealed new benchmarks for its chips and published technical documentation about its MLX AI framework's ability to split open-source models across multiple machines.
Mac Studios aren't cheap though, and this AI model requires the fastest Apple chips and as much memory as possible.
Currently, a Mac Studio with the required M5 Ultra chip and 256GB of memory costs at least $10,799. A more expensive version with 512GB of RAM will be released later this month.
Plus, users will need to buy multiple machines.
Common ground on open source
The two companies are collaborating on open-source AI, which has become a point of contention in Washington as politicians worry that free Chinese models could undercut American AI. Although Meta once centered its AI strategy on its older open-weight Llama family of models, it has since focused on creating proprietary models under the leadership of Wang, who joined Meta when the company invested more than $14 billion into his former startup Scale AI last year.
While Apple and Meta, then known as Facebook, partnered on iPhone extensions over a decade ago, they haven't struck any public partnerships since 2017 after Apple removed system-level Facebook integration from the iPhone.
"Most of the animosity predates my tenure at the company, but obviously there's been a long history between Meta and Apple," Wang said, pointing to one member of his team, AI researcher and former Apple director Daniel Gross, as a reason for the collaboration. Gross, along with former GitHub CEO Nat Friedman, was a major Zuckerberg hire last year as the Facebook founder was overhauling his company's AI strategy.
Their leaders have also traded harsh words.
Cook, who was Apple CEO until Ternus succeeded him last month, took a shot at Zuckerberg in 2018, during the Cambridge Analytica scandal, saying, "I wouldn't be in this situation." Cook often criticized Meta for compromising user privacy.
Zuckerberg has also insulted Apple in public, telling Joe Rogan last year that the company "hasn't invented anything great since the iPhone." Zuckerberg has long sought to find a platform that Meta can own so it's not beholden to Apple.
Ternus, a hardware engineer, has already started changing things at Apple, including when it releases products.
And Meta's developers haven't been able to resist Apple's products. The company bought hundreds of Mac computers so its Superintelligence team could experiment with local AI and agents earlier this year.
Apple's multiple partners
Meta is just the latest AI model developer to team up with Apple.
In 2024, Apple announced a partnership with OpenAI to integrate ChatGPT into Siri, although the integration "dramatically underperformed" and didn't lead to OpenAI user growth, OpenAI said in a filing that's part of a legal dispute with Elon Musk's xAI. Apple sued OpenAI in July, alleging trade secret theft, a claim OpenAI denied.
Earlier this year, Apple announced a deal with Google, to use its Gemini models in Apple Intelligence as well as Google Cloud infrastructure.
Still, Apple's AI strategy has drawn criticism from investors and customers in part because its new version of Siri, released last month, isn't as advanced as chatbots and agents from leading labs.
Meanwhile, Meta has bet big on becoming a leading lab but has struggled to keep up with the competition and its business remains almost entirely reliant on ads. Recent developments, such as Meta's Muse personal agent app and its latest proprietary foundation model, Muse Wonder, released earlier this week, have begun to excite investors who are optimistic about new AI business opportunities.
Open source remains part of Zuckerberg's AI strategy. In August, Meta debuted a small open-weight AI model dubbed Muse Glimmer, with Zuckerberg pledging to eventually release something bigger and more powerful.
Muse Spark Open isn't as advanced as Muse Wonder, a proprietary offering, but Wang said it's good enough to potentially entice more coders to upgrade.
"These aren't the most capable models that we've developed or released," Wang said. "But we think that there will be a lot of companies and developers who sort of use this model and tinker with it at small scale and then seek to ramp up and scale up their usage."

PM Carney urges Canadian unity ahead of Alberta secession vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
17:46:00 UTC
02:46:00 KST

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney made a push for national unity in oil-rich Alberta on Thursday as the province prepared to vote on whether to pursue a binding referendum on independence from Canada.
Polling indicates less than a quarter of Alberta's roughly five million people want to break away from Canada, but Carney, who grew up in the western province, said: "polls don't vote."
"We need people to show up and vote and stand up for Alberta, stand up for Canada," he said during a television interview in Calgary.
Speaking later with local business leaders, Carney said he couldn't think of a "worse time to have a referendum," citing a "more dangerously divided world" and friction with the United States.
Alberta's right-wing Premier Danielle Smith says she is against independence but called Monday's non-binding vote to settle a divisive issue.
If a majority votes for independence, she has committed to launching a legally binding separation process. If a majority votes to stay, Smith says she won't approve another referendum.
Mitch Sylvestre, who heads the Alberta Prosperity Project, a prominent separatist organization, told AFP his side might "actually win this referendum."
"I would be very surprised if we got less than 40%," he said in an interview on Tuesday.
Carney has put Alberta's oil industry at the center of his plans to solidify Canada's economy and reduce dependence on the United States, warning close economic ties have been permanently fractured by President Donald Trump.
Carney has backed a new pipeline and other projects to increase crude production, marking a clear break from his predecessor, Justin Trudeau, who was broadly reviled in Alberta over allegations he stifled oil industry growth in favor of environmental policies.
Carney has repeatedly cited the proposed pipeline to argue for Alberta's future prosperity within a united Canada.
Alberta separatists voice familiar conservative frustrations, from concerns about immigration levels to generalized fears about fraying individual liberty, but their grievances often hinge on oil industry management.
Smith told the CBC that Alberta separatists stepped up mobilization because Trudeau, who left office last year, was "actively trying to kill" the oil industry.
Oil's dominance in separatist discussion makes Alberta "mostly an outlier," said Syracuse University professor Ryan Griffiths, an expert on global secessionist groups.
Secessionist movements regularly have "economic motivations," but typically those are married to a linguistic or nationalist component, Griffiths said.
"There's no magic line" dictating what defines a nation, he told AFP, but noted Alberta's case for nationhood appears harder to make than that of other groups, like Catalans, Scots and French-speaking Canadians in Quebec.
The alleged influence of Trump allies in Alberta has attracted intense scrutiny in Canada.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has called Alberta a "natural partner" for the United States, and Alberta Prosperity Project leaders held several meetings at the State Department.
Earlier this month, Canada's Globe and Mail newspaper detailed contacts between Sylvestre, his team and Republican Party operatives.
Sylvestre told AFP that, for him, U.S. interests "don't play any role" in Alberta "until we win and become government," at which point he would work to ensure free-flowing trade.
"There's no animosity towards America here," he said. "I can't see why we wouldn't want to continue trading with the biggest economy in the world."
Asked about alleged foreign interference on Thursday, Carney said: "our expectation is – to be absolutely clear on foreign governments, United States included – we don't get ourselves involved in their elections, they don't get themselves involved in our elections."

Saudi Arabia accuses Iran of encouraging Houthis in latest escalation
Saudi Arabia on Thursday accused Iran of encouraging Yemen's Houthis in the dramatic escalation of their fight with the kingdom, adding that the Islamic republic continued to arm and train the group.
In a virtual briefing with reporters including AFP journalists, Saudi Arabia's deputy minister for public diplomacy at the foreign ministry said Riyadh was still in touch with Iran, but that Tehran did not appear ready to make concessions.
Saudi Arabia, the world's top crude oil exporter, has come under sustained attack by the Houthis in recent days, shifting the focus of the Middle East war that erupted with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in February.
It has launched retaliatory strikes on Houthi strongholds in Yemen - one of the world's poorest countries - but the Iran-backed group remains undeterred.
"Iran continues to arm, train and support the Houthi militia in violation of UN security council resolutions," said Dr. Rayed Krimly, the deputy minister.
"We think that the escalation by the Houthis at this latest stage of the conflict is encouraged by Iran," he added.
The official said the kingdom continued "to have direct communications with Iran", but added: "Overall, it doesn't seem yet that the Iranians are able to provide the necessary concessions for a solution."
In 2023, regional rivals Iran and Saudi Arabia reached a deal mediated by China to thaw a longstanding freeze in ties, but the latest violence might threaten to upend the entente.
The Saudi official went on to accuse the Houthis of refusing to meet in Oman in recent weeks as fighting ramped up between the two sides.
"At the beginning of this escalation, we asked them to meet in Muscat, Oman and they refused," he added.
"This was the last communication which happened a few weeks ago."
Airport strikes
On Saturday, a strike hit Riyadh's international airport, killing 13 people and wounding around 300 others, in the deadliest attack on Saudi Arabia in a decade.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis on Thursday said the group had attacked Riyadh's airport 20 times in October.
During a presentation in Riyadh covering the strikes, coalition spokesman Turki Al-Malki said "the Houthis must immediately cease all terrorist operations targeting civilians and civilian facilities, including airports, ports, oil facilities, and infrastructure".
"The terrorist Houthi militias have worked to obtain advanced technologies with the help of regional actors," he said, adding that the group now had "ballistic missiles, attack and suicide drones, and fast explosive-laden boats".
Yemen's civil war reignited in July after a years-long UN-brokered truce collapsed, months into a wider Middle East war that has rocked the region and roiled energy supplies and markets.
The situation took a sharp turn for the worse in September, when the Houthis launched a lightning offensive that saw them capture swathes of new territory in Yemen, including along the Red Sea coast where a waterway crucial to global energy flows is located.
On Thursday, the Houthis fired missiles at the presidential palace in Aden, which also serves as the headquarters of the internationally recognised government, security sources told AFP, while a journalist saw smoke rising from the site.
"Houthi missiles targeted the Al-Maashiq presidential palace in Aden," the government's interim capital, three local police sources said on condition of anonymity, after residents of the southern city reported hearing explosions.
Since their offensive began, the Houthis have also repeatedly targeted Saudi Arabia, which backs the internationally recognised government whose forces they are battling on the ground.
The attacks on Saudi Arabia have tested the country's infrastructure and resilience, the energy minister acknowledged earlier this week.
Riyadh usually hosts a packed calendar of events this time of year, including its flagship investment conference drawing foreign leaders and business titans.
In Yemen, the conflict has caused what the United Nations calls one of the world's worst humanitarian crises, leaving most of the nation's population dependent on aid.

A mother’s touch helps premature babies grow strong in Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
17:43:01 UTC
02:43:01 KST

A mother’s touch helps premature babies grow strong in Gaza
At Nasser Hospital, a kangaroo mother care pilot programme helps vulnerable newborns as Gaza’s healthcare system struggles with shortages.
Khan Younis, Gaza Strip – For 11 days after giving birth last month, Rania Fadel could not hold her newborn son.
The 24-year-old gave birth to twin boys, Ilyas and Yahya, on September 25.
While Yahya was born healthy, Ilyas was admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit at Nasser Medical Complex in Khan Younis, in southern Gaza, where he remained for nearly two weeks.
Born prematurely, Ilyas weighed just 1.4 kilogrammes (3 pounds) at birth, according to his mother. He had medical issues affecting his blood and lungs, she said, and needed specialised care in an incubator.
Rania herself was recovering from a Caesarean section when her son was taken into intensive care. For days, she could not hold him.
“When they called me to hold him, I rushed over,” she recalled. “I was in a hurry to get to him. It was such a feeling.”
As Ilyas’s condition improved and he moved from intensive care to the hospital’s neonatal care unit, Rania was able to hold him against her bare chest, introducing her to a form of care for low-birthweight newborns known as kangaroo mother care, part of a newly-launched programme at the hospital.
It involves prolonged skin-to-skin contact between a caregiver – ideally the mother – and baby, with exclusive breast milk feeding, and has been shown to have important health benefits for premature and low-birthweight babies.
“I was so happy. It was such a beautiful feeling,” Rania said.
During the session, a nurse helped Rania position Ilyas against her chest, with his skin touching hers. Rania said he remained there for about 90 minutes.
“He started breastfeeding from me, and he stayed a little longer,” she said. “I felt he was improving.”
For Rania, the contact also brought a sense of closeness after days of separation.
“The baby feels that his mother is there,” she said. “He feels safe. Honestly, it makes me very happy.”
Skin-to-skin
Kangaroo mother care involves placing a baby against a parent’s bare chest for skin-to-skin contact, alongside breastfeeding and appropriate medical care.
For premature and low-birthweight babies, it can help regulate body temperature, support breastfeeding and improve health outcomes.
World Health Organization (WHO) guidance says that kangaroo mother care has been shown to reduce neonatal mortality by 32 percent, and mortality by six months of age by 25 percent, compared with conventional care.
At Nasser Medical Complex, Khawla al-Madhoun, director of nursing at the hospital’s maternity and neonatal departments, described it as an integrated approach to newborn care that supports growth and strengthens the bond between mother and baby.
“When we place a baby on the mother’s chest, it helps the baby grow,” she said.
“We have seen babies who were unwell or underweight begin to grow faster with kangaroo care. This can help them leave the hospital sooner.”
The hospital has begun introducing kangaroo care through a pilot programme supported by WHO, the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), and the UN Population Fund (UNFPA). The agencies announced the initiative at Nasser Hospital in September, but the practice is being introduced gradually in its external neonatal care unit, where babies stay with their mothers, and in maternity wards after delivery.
Al-Madhoun said the team was also preparing a dedicated room and seeking equipment to make the sessions more comfortable.
The team aims for longer periods of skin-to-skin contact – WHO recommends at least eight hours per day – although its immediate target is at least two hours, depending on each family’s circumstances.
At Nasser, the team is currently prioritising babies who are medically stable and do not require oxygen support. Nurses monitor their vital signs and assess them throughout the process.
Al-Madhoun stressed that the technique cannot replace an incubator or other treatment when a baby needs intensive care.
“It can help babies grow, gain weight and leave the hospital earlier, but some babies need other interventions, such as respiratory support,” she said. “Those babies still need the incubator and the care it provides.”
Shortage of neonatal equipment
The need for specialised newborn care comes as Gaza’s health system continues to struggle with damaged facilities, shortages of equipment and overcrowded neonatal units.
Before Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began in October 2023, Gaza had eight neonatal intensive care units with a total of 178 incubators, according to UNICEF.
By November 2024, three of those units had been destroyed by Israel, and the number of available incubators had fallen to about 54, a reduction of 70 percent. The shortage of equipment, compounded by limited supplies of fuel and electricity as a result of Israeli restrictions, put premature newborns at serious risk.
Israeli strikes have continued since an October 2025 “ceasefire”. Despite this supposed truce, and despite the delivery of some new equipment, the shortage of incubators and other equipment has persisted.
In May, UNICEF said it and its partners had supplied incubators and ventilators to hospitals in Gaza, while warning that neonatal units were still managing large numbers of fragile infants with limited equipment, space and power.
The war in Gaza has worsened living conditions for pregnant women with economic hardship, food shortages, poor nutrition and the harsh realities of displacement, including cooking over open fires and carrying water.
“These conditions have contributed to the rise in premature births and babies born with low birth weight who need specialised neonatal care,” al-Madhoun said.
Meanwhile, repeated displacement and overcrowding have placed further pressure on hospitals, including Nasser Medical Complex, which is already struggling with limited space and shortages of incubators and other essential neonatal equipment.
Newborn in a tent
Linda Abu Nasira’s baby girl is only three days old.
The infant initially developed a fever, which has since subsided, according to 23-year-old Linda.
As her daughter was being treated and breastfed, Linda was learning how to hold her against her chest under the guidance of the medical team.
The sessions were brief. Linda said she held her daughter against her chest for about 30 minutes at a time, repeating the process roughly every two hours, according to the instructions she had received.
“She is a little better than yesterday,” Linda said. “Little by little.”
Away from the hospital, Linda lives in a tent in al-Mawasi, in Khan Younis, where she is raising her two older children – aged three and two – while caring for her newborn.
She described the conditions as difficult, particularly when it comes to securing food and drinking water.
“We try to manage,” she said. “But it is not like before, or like the conditions you would expect when giving birth.”
She does not know how long the baby will need to remain under observation in the hospital’s external neonatal care unit.
“As a mother, it means a lot to me to feel that I am helping my daughter recover,” Linda said. “I hope she will recover and be discharged as soon as possible.”

In 100th lawsuit against Trump, California challenges immigration arrests near courthouses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
17:41:13 UTC
02:41:13 KST

In 100th lawsuit against Trump, California challenges immigration arrests near courthouses
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- California is challenging the practice of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents arresting people for alleged civil immigration violations at or near state courthouses.
- State Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta said such arrests have long been barred because they are unconstitutional and deeply disruptive to the rule of law and the rights of victims, witnesses, defendants and other parties to court proceedings.
- Bonta said his office having to take the Trump administration to court 100 times in less than two years, often alongside other Democrat-led states, was a ‘sobering milestone.’
California sued the Trump administration for the 100th time in under two years Thursday, challenging the practice of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents arresting people for alleged civil immigration violations at or near state courthouses.
California Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta said such arrests have long been barred because they are unconstitutional and deeply disruptive to the rule of law and the rights of victims, witnesses, defendants and other parties to court proceedings.
“We’ve seen serious criminal charges dropped and entire cases jeopardized because victims and witnesses are too scared to come to the courthouse to testify,” Bonta said. “Our justice system cannot function this way.”
Bonta said his office having to take the Trump administration to court 100 times in less than two years, often alongside other Democrat-led states, was a “sobering milestone” and a reflection not of political interference on California’s part — as the president and his supporters have cast it — but of Trump’s nearly unbridled lawlessness.
“It’s very troubling when the most powerful person on the planet and the president of our country is the one trampling over the Constitution, breaking the law so blatantly and brazenly, so consistently, so frequently,” Bonta said.
Independent legal experts said several factors have driven the wave of lawsuits.
Federal officials have given California election officials 48 hours to prove the citizenship of voters flagged as potential noncitizens, or withhold their ballots.
Presidents from both parties have increasingly flexed their executive power, and state attorneys general have increasingly sued in response. During Trump’s first term in office, California — under the leadership of then-Atty. Gen. Xavier Becerra, a current gubernatorial candidate — sued the Trump administration more than 120 times over four years. Texas Atty. Gen. Ken Paxton — now a Republican candidate for Senate — sued the Biden administration just over 100 times in four years.
Trump in this term quickly began implementing an array of policies left over from his first term or outlined in the Project 2025 policy blueprint, many of which Bonta and other Democratic attorneys general were prepared to sue over, experts said.
Trump was also able to appoint a host of loyalists with the help of the Republican-controlled Congress, who helped advance policies that less loyal agency heads would have balked at, and which were sure to draw additional legal challenges, experts said.
Daniel Farber, a professor at UC Berkeley Law School and author of “Contested Ground: How to Understand the Limits of Presidential Power,” said California’s raft of lawsuits is a result of the current Trump administration “doing more aggressive things right off the starting block” — but also repeatedly targeting California specifically.
Bonta claimed in August that his lawsuits had saved California more than $200 billion, namely by reversing Trump cuts to federal funding meant for the state.
The White House has consistently derided Bonta’s litigation against the administration as baseless and misguided. White House spokesperson Lauren Bis on Thursday said Bonta should stop bragging about “filing frivolous lawsuits” and “focus on addressing problems in his own state.”
“The reality is, with well over 25 Supreme Court victories, the administration’s policies have been consistently upheld as lawful, despite some lower courts issuing an unprecedented number of lawless injunctions,” Bis said.
ICE, which did not immediately respond to a request for comment, has defended its arrests near courthouses as a “common sense” approach to apprehending offenders at times and locations where authorities know they will be.
The 100th case
Bonta’s lawsuit argues that such arrests are arbitrary and capricious given the chilling effect they have on justice in the state. They violate the Immigration and Nationality Act as intended by Congress, and interfere with California’s rights under the 10th Amendment to execute its “core sovereign judicial and police functions,” Bonta’s office said.
His arguments echo those made by other state officials in the past. During Trump’s first term, for example, then-California Supreme Court Chief Justice Tani G. Cantil-Sakauye called the arrests “disruptive, shortsighted and counterproductive.”
Arrests at or near courthouses began to rise again after Trump took office in January 2025. An ICE memo, issued in May 2025, said agents could conduct “civil immigration enforcement actions in or near courthouses when they have credible information that leads them to believe the targeted alien(s) is or will be present at a specific location.”
Incidents quickly began cropping up. In June 2025, ICE agents arrested two women outside a Los Angeles County courthouse after a hearing in a local criminal case. The same unfolded across the state.
Alejandro Barraza, a criminal defense and immigration attorney, said he has witnessed the effect firsthand.
In October 2025, a client was arrested driving home from a hearing at the Riverside County Hall of Justice. In December, another client was arrested leaving the Rancho Cucamonga courthouse. And a third client chose to plead guilty in his criminal case rather than go to jury trial, despite Barraza’s advice that the case was worth fighting, for fear of being arrested by ICE.
“The victims are losing,” Barraza said. “Our clients are losing their rights to due process. Everyone is losing.”
In June, U.S. District Judge P. Casey Pitts in San Francisco struck down ICE’s expanded courthouse arrest policies nationwide. Although the lawsuit focused on immigration courthouses, the ruling also covered state criminal courthouses, restoring earlier restrictions that barred civil immigration arrests in or near courthouses except in limited circumstances. The Trump administration is appealing the ruling.
Since then, California court officials have tracked arrests by federal agents and reported them to the Judicial Council of California. Thirty people were taken into custody in June, 29 in July, 19 in August and 14 in September.
Three lawsuits filed Friday challenge the Trump administration’s rollback of vehicle mileage rules as illegal, including one led by California.
State legislators have tried to push back. Last month, Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a law strengthening California’s protections against civil arrests for people traveling to, attending or leaving courthouses for lawful purposes. The measure extends those protections to public ways within 1,000 feet of court facilities, while preserving an exception for arrests made under a valid judicial warrant.
Bonta said his lawsuit is necessary despite the new California law, in part because the Trump administration thinks that “no state law applies to them,” and courts have in some cases agreed — including the U.S. 9th Circuit Court of Appeals, which this week blocked a state law that would have required federal immigration agents to display identification while working in the state.
The wider legal battle
Bonta’s office has had substantial success in halting some of the Trump administration’s biggest policy moves — including its plans to end birthright citizenship for the U.S.-born children of immigrants, its worldwide tariffs, its deployment of National Guard troops in Los Angeles and other U.S. cities, and its withholding of billions of dollars in federal funding allocated to the state by Congress.
Michael McConnell, director of the Constitutional Law Center at Stanford Law School, said many of California’s lawsuits have been “legally meritorious,” as there is a “whole lot of legal error” coming out of the Trump administration — with a “lot of the overreach” having been “facilitated by the lack of internal checks” from loyal Trump agency heads.
However, he also said that as a California taxpayer, he doesn’t “appreciate having government using my tax dollars for what essentially are in many cases ideological lawsuits, even if meritorious,” because private litigants can and often do bring lawsuits of their own. He said he felt the same way about many of the lawsuits brought against the Biden administration by Republican states.
Bonta said he is proud of his team for challenging the Trump administration every time they believed it had broken the law and harmed California, despite Trump’s intentional effort to make that difficult.
“It was a shock and awe,” he said. “It was flood the zone. It was trying to overwhelm with speed and volume, and we kept pace every time.”
What happens next, he said, will depend on Trump. If he keeps breaking the law in ways that hurt the state or its residents, Bonta said he’ll keep getting sued by California.

Two ships sink near Hormuz after being hit by projectiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
17:38:56 UTC
02:38:56 KST

Breadcrumb
Two ships sink near Hormuz after being hit by projectiles
A container ship and a dry bulk carrier sunk near the Strait of Hormuz inside 24 hours on Wednesday after being hit by projectiles in separate incidents, maritime officials said on Wednesday.
Attacks around the waterway have surged over the past 10 days, with Iran saying it is stepping up strikes in response to the US blockade of its ports and tougher sanctions introduced last month.
The Singapore-flagged GFS Pride, a small container vessel with a capacity of 2,824 20-foot equivalent units (TEU), sank while sailing through the strait, according to maritime security sources.
"GFS PRIDE sustained damage and a fire on board, and has since sunk. All 21 crew members were safely evacuated. No injuries have been reported," the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA) said in a statement on Wednesday, adding that the vessel had been sailing through the strait on Tuesday.
In a separate incident, the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged Cape Dao sank close to the strait, weeks after being struck by a projectile on September 23, data from UN shipping agency the International Maritime Organisation showed on Wednesday.
One crew member was killed, the rest of the crew evacuated straight after the strike, maritime sources said.
Its UAE-based manager Peonies Shipmanagement FZE could not be immediately reached for comment.
The GFS Pride and Cape Dao are the second and third vessels to have sunk since the US-Iran war began on February 28, according to an analysis of IMO casualty data.
"MPA is deeply concerned about the continued attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz," the Singapore authority said.
"Such attacks are unprovoked, unjustifiable, and a breach of international law."
GFS Pride's United Arab Emirates-based manager, GFS Ship Management FZE, could not be immediately reached for comment.
"The latest incidents reinforce the continuing threat to commercial shipping transiting the Strait of Hormuz," maritime risk management company MARISKS said on Wednesday.
"The threat is not confined to tankers, with container vessels and bulk carriers also sustaining serious damage."
A sharp escalation in threats to commercial shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz, through which about a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas trade passed before the war, has heightened concerns about security in the waterway.
Tehran has sought to tighten its grip on the waterway since US and Israeli strikes on Iran on 28 February, restricting transit in an effort to gain leverage over Washington.
Iran is increasingly deploying new tactics against vessels transiting the strait as it seeks to keep oil prices elevated and influence US midterm elections, two senior Iranian officials told Reuters.
While Iran and the US have focused their attacks on tankers, cargo and container vessels have also been attacked, immobilised or sunk.
The Maltese-flagged container ship Safeen Prestige was hit by a projectile in March and later sank north of the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards attacked and seized the container ship MSC Francesca in April.
(Reuters)

Netherlands opens nuclear deterrence talks with France
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
17:26:45 UTC
02:26:45 KST

- The Netherlands and France held the first meeting of a bilateral Nuclear Steering Group on Oct. 14, discussing European nuclear and conventional deterrence.
- The talks follow Macron’s March offer of a strategic dialogue, which the Dutch government says complements NATO deterrence instead of replacing it.
The Netherlands and France held the first meeting of a new bilateral Nuclear Steering Group on Oct. 14, opening high-level talks on how French nuclear forces and European conventional forces could work together to deter attacks on Europe, the Dutch Ministry of Defence said.
The ministry announced the meeting in a statement on Oct. 15, saying it was the first time the two countries had held talks on the subject at this level. Senior French government officials attended, while the Dutch delegation was drawn from the Ministry of General Affairs, which is the prime minister’s office, along with the defense and foreign ministries. The two sides discussed ways to strengthen the European dimension of nuclear and conventional deterrence, according to the statement, which did not describe any specific decisions.
The talks follow an offer French President Emmanuel Macron made in early March to a group of European countries, including the Netherlands. The Dutch government accepted the French offer in line with its coalition agreement.
Macron set out the plan in a speech on March 2 at the Île Longue base in Brittany, home to France’s ballistic missile submarines. He said France would increase the number of its nuclear warheads and adopt what he called advanced deterrence, under which elements of France’s nuclear-capable air forces could be temporarily deployed to allied countries, Defense News reported. He named Germany as a key partner alongside Poland, the Netherlands and several other European states, and said partners could contribute early warning, air defense and long-range strike capabilities while their territory would gain a clearer link to French deterrence.
The Dutch government said Russia’s war against Ukraine has fundamentally worsened European security and requires Europe to take more responsibility for its own defense, and that the French offer fits that goal. It stressed that cooperation with France is meant to add to NATO’s collective defense and deterrence, and does not replace it.
France is the only nuclear-armed member of the European Union. Its arsenal is kept under exclusive national control, with the president alone authorized to order its use, and Macron has said that will not change under the new arrangements.
The Netherlands already takes part in NATO’s nuclear sharing arrangements, under which some allies provide aircraft and crews for the alliance’s nuclear mission while the United States retains control of the weapons.

Army looks at off the shelf kit to stop drones over bases
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
18:25:32 BST
02:25:32 KST

An Army-led project called Halo Shield is examining how commercially available counter-drone technology could protect British military sites, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked for the full scope of the project.
Louise Sandher-Jones, Parliamentary Under-Secretary and Minister for the Armed Forces, said: “Project HALO SHIELD is an Army-led initiative examining how commercially available Counter-Uncrewed Aircraft System (C-UAS) technologies can improve the protection of UK military sites from the growing threat posed by uncrewed aircraft systems.”
Halo Shield sits alongside Project PRESAGIUM, the £240 million enhanced counter-drone system the department described in a separate answer, which it says will provide detection and defeat of emerging drone threats.
Drone activity over British bases has moved from an irritant to an operational concern over the past two years, with incursions reported over sites including RAF Lakenheath and RAF Mildenhall, and the Prime Minister this week attributing the September incident at RAF Fairford to direction by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
Counter uncrewed aircraft systems generally pair radar, radio frequency and optical sensors to spot and identify a drone with a mix of jamming, spoofing, nets, guns and directed energy to bring it down.
Protecting a fixed site is awkward because commercial quadcopters return almost no radar signature, because anything shot down has to come down somewhere, and because jamming radio transmissions over British soil runs into civil aviation and telecommunications law.

The 71-year-old had part of his right lung removed after a lengthy operation on Tuesday following doctors identifying a suspected cancerous nodule.

Doctors are still awaiting the results of tests to understand the precise molecular makeup of the cancer, whether it has spread beyond the lobe and whether any further treatment is necessary.
Pope Leo attracted a following of almost one million people at a Mass in Paris during a four-day visit to France last month before announcing he was to undergo surgery.

Türkiye welcomes Baku Declaration at 7th CICA Summit, reaffirms commitment to peace in Asia

After Oct. 7, Israel’s border communities need long-term philanthropy - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
17:23:46 UTC
02:23:46 KST

In the months after the October 7 massacre, Jewish communities around the world responded with extraordinary generosity. Emergency funds were created almost overnight. Philanthropic foundations accelerated decisions that would normally take months.
Donors asked a simple question: What is needed now?
That response mattered enormously. It allowed organizations working in Israel’s border communities to act quickly, respond to changing needs, and build new initiatives in places facing evacuation, loss, and profound uncertainty.
Three years later, we are entering a very different stage.
The emergency is no longer new. Philanthropic institutions are understandably asking different questions. They are returning to strategic priorities, long-term planning, and more conventional funding cycles.
At the same time, Israel is approaching an election period, creating uncertainty around government commitments that many organizations assumed would help carry emergency initiatives into the next stage.
The problem is that communities do not recover according to either philanthropic or political calendars.
Across Israel’s border regions, projects launched during the emergency are only now reaching the point at which they can become sustainable. The danger is that the bridge between emergency response and long-term recovery may disappear precisely when communities are ready to cross it.
In one community along Israel’s border with Gaza, a compound is already waiting to become a new Kedma student village. The community has opened its doors. Students are ready to move in, become part of local life, and contribute to education and community rebuilding.
But the village has not opened.
Additional protective shelters are still required, and while we wait for the necessary arrangements, the emergency funding that allowed us to begin this process is running out.
On paper, this may look like a delayed project. In reality, much more is at stake.
Entering a community recovering from war takes time. An organization cannot simply arrive with a program. Local leaders and residents must first decide to trust it: to share what they need, to allow outsiders into a deeply disrupted community, and eventually to make room for a new group of young people within their daily lives.
That trust is built slowly.
The same dynamic can be seen elsewhere. In Menara, on the Lebanese border, where residents have endured evacuation and enormous destruction, rebuilding a student village is not simply about providing accommodation for young people. It is about helping restore a living community.
In Sufa and Urim, in the western Negev, programs bringing young adults and discharged soldiers to live, volunteer, and become part of local life similarly depend on relationships that cannot be created overnight.
These programs were born or expanded during an extraordinary period, when philanthropy understood that extraordinary measures were necessary. Government ministries also made commitments based on the assumption that the emergency phase would eventually be followed by sustained reconstruction.
But that handover is not automatic.
We need a transition period to sustain trust
An election year makes the problem more acute. Budgets can change. Priorities can shift. Decisions that appeared secure can be delayed or reconsidered. Organizations that expanded in response to national needs can suddenly find themselves caught between emergency philanthropic grants that are ending and government commitments that have not yet materialized.
The result is not primarily an organizational problem. It is a community problem.
If a program closes, staff positions can eventually be recreated. A new grant can finance new activities. But when an organization has spent months or years entering a traumatized community, listening to residents and earning their confidence, withdrawing has consequences that cannot be measured only in budget lines.
It tells a community that another partner has come and gone.
For communities that have already experienced evacuation, uncertainty, and the collapse of so many assumptions about their security and their future, that matters.
This is why the next phase of philanthropy in Israel should not be understood simply as a return from “emergency giving” to normal giving. The challenge now is to build a transition period between the two.
That does not mean every emergency initiative should continue indefinitely. Nor does it mean philanthropy should replace government responsibility. On the contrary: long-term recovery requires government, philanthropy, local authorities, and civil society to understand where each one’s responsibility begins and ends.
But transitions need time.
A responsible philanthropic strategy for the coming year should ask not only which new projects deserve support, but which successful emergency investments are currently standing at the edge of a funding gap. Which initiatives have already earned the communities’ trust? Which are waiting for government funding or infrastructure to catch up?
And where could one additional year of support make the difference between an emergency intervention that disappears and an institution that becomes locally sustainable?
The years since October 7 demonstrated the extraordinary capacity of Jewish philanthropy to respond quickly when Israel was in crisis. The next test may be less dramatic, but no less important: whether we can stay long enough for recovery to take root.
Because funding may return.
Trust is much harder to rebuild.
The writer is the president and founder of the Kedma pioneering social-Zionist organization.

He was just a plumber. Then he helped save a plane full of passengers - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
17:23:39 UTC
02:23:39 KST

JERUSALEM — He is a plumber by profession, a husband and father by nature, and a hero because of the decision he made when lives hung in the balance.
Yaniv Hayoun never boarded a plane expecting to become a hero. He was traveling home to Israel when violence erupted aboard a flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv. When the captain was seriously injured and the aircraft began descending dangerously, Hayoun faced a choice that would test his courage: remain in his seat and hope someone else would act, or move toward the danger.
He chose to act.
Hayoun joined other passengers in confronting the attacker inside the cockpit. After helping restrain him, Hayoun returned to the cockpit and pulled back on the aircraft's controls in an effort to stabilize the plane until another pilot could take over. The aircraft was diverted to Saudi Arabia and landed safely. Everyone aboard survived.
Hayoun was not a commercial pilot. He was a plumber who suddenly found himself in a situation few people could imagine. Yet when lives were at stake, he refused to stand by. He acted alongside fellow passengers who were willing to risk their own safety to protect others.
His courage demonstrates a powerful truth: heroism does not depend on a title, a uniform, or professional training. Sometimes it begins with an ordinary person recognizing that others are in danger and refusing to look away.
A hero honored in Jerusalem
Just one week after the harrowing flight, Hayoun's story became part of a historic gathering in Jerusalem.
On October 7, 2026, the third anniversary of the Hamas-led attacks on Israel, more than 2,100 Christian leaders gathered in Jerusalem for the Global Prayer Event, an international gathering of remembrance, prayer, and solidarity with the Jewish people. The event was part of a 24-hour global prayer broadcast, hosted by Friends of Zion, that united leaders across nations around a common message: Israel is not alone.
During the gathering, Hayoun received the Hineni Award, named for the Hebrew expression Hineni, meaning “Here I am.”
Throughout Scripture, Hineni expresses a willingness to answer a call and step forward, even when the outcome is uncertain, and the cost may be great.
Hayoun embodied that spirit aboard the aircraft. He could not have known how the confrontation would end or whether he would survive. But he moved toward those who needed help, putting his own safety at risk to protect the lives of others.
His recognition in Jerusalem was especially meaningful on a day devoted to remembering the victims of October 7, honoring survivors, and standing with families still carrying the pain of that terrible day.
Yet Hayoun was not the only person whose story of courage and survival was honored.
Honoring the survivors and former hostages of October 7
Among those who joined the Jerusalem gathering were four former hostages whose lives were forever changed by the October 7 attacks: Agam Berger, Sagui Dekel-Chen, Bar Kupershtein, and Evyatar David. Each represented a deeply personal story of captivity, survival, and the difficult journey of rebuilding life after unimaginable trauma.
Their presence gave the gathering a significance that extended beyond speeches and ceremonies. These were people whose lives had been directly affected by the attacks, whose families had endured extraordinary anguish, and whose survival carried a meaning that no statistic could fully convey.
Together with Hayoun, they represented different expressions of courage: the courage to intervene when lives are threatened, the courage to endure captivity, and the courage to begin again after profound suffering.
A message the world must never forget
The October 7, 2023, attacks claimed more than 1,200 lives and resulted in 251 people being taken hostage. The tragedy left families shattered, communities devastated, and survivors facing a long road toward healing.
Three years later, the pain remains. Remembering those who were murdered, listening to survivors, and honoring the former hostages are essential to preserving the truth of what happened and recognizing the humanity of those whose lives were changed forever.
For the organizers of the Global Prayer Event, bringing thousands together in Jerusalem was about more than marking an anniversary. It was a declaration that the Jewish people must never be abandoned to hatred or left to believe the world has forgotten their suffering.
The former hostages who joined the gathering offered a powerful reminder: survival is not the end of the story. Healing, rebuilding, and finding the strength to move forward can take years, and the support of others matters.
In honoring these men and women, Jerusalem became a place where courage, remembrance, and solidarity met. Their stories reminded those gathered that behind every headline are human beings whose lives deserve to be remembered and whose dignity must never be forgotten.
For Yaniv Hayoun, the journey from an ordinary day of travel to an extraordinary act of courage culminated in recognition in the very city where thousands had gathered to stand with Israel.
He did not act because he expected an award. He acted because people were in danger and someone needed to help.
That is what makes his story so powerful.
When lives are in danger, someone must be willing to say, “Here I am.”
Yaniv Hayoun answered that call. In Jerusalem, alongside survivors and former hostages whose courage continues to inspire, his story became part of a larger message to the world: even in the face of terror, courage can prevail, hope can endure, and no one should have to stand alone.
Dr. Mike Evans has written 120 books and is a #1 New York Times bestselling author. He is the founder of the Friends of Zion Museum in Jerusalem, the Ten Boom Museum in Holland, and Churches United with Israel, one of the largest Christian Zionist networks in America, with more than 30 million followers.

China’s Rare Earth Strategy and the Future of the South China Sea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
17:21:00 UTC
02:21:00 KST

In August 2026, Japan and the United States worked together to explore extracting rare-earth-rich mud from the seabed near Minamitorishima. It offered a glimpse into the next phase of critical minerals competition. The race for rare earths is no longer confined to land mines and export control policies. As deep-sea minerals become part of national security planning, maritime spaces that were once mainly discussed in terms of sovereignty, shipping lanes, and fisheries may acquire a new layer of strategic value.
The South China Sea is not currently central to China’s rare earth advantage, but it may become increasingly relevant to how Beijing and its competitors think about the future geography of critical minerals security.
For now, China’s rare earth strategy and its South China Sea strategy remain largely distinct. China’s leverage in rare earths comes less from pure geology than from the country’s dominant position in refining, separation, and magnet production, combined with regulatory instruments that allow Beijing to manage outward flows of selected minerals. The April 2025 export control measures on several medium and heavy rare-earth-related items underscored how critical minerals have become part of China’s national security toolbox.
By contrast, the South China Sea has traditionally been discussed and understood through a different strategic vocabulary: sovereignty claims, maritime jurisdiction, military presence, fisheries, hydrocarbons, and sea lanes of communication. This kind of separation, however, may not hold indefinitely, because the critical minerals competition is acquiring an increasingly prominent maritime dimension.
As governments search for ways to reduce dependence on existing rare earth supply chains, attention is gradually shifting toward deep-sea muds, polymetallic nodules, cobalt-rich crusts, and other seabed resources. These resources are not immediate substitutes for today’s land-based mines and processing systems, but they are entering strategic planning and industrial policy. Once critical minerals are imagined not only as terrestrial commodities but also as seabed resources, the boundary between resource security and maritime security begins to blur.
The South China Sea disputes have always had a strategic dimension, in addition to the sovereignty disputes alone. Yet oil, gas, fisheries, and shipping are the dominant drivers of maritime competition; seabed resources have thus far remained a less developed part of the story. Studies of Fe-Mn crusts and polymetallic nodules in the South China Sea have identified the presence of cobalt, nickel, rare earth elements, yttrium, and other critical materials.
That does not mean that the South China Sea is about to become a commercially viable rare earth mining zone. But as deep-sea mineral technologies and governance frameworks mature, the South China Sea’s significance may be reinterpreted through the language of critical minerals security.
That shift, if it occurs, would not replace the existing logic of South China Sea competition but add another layer to it. Critical minerals could make seabed mapping, marine scientific research, environmental regulation, and deep-sea mining rules more politically sensitive. Activities that once appeared primarily scientific or commercial could come to be viewed through the lens of supply chain resilience and national security.
China is especially well placed to think across these domains because it already possesses capabilities on both sides of the equation. It is not only a central actor in the rare earth supply chain, but also an active participant in deep-sea exploration and seabed governance. China adopted a national law on deep seabed resource exploration and development in 2016. Chinese entities already hold exploration contracts with the International Seabed Authority for polymetallic nodules, polymetallic sulphides, and cobalt-rich Fe-Mn crusts. Its deep-sea technological capacity has also expanded, symbolized by the Fendouzhe manned submersible’s dive to more than 10,000 meters in the Mariana Trench.
Rare earths are not about to become the central driver of South China Sea disputes. The more important trend is that two strategic arenas for competition are beginning to converge. China’s rare earth strategy is about control over critical supply chains, while its South China Sea strategy is about control over maritime space, rights, and access. As critical minerals competition expands offshore, these two forms of strategic control may begin to interact. The South China Sea, in the longer term, may become part of a broader debate over who maps, governs, regulates, and eventually exploits the seabed resources that underpin future industrial and military power.
Rare earths may not define the South China Sea today, but they could help reshape how its strategic value is imagined tomorrow.

Lockheed adds 6,000 jobs to speed up missile production
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
17:19:32 UTC
02:19:32 KST

- Lockheed Martin will invest $300 million to expand its Grand Prairie, Texas, missile parts plant as part of a plan to create 6,000 U.S. jobs.
- Hadrian will install a 24-machine automated cell at the plant in early 2027 to boost parts output for PAC-3 MSE, THAAD and other missiles.
Lockheed Martin plans to create 6,000 jobs across the United States, including 2,000 in Texas, as it expands munitions production. At the center of the plan is a $300 million expansion of its Grand Prairie missile parts plant, where defense manufacturing startup Hadrian will install an automated machining cell.
The company announced the plan on Oct. 14. The Grand Prairie expansion will grow the site to more than 68,000 square meters (735,000 square feet), including about 9,300 square meters (100,000 square feet) of new space and roughly 7,900 square meters (85,000 square feet) of former offices converted into production floor for automation, digital manufacturing and high-precision machining.
Grand Prairie, between Dallas and Fort Worth, is the headquarters of Lockheed’s Missiles and Fire Control business. It machines components for all of the unit’s programs, including the PAC-3 MSE interceptor fired by Patriot air defense batteries, the THAAD missile defense interceptor, the U.S. Army’s Precision Strike Missile and the Joint Advanced Tactical Missile. Parts made there go to final assembly lines in Camden, Arkansas, and Troy, Alabama.
Nearly 800 production workers at the plant made 250,000 parts in 2025. Over the past few months, Lockheed has installed more than 30 additional high-precision machines in converted office space that now turn out thousands of components a week, and it expects to add nearly 100 new machines across the site by the end of 2026.
Hadrian’s cell will hold 24 machines and is expected to start running in early 2027, staffed by Lockheed’s own production workers. The Los Angeles-area startup builds highly automated factories driven by its own software and sells what it calls a factory-as-a-service model, and the two companies signed a seven-year agreement in 2025 for Hadrian to embed a machining and inspection cell at a Missiles and Fire Control site.
“The warfighter can’t wait on peacetime timelines,” said Chris Power, CEO of Hadrian.
Michael Duffey, under secretary of war for acquisition and sustainment, attended the event in Grand Prairie. Tim Cahill, president of Lockheed’s Missiles and Fire Control business, said in a LinkedIn post the next day that the company had marked the investment together with Hadrian, the plant’s workforce and GM Defense, which Lockheed recently brought in to apply automotive manufacturing methods to defense production.
“This expansion is more than just a new facility; it is a stronger supply chain and a more resilient industrial base,” said Duffey.
The investment is aimed at meeting production targets set under new long-term agreements with the U.S. Department of War. Under a seven-year deal, Lockheed is working to raise PAC-3 MSE output from roughly 600 interceptors in 2025 to about 2,000 a year, backed by a multiyear award now worth $58.62 billion. A separate framework signed in January calls for quadrupling THAAD production from 96 to 400 interceptors a year.
“By combining advanced technology with the expertise of our American workforce, we’re transforming manufacturing to deliver critical munitions at speed and scale,” said Jim Taiclet, chairman, president and CEO of Lockheed Martin.
The Grand Prairie project is one piece of Lockheed’s plan to spend $8 billion to $9 billion through 2030 to expand munitions production and modernize or expand more than 20 facilities nationwide, with the Hadrian cell due to come online at the Texas plant in early 2027.

Valid ID cards, 'impartial' reporting, basic first-aid: Press Council issues guidelines for journalists covering anti-SIR protests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:43:11 UTC
21:43:11 KST

NEW DELHI: The Press Council of India (PCI) has issued guidelines for journalists covering the ongoing protests in Delhi against the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, saying the measures are aimed at "ensuring the safety of media personnel while enabling them to carry out their professional duties effectively."According to a PCI release, the council adopted the "Guidelines for Journalists Covering Protests and Demonstrations" at a meeting on Thursday.The guidelines advise journalists to carry valid identity cards issued by their organisations or accreditation from the Press Information Bureau (PIB) or the Directorate of Information and Publicity (DIP), and keep them visibly displayed. They should calmly identify themselves to law enforcement personnel, maintain neutrality, avoid provoking confrontations and follow lawful instructions, particularly those issued for safety reasons.On safety, the PCI urged journalists to maintain a reasonable distance from confrontations, move cautiously through crowds and continually reassess their surroundings. It also cautioned against attaching cameras or recording equipment to police barricades, vehicles or other equipment in ways that obstruct movement or damage property.“Move carefully through crowds, taking short steps to reduce the risk of falling or being trampled.
Continuously reassess your position in relation to protesters, counter-protesters, police, and other potential sources of danger,” the guidelines said.Journalists should remain alert to changes in crowd behaviour, approaching individuals, potential confrontations, shifts in crowd noise and emerging hazards. They should also identify and regularly reassess escape routes, including nearby exits, open streets, sidewalks and safe locations. In the event of smoke or tear gas, they should use visible landmarks and safe routes to leave the affected area without moving further into the crowd.The PCI also advised journalists to carry a compact safety kit containing first-aid supplies, water, snacks, a flashlight, a washcloth and eye protection. Depending on the assessed threat, they should consider wearing protective headgear and body armour. Journalists should learn basic first aid and avoid touching tear-gas canisters, flash-bang devices or smoke grenades.On coordination, the guidelines call on newsrooms to designate a point of contact to track journalists’ locations and respond to emergencies. Freelancers, meanwhile, should ensure that a trusted editor or contact knows their location, assignment plan and expected return time.
For planned demonstrations, media organisations should coordinate with police and public information officers to clarify communication protocols and identify designated media staging areas.Emphasising journalistic ethics, the Council called for accurate and impartial reporting, urging journalists to distinguish verified facts from allegations and unconfirmed claims and to verify information through multiple sources. Statements from protesters, organisers, police and government authorities should be subjected to equal journalistic scrutiny, with claims clearly attributed.The guidelines also caution against publishing real-time police positions or escape routes if doing so could compromise safety. Journalists should describe observable actions rather than speculate about motives and exercise particular care when filming minors, injured people and private citizens in distress.The council stressed that equipment, live-broadcast commitments and pressure to obtain exclusive footage should never take precedence over journalists’ safety.(With ANI inputs)
Karan Manral is a journalist at the Times of India. He covers politics, social issues, and international affairs, exploring stories that affect people’s everyday lives. He also writes explainers to make these stories easier for readers to follow.

Hong Kong authorities have uncovered alleged corner-cutting and false declarations involving fire-safety components in a contractor’s replacement of 48 lifts at two public housing estates.
The Electrical and Mechanical Services Department said on Thursday that surprise inspections had found serious deficiencies in projects carried out by Taizoom Elevator (Hong Kong) at Tsui Ping (North) Estate in Kwun Tong and Pok Hong Estate in Sha Tin.
It said 39 lifts replaced between May 2025 and July this year were affected at Pok Hong Estate. Nine lifts replaced between February and July at Tsui Ping (North) Estate were also affected.
The department said that although Taizoom had submitted fire-resistance test reports, inspectors found that it had only installed fire-resisting doors and not the corresponding door-frame components required before reporting the works as completed.
