The UK's Green Party declare Zionism racism, exposing their double standards - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
17:00:00 UTC
02:00:00 KST

In The Man of Destiny (1898), George Bernard Shaw gave Napoleon the definitive line on the English: “You will never find an Englishman in the wrong. He does everything on principle. He fights you on patriotic principles; he robs you on business principles; he enslaves you on imperial principles; he bullies you on manly principles; he supports his king on loyal principles, and cuts off his king’s head on republican principles.” Britain has spent a fortnight proving him right.
On October 4, in Brighton, the Green Party of England and Wales adopted a “Zionism is Racism” motion by 1,022 votes to 813. The party now “declares itself to be an anti-Zionist party,” resolves that Zionism “will be treated as any other form of racism,” and calls for “a single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine.”
An amendment to protect members of synagogues that identify as Zionist was defeated, 1,026 to 684. Outside, supporters chanted: “Say it loud, say it clear, Zionists are not welcome here.”
The motion’s brochure is franker still. It invokes “struggling by all available means, including armed struggle,” and asserts: “Only racists, genocidaires and supporters of apartheid can argue (and kill) for the continuation of Zionism.”
The lead author’s signed text ends with “Free Palestine, from the river to the sea!” – repeated on the endorsements page. The river is the Jordan, the sea the Mediterranean; between them lies Israel, which the slogan erases.
Zionism is nothing other than the right of the Jewish people to self-determination in the land where it became a people. By a grim twist of fate, the very same tireless champions of the right of return and of self-determination for every people deny both to the Jews alone.
And the “racism” Brighton denounces has a face: according to the Institute for Jewish Policy Research, 64% of British Jews identify as Zionists. The Board of Deputies and the Jewish Leadership Council called the motion “an attack on the Jewish community” and answered in three words: “Zionism is anti-racism.”
Brighton is no island. That same weekend, the Royal College of Nursing cut ties with Teva UK, the Israeli drugmaker’s subsidiary, after a Nurses for Palestine campaign.
Days earlier, The Sunday Times revealed Britain had granted asylum, then citizenship, to a former bodyguard of Hamas chief Ismail Haniyeh – accused by German prosecutors of helping prepare attacks on Jewish and Israeli targets in Europe.
A former Hamas bodyguard naturalized, an Israeli company shown the door, Zionism outlawed: each decision has its principle, and none is in the wrong.
Green Europe refused to follow. The European Green Party said: “As EGP we unequivocally distance ourselves from it” – while lambasting Israel’s government. German Greens co-leader Felix Banaszak called the motion “intolerable and unacceptable.” At home, a councillor, a former opposition leader in Richmond, and Amnesty International UK’s board chair have quit the party.
The J50, a forum of Diaspora Jewish leaders convened by Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar, which declared in September that “Zionism is part of Jewish identity,” is working to keep the other Green parties apart from Brighton. Its aim is plain: Brighton must stand alone.
Israel has answered the Labour government – not Brighton. On October 8, Sa’ar confirmed the four measures announced on September 8 were implemented: British representatives removed from the International Gaza Support Center in Kiryat Gat; British training of Palestinian Authority forces in Judea and Samaria terminated; 12 British elected officials and other Britons involved in antisemitic and anti-Israel activity denied entry; and the British Consulate in Jerusalem closed, its sign taken down.
'Labour Government brought us here'
London is saving face: Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband says the building “will be known as the UK Mission, Jerusalem,” its staff only “temporarily withdrawn,” and pledges no “reciprocal action while such discussions are underway and credible.” The consul general and 19 diplomats are leaving all the same.
“We did not want to reach this point,” Sa’ar said, “but the actions of the UK Labour Government brought us here.”
Since July 2024, that government has recognized a virtual “Palestinian state,” restored UNRWA funding, suspended defense export licenses and free trade talks, sanctioned Israeli ministers, frozen military dialogue, kept IDF officers out of the Royal College of Defence Studies and, lately, imposed far-reaching sanctions on Judea and Samaria’s communities, amid accusations of “ethnic cleansing.”
Israel does not confuse a government with a nation. Sa’ar stressed that relations with Britain “are important and have repeatedly proven their value also in protecting the lives and interests of British citizens” – most recently with vital information in the RAF Fairford affair. Yet he warns: “any country that acts against Israel must know that there will be a price for doing so. … Israel will no longer turn its cheek to diplomatic attacks against it.”
That is how duplicity is sanctioned: not with invective, but with measured acts of state. The rest must follow – politically, at the ballot box; legally, wherever British equality and nationality law offers a foothold.
The self-determination of peoples is enshrined in Article 1 of the UN Charter; Britain’s Greens grant it to every people but one. Denying to Jews alone what is granted to everyone else has a precise legal name. That name is not “Zionism.” It is “discrimination.”
Shaw’s Englishman is never in the wrong. This time, he is simply wrong in law.
The writer is a Portugal- and Israel-based French entrepreneur, legal adviser, and expert in crypto assets, information security, and computer warfare. A former lecturer at the Institut des Hautes Études de Défense Nationale (IHEDN) on influence operations, he has participated in French parliamentary missions on economic intelligence and advised on digital threats facing France and European institutions. He regularly comments on French foreign policy and Middle East affairs.

Dying in Detention
Fault Lines investigates the soaring death rates in immigration detention centers following President Trump’s crackdown.
In September 2025, 39-year-old Ismael Ayala-Uribe died just one month after entering California’s Adelanto ICE Processing Center.
He was one of more than 50 people to die in immigration custody during Donald Trump’s first 500 days back in office.
His family says he repeatedly complained of intense pain and asked for medical help, but received little beyond Tylenol. When he finally reached a hospital, his heart stopped within minutes.
The Trump administration is detaining record numbers of immigrants, and deaths in custody are soaring. Fault Lines investigates failures in medical care and oversight, allegations of retaliation against hunger strikers and the role of private prison companies in the rapid expansion of immigration detention.

EU freezes assets of three individuals and nine companies circumventing sanctions against Russia
Ukraine

EU freezes assets of three individuals and nine companies circumventing sanctions against Russia
The European Council has adopted additional restrictive measures against three individuals and nine entities involved in the import of sanctioned goods to Russia, as well as in the circumvention of EU sanctions regarding oil and financial transactions.
Source: European Pravda, citing the press service for the European Council
Details: The sanctions lists were approved under the EU's restrictive measures framework aimed at actions undermining or threatening the territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence of Ukraine.
Quote from Kaja Kallas, EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy: "Circumventing EU sanctions is akin to aiding and abetting Russia's illegal war of aggression. Today we are taking further action against individuals and companies who are doing this. Sanctions have already denied Moscow over one trillion euro, but they can be even more effective when we fully enforce them".
Details: The list includes Movers Group LLC, a Russia-based cargo delivery company involved in the parallel import to Russia of goods subject to EU restrictive measures, and its general director, Dmitry Chudovsky.
The European Council also listed DT Inier LLC and its majority shareholder, Ivanna Savchuk. DT Inier LLC is a licensed Russian customs broker and full-cycle logistics operator involved in decentralised sanctions circumvention schemes, as are other entities added to the list today: Begler Tekstil Insaat Elektronik VE DIS Ticaret LTD and Medse Group LLC. Both of these companies are trade enterprises based in Türkiye but operating a global network.
Furthermore, the EU is imposing sanctions on United Stream LLC and its founder and director, Svetlana Gumenyuk. United Stream is a financial services company registered in the Russian Federation that acts as a payment agent and intermediary, also facilitating the import of EU goods subject to restrictive measures.
In addition, the European Council imposed sanctions on entities based in the United Arab Emirates, India and the Seychelles. This list includes DIS Logistics DMCC, Vigor Marine Services LLP and Shiva Shipping LTD, which are part of the "shadow fleet" ecosystem, as well as Hurus Trade FZE, a trading intermediary supplying Russian-origin oil to India.
The individuals and entities included in the list are subject to an asset freeze, and the provision of funds or economic resources, directly or indirectly, to them or for their benefit is prohibited. Additionally, a travel ban to the EU applies to the listed individuals.
Background:
- On Thursday 15 October, following court decisions, the EU lifted sanctions on businessmen Mikhail Gutseriev and Viktor Shevtsov, who are described as a friend and the "wallet" of Belarusian ruler Alexander Lukashenko.
- On 12 October, the EU approved the largest expansion of personal sanctions against Russia, with nearly 1,600 individuals and legal entities included in the new list.

            Lead Architects: Alziro Carvalho Neto, Felipe Rio Branco
Text description provided by the architects. The Ibitipoca House is born from the logic of reuse. Faced with an old ruined building in the Serra do Ibitipoca, in Minas Gerais, the project begins with a disassembly operation that seeks to preserve, reconfigure, and re-inscribe the materials and traces of what already existed into the present. Instead of erasing the previous construction, the proposal transforms it into the material and conceptual origin of the new house.

New joint venture targets Army light vehicle programme
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
17:53:01 BST
01:53:01 KST

Two family-run British engineering firms have formed a joint venture to manufacture composite vehicle bodies in Tamworth, positioning themselves ahead of the British Army’s Land Mobility Vehicle competition, according to the companies.
North Strong brings together North Defence, the light mobility vehicle specialist founded by the former Royal Engineer Oliver North, and Strongs Plastic Products, the Midlands polymer engineering company founded in 1978 by the late Barry Strong and now run by his son James. The two have worked alongside each other since 2023, and the venture is incorporated at Companies House as North Strong Defence Limited.
The Tamworth facility will build North Defence’s co-polymer vehicle bodies, the component the company describes as central to the performance, survivability and adaptability of its platforms.
Oliver North, chief executive of North Defence, said: “This is about delivering real, sovereign capability, not just intent.
“For years, we’ve evolved our vehicles at a pace traditional primes struggle to match, because our model allows us to respond immediately to changing battlefield demands. North Strong now gives us the ability to scale that agility, rapidly, reliably, and here in the UK, across multiple platforms. It proves we’re a key industrial partner within the LMV ecosystem and it ensures we’re ready to deliver when the Army needs it most.”
James Strong, managing director of Strongs, said: “This is a golden opportunity for us to take what we have learned over the decades, to better help and support UK and NATO forces in these troubled times. Strongs has always prided itself on innovation in the use of polymers and we see this as another opportunity to develop and grow our capabilities in a new market sector with the help of North Defence.”
The announcement lands alongside the North Defence LMV MKIII, which the company says can be built on Toyota, Ford, INEOS Grenadier and Mercedes-Benz base chassis, all using the same North Strong body. Decoupling the military capability from a single original equipment manufacturer is the pitch, and the company argues it brings faster procurement cycles, greater supply chain resilience and more flexibility across operating environments.
The Land Mobility Vehicle programme is the Army’s effort to replace the ageing Land Rover-derived fleet that has carried infantry, engineers and support units for decades, and it has drawn a competitive field.

Over 70 groups urge Egypt to release Matsad2sh journalists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:52:24 UTC
01:52:24 KST

Breadcrumb
Over 70 rights groups urge Egypt to release Matsad2sh journalists
Over 70 organisations, including news outlets, human rights groups, international foundations and syndicates, have issued a statement condemning the detention of six journalists from a Cairo-based fact-checking newsroom by security forces in late September and calling for their urgent release.
The organisations shed light on the escalating crackdown on the Matsad2sh platform (Arabic for ‘don’t believe’) and the six journalists who were detained following raids on their homes on 28 and 29 September.
The journalists have been identified as Abdallah Qadri, Mohamed Ashraf Abu Emeira, Mohamed Adel, Islam Barakat, Mohamed Mahmoud and Omar Helal. All remain behind bars, with some telling their lawyers that they have faced torture and beatings.
“Independent journalism is critical in any free society and Egyptian authorities’ failure to allow the free exercise of the right to expression goes against a purported commitment to dialogue, transparency, anti-corruption, and regional leadership,” the joint statement from the 79 organisations reads.
“The crackdown on the Matsadaash platform and these arrests are alarming escalations on independent media and freedom of expression that cannot be allowed to stand,” the statement adds.
Some of the signatories include Access Now, Daraj Media, Democracy for the Arab World Now, Global Voices, Greece Fact Check, Human Rights Watch, Mada Masr, Kawaakibi Foundation, PEN Lebanon and Raseef22, among others.
The development comes after the head of Egypt’s Journalists Syndicate reiterated that it would continue to push for press freedom.
Detention renewed
It also comes after Egypt’s state security prosecution on Tuesday renewed the detention of the six journalists for 15 days, pending further investigations.
The journalists’ lawyers confirmed to local media that the renewal was ordered on Tuesday following questioning that started at 1pm and continued into the evening. The questioning touched on their wages, the structure of the fact-checking platform and their work. However, no evidence related to the allegations was presented.
Egyptian prosecutors have accused the journalists of being linked to the Muslim Brotherhood, a group which the government has targeted for years, claiming it is a “terrorist” organisation, which the movement has strongly denied. The co-founder of Matsad2sh, Abdelrahman Mansour, has also rejected any links between the platform and the Muslim Brotherhood.
The prosecution has also accused them of spreading false news, misusing social media and receiving foreign funding.
The journalists’ lawyers say they are due to receive family visits from today and be granted time for exercise.
According to MENA Rights Group, the fact-checking platform was previously targeted by Egyptian authorities in 2023, when an editor was arrested and then released after 48 hours. The group says the platform has also been subjected to smear campaigns.
Egypt is one of the world’s leading jailers of journalists, with at least 19 currently behind bars.

Venezuela’s Maduro and wife plead not guilty to US torture charges
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:51:10 UTC
01:51:10 KST

Venezuela’s Maduro and wife plead not guilty to US torture charges
NEW YORK – Ousted Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores pleaded not guilty on Oct 15 to a new US indictment accusing them of conspiring to torture political opponents.
The additional charges, brought on Oct 15, significantly expanded the US criminal case against Maduro, 63, and Flores, 70. They previously pleaded not guilty to charges that they abused their power to help drug traffickers ship cocaine.
Maduro and Flores, captured by the US military in a January raid ordered by US President Donald Trump and flown to New York, entered their pleas at an arraignment before District Judge Alvin Hellerstein in Manhattan federal court. They wore tan prison garb and were shackled at the ankles during the hearing.
When Hellerstein asked for his plea, Maduro said the accusations had been made previously and were false.
“I have seen it in its entirety, Judge Hellerstein,” Maduro said, referring to the indictment. “I reject this document in its entirety.”
The judge cut Maduro off as he spoke and said a plea of not guilty would be entered on his behalf.
Flores said: “I am completely innocent. I am not guilty.”
Maduro and Flores are not accused of personally carrying out any acts of torture. They would each face a mandatory minimum sentence of 50 years in prison if convicted on all charges.
Hellerstein postponed the trial start date by two weeks to June 14, 2027, due to the new charges.
‘Squeeze them harder’
Prosecutors with the Manhattan US Attorney’s office say Maduro directed Venezuelan officials to torture opposition politicians and military personnel accused of plotting against him to maintain power in the South American country.
In one alleged incident described in the indictment, Maduro in 2014 directed officials to kidnap military personnel to draw information out of them about possible dissidents, and told officials to “squeeze them harder” when some remained defiant.
Flores agreed with the plan in the meeting, and dismissed a suggested alternative plan to glean information by infiltrating the ranks, according to the indictment.
Relations between Maduro, a socialist, and the US were tense during his 13 years in power leading the oil-rich country.
Successive US administrations imposed sanctions on top Venezuelan officials and key state companies, citing alleged human rights violations, corruption and election-rigging. Maduro accused the US of seeking his ouster to gain greater control of the South American country’s natural resources.
Captured at home
The pressure campaign culminated in the Jan 3 raid, when the US military captured Maduro and Flores at their Caracas home and brought them to the US to face drug trafficking charges announced that same day. Since then, they have been held at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn.
Maduro’s former vice-president, Delcy Rodriguez, has led Venezuela since his capture and has ramped up cooperation with the US. Trump has touted Maduro’s capture and the reset of relations with Venezuela as a key foreign policy success heading into the Nov 3 midterm elections in which his fellow Republicans are fighting to retain control of Congress. Farmer's discovery in Egypt leads to pieces of statues for ancient king
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:51:08 UTC
01:51:08 KST

An Egyptian farmer found "an unusual stone." It led archaeologists to pieces of statues for an ancient king.
Cairo — Egyptian farmer Khaled al-Shahat was working on his land when he came across something he hadn't seen before. The unusual pink rock led archaeologists to unearth pieces of statues for King Ramses II, who ruled Egypt from 1279 B.C. to 1213 B.C.
"I was working on my land on Friday when I came across an unusual stone," al-Shahat told CBS News. "I informed the relevant authorities, and they came to examine it."
The stone turned out to be an ancient pink granite block measuring approximately 1.3 meters long (around 4.26 feet) and bearing two royal titles of Ramses II: "Nesw-Bity" (King of Upper and Lower Egypt) and "Sa-Ra" (Son of Ra, the sun god), the Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities said.
Archaeologists began excavations, and near the block they uncovered a colossal head of a statue of Ramses II, measuring approximately 1.6 meters high (around 5.25 feet). The king is depicted wearing the double crown, a symbol of the unification of Upper and Lower Egypt around 3100 B.C.
On Wednesday, Minister of Tourism and Antiquities Sherif Fathy visited al-Shahat's hometown in Al Gharbia Governorate in the Nile Delta to honor him.
The minister presented al-Shahat and his wife with certificates of appreciation, and awarded them a trip to Saudi Arabia to perform the Umrah pilgrimage in recognition of his honesty and responsible conduct for not keeping the discovery to himself.
"The minister insisted that the citizen be honored in his village, on his own land, and among his family and fellow villagers, in recognition of his honesty, awareness, and sense of responsibility," the ministry said in a statement.
Archaeologists also unearthed the remains of the upper part of the statue's back pillar, bearing Ramses II's formal royal title, or Horus name: Hor Ka Nakht Mery Maat.
The size of the head suggests the complete statue was about 28 feet tall, according to archaeologists.
"I was surprised and happy when they discovered more antiquities," al-Shahat told CBS News. "They told me this might change the history of the area."
Most of a second royal statue, also believed to depict Ramses II, was uncovered. Measuring approximately 2.4 meters long (around 7.87 feet), it is missing its legs and base, as well as part of the upper section of its royal nemes headdress. Its head has clearly visible, well-preserved facial features resembling those of the first statue, the ministry said.
Excavations and archaeological studies are continuing on al-Shahat's land to learn more about the statues, the area's history and its architectural development in ancient Egypt.

At least 5 killed in Houthi attack on Yemen’s presidential palace in Aden
Saudi-led coalition accuses Houthis of obtaining missile parts from regional states.
At least five people have been killed in the vicinity of the al-Maashiq presidential palace in Yemen’s port city of Aden after Houthi missile strikes.
Yemeni health minister says five people were killed and 16 others injured in the Houthi missile attack that targeted the al-Maashiq Presidential Palace in Yemen’s Aden on Thursday.
The Yemeni Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani said in a social media post on Thursday that Houthis had targeted the al-Maashiq presidential palace with five missiles.
The government says the prime minister and other officials are safe, but two of his bodyguards were killed in the attack.
Plumes of smoke could be seen rising from the vicinity of the palace.
Al Jazeera correspondents reported earlier on Thursday that there were explosions near the palace.
The palace is considered the headquarters and the seat of power for the Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government.
Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry, reporting from the Houthi-controlled capital Sanaa, said the attacks on the headquarters of the internationally recognised government are the “first of their kind” by the Houthis.
“This is an indication that the escalation is going to intensify between both sides,” Mawry said, adding that fears are now growing inside the country of “an all-out civil war” that could potentially drag in other regional powers besides Saudi Arabia.
The attack in Aden came as fighting between the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), and Saudi-backed forces intensified in Taiz, which is effectively under siege by the Houthis.
Controlling Taiz, Yemen’s third city and the broader Taiz governorate, in the southwest of the country would ensure control over the critical Bab al-Mandeb strait for either side.
Forces allied with the Yemeni government said they are repelling a Houthi attack on Dhubab airport.
The pro-government Homeland Shield Force said in a statement that they are, along with the Southern Giants Brigades, securing the airport in the coastal city of Dhubab in Taiz governorate.
Aid agencies say the escalating violence in Taiz is pushing the healthcare system towards breaking point.
On Sunday, the Ministry of Public Health warned of a “humanitarian catastrophe” there.
Meanwhile, the Saudi-led coalition says Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport has come under at least 20 Houthi attacks over the past 11 days with dozens of other airports, oil facilities and ports also targeted.
Major-General Turki al-Maliki, the spokesperson for the alliance, released footage showing strikes on the main airport with passengers seen fleeing for safety, during a news conference in the Saudi capital,
The coalition says the Houthi attacks have killed 17 people and injured more than 300.
Al-Maliki also accused the Houthis of obtaining ballistic missiles from other countries in the region.
Mohamad Elmasry, a professor at the Doha Institute for Graduate Studies, said the Saudi-led coalition’s news conference was intended as a response “to some of the, perhaps, military and security failures”.
“There’s kind of an image problem there because this is maybe affecting the perception of Saudi deterrence, the fact that missiles are getting through,” he told Al Jazeera.
Elmasry said the Houthis also have an image crisis, with the global community viewing their actions as “reprehensible, in particular these targeting civilian infrastructure”.

How RSF defections are reshaping Sudan's fragmented battlefield
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:49:50 UTC
01:49:50 KST

Breadcrumb
How RSF defections are reshaping Sudan's fragmented battlefield
On 8 October, Mohamed Azraq al-Fangari defected from the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and joined the Sudanese Armed Forces, the national army.
The special forces commander was accompanied by some 300 fighters from Kordofan, a region in central Sudan where the army has made advances in recent weeks.
Al-Fangari’s forces played a key role in besieging North Darfur’s capital of El-Fasher in April 2024.
The chokehold lasted 18 months and culminated in the mass killing of sedentary farming ‘non-Arab’ civilians. A UN probe found that the atrocities bore the ‘hallmarks of genocide’.
By then, al-Fangari had long been living in neighbouring Chad, where he was lobbying the RSF’s leadership for better equipment, higher salaries, and medical treatment for his fighters, according to Ahmed Gouja, a local journalist who hails from the same nomadic ‘Arab’ Hawzama tribe as al-Fangari.
“Al-Fangari had a lot of fighters who were injured in his special forces, but the RSF’s leaders treated them as an afterthought,” Gouja told The New Arab. “For those reasons, he defected.”
Dozens of disgruntled RSF officers have defected to the SAF in recent months, a trend that could fragment the RSF across tribal lines, according to local journalists and analysts from Darfur.
Like al-Fangari, most defected fighters hail from nomadic Arab tribes that the RSF’s top brass excludes from powerful positions. The RSF’s leadership is made up almost entirely of the Dagalo family, which hails from the nomadic ‘Arab’ Mahariya tribe.
The family’s grip on power has exacerbated tensions between its own tribe and other Arab communities, which the RSF leans on to fight the SAF.
The SAF’s warm embrace of RSF defectors is also stoking tensions within its own camp, which includes dozens of militias from various ethnic backgrounds and ideological leanings.
Defectors have been awarded impunity, arms and vehicles as a way to tempt other RSF commanders to change sides.
This has agitated some SAF-aligned militias who fear losing power and resources to RSF defectors, analysts say.
Favouritism and neglect
Throughout the war, the RSF’s leaders have sidelined ground commanders despite their role in spearheading major battlefield victories, which they achieved by committing systematic atrocities.
Former RSF commander Al-Nour ‘al-Gubba’ Ahmed Adam expected to be appointed governor of North Darfur for playing a substantial role in the RSF’s genocidal campaign to capture El-Fasher in October 2025.
Yet as a member of the nomadic ‘Arab’ Mahamid tribe - a community divided over its support between the RSF and the SAF – he was passed over for a fighter from the Mahariya.
In April 2026, al-Gubba defected to the SAF, partially because he was denied that powerful post. Many others have followed suit for similar reasons.
“Many [Arab] community leaders have come out and said publicly that these defections don’t represent the position of their tribes, but merely the self-interest of the officers who defected,” said Gouja.
Despite these statements, Gouja added that the RSF has stigmatised these communities, often arresting young men based on unfounded allegations that they are collaborating with the SAF by helping commanders defect.
This has compounded grievances among many nomadic Arab communities, who believe they are shouldering an unfair burden in the war against the SAF.
Many have sent their sons and fathers to either die or suffer life-altering injuries on the front lines, according to Abdel Nasser Suluk Hamid, an analyst from Darfur who is in touch with many Arab tribal leaders and civilians across the region.
“Fighters belonging to [the Mahariya] are sent abroad for life-saving hospital treatment, while the rest of the fighters are abandoned in South Darfur’s capital of Nyala or in Kordofan,” Suluk Hamid told The New Arab.
Despite the discriminatory treatment, Suluk Hamid believes that nomadic Arab tribes won’t turn against the RSF any time soon. Most still fear that the army will subject them to collective punishment if it recaptures Darfur - a fear the RSF stokes to keep them aligned and to attract new recruits.
“Arab communities in Darfur are told that SAF will rape their mothers and loot their lands,” Suluk Hamid told The New Arab.
The irony is that while both sides have committed atrocities such as torture and summary executions, the RSF is disproportionately responsible for systemic sexual violence and mass looting, according to human rights groups and media reports.
Simmering tensions
The wave of RSF defections could also lead to infighting within the delicate alliance of armed groups fighting under the banner of the SAF.
On 8 October, Minni Arko Minnawi, the leader of the SAF-aligned Joint Forces, which is composed of non-Arab militias that rebelled against the state in 2003, warned that he would rebel again if the army supported the creation of new militias.
“We are against any militias that are supported by the state with our money and taxes,” he said during an address to reporters from his residence in Khartoum.
Noon al-Baramkee, a journalist from Darfur, said that many of the RSF’s defectors are present across Sudan’s capital of Khartoum and in eastern Sudan. She said that Minnawi’s speech was likely prompted by fear that these groups would be empowered at the expense of the Joint Forces.
In addition, she believes Minnawi is agitated by the racist rhetoric of vocal SAF supporters, who are calling on the SAF to replace non-Arab armed groups with a new force.
Still, al-Baramkee said that Minnawi’s speech had exacerbated ethnic tensions.
“His speech was very dangerous and poorly timed. Many people now believe that Minnawi may be planning another rebellion [against the army again],” she told The New Arab.
A day after Minnawi’s speech, he walked back his threat of rebelling against the state, saying that he supports one state and one army. However, Gouja believes that Minnawi succeeded in warning the SAF against diluting his power and influence.
He noted that the Joint Forces remain a pivotal force, leading ground battles against the RSF in the broader Kordofan region, and that the SAF can’t afford to betray them.
“There are members of the SAF and of Sudan’s deep state that don’t view Minnawi as a trusted partner,” Gouja told The New Arab.
“But the leadership in the SAF knows that they would be weaker without him.”

Fiji is enlisting New Zealand’s intelligence agency to help overhaul its fragmented security sector, Suva said on Wednesday, as US warnings of suspected China-linked cyberintrusions highlight concerns about vulnerabilities in the nation.
The Fijian Cabinet approved a six-month partnership with the New Zealand Security Intelligence Service (NZSIS), funded by Wellington, to assess Fiji’s intelligence structure and recommend reforms, Fiji’s government said in a statement.
The review is designed to improve information-sharing and coordination across agencies, and reforms would create a more sustainable intelligence framework with clearer roles and improved support for security decisionmaking, the statement said.
Photo: AFP
Fiji did not identify a specific threat behind the review.
The NZSIS said in a separate statement that it was working on the review.
A spokesperson said its mission included keeping New Zealand safe and contributing to an open, stable and resilient Pacific region, and that meant working with Pacific partners on shared security challenges and supporting them to build resilience.
The US embassy in Suva earlier this week said that it had alerted Fiji and a regional organization based in the capital to a suspected network compromise between July and August.
Hackers linked to China maintained access to the organization’s network for several days, while Washington had provided technical recommendations to help Fiji and the affected entity protect their systems, the embassy said.
The US had continued to observe China-linked state-sponsored cyberactors targeting foreign governments, multilateral organizations and telecommunications networks in the Pacific, it said.
Stolen data could expose sensitive communications among Pacific island countries and territories, it added.
China’s embassy in Suva rejected the allegations, saying on Tuesday that Beijing opposed hacking and the politicization of cybersecurity.
“China firmly opposes and combats hacking activities in accordance with law,” the Chinese embassy said, accusing the US of making allegations without evidence and calling for dialogue to manage cyberrisks.
The intelligence review comes as Pacific governments face growing pressure to protect government networks and critical communications while navigating sharpening competition for influence between China, the US and its regional partners.

TSMC eyes adding facilities in Texas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:43:40 UTC
01:43:40 KST

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC, 台積電) yesterday said it is in discussions with a customer to secure wafer capacity supply in Texas, potentially extending its US manufacturing footprint beyond Arizona to satisfy surging demand from customers for artificial intelligence (AI) chips.
“Recently, we did expand our capacity consideration to see whether we can get another chance to expand our capacity outside Arizona, and Texas is the one,” TSMC chief executive officer C.C. Wei (魏哲家) said at the company’s earnings conference.
“So we sent our teams to Texas to do all the evaluation and we also talked to one of our customers who is trying to build a fab, TeraFab. And we are discussing with them to see whether we can utilize that actual capacity,” Wei said.
Photo: Cheng I-hwa, AFP
The main principle is that “the fab [has] got to be run by TSMC,” no matter the framework — whether it is similar to the company’s joint venture in Japan or the structure adopted in Europe, he said.
TSMC believes accelerating capacity in the US is “necessary,” he said, citing demand to ramp up onshore production from major customers there.
The company in July increased its US investment to US$265 billion.
TSMC yesterday said it remains committed to the AI mega trend, rebuffing skepticism over the profitability and sustainability of such investments.
“We observe increasing AI demand fueled by the rising adoption of agentic AI as we transition from chatbots to AI assistants,” Wei said.
“In addition, we are observing greater adoption of open-source AI models. This will drive greater efficiency and help lower the barrier to future AI usage, and result in more and more demand for leading-edge silicon,” he added.
Customer demand is far higher than what TSMC can supply, the company said, adding that it is adopting many approaches to maximize capacity support. "The AI demand is a very extremely robust. And we did not see any sign of slowdown," Wei said. “We have no intention to leave food on the table for others and we want to capture every piece of business possible."
Addressing competition from Intel Corp’s EMIB-T packaging technology, Wei highlighted TSMC’s unmatched market position, saying that the company offers highly competitive packaging technologies — producing 5.5-reticle size chip-on-wafer-on-substrate (CoWoS) and planning larger versions.
“I don’t believe that any company can do that today except TSMC. And the yield is excellent,” he said, adding that the company’s CoWoS products are the “No. 1 choice” for customers.
Asked if TSMC would provide CoWoS capacity as a contingency for customers should Intel fail to deliver its EMIB-T solutions, Wei said that it would.
TSMC’s ultimate priority is ensuring customers have smooth product rollouts, he said.
The company said it expects revenue this quarter to expand to US$52.3 billion to US$54.3 billion due to increasing demand for its leading-edge technologies, including the 2-nanometer process.
The mid-point of the revenue projection would represent sequential growth of 14 percent from US$46.72 billion last quarter.
Revenue is expected to expand about 44 percent in US dollar terms annually for the whole of this year, TSMC said.
It said it expects its 2-nanometer capacity to more than double next year from this year.
The company said it plans to build one more 3-nanometer plant in Tainan, with volume production scheduled in the first half of 2028.
Gross margin is forecast at 65 to 67 percent, compared with 66.4 percent last quarter, due to dilution from the steep ramp-up of 2-nanometer technology, TSMC said.
Net profit last quarter hit a new record at NT$763.06 billion (US$23.65 billion), up 8 percent from NT$706.56 billion a quarter earlier and 68.7 percent from NT$452.3 billion in the same period last year.
Earnings per share advanced to NT$29.43 from NT$27.25 in the second quarter and NT$17.44 a year earlier.

====================================================================================================

‘Misty Green’ nicely skewers Hollywood
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:43:38 UTC
01:43:38 KST

Ten years ago moviegoers got a love letter to Los Angeles in the achingly sweet La La Land, where characters danced on air. Gravity arrives a decade later in Chris Rock’s terrific poison pen letter to the city, Misty Green.
Rock, who directs and stars in the film as well as having written the screenplay, holds a mirror up to modern-day Los Angeles and shows us a metropolis that acts as a meat-grinder for a never-ending wave of wannabes. The city may as well use that mirror to cut another line of coke and snort it off someone’s thigh in a dingy bathroom.
Misty Green is an almost noirish take on Hollywood and the chase for fame. The result is one of Rock’s best projects, boosted by the ferocious abilities of Rosalind Eleazar as Misty. She turns a star-seeking character into a star-making part.
Photo: AP
Eleazar’s Misty Green is a mess when we first meet her: A once white-hot actor-singer who won a supporting Emmy trophy years before but is now approaching 40 and struggling to keep her career going.
Misty has poor impulse control, a long line of grudges and finds herself somewhat trapped: “Too Black to be with Leo (Leonardo DiCaprio), not Black enough to be with Damson (Idris), not a nepo baby or a Brit,” she says, which is a little meta because Eleazar is, in fact, a Brit.
Topher Grace, who plays Misty’s unhelpful agent, is out of ideas for his struggling client.
“You’re not exactly unknown,” he tells her. “I don’t know if I could get you on Law & Order.”
Hope arrives in Rock, who plays a movie director trying to recover from his last flop, starring Nicolas Cage, one of several celebs who catch strays in this movie. (Others include Victoria Beckham, J. Lo and Nicole Kidman. Speaking of celebs, look for a hysterical Ice-T cameo and, in an apparent nod to nepo babies, Rock’s daughter, Zahra, also has a small part.)
Rock’s easygoing director fired Misty years ago when she assaulted a makeup artist while coked up during his remake of Cinderella. Misty chalks up the incident to “creative differences,” and Rock may be willing to give her a second chance in his remake of the musical Dreamgirls.
Adding to Misty’s stress levels are the need to find new housing, stat, and the arrival of her bipolar brother, heartbreakingly played by Daniel Kaluuya. His character can be very dangerous when not on his meds and he has an irritating tendency of throwing plastic spiders at people.
Others in Misty’s orbit include an actor friend played by Anna Kendrick, who’s growing disillusioned by show biz.
“I really can’t do this anymore. I love acting, but riding the line between ’ho and hostess, I’m out,” she says.
Then there’s Misty’s hook-up/drug dealer friend played by Adam Driver. Both actors are terrific. Rock, bless him, is out of his depth, showing a lot of Progressive car insurance actor energy.
Rock puts Misty in a city divided by haves and have-nots — homeless encampments on one side juxtaposed by men in suits who keep telling people experiencing homelessness that they’re not carrying any cash. Everyone here is cheating, gossiping and judging. A Birkin bag is the coin of the realm.
It’s the kind of town where the emergency room doctor tending to your wounds confesses that she’s a fan of your TV work and wants a selfie, or the young woman auditioning for the same part as you are remarking that her dad — her dad — really loves your work.
Early on, the widow of Misty’s sugar daddy bursts into their love nest apartment, demanding she leave immediately and cursing up a storm, but soon offers to run dialogue with Misty ahead of her audition. “Memorize your lines,” she advises. Hollywood, right?
Rock has created a complicated character in Misty, a talented singer and actor who delivers a brave cover of Radiohead’s Creep at a piano lounge, but who is also an egotistical, party-loving starlet. She really should stay home and memorize her scenes, yet ends up lured to a nightclub all night. Eleazar shows us all her flaws and yet we root for her; it’s a stunning performance from the Slow Horses star.
Rock slyly examines race in this setting, too, with a casting agent blurting out to Misty: “Are you mixed?” Seemingly every role for Black women is exploitative. Rock notes wryly that wherever you go, at some point in history, Black people weren’t allowed there. The TV news is blaring about a dead white college student and a manhunt for her killer; Misty’s brother suspects they’ll railroad a Black man.
Misty’s money, family and career woes all build to an almost-operatic decision — follow her craft and career or debase herself and earn a lot of money. Whatever happens, no one in this tawdry town will be dancing on air.

US to account for over 20% of LNG imports: minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:43:36 UTC
01:43:36 KST

US liquefied natural gas (LNG) is expected to account for more than 20 percent of Taiwan’s LNG imports this year, up from 10 percent last year, and rise to 25 percent by 2029, Minister of Economic Affairs Kung Ming-hsin (龔明鑫) said yesterday.
If talks to purchase LNG from an Alaskan project proceed smoothly, supply could begin as early as 2032, potentially raising the US share in Taiwan’s LNG imports to 30 percent or more, Kung said.
Under a planned investment of up to US$4.4 billion in the project, CPC Corp, Taiwan (台灣中油) would purchase 6 million tonnes of LNG from Alaska annually once production begins, the ministry said.
Photo: Lin Jing-hua, Taipei Times
As Taiwan’s natural gas demand continues to rise, with 25 additional large gas-fired power units expected to be added by 2035, the government needs to secure supplies in advance and diversify procurement sources to strengthen energy resilience, Kung said.
In addition, securing stable supplies through long-term contracts could help reduce price volatility in LNG imports, he said.
Alaska is also relatively close to Taiwan, with a shipping time of about 10 days, which could reduce transportation time and shipping risks, Kung said.
For the US$4.4 billion investment, the government has a preliminary plan and an investment ceiling, but the actual amount, equity stake and other terms still need to be determined through negotiations, he said.
Kung said he is confident in CPC’s ability to negotiate favorable investment terms, but declined to disclose pricing because of commercial confidentiality.
The source of funding for the investment would depend on the final investment structure, timetable and CPC’s financial position, and could include capital injections, capitalization of retained earnings or loans, he said.
Funds would also be committed in stages in line with project progress rather than paid in a lump sum, he said.
As Taiwan’s trade surplus with the US has widened, increasing energy purchases from the US could also help narrow the imbalance, Kung said.
Separately, asked about Pegatron Corp (和碩) chairman Tung Tzu-hsien’s (童子賢) suggestion of developing an artificial intelligence (AI) park in the Danhai New Town (淡海新市鎮) area of New Taipei City’s Tamsui District (淡水), Kung said it was “a pretty good idea.”
The area has advantages including large contiguous parcels of land, convenient transportation and access to labor, he said.
The Danjiang Bridge would also improve access to the Port of Taipei and provide links to Taiwan Taoyuan International Airport, improving the area’s transportation advantages, he said.
In contrast, Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an’s (蔣萬安) proposal to develop an AI park on the site of Taipei International Airport (Songshan airport) could remain in the discussion phase for another decade because opinions remain divided, Kung said.
Taiwan’s AI industry cannot afford to wait for a consensus before moving ahead, he added.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:43:36 UTC
01:43:36 KST

The Ministry of Sports is working with the Chinese Taipei Skating Union (CTSU) to review the eligibility of five junior short-track speed skaters who were left out of international competitions, Minister of Sports Lee Yang (李洋) said yesterday.
Parents and coaches of the five skaters said the athletes met the International Skating Union’s qualifying standards for this year and next year’s Junior World Cups and World Junior Championships, but were excluded, as the union insisted on using results from a single domestic spring competition as the sole selection criterion.
The dispute has left Taiwan without skaters eligible to compete in the events, potentially jeopardizing the athletes’ chances of qualifying for the Youth Olympic Games, they said.
Photo: CNA
Democratic Progressive Party Legislator Chen Hsiu-pao (陳秀?) said the dispute was the third recent incident in which a sports association had jeopardized athletes’ opportunities to compete internationally.
Last month, the Chinese Taipei Gymnastics Association declined replacement spots for Pan Tsai-chen (潘采宸) and Lee Chia-wei (李佳蔚) at the World Championships without confirming whether they were willing to compete.
The Chinese Taipei Archery Association also warned that funding delays could affect registration for this year’s Asian Cup and Asian Youth and Cadet Championships, potentially forcing athletes to pay their own expenses.
The cases have raised questions about sports associations’ selection decisions, funding arrangements and responsibility of protecting athletes’ opportunities to compete, Chen said.
Lee said the CTSU had announced its selection rules before February and that the ministry was discussing with the union the possibility of reconvening the Selection and Training Committee to review the appeals and prevent similar disputes.
Chen questioned whether there was enough time to resolve the matter, as the registration deadline for the competitions is on Oct. 25.
Lee said the ministry had asked the union to reconvene the committee soon and would seek to secure the athletes’ right to compete before the deadline.
Chen also said participation in this year’s World Cup events affected applications for the government’s promising-athlete development program.
Last year, skaters who did not compete at the World Junior Championships were denied eligibility for the program, and those unable to compete this year could lose their eligibility, she said.
Lee said eligibility should be assessed based on each sport’s overall results and that missing the World Junior Championships would not automatically disqualify an athlete.

Unknown

2026-10-15
16:43:33 UTC
01:43:33 KST

Formula One driver Franco Colapinto has called on his fans to stop social media campaigns attacking other drivers and his Alpine team staff, saying they are holding back his career.
Since the Argentine driver’s F1 debut in 2024, fans have sent negative and sometimes abusive comments on social media targeting drivers who clashed with him on the track. Among them were champion Lando Norris and FIA race stewards who penalized Colapinto.
Alpine also stepped in this year to condemn online abuse and deny claims it was trying to “sabotage” Colapinto to favor teammate Pierre Gasly.
Photo: AFP
“I know it makes you feel very proud when things go well for me, when I score points, for me and for the whole team, and I’ll always be very grateful for that,” Colapinto said in a video posted on Instagram late on Wednesday. “But there are times when we go over the line, when instead of supporting me we end up criticizing, we end up attacking other drivers, other colleagues, my teammates, my mechanics, my engineers, people I work with day in and day out.”
“I know you’re thinking that you’re defending me, but you’re actually doing the opposite,” he said. “You don’t help me or my future, and I really want you to understand that this is what we have to change, all of us together.”
Colapinto became racing-mad Argentina’s first F1 driver in 23 years when he made his debut in 2024 with Williams.
He moved to Alpine the following year, initially as a reserve, then was promoted when the team fired Jack Doohan, who later complained he had received death threats around that time.
Colapinto is having his most successful season this year and is 12th in the standings, as well as picking up a best career race finish of sixth.

The new Darth Vader: how tech execs became the film villains of our age
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:43:32 UTC
01:43:32 KST

When The Social Network came out, Mark Zuckerberg organized a staff viewing of a film he described as “fun.”
A group corporate outing to the sequel is unlikely.
The Social Network hardly portrayed the Facebook founder and his company in a hagiographical light (Zuckerberg later described the film as “hurtful”), but there was at least an element of the plucky upstart to the rise of Zuckerberg as he takes Facebook to 500 million users and a valuation of US$25 billion (ridiculously small numbers now — Meta has 3.6 billion users and is worth US$1.8 trillion).
Photo: AP
By the end of that film, though, a steely CEO is emerging and his company is on the brink of global hegemony. The Social Reckoning picks up from there, with a clear perspective that both the founder and his company — as well as the industry they represent — are corporate villains now.
This is set to be underlined by the release of the OpenAI drama, Artificial, where its CEO, Sam Altman, is reportedly given a deeply unflattering portrayal. Elon Musk completes the villainous trilogy by appearing as himself — aside from the odd deployment of an AI avatar — in Alex Gibney’s four-hour documentary, Musk, about the world’s first trillionaire.
Tech is the obvious thread joining these films, but another is the scathing portrayal of the company leaders in them. Film villains used to be hoodlums, ex-deep state operatives, people with posh British accents. Tech execs are the new Darth Vader.
This is underlined by the casting of Jeremy Strong, who looks a touch on the old side to be playing 2019-2021-era Zuckerberg (the Meta CEO was in his mid-30s at the time of the film’s events whereas Strong is 47), but is embedded in our minds as the tortured Roy family scion Kendall in Succession.
Strong also brings a straitjacketed simmer to the role here, one that breaks slightly at the end as he backtracks on being a “free speech absolutist.” It is the most human Zuckerberg moment in the entire film.
Peter Bradshaw describes Strong’s performance as a “very interesting Zuckerberg impersonation, standing and sitting like a Thunderbird puppet.” It is much less sympathetic than Jesse Eisenberg’s in The Social Network and is a sort of corporeal representation of Meta as the monolithic, corporate bad guy.
Elements of the portrayal chime with some former Meta employees, including a whistleblower, Arturo Bejar, who describes it as “accurate.” Another former employee tells the Guardian that Zuckerberg was “unemotional” in meetings (perhaps what you’d expect from a US$1.8 trillion company CEO, admittedly). Well, Strong’s performance certainly is that.
There had already been a turning point in public perception of Facebook before the Haugen leaks, with the Cambridge Analytica scandal, which raised questions about the privacy of account holders’ data and how it is used.
Haugen’s revelations in 2021 compounded this disquiet. By the time of the 2022 inquest for British teenager Molly Russell, who took her own life after watching harmful content on Instagram, regulation of social media around the world was inevitable.
The tone of the film and Strong’s performance reflect this shift. In the UK, screenings of the film are carrying an advert for the online safety charity established by Molly’s family, in which her father says: “‘Instagram helped kill my daughter.”
Responding to Russell, Meta says it has worked to improve the safety of its platforms.
The regulatory, legal and political backlash against social media — as well as the release of The Social Reckoning — reflects a lack of trust in such statements.
Strong’s Zuckerberg says in the film that “the debate is over.” If it is, The Social Reckoning portrays a world where Meta is on the wrong side of it.

Taiwan blocks Coinbase, Kalshi over suspected election bets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:43:32 UTC
01:43:32 KST

Taiwan has blocked the Web sites of Coinbase Global Inc and Kalshi Inc over suspected election betting, weeks before local polls that will test support for President William Lai’s (賴清德) government.
A New Taipei City court authorized the Taiwanese communications regulator and Internet registry to bar domestic access to the platforms, according to a ruling seen by Bloomberg News.
Some Coinbase users in Taiwan reported being unable to access the site since Wednesday.
Photo: Reuters
The Criminal Investigation Bureau, which sought the order, said in response to questions from Bloomberg that the Web sites were suspected of violating the Public Officials Election and Recall Act (公職人員選舉罷免法).
The law prohibits operating gambling for profit based on the outcome of an election or recall.
Coinbase and Kalshi did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The bureau said it requested the restrictions to protect election integrity and prevent “overseas interference,” without giving further details.
Taiwanese authorities have separately warned that money from China could enter the nation through underground financial channels and be used to influence elections.
The government has stepped up scrutiny of illicit financial flows ahead of the Nov. 28 vote, including underground gambling operations.
Authorities have not alleged that Coinbase or Kalshi handled funds from China.
China’s Taiwan Affairs Office did not immediately respond to a request for comment sent outside normal office hours.
Taiwan is among the jurisdictions that criminalize election wagering. Under a 2023 amendment to the election act, bettors can face as long as six months in prison, while gambling operators can receive up to five years.
Authorities have increasingly targeted election wagering on prediction markets. Polymarket, the main rival to Kalshi, has also been blocked in Taiwan.
Cryptocurrencies are often used to place bets on such platforms.
Taiwanese voters are to choose local officials ranging from mayors and city councilors to village chiefs.
The elections would be the first nationwide electoral test for Lai since he took office in 2024 and could offer an early indication of the political landscape ahead of the 2028 presidential election.

Spain’s Poncelet achieves ‘dream’ with speed record
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:43:31 UTC
01:43:31 KST

Spanish downhill skateboarder Diego Poncelet did not just want to set a standing world speed record; he wanted to know what it felt like going 150kph with no brakes.
The two-time world champion finally achieved that goal on Sept. 22 in Canada when he reached a speed of 151.83kph, nine years after Pete Connolly clocked 146.73kph on the same road.
“If a record has stood for nine years, you don’t just break it by a little bit, you destroy it,” Poncelet said in an interview on Wednesday. “If I’m honest with myself, my real objective was 150kph. That was the dream.”
Photo: Reuters
The Red Bull athlete began work on the attempt four years ago, but his search for a road with the required gradient to spur him to record speeds came to nothing.
Finally, Poncelet had to accept that Route 362 in Les Eboulements, two hours northeast of Quebec City, is a “miracle.”
“A lot of people told me it wasn’t possible anymore because of large cracks and potholes,” the 27-year-old said. “There was a real question over whether the road had deteriorated too much.”
On a specially designed 14kg skateboard, in shoes soled with car tire rubber, Poncelet launched himself into the abyss.
“That road in particular was terrifying because you’re doing about 110kph and suddenly the road disappears, you can’t see it. All you can see is the St Lawrence River,” Poncelet said.
Usually when Poncelet plunges downhill, he has two plastic slide pucks attached to gloves he uses to slow himself.
Not this time.
“It was very difficult mentally, because of how steep it is and because of the equipment I was using, I couldn’t brake. Once you start the run, whatever happens, you have to get to the bottom at full speed,” he said. “You can’t brake because at those speeds you would go flying.”
Poncelet, who has a degree in international relations, says it is almost as if he enters a Zen-like state when traveling at such frightening speeds.
“I like to say it’s as if there’s a wise person inside your mind and you let that person take control,” he added. “That wise person is your subconscious. It’s an incredible feeling, everything feels perfect.”
“It’s like high-consequence meditation,” he said with a grin.

Real wage growth in Taiwan hits an 11-year high
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:43:30 UTC
01:43:30 KST

Real wage growth in Taiwan reached an 11-year high in the first eight months of this year as robust exports supported earnings gains and inflation remained relatively moderate, helping improve purchasing power despite wide differences across industries, the Directorate-General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics (DGBAS) said yesterday.
The average regular monthly wage rose 3.28 percent from a year earlier to NT$52,523 in August, while the total monthly wage — including bonuses, overtime pay and other compensation — climbed 6.64 percent to NT$69,520 on average, the agency said.
DGBAS Census Department Deputy Director Tan Wen-ling (譚文玲) attributed the gains to robust export growth, saying employment, regular wages and total earnings had all increased from a year earlier.
Photo: CNA
Overtime hours also continued to rise, she said.
“Wage increases and bonus payments, coupled with moderate inflation and government efforts to stabilize prices, have helped wages outpace consumer prices and support workers’ purchasing power,” Tan said.
However, the gap between average and median wages suggests that typical workers earn considerably less than the overall average.
The median regular monthly wage, a statistic that is less affected by outliers, rose 3.46 percent year-on-year to NT$41,353 in August, notably lower than the average wage of NT$52,523, DGBAS data showed.
Over the first eight months of the year, the median regular monthly wage increased 3.06 percent to NT$39,383, while the average regular monthly wage rose 2.94 percent to NT$49,110 and the total monthly wage increased 4.55 percent to NT$549,200.
After adjusting for inflation, the increase was 1.2 percent for the median regular monthly wage, 1.08 percent for the average regular monthly wage and 2.66 percent for the total monthly wage, which was an 11-year high, the agency said.
Wage growth also varied considerably by industry. Financial and insurance services recorded the strongest increase among major industries in the first eight months, with average regular monthly wages rising 5.85 percent from a year earlier to NT$75,313, the data showed.
Wholesale and retail trade wages increased 3.52 percent to NT$50,414 on average, while manufacturing wages rose 3.47 percent to NT$51,661 on average, it said.
Accommodation and food services recorded the weakest growth, with the average regular monthly wage rising just 0.4 percent to NT$38,871, underscoring the uneven distribution of wage gains across industries, the data showed.
Average working hours totaled 172.9 in August, up 0.5 hours from a year earlier, while average overtime hours increased by 0.1 hours to 8.9, reflecting sustained demand for labor amid strong demand for artificial intelligence hardware, the DGBAS said.

‘Democratic Taiwan’ badges sell out, more to come
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:43:29 UTC
01:43:29 KST

“Democratic Taiwan” souvenir badges created by the National Cultural Association of Taiwan for the Double Ten National Day holiday have sold out, with more to go on sale in December.
The 11 badges would be available along with additional new designs on UN Human Rights Day on Dec. 10, the association said on Monday.
The badges, designed by Chiu Hsi-min (邱璽民) and a group of young designers on the invitation of the association, were created for the Presidential Office Building’s National Day projection mapping show this year, echoing the show’s theme of “Democratic Taiwan, the Heartbeat of the World.”
Photo: CNA
While this year marks the 30th anniversary of Taiwan’s direct presidential election, the 11 badge designs all revolve around important democracy movements in the nation’s history.
For example, the 228 Incident badge commemorates the shooting of protesters by security personnel at the at the Governor-General’s Office in Taipei (currently the Executive Yuan building) on Feb. 28, 1947, while the Formosa Incident” badge reminds Taiwanese of the pursuit of democracy under ruthless authoritarian rule.
Other designs were inspired by critical historical events marking democratic shifts, including the lifting of martial law in 1987, the abolition of article 100 of the Criminal Code in 1992 and Taiwan’s first direct presidential election in 1996.
Photo: Liu Hsin-de, Taipei Times
Article 100 of the Criminal Code was used as justification to penalize people for “intending” to commit a crime of sedition, and was a primary legal tool of repression during the Martial Law era.
Pro-democracy student movements were also included, such as the Wild Lily movement in 1990, the Wild Strawberries movement in 2008 and the Sunflower movement in 2014.
One of the designs features the 228 Hand-in-Hand rally held on Feb. 28, 2004 — a large-scale demonstration against Chinese military threats famous for its 500km-long hand-in-hand human chain.
The designers said that it was a wonderful journey creating the badges.
They revisited the commonly known historical events and gained a new understanding of the past, which prompted them to rethink the Taiwanese values of today, they said.
Visiting the history of Taiwan through the badges was like taking a make-up class on the nation’s democratization journey, the designers said.
The association on Oct. 2 launched a capsule vending machine containing the badges at the South Taipei Space No. 1 exhibition room in its building.
The machine sold out of badges on launch day.
Two capsule vending machines featuring the badges were also set up near the Presidential Office Building alongside the projection mapping show, which ran from Oct. 7 to Saturday last week.
The two machines’ badges were offered in limited volume capped at a collective total of 250 badges per day, with each person allowed to draw two capsules each time.
People waited in line from as early as 5pm and waited for the machines to open at 6pm.
The line ran from Ketagalan Boulevard down Guiyang Street.
The association said the badges were manufactured by local Taiwanese companies, adding that the 11 badges would be available again on UN Human Rights Day and new designs would also be introduced.

Political unrest surges in S Africa as elections loom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:43:27 UTC
01:43:27 KST

Gunmen in August opened fire on local government candidate Khethelo Mdluli outside his rural home as he was with his young children, one incident amid a surge of suspected political assassinations ahead of South Africa’s polls next month.
The 40-year-old died in hospital at the end of August, with his family telling reporters they did not know why he was targeted.
“My brother was not a violent man,” said Sifiso Mdluli, a representative of the family.
Photo: AFP
Mdluli was running as a ward councilor for the veteran Inkatha Freedom Party (IFP) in the Nov. 4 local elections, seen as a test of support for the African National Congress (ANC) after it lost its national parliamentary majority in 2024.
“One of his IFP colleagues, who was speaking at the funeral, said he had alerted them that there were people threatening him in the days leading to his murder,” his brother said.
The day after Mdluli died, another IFP ward council candidate was gunned down after arriving home in the same province, the politically volatile KwaZulu-Natal.
“He was a good man. We are scared,” said a relative of 34-year-old Lucky Sokhela who declined to be identified for fear of reprisals.
The party called a special Political Killings Task Team (PKTT), established in 2018, to investigate.
“The killing of political candidates cannot be treated as ordinary criminality,” it said. “Let the ballot, not the bullet, decide.”
In a new killing this week also referred to the PKTT, four members of the ANC youth division died after a gunman opened fire on them on Tuesday outside Johannesburg.
The motive was unknown and the attacker had turned himself in, police said.
At least 43 people were killed in 45 suspected political attacks in the first nine months of this year, according to the Geneva, Switzerland-based Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC).
The tally topped the full-year total of 30 for 2021, the year of the previous municipal elections, and 33 in 2024, when the most recent national election was held, the independent civil society group said in a report.
The targets included ward councilors, party officials or traditional leaders — figures with influence over local issues such as the allocation of houses and contracts.
“The focus shifted from ideological divides to contestation over access to resources,” said researcher Crispin Hemson, who documented KwaZulu-Natal’s bloody political wars in the final years of apartheid.
“The market for killing, the networks, the guns, they were already there. Now the ideology is gone and the motive is a tender, a ward, a job,” Hemson told reporters.
The trial of two men sentenced to life imprisonment last month for the 2023 murder of KwaZulu-Natal Democratic Alliance councilor Nhlalayenza Ndlovu heard that the hit was ordered by a traditional chief over disputed land sales and electricity connections.
A ward councilor’s job comes with a salary of more than 25,000 rand (US$1,500) a month before allowances, according to government figures.
The official national unemployment rate is 33 percent and the minimum wage is nearly 6,000 rand.
“The struggle for employment is such that many people see being a councilor as escaping poverty,” said Zakhele Ndlovu, a political analyst and lecturer at the University of KwaZulu-Natal. “Hence there is such competition for councilor posts, with others prepared to kill or be killed in pursuance of this position.”
Most of the attacks (16) recorded by GI-TOC to the end of last month were in KwaZulu-Natal, but there were also 10 in Gauteng, where Johannesburg is.
Of several political movements affected, most of those killed (13) were from the ANC, followed by eight from former South African president Jacob Zuma’s uMkhonto weSizwe Party (MKP), based in KwaZulu-Natal.
“Quite a few of these killings speak to the criminalization of politics, particularly at a local government level, where it’s about contestation for access to power and the money that comes with it,” said Julian Rademeyerthe, author of the GI-TOC report Ballots and bullets.
There is an “intersection between politics and organized crime” that “damages the constitutional democracy that South Africa is,” GI-TOC executive director Mark Shaw told a public hearing last month.

Sunak invokes Lee Kuan Yew’s ‘poisonous shrimp’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:43:26 UTC
01:43:26 KST

Former British prime minister Rishi Sunak on Wednesday urged so-called middle powers to become a “poisonous shrimp” to carve out strategic economic leverage in a more turbulent global environment.
Sunak drew from a metaphor by former Singaporean prime minister Lee Kuan Yew (李光耀): A big fish will eat a smaller fish, and the smaller fish will eat the shrimp.
Lee made the point a year after the Asian nation’s independence in 1966 that the city-state needed to build up its defense mechanisms — like a shrimp that stings — so it would be left alone by predators.
Photo: Bloomberg
“He was thinking about what Singapore’s path [was] going to be in that world, and it was: We have to make ourselves a poisonous shrimp,” Sunak said in a panel discussion at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum in New Delhi.
Middle powers “can’t operate at the scale of the big ones. What they can do is make themselves indispensable,” he said.
The approach reflects a more transactional view of economic security, where access to essential technologies can help smaller nations preserve their autonomy and secure a place in negotiations with larger powers, he said.
As competition between major economies reshapes global supply chains, Sunak’s message was that survival for middle powers might depend on becoming a “choke point” that other countries cannot do without.
The strategy does not require dominating an entire industry, but controlling a critical part of it, he said.
“That is how you make sure you have a seat at the table that you can’t be eaten like the little shrimp,” he said. “You bring something to the table that everyone else needs and wants — you don’t have to provide the whole buffet.”
The competitive mindset persisted after Lee’s death in 2015.
In an interview in the Indian capital, Singaporean Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong (顏金勇) said that the island nation must work faster and harder as it competes with other global wealth hubs.
“We have always been competing with financial centers around the world, in Hong Kong, Dubai, London or New York,” Gan told Bloomberg TV’s Haslinda Amin. “We can move fast and that is our strength.”
Back on Sunak’s panel, which included foreign ministers from Canada and India, former Australian prime minister Kevin Rudd repeatedly returned to the idea first introduced by Lee.
“I’m still struggling with the concept of poisonous shrimp,” Rudd said, drawing laughter from the audience.

The Legislative Yuan in August passed the Act for Strengthening Defense Autonomy and Unmanned Vehicle Industry Development (強化國防自主暨無人載具產業發展條例) after heated debate over how to balance national defense procurement with industrial development, Chiang told the Chinese-language Liberty Times (sister paper of the Taipei Times).

Photo: Chang Chia-jui, Taipei Times

The compromise includes a NT$240 billion (US$7.4 billion) budget over six years, and mandates that domestic production rates reach 50 percent within two years and 80 percent within four years, he said, adding that all party caucuses would support the budget as long as it benefits industrial development.
Taichung is well positioned to develop uncrewed vehicles and robots because of its strong manufacturing base, Chiang said.

Proper use of the funding under the act would benefit Taichung’s industries, Chiang said.
Turning to politics, Chiang said next month’s local elections would serve as a warm-up for those seeking the presidency or legislative seats in 2028.
Winning this year would not guarantee victory in 2028, as the elections would be fought on different political terrain and voters’ views could change with events and government performance, he said.

President William Lai (賴清德) yesterday called for US memory maker Micron Technology Inc and its workers to negotiate “sincerely” ahead of a possible strike by the company’s union in Taiwan.
Last week, a Taiwanese union representing workers at Micron said it had secured authorization from its members to strike over a dispute concerning the company’s bonus scheme, escalating a labor conflict at the chipmaker’s largest manufacturing hub.
Micron employs about 15,000 people in Taiwan and has said it invested more than NT$1.6 trillion (US$49.6 billion) in the country.
Photo: Ann Wang, Reuters
Speaking in Taichung at the opening of a new Micron advanced assembly and testing facility, Lai said he hoped the government and the private sector could work together to promote better communication between labor and management.
“We also hope both labor and management will uphold the spirit that fish need water and water needs fish, continuing to negotiate sincerely and in good faith to build the broadest possible consensus,” he added.
“Only by creating harmonious labor relations can both sides win, allowing employees to work with peace of mind and businesses to move steadily and go further,” he said.
Lai said he appreciated Micron’s commitment to Taiwan and hoped it would continue investing in the country, adding that Micron had secured government support for high-bandwidth memory (HBM) research and development.
Taiwan is a crucial production hub for Micron’s DRAM and HBM chips, which are used in artificial intelligence servers.
“Micron values its team members and remains committed to listening to their perspectives and engaging with them constructively,” the company said in a statement, when asked about Lai’s remarks.
Micron’s Taichung union said that it looked forward to the company engaging in “more substantive dialogue and negotiations” with them.
Micron president and chief operating officer Manish Bhatia made no mention of a possible strike action in his comments delivered shortly before Lai’s.
“We have already sold out all the capacity for 2027 that this factory will build and we expect high-bandwidth memory to grow faster than the rest of the DRAM industry all the way through 2028,” he said.
Last week, the two unions representing workers at Micron’s Taoyuan and Taichung operations said they hoped the company would put forward a concrete profit-sharing proposal for employees.
Mediation with the Taoyuan union ended without agreement last month, while the Taichung union remains in negotiations.
The unions are encouraging members to take a day off on Monday to join a rally in Taipei, which they said would not be a strike.

Smartphone shipments crash 22% in worst quarter ever, research group says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:43:24 UTC
01:43:24 KST

The smartphone market suffered its worst decline on record in the third quarter, after rising memory costs pushed global shipments down 22 percent year-on-year to 255.3 million units with worse to come, market researcher International Data Corp (IDC) said in a report released on Wednesday.
The higher cost of storage over the past year, led by demand from artificial intelligence industry orders, has hurt profitability across the mobile sector and forced companies to raise prices, cut back specifications and discard budget-focused models, IDC said.
Chinese brands like Xiaomi Corp (小米) and Oppo Mobile Telecommunications Corp (歐珀) took the worst hit among the top names, while Apple Inc and Samsung Electronics Co fared better due to their larger premium handset portfolios, the preliminary data from IDC’s Worldwide Quarterly Mobile Phone Tracker showed.
Photo: AP
Device manufacturers are increasingly recognizing that they are facing a permanent structural shift and IDC expects market growth to be constrained through next year and any recovery in growth would not come until 2028 at the earliest, the report said.
As companies increase prices and push consumers toward flagship or high-end models, the long-term trend is seen translating into greater share of a smaller market for Apple and other vendors with large-scale distribution and a premium mix of products, it said.
“Current indicators suggest that the market has not yet reached the bottom,” IDC research director Nabila Popal said. “Memory costs have surged approximately 350 percent since last year and are still rising, creating substantial pressure on vendor margins and shipments. The worst is yet to come.”
