Don’t Call It a Reset: The Modi-Xi Meeting Wasn’t a Turning Point
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
15:42:00 UTC
00:42:00 KST

Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to New Delhi last month for the BRICS summit prompted speculation that India and China are moving toward a reset. Some see an opening for rapprochement, while others attribute the renewed engagement to deteriorating India-U.S. relations. Both interpretations overstate the shift in bilateral ties. Xi’s visit was important, but it did not mark a turning point.
Xi came to New Delhi for the BRICS summit in September, which also gave him an opportunity to meet Prime Minister Narendra Modi. India and China’s participation in BRICS and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) should not be mistaken for an alignment of interests. India’s engagement within multilateral organizations is a longstanding feature of its foreign policy, and China has not been a decisive factor in that approach.
Since the 2020 Galwan clashes, India has sought to stabilize ties and manage differences with China. These efforts have gained momentum amid U.S President Donald Trump’s increasingly hostile policies toward India and much of Asia. Yet the reasons for renewed engagement with Beijing go beyond the state of India-U.S. relations.
The resumption of high-level dialogue, leadership meetings, and direct connectivity are important developments. Another Galwan-like border confrontation would carry heavy domestic costs and could be difficult to recover from. Preventing a recurrence of such violence is a priority. But this does not require India to reconsider its position on the underlying differences.
It is also important to note that India never abandoned dialogue with China after Galwan. Keeping communication channel open has remained part of its approach, even as tensions persisted along the border. The latest meetings continue that policy; they do not demonstrate that the relationship or India’s approach to it has fundamentally changed.
The border remains the principal obstacle. China’s recent statement that it does not recognize the Union Territory of Ladakh underlined the depth of the disagreement. There is little basis for expecting a reset while the two sides remain so far apart on territorial issues. Nor is the border the only source of friction. China’s relationship with Pakistan and the persistent trade imbalance remain contentious issues, too. There is little evidence of progress on any of these fundamental differences.
The separate readouts issued after the Modi-Xi meeting offered further evidence of the distance between them. There was no joint statement. The Chinese readout included a reference to Tibet and Taiwan that was absent from the Indian account. Beijing described India as a partner, but the Indian readout did not use the same language. The differences in wording hardly suggest a shared political understanding.
Deteriorating India-U.S. relations and uncertainty over Washington’s commitment to Indo-Pacific security have shaped the circumstances in which New Delhi engages Beijing. But it would be a mistake to explain India’s China policy primarily through its relationship with the United States. India has its own reasons to avoid another border crisis, and its willingness to maintain dialogue with China predates the current difficulties with Washington.
The suggestion that worsening ties with the U.S. have left India isolated, or made the Indo-Pacific less relevant, also overlooks the agency of regional countries. Their security concerns remain, regardless of changes in Washington’s priorities. The U.S. remains important to collective regional security, but uncertainty over its commitments does not remove the need for cooperation among countries in the region. The more immediate concern for Washington is the effect of its policies on its credibility among regional allies and partners. If confidence in the U.S. weakens, the consequences could extend across the Indo-Pacific.
India’s security interests do not begin and end with its relationship with the U.S. Even as ties with Washington come under strain, New Delhi must contend with its own regional challenges. This does not mean India and China will draw closer. New Delhi can manage relations with Beijing while reassessing its ties with Washington; neither relationship necessarily dictates the other. Efforts to manage differences with China are consistent with India’s longstanding approach of preserving options without compromising its security concerns.
China-India relations are still short of their pre-2020 status quo. Security cooperation is limited, and military exercises such as Hand-in-Hand remain suspended. The trust needed for closer cooperation has yet to be restored, and the prospects seem far-fetched for now.
For India, the unresolved border dispute remains a central security concern. The Galwan clashes changed India’s view of and threat perception from China and raised serious questions about the viability of the existing arrangements in ensuring peace along the Line of Actual Control (LAC). High-level meetings can help manage tensions for the time being, but they cannot substitute for progress on the ground. India is also unlikely to return to its previous position on the One China policy without some reference to, or assurance regarding, a corresponding One India policy from Beijing. Such an assurance appears unlikely in the foreseeable future.
Just a couple of years ago, a meeting between Xi and Modi on Indian soil seemed difficult to imagine. That is one of the reasons why their meeting drew so much attention. But it has not changed the scope or nature of the issues dividing the two countries. For now, both sides are trying to prevent another crisis while their core disagreements remain unresolved. Until those differences are addressed, dialogue may keep the relationship from deteriorating further, but it will not put China-India ties on the path to a reset.

Venice Biennale Sessions event puts Arab artists in focus
Unknown

Breadcrumb
Venice Biennale Sessions event puts Arab artists in focus
At an event held in Venice that explored Arab artistic expression, cultural identity and solidarity with Palestine, the growing influence of Arab artists and curators on the global contemporary art scene took centre stage.
Around 100 students, researchers, academics and art enthusiasts gathered in Venice on 10 October for Rewriting Contemporary Art: Shifting Paradigms through Arab Artistic and Curatorial Practices, an initiative aimed at highlighting the expanding role of Arab artists and curators within the Biennale and the wider international art world.
Organised by curator and journalist Alba Nabulsi in collaboration with Ca’ Foscari University, the event formed part of the Biennale Sessions programme, which seeks to engage students and universities with contemporary art.
The initiative, supported by The New Arab and its Arabic-language edition Al-Araby Al-Jadeed, also involved the University of Padua, Iscte University Institute of Lisbon and Cosmos Lab at the Scuola Normale Superiore.
Growing Arab presence at the Venice Biennale
The programme began with a guided tour of Arab national pavilions at the Giardini, offering participants an opportunity to explore how artists from the region are challenging established narratives and bringing new perspectives to contemporary art.
Among the highlights was Qatar's debut pavilion, the first new national pavilion space to be introduced at the Giardini in more than three decades.
Titled Untitled 2026 (a gathering of remarkable people), the pavilion brings together music, film and food in a multidisciplinary programme celebrating artistic exchange.
Participants met members of the pavilion's team and discussed the project with its public relations adviser, Dr Laura Alfieri.
The group also visited Egypt's pavilion, one of the oldest national presences at the Giardini, where artist Armen Agop presented Silence Pavilion: Between the Intangible and the Tangible, an exhibition inviting visitors to reflect on time, stillness and human presence.
The tour continued at the Arsenale, where participants explored a selection of Arab national pavilions showcasing the region's diverse artistic traditions and cultural heritage.
Saudi Arabia's presentation drew on ancestral knowledge rooted in Islamic and Arab art, seeking to connect historical traditions with contemporary expression.
Morocco's pavilion focused on ritual weaving, while Oman's explored the country's tradition of crafting silver ornaments for horses.
The programme also highlighted the growing visibility of artists with Arab roots beyond the region, including Khaled Sabsabi and Yto Barrada, whose work featured in the Australian and French pavilions respectively.
Across the international exhibition, participants encountered expressions of solidarity with Palestine, reflecting the role of art in engaging with political struggles and questions of identity.
Art, resistance and the legacy of Koyo Kouoh
The afternoon programme shifted to discussions at the Arsenale, where curators and academics examined the changing place of Arab artistic practices within international institutions.
A central focus was the legacy of the late Biennale curator Koyo Kouoh and her exhibition In Minor Keys, which encouraged audiences to approach art through empathy, spirituality and postcolonial perspectives.
Rasha Salti, an adviser to the Biennale Arte curator, opened the first panel by reflecting on Kouoh's influence and her own experience as an Arab cultural practitioner.
Tom Eccles, co-curator of Qatar's pavilion, discussed the ideas behind its presentation, describing the exhibition as a symbol of resilience amid the wars affecting the Middle East.
The relationship between art and political resistance also featured prominently.
Marco Baravalle, founder and curator of S.a.L.E. Docks, discussed his involvement with the Art Not Genocide Alliance and the grassroots process behind People's Liberation, an exhibition by Indonesian art collective Taring Padi.
Dr Bishara Ebeid of Ca’ Foscari University explored the importance of contemporary art in education, highlighting how artistic expression can help students engage with language, culture and evolving ideas.
Curator Hesperia Iliadou also discussed her work on Aghrab Idrāk: Thresholds of Perception, an exhibition by Virginia Commonwealth University School of the Arts in Qatar presented as a collateral event at the Biennale.
She reflected on her curatorial relationship with the Mediterranean and Arab region, and the importance of cultural exchange in shaping contemporary artistic practices.
Amplifying Arab voices through literature, media and music
A second panel broadened the discussion beyond visual art to examine how literature, journalism and music can contribute to the visibility of Arab cultural expression.
Algerian literary author Amal Bouchareb reflected on the responsibilities and challenges facing Arab writers, while Ibrahim Fakhri, creative manager at The New Arab and an artist, explored the role of media and artistic production in amplifying Arab voices.
Fakhri also addressed the challenges of producing art amid political conflict and the importance of creating spaces where artists from the region can tell their own stories.
The event concluded with two musical performances connecting Arab artistic heritage with contemporary experimentation.
Accordionist Margherita Berlanda performed TSLALIM by composer Samir Odeh-Tamimi, bringing together Western instrumental traditions and Arab musical influences.
Italian musician Toni Cutrone, performing under the name MaiMaiMai, presented music from his latest record, Karakoz, which was recorded in Bethlehem during Israel's war on Gaza.
The performances were accompanied by discussions with the musicians about the cultural and personal meanings behind their work.

Iran, Turkey, Kuwait, Pakistan, PA leave Baku conference when Herzog spoke, but Qatari Emir stayed

Representatives from Iran, Turkey, Kuwait, Pakistan, and the Palestinian Authority walked out of President Isaac Herzog's Thursday speech at the Conference on Interaction and Confidence-Building Measures in Asia (CICA) in Baku, Azerbaijan.
At the same time, questions arose about the reported behavior of the Qatari delegation. The Iranian newspaper Tehran Times claimed the Qatari delegation also exited the hall, while eyewitnesses at the conference said the Emir of Qatar, Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, remained in his seat and listened to Herzog's remarks.
The summit was attended by senior representatives from Asian and Middle Eastern nations, including countries that do not maintain diplomatic relations with Israel.
Turkey was represented by Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, the Palestinian Authority by its foreign minister, Kuwait by its deputy foreign minister, Iran by its deputy minister for legal and International affairs, and Pakistan by its ambassador to Azerbaijan.
Representatives from Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates remained in the hall. The decision of the Emir of Qatar to remain seated drew particular attention due to the absence of formal diplomatic ties between Doha and Jerusalem, as well as Qatar's role in mediating sensitive regional issues.
Discrepancy between Iranian media, eyewitness accounts
The discrepancy between the Iranian media report and eyewitness accounts raises questions regarding Iran's motivation in framing Qatar's actions toward Israel.
The original text of the Iranian report has not been independently verified, and it remains unclear whether it referred to the Emir himself or to other delegation members. Other members of the Qatari delegation may have left while the Emir stayed. As of now, no official statement has been issued by Qatar to reconcile the contrasting accounts.
Dr. Ariel Admoni of Ariel University, Bar-Ilan University, and the Jerusalem Institute for Strategy and Security noted that the Iranian newspaper's framing reflects the delicate relationship between Doha and Tehran.
Within this framework, Iran relies on Qatari mediation and thus seeks to portray Qatar as taking a more anti-Israel stance than its actual policy dictates, enabling Iran to maintain public relations with Doha.
From Tehran's perspective, Qatar is a crucial regional partner, largely because it can engage with actors with whom Iran cannot maintain direct contact. Portraying Doha as taking a firm public stance against Israel helps the Iranian regime justify its ongoing ties with Qatar to both the Iranian public and anti-Israel factions.
This analysis serves as an explanatory interpretation of a potential narrative motive and does not constitute proof that the report was directly dictated by authorities in Tehran.
Qatar maintains close ties with Tehran, mediates with Washington
Qatar maintains close ties with Tehran, keeps open communication channels with the United States and Western governments, and plays a mediating role between opposing sides. The Qatari Emir refrained from joining the public protest against Herzog's speech.
The summit brought together representatives of nations engaged in severe political conflict. According to the seating chart, Herzog and the Iranian representative sat on the same side of the conference table, separated by four seats, including those of the foreign ministers of Turkey and Bahrain. The Emir of Qatar was seated on the other side of the host President, Ilham Aliyev.
During his diplomatic visit to Azerbaijan, Herzog met with President Ilham Aliyev to discuss strengthening strategic relations and regional stability. Herzog also met with Bahraini Foreign Minister Abdullatif bin Rashid al-Zayani to discuss expanding regional cooperation and the Abraham Accords.
Azerbaijan maintains close relations with Israel while also preserving diplomatic ties with Turkey and Iran.
The visit also drew attention in Turkey after it emerged that Herzog arrived in Baku aboard a flight operated by Azerbaijan's national carrier, AZAL, which flew through Turkish airspace despite restrictions on Israeli government aircraft. A Turkish official stated that Ankara was not informed that the Herzog was aboard the aircraft.
Herzog departed Israel on Wednesday via a commercial Boeing 787 flight operated by AZAL. Overflight through Turkish airspace was permitted under standard commercial flight regulations, which differ from the restrictions applied to Israeli state aircraft.
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan did not attend the summit; his country was represented by Foreign Minister Fidan, whose delegation was among those that walked out prior to Herzog's address.

More than half of Palestinians support a two-state agreement with east Jerusalem serving as the capital of a Palestinian state, according to a new poll published on Wednesday by the Ramallah-based Palestinian Center for Policy and Survey Research think tank.
Though 53% overall support two states, with 56% endorsing consultative talks with Israeli figures they deemed “anti-occupation,” only 48% of Gazan respondents said they would agree with the establishment of a Palestinian state alongside a Jewish one.
The survey collected data from 909 Palestinians in the West Bank and 488 in the Gaza Strip, living outside Israel-controlled territory, and had a margin of error of 3.5%.
Asked what the current obstacle to Palestinian statehood was, 41% said it was the expansion of Israeli settlements while only 23% said it was internal Palestinian divisions.
The Palestinian think tank attributed the increase in support for armed resistance among Gaza residents to ongoing Israeli strikes in the Gaza Strip. Compared with the August poll, support for armed resistance rose from 21% to 37%, slightly above the overall average of 33% recorded across both Palestinian territories. Diplomacy remained the most popular option, however, with 42% of Palestinians supporting it and a further 18% supporting popular nonviolent resistance as the most effective path toward establishing a Palestinian state.
Neither Hamas nor Israel won the war, say 62% of Palestinians
Despite the increase in support for armed “resistance,” 62% of Palestinians polled said neither Israel nor Hamas had won the war. While 17% said Israel had emerged victorious, only 16% viewed Hamas as the winner. Still, around three-quarters of Palestinians overall, 69% in the Gaza Strip and 78% in the West Bank, felt Israel should withdraw from the Gaza Strip before Hamas disarms.
Most Palestinians were also pessimistic about the ceasefire’s prospects, with 61% expecting insecurity to continue. Only 42% said they trusted the technocratic committee to govern Gaza. Trust in the committee was significantly higher among Palestinians in Gaza than among those in the West Bank, at 60% and 29%, respectively.
In terms of party affiliation, only 19% of Palestinians identified with Hamas, down from 24% in August and 35% ten months earlier. Less than a quarter (22%) said they supported Fatah, but a commanding 33% identified with none of the listed parties.
Additionally, while the August poll found a three-way race for leadership between Marwan Barghouti, Hamas leader Khalil al-Hayya, and Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas, the latest poll suggests growing support for independent figures. Only 34% said they would support Barghouti’s leadership, while 13% backed Palestinian businessman Bashar Masri nationwide, rising to 21% among respondents in Gaza. Mustafa Barghouti received 12% support.
PA elections pushed back to next September
There is also still a strong desire for the Palestinian Authority to move ahead with the elections in November, which Abbas has pushed back to September next year. More than half, 53%, support holding elections on schedule on November 28 without delay, and an additional 21% favor a short operational postponement of under six months to ensure administrative inclusivity, while 20% oppose holding elections altogether.
Overall voter turnout intention was found to be around 55% among eligible voters, though only 31% of young citizens aged 18–22 report being registered on the voter rolls, and their overall voting intention lags at just 46%.
There is also significant willingness to vote for a newly formed candidate list, around 56%, and when testing nine candidate lists among likely voters who have finalized their choices, the National Independent List led by Bashar Masri tied for first place with the list backed by imprisoned leader Marwan Barghouti, each securing 22% of the vote.
Both the independent figure and imprisoned Fatah leader hold more support than the joint
Hamas-Dahlan List, which only received 20% support, and the official Fatah list led by Palestinian Vice-President Hussein al-Sheikh and backed by President Abbas (13%), and the National Initiative led by Mustafa Barghouti (13%).
According to the survey, Masri’s appeal was closely linked to confidence in his ability to manage Gaza’s economic recovery and improve the cost of living, with 30% saying they trusted him to do so. Mustafa Barghouti received a similar level of trust, at 29%. Confidence in senior Palestinian Authority figures was considerably lower, with only 6% trusting Hussein al-Sheikh and 8% trusting Jibril Rajoub to manage these challenges.

Scotland to match funding for two defence skills colleges
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:37:59 BST
00:37:59 KST

The Scottish Government has confirmed it will match the £10 million offered by the Ministry of Defence to establish two Defence Technical Excellence Colleges in Scotland.
Alyn Smith, the Innovation Minister, has written jointly with Economy Secretary Stephen Flynn to Luke Pollard, the Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, and to Douglas Alexander, the Secretary of State for Scotland, confirming that Edinburgh will put up the money needed to unlock the UK Government contribution. We understand that plans are underway to allocate sites in the east and west of the country, supporting skills for careers in defence engineering, advanced manufacturing and maritime technology.
Smith said: “Scotland is well placed to seize the opportunities arising out of the defence industry, with a highly skilled workforce, world-class colleges and universities and internationally recognised manufacturing. DTECs will allow workers to upskill and connect the next generation to opportunities in sectors where demand for a highly-skilled workforce is rising rapidly.
“I am pleased to confirm we will partner with the UK Government to develop plans for DTECs in Scotland and build on the £3.7 billion to Scotland’s economy provided by the defence sector.
“Our Programme for Government committed to establishing a responsible defence industrial growth programme to maximise the economic opportunities arising from increased defence spending. We will work with partners to ensure our workers are equipped with the right skills for emerging jobs in this vital sector.”
A consultation will now be held to work out which colleges can achieve DTEC status and how the scheme is implemented.
The offer being accepted dates back to 12 March, when the Ministry of Defence set out plans for two colleges aligned to the defence clusters in the east and west of Scotland, developed with Colleges Scotland. The £10 million came from the £20 million allocated to Scotland out of the £182 million Defence Industry Skills Package, and it was contingent from the outset on Edinburgh providing match funding.
Scotland’s defence industry contributes around £3.7 billion a year to the economy, and its geography accounts for the east and west split. The west has BAE Systems at Govan and Scotstoun building the Type 26 frigates, Thales at Govan, and the submarine base at Faslane with its associated armaments depot at Coulport. The east has Babcock at Rosyth assembling the Type 31 frigates, Leonardo in Edinburgh producing radar and electronic warfare equipment, and Raytheon at Glenrothes. All of them compete for the same pool of welders, electrical technicians, systems engineers and naval architects, and all of them have warned about the pipeline.
Defence Technical Excellence Colleges were created under the Defence Industrial Strategy to put defence-specific training into the further education system, so that employers draw on a shared pipeline instead of each running its own apprenticeship scheme in isolation. Colleges carrying the designation in England include Telford College, close to the Rheinmetall BAE Systems Land plant, Rotherham College and Furness College, next to the submarine yard at Barrow.

Economists: Hot PPI shows Fed's work is not done
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
15:37:59 UTC
00:37:59 KST

Wall Street estimates for the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation indicator now expect an acceleration from the level that prompted the central bank to hike rates last month.
The estimates come after a hotter-than-expected producer price index came in at 1.3% Thursday, the biggest monthly gain since March 2022 and more than double the 0.6% consensus.
That drove the year-over-year increase to 6.3%, the biggest jump since December 2022. The increase was paced by a 20% rise in gasoline prices. But taking out food, energy and trade services, prices still rose a healthy 0.5%, indicating that inflation was broader than just energy.
Seven Wall Street estimates gathered by CNBC show core personal consumption expenditures inflation for September, which will be published later this month, is forecast to rise 0.32%, up from 0.25% in August. Wall Street economists use the consumer price index, released Wednesday, and the PPI to estimate the PCE.
"We see real risks the Fed will deliver another rate hike in two weeks' time even as recent Fedspeak tempered expectations for back-to-back increases,'' wrote Kathy Bostjancic, chief economist at Nationwide.
Several Fed officials have argued that the Fed does not need to hurry to hike rates, though they have suggested more rate hikes are needed. As a result, Fed futures on Thursday showed just a 29% probability of a hike at the Fed meeting at the end of this month, but a 91% probability of at least one hike by December.
A 0.32% increase in PCE would boost the year-over-year core inflation rate to 3.1%, up from 3.01% in August. Estimates ranged from a high of 0.35% from Barclays to a low of 0.29% from Oxford Economics.
"The picture is not benign with inflation elevated and intensifying," wrote Alex Pelle, senior U.S. economist at Mizuho Securities. "On the economic data alone, there is little reason for the Fed to hesitate to continue moving the policy rate higher."
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh has suggested one litmus test for not hiking is confidence that inflation will return in a timely manner to the Fed's 2% target. Both headline and core PCE inflation have been above target since 2021. They have inched steadily higher since tariffs were introduced in April 2025. The gains have accelerated since the beginning of the Iran war.
The Fed prefers the PCE because, compared to the CPI, it believes it more closely resembles how Americans actually spend their money and changes its weightings when consumers change their spending patterns.

Wikipedia left biased edits on Israel, Hamas, and Zionism pages intact despite bans, ADL finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
15:37:33 UTC
00:37:33 KST

Uncorrected past biased edits remain embedded across Wikipedia’s most-read pages concerning Israel, Zionism, Hamas, and Jewish history, according to a follow-up report published by the Anti-Defamation League (ADL) Center for Technology and Society on Thursday.
The report, titled “Damage Done: Wikipedia Leaves Biased Edits Unchecked Despite Editor Bans,” follows an initial investigation released in March 2025 titled “Editing for Hate,” which documented a coordinated campaign by approximately 30 bad-faith editors to manipulate entries related to Israel, Jewish history, and the Israel-Palestinian conflict.
Following the release of that initial investigation, the findings became the subject of extensive external pressure, including a US House Committee on Oversight investigation, a bipartisan congressional letter signed by 23 members, and federal inquiries from the Justice Department and the Senate Commerce Committee, alongside widespread media reporting and scrutiny from Wikipedia’s own neutral-point-of-view editors.
To understand how editor behavior and article content have changed since their previous investigation, researchers analyzed platform activity using five separate data collections gathered between July and August this year. These methods included tracking whether edits made by banned users remained live on major pages, comparing editing volumes before and after the 2025 report, and reviewing thousands of revisions and discussion logs across conflict-related entries.
As part of this methodological analysis, the ADL examined public platform communication records and collaboration patterns on Wikipedia.
Following the intense external scrutiny, visible coordination metrics among the bad-faith editors dropped sharply. Public user-talk page messaging between group members fell 95.41%, from 501 to 23, and same-page tandem editing dropped 87.91%, from 6,218 to 752. Total combined edits across the group decreased by 26.65%, from 182,440 to 133,817.
Wikipedia retains 91% of banned editor's changes to key Israel-related articles
According to the report, although Wikipedia’s Arbitration Committee topic-banned six editors and site-banned three, none of their work was systematically reviewed or corrected.
On six flagship articles, including Hamas, Gaza war, Zionism, and October 7 attacks, 91% of past edits made by Iskandar323, an editor identified in the original 2025 report and subsequently site-banned for violating platform rules in the topic area, remain intact in the live text.
A review conducted in July identified 19 active accounts shaping conflict-related pages, consisting of eight unsanctioned members from the original cohort and 11 newly identified editors.
These accounts employ subtler techniques, such as gatekeeping through frequent reverts to undo neutral updates, hedging factual claims with qualifiers to turn documented facts into contested opinions, and gradually rewriting or restructuring page sections over time, so that no single edit draws administrator attention.
When looking at how these active accounts influence the current content, researchers tracked who made the most recent change across these Wikipedia pages. Out of 229 articles touched by these accounts, newly identified editors hold the final and current version on roughly six-in-10 pages (144 pages out of 229), as well as two-thirds of the pages edited by both the old and new cohorts (95 out of 142).
Furthermore, editors flagged in the report heavily rewrote and managed the content on October 7 sexual violence, accounting for 832 out of 9,576 total revisions, roughly one out of every 11 edits, across those specific articles and their accompanying discussion boards, where disputed wording is actively negotiated.
The report detailed several notable examples of enduring distortion.
Three days after the October 7, 2023, attacks, on October 10, an editor relocated material concerning Hamas’s antisemitism, human shields, child combatants, and human rights abuses into a far less-read page titled Criticism of Hamas. At the time, the main Hamas page was drawing close to one million views per day, meaning readers arriving at the primary entry no longer encountered that critical material unless they navigated to the secondary article. Consequently, the main page’s lead section does not identify Hamas as a designated terrorist organization until its very end.
Wikipedia edits remove details of Hamas atrocities, alter Zionism article
In November 2023, approximately 17,000 characters were removed from the Gaza war article, deleting forensic documentation of victims bound with wire, burned bodies, and attempted decapitations, followed by another cut of roughly 7,400 characters. What remains is a single line stating that terrorists “reportedly engaged” in such violence.
A newly identified account made 543 edits to the Zionism article, adding roughly 193,000 characters and removing approximately 188,000. The resulting lead defines Zionism as achieved “through colonization” and states as fact that Zionists sought a state with “as few Palestinian Arabs as possible.” Wikipedia’s own editors had internally flagged the article as disputed, and it was locked in place after a 12-month administrative moratorium.
Following the February 2025 return of the bodies of Shiri Bibas and her young sons Ariel and Kfir, an unsanctioned original-cohort editor made 64 edits to their article and discussion page, holding the manner of their deaths open, despite Israeli forensic conclusions that they were murdered in captivity.
Daniel Kelley, senior director of the ADL Center for Technology and Society, said, “Even in cases where the Wikipedia community took some modicum of action against editors who went against their policies, the activities of that banned editor remain in this case activity over numerous years driving an ideological narrative in flagrant violation of the neutral point of view policy of the platform.”
“This speaks to a systematic issue with how Wikipedia allows their platform to operate, and it is something they have the responsibility to address,” Kelley added.
ADL calls for Wikipedia reforms over enduring bias, AI concerns
ADL CEO Jonathan Greenblatt said, “Banning individual editors was never going to be enough. The pages that millions of people read, and that AI tools learn from, still bear the marks of a systematic disinformation campaign that Wikipedia itself has sanctioned but never cleaned up.”
Greenblatt further stated, “The most visited online encyclopedia that claims neutrality has to be willing to repair its own record. The Wikimedia Foundation should audit this work, and the companies that build search and AI products should stop presenting contested framing as settled fact.”
Because Wikipedia feeds directly into AI training pipelines, Large Language Model (LLM) outputs, and search engine results, the ADL has renewed calls for structural reforms. These recommendations include private identity verification for editors in contentious topic areas, ending anonymous IP-address editing, establishing a dedicated task force on antisemitic bias, and conducting structured content audits of heavily edited articles.

How Green Party insiders aided the media's Zionism witch hunt
Some years ago, probably around 2014, my student society at Sussex University invited then Green MP Caroline Lucas to speak on campus. I don’t recall much of her talk, but one thing she said has stayed with me.
A student, clearly trolling, asked her if she believed everyone should be vegetarian during the audience question portion of the event. Lucas’s response was refreshingly candid for a politician. Yes, she said, she did believe everyone should be vegetarian, but that did not mean she would ever push to legislate it. Her straightforward answer shut down the joker very quickly. Inspired, I even joined the Green Party for a few years until the bottom fell out of British politics.
Today Lucas cuts an isolated, bitter figure, clearly adrift in a party she no longer recognises after the groundswell under Zack Polanski’s leadership. The straight shooter I remember is gone. Lucas seems perfectly content to get in the muck to drag her party back to irrelevancy.
Party insiders I’ve spoken to say she has been unhappy for months, worried that the party’s pivot toward mass-movement politics was taking away from its focus on the environment. The breaking point was the adoption of the motion Zionism is Racism at the party’s conference in Brighton in early October. The motion defined Zionism as a form of racism to be dealt with accordingly, positioned the party as an explicitly anti-Zionist party, called for the de-proscription of Palestine Action, called for the release of all Palestinian political prisoners, and endorsed a single Palestinian state with equal rights for all.
For critics of the motion, it was a step too far. Many argued that in baiting the opposition, the motion undermined the work for Palestine the party could achieve without the inevitable scrutiny. They worried it would alienate Jewish members and that it wasn’t strategic. Ultimately, the motion passed 1,022 to 813.
Contradictions
Lucas posted her bizarre, contradictory speech from the conference on Twitter late that Sunday. “Is the Israeli government racist? Yes,” she said, after presenting her pro-Palestinian bona fides. “Is Zionism racist? It is both racist AND a response to racism.” She went on to explain that, because of this duality, Zionism is far too complex for such a pointed motion.
It’s a difficult position to triangulate. Yes, this ideology is racist. No, we shouldn’t say so. Yes, the de facto single state is a genocidal settler-colony. No, we shouldn’t challenge its hegemony. There is an obvious asymmetry here to which she even concedes. The inciting racism came at the hands of Europeans; Palestinians simply footed the bill. “Of course that [persecution] doesn’t justify the appalling treatment of the Palestinians. Nothing possibly could.” And yet.
Lucas, the sole Green MP from 2010 to 2024, who failed to get a single other MP elected in either of her leadership stints, went on to chum the water ahead of Polanski’s defeat in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election. Appearing on BBC Newsnight on 8 October, Lucas said, in response to a question about whether Polanski should step down, “I think let’s just see what happens in the coming days and weeks.”
She accused him of showing a lack of leadership the previous Sunday in regard to the Zionism is Racism motion, which she said was dangerous, divisive, and “flawed top to bottom.” She stated the motion “tries to have a singular definition of Zionism when we know that there are many,” parroting a line being pushed by many embarrassed Zionists regarding the motion.
Setting off the witch hunt
The talking point, as far as I understand it, is that Zionism can mean many things to different people, and therefore, cannot be subject to critique. If there could, theoretically, be a strand of Zionism not predicated on the subjugation of Palestinians, then it cannot be considered racist. The problem with this being that the world has seen Zionism in practice for a century, and we know that the ideology — as it exists, manifested in the Israeli state — requires death, dispossession, and racial oppression. To claim it is impolite to point this out because of an imagined alternative is an absurdity.
The following day, with a sliminess usually reserved for the Labour right, Lucas took to Twitter to hedge: “To be clear I’m not calling on Zack to step down. Today he's indicated he shares some of my concerns on the Zionism motion & I welcome that. Now the party needs to come together to make the urgent changes needed to take us forward,” she posted.
By then, the damage was done, and she had served her purpose. The British press took no time to spin a trebling of the vote share in the by-election into a leadership crisis. The 2018 playbook lay annotated and earmarked at hand. Claims of systemic antisemitism and entryism flowed. Green Party representatives were asked ad nauseam whether Zack should step down.
Rumours also swirled that Mothin Ali would make a move. Disgruntled Zionist councillors were given their requisite column inches, and obscure MEPs came out of the woodwork with statements.
Despite the rehashed tactics, Green Party veterans and leadership appeared woefully unprepared. Former leader Natalie Bennet failed to shut down repeated questions from Cathy Newman regarding that old chestnut of Israel’s right to exist. Polanski understandably squirmed as Nick Robinson hounded him with all of the professional integrity we’ve come to expect from the BBC on the subject, asking repeated variations of, “Do you think that the state of Israel, as a safe home for Jews after the Holocaust and after the pogroms, has a right to exist?"
Elsewhere, Jonathan Freedland, the eternal hand-wringer, for whom Israel is always on the cusp of crossing the line but never over it, accused the Greens of trying to “tell Jews how we should think.” He pushed back on the idea that Zionism can be a wholly political ideology, invoking the Kaddish prayer he was to say in remembrance of his father. “The prayer book in my hand will be full of references to Jerusalem and indeed to Zion, expressing in a hundred poetic ways a yearning to return. This is not some new, political thing.”
At the same time, Angela Epstein impugned Polanski’s claim that his family had fled the Holocaust on her Twitter account. “Polanski has repeatedly weaponised his Jewish background, so was the Greens’ useful idiot,” she wrote. “After his by-election defeat, what use will he be to a party riven by antisemitism, when the ‘AsAJew’ defence for their toxic policies doesn’t wash?” Identitarian politics for me and not for thee.
Patrick Spencer, MP for Central Suffolk and North Ipswich, put it more precisely on Twitter over the weekend: “Polanksi is an anti-Semite and a racist”.
Shutting down criticism of Israel
To borrow from Ecclesiastes, there is nothing new under the sun. This is the same pincer movement deployed under the Corbyn era to make all criticism of Israel impossible. The feelings and opinions of Zionist Jews must be endlessly entertained, while those of anti-Zionist Jews are disingenuous ploys. The voices of Palestinians are, naturally, completely absent.
As things reached a fever pitch, reports of plots abounded. Leaked Greens for Palestine chats showed the group considering formal complaints against Lucas, who, in turn, had to deny staging a coup with former party co-leader Adrian Ramsay.
A YouGov voting intention poll released Tuesday finally showed the extent of the damage nationally, with the Greens on 11% (no change). For all the noise, the party's most likely path forward seems to be reforms to its democratic processes to gain central control.
But the mass media hysteria was not without some success. YouGov also announced that 34% of those polled now believe the Green Party has a problem with antisemitism, up from 25% in May. The furore surrounding a party that has historically struggled to secure a debate podium highlights how deeply the motion has struck a nerve. For the first time, adherents to the ideology that has produced the ongoing genocide are being forced to defend themselves from accusations of racism. They hate it.
The motion has also undercut one of the main tactics soft Zionists have deployed to limit the fallout from the genocide: acknowledge the crimes, never the criminal. The situation in Gaza is ascribed to some vague, blameless catastrophe. At most, they will attempt to scapegoat Netanyahu. Now Green Party members have named the perpetrator and the ideology that motivates it, even if the party establishment would rather they hadn’t.
Alex Foley is a researcher and painter living in Brighton, UK. They have a background in molecular biology of health and disease. They are the co-founder of the Accountability Archive, a web tool preserving fragile digital evidence of pro-genocidal rhetoric from power holders.

Ukrainian Military Links Air, Sea and Underwater Drones Through DELTA System at NATO Exercise
Ukraine’s military used its DELTA battlefield management system to coordinate maritime operations during NATO’s REPMUS 2026 exercises, successfully integrating aerial, surface, and underwater drones as well as radars, Ukraine’s Defense Ministry reported on October 14.
REPMUS, or Robotic Experimentation and Prototyping with Maritime Unmanned Systems, is an annual NATO exercise led by the Portuguese Navy. Ukraine participated for the third time this year.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The Ukrainian team used DELTA to coordinate reconnaissance, maritime monitoring, maneuvering, escort exercises, and simulated strikes alongside allied forces.
The Defense Ministry reported that all systems transmitting telemetry under NATO’s STANAG 4817 standard were successfully integrated into DELTA during the exercises.
Ukrainian specialists also shared combat experience with NATO partners, including lessons from the use of unmanned systems in maritime operations.
The ministry noted that DELTA continued operating without interruption under unstable communications conditions. Ukrainian personnel also highlighted the convenience of streaming through the system’s Vezha module compared with other platforms.
DELTA had already served as the main command-and-control platform during REPMUS 2025, when it integrated more than 100 unmanned systems operating across multiple domains.
The Defense Ministry stated that this year’s testing again demonstrated DELTA’s compatibility with NATO systems and moved Ukrainian solutions closer to broader standardization within the Alliance.
Ukraine plans to continue sharing combat experience from unmanned operations while expanding interoperability with NATO member forces.
In June, DELTA logged more than 200,000 drone-confirmed strikes on Russian targets, averaging over 6,600 per day. The system also processed more than 75,000 video streams daily and used its built-in Avengers platform to automatically detect enemy objects in battlefield footage.

Russia Loses Over 350,000 Troops in 2026 as Battlefield Losses Accelerate
Russia has lost 350,260 military personnel since the beginning of 2026, according to the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine on October 15.
The General Staff said September saw the highest Russian personnel losses of the year, with 46,230 recorded.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The monthly figures show a substantial increase in Russian losses during the summer and early autumn, rising from 26,090 in February to more than 42,000 in both July and August.
According to the figures provided, Russian personnel losses totaled 326,900 from January through September, with another 23,360 recorded in October as of October 15.
The latest figures published by Ukraine's Ministry of Defense provide additional context: estimated Russian personnel losses since the full-scale invasion began on February 24, 2022, reached 1,559,230 as of October 15, 2026, including 1,880 over the preceding day.
The September figure translates to approximately 1,541 Russian personnel losses per day, compared with 932 in February.
The September surge included the highest reported daily toll of the full-scale war, with 2,090 Russian troops killed or wounded on September 28, surpassing three daily totals above 2,000 recorded in 2024.
Another 1,960 casualties were logged on September 16 as Russia maintained its offensive intensity in the fortress belt region, particularly around the Ukrainian stronghold of Dobropillia.
Russia's overall losses in Ukraine are estimated at roughly 100 times Soviet losses in Afghanistan, and 125 times Moscow's officially acknowledged toll in the two Chechen wars.
Internal documents from Russia's 127th Motor Rifle Division also point to widespread unauthorized absences, suicides, and serious disciplinary problems, suggesting official casualty records may lag well behind losses at the front.

Russia Wants FSB Encryption Built Into Every 5G Smartphone—From iPhones to Samsung
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
15:31:07 UTC
00:31:07 KST

- Category
- World
Russia Wants FSB Encryption Built Into Every 5G Smartphone—From iPhones to Samsung
Russia is preparing to require smartphone manufacturers to build an encryption algorithm developed by the FSB directly into devices that use the country’s future 5G networks, a move that could affect virtually every major smartphone brand sold in Russia, including Apple, Samsung, and Chinese manufacturers.
The proposed requirement appears in a draft order from Russia’s Ministry of Digital Development cited by Russian media outlet RBC on October 15.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
It would make support for the Russian encryption algorithm known as Kuznyechik mandatory beginning March 1, 2032.
Under the plan, Kuznyechik would be used in 5G networks to encrypt mobile traffic and verify its integrity. Until the 2032 deadline, foreign smartphones that do not support the algorithm would continue operating on Russian 5G networks normally. During that transition period, Russian encryption would only be activated when both the smartphone and the network’s base station support it.
The technical challenge is that mobile-network encryption takes place directly inside a smartphone’s modem chipset. Current foreign devices using Qualcomm and Unisoc hardware do not include Kuznyechik, RBC noted, meaning support cannot simply be added through an ordinary software update or by replacing a SIM card.
For mass-market smartphones, the Russian algorithm would have to be implemented at the modem hardware level. That would require cooperation from chipmakers and device manufacturers, potentially forcing companies to produce Russia-specific hardware or alter future global modem designs.
The task is further complicated by the fact that Kuznyechik is not part of the international 3GPP standards that define how modern mobile networks operate.
Alexei Alyasev, CEO of Russian base-station manufacturer Signaltek, said implementation in smartphones would likely not be technically possible before 2030 and would require significant investment.
Russia’s own telecommunications infrastructure is also only partly ready. Domestically produced base stations can already support Kuznyechik at the software level, according to RBC, but additional modifications would be required to use the algorithm to protect the radio connection between phones and cellular infrastructure. That work could take another one to two years.
Previously, Russia’s Federal Antimonopoly Service (FAS) opened a case against Apple over the company’s failure to enable the preinstallation of two Russian applications—the Max messenger and the RuStore app marketplace —on iPhones and iPads.

Fewer than one in thirty reservists deployed last year
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:30:15 BST
00:30:15 KST

Just under three per cent of Britain’s reservists were mobilised for operations in the last financial year, with the proportion falling for a second year running as overall reserve strength declined, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Gordon McKee, the Labour member for Glasgow South, asked what proportion of reservists had been mobilised for operations in each of the last five years.
Calvin Bailey, Parliamentary Under-Secretary and Minister for Veterans and People, said: “Our Reservists make a vital contribution to the nation’s security, supporting operations at home and overseas.”
The figures he supplied cover Future Reserves 2020 personnel and serving ex-regular reserves. Strength stood at 39,400 at the end of the 2021/22 financial year, 37,460 a year later, 36,220 at the end of 2023/24, 35,940 at the end of 2024/25 and 36,280 at the end of 2025/26, the first rise in the series.
Deployments over the same period moved on a different curve. In 2021/22 a total of 920 reservists deployed, which was 2.3 per cent of the force. That rose to 1,730 in 2022/23, or 4.6 per cent, and peaked at 1,850 in 2023/24, or 5.1 per cent. The figure then dropped to 1,160 in 2024/25, which was 3.2 per cent, and to 1,060 in 2025/26, or 2.9 per cent.
The peak years coincide with the heaviest period of British support to Ukraine, including Operation Interflex, the training mission for Ukrainian recruits run from sites across the UK, which drew on reservists alongside regulars and allied instructors.
Reserve strength has been a persistent problem for the department for well over a decade. The Future Reserves 2020 programme set a target of 30,000 trained Army Reserve soldiers that proved difficult to hit, and the services have struggled with the recruitment and retention of part-time personnel for most of the past decade. The Strategic Defence Review last year committed to growing the reserves and gave them a larger role in homeland defence, including the protection of critical national infrastructure, and the department has since set out investment in equipment for reserve units.
Mobilisation of a reservist can be compulsory or voluntary, and employers have statutory obligations and rights around it.

Moving Taiwan beyond Double Ten
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
15:26:35 UTC
00:26:35 KST

Last weekend, Taiwan celebrated Double Ten National Day, marking 115 years since the Wuchang Uprising.
An Army CH-47SD Chinook carried a massive 12-by-18-meter ROC flag across downtown Taipei, accompanied by two UH-60M Black Hawk helicopters, passing over vibrant celebrations in front of the Presidential Office Building.
The spectacle made global headlines, with Reuters even titling its report “Giant Taiwan flag flies from helicopter for national day, defying Beijing.”
Yet the irony is that the flag is not originally Taiwanese, and its display hardly represents defiance of Beijing given that ROC flags have filled Double Ten celebrations in Taiwan for decades.
There is a deeper paradox. Double Ten commemorates an event that did not take place in Taiwan and did not significantly involve Taiwanese people.
Double Ten commemorates the 1911 Wuchang Uprising in Wuhan, China. It took place while Taiwan was under Japanese rule.
A historical event fundamentally external to Taiwan’s own historical narrative and collective memory will inevitably struggle to resonate widely with Taiwanese.
The uprising helped overthrow the Qing dynasty and paved the way for the establishment of the Republic of China. It was not until 1949 that the ROC government relocated to Taiwan.
Although Double Ten distinguishes Taiwan’s national commemoration from the People’s Republic of China’s Oct. 1 National Day, it continues to tie Taiwan to an outdated pan-Chinese political ideology.
To solidify Taiwan’s identity, break free from historical constraints, and signal its separate sovereignty to the international community, the country should establish a new and genuinely Taiwanese national day.
More troubling is that the giant flags flown over Taipei last Saturday still serve as a stark reminder to many Taiwanese of the KMT’s authoritarian legacy.
The upper-left “blue sky, white sun” portion of the ROC flag is also used by the KMT as its party emblem. After the ROC took control of Taiwan in 1945 and the KMT government relocated there in 1949, the party-state embedded ROC institutions and symbols throughout Taiwan.
As a minority regime ruling over a largely local Taiwanese population, the KMT imposed martial law to maintain political control and suppress threats to its rule.
Its central narrative for justifying the suspension of constitutional democracy, freezing elections, and almost four decades of authoritarian one-party rule was that the ROC government remained the sole legitimate government of all China and Taiwan was merely a temporary base from which it would eventually launch a counteroffensive to recover the “mainland.”
No other day of the year displayed that narrative more vividly.
To project legitimacy, the authoritarian KMT government gathered foreign dignitaries and overseas Chinese delegates for grand Double Ten celebrations in Taipei.
Outside this elite circle, many of whom had little or no connection to Taiwan, many Taiwanese looked on with indifference or quietly shook their heads for fear of the repercussions of disrupting the regime’s manufactured narrative.
Many local Taiwanese also felt alienated by Double Ten celebrations during martial law, which centered on a China-focused national narrative expressed overwhelmingly in Mandarin.
This excluded Hoklo, Hakka, and Indigenous Taiwanese communities, many of whose members did not speak Mandarin. For many, authoritarian ROC governance represented language erasure and suppression of culture and identity rather than national liberation.
Although the holiday can counter Beijing’s narrative by emphasizing the distinction between the ROC and PRC, Double Ten nevertheless commemorates the founding story of a political system born in China.
Celebrating a national day with origins in the heart of China continues to tie Taiwan to a Greater China political framework. Beijing can exploit this ambiguity to bolster its narrative that Taiwan is an integral part of China that must ultimately be “unified,” by force if necessary.
It also reinforces the international ambiguity Beijing has worked to shape.
When international media report that Taiwan is celebrating a Chinese uprising as its national day, it can blur the reality of Taiwan’s current de facto independence and its existence as a sovereign political entity separate from China.
Breaking free of this Greater China framework will require a new national anchor.
Double Ten represents to many Taiwanese an imported historical narrative and a dark authoritarian past. Taiwan deserves better.
The country is no longer an authoritarian regime in exile, but a vibrant modern democracy. Celebrating a violent historical event that did not even take place in Taiwan sits awkwardly beside the democratic values that distinguish modern Taiwan so sharply from China.
While Taiwan’s government and civil society promote those values, celebrating a date tied to bloodshed in China more than a century ago risks confusing the story Taiwan tells about itself to the world.
A national day should also belong to the land and the people living on it. The Wuchang Uprising obviously did not take place in Taiwan.
Without the coercive machinery that once imposed a singular national narrative, it is difficult to expect Taiwan’s diverse communities to rally around a commemoration so distant from their own histories.
The national fabric would be better woven around a Taiwan-centered cause that people of different languages, cultures, backgrounds, generations, and newer immigrant communities can share. It would also help disentangle Taiwan’s statehood from the ROC’s founding history in China.
Taiwan needs a forward-looking national day that celebrates its democratic progress.
March 23 or May 20 could serve as alternatives. March 23 marks Taiwan’s first direct presidential election in 1996, while May 20 is the traditional inauguration day for Taiwan’s democratically elected presidents.
Either could serve as a reminder of the democratic mandate of Taiwan’s people and their collective journey toward self-government. May 20 could even allow national celebrations to coincide with presidential inaugurations every four years.
With China increasing pressure to distort Taiwan’s political reality, there is an even greater need for the country to step out of Double Ten’s Chinese shadow and tell the world that Taiwan is Taiwan.
A genuinely Taiwanese national day would make clear that Taiwan’s modern identity is rooted in the history, democratic choices, and political sovereignty of the people who live here.
Rath Wang is a political commentator based in Taipei focusing on Taiwan’s politics, media, civil society, and key issues influencing Taiwan’s future. He is a media producer and host of current affairs talk shows and podcasts and has worked on political campaigns and lived in Taiwan, Japan, Thailand, and the US.

El Nino a 'terrifying' threat to coral reefs: UN biodiversity expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
15:23:16 UTC
00:23:16 KST

El Nino a ‘terrifying’ threat to coral reefs: UN biodiversity expert
PARIS, France – A super El Nino fuelling record ocean temperatures poses a “terrifying” threat to the world’s fragile coral reefs, the chair of the UN’s expert nature panel told AFP.
Marine scientist David Obura said the exceptional El Nino pattern building strength in the tropical Pacific could drive vulnerable coral species even closer toward extinction.
Corals are heat sensitive and particularly vulnerable to climate change, which is heating the world’s oceans and increasing the frequency and intensity of damaging bleaching events.
But 2026’s El Nino layers “a terrifying level of additional risk”, said Obura, a Kenyan reef expert and chair of IPBES, the UN’s expert scientific panel on biodiversity.
The warming phase of a natural climate cycle, El Nino events temporarily elevate global temperatures, altering cloud and wind patterns, and raise the risk of damaging weather.
Global forecasters expect this episode to be the strongest on record, and sea surface temperatures in parts of the Pacific have already hit all-time highs months before its expected peak.
That greatly concerns Obura, who recalled the damaging impact of a previous super El Nino episode in 1997/98.
“That this coming event is worse than that, after three intervening global bleaching events ... is a terrifying reality,” he said.
Significant worsening
Obura led a major reassessment of coral health published in Nature on Thursday that reported a sharp deterioration in reef-building species since the last global census in 2008.
“Our results show that by 2020, nearly half of coral species were at elevated relative risk of extinction” with climate change the main driver of this decline, wrote Obura and dozens of top scientists.
The review covered hundreds of species on the IUCN’s “red list” – icons like staghorn and table corals whose mineral skeletons give reefs their dazzling three-dimensional complexity.
This “indicates conditions for corals are worsening significantly... not at all surprising given the accelerated warming and lack of abatement of global drivers of coral decline”, said Obura.
But the study was completed in 2020 and the findings today would be even bleaker, he said.
Since then, global ocean temperatures have soared to unprecedented highs and the worst coral bleaching episode on record between 2023 and 2025 caused widespread mortality across reefs.
“It is entirely possible that reassessing the status of corals just after this coming El Nino may show them to have crossed the 50 percent mark of the proportion of species at elevated risk of extinction,” said Obura.
In 2025, scientists warned that warm-water coral reefs had almost certainly crossed a point of no return as oceans warm beyond a level most can survive.
The study in Nature said that projected rises in ocean temperatures and other pressures “primarily determined when and where, rather than if, conditions will become unviable for corals”.
“When they hit their threshold the collapse of reefs in that region could be precipitous and we don’t know if that is five, 15 or 30 years into the future, or maybe this year with the super El Nino ramping up,” said Obura. AFP

Man with suitcase full of snakes stopped at German airport
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:21:32 BST
00:21:32 KST

Man with suitcase full of snakes stopped at German airport
- Published
A man has been stopped at Cologne Bonn Airport in Germany after trying to smuggle in more than 90 lizards and venomous snakes.
Customs officials said the 45-year-old Mexican firefighter had looked "conspicuously nervous" as he tried to go through the green - nothing to declare - exit at the airport.
They conducted a drugs test on the man - which came back positive for cocaine - before proceeding to check his suitcase.
They did not find any drugs, but vipers, rattlesnakes and other species of snakes and lizards, including iguanas, hidden in shampoo and cream bottles, plastic containers and balls of socks.
"My colleagues at the airport are used to a lot when it comes to souvenirs in suitcases, but we've never had 37 live venomous snakes and 55 lizards from Mexico before," said Jens Ahland, spokesman for the Cologne Customs office.
Some were being kept "in inhumane conditions", Ahland said. Others had died during the journey from Mexico City via Istanbul.
The man, who has not been named, told officers that he had brought the animals back as a favour for a Brazilian acquaintance.
He was denied entry to Germany and flown back to Istanbul.
As for the surviving animals, they are being looked after at a snake farm in Germany.
"Last year, we had over 1,300 seizures nationwide involving more than 56,600 protected animals and plants or products made from them," the Customs spokesman said.
Six years ago, 26 rare reptiles - 10 of them dead - smuggled inside parcels of toys and sweets from Mexico, were found by customs officials at Cologne Bonn Airport.
They were destined for private buyers in Germany.

Rosatom says UN atomic agency-mediated ceasefire implemented near Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Burç Eruygur
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
The head of Russia’s state nuclear corporation Rosatom said Thursday that a local ceasefire is being implemented near the Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant (ZNPP) to allow repairs at the facility under Moscow’s control.
Alexey Likhachev told reporters in Moscow that power supply to the ZNPP via the 330kV Ferosplavnaya-1 backup external power line is “extremely unstable and fraught with risks,” noting a “very high probability” of recurring loss of a stable power supply to the plant due to the “semi-destroyed state” of the nearby Zaporizhzhia Thermal Power Plant (ZTPP).
Likhachev said Russia began efforts to arrange a localized ceasefire days ago to facilitate repairs at the ZTPP, and that the plant’s switchgear is essential for ensuring safety and power supply, including for the ZNPP.
“By engaging the IAEA (International Atomic Energy Agency) and coordinating with our relevant ministries … we have successfully established a ‘regime of silence’ at the ZTPP today,” Likhachev was quoted by Russian media outlets, including state news agency Tass.
He went on to say that Rosatom specialists are heading to the site to begin repairing technical equipment, which he said will help strengthen power supply to the ZNPP.
The situation around the ZNPP, Europe’s largest nuclear power plant and one of the world’s 10 largest, remains tense amid persistent concerns about a potential nuclear disaster, as Moscow and Kyiv frequently accuse each other of carrying out attacks around the facility in southeastern Ukraine.
Since Sept. 1, 2022, IAEA personnel have been stationed at the plant, which Russia has controlled since March 2022.
IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi announced earlier this month that he was negotiating a localized ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine to allow repairs at the ZTPP.

Syrian court sentences two to death over 2025 coastal violence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
15:19:18 UTC
00:19:18 KST

Syrian court sentences two to death over 2025 coastal violence
Court rulings concern violence and killings during March 2025 uprising by pro-Assad forces, and retaliatory attacks.
A court in Syria has sentenced to death two supporters of the ousted Bashar al-Assad regime for inciting an uprising last year, and handed hefty sentences to members of the current government’s security forces for the killing of hundreds of civilians from the Alawite religious minority.
The Military Criminal Court at the Justice Palace in the northern city of Aleppo gave death sentences to Al-Waddah Ismail and Maher Ali, according to state media.
The Syrian Arab News Agency (SANA) reported that the pair were convicted of seeking to incite civil war and sectarian fighting and for leading armed gangs with the intent to attack public forces.
A third defendant, Maher Othman, was sentenced to 12 years in prison, the court also announced on Thursday without immediately specifying the charges on which he was convicted.
In separate rulings, the court sentenced Mohammed Bakour, a member of the Defence Ministry’s 82nd Division in the new government, to 20 years in prison after convicting him of intentional homicide.
It also sentenced Ammar Abdul Aal to three years for torture and acquitted Abdul Raouf Bakrjan and Mohammed Zarzouri, SANA said.
The rulings concern investigations carried out by a government committee into attacks in March last year. At least 1,426 people, mostly civilians, were killed in several days of sectarian violence in the predominantly Alawite areas of Syria’s coastal regions.
The defendants included loyalists to the former al-Assad regime and members of the new government’s security forces. It is the first time government-linked personnel have been put on trial for acts of violence.
The government committee said it had identified 298 suspects implicated in serious violations during the violence in the Alawite heartland.
The committee’s investigation documented “serious violations against civilians on March 7, 8 and 9 [2025], including murder, premeditated murder, looting, destruction and burning of homes, torture and sectarian insults”.
The committee said 238 members of the army and security forces were killed by pro-Assad fighters in the attacks in the provinces of Tartous, Latakia and Hama.
About 200,000 pro-government military reinforcements then converged on the area, carrying out alleged revenge killings.
Al Jazeera’s Heidi Pett, reporting from the Syrian capital, Damascus, said the uprising was started by individuals still loyal to the regime of al-Assad, who himself is from the Alawite religious minority.
“After the Assad regime fell and its leadership fled the country at the end of 2024, supporters including loyal soldiers from the ousted regime as well as militia members fled to the mountains from where they launched an uprising in March 2025 against the new government”, Pett said.
She added that forces loyal to the new government are accused of killing civilians from the Alawite minority group in revenge attacks.
“These trials are for seven men who took part in the initial pro-Assad uprising, and also seven members of the new government’s security forces who were subsequently deployed into the area and are accused of carrying out revenge attacks,” she said.
SANA reported that on September 17, the court issued verdicts in cases involving four other defendants accused of violations during the events in the coastal region last March. One was sentenced to death, one to life imprisonment and one to 20 years in prison; the fourth was acquitted.

Interview: Chinese desertification control expert calls for global unity to protect planet
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
23:19:11 CST
00:19:11 KST

ROME, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- A leading Chinese expert on desertification control has called for global unity to protect food security and the environment.
Yin Yuzhen, who has spent more than four decades restoring the Maowusu Sandy Land in north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, said in a recent interview with Xinhua that she hopes to share her experience and inspire collective efforts to safeguard the future of the planet.
Yin was named one of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations' (FAO) 100 Women Heroes in Agrifood Systems and Rural Development on Thursday.
Speaking to Xinhua in Rome, she said desertification control has not only transformed the local environment but also created new opportunities for rural residents to improve their livelihoods.
"I have spent more than 40 years transforming this desert, and now all kinds of food can grow here," Yin said.
Since planting her first tree in 1986, Yin has helped green over 70,000 mu (around 4,667 hectares) -- an area roughly the size of 6,500 standard soccer pitches -- of sandy land. Today, the area supports a greater variety of crops and plants, including cherries and roses, creating new opportunities for agricultural production and income growth.
For Yin, combating desertification is closely linked to food security. "If we cannot control the sand, how can we grow good crops when sandstorms come? How can we improve the soil?" she said, stressing that protecting the land is essential to producing quality agricultural products and ensuring that ecological restoration benefits local communities.
"The Maowusu Sandy Land has turned green, and now it is becoming a land of gold," she said, describing the transformation as an example of the Chinese concept that lucid waters and lush mountains are invaluable assets.
Yin's work has also fostered a friendship that transcends national borders. In 1999, Ronald Sakolsky, an American teaching in China at the time, saw a television report on Yin's tree-planting efforts and raised 5,000 U.S. dollars to support her work.
Like the trees, their friendship has grown and endured.
"Although we come from two different countries and speak different languages, our hearts are connected," Yin said.
She sees their friendship as a reflection of the need for international cooperation in environmental protection.
"It is like the vision of a community with a shared future for humanity proposed by China. Although we come from different countries, we live on the same planet," she said. "We must unite to cherish nature and protect our planet."
Yin hopes to share her experience with communities facing land degradation, drought and desertification. Although conditions vary across regions, she believes that determination, and locally adapted approaches can help restore degraded land and improve people's lives.
The year 2026 has been designated by the United Nations as the International Year of the Woman Farmer. Yin said women play an important role in families and society and deserve greater support and opportunities in agriculture and rural development.
"They need not only equal status, but also more opportunities to put their abilities to use," she said. "Give them a little sunshine, and they will flourish."
Being named one of the FAO's 100 Women Heroes is both a recognition of Yin's past efforts, and an encouragement to continue her work, which shows that perseverance and cooperation can transform barren land into a fertile landscape.
"Like a Mongolian horse, I will keep pressing forward with perseverance and determination," she said. ■

ACC Mulls Commercial Counter-Drone Services for Air Base Defense
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
15:15:36 UTC
00:15:36 KST

Air Combat Command is looking for defense firms capable of providing a private counter-drone service, complete with the personnel to operate it, for defending air bases across the Air Force.
ACC, which oversees the service’s Point Defense Task Force, is conducting a market survey to identify companies specializing in counter-small unmanned aerial systems defense technology that can provide “C-sUAS as a Service,” according to an Oct. 13 solicitation.
According to the solicitation, the intent of the service model is to:
- Provide organic, resilient, sustainable, and agile Point Defense capabilities across Department of the Air Force installations
- Implement a flexible, scalable architecture allowing installations to scale operational capacity up or down based on dynamic threat levels
- Leverage mature, commercially available or rapidly adaptable systems rather than initiating high-risk developmental programs
The market survey comes as the Air Force races to develop an arsenal of capabilities to defend its installations against drone threat.
“The Government envisions an initial prototype deployment at two designated Continental United States Air Force installations, with option mechanisms to scale across additional ACC installations upon proven performance,” the document states.
Interested firms have until Oct. 31 to respond to the solicitation. ACC is interested in companies that can provide technology for detecting, tracking, and identifying drones—ranging from small quadcopters to larger, Group 3 systems like the Iranian Shahed one-way attack drones that weight up to 1,320 pounds—at distances of up to five miles from a base perimeter, the document states.
Firms should also be capable of incorporating “government-approved kinetic and/or nonkinetic” effectors that range from radio frequency jamming to directed-energy such as lasers and high-powered microwave systems, the document states. Interested defense firms would also have to show they would continuously refresh software and hardware “within a multiyear service contract without frequent contract modifications,” according to the document.
ACC would also want a commercial capability to have the built-in logistical support to be self-sufficient for up to 96 hours, the document states.
The concept would require the contractor to “provide a complete, integrated, turn-key service solution covering materiel, personnel, training, sustainment, and ongoing modernization,” the solicitation states.
It’s unclear how this commercial service would align with the service’s intent to create a new point defense career field for enlisted Airmen, training and equipping them to defend air bases from drone and missile attack. The Air Force is slated to start designating Airmen with the new specialty within two years. As a short-term fix, the service has established point defense flights, specialized units of roughly 20 Airmen each, trained to rapidly deploy to hotspots and defend air bases against drone attacks.
Currently, the Air Force is equipping installations with the Small Unmanned Air Defense Systems, or SUADS, for countering drones. The system is capable of identifying and tracking enemy missiles or drones of multiple sizes, and downing incoming drones with an electronic warfare weapon. To stop missiles, it uses both electronic warfare and kinetic effectors. It can also interface with commercial counter-drone systems and other air defense systems, depending on the needs of a commander.
The service is also acquiring additional counter-drone systems through the Pentagon’s Joint Interagency Task Force 401. In the future, counter-drone technology will fall under the “point defense weapon system,” a classification to manage multiple counter-drone systems that range from sensors, radars, and command and control architecture to kinetic and non-kinetic effectors for disabling or destroying incoming drones.
