A Syrian military court has handed down sentences ranging from two months in prison to the death penalty against several defendants, including defence ministry personnel, over violations committed during deadly violence along the country’s coast in March 2025.
The Military Criminal Court in Aleppo sentenced al-Waddah Ismail and Maher Ali to death at a hearing at the city’s Justice Palace on Thursday, state-run Alikhbaria TV reported.
The court convicted both men of acts intended to “provoke civil war and sectarian fighting” and of leading armed groups to attack government forces, the broadcaster quoted the presiding judge as saying.
A third defendant, Maher Othman, was sentenced to 12 years in prison, though the court did not immediately specify the charges on which he was convicted.
In rulings involving defence ministry personnel, Mohammed Bakour, a member of the ministry’s 82nd Division, received a 20-year prison sentence for intentional homicide.
Captain Mustafa Shannan and Khaled Muhaimeed, both from the 54th Division, were each sentenced to two years in prison for involvement in torture. Another ministry member, Mahmoud Shaheen, received a two-month sentence for causing bodily harm.
The court acquitted Abdul Raouf Bakr Jan and Mohammed Louay Zarzouri, members of the 50th and 54th divisions respectively, of intentional homicide charges “due to insufficient evidence”.
Widespread abuses against civilians
The rulings are part of proceedings against former regime members and personnel serving under Syria’s current defence ministry accused of violations during the coastal violence.
The violence erupted in March 2025 after armed groups loyal to ousted president Bashar al Assad attacked government security forces in the coastal provinces of Latakia and Tartus, triggering clashes and widespread abuses against civilians.
The violence killed hundreds of civilians and security forces personnel.
Public trials began at Aleppo’s Justice Palace in November 2025, with defendants facing charges including incitement to sectarian strife, homicide, theft and attacks on security forces.
On September 17, the same court sentenced one defendant to death, another to life in prison and a third to 20 years, while acquitting a fourth.

Türkiye plans to present local climate projects at next month’s COP31 summit in Antalya, Climate Change Directorate head Halil Hasar said on Oct. 15.
Speaking at the opening of the Ankara Climate Transition Forum, Hasar stressed the need for early warning systems and scientific data to help local authorities prepare for changing climate conditions.

The two-day forum brings together municipalities, representatives of the European Union and U.N. Development Program, international financial institutions and scientists. It aims to identify local initiatives for presentation at the conference, supporting the presidency’s emphasis on implementation.
Türkiye recorded its hottest year in 2024 and its driest since 1964 in 2025, according to official meteorological data. Precipitation last year was 27.6 percent below the 1991–2020 average.
COP31 will take place in Antalya on Nov. 9–20. Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change Minister Murat Kurum is the conference’s president-designate.

====================================================================================================

Gaza’s child amputees are growing faster than their prosthetics allow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
14:13:03 UTC
23:13:03 KST

Abdul-Rahman al-Nashash, 11, holds onto the edge of a chair and pushes his left leg into a plastic prosthetic that doesn’t fit him anymore. The bone that was cut two years ago has kept growing inside, and it presses painfully against his skin.
His doctors told him to stop wearing it. He wears it anyway, every morning, pulling the straps tight and rolling his pants down so no one sees the plastic before he takes his first step. He bites his lip when it hurts and holds his shoulders straight so no one can tell he is limping.
“He forces himself to wear it,” his mother said, “just so no one knows he has a disability.”
Before the genocide, al-Nashash played for a local soccer club, and he would chase the ball across a dirt field until the sun went down. He is the eldest son in his family, and he was the one his mother leaned on at home. When she needed water, he was the one who ran to carry the heavy gallon of water, and he never got tired. Now, he is not able.
When he finally takes the prosthetic off, he sits curled up. He is waiting for his third surgery, and his mother said he will need one every year.
As a child grows, the bone in the amputated leg grows too, but the prosthetic doesn’t. At some point it stops fitting, and sometimes the child needs another operation before he can get a new one. In Gaza, that often means starting over with surgery, then rehabilitation, then a new limb if one can be made at all, because Israel restricts the parts and materials needed to make and repair them. Some children in Gaza have outgrown their limbs and are waiting for new ones. Others never received one, because there are none in Gaza that fit them.
Al-Nashash’s family was forced to evacuate from al-Bureij refugee camp in Central Gaza in 2023 and took shelter in UNRWA schools. His father stayed behind. Two days after they left, on October 20, the house was struck, and his father was killed along with several relatives. The three-wheeled motorcycle that had been the family’s only source of income was parked in the storeroom and was destroyed in the same strike.
From there, the family moved from school to school and tent to tent. They spent about three months in Rafah, then moved to schools in Nuseirat. With no money coming in, his mother opened a small stall with her brother-in-law, selling a variety of canned beans.
Around noon on July 16, 2024, her sister asked her to come light a fire and cook, so she left her son to mind the stall in her place. An Israeli airstrike hit the tents in the middle of al-Razi school, a UNRWA shelter in Nuseirat camp, killing 23 people, according to Gaza’s Government Media Office. A piece of shrapnel struck his leg directly. His mother said his injured left foot was split in two, the bones of his toes exposed, and she kept screaming that her son had been killed.
At first, she said, she was told doctors hoped to fix the leg with metal plates rather than amputate. At Al-Aqsa Hospital, one doctor told her the leg would have to be amputated, and she asked them to cut off her own leg and give it to him, because he was the one who took care of her. He was then taken by an ambulance to a hospital by the sea in Deir al-Balah where a foreign medical team was working. There they told her nothing more could be done. The amputation needed her consent. She signed, because there was no other choice.
When al-Nashash woke from the anesthesia, he kept staring at himself as if he were losing his mind. It was only after counselors came and he began to see other children like him that he slowly started to adjust.
After the amputation, therapists from local rehabilitation programs came to work with him regularly. But his natural childhood growth worked against his recovery. “My son grows fast,” his mother said. By March 2025, just eight months after he lost his leg, the bone had already grown too long.
They traveled to Jordan, where surgeons cut the bone back and fitted him with his first prosthetic, the one he still wears today. The trip lasted five months. When al-Nashash returned to Gaza, the boy who used to sprint on the soccer field had to start physical therapy from scratch, learning how to balance and walk all over again.
Today, that same cycle is about to restart. Once he manages to get his next surgery, he will face three more months of physical therapy before he can even begin training to walk again. His mother has applied for a medical evacuation out of Gaza, hoping he can be treated abroad. “I wish I could see my son walk like other children,” she told Mondoweiss.
Until that approval comes, al-Nashash also uses a pair of forearm crutches that are are breaking down. The soft material on the hand grips has completely worn away, leaving his hands to rub against the hard surface. “There are no spare parts for the grips,” his mother said.
The indefinite wait for prosthetics
Mahmoud al-Darbali, 10, lost his right leg up to the hip when he was nine, and over a year later, he is still waiting to receive his first prosthetic.
Al-Darbali’s family home near the Zeitoun car market was bombed a week after they evacuated. After being displaced south more than ten times, the family returned north, squeezing into a single room in his grandmother’s house on Kishko Street, in the Zeitoun neighborhood of Gaza City. “We were happy,” his mother told Mondoweiss.
On July 5, 2025, three shells struck the house. The blast killed several relatives, including al-Darbali’s 14-year-old sister. “I didn’t get to say goodbye. She died hungry,” his mother said. The explosion severed Mahmoud’s right leg instantly and burned his left thigh. Shrapnel hit his seven-year-old brother’s lung and struck his mother’s knee. His 16-year-old brother still has shrapnel near his spine, and he cannot sleep without painkillers.
They spent over two months at Al-Ahli Arab Baptist Hospital, where al-Darbali was taken to the operating room daily just to change his bandages. The mother and her five surviving children shared a single hospital bed. In July 2025, the same month Mahmoud was injured, Doctors Without Borders (MSF) said injured patients at its clinics in Gaza were asking for food instead of medicine, because their wounds were not healing without enough protein.
After leaving the hospital, the family managed on the street. Al-Darbali relies on crutches and a wheelchair, yet he cannot walk more than a hundred meters on the crutches. Without electricity, he often loses his balance in the dark. “Many times I wake up to his terrified voice as he hits the ground,” his mother says.
He still feels the missing leg. “Mom, my heel hurts,” he tells her, his mother said. His brother holds the empty space where Mahmoud’s leg used to be and presses on it. “I feel better,” Mahmoud says. He receives no psychological support. When he is given paper, he draws tanks, missiles and blood.
Because the amputation reaches his pelvis, leaving only a tiny fraction of the thigh bone, the family has been told no prosthetic in Gaza can fit him. He has been referred for medical evacuation abroad, but no country has accepted his case yet. “The situation is hard,” his mother said, “and there is no food.”
A shortage by design
Dr. Mohammed Abu Mansi, a physical therapy and rehabilitation specialist at Sheikh Hamad Bin Khalifa Al Thani Hospital for Rehabilitation and Prosthetics in Gaza City, explained that while not every child requires annual revision surgeries, bone overgrowth causes complications in some children. For patients like al-Nashash, the growing bone creates a protrusion. “When the child puts weight on the prosthetic, this spot becomes very painful,” he said. “The pressure inside the prosthetic becomes unbearable.”
Revision surgeries can be done in Gaza, he said, but only within what is available in operating rooms, anesthesia and follow-up care. Complicated cases need to travel abroad.
For hip-level amputations like al-Darbali’s, the problem is the materials. “We used to fit this type of prosthetic inside Gaza before the war,” Dr. Abu Mansi told Mondoweiss. “But now the materials needed to make a prosthetic for an amputation up to the hip are not available.” Before the war, he said, prosthetic parts and materials came in regularly, and the hospital could provide steady care to amputees.
Children like al-Darbali, left without a prosthetic, he said, develop muscle weakness, muscle contractures, limited movement and changes in the shape of the amputated limb as their bodies continue to grow. Relying on crutches and wheelchairs for a long time also causes other complications.
Al-Nashash and al-Darbali are among thousands of amputees. The World Health Organization estimates that more than 5,000 people in Gaza have lost limbs since October 2023, and that one in five of them is a child. Of 2,277 amputees the WHO evaluated between September 2024 and May 2026, only 502 had been fitted with a prosthetic. Eighteen percent were children, and 32 percent had above-knee amputations. 225 needed revision surgery on what remained of their limb, and only eight prosthetists were working in the entire Strip.
According to the same report, no rehabilitation equipment entered Gaza between May 2024 and April 14, 2026. By that date, 18 shipments, including prosthetic limbs and children’s wheelchairs, were still waiting for clearance, for 136 days on average and 526 days in the longest case. In the six months before that, four shipments were rejected. In June, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs reported that Israeli authorities had denied prosthetic hand, knee and ankle joints, silicone liners and medical shoes, despite repeated requests.
Treatment abroad is not guaranteed either. A medical referral is only the first step. A host country has to select the patient, and the list then goes to Israeli authorities for clearance. By mid-September, 13,555 patients had been evacuated since October 2023, including 6,326 children. Before the war, 50 to 100 patients left Gaza every day for treatment. In January, WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said more than 18,500 patients, including 4,000 children, still needed urgent medical evacuation. Citing Gaza’s Ministry of Health, he said 1,092 patients had died while waiting between July 2024 and November 2025.
Al-Darbali turned 10 in July. His mother is still waiting for a call from the officials handling his referral to tell her that his evacuation has been approved. “Every second, I pray my phone will ring, and they’ll tell me to get ready,” she said.
Now, when al-Darbali is taken to the hospital, he refuses to be put to sleep. His left leg, the only one he has left, is scarred from the burns.
“I don’t want to sleep,” Mahmoud said. “They’ll cut off my other leg.”

Israel moves to extend state of emergency beyond Oct. 27 elections

15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
The Israeli government is set to vote Thursday on extending the state of emergency on the home front until Nov. 3, past the Oct. 27 elections, citing “uncertainty over the situation,” particularly on the Iran and Lebanon fronts.  
The state of emergency was imposed when the Israeli-US war on Iran began Feb. 28. Tehran responded with attacks on Israel and US military facilities in Arab countries.  
Israeli public broadcaster KAN reported that ministers will vote on extending the declaration of a “special state of emergency” beyond the Oct. 27 general elections.  
It added that a document submitted by the cabinet secretary cited “uncertainty over the situation, particularly regarding the fronts in Iran and Lebanon.”  
The document, according to the broadcaster, stated that “according to security officials’ assessments, there remains a high likelihood of an attack” against Israel.

Mucahithan Avcioglu
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
International Energy Agency (IEA) members agreed Thursday to accelerate the release of around 100 million barrels of remaining emergency oil stocks, including more than 20 million barrels of diesel as soon as possible amid continued tightness in global energy markets.
The agency's Governing Board said its latest assessments pointed to persistent tightness in oil markets, particularly diesel, following a meeting on energy markets and security.
Approximately 330 million barrels have already been released under the collective action launched in March in response to the Strait of Hormuz crisis.
Total releases will exceed the original commitment of 400 million barrels, as some members have released more than initially pledged and others intend to do so, the board said.
Members agreed to take all necessary steps to complete the remaining releases in a timely manner consistent with national circumstances, with specific acceleration plans already in place.
The board also encouraged members with oil production and refining capacity to boost supplies of crude and refined products, particularly diesel, and emphasized the importance of the free flow of energy trade.
Reaffirming their commitment to international energy security, members expressed willingness to take further action to address global energy market challenges, building on the G7 statement of Oct. 2.
The IEA Secretariat will monitor progress and inform G7 leaders and the Governing Board of further action needed, drawing on an updated oil market assessment focused on diesel.

====================================================================================================

Puberty may mark a turning point for sex differences in the brain’s emotion and memory centers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
14:00:08 UTC
23:00:08 KST

Differences between males and females in the fine-grained tissue structure of deep brain regions are minimal at ages 9 to 12 but emerge and widen during adolescence, according to a new brain imaging study. The timing coincides with puberty and with the period when sex differences in conditions like anxiety and depression begin to appear, though the study could not determine what drives the brain changes. The findings were published in Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience.
Deep gray matter refers to a collection of structures located beneath the outer layer of the brain. These areas include the amygdala, which processes emotions, the hippocampus, which is central to memory, and the nucleus accumbens, which plays a role in reward and motivation. The study also examined the thalamus, a relay hub for sensory signals, and the caudate and putamen, which help control movement and habits. In human populations, many mental health conditions tied to these brain functions show different rates of diagnosis between men and women, but the biological reasons behind these differences remain poorly understood.
Animal research points to puberty as a key period for these changes: a 2008 study in rats found that sex hormones during puberty drive the addition of new cells to brain regions that differ between the sexes. In humans, a 2014 study that followed young people over time found that pubertal development was linked to the size of these deep brain regions in both boys and girls, independent of age.
While overall volume provides part of the picture, scientists have sought to understand the microscopic layout of brain tissue. Earlier work by the same research team, covered by PsyPost in 2024, found large differences between young adult men and women in measures of tissue microstructure, with men showing signs of more densely packed cells in regions like the hippocampus. The new research, led by Christopher G. Filippi of The Hospital for Sick Children and Richard Watts of the University of Canterbury, aimed to pinpoint when those microscopic differences first develop.
The research team examined brain scan data from 1,643 individuals aged 9 to 35. The participants were drawn from two large public databases: the Human Connectome Project Development dataset for children and teens, and the Young Adult dataset for older participants. In their analyses, the scientists statistically controlled for age and body mass index, and they accounted for family relationships among the many twins included in the adult sample.
To evaluate tissue microstructure, the researchers used an advanced magnetic resonance imaging technique called Restriction Spectrum Imaging. This method measures how water molecules diffuse through brain tissue. Water trapped inside a cell encounters barriers, producing a restricted diffusion signal that reflects cell packing. Water in the spaces between cells encounters fewer obstacles, producing a hindered diffusion signal that reflects the extracellular environment.
For the youngest participants, aged 9 to 12, the researchers observed no statistically significant differences between boys and girls in these diffusion measures. Across the deep gray matter structures, the tissue composition in childhood appeared similar between the sexes.
However, differences began to emerge between ages 13 and 16, first in the hippocampus, amygdala, and thalamus. Restricted diffusion rose with age in both sexes, but from puberty onward it was consistently higher in males, a pattern the researchers suggest may reflect more densely packed cells or larger cell bodies. By ages 17 to 21, sex accounted for roughly 13 to 33 percent of the variation in restricted diffusion across all six regions, and in adults it explained 32 to 37 percent in the hippocampus and amygdala.
Females, in turn, showed a larger hindered component, meaning a greater share of the water signal came from the spaces between cells. Because both measures are expressed as shares of the total signal, the two patterns largely mirror each other.
In regions such as the nucleus accumbens, caudate, and putamen, females showed a slowing in development in their late teens before accelerating again in their early 20s, while males followed a more steady progression. By the mid-20s, the size of the sex difference in the hippocampus and amygdala had leveled off, though the measures themselves were still changing in both sexes. In the thalamus, the divergence between the sexes continued to widen up to age 35.
“Sex differences in the brain have so far been primarily investigated at the macro-structural level (i.e., differences in overall brain size or differences in the size of specific regions),” said Yumnah Khan, a doctoral scientist at the Autism Research Centre at the University of Cambridge who was not involved in the research. “What is interesting about this work is it provides evidence for differences in brain microstructure (i.e., what is happening at a finer level within brain tissue), which gives us a more detailed picture of sex differences in the brain.”
Marco Balducci, a senior researcher at the University of Turku who was not involved in the study, said the findings build on earlier work. “Earlier studies had identified sex differences in subcortical brain structure and, more recently, in diffusion-derived microstructure in young adults,” Balducci told PsyPost. “This study extends that work by showing that the differences emerge during adolescence rather than simply being present in adulthood.”
The timing of these changes aligns with the pubertal transition, leading the study authors to speculate about biological drivers. Earlier animal work indicates that sex hormones can influence synapses and dendrites, the connection points and branching extensions of nerve cells. Because these adolescent brain shifts occur alongside the emergence of sex-biased mental health conditions, identifying typical developmental paths could help clarify underlying vulnerabilities.
Khan told PsyPost that considering human imaging alongside animal research helps connect biology to observation. “Animal studies can provide much stronger evidence about causality and specific mechanisms, while human studies are generally observational and correlational,” she said. “However, when both of these lines of research are considered and interpreted together, we get a better picture of the mechanisms underlying sex differences in brain development.”
Balducci noted that the broad descriptive findings appear well-supported. “The main descriptive finding appears robust because the study uses a large combined sample, finds a consistent developmental pattern across several brain regions, and applies correction for multiple comparisons,” he said. “However, the reasons for these differences remain uncertain because the data are cross-sectional, and in this setting it is difficult to distinguish age-related changes from pubertal development or establish a hormonal cause.”
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The study relied on cross-sectional data from different individuals at each age, rather than following the same individuals across their development. Additionally, puberty was measured using ratings of physical development, which rose so closely with age that the researchers could not separate the effects of puberty from those of getting older, and hormone levels were not measured. The researchers did find an association between a girl’s first menstrual period and a specific measure in the thalamus, but they describe any role of sex hormones as speculative.
The researchers also had to combine two projects that used different scanners and imaging settings. Because one covered ages 9 to 21 and the other ages 22 to 36, the statistical adjustments for those differences fall at the same point as the transition into adulthood, so features of the age trajectories near that point, such as the slowdown seen in females, should be read with some caution. Comparisons between males and females within each age group are less affected.
“I think the biggest risk is interpreting these findings as showing that male and female brains are fundamentally different,” Khan said. “In reality, sex differences in the brain tend to be relatively small, with a lot of overlap between the sexes.”
She added that the timing of differences depends on which ages a study covers. “It is also important not to assume that adolescence is when these differences necessarily begin,” Khan noted. “Although the study found minimal differences early in childhood, sex-by-age effects can be highly sensitive to the particular age range that is being studied. As such, the findings do not necessarily mean that differences are entirely absent earlier in development.”
Balducci also cautioned against reading too much into what the scans can show.
“The findings do not show that differences in water diffusion directly cause differences in behavior or mental health,” Balducci pointed out. “Diffusion MRI provides an indirect measure of tissue microstructure.”
“Also, as with many sex differences, males and females vary on average,” Balducci added. “However, when multiple small differences are considered together, the overall profiles of males and females can become considerably more distinct.”
To address these remaining questions, both outside researchers point toward the need for investigations that capture earlier and more detailed developmental data.
“The most important next step would be a longitudinal study that repeatedly scans the same individuals before, during, and after puberty, while also measuring pubertal hormones and developmental phases,” Balducci told PsyPost. “That would help determine whether the observed diffusion changes track individual pubertal development and whether they are related to later mental-health outcomes.”
“It would be very interesting to see this approach being used in earlier stages of development, such as the prenatal period,” Khan said. “The prenatal period is another critical window for the emergence of sex differences in the brain. Moreover, male and female fetuses are exposed to different levels of sex hormones, which may contribute to differences in early brain development.”
The researchers say the sex-specific trajectories they describe could serve as a reference point for future studies exploring how departures from typical development might relate to mental health conditions.
The study, “Sex Differences in Human Deep Grey Matter Microstructure Emerge During Adolescence,” was authored by Christopher G. Filippi, Jay N. Giedd, Aziz M. Uluğ, and Richard Watts.

LONDON – A “severe drought” was declared in parts of southern England on Oct 15 by the British government, which said it took the decision following an “unprecedented period of extreme weather”.
The United Kingdom experienced its hottest summer on record in 2026, featuring several heatwaves and an exceptional drought that resulted from a lack of rainfall not seen since records began in 1836.
More than 80% of England is currently in a state of drought as it continues to experience below average levels of rainfall into the autumn months.
“Record-breaking summer heat and severe drought have put our water resources under immense pressure,” said Environment Agency head Philip Duffy.
The “severe drought” status was declared in the English counties of Cornwall, Devon, Dorset, Somerset, East Sussex and West Sussex. It is the worst stage triggered by “exceptionally low indicators over a long period of time”.
The declaration came as two major reservoirs in south-west England serving nearly 400,000 properties were below 20% of their storage capacity.
The Environment Agency said it “would expect reservoir storage to be around 75% for this time of year”.
South-east and south-west England have experienced their driest April to September period in more than a century, according to the government.
Scientists say climate change is intensifying weather events such as drought and heatwaves, resulting in records being broken more frequently.
As of last week, average reservoir levels across England stood at 54%, with the nation receiving just 10% of average October rainfall.
The government has urged water companies to monitor their water intake from natural resources and encouraged customers to cut their consumption, with usage restrictions already imposed in several regions.
“This level of drought is something we have not experienced for decades,” environment minister Angela Eagle said.
Months of drought have piled pressure on everyone from farmers and anglers to firefighters, who say tinder-dry conditions resulted in challenging wildfires this summer.

====================================================================================================

From underground wealth to diplomatic power: Azerbaijan’s energy strategy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:53:03 UTC
22:53:03 KST

Azerbaijani oil passes through Turkiye to Israel, its gas reaches European markets, and Emirati and Saudi capital finances its power plants. This network places Azerbaijan at the intersection of interests that do not always align. Baku has made itself relevant to several competing actors. Its harder task is to turn those relationships into lasting influence while preserving strategic autonomy.
Continued oil deliveries to Israel, despite Ankara’s trade restrictions, illustrate the challenge. Infrastructure, contracts and commercial interests can sustain connections across political divisions. Azerbaijan gains revenue and strategic importance, while becoming exposed to disputes among its partners.
Ankara and Tel Aviv: Two relationships, one route
Turkiye is both a political partner and Azerbaijan’s gateway to overseas markets. The Baku–Tbilisi–Ceyhan pipeline carries Caspian oil to the Mediterranean, while the Trans-Anatolian pipeline forms part of the Southern Gas Corridor, connecting Azerbaijani gas to Europe. These assets give the Baku–Ankara relationship a durability extending beyond immediate political positions.
The route’s importance to Israel is measurable. Azerbaijani crude accounted for 46.4 per cent of Israeli oil imports in 2025. Reuters reported in January 2026, citing Kpler data, that imports through Ceyhan reached approximately 94,000 barrels a day, up 31 per cent from the previous year. It also described vessels declaring alternative destinations and switching off tracking systems.
These shipments expose a gap between Ankara’s declared restrictions and the operation of a multinational oil supply chain. Cargo ownership, pipeline operations and final delivery involve different commercial and regulatory arrangements. In November 2024, Turkiye’s energy ministry stated that BTC operates under the 1999 intergovernmental agreement and associated host government agreements, and that its Turkish operator has no involvement in oil purchases or sales. It also denied loading cargoes with Israel as their declared destination.
The contrast with final-destination tracking data raises questions about enforcement and oversight. Distinguishing transit operations from oil sales explains part of the commercial structure; it does not settle the extent of the Turkish state’s authority or responsibility.
Energy supplies and defence cooperation give Baku’s relationship with Israel strategic depth. According to SIPRI, Israel supplied 69 per cent of Azerbaijan’s imports of major arms in 2016–2020. Azerbaijan occupies an important place in Israel’s oil supply, while Israeli arms have contributed to Baku’s military capabilities.
These interests raise the cost of political disengagement for both sides.
For Baku, the benefits come with political costs. Against the backdrop of the Gaza war, supplying Israel with oil raises serious ethical and political questions. Azerbaijan must manage a partnership important to its trade and defence while facing scrutiny from regional publics.
Iran: Geography needs workable agreements
Iran demonstrates another feature of Baku’s energy diplomacy: neighbours with political differences can still need each other’s infrastructure. The November 2021 gas swap agreement envisaged Iran receiving 1.5–2 billion cubic metres of Turkmen gas annually and delivering an equivalent volume to Azerbaijan. Existing networks enabled cooperation without constructing a new pipeline along the entire route.
READ: Azerbaijani president approves financial aid for Palestinian Embassy
The arrangement’s temporary suspension in early 2024 exposed its commercial limits. Trend reported at the time that Baku and Ashgabat had not agreed the terms for that year. Geography creates an opportunity for exchange; prices and contracts determine whether gas flows.
This lesson also applies to proposed connections with Nakhchivan. Routes through Iran and southern Armenia involve different geographical and legal arrangements. Their value depends on sovereignty, security and investment. For Tehran and Baku, durable cooperation requires clearly shared benefits and reliable implementation.
Gulf capital expands Baku’s options
Emirati and Saudi investment has widened Azerbaijan’s energy partnerships. Masdar announced the inauguration of the 230-megawatt Garadagh solar plant in October 2023. The 240-megawatt Khizi–Absheron wind plant, developed by Saudi Arabia’s ACWA Power, was officially inaugurated in January 2026. These projects anchor Gulf relationships in long-term economic assets.
Baku gains capital and a broader choice of partners. Gulf investors gain opportunities to expand in the Caucasus. The practical value of these partnerships will emerge through electricity production, grid development and domestic capabilities.
Renewables offer another benefit. The International Energy Agency notes that their expansion could conserve gas for exports and petrochemical production. Green investment therefore also supports the management of Azerbaijan’s export resources.
Europe and the credibility test
Europe adds weight to this network. The 2022 energy memorandum set an ambition to expand corridor capacity to deliver at least 20 billion cubic metres annually to the EU by 2027. Achieving it requires additional gas production, infrastructure and commercial commitments.
TAP’s March 2026 announcement confirmed that its first expansion phase was operational, adding 1.2 billion cubic metres of annually booked long-term capacity. This is a concrete advance, but it does not by itself establish a delivery pathway to the 2027 ambition. Meeting that target requires further transport capacity, additional exportable gas and firm purchasing commitments.
Reliable delivery strengthens Baku’s bargaining position. Political promises unsupported by the necessary investment risk weakening the credibility on which that position depends.
Today’s wealth, tomorrow’s power
The World Bank’s 2023 assessment placed oil and gas at around 90 per cent of Azerbaijan’s exports. Such concentration leaves the economy exposed to market volatility and the global energy transition.
Baku has made its resources matter abroad. Its next test is to build an economy that can sustain that influence as hydrocarbon revenues decline. Diplomatic power will endure only if Azerbaijan converts today’s resource income into productive capacity beyond the extractive sector.

One Night, Six Su-34s Hit—More Than Russia’s Entire Known 2026 Supply
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:46:32 UTC
22:46:32 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
One Night, Six Su-34s Hit—More Than Russia’s Entire Known 2026 Supply
Russia may have lost more Su-34s in one night at Borisoglebsk than it received during the entire year—a brutal production-versus-loss imbalance.
A Ukrainian Neptune missile strike on Russia’s Borisoglebsk airbase may have knocked out more Su-34 fighter-bombers in a single night than Moscow has received from its defense industry during all of 2026, according to an analysis by Defense Express on October 15.
Ukraine’s Navy reported that six Su-34s were struck during the overnight attack on the airfield in Russia’s Voronezh region.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The aircraft are among Russia’s principal platforms for launching guided aerial bombs fitted with UMPK glide-and-guidance kits against Ukrainian positions and frontline communities.
Defense Express argues that the scale of the reported losses is particularly significant when compared with Russia’s current production rate. Russian aircraft manufacturers typically deliver new tactical combat aircraft to the Aerospace Forces in small batches of two or three jets at a time.
Russia replacing Su-34s only a few at a time
In 2025, Russia publicly announced seven Su-34 deliveries totaling about 18 aircraft. Defense Express reviewed the available Russian announcements for 2026 and estimates that only four to five new Su-34s have been delivered so far this year.
That means the six aircraft Ukraine says were hit at Borisoglebsk would exceed all publicly known Su-34 deliveries to the Russian Aerospace Forces in 2026.
Why Su-34 loss matters for Russia’s glide-bomb campaign
The comparison is important because the Su-34 is not simply another combat aircraft in Russia’s inventory. Moscow relies heavily on the type to launch large numbers of guided glide bombs from outside the immediate reach of many Ukrainian frontline air defense systems.
Those weapons have become one of Russia’s most heavily used tools for striking Ukrainian defensive positions, towns, and cities close to the front.
At least nine Su-34s hit or lost in 2026
Defense Express also notes that Russia had already lost at least three Su-34s destroyed or damaged earlier in 2026, based on publicly available information. Adding the six aircraft reported hit at Borisoglebsk would bring the number of Su-34s affected this year to at least nine.
The Ukrainian Navy has not yet provided a detailed breakdown of how many of the six aircraft were destroyed versus damaged, and the full results of the strike remain under assessment.
Even at the lower figure, however, the losses would represent a substantial portion of Russia’s annual replacement capacity. At the six-aircraft figure reported by Ukraine’s Navy, one Neptune strike would have inflicted Su-34 losses exceeding Russia’s entire known production output for the year.
With at least nine Su-34s reportedly destroyed or damaged during 2026, the attrition is also gradually reducing the pool of aircraft available for Russia’s intensive guided-bomb campaign against Ukraine.
Previously, new satellite imagery showed the aftermath of Ukraine’s strike on Russia’s Borisoglebsk military airfield in the Voronezh region, with open-source intelligence analysts assessing that at least four Su-34 fighter-bombers were likely destroyed.

French supermarkets’ cyber insurance unlikely to cover food losses, insurers say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:46:00 UTC
22:46:00 KST

French supermarkets’ cyber insurance unlikely to cover food losses, insurers say
- French supermarkets lost food after a cyberattack hit cooling systems at about 350 stores, forcing fridges and freezers up to 50C and causing losses of tens of millions of euros.
- Insurers said standard cyber cover usually excludes physical losses like spoiled food, though claims may depend on software updates, contract terms, and whether a state actor was involved.
- Experts said the attack is a warning for retailers using connected equipment, and could push higher premiums and more insurance products that cover perishable stock and physical damage.
AI generated
LONDON/PARIS – French supermarkets are facing millions of euros in losses after a cyberattack forced them to throw away food, in a crisis that is not typically covered by cyber insurance policies but could still lead to higher premiums in future, insurers told Reuters.
Hackers – whose identity remains unknown – took control of cooling units at around 350 French supermarkets on the night of Oct 11, raising the temperature of internet-connected fridges and freezers to 50 deg C.
The attack’s total costs could add up to tens of millions of euros nationwide, Thierry Cotillard, president of Intermarche owner Les Mousquetaires, estimated on Oct 12, saying that supermarkets will begin a legal battle over who is responsible for the losses.
Cyber insurance typically does not cover physical losses from attacks and supermarkets’ claims could be affected if they lacked the latest software updates, four insurance brokers told Reuters.
If a state actor turns out to be behind the hack, it could complicate supermarkets’ insurance claims because cyber policies typically do not cover acts of war, according to a cyber underwriter, who requested anonymity as they were not authorised to speak publicly.
As companies have embraced the so-called Internet of Things, the growing connectivity of once largely mechanical equipment has exposed them to new security threats compounded by technological advancements including AI.
Between 2020 and 2025, cyberattacks in France, Germany, Italy and Spain cost over €300 billion (S$431 billion) in economic losses, insurance broker Howden estimates.
David Molony, head of cyber and financial sponsors at insurance broker Aon, said he recommended for companies in some sectors, including retail and pharmaceuticals, specific cover for perishable goods that need to be stored in tightly controlled physical conditions.
“Given the increasing digitisation of operational technology and connected systems, this is an area that businesses should review carefully,” he said.
Cyberattack, physical losses
Supermarkets’ cyber insurance policies may cover some costs, such as investigating internally or hiring PR advisors, but typically exclude physical losses.
Intermarche told AFP on Oct 12 that its insurance did not cover this type of incident. Asked by Reuters, Les Mousquetaires did not disclose its insurance arrangements. Carrefour, Monoprix, Cooperative U and E.Leclerc did not respond to requests for comment.
The hack affected fridges using software supplied by Danish firm Danfoss, as well as Copeland and Dixell, France’s cybersecurity agency said. Danfoss said many of the appliances were using out-of-date software or had “reached end of life and no longer receive software or security updates”.
Whether failing to update the software could affect the insurance depends on the details of the contract, insurers said.
Typically a company taking out a cyber insurance policy would declare its policy on software updates, for example committing to critical updates within a particular time period, said Emma Pleut, head of cyber for France at WTW.
Paul Gooch, deputy departmental head at Tokio Marine Kiln, said outdated software is not usually in itself a reason to reject a claim.
Higher premiums, new products
Retailers are increasingly seeking cyber insurance which covers physical damage, Aon’s Molony said. Such policies are already used in the energy, marine cargo, and defence sectors.
Aon has advised large retailers and other clients to get insurance that extends to “perishable stock”, and has recently arranged “high-value towers” – policies with large maximum payouts – in the London market with such cover included, Molony said.
Recent cyberattacks on retailers in Britain and France could also lead to higher premiums, underwriters said.
Asked whether European retailers could face higher insurance prices following cyberattacks, Sydonie Williams, head of international cyber risks at Beazley, said: “I absolutely think that could happen.”
TMK’s Gooch said that he expected greater focus on insurance products that specifically address physical losses from attacks.
“The recent cyberattack impacting refrigeration systems across France should act as a wake-up call to those who underestimate the potential physical consequences of cyber incidents,” he said. REUTERS

Who Are the Houthis and Why Are They Attacking Saudi Arabia’s Airports?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:43:41 UTC
22:43:41 KST

The European Union and Gulf Cooperation Council on Thursday announced the postponement of a joint summit set to take place in Saudi Arabia next week, amid safety concerns prompted by Houthi attacks on airports in the kingdom.
Citing the “continued attempts by the terrorist Houthi militia to target the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and its civilian infrastructure, which threatens the security and safety of innocent civilians,” the council said the Gulf-European Summit will be rescheduled.
The postponement comes after Yemen’s Houthi rebels on Wednesday vowed to forge ahead with the attacks on Saudi Arabia’s airports and oil facilities, just hours after striking oil giant Saudi Aramco’s headquarters.
“Operations toward Saudi depths will continue in the coming days,” said Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree, describing the locations as “legitimate targets” and framing their attacks as a direct response to Saudi strikes on Yemen. Saudi-led forces said they had intercepted a ballistic missile fired by the Houthis towards Riyadh on Wednesday and local journalists reported hearing “loud blasts” in the Saudi capital.
The escalation follows weeks of fighting between the Iran-backed Houthis and the Saudi-backed government of Yemen, shattering a four-year informal cease-fire in the country's civil war. The conflict reignited amid the widespread fallout of the U.S.-Iran war, bringing further instability to the Gulf region. In September, the Houthis said they had captured the strategic Perim Island that sits in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a critical maritime chokepoint. They also seized other islands in a bid to tighten their grip on the Red Sea coastline. Amid fears that a stronger Houthi position along the coast could further constrain global energy supplies, Saudi-backed forces recaptured key areas around the strait in early October. The Houthis have since ramped up their focus on Saudi Arabia’s airports and energy infrastructure.
Tuesday night’s attack on Aramco’s executive offices in the eastern city of Dhahran caused a limited fire, Saudi’s Ministry of Energy confirmed. No injuries were reported. TIME has reached out to Aramco and the Saudi government’s media office for further information. Saudi authorities said several missiles and drones had been intercepted elsewhere, and that falling debris injured four people in the capital of Riyadh. Saudi Arabia launched strikes on an oil depot on the outskirts of Yemen’s capital Sanaa on Tuesday, as the tit-for-tat attacks escalated.
The Saudi strike on the oil depot appeared to be in response to the Houthis’ attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Saturday that killed 13 people and left over 300 injured. A projectile hit that same airport on Sunday, killing one person, Saudi Arabia's General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) confirmed. The week before, an attack on Abha International Airport killed two people and wounded 28, said GACA.
Saudi Arabia is the world’s top purchaser of American weapons, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute. However, it is struggling to defend itself against the Houthis, who are positioned to strike deep into the kingdom. The Saudis are currently investigating how their defense systems failed to stop the deadly attacks. Experts cite the vast mass of Saudi land as one reason why defensive measures may have failed. The Saudi border with Yemen stretches more than 800 miles. “Expecting a country the size of Saudi Arabia to intercept every missile is simply unrealistic. No defense can guarantee complete protection,” said Ali Shihabi, a Saudi analyst, in an online post.
Operations at King Khalid remain suspended in the wake of the attacks. Etihad Airways, Qatar Airways, and Philippine Airlines are among the carriers to announce a suspension of flights to Riyadh.
The U.S. embassy in Riyadh has warned Americans in the country of “potential flight cancelations, airspace closures, and travel disruptions,” stipulating that U.S. government employees now require “special authorization” to use any airport in the country.
President Donald Trump on Tuesday said the Houthis “are behaving very badly.” In a Truth Social post, he continued, “I thought they learned their lesson a year ago when we bombed the hell out of them and, at their request, stopped,” seemingly referencing the U.S. strikes between March and May last year, which came in response to the Houthis attacking vessels in the Red Sea and disrupting global trade. Weeks after the strikes began, a cease-fire between the U.S. and the Houthis was reached via Omani mediations.
On Saturday, Trump suggested that the U.S. may join Saudi strikes on the Houthis. Asked about the possibility of U.S. strikes, a senior U.S. official told TIME that Washington is “in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the Republic of Yemen Government regarding regional stability and we will always fulfill our commitments to our partners.”
As tensions in the region continue to escalate, here’s what to know about the Houthis, their history with Saudi Arabia, and why they are attacking airports.
Who are the Houthis?
The Houthis are a political and armed group in Yemen that first emerged in the 1990s and have been fighting the country’s internationally recognized government for around two decades. The group is a revivalist movement for Zaidism, a branch of Shi‘ite Islam. The Zaidi muslim population in the country represents around 35% of the Yemeni population.
The Houthi movement was largely born from a transformation of the Believing Youth Forum (BYF), according to the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. The group became known as the Houthis in honor of their founder and leader, Hussein al-Houthi. Before he was killed by Yemeni forces in 2004, al-Houthi had developed the group into a more militarized movement. The group is now led by his brother, Abdul-Malik al-Houthi.
Civil war broke out in 2014 after the Houthis seized Sanaa, forcing the government to flee to the southern city of Aden. Since then, the group has been engaged in fighting against a Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen’s government. The Houthis currently have control of most of the country’s west, including Sanaa.
Experts compare the Houthis to authoritarian regimes on account of the social restrictions imposed in areas under the group’s control and alleged human rights abuses.
“The Houthis are dominated with very ideological and radical ideas, like a Zaidi ISIS. They have similarities also with the Taliban in terms of social control," says Mahmoud Shehrah, a Yemeni political analyst at London-based think tank Chatham House.
How are the Houthi rebels linked to Iran?
The Houthis hold strong ties to Iran, often taking action in line with Tehran’s objectives.
“Since 2009, Iran [has] started to speed up weapons supplies, training, but also a lot of funding to the Houthis,” says Farea Al-Muslimi, a Yemeni research fellow at Chatham House, noting that links between the two began as early as the 1990s.
The Houthis are often considered part of Iran’s proxy network, known as the “Axis of Resistance,” which also includes Hezbollah in Lebanon, the Islamic Resistance network in Iraq, and previously the Assad regime in Syria, until its collapse in December 2024.
In response to the Israel-Hamas war, the Yemeni militia launched several strikes on shipping vessels in the Red Sea, disrupting global trade in late 2023 and the early months of 2024. The U.S. and U.K. joined forces in January 2024 for a series of strikes on Houthi targets across Yemen in retaliation for the attacks on unarmed vessels. The U.S. carried out an additional campaign against Houthi targets later that year.
The Houthis entered the Iran war in March by firing a barrage of ballistic missiles at southern Israel. In the months since, the group’s advances along the Red Sea are widely considered to serve the interests of Iran. A Houthi blockade in the region against Saudi Arabia was declared in July, and several vessels have been attacked. The threat that the Houthis could bring another critical maritime chokepoint to a standstill, much like Iran has done with the Strait of Hormuz, could give Tehran significant leverage in its negotiations with Washington.
However, experts say it’s not entirely accurate to call the Houthis a direct proxy.
"The Houthis are one of the more independent regional allies of Iran in the Middle East. They have their own independent interests, even though their interests converge regionally and globally,” says Fawaz Gerges, a professor of international relations at the London School of Economics.
Even so, the Houthis have become increasingly vital for Iran. “With the fall of Assad, with the weakening of Hezbollah, the Houthis became the most important regional ally Iran has,” says Al Muslimi, pointing specifically toward the Houthis' ability to disrupt trade in the Red Sea.
What do the Houthis want?
The group’s goals have changed over time, as regional developments have unfolded, experts note.
“The Houthi's ultimate goal is to be a regional power,” says Al-Muslimi. With regard to the reignited civil war, the Houthis ultimately want an end to what they call a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory.
“The Houthis want to have the skies and the ports of the country open for trade, for goods and services,” says Gerges. “They want money to flow into the coffers of the Houthis.”
The civil war has had a disastrous effect on Yemen, with nearly half of the population in government-controlled areas facing high levels of acute food insecurity, according to the United Nations. “The current situation is very dire for the Yemeni population, but also for the ability of the Houthis to rule Yemen effectively,” says Gerges.
“The Houthis want to consolidate rule and regime. They want to be recognized as the legitimate government in Sanaa, as opposed to being considered a non-state actor,” he adds.
When did the Houthis and Saudi Arabia begin fighting again?
A cease-fire brokered by the United Nations in April 2022 largely held for over four years, before collapsing in July. The Houthis claimed Saudi Arabia had launched strikes on Sanaa Airport, targeting a Houthi delegation returning from Iran. In a move they framed as retaliatory, the Houthi rebels launched ballistic missiles toward Saudi Arabia.
“The Houthis saw this as a golden opportunity to change the balance of power against Saudi Arabia and Yemen itself and launch a lightning offensive,” says Gerges.
Following further strikes on Houthi targets later that month, the militia group began striking oil refineries in Saudi Arabia, belonging to the state-owned petroleum company Aramco.
In September, strikes on oil refineries and other related facilities ramped up, and Saudi Arabia’s airports became a target.
Why are the Houthis attacking Saudi airports?
Prior to the 2022 cease-fire, attacks on airports were largely considered a signature move of the Houthis.
In a highly-publicized attack, the group struck Abha International Airport in June 2019, injuring at least 26 people, Saudi authorities said. The strike earned international condemnation and was deemed a possible war crime by Human Rights Watch.
Now, after fatal strikes on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport, the Houthis have threatened to keep targeting airports. The main motivation behind these attacks is the economic and geopolitical pressure they apply to Saudi Arabia, experts say.
“The Houthis want to put severe pressure on the Saudi Arabia economy, airport infrastructure, and security,” says Shehrah. “They want to squeeze Saudi Arabia's arms to push them to a political settlement.”
The unrest threatens to have a strong economic and political impact on Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed Bin Salman's governance. The disruption is “costly” to him, says Al-Muslimi, who notes that Bin Salman is eager for Saudi Arabia to be seen as a “safe harbor.”
The financial and reputational damage of these strikes has also put the Saudi public on the frontline of the conflict. It’s a “shock, because it's the first time in years that such major attacks have targeted deep inside Saudi Arabia,” says Gerges.
“The Houthis are trying to exert tremendous pressure on the leaders of Saudi Arabia to force them to accept conditions for lifting the blockade on Yemen and recognizing their legitimacy,” he continues. “Although, I doubt that the Saudi leadership will concede to Houthi demands… this would be seen as a surrender and humiliation."

Thursday saw a timely withdrawal of the Summer Monsoon (Photo: PTI).
NEW DELHI: The southwest (summer) monsoon withdrew from the entire country on Thursday, exactly on the date of its normal withdrawal, while the northeast (winter) monsoon rainfall activity simultaneously commenced over part of south Peninsular India, IMD said.Summer monsoon normally starts withdrawing from west Rajasthan on Sept 17 and its withdrawal process ends on Oct 15. This year, the withdrawal started on Sept 19. Last year, the complete monsoon withdrawal happened by Oct 16.
A diagrammatic representation of the Southwest Monsoon withdrawal.
“With the onset of the northeast Monsoon, a wet spell with isolated heavy falls is likely over many parts of south Peninsular India till Oct 21,” said the Met department. The parts of south India that witnessed winter rainfall showers on Thursday include Tamil Nadu, Puducherry, coastal Andhra Pradesh, south interior Karnataka and Kerala.IMD has already predicted a ‘normal’ winter monsoon in south Peninsular India during the Oct-Dec period. Overall, south Peninsular India receives about 30% of its annual rainfall during the northeast monsoon season (Oct to Dec). Tamil Nadu, Puducherry and Karaikal receive approximately 48% of their annual rainfall during the season.
Normal winter monsoon rainfall this year may bring some relief to the region, which received the fourth-lowest summer monsoon rainfall since 1901 and the second-lowest since 2001.
Though the country as a whole recorded a deficit of nearly 13% during the June-Sept summer monsoon period — the fourth-lowest season since 2001 and 13th lowest since 1901 — the deficit in Karnataka was as high as 30% followed by 28% in Kerala, 25% in Andhra Pradesh and 20% in Tamil Nadu.

Germany's trade deficit with China set to hit record as automotive surplus collapses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:41:14 UTC
22:41:14 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
Germany's trade deficit with China is expected to exceed €100 billion ($112 billion) for the first time this year, driven by widening imbalances in key industrial sectors, the German Economic Institute (IW) said Thursday.
The deficit would be more than seven times its 2019 level of €14.1 billion if trade trends from the first half of 2026 continue through the rest of the year, the institute said.
Germany imported almost 2.5 times as much from China as it exported to the country in the first six months. The projected annual deficit would surpass the previous record of about €90 billion in 2025.
German goods exports to China are projected to be roughly 25% below their 2019 level, while imports from China are expected to be about 62% higher.
Core industrial sectors under pressure
The automotive industry accounts for almost 24% of the projected increase in the deficit since 2019, making it the largest individual contributor.
Germany's automotive trade surplus with China is expected to shrink from more than €23 billion in 2019 to about €1 billion this year. Automotive exports to China are projected to fall 54% over that period, while imports of Chinese vehicles and parts are expected to rise more than 475%.
The trade deficit in electrical equipment is forecast to exceed €24 billion, compared with €4.8 billion in 2019.
Machinery manufacturing is also expected to record its first trade deficit with China, at slightly more than €1 billion, reversing a surplus of nearly €10 billion in 2019.
Energy-intensive industries, including chemicals, paper, glass and metals, account for only around €4 billion of the widening gap, IW said, arguing that higher energy costs explain only a small part of the deterioration.
The institute attributed the shift to China's technological advances and what it described as competitive distortions, including substantial subsidies and a sharply undervalued currency.
IW foreign trade expert Jurgen Matthes called for domestic reforms and broad countervailing tariffs that could be implemented quickly.
He urged the European Council to ask the European Commission to develop a new trade instrument, arguing that such measures would restore fair competition.

Ukraine's Ministry of Defence has received 389 applications from foreign manufacturers of military equipment and weapons seeking to register on TrophyLab, a unified web portal for research into Russian equipment.
Source: Ukraine's Ministry of Defence
Details: More than 650 applications have been submitted in total. Ukrainian manufacturers, military units and government institutions can also register on the portal.
The Defence Ministry said TrophyLab contains data on captured Russian weapons that engineers, scientists and defence technology manufacturers in Ukraine and partner countries can use.
The database is populated by units of Ukraine's defence forces, Defence Intelligence of Ukraine, the Security Service of Ukraine and specialised research institutions.
"Every registered researcher can request a sample or a fragment of it for independent study," the ministry said.
Users can access research findings online or request weapon samples for offline analysis.
To gain access to TrophyLab, applicants must complete a form on the platform's website. The Defence Ministry explained that applicants are screened for links to Russia, Ukrainian or international sanctions, and compliance with other mandatory criteria.
Once they pass the checks, users gain access to the catalogue of Russian weapons and the findings of research into them.
The Defence Ministry said that access to TrophyLab enables faster and safer exchanges of information on Russian weapons, helping accelerate the development of effective countermeasures for Ukraine's defence forces. It also contributes to international security and strengthens the defence capabilities of partner countries.
Background:
- As of late August, more than 130 Ukrainian weapons manufacturers and over 300 foreign companies had applied for access to TrophyLab.

Turkish army gets three more E-ZPT electric armored carriers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:38:48 UTC
22:38:48 KST

- MKE delivered three more E-ZPT electric armored personnel carriers, rebuilt from M113s, to the Turkish Land Forces Command on Oct. 15.
- The E-ZPT carries seven people, travels about 150 km on battery power and up to 650 km with its onboard generator.
Türkiye’s state-owned defense company MKE has delivered three more E-ZPT electric armored personnel carriers to the Turkish Land Forces Command, adding to a small fleet of rebuilt M113s that run on battery power instead of a diesel engine alone.
MKE announced the handover in a post on X on Oct. 15, describing the E-ZPT as Türkiye’s first electric armored personnel carrier. The company said the vehicle’s all-electric drive gives it lower acoustic and thermal signatures, making it harder for enemy troops and sensors to hear or spot, and that maintenance and repair costs are lower than for conventional vehicles.
The E-ZPT is a modernized version of the M113, the tracked American-designed troop carrier that has served in the Turkish military for decades. MKE kept the original armored hull and replaced the powertrain with electric motors fed by battery packs mounted on both sides of the vehicle, an approach that lets the army reuse existing hulls.
On battery power alone, the vehicle can travel about 150 km (93 miles), Turdef reported, and an onboard diesel generator that recharges the batteries on the move stretches total range to 650 km (404 miles). MKE said fast charging takes the batteries from 20% to 80% in 1.5 hours. The E-ZPT carries seven people, including a driver, a commander, a gunner and four more crew members, and is armed with a 12.7 mm remote-controlled weapon station.
The vehicle has a combat weight of around 15 tonnes and can carry 2.5 tonnes of payload. Before acceptance, MKE put it through a qualification program that began in October 2024 and covered about 3,000 km (1,860 miles) of driving on asphalt and off-road terrain, along with climbs on 60% gradients, 30% side slopes, trench crossings and testing in hot and cold weather.
Türkiye’s Ministry of National Defense announced the delivery of the first serial-production E-ZPT in January 2026, and MKE handed over its first batch of three vehicles to the Land Forces in July. The program calls for 50 E-ZPTs in total, C Savunma reported, and MKE has also developed an armed version of the electric M113 called the E-ZMA.
With the latest handover, MKE has now delivered two batches of three E-ZPTs to the Turkish Land Forces this year, as it works toward the planned fleet of 50 electric carriers.

15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
European Parliament President Roberta Metsola on Thursday criticized proposed cuts in the EU's next long-term budget, saying reductions in funding for civil protection, research and strategic infrastructure, and defense were incompatible with the bloc's growing challenges.
Speaking at a news conference on the sidelines of the European Council summit in Brussels, Metsola warned that the proposed cuts risk undermining the balance between new priorities and traditional EU policies.
"We cannot agree on Europe's ambitions and then cut the means to achieve them," she said.
Metsola highlighted a proposed 35% cut to civil protection funding, a 10% cut to the Horizon research programme, and a 14% cut to funding for strategic infrastructure and defense.
"This, in our opinion, doesn't fly for us," she said.
Her remarks came amid an ongoing dispute between member states and the European Parliament on the bloc's next multiannual financial framework (MFF), with disagreements about funding priorities and how to finance the union's growing ambitions.
The EU aims to reach a political agreement on the 2028-2034 MFF by the end of 2026, allowing the necessary legislative acts to be adopted in 2027 and ensuring the new budget takes effect Jan. 1, 2028.
Deep divisions among member states and disagreements with parliament, however, could complicate the timeline.
Metsola said parliament was ready to work with EU leaders to reach a compromise but stressed that lawmakers would not simply endorse an agreement reached by member states.
"The parliament is not a rubber stamp and never will be," she said, adding that securing the necessary majority in the assembly would be challenging.
She noted that approving the next long-term budget would require 361 votes in parliament, stressing that any agreement must have the support of directly elected representatives.
Metsola also urged the introduction of new EU resources to help finance the next budget, saying it would ease pressure on national budgets and prevent the financial burden from being passed on to future generations.

Why Azerbaijan, Bahrain's Baku meetings with President Herzog are important - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15

22:38:16 KST

Israel’s President Isaac Herzog met in Baku on Wednesday with Azerbaijan's President Ilham Aliyev and Bahrain’s Foreign Minister Abdullatif bin Rashid al-Zayani during his attendance at the seventh summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (CICA).
These meetings, of importance for Israel, come amid a number of diplomatic and other recent successes, such as Colombia inaugurating its embassy in Jerusalem. Colombia’s Foreign Minister Omar Bula Escobar came to Israel for the event. Additionally, on October 8, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu met with Paraguay's Vice President, Pedro Alliana, in Jerusalem.
These are historic days for the Jewish state. Three years after the October 7 attacks, Israel is increasing its engagement with several countries. This comes as the media discusses whether fighting will resume against the Islamic Republic. In this context, the meetings between Herzog and the president of Azerbaijan, as well as Bahrain’s foreign minister, are important. Azerbaijan is a rising power in the Caucasus, with influence that extends to Europe, Central Asia, and beyond. It also borders Iran.
Bahrain is an important Gulf country. It joined the Abraham Accords in 2020. About the Wednesday meeting between Herzog and Aliyev, the President’s Office, in a statement distributed by Israel’s Government press Office, noted that Herzog had attended the summit “at the invitation of President Aliyev” and that he “thanked President Aliyev for the warm welcome and noted that Azerbaijan is a model of stability and an important and respected voice in the international community.”
Azerbaijan is an important country for many reasons
The leaders looked at “ways to deepen the strategic relationship between Israel and Azerbaijan, which is rooted in mutual respect, shared interests, and the deep historical ties between the two peoples. They also discussed recent regional developments and their countries’ shared commitment to stability and security in the region.”
Azerbaijan is strategically important: It has been reaching out to Syria recently, and it is a close friend of Turkey’s. Turkey has tended to be critical of Israel; and Israel has concerns about Turkey’s role in Syria. Baku can potentially play an important role in reducing tensions between the two.
Herzog’s office noted that “President Aliyev thanked President Herzog for his words of appreciation regarding Azerbaijan’s chairmanship of CICA, and emphasized that his country continues to work to strengthen mutual trust among CICA member states and to advance practical cooperation between them.”
Herzog said, “Israel and Azerbaijan share a unique relationship, one that has been developed over many years and has proven its importance in complex times as well. I thank President Ilham Aliyev for our partnership and for the open dialogue between us, and I believe we have much more to achieve together: strengthening the ties between our peoples, expanding our cooperation, and creating new opportunities for generations to come.”
In the meeting with Bahrain, Herzog also brought up the importance of strengthening the Abraham Accords. The October 7 massacre and the ensuing Israel-Hamas War created a backdrop against which it was difficult for expansion of the accords to take place. Currently, though, there are many opportunities.
“President Herzog emphasized the great importance Israel attaches to its relations with the Kingdom of Bahrain and commended the courageous leadership of His Majesty King Hamad bin Isa Al Khalifa and the Government of Bahrain. The President conveyed his warmest wishes to His Majesty the King and the Bahraini people,” Herzog’s office said.
The important relationship between Israel and Azerbaijan
It is worth recalling the important relationship between Israel and Azerbaijan that has developed over the last decades. They established diplomatic relations in April 1992, shortly after Azerbaijan gained independence, following the collapse of the Soviet Union.
The relationship expanded over the years: Energy trade and defense sales have been important building blocks. Azerbaijan has become a modern military power and has showcased Israeli defense technology during events in the past. In 2023, Azerbaijan opened an embassy in Israel. George Deek played a key role as ambassador to Azerbaijan from 2018 to 2025.
Bahrain-Israel ties are also important, though less in the spotlight than Israel-UAE ties or even Israel-Morocco ties. However, Bahrain is an important part of the Abraham Accords. It is a cautious country, and this caution means it is not often in the spotlight in the Gulf. However, it has also suffered from threats during the recent Iran conflict. Israel opened an embassy in Manama in 2021, following the signing of the Abraham Accords. Its first ambassador, Eitan Na’eh, was a former ambassador to Azerbaijan and Turkey – as well as Israel’s first envoy to the United Arab Emirates in 2021. (He died of a heart attack in January.)
There has been cooperation between Israel and Bahrain in recent years.
The meetings in Baku are important in terms of the larger regional context. Israeli defense companies also had a major role at the Marrakesh Air Show this week in Morocco. As such, there is a growing perception that Israeli ties with various Muslim countries are now improving and have become more public than they were in the past several years.

Israelis and Diaspora Jews are donating more since Oct. 7, says JGive founder
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:37:47 UTC
22:37:47 KST

Charitable giving to and within Israel has not fallen since the surge that followed October 7, but has kept rising, JGive founder and CEO Ori Ben-Shlomo said on The Deep Dive this week.
Ben-Shlomo said the platform expects to finish this year at more than four times its pre-war volume, with over 250,000 Israeli and Diaspora donors giving about NIS 500 million.
"It changed society," he said. He added that Israelis now see civil society organizations as a "must-have" rather than a nice extra. Ben-Shlomo, a lawyer who was general counsel at a major Israeli media group, founded JGive after serving in Gaza as a reservist during Operation Protective Edge in 2014. There, he said, he saw how much donated goodwill was lost to poor coordination.
On October 7, as calls came in from New York, Los Angeles and London, JGive helped thousands of charities raise emergency funds. It also set up a national emergency fund whose leadership included a former Israel Air Force commander and a former Supreme Court justice. The fund began with basic needs, such as food, clothing and medication for evacuees from the kibbutzim, including Holocaust survivors, before moving on to education and rehabilitation.
The way Diaspora Jews give has also changed, Ben-Shlomo said. Their grandparents' generation wrote checks to large institutions. Younger donors want to give "without the middleman," to specific causes they have researched themselves, and increasingly alongside Israelis rather than simply to them. "Israel is not a young state," he noted. "We're close to 80." He said young people are now among JGive's top donors, the same group that major charities had once told him they could not reach.
Israeli elections two weeks away
With Israel's elections two weeks away, the conversation turned to Diaspora Jews who feel tied to the country's future but cannot vote. Ben-Shlomo argued that giving is "the best way" for them to have a say, and said it does more to shape the country than politics does. "Politics divides people, and giving connects people," he said. He also addressed the strain that rising antisemitism has placed on Jewish communities abroad, which must fund their own security while still supporting Israel. He said those donors have shifted the balance toward their own communities without stopping their support for Israel, and argued that the Israeli government and Israeli donors should now help Diaspora communities in return.
Ben-Shlomo described working with Israel's Tax Authority to introduce donor-advised funds, a tool familiar in the US, and to allow donations of stocks and other assets, which he called "a game changer." He said further reform is still needed, including ceilings on tax benefits for major donors. He framed the larger task as building what he called Israel's "fourth power." After defense, the economy and technology, he said, the country now needs the strength of a society "that makes sure no one is left behind," built from the ground up, much like the start-up nation.
Asked whether he is optimistic about the next generation, he answered with the story of a reserve officer badly wounded in Lebanon who, while still in rehabilitation, organized a campaign for a fellow patient.
