Europe distinguishes Iranians from Iran. Why not Israelis from Israel? - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:37:40 UTC
22:37:40 KST

Europe knows how to condemn a government without condemning everyone it governs.
When Iranians take to the streets, European leaders do not tell them they are responsible for the Islamic Republic. They condemn the regime and express solidarity with the protesters. Europe sanctions North Korea while speaking of North Koreans as victims of repression. It condemns Hezbollah without pretending that Lebanon and Hezbollah are the same thing.
The distinction has been particularly clear in the Palestinian case. After the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led massacres in Israel, the European Union (EU) repeatedly separated Hamas, the Palestinian Authority, and the Palestinian people. Josep Borrell, then the EU’s foreign policy chief, warned against collective punishment and reminded Europeans that “not all the Palestinian people are terrorists.”
Russia complicates the picture. Even before the invasion of Ukraine, the European Parliament distinguished “between the Russian people and President Putin’s regime.” After the invasion, ordinary Russians faced visa restrictions and exclusions from sports and culture. Still, European leaders continued to talk about Russian President Vladimir Putin’s war and Putin’s regime.
None of these comparisons is exact. Iran, Russia, and North Korea are authoritarian states. Hezbollah is a terrorist organization whose weapons answer to no electorate. Hamas won Palestinian elections in 2006 and has not faced voters in two decades.
Israel is different. It is a democracy. Israelis choose their governments.
And this is where things get uncomfortable
Across parts of Europe, Israeli universities are treated as extensions of the state. Israeli artists and cultural institutions face calls for exclusion. Broadcasters withdrew from the 2026 Eurovision Song Contest because Israel’s public broadcaster, KAN, was taking part. There is growing pressure to keep Israeli athletes out of international competitions.
Official Europe is more careful. When European Council President António Costa supported proposed measures against Israel in September 2025, he stressed that they were “not aimed at the Israeli people,” but were a response to the government’s actions in Gaza and the West Bank.
Outside Brussels, that distinction is less secure. In debates over universities, culture, broadcasting, and sports, the categories slide into one another. The Israeli government becomes Israel. Israel becomes its institutions. Its institutions become its citizens.
Why? The obvious answer is democracy.
ISRAELIS VOTE, pay taxes, and elect the politicians who govern them. Many serve in the military. Perhaps Europeans are, therefore, entitled to hold Israelis responsible in a way they would hesitate to hold Iranians responsible for the ayatollahs.
There is something to that argument. Israelis cannot have democracy both ways. We cannot celebrate democratic choice when it produces governments we like, and then pretend that governments we dislike have nothing to do with the society that elected them. The death, displacement, and destruction in Gaza resulted from decisions made by an elected Israeli government. European anger at Israel did not come from nowhere.
But there is a long distance between political responsibility and collective guilt.
Hundreds of thousands of Israelis protested against the judicial overhaul. Israelis have demonstrated for the hostages and demanded accountability for October 7. Israel’s research universities went on strike against the judicial overhaul in 2023. Supporting a war does not mean supporting everything done in its course.
And what about the roughly one-fifth of Israeli citizens who are Arab, many among the government’s strongest critics? If responsibility follows automatically from an Israeli passport, where do they fit?
Citizens in a democracy have a relationship with state power. But they are not the state.
Still, democracy is not the whole explanation. Israel occupies a peculiar place in the European imagination. It is not European, but neither does it feel entirely foreign.
Much of its early political leadership came from Europe. Its universities, political parties, trade unions, legal traditions, and public culture were deeply influenced by European ideas. The Holocaust sits at the heart of both Israeli political memory and Europe’s understanding of its postwar self. Israel participates extensively in European research, culture, trade, and sports.
That closeness does not always work in Israel’s favor.
When many Europeans look at Israel’s rule over Palestinians, they see things they recognize from their own history: a powerful state ruling another people, settlements, contested land, and a profound imbalance of power. Much of the language now used to describe Israel comes from Europe’s arguments about its past: colonialism, occupation, settler colonialism.
Europe spent centuries ruling other peoples, building settlements, drawing borders, and calling domination civilization. Much of postwar Europe was built around the determination not to be that Europe anymore.
Israel, therefore, does something unusual. It does not confront Europe only with the Middle East. It confronts Europe with Europe.
Perhaps that is part of what makes Israel so difficult for Europeans to discuss. It is familiar enough to be judged by European standards, yet different enough to carry meanings beyond the country itself. Arguments about Israel become arguments about colonialism, nationalism, war, memory, and Europe’s own past.
The settler-colonial argument takes this further. If the problem is understood not as the policy of one government but as something built into Israeli society itself, the Israeli citizen becomes part of the structure being condemned. The distinction between government and people begins to disappear.
THIS DID NOT begin with Gaza. Before October 7, an EU Agency for Fundamental Rights survey found that 75% of Jewish respondents felt people held them responsible for the Israeli government’s actions because they were Jewish. The war did not invent this tendency. It intensified it.
Government becomes country. Country becomes citizens. Citizens become Jews.
Yet democracy should push us in the opposite direction. Elections create responsibility, but they also reveal disagreement. A democracy contains those who voted for the government and those who voted against it, majorities and minorities, supporters and protesters.
None of this means Israel should be shielded from criticism. Israeli governments should answer for their decisions. Israeli institutions should be judged for what they do. Israelis who commit crimes should be held responsible.
But responsibility should be attached to conduct.
That should also guide European decisions about “Horizon Europe,” cultural programs, universities, and artists. If an Israeli institution is complicit in wrongdoing, make the case and act accordingly. If an individual has done something that warrants exclusion, demonstrate it. Nationality itself should not become the evidence.
And Israelis cannot demand this distinction only for themselves.
Palestinians are not Hamas. Criticism of Israeli policy is not necessarily hostility toward Israel. Hostility toward Israel is not automatically antisemitism. If we insist that Europeans distinguish between Israel and Israelis, we must be equally serious about distinguishing between Palestinians and those who claim to act in their name.
Otherwise, this is not a principle. It is simply an argument we use when it suits us.
Europe knows how to make these distinctions, imperfectly but deliberately.
It should be able to make them with Israel too.
The writer is a senior fellow at the Jewish People Policy Institute and a professor of European studies and international relations in the Department of Politics and Government at Ben-Gurion University of the Negev.

‘Hope is still mandatory’: Israel’s resilience three years after October 7 - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:37:39 UTC
22:37:39 KST

Over two years into my second term as Israel’s ambassador to the United Nations, I have heard countless speeches and witnessed countless moments. But some words stay with you.
“Hope is still mandatory.”
Those words were spoken by Rachel Goldberg-Polin, the mother of Hersh Goldberg-Polin, who was murdered in Hamas captivity. A few months ago, we invited Rachel to address an international gathering of counterterrorism agency heads from UN member states in New York, making her the first Israeli to address the conference in years.
I remember listening to her and asking myself: After everything she has endured, how can she still hold on to hope? The answer became clear: resilience.
Resilience: The secret to holding onto hope after October 7
Three years ago, on October 7, Hamas invaded Israel and tried to destroy the Jewish state.
It murdered families in their homes, burned people alive in safe rooms, slaughtered young people at a music festival, and fired thousands of rockets at Israeli communities. It dragged 251 men, women, and children into Gaza and subjected them to unimaginable cruelty.
October 7 changed Israel forever. It wounded us. It left scars that will never fully disappear. But it did not break us.
Three years later, the defining story of October 7 is not only what Hamas did to us. It is the resilience we showed afterward. We chose to rebuild.
Resilience is part of our DNA. Our history has taught us that resilience is more than surviving tragedy. It is the strength to rise from it, rebuild, and choose life.
We have seen that resilience throughout our history. We saw it in the generations that survived persecution and exile. We saw it in Holocaust survivors who, after losing everything, dedicated themselves to rebuilding Jewish life and building the State of Israel.
On October 7, we saw that same resilience. Parents protected their children. Soldiers rushed into battle. Ordinary citizens became heroes, saving strangers and carrying the wounded to safety.
While Israel fought against its enemies, its people refused to leave its hostages behind. That determination showed who we are: a nation that leaves nobody behind. A nation that couldn’t move forward until all our loved ones came home.
Eliya Cohen and Ziv Abud exemplified that resilience better than most. On October 7, the couple was at the Nova music festival when Hamas terrorists attacked. They fled to a bomb shelter, where they faced grenades and gunfire. Abud survived by hiding among the bodies of those who had been murdered. Cohen was taken hostage and spent 505 days in captivity.
For months, Abud advocated relentlessly for Cohen’s return. When Cohen finally came home, their ordeal was not over. They had to begin the difficult process of rebuilding lives that were shattered by an experience neither of them should ever have endured.
And yet, they chose to build. On August 19, they celebrated their wedding and the future they had fought so hard to reach. Their marriage was not a denial of their pain or an attempt to leave October 7 behind. It was a declaration that what happened to them would not determine the rest of their lives. They chose each other. They chose a future. They chose life.
This year, I invited Abud and Cohen to speak together for the first time as a married couple at the United Nations. I wanted their resilience to be heard.
Their story is also the story of thousands of Israelis carrying invisible wounds. It is the families who spent sleepless nights with their children in bomb shelters, and the parents who still flinch when they hear a siren. It is the soldiers who lost lifelong friends and returned from battle with life-altering injuries. It is the families who lost sons and daughters and nevertheless found the strength to keep raising their children and moving forward.
Their sacrifices were not in vain. Three years after October 7, Israel is stronger than it was on that terrible morning. We have confronted threats from Hamas, Hezbollah, Iran, and other forces determined to destroy us. We have strengthened our alliances and expanded our circle of peace.
Despite these accomplishments, Israel still faces challenges. Hamas and Hezbollah must be disarmed. Iran continues to seek Israel’s destruction.
At the United Nations, the campaign to demonize Israel continues. The country that suffered one of the worst terrorist attacks of the 21st century now faces accusations of genocide, war crimes, and starvation. Those who should be defending the truth have instead turned the victim into the accused.
Today, we have one message: Israel is still here. We are raising our children, building our communities, developing our hi-tech sector, strengthening our alliances, and expanding our circle of peace.
After everything we have endured, we continue to choose life.
Three years later, we remember the victims. We honor the survivors. We stand with the families who continue to carry unimaginable pain because hope is still mandatory.
We do what the Jewish people have always done. We rise. We rebuild. And we choose life.
The writer is the Israeli ambassador to the United Nations.

Saudi Arabia could help unlock the next phase of Trump's Gaza plan - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:37:30 UTC
22:37:30 KST

In September 2025, US President Donald Trump introduced the 20-point Comprehensive Plan to End the Gaza Conflict, which established a framework for ending the war, returning the remaining hostages, providing humanitarian assistance, establishing transitional governance, and ultimately demilitarizing Gaza and facilitating its reconstruction.
On November 17, 2025, the UN Security Council adopted this plan through Resolution 2803, which also welcomed the establishment of the Board of Peace.
However, nearly one year after the ceasefire, the UN reported in September 2026 that Hamas and other armed groups had not disarmed, the transitional governance arrangements had not yet become operational in Gaza, and the International Stabilization Force had not deployed.
The main obstacle has been disagreement over the sequencing and implementation of the second phase.
While the US and Israel insist on dismantling Hamas as an initial step according to the plan, and before a complete withdrawal of the IDF, leaders of Arab states maintain that the second phase must include immediate delivery of humanitarian assistance, rehabilitation of critical infrastructure, and a clear path to the two-state solution.
These gaps have created a significant financing problem, as the failure to establish the security and governance conditions has prevented reconstruction from proceeding.
On February 19, 2026, Saudi Arabia joined eight other founding donors in signing the Declaration of the Founding Donors to the Board of Peace.
Riyadh committed to providing core financial support to implement the plan and pledged $1 billion toward peace and reconstruction.
However, it has since withheld these funds, making full delivery of humanitarian aid and a clear path to a two-state solution preconditions for its support.
The impasse therefore threatens to prolong humanitarian suffering, delay reconstruction, and perpetuate the broader regional instability that emerged from the Gaza war.
Saudi Arabia is the country best placed to break the diplomatic deadlock and restore US credibility in the region. Saudi Arabia has agreed that proceeding to phase two won’t happen as long as Hamas holds military capabilities. Additionally, strengthening Saudi security serves a core US interest in regional stability, which is why the two countries signed the Strategic Defense Agreement in November 2025.
Houthis pose a threat to Saudi Arabia
Saudi Arabia faces an increasingly serious security challenge from the Houthis in Yemen. By September, the Houthis escalated attacks on Riyadh. While Pakistan and Turkey remained cautious about the extent of their involvement under the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, Saudi Arabia may seek alternatives.
Since the US has already considered a military campaign against the Houthis, Washington should now go further and turn that readiness into a more strategic course of action that serves long-term US interests. It should offer Riyadh security guarantees that are stronger than the 2025 agreement and more credible than the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement.
In exchange, Riyadh would recommit to implementing phase two of the 20-point plan without further preconditions.
The subsequent escalation of Houthi activity and the abstention of Pakistan and Turkey from taking an active part in the defense alliance have exposed the limits of relying exclusively on regional partners.
Israel and Saudi Arabia have already shown an intention to collaborate and share intelligence against the Houthis. The US could exploit Pakistan’s and Turkey’s hesitancy by offering Saudi Arabia an alternative: a US-Saudi joint defense agreement that commits US forces to direct action against the Houthis while deepening the US-mediated channel for Israeli-Saudi security cooperation.
This course of action would demonstrate that the US remains the only credible security guarantor capable of assisting Saudi Arabia’s national security. A joint defense treaty with the US would give the Saudis the ultimate strategic “carrot.” This would give Riyadh the political cover to translate its commitment into concrete action on phase two of the 20-point Comprehensive Plan.
Bringing the US and Saudi Arabia into direct ties through a joint defense agreement could lead to the most desirable outcome in aggregate terms.
Sharing responsibilities with Israel, which has a strong incentive to eliminate the Houthi threat, the US could create a framework for gradual engagement, allowing Israel to serve as their frontliner in the Middle East. In other words, the US could devise a plan of escalating measures, providing an initial, indirect response through intelligence, weaponry, and advanced defense systems, while intervening actively only when necessary.
This framework could also strengthen Saudi-Israeli ties and improve the prospects for normalization, which Washington has declared a US national security interest.
Finally, by giving Saudi Arabia incentives to reengage with the 20-point plan, the US could restore the plan’s credibility, encourage other members of the Board of Peace to follow suit, and strengthen regional stability.
This course of action reflects the understanding that a two-state pathway is a possible outcome that should be discussed simultaneously through diplomatic means, but not as a precondition for implementing the plan. It depends on both sides implementing the plan in good faith, which would create the conditions for Palestinian self-determination.
The writer is an Israeli attorney and an MA candidate in international relations at Johns Hopkins University, School of Advanced International Studies, specializing in International economics and finance. The writer has a comprehensive security background, with about eight years of service as an officer and combatant commander in the IDF.

Al Jazeera probe exposes fake viewing numbers for Israeli counter-film
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:35:46 UTC
22:35:46 KST

Al Jazeera probe exposes fake viewing numbers for Israeli counter-film
An Al Jazeera data investigation raises questions about claims that an Israeli counter-documentary to NAZA got 40mn views.
An Al Jazeera investigation has exposed holes in claims that an Israeli counter-film to the acclaimed documentary NAZA achieved more than 44 million views. By examining domain registries, web archives, source code, and three independent traffic tools, the investigation exposed the fabricated numbers adopted by official Israeli entities to promote the film.
The original award-winning film, NAZA, draws on testimony from 24 unnamed Israeli military whistleblowers, accusing the army of using artificial intelligence-powered targeting systems to kill numerous civilians in Gaza. The documentary takes its name from the Israeli military term for civilian casualties expected in air strikes. After winning the special jury prize at the Venice International Film Festival and receiving a historic 25-minute standing ovation, the film was scheduled to screen in 56 countries.
Official backlash
The success of the original documentary triggered a political storm in Israel. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu demanded that the chief of general staff, the head of the Shin Bet, and the attorney general launch a comprehensive investigation into the participants and prosecute them for information security violations.
The film’s directors, Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, were accused of treason, and Netanyahu and Culture Minister Miki Zohar threatened to revoke their Israeli citizenship.
Network of domains
To counter the film’s global resonance, opponents created a counter-film. On September 16, just days after NAZA premiered, the domain nazadocumentary.com was registered via Cloudflare, with the owner’s details hidden.
The Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine revealed the site initially disguised itself as the official NAZA website, listing the directors’ names and information on screenings and press. However, it described the film as exposing the systems behind the calculated mass killing of terrorists in Gaza. By September 30, this deceptive page vanished, replaced by a new title, “NAZA: The Real Story”.
The individuals behind the 49-minute counter-film are Ariel Averbuch, Roy Danino, and Hagai Gutman, who claimed the work was self-funded. Later, two more domains, whatisnaza.com and watchnaza.com, were registered to redirect users to the counter-film.
The fake counter
By the morning of October 14, the nazadocumentary.com website’s counter displayed 43,758,421 views, without disclosing the source of the number or how it was calculated.
Public platforms told a drastically different story. The full 49-minute version of the film on its official YouTube channel had not exceeded 130,000 views by the same date. This means the website’s counter displayed roughly 336 times the actual viewership. The YouTube channel had fewer than 2,000 subscribers, and the film’s account on X had only 170 followers.
Independent traffic analysis platforms confirmed the discrepancy. The US-based platform Semrush estimated the site’s total visits by October 8 at about half a million. Israeli-founded Similarweb estimated only 326 visits for September. Furthermore, the film’s domains were absent from the Tranco list of the world’s top one million visited domains.
Discrepancies and code
An examination of the page’s source code revealed that the element displaying the huge number was internally tagged as “visitors” but displayed to users as “views”. The number is delivered directly from the site’s server, making its calculation method invisible from the outside. Upon opening the page, the counter begins at 97 percent of its value and counts up for three seconds, creating the illusion of a live counter.
Additionally, the site collects actual viewing data without publishing it, sending a “watch-tracker” file after about 25 seconds of video playback to identify the viewing session and parts watched, leaving it unknown whether the counter is based on this data.
State promotion
Despite the seemingly fabricated metrics, official Israeli accounts spearheaded the promotion of the counter-film. The Israeli Embassy in Washington promoted it on October 3 on social media.
Tzipi Hotovely, head of Israel’s National Public Diplomacy Directorate, awarded the three creators certificates of recognition for countering the original film. Hotovely said the film had garnered tens of millions of views, transforming an unsupported, fabricated number into an official talking point.
This elaborate digital campaign unfolds against the backdrop of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, which began in October 2023. Since the conflict started, Israel has killed at least 74,000 Palestinians, including at least 21,000 children, according to Gaza’s Ministry of Health.

Chinese sand-control pioneer Yin Yuzhen named among FAO's 100 women heroes
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
21:34:08 CST
22:34:08 KST

Chinese sand-control pioneer Yin Yuzhen (2nd L, front) attends a ceremony in Rome, Italy, Oct. 15, 2026. Chinese sand-control pioneer Yin Yuzhen was named on Thursday among the FAO's 100 Women Heroes in Agrifood Systems and Rural Development, a global recognition initiative launched by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO). (Xinhua/Li Jing)
ROME, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- Chinese sand-control pioneer Yin Yuzhen has been named among the FAO's 100 Women Heroes in Agrifood Systems and Rural Development, a global recognition initiative launched by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO).
The honorees were celebrated at a ceremony on Thursday at the FAO headquarters in Rome as part of this year's World Food Forum.
Yin has spent more than four decades combating desertification in the Maowusu Sandy Land in north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region. After decades of persistent tree planting, she and her family have transformed stretches of the once-barren landscape into a green expanse, overcoming harsh conditions and shifting sands.
Her story also forged an enduring friendship with retired U.S. teacher Ronald Sakolsky, who raised 5,000 U.S. dollars decades ago to support her afforestation work.
Yin told Xinhua that the recognition had strengthened her resolve to continue her work. "Like a Mongolian horse, I will keep pressing forward with perseverance and determination, doing my work well and giving back to nature," she said.
Sitting in the audience at the ceremony, Sakolsky applauded Yin's achievement. "Yin deserves everything that she gets. She is the heroine," he told Xinhua.
Launched by the FAO to mark the International Year of the Woman Farmer 2026, the global initiative recognizes 100 women for their outstanding contributions to agriculture, food systems and rural development. ■

World Insights: Black Sea drone attacks add to global energy, shipping strains
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
21:34:07 CST
22:34:07 KST

SOFIA, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- A fresh wave of drone attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea, an alternative shipping route to the disrupted Strait of Hormuz, is deepening insecurity along the European Union's (EU's) eastern flank and compounding pressures on an already stretched global shipping network.
A San Marino-flagged vessel caught fire in the Black Sea early Thursday morning, with eight of its 12 crew members still missing, according to Romanian maritime authorities. The incident came just hours after a suspected drone strike on a Comoros-flagged tanker in Romanian waters on Wednesday.
Despite reports about drones detected in the area overnight, Romania's Ministry of National Defense has not confirmed the two vessels were struck by drones. However, over the past week, drones have struck multiple vessels off Bulgaria's coast, leaving 11 crew missing and 10 presumed dead. Both Russia and Ukraine have denied involvement in the recent attacks.
DIPLOMATIC FALLOUT
The strikes have triggered a diplomatic row. Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev has summoned Russian Ambassador to Bulgaria Eleonora Mitrofanova, saying that although there was "no conclusive evidence," "the logic suggests that the outcome benefits the Russian Federation."
Mitrofanova denied knowledge of the strikes and suggested a "provocation by a third party." Moscow rejected a limited naval ceasefire proposal brokered by Türkiye and the UN, saying it lacked guarantees against arms shipments to Ukraine by sea, and blaming Kyiv for refusing comprehensive agreements.
On Thursday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told British media that Kyiv would resume strikes on Russia's oil refineries, citing Russia's attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure as violations against the U.S.-announced "energy ceasefire."
In response, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said the alliance would "adjust our deterrence and defense posture as needed." European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called the Black Sea "another front of escalation" of the Russia-Ukraine war, which is "unacceptable." France and Germany also urged a halt to attacks on commercial vessels.
Bulgarian President Iliana Iotova and Romanian President Nicusor Dan have agreed to jointly push for an emergency item on the Black Sea at the European Council. On Thursday afternoon, the Bulgarian prime minister and the Romanian president met with Mark Rutte in Brussels for regional security discussions. The three NATO littoral states -- Bulgaria, Romania and Türkiye -- have also agreed to boost surveillance and intelligence-sharing.
FROM ONE CHOKEPOINT TO ANOTHER
The attacks are compounding a crisis that began thousands of miles away. The Strait of Hormuz, which normally carries about a fifth of global oil and gas supplies, has faced repeated attacks on tankers since late February. This has pushed some energy and grain cargoes toward alternative routes -- including the Black Sea corridor, now itself in jeopardy.
The Black Sea handles roughly 25 to 30 percent of global wheat exports, over 10 percent of corn and two-thirds of sunflower oil. Russia and Ukraine together normally supply about 27 percent of the world's wheat, most of it shipped through the Black Sea. Their combined wheat shipments from July to September were 6.5 million tons below the same period a year earlier, according to estimates from the International Food Policy Research Institute and the Agricultural Market Information System. Separately, Barva Invest has warned that up to 38 million tons of wheat and corn exports could be at risk in 2026/27 if deep-sea port restrictions persist.
"We see three concerning chokepoints right now that are driving up food prices across the world," said Carl Skau, acting executive director of the UN World Food Programme, referring to the Strait of Hormuz, the Bab Al Mandeb strait and the Black Sea. "All those three are causing disruptions to maritime trade, which is pushing up the price of energy and of food." Countries dependent on Black Sea grain, including Egypt, Türkiye and other parts of the Middle East, face the sharpest impact.
Insurance costs reflect the escalation of the conflict. War-risk premiums for Black Sea voyages have jumped from about 200,000 U.S. dollars to 2.5 million dollars per vessel, according to Lukoil's commercial manager in Bulgaria. Meanwhile, London-based insurance body Joint War Committee has expanded its high-risk zone to cover almost the entire basin.
"The Black Sea didn't become more expensive; it became just harder to access," Alexey Zavarskiy, a ship operator at Angara Denizcilik, said at an industry conference held on Sept. 22. He estimated that around 90 percent of shipowners had suspended calls at affected ports.
Washington's decision on Oct. 9 to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian diesel exports illustrates the dilemma. On paper, it appears to be a release valve for a tight global diesel market: U.S. diesel prices are up 70 percent since February. However, the relief depends on a route that is itself under attack -- Russian diesel loads primarily at Black Sea ports such as Novorossiysk, the same waters where drones are now striking commercial vessels.
The first tranche of about 2.25 million barrels is less than a single day of U.S. diesel demand, and analysts from Quilter Cheviot to Wood Mackenzie have dismissed it as too small and too exposed to make a difference.
CALL FOR NEW FRAMEWORK
Military analysts warn the Black Sea has become one of the world's most dangerous shipping routes, with drone attacks having overtaken sea mines as the primary risk.
Retired Romanian Navy commander Sandu Valentin Mateiu told local media that the density of incidents pointed to a deliberate hybrid campaign. Mateiu said Romania should prepare a serious case for diplomatic protest, potentially raising the issue even at the level of NATO's Article 4. Poland took this step in September 2025 after drones violated its airspace, leading to emergency consultations and the deployment of allied fighter jets and air defense systems to the alliance's eastern flank under the "Eastern Sentry" mission.
Murat Ersavci, director of the International Studies Center at the Economic Policy Research Foundation of Türkiye, said the changing nature of the conflict is reshaping the Black Sea into a "multilayered security environment," with the boundary between trade and security becoming increasingly blurred.
Ersavci called for a comprehensive maritime security arrangement to ensure safe, predictable commercial navigation, distinguish civilian vessels from military targets, and coordinate efforts among littoral states to protect energy and food shipments.
Canan Tercan, a foreign policy expert at Istanbul Aydin University, warned that the Black Sea risked mirroring the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz, and that navigational safety "must be secured through an international non-combat agreement, not through naval forces." ■

Chinese medical team brings care to South Sudan communities
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
21:33:52 CST
22:33:52 KST

JUBA, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- The 14th batch of the Chinese medical team in South Sudan delivered healthcare services to communities at the latest weekly clinical outreach session on Wednesday.
Conducted at the University of Juba clinic in the capital city, the session benefited not only enrolled students but also vulnerable people from surrounding communities.
Sonia Laku, 25, a medical student at the University of Juba, returned to the outreach clinic for follow-up care two months after her first visit.
Laku sought pain-relief plasters for her knee. Although the plasters she sought were temporarily unavailable, doctors prescribed alternative pain medication.
"Whenever I come here, I find not only students but also people from neighboring communities. The Chinese medical team has been providing great services to vulnerable people who are unable to access proper medical care due to the prevailing economic hardship," she said.
Chinese medicated pain plasters are widely utilized to provide temporary relief for minor muscle aches, joint stiffness, backaches, sprains, and bruises.
Margret Tabu Tereza, an engineering student who sought treatment for a severe headache, said Chinese doctors reassessed an elderly woman who had previously been diagnosed with diabetes at a private clinic.
"It was my first time visiting the clinic, and I saw Chinese doctors helping our people. I met an elderly woman who had been wrongly diagnosed with diabetes. The Chinese doctors noticed the anomaly and rectified this grave mistake," Tabu said.
The medical team's evaluation found that the woman did not have diabetes, and doctors prescribed medication for her actual condition.
Alfred Angwet Gai, a waste management supervisor at the University of Juba, returned to the campus clinic for a follow-up visit after receiving treatment for severe chest pain in the last session.
"I came here last week with terrible chest pain. The Chinese doctors examined me and gave me medicine that relieved the pain," Angwet said.
He said the team's outreach efforts also extend beyond the university, bringing health care services to communities in other parts of the country.
Li Zheng, a gynecologist in the 14th batch of the Chinese medical team, said that many patients arrive with advanced or deteriorated conditions primarily due to delays in receiving timely medical intervention.
Individuals seeking care at the outreach clinics frequently present with a wide range of ailments, including chronic abdominal discomfort, joint and musculoskeletal pain, hypertension, and diabetes, Li added.
"We not only treat the patients but also provide them with medical advice on healthy living such as good eating habits and adequate rest," Li said. ■

ABIDJAN, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- The Chinese People's Liberation Army Navy hospital ship Auspicious Ark arrived in Abidjan, the economic capital of Cote d'Ivoire, on Wednesday to begin a friendly visit and provide medical services, marking the first visit by a Chinese naval hospital ship to the country.
The hospital ship, which is carrying out Mission Harmony-2026, docked at Abidjan at about 10:00 a.m. local time (1000 GMT).
Ivorian military and government officials, China's ambassador to Cote d'Ivoire, the defense attache and embassy staff, as well as representatives of the Chinese community and Chinese enterprises welcomed the ship at the port.
On board, Chinese naval personnel and civilian staff stood in formation and waved to the welcoming crowd at the port.
At the welcoming ceremony, local residents held banners and waved the national flags of China and Cote d'Ivoire to welcome the Chinese naval hospital ship. After the ceremony, the Chief of Staff of the Ivorian Navy boarded the Auspicious Ark and toured the hospital ship.
During the seven-day visit, the hospital ship will provide medical treatment for local patients aboard the vessel, while medical personnel will visit the Abidjan Military Hospital and a local university, among other places, for medical exchanges and medical services.
The mission will also organize a deck reception to strengthen friendship and mutual trust with the Ivorian side.
China and Cote d'Ivoire established diplomatic relations in March 1983 and formally established a strategic partnership in September 2024. ■

China Focus: Long March legacy takes root in greener landscapes of revolutionary heartlands
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
21:33:31 CST
22:33:31 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- Perched on a hillside in Changting County of southern China, visitors soak in lush scenery stretching beside the glistening Tingjiang River.
But things weren't always so picturesque.
Changting, an old revolutionary base area in Fujian Province, was among the counties hardest hit by soil erosion in China's red-soil region, which threatened local people's livelihoods and left the landscape degraded.
Efforts to improve the local environment began nearly a century ago.
In November 1931, the Communist Party of China (CPC) established the Provisional Central Government of the Chinese Soviet Republic in Ruijin, Jiangxi Province, where the CPC put its revolutionary ideals into governance experimentation. The following year, it launched a tree-planting campaign to protect farmland from floods and droughts, reclaim barren hills and benefit local people.
During this campaign, CPC-led Red Army soldiers in Changting, which neighbors Ruijin, taught residents how to plant trees. In turn, residents brought food and seedlings to the soldiers and joined the planting campaign voluntarily.
"Even amid the turmoil of war, the Party still called for tree planting with great vigor," said Chen Liping, a researcher of CPC history and local chronicles in the county. "It reflects the Party's commitment to putting people's interests first and laying the foundations for future development."
As the war intensified, however, the tree-planting campaign had to be halted. The Red Army then embarked on the Long March, an epic military trek from 1934 to 1936 that broke through the encirclement of Kuomintang (Nationalist Party) forces. With some marching as far as 12,500 kilometers, the arduous journey helped lay the foundation for the eventual victory of the Chinese revolution.
As one of the starting points of the Long March, Changting has carried forward the Red Army's legacy in its decades-long efforts to combat soil erosion.
Tree planting, as the Red Army had practiced earlier, remained an effective method to tackle the problem. However, in severely eroded areas, ground temperatures can soar above 70 degrees Celsius, making it difficult for trees to survive.
Through experimentation, the county developed a phased approach suited to its natural conditions: first planting grass, then shrubs, and next trees, bringing the barren hills back to life step by step.
"Grass helps lower ground temperatures and create favorable conditions for other vegetation, allowing a mix of tree species to take root," said Shangguan Yuanbin, deputy head of the county's soil and water conservation station.
Over the years, local people adapted to changing conditions and met emerging problems with determination, patience and ingenuity.
Years of effort have paid off. To date, Changting has reduced the area affected by soil erosion by about 1.17 million mu (about 78,000 hectares), while its soil erosion rate fell from 31.47 percent to 6.31 percent, according to local authorities.
"Had we given up at any point over these decades, we would not have achieved such results today," said Shangguan. "We've applied the fearless Long March spirit to soil and water conservation."
Changting's transformation epitomizes a broader greening trend in China, which marks a national tree-planting day annually. Official data showed that between 2021 and 2025, China accounted for roughly one-quarter of the world's increase in green vegetation, while its forest and grass coverage rate exceeded 56 percent in 2025.
China's greening endeavor has gained international recognition. In 2021, Changting's comprehensive soil erosion control and ecological restoration practices were selected as a model case at the 15th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (COP15).
But restoring the land is not the end of the story. The next challenge is to turn environmental recovery into lasting economic opportunities for local communities.
One of these places is Xikuangshan, an old mining area in central China's Hunan Province. During the Long March, about 1,500 well-disciplined Red Army soldiers were stationed there for a week. Through their words and deeds, they gained the trust of locals, who went from hiding from the Red Army to following it.
Dubbed the "World's Capital of Antimony," Xikuangshan has witnessed decades of intensive underground mining dating back to 1897, which led to vegetation loss, air and water pollution, and ground subsidence. Some even joked that "a white bird flying across Xikuangshan could turn black."
In 2004, local people mounted an all-out campaign for ecological restoration. Inspired by the perseverance shown by the Red Army, a research team conducted countless experiments and finally achieved a breakthrough in the treatment of harmful residue generated during antimony refining, a challenge that has long confronted the industry worldwide.
The once-scarred mining landscape gradually regained its vitality. The improved environment, together with its revolutionary history and mining culture, helped Xikuangshan to develop into a well-known tourist destination with around 300 million yuan (about 44.6 million U.S. dollars) in tourism revenue annually.
Yang Lijun is among those who have benefited. After more than a decade, he decided to return home in 2021 upon seeing his hometown's blue skies and clear waters. He rented an abandoned rural house and opened a tourist restaurant featuring local specialties, which now generates an annual income of more than 100,000 yuan.
"In the past, many residents, myself included, left home because of worsening environmental conditions," he recalled. "Now, with the environment improving, more tourists are coming, bringing new opportunities for a better life."
For places like Changting and Xikuangshan, ecological restoration is therefore not simply about bringing back greenery, but also about higher-quality lives and new development paths for former revolutionary base areas.
Earlier this year, China issued guidelines on accelerating the development of such areas, with measures to support systematic environmental protection and encourage eco-tourism.
For Yue Hui, director of the soil and water conservation center in Changting, the changes are encouraging, but the work is far from over.
"Combating soil erosion requires sustained effort. We will continue our march toward a greener future," Yue said. ■

Fifth Congress of Chinese Archaeology opens in north China's Shanxi Province
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
21:33:30 CST
22:33:30 KST

TAIYUAN, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- The Fifth Congress of Chinese Archaeology opened on Thursday in Yuncheng, north China's Shanxi Province, under the theme of "Archaeology: The Past and the Future."
Scheduled to run through Saturday, the congress draws hundreds of archaeologists from home and abroad, featuring keynote speeches and 28 parallel sessions, with more than 570 academic presentations and 22 public lectures.
Yuncheng, the host city, is where the Xiyin site in Xia County was excavated 100 years ago. The site dates back to the Neolithic Age. The excavation unearthed thousands of pottery fragments and other artifacts associated with the Yangshao culture, which originated around the middle reaches of the Yellow River and dates back 4,700 to 7,000 years.
Led by Chinese archaeologist Li Ji and geologist Yuan Fuli, it was the first modern scientific archaeological excavation independently conducted by Chinese scholars, ushering in a new era for Chinese archaeology and becoming a landmark in modern Chinese archaeology.
Marie Louise Stig Sørensen, professor of Prehistoric Europe and Heritage Studies at the University of Cambridge's Department of Archaeology and a guest at the congress, said she became interested in archaeology related to the Yangshao Culture after working with some young scholars about the importance of the culture.
"It is such a fascinating part of our world history, and at the same time, its archaeology is so similar in some way to what I do in Europe," she said.
Established in 2016, the Congress of Chinese Archaeology aims to showcase the current state and achievements of Chinese archaeology, promote greater openness and international academic exchanges, and advance the overall development of Chinese archaeology. ■

South Korea's Choi takes early lead at Buick LPGA Shanghai, China's Yin tied for third
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
21:33:20 CST
22:33:20 KST

SHANGHAI, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's Choi Hye-jin fired a bogey-free 8-under 64 to take the outright lead after the opening round of the Buick LPGA Shanghai on Thursday, while China's Yin Ruoning finished four shots back in a tie for third.
Choi made a flying start at Sheshan International Golf Club, birdieing the opening hole before adding three more birdies on the front nine. She maintained her momentum after the turn with another four birdies to complete a flawless round.
"The course is long, and it's quite challenging. A lot of my long putts went in today, which was key to my good score," Choi said.
"Over the next three rounds, I'll try to maintain this form and stick to my game plan."
Now in her fifth season on the LPGA Tour, Choi is still seeking her first title on the circuit after several near misses.
"I really want to win my first LPGA title, and I'll give it everything I've got. But for now, I just want to focus on my own game and play each round well," she said.
Yin, a former tournament champion, recovered from an uneven front nine to shoot a 4-under 68.
Playing alongside Thailand's world No. 2 Jeeno Thitikul, another former winner of the event, Yin made one birdie on the front nine but gave the shot back with a three-putt bogey at the ninth.
The Chinese responded with five birdies and one bogey on the back nine to move into a tie for third.
"I ended up the ninth hole by taking three putts, so I was a bit angry with myself," Yin said.
She credited a crucial putt on the 17th with restoring her confidence heading into the final hole.
"I made that putt with a lot of conviction, and it gave me a great deal of confidence. Because I made the putt on the 17th, I was able to make the one on the 18th."
The tournament is being staged at Sheshan International Golf Club for the first time. The venue has previously hosted major men's events, including the WGC-HSBC Champions.
Yin admitted she had been surprised by Choi's low opening score on the demanding layout.
"I couldn't imagine anyone shooting eight under here. Now that someone has done it, I know it's achievable. I'll aim to chase that score tomorrow," she said.
"My strategy will remain the same, but I need to be more attentive and decisive with my putting."
Thitikul also pointed to the course's length as a significant challenge for the field.
"This is a long course, and it probably suits the men's game better. But the challenge is the same for everyone, and I'm looking forward to seeing what happens over the next three days," she said. ■

(Str/Xinhua)
ISLAMABAD, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- The death toll from a school roof collapse in Pakistan's northwest Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province on Thursday has reached 33, with 17 injured people discharged after observation, hospital officials and a rescue service spokesperson confirmed to Xinhua.
According to a report from the Bed Management Office of Lady Reading Hospital in Peshawar, 53 patients were brought to the hospital, including 33 who died and three who remained under observation. Seventeen others were discharged after observation.
The hospital list included children aged 4 to 14, as well as a 25-year-old woman.
Bilal Ahmed Faizi, spokesperson for Rescue 1122, told Xinhua that police were investigating the incident. Initial investigations suggested that heavy rainfall had caused the roof of the two-story school building in Dir Colony to collapse.
President Asif Ali Zardari expressed condolences over the loss of lives and directed the authorities to ensure medical facilities for the injured, according to his office. In a post on X, he also called for a comprehensive investigation into building safety standards at educational institutions.
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif ordered expedited relief operations and directed that all possible medical assistance be provided to the injured.
Meanwhile, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Governor Faisal Karim Kundi ordered an inquiry into the incident. ■

Cyber hit on a defence prime would cost capacity, warns MP
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
14:32:59 BST
22:32:59 KST

A cyber attack on the scale of the one that stopped Jaguar Land Rover would, if it struck a defence prime or a munitions supplier, take British industrial capacity out of the fight as well as money out of the economy, the Labour MP Graeme Downie has told the UK Defence Journal.
Downie, the member for Dunfermline and Dollar, was asked what an attack of that size against a defence manufacturer would mean for the country.
“I think the implications are the same, but with the added that you’ve probably taken down or reduced direct UK industrial capacity,” he said. “That obviously has a short-term impact, but also then huge knock-on effects to supply chain, availability of skills, raw materials, and lots of other things. So it would be a more direct attack, but it would nonetheless still have a huge economic impact, and then possibly knock on down to our industrial capacity.”
The comparison he was working from is the attack on Jaguar Land Rover, which his report identifies as the costliest cyber attack in British history. Downie said its effects travelled a long way past the company’s own balance sheet.
“What was striking is not only did that meaningfully affect UK GDP, reducing it by I think it was 0.1 per cent, in an economy that’s only growing by you know 1 per cent a year, that’s a significant number,” he said. “It’s noteworthy that it also affected Bank of England interest rate decisions and could have delayed an interest rate cut because of the performance of the economy. So not only was it costly to a large British company and all of the knock-on to supply chain and everything else, but that actually hit British mortgage payers potentially and cost them money.”
Asked what defence firms themselves could do about the risk while government works out how to measure it, Downie said the burden does not sit with them.
“I don’t think there’s anything defence firms can do in the meantime. I think at the moment this is something that really is on government to start publishing the cost of attacks,” he said. “I think there’s probably things government can do with businesses to not compel them to publish the cost of a cyber attack, for example, because that is difficult. But I think you can probably compel them much faster to have in place the right protections against cyber attack, and I think government just needs to be much quicker and more proactive.”
His prescription for the National Cyber Security Centre is that it should arrive without being asked, and leave with a number. “NCSC and other parts of government need to be much stronger at not only being there to assist when asked, but actually going in and assisting, not only to fix the problem as they did with JLR, for example, but also, while we’re here, we are going to find out how much this has cost your business, and then find a way to publish that.”
Downie’s report puts the cost of Russian hostile activity to the British economy at between £2 billion and £2.5 billion, a figure that excludes the additional defence spending the Russian threat has driven. He said the exclusions were deliberate and the real number is a good deal larger.
“What we did with all the figures was we took very conservative estimates because I wanted to make sure these figures were credible and were only what we could absolutely find,” he said. “I’m hoping that we will have more information out in the coming weeks and months as other information becomes available to us. I think it will be significantly bigger. But as I say, what’s important is that we don’t start spreading misinformation and unattributed sources. I think we’ve got to be really careful as we’re introducing this concept to the British public about how much Russian activity costs us.”
The Jaguar Land Rover attack halted production for weeks from the end of August last year and has been estimated by the Cyber Monitoring Centre at around £1.9 billion, the largest figure it has put on a single cyber event in the United Kingdom. Britain’s defence manufacturers sit on the same kind of integrated production systems, with the added exposure of long single-source supply chains for forgings, energetics and specialist components, where the loss of one plant for a few weeks cannot be made up elsewhere.
One of the four recommendations in The Putin Tax, published this month, asks the Ministry of Defence to begin costing physical attacks on British interests.

Kuwait drone shield to cover the sea as well as the air
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
14:32:41 BST
22:32:41 KST

The counter-drone system Kuwait is buying from the British firm MARSS will defend against seaborne drones along the coast as well as airborne ones, using sonar alongside radar and electro-optical sensors feeding a network of command centres, according to the company.
MARSS, an EOS company, will act as prime contractor and systems integrator on the £370 million contract, installing sensors across a network of sites that report into central command centres. Its NiDAR command and control platform fuses that data into threat assessments and provides what the company describes as hemispherical coverage against airborne and coastal seaborne drones. The contract also covers an initial supply of hard-kill interceptors and soft-kill jammers.
Johannes Pinl, chief executive of MARSS, said: “Countering drones and aerial threats is not about any single system. It is about an intelligent, layered architecture that detects, decides and defeats within seconds, and MARSS has built exactly that.
“Over the coming 24 months, MARSS will integrate the sensors and effectors that protect Kuwait’s people, critical infrastructure and national assets, backed by British engineering and new skilled jobs here in the UK.”
Doctor Andreas Schwer, chief executive of EOS, said: “Air defence is being redefined by the drone. Nations can no longer afford to answer low-cost threats with high-cost interceptors, and they need integrated systems that can respond faster than the threat. MARSS’ NiDAR is the intelligence layer in EOS’ counter-drone strategy, connecting sensors and effectors into a single, scalable architecture. Kuwait’s decision to deploy this capability nationwide shows where the market is heading, and it positions EOS as a leading provider of integrated counter-drone defence.”
Having both soft-kill and hard-kill effectors run through the same command system gives operators layered defeat options and a choice of response for each engagement, the company said, with NiDAR using AI to classify threats automatically and recommend an engagement, shortening the time between detection and defeat.
MARSS said the contract builds on NiDAR systems it has already fielded in the Gulf, which it said have been in operational use throughout the recent crisis in the region, and extends that approach to a national scale.
Delivery will be phased over 24 months and followed by a multi-year integrated logistic support programme. A training package running over several months will put MARSS personnel on the ground to train Kuwaiti operators across the sensors, the effectors and NiDAR itself, and a team will deploy to Kuwait for the duration, with recruitment already under way.
The commercial side of the deal was announced by the Ministry of Defence earlier, including the £370 million value, the roughly one hundred jobs expected across MARSS and its British supply chain, production proposed for Bristol, and the contract’s place within Taskforce Sabre, the government and industry effort to help Gulf states buy what they need quickly. Britain has already supplied Kuwait with the Rapid Sentry ground-based air defence missile system, and the Royal Air Force’s ORCUS counter-drone system is operating in the country.
NiDAR itself covers air, surface, sub-surface and land, detecting, tracking and classifying threats and recommending responses, and MARSS says it has more than sixty deployments worldwide. The company has been working on AI-enabled command and control for around twenty years, including research with the European Union, NATO and defence agencies.
EOS is an Australian group listed on the ASX with divisions covering defence and space. Its defence products include remote weapon stations, high energy laser weapons and drone interceptors, and NiDAR sits inside that portfolio as the command layer. MARSS is exhibiting NiDAR at SOFEX in Jordan from 27 to 29 October, where it will be shown integrated onto vehicle platforms alongside EOS remote weapon stations.

What is Starshield, and who limited Ukraine’s access to it?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:32:16 UTC
22:32:16 KST

What is Starshield, and who limited Ukraine’s access to it?
Ukraine relies on Starshield, the military-grade version of Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite service, to fight Russia.
Ukraine’s military Starshield satellite connection has been restored, a Ukrainian Ministry of Defence source says, just days after the United States reportedly restricted the service.
The Reuters news agency, quoting a source, reported that Kyiv is still seeking clarifications from Starshield’s parent company, SpaceX, as to why its service was disrupted between Tuesday and Wednesday.
Ukraine relies on Starshield, the military-grade version of SpaceX’s internet service, Starlink, to provide intelligence amid its war with Russia.
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has denied the company’s involvement and suggested only the US government could have disrupted it, despite President Donald Trump’s insistence that Washington is still sharing intelligence with Kyiv.
Here’s what we know:
What is Starshield?
Starshield is a sister service to Starlink, an array of 11,000 satellites placed by SpaceX into Earth’s low orbit to provide high-speed internet connectivity even in remote areas.
Starshield, launched in 2022 and provided to the US government, is designed for military use as it allows for deeper encryption to process sensitive information. SpaceX says it is primarily used by US defence agencies and other “government partners”.
Ukraine’s military relies on Starshield, especially to guide its drones, on which it relies heavily to attack Russia.
What happened to Ukraine’s access to Starshield?
On Tuesday, Ukrainian defence officials said they had lost access to important satellite-based communications and that the disruptions had affected military missions. This came in the wake of heavy Russian strikes, which hit the country with more than 100 drones and five ballistic missiles, for which Ukraine said it had received no prior warning.
“Intelligence on Russian ballistic missile launches helps save lives, and this is one of the most critical issues. This is precisely what helps prevent people from being killed – when there is an early warning about ballistic missiles,” President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote on X. “Regarding this strike, unfortunately, there was no warning from partners.”
Serhiy Beskrestnov, a defence adviser to Zelenskyy, posted on Telegram that SpaceX had also “implemented a speed limit” on Starlink terminals, capping internet speeds at 100mph (160km/h).
That meant any drones or missiles flying at more than 100mph lost their guidance connection.
“Our armed forces did not receive a warning about these restrictions, and this led to the failure of a number of missions,” he said, adding that this was clearly “related to the current political situation”.
Officials said the restrictions also reduced capabilities for front-line logistics, reconnaissance and relaying signals.
Who controls Starshield?
On Wednesday, Musk denied any involvement in the incident, insisting that the service is “controlled by the US government”.
Responding to a post on X by Ukraine’s former Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, who said the speed limits were being lifted and demanded unrestricted internet speed, Musk wrote, “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government.”
“Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” he said, referring to the US president.
Musk further clarified that Starlink is for “civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company” – an apparent attempt to differentiate it from Starshield, which Kyiv also deploys but is not allowed to use for offensive operations.
Last year, Starlink cut off access for Russian troops who were covertly using the service on the battlefront in Ukraine.
Is Musk supportive of Ukraine?
The SpaceX boss has shown an active interest in the Russia-Ukraine war since it began, but has not been particularly favourable towards Kyiv. In 2022 – just after Russia invaded Ukraine – he proposed a “peace plan” under which Kyiv would end its claim to Russia-occupied Crimea and would drop hopes for joining NATO. Zelenskyy criticised Musk’s comments, and tensions between the two have remained.
On Sunday, the billionaire, who is also the CEO of Tesla and owns X, said Zelenskyy “has gone too far”, in a response to Trump’s comments that the Ukrainian president should leave office.
On Wednesday, Musk appeared to blame Zelenskyy for deaths in the war. “And so the slaughter continues,” he wrote on X. “Time for Zelensky to go.”
Does Ukraine blame the US for restricting intelligence?
Ukrainian officials have complained that the country received no warning in advance of Russian ballistic missile strikes on Tuesday and Wednesday. Usually, the US provides crucial early-warning alerts that allow Kyiv to issue evacuation orders.
Zelenskyy said in an interview with the Financial Times on Thursday that US military officials had earlier warned Kyiv that Washington would block intelligence unless attacks on Russian energy infrastructure stop.
The Ukrainian leader added that he did not accept suggestions that the Starshield incident could have been a glitch. “It was not a technical problem; it was the will,” he said.
Why might the US restrict intelligence from Ukraine?
Tensions between Kyiv and Washington have been building since Trump took office last year over a host of issues, including weapons transfers and the US’s increasing closeness to Russia.
In recent weeks, Washington has pressured Ukraine to stop attacks on Russian oil refineries to allow more oil into global markets. In particular, Trump has sought to blame Ukrainian attacks on Russian diesel facilities for the rising price of the fuel globally ahead of November midterm elections.
Trump said last week he had agreed to a deal with President Vladimir Putin to release Russian diesel stocks into the US and global markets, despite existing sanctions on Russian oil.
Zelenskyy criticised the move and said it would embolden Putin.
Over the weekend, Trump unilaterally announced an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine, apparently without consulting Zelenskyy, who told reporters the deal was “news to me”. Russia also did not confirm it. Angered, Trump called for Ukraine to replace its president and blamed Ukraine’s attacks on Russian oil infrastructure for global energy disruptions.
Ukraine said it had, in fact, refrained from attacking Russian refineries and would continue to do so if Russia did the same. However, Russian strikes have continued. On Wednesday, Zelenskyy said strikes on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure had caused blackouts affecting 600,000 people.
“We’re done,” the Ukrainian president said in the FT interview, confirming that Kyiv had subsequently resumed attacking Russia’s oil infrastructure.

Ex-IAS Divya Mittal launches own party: 10 civil servants who quit service to enter politics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:31:31 UTC
22:31:31 KST

Mittal launched her party, the Jan Neeti Bharat Party.
NEW DELHI: Former IAS officer Divya Mittal on Thursday launched the Jan Neeti Bharat party and announced that it would contest the 2027 Uttar Pradesh assembly elections. Her announcement comes nearly a month after she took voluntary retirement from the civil services, ending a 13-year administrative career to pursue politics independently.In a video message on X, Mittal said the party will focus on making people central to policymaking and ensuring that the government remains accountable to them throughout its five-year term, rather than only on election day.
"Politics rules over you. In Jan Neeti, you will be the ones who rule," she said, announcing the party's name and its decision to contest the state polls due early next year.
Her decision to launch a party of her own places her among a group of civil servants who left government service before their scheduled retirement to enter politics.Here are 10 former civil servants who made the transition from bureaucracy to politics before completing their service.
1. Yashwant Sinha
Yashwant Sinha resigned from the Indian Administrative Service in 1984 to enter active politics. He joined the Janata Party and subsequently became associated with the Janata Dal before joining the BJP.Sinha first served as Union finance minister in the Chandra Shekhar government in 1990-91.
Under Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee, he returned to the finance ministry in 1998 and held the portfolio until 2002, when he became external affairs minister.His political career also included membership of the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha. Sinha later distanced himself from the BJP and joined the Trinamool Congress in 2021, before contesting the 2022 presidential election as the opposition's joint candidate.
2. Ajit Jogi
Ajit Jogi left the IAS in 1986 to enter politics and joined the Congress. He had served as a district collector before moving into political life and was subsequently elected to the Rajya Sabha.Jogi's biggest political breakthrough came in 2000, when Chhattisgarh was carved out of Madhya Pradesh. He became the newly created state's first chief minister, holding office until 2003.After years in the Congress, Jogi broke away from the party in 2016 and founded the Janata Congress Chhattisgarh, seeking to establish an independent regional political platform.His career stands out as an example of a former administrator moving from district-level governance to the leadership of a newly formed state and later attempting to build a party of his own.
3. Mani Shankar Aiyar
Mani Shankar Aiyar resigned from the Indian Foreign Service in 1989 to enter politics. He had served as a diplomat for more than two decades and spent part of his career on deputation to the Prime Minister's Office under Rajiv Gandhi.Aiyar joined the Congress and won the Mayiladuthurai Lok Sabha seat in Tamil Nadu in 1991. He went on to become a prominent party leader and served as Union minister for petroleum and natural gas during the UPA government.He also held the panchayati raj portfolio and was involved in efforts to strengthen local self-government institutions.
4. Arvind Kejriwal
Arvind Kejriwal resigned from the Indian Revenue Service in 2006 after working in the income tax department. He had become involved in the Right to Information movement and founded the non-governmental organisation Parivartan to address citizens' grievances.His political journey gathered momentum during the Ana Hazare-led India Against Corruption movement, which campaigned for a stronger anti-corruption law. In 2012, Kejriwal founded the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP), choosing to build a political organisation rather than join an established party.AAP made its electoral debut in the 2013 Delhi assembly elections, when Kejriwal defeated then chief minister Sheila Dikshit. He became Delhi chief minister in December 2013 and returned to the post after the party's victories in 2015 and 2020.
5. KJ Alphons
KJ Alphons took voluntary retirement from the IAS in 2006 and entered electoral politics in Kerala. He contested the Kanjirappally assembly seat in Kerala as an independent candidate supported by the Left Democratic Front and won.Alphons later founded the Jana Shakti platform before joining the BJP in 2011. His political journey subsequently took him to Parliament, when he became a Rajya Sabha member.In 2017, he was inducted into the Narendra Modi government as Union minister of state for tourism, with independent charge, and also handled electronics and information technology.His transition from a civil servant known for urban development initiatives to a state-level politician and Union minister is an example of an officer moving across political formations during his career.
6. Satyapal Singh
Satyapal Singh, a 1980-batch IPS officer of the Maharashtra cadre, opted for voluntary retirement in January 2014 while serving as Mumbai police commissioner, ahead of the Lok Sabha elections.He joined the BJP and contested the Baghpat Lok Sabha seat in Uttar Pradesh in 2014, defeating Rashtriya Lok Dal chief Ajit Singh. He retained the constituency in the 2019 general election.Singh served as Union minister of state for human resource development and water resources during the Modi government's first term. Before entering politics, he had served in several police leadership roles and was known for his work in law enforcement.
7. OP Choudhary
OP Choudhary, a 2005-batch IAS officer, resigned from the service in 2018 while serving as Raipur collector to enter politics. He joined the BJP and contested the Kharsia assembly constituency in Chhattisgarh in the same year.Choudhary lost that election but returned to the electoral contest in 2023, this time winning the Raipur City South seat. He was subsequently inducted into the Chhattisgarh government as a minister.His career highlights the uncertain transition from administration to politics. Unlike officers who win their first election, Choudhary's initial defeat did not end his political ambitions. He returned five years later and secured a place in the state Cabinet.
8. Aparajita Sarangi
Aparajita Sarangi, a 1994-batch IAS officer of the Odisha cadre, took voluntary retirement in 2018 while serving as joint secretary in the Union rural development ministry.She joined the BJP in November that year and contested the 2019 Lok Sabha election from Bhubaneswar. Sarangi won the seat, defeating Biju Janata Dal candidate Arup Patnaik.She retained the constituency in the 2024 general election, establishing herself as a BJP leader in Odisha.Sarangi's transition was particularly swift: she moved from a senior central government position to an electoral contest within months of leaving the service and subsequently secured two consecutive Lok Sabha victories.
9. AK Sharma
AK Sharma, a 1988-batch IAS officer of the Gujarat cadre, took voluntary retirement in January 2021, around 18 months before his scheduled superannuation.Sharma had spent a substantial part of his career working in the Prime Minister's Office and was associated with Narendra Modi's administration during his tenure as Gujarat chief minister and later as prime minister.After leaving the service, Sharma joined the BJP and was elected to the Uttar Pradesh Legislative Council. He subsequently became a minister in the Yogi Adityanath government, handling portfolios including urban development and energy.His move demonstrated how a senior bureaucrat with experience in the central administration could enter state politics and secure a position in the Cabinet without first contesting a direct assembly election.
10. Asim Arun
Asim Arun, a 1994-batch IPS officer, took voluntary retirement in January 2022 while serving as Kanpur police commissioner. He joined the BJP soon afterwards, ahead of the Uttar Pradesh assembly elections.Arun contested the Kannauj assembly seat and won, entering a constituency associated with the Samajwadi Party. He was subsequently inducted into the Yogi Adityanath government.His political entry came within weeks of his voluntary retirement, making him one of the clearest recent examples of a serving police officer moving directly into electoral politics before the end of his career.
Bonus: K Annamalai
K Annamalai, a 2011-batch IPS officer of the Karnataka cadre, resigned from the police service in September 2019, before completing his tenure. He had served as superintendent of police in Udupi and Chikkamagaluru districts before leaving the force.
He joined the BJP in August 2020 and rose rapidly through the party's ranks. In July 2021, he was appointed the BJP's Tamil Nadu president, becoming one of the party's most prominent faces in the state.Annamalai contested the 2021 Tamil Nadu assembly election from Aravakurichi but lost to the DMK's R Elango. In the 2024 Lok Sabha election, he contested from Coimbatore but lost to DMK candidate Ganapathi P Rajkumar.In June 2026, Annamalai quit the BJP following differences with the party leadership over its political strategy in Tamil Nadu and launched a new political movement, 'We The Leaders'. He said the movement would focus on "common man politics", challenge what he described as "cult and dynastic politics", and eventually evolve into a political party. He has outlined plans to contest the 2031 Tamil Nadu assembly elections.
