Lula or Bolsonaro: Why Brazil's presidential election matters for Brics and India
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:08:21 UTC
22:08:21 KST

When 
Brics
 leaders met in New Delhi last month, Brazil’s President Lula da Silva was conspicuously absent from the Bharat Mandapam. He was campaigning for the crucial fourth term back home, so his foreign minister Mauro Vieira arrived in the capital for the "non-West" summit.
That absence could now highlight the Brics' road ahead, at least for the time US President Donald Trump occupies the White House.
Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability. This is what Brics stood for when India hosted it on September 12. However, the real B of Brics, which is Brazil, has the world's attention.
(From left) Egyptian president Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, Russian president Vladimir Putin, Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Chinese president Xi Jinping and South African president Cyril Ramaphosa during a joint tree plantation initiative during the 18th Brics Summit, at the Bharat Mandapam, in New Delhi.
On 25 October, Brazilians will choose between Lula and Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, son of jailed ex-president Jair Bolsonaro, and the winner will decide how deeply one of the bloc’s founding members keeps investing in it.
Flávio Bolsonaro leads the race into the runoff (second round of voting) after securing 47 per cent of the first-round vote, against Lula’s 45 per cent. Brazil mandates a second round of voting if no candidate secures a majority (more than 50 per cent) in the first round. Therefore, for a grouping already stretched by its own expansion, the result matters well beyond South America.
Results after first round of voting in Brazil.
A bloc pulled in three directions
Brics began with five members and grew to eleven after the 2024 expansion, with Indonesia the newest, joining in 2025. 
Brazil opposed the enlargement, particularly because of the one nation. Iran. It feared that adding the avowedly anti-West Islamic Republic would cost the group its cohesion. Like India, Brazil wants Brics to be reformist and not revolutionary, thereby limiting it to a body that argues for change inside the existing order rather than one that tries to replace it.
Vieira, putting the Brazilian view plainly in the run-up to the 2026 summit, said that “a multipolar world that promises peace and prosperity must not be confused with a world of spheres of influence.” In other words, Brasília wants rules that bind the strong as well as the weak.
Brazil had some success as the New Delhi declaration reaffirmed support for the United Nations system and the Paris climate agreement, going further than the G7, whose latest declarations did not mention the climate pact.
However, these are words and not actions, and Russia, a Brics member, has ignored the UN Charter in recent years. Even so, agreeing to acknowledge the UN’s legitimacy was a better outcome than blocking any mention of it.
Brics continues to expand unlike the West-dominated G7.
Those gains on paper may not last, as Brazil’s place in the bloc will depend largely on its next president. The world’s two biggest powers have very different visions for what Brics should become. Both Washington and Beijing are seeking to tilt the balance in their favour.
The United States, under Donald Trump, has made clear what it wants from Brazil. The Trump administration imposed heavy trade duties on Brazilian exports in July 2025, in retaliation for what it called a judicial “witch hunt” against former President Jair Bolsonaro, who Trump see as his "ally".
It has sanctioned the Supreme Court justice who prosecuted him and revoked the visas of several justices. It also accepted Flávio Bolsonaro’s appeal in May to designate two Brazilian criminal groups as foreign terrorist organisations, while Lula’s alternative proposals went unanswered.
Beyond one man’s fate
A Bolsonaro win would help realign Latin America behind an America First agenda of militarised approaches to crime, crackdowns on migration and preferential access to critical minerals and energy. Brazil holds the world’s second-largest rare earth reserves, and Washington wants to reduce its dependence on China for them.
On the trade and commerce front, Bolsonaro has criticised non-dollar initiatives, which is exactly the kind of de-dollarisation talk that makes some Brics ideas unwelcome in Washington. His platform does not mention Brics at all, and he has entertained the idea of leaving the group.
Beijing sits on the other side of the ledger, and its leverage is economic. China has been Brazil’s largest trading partner since 2009. It buys nearly 30 per cent of Brazil’s total exports, including soybeans, crude oil and iron ore, and it has become a major investor in electricity, mining, cars and oil.
The Brics has outperformed G7 over the last two decades.
A Brics that China hopes to make firmer and more assertive is difficult to build without Brazil, the largest economy in Latin America. That is why a Brazilian drift towards Washington would be felt in Beijing, even if it never became a formal exit.
Nevertheless, the challenge with China is intricate, as even under Jair Bolsonaro, anti-Beijing rhetoric did not stop bilateral trade from reaching record levels, and Brazil resisted US pressure to exclude Huawei from its 5G rollout. Flávio Bolsonaro’s own programme envisages continued commercial engagement with China. A withdrawal from Brics, in short, is possible but far from inevitable.
Therefore, a Bolsonaro government could stay inside the main multilateral bodies while withdrawing from the effort to give them energy, shifting from coalition-building among middle powers to a transactional, bilateral relationship with Washington.
Lula, by contrast, has pursued what officials call “multi-alignment”, keeping a working relationship with the United States, expanding trade with China and using Brics, the G20 and UN climate talks to widen Brazil’s room for manoeuvre.
Brics constitutes 40% of the global GDP.
A state under strain
The foreign policy debate is real, but it is not what most Brazilians say drives their vote. Crime is a central worry, and Bolsonaro’s “mano dura”, or iron fist, approach appeals to voters tired of violence in their neighbourhoods.
Education is another concern, as a recent poll found that 71 per cent of Brazilians are weighing it in their vote, and 83 per cent believe it should be among the next government’s top three priorities.
Only 66 per cent of Grade 2 children met basic literacy requirements in 2025, well short of the 80 per cent target for 2030.
On the US relationship, voters appear to lean towards Lula. Polls show his popularity rose after his frequent disagreements with Trump over trade and security, and other surveys found Brazilians blamed Bolsonaro more for the tariffs imposed in July.
A woman at a voting centre in US to participate in Brazil's general election. (Reuters photo)
The Brazilian Association of Institutional and Governmental Relations says the same pressure would follow Bolsonaro into office.
Its president, Jean Castro, said: “He cannot adopt a stance that could be mistaken for subservience.”
Behind these campaign themes lies a harder question. Can Brazil actually deliver on what it promises abroad? Brasilia's influence depends on partners believing that today’s deals will survive tomorrow’s politics, and that this belief is eroding.
More than 90 per cent of the federal government’s non-interest spending is mandatory, leaving little room for infrastructure, which Brazil needs if it is to make use of its mineral reserves.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) projects that government debt will reach about 98 per cent of GDP by the end of 2026. Real interest rates sit near 10 per cent, so servicing that debt consumes funds that could strengthen security forces or support strategic goals.
Adding to that, criminal networks operate across more than 1,500 clandestine airstrips in the Amazon basin and move drugs, gold and weapons across borders with Brazil’s ten neighbours.
Responsibility for fighting them is split among federal police, highway police, an intelligence agency, police forces in 26 states and the federal district, the armed forces and prosecutors. Efforts to bring them under one authority have failed in Congress. The result is that decisions about gangs operating from Brazilian soil are increasingly taken elsewhere, as Washington’s terrorist designations show.
The third problem is trust in the courts because since late 2025, the public has learned how far parts of the judiciary became entangled with the Banco Master affair.
The bank’s owner is alleged to have made side payments and awarded lucrative contracts to families of Supreme Court justices, and to have lent his private jets to justices.
Flavio Bolsonaro is himself under investigation over alleged links to the bank, and figures close to Lula’s government have also been drawn in.
The winner will appoint at least three of the court’s 11 justices, reshaping the institution that is meant to hold the next government to account.
The neighbourhood also offers little relief. Brazil once led the creation of regional institutions such as Mercosur, but it is now increasingly isolated in South America. Its relationship with Argentina, which helped underpin four decades of regional stability, has deteriorated to the point that neither country has an ambassador in the other’s capital.
Where India stands
India could probably be the member with the most to lose from a Brics that becomes either a Chinese-led counterweight to the West or an empty shell.
India has a significant interest in Brazil's political direction, given its economic ties with the Latin American nation. Bilateral trade exceeded $15 billion in 2025, making Brazil India's biggest trading partner in Latin America. Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva have set a target of taking bilateral trade to $20 billion by 2030.
Brazil's importance also extends to the steel sector, as the country is a major global supplier of iron ore and has substantial reserves of minerals used in steel production. Stronger cooperation could help India secure vital raw materials and access technologies needed to support the long-term expansion of its steel industry, according to a government statement.
One in every four overseas Indians lives in Brics nation.
Flavio Bolsonaro, meanwhile, has indicated that he would not align himself exclusively with any side, naming India among the countries with which he would maintain engagement.
India and Brazil have shared a strategic partnership since 2006, with collaboration covering areas such as defence, energy, agriculture, healthcare, critical minerals, technology and digital infrastructure.
Beyond trade, the two countries coordinate on several international issues, including reform of the United Nations, climate change and counter-terrorism. Brazil is also India's largest trading partner across Latin America and the Caribbean.
India hosted this year’s summit, where the Iranian and Emirati presidents both turned up, and it shares Brazil’s view that the bloc should push for reform rather than confrontation.
ALSO READ | Bombs without brakes? Why the US-China AI race may be harder to control than the nuclear one
The two countries also sit together in Partners for Multilateralism, launched on 21 September alongside Canada, Australia, Barbados, the European Union and Kenya.
The framework is meant to support international law and institutional reform, and it links western and Global South middle powers without forcing any of them to pick a camp.
That makes Lula a natural partner for New Delhi, and a Bolsonaro victory a quiet setback that could probably interrupt the bloc's ambitions.
India would lose a like-minded voice for a measured, rules-based Brics, leaving it with partners who are either more radical or more distant. Its own position, balancing Washington and Beijing, depends on a bloc that can talk to both.
However, whichever way Brazil votes, nobody expects an immediate revolution in its foreign policy.
Rubens Ricupero, a former Brazilian diplomat, calls Bolsonaro’s approach a “blank slate”, while Lula’s is well established. The market for Brazil’s minerals, the weight of its trade with China and the limits on its finances will constrain either man. The pressure will come from outside.
Rubens Barbosa, a former Brazilian ambassador to the US, warns that “the Americans may prove reluctant to yield anything to Lula, preferring to wait and negotiate with Bolsonaro.”
Economist Monica de Bolle argues that a re-elected Lula facing a right-leaning Congress would feel “a lot of pressure” to give in “to some US demands regarding natural resources, as well as other issues.”
That is the real stake for Brics on 25 October. The bloc’s future will turn on whether Brazil stays a champion of its reformist wing or becomes a member that merely turns up.

Could the US exit from Iraq fuel an Islamic State resurgence?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:06:56 UTC
22:06:56 KST

Breadcrumb
Could the US exit from Iraq fuel an Islamic State resurgence?
Erbil, Iraq - The US completed its planned troop withdrawal from Iraq by 30 September, with the last of the remaining anti-Islamic State (IS) coalition troops leaving Iraqi Kurdistan’s capital, Erbil, ahead of that deadline.
The withdrawal, however, has renewed anxieties in Iraq that IS could exploit the inevitable power vacuum and regional crises to reorganise and regroup, threatening the region and its peoples once again.
In late September, veteran Kurdish leader Masoud Barzani warned that the withdrawal reopens the risk of another IS resurgence. He recalled how the previous 2011 American withdrawal led to the infamous IS invasion of Iraq in mid-2014. “I fear the same scenario will happen,” he said.
Barzani isn’t the only one concerned about IS. Former Iraqi Interior Minister Baqir Jabr, a veteran Shia politician, claimed in early October that IS remnants in Syria have increased to as many as 10,000 fighters since the former regime of Bashar Al-Assad collapsed in December 2024.
IS initially seized territory in Syria and expanded by invading northern Iraq in June 2014, declaring a caliphate on those vast swathes of territory it conquered and symbolically dismantling the Iraq-Syria border.
While a restoration of that self-styled caliphate isn’t imminent today, analysts warn that multiple factors must be addressed to prevent a significant IS resurgence.
Obstacles
“IS is definitely trying to make its presence known in Iraq with the US withdrawal, but it is still small and relegated to mostly rural areas of northern Iraq with very little support,” Joel Wing, author of the Musings on Iraq blog, told The New Arab.
“There are no signs that Sunni Arabs are backing the group once again,” he said. “During the war, the government forces carried out widespread Sunni cleansing and still occupy many Sunni areas, making it far too costly for people to back the insurgents again.”
Mohammed A. Salih, a non-resident senior fellow at the Foreign Policy Research Institute, noted that conditions in Iraq and Syria are markedly different from those in 2012-14.
“Iraqi Sunnis participate in the political process despite ongoing grievances, while security forces are more capable, particularly with the presence of the ideologically driven Popular Mobilisation Forces,” Salih told The New Arab.
“Syria also has a generally functioning government rather than a full-scale civil war.”
The PMF consists of several mainly Shia militias mobilised in 2014 to help combat IS. Many powerful Iran-backed groups operate within the state-sanctioned paramilitaries and have refused recent efforts by incumbent Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi to disarm them.
Despite the significantly different circumstances between today and 2014, Salih still sees a significant risk of an IS resurgence. Stopping it will very much depend on continued support from the US-led coalition and security cooperation between Iraqi and Kurdish forces.
Across the border, Syria's new security forces must also show the “willingness and capacity” to contain IS.
“Ideological overlap between some elements of Syria’s security apparatus and IS could also create openings, especially amid economic hardship and growing public frustration over the government’s approach to dealing with Israel,” Salih said.
To Iraq’s east, any collapse or substantial weakening of the regime in Iran could undermine Iraq’s ruling Shia elite, potentially creating opportunities for IS.
“Some regional actors might also be tempted to support a Sunni insurgency if Iran-backed Iraqi militias continue attacking neighbouring countries, further increasing the risk of instability,” Salih said.
Security gaps
In 2014, the Iraqi Security Forces (ISF) infamously failed to prevent a comparably small number of IS militants from swiftly seizing Mosul.
Today, Wing believes the ISF are “far more competent,” noting that they are no longer reactive and are “mostly carrying out pre-emptive raids and operations”.
After losing all of the territory it captured in Iraq in 2017, IS remnants were still able to operate within security gaps in the disputed territories between federal Iraq and Iraqi Kurdistan, such as Kirkuk.
IS benefited from the lack of cooperation between the ISF and the Kurdish Peshmerga, particularly in the aftermath of Iraq’s forceful seizure of Kirkuk from the Peshmerga in October 2017.
Iraqi lawmaker Mazen Gharib warned this October that the group is once again doing this following the coalition’s withdrawal, pointing to increased movements in Kirkuk province and the existence of “active detachments.” On 10 October, Iraq’s security forces and IS clashed in Kirkuk’s Hawija district.
According to Wing, the gap between the Iraqi forces and the Peshmerga continues to be a security concern in Iraq.
“There are some areas where the space between the two forces is quite large, and IS has exploited this for years,” he said.
“The problem is this is in the disputed territories and the Kurds want to move back into them after they were forced out following the 2017 Kurdish independence referendum and Baghdad does not want them to return,” he added.
“This dispute has resulted in the security gap between the two sides.”
Sectarian fault lines
FPRI’s Salih concurs that the ISF is more prepared than before. “At the federal level, the presence of the PMF, as an ideologically driven and predominantly Shia force, has strengthened the ISF’s overall capabilities,” he said.
“However, effective coordination between federal and Kurdish forces remains critical to denying IS the operational space it needs in the disputed territories.”
Security coordination between Iraq and Syria is also “hugely important” for containing IS. Such cross-border cooperation is essential since the “predominantly Sunni Arab borderlands” between them have served as a “core breeding ground and operational hub” for IS for several years.
Wing noted that the two neighbours are trying to cooperate on border security for the first time in decades. “How thorough that is remains to be seen, but it can’t do anything but help,” he said.
Still, some of the forces deeply distrust one another. Iran-backed PMF groups entered Syria during the civil war to fight for President Bashar Al-Assad while the former militias that make up the new Syrian armed forces fought against Assad.
“The two definitely don't like each other, but there have not been reports of the two clashing,” Wing said.
“I think with everything else going on in the region such as the Iran war, Prime Minister Zaidi demanding the PMF to disarm, etc., the distaste for the new Syrian government has simply not been a priority.”
Independent Iraqi analyst Lawk Ghafuri noted that while IS was militarily defeated in Iraq in 2017, its ideology was never eliminated.
“Since December 2024, Syria has become an increasingly concerning environment, with foreign extremists, including individuals with IS and al-Qaeda backgrounds, potentially embedded within the new security structures,” Ghafuri told The New Arab.
“The presence of the PMF in Iraq and hostile forces across the Syrian border creates a dangerous sectarian fault line.”
Islamic State prisoners
Iraq presently holds thousands of suspected IS militants and their families in its prisons. Thousands of them were airlifted by the US military from Syria in January, including from the infamous al-Hol camp.
These militants previously attempted a well-planned, coordinated jailbreak in Syria’s Hasakah in January 2022, which took local Kurdish-led security forces more than a week to suppress.
Human Rights Watch released a report in early September charging that these detained IS suspects in Iraq face abuse, unfair trials, and executions.
The report also noted that dozens of countries are stalling on repatriating their national suspects, pledging aid instead. Baghdad rejected a Syrian request to repatriate 4,000 Syrian suspects in Iraqi custody, declaring that any of those Syrians who committed crimes in Iraq will be tried there under Iraqi law.
FPRI’s Salih argued that it is critically important for countries with nationals among the IS prisoner population in Iraq to repatriate them, noting that Iraq is already “overwhelmed by the sheer number” of these inmates.
“Iraq should not be treated as a dumping ground for unwanted IS elements and prisoners,” he said.
“In the event of major instability or chaos in Iraq, particularly as a consequence of the Iran-US-Israel war, these prisoners could become a readily available pool of battle-hardened and highly motivated manpower for IS,” he added.
There are concerns in Iraq that these prisoners could return to the battlefield in the event of a prison break, or if regional tensions spill into Iraq, Salih notes.
“That said, it is important that other countries repatriate their nationals held among IS prisoners and help alleviate some of the enormous burden Iraq is shouldering.”
Ghafuri pointed out that the US-Iran war has undoubtedly shifted regional attention further away from counterterrorism, giving IS elements a potential “opportunity to regroup” and prepare for their next phase.
“IS may no longer face the same international military pressure, while regional governments are preoccupied with Iran, oil, and wider geopolitical rivalries,” he said.
“The greatest danger is not simply that IS could return, but that the regional conditions that once enabled its rise are beginning to re-emerge.”
Paul Iddon is a freelance journalist based in Erbil, Iraqi Kurdistan, who writes about Middle East affairs.

Turkish parliament speaker meets Moldovan counterpart in Rome
Unknown

Norway: Proposed sovereign wealth fund reforms would mark biggest setback for its human rights safeguards in 20 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:04:07 UTC
22:04:07 KST

The new proposals to change the ethical framework governing Norway’s Government Pension Fund Global could significantly weaken independent human rights oversight, reduce transparency and make it harder to exclude companies linked to serious abuses, Amnesty International said today.
Norway’s Government Pension Fund Global, the world’s largest sovereign wealth fund, is reviewing its ethical governance framework. The Gjedrem Committee, set up for this purpose, has proposed weakening the independent Council on Ethics, allowing some of its assessments to remain confidential, and making it harder to exclude companies linked to serious human rights risks.
“The proposed ethical governance changes in the Norwegian fund risk weakening accountability and integrity and dismantling key human rights protections and amount to the most significant weakening of its human rights safeguards in two decades. When the world’s largest sovereign wealth fund changes its standards, the consequences do not stop at Norway’s borders. Other investors pay attention, and companies do too,” said John Peder Egenæs, Secretary General of Amnesty International Norway.
“Under the new proposals, the Council on Ethics would lose its ability to recommend exclusion, while some companies could remain in the portfolio despite serious human rights risks and failed engagement efforts. This risks weakening independent ethical scrutiny precisely when it is most needed and making certain investments too big to exclude. This is a dangerous approach and in practice imply that companies at risk of contributing to serious violations of international law are never excluded from the fund.”
When the world’s largest sovereign wealth fund changes its standards, the consequences do not stop at Norway’s borders. Other investors pay attention, and companies do too.
John Peder Egenæs, Secretary General of Amnesty International Norway
Greater discretion demands greater scrutiny
The new proposals recommend that the Council of Ethics would continue to assess the risk of companies contributing to or being responsible for serious ethical violations, but without recommending exclusion or observation. Instead, the central bank of Norway, the Norges Bank (NBIM), would determine the response.
The proposals also allow the Council’s risk assessments to be withheld from public disclosure where specified conditions relating to the fund’s economic interests or NBIM’s ability to fulfil its management responsibilities are met. This is a major setback for transparency, integrity and accountability.
“First, the watchdog loses its teeth. Then the curtains are drawn. The fund belongs to the Norwegian people, yet they risk losing access to information about any serious abuses that their money could be linked to,” said Egenæs.
While limited confidentiality during company engagement may sometimes be justified, the public must still be able to scrutinize why NBIM retains investments in companies linked to serious human rights risks.
“The Norwegian people have a right to know what the bank is asking companies to change, whether those changes are actually implemented, and why it continues to invest when serious human rights risks remain,” said Egenæs.
First, the watchdog loses its teeth. Then the curtains are drawn. The fund belongs to the Norwegian people, yet they risk losing access to information about any serious abuses that their money could be linked to.
John Peder Egenæs
Technology suppliers’ ongoing role must be examined
The Gjedrem Committee report recognizes that cloud computing, artificial intelligence and data analysis can be used in surveillance, intelligence gathering and military targeting, but proposes that sales of generic products should normally fall outside conduct-based exclusion criteria.
For major technology companies, the committee states that diversification considerations may carry decisive weight when assessing exclusion.
“Military use alone is insufficient to establish a company’s involvement in human rights abuses. But civilian applications cannot be used to avoid scrutiny of the role technology may play in any serious rights violations. Too often, the dual-use nature of these technologies is invoked to avoid meaningful scrutiny of the risks they create,” said Egenæs.
“The fund must examine what the supplier knows, how its services are used, and what it does to prevent or stop the misuse. There is an important distinction between selling a standard product and continuing to operate, adapt and support services used in serious abuses.”
Engagement cannot justify indefinite delay
Under the proposed framework, engagement with the company in order to address ethical concerns would replace exclusion as the primary response when risks of serious ethical violations are identified. NBIM would be required to exclude a company only where engagement has failed or has no realistic prospect of succeeding within a reasonable time, unless exclusion would limit the fund’s ability to remain broadly diversified globally. This exception risks allowing financial considerations to override human rights concerns. It also risks weakening the fund’s leverage over companies.
“An abuse does not become less serious because a company is large or an investment profitable. Applying the same ethical standard means little if the fund can retain the investment after efforts to secure change have failed,” said Egenæs.
“Engagement is a tool, not an end in itself. Without a credible possibility of exclusion, engagement risks becoming a conversation without consequences. In situations of armed conflict or occupation, the urgency of protecting people must guide the response. An ongoing dialogue is not, by itself, evidence that risks are being reduced.”
An abuse does not become less serious because a company is large or an investment profitable.
John Peder Egenæs
Weapons safeguards would be weakened
The committee further proposes an exception to the nuclear weapons exclusion criterion for producers based in states that are both recognized nuclear-weapon states under the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty and NATO allies of Norway. This would allow certain producers based in the United States, the United Kingdom and France to become eligible for investment.
“The catastrophic humanitarian consequences of nuclear weapons – the most inhumane and destructive weapons ever to be created – do not change with the nationality of their producer. Norway’s alliances must not determine which nuclear weapons producers the fund considers acceptable investments; all companies involved must be excluded,” said Egenæs.
The committee also recommends removing the specific criterion addressing arms sales to states that use those weapons to commit serious and systematic violations of international humanitarian law.
It proposes retaining the criterion concerning serious violations of individuals’ rights in war and conflict, and expanding a separate criterion concerning arms sales to states subject to sanctions or arms embargoes supported by Norway.
“These remaining safeguards matter. But removing an explicit criterion addressing arms transfers used in serious violations of international humanitarian law risks weakening scrutiny of suppliers and the human rights impacts of their products,” said Egenæs.
Amnesty International is calling on the Norwegian government and parliament to ensure and maintain strong, independent, ethical oversight of the fund, ensure meaningful public transparency and participation and preserve exclusion as a vital safeguard when engagement cannot effectively mitigate serious human rights risks.
The revised framework must be grounded in the United Nations Convention against Corruption, UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights and the OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises on Responsible Business Conduct, including risk-based and heightened human rights due diligence in conflict-affected settings.
“Human rights and independent oversight cannot be optional when they become inconvenient or costly. Norway should apply the same principles to the management of its own wealth that it expects others to uphold. It must ensure that transparency, accountability and human rights remain at the heart of how its wealth is managed. The Gjedrem Committee proposal must not be operationalized,” said Egenæs.
Human rights and independent oversight cannot be optional when they become inconvenient or costly.
John Peder Egenæs
Background
The Norwegian government appointed the committee, chaired by former central bank governor Svein Gjedrem, in November 2025 to review the ethical framework governing the Government Pension Fund Global. The committee submitted its unanimous report on 15 October 2026. Its recommendations do not themselves change the fund’s rules.
Amnesty International has previously called on Norway to divest the fund from companies involved in maintaining Israel’s unlawful occupation of the Occupied Palestinian Territory and to rigorously screen investments in line with international business and human rights standards.

UK threatens visa ban on Eritreans over migrant returns dispute

- Fast-track visas for senior officials and other VIPs to be suspended
The UK government has threatened to ban all Eritrean nationals from entering the country unless Eritrea agrees to accept the return of more of its citizens who arrive in the UK by small boats or have been convicted of crimes, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said Thursday.
Starting Thursday, Eritrean diplomats will face restrictions on their movements outside London, while fast-track visas for senior officials and other VIPs will be suspended, according to the government.
Under the new measures, Eritrean diplomats will be prohibited from travelling more than 60 kilometers (37 miles) outside London without permission. The Home Office said the restrictions mirror those imposed on British officials in Eritrea’s capital, Asmara.
Speaking to The Telegraph, Mahmood said Eritrea had repeatedly refused to cooperate with the return of individuals who have committed crimes or have no legal right to remain in the UK.
“Eritrea has had every chance to accept the return of criminals and those with no right to be in the UK. Unlike other countries, it has refused,” she said, adding that she would consider further measures against countries that refuse to cooperate.
The UK government accused Eritrean authorities of abruptly withdrawing cooperation earlier this year. London has previously used the threat of visa restrictions to pressure other countries into accepting the return of their nationals.
Eritreans were the largest nationality group among small-boat arrivals in the UK in the 12 months to June, accounting for 18% of arrivals, according to figures cited by the House of Commons Library.
Eritrea, a one-party state, has seen many young people attempt to leave the country to escape military conscription, which can last for decades.
The UK government earlier this year threatened visa restrictions against Angola, Namibia and the Democratic Republic of Congo.
Restrictions imposed on the Congo last year were lifted after cooperation on returns improved, according to the Home Office. Angola and Namibia agreed to changes before the threatened restrictions were introduced.
In November, Mahmood announced plans to reform the UK’s asylum system, warning that visa penalties would be imposed on countries that failed to cooperate with the return of their nationals.
The proposed measures included an “emergency brake” on visas for countries with high numbers of asylum claims, which would remain in place until they agreed to take back citizens living in the UK illegally.

Ukraine passes key laws to help unlock billions in aid from EU, IMF
KYIV, Oct 15 - Ukraine's parliament passed a package of legislation on Thursday to advance the implementation of key demands from the European Union and the International Monetary Fund to unlock billions in foreign aid.
As the war with Russia is in its fifth year, Ukraine faces a budget crisis driven by a huge military funding deficit, stalled economic growth, and domestic revenue shortfalls due to intensified Russian strikes on businesses and infrastructure.
Lawmakers approved bills to raise taxes on foreign parcels, increase e-commerce transparency, and amend financial monitoring rules for politicians.
"The laws approved today establish a modern model for the taxation of e-commerce, which is in line with the European Union’s approach and is fair to domestic businesses," said Finance Minister Sergii Marchenko.
"The reform is also part of the cooperation programme with the IMF and a condition for macro-financial support from the EU."
As the war gets more expensive and demand for weapons, drones and ammunition continues to grow, Ukraine is struggling to cover its defence spending with domestic revenue and crucially depends on financial aid from its Western allies.
Last month, the government was forced to delay some of the budget spending – like reconstruction work and preparations for winter – due to a budget liquidity crisis. Domestic tax revenue fell by 32 billion hryvnias ($711 million) in August and September as Russia intensified its strikes on the Ukrainian infrastructure, logistics and businesses.
Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi said that the results of this week's parliamentary work gave the government cause for optimism, but there was still a lot of work to do to meet all the requirements of the country's lenders.
For the remainder of this year, Ukraine has around $29 billion available in EU financial support waiting for continued disbursement.
The finance ministry said that the new rules for foreign parcels, introducing a 20% value-added tax, would take effect no earlier than July 2027. It was expected to generate an additional 20-30 billion hryvnias in budget revenue, lawmakers estimated. REUTERS

Brain implants are helping people who’ve lost their voice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

Brain implants are helping people who’ve lost their voice
The technology could get those with ALS, Parkinson’s disease and brain injuries “talking” again
This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)
On paper, my interview with Casey Harrell looks like any other.
I ask the questions, he answers them. He tells me about his background as a climate activist, his Southern roots and his daughter, who as a preschooler loved to dress up like a cheetah and roar around the house. “My daughter was incredibly cute in her cheetah outfit,” Harrell says.
The transcript tells the story of our conversation. But between the lines is an entirely different story — the story of where Harrell’s words come from.
Harrell started losing his ability to speak in his early 40s, nearly six years ago. He talked to me using a brain implant that can decode his words directly from his thoughts. The device, called a brain-computer interface, is experimental. But it has transformed Harrell’s life. And it could soon transform others. Advances in computing power and AI, lessons gleaned from patient experience and investments from neurotechnology companies are starting to yield real progress on brain-computer interfaces for people who can no longer talk. In other words, Harrell’s new voice might not be so singular in the future.
“There’s a lot of excitement and hope in the field right now,” says Matthew Willsey, a neurosurgeon and biomedical engineer at the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor, who recently implanted a new type of speech interface in a woman’s brain. For years, Willsey says, scientists didn’t know whether attempts to decode speech would be successful; now, a body of research results points clearly to yes. “They’re thinking, ‘Wow, this is actually a usable technology that addresses a real problem that people suffer from.’”
Harrell has amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or ALS. The progressive neurodegenerative disease, which affects an estimated 35,000 people in the United States, kills nerve cells in the brain and spinal cord that control muscles. As the neural connections between Harrell’s brain and body began to falter, he gradually lost his ability to move his muscles, leaving him confined to his bed or a wheelchair. Some of those dropped signals directed the muscles in his throat and mouth, the ones that allow him to speak.
“I began to lose my ability to talk shortly after my diagnosis in 2020,” Harrell says. After that, it was “a slow-motion car crash” as fewer and fewer people could understand him. “[My voice] is the most important thing I have lost in this whole disease,” he says.
In a stroke of luck, Harrell learned through a family member about a clinical trial happening at the University of California, Davis — one that attempted to restore speech with a brain-computer interface. In 2023, Harrell had four small devices implanted on the left side of his brain. These grids of electrodes reside on Harrell’s speech motor cortex, a stretch of brain along the precentral gyrus that controls the movements required for speech.
Today, Harrell uses his system for about 10 to 14 hours daily, making him, as he puts it, “the world’s biggest power user of the brain-to-computer interface known to man.” Hard data suggest he’s right. A recent count shows that Harrell has used his system to communicate nearly 2 million words, the scientists working with him reported in June in Nature Medicine.
The very existence of Harrell’s words shows it may be possible to restore speech for people with ALS, as well as for those whose speech is impaired by stroke, paralysis, cerebral palsy and Parkinson’s disease. “This kind of technology has the potential to dramatically change the conversation,” says David Brandman, a UC Davis neurosurgeon and neuroscientist who works with Harrell.
Harrell’s interface still has room for improvement. It’s bulky, relatively slow and limited in what sorts of nonword sounds it can decode.
But it is a “beginning,” says Leigh Hochberg, a neuroscientist at Brown University who works with Harrell. “It’s still early days. There’s a lot of research to happen, and it’s going to be very exciting.” The end game, Hochberg says, is a world in which people could use a device to communicate seamlessly, quickly, clearly — and in their former voices.
Success would mean restoring more than just people’s words, Brandman says. It would mean restoring their ability to connect in all the ineffable ways that make us human. “Speech is so fundamental to who we are,” he says. “Imagine living in a world where you couldn’t tell someone you’re in pain, or you couldn’t say that you love them … It’s not hard to imagine how devastating that would be for your quality of life.”
The voice inside
On the path to a technology that enables fast, natural speech, scientists first had to answer a more basic question: Could the brain’s electrical chatter be decoded and translated into action outside of the head?
Nerve cells speak to each other with tiny pulses of electricity, signals that can be picked up with electrodes. The existence of this electrical language raised the tantalizing idea that electrical messages could be decoded straight from where they originate in the brain, bypassing damaged links to the rest of the body.
“This has really started as early as the 1950s, the first time scientists put electrodes into brains to record neural activity,” says Sergey Stavisky, a neuroscientist and neural engineer at UC Davis. “You can record the electrical activity of brain cells or parts of the brain. And that’s really when modern neuroscience started trying to study, how does the brain compute? How does it allow us to move our muscles?”
Figuring out how to decode simple neural commands was the first step. Animal studies paved the way, including experiments in which rhesus monkeys consciously controlled the movements of a robotic arm using only brain signals detected by implanted electrodes.
The Deep End podcast explores what makes your voice yours
What if you lost your voice? Today, AI can re-create it, and brain implants can turn thoughts into speech. This season of The Deep End follows people living through these vocal transformations — and asks what these remarkable technologies can teach us about why our voices matter in the first place.
By 2004, scientists had enough confidence in the approach to launch a clinical trial in humans called BrainGate. Researchers implanted a grid of electrodes in the brain of a paralyzed man named Matthew Nagle. A former star athlete, Nagle was able to control a computer cursor with his thoughts alone. “That was really the starting gun of the modern version of the brain-computer interface field,” Stavisky says.
From there, attempts to link brain activity with some physical outcome — such as moving a computer mouse, a wheelchair or a robotic arm — blossomed. Some of these efforts focused on the brain signals and regions that controlled movements of the hands and arms. Others focused on a very tricky version of the same basic problem: talking.
A brain-computer interface that could detect the intention to say a word and bypass the muscles needed to say it would be a powerful workaround for people with diseases like ALS or brain injuries. And it is no small thing to people who can no longer talk. “Losing their speech is way more devastating than losing their mobility,” says Jessica Pietrowski, a speech and language pathologist at UC Davis who has worked with many such patients. “Speech is how they maintain their identity in their relationships.”
Harrell emphasizes this point. “What does my voice mean to me? It means so much,” he says. “It is the ability to parent my daughter. It is the ability to connect with my wife. It is the ability to make a wry joke with my friends.”
Looking for a cheetah
Talking feels effortless to most of us, but just saying hello involves a sweeping array of actions — and upwards of 100 muscles. “It’s incredibly complex and intricate, and really, an incredible human feat,” Pietrowski says.
Consider the “h” sound in “hello.” Known as a glottal fricative, it involves an orchestra of tiny movements. First, the diaphragm contracts to fill the lungs with air. Chest and abdominal muscles push air up through relaxed vocal cords and surrounding tissues. This puff of air then travels to the mouth, where lips, jaw and tongue execute complex sequences of movements that create the rest of the sound. Finally, air waves, perfectly shaped, ripple from the mouth. Then, and only then, “you have speech,” Pietrowski says.
But the beginnings of this nearly miraculous transformation start in the brain, where tiny electrical nerve pulses command the body to speak. In Harrell’s trial, he would attempt to speak words, prompting his motor cortex to send signals to his body. The implanted electrodes would detect the patterns and send them to a computer to interpret. With this work-around, it didn’t matter that Harrell’s muscles didn’t get the message; the computer would.
After Harrell recovered from surgery, researchers began testing the system in his home. They collected his neural data and streamed it to computers on a nearby cart, where machine learning algorithms attempted to match Harrell’s brain activity patterns to those that predictably occur with certain sounds. Called phonemes, these sound units are the building blocks of words. The algorithm assembled the phonemes into words, as it made its best guess about what Harrell was trying to say. To limit the computational power required, the algorithm used a vocabulary of just 50 words.
When the system was plugged in and ready to go, scientists asked Harrell to try and say a specific, random sentence built from that library: “What good is that?”
Harrell got to work. His eyebrows shot up as he saw the words appear on a screen in front of him in response to his thoughts. The decoder worked.
Everyone paused. Some of the researchers started to cry. Harrell and his family became emotional. Being in the room when the switch was flipped on was “incredible,” Brandman says. “The majority of my adult life was working up to that moment, and to see it come to fruition was an incredible experience. But more than that was seeing what impact it immediately had for Casey and his family.”
Harrell remembers his feelings that day, too: “Pure joy.” Even though he wasn’t choosing his words for that first test, “it was a profound moment,” he says. “The possibilities for the near future for me and the rest of humanity were overwhelming to realize.”
The second day of testing was even more profound, but in a personal way. This time, the system’s algorithm was using a vocabulary of over 125,000 words. This would be more challenging for the decoder, but it would give Harrell more autonomy to say what he wanted.
Harrell started the session with a joke, Hochberg recalls, along the lines of, “Is this thing on?” But his next line was a real puzzler: “I’m looking for a cheetah.”
Hochberg, who had joined remotely on a video call, was sure it was a mistake. “There’s no way that the second sentence on the second day of using a brain-to-computer interface is going to say anything about a cheetah,” Hochberg says. “That’s obviously a decoding error.”
But there was something the scientist couldn’t see. Harrell’s 4-year-old daughter had bounded into the room, dressed as a cheetah.
The discovery was big scientifically, but it was bigger for what it represented to Harrell. Brain technology could restore not just his words, but also the spontaneous exchanges that had once made up his everyday life.
“It was so amazing to be able to be understood right from the get-go and to be able to talk and respond to my daughter,” Harrell says, “especially because that was lacking completely from my life.”
Hochberg says moments like that represent the promise that brain-computer interfaces hold. “To me, seeing it work that quickly and that powerfully really, really emphasized that these are technologies that are going to be able to restore not only activities of daily living,” he says, “but they’re going to restore communication between parent and child.”
From thoughts to words
Casey Harrell’s brain-computer interface extracts neural signals from his brain and, through a few key steps, transforms them into
words. Electrodes implanted in Harrell’s speech motor cortex detect neurons’ electrical signals (1), generating raw neural data (2). Advanced machine learning efforts (3) map chunks of the data to phonemes, the building blocks of words (4). Those phonemes are then assembled into sentences by a predictive language model, or LM (5), and put on a screen where they can be read or spoken.
Harrell uses his interface to send email and Slack messages and play Wordle with his wife and child. He uses it to work; in fact, he’s just getting started on a new climate consultancy project. Harrell’s interface has connected him to the world in a way that would have been impossible even a few years ago.
But the system is still a research device. And like any early design, it comes with limitations. First, it isn’t portable; Harrell has wires coming from a port that sits on the top of his head, and he can use it only at home. And it is slow by the standards of typical conversation. You can’t tell from the written transcript of our interview, but our conversations always came with built-in delays.
For example, as we chatted, we discovered that we had both worked in the same part of Washington, D.C. I asked him if he remembered his old address. The answer came some two minutes later.
“I make a very simple analogy where I talk about having the brain-to-computer interface being akin to trying to catch a train, running to get the last car before it leaves the station,” Harrell says. With the current interface, “if people are patient and wait for my sentence correction, I can [catch the train and] be a part of the conversation.”
Harrell’s system translates his neural activity into words on a screen. If he chooses to do so, he can then use a computerized voice to say the words out loud. “It is brain-to-text, and then it gets translated to the voice,” Harrell says. A brain-to-voice system, in which a person’s thoughts are translated directly into spoken words, he adds, “is the holy grail of what this will become.”
More than words
Harrell and the scientists working with him are getting closer to this very type of real-time communication. Last year in Nature, they debuted a new algorithm that attempted to turn Harrell’s brain signals straight into sounds. The results: He could speak his mind with a delay of just 10 milliseconds. That’s very close to a real-time conversation. But the sounds Harrell made were hard to understand, with just over half of them being intelligible to listeners.
The next generation of devices aims to do better. Willsey, the University of Michigan neurosurgeon, is working on one such device, a fully implantable array. In June, he implanted what’s called the “cortical module,” about the size of a dime, in the brain of a 68-year-old woman. Like Harrell, the woman could no longer talk in a way that most people could understand.
Unlike the BrainGate system, this new device — made by Austin, Texas–based neurotechnology company Paradromics — is portable. Surgeons implanted it in a stretch of brain tissue that made up the woman’s speech motor cortex, along the precentral gyrus. The cortical module collects neural data and sends it to another device implanted in the chest called a transceiver. From there, signals shoot to a receiver on her chest, where the data gets transformed into sounds — spoken words that play out of speakers on a nearby computer.
Paradromics’ priority is to test whether the implant is safe. If so, scientists can turn to the goal of restoring speech in real time. “The moment that you’re thinking the words, you don’t have to wait for the sentence to complete,” says Willsey, who, like Brandman, is a site investigator for the Paradromics clinical trial. “You can let the words kind of flow out as they would in a normal conversation.”
Scientists also want to decode more than words. Qualities of voice, such as pitch, are important for marking questions, says Vikash Gilja, a Paradromics neuroscientist. Speakers can also alter or pace their conversation to show sarcasm or concern. These sounds are all made by moving muscles, Gilja says, and can therefore be decoded from the brain.
“Our near-term goal right now is just to restore speech,” says Paradromics neurosurgeon Stephen Ryu. “But eventually, we’re hoping that we can actually restore someone’s ability to be fully involved in a conversation, to basically decode things like their timing, their emotions, their personality.”
Other researchers are trying to incorporate the gestures that many of us use to communicate.
“Some gestures can substitute for speech entirely, like nodding yes, shaking your head no, waving, shrugging, giving a thumbs up,” says bioengineer Samantha Brosler of the University of California, San Fransico. Gestures can also change the meaning of words; a “maybe” with a head nod is close to a yes, for instance. “I think of gestures and body movements as an additional communication channel that can work together with speech,” Brosler says.
In a new study, Brosler and colleagues enabled two people with paralysis who had lost their speaking ability to instead use their brain signals to control both the words and gestures of digital avatars. The advance, reported in September in Nature Neuroscience, adds to the repertoire of signals that could be decoded and turned into action.
And as all this is happening, scientists are creating smaller, more stable types of electrodes to embed in the brain; more powerful computational algorithms to handle larger amounts of data; and better models of how those signals relate to sounds, words and gestures, Gilja says. “We can see all the pieces coming together.”
There are many reasons to be optimistic about the future, says Brandman, who is an investigator for the clinical trial led by Paradromics. “I think I’m about five years away from being able to meet a patient with ALS and having the following conversation,” he says. “‘Ms. Smith, I’m sorry you’ve been diagnosed with ALS. I don’t have a cure for you, but I do have a device that I can implant that can help you communicate.’”
That conversation is tantalizing. But there are no guarantees that these systems will work as hoped, or that they will be widely available. Such implants would probably come with hefty price tags, invasive brain surgeries and perhaps more demand than the few capable clinicians and technologists could meet.
And there are underlying questions about the brain itself. One concern is that changes to the brain over time might render neural signals unreliable, especially as diseases progress. If that happens, a person’s interface might produce a scrambled message — or be left without enough neural data to decode.
“These are real challenges, and the field is working on them,” Stavisky says. “But they’re not solved yet.”
Despite these hurdles, the push for voice-restoring technology can’t come soon enough for people who have lost theirs. In September, researchers reported that the woman with the Paradromics implant had a message for them. “OK,” she used her brain-computer interface to tell researchers. “I have a lot to say.” With her system, she was able to call her grandchildren on the telephone.
And Harrell is now living a life that looks very different from the one he might have imagined six years ago. Although his disease keeps him close to home, he can now share his thoughts with the world — and his family — instead of locking them away inside.
“The ability to scream when you are running and want to get out some stress, the ability to say sweet nothings into your partner’s ear,” Harrell says. “These are the things that life is all about, and when you are robbed of those times, you want them back at all costs. And this is why this is good enough for now.”
But he too has a vision, a day when these devices are commonplace, “when I am one of many, instead of being one of one.”
For more about the human voice and to hear from Casey Harrell himself, listen to The Deep End podcast Season Two, called Talk to Me. It’s free wherever you get your podcasts.

DPP's Lai Jui-lung campaigns on experience in Kaohsiung mayoral race

2026-10-15
12:58:04 UTC
21:58:04 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — DPP Kaohsiung mayoral candidate Lai Jui-lung (賴瑞隆) will launch his campaign headquarters Saturday, highlighting two decades of experience in city government and the legislature.
CNA reported that Lai has represented Kaohsiung in the legislature since 2016. He secured the DPP mayoral nomination in January after defeating fellow legislators Chiu Yi-ying (邱議瑩), Hsu Chih-chieh (許智傑), and Lin Tai-hua (林岱樺) in the party's primary.
Lai studied political science at Soochow University and earned a master's degree from National Taiwan University. The Changhua-born candidate began his political career as a legislative aide before holding posts in several central government agencies, per FTV News.
He later spent about a decade in Kaohsiung City Government under former Mayor Chen Chu (陳菊). His work covered economic development, tourism, public information, and marine affairs, per Knews.
Lai helped organize the 2009 World Games in Kaohsiung and promoted major tourism events, including the giant yellow duck exhibition in 2013. He has cited these projects as examples of his experience in attracting visitors and raising the city's international profile, per Taisounds.
Lai entered the legislature in 2016 and won re-election in 2020 and 2024. He has chaired the legislature's interior and economic affairs committees and served as deputy secretary-general of the DPP legislative caucus.
Economic development is a central part of Lai's mayoral campaign. He wants to expand Kaohsiung's semiconductor and artificial intelligence industries, including plans for an AI industry hub in the Asia New Bay Area, per UDN.
Lai has also proposed building an indoor stadium and a large forest park, along with improving transport links in the Asia New Bay Area. He said the projects would attract investment, create jobs, and improve residents' quality of life.
However, Lai faced controversy in December 2025 after his child was accused of bullying a classmate. He publicly apologized and acknowledged spending too little time on parenting because of his political work, TVBS reported.
Lai later said the families had reached an agreement through the school's procedures and described the incident as a conflict rather than bullying. A relative of the other child disputed his account, saying the family had accepted an apology but had not agreed that bullying did not occur.
Lai has made his experience in city government and the legislature central to his campaign. He said he wants to build on the work of previous DPP mayors and guide Kaohsiung's next stage of development.

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said Thursday that Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (CICA) member states must take a firm stance in supporting the rights of Palestine, which is among the group’s members, as well as in opposing ongoing oppression and grave violations.
Addressing the 7th CICA Summit in Azerbaijan’s capital Baku, Hakan Fidan said: “We cannot uphold this commitment while Israel, a CICA member, violates the fundamental rights of the Palestinian people through a systematic policy of oppression.”
“A lasting solution requires the establishment of an independent and sovereign Palestinian state based on the 1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital,” he stressed.
Stronger CICA essential for Asia’s security, prosperity
Fidan stressed that a stronger CICA is essential to ensuring peace and prosperity at a time when Asia’s rise is shaping the global landscape.
“Türkiye is committed to strengthening CICA as Asia’s most inclusive security forum,” he said.
“We must enhance economic security and improve connectivity by expanding transport links and diversifying energy corridors,” he said.
Fidan highlighted the importance of the Middle Corridor project, saying it would significantly boost the effectiveness of China’s Belt and Road Initiative.
“This will not only facilitate trade between Asia and Europe but also help us build new bridges for people-to-people contacts,” he said.
On the Development Road project from Iraq’s Grand Faw Port through Türkiye, Fidan said: “This project will connect the Gulf to Europe through Iraq and Türkiye while also supporting stability and prosperity in the region and beyond.”
Fidan also highlighted the importance of enhancing synergies among different regional cooperation mechanisms in Asia.
“Improving coordination among CICA, the Organization of Turkic States, the Economic Cooperation Organization, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization will undoubtedly strengthen connectivity across the continent,” he said.
Noting that connectivity also extends to the digital world, Fidan said cooperation in science, technology, and innovation should be deepened under CICA to ensure that artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies benefit people not only in Asia but around the world.
The Turkish foreign minister also said sustainable development requires action to address environmental challenges, noting that Türkiye continues to play a leading role in tackling the effects of climate change.

Taiwan's ITRI and eJoule improve drone battery manufacturing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
12:57:44 UTC
21:57:44 KST

TAIPEI (TAIPEI NEWS) – Hsinchu-based Industrial Technology Research Institute said Thursday that it has partnered with local battery maker eJoule to make high-capacity batteries for drones and electric vehicles.
Medium-and high-lithium ternary batteries use nickel, cobalt, and manganese. Higher lithium content means greater storage capacity, making them suitable for drones, robotics, and electric vehicles.
According to a press release, drones and EVs are driving demand for lighter, longer-lasting batteries. Although ternary batteries are valued for their capacity, there are lifecycle and safety bottlenecks that need to be addressed before commercialization.
ITRI and eJoule co-developed a solution using single-crystal structures, electrode fabrication, and power cell certification to speed commercialization for drones, robotics, and storage applications. The project also aims to achieve production and supply chain self-reliance.
Electrode fabrication combines raw materials with metal foils to create the positive and negative charges required for batteries to function. The common method involves mixing the materials with additives and solvents such as water for coating onto the foils, which are then vacuumed and pressed into batteries.
ITRI Material and Chemical Research Laboratories Director Chiu Kuo-chan (邱國展) said eJoule provided the material while ITRI designed battery specifications and conducted performance tests. He noted that the material proved stable after extensive, repetitive cycles of charging and discharging, making it a suitable candidate comparable to lithium iron phosphate batteries in terms of lifespan as well as safer than traditional ternary materials.
ITRI said eJoule’s patented dynamic crystallization process yields simple, high-performing structures without using toxic precursors. eJoule Vice President Liu Min-tuan (劉敏端) said the initiative would combine ITRI's battery expertise to speed material applications from laboratory settings to commercially viable products.

Taiwan’s Delta Electronics warns power shortages could constrain AI growth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
12:57:39 UTC
21:57:39 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Delta Electronics Chair Cheng Ping (鄭平) said Thursday that power infrastructure is failing to keep pace with the rapid expansion of AI data centers.
Four major US cloud service providers are expected to spend 4.7 times as much on capital expenditures this year as in 2022, while investment in power systems has grown only 1.8-fold, Cheng said at a forum, per CNA.
Cheng said global electrification stands at about 21%, compared with 30% in Taiwan, and electricity demand will continue rising as transportation, industry, and data centers expand. He projected that EV power consumption could increase fivefold over the next decade, while data center electricity use could triple from last year’s level by 2030.
Citing estimates, Cheng said US data centers are expected to add 44 GW of electricity demand by 2028, while the power grid is projected to add only 25 GW in supply capacity, leaving a 19 GW gap. He attributed the infrastructure lag partly to regulations, equipment lifespans, and investment returns.
Cheng said improving energy efficiency is essential to stable power supplies. He noted that Delta has invested in solid oxide fuel cells, which generate electricity using hydrogen or natural gas and can achieve overall efficiency of up to 85%, per Anue.
Cheng said the company is also developing solid-state transformers that convert medium-voltage alternating current directly into 800-volt direct current, reducing conversion losses in data centers. He added that the company’s new prefabricated power solution can cut on-site deployment time by 50%.

Euro area industrial output unexpectedly falls 0.5% in August
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
12:56:35 UTC
21:56:35 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
Industrial production in the euro area fell 0.5% month-on-month in August, against expectations of stagnation, according to Eurostat data released Thursday.
The decline followed a 0.3% contraction in July and a 0.1% drop in June, marking the third consecutive monthly fall.
Across the EU, seasonally adjusted industrial output decreased 0.3% in August, following a 0.4% drop in July.
Euro area production of non-durable consumer goods saw the sharpest monthly decline among the main industrial groupings, down 2.7%. Intermediate goods output decreased 0.8%, while energy production slipped 0.6%.
Capital goods production, however, rose 0.4%, and durable consumer goods output climbed 0.2%.
Across the EU, non-durable consumer goods production fell 2.3%, energy output declined 0.5%, and intermediate goods production dropped 0.3%. Capital goods output rose 0.7%, while durable consumer goods production remained unchanged.
Among member states, Belgium saw the largest monthly decline at 5.1%, followed by Ireland at 3.1% and Portugal at 2%.
Sweden posted the strongest increase at 6.5%, followed by Estonia at 4.3% and the Netherlands at 2.6%.
Among the bloc’s largest economies, industrial output rose 0.4% in Germany but fell 0.3% in France, 1.3% in Italy, and 0.8% in Spain.
On an annual basis, industrial production declined 1.1% in the euro area and 0.2% across the EU.
Euro area non-durable consumer goods output dropped 9.1% from August 2025, while intermediate goods production fell 0.4%. Energy, capital goods, and durable consumer goods output climbed 3.1%, 3%, and 0.4%, respectively.
Ireland saw the steepest annual contraction at 15%, followed by Belgium at 7.1% and Bulgaria at 5.4%. The Netherlands saw the largest jump at 9.8%, ahead of Hungary at 8.8% and Denmark at 8.3%.

Berk Kutay Gökmen
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
Former US President Barack Obama has criticized Israel’s handling of the Middle East conflict, warning that military strength cannot guarantee lasting security and that refusing concessions to Palestinians risks undermining its moral standing.
The former president made the remarks on Tuesday during a discussion with award-winning writer and journalist Susan McKay at Belfast, northern Ireland, according to the Belfast Telegraph.
Speaking about the Israeli war on Gaza, Obama said the violence should “pain everybody”, describing it as a destructive cycle driven by historical grievances, hardened attitudes and deep divisions.
He acknowledged the long history of persecution faced by Jewish people in Europe. However, he also stressed that Palestinians had suffered injustice through the loss of their land.
“That is undeniable. What is also undeniable is that they took land off people and they were excessive. And those people understandably said: ‘This is injustice and I want my land back,’” he said.
Obama argued that the stronger side carries a greater responsibility to help break the cycle of violence, rather than relying solely on its military and technological superiority.
“If the attitude of Israel is, now that we are the strongest, the most technologically advanced in the region, then our security will depend on us simply doing whatever we need and taking whatever we want, and not making any concessions to anyone,” he said.
“That may work short-term... but you have ceded moral ground if that is the position you take.”
He said the current Israeli government appeared to have adopted that approach and urged it to recognize that millions of Palestinians would remain in the region.
“I would say the current Israeli government appears to have taken that. It is incumbent on them to recognise that 7 million Palestinians are not going anywhere,” Obama said.
“It is not sustainable to press upon them a condition that no-one would accept for themselves.”
Earlier on Tuesday, Obama received an honorary doctorate from Queen’s University Belfast.

Photos: China and North Korea open new border bridge amid deepening ties
The New Yalu River Bridge connects Dandong, China, and Sinuiju, North Korea, enhancing regional trade and collaboration.
The opening of a long-delayed bridge linking China and North Korea underscores the deepening ties between the two neighbours as Pyongyang courts both Beijing and Moscow to ease its economic isolation.
China’s official Xinhua news agency said a launch ceremony was held on Thursday for the New Yalu River Bridge, which connects the northeastern Chinese city of Dandong with the North Korean border city of Sinuiju.
Video from state media showed trucks decorated with the national flags of both countries lined up on the four-lane span, which itself was festooned with Chinese and North Korean flags.

North Korean Premier Pak Thae Song also delivered a video message.
The 3km (1.8-mile) road bridge is expected to ease pressure on the ageing Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge, a decades-old structure on the same route that carries a railway line and vehicles but can accommodate only one-way traffic at a time.
More than 70 percent of official trade between the two countries currently goes through that crossing, according to Chinese data. The South Korean government has counted at least 17 active road and rail links along the 1,400km (870-mile) North Korea-China border.

Sally Rooney books withdrawn from sale in UK over Palestine Action support
Publisher Faber says withdrawal due to ‘circumstances where Faber cannot pass on UK earnings to Sally Rooney’.
Irish novelist Sally Rooney says her books have been withdrawn from sale in the United Kingdom due to her public support for Palestine Action, a group the British government has designated as a terrorist organisation.
Rooney’s publisher Faber said on Wednesday that the withdrawal was due to “circumstances where Faber cannot pass on UK earnings to Sally Rooney for her work”, calling it an “unconscionable situation for a publisher”.
Rooney told BBC News that the further publication of her work could constitute a “serious criminal offence”.
She added that she made “every effort to be honest” with the public about her beliefs and intentions and that she is “wholly prepared to accept the consequences”.
The Ebook editions of her work have been removed from sale in the UK, but a number of physical copies of her books are still available in shops.
Rooney has received critical acclaim for her novels, including Normal People and Conversations With Friends, which have sold millions of copies globally. The two novels were adapted for television by the BBC.
The UK government outlawed Palestine Action in July 2025, after activists from the group broke into a Royal Air Force base and sprayed red paint on two aircraft to protest against Britain’s military support for Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.
Being a member or a supporter of the group in the UK is punishable by up to 14 years in prison.
After the ban took effect, Rooney wrote in the Irish Times that she would continue to support Palestine Action and if that makes her a “‘supporter of terror’ under UK law, so be it”.
She has publicly said she would use her earnings from her novels and adaptations to support the group. In September 2025, Rooney could not travel to the UK to receive an award due to fear of arrest.
Independent Member of Parliament Jeremy Corbyn, who has recently been banned from entering Israel for his support for Palestine, said the situation showed the “complete absurdity of the proscription of Palestine Action”.
“What a stain on this government that people in this country are unable to buy and enjoy the work of one of this generation’s greatest writing talents,” he wrote in a statement on X.
John McDonnell, a Labour MP, released a statement saying he does not want anyone in the UK “to miss out on her wonderful writing”.

Limburg named the world’s “most intelligent region”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:47:29 UTC
21:47:29 KST

Limburg named the world’s “most intelligent region”
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Limburg has been named the world’s smartest region by the US-based think tank Intelligent Community Forum (ICF). The southern province, known for its hills and regional dialects, beat finalists from countries like Taiwan and Canada.
The award was presented to Brightlands, a network of four business and research campuses in the province that focus on health, AI, sustainable chemistry and food research. The ICF, a federation of 200 cities and regions, ranks areas around the globe each year on factors like economic and social development.
The jury praised the cooperation between government, business and research institutions at the campuses, as well as the way Limburg rebuilt itself after its coal mines closed half a century ago. After natural gas was discovered in 1959, “the region lost not only jobs but also security and hope,” ICF founder Robert Bell said.
Brightlands was set up in 2014 by the provincial government, education institutions and local businesses, according to L1 Nieuws.
The Maastricht campus focuses on health and is linked to the university hospital, while Heerlen, home to pension fund ABP and the national statistics office CBS, specialises in data and AI.
The materials campus is on the Chemelot chemical site in Sittard-Geleen, and Venlo’s food campus uses infrastructure left over from the 2012 Floriade horticultural expo.
Limburg beat six other finalists, from Brazil, Turkey, the US, Canada, Spain and Taiwan. Last year’s winner was Durham Region in Canada. The Brainport region around Eindhoven won in 2011.

A teenage hitman who travelled from Norway to the UK with the intention of carrying out a murder on behalf of an Iran-backed international crime gang has been jailed for 20 years.
Johannes Kongsnes Natland, 19, a talented footballer, had agreed to shoot an unknown target in return for €25,000 (£21,500).
He travelled to the UK in March last year from his home in Stavanger, and two days later – before he could carry out the hit – armed police arrested him at a hotel in Huddersfield, West Yorkshire.
Officers found him in possession of a semi-automatic pistol, a revolver, 12 rounds of live ammunition and gloves.
Natland admitted possessing the firearms and ammunition and said he had intended to shoot himself in the foot to get out of the “pickle” he was in. However, he was found guilty of conspiracy to murder and on Friday was sentenced to 20 years in detention.
The court heard that Natland had been recruited by another teenager, referred to as Generalen, who was working for the proscribed Swedish Foxtrot gang, which is backed by the Iranian regime and known for recruiting children as young as 13 to become involved in drug smuggling and violent crimes.
Natland had been controlled by an English-speaking boss called Agent 47, an apparent reference to the Hitman gaming and film franchise. The identity and whereabouts of Agent 47 remain unknown.
Natland flew into Manchester on a temporary passport and was stopped by Border Force officials, who bailed him to return to the airport to catch the next direct flight home.
Instead, he travelled by taxi to Huddersfield where he booked into the Briar Court hotel and picked up the guns and ammunition, as well as £2,000 in cash. He was directed to a stolen Nissan with false number plates, which was to be used in the murder.
While in the hotel, Natland took selfies with the guns and cash spread out on his bed, and bragged to his girlfriend that he had the “bangs in the bag”. Armed police arrived to arrest him at 5.15am the next day.
Paul Hynes KC, defending, pointed to Natland’s age at the time of the offending and said he had been a “young, popular, successful student and sportsman” before he went “off the rails” after he became addicted to drugs.
Giving evidence, Natland told jurors: “I wasn’t an international assassin. I thought people had this impression and expected me to be this guy. I knew I wasn’t.”
However, in a televised sentencing at Woolwich crown court in south-east London, Mrs Justice Cheema-Grubb said messages he had sent showed “not only participation but at points excitement” about what he had been planning to do.
“You agreed to be the enforcer and pursued it, despite numerous opportunities to extricate yourself,” she said. “Although the fact that no one was shot dead or physically harmed is important, I am sure had the intervention of the police not prevented the plan from proceeding, you would have done what you had agreed to.”
