British food and drink exports to EU collapse by more than a third since Brexit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:34:37 UTC
21:34:37 KST

Exports of British food and drink to the EU have collapsed by more than a third since Brexit with eggs, chicken and potato producers badly hit, new figures show.
Analysis by the National Farmers’ Union (NFU) of HMRC data shows a sharp fall in exports in the year to July compared with the same period in 2019, with sugar dropping the most, down 70%.
Data for the first seven months also shows poultry exports fell 53%, with eggs and egg products sold for confectionary and baking industries down 65% for the same period.
Full-year data from 2019 to 2025 showed an even deeper impact since Brexit with exports of eggs and egg products down 74%.
The NFU president, Tom Bradshaw, said: “The EU is our largest trading partner for agri-food products, accounting for 68% of agri-food exports last year, but trade volumes have fallen over a third since 2019.”
Boris Johnson’s government signed a deal on the UK’s future trading and security relationship with the EU in late 2020, after the UK’s formal exit earlier that year.
Andy Burnham is reconsidering Labour’s red lines on EU membership under pressure to repair the economic damage of Brexit. Economists estimate the cost to the UK economy has been up to £240bn so far.
Food exporters have long complained over the added paperwork that Britain’s exit has brought. Since Brexit all food exports are required to have customs paperwork with different codes for every single product. This includes, for example, every variation of an egg product, whether it is fresh, dried, steamed, shelled, or contains added water or sugar. The paper pulp used in egg cartons as well as the eggs also need health certification to show they are free of disease.
Also hit hard by Brexit is the horticultural sector with seed potatoes from Britain, mainly Scotland, banned from the EU after trade negotiators failed to agree on equivalent standards in the Brexit trade and cooperation agreement in 2020. Horticultural exports fell more than 50%.
Pre-Brexit, Scotland exported around 20,000 tonnes of seed potatoes, worth almost £11m, to Europe each year.
Speaking in parliament earlier this week Andy Burnham said that Brexit trade barriers meant “entire truckloads of plants or fresh product can be destroyed because of a single missing stamp or minor paperwork delay”.
He hoped to “land a positive outcome” in the upcoming UK-EU reset talks with a new agreement removing many of the sanitary and phytosanitary checks on fresh farm produce exports that came in after Brexit.
Burnham told MPs: “Our largest food export, Scottish salmon, faces a 100% rate of document checks at the border, costing us around £100m in lost exports.
“British burgers and other fresh meat products cannot be sold in the EU. Seed potatoes from Scotland and shellfish from Wales are banned. This is having a real impact on businesses and the agreement on the table could reverse some of that damage.”
A deal to ease sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) checks was largely agreed in May giving food producers time to prepare for changes expected to come in next summer, but key details remain to be finalised.
The NFU is calling for “transition arrangements” for some UK crops that have been grown with fungicides or breeding techniques not yet approved in the EU.
This is to allow those harvesting this autumn and winter to make use of the new export freedoms when they come in next year.
Bradshaw said: “British farmers and growers must retain access to precision breeding technologies that will help to strengthen food resilience to extreme weather and to science-based plant protection products that help protect food being grown for 29m households from pests and diseases.
“Any changes must also provide an appropriate transition period to minimise disruption for farm businesses and we will continue to make this case to government while we await the final agreement.”

IMF, World Bank warn of mounting debt, divergent AI boom at Bangkok annual meetings
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
20:56:55 CST
21:56:55 KST

BANGKOK, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- Global economic leaders gathering in the Thai capital on Friday warned that escalating sovereign debt burdens, geopolitical conflict, and rapid technological disruption risk fragmenting the world economy, even as headline global growth holds steady at 3.1 percent.
Speaking at the plenary session of the 2026 Annual Meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank Group, policymakers emphasized that while artificial intelligence (AI) is delivering unprecedented productivity momentum to select advanced economies, the broader global financial architecture faces mounting strain from high borrowing costs and shrinking fiscal buffers.
The summit marks the return of the Bretton Woods institutions to the Queen Sirikit National Convention Center in Bangkok 35 years after the city first hosted the gathering in 1991.
Delivering her annual address to the Board of Governors, IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva described the global economy as navigating between "two big opposing forces": a drag caused by ongoing energy supply shocks and a countervailing surge driven by AI-led investment.
A year ago, in October 2025, the projection for 2026 economic output stood at 3.1 percent. Today, that estimate is holding steady at 3.1 percent, Georgieva told delegates, adding that "trade, meanwhile, has flown around all obstacles."
However, Georgieva cautioned that the headline stability masks sharp underlying divergence. While technology leaders in the United States, China, India, and parts of Asia are capturing substantial growth upgrades, economies battered by conflict and persistent inflation are experiencing severe downgrades.
"Our boat is being lashed by the waves of technology and geopolitics. Our ability to twist and turn and maneuver is impaired by a heavy load of public debt," she said, urging central banks to remain restrictive where inflation persists and calling on finance ministers to pursue decisive fiscal consolidation to rebuild depleted buffers.
World Bank Group President Ajay Banga underscored the growing financing shortfall facing developing economies, warning that public balance sheets alone cannot bridge the gap.
Banga reported that the World Bank more than tripled its private capital mobilization in fiscal year 2026 by deploying reformed guarantee instruments and blended finance structures.
He focused specifically on an impending demographic challenge across the developing world, noting that 1.2 billion young people will reach working age over the coming decade against current projections of only 420 million new jobs.
"A good job is the surest way out of poverty," Banga said. "We are refocusing our investments on foundational skills, infrastructure, digital connectivity, and entrepreneurship to close this jobs gap."
Welcoming delegates, Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul contrasted the global integration that characterized the 1991 meetings with today's fractured geopolitical environment.
"Back then, the fax machine represented speed. Today, AI is transforming our activities and our way of life," Anutin said. "The world was moving toward greater economic integration. Today, geopolitical fragmentation is reshaping trade and investment."
Anutin called on member nations to resist insular trade policies and leverage regional groupings such as the Association of Southeast Asian Nations to maintain cross-border economic ties.
Annual Meetings Chairman Carlos Carvallo Spalding, president of the Central Bank of Paraguay, pointed to his country's transition from high inflation and recession in previous decades to recently achieving investment-grade credit status as proof that multilateral reform programs remain effective.
"The challenges we face are impossible to solve alone," Carvallo said, pointing to recent overhauls of the joint Debt Sustainability Framework for Low-Income Countries as essential steps to shield the most fragile economies from external shocks.
The Bangkok meetings continue through Sunday, with discussions focused on harnessing the benefits of AI while managing its economic and social risks, debt governance, and financing a resilient green economy. ■

Explainer-Will a new leader and a new name boost the rebellion in eastern Congo?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:55:44 UTC
21:55:44 KST

Explainer-Will a new leader and a new name boost the rebellion in eastern Congo?
DAKAR, Oct 16 - The former president of the Democratic Republic of Congo, Joseph Kabila, took over leadership of rebel forces occupying eastern regions this week, in the most significant shake-up of the uprising in years.
The move gives the rebels a highly prominent Congolese figurehead and could boost their efforts to present themselves as a national movement rather than a Rwandan proxy, diplomats, rebel sources and analysts said.
The big questions now are whether Kabila can translate his political stature and regional connections into broader support for the rebellion, and whether his leadership will significantly alter the balance of power on the ground in the fractured country.
WHAT DOES KABILA'S LEADERSHIP CHANGE?
The most obvious change is the name.
After Monday's announcement of Kabila's new role, the rebels — an alliance of the Alliance Fleuve Congo coalition and the M23 armed group — said they would now be known as the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN).
The name suggests a greater focus on national Congolese, not regional, affairs.
Even before the leadership change, the rebels said their main aim was to remove Congo's current president, Felix Tshisekedi, from power, accusing his administration of corruption, discriminatory policies and crackdowns on opponents.
But UN experts and analysts said the violence has been primarily driven by long conflicts over power, identity and resources dating back to the 1990s genocide in neighbouring Rwanda and even earlier.
Western countries and UN experts have accused Kigali of backing M23. Rwanda denies the allegations, but has acknowledged coordinating with the rebels on security matters.
Much of the rebel leadership remains in place. Kabila takes over as president, while former Alliance Fleuve Congo coordinator Corneille Nangaa and M23 political leader Bertrand Bisimwa become vice presidents.
Veteran M23 leader Sultani Makenga also takes a vice-presidential role, and remains chief of the rebel armed wing, preserving his central role in the movement.
WHY IS KABILA STILL IMPORTANT YEARS AFTER HE LEFT POWER?
The appointment of Kabila — who led Congo from 2001 to 2019 — puts a high-profile Congolese face on the rebellion.
It could also broaden the rebellion's appeal beyond its eastern stronghold. Kabila is from the southern Katanga region, where there is mounting resentment towards the administration of his successor as president, Tshisekedi. But the rebellion has not yet reached the province.
Kabila also brings greater political weight than Nangaa, as well as influential connections in Congo and beyond, particularly in Namibia, Kenya, South Africa and other parts of the region, which he regularly visits. But it is not yet clear if they would translate into tangible support.
HOW WILL THIS AFFECT THE REBELLION ON THE GROUND?
It remains to be seen how much support Kabila will be able to rally around the rebellion.
After remaining in power for two years beyond his mandate, Kabila left office deeply unpopular in much of Congo, including in Katanga.
His political network has weakened in recent years. Many former allies have switched allegiance to Tshisekedi, gone into exile or been imprisoned.
Since Monday's announcement, several prominent figures from his political camp have publicly broken ranks with him.
A Congolese court sentenced Kabila to death in absentia for treason a year ago after allegations that he had joined the rebels. He was also placed under US sanctions in April for providing material support to the rebels and destabilizing eastern Congo.
A 2021 investigation by international media outlets and anti-corruption groups based on millions of leaked bank documents showed that Kabila and his family amassed significant wealth during his nearly two decades in power. It is not clear where this money is held and how he could mobilise it.
WHAT DOES THIS MEAN FOR PEACE TALKS?
AFC/M23 had been negotiating with the Congolese government in Qatari-mediated talks and signed a declaration last year committing both sides to a permanent ceasefire and broader peace negotiations.
The FRN said on Wednesday it "assumes all of the rights, obligations, and commitments" of AFC/M23, "including those undertaken in the context of the Doha negotiations."
At a UN Security Council meeting on Tuesday, Congo stressed the need for all parties to make good on promises, while the US called for the pursuit of negotiations.
It remains unclear how much either side is committed to the peace process, with both blaming the other for the continued fighting. REUTERS

Thousands march in Albanian capital as anti-government protests spread
TIRANA, Oct 16 - Thousands of young Albanians marched through Tirana on Friday, breaking some windows and traffic lights on the fourth day of an increasingly violent student-led campaign to force Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign.
The demonstrations, which are spreading through the country, turned into a riot in the capital on Thursday, with protesters smashing windows, raiding a bank and clashing with police. They follow months of mostly peaceful demonstrations that the students say the government ignored.
"They are pushing us to the limits," said 19-year-old protester Enea, declining to give a second name for fear of arrest. He said his message to Rama was: "To resign as fast as possible before everything burns down."
The students accuse officials of corruption and neglecting education and say they are angry about the sale of pristine parts of Albania's coast to a luxury resort development backed by US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner.
The unrest is a challenge for Rama, who won a fourth term last year on promises to take Albania into the European Union and is aiming for membership as early as 2028.
"We will not bow to violence," he said on Facebook.
BUSINESSES APPEAL TO PROTESTERS TO LEAVE THEM ALONE
The students, many wearing masks, faced off against lines of riot police in front of the Education Ministry building. Some small businesses had their shutters down and notes on their facades saying: "We are with you. Do not damage our business all over the town."
In the coastal town of Lezha, police clashed with stone-hurling protesters. Protests have also spread to Elbasan, Skhodra and Korca, where demonstrators broke windows and set fire to garbage bins, local media reported.
"We've been protesting peacefully for 140 days, and nothing was heard. So this is our only chance to be heard and get our rights that we deserve," a 19-year-old protester who gave her name only as Klea said.
The demonstrations were sparked by the plans to build the resort, which has faced legal challenges.
Villagers told Reuters in July that their land was wrongfully sold for development. Reuters later reported that the man who sold the land was wanted by prosecutors for drug trafficking, charges his lawyer denied.
Reuters found no evidence of wrongdoing by Kushner, who is not directly involved in the villagers' dispute.
Political analyst Afrim Krasniqi said younger generations saw no future in Albania. "They see that all resources in the country, political resources, economic, everything is in the hands of oligarchs," he told Reuters.
Corruption scandals have tarnised Albania's image over the years and analysts say the country is a hub for gangs seeking to launder money from drugs and weapons trafficking, complicating its efforts to join the EU.
Along with Montenegro, Albania is leading the accession process among Balkan countries.
The unrest is part of a wave of student activism in Europe. In France, high school students have staged weeks of protests and school blockades demanding more teachers and better facilities, arguing that deteriorating school buildings and overcrowded classrooms are undermining education. REUTERS

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan plans to tighten controls on advanced AI chips and servers exported to China, bringing its rules closer to US restrictions, Economics Minister Kung Ming-hsin (龔明鑫) said.
In a Monday interview with Bloomberg, Kung said the country would add advanced semiconductors and AI servers to its export control list. Unauthorized shipments of restricted equipment could then lead to criminal charges under the Foreign Trade Act, the minister said.
Kung said the changes are part of the commitments under the Taiwan-US Agreement on Reciprocal Trade, which covers economic cooperation and security. He said some export controls would follow US rules but did not say when the new measures would take effect.
CNA reported that the country already requires permits for exports of sensitive technologies, particularly those with potential military uses. However, advanced AI chips and servers are not specifically covered by the proposed restrictions, making some unauthorized shipments difficult to prosecute under existing export laws.
The planned changes come as concerns over efforts to smuggle restricted AI equipment into China grow. The US has tightened controls on advanced semiconductor exports since 2022, citing concerns that the technology could strengthen China's military, per Reuters.
In August, prosecutors indicted nine people over an alleged scheme to illegally export AI servers to China. Authorities said the case involved 130 servers, including 74 allegedly shipped to China through other countries using false documents.
Prosecutors filed charges including breach of trust and document forgery, rather than offenses specifically involving unauthorized AI hardware exports. The case highlighted difficulties in enforcing US technology restrictions through Taiwan's existing laws.
A separate US investigation also uncovered attempts to bypass export restrictions. Reuters reported that a contractor linked to Super Micro Computer pleaded guilty in a case involving the diversion of Nvidia-powered AI servers to China.

How Probate Timelines Differ Between Countries and What Families Should Know  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:44:29 UTC
21:44:29 KST

Six weeks in one country. Three years in another. Same estate value, same number of heirs, wildly different outcomes. The gap is not luck, and it is not the lawyer.
Probate moves at the speed of the local court system, and court systems are built on very different assumptions. Get a handle on which assumption applies to your situation and the whole process gets easier to plan for. Money stops sitting in limbo. Siblings stop calling you every week asking why nothing has happened.
Most estates clear the system without a fight, but the ones that stall usually stall for predictable reasons. If you are navigating a Florida estate right now, working with an experienced probate lawyer davie residents can count on keeps the local filings on schedule while you sort out anything happening abroad.
What Actually Drives the Clock
Three things decide how long an estate sits open: whether there is a will, whether anyone contests it, and how much the government wants to review before it lets assets move. That last one varies enormously.
In the United States, probate is a state court function, so the timeline you get in one state tells you almost nothing about another. Some states run simplified procedures for smaller estates that take weeks. Others have a mandatory creditor claim window that alone can stretch past six months, and nothing in the system lets you shorten it. The Florida Courts system publishes its own guidance on how estate administration is handled within the state, and it is worth reading before you assume a timeline you heard from a friend in a different state applies to you.
Here is what almost nobody explains up front. The clock rarely starts when your loved one dies. It starts when the executor formally opens the case, and that can be weeks later if the family is still searching for documents or waiting on a death certificate. Everything after that is measured from a date the family controls.
Translation? Get organized early. Not later.
Why Some Countries Take Years
Civil law countries, including Germany, France, and much of Southern Europe, handle succession quite differently from the common law tradition in the US, the UK, and Australia. In several European systems, heirs may need formal notarized acceptance of the estate before assets transfer, and that paperwork can crawl through notary offices with heavy backlogs.
The European Union has worked to simplify cross-border succession through its Succession Regulation, which lets families designate a single applicable law for an estate spanning multiple member states. Streamlined on paper. Slow in practice, because notaries in different countries still coordinate on their own schedules.
I have watched a family wait eighteen months for a notary appointment in one member state while a sibling in another country had already filed taxes on their share. That is not a failure of the system. That is the system working exactly as designed, just slowly. If you have relatives in multiple countries, assume the slowest jurisdiction sets your real timeline, and plan your cash flow around that.
Small Estate Shortcuts Worth Knowing
Many jurisdictions offer a fast lane for smaller estates, and too many families never ask about it. In Florida, for example, an estate may qualify for summary administration when the non-exempt assets fall under a set threshold or when enough time has passed since the death. Do not assume the threshold mentioned in one conversation applies to you. Ask directly and confirm the current number.
Questions to ask an attorney before you assume you are stuck in full formal probate:
- Do the non-exempt assets fall below the local small estate threshold?
- Has enough time passed since the date of death to qualify for a shortened process?
- Are any assets held in a trust or with a named beneficiary, and do those skip probate entirely?
- Are there out-of-state properties that would need a separate ancillary filing?
- What is the mandatory creditor claim window in this jurisdiction, and is it waivable?
That fourth question trips up a lot of people. A vacation cabin or a rental property in another state is not covered by the primary probate case. It needs its own filing, in its own court, under its own rules. Families discover this months in, right when they thought they were almost done.
The Cross-Border Scenario Nobody Plans For
Consider a family in Davie with a parent who owned a condo in Florida and an apartment in São Paulo. Two estates, two legal systems, two sets of heirs who may not share the same assumptions about who gets what. If a will exists but was drafted abroad, a local court may need to determine whether it is valid under the laws of the state where it is being submitted. That determination alone can take months.
The practical move is to treat each jurisdiction separately from day one. Line up a professional in each place rather than asking one attorney to handle everything. Coordinate on the sequence, not on the paperwork, because the forms do not translate. Getting an estate valuation done for the foreign property early saves you from redoing it later when the market has moved.
What This Means for Your Planning
If probate is already open, your job is simple: keep answering the attorney, keep providing documents, and stay ahead of deadlines. The estate does not close any faster because you sent a frustrated email. It closes faster when nothing sits on your desk.
If you are still in the planning stage, this is where a conversation pays for itself. Estate values shift, tax rules change, and a will drafted a decade ago in a different country may not reflect what you want today. According to the World Bank, sound legal and judicial institutions are a foundational part of how economies function, which is a formal way of saying: the courts matter, and they behave differently everywhere.
Here is the part I would push back on if a client insisted otherwise. Everyone wants the cheapest option, and in a single-jurisdiction estate with a straightforward will, the cheap option is often fine. Cross a border, though, and the money you save up front rarely survives the first delay. I have watched a family try to handle two countries with one attorney and spend more on rework than they would have spent on both professionals combined.
What to Do in the First Two Weeks
1. Order at least ten certified copies of the death certificate. You will run out of the first six, guaranteed.
2. Locate every will, and find out whether the original exists or only a copy. Courts care about the difference.
3. List every asset by location, not just by value. The location drives which process you need.
4. Identify the named beneficiaries and confirm whether any accounts have designated beneficiaries, since those skip probate.
5. Confirm the small estate threshold in each relevant jurisdiction and ask whether you qualify.
Skip step three and you will discover a second filing at the worst possible moment. I have seen it happen twice in one year. Neither family was careless. They just assumed everything sat in one state because their parent only ever mentioned one address.
The Bottom Line
Speed in probate is not a measure of how good the estate plan was. It is a measure of how well you understood the rules before you started. A well-prepared family can move through a slow jurisdiction faster than an unprepared family moves through a fast one, and the difference shows up in weeks, not days.
So here is the question worth sitting with: if your estate landed in court tomorrow, would your family know which jurisdictions are involved, which documents matter, and who to call first? If the answer is no, you already know what to do this month.

Why Commercial Buildings Lose Heat on the Coldest Nights  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:44:26 UTC
21:44:26 KST

The building didn't fail in January. It failed in the ten months before January, a fraction of a degree at a time. Nobody filed a work order because nobody felt anything yet. That's the pattern I've watched play out in warehouses, restaurants, and small office parks along Lake Erie's snowbelt. Heat loss in commercial spaces is almost never a single dramatic breakdown. It's slow drift: a heat exchanger sooting up, burners running a little rich, a vent damper stuck half open, and a filter rack that hasn't been touched since the last tenant moved out. You don't notice a 4 percent drop in output. You notice the Monday after Christmas, when the building hasn't held 65 degrees and your whole crew is standing around in coats.
Here's what actually happens in that moment, and this is where owners get taken advantage of. Somebody calls the first number that answers and asks for prompt commercial furnace repair, and a truck shows up with a guy who knows rooftop units but has never touched a 40-year-old boiler. He replaces a $200 part. The heat comes back. Three weeks later it's out again, and now you've paid twice for one diagnosis. If you get a sense the tech on your roof is guessing, ask them to walk you through the combustion readings before they touch the gas valve. Any professional will. A parts-swapper won't. So why does heat choose the worst possible week to quit? Physics and scheduling, mostly. Here's the trifecta.
Load, Pressure, and the Calendar Stack Against You
When the outdoor temperature sits in the teens, your heating unit is running close to 100 percent of its rated capacity for hours. There's no headroom left. Any small deficiency that stayed invisible at 40 degrees, like a partially clogged burner orifice, becomes a real problem at 12 degrees. You can see how outdoor conditions drive building loads in the basics laid out by the Department of Energy. I'd read the load material before I'd read anything a vendor hands me.
The second factor is pressure. Commercial buildings pull air in and out constantly. Kitchens exhaust enormous volumes. Bathroom fans, dock doors, and lobby entrances all fight for make-up air. That imbalance can pull combustion gases back down a flue or starve a unit of the air it needs to burn cleanly. Then the pressure safety switch trips, and your furnace shuts down on its own. That's not a furnace that broke. That's a building that stopped being a closed system. If your unit keeps locking out without a clear reason, ask about building pressure before anybody replaces the control board.
The calendar part is simpler and more painful. Every commercial property manager schedules fall maintenance in the same six-week window, then trusts it for the rest of the winter. New tenants move in during November, a wall gets cut for a new network closet, a dock shelter tears and never gets patched. Your building changed. Your heating load changed with it. Your service contract didn't.
What Healthier Buildings Do Differently
The facilities I've seen go through a serious cold snap without a crisis aren't the ones with the newest equipment. They're the ones with a short, unglamorous inspection habit and a clear escalation path. The U.S. General Services Administration is worth a read if you want an institutional benchmark for how high-performing facilities approach operations and tenant comfort. It's public, and it's free of a sales angle.
Start with a two-part triage. First, decide whether you have a building problem or a unit problem. Cold complaints clustered in one zone with everything else fine means a unit. Complaints spread across zones, or a whole floor that won't hold temperature, means a building problem, and you'll waste money chasing the equipment.
Second, get hard numbers before you authorize anything. Ask for combustion analysis, temperature rise across the heat exchanger, and static pressure. Those three readings tell a competent tech almost everything about whether a unit is underperforming or just undersized.
Two small things you can check today without a ladder: whether last winter's roof unit filters were actually changed on the schedule someone wrote down, and whether every exterior door you own still closes on its own.
A Framework I Actually Use: The Four-Leaf Diagnostic
I built this after watching too many owners pay for the same repair twice. Picture four leaves, and you only get to fall back on a service call when you've checked all four.
Leaf 1, Thermal: Is the unit producing heat at all, and is that heat reaching the spaces that need it? This is where airflow, duct leakage, and zoning get tested.
Leaf 2, Fuel: Is the burn clean, and is the supply pressure right? Soot on a heat exchanger is a symptom, not a problem to wipe off.
Leaf 3, Safety: Is every interlock, roll-out switch, and pressure switch doing what it was built to do, and is the flame proving properly? You never bypass these for a quick fix, no matter what a tenant says.
Leaf 4, Environment: What's the building doing to the equipment? Negative pressure, dirty make-up air, and unbalanced exhaust all belong here.
Most failures I've seen land in Leaf 1 or Leaf 4, and both are cheap to fix once you know where the problem lives. My honest take: if a technician can't tell you which leaf the problem sits on before they start talking about parts, get a different technician.
How to Pick a Vendor Before the Crisis Hits
Do this in October, not at 2 a.m. Nobody answers the phone well when the pipes are already cold.
- Ask for the names of two commercial accounts they service in your building class, and call them without warning.
- Request a written diagnosis before work starts, not a verbal estimate.
- Confirm their techs are trained and certified on the specific brand on your roof, not just heating in general.
- Check whether they carry the parts that fail most on your equipment, or whether you'll wait four days to order them.
- Ask who answers at night, and whether that person can authorize the repair.
I'd add one more that most owners skip: ask whether they test the building or just the box. A vendor who only looks at the furnace will fix it, and you'll call them back next winter. A vendor who reads static pressure and building balance will tell you the furnace was never the whole story.
Diagnostics Should Follow a Standard, Not a Gut Feeling
If you want to know whether the work is being done to a real benchmark, look at what the National Institute of Standards and Technology publishes on building performance and measurement. You don't need to read a technical report to get value from it. You need to know that measurement standards exist, so you can ask whether your vendor is using one or just going by feel.
A vendor who can point to a method is easier to hold accountable than one who says "we just know." That's not a small difference when you're the person signing the invoice.
Before You Sign Anything This Winter
Commercial heat failures trace back to drift, and drift is invisible until the temperature drops. Keep a simple log of what your building's heating load looks like in shoulder seasons, so you know when something changed. Check pressure balance annually, especially after a tenant build-out. And when a unit does go down, get the diagnosis in writing before you approve a repair.
The next cold snap is already on the calendar. What's the one reading you don't have yet on your building, and who would you trust to walk you through it without selling you something you don't need?

TALLINN - Led by Telia Estonia, partners of the 5G-BALTICS project from the three Baltic states convened in Tallinn to review the progress of establishing 5G infrastructure along the Via Baltica transport corridor and to plan the next phases.
Following an extensive planning and preparation phase, the project in Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania is now entering the practical implementation stage, with construction work already underway in several regions.
The project aims to provide uninterrupted 5G coverage along the entire 663-kilometer Via Baltica transport corridor, from Tallinn to the Lithuanian-Polish border. The establishment of this unified digital corridor will enhance cross-border digital connectivity and network reliability among the three Baltic states, pave the way for new digital services, and support regional economic development.
In August, following a detailed planning and design phase, Latvian company Tet began constructing a fiber-optic communication network along the Via Baltica route. The work is being carried out in five sections, employing technical solutions best suited to local conditions. In total, 180 kilometers of high-capacity communication infrastructure will be built in Latvia.
In Estonia, construction of the fiber-optic network and 5G masts has commenced in multiple locations. Concurrently, preparations are underway for the deployment of active 5G network equipment.
In Lithuania, work is ongoing to achieve the project's two primary infrastructure objectives: building communication masts with the required electrical connections and rolling out the fiber-optic communication network.
Once construction and setup are complete, the project will move into its next crucial phase: the practical testing of the 5G network, currently scheduled for 2027.
During the testing phase, project partners will evaluate the network's performance, connection stability, and service quality across the entire transport corridor, with a special focus on cross-border areas. The tests will include assessing the network's performance with everyday digital services, such as music and video streaming, participating in online meetings, using navigation apps, and playing online games.
5G-BALTICS (uninterrupted 5G coverage across the entire Via Baltica corridor) is a Connecting Europe Facility (CEF) project aimed at establishing seamless 5G coverage along the Via Baltica transport corridor in Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania. The project (No. 101181148) is implemented with the support of the European Union (EU).

Best UK Websites for Finding Local Services  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16

21:44:15 KST

Quick Answer
Finding the best websites to find local services in the UK depends largely on the type of job you need done, your budget, and how much vetting you require. For heavily vetted tradespeople with verified qualifications and insurance, dedicated trade directories like Checkatrade and Rated People are often the strongest choices. If you are looking for flexible help with everyday tasks, odd jobs, or affordable local services such as cleaners, gardeners, and handymen, Gumtree is a highly practical option that connects you directly with nearby providers. Meanwhile, lead-generation platforms like Bark and general business directories like Yell offer broad coverage across multiple service categories. Ultimately, the right platform balances your need for speed, cost-effectiveness, and peace of mind.
Comparison of the Best Websites for Local Services in the UK
Top Platforms for Finding Trusted Tradespeople and Services
When wondering where you can find reliable local services in the UK, it helps to understand how each platform operates. Some sites focus heavily on accreditation and insurance, while others prioritise speed, affordability, and direct communication between households and providers.
Checkatrade
Checkatrade is widely recognised for its strict vetting process. It is particularly useful for homeowners seeking trusted tradespeople for plumbing, electrical work, roofing, and building projects. Every professional listed undergoes checks on qualifications, insurance, and trading history. Customer reviews are monitored to reduce fake feedback. If your priority is minimising risk for complex or high-value home improvements, Checkatrade provides a strong layer of reassurance. However, the thorough vetting and membership model mean that prices can sometimes be higher than independent local providers.
Gumtree
Gumtree is a leading UK local marketplace that excels at connecting users directly with nearby service providers. It is particularly relevant for finding a local handyman, cleaner, or gardener online without navigating complex booking systems or paying platform commissions. Because listings are posted by both independent providers and small businesses, you can often find flexible availability and competitive rates. The platform allows direct messaging, making it easy to discuss job specifics, request photos of previous work, and negotiate quotes. While it does not enforce trade accreditation, its local focus and straightforward layout make it a strong option for everyday maintenance, one-off tasks, and community-based services.
Rated People
Rated People operates on a quote-matching model. You post a description of your job, and interested tradespeople purchase the lead to contact you. This system is efficient for comparing multiple quotes for larger projects like kitchen refits, bathroom installations, or landscaping. The platform includes customer ratings and allows you to view a tradesperson’s history before replying. It is best suited for planned home improvements where you have time to evaluate several proposals. Keep in mind that because tradespeople pay to access leads, they may be selective about the jobs they pursue.
Bark
Bark covers an exceptionally wide range of services, from web design and accounting to house cleaning and personal training. Instead of browsing listings, you answer a series of questions about your project, and Bark matches you with professionals who then reach out with quotes. This approach saves time if you are unsure which websites are best for comparing local service providers across different industries. The trade-off is that you may receive numerous calls or messages, and the level of experience can vary significantly between respondents.
Taskrabbit
Taskrabbit is ideal for quick, smaller jobs that do not require a fully licensed contractor. Whether you need furniture assembled, shelves mounted, or a quick deep clean, Taskrabbit connects you with local “Taskers” who charge by the hour. The app handles booking and payment, and Taskers undergo identity checks. It is highly convenient for urban users who need same-day assistance, though the platform fees and hourly rates may add up for larger or multi-day projects.
Yell
Yell functions as a comprehensive digital business directory. It is useful for locating established local companies with physical premises, such as garages, solicitors, or commercial cleaning firms. Listings typically include contact details, opening hours, and links to company websites. While Yell provides a broad overview of businesses operating in your postcode, it is less tailored to individual self-employed tradespeople and does not facilitate direct quote comparisons in the same way as dedicated trade platforms.
As an emerging classifieds platform in the UK, OK offers a streamlined space for local buying, selling, and service discovery. It may suit users who prefer a straightforward marketplace environment to browse local adverts and contact providers directly. While its service category is still growing compared to long-established directories, it provides another viable avenue for finding independent local operators and community-based listings.
How to Choose the Right Platform for Your Needs
Knowing how to find trusted tradespeople near you in the UK requires matching your project to the right platform features. Consider the following factors before posting a job or making an enquiry:
· Scope and complexity: Major structural work, gas installations, or electrical rewiring should be sourced through platforms that verify qualifications and insurance, such as Checkatrade or Rated People. For general maintenance, gardening, or cleaning, broader marketplaces like Gumtree offer greater flexibility and faster local responses.
· Speed versus comparison: If you need help immediately, apps like Taskrabbit or direct-messaging classifieds allow you to secure someone quickly. If you want to compare three or four detailed quotes, lead-generation sites give you a structured way to evaluate options over a few days.
· Budget and fees: Some platforms charge service fees or booking commissions, which can inflate the final cost. Direct-enquiry marketplaces typically allow you to negotiate prices directly with the provider, which can be more cost-effective for straightforward tasks.
· Local availability: National directories sometimes prioritise larger firms that cover wide areas. If you prefer a neighbourhood provider who can visit on short notice, local classifieds and community marketplaces often yield faster, more personal responses.
· Communication style: Decide whether you prefer a managed booking system with in-app payments or direct phone and email contact. Direct communication speeds up negotiations but requires you to manage the agreement and payment terms yourself.
When Gumtree Can Be a Good Option
Gumtree is particularly useful when you value direct interaction and local convenience. It is a strong choice if you are looking for:
· Flexible, affordable help: Independent handymen, cleaners, and gardeners often advertise here to avoid high commission fees, which can result in more competitive quotes for you.
· One-off or unusual tasks: Whether you need a single room painted, a fence repaired, or rubbish cleared after a renovation, local providers on classified sites are often willing to take on smaller jobs that larger firms might decline.
· Direct negotiation: The platform allows you to message providers instantly, ask for availability, and agree on a price without intermediaries. This is ideal for users who prefer to manage the hiring process themselves.
· Community-based services: Many local tutors, beauty therapists, and pet sitters use community marketplaces to build their client base. Browsing local adverts can help you discover independent professionals operating right in your neighbourhood.
For users who want to browse local listings or post an ad requesting help, Gumtree provides a low-barrier, highly accessible way to connect with nearby service providers across the UK.
How to Check Reviews, Qualifications and Stay Safe
Regardless of which website you use, verifying a provider’s background is essential. Here is how you can check reviews and qualifications for local service providers while protecting yourself from poor workmanship or scams:
· Verify trade credentials: For regulated work, always ask for proof of accreditation. Gas engineers must be on the Gas Safe Register, and electricians should hold NICEIC or NAPIT certification. Reputable tradespeople will gladly provide their registration numbers.
· Check independent reviews: Do not rely solely on testimonials hosted on a provider’s own website. Look for feedback across multiple platforms, and pay attention to how the provider responds to negative reviews or complaints.
· Request references and portfolios: For larger projects, ask for contact details of recent clients or photos of completed jobs. A trustworthy professional will have a track record they are happy to share.
· Get written quotes: Avoid vague verbal estimates. Request a detailed breakdown of labour, materials, and potential extra costs. This prevents disputes if the scope of the job changes midway through.
· Avoid large upfront payments: Be cautious of anyone demanding full payment before starting work. A small deposit for materials is common, but the majority of the fee should be paid upon satisfactory completion.
· Meet safely and securely: When hiring through open marketplaces, arrange initial meetings during daylight hours and keep communications within the platform until you are comfortable sharing personal contact details.
· Trust your instincts: If a deal seems unusually cheap, the provider is reluctant to provide a written agreement, or they pressure you to decide immediately, it is best to walk away and explore other options.
FAQ
Where can I find reliable local services in the UK?
Dedicated trade directories like Checkatrade and Rated People are excellent for vetted professionals, while local marketplaces like Gumtree are highly effective for finding affordable, independent providers for everyday tasks and maintenance.
Which websites are best for comparing local service providers?
Lead-generation platforms such as Bark and Rated People allow you to post a job and receive multiple quotes, making it easy to compare prices and approaches. General directories like Yell are better for researching established companies with physical premises.
How do I find trusted tradespeople near me in the UK?
Start by filtering searches to your specific postcode. Look for providers with a history of positive reviews, verified qualifications, and clear communication. Asking neighbours for recommendations alongside online searches often yields the most reliable results.
How can I check reviews and qualifications for local service providers?
Cross-reference reviews across different websites and check official registers for regulated trades (e.g., Gas Safe for engineers, NICEIC for electricians). Always ask to see physical certificates or registration cards before work begins.
Where can I find a local handyman, cleaner or gardener online?
Community classifieds and local marketplaces are ideal for these roles. Platforms like Gumtree host thousands of adverts from independent handymen, cleaners, and gardeners who offer flexible scheduling and direct booking without agency fees.
Is it safe to hire service providers through classified websites?
Yes, provided you take sensible precautions. Verify their identity, check references, agree on a written scope of work, and avoid paying the full amount upfront. Meeting in person and trusting your judgement are key to a safe hiring experience.

Political developments in Europe run counter to solutions needed to address today's challenges - director of Carnegie Europe  - The Baltic Times

RIGA - European countries and their societies are currently at a critical crossroads, as national policies are ill-suited to addressing current transnational challenges, Rosa Balfour, director of the Carnegie Europe think tank, said in an interview LETA.
The expert believes that Europe has fallen into a kind of vicious cycle, because, due to public dissatisfaction, the policies and developments in individual countries are not suited to addressing current transnational issues, even though these are precisely the problems that must be resolved to alleviate this underlying public discontent.
"Some of these incongruities arise domestically, while others have international origins. It is precisely these incongruities that concern me the most. Moreover, the fact that this situation has persisted for so long has deprived governments of the ability to act with the tools necessary to address the problems and their causes," Balfour told LETA.
In her view, there are many politicians in Europe who genuinely want to work for the common good and achieve results to solve the problems of ordinary people, but they lack an accurate diagnosis of what is wrong, and that is precisely why they are often unable to find solutions to these problems.
The director of Carnegie Europe pointed out that there is a significant inconsistency regarding how issues can be addressed at the European level.
"The European Union (EU) has been driving European integration for decades and has sought solutions to problems through this very process - through cooperation, through economic integration, and through the expansion of the single market. Today, there are many problems that could be solved, or at least alleviated, through greater integration. By unifying not only the market of goods but also the financial sector, and by supporting greater mobility and immigration. However, we have reached a point where politicians do not want this," Balfour concluded.
As an example, she cited bank mergers, which are often blocked by politicians, because they are concerned about their own power, about control over the banking system in their country, and about the possibility that a bank might be owned by another country or another conglomerate.

Reading an ALTA Survey Like an Underwriter: What the Lines and Notes Actually Say  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:43:55 UTC
21:43:55 KST

Most people open an ALTA survey, flip to page one, find the boundary line, and close the file. I've watched a lender's credit committee do the opposite. They start at Table A, work backward into the notes, and treat the drawing as the last thing worth reading.
That habit isn't paranoia. It's how you catch the easement that runs straight through your planned loading dock before you've wired the deposit. A survey isn't a picture of a piece of dirt. It's an inventory of every claim, restriction, and gap in the record that could cost you money after closing. If you're spending the money on a survey anyway, you should be getting real understanding ALTA land surveys out of it, not a PDF you skim and archive.
Here's the cold-open truth: the drawing tells you where things are, and the notes tell you what will hurt you. Almost every surprise I've seen on a closing statement came from a note, not a line.
What Table A Actually Controls
Table A is the first thing an underwriter checks because it defines the scope. Every checked box is a promise the surveyor made to look. Every unchecked box is something nobody looked for. That distinction matters more than any individual measurement on the map.
When a survey is ordered, the client picks which Table A items apply. If item 11, utilities, isn't checked, the surveyor isn't obligated to locate buried lines. If item 13 is skipped, the flood zone determination isn't part of the deliverable. You can have a completely clean survey that simply never asked the right questions.
Read it like this: scan Table A first and ask which items your lender required. If your loan commitment lists a Table A item that isn't checked on the survey, that's a real problem, and it's cheaper to fix it now than at the closing table.
Every Note Is a Conditional Answer
Surveyors write notes the way lawyers write contracts, carefully, and for the same reason. "No encroachments observed" is not the same as "no encroachments exist." The first is a statement about what someone could see. The second is a statement about reality, and a surveyor almost never makes it.
Look for notes that add a condition to the drawing. Words like "per record," "not field verified," and "as shown on the recorded plat" mean the surveyor relied on documents instead of walking the boundary. That's normal and legitimate. It's also the exact place where a bad legal description or a stale plat quietly becomes your problem.
Easements and the Language That Hides Them
Easements are where deals actually die, and they rarely announce themselves as easements. A right of way, a utility corridor, a drainage ditch, an access agreement, and a party wall clause can all encumber your land without the word "easement" appearing anywhere on the page.
An underwriter asks three questions about each one. Where does it physically run? Who has the right to use it and for what? Does it conflict with what you intend to build or how you intend to use the property? A ten foot utility easement along the rear of a warehouse is background noise. The same easement cutting across the only place a fire lane can go is a redesign.
Cross-check the survey against the title commitment. The survey should show the location of recorded easements, and the title commitment should list them as exceptions. When the two documents disagree, the survey is usually the more physical truth and the title commitment is the more legal one. Get both in front of your attorney before you sign anything.
The Lines Nobody Prints Explicitly
Setback and boundary lines are the obvious ones. What gets missed: line of sight, site distance, and access. If the parcel is a pad site in a shopping center, the survey might show a legal boundary but not whether a delivery truck can physically turn into it. A surveyor will draw what exists. Whether a fire apparatus can reach the building is a planning question, but the drawing is where you catch the problem first.
Here's a scenario that has cost real money. A buyer reviewed a survey showing a clean rectangular boundary and a utility easement along the back. Everything checked out. What the survey also showed, in a note rather than the drawing, was that the recorded plat described the rear line "as per document 2014-1187" instead of by metes and bounds. That document turned out to describe a line twenty-two feet north of where the fence sat. The seller believed they owned the dirt up to the fence. They didn't. The deal closed, but the buyer financed the purchase of a strip of land the seller never owned, and the survey had said so in plain English.
That's the whole game. The survey informed everyone. Nobody read the note.
A Practical Field Guide for Your Next Survey
Here's the sequence I'd run before closing, in order:
1. Read Table A out loud. Confirm every item your lender or attorney required is checked. Mark anything missing in red.
2. Read every note, top to bottom, before looking at the drawing. Highlight any phrase that limits the surveyor's confirmation, like "per record" or "not field verified."
3. List every easement, right of way, and encroachment. For each one, write where it physically sits and what it blocks. If you can't answer, call the surveyor.
4. Match the survey against the title commitment. Easements on one should appear on the other. Discrepancies go to your attorney before you sign.
5. Walk the property with the survey in hand. If the drawing and the ground disagree, that's the single most important phone call you'll make this month.
It's a boring hour of work. It's also the cheapest insurance policy in commercial real estate, because it catches the problem while you still have leverage to renegotiate, reprice, or walk.
Why the Notes Outrank the Drawing
The drawing shows geometry. The notes show the limits of what anyone actually verified. Underwriters read in that order because the second one is what a court, a lender, or a future buyer will scrutinize if something goes wrong.
Technical standards for how survey data is captured and communicated follow documented conventions rather than local habit. The National Institute of Standards and Technology publishes foundational work on measurement standards that shapes how surveying and spatial data are handled in the United States. If a surveyor's notes feel vague, that's not a stylistic choice. It's a signal about the limits of the work.
Recorded documents are the other half of the picture. Land records, plats, and prior surveys live in county archives, and the reliability of any ALTA land surveys partly depends on how faithfully those records were kept. The National Archives and Records Administration maintains the standards framework that public records offices across the country generally follow, and it's worth remembering that older plats vary wildly in quality depending on when and where they were recorded. A 1958 plat drawn from a hand-drawn metes and bounds description is not the same tool as a modern GPS-located survey.
Scale matters here too. As parcels get subdivided, density increases, and the number of overlapping easements, rights of way, and access agreements climbs with it. The U.S. Census Bureau tracks land use and parcel patterns across the country, and the broad trend has been more subdivision, more shared infrastructure, and more recorded claims on any given acre. More claims on the land means more notes on the survey. That's the world you're reading.
What to Do With What You Find
You don't need to be a surveyor to read a survey like one of the people signing off on the loan. You need to read in the right order, ask the right questions, and treat every note as a fact about risk rather than a piece of boilerplate.
The lines tell you where the land is. The notes tell you whether the land is really yours, and on what terms. Which one are you going to read first on your next deal?

TALLINN - Next week, members of parliament, speakers, and government representatives from the Baltic states will gather in Tallinn for the 45th Session of the Baltic Assembly and the 32nd Baltic Council to discuss the security of the Baltic states and strengthening defense cooperation.
The gathering will begin on Thursday, October 22, with a formal ceremony where the Baltic Assembly (BA) prizes and medals will be awarded. This year's BA Prize for the Arts was awarded to jewelry and video artist Darja Popolitova. The Prize for Literature was awarded to Latvian poet Karlis Verdins and translator Valts Ernstreits for the poetry collection "Libiesu balades/Livod baladod", or "Livonian Ballads". The ceremony will begin at 7 p.m. in the House of the Knighthoods.

Also on Friday, the 32nd meeting of the Baltic Council, the cooperation body for the governments and parliaments of the Baltic states, will take place. The Baltic Council session will be chaired by Baltic Assembly President Timo Suslov and the representative of Estonia, the presiding country of the Baltic Council of Ministers. Representatives from the Latvian and Lithuanian governments will also deliver addresses.
A press conference will begin at 1 p.m. on Friday in the White Hall of the Riigikogu, where journalists will have the opportunity to ask questions to the three representatives of the Baltic Council of Ministers and the heads of the Baltic Assembly delegations. Immediately before the press conference, Baltic Assembly President Timo Suslov and the representative of Estonia, the presiding country of the Baltic Council of Ministers, will sign a joint statement of the Baltic Assembly and the Baltic Council of Ministers.
The BA session will continue in the afternoon, with discussions on ensuring the security of the Baltic states and the next steps needed to strengthen defense cooperation. At the end of the session, a new BA president will be elected, and the 45th resolution and final documents of the Baltic Assembly will be signed. After the session concludes, Estonia will hand over the presidency of the Baltic Assembly and the Baltic Council of Ministers to Lithuania.
The Baltic Assembly is a consultative cooperation organization of the parliaments of the three Baltic states, which discusses issues of mutual interest.

Valid ID cards, 'impartial' reporting, basic first-aid: Press Council issues guidelines for journalists covering anti-SIR protests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:43:11 UTC
21:43:11 KST

NEW DELHI: The Press Council of India (PCI) has issued guidelines for journalists covering the ongoing protests in Delhi against the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, saying the measures are aimed at "ensuring the safety of media personnel while enabling them to carry out their professional duties effectively."According to a PCI release, the council adopted the "Guidelines for Journalists Covering Protests and Demonstrations" at a meeting on Thursday.The guidelines advise journalists to carry valid identity cards issued by their organisations or accreditation from the Press Information Bureau (PIB) or the Directorate of Information and Publicity (DIP), and keep them visibly displayed. They should calmly identify themselves to law enforcement personnel, maintain neutrality, avoid provoking confrontations and follow lawful instructions, particularly those issued for safety reasons.On safety, the PCI urged journalists to maintain a reasonable distance from confrontations, move cautiously through crowds and continually reassess their surroundings. It also cautioned against attaching cameras or recording equipment to police barricades, vehicles or other equipment in ways that obstruct movement or damage property.“Move carefully through crowds, taking short steps to reduce the risk of falling or being trampled.
Continuously reassess your position in relation to protesters, counter-protesters, police, and other potential sources of danger,” the guidelines said.Journalists should remain alert to changes in crowd behaviour, approaching individuals, potential confrontations, shifts in crowd noise and emerging hazards. They should also identify and regularly reassess escape routes, including nearby exits, open streets, sidewalks and safe locations. In the event of smoke or tear gas, they should use visible landmarks and safe routes to leave the affected area without moving further into the crowd.The PCI also advised journalists to carry a compact safety kit containing first-aid supplies, water, snacks, a flashlight, a washcloth and eye protection. Depending on the assessed threat, they should consider wearing protective headgear and body armour. Journalists should learn basic first aid and avoid touching tear-gas canisters, flash-bang devices or smoke grenades.On coordination, the guidelines call on newsrooms to designate a point of contact to track journalists’ locations and respond to emergencies. Freelancers, meanwhile, should ensure that a trusted editor or contact knows their location, assignment plan and expected return time.
For planned demonstrations, media organisations should coordinate with police and public information officers to clarify communication protocols and identify designated media staging areas.Emphasising journalistic ethics, the Council called for accurate and impartial reporting, urging journalists to distinguish verified facts from allegations and unconfirmed claims and to verify information through multiple sources. Statements from protesters, organisers, police and government authorities should be subjected to equal journalistic scrutiny, with claims clearly attributed.The guidelines also caution against publishing real-time police positions or escape routes if doing so could compromise safety. Journalists should describe observable actions rather than speculate about motives and exercise particular care when filming minors, injured people and private citizens in distress.The council stressed that equipment, live-broadcast commitments and pressure to obtain exclusive footage should never take precedence over journalists’ safety.(With ANI inputs)
Karan Manral is a journalist at the Times of India. He covers politics, social issues, and international affairs, exploring stories that affect people’s everyday lives. He also writes explainers to make these stories easier for readers to follow.

Albanian protests turn violent: What we know
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:26:15 BST
21:26:15 KST

Albanian protests turn violent: What we know
- Published
Protesters and anti-riot police have clashed in Albania's main cities in scenes not witnessed for a long time.
Government buildings have been attacked and some private businesses, too.
So what is happening?
How big and unusual are these protests?
Albania's capital Tirana has seen months of protests from an anti-government "Flamingo" movement, but what started on Tuesday this week was on a different scale.
And the clashes have spread beyond Tirana - to include the main cities of Durrës, Shkodër, Korçë and Vlora.
The new demonstrations were announced as a student movement, ostensibly demanding action by the government to help with the high cost of education fees and books - and the higher cost of living.
Secondary schools joined in, swelling the numbers.
Before too long, masked protesters threw stones at police, and they responded with water cannon, tear gas and batons.
Many were incensed by scenes of a young man being carried away, his broken leg dangling with him in agony.
Apologies were expressed but failed to calm the situation.
A floor of the education ministry was set on fire, with other government institutions ablaze, too.
Every evening, throughout the summer for some 140 days in a row, Albanians in central Tirana would hold pictures of a pink flamingo, calling on Prime Minister Edi Rama - now in his fourth term - to resign.
The protests began over a mega-tourism project on the Adriatic coast linked to US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner. Demonstrators said the bird would become extinct on an island near the coastal city of Vlora, if the plans for a luxury development went ahead.
The public anger comes as allegations of corruption among ministers and other senior officials grow louder.
One deputy prime minister has fled the country, another has been ordered to step down as investigations continue.
- Student protesters attack government buildings in Albania 
  - Published1 day ago
- Kushner-backed luxury resort plan sparks protests in Albania 
  - Published4 June
So has the Flamingo movement radicalised?
The flamingo protesters say they have no links to any political party - one of their slogans being "Rama in jail, Berisha in jail". While Rama is prime minister, Sali Berisha is Albania's main opposition leader - as well as a former prime minister and president.
They were attended by young and old, parents with children and sometimes their grandparents. Some of the participants took pride in cleaning up after every night.
But after months and an unusually hot summer, their numbers dwindled - with no sign that the government was meeting their demands.
The current movement appears far more violent. Dozens of police have been hurt, and the eyes of Europe are now watching what happens next in a country viewed as one of the top candidates for EU membership.
Several young protesters told the BBC that what was going on now was a new phase born of the previous movement.
Five months of peaceful protest had been "met with humiliation, ridicule, mockery," complained one young woman called Livia. "That was a clear message from the government that our voice will not be allowed to be heard."
Another called Brunela said she was worried about what might happen next: "I am very terrified because the media and the government is reacting, especially now. It was not just my voice, it is the voice of Albanian youth."
An overlap between the two sets of protests may well have occurred, even though flamingo leaders have not publicly stated so and no representative of the student movement has come forward.
After all, their main concerns relate to corruption, which the prime minister says must be investigated by the justice system.
How is the government handling the unrest?
Rama has been touring some of the damaged buildings and blaming Sali Berisha for instigating chaos.
"All of this is the work of the very same hand - the hand that has gripped the Albanian opposition by the throat, the hand that has burned and destroyed Albania more than once, and is now prepared to burn and destroy it again to prevent any progress. It is a blind struggle, fuelled by the most irrational hatred," he said on Friday.
The prime minister has ruled out resigning, promising to "listen, address legitimate concerns and keep Albania moving forward".
Berisha's Democratic Party has often tried to get people out to oust Rama.
But the number of his loyal supporters, who have also protested for months and at times clashed with police, has been low in comparison to the current attendance.
So there is some scepticism about Berisha's ability to mastermind the trouble, though he may well seek to capitalise on it.
On the other hand, the Albanian media have suggested that secret services of foreign countries may be involved.
Unfounded allegations have been made against Serbia, with commentators suggesting Belgrade is envious of Albania being often cited as potentially next in line to join the EU.
Indeed, without mentioning names, Prime Minister Rama echoed the allegation on Friday.
"These are foreign hands that do not wish for Albania to be at peace... they do not want Albania to be part of the united European family," he said, adding: "Do you think it is a coincidence that every time Albania receives another green light... or draws closer to that great ambition - that historic objective - flames suddenly erupt? It is no coincidence at all! None of what is happening now is a coincidence."
Is Albania safe to visit?
Although the street violence has taken place in many cities, it remains contained for the time being.
The UK government has urged visitors to check media, external for latest information, stay away from "demonstrations, large-scale gatherings or political rallies" and follow advice of local authorities.
Albania is a popular tourist destination, and the government in Tirana has warned that violence tarnishes the country's image, affecting both tourism and its European path.

MP: Eesti 200 should 'lick its wounds' and sit out 2027 elections

MP: Eesti 200 should 'lick its wounds' and sit out 2027 elections
Eesti 200 MPs Ando Kiviberg and Toomas Uibo say their struggling coalition party should skip next March's Riigikogu elections and instead focus on rebuilding for 2031.
Kiviberg told ERR he has not decided whether to run for reelection in March, but if the party decides to run, he would have to act as a team player.
Still, he sees little sense in the party throwing money away at this point, believing Eesti 200 should sit out the 2027 elections instead.
"The party should lick its wounds, do a little soul-searching and commit to preparing properly for 2031," Kiviberg said. He added that he has already discussed the issue with other party members but expects a final decision to be made at Sunday's party council meeting.
Party whip Toomas Uibo, meanwhile, said voters have already made up their minds about Eesti 200, as their rating hit a historic 1.3 percent low in Norstat polls earlier this month.
"I don't know if miracles like this happen, but right now I don't see any point in wasting taxpayer money on running in the elections," he admitted.
While members may still decide on a different course on Sunday, Uibo likewise believes Eesti 200 should instead regroup and focus on the 2031 elections.
Potential Greens merger raises questions
Eesti 200 and the nonparliamentary Estonian Greens are discussing a possible merger, but Kiviberg said this may not necessarily be the right move. "Several party members I've spoken with share my views," he said.
Uibo noted he was unsure whether the two parties have enough in common to unite.
"Of course, you can't expect two different parties to come together and agree on absolutely everything," he said, adding that the question is whether both parties are willing to set enough aside and compromise. "It's still unclear how much common ground we have."
Kiviberg nonetheless ruled out running on another party's ticket next spring and said he has received no such offers. He said he remains committed to Eesti 200 because he believes its ideas are necessary and sound, and will ultimately benefit the country. The question, he said, is how effectively the party has put those ideas into practice.
While Uibo and Kiviberg argued that Eesti 200 should sit out the upcoming elections, fellow MP Peeter Tali told ERR he currently intends to run.
"A politician has to run," Tali said. "If they're no longer a politician, then they don't have to."

On 9 October, according to multiple reports, the presidential aircraft carrying Vladimir Putin — returning from a summit in Turkmenistan — was unable to land in Moscow due to a drone attack and was diverted to St Petersburg. Putin's plane was not reported to have been a direct target.
Russian officials have neither confirmed nor denied the reports.
Ukraine has not officially confirmed any organised campaign to shut down Russian airports, in what media outlets have dubbed "Operation M&Ms".
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has not yet authorised the military to proceed with an original, more aggressive plan for such a campaign, according to reports.
In September, Zelenskyy said Russian skies "are becoming unsafe" and that "drones will appear in the skies over Russia, and that will have to be taken into account", urging international airlines to stop flying to Russian airports.
Kyiv has targeted Russia's military, energy and commercial facilities in a bid to defund Moscow's war machine, as its all-out war in Ukraine continued well into its fifth year.
Yet US President Donald Trump reiterated criticism of Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries in an interview, calling them "a disgrace" after his shock announcement of a deal to purchase diesel from the Kremlin.
"There are many targets that can be hit. But when you shell oil refineries that produce, you know, diesel fuel, and we and the whole world need that, (Zelenskyy) is not doing the world a favour," Trump said.

Russian strikes and winter hardship may drive more Ukrainians from homes, UN agency warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Russian strikes and winter hardship may drive more Ukrainians from homes, UN agency warns
GENEVA, Oct 16 - Millions of Ukrainians face another winter of hardship as attacks on critical infrastructure, damaged housing and rising living costs threaten to force more people from their homes, the United Nations migration agency said on Friday.
With temperatures set to fall in the coming months, many families are struggling to secure reliable heating, electricity and water after years of war, the International Organization for Migration said.
This week, Russian missiles and drones have rained down on Ukrainian cities, amid fears that the US could pull back intelligence sharing and weapons support from Kyiv.
"Winter is fast approaching in Ukraine, and for many Ukrainians, the months ahead could be the most difficult since the full-scale war began," Dejan Keserovic, IOM deputy chief of mission in Ukraine, told reporters in Geneva via video link from Kyiv.
Nearly 3.6 million people remain internally displaced across Ukraine since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, while an estimated 3.8 million have returned after displacement, often to damaged or partially destroyed homes, according to the latest IOM figures.
Ukrainians who returned to their homes within the last three months are the most likely to say they intend to leave again, reflecting growing concerns about deteriorating living conditions, the IOM said.
European countries such as Poland, Germany and the Czech Republic currently host around 6 million Ukrainian refugees.
Keserovic said he expected host countries to be preparing for more Ukrainians to leave if the situation got worse.
Repeated Russian strikes on energy and other critical infrastructure have put increasing pressure on Ukraine's electricity, heating and water systems, while drone and missile attacks continue to kill and injure civilians across the country, the IOM said.
Reliable access to water is emerging as a major concern because water systems depend heavily on electricity, the IOM said. The UN agency has installed 31 solar power stations to support water systems across Ukraine, but warned that needs remain immense.
The IOM also warned that funding shortages could hamper aid efforts, with less than 7% of its 2026 Ukraine response plan funded so far, and said urgent resources were needed to improve insulation as households face freezing conditions. REUTERS
