American journalist, Palestinians injured in clashes with masked Israeli settlers in West Bank
Several Palestinians and an American photojournalist working for the Washington Post were injured after a group of masked Israeli men clashed with Palestinians harvesting olives in the West Bank, according to videos, eye-witnesses and Palestinian authorities.
Video of the incident obtained by CBS News showed a group of around 20 masked men clad in black or grey clothes descending a hill from the area of an Israeli settlement outpost into an olive grove near the Palestinian village of Abu Falah.
Another video from the incident showed two vehicles set on fire and a Palestinian man with a bloodied face being escorted away from the area by a woman and a man.
Among the injured was Heidi Levine, a veteran American photojournalist working with the Washington Post.
Video shared by the Foreign Press Association showed Levine was surrounded by masked men, pushed to the ground and beaten, and her camera equipment taken from her.
While Levine was on the ground, the masked men launched stones with their arms and slingshots at Palestinians and the Palestinians threw stones at the masked men, the video showed
Levine was taken to a hospital in Ramallah for medical treatment.
Footage of Levine in her hospital bed showed she had a large wound on one of her legs and one of her hands had been bandaged.
"I was attacked, pushed to the ground. Luckily I had my flak jacket and helmet, otherwise I probably wouldn't even be here, because they just kept kicking and kicking me," Levine said from her hospital bed.
The Israeli military said it was looking into the incident and would soon issue a statement.
The Palestine Red Crescent Society said it treated three Palestinians for injuries at Abu Falah. The wounded included a man who had been shot in the thigh, according to WAFA, the official media arm of the Palestinian Authority.
Clashes between Israeli settlers and Palestinian olive pickers also took place near the villages of Burqa and Turmus Ayya, which are located in the central West Bank, WAFA reported. The Palestine Red Crescent treated four people for injuries sustained at the clashes near Burqa, WAFA said.
Attacks against Palestinians in the West Bank have surged in recent years, particularly after the establishment of Israel's current hard-right government in late 2022, according to statistics released by the United Nations humanitarian office.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has condemned the violence and vowed a crackdown against what he says is a small group of several hundred wayward youths responsible for attacks on Palestinians.
Despite those public promises by Netanyahu, the violence has continued in recent weeks.
Over the past 18 days, Yesh Din, an Israeli settlement monitoring group, says it has documented 486 violent incidents against Palestinians across 181 different Palestinian localities, and that 234 of these incidents were related to the olive harvest.
In August, three journalists from NBC and a Palestinian woman they were interviewing were attacked by Israeli settlers in the IWest Bank.

Defence official: Front heats up, energy truce fails as US-Kyiv strain grows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:24:00 UTC
21:24:00 KST

Defence official: Front heats up, energy truce fails as US-Kyiv strain grows
The recent US–Russia diesel deal and a failed energy truce have strained ties with Kyiv at a time when fighting has been escalating at the front, the defense ministry said.
The ministry's intelligence review points to growing friction between Washington and Kyiv as battlefield intensity rises alongside the stalled energy ceasefire.
Speaking at the regular Ministry of Defense Friday press conference, Gert Kaju, head of the ministry's defense readiness department, said a number of significant events had taken place at the strategic level over the past week. He said it became known last Friday that the U.S. had issued the Russian Federation a temporary permit to supply diesel fuel to its market and to the global markets. "According to the expectations of the U.S. leadership, Russia should supply 3 million tons of diesel fuel as quickly as possible, which the U.S. leadership believes should lead to a decline in fuel prices on the U.S. domestic market," Kaju said.
Just over a week earlier the U.S. president had announced a ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia so far as attacks on energy facilities went, but it later emerged that this was a ceasefire arrangement which neither side had agreed to.
Ukraine did attempt to observe the energy ceasefire and refrained from striking Russian oil refineries for three days on the condition that Russia stop attacking Ukraine's electricity generation facilities and transmission networks.
Russia, however, interpreted the agreement as a suspension of attacks only on oil refineries and fuel transportation infrastructure only, and continued striking Ukraine's energy infrastructure. According to Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov, the energy ceasefire proposed by President Donald Trump had not been specified in detail.
The U.S.-Russia diesel supply agreement drew international criticism, some of it from Kyiv. In response, the U.S. raised the question of the need to hold elections and change the government in Ukraine. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy agreed to hold elections on the condition that a 60-day ceasefire be established, but Moscow refused. Russia's leadership believed Ukraine would use the ceasefire to rebuild its forces, and according to Peskov, Moscow was prepared to establish a ceasefire for only 24 hours.
Since Russia had not observed the energy ceasefire, President Zelenskyy announced on October 15 that Ukraine would resume strikes against Russian oil refineries, saying it would be prepared to consider suspending such strikes only if it received assistance in strengthening its missile defense capabilities.
Ukraine counterattacked in the Lyman and Sloviansk sectors in Donetsk oblast
Nearly 230 combat engagements took place per day on the front line over the past week, a rise on the previous week. The most intense fighting took place in Donetsk oblast in the Pokrovsk and Kostiantynivka directions, followed by the Huliaipole direction in Zaporizhzhia oblast, the Southern Slobozhanshchyna direction in Kharkiv oblast and the Lyman sector in Donetsk oblast.
Ukrainian counterattacks took place mainly in the Lyman and Sloviansk directions in Donetsk oblast, the Oleksandrivka area in Dnipropetrovsk oblast and in Sumy oblast. Ukrainian forces pushed back Russian units in the Sloviansk and Kramatorsk sections and strengthened the front line in that sector.
The Russian armed forces' objective remains to reach the borders of Donetsk, Luhansk and Zaporizhzhia oblasts and restore their positions in Dnipropetrovsk oblast, while simultaneously attempting to expand the territory under their control in Sumy and Kharkiv oblasts. At the same time, the Russian Federation lost an average of 1,600 military personnel per day. Russian armed forces' losses remained above 10,000 troops per week, marking the seventh consecutive week that losses had reached this level, the ministry said.
The fighting was also accompanied by extensive airstrikes despite the recent stalled truce. The Russian Federation attacked various targets in at least 19 Ukrainian oblasts (out of a total of 24). Targets of long-range precision strikes included critical infrastructure, residential buildings, government, commercial, educational and medical institutions, the transportation system, the fuel industry and the energy system.
Russia intensively attacks energy infrastructure
The number of strikes against Ukraine's energy infrastructure has steadily increased in recent weeks and multiplied in Kyiv. Between October 4 and 11, Russia attacked Ukraine's energy infrastructure 196 times and its fuel infrastructure 20 times, while Ukrainian energy workers restored electricity supplies to 1.9 million households.
Intensive attacks continued overnight on October 13-14 in Kyiv and Kharkiv oblasts, where 26 energy infrastructure facilities were damaged, including three combined heat and power plants in Kyiv, and according to President Zelenskyy, 600,000 people were left without electricity.
Ukraine responded with extensive long-range strikes. Between October 8 and 10, attacks hit Russian oil refineries in Omsk oblast, Bashkortostan and the Komi Republic, an oil terminal in Rostov oblast and a distribution station in Samara oblast. Attacks resumed on October 15, when a long-range strike hit the Ryazan oil refinery.
In the 242nd week of the war, Ukrainian long-range strikes targeted Yandex data centers in Ryazan, Kaluga and Vladimir oblasts and a Sberbank data center in Saratov oblast for the first time.
Ukraine also attacked companies important to Russia's military-industrial complex in Tver, Nizhny Novgorod and Rostov oblasts, as well as military targets and transport routes in occupied and border areas.
Away from the front line, Russia continued its hybrid activities against countries supporting Ukraine. The Danish Security and Intelligence Service also warned that Russia had launched operations against Danish companies supporting Ukraine in repelling the aggression.
"At the same time, the Finnish Security Intelligence Service noted that Russia poses a real, although not yet immediate, threat to the country's defense industry, which the agency considers an expected development, as Finnish companies operate in the same security environment as the rest of Europe," Kaju added.

EU summit: European leaders pledge support for Ukraine's Zelenskyy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16

21:10:00 KST

EU summit: European leaders pledge support for Ukraine's Zelenskyy
October 16, 2026
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy attended the final day of an EU summit in Brussels on Friday as European leaders pledged continued support for the Ukrainian leader and his country in a turbulent week.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa both took the fore in calling on allies to continue their support of Kyiv as it faces increased Russian attacks and detrimental US foreign policy decisions.
What did EU leaders say about the bloc's support for Ukraine?
"This is no time to withdraw support to Ukraine," said Costa as he stood next to the Ukrainian president. "This is no time to relieve Russia's sanctions. Now it is time to increase our support, to increase our pressure."
"One thing is absolutely clear," pledged von der Leyen, "we will not lift any sanctions unless Russia stops this war."
The EU leaders' remarks come just one week after Ukraine and its European allies were blindsided by US President Donald Trump's unilateral decision to lift sanctions on Russian oil exports and purchase diesel from the Kremlin after a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
On Wednesday, a US official said Washington was also considering easing sanctions on Russia's shadow fleet — unflagged tankers that turn off transponders to transport and transfer illicit oil while circumventing international export sanctions.
After undermining years of Western sanctions against Russia over its illegal invasion of Ukraine, Trump is now seeking to increase pressure on Ukraine — calling for Zelenskyy to be replaced as its leader and blasting Kyiv's targeting of Russian energy infrastructure as a "disgrace."
Trump seeks to deflect blame for high energy prices onto Ukraine
Upon arrival at Friday's Brussels summit, Zelenskyy said, "We want to end this war as quick as possible. We don't see now signals from the Russian side that they are ready for this, to end this war, that's why we have to prepare for the winter."
"The winter package is not only energy, it's also air defense and funding," he added.
During his speech at the summit, Zelenskyy asked European Union leaders to provide an additional €70 billion ($79 billion) in funding to Kyiv next year to help it continue fighting Russia.
"The war will cost €155 billion next year. And we need at least €70 billion euros more from you — for defence, for weapons, and for our resilience. This is a realistic amount. And I ask you to find this support," the Ukrainian president said.
When asked after his meeting with EU leaders if Trump was scapegoating him for troubles in the US, Zelensky gave a knowing smile and stayed mum. "This is my answer," the Ukrainian president said, as journalists broke into laughter at a press conference in Brussels.
Trump last week justified his calls for Zelenskyy to be removed from office by claiming the Ukrainian leader did not want to stop the war — which Russia launched on February 24, 2022 — as well as attempting to divert anger over high global fuel prices away from his own war in Iran, which triggered the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and sent global oil and gas prices through the roof.
"All he's doing is making the world oil price higher," Trump told far-right US media outlet Newsmax on Thursday. Asked about Ukraine resuming attacks on Russian energy infrastructure, Trump said, "Well, I think that's a disgrace."
Earlier this week, Kyiv reported restrictions on its use of Elon Musk's Starshield system, Starlink's military-grade satellite service which Ukraine relies on for its battlefield communications, mid-range strikes on Russian-occupied territories and interceptor drones.
Zelenskyy hails 'very good' meeting with Hungary PM
The Ukrainian president also praised his first bilateral meeting with Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar on the sidelines of the summit.
"We had a very good meeting," Zelenskyy told reporters in Brussels. He added that he and Magyar had discussed "many things, including relations, the economy, and logistics — all of which are important to our two countries."
Zelenskyy also said that he "won't mind" visiting Budapest.
After meeting, Magyar announced that Budapest and Kyiv had agreed to put their relations on a new footing.
"I assured the Ukrainian president of my full solidarity over the inhuman Russian aggression against his country," Magyar wrote in a Facebook post. He also said that Hungary was ready to assist Ukraine by all possible diplomatic means to reach a ceasefire and lasting peace.
The meeting occurred just days after Kyiv passed legislation addressing Budapest's long-standing concerns regarding the rights of the ethnic Hungarian minority in western Ukraine.

Europe's far right has a Putin problem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:09:43 UTC
21:09:43 KST

Europe's far right has a Putin problem
Rassemblement National (RN) candidate Marine Le Pen in Paris, France, on Sept. 28, 2026. (Anne-Christine Poujoulat / AFP via Getty Images)
Europe's far-right parties grow increasingly divided on something that once united them — sympathies for Vladimir Putin's Russia.
As nationalists and right-wing populists across Western Europe move closer to power, many are seeking to distance themselves from their past admiration for a country waging Europe's largest war since 1945 while conducting hybrid attacks against much of the continent.
Despite finding common ground on dislike of liberalism, NATO, and the EU, Europe's far right is being forced to rethink its relationship with Moscow — much like it had to do with U.S. President Donald Trump.
France's National Rally (RN) and the U.K.'s Nigel Farage now harden rhetoric on Russia while signaling a more conditional, rather than simply hostile, approach to Ukraine, as part of a strategy to cast a wider net of voters.
But the Alternative for Germany (AfD), which has emerged as Europe's largest and most extreme nationalist party, is moving in the opposite direction.
The split comes at a critical moment. The National Rally's Marine Le Pen is a frontrunner for the French presidential election next April, the AfD is leading the German polls, and Farage's Reform party was, until very recently, a favorite to win the next elections in Britain.
Experts who spoke to the Kyiv Independent explain the reasons behind this divide and what the coming string of European elections could mean for Ukraine.
Farage, Le Pen seek Russia detox
For years, far-right leaders have been ranked among the most Moscow-friendly voices in European politics.
In 2014, Farage, the man who later led a campaign to push the U.K. out of the EU and whose Reform party now polls second at 22%, expressed his admiration for Putin as an "operator."
As recently as 2024, while Russia’s full-scale invasion had already been raging for two years, he suggested that the eastward expansion of the EU and NATO provoked the war.
Comments like these have made it easy for his opponents to blast him as a Putin fan.
Now, Farage seems intent on proving he is no such thing.
"Russia in general and Putin in particular are extremely unpopular with Brits, so why would they want to convey the impression that they have any sympathy with them?"
Last year, the Reform leader called the Russian dictator a "very bad dude" and said NATO should shoot down Russian jets intruding into its airspace.
On Ukraine, he has cautiously affirmed support for Ukraine — even backing the idea of using frozen Russian assets for Kyiv's benefit.
And while he criticized plans for a post-war "reassurance" force in Ukraine as outlined by the Labor government, Farage backed sending British troops to the country, if on a temporary basis and as part of a U.N. peacekeeping mission.
Reports have emerged that Farage is even considering a trip to Ukraine as part of his quest to brush off his Russia-friendly image.
A similar shift is taking place across the English Channel.
Prior to 2022, Le Pen said that the Russian occupation of Crimea was not illegal, and her party took out a loan from a Russian bank.
But after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, she backpedaled.
Now, the three-time failed presidential candidate sees she has a real chance to win, with a court clearing a path to her candidacy despite last year's embezzlement conviction.
As the vote nears, she is treading cautiously on foreign policy.
Le Pen has condemned Russian aggression and has backed continued military assistance to Ukraine, even as she wants Paris to cut financial aid — citing France's own budget constraints — opposes Kyiv's EU membership, and is skeptical about future EU aid if it burdens France.
She also said she would be happy to visit Ukraine for talks with President Volodymyr Zelensky.
The RN's younger co-leader, Jordan Bardella, has taken a tougher stance on Russia, naming the country a threat — something that Le Pen avoided in a recent interview with the Financial Times.
Both party chiefs also blasted Moscow in September over its seizure of European business assets in the country and denounced Russian interference and destabilization efforts.
Elsewhere in Europe, far-right parties have proved they can tone down their views on Russia and Ukraine in exchange for government seats.
Matteo Salvini, head of Italy's League party, remembered for once sporting a T-shirt with Putin's likeness, has largely fallen in line behind Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's firmly pro-Western, pro-Ukraine course, save for some symbolic resistance.
And the former Dutch government also maintained its support for Kyiv, even though Geert Wilders's far-right Party for Freedom (PVV) was the strongest party in a short-lived coalition.
Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis, a right-wing populist, while expressing his disdain for EU plans to earmark billions of euros of support for Ukraine, echoed Zelensky's take on a set of recent pro-Russian moves made by the U.S.
"Trump effectively betrayed us by concluding the business deal with Putin, and we have to do something," Babis said on Oct. 16.
Elsewhere, the far right doubles down
This shift is far from uniform, however.
As Meloni, Italy's right-wing, anti-immigration prime minister, prepares for the 2027 elections, she faces a new pro-Kremlin challenger.
Roberto Vannacci, a retired army general, left the League in February to found his own nationalist party, National Future.
Vannacci, a former military attaché in Moscow, has famously said he prefers Putin over Zelensky.
With support reaching as high as 8% in recent polls, National Future has already surpassed Meloni's junior coalition partners.
But the most striking example is the AfD, currently the strongest opposition party in Germany, nearing 30% in polls.
The AfD was seen as so extreme that the far-right European Parliament group expelled it at the RN's urging in 2024, prompting the AfD to form a new ultranationalist coalition, Europe of Sovereign Nations (ESN).
The party campaigns on a halt to military and financial aid to Ukraine, the lifting of sanctions against Russia, and the resumption of Russian energy purchases.
Given the AfD's particular brand of extremism and Berlin's role as the leading military donor to Ukraine, this is an especially worrying signal for Kyiv and Europe.
Like in the U.K., the next German parliamentary elections are expected no later than 2029.
Why the difference
With Russia's full-scale war nearing its fifth anniversary, many countries have seen the public's support for Ukraine cool — but not collapse.
Politicians vying for victory in upcoming elections have to take this into account, with the U.K. being a prime example.
Farage's party certainly has a reputation to fix, after its former leader in Wales, Nathan Gill, was sentenced to prison for taking bribes from pro-Russian Ukrainian politicians.
"Russia in general and Putin in particular are extremely unpopular with Brits, so why would they want to convey the impression that they have any sympathy with them?" Tim Bale, a professor of politics at Queen Mary University of London, comments on Reform's strategy.
A poll from last fall shows that 59% of Brits support continued assistance to Ukraine, and slightly over half back sanctions even at the cost of paying more for energy and food.
The support is somewhat cooler in France, where 47% favor continued arms deliveries to Ukraine, down from 65% in 2022.
Yet this is not an insignificant number, and the majority of French people — including a little over half of RN voters — see Russia as an enemy, according to polls.
Anton Shekhovtsov, a visiting senior fellow at Central European University in Vienna, notes that Le Pen likely remembers well the "reputational nightmare" her Russian loan has caused.
"Everybody just pointed to that loan and said, 'you're all Russian Trojan horses in France,'" Shekhovtsov said in comments for the Kyiv Independent.
Now, Le Pen likely sees an example in Meloni — a politician who emerged from a similar far-right background but maintained a pro-Western course, the expert notes. Meloni's government has been Italy's longest-serving since World War II.
But the AfD has doubled down on its pro-Russian course, despite the majority of Germans continuing to support Ukraine. It does not seem to be hindering its rise.
Jakub Wondreys, a researcher at the Hannah Arendt Institute for the Research on Totalitarianism in Dresden, offers an explanation.
"The key factor is the party's internal division, which we don't see elsewhere. It is specific to German politics, and to the AfD itself," Wondreys tells the Kyiv Independent.
While all parties have different wings, the AfD is notably decentralized, with the former border between West and East Germany surviving as a key divide.
The AfD's extremist, more Moscow-friendly wing is rooted in East Germany, a former Soviet satellite state. The "moderates" are stronger in the west, the researcher explains.
The AfD is growing nationwide, but the east remains its main stronghold — as evidenced by its recent victories in regional elections there. This means that the more extreme wing of the party is also its loudest and most influential one.
This split was laid bare when the AfD's two leaders, Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla, disagreed over a trip by a group of their colleagues to Sochi last November.
Weidel, who hails from what was West Germany, criticized the visit, while Chrupalla, himself born in socialist East Germany, downplayed it, adding that he does not consider Russia a threat.
Recent polls show that 54% of Germans from what was East Germany think aid to Ukraine has gone too far, compared to 39% in the west. Eastern Germans are also less likely to see Russia as a threat.
Yet even an RN or Reform victory would not bode well for Ukraine, regardless of their change of rhetoric, experts warn.
As Bale points out, no matter its public posturing, a Reform government "might try to spend less money on defense aid behind everyone's back."
Just on Oct. 12, Farage pledged to take a "keen look" at whether British aid to Ukraine is being swallowed up by corruption there and signaled that London's support cannot be limitless.
The RN's victory might not end military support for Ukraine, but it will likely curtail the financial assistance and weaken the European sanctions push against Moscow.
And Shekhovtsov warns that even if Le Pen does not adopt overtly pro-Russian positions after the elections, her victory could be such an upset for France and Europe that it might shift political attention away from supporting Ukraine.
The coming election season has the potential to shake the European pro-Ukraine coalition to its core.

Tokayev calls for greater international cooperation to preserve biodiversity
Head of State Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has addressed the COP17 Leaders’ Summit on Biodiversity in Yerevan, Armenia, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing the press service of Akorda.
Welcoming the Summit participants, the Head of State thanked the Prime Minister of Armenia, Nikol Pashinyan, for a warm welcome and a high level of organization of the event.
In his remarks, the President emphasized the need to coordinate international efforts and uphold a shared responsibility to future generations for preserving the environment
"We have gathered here to expand international cooperation aimed at preserving our shared natural heritage. This is a collective responsibility to future generations, who may face serious challenges and threats. It is also a matter of survival for our civilization, as biodiversity is vital to human well-being, economic resilience, and long-term security. Healthy ecosystems play a crucial role in food production, the protection of water resources, and the livelihoods of millions of people.
At the same time, desertification, water scarcity, and other environmental challenges pose a serious threat to the fragile balance between people and nature. For millions, water shortages and land degradation have already become an everyday reality. Most concerning is that these processes transcend national borders, undermining sustainable development and threatening global stability.
Environmental agenda, based on a balanced approach and concrete action, must take precedence over political differences. Our shared priority should be international cooperation based on true partnership, impartiality, and, above all, a commitment to achieve practical results," the President said.
Earlier, it was reported that Kassym-Jomart Tokayev arrived at the Meridian Expo and Event Center in Yerevan to attend the COP17 Leaders' Summit on Biodiversity.

Tokayev highlights Kazakhstan's success in restoring rare animal populations

Tokayev highlights Kazakhstan's success in restoring rare animal populations
President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said Kazakhstan has achieved significant progress in biodiversity conservation, citing the recovery of populations of the saiga antelope, snow leopard, Turan tiger, Przewalski's horse and Caspian seal, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing the press service of Akorda.
The President described the revival of the saiga population as one of the country's greatest conservation achievements.
“This ancient animal survived the last Ice Age and remains very essential to the natural balance of our steppes. Today Kazakhstan is home to around 98 percent of the world’s saiga population. In 2003, just 21,000 species remained in our country. By the spring of this year, their numbers had reached an estimated 4.7 million,” Tokayev said.
He also noted encouraging signs in the recovery of the snow leopard, “a proud symbol of our mountain heritage.”
“Around 70 percent of its range in our country are within protected areas. Reliable and sustained protection and systematic scientific monitoring have helped its population grow from critically low levels of 90s last century to nearly 190 animals today. Behind all these recoveries are years of hard and dedicated, determined work by the authorities, scientists and international partners,” he noted.
Kassym-Jomart Tokayev expressed his gratitude to the Russian Federation and its President, as well as the United Nations Development Programme, the World Wildlife Fund, and other international partners, including NGOs, for their assistance in restoring the population of the Turan tiger.
He emphasized that in July this year, a tiger was released into the wild for the first time in 70 years, marking a milestone for Kazakhstan.
The Head of State also noted that efforts are underway, in cooperation with Czech, German and Hungarian partners, to reintroduce the Przewalski’s horse to Kazakhstan.
The President also highlighted the need to protect the Caspian Sea and its unique biodiversity.
“At the recent first Caspian Environmental Summit in Turkmenistan, I called for urgent, coordinated action to prevent fatal damage to this fragile ecosystem. The future of Caspian seals causes a particular concern. Its population has fallen from one million to 270,000 over the past century. In Kazakhstan, the Caspian seal has been officially listed as a rare and endangered animal. We urge all five littoral states and international community to increase efforts to protect these species. The tragedy of the Aral Sea is a stark reminder of the devastating cost of reckless exploitation of nature and we must not allow the Caspian Sea to suffer the same fate,” Kassym-Jomart Tokayev emphasized
Earlier, it was reported that Kassym-Jomart Tokayev arrived at the Meridian Expo and Event Center in Yerevan, Armenia, to attend the COP17 Leaders' Summit on Biodiversity.
Addressing the summit, the President called for greater international cooperation to preserve biodiversity and presented the Taza Qazaqstan initiative.

(Xinhua/Chen Junfeng)
BAKU, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi met with Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan on Thursday in Baku, the capital of Azerbaijan, on the sidelines of the Seventh Summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia.
Wang, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, said China and Türkiye enjoy a traditional friendship, and deepening strategic cooperation between Beijing and Ankara serves the interests of both countries and their peoples and will also contribute to global economic recovery.
China has always attached great importance to its relations with Türkiye and stands ready to work with Ankara to take the 55th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations between the two countries as an opportunity to implement the important consensus reached by the two heads of state and advance China-Türkiye strategic cooperation to a new level, Wang said.

Sorry, Darwin: Chinese fossil shows that not all early birds evolved to fly
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:00:08 UTC
21:00:08 KST

Sorry, Darwin: Chinese fossil shows that not all early birds evolved to fly
Discovery suggests that adaptation branched out into more diverse, terrestrial non-flying niches much earlier than previously thought
Chinese scientists have unearthed a fossil of the earliest known flightless bird, offering compelling evidence that not all early birds evolved to take to the skies.
The discovery could also challenge long-held assumptions – including ideas dating back to evolutionary theorist Charles Darwin – that flightlessness in birds arose only as a secondary adaptation after earlier species had mastered flight.
The 150 million-year-old fossil of the Late Jurassic avialan Yuezhuornis yangyuanensis found in China’s southeastern Fujian province suggests that early bird adaptation branched out into more diverse, terrestrial non-flying niches much earlier than previously thought.
“Selection for powered flight has been viewed as the main driver of early avialan skeletal modifications,” the researchers said in a paper published in the peer-reviewed journal Nature on October 14.

Heavy cost for US to return to confrontation with Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:00:03 UTC
21:00:03 KST

The experience of recent conflicts has demonstrated that possessing advanced weaponry and massive firepower does not necessarily equate to achieving strategic objectives. Factors such as depletion of military stockpiles, damage to military equipment, need to procure replacement ammunition, and Iran’s capacity to restore its defensive capabilities all serve to complicate the White House’s calculations regarding a potential re-engagement in military confrontation with powerful Iran.
In a report citing the financial and military costs of past US strikes against Iran, the British newspaper “The Times” highlights the significant strain this conflict has placed on Washington’s military resources. According to the report, US expenditures have exceeded $43 billion in this war, dozens of American aircraft have sustained damage, and the US stockpiles of interceptor missiles have come under pressure. Regardless of the final assessment of the conflict's military outcomes, these figures indicate that sustaining large-scale operations against Iran requires substantial financial and material resources, the resources that cannot be replaced or replenishment in the short term is impossible.
The significance of this issue becomes even greater when the direct costs of military operations are weighed alongside their strategic consequences. In military calculations, the number of attacks carried out or the volume of ammunition expended is not, in itself, the definitive measure of victory. What truly matters is the ratio between the costs incurred and the objectives intended to be achieved through those expenditures. If a military operation entails the extensive use of ammunition and damage to equipment, yet fails to eliminate the adversary’s capacity to continue their resistance, persisting with the same approach may simply lead to mounting costs with no guarantee that the desired outcome will ever be attained.
Erosion of Military Stockpiles: Washington’s Hidden Challenge
One of the most significant consequences of a military conflict is the strain placed on stockpiles of weapons and ammunition. The extensive use of interceptor missiles to counter threats from missiles and drones, particularly when attacks are sustained, can deplete ready-to-use stockpiles, thereby increasing the need for production and resupply. This issue is of particular importance to the United States. In addition to its military commitments in West Asia, Washington must also ensure its forces remain prepared to address potential crises in other parts of the world.
Replenishing arms stockpiles is not merely a matter of securing funding. The production of certain advanced systems and the ammunition they utilize requires complex supply chains, specialized raw materials, and specialized industrial capacity. However, even if new budget allocations are made, rapidly replacing expended stocks is not necessarily feasible. The higher the rate of ammunition consumption in a conflict, the greater pressure placed on production schedules, the prioritization of arms deliveries, and the allocation of resources toward other military missions.
Under such circumstances, Washington’s decision to launch a new round of strikes is not limited merely to an assessment of operational capability; rather, it must also account for the opportunity cost of expending munitions and the subsequent impact on US military readiness. In other words, every missile used in an operation must be evaluated within the context of the United States’ broader defense requirements.
Iran’s Capacity for Recovery and Difficulty of Achieving a Definitive Outcome
On the other side of this equation lies Iran’s capacity to maintain and restore its defensive capabilities. In a report, “The Times” notes that, despite military attacks and pressures, Iran has managed to recover a portion of its missile and drone capabilities. This is significant from the perspective of military calculations, as the effectiveness of an offensive operation depends, to a large extent, on the degree of its lasting impact on the adversary’s capabilities.
If military strikes fail to permanently dismantle a nation’s defensive capacity, inflicting damage at a specific point in time does not necessarily equate to eliminating that nation’s ability to continue its resistance. The potential to repair equipment, restore certain operational capabilities, and maintain the capacity to produce or deploy weaponry can alter the conflict’s equation over time. In such a scenario, the aggressor may be compelled to repeatedly expend further munitions and equipment to sustain military pressure—all while the ultimate outcome of this process remains uncertain. The strategic implication is clear: as long as the adversary retains the ability to continue resisting, one cannot conclude that their defensive capacity has been exhausted based solely on the volume of attacks carried out.
Why could a renewed attack be more costly?
The United States re-engaging in a confrontation with Iran could trigger a repeat of that same costly cycle. New operations would require ammunition, logistics equipment, fuel supplies, the movement of troops, and the protection of military bases and facilities. Should equipment sustain damage or the scope of the conflict expand, costs would rise accordingly. Furthermore, a prolonged crisis could impact energy markets and economic expectations, extending the repercussions well beyond the military battlefield.
On the other hand, the United States must also consider the possibility of a prolonged conflict and the need to remain prepared for unforeseen scenarios. Military operations might begin with limited objectives, but reciprocal responses and shifting conditions could expand their scope. Under such circumstances, the final cost will not necessarily align with initial estimates.
The fundamental question for the White House is whether the costs of a new confrontation would yield commensurate gains. If the objective is to durably weaken Iran’s defensive capabilities, the persistence of its missile and drone capacities could make achieving this goal more difficult. Furthermore, if the aim is to compel Tehran to accede to Washington’s demands, it remains to be seen whether military pressure would truly lead to such an outcome, or if it would merely generate additional costs.
The White House’s Strategic Calculus Test
A report by “The Times” once again draws attention to the gap between military superiority and the achievement of strategic outcomes. Possessing extensive military capabilities enables the infliction of damage, but it does not, in itself, guarantee that the adversary will cease resistance or that the aggressor’s political objectives will be realized. When assessing a conflict, one must simultaneously consider the costs incurred, the resilience of the parties involved, and the extent to which objectives have been achieved.
For Washington, returning to a confrontation with Iran—without regard for the lessons of past costs—means re-entering a path with a predetermined outcome. The strain on U.S. military stockpiles, combined with Iran’s ability to restore parts of its defensive capabilities, suggests that repeating such attacks will not necessarily shift the equation in favor of the aggressor.
Ultimately, the primary challenge for the United States is not merely the capacity to launch a new operation, but the ability to achieve a sustainable outcome at a manageable cost. If previous strikes failed to realize Washington’s intended objectives, any decision to follow the same path requires a clear answer to the question: what will be different this time? Absent such an answer, a renewed attack risks becoming less of a solution to the crisis and more the beginning of another phase of resource depletion and escalating strategic costs for the United States.

Friday, 16 October 2026, 13:17
The main building of the Bulgarian Academy of Sciences in central Sofia
PHOTO bas.bg
Font size
A total of 64 scientists affiliated with the Bulgarian Academy of Sciences (BAS) have been ranked among the world’s top 2% of researchers in the latest edition of the Stanford ranking, which assesses scientists’ career-long impact and is compiled by Stanford University in the United States.
Twenty of these scientists are BAS academicians and corresponding members, while the remainder are professors at the Academy’s institutes. The latest Stanford ranking includes a total of 102 Bulgarian researchers, BAS announced.
The ranking is compiled annually based on an analysis of scientometric indicators for more than 12 million scientists whose publications are indexed in Scopus. It reflects the impact individual researchers have had on the advancement of science.
A separate ranking assesses scientific impact over the previous year. It includes another 10 BAS scientists and members who do not feature in the career-long ranking. This brings the total number of scientists affiliated with BAS included in the two rankings to 74.

Zagreb sets eight conditions for Montenegro’s EU accession
Croatia has sent EU member states a document setting out eight conditions that Montenegro must meet before joining the bloc, Radio Free Europe reports, citing diplomatic sources. The demands concern negotiating Chapters 23 and 31, which cover fundamental rights and foreign policy, security and defence.
The conditions include compensation for Croatian citizens held by the Yugoslav army at the Morinj camp near Kotor in 1991–1992. Zagreb is also calling for clarification of the fate of 14 missing Croatian citizens, access to archives, the prosecution of war crimes and the settlement of property claims by Croatian families in Montenegro. Another demand concerns the return of the Yugoslav training ship Jadran.
PHOTO BGNES
Turkish police raid opposition TV
On 14 October, police raided the Istanbul offices of Halk TV, a leading Turkish television channel close to the opposition. The broadcaster will be placed under the management of a trustee. The operation took place in the early morning, when the channel’s broadcasts were suspened, the Bulgarian News Agency (BTA) reported.
According to a statement by the Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office, Halk TV Board Chairman Cafer Mahiroğlu is under investigation on suspicion of bribery and bid-rigging in Izmir.
Last year, Halk TV was also sanctioned by Türkiye’s media regulator, with a court ordering the channel to suspend broadcasting for 10 days.
The channel’s journalists issued a joint statement saying that “the appointment of a trustee and the suspension of the channel’s broadcasts constitute an attack on freedom of expression and the public’s right to receive information.”
PHOTO AP/BTA
Romanian government ordered to pay judiciary nearly EUR 1 billion
Romania’s High Court of Cassation and Justice has upheld a ruling by the Bucharest Court of Appeal, in a case brought by the judiciary against the government and the Ministry of Finance over the back payment of overdue salaries to magistrates.
The government now owes nearly EUR 1 billion. The High Court’s ruling is final, and Romania’s Constitutional Court has also dismissed the government’s appeal in the case.
The funds must be allocated, even if this means amending the state budget. The government has 10 days to comply with the court order. It it fails to meet the deadline, it will face a penalty of 1% of the amount owed for each day of delay, the Bulgarian News Agency (BTA) reported.

In southern Odesa Oblast, four people were injured in Russian attacks over the past day, according to regional governor Oleh Kiper. Russia struck private houses, a manufacturing enterprise, as well as energy infrastructure, the governor added.

Homeless man reportedly insults Erdogan to get food, bed in jail
- A homeless Turkish man said he insulted President Recep Tayyip Erdogan on purpose to get food and a bed in jail, after saying, "I have nowhere to stay, I sleep in rubbish dumps."
- He was detained in Alanya and jailed pending trial, after three failed attempts to get pre-trial detention, according to Sozcu.
- The case highlights Turkey's insult laws, which have been used against critics. Justice ministry data show nearly 83,000 cases since 2016 under articles 299 to 301.
AI generated
ANKARA – A Turkish homeless man admitted to intentionally committing the offence of insulting President Recep Tayyip Erdogan in order to get access to food and a bed in jail, media reports said on Oct 16.
The 66-year-old was detained for the offence in a park in the southern resort town of Alanya, near the city of Antalya.
“I have nowhere to stay, I sleep in rubbish dumps. That is why I did it,” he told a court, which jailed him pending trial for the offence, according to newspaper Sozcu.
He had reportedly tried three times before but until now had not succeeded in being placed in pre-trial detention.
Insulting the president is a criminal offence in Turkey that has often been used against critics.
The authorities have charged many thousands with the crime, from journalists to teenagers and even a former Miss Turkey.
Although the offence has been part of Turkish law for decades, its use has risen significantly since Turkey transitioned to a presidential system in 2018.
Between 2016 and the end of 2025, justice ministry statistics show prosecutors opened nearly 83,000 cases into offences under articles 299 to 301 of the Turkish penal code, which cover insulting the president, insulting the Turkish flag and state symbols, and insulting the Turkish nation and state institutions.
Under article 299, the offence of insulting the president carries a prison term of between one and four years. AFP

Why is China buying up gold?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:38:11 UTC
20:38:11 KST

Why is China buying up gold?
Beijing’s gold purchases reflect a shift away from reliance on US dollar assets, experts say.
China is increasing its gold reserves in a bid to reduce its dependence on US dollar assets and protect against financial and geopolitical risks, analysts say, while households are turning to the precious metal amid uncertainty over the domestic economy.
The People’s Bank of China reported buying gold for a 23rd consecutive month in September, when the country’s central bank also made its largest monthly purchase in nearly three years. The sustained buying points to a longer-term effort to spread risk associated with its vast reserves, experts say.
Among concerns is high US debt and Western governments’ freezing of assets, which has highlighted the inherent risk in holding money overseas, particularly for emerging market and Global South economies. Gold bought and stored domestically offers protection against that risk because access does not depend on the will of another government.
But central bank buying and household demand for gold in China have different drivers. While Beijing is managing its financial exposure, private investors are seeking somewhere to preserve their savings. Here is what we know.
How much gold has China bought?
China’s central bank added approximately 23 tonnes of gold in September, bringing its reported holdings to about 2,410 tonnes, according to the World Gold Council. That was its largest monthly purchase since October 2023. Gold accounted for 8.5 percent of China’s total official reserves at the end of September, compared with 5.5 percent at the end of 2024.
Reserves are assets central banks hold to ensure they can meet international payments and respond to financial disruption. They usually include foreign currencies, foreign government debt and gold.
Private demand for gold within China has also risen, with purchases of gold bars and coins 28.4 percent higher in the first half of 2026 than during the same period last year, according to the China Gold Association. The buying of gold has continued amid falling prices, with gold down around 8.5 percent over the month.
The World Gold Council attributed the decline in gold prices partly to a stronger dollar and higher returns on US government debt. With interest rates going up in an attempt to curb inflation, these investments are attractive for buyers as they pay interest, making them more attractive to private investors than gold, which does not.
Why is China buying more gold?
A key objective is to reduce dependence on US government debt, known as Treasuries, according to Thu Lan Nguyen, head of commodity research at Commerzbank in Frankfurt.
China holds substantial reserves in dollar-based assets and, therefore, buying gold reduces its exposure to decisions taken in Washington. “China’s gold purchases are part of a broader effort to make its reserves more resilient,” Nguyen told Al Jazeera.
The freezing by Western countries of roughly $300bn in Russian Central Bank overseas assets following Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 demonstrated how reserves held abroad can quickly become inaccessible.
The concern for China may be that a future confrontation with Washington could expose some of its overseas assets to similar restrictions. “Gold held domestically has a crucial advantage in this respect: it does not represent a claim on another country and is therefore much less exposed to sanctions or asset freezes,” Nguyen said.
“I would interpret it primarily as risk management,” she added, pointing to increased geopolitical tensions and economic and fiscal risks.
America’s rising debt, which hit $40 trillion for the first time in history earlier this year, adds another source of uncertainty. In February, the US Congressional Budget Office projected that federal debt held by the public would rise from 101 percent of the size of the US economy in 2026 to 120 percent in 2036. That provides context for concerns about Washington’s ability to repay that debt going forward should an economic crash occur. Much of this debt is held by China. Gold, therefore, offers a less volatile and risky asset to hold.
Chinese households have different motivations for buying gold. When confidence in other investments weakens, gold can become more attractive as a way to hold savings. “Strong demand for gold can partly reflect a search for alternative stores of value,” Nguyen said.
The World Gold Council has identified weak Chinese share markets as one factor supporting domestic demand for gold, while its property market is burdened by heavy borrowing and overbuilding, contributing to a fall in housing prices, making it a poorer investment.
What this means for the US dollar
Analysts warned that China’s increased buying of gold does not signal an imminent end to the dollar’s global dominance. “I would be cautious about describing this as a major shift away from the dollar,” Nguyen said. “The dollar remains by far the dominant global reserve currency.”
But a gradual shift could still matter if China and other central banks put more of their new reserves into gold, buying fewer US assets than they normally would. That could weaken one source of demand for US government debt. But the effect would depend on how widely and quickly the shift developed.
“The key point is, therefore, that this is likely to be a slow diversification process rather than a sudden abandonment of the dollar,” Nguyen said. She added that the consequences for the US economy would remain limited unless the trend broadened and accelerated substantially.
Central banks also need readily available foreign currency to support international payments and the dollar remains central to those transactions. So gold can provide financial protection, but it cannot directly replace all the functions of dollar reserves.
Who else is buying gold?
China is part of a wider trend, particularly among central banks in emerging economies, Nguyen said.
“The trend is particularly visible among emerging market central banks,” Nguyen said. “But sanctions are only part of the story.”
Poland has also become a more prominent buyer. Its central bank purchased 31 tonnes in the first quarter of 2026 and another eight tonnes in July, according to the World Gold Council.
Large holdings do not necessarily indicate recent purchases. India, for example, confirmed in June that its physical gold stock remained unchanged at about 880.5 tonnes. India’s gold reserves have changed little since mid-2025, according to the World Gold Council. It bought about four tonnes in 2025, down from 73 tonnes in 2024.
Despite China’s sustained buying, its reserves remain far smaller than those of the United States. Its holdings of about 2,300 tonnes at the end of 2025 amounted to less than one-third of the US stockpile of approximately 8,133 tonnes.

Two Israeli women accused of smuggling 100 kg of khat released on bail in Poland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:37:04 UTC
20:37:04 KST

After three and a half months in detention, a court in Krakow has released on bail two young ultra-Orthodox Israeli women arrested on suspicion of smuggling 100 kilograms of khat, a plant classified as an illegal drug in Poland and the European Union.
The court accepted an argument from their Polish lawyer, Wit Steidler, in favor of their release. The women must report to police weekly and are prohibited from leaving Poland until the legal proceedings are concluded.
Steidler said that under Polish law, the amount of khat found in their suitcases was enormous. "This is a very serious crime in Poland," he explained. "Khat is included on the list of prohibited substances and is classified as a drug. If they are convicted, they could face between three and 23 years in prison. We managed to convince the court that it was inappropriate to continue holding them in detention.
"Even I, as their lawyer, was surprised by the court's decision to release them. But they are young women, this is the first time they have done something so foolish, and there is no point in keeping them isolated. We proposed bail and weekly police supervision. I was lucky the judge listened to me."
The two women, ages 23 and 24, were arrested on June 19 after arriving in Krakow on a flight from Israel. Each was carrying 50 kilograms of khat in her luggage.
There is considerable demand for khat in Europe among immigrants from Ethiopia and Eritrea. According to the report, individuals in Israel recruit young people, usually from the ultra-Orthodox community, to transport the plant in exchange for airfare and a payment of 5,000 shekels. They tell the recruits that if they are caught, the worst they can expect is a small fine or confiscation of their luggage.
However, Poland is considered one of the strictest countries when it comes to khat smuggling. In practice, the immediate consequence is often harsh pretrial detention. As soon as suitcases containing khat are discovered, typically weighing between 40 and 80 kilograms, the couriers are arrested and sent to detention facilities in Poland for periods ranging from several weeks to several months while their cases are examined.
For young people with no previous involvement in crime, the experience can be extremely traumatic: harsh detention conditions in a foreign country, separation from family, a lack of kosher food for those who observe Jewish dietary laws, and language barriers. Polish law enforcement authorities use detention as a form of shock treatment and as a punitive measure in itself, even before a trial begins.
Attorney Mordechai Tzivin, who represents Israelis facing legal difficulties abroad and assisted one of the women voluntarily alongside the Polish lawyer, said the Polish law enforcement authorities deserved thanks for the humane treatment they had shown his client, recognizing that numerous mitigating circumstances should be taken into account.

The EU is discussing the use of frozen Russian assets for Ukraine again — who is for it and who is against it
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
14:30:52 EEST
20:30:52 KST

The EU is discussing the use of frozen Russian assets for Ukraine again — who is for it and who is against it
Kyiv • UNN
EU leaders have resumed discussions on using Russian assets to support Ukraine. Belgium stated that its position remains unchanged.
European leaders on Friday, October 16, resumed discussions on using frozen Russian sovereign assets to support Ukraine, despite Belgium's continued opposition to the scheme, which it successfully blocked last year. Rapporteur reports, as cited by UNN.
Details
"The frozen assets are there: they should be used to support Ukraine. It's that simple," Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs said ahead of the second day of the EU summit in Brussels on Friday, where Ukraine's financial needs were to be discussed with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen also noted that these assets, the vast majority of which are located in Belgium, are the "most obvious place to turn to" in order to support Ukraine, which, according to the publication's estimates, will face a $78 billion funding shortfall next year.
These assets "serve a dual purpose: they will finance Europe's defense, but they will also mean that Russia, which is currently causing so much destruction both in Ukraine and in Europe, will itself pay for everything it is doing," Frederiksen said.
The EU's chief diplomat, Kaja Kallas, also proposed using Russian assets to cover Ukraine's impending budget shortfall. "I am sure that [the leaders] will raise this [issue] today," she said. "Ukraine needs this money right now."
The comments came several weeks after Sweden, Spain, Poland and the Netherlands wrote to the European Commission, urging it to revive last year's heated debate on using these assets to support Ukraine.
Belgium rejected Germany's initiative last year to provide a "reparations loan" backed by the assets, citing legal and financial risks for Euroclear, the Brussels-based securities depository that holds €190 billion in Kremlin funds intended for use in the loan.
Ultimately, EU leaders decided to issue €90 billion in joint debt to finance Ukraine, as well as to freeze the Russian assets indefinitely.
The remarks also came several hours after Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever told reporters that his country's position remained unchanged.
"At the end of a conflict, there is always a peace agreement, and part of that peace agreement is the use of immobilized assets," De Wever said at a press conference that began after midnight on Friday.
"Are there people on this planet who might dream of doing this differently this time and using these assets earlier for certain purposes? The answer to that question is: yes, there are. Are they in this building? They are. Are there [some] outside this building? Yes, there are. Do I want to talk about it? No, I don't," he said.
Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin also hinted that he did not want to resume discussions on the frozen assets on Friday.
"We strongly supported the issue of seizing [these] assets and the possibility of using them, but ultimately it produced no results," said Martin, whose country currently holds the presidency of the Council of the EU.
"I recognize the amount of energy and effort that went into this last time. I would be more supportive of doing something effective, efficient and as quickly as possible on this issue," Martin said.

Nuremberg at 80: How do you put a death machine on trial?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:29:28 UTC
20:29:28 KST

Nuremberg at 80: How do you put a death machine on trial?
On the night of October 16, 1946, 10 individuals were hanged in the Nuremberg prison. These were the main Nazi criminals who had been captured and brought to trial.
Despite the horrifying scale and brutality of the crimes, the Nuremberg Trials remain one of the most controversial proceedings in world history.
Justice instead of revenge
The idea of an international tribunal to address Nazi atrocities had been considered for some time. In 1942, the Soviet Union established a special Extraordinary Commission that gathered information about these crimes. Tragically, it had a lot of work to do. The USSR became the primary battleground for the bloodiest and most brutal war in Europe.
The range and nature of the crimes committed on Soviet soil were staggering: genocide against multiple peoples, mass killings on various grounds, all sorts of war crimes, deliberate attacks on medical facilities and civilian infrastructure, arbitrary executions, economic exploitation, and sexual violence. Essentially, every town liberated from the Nazis had enough evidence to warrant its own tribunal. When the concentration camps were liberated, it became clear that Allied propaganda had not exaggerated but rather understated the extent of Nazi atrocities.
In addition to the Soviet government, the exiled governments of occupied countries – Belgium, Czechoslovakia, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Poland, Norway, France, and Yugoslavia – also wanted to hold the Nazis legally accountable for their crimes.
The outlines of the future tribunal began to take shape in the fall of 1943 during a conference in Moscow attended by the foreign ministers of the ‘Big Three’ – the USSR, the UK, and the US. The three powers agreed that Nazi leaders who committed crimes across multiple nations should be tried by an international court.
At that time, even the idea of lynching Nazi leaders seemed valid. Benito Mussolini was executed along with his mistress by Italian partisans on April 28, 1945, without any trial. Their mutilated bodies were publicly displayed. No one mourned Mussolini; similarly, no one would have objected if a Red Army soldier had shot Hitler.
Sporadic acts of vigilante justice also occurred as the war neared its end. A well-known incident involved American soldiers executing the staff of the Dachau concentration camp. Polish troops beat to death Oscar Dirlewanger, the commander of a punitive brigade responsible for countless deaths in Belarus and Poland.
Yet vigilante justice was not what the Allied leaders envisioned.
The men in the dock – and those who escaped it
It became clear that the crimes committed were not only widespread but complex. Determining individual responsibility was not always an easy task. The Nazis had taken measures to conceal their atrocities whenever possible; for example, they buried the remains of over 100,000 people, mostly Jews, after executing them at Babi Yar ravine near Kiev. Furthermore, once the Reich collapsed and arrests began, everyone began shifting blame onto one another, particularly onto those who had already died.
By April and May of 1945, most of the individuals who would eventually be tried at Nuremberg had been apprehended. Of course, many key figures were never tried.
For obvious reasons, Minister of Propaganda Joseph Goebbels and Hitler himself were absent from the trial: both had committed suicide before they could face justice. Heinrich Himmler, the head of the SS, was captured by two freed Soviet prisoners, yet during a medical examination, he swallowed a poison capsule and died. Heinrich Müller, the leader of the Gestapo, likely shot himself in late April or early May 1945. His body was discovered months later in a temporary grave.
The fate of Martin Bormann, Hitler’s private secretary and head of the party chancellery, was unknown for many years. He went missing, which in 1945 could imply that he had fled under an assumed identity. However, today we can say with certainty that Bormann was killed in the final hours of the defense of Berlin, while attempting to break out of the encircled city alongside a column of German troops.
Twenty-four people were tried in Nuremberg. The most prominent among them was Hermann Göring, the commander of the Luftwaffe, who held numerous official and unofficial positions, served as Hitler’s close associate, and was considered the second most powerful man in the Reich.
Other figures included the Minister for Occupied Eastern Territories and the Nazis’ chief ideologist Alfred Rosenberg; Chief of the Armed Forces Command Wilhelm Keitel; Minister of Foreign Affairs Joachim von Ribbentrop; and the head of the security service Ernst Kaltenbrunner.
Nuremberg’s Palace of Justice was chosen for the trials for several practical reasons. It had direct access to the prison, was in relatively good condition, and was well-equipped to accommodate large numbers of people.
Unprecedented crimes, untested law
The decision was made to conduct the trials according to established legal standards, allowing the defendants the right to defend themselves. The Nazis found attorneys to represent them. Admiral Karl Dönitz took an interesting approach: he secured a maritime law specialist as his lawyer, but said that if he were not allowed to work with him, he would choose the admiral of the Allied forces who commanded submarines as his lawyer.
Rosenberg pursued a different strategy by trying to recruit Hans Frank, who was also being tried for war crimes as the governor of occupied Poland, and happened to be a lawyer by training. However, this request was denied. Furthermore, since the court needed to address the criminal status of certain organizations, and Martin Bormann was absent from the trial, the court appointed its own attorneys. The judges were from the USSR, the US, the UK, and France.
A significant challenge arose from the fact that some legal norms were developed during the trial itself. As a result, defense attorneys argued that the court was fundamentally unlawful since it relied on laws that did not exist at the time the defendants committed their crimes. Certain participants stated that Nuremberg represented “victor’s justice.” This sentiment partly fueled Winston Churchill’s earlier wartime suggestion to execute the political leadership of the Reich outright. The problem was that such a trial was unprecedented – nothing similar had ever been attempted before – and required the unveiling of many layers of guilt to find the responsible persons.
For example, one of the most repugnant acts leading to the mass death of people was the so-called Barbarossa Decree issued in May 1941. This document was signed by Field Marshal Wilhelm Keitel, chief of the German armed forces. It effectively removed accountability for crimes committed by Wehrmacht soldiers and officers against Soviet civilians. Such actions could only be punished if they harmed German interests. If a soldier looted and killed a peasant, Keitel technically bore no responsibility, as the soldier operated within the legal framework that existed at the time.
Additionally, during the trial, Keitel’s attorney attempted to shift all blame onto the dead Hitler, citing that Keitel “was just following orders.” Moreover, the fact that the USSR did not sign several international agreements designed to protect war participants, especially prisoners of war, compounded the issue. The mortality rate among Soviet POWs during WWII exceeded 50%; in absolute terms, 3.3 million out of 5.7 million documented prisoners died. And this was just a small part of the challenges faced by the judges at Nuremberg.
The prosecution comprised four categories of crimes: crimes against humanity, crimes against peace, war crimes, and general conspiracy crimes. There was a significant challenge in aligning the legal positions of the USSR, the UK, and the US. Soviet law existed as an independent branch but was rooted in continental legal principles; meanwhile, the British and Americans relied on their own legal frameworks; for instance, the concept of ‘conspiracy’ was unique to these countries and was not typical in Soviet or German law.
Additionally, the Allies often favored a compromise stance whenever they could have been held accountable for similar actions themselves. This enabled Admiral Dönitz to mitigate his own sentence: although German submarine forces under his command fought ruthlessly, British and American submarine forces could have been accused of similar conduct.
Witnesses, evidence and Göring’s defiance
In some cases, the Allies had to make real compromises with their conscience. One such case involved Erich von dem Bach-Zelewski, who participated in the proceedings as a witness. This man had directly overseen mass killings during counter-partisan operations in Belarus, Russia, Ukraine, and Poland.
A horrifying tactic employed by his subordinates involved rounding up villagers in partisan areas into one building, which was then set ablaze. The mass slaughter of Poles during the Warsaw Uprising in 1944 is another example of his policy – about 15 civilians were killed for every lost insurgent.
Zelewski understood that his survival depended on betraying others, so he turned on everyone, revealing their darkest secrets. Hermann Göring shouted from the defendant’s stand, “You disgusting traitor, swine!” but there was nothing he could do. Ultimately, a German court sentenced him to life in prison, not only for his wartime actions but also for murders committed during the power struggles in Germany in the 1930s.
The tribunal had volumes of documents to examine. American judge Robert Jackson later recalled that he had approached stories of Nazi atrocities with skepticism before the trial, but was horrified by the reality that unfolded before him. He was particularly struck by an SS report detailing the destruction of ghettos – Jews leapt from burning buildings, and some attempted to crawl away on broken legs; they were hunted down like game.
While most defendants tried to speak evasively, Hermann Göring stood his ground until the very end. He was informally dubbed ‘Fuhrer of the Defendants’. Göring urged his co-defendants to remain defiant and not to confess. He showcased his skills as an orator, made sarcastic remarks, and effortlessly parried the initial accusations.
According to him, Gestapo actions and concentration camps were just a response to the terrorist actions of the communists; and the extermination of Jews was merely harsh rhetoric, there were no actual plans for their annihilation. He claimed to have had no hand in any acts of aggression, insisting he was always taken by surprise by such acts. He also maintained that the Reich had to strike preemptively against the USSR to defend itself from potential Soviet aggression. As for the humanitarian catastrophe in occupied territories – that was the fault of the Soviet authorities and their scorched-earth tactics; and any crimes committed by German soldiers were merely isolated incidents.
Göring steamrolled over Justice Robert Jackson with his shameless demagoguery. However, the Allies had seized enough documents to bring down the Reichsmarschall. Soviet prosecutor Roman Rudenko and British prosecutor David Maxwell-Fyfe hammered Göring with his own orders that led to mass starvation. Göring knew that he intended to starve millions and openly discussed it in his circles.
In contrast, Albert Speer, the Minister of Armaments, didn’t plead for mercy; he acknowledged his guilt and presented himself as a humble technocrat, successfully avoiding the gallows.
The defense generally argued that the Nuremberg Tribunal established no new legal norms, yet the entire legal framework had been crafted specifically for this trial. Moreover, the conspiracy concept (one of the four main charges) allowed individuals to be condemned for being affiliated with criminal organizations. This was an unprecedented model in continental European law, including German law, and many lawyers deemed it inapplicable.
Even the term ‘genocide’ was used retroactively, having only emerged during the trial itself. Additionally, the defense reduced the discourse to the notion that the defendants were either uninformed or inadequately aware of the crimes being committed, while the actual perpetrators were presumably already in their graves.
The verdicts and the gallows
Out of 24 defendants, only 12, including Göring and Keitel, received death sentences. In reality, there were only 11, as the fate of Bormann remained unknown. Three others received life sentences – including naval commander Erich Raeder and Minister of Economics Walther Funk – but both were released in the 1950s. Rudolf Hess, one of Hitler’s associates, was sentenced to life in prison and committed suicide in 1987 at age 93. Albert Speer and the leader of the Hitler Youth organization Baldur von Schirach both received 20-year sentences. Interestingly, three people were acquitted: propagandist Hans Fritzsche, diplomat Franz von Papen, and financier Hjalmar Schacht.
Two others managed to evade justice altogether. Party official Robert Ley committed suicide before the trial even began, while Göring somehow obtained poison and took it just hours before his execution.
On the evening of October 15th, three gallows were erected in the prison gymnasium. Before midnight, the condemned were roused from their cells and led out. Execution began just after one o’clock, and by 2:45 AM, it was all over. The bodies were transported to Munich for cremation, and their ashes were scattered.
But that wasn’t the end of it. Following the main trial, there were 12 ‘mini-trials’ which focused on Nazi doctors, judges, and the case of the Einsatzgruppen (paramilitary death squads), among others. In total, 142 more individuals were found guilty, with 13 sentenced to execution. Many of these defendants were just as monstrous as those hanged in the primary trial. For instance, doctors were accused of a range of inhumane experiments on human subjects, including frostbite experiments, the deliberate poisoning of victims, and intentional infection with deadly diseases, among other atrocities.
Among those hanged was Waldemar Hoven, the chief physician at the Buchenwald concentration camp, who conducted gas poisoning experiments on inmates. A whole team of SS officers was convicted in connection to the Einsatzgruppen case. For unclear reasons, out of 24 individuals, only a few were actually executed, despite all being directly responsible for the murders. Among those executed was Paul Blobel, who organized the mass killings at Babi Yar. Additionally, separate trials occurred in various countries under their national laws. In Norway, 12 Germans and 25 collaborators were executed. In Poland, Rudolf Höss, the commandant of Auschwitz, was hanged following a separate trial.
***
The Nuremberg Tribunal was an impressive judicial process, and the Allies’ decision to hold it deserves commendation. The trial wasn’t perfect and it’s true that it departed from traditional methods of justice. Many legal norms were established retroactively; moreover, in the subsequent trials, many Nazi criminals managed to escape justice. However, Nuremberg wasn’t merely about ‘victor’s justice’. No one would dare say that those horrific criminals were hanged unjustly. Most importantly, while the principles of justice established in Nuremberg may have been imperfect, they are still effective in situations reminiscent of the horrors perpetrated by the Nazis.

German parliament backs tobacco tax hike for revenue, public health
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:28:41 UTC
20:28:41 KST

Ayhan Simsek
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
Germany’s lower house of parliament late Thursday approved a phased-in increase in the tobacco tax that is expected to raise the average price of a pack of 20 cigarettes from roughly €8 ($9) now to about €9 next year and nearly €12 by 2030.
The Bundestag backed the measure with votes from the governing coalition of Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s center-right CDU/CSU alliance and the center-left SPD. Officials project the step will generate roughly €12 billion in extra federal revenue over the four years.
The increases will take effect step by step each January from 2027 through 2030. Brand cigarettes could cost as much as €14 by the end of the period. Fine-cut tobacco used for rolling cigarettes will also become significantly more expensive.
The figures are average projections based on the higher rates the coalition approved; manufacturers will set the actual retail prices, which can vary by brand.
The government has cited both the need to consolidate the federal budget and protecting public health. The additional revenue is not earmarked and will enter the general budget. Past tobacco tax rises have mainly helped close fiscal gaps.
Health experts see higher prices as an effective way to encourage people to quit. The German Cancer Research Center has reported that about 131,000 people died in Germany in 2023 from tobacco-related diseases. A 2025 survey found that 19% of people age 15 and older in the country smoke.
