In Spain, the organizer of a scheme to embezzle UAH 71 million from the heat supply system of Ivano-Frankivsk was detained
Kyiv • UNN
In Spain, a 40-year-old resident of Kyiv Oblast suspected of organizing a scheme to inflate heat tariffs was detained. Ukraine is preparing an extradition request.
In Spain, a resident of Kyiv region suspected of leading a criminal organization that seized more than UAH 71 million while setting district heating tariffs in Ivano-Frankivsk has been detained. Ukrainian prosecutors are currently preparing a request for his extradition. The Prosecutor General’s Office reported this, UNN writes.
On October 14, a 40-year-old resident of Kyiv region was detained in Spain. He is suspected of establishing and leading a criminal organization, as well as seizing more than UAH 71 million while setting district heating tariffs in Ivano-Frankivsk. Since January 2026, he had been wanted internationally
According to the investigation, the man headed a criminal organization of five people, including the founder and executives of private companies that produced and transported thermal energy in the Ivano-Frankivsk municipality. The organizer was the ultimate beneficial owner of the affiliated enterprises.
During the 2021–2023 heating seasons, the participants submitted inaccurate calculations to local government bodies for setting tariffs: they artificially inflated heat production costs and concealed the actual losses incurred during its transportation.
As a result, the budget of Ivano-Frankivsk suffered losses of more than UAH 71 million, while city residents paid for heat they did not actually receive.
In December 2025, the man was notified in absentia that he was suspected of misappropriating property on an especially large scale through abuse of office. In January 2026, he was notified of new charges—establishing and leading a criminal organization, misappropriating property on an especially large scale, and entering knowingly false information into official documents (Part 1 of Article 255, Part 4 of Article 28, Part 5 of Article 191, Part 1 of Article 366 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine). The investigation established that the suspect had left Ukraine back in June 2025. On January 22, 2026, he was placed on an international wanted list
Prosecutors from the Ivano-Frankivsk Regional Prosecutor’s Office are currently preparing a request to the competent Spanish authorities for his extradition to Ukraine.
In March 2026, prosecutors referred the indictment against the other four members of the organization to court. The trial is ongoing.

US in ‘denuclearisation’ talks with Russia and China: Trump
The US and Russia each have more than 4,000 warheads. China is set to catch up with them within five years, Trump says.
The United States is engaged in talks with Russia and China regarding nuclear disarmament, President Donald Trump has announced.
Trump said on Thursday that China – which lags behind the US and Russia in terms of the number of warheads it has – is racing to catch up. He added during an interview with US broadcaster Newsmax that Washington is discussing with its peers a route to “denuclearise”.
China’s nuclear stockpile of about 620 warheads is dwarfed by those of the US and Russia, which each have more than 4,000, but Trump said he thinks China will “catch up” within five years.
“The whole thing is a shame because I’d love to denuclearise if possible,” Trump said. “We’re actually talking to Russia about that, and we’re talking to China about that denuclearisation.”
China doesn’t seem willing to disarm, he noted, but said talks have continued. Newsmax reported that Trump spoke with Chinese President Xi Jinping on the subject, but no further details regarding the talks with either Russia or China were revealed.
Russia has the world’s largest stockpile of nuclear warheads, and the US is close behind, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI).
The two countries together possess an estimated 86 percent of all nuclear weapons globally.
China has the third largest nuclear arsenal, according to SIPRI, having expanded it to 620 warheads in the past year.
Trump’s claims came shortly after the expiration of the Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty, an arms control agreement between the US and Russia to limit their nuclear arsenals.
A month after the treaty expired, French President Emmanuel Macron announced the Forward Deterrence Initiative as Russia’s nuclear sabre-rattling during its war on Ukraine has spooked Europe.
Former Australian Minister of Foreign Affairs Gareth Evans told Al Jazeera that the world’s interest in the risk of nuclear weapons has waned.
“[The] world … has become alarmingly complacent about the risks of nuclear war with every major nuclear arms control agreement dead, dying or on life support and the longstanding taboo against threat or use eroding,” he said

Europe’s best party cities for a Halloween night out, according to a new ranking
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:26:02 UTC
20:26:02 KST

From Edinburgh’s fiery Samhuinn festival to Dublin’s Gothic celebrations, Europe has plenty of ways to get into the Halloween spirit.
Halloween falling on a Saturday in 2026 means plenty of us will be keen to make the most of the spooky holiday, even travelling abroad to celebrate it.
Now, a new ranking has revealed the best party places to experience All Hallows' Eve across the globe.
Travel experts at Adventure360 analysed some 113 cities worldwide to uncover where travellers can find the biggest Halloween celebrations this year.
Each individual city was scored on the number of Halloween events happening between 30 October and 1 November, as well as the size of its nightlife offering and late-night restaurant scene.
The safety of the city was examined, too, and the report noted whether or not the destination hosts a signature Halloween or Day of the Dead event. In the end, each city was given a score out of 100.
In first place was New York, with a score of 91.1 out of 100, and it was followed by another US city, Chicago, which got a score of 80.1.
In terms of countries, the US had the most showings in the top 10, with New Orleans coming in at number nine but, continent-wise, Europe was revealed to be far and away the best Halloween destination, with five spots on the list.
Edinburgh is in third place, thanks in part to its legendary Samhuinn Fire festival, while Dublin follows close behind, partially because of its Bram Stoker festival.
Madrid, London and Prague also feature in the top 10, despite none of them actually offering a signature Halloween event; they’re just that spooky!
Within the Halloween top 20, other European cities included Rome, Berlin, Amsterdam, Barcelona, Budapest, and Lisbon
The world's best Halloween party cities 2026
How the cities rank out of a score of 100, according to the Adventure360 study:
- 1. New York, USA – 91.1/100
- 2. Chicago, USA – 80.1/100
- 3. Edinburgh, UK – 79.2/100
- 4. Dublin, Ireland – 73.0/100
- 5. Tokyo, Japan – 72.3/100
- 6. Mexico City, Mexico – 71.8/100
- 7. Madrid, Spain – 70.7/100
- 8. London, UK – 69.6/100
- 9. New Orleans, USA – 69.2/100
- 10. Prague, Czechia – 69.0/100
- 11. Rome, Italy – 68.6/100
- 12. Berlin, Germany – 67.4/100
- 13. Amsterdam, Netherlands – 66.7/100
- 14. Osaka, Japan – 66.4/100
- 15. Barcelona, Spain – 65.6/100
- 16. Washington D.C., USA – 65.5/100
- 17. Dubai, UAE – 65.4/100
- 18. Budapest, Hungary – 65.4/100
- 19. Sydney, Australia – 64.3/100
- 20. Lisbon, Portugal – 64.1/100
Europe’s top five cities for Halloween parties
Following the ranking, these are the five best cities to spend Halloween in Europe this year – and the reasons why.
Edinburgh, United Kingdom
Scotland’s capital Edinburgh may only have a relatively small number of nightlife venues and late-night restaurants, but it boasts plenty of Halloween-themed events, not least the Samhuinn Fire festival.
The event brings a dramatic twist to Halloween, with Calton Hill transformed by fire, drumming, acrobatics and elaborate costumes.
Taking place on 31 October, the event reimagines ancient Celtic traditions marking the end of summer and the arrival of winter, with performers acting out the battle between the Summer King and Winter Queen.
Dublin, Ireland
Dublin has just seven Halloween-themed events – one of the lowest amounts in the top 10 – but it makes up for it with its legendary Bram Stoker festival.
This year, the celebration of the city’s Gothic heritage will take place from 23-26 October, with four days of spooky events inspired by the author of Dracula.
Expect haunted walking tours, horror theatre, candlelit library visits and a spectacular parade. There’s family-friendly fun, too, including Stokerland, a free gothic-themed park at St Patrick’s Park.
Madrid, Spain
Madrid may not have one big signature Halloween celebration, but there’s plenty to get stuck into.
For a dose of horror, head to MADHORROR at IFEMA Madrid, running from 30 October to 2 November, with haunted houses, horror films, gaming and comic-book events.
After dark, join a ghost and legends walking tour through the old town, or head to Malasaña for costume parties and late-night drinks and eats.
London, United Kingdom
Although England’s capital doesn’t have a signature Halloween event, it does have some 22 themed happenings, as well as more than 1,000 nightlife venues and 2,600 late-night restaurants, which is the highest number in the top 10.
Head to Kew Gardens for its illuminated Halloween trail, featuring Dracula’s Lair, live performers and a Headless Horseman, or explore the capital’s darker history on a Jack the Ripper walking tour.
For something quirky, the London Transport Museum is holding a Halloween silent disco among its historic trains and buses.
Prague, Czechia
Prague’s Gothic streets make a fitting backdrop for Halloween, with plenty of ways to get into the spooky spirit.
While the Czech capital doesn’t have a signature event, Wonderland Halloween takes over the historic Lucerna Great Hall on 30 October for a night of elaborate costumes, live performances, DJs and theatrical decorations.
For something more low-key, join a ghost tour through the Old Town’s narrow lanes and medieval underground passages, where guides share tales of murder, alchemy and restless spirits.
On 30 October and on Halloween night itself, the legendary five-floor nightclub Karlovy Lázně will play host to its annual Wicked Weekend event.

Swiss journalist risks court sentence for exposing top banker
ZURICH, Oct 16 - Zurich prosecutors this week charged Swiss journalist Lukas Haessig with violating banking secrecy over reporting that set off a high-profile corporate criminal trial of the former boss of Raiffeisen Bank Switzerland, Haessig said on his financial blog Inside Paradeplatz.
• Zurich-based Inside Paradeplatz published a series of articles in 2016 about Pierin Vincenz, former CEO of Raiffeisen Bank Switzerland, and his business partner Beat Stocker, who were found guilty of fraud in April 2022
• That verdict is currently under review by a higher court expected to rule in January 2027
• Police in June 2025 searched the blog's Zurich office and home of its founder, seizing evidence linked to suspected violation of Swiss banking law
• Prosecutors had dropped the case in December 2025, but Zurich's High Court in April said a court must decide how the banking secrecy provision should be interpreted after a complaint by Stocker
• Article 47 of the Swiss Banking Act criminalises disclosure of confidential information leaked by bank insiders, with penalties of up to three years in prison or a fine
• Press freedom group Reporters Without Borders Switzerland called the charges troubling and said Article 47 of the Swiss banking act must not be used to prosecute journalists
• Inside Paradeplatz's reporting was clearly in the public interest, Reporters Without Borders said, adding the banking secrecy law had a chilling effect and pointing to "legal shortcomings" in Switzerland on press freedom
• Prosecutors said the presumption of innocence applies to Haessig. No court date has yet been set REUTERS

Türkiye calls for international action over Israel's violations of international law

The international community cannot remain silent in the face of persistent Israeli violations of international law, Turkish Parliament Speaker Numan Kurtulmus said on Friday.
Addressing a meeting of the European Conference of Presidents of Parliament in Rome, Kurtulmus said: “We cannot let impunity go unpunished. “
Kurtulmus called upon the international community to take concrete steps to uphold international law.
The erosion of the rules-based international order is starkly reflected in the years-long humanitarian catastrophe and genocide in Gaza, he said.
“We can no longer turn a blind eye to the humanitarian catastrophe in Gaza and the wider region and the blatant human rights violations and crimes against humanity perpetrated by the Israeli government against the people of Palestine,” Kurtulmus said.
“This is not merely a political question but also a test for the humanity's common conscience,” he added.
Underlining that the Israeli aggression is not confined to Gaza, Kurtulmus said: “Destruction, displacement, and settlers' violence persist in the West Bank, and Israel continues to threaten the territorial integrity and sovereignty of regional countries, including Syria and Lebanon.”
It is imperative that parliaments step up and assume an active role to help put an immediate end to the suffering of the Gazan people and the violations of international humanitarian law, he stressed.
Kurtulmus called on parliaments to take an active role in urgently ending the suffering of the people of Gaza and violations of international humanitarian law.
“We believe that coordinated action by parliaments can strengthen international efforts to uphold international law and confront persistent violations,” he added.
International order fails to prevent conflicts
The current international order has proved its inability to prevent conflicts and wars, even in Europe's immediate territory, according to Kurtulmus.
“The war between Russia and Ukraine, continuing for almost five years now, has turned to a war of attrition affecting all of Europe rather than a conflict between two nations,” he said.

Editor's note: The story has been updated with the latest details.
President Volodymyr Zelensky and Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar met for their first bilateral talks in Brussels on Oct. 16, as their countries seek to open a "new chapter" in relations.
Both leaders are in Brussels for a two-day EU summit, where Kyiv seeks to drum up European support amid deteriorating ties with the U.S.
The meeting comes the same week Zelensky signed a law on the educational rights of Ukraine's national minorities, a step Hungary had demanded before allowing Kyiv's EU accession talks to proceed.
"We see the Ukrainian parliament's adoption of the minority education law and the immediate start of its implementation as a first step towards rebuilding mutual trust," Magyar said on X after the meeting.
The Hungarian prime minister also said that both countries would continue talks at the ministerial level, focusing on the situation of national minorities.
Magyar underscored that both countries agreed on the need "to build a new foundation for our political and economic relations" and expressed solidarity with Ukraine in the face of "Russia's brutal aggression."
After Ukraine passed the minorities bill, Hungary lifted its veto on the opening of two more negotiation clusters for Ukraine, allowing their official launch on Oct. 13.
The law gives Ukraine's Hungarian-speaking minority and other EU-language minorities more room to use their native language in education.
Ukrainian officials have said it would formalize existing education rights for national minorities rather than bring major practical changes.
Roughly 80,000 ethnic Hungarians live in Ukraine's westernmost Zakarpattia Oblast.
Zelensky said the meeting focused on Ukraine's EU accession efforts, as well as opportunities for bilateral cooperation, trade, and agricultural issues.
"We also discussed diplomacy and efforts to end Russia's war," the president said, adding that the leaders agreed to exchange visits.
"We're moving on our relationship with Hungary; we had a very good meeting," Zelensky said later at a press conference in Brussels. He did not rule out traveling to Budapest.
"I hope that we will get to the point where a new chapter opens (in Hungarian-Ukrainian relations)," Magyar said about his meeting with Zelensky a day prior, saying the two could then meet again in Berehove, a Zakarpattia Oblast town considered the heart of the Hungarian-speaking community in Ukraine.
Magyar has floated a meeting in Berehove since the spring, but no firm date has been set so far. The two held brief conversations in June in Brussels, and then again in July at the NATO summit in Ankara.

Swiss postal revamp plan faces fire during consultation
A revision of legislation governing the Swiss postal service has drawn criticism from both the left and the right of the political spectrum during a consultation process., which concluded on Thursday.
Swiss Post said it welcomed the government’s proposed changes as the consultation period ended on Thursday.
By putting its draft proposal out for consultation in June, the government was responding to the decline in demand for traditional postal services and to Swiss Post’s expansion of commercial activities beyond its core remit.
Business circles have criticised the insufficient opening up of the market and the overly lax restrictions on corporate takeovers.
Left-wing parties and the regions, for their part, have condemned the planned reduction in services from 2030 onwards, fearing a less dense postal network and a reduction in the number of delivery days.
Swiss Post has welcomed the planned changes, describing them as “dynamic regulation”. It has emphasised the importance of having room for manoeuvre.

UNDP local governance project to cover five regions of Kazakhstan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16

UNDP local governance project to cover five regions of Kazakhstan
Five regions of Kazakhstan will join a new UNDP-backed initiative aimed at strengthening local self-government, officials said at the 11th meeting of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) Coordination Council chaired by Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Economy Serik Zhumangarin, Qazinform News Agency reports.
The meeting brought together UN representatives, heads of central government agencies, and regional administrations.
Zhumangarin said Kazakhstan remains strongly committed to the global sustainable development agenda and has established itself as a regional leader in Central Asia, enhancing its positions at the international arena.
“As President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has repeatedly emphasized, the implementation of the SDGs is directly linked to our national priorities. Speaking at the 80th session of the UN General Assembly, the President noted that Kazakhstan had integrated sustainable development goals into state planning and budgeting processes. We attach particular importance to cooperation with international organizations in achieving these objectives,” he said.
UN Resident Coordinator in Kazakhstan Sarangoo Radnaaragchaa highlighted the importance of preparing an annual national SDG report, aligning budget planning with sustainable development goals, and strengthening regional cooperation. She also emphasized joint efforts between Kazakhstan and the United Nations on climate change and water resource management.
UNDP Resident Representative in Kazakhstan Katarzyna Wawiernia underscored the country’s progress in integrating the SDGs into the national planning system. She said the next key step would be adapting national priorities to the specific needs of each region, expanding local self-government, and unlocking territorial economic potential.
With support from the European Union, a three-year initiative to advance local self-government reform has been launched. The project will be implemented jointly with the Ministry of National Economy and local executive authorities in five regions: Abai, Zhetysu, Turkistan, Mangystau, and Kostanay. The initiative aims to stimulate local economies, strengthen regional capacity, expand employment opportunities, and increase household incomes.
Participants reviewed interim SDG implementation indicators and discussed future priorities. Among the achievements highlighted was progress in the SDG indicator measuring population coverage by the social protection system. The number of beneficiary families declined from 54,400 in 2025 to 41,300 currently.
In Kyzylorda кegion, 99.3% of schools have created conditions for inclusive education, while issues related to three-shift and dilapidated schools have been fully resolved.
In Zhetysu region, 110 settlements have been gasified, up from just five in 2022. Regional gasification has reached 67.2%, covering 467,000 people. Authorities plan to gasify another 16 settlements this year, increasing coverage to 72%.
Participants identified the development of a comprehensive national system for regular monitoring and evaluation of SDG implementation as a key priority, with efforts to localize SDG indicators set to continue at the regional level.
Earlier, it was reported that the Kazakh Energy Ministry together with the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) proceeded to developing a project initiative on digital intelligent power grids.

Reforms and financing assurances from partners are prerequisites for receiving EFF tranche – IMF
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
14:07:38 EEST
20:07:38 KST

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) welcomes the efforts of the government and the Verkhovna Rada to reinvigorate reforms in Ukraine. Resuming these reforms is a key condition for the successful completion of the combined second and third reviews of the Extended Fund Facility (EFF) program by the end of this year. A second essential condition is the provision of financing assurances from partners, stated Mateusz Szczurek, Director of the IMF’s European Department.
"We plan to conduct the second and third reviews of the program by the end of this year. Naturally, this depends on the resumption of reforms, as well as on the provision of financing assurances by partners," he said during a press conference held on the sidelines of the IMF and World Bank Group Annual Meetings in Bangkok on Friday, according to an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent.
Szczurek emphasized the critical importance of adopting legislation and implementing other measures related to revenue mobilization and public administration, as these are vital for securing further donor financing, starting as early as 2026.
Regarding new assumptions and the potential need to revise the EFF program, the IMF European Department Director pointed to the Ukrainian government’s draft state budget for 2027, currently submitted to parliament, which is based on the assumption that the war will continue for a longer period.
"This, of course, increases the financing requirement for 2027 (...) As for the structuring aspects, that is a topic for discussion during the combined second and third reviews of the program, so we will provide details once they are made public," noted Szczurek.
During this year’s IMF Annual Meetings, held from October 12–18, the Ukrainian delegation is discussing with the Fund the implementation of the new four-year Extended Fund Facility (EFF) program, valued at $8.1 billion, which was approved at the end of February this year. This program is part of a broader $136.5 billion external financing package for the 2026–2029 period, based on the baseline scenario.
In July, the IMF completed the first review of the program and disbursed a second tranche of approximately $690 million, bringing the total funding received under the new program to $2.2 billion. At the same time, it was noted that some of the program’s structural benchmarks had not been met by their respective deadlines. Following the first review, the EFF program was updated to include eight additional structural benchmarks, seven of which are fiscal in nature.
Discussions are currently underway to combine the second and third program reviews, with the aim of presenting the matter to the Executive Board before the end of this year. This would coincide with the approval of a combined third and fourth tranche disbursement, totaling approximately $1.65 billion.
"Bringing this to the Board depends on receiving sufficient and credible financing assurances to cover the projected funding gap, on terms that are consistent with maintaining Ukraine’s debt sustainability," IMF spokesperson Julie Kozack stated in early October.
Finance Minister Marchenko noted that, ahead of the expected IMF mission visit in November, it would be desirable to secure confirmation for all sources of the $52.6 billion in external financing required for the 2027 state budget; currently, about $32.6 billion of that total still awaits confirmation.
According to Marchenko, Kyiv expects the European Union to fulfill its commitment to cover two-thirds of Ukraine’s external financing needs for next year as well—a move that would increase confirmed funding by approximately $17.5 billion. As for the remaining balance of roughly $15 billion, the minister explained that there are several potential sources to cover it, including bilateral financing, guarantees, and programs with international financial institutions.

A Houthi commander was killed in clashes with Yemeni government forces near Mount Han in the southwestern city of Taiz, a Yemeni official said Friday.
Fayyad al-Noman, a Yemeni media spokesman, said on US social media platform X that Abdulrahman Mohammed Sufyan Wajih al-Din, also known as Abu al-Karrar, was killed by government troops near Mount Han.
Al-Noman identified the slain Houthi commander as a brigadier general and director of Dhi al-Sufal in the Ibb province.
He did not specify when the incident occurred or provide further details on the circumstances of the killing.
There was no immediate comment from the Houthis.
Taiz has remained a major front line in Yemen's conflict, with government forces and the Houthis engaged in repeated clashes around the city.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and several other provinces in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene the following year in support of the internationally recognized government.

Sudan: Over 6,500 detainees held by RSF in West Darfur face major food shortages
Over 6,500 detainees held by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) paramilitary group in West Darfur are facing major food shortages and dire conditions, The Sudanese Doctor’s Network warned on Thursday.
The detainees are being held in El Geneina, an area that has witnessed horrors amid the war between the Sudanese army and the RSF which started in April 2023. Clashes in the area have killed over 10,000 people, mostly from the Masalit population, while mass graves have also been found in the region.
In a statement, the medical network said the information it had was based on details from reliable sources, who indicated that the detainees are being held in several detention centres.
It specified that there are 709 women and approximately 500 children under the age of 18 in the detention facilities.
The network has previously raised the alarm over the welfare of civilian detainees across Sudan, and reiterated its concerns over the food shortages and worsening health conditions in detention centres on Thursday.
It noted that there was a rising death toll in detention centres, as well as many cases of serious health and humanitarian issues threatening the lives of thousands.
The Sudanese Doctor’s Network issued an urgent call for an investigation to be carried out into the causes of the poor conditions and for international groups to ensure they receive adequate medical care and food.
It further pushed for humanitarian organisations to be granted access to the detention centres and for transparency regarding the safety and whereabouts of the detainees, which comes amid reports of torture and ill-treatment of thousands of them.
Sudanese authorities and human rights organisations estimate that the RSF are holding around 19,800 people in their prisons, including military personnel, civilians, women and children under the age of 18.
Last month, the RSF stepped up its deadly drone attacks in government-held towns in the frontline state of North Kordofan.
Reports state that drone attacks have become the weapon of choice increasingly when it comes to the conflict in Sudan. The UN also said last month that drone attacks by both sides killed more than 1,000 civilians in the first half of this year.

Pezeshkian urges ‘peace diplomacy’ to protect biodiversity, condemns ecocide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:05:55 UTC
20:05:55 KST

Pezeshkian urges ‘peace diplomacy’ to protect biodiversity, condemns ecocide
TEHRAN – President Masoud Pezeshkian has called for “peace diplomacy” to protect biodiversity, condemning the devastating environmental impact of wars of aggression as ecocide and urging the international community to establish effective, transparent and enforceable mechanisms to safeguard natural heritage during wartime.
Speaking on Friday, October 16, at the summit of heads of state and government held as part of the 17th Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17) in Yerevan, Pezeshkian said war is not only a threat to people and infrastructure but also a direct driver of environmental destruction. “War burns forests, destroys wetlands, contaminates soil and water, and displaces wildlife,” he said.
Pezeshkian described environmental cooperation as a bridge between nations, stressing that biodiversity conservation could serve as an important pillar of “peace diplomacy.”
“In a region facing security crises stemming from the illegal and expansionist presence of powers, as well as climate change, water scarcity and ecosystem degradation, environmental cooperation can build bridges between nations,” he said.
Such cooperation, he added, can pave the way for peace and security for all, peace with nature, and a future in which human life is aligned and in harmony with the natural world.
“Today, we stand at a pivotal moment in history when biodiversity is no longer merely a scientific or environmental concern. It is also an issue of peace and security, human health, food and water security, and intergenerational justice for all the inhabitants of our planet,” Pezeshkian stressed.
“The Islamic Republic of Iran was among the first countries to recognize the legal and international significance of this issue and become a party to the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD). However, Iran’s relationship with biodiversity goes far beyond its membership in an international convention.
With an ancient tradition of living in harmony with nature and an extraordinary diversity of ecosystems, species and genetic resources, Iran is the custodian of an invaluable and irreplaceable natural wealth. This heritage is the result of millions of years of evolution, natural dynamism and adaptation, and is reflected in the culture, customs, livelihoods, indigenous knowledge and historical identity of the people of this land.
Owing to its exceptional geographical location, Iran lies at the intersection of several biogeographical regions. From the Hyrcanian and Arasbaran forests to the Zagros Mountains, and from arid and desert landscapes to the coasts of the Persian Gulf, the Sea of Oman and the Caspian Sea, Iran is home to thousands of plant and animal species, as well as valuable genetic resources. These natural assets underpin the country’s ecological stability and sustainability, provide a vital foundation for water and food security and human health, strengthen resilience to natural hazards, and serve as a cornerstone of sustainable development.
In Iran, biodiversity, together with climatic and geographical diversity, is deeply intertwined with human history and civilization. Friendship with, respect for and protection of nature are integral to the cultural, religious and ritual identity of Iranians. Nature has long been regarded as an inseparable part of human life and a trust to be preserved for future generations. Many traditional ways of life, agricultural and livestock-raising practices, the use of medicinal plants, and the indigenous knowledge of Iranian communities have evolved over time through an understanding of and adaptation to nature, reflecting thousands of years of interaction between humans and the natural world.
For Iran, therefore, biodiversity conservation means far more than protecting species and their habitats. It means safeguarding a natural, cultural and civilizational heritage.
In my country, drawing on a long-standing culture of respect for nature and in line with national and international goals and commitments, the National Biodiversity Strategies and Action Plan has been developed and approved. The Department of Environment has been designated as the national coordinating authority, while a mechanism for non-governmental participation, with priority given to local communities, has also received government approval.”
He highlighted that protecting threatened species and restoring vulnerable populations are among the key priorities. These efforts include expanding protected areas and monitoring flagship wildlife species.
“War does not target only human lives and economic infrastructure. It also damages nature: burning forests, destroying wetlands, contaminating soil, threatening water resources, destroying habitats, displacing wildlife, and introducing chemicals and heavy metals into natural cycles. The environmental consequences of war can persist for years after hostilities have ended.
The international community now recognizes that environmental destruction during armed conflicts is not a minor or incidental consequence of war. Such damage is directly linked to the security and well-being of future generations.
In our region, including Iran, the environmental consequences of military conflicts must receive greater attention from the international community. The war of aggression launched by the United States and the Israeli regime in our region has threatened natural ecosystems and damaged environmental protection infrastructure built over years of efforts to conserve biodiversity. Attacks on industrial and energy facilities, fires, pollutant emissions, and soil and water contamination have all contributed to these threats.
This is not merely a domestic issue or one confined within a country's political borders. Nature recognizes no political boundaries, and the spread of water, soil, and air pollution does not stop at national frontiers. The environmental damage caused by war is therefore global in nature and requires international solutions.”
The effects of war on ecosystems can persist for years or even generations, affecting areas hundreds or thousands of kilometers away. One stark example is the scale of destruction in Gaza, where, according to experts, parts of the territory's soil may remain incapable of supporting natural life, vegetation, and ecological cycles for hundreds of years. The destruction caused by wars of aggression in our region amounts to what is known as “ecocide,” or environmental genocide, and must be condemned, Pezeshkian underlined.
“The international community is expected to establish effective, transparent, and enforceable mechanisms to protect natural heritage and biodiversity. No country should be allowed to treat nature as a silent and defenseless victim of war.
The Islamic Republic of Iran is committed to implementing the Convention on Biological Diversity and advancing global goals for nature conservation. In Iran, we pursue the protection of natural areas, wetlands, forests, rangelands, wildlife habitats, and genetic resources alongside sustainable development.
However, we must be realistic and fair. A country facing the mounting pressures of climate change, drought, water scarcity, desertification, and dwindling natural resources, while also grappling with the effects of economic sanctions and restricted access to technology and financial resources, needs genuine international cooperation to implement its environmental programs and repair the damage it has sustained. This is particularly true when the country has been targeted in two consecutive years by what it describes as criminal wars involving the extensive use of destructive and prohibited weapons, with attacks in many cases allegedly intended to cause environmental damage, including strikes on fuel storage facilities in the capital.”
He emphasized that biodiversity conservation will remain confined to negotiations, resolutions, and the setting of targets unless it is backed by adequate financial resources, equitable access to knowledge and technology, and capacity-building.
“If developing countries are expected to protect their forests, wetlands, species, and genetic resources, they must also be provided with the means to fulfill that responsibility. This is the true meaning of environmental justice.
We therefore call on United Nations agencies, international financial institutions, and relevant organizations and bodies working in environmental protection and sustainable development to strengthen mechanisms for mobilizing financial resources, assessing environmental damage, restoring damaged ecosystems, and supporting affected countries in addressing the environmental consequences of armed conflicts.”
In conclusion, Pezeshkian said that the Islamic Republic of Iran stands ready to cooperate constructively with the international community in this joint effort by sharing its scientific and academic capacities and experience with other countries. “We believe that biodiversity conservation can serve as an important pillar of “peace diplomacy.”
In a region grappling with security crises stemming from the unlawful and expansionist presence of powers, climate change, water scarcity, and ecosystem degradation, environmental cooperation can build bridges between nations. These bridges can pave the way toward peace and security for all, peace with nature, and a future in which human life is aligned with and harmonious with the natural world.
 
It is a future free from war, bloodshed, and destruction, in which biodiversity serves as a shared foundation for the well-being and prosperity of present and future generations.”

‘It was fake’: Indian villagers allege forgery behind Adani mine project
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:05:45 UTC
20:05:45 KST

‘It was fake’: Indian villagers allege forgery behind Adani mine project
Forged signatures and thumbprints – even of dead and fictitious people – allegedly used to get land for bauxite mine.
Koraput, India – Raghunath Khara was shocked to look at his thumb impression on a piece of paper that declared he had consented to a government proposal to mine his village’s pristine forest land for bauxite.
He says he never gave that thumb impression.
“I always sign in English. It was someone else’s thumb,” alleged Khara, a shopkeeper in Balda village in the tribal-dominated Koraput district of Odisha state in eastern India.
Khara is among hundreds of people from Indigenous tribes in Balda and neighbouring Bannur village who have lost their lands to the new bauxite mine. It is being developed by Kalinga Alumina Limited, a subsidiary of Adani Enterprises Limited, a conglomerate owned by Gautam Adani, India’s second richest businessman and close to Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
The $24m project will consume a large chunk of the tabletop Balda Hill – home to forests, grasslands and caves that are considered sacred by at least 10 tribal villages surrounding it.
To push the project, the purported signatures and thumb impressions of nearly 600 tribals were allegedly collected during village council meetings in Balda and Bannur held on October 9 last year. Bannur is 5km from Balda.
Khara says he never attended the meeting at Balda and was instead protesting against the proposed mine with his wife, sister and other villagers about 100 metres from the village council office.
“It [thumb impression] was fake. We didn’t attend the village meeting at all. We were all busy protesting outside,” he told Al Jazeera.
India’s constitution recognises the rights of Indigenous communities over their traditional lands. Forest laws and laws granting autonomy to tribal areas dictate that village council resolutions are mandatory for any diversion of such lands for other purposes.
A resolution passed in a village council meeting is valid only if 50 percent of all the adults in the village consent to it in writing. Government documents claim all the 580 adults – 360 in Balda and 227 in Bannur – agreed to give up their land for the Adani mine. But the elected village heads in both villages denied any signatures were collected and called the two meetings “invalid”.
Even photographs taken by villagers at both council meetings show a combined attendance of about 100 people – nearly 40 in Balda and 68 in Bannur – far below the minimum 50 percent quorum required to pass a valid resolution.
Moreover, the villagers allege that most signatures on the resolution documents are fake, forged or impersonated.
They also claim the documents contain signatures of fictitious persons and even the names of people who died years ago. Some even said their signatures from a previous, unrelated village council meeting were fraudulently pasted onto the bauxite mine document.
Al Jazeera emailed the Adani group and its communications chief on August 18 seeking responses to the accusations of forgery and fraud. Then we followed up with a second request for comments on September 25, but did not receive any response. Al Jazeera also sought responses from Manoj Satyawan Mahajan, the district magistrate — the most senior bureaucrat in Koraput – to the concerns raised by villagers but did not receive a response. Rohit Varma, the superintendent of police for Koraput district, also did not respond to Al Jazeera’s queries.
‘They took the paper away from me’
Many of those who attended the meetings said they were opposed to the mining project.
“We were told that if mining was allowed, the village would get roads, jobs, drainage and water connections and a school built,” said Madhav Kuntili, a farmer in Bannur.
Koraput is one of India’s least developed districts and similar promises often have a significant sway. Kuntili said a document was passed around, seeking signatures.
“I said if the forest was being diverted, then I would not sign it. They took the paper away from me,” he told Al Jazeera.
Across Balda and Bannur, Al Jazeera met many villagers who said they were shocked to find their signatures or thumb impressions on the resolution.
Rama Hantal sat motionless by the doorway of his rusted tin-and-wood hut. The 60-year-old has been paralysed for several years and is unable to talk.
“There is no chance he could have attended the meeting or even signed,” said Chandrama Hantal, his daughter-in-law.
While Hantal had apparently signed the consent form in Odia, Odisha’s official language, Chandrama saw a thumb impression against her name. She also denied attending the meeting.
Among the signatories are three Gurubari Kharas – their purported thumb impressions in support of the mining project.
In Balda, villagers could only track two “Gurubaris” – one living 3km away who denied attending the meeting – and another from the village itself, who had died well before the village council meeting was held.
“My mother died in February 2025. How can they forge her presence and signature eight months later?” asked her son, Sahdev. She was nearly 75 when she died of natural causes.
Two other persons from the first Gurubari’s family are also listed as signatories – her bedridden husband, who has been paralysed since falling from a tree three months before the council meeting and her nephew. Both deny attending the October 9 meeting.
The third Gurubari remains untraced.
Al Jazeera interviewed more than 20 people and accessed records from both Balda and Bannur villages, but could not trace at least 67 persons named as signatories in the resolution.
In Bannur, at least three deceased persons were represented through thumbprints. The families of all three – who are also listed in the documents as consenters – confirmed the deaths of their kin.
“My mother died four years ago,” said Nakul Alang, the 35-year-old son of Sanai Alang who is listed at serial number 108 in the Bannur resolution.
Nakul’s signature appears in Odia, but he says he was working at a construction site in Visakhapatnam, a coastal city in Odisha’s neighbouring Andhra Pradesh state 170km (105 miles) from Koraput.
“I don’t know who put our names and signatures,” he told Al Jazeera.
Hurried, ‘fraudulent’ meeting
On page 10 of the 16-page Bannur resolution document, 13 names are written by the same hand, followed by a neat array of thumb impressions next to them.
When Sunadhar Muduli, a 50-year-old farmer, saw the sheet, he immediately recognised that it was his own handwriting.
“But none of us ever attended the Gram Sabha meeting,” he said.
Muduli said Ramnath Pungi, who works for the local revenue office on contract, visited the village in December and handed him a registry. He was asked to fill the names of those residents who wanted to get their traditional lands recognised by the government.
Many tribal communities, who have been historically kept out of land documentation, have been cultivating on “government-owned” lands for generations. There have been frequent promises to transfer such lands to their names, and it is not uncommon practice in the region to send contracted officials to collect information about farmers.
“He said he needed everyone’s signatures. I told him I would gather the residents, but he said that was not necessary. That I could sign on their behalf,” said Muduli, who then called some residents to get their permission.
“I wrote down the names on one side of the page and then he and I placed our thumbs alternatively against the name. It was his idea and I just followed the instructions,” he said.
It was only in June when Al Jazeera visited Bannur that Muduli saw the inclusion of the same sheet as part of the mining resolution draft.
Pungi also confirmed to Al Jazeera that the signatures were taken on another pretext.
“I was paid 3,000 rupees to collect documents and sign land settlement documents from each village. That’s what I did. I only submitted the signed sheet to the [revenue] office,” he said.
“I did not know they would use it for this [Adani project]. I am also against mining in our region.”
Official guidelines state that the announcement of a Gram Sabha meeting should be made two weeks before the scheduled date in order to ensure a quorum.
However, several residents told Al Jazeera that the notices announcing the meeting were pasted outside the village council offices on October 8, only a day before the meeting. The notices, accessed by Al Jazeera, were dated September 22 and September 23, 2025.
‘Abnormally rushed’ mining approval
Meanwhile, the government pushed the Adani mining project in Odisha – hastily, according to the residents and activists.
In February 2023, the Odisha government declared Adani Enterprises as the preferred bidder for the mine at Koraput, triggering immediate protests by the tribal people in Balda and Bannur. They marched to the local government office to protest against the mining of 157 hectares of forest land by destroying the trees around them and displacing residents.
Two years later, on March 6, 2025, the state government held a public hearing – a mandatory process to obtain approvals where villagers are given details of the project and their objections formally recorded. An overwhelming number of villagers expressed their opposition to the mining project.
Despite the objections, an environmental clearance – a key approval given by the government after assessing possible ecological damage of a project – was granted a few months later.
Under Indian laws, forest-dwelling communities who have been historically left out of land -ownership can seek individual or community rights over traditional forest lands. Balda and neighbouring communities applied for rights over 2,500 hectares of forest land in 2025. A majority of those claims overlapped with the mining lease area.
Usually, the settlement of claims involves the collation of claims and documents, approval from local bodies, verification by officials and ample time for appeals if the claims are modified or rejected. The process is usually notoriously slow.
In January, authorities “settled” these community rights claims without informing the village councils in the area. Less than one-fifth of the claimed area was recognised while the entirety of the mining area was excluded from the claims. Villagers are usually given time to appeal.
However, in this case, two appeals committees affirmed the decision in just three days, without even allowing the villagers time to submit their appeals, allege the villagers.
Ajaya Muduli is part of a three-member team authorised by the affected villages to approach any court in India, sign documents, take necessary legal steps and liaise with government committees in their fight to prevent the takeover of their lands.
Muduli told Al Jazeera that the land acquisition process was “abnormally rushed”.
“We have safeguarded this sacred land for centuries and yet were not even consulted,” Muduli told Al Jazeera. “This is a clear tactic forcing the mines on us without our consent while snatching our rights.”
Immediately after the October 9 Gram Sabha meetings, the villagers wrote to the local authorities asking for the deliberations to be held again. They flagged the hurried nature of the meetings and pointed to the fact that the village heads had declared them “invalid”.
Yet, on October 15, the allegedly forged resolutions were added to the official file. It was only on February 11 this year that those documents were made public on the environment ministry’s website.
So far, more than 50 people from several villages in Koraput have issued sworn affidavits declaring that they did not attend the village council meetings and that their signatures or thumb impressions were forged. They have also filed petitions in court and with district authorities, as well as complaints with the police, alleging forgery and demanding an investigation into the land given for the Adani mine.
In March, the 10 affected villages around Balda Hill held meetings where they rejected the previous resolutions passed by their village councils and reiterated their opposition to the proposed bauxite mine.
In May, Muduli approached the court on behalf of the villagers. But it was too late.
On May 7, all required approvals were granted to Kalinga Alumina Limited and the forest land was handed over for the $24m bauxite mining project, with an associated alumina refinery on a lease of 50 years. No compensation has been promised to the villagers.
“What they have done is illegal, but we will not back off,” Balda resident Rajendra Khara told Al Jazeera.
While the approvals have been granted, actual work has not started on the ground. Villagers have vowed to stop construction. “Whatever happens, we are never going to give it to Adani. This is our ancestral land,” Rajendra said.
‘Deeply troubling trend’
Arpitha Kodiveri, assistant professor of political science at Vassar College in the United States who has worked on environmental law and justice related to mining in India, told Al Jazeera that bypassing the consent of landowners sets a trend for illegal practice.
“What you are starting to see across multiple jurisdictions is an administrative approach to bypassing the consent provision. What I fear is that it has become an illegal administrative practice of implementing the consent provision without adhering to procedure and law, and that is something we should be worried about,” she said.
Kodiveri said alleged irregularities in the consent process could also provide grounds for the affected parties to challenge the government clearance granted to such mining projects. She also argued that the rules should make consequences for irregular consent practices clearer and must seek accountability when mandatory provisions are bypassed.
“Guidelines must be established so this process is implemented in spirit and not just in letter, and to signal to administrative actors that there are consequences for practising fraudulent signatures or taking signatures of the deceased. This has happened so many times in Odisha and elsewhere that it is a deeply troubling trend.”
Land Conflict Watch, a New Delhi-based research organisation, has tracked at least 28 instances of consent-related “conflicts” from projects such as mining, plantation, energy and other infrastructure across India since 2003. The organisation also found allegations of forgery, evasion of mandatory public consultations and forceful mining of ancestral land while studying such conflicts.
Even the studies conducted by the government show a similar trend.
A 2024 report by India’s Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG), an independent constitutional authority, on land management in tribal-dominated areas revealed 136 consent violations in mining and other projects. In 73 of these violations, no Gram Sabha meetings were held, while in another 29, land acquisition was done while disregarding the views of the village council.
Over the past few years, however, allegations of outright forgeries of Gram Sabha resolutions have emerged.
In 2023 in Sijimali, about 180km from Balda, villagers discovered similar forged consents and meetings for a bauxite mine by Vedanta Resources, India’s largest mining company backed by a London-based conglomerate. At least eight villages denied consent to hand over 708 hectares of forest land, despite official documents claiming otherwise.
Sijimali has seen near-continuous protests since, escalating to violence in April when clashes between the police and protesters injured 70.
“If the Gram Sabha has not given consent, then the forest clearance given is illegal. It has to be quashed. They are making a mockery of the law,” Shomona Khanna, a Supreme Court lawyer specialising in environmental and tribal law, told Al Jazeera.
“These are criminal offences … Any person who dispossesses a forest dweller of their forest right or interferes in the enjoyment of the forest right is committing a crime, which is called an atrocity under Indian law,” she said.
Back in Balda, the villagers fear that if mining starts, the rainwater-fed streams that sustain paddy cultivation will dry up. Forests that provided gourds, fruits, flowers, bark, firewood and medicinal plants will be affected.
Like many Indigenous tribal communities, their animist faith is linked to the surrounding forests – home to small shrines, idols and caves considered to be sacred.
“The forest is everything for us,” said Raghunath Hanthal, a 70-year-old priest in Balda. “Our maa [goddess] is here.”
On the official document, the priest’s name is listed as serial number 171, with his purported signature in Odia.
“I did not even go to the meeting. We were here, protesting that day,” he said. “Taking away our forests will not just destroy our livelihood, but it will incur the wrath of our goddess.”

India-Russia trade jumps in first half of 2026 – envoy

India-Russia trade jumps in first half of 2026 – envoy
Trade between India and Russia reached $38 billion in the first half of this year and is on track to reach the $100 billion annual target set for 2030, Indian Ambassador to Russia Vinay Kumar has said. 
“We think we are on the right path to achieve the target,” Kumar told The Tribune newspaper on the sidelines of the second Russia-India TIME Business Forum in Kazan on Thursday. He said India was sourcing energy and fertilizers from Russia while exporting pharmaceuticals and expanding opportunities for skilled workers. 
The two countries are making a concerted effort to diversify trade and deepen economic ties, with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Russian President Vladimir Putin giving personal attention to the relationship. The Kazan forum, in the Russian Republic of Tatarstan, follows the INNOPROM.India trade fair held in New Delhi last month. 
The $100 billion trade target was set during Modi’s visit to Moscow in July 2024.
15 октября 2026 года в Казани состоялось торжественное открытие II Российско-индийского бизнес-форума «TIME: Индия – Россия. Взаимная эффективность», организованного Генеральным консульством Индии в Казани совместно с Агентством инвестиционного развития Республики Татарстан. Форум объединяет представителей органов государственной власти, деловых объединений и ведущих компаний Индии и России, преследующих общую цель — укрепление практического сотрудничества и разработку новых совместных проектов. В церемонии открытия приняли участие Председатель Государственного Совета Республики Татарстан г-н Ф.Х. Абдулганиев, Чрезвычайный и Полномочный Посол Индии в Российской Федерации Его Превосходительство г-н Винай Кумар, член Законодательного собрания Дели Шри Хариш Кхурана, а также другие высокопоставленные представители органов власти и деловых кругов. The strong growth in trade has continued beyond the six-month period cited by the Indian envoy. Bilateral commerce reached $47.7 billion in January-July, up 24.3% year-on-year, according to Indian Commerce Ministry figures cited by Russian lender Sberbank.
India’s imports from Russia totaled $44.9 billion during the seven months, including $36 billion in crude oil purchases. Indian exports reached $2.8 billion as Russia bought more chemicals, electrical goods, medical equipment, seafood, tea, and spices.
Bilateral goods trade grew from around $13 billion in 2021-22 to nearly $60 billion in 2025-26, Indian Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar said in August. However, the trade imbalance also widened as India bought Russian oil in huge quantities amid disruptions in the Middle East caused by the US-Israeli attacks on Iran.
New Delhi is seeking to expand shipments of pharmaceuticals, engineering goods, chemicals, food products, and auto components to Russia to lower the deficit.
Both sides are working on a bilateral investment treaty and strengthening local currency payment mechanisms to facilitate trade. India has also launched free trade negotiations with the Eurasian Economic Union, which includes Russia, to expand market access.

Estonia wants to block Russian gas transit through Baltics for good

Estonia wants to block Russian gas transit through Baltics for good
Energy minister Erkki Keldo (Reform) wants to work with Latvia to permanently stop Russian gas transit through the Baltics, with other options on the table if talks fail.
Speaking to ERR, the Estonian energy and environment minister said he plans to meet his Latvian counterpart as soon as Latvia's new government is in place.
"The valve, so to speak, that we can physically control on the Estonian side is closed, so nothing can flow through there," Keldo explained, referring to a natural gas pipeline that runs through Southeastern Estonia. "But the other physical pipe and valve are on the Latvian side, and we need to discuss this with the Latvians and Lithuanians."
He noted that the section of pipeline belongs to state-owned grid operator Elering and is used solely for transit, stressing that no gas from it can enter Estonia's domestic network.
Keldo declined to speculate before the two ministers met on whether Latvia would agree to shut off the supply, but he made his own position clear.
"We'll look at what intervention options and solutions are available," he said. "Since, unfortunately, [the pipeline] is operated by a Latvian state-owned operator, this is also a matter for negotiations with our neighbors and allies. But I can certainly say that I don't think this is right."
The minister said sanctions or other measures should be considered only after talks with Latvia.
The two countries have both advocated raising the cost of Russia's continued aggression in Ukraine through sanctions and additional tariffs, Keldo noted.
In light of this, while no Russian gas has flowed through the pipeline for more than two years already, he hoped his Latvian counterpart would help find a way to ensure it won't resume in the future either.
"I believe and hope we can reach an agreement with the Latvians," the minister said. "But if we can't, we'll have to look at what other options are available."
Sector politicians unaware
Earlier this week, Eesti Ekspress reported that Estonia is maintaining a natural gas pipeline running through Võru County that Russia can use to supply its exclave of Kaliningrad Oblast.
The paper noted that none of the Estonian politicians responsible for overseeing the sector in recent years were aware of the Russian gas pipeline arrangement.
Kaliningrad relies on Russian gas to fuel its power plants. After Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania disconnected from the Russian-controlled power grid in February 2025, the exclave was left as an isolated energy system.

INTERVIEW – Armenian church official sees Türkiye-Armenia normalization as path to ‘stronger friendships’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:57:32 UTC
19:57:32 KST

INTERVIEW – Armenian church official sees Türkiye-Armenia normalization as path to ‘stronger friendships’
Vice president of Surp Giragos Armenian Church Foundation welcomes efforts to improve bilateral ties, expresses hope that land border will soon reopen
Beril Canakci
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
DIYARBAKIR, Türkiye
A senior official of the Armenian church foundation in southeastern Türkiye’s Diyarbakir province has voiced support for the ongoing normalization process between Ankara and Yerevan, saying growing contact between the two sides will deepen friendship.
“We view the ongoing rapprochement between Armenia and Türkiye very positively,” Ohannes Gafur Ohanyan, vice president of the Surp Giragos Armenian Church Foundation, told Anadolu.
Ohanyan spoke during a visit by 7 Turkish and 7 Armenian journalists to Surp Giragos Armenian Church in Diyarbakir’s historic Sur district as part of an EU-funded media tour aimed at supporting normalization between Türkiye and Armenia.
“We believe that as these kinds of visits and events increase, the friendship between the two countries will grow even stronger,” he said. “Hopefully, the borders will open soon too.”
Türkiye and Armenia do not have diplomatic relations, and their land border has been closed since 1993. The two countries launched a normalization initiative in late 2021, appointing retired Turkish Ambassador Serdar Kilic and Armenian parliament Deputy Speaker Ruben Rubinyan as special envoys.
Türkiye’s Foreign Ministry said in May that technical and bureaucratic work to reopen the shared border with Armenia was still ongoing, although preparations for direct trade had been completed.
In early May, Turkish Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz visited Armenia, where officials signed a memorandum on the joint restoration of the historic Ani Bridge, a medieval structure spanning the border between the two countries.
During a meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York last month, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan also discussed advancing normalization, strengthening trade and economic ties, and improving regional transport links.
Center of attraction for Armenians worldwide
The local Armenian community in Diyarbakir comprises roughly 60 to 65 people, according to Ohanyan. Despite its compact size, social and community life surrounding the church remains active, with regular religious services organized around major holidays.
"Because we do not have a permanent resident clergyman here, we hold around 8 to 10 services a year during important religious holidays," Ohanyan said.
Describing Surp Giragos as an 800-year-old church and the largest Armenian church in the Middle East, he said it draws Armenians from Armenia as well as from the diaspora in Europe and the US.
Following decades of disuse, comprehensive restoration initiatives spearheaded by the local foundation and supported in subsequent years by Turkish state institutions including the Culture and Tourism Ministry, allowed the site to formally reopen for worship.
The church was later damaged during 2015 clashes in Sur involving the terrorist group PKK. It was restored with funding from Türkiye’s Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change Ministry, under the coordination of the General Directorate of Foundations, and reopened for worship after seven years.
The foundation’s second church, the roughly 500-year-old Surp Sarkis in the Alipasa neighborhood, fell into disrepair over time because it had no congregation and was further damaged in the February 2023 earthquakes centered in Kahramanmaras. Restoration work began in 2024 with a grant from the Culture and Tourism Ministry.
"Surp Sarkis has been in ruins for nearly a century," Ohanyan noted. "We have made considerable progress and have largely completed the structural work on the main building."
Ohanyan also called on businesspeople, philanthropists and the wider public for further support.

Ukrainian children abroad will be able to receive a school-leaving certificate without repeating their studies: the government explained the mechanism
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:56:53 EEST
19:56:53 KST

Ukrainian children abroad will be able to receive a school-leaving certificate without repeating their studies: the government explained the mechanism
Kyiv • UNN
Ukrainian children abroad will be able to receive a school-leaving certificate through recognition of their foreign education and a Ukrainian studies component. The program can be completed in person or remotely.
Ukrainian schoolchildren who are abroad because of the full-scale war can obtain a Ukrainian certificate of completion of secondary education without having to repeat the full educational program. Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said this during his speech in parliament on October 16, UNN reports.
To this end, the state has provided for the possibility of recognizing the results of education at foreign schools in combination with the study of Ukrainian studies subjects.
Details
The issue of providing education to Ukrainian children abroad was raised by Deputy Speaker of the Verkhovna Rada Olena Kondratiuk. According to her, based on estimates cited in a report by the Ministry of Education and Science of Ukraine and the Accounting Chamber for September 2026, between 320,000 and 400,000 Ukrainian children are currently studying outside Ukraine. Kondratiuk emphasized that one of the state's key tasks remains preserving these children's connection with the Ukrainian education system, as well as creating conditions for their return after the war ends.
In particular, she asked how effectively the mechanisms for reintegrating schoolchildren, simplifying the recognition of education documents, and providing opportunities to study the Ukrainian language at educational institutions in other countries are working.
Answering the question, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi emphasized that Ukrainian children abroad remain one of the priorities of the state's education policy.
Our children abroad are our children; they are Ukrainian children. And we must do everything so that, once the danger of war has ended, they return to Ukraine and support and develop the Ukrainian economy
According to the head of government, education is one of the most important tools for preserving the younger generation's connection with Ukraine. At the same time, he acknowledged that children who are already studying at schools in their host countries often do not have the opportunity to fully master the Ukrainian educational program in parallel because of the excessive workload.
How Ukrainian schoolchildren abroad can obtain a certificate
To solve this problem, the state proposed a Ukrainian studies component that makes it possible to combine education at a foreign school with the study of subjects necessary to preserve ties with Ukrainian education. According to the head of government, the relevant program can be completed either directly at educational centers abroad or remotely through Ukrainian schools.
It (the program, — ed.) can be completed at verified centers operating in other countries—there are already more than 120 of them that have been verified by the Ministry of Education. It can also be done remotely through Ukrainian schools operating in a remote-learning format
The program provides that, in their free time outside their main studies, Ukrainian children study the Ukrainian language, the history of Ukraine, the geography of Ukraine, cultural studies, as well as individual subjects of their choice. In other words, schoolchildren do not need to repeat the entire program they are already studying at educational institutions in their host countries.
As the head of government explained, under the agreements reached, the Ukrainian side may recognize the results of education obtained abroad. After completing the Ukrainian studies component, the child will also be able to receive a Ukrainian document certifying completion of secondary education. This, in particular, opens the possibility of admission to Ukrainian universities and allows schoolchildren to remain part of the Ukrainian educational and cultural environment.
In addition, the government is cooperating with Ukrainian communities abroad, including religious communities, to support the activities of educational centers and provide them with educational literature.
Ukrainian as a second foreign language in European schools
Particular attention during the discussion was devoted to the possibility of studying Ukrainian as a second foreign language in schools in European countries.
Olena Kondratiuk noted that the relevant practice already exists in a number of countries that have taken in Ukrainian refugees. According to her, approximately 45 Polish schools are already working in this direction. Similar approaches are being applied in certain educational institutions in the United Kingdom and Austria. The lawmaker also noted France's active involvement. In her view, expanding such opportunities will allow Ukrainian children to take relevant exams in their host countries while maintaining their knowledge of their native language.
Kondratiuk also emphasized that introducing Ukrainian as a second foreign language could become an alternative to studying Russian in European schools. She urged the Ukrainian authorities to intensify cooperation with the education ministries of European Union states to expand this practice.
Some Ukrainian children abroad may remain outside the education system
Another problem highlighted by the Deputy Chairperson of the Verkhovna Rada was the absence of some Ukrainian children from education institution registration systems.
Kondratiuk emphasized that meetings with the education ministers of European countries revealed that some Ukrainian children are studying neither in local schools nor remotely at Ukrainian educational institutions. She called this a serious gap requiring the attention of the Ukrainian authorities and the education agencies of the host countries.
In Kondratiuk's view, Ukraine should maintain regular contact with such children, ensure their access to education, and create conditions enabling them to remain part of the Ukrainian educational space even during an extended stay abroad.
Previously
Earlier, UNN reported that due to the war and the search for prospects, female graduates are leaving Ukraine en masse to study abroad.

NATO tries to propagate its interests

Iran ships some LPG, jet fuel despite US blockade, data shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:55:27 UTC
19:55:27 KST

Iran ships some LPG, jet fuel despite US blockade, data shows
DAMASCUS/LONDON, Oct 16 - Iran has managed to export some liquefied petroleum gas and jet fuel since July, despite a US naval blockade, shipping intelligence showed and people involved in security said.
Tehran has in recent weeks been concealing such cargoes among a growing volume of ship-to-ship transfers by other Gulf producers off Oman, four people in maritime security who track Gulf oil movements told Reuters.
The Iranian exports and methodology are reported for the first time here. While a fraction of its former energy exports, the cargoes are rare evidence of petroleum products getting through a blockade that has halted Iran's crude exports.
Analysis by US advocacy group United Against Nuclear Iran (UANI), which monitors Iran-related tanker traffic using ship and satellite tracking, shows at least eight gas tankers carrying Iranian LPG have left the Gulf of Oman since mid-July.
Another tanker carrying Iranian jet fuel reached Myanmar in September, additional satellite imagery and analysis by maritime intelligence group SynMax show.
The US imposed targeted sanctions in 2023 on Myanmar's jet-fuel industry, citing military airstrikes on civilians that the United Nations says have killed thousands of people. Myanmar's military government has repeatedly denied targeting civilians, saying its operations are directed against armed groups.
Six of the eight gas tankers and the jet fuel tanker are under US sanctions for transporting Iranian petroleum and petrochemical products, a Reuters analysis of the vessels and sanctions imposed on ships by the US Treasury showed.
"What we have seen passing is a handful of tankers carrying Iranian LPG, but the overwhelming majority of tankers laden with Iranian products have been redirected by US forces," said Jemima Shelley, senior research analyst with UANI.
Shelley said some Iranian LPG tankers transferred cargoes near the Omani coastal towns of Shinas and Sohar, while others waited in the Gulf of Oman before heading past the US blockade, which US Central Command has said sits across the Gulf of Oman near the Iran-Pakistan border.
The total amount of these LPG cargoes was estimated at 4.1 million barrels, Shelley said.
Shelley said the shipments were driven "more by opportunism" than showing a new trend of Iran trying to export its oil and petrochemicals by using smaller ships.
Most of the cargoes sailed to Malaysia's Eastern Outer Port Limits to conduct further STS transfers for likely destinations in China, Shelley said, based on UANI's analysis.
The Iranian government did not respond to a request for comment. Myanmar's military-backed government did not respond to a request for comment on whether the country had received Iranian jet fuel.
US MILITARY SAYS BLOCKADE 'IRONCLAD'
The US military's Centcom said its naval blockade, which was first imposed on Iran-related oil exports on April 13, is "ironclad". The blockade was lifted in June after the US reached a draft understanding with Iran, but it was reimposed on July 14 following the collapse of the agreement.
A US military official told Reuters that the passage of a vessel does not necessarily mean it had evaded the blockade. Every ship was assessed individually, including through a review of its papers, and some vessels could be allowed through for humanitarian reasons, the official added.
The official said the appearance of a vessel on US sanctions lists is not the only factor to make it subject to the blockade, adding that US forces are also closely monitoring some ships without taking action against them for operational reasons.
Centcom said in an update on October 13 that during the three months of the latest blockade, four commercial vessels had been disabled and 135 ships had been turned around by US forces.
The US military has turned around ships from Asia and also seized some tankers, previous Centcom statements said.
Washington has coupled its blockade with a sanctions campaign aimed at severing Iran's remaining financial links and depriving it of revenue. Last week, it imposed fresh sanctions on 17 vessels involved in transporting Iranian crude, petrochemicals and petroleum products.
A US Treasury spokesperson questioned shipping data suggesting vessels had evaded the blockade, saying ships could spoof their locations or use false identities when loading.
Such data "should be taken with a grain of salt", the spokesperson said.
The Treasury spokesperson said Operation Economic Outcast, together with the blockade, was "suffocating the Iranian regime".
Torbjorn Soltvedt, principal Middle East analyst at risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft, said although there was no sign of Washington easing its blockade, worsening economic conditions in Iran could push Tehran to take greater risks.
"If Iran can move product tankers through, even in small numbers, jet fuel may be a good option. Iran's aviation industry is under increasing pressure from US sanctions, with a growing number of planes grounded, and a potential surplus of jet fuel at Iranian refineries," Soltvedt added.
Iranian crude exports fell to zero in September, according to Kpler, the first month without a shipment since the analytics firm began tracking the producer in 2013.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has said the blockade prevented most Chinese purchases of Iranian oil and left Iran unable to deliver crude to customers. REUTERS
