Romanian Institutions Bought Banned Russian Cybersecurity Software
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:54:00 UTC
19:54:00 KST

Reported by
More than 80 Romanian public institutions continued to purchase cybersecurity software from a Russian-founded company after the government explicitly banned its use over national security concerns, a review of public procurement records reveals.
Following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Romania passed a 2022 law prohibiting public entities from acquiring cybersecurity software originating fromRussian individuals or entities. In March 2023, a government order officially blacklisted a broad range of products from Kaspersky, a Russian cybersecurity firm.
However, procurement data shows that between March 2023 and September 2026, 83 public institutions and authorities made 131 purchases of prohibited software.
In an emailed statement, Kaspersky said it “does not have any inappropriate ties to any government.”
“Kaspersky has maintained that the claims about alleged security risks that the company’s products might have and related restrictions are based on the current geopolitical climate rather than a technical analysis of Kaspersky software security,” the company said.
“To date, no party has presented any public evidence that the company’s products might pose a threat to corporate or private users,” Kaspersky added.
The Romanian buyers of Kaspersky software included hospitals, municipal governments, schools, and other public institutions.
Notably, less than two months after the blacklist was published, the National Institute for Laser, Plasma and Radiation Physics bought two-year Kaspersky antivirus licenses for three devices. According to its annual reports, the research institute generates classified information and works under contracts with the Ministry of National Defense, the "Ferdinand I" Military Technical Academy, and NATO.
“We would like to clarify that the purchased product has never been installed or actually used on any computer, server, or other IT system belonging to the institute,” the institute said in an emailed response to questions.
Sebastian Burduja, who headed Romania's Ministry of Research, Innovation and Digitalization when the rules were introduced, attributed the continued purchases to a lack of enforcement staff.
"On the other hand, as we all suspect, we likely have a pro-Russian strain within Romanian state institutions," said Burduja said, who is now a deputy in the country’s parliament.
Kaspersky is named after its founder, Eugene Kaspersky, a former software engineer for the Soviet Union Defense Ministry who studied mathematics at a school sponsored by state authorities like the KGB, the secret police and intelligence agency. From its founding in 1997, Kaspersky grew into one of the world's largest cybersecurity providers. But the company’s business has been hampered by international restrictions, including a 2024 action by several countries.
The U.S. prohibited the sale of many Kaspersky products, citing risks to national security. The company rejected the allegations, claiming the ban was based on the "geopolitical climate and theoretical concerns" rather than product integrity.
Germany, Lithuania, and Italy have also issued formal warnings or implemented measures to phase out the software from critical infrastructure.
Under Romanian law, violating the ban on Kaspersky products is an administrative offense carrying fines between 50,000 and 200,000 lei (between $10,500 and $42,000).

3D-printed brick phone brings back the art of simply answering calls
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:53:37 UTC
19:53:37 KST

3D-printed brick phone brings back the art of simply answering calls
designer kevin noki recreates the 1980s brick phone as a 3D-printed bluetooth handset with 19 physical keys, allowing users to answer iphone calls without the usual smartphone distractions.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
ADHD ONE REVISITS THE 1980S BRICK PHONE
As smartphones become increasingly difficult to put down, Cologne-based designer and maker Kevin Noki has taken a rather unconventional approach to digital detox: building a handset that looks straight out of the 1980s. Named ADHD ONE, short for Anti Distraction Handset Device, the project revisits the oversized brick phones of early mobile communication, complete with a physical keypad, compact display, and unmistakably chunky silhouette. Unlike most contemporary devices, however, its purpose is to offer fewer features rather than more.
The concept is relatively straightforward. Instead of replacing a smartphone, ADHD ONE connects to an iPhone via Bluetooth, allowing users to receive and answer calls while keeping the original device out of sight. By configuring the iPhone’s Do Not Disturb settings to permit calls from selected contacts, Noki creates a more controlled communication experience. The handset has no independent cellular connection and relies on the paired smartphone to function. In practice, it preserves one of the phone’s most basic purposes without inviting its owner into another endless round of scrolling.
BLUETOOTH TECHNOLOGY MEETS 3D-PRINTED RETRO DESIGN
Despite its deliberately outdated appearance, ADHD ONE relies on contemporary electronics. At its core is an FSC-BT1026C Bluetooth module based on Qualcomm’s QCC3024 chip, which uses the Hands-Free Profile (HFP) to transmit call audio between the handset and the connected iPhone. A Raspberry Pi Pico development board manages the device’s functions, while additional components include an OLED display, a microphone, a speaker, a rechargeable lithium battery, and a charging controller. A custom printed circuit board brings the electronics together inside the compact housing.
Kevin Noki designed the enclosure in Autodesk Fusion before producing its components through 3D printing. The housing draws heavily on the visual language of early mobile phones, with substantial proportions, a prominent antenna, and tactile buttons replacing the smooth surfaces of contemporary smartphones. The design incorporates a 19-key keypad and offers several possibilities for customization, including three speaker grille styles (Classic, Holes, and Stripes) and three antenna designs (Retro, Slim, and Screw). An alternative housing even eliminates the antenna entirely, although that arguably takes away some of the brick phone’s charm.
KEVIN NOKI RELEASES DIY FILES FOR HIS RETRO HANDSET
For those interested in building their own version, Noki has made the digital construction files available through his website. The downloadable package includes 3D-printable STL files for the housing, back panels, internal mounting frame, display cover, battery holder, and keypad, alongside ready-to-flash firmware in UF2 format. Gerber and drill files allow users to order the custom PCB from a manufacturer, while a bill of materials and quick start guide provide the necessary references for sourcing components and assembling the device. The package does not include physical parts, editable CAD or PCB files, or the firmware’s source code, and is licensed for personal use only. A separate physical DIY kit is listed on the website but is not yet available.
Ultimately, ADHD ONE occupies an interesting position between nostalgia, experimental product design, and the growing desire for simpler digital experiences. It does not eliminate the smartphone, which must remain within Bluetooth range, nor does it attempt to recreate the independence of an actual 1980s mobile phone. Instead, it rethinks how people physically interact with technology they already own, turning a familiar communication function into a deliberately limited experience. There is a certain irony in designing, printing, and assembling an entirely new electronic device just to avoid using another one. Then again, perhaps that is precisely the point.

 name: ADHD ONE – Retro Brick Handset
designer: Kevin Noki | @kevinnoki
location: Cologne, Germany

The Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO) and the National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) have completed the pre-trial investigation in the case of former Deputy Prime Minister for European and Euro-Atlantic Integration – Minister of Justice of Ukraine Olha Stefanishyna concerning illicit enrichment amounting to UAH 13.9 million.
"On October 15, 2026, the SAPO prosecutor decided to complete the pre-trial investigation in the case against the former Deputy Prime Minister – Minister of Justice of Ukraine. The individual is suspected of illicit enrichment totaling over UAH 13.9 million and submission of inaccurate declarations (Articles 368-5 and Part 2 of Article 366-2 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine)," SAPO reported in a Telegram post on Friday.
According to the pre-trial investigation, in 2024–2025, the individual acquired two apartments in the Faina Town residential complex valued at UAH 6.9 million, registering them in the name of a close female friend, as well as UAH 7 million in cash, part of which was spent on renovating these properties.
"It also transpired that she was negotiating the purchase of a house near Kyiv with an estimated value of $550,000, intending to pay with cash ($250,000) and the two aforementioned apartments. However, she later abandoned the deal, presumably due to her appointment to a diplomatic position abroad," the statement notes.
According to SAPO, an analysis of income and expenses confirmed that despite an official income of about UAH 3.7 million (recorded from early 2024 to mid-2025), approximately UAH 4.2 million was spent solely from bank accounts.
Furthermore, the anti-corruption prosecution emphasized that the individual failed to declare information regarding the use, at various times, of assets registered in third parties' names.
This concerns an apartment in the capital's business-class residential complex Lvivska Ploshcha (registered in her mother's name) and a "MERCEDES-BENZ GLC 220D" vehicle (registered in the name of a subordinate).
"Currently, upon the prosecutor's instruction, NABU detectives have disclosed the case materials to the defense counsel for review," SAPO informed.
As reported, on August 6, the High Anti-Corruption Court (HACC) selected a preventive measure for Stefanishyna in the form of bail totaling UAH 6 million. The prosecutor's office had requested a bail of UAH 13.3 million. She is suspected of illicit enrichment and false declaration. According to the investigation, she failed to declare two apartments in Kyiv, renovation expenses, housing rental costs, the use of a Mercedes-Benz, as well as payments for plane tickets and her mother's medical treatment.
Stefanishyna stated that she did not have the funds for the bail set by HACC but would look for them, and that she would consult with lawyers regarding a possible appeal. On August 13, the "Ilyashev & Partners" law firm posted the designated bail for Stefanishyna.
On August 20, the HACC Appeals Chamber upheld the preventive measure for Stefanishyna. Since the bail was paid, procedural obligations were imposed on the suspect, including reporting to detectives, prosecutors, and the court upon summons, notifying them of any change of residence, and refraining from communicating with a specified circle of persons.
On June 4, Ukrayinska Pravda published an investigation stating that the Asset Recovery and Management Agency (ARMA) had selected a management company for the Trade Unions House in Kyiv that may be linked to Stefanishyna's family, specifically her former husband. According to the investigation, this is already the fourth valuable asset acquired by the same company.
Stefanishyna stated that she was not connected to her ex-husband's activities, complained of information pressure, and emphasized that she had no conflict of interest regarding ARMA. In turn, ARMA Head Olena Duma stated that there were no links between the individuals mentioned in the media and ARMA, nor with participants in the competitive procedures for selecting managers of seized assets.

Merz und Macron bestätigen Einigung zum Verbrenner-Aus und „Made in Europe“
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:41:40 UTC
19:41:40 KST

Der französische Präsident Emmanuel Macron und Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz haben sich zu „Made in Europe“ für Autos geeinigt. Zudem soll das Verbrenner-Aus aufgeweicht werden. | Ludovic Marin/AFP via Getty Images
BERLIN – Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz und der französische Präsident Emmanuel Macron haben sich auf ein gemeinsames Vorgehen zum Auflockern des Verbrenner-Aus und zu „Made in Europe“ für Autos geeinigt, teilten beide Regierungen in einer gemeinsamen Erklärung mit.
„Unser Kurs bleibt unverändert: Wir streben eine deutliche Senkung der CO2-Emissionen an und stärken zugleich Europas Kapazitäten für die Entwicklung und Fertigung der nächsten Generation von Elektrofahrzeugen“, heißt es in der Erklärung.
Die beiden Regierungen wollen „mit ihren europäischen Partnern zügig auf eine Einigung hinarbeiten“. Das Paket verbinde „einen ehrgeizigen europäischen Dekarbonisierungspfad mit der nötigen regulatorischen Flexibilität, um unterschiedlichen Marktgegebenheiten und Technologieoffenheit Rechnung zu tragen“.
Umweltminister Carsten Schneider hatte die Einigung jedoch zunächst mit einem Brief an Kanzler Friedrich Merz am Mittwoch aufgehalten. Darin verlangte der SPD-Minister mehr Konditionierung für grünen Stahl, erzählten mehrere Beteiligte POLITICO. Am Freitagmorgen gab es Gespräche der SPD-Minister über das weitere Vorgehen. Im Anschluss daran gab Schneider seinen Widerstand schließlich auf. Aus Kreisen des Umweltministeriums hieß es, die Beschaffung von grünem und recyceltem Stahl könne man auch national regeln.
„Mir war wichtig, dass wir bei dieser Gelegenheit auch klima- und industriepolitische Fortschritte für die Stahlindustrie erreichen“, sagte Schneider in einer Mitteilung. „Es soll Anreize geben, damit Autos künftig mit klimafreundlichem grünem Stahl gebaut werden.“
Laut dem Abkommen würde Deutschland strengere „Made in Europe“-Kriterien für den Automobilsektor im „Industrial Accelerator Act“ akzeptieren, auf die Frankreich gedrängt hat, im Gegenzug wird das Verbrennerverbot weiter aufgeweicht, eine der langen Forderungen Berlins.
„Wir wollen nicht, dass in Deutschland nur noch Komponenten aus Asien zusammengeschraubt werden, sondern dass entscheidende Komponenten hier entwickelt und hier produziert werden“, sagte Vizekanzler und Finanzminister Lars Klingbeil in einer Mitteilung. „Dazu gehört auch die Batteriezellfertigung und alles, was wir für deutsche E-Autos brauchen. Er verspricht der Autoindustrie „mehr ‚made in Germany’ und ‚made in Europe’“. Nun seien die Automobilhersteller in der Verantwortung, „in die Zukunft der deutschen Standorte zu investieren und Arbeitsplätze zu sichern“, so Klingbeil.
Derzeit sieht das Ziel der EU vor, dass Unternehmen die Emissionen von Verbrennungsmotoren bis 2035 um 100 Prozent gegenüber dem Niveau von 2021 senken, wobei sie die Möglichkeit haben, sich durch Initiativen wie Ausgleichsmaßnahmen und Investitionen einen Spielraum von 10 Prozent bei den Emissionen zu „erwerben“.
Im Rahmen des vorgeschlagenen Abkommens wollen Frankreich und Deutschland das Ziel für 2035 auf 90 Prozent absenken und im Gegenzug für Investitionen in alternative Kraftstoffe einen zusätzlichen Spielraum von 10 Prozent einräumen (was insgesamt 80 Prozent ergibt).
Jordyn Dahl und Georgio Leali haben zu diesem Artikel beigetragen.

How prepared is Kenya for an Ebola outbreak?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:41:00 UTC
19:41:00 KST

How prepared is Kenya for an Ebola outbreak?
October 16, 2026
Kenyais rushing to contain Ebola linked to the deadliest outbreak on record in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) . The East African nation has reported two cases and one death, while the DRC has reported over 9,000 cases and 4,400 deaths.
Kenya's first Ebola patient died at Nairobi hospital on October 5. The 40-year-old Kenyan had traveled by road from the DRC to Uganda before boarding a flight to Nairobi in Entebbe on October 3.
One of his relatives is now confirmed to have contracted the virus. The 39-year-old was under quarantine when he developed symptoms on October 13. "Both cases are linked, and there is no evidence of spread in the wider community," Kenya's health ministry said.
Contact tracing has been ongoing since officials first detected the case. Of the 128 people who came into contact with the first Ebola patient, 113 have been identified, according to the health ministry. All, except five—who are in unspecified countries abroad—have been quarantined.
Should Kenyans worry about Ebola spreading?
Public anxiety is rising, with fears of lockdowns and economic disruption and skepticism about government readiness.
"It's a very dangerous disease, so it's very shocking," a Nairobi resident told DW. Another citizen said he was disappointed: "The government has been caught unaware. It appears to me that the government was not prepared, especially at the entry point of this particular person who was found to be suffering from Ebola."
One woman said she felt there was a lack of public information on the disease. "The government should do more in educating and sensitizing about it, and raising awareness," she said.
Kenya's Health Ministry, through its Cabinet Secretary, Aden Duale, has been seeking to allay fears, urging Kenyans to remain vigilant and encouraging anyone who develops symptoms to report to the nearest medical facility. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), symptoms can develop between 2 and 21 days after infection.
Early symptoms include: fever, fatigue, malaise, muscle pain, headache and sore throat. Later, a patient may suffer from vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, and kidney and liver infection.
However, these symptoms might be similar to other illnesses such as malaria or typhoid, and only an Ebola test can confirm if one has been exposed to the virus.
Criticism and calls to improve screening
Several prominent figures, medical unions and opposition politicians have criticized Kenya's response to its first Ebola cases. Former Chief Justice David Maraga, who has declared interest in running for the presidency in the 2027 election, questioned how a man carrying the Ebola virus could pass through screening at Jomo Kenyatta International Airport, Nairobi.
"We don't know how many have been infected. We must demand appropriate action be taken so that we don't have deaths arising from that disease," Maraga told The Standard.
Kalonzo Musyoka, Kenya's vice president from 2008 to 2013, meanwhile noted that doctors at Nairobi Hospital, not border systems, detected the danger.
Dr. Dennis Miskellah of the Kenya Medical Practitioners, Pharmacists and Dentists Union believes that the Ebola cases show that Kenya's health system is not pandemic-ready. "This system is not yet resilient. This system did not learn from the COVID pandemic that we had a few years ago," he said.
"Since May, we've had this outbreak in the region. Uganda, our immediate neighbor, had almost 20 cases. So, we had ample time to prepare adequately. But it seems like somebody dropped the ball."
Kenya went on high alert after the DRC declared the Ebola outbreak in May. The government designated several hospitals as isolation centers.
It also enhanced screening at airports and border points, deploying mobile labs. Flights from several African countries were ordered to land in designated airport wings for screening.
Where are the gaps in Kenya's health system?
"Top of it all is that there's has been a serious lapse of leadership in governance of healthcare this country," said Miskellah. "All those broken pillars, there's no clear responsibility or chain of command, whether its the Ministry of Health or the 47 county governments who are semi-automous."
Capacity at some isolation centers is limited. Rural facilities lack resources such as the protective gear available at major hospitals, according to Miskellah. And there's also a shortage of health workers due to a freeze on public service workers.
Meanwhile, healthcare workers, many of whom have no healthcare cover, are reportedly wary of putting their lives at risk. Dozens of Kenyan nurses and doctors lost their lives during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Kenya's agreements on Ebola with its neighbors are being called into question since the first case was recorded in Kenya, which has one of the strongest healthcare systems in the region.
Experts are questioning the state of regional cooperation on Ebola, where borders have largely remained open despite the surge in cases and deaths. "Before we trust these agreements and cooperation, then we have have to audit them and question them so that we don't just blindly believe that Kenya is doing the right thing, or that the DRC is doing the right thing," said Miskellah.
Then, there's the question of individual responsibility. Kenya requires travelers arriving from Congo, Uganda, Tanzania, Ethiopia, Angola, Zambia, Rwanda, Burundi, Central African Republic and South Sudan to complete a health declaration form — truthfully.

BNN IN FOCUS | Political scientist’s view: Real action to weaken Russia is needed, not politicised slogans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:40:41 UTC
19:40:41 KST

This week, Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs suddenly appeared to realise that grain transported in transit from Russia and Belarus does not belong to Russian companies but to major international traders from the United States and other countries. Moreover, grain transit through the European Union has never been prohibited. The Ministry of Transport also finally released calculations showing that banning grain transit through Latvia would cost the country 290 million euros annually and could increase domestic rail freight costs by up to three times. Since the government had already been aware of these figures in early September, it appears that ministers first familiarised themselves with the consequences, then announced their determined fight against Russian grain transit, and only afterwards explained to the public why that fight could not be won.
What was really behind this sequence of events? BNN asked political scientist Filips Rajevskis, co-owner of the company Mediju tilts.
“I think all these issues related to grain and sanctions have become excessively politicised in Latvia,” the political scientist said. “Instead of pursuing sensible policies genuinely aimed at taking effective action to weaken Russia and help Ukraine, we have turned the issue into shouting politicised slogans while concealing and withholding the true situation. And that is much worse than simply addressing the problem rationally.”
“Who tried to introduce a voice of reason by asking whether we are doing everything possible, and whether we are doing the right things, to restrict Russia and inflict maximum damage on it?” Rajevskis asked rhetorically, adding that this was precisely the problem.
Asked by BNN whether the prime minister genuinely had no knowledge of EU regulations governing grain transit until this week, Rajevskis replied: 
“I am absolutely convinced that he knew. But he had to play by the rules established during the election campaign.
 If he had told the truth then, what he is saying now, all the politically aligned media would most likely have attacked Kulbergs, creating problems for him during the election campaign. It is clear that policy in this area will not change at the European level either.”
Asked whether public controversies such as the “Russian grain affair” and the “timber industry scandal” could be regarded as instruments of domestic political competition, Rajevskis agreed. “For example, the entire grain and sanctions issue was important to New Unity, while the timber industry affair was important to the Progressives. This correlates very directly with the ministries controlled by these parties and the ministries that distribute funding to the media.”
What should be done to put an end to such practices?
According to Rajevskis, the first fundamental question that needs to be reconsidered is whether such substantial amounts of public money should be allocated to the media.
 “We can see that the more money the media receive nowadays, the more their audiences decline. Instead of informing society, they engage in ‘conditioning’ people, as we remember very well, spreading certain ideas and propaganda. This is actually very dangerous. As a result, alternative information environments emerge, beyond the state’s reach, where the real dialogue with society takes place. These environments remain invisible, and consequently all sorts of unusual individuals get elected to parliament, leaving everyone asking: how did they get there?“The answer is that they are capable of establishing their own dialogue with society.”
BNN pointed out that Latvia’s parliament currently includes a rather unusual political party whose leader is facing legal proceedings and has fled the country.
Rajevskis responded that this party was among those attempting to establish alternative channels of communication. “Until its leader started making obscene gestures from the Saeima rostrum and speaking Russian, he was actually doing quite well at it.”
Could all the controversy surrounding Russian grain, the timber industry affair, the proposed buyout of shares in Swedish-owned Tet and LMT, and other major economic issues ultimately lead to a split within the United List?
Rajevskis is convinced that attempts to create such a division will occur.
 “To create a split, or at least the impression of one, they will use media outlets controlled through funding and people placed in key positions. There will certainly be pressure. The important thing is that the United List should understand the need to use more modern tools, including sociological research, to determine what society actually thinks. If your only understanding of public opinion comes from the media and social networks, you cannot build successful policies,” Rajevskis said.
He added that studies have shown people support pragmatic policymaking. “The question is what people mean by that, how they understand it, and how to respond to this demand for both change and pragmatic policies that would benefit the country and society.”

Ukrainian military tests new SkyFall drone for aerial evacuation of wounded soldiers – AP
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:38:00 EEST
19:38:00 KST

Ukrainian military tests new SkyFall drone for aerial evacuation of wounded soldiers – AP
Ukrainian company SkyFall has developed the StarGate drone for aerial evacuation of wounded soldiers and handed it over to the military this week for frontline testing.
Source: Associated Press
Details: A SkyFall spokesperson said the idea emerged after a request from the military.
Quote from AP: "Last year, Flint, commander of the 475th Separate Assault Regiment, known as Code 9.2, approached SkyFall's founder about developing a safer way to evacuate wounded soldiers from hard-to-reach positions."
Details: In some parts of the front line, the so-called kill zone – an area constantly exposed to drone and artillery fire – extends 10-15 km (6-9 miles) or more. StarGate can fly up to 15 km one way, potentially reaching critically wounded troops stranded deep within this dangerous zone.
According to a unit commander with the alias "KVN", ground robots usually take two to three hours to reach a position.
"Covering 10 km in minutes would be a drastic change on the front line," he said.
StarGate has a maximum payload capacity of 150 kg (330 pounds), the manufacturer says, enough to transport a wounded soldier in body armour with their combat gear.
The drone has a cruising speed of 65 km/h (40 mph) and a maximum speed of 105 km/h (65 mph). Preparing it for flight takes about 10 minutes.
The StarGate has two communication channels: Starlink and its own L-Link system. The drone is operated remotely, while AI features help it function without GPS and in conditions of electronic warfare interference. According to the developers, if communication is completely lost, the drone can independently plot a route to a safe area.
During a field demonstration, a StarGate took off carrying a stretcher loaded with equipment simulating a wounded soldier wearing body armour. The test range also simulated an FPV drone attack and activated electronic warfare systems. When one of the drones approached, StarGate fired a net that entangled it and knocked it off course.
SkyFall estimates that one system will cost at least US$50,000, depending on its configuration. The company plans to ramp up production to as many as 1,000 units per month by the end of 2026.
The military is currently testing the StarGate in frontline conditions. KVN said at least a month of use will be needed to assess the drone's effectiveness.
SkyFall is a Ukrainian manufacturer of heavy Vampire drones, known as Baba Yaga, and Shrike FPV drones. The company has also developed the P1-SUN interceptor drone.
Background: In March, Ukrainian company Gurzuf Defence unveiled the Ayudag-6 heavy drone, capable of carrying up to 90 kg of cargo. The multicopter is also being considered for evacuating wounded soldiers from the battlefield.

Mansour Abbas, leader of the Islamist Ra’am party, broke a longstanding taboo in 2021 by bringing an Arab party into an Israeli coalition government.

Palestinian citizens and their descendants make up about 20 percent of Israel’s population. Although they hold citizenship and voting rights, activists say they face discrimination and inadequate protection from violent crime.
The homicide rate among Palestinian citizens is more than 22 times higher than among Jewish Israelis. The Abraham Initiatives, an Israeli organization advocating equal rights, has recorded 184 crime-related killings in Arab communities so far this year, with only 12% of cases reported in the first half of 2026 solved.
Authorities have also restricted anti-war protests, displays of Palestinian flags and online expression, according to the rights group Adalah.
The Israeli government maintains that minorities have equal rights and says restrictions are rooted in security concerns.
Tensions have worsened since the 2023 attack and Israel’s subsequent offensive in Gaza, which has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, according to local health authorities. Mohammad
Darawshe, a director at the Givat Haviva Center for a Shared Society, said an initial period of solidarity between Jewish and Palestinian citizens faded as Israel’s military response alienated many Palestinians.
Arab parties could hold significant leverage in the election because no single party is expected to secure the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset.
However, Netanyahu, centrist opposition figure Gadi Eisenkot and former coalition leader Yair Lapid have all ruled out forming a government with Arab-led parties. A deadlock could force another election, leaving Netanyahu’s government in a caretaker role.
Despite their political marginalization, some Palestinian citizens say voting remains essential to securing better representation and addressing local problems. Ahmed Kadan, a 50-year-old guidance counselor in Baqa al-Gharbiyye, plans to vote for Ra’am, saying the government has neglected Arab communities despite their contributions to Israeli society.
“We live in this state and not in any other place,” Kadan said. “We’re doing our duty but not getting what we need.”

The Asset Recovery and Management Agency (ARMA) is preparing for the sale of the seized dry-cargo vessel EMMAKRIS III, which is owned by a company based in Rostov-on-Don (Russian Federation).
According to the agency’s website, the vessel is currently located within the waters of the Chornomorsk seaport in Odesa region.

Spaces by Manah signposts Chennai community centre with barrel-vaulted roof
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:30:32 UTC
19:30:32 KST

Spaces by Manah signposts Chennai community centre with barrel-vaulted roof
Local architecture studio Spaces by Manah has completed The Soil & Sea community centre in Chennai, India, with a brick barrel-vaulted roof that serves as a "visible landmark" on the site.
The 4,330-square-metre building was designed to provide learning space for a local education centre, as well as to house community workshops and events.
Spaces by Manah designed its single-storey masonry structure to appear as though it were "growing out of the existing landscape", creating a series of outdoor and open-air spaces that overlook its lush surroundings.
"The project sits within a lush, tree-lined parcel of land with the design growing out of the existing landscape," the studio told Dezeen.
"The building is positioned to retain its connection with the trees and outdoor spaces through a sequence of shaded, open and enclosed spaces, while the dominant barrel vault rises above the canopy to create a visible landmark within the site," it added.
Raised on a rubble stone foundation, the centre is organised around a flat-roofed volume, flanked on two sides by an L-shaped verandah that was conceived by the studio as an "intermediate, informal zone" between the building and landscape.
Steps and a ramp at the building's front lead up to the verandah, which is sheltered by the barrel-vaulted roof on one side to form a main gathering space for the community.
Meanwhile, its other edge is topped with a sloping, tiled roof. A series of granite stone pillars frame the space, along with built-in seating.
"The architecture responds to this idea through a strong central gathering space, expressed by the barrel vault, with more intimate and informal spaces arranged around it," the studio said.
"An L-shaped veranda acts as an intermediate, informal zone between the enclosed spaces and the landscape, with built-in seating and ramps supporting movement, accessibility and interaction throughout the building."
The bricks used for the structure's load-bearing walls were left exposed throughout the space. To complement the brick design, the studio sourced doors, windows and Mangalore floor tiles locally and repurposed them throughout the building.
This materiality extends to the building's interior, where exposed brick walls and roof elements are set off by glossy tiles.
"The material palette was intentionally kept natural, tactile and largely raw, allowing the building to sit comfortably within its landscape," the studio said.
Also on the site is a separate toilet block, which is similarly perched atop a stone foundation, and complete with load-bearing brick walls and a tiled canopy roof.
Elsewhere in Chennai, Ekarth Studio has used bamboo to form a sculptural venue for the Maestro Ilaiyaraaja Centre for Music Learning and Research, while Habitat Collaborative has threaded a curved school through a tree-filled site in Vadodara.
The photography is by Sreenag Pictures.

Dad fined after son, 2, died in Cyprus hotel fall
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16

Dad fined after son, 2, died in Cyprus hotel fall
- Published
A father whose two-year-old boy fell from a fourth floor window at a hotel in Cyprus has been fined €3,000 (£2,500) for causing his death.
Joshua Foster thought the window was closed when he placed his son on a sill to show him the view of a waterpark and "lost control" of him, Paphos District Court previously heard.
The toddler fell nearly 40ft (12.1m) at the five-star King Evelthon Beach Hotel and Resort on 12 July, the first day of the family's holiday in Chlorakas.
Foster, 37, from Essex, admitted causing death through a reckless, rash or dangerous act and was sentenced on Friday morning.
He told reporters afterwards: "Thank you for the support. I'm looking forward to going home and being with my wife and daughter."
Foster, an auditor, arrived in Cyprus hours before the incident with his wife, two children and in-laws.
They enjoyed various activities and swimming, before getting ready for dinner in the evening.
At about 18:00, Foster, his father-in-law and son were walking towards a lift when the boy noticed a waterpark outside.
Foster pushed the lift button, placed the child on the windowsill and the "inconceivable" unfolded before he could react, the court heard.
The boy was taken to Paphos General Hospital and later pronounced dead.
"The window did not appear to carry markings that would necessarily have alerted the defendant to the fact that one section was open," said District Judge Froso Christodoulidou.
His failure to establish that the window was closed led to the tragic result, the judge added.
"It was a momentary error which created a dangerous situation with fatal consequences."
The judge said there was "no evidence that the defendant deliberately exposed the child to danger", according to a translation of proceedings.
She added no sentence could outweigh the "personal consequences of the loss of his child".
In a voluntary statement to police, Foster said when he placed his son on the windowsill, the boy "fell before he had a chance to grab him".
While Foster had alcohol in his system, it did not form a significant part of the case against him - and his lawyer said there was no testimony he was drunk.
After the sentencing, Foster's lawyer, Alexandros Alexandrou, told reporters the case should have "never gone to court".
He said Foster was held in custody for eight days immediately after the incident and had to call his daughter from custody to explain what had happened.
"Within this three months, there was a lost opportunity for this man to grieve as he wanted to, to be with his family," he said.
He described his client as an "incredible father".
"[He is] an exemplary family man with a beautiful family behind him, that support him, that embraces him, that has always been by his side."

Türkiye targets 4.2% growth in 2027 as government unveils budget proposal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:27:45 UTC
19:27:45 KST

Türkiye expects economic growth to accelerate to 4.2% in 2027 from a projected 3.3% this year, supported by an improving global outlook and a recovery in external demand, Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz said Friday with next year's proposed budget in hand.
Presenting the government's 2027 budget proposal at the presidential complex in Ankara, Yilmaz said stronger growth among Türkiye's trading partners would create opportunities for exports and support balanced economic expansion.
The Turkish economy grew 3.7% in 2025, he said, adding that investment outpacing private consumption had strengthened production capacity and improved the composition of growth.
“In 2027, we expect our growth to rise to 4.2%, supported by the anticipated improvement in the global outlook and the recovery in external demand,” Yilmaz said.
The government aims to gradually accelerate growth to 5% by the end of its medium-term program through policies focused on productivity, technological transformation, and innovation, he said.
Employment is expected to increase by 657,000 people next year, with labor force participation reaching 53.4% and unemployment declining to 8%, from a projected 8.1% in 2026.
 
Inflation forecast to decline to 21%
Yilmaz said annual inflation, which fell below 30% in September, was expected to reach 28.4% by the end of this year before declining to 21% by the end of 2027.
“Price stability is the fundamental priority of our program,” he said.
Fiscal discipline and incomes policies will continue to support monetary policy, while supply-side measures, particularly in social housing and food, will reinforce disinflation.
Despite fluctuations stemming from energy and commodity prices, the underlying inflation trend continues to improve, Yilmaz said, reiterating the government's medium-term goal of achieving lasting single-digit inflation.
He said the current account deficit was expected to fall below 2% of gross domestic product next year from a projected 2.6% in 2026.
Türkiye will continue policies to boost exports, strengthen energy supply security, and reduce dependence on energy imports, he added.
Goods exports this January-September rose 5.2% year-on-year to $211 billion, bringing the rolling annual total to a record $283.7 billion, Yilmaz said.
The share of medium-high- and high-technology products in exports reached 44%, compared with around 28% in the early 2000s, he added.
 
Budget spending projected at $551.2B
The 2027 budget proposal projects expenditures of 27.276 trillion Turkish liras and revenues of 23.408 trillion liras ($551.2 billion), with national income expected to reach $2.24 trillion.
The figures imply a budget shortfall of $78.1 billion, equivalent to a projected 3.5% of GDP. Excluding earthquake-related expenditure, the deficit is forecast at 2.8% of GDP.
Yilmaz said the proposal would be submitted to parliament with President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's signature, calling it a budget of “resilience, prosperity and transformation.”
Interest expenditures are projected at $80.2 billion, personnel spending at $143.7 billion, and current transfers at $206.7 billion. The budget is expected to maintain a primary surplus next year.
For 2026, the government forecasts a deficit of 3.1% of GDP, below the initial 3.5% projection, despite spending pressures from higher energy and commodity prices.
Urban transformation funding will rise 176% to $5.57 billion in 2027, Yilmaz said, with disaster resilience remaining a priority alongside expanded social and rental housing provision.
Earthquake reconstruction spending over 2023-2026 totaled $109 billion at current prices, equivalent to $104 billion, he said, with 455,357 independent units completed and delivered.
Türkiye's EU-defined general government debt declined to 22.3% of GDP in the second quarter from 23.1% in the first, Yilmaz added, describing low public indebtedness as an important advantage amid global uncertainty.

NCP parliamentary group proposes tightening Finland's asylum rules
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:27:07 EEST
19:27:07 KST

The National Coalition Party's (NCP) parliamentary group wants Finland to move towards a policy of selective immigration, in an aim to give the country more control over who can enter and remain in Finland.
The group published its new immigration policy guidelines on Friday, with proposals prepared under the leadership of MP Atte Kaleva (NCP), who has led the work since January.
They have proposed moving asylum processing outside the EU and tightening the conditions for family reunification and access to social security.
"This means that Finland must be able to decide under all circumstances who is allowed to enter the country and under what conditions, as well as who is allowed to remain here," Kaleva said.
The proposals include linking immigrants' eligibility for unemployment benefits to their employment history in Finland and tightening the conditions for receiving the national pension and guarantee pension.
Asylum processing outside the EU
The parliamentary group proposes transferring asylum processing entirely to reception and return centres outside the EU.
It also wants to restrict repeated asylum applications deemed unfounded and make returns more efficient.
"Asylum has been misused as a channel for mass migration, which it was never intended to be. We are returning to protecting individual people who are in need of protection. This also removes the market for people smuggling," he said.
The group further proposes that serious or repeated criminal offences could lead to the revocation of a person's residence permit and their deportation.
Regarding quota refugees, the group proposes that authorities also take into account their prospects for integrating into Finnish society and culture.
"We have certain fundamental values in Finland that we cannot compromise on: democracy, individual freedoms, equality, the equality of women and girls, and minority rights," Kaleva said.
"If a person is unable to adapt to these values, then of course they cannot be accepted into Finland," he added.
Unemployment benefits linked to work in Finland
Under the proposals, immigrants' eligibility for unemployment benefits would depend on the work they had done in Finland. The level of support would vary according to the length of their employment.
The group also proposes tightening family reunification rules by requiring the person bringing family members to Finland to be able to support them through employment or business activities.
Kaleva said the party wanted to encourage work-based immigration, but opposed the creation of a low-wage labour market in Finland.
"We cannot create a cheap labour market in Finland, where people come here to work for companies that do not pay a sufficient salary," he said.
Kaleva said responsibility for integration should lie primarily with immigrants themselves, but also with their employers.
The parliamentary group's proposals were outlined in its new immigration policy programme, titled 'Towards Selective Immigration' (Kohti valikoivaa maahanmuuttoa), included in their press release (in Finnish).

Ukraine makes its anti-drone road nets a national standard in a new strategy for defensive lines through 2028. It has already strung over more than 1,000 kilometers of road
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:26:04 UTC
19:26:04 KST

Ukraine’s government has approved a Strategy for the Engineering Equipment of Defensive Lines through 2028. It makes strengthening anti-drone protection of logistics routes one of its priorities, the Defense Ministry says.
Russian FPV drones hunt almost anything that moves within 15 to 30 kilometers of the front, which has forced Ukraine to drape its logistics roads in overhead netting, wire-mesh canopies and reinforced barriers that catch an attacking drone before it reaches a vehicle. Ukraine had already built more than 1,066 kilometers of such protection by mid-July and aims for 4,000 kilometers by the end of 2026.
The new strategy turns that scramble into a single national standard, setting deadlines, assigning responsibility, and building control mechanisms, the ministry explained.
“Solutions that have proven effective we will scale. But we will also account for new challenges, threats and changes in Russian tactics. The main goal is the protection of our service members and civilians,” the Defense Ministry says.
One digital map for every trench and net
The plan puts the entire defensive network onto a screen. To track and monitor the state of defensive lines, Ukraine will introduce a single digital geographic information platform, built on and expanding existing systems, including the DELTA situational-awareness system.
The database will hold object passports, photographs, and data on each structure’s location and condition, helping officials verify that work is done, identify repair needs, and distribute resources on evidence rather than guesswork.
From trenches to supply roads, one cycle
The strategy covers the full span of military engineering. Its main lines of work are building and maintaining fortifications, laying engineering obstacles, strengthening anti-drone protection of logistics routes, using modern designs, materials and camouflage, creating a reserve of construction materials, and maintaining digital records of the work.
Developed on the Defense Ministry’s initiative based on combat experience, the document spans the entire cycle from planning and construction to accounting, upkeep, and restoration, the ministry noted. Financing will come from the state and local budgets for the relevant year and from other sources not prohibited by law.

“Russia has lost more than 100 fighter aircraft in the Ukraine conflict since February 2022.”
Russia will find the Bear the harder of the two losses to absorb, because production of the Tu-95MS ended in the early nineteen nineties. They fly the Kh-101 cruise missile strikes that have hit Ukrainian cities through the war, launching from well inside Russian airspace and turning for home without entering contested air.
Khanskaya sits in the Republic of Adygea in southern Russia, well outside the range at which Russian commanders had been willing to disperse aircraft earlier in the war. Ukraine’s long-range one-way attack drones have steadily pushed that calculation back, and airfields that were treated as rear areas have had to adopt the revetments, decoys and dispersal that frontline bases adopted years ago.

Türkiye targets 4.2 percent growth in 2027 as government unveils budget proposal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:16:26 UTC
19:16:26 KST

Türkiye expects economic growth to accelerate to 4.2 percent in 2027 from a projected 3.3 percent this year, supported by an improving global outlook and a recovery in external demand, Vice President Cevdet Yılmaz said on Oct. 16 with next year’s proposed budget in hand.
Presenting the government’s 2027 budget proposal at the presidential complex in Ankara, Yılmaz said stronger growth among Türkiye’s trading partners would create opportunities for exports and support balanced economic expansion.
The Turkish economy grew 3.7 percent in 2025, he said, adding that investment outpacing private consumption had strengthened production capacity and improved the composition of growth.
“In 2027, we expect our growth to rise to 4.2 percent, supported by the anticipated improvement in the global outlook and the recovery in external demand,” Yılmaz said.
The government aims to gradually accelerate growth to 5 percent by the end of its medium-term program through policies focused on productivity, technological transformation and innovation, he said.
Yılmaz said annual inflation, which fell below 30 percent in September, was expected to reach 28.4 percent by the end of this year before declining to 21 percent by the end of 2027.
“Price stability is the fundamental priority of our program,” he said.
Fiscal discipline and incomes policies will continue to support monetary policy, while supply-side measures, particularly in social housing and food, will reinforce disinflation.
Despite fluctuations stemming from energy and commodity prices, the underlying inflation trend continues to improve, Yılmaz said, reiterating the government’s medium-term goal of achieving lasting single-digit inflation.
He said the current account deficit was expected to fall below 2 percent of gross domestic product next year from a projected 2.6 percent in 2026.
Türkiye will continue policies to boost exports, strengthen energy supply security and reduce dependence on energy imports, he added.
The 2027 budget proposal projects expenditures of 27.28 trillion Turkish liras and revenues of 23.41 trillion liras ($551.2 billion), with national income expected to reach $2.24 trillion.
The figures imply a budget shortfall of $78.1 billion, equivalent to a projected 3.5 percent of GDP. Excluding earthquake-related expenditure, the deficit is forecast at 2.8 percent of GDP.
Yılmaz said the proposal would be submitted to parliament with President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan’s signature, calling it a budget of “resilience, prosperity and transformation.”
Interest expenditures are projected at $80.2 billion. The budget is expected to maintain a primary surplus next year.
For 2026, the government forecasts a deficit of 3.1 percent of GDP, below the initial 3.5 percent projection, despite spending pressures from higher energy and commodity prices.
Urban transformation funding will rise 176 percent to $5.57 billion in 2027, Yilmaz said, with disaster resilience remaining a priority alongside expanded social and rental housing provision.
Earthquake reconstruction spending over 2023-2026 totaled $109 billion at current prices, equivalent to $104 billion, he said, with 455,357 independent units completed and delivered.

Dinh identified banking restrictions as the main operational concern. Official Vietnam–Iran trade is around $170 million, but much of the real trade may pass through third countries. &quot;We can no longer do this&quot;: Le Pen opposes further financial support for Ukraine
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:15:35 EEST
19:15:35 KST

"We can no longer do this": Le Pen opposes further financial support for Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
Marine Le Pen said that after winning in 2027, she would end financial aid to Ukraine within six months. She is also opposed to Ukraine joining the EU.
French far-right politician and representative of the National Rally party Marine Le Pen said that Europe, and France in particular, can no longer increase its financial support for Ukraine. UNN reports this, citing Financial Times and French media.
Details
If she wins the 2027 presidential election, she plans to stop direct financial aid to Kyiv six months after taking office. The politician also opposes Ukraine's membership in the European Union and any further increase in European countries' financial commitments.
In an interview with the Financial Times published on October 14, Marine Le Pen said that European states had already undertaken significant financial commitments to support Ukraine and that the possibilities for further increasing aid were limited. According to the French politician, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy needs to be openly told about the financial constraints faced by European partners.
To deal honestly with Mr. Zelenskyy is to tell him, in fact to warn him: listen, we cannot do more. We have already provided loans totaling €90 billion, of which €18 billion falls to France. That is a truly large sum
She emphasized that France could no longer afford to support Ukraine at previous levels because of the difficult situation with its public finances. In addition, Le Pen questioned the rationale for further financing Kyiv through the European Union if this would result in an additional financial burden on the French budget.
The politician also called for a significant reduction in the EU budget and a limitation of the powers of European institutions.
Le Pen promised to stop funding Ukraine six months after winning the election
On October 14, while in Brussels, Marine Le Pen clarified her position in an interview with the Belgian television channel VRT News. She said that if elected president of France, she would not stop financial support for Ukraine immediately after taking power. Instead, she envisages a six-month transition period.
From the moment of my election, for six months we will maintain aid so as not to leave anyone in an impossible situation. But after that, we will stop financial aid to Ukraine, because we no longer have the ability to provide it
At the same time, she did not rule out maintaining certain forms of military cooperation, including operational support and the training of Ukrainian service members.
Le Pen opposed Ukraine joining the EU
The politician separately criticized the prospect of Ukraine's membership in the European Union. According to her, Ukraine's accession to the EU could lead to significant economic losses for France, particularly in the agricultural sector. Le Pen claims that Ukrainian agricultural products would create additional competition for French farmers and that the distribution of European subsidies would change to France's disadvantage.
In her conversation with the Financial Times, she called Ukraine's possible accession to the European Union a "harakiri" for France, linking it to threats to national sovereignty and significant economic losses.
What Volodymyr Zelenskyy replied to Le Pen
On October 15, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy commented on the French politician's statements in an interview with the Financial Times. The head of state emphasized that Ukraine's cooperation with France and other Western partners is not limited to financial support. According to him, European states are gaining valuable experience from the Ukrainian military that can be used to develop their own defense technologies and improve the combat readiness of their armies.
In particular, the president mentioned the Franco-Italian SAMP/T air defense systems, which were improved based on experience from combat use, as well as SCALP/Storm Shadow cruise missiles. Zelenskyy emphasized that Ukraine's experience of modern warfare has practical value for European defense companies.
We also give something in return
In his view, French industry could benefit from the joint production of weapons, technological cooperation, and the use of Ukrainian military expertise.
The president also expressed the conviction that Le Pen does not fully take into account certain aspects of defense cooperation between the countries.
What is known about financial support for Ukraine from the EU
Despite Le Pen's statements, the European Union continues to provide Ukraine with military, economic, and budgetary assistance. In particular, the EU approved a €90 billion loan program for 2026–2027. It provides funding for Ukraine's defense needs and support for the state budget. However, funds under this program are disbursed gradually, and their allocation depends on the agreed conditions and Ukraine's implementation of the necessary reforms.
In addition, European institutions are considering mechanisms for further financing Ukraine in view of the country's significant needs amid the continuation of the full-scale war with Russia.
Context
Marine Le Pen is one of the leading representatives of France's far-right forces and has consistently advocated reducing France's financial contributions to the European Union budget. She has repeatedly criticized European sanctions against Russia while stating that she condemns Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Against the backdrop of preparations for the 2027 presidential election, Le Pen has stepped up statements regarding the need to review France's foreign policy and budgetary priorities.

Ethiopia's Abiy names new Tigray government, wants polls in six months
NAIROBI, Oct 16 - Ethiopia's Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has named a caretaker government to stabilise the northern Tigray region and prepare for an election within six months, after fighting erupted between a rebel alliance and federal troops.
The Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) led an offensive last month against Abiy's government, reigniting a war that killed hundreds of thousands between 2020-22.
Renewed conflict has led to the severing of ties between Ethiopia and Eritrea. Addis Ababa accuses Asmara of backing the rebels, which Eritrea denies.
The TPLF, Tigray's ruling party, dominated Ethiopian politics for decades until Abiy took office in 2018. Since fighting erupted, Ethiopia's military and a pro-government militia have made significant advances and taken control of large parts of Tigray including the regional capital Mekelle.
The temporary administration will be in office for six months, Abiy's office said, to create a stable political climate for free and transparent elections within six months.
"To attain the peace that has long eluded them, to secure their right to self-administration, and to finally enjoy the fruits of development — which have been out of reach for many years — the people of Tigray must break free from this cycle of conflict," Abiy said in a statement posted on X.
The administration will also repair damaged infrastructure and help displaced people return to their homes, he said.
A TPLF spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Tigray is yet to recover from the humanitarian toll of the previous war, which pushed hundreds of thousands into famine. Around 750,000 Tigrayans were still internally displaced as of February, according to the UN refugee agency, and the region faces drought linked to El Nino.
There are fears that unrest could spread beyond Ethiopia’s borders in the fragile Horn of Africa region where other powers vie for influence.
In addition to Eritrea, Ethiopia's government has accused Egypt and Sudan of supporting the rebel alliance.
They have denied the allegations. REUTERS

ICC serves Europe’s ‘colonialist interests’ – analyst (VIDEO)
The International Criminal Court (ICC) has become a tool of Western influence that selectively targets countries of the Global South while shielding European interests and ignoring crimes in Ukraine, international legal analyst and academic Alexandre Guerreiro has said. He accused the tribunal of applying double standards rather than delivering universal justice.
Criticism of the ICC has intensified in recent months amid growing accusations of political bias and selective justice. Venezuela, Chad, Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger have moved to withdraw, accusing the court of serving Western interests and engaging in “neocolonial repression.”
In an interview with RT on Thursday, Guerreiro argued that the court had abandoned its original purpose as an independent institution capable of holding perpetrators accountable regardless of nationality, and has become increasingly politicized and dominated by European powers.
“In practice, what we have is a court that serves European interests, colonialist interests,” he said, arguing that the tribunal is used to pressure Global South nations while avoiding similar scrutiny of European countries.
Guerreiro pointed to the court’s handling of cases involving Afghanistan, Iraq and Kenya, arguing that political interference had repeatedly undermined the principles of impartial justice.
He also accused the ICC of ignoring alleged crimes in Ukraine, including the deadly May 2014 Odessa clashes between Ukrainian nationalists and opponents of the Western-backed coup in Kiev, as well as the sniper shootings during the preceding Maidan unrest.
“This is not justice,” he said, arguing that the court only pursues cases that serve the interests of the current Ukrainian authorities and the Western bloc as a whole.
The remarks come days after Washington imposed sweeping new sanctions on the ICC, accusing it of overstepping its jurisdiction in cases involving American and Israeli nationals. The court issued arrest warrants in 2024 for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.
Meanwhile, the ICC’s investigation into alleged war crimes by American forces in Afghanistan has produced no criminal charges against US personnel.

Europe Has No Starlink Replacement as Ukraine Faces Satellite Disruptions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:14:27 UTC
19:14:27 KST

Europe cannot replace Starlink anytime soon, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas warned Friday, as disruptions to Elon Musk’s satellite network raised concerns over Ukraine’s battlefield communications.
“Starlink is really necessary for Ukraine and unfortunately in the short term Europe can’t replace this capability,” Kallas told reporters ahead of an EU summit attended by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Ukraine relies on Starlink and its military-grade counterpart, Starshield, for battlefield communications, mid-range strikes on Russian-occupied territory and interceptor drones used to shoot down Russian attack drones.
Starlink’s satellite network is unmatched in scale, while its business model and portable, affordable terminals give it a major advantage over competitors that rely on bulkier, more expensive equipment.
Kyiv reported restrictions on military Starlink connections this week, with Ukrainian officials reporting slower speeds on some terminals on Wednesday. Musk said any disruption was the responsibility of the US government, not his SpaceX company.
Europe scrambles for alternatives
Kallas said the European Defence Agency had mapped the critical military capabilities Europe lacks and must develop.
“We need to fill these gaps as soon as possible,” she said.
Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs acknowledged that Europe was not yet equipped to provide a full alternative.
Le Pen Looms Large as Macron Enters Final Months on EU Stage
“Starlink is the key for Ukraine actually to fight or fight back,” he told reporters on Friday, according to AFP. Europe has some comparable capabilities, but not enough to meet Ukraine’s needs.
Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten told AFP he had discussed the issue with French President Emmanuel Macron on Thursday, focusing on how European countries could provide more satellite communications services in the near future.
EU eyes satellite backup
The European Commission is negotiating Ukraine’s participation in GOVSATCOM, an EU program that pools satellite resources to provide secure communications for government users.
“We are currently in talks with Ukraine to fully associate Ukraine to GOVSATCOM,” Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier said Wednesday.
The system could give Kyiv another way to maintain secure communications during Russian attacks on infrastructure and disruptions to conventional networks. But Brussels has yet to confirm whether it can match Starlink’s capabilities for combat operations.
The EU could add commercial satellite services as early as 2027, potentially helping meet military needs, Regnier said. Its longer-term plan, the IRIS² constellation of more than 300 satellites, is expected to become fully operational in 2029.
Until then, Ukraine remains heavily reliant on Starlink – and Europe has no immediate replacement for a system critical to its war effort.
Why Ukraine needs another option
The European discussions have gained urgency after restrictions detected overnight on Oct. 13–14 disrupted Ukrainian drone operations.
Ukrainian Defense Ministry sources said units received no advance warning and reported connections dropping at different movement speeds, approximately 72 to 161 kilometers per hour.
The ministry contacted the United States, SpaceX and NATO partners while checking backup communications channels.
The disruption affected interceptor and medium-range strike drones, alongside reconnaissance, logistics and communications relay missions.
The reported speed limits concern how fast a terminal is moving, rather than its internet download speed.
Former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov said on Wednesday evening that connectivity at speeds of up to 160 kilometers per hour was being restored, while calling for Starshield’s speed restriction to be removed entirely.
That partial restoration does not resolve every operational requirement. Two Ukrainian officials told RFE/RL that connections had improved below the threshold, but restrictions continued to complicate interception of Russia’s jet-powered drones.
One Ukrainian source said operating speeds needed to reach at least 450 kilometers per hour.
President Volodymyr Zelensky has accused those responsible of deliberately restricting the service during Russian attacks, saying the disruption weakened Ukraine’s defenses and endangered civilians. Who authorized the restrictions remains disputed.
Musk said Starshield systems are controlled by the US government and that their operational limits are determined by the US military and ultimately the president. A senior White House official, however, told Axios that the Trump administration was not involved.
Why switching networks will take time
According to Reuters, Europe has no ready-made replacement that Ukrainian troops can immediately attach to their drones.
Eutelsat already provides connectivity in Ukraine through its low Earth orbit and geostationary networks.
But independent satellite consultant Christian Freiherr von der Ropp told Reuters that OneWeb faces capacity and performance constraints, while terminal cost, weight, size and power consumption limit frontline suitability.
Switching would also require replacing thousands of terminals: Starlink equipment uses proprietary technology and cannot simply connect to OneWeb.
European political pressure to develop alternatives is growing. In a statement on Thursday, Oct. 15, Renew Europe President Valérie Hayer urged EU leaders to strengthen support for Ukraine and address dependence on American satellite services.
“Recent days have also shown the urgent need for a European alternative to Starlink,” she said.
Russia races to build its own Starlink
Russia could deploy an alternative to Starlink across the front line within a year, Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces commander Robert “Madyar” Brovdi warned in May.
Russia’s main project is Rassvet, developed by Russian company Bureau 1440. The company launched 16 spacecraft in March 2026, while six Rassvet satellites were in orbit at the time, according to Russian media outlet Kommersant.
Despite the limited constellation, Ukrainian defense outlet Militarnyi reported that the satellites’ regular passes over Ukraine could provide usable coverage for some frontline applications. However, Rassvet remains far behind Starlink in scale and established operational capability.
Russian troops have also relied on alternative equipment, including terminals referred to as “Gazprom.” In an intercepted conversation published by Kyiv Post in February, a Russian serviceman dismissed one such terminal as “f**king shit.”
Starlink operates more than 7,800 satellites, while Russia is still building its network. Moscow’s ability to expand Rassvet and improve its terminals could nevertheless become a growing concern for Ukraine, particularly as both sides depend increasingly on satellite connectivity to control drones and coordinate battlefield operations.

Türkiye’s exports to the 10 member states of the BRICS grouping totaled $18.2 billion in the first nine months of the year, according to the Turkish Exporters’ Assembly (TİM).
While Türkiye’s total global exports this January-September grew 5.2 percent to $210.9 billion, Russia was the largest destination among other BRICS member states, receiving $4.1 billion in exports despite a 2.5 percent annual decline.
BRICS includes longtime members Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa, plus recent additions Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, and the United Arab Emirates.
The UAE followed Russia as the second-largest destination for Turkish exports to BRICS, accounting for $3.3 billion even after a 4.12 percent contraction in export volume.

Turkish exports increased in eight of the 10 BRICS member states, with shipments in Ethiopia surging the most by 79.6 percent.
The chemicals and chemical products sector accounted for most of these exports to the bloc, generating $3.5 billion in the first nine months of the year, the data showed.
Mining exports grew 33.5 percent to $2.1 billion, a net gain of roughly $539 million, followed by the jewelry sector, whose exports fell 45 percent to $1.3 billion.
The textiles and raw material exports climbed 8.7 percent to $1.2 billion at the same time.

Social media favourites, Pompeii's cats star in new photo book
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:06:50 UTC
19:06:50 KST

Photographed by thousands of visitors every year, the cats of Pompeii’s Archaeological Park now star in a new book. Around 50 live among the ruins.
After charming thousands of visitors and turning into genuine social media celebrities, the cats that live inside the archaeological area of Pompeii have now become the stars of a photographic book dedicated to them.
The book, entitled Cats of Pompeii, is published by Giunti Editore in collaboration with the Pompeii Archaeological Park. Richly illustrated, it tells the stories of the everyday life of the feline colony that inhabits the UNESCO World Heritage site.
The volume grew out of photographs donated to the Park by archaeologist and photographer Silvia Vacca and offers a journey into the most unusual and captivating side of the ancient city. The shots capture the cats as they roam among domus, gardens and Roman streets, providing an original perspective on a presence that has long since become an integral part of the Pompeian landscape.
The Park’s feline colony numbers between forty and fifty animals, and their presence is constantly monitored through a management and protection system that makes it possible to combine animal welfare with the conservation of the archaeological heritage and the safety of visitors. The Park has also introduced a video surveillance system to prevent animals being abandoned.
Thanks to cooperation with the charity Archeogatti Onlus, chaired by Antonella Carotenuto, the Archaeological Park also ensures sterilisation campaigns, health checks, measures to prevent abandonment, and the management of feeding the colony and arranging adoptions for some of the "archaeologist" cats.
Cats in ancient Pompeii
The presence of cats in Pompeii is a symbolic feature of life at the site. Ongoing archaeological research sheds light on the relationship between humans and felines in the ancient world, while today these animals remain a familiar sight and are much appreciated by visitors from all over the globe.
The camera lens reveals intimate, evocative images taken during the Park’s quietest moments, when the streets of the ancient city fall silent once more. Out of this comes a portrait of a different Pompeii, where safeguarding cultural heritage goes hand in hand with protecting the animals that have inhabited its spaces for years.
"Cats of Pompeii" is available at sales points in the Pompeii Archaeological Park and through Giunti’s distribution channels.

A British man has been handed a €3,000 (£2,500) fine after his two-year-old son fell nearly 12 metres (40ft) to his death from the fourth floor window of a hotel in Cyprus.
Joshua Foster thought the window was closed when he placed the boy on a sill to show him the view of a waterpark and “lost control” of him, the court previously heard.
The 37-year-old appeared at Paphos district court on Friday for sentencing having pleaded guilty to a charge of causing death through a reckless, rash or dangerous act.
Foster, an auditor, held back tears as his sentence was read out by the district judge Froso Christodoulidou.
After the 25-minute hearing, Foster hugged his lawyer before embracing his parents.
The boy fell from the fourth floor of the five-star King Evelthon Beach Hotel and Resort in Chlorakas on 12 July, the first day of the family’s holiday.
The court previously heard that Foster, his wife, two children and in-laws had arrived in Cyprus in the early hours of the morning on the date of the incident.
After various activities, including visiting the pool, the family returned to their rooms to get ready to go out for dinner.
At about 6pm, Foster, his father-in-law and son walked towards the lift, and his lawyer Alexandros Alexandrou told the court that the defendant was in a “good mood” and was playing with his son.
The court was told that as they approached the lift, the boy noticed a waterpark outside.
It was said that Foster pushed the lift button, placed the child on the windowsill, the boy looked out, and the “inconceivable” unfolded before Foster had a chance to react.
Alexandrou told the hearing, which took place on 6 October, that Foster’s life “changed for ever” from that moment.
It was heard that Foster had not realised that the section of the window was open, and that he thought there was protective glass.
Prosecutor Chryso Pergandi said that at around 6.40pm, police received reports that a child had fallen from the fourth floor of the beachfront hotel under unknown circumstances.
The boy was taken to Paphos general hospital where, despite efforts to resuscitate him, he was pronounced dead.
In a voluntary statement to police, Foster said that when he placed his son on the windowsill, the boy “fell before he had a chance to grab him”.
After the incident, Foster was taken to Paphos general hospital and a blood sample to detect drugs and alcohol was taken.
Tests showed that the alcohol concentration in his blood was an estimated 124mg.
Alcohol consumption did not form a significant part of the case against Foster, and his lawyer said there was no testimony that he was drunk.
The lawyer told the court that Foster had no previous convictions and his remorse “is clear”.
He said he was held in custody for eight days immediately after the incident, adding that while grieving for his child he had to call his daughter from custody to explain what had happened.
The court heard the window was 2.85 metres wide and 1.2 metres high.

Hegseth's TV instincts backfire as Trump rejects execution livestream

2026-10-16
