Hegseth's TV instincts backfire as Trump rejects execution livestream
WASHINGTON, Oct 16 - As he took to the stage this week at an Army event, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth remarked how much it looked like a TV set. The former Fox News host said that put him at ease, even as the first in a series of anti-war protesters shouted at him.
But Hegseth's TV instincts, while perhaps one of the tools he relies on most in his Pentagon role, appear to have failed him on Thursday when President Donald Trump pulled the plug on his plans, announced last week, to livestream the Army's firing-squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan.
Trump had been unaware of Hegseth's unprecedented plan to broadcast the execution, said a White House official who spoke on condition of anonymity. Many fellow Republicans, along with religious leaders and international observers, raised objections to the plan, and defense officials who spoke to Reuters on Thursday expressed relief that the livestreaming would not go forward.
Defense secretaries often cycle out after a couple of years in the job and speculation in Washington has mounted whether Trump might see value in bringing new management to the Pentagon after November's midterm elections.
But Republican strategists said it was too soon to say whether Trump's decision to overrule Hegseth would affect their relationship, which has remained strong despite mounting public opposition to the war in Iran.
"They've been kind of very closely knit and I don't know whether it means anything at all," Republican strategist Douglas Heye said. Charlie Black, a veteran Republican strategist, said it would likely blow over.
"It's a wild thing but nobody will remember it next week," Black said, adding Trump "did the right thing."
The Pentagon sought to downplay the first major public split between Trump and Hegseth, saying the two spoke before the US president posted his decision on Truth Social.
"The Secretary supports the President's decision, and they are completely aligned," said Sean Parnell, the Pentagon's chief spokesperson.
CONGRESSIONAL WORRIES
Trump regularly extols Hegseth publicly, and has given the former Army National Guard soldier significant leeway as he seeks to reshape the Pentagon, including by firing its most senior officers.
But after narrowly winning Senate confirmation, Hegseth has failed to win over many Republicans who voiced concerns over his qualifications for the job. Some Republican lawmakers and congressional aides have expressed worries over his expected plans to draw down forces in Europe.
One Republican lawmaker filed articles of impeachment against Hegseth last month, accusing him of abusing his office by executing an order for hostilities against Iran without approval by Congress.
While Representative Thomas Massie's measure is not expected to succeed, Democrats could look to move forward with impeachment proceedings if they win control of the House in the upcoming elections in November.
At times, the conflict between Hegseth and members of Congress has become personal. Last year, Hegseth sought to prosecute Democratic Senator Mark Kelly after he and five other Democrats in Congress with backgrounds in the military and intelligence community urged US troops to refuse illegal orders.
Kelly on Thursday introduced a bill that would prohibit livestreamed executions.
"Livestreaming an execution is un-American and dangerous. It is the kind of thing we see with regimes like Iran and the Taliban in Afghanistan," Kelly said in a statement.
The event would have been extraordinary, even for a country that has long employed capital punishment. A government execution has never been broadcast or livestreamed, according to death penalty experts, and the US military has not executed anyone by firing squad since 1945.
Hasan was convicted of premeditated murder for shooting dead 13 people and wounding 32 others in a medical facility at the vast Fort Hood base in 2009. Now 56, he requires a wheelchair, having been shot by police during his arrest.
Hegseth had argued that making the event public would help show "there's serious consequences for these types of things."
Trump appeared to accept Hegseth's argument, saying on Thursday livestreaming it "might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan."
But Trump, who is himself a former reality television star, ultimately decided a public show went too far.
"Many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device. He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed," Trump wrote. REUTERS

Brazil's incoming right-wing Congress takes aim at judge who jailed Bolsonaro
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:05:36 UTC
19:05:36 KST

Brazil's incoming right-wing Congress takes aim at judge who jailed Bolsonaro
BRASILIA, Oct 16 - Brazil's next Congress is spoiling for a fight with the Supreme Court, including plans for an unprecedented impeachment of one of its justices that could dramatically expand the reach of a right-wing agenda, more than a dozen experts and officials at both the Senate and court told Reuters.
Driving the effort are allies of far-right former President Jair Bolsonaro who dominated legislative elections this month and plan to take aim at Alexandre de Moraes, the Supreme Court justice responsible for the ex-president's arrest and conviction on coup-plotting charges.
That would represent a major escalation by the legislative branch in a years-long power struggle with an empowered Brazilian judiciary, reasserting the influence of Congress and potentially pushing the court to the right for years to come.
If Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the former president's son, beats leftist incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in an October 25 runoff as polls now suggest, a defanged judiciary would also reduce one of the main checks on his power.
BLOCKING RIGHT-WING POLICIES
Brazil's Supreme Court was the main obstacle to his father's agenda during his 2019-2023 presidency, blocking efforts to weaken environmental protections, ease pandemic restrictions and facilitate gun purchases, for example.
The top court continues to hold back some of the most strident right-wing legislation, effectively defining policy on matters from Indigenous rights to regulating the internet.
This month's election could prove pivotal, as the next president could name at least 4 of the court's 11 justices, including an already vacant seat and replacements for 3 justices who will reach the mandatory retirement age of 75 before the president's term ends.
After former President Bolsonaro named two justices to the court, a victory by his son could spell a majority of the court appointed by the Bolsonaro family by the time he would leave office in 2031.
Impeaching Moraes, 57, would hasten that majority's arrival.
"Should Flavio win, the next administration and the Senate can reshape the majority of the 11-member bench, which means defining, literally, the balance of power in Brazilian democracy for a generation," said Bruna Santos, director of the Brazil Program at the Inter-American Dialogue.
SCORNED BY TRUMP, MUSK
Ex-President Bolsonaro has been in jail since November for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election to Lula. Moraes, who oversaw the case, became one of Brazil's most polarizing figures, drawing even the ire of US President Donald Trump, who described the case as a "witch hunt" and briefly sanctioned the judge in 2025.
Moraes also drew criticism when he ordered X suspended in Brazil in 2024, after the platform defied court orders. Its owner Elon Musk accused him of censorship and authoritarianism.
Bolsonaro supporters have rallied to remove the judge after a federal police report revealed communications between Moraes and a jailed banker accused of the country's biggest-ever banking fraud. Bolsonaro, who himself is being investigated for ties to the same banker, has also called for Moraes' removal.
"Defending the Judiciary means confronting this problem — opening an impeachment process and giving him the right to a defense, concluding it and turning this page," Senator-elect Domingos Savio, from Bolsonaro's Liberal Party (PL), told Reuters.
Lula has publicly supported unsealing the investigation, calling for transparency, disclosure, and an impartial investigation into all allegations of corruption.
Neither Moraes nor the Supreme Court responded to questions from Reuters. He and the wider court have defended their actions as necessary to uphold Brazilian law and protect democratic institutions. He has referred to the probes as politically and electorally motivated as revenge for the conviction of former President Bolsonaro, and requested his own investigation into another justice who released the reports.
LEGISLATIVE FIREPOWER
Senator Bolsonaro's running mate, lawmaker Alfredo Gaspar, told Reuters there is "a need to review what is happening today in the relationship between the Supreme Court and the other branches of government, and that involves examining whether justices have committed impeachable offenses."
Brazil's constitution allows the Senate to try Supreme Court justices for infractions that violate the constitution or risk public security. Votes from two-thirds of the 81-member Senate — 54 senators — are needed to convict and remove a justice.
Senator Bolsonaro's allies may already be close when the next Senate takes office in February. His party won a record 28 seats, and the senator has already secured backing from five other parties that together hold another 22 seats.
That would bring the conservative coalition to 50 senators. The remaining four votes could come from the 15 senators with non-aligned parties.
Since 2023, there have been 48 unsuccessful requests to impeach Moraes within the Senate, which never made it to trial because the Senate president must choose to advance a complaint against a justice.
That could change, as Senator Bolsonaro's campaign manager Rogerio Marinho is likely to become the next Senate president.
Marinho has in recent days told several Supreme Court justices that Brazil's upper house will not seek opportunities for revenge, he said to journalists, though adding that the current Senate is "failing to act" to hold justices accountable.
"If impeachable offenses are committed, they must be investigated. No one is above the law," Marinho said. REUTERS

Reservations under the new system: why the government’s assurances failed to allay the concerns of business and parliament
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:05:31 EEST
19:05:31 KST

Reservations under the new system: why the government’s assurances failed to allay the concerns of business and parliament
Kyiv • UNN
The Cabinet of Ministers is finalizing amendments to the rules for reserving employees of critical enterprises, despite warnings from businesses and members of parliament about risks to defense capabilities and the economy. At the same time, the National Agency for the Prevention of Corruption identified a number of corruption risks in the government initiative.
The government resolution on reducing reservation quotas for critical enterprises has sparked a wave of outrage among business representatives, the public, and parliament. Today it became known that the Cabinet of Ministers has not yet made a final decision, but the debate around the proposed changes is gaining momentum. Despite assurances from Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi that there would be no radical changes for the defense industry and energy sector, business representatives and members of parliament continue to insist that the initiative be canceled and that consultations be held with business representatives, reports UNN.
Government decision to restrict reservations
On October 13, the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine considered amendments to Resolution No. 76, which regulates the procedure for reserving military-liable employees. According to media reports, during the meeting the government did not make a final decision on reducing reservation quotas for critically important enterprises.
The draft resolution proposed reducing the percentage quotas for reservations for enterprises in the defense-industrial complex and energy sector—from 100% to 85%, and for the municipal sector—from 75% to 60%. The relevant changes are to be revised within 5 days.
The document removed the provision excluding employees who have a deferment (students, parents of many children, and others) from the calculation.
The government decided to establish a Coordination Center involving the Security Service of Ukraine, the Defence Intelligence of Ukraine, the Foreign Intelligence Service, and the National Police, with the relevant decision to be further revised.
At the same time, business representatives pointed out that the proposed changes had not been discussed with them and that business had not received any official clarifications regarding the decisions made. Business associations sharply criticized the government initiative, noting that such a decision would deepen the personnel shortage in critical sectors and cause economic losses for the state.
The details will be provided when they are made public
Commenting on the issue of reducing reservation quotas for critical enterprises, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi confirmed that the government had not discussed this initiative with business.
This resolution is currently being worked on; it will definitely be revised, adopted, and published. There is no betrayal here. All the details will be provided exactly when they are published and all the relevant decisions are made. So the skepticism currently being discussed in society has no basis. There are no official decisions, so there is nothing to criticize at this point
At the same time, Koretskyi added that the mobilization process needs improvement.
There is no need for critical enterprises that are genuinely critical for both the defense complex and the energy complex to worry. I can say with great confidence that there will be no radical changes for these people, these enterprises, or these production facilities
At the same time, Koretskyi did not mention other critically important sectors that had already expressed concern about changes to the reservation rules and reductions in quotas.
According to the Prime Minister, 100% reservations create opportunities for manipulation, and enterprises with critical status can endlessly expand their workforce and reserve employees regardless of their qualifications.
Unfortunately, this system has already grown to a considerable scale. Therefore, this is the only reason why we are considering the 100% threshold—whether to modify it or nevertheless leave it as it is, because, unfortunately, there are many abuses
Koretskyi said that he considers enterprises that support defense capability and life-sustaining services to be critical. At the same time, the Prime Minister did not mention enterprises in related sectors that also help provide for the army or fulfill government contracts.
As an example, he cited a company that carries out work for "Ukrenergo", where all personnel are reserved. According to him, only some of the employees work under contracts for the energy company, while the rest are engaged in business.
At the same time, Koretskyi is evidently deliberately ignoring the fact that, in order to be able to operate, private companies also need to have funds to maintain their personnel.
Parliament plans to cancel the government's decision
Just now, Resolution No. 16160 was registered in parliament, authored by me and 62 other MPs from all factions and groups. (…) I will not put the adoption of this resolution to a vote because I understand that it needs to be prepared, but I have an appeal and a request to the Prime Minister and the members of the Cabinet of Ministers. This is not only the position of members of parliament; it is the position of business, think tanks, local government and, most importantly, energy workers and the defense-industrial complex — stop this decision, hold consultations, and only after that adopt the final document
Iryna Friz, a member of the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine Committee on National Security, Defense and Intelligence, said that the committee had considered the issue of changes to the reservation system announced by the government.
According to the report by representatives of the Ministry of Economy and the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine, as of now, there is still no final text of the Cabinet of Ministers' Resolution. It is still being coordinated, revised and awaiting a political decision….
According to her, during the discussion, parliamentarians pointed out that government officials had not substantiated the need to reduce reservation percentages for critical enterprises in certain sectors, nor provided methodological calculations or modeling of the consequences of such a decision.
She recalled that the Ministry of Defense had opposed reducing the reservation limits in the defense-industrial complex from 100% to 85%. In addition, according to her, committee members did not receive exhaustive arguments from government officials regarding the expediency of creating a Coordination Center, its functions and powers. The committee's decision points to the lack of justification and the risks of reducing quotas for the defense-industrial complex.
I must emphasize that the government's proposed reduction of reservation quotas to 85% for defense and energy enterprises and to 60% for heat and water supply enterprises and other utility services creates risks for the stable operation of both defense-industry enterprises and critical infrastructure
She added that the state's mobilization needs and the capabilities of the defense industry and critical infrastructure must be balanced.
The government must finally understand that without the people who produce weapons, restore the energy system and ensure the country's vital functions, it is impossible to guarantee the state's resilience during wartime. That is why changes must be developed and adopted exclusively on the basis of sectoral audits, an analysis of compliance with criticality criteria, and accountability and the inevitability of punishment for corrupt schemes involving personnel reservations
NACP warns: the government's decision carries corruption risks
The UNN editorial office has a decision by the National Agency on Corruption Prevention at its disposal, which contains comments on the government resolution.
In particular, the NACP recommended removing the provision under which the government proposed excluding employees with deferments from the calculations of the quotas, which significantly reduced the calculation base. In this regard, the Cabinet of Ministers took the comments into account and, as already mentioned, the provision was removed.
In addition, the Agency pointed out that the creation of a Coordination Center in the version proposed by the Cabinet of Ministers — without specifying the rules of operation, the deadlines for granting enterprises critical-importance status, and the grounds for refusal — "creates preconditions for corrupt practices".
According to the government resolution, the Coordination Center will provide recommendations, while the final decision on critical status will be made by the ministry. The NACP also has comments on this provision; the Agency believes that under such conditions, the recommendations should be mandatory in order to eliminate opportunities for abuse.
Thus, despite the government's assurances that there will be no radical changes for critically important enterprises, the proposed amendments to the reservation rules continue to raise a number of questions. The lack of economic calculations, proper consultations with businesses, and the NACP's comments regarding corruption risks indicate that the document requires further work. The government has not modeled the consequences of the changes either for the defense industry and energy sectors or for related critically important industries. Clearly, combating abuse in the reservation system is necessary, but it should not create new risks for enterprises on which the state's resilience during the war depends.

Former parliamentarian targeted for banned Israeli wine purchase
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
A complaint has been filed against former orthodox Protestant SGP MP Roelof Bisschop, who said publicly that he had bought wine in protest against the Dutch ban on goods from illegal Israeli settlements, public broadcaster NOS reported.
Pro-Palestinian group BDS Netherlands (Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions) filed the criminal complaint with the public prosecution service (OM). Activists had earlier reported Bisschop to the fiscal investigation service FIOD.
Bisschop bought two bottles on September 23, the day after the ban took effect, and posted a photo of them on social media. Two days later he told Christian television channel Family7 that the purchase was a “statement” against the ban.
Since September 22, the Netherlands has banned imports of goods from illegal settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories and the Golan Heights. The rules also ban buying and selling such goods, intermediary trade and any form of circumvention.
In its complaint, BDS Netherlands said Bisschop had deliberately acted against the sanctions policy and promoted this on several platforms.
“Anyone who, as a former MP, publicly announces they are deliberately testing the law can expect the OM to look at whether that is a criminal offence,” the group said in the complaint.
It is not yet clear whether the wine is covered by the ban. The producer, Teperberg Winery, has vineyards in the occupied West Bank and is on a UN list of companies active in settlements. However, it says these wines are made just inside Israel. Bisschop told NOS he did not know exactly where the bottles came from.
The OM said it is aware of the complaint and will assess whether there are grounds to open an investigation.

Dinosaur fossil hidden in London’s Natural History Museum for 100 years identified as new species
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:58:55 UTC
18:58:55 KST

The 120-million-year-old skull fragment belongs to Europe’s first known megaraptoran, a predator featuring powerful arms and sharp claws.
A dinosaur fossil that spent almost a century in the collections of London’s Natural History Museum has been identified as a new species.
The skull fragment belonged to Invictibellatrix amberina, a previously unknown carnivorous dinosaur that lived around 120 million years ago. It’s also the first confirmed evidence of a megaraptoran dinosaur in Europe.
The fossil was originally discovered at the foot of a cliff on the southwest coast of the Isle of Wight by amateur fossil hunter Reginald Walter Tooley. After his death in 1924, the Natural History Museum acquired more than 1,000 specimens from his collection, including the fragment.
Although scientists knew it belonged to a dinosaur, exactly which one remained a mystery for decades.
Now, researchers have taken another look at the fossil using CT scanning technology, allowing them to examine its internal structure and create a 3D model. Their full findings were published in the journal Royal Society Open Science.
"More dangerous than a T.rex"
Professor Paul Barrett, the study’s senior author from the Natural History Museum, says, "Despite over 200 years of collecting, the Isle of Wight continues to surprise us with new dinosaur species, and finds of carnivorous dinosaurs, such as Invictibellatrix, have been particularly elusive."
"Work like this shows the exceptional value of working with historical museum collections where there are still many discoveries to be made," he added.
Despite their name, megaraptorans were not the small, bird-like dinosaurs we commonly associate with the word "raptor". They were larger predators, more closely related to tyrannosaurs, with "slender heads", "large arms" and "giant curved claws", according to the Natural History Museum.
Invictibellatrix amberina is estimated to have measured between 3 and 4 metres (10 and 13 feet) in length and stood around 1.5 metres (5 feet) tall. It lived during the Early Cretaceous period, when dinosaurs dominated terrestrial ecosystems.
Researchers have also suggested that it may have had feathers, although its exact appearance still remains uncertain.
According to Dr Cassius Morrison, a researcher at the University College London's (UCL) Earth Sciences department, the species would have eaten small dinosaurs, lizards and mammals - similar to the role in the food chain a hyena holds today.
"It was not the apex predator of its time, but for humans this dinosaur would have been more dangerous than a T. rex. We would have been perfectly sized prey, about a third of their body weight. They definitely would have chased us. A T. rex would not have bothered, as we would have been too small," explains Dr Cassius Morrison, who led the study.
The discovery is particularly exciting because megaraptorans have previously been identified in Asia, Australia and South America, but never conclusively in Europe.

US greenlights Iraqi cabinet with blacklisted factions: diplomatic sources
Iraq's prime minister completed his cabinet line-up by appointing a US-designated terrorist after receiving Washington's approval, in a bid to advance efforts to disarm Iran-backed groups in the country, diplomatic sources told AFP.
On Thursday night, Zaidi announced the completion of his government, appointing Laith al-Khazali, a senior leader in the US-blacklisted Asaib Ahl al-Haq group, as one of his deputies.
Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi "secured tacit US approval during his visit to the United States in September" for the UN General Assembly, and during which he met President Donald Trump, a diplomatic source said on Friday.
The US agreed to the participation of some pro-Iran factions in the government "after the prime minister promised to move forward with his disarmament plans and provided guarantees that the groups will not attack US interests in Iraq", the source added.
The US, which wields significant influence in Iraq, "wants to help him advance his plans".
Khazali and his brother Qais, the leader of Asaib Ahl al-Haq, are both designated as "global terrorists" by Washington, which sees them as "violent proxies" of Iran.
But their group has emerged as a major political force, winning 27 seats in the latest parliamentary elections.
It was among the first to back Zaidi's plan to bring all arms under state control, says it has begun handing over its own weapons, and has not been publicly linked to recent attacks on US interests.
Ex-detainees
Washington accuses the Khazali brothers, both former US detainees, of attacks on its forces after the 2003 invasion of Iraq, including a 2007 attack that led to the capture and killing of five American soldiers.
A second diplomatic source confirmed that the US had given Zaidi the green light to complete his government with the participation of some factions.
One such faction, the Iran-backed Kataeb Sayyid al-Shuhada, part of the Islamic Resistance in Iraq that has recently claimed hundreds of attacks on US interests, secured the tourism ministry.
The US has previously turned a blind eye to the participation of some blacklisted factions in Iraqi governments.
But, this time the shift came after months of mounting pressure on Zaidi to disarm Iran-backed groups, which have long targeted US interests in Iraq and stepped up their attacks during the Middle East war in support of Tehran.
"Things changed," the first diplomatic source said, adding that the US had already shown in Syria its willingness to shift tactics, with its support for Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa, who was previously designated a terrorist.
Zaidi, who assumed office earlier this year with US blessing, initially set 30 September, the date marking the end of the US-led coalition mission in Iraq, as the deadline for factions to hand over their weapons.
He later withdrew it as talks continued, and then set a new deadline of 30 June.
Zaidi announced part of his cabinet in May, but the remaining portfolios were held up by negotiations among political parties, including demands from some factions for government representation.

One Ukraine out-produced third of EU’s steel. Russian strikes have now cut its output to zero
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:55:49 UTC
18:55:49 KST

Ukraine produced no steel at all last month, Oleksandr Kalenkov, president of the Ukrmetalurgprom association, says, according to Ukrainian Radio. Russian missiles have destroyed the blast furnaces at its plants, stopping an industry that ran for more than 150 years.
Over its independence, Ukraine smelted more than 42 million tons of steel a year, more than a third of what the entire 27-nation EU produces now. That industry is now in catastrophe: before the war, it accounted for over a third of Ukraine’s exports and up to 12% of GDP, and a month of zero output tears a hole in the entire economy.
“What is happening now is not just a hard or critical situation. It is a tragic situation when an industry more than 150 years old produced zero steel last month,” Kalenkov says.
The collapse is the end of a long descent, and 15 years ago the sector earned half the country’s foreign currency, Kalenkov notes.
Steel remains Ukraine’s second-largest foreign-currency earner, employing more than 70,000 people directly and paying close to $1 billion a year in taxes.
A pillar knocked out piece by piece since 2014
The war has chipped at the industry for more than a decade. Ukraine lost about a third of its capacity in 2014, including almost all its coking-coal mines and finally the Pokrovske mine, and in 2022 it lost the Mariupol production site, another 40% of what it then made, he recalls.
Even the plants left on government-controlled land have worked in survival mode since.
In 2021, the last year before the invasion, the mining and metals complex still accounted for more than a third of all exports and accounted for up to 12% of GDP, rising above 40% of regional output in Zaporizhzhia, Donetsk and Dnipropetrovsk oblasts.
The strikes that finished the furnaces
The decisive blow came from the air. Since August, a huge number of missiles, both ballistic and cruise, have targeted the plants, and practically all the blast furnaces still working were destroyed, he adds.
Ukraine’s largest steelworks, ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih, began a cold shutdown after four Russian attacks that killed six workers and halted primary steel production, while September output fell 4.7-fold year on year to 131,000 tons

How a Ukrainian Developer Built an FPV Simulator to Hunt Russian Shaheds
Ukrainian FPV combat drone simulator Remote Reaper officially launched out of Steam Early Access with version 1.0, marking the software’s largest update since development began.
The full release introduces airborne targets—specifically Shahed drones—alongside a time trial racing mode, new missions, and various technical enhancements, according to dev.ua.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Developer Vladyslav Fomenko built the project independently in direct collaboration with active military drone operators. To recreate flight mechanics with high accuracy, Fomenko personally tested uncrewed aerial vehicles at training grounds.
The software recreates real operational conditions, simulating the impact of electronic warfare systems, adverse weather, armored vehicle protection, and terrain topography.
"Shooting down Shaheds is more fun with friends," Fomenko noted, highlighting the simulator's online cooperative multiplayer feature, as reported by dev.ua.
The addition of aerial targets stands out as the core upgrade in version 1.0. Intercepting Iranian-designed attack drones requires operators to apply distinct handling techniques and approach vectors compared to ground strikes, alongside detonating the payload while airborne.
The update also incorporates a time trial mode featuring three dedicated tracks for flight skill practice, as well as new combat scenarios covering multiple rocket launcher hunting, infantry engagements in foggy conditions, and expanded tutorial courses.
Visual damage displays appear on struck targets, while opposing infantry can now deploy smoke screens to break line of sight.
Control options expanded to include gamepad support within a simplified control scheme, improved navigation on Steam Deck devices, and an updated flight compass with target tracking markers.
The program retains a detailed drone builder that factors component weight into flight duration, alongside a custom mission editor supported by Steam Workshop integration.
Previously, it was reported that Ukrainian defense company TENETA developed a new lightweight, single-use anti-drone device designed to counter enemy FPV drones and reconnaissance quadcopters.

Nearly 400 Foreign Companies Request Access to Ukraine’s Russian Weapon Intelligence
The Ministry of Defense of Ukraine has received more than 650 registration applications for its unified research portal for captured adversary hardware, known as TrophyLab.
Among these requests, 389 applications have come from foreign manufacturers of military equipment and weaponry. Registration on the portal is also accessible to Ukrainian manufacturers, military units, and government institutions, according to the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
TrophyLab gathers unique information regarding captured Russian military hardware to support engineers, scientists, and defense technology producers from Ukraine and partner nations.
The database is actively populated by units of the Defense Forces of Ukraine, the Main Directorate of Intelligence of the Ministry of Defense, the Security Service of Ukraine, and specialized scientific institutions.
Every registered researcher has the opportunity to submit a request to receive a sample or its physical fragment for independent evaluation.
According to the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine, access to TrophyLab enables faster and secure information sharing regarding Russian hardware to accelerate the creation of effective countermeasures for the Defense Forces of Ukraine.
The development comes as Russia continues introducing new weapons into its arsenal. Ukrainian military technology expert and defense adviser Serhii Flash said on July 14 that Russia has begun deploying the low-cost, highly maneuverable Banderol cruise missile, although production has yet to reach the planned rate of 120 missiles per month.
According to Flash, achieving that production target would allow Russia to launch an average of four Banderol missiles per day. However, he said the manufacturing facility has not yet reached the required output. The missile is launched from airborne platforms, primarily the Orion medium-altitude, long-endurance unmanned aerial vehicle.

WASHINGTON -- A bipartisan group of nine US senators has called for an investigation into disruptions to satellite systems supporting Ukraine's military as European officials rallied around Kyiv after President Donald Trump again attacked his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
The senators, including Senate Foreign Relations Committee Ranking Member Jeanne Shaheen (D), Thom Tillis (R), Dick Durbin (D), Susan Collins (R), Jack Reed (D), John Cornyn (R), Chris Coons (D), Lisa Murkowski (R), and Richard Blumenthal (D), sent a letter to the Department of Defense inspector-general calling for an investigation into disruptions to SpaceX's Starshield satellite system, which is overseen by the US government.
"We write with grave concern regarding reported disruptions to critical US-supported communications and intelligence-sharing capabilities in Ukraine that have endangered American personnel and potentially compromised Ukraine’s ability to defend against Russian missile and drone attacks," the letter read.
The senators urged an immediate probe to determine whether any US officials "directed, authorized, approved, or had advance knowledge of changes to intelligence-sharing arrangements, warning capabilities, or Starlink and Starshield services affecting Ukraine."
Elon Musk's SpaceX owns the Starlink system. Musk wrote on X, which he also owns, that "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS (President Trump)."
Zelenskyy criticized the throttling of Starshield, telling the Financial Times in an interview published on October 15 that such a move was "dangerous."
He also said Ukraine would defy an "energy cease-fire" unilaterally imposed by Trump -- which neither Russia nor Ukraine officially confirmed -- over the weekend and resume attacks on Russian energy facilities because Moscow had not halted strikes on Ukrainian energy sites.
"We're done," Zelenskyy told the FT after saying Ukraine had halted strikes on Russian refining operations for three days.
In response, Trump, who recently eased sanctions on Russian diesel exports in an attempt to bring down fuel prices -- told the staunchly conservative US media outlet Newsmax on October 15 that peace between Russia and Ukraine would only be possible if Zelenskyy left office.
"Zelenskyy is not a good guy for us to deal with," he said in an interview.
"He doesn't want to settle. He says he wants to settle, but he doesn't. No, I'm not a big fan of Zelenskyy," Trump said, adding that he believes both leaders wanted peace but found Zelenskyy more difficult to negotiate with than his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin.
Alexander Gray, chief executive officer of American Global Strategies, suggested that Zelenskyy should have delivered those messages to President Trump privately.
Speaking to RFE/RL on October 16, Gray said Zelenskyy should do so in a way that "doesn't make President Trump feel that he has to publicly counterpunch and create a cycle that does not serve Ukraine's interests."
He also argued that Zelenskyy's decision to resume strikes on Russian oil refineries posed a risk of creating a deeper rift between Kyiv and the Trump administration.
The sparing came as Zelenskyy arrived in Brussels for the second day of a summit of European Union leaders, where discussions are expected to focus on continued support for Ukraine, including protecting critical infrastructure ahead of winter.
Ahead of the talks, Zelenskyy said Ukraine's main priority was meeting its energy needs, while also noting the country requires additional air defense systems and funding for the rest of the year and 2027.
Speaking to reporters alongside Zelenskyy in Brussels on October 16, European Council President Antonio Costa reaffirmed that the EU's support for Ukraine was stronger than ever, stressing that this was no time to withdraw assistance or ease sanctions on Russia.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen added that the EU had supported Trump's proposed energy cease-fire but Russia had failed to respect it "for a single minute."
She added that EU sanctions would remain in place until Russia stopped the war.
Meanwhile, overnight Russian attacks injured five people in Ukraine's central Cherkasy region, where a drone strike set fire to an apartment building in Uman, regional officials reported on October 16.
Lutsk, in Ukraine's Volyn region, was left without electricity following a Russian drone attack, according to city authorities.
Russian authorities said their defense forces had repelled a Ukrainian drone attack targeting heating infrastructure in the Vladimir region.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin reported that 94 Ukrainian drones had been shot down near the capital over period of eight hours, while four were downed over the Leningrad region, according to the regional governor.
All four Moscow airports were temporarily closed amid the drone attacks, with flights diverted to other cities, Russia's Federal Air Transport Agency reported. An air raid alert was also declared in the Leningrad region.

====================================================================================================

Platform workers' grueling hours raising health and safety concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:39:00 UTC
18:39:00 KST

Platform workers' grueling hours raising health and safety concerns
Many food couriers and ride-hailing drivers in Estonia work exhausting hours that put their health and road safety at risk, but the government has no plans to intervene.
A recent study by the Foresight Center and the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications (MKM) found that a quarter of food couriers and ride-hailing drivers work more than 50 hours a week, well above Estonia's standard 40-hour workweek.
"The study also found that many couriers and drivers were working more than 100 hours a week," said Olavi Miller, an expert at the Foresight Center.
Such workloads can harm workers' health and raise concerns about road safety. But while the MKM doesn't condone excessive workloads, Hedi Arukase, the ministry's deputy secretary general for labor and equality, says platform workers are independent contractors, not traditional employees, and thus are free to set their own hours.
"Unfortunately, there isn't much we can do about it," she said.
Money is a major reason workers put in such long hours. About 90 percent earn additional income elsewhere, while platform work is the sole source of income for roughly 2,000 people. Two-thirds earn less than €1,200 a month.
Social protections are another concern. Not all platform workers contribute to pensions, and most rely on other jobs or educational institutions to qualify for Estonian Health Insurance Fund (EHIF) coverage. Fourteen percent have no health insurance at all.
Ex-minister: They chose this job
MP Signe Riisalo (Reform), chair of the Riigikogu's Social Affairs Committee and former minister of social protection, said platform workers are all independent, capable adults who have chosen this form of employment, but did also acknowledge a broader problem.
"Is this a broader problem for society? Yes, it is," Riisalo said. "And do we need to look for solutions? Yes, we do."
One option would be for platform workers to unionize, she said, "because social protections can be provided by an employer, which in their case is the platform."
A new EU directive aims to make platform work more transparent, and legislation to implement it in Estonia is currently pending in the Riigikogu. Arukase said the bill should help workers better understand their employment conditions and figure out how to earn more in less time.
--
Editor: Merilin Leetna, Aili Vahtla

Whatever Russia may say, sanctions are working, and we know that. They will gradually have a critical impact on the Russian economy. Even if the Russians circumvent sanctions, even if they adapt, this still hurts any economy – all the more so the economy of a country waging such aggression,” the Foreign Minister stressed.
According to Sybiha, Ukraine is proposing tougher restrictions on Russia’s “shadow fleet,” including a complete ban on maritime services and sanctions against the captains of such vessels.
“This is also a very sensitive issue. We know that many captains refuse to work on shadow fleet tankers because doing so poses a serious reputational risk. We will continue working in this area,” Ukraine’s top diplomat said.
Kyiv is also calling for a ban on the transit of Russian grain and other agricultural products through Europe, including Baltic ports, as well as further restrictions on Russian banks’ access to the SWIFT system.
“Russia still uses SWIFT, and Russian banks need to be disconnected from the system to the greatest extent possible. It is important to keep up the pressure on Russia to ensure that these sanctions have a truly shocking and devastating effect. There is still room to do more,” Sybiha said.
He stressed that sanctions pressure must raise the cost of Russia’s continued aggression. According to Ukrainian estimates, the war costs Russia about $1 billion a day.
“Putin understands only strength. To seriously force him to negotiate, pressure is needed, and the cost of continued military action must be raised,” the minister said, citing sanctions, the use of frozen Russian assets, international isolation and restrictions on access to technology as tools of such pressure.
Sybiha recalled that an EU sanctions package covering around 1,600 individuals and legal entities was adopted at a meeting of EU Foreign Ministers in Luxembourg. He said particular attention was paid to Russia’s defense industry and efforts to counter sanctions evasion.
The Ukrainian Foreign Minister also criticized the decision to remove Russian oligarchs Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from the EU sanctions list. Ukraine, he said, will seek to have both men reinstated and is proposing sanctions against more than ten other Russian oligarchs linked to Russia’s military-industrial complex and Putin’s inner circle.
Sybiha added that the United Kingdom had assured Ukraine it intended to maintain sanctions against Usmanov and Fridman. He emphasized that Kyiv would continue working with its partners to strengthen and expand restrictions against Russia.
As Ukrinform reported, the Council of the EU adopted additional restrictive measures against 1,569 individuals and entities linked to Russia’s military-industrial complex.

Study finds enriching life experiences may ease impacts of trauma on aging brain
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
17:29:59 CST
18:29:59 KST

CANBERRA, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- An Australian study has found that developing cognitive reserve via enriching life experiences could reduce overall cognitive and psychological impacts of traumatic experiences in later life.
The study, involving 745 adults aged 50 to 86, explored the effect of traumatic events on cognitive function. Participants completed several assessments to measure their traumatic event exposure, post-traumatic stress symptoms and cognitive performance, according to a statement released recently by Australia's Adelaide University.
About 87 percent of participants reported at least one direct traumatic experience, said Sabrina Sghirripa, a researcher at Adelaide University and lead author of the study published in the Journal of Affective Disorders.
"However, not everyone who experiences trauma develops cognitive deficits in later life, suggesting protective factors, including cognitive reserve, may promote resilience," Sghirripa said.
Researchers found that people with higher cognitive reserve were less likely to be affected by post-traumatic stress symptoms and maintained better cognition in the face of exposure to traumatic events.
Cognitive reserve refers to the brain's adaptability in maintaining cognitive abilities as it ages. It can be built throughout life by enriching experiences such as education and leisure activities, the study showed.
The findings suggest that developing cognitive reserve may help reduce the cognitive and psychological impacts of trauma, Sghirripa said, adding that interventions like leisure activities and social engagement could benefit older members of the community in building cognitive reserve.
"Staying socially connected and engaged in meaningful activities may help protect cognitive and mental health in later life," even among people who have had many adverse life experiences, she said. ■

EU leaders demand joint action to tackle soaring energy prices
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:28:19 UTC
18:28:19 KST

EU leaders are pressing Brussels for coordinated measures to ease soaring energy costs, bolster fuel supplies and support struggling industries, as the crisis strains national budgets and tests the bloc's climate ambitions.
EU leaders have called for a coordinated European response to the energy crisis, urging the European Commission to introduce targeted, temporary measures to ease the burden on households and businesses, including extending financial support to industries hardest hit by soaring energy prices.
After European Council summit negotiations that went into the night on Thursday, the leaders also raised concerns about the security of energy supplies, asking the Commission to improve the capacity and efficiency of European oil refineries, which have been in decline since 2009.
They also expressed interest in exploring voluntary joint energy purchasing, similar to the platform launched by the Commission to help replace Russian gas supplies following Moscow's invasion of Ukraine.
The calls came amid a severe energy crisis threatening European industry and leaving millions of households at risk of energy poverty this winter.
Rising energy prices and inflation rates have prompted several EU capitals to ask the European Commission for more support.
Italy and Greece recently urged Brussels to allow for extra spending without incurring infringements due to the extraordinary circumstances posed by the energy shock.
Diesel markets are expected to remain tight well into 2027, the International Energy Agency (IEA) warned on 14 October, and wholesale diesel prices in Europe could rise again in the coming weeks.
Diesel prices have retreated from September’s records above $200 a barrel, but benchmarks "remain nearly double the price of crude oil and their pre-crisis levels", the IEA stated.
EU countries received in May the green light from the Commission to offer direct financial support to the hardest-hit, energy-intensive sectors, including farmers, heavy manufacturing, and haulers. But as the energy crisis lingers, public funds shrink.
Greece’s PM Kyriakos Mitsotais called for a coordinated EU response rather than relying solely on national measures.
“Energy costs have fueled a new surge in European inflation,” he said on Thursday, arguing that Brussels must consider “additional measures and further flexibility” to help the most vulnerable households and businesses.
The Greek leader cautioned that negotiations would take time, saying he did not expect a deal “today or tomorrow”.
Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo has also called for immediate action from the EU to address soaring energy prices.
"We need short-term measures because we have to guarantee cheap prices for people and companies," he said.
Energy crisis squeezing finances
The measures are intended to cushion the immediate economic impact of the crisis, but they also expose the limits of EU governments’ ability to insulate their economies from geopolitical shocks.
Desmond Lawrence, senior investment strategist at the US asset manager State Street Investment Management, warned on 14 October that France and Belgium are slowly heading towards an unsustainable debt burden.
The shockwaves from the escalation in the Middle East have renewed concerns about disruptions to energy supplies and strategic shipping routes, particularly the Strait of Hormuz. Ukraine's military strikes on Russian refineries are also aggravating the fuel crisis.
EU leaders warned that the Middle East crisis risks causing lasting disruption to global supply chains, especially for energy, fertilisers and food — a predicament that may stretch the Commission's "targeted and temporary" measures indefinitely.
Such a scenario adds another headache to ongoing political talks on the bloc's next multi-annual budget, which was recently met with backlash from net contributors Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden for being overly ambitious.
The outcome of the talks will influence the EU's energy transition goals, which the Commission stands by as the most effective way to strengthen strategic autonomy and lower energy prices in the long term.
However, EU leaders also welcomed the Commission's proposal to delay one-year monitoring and reporting methane rules for oil and gas importers.
The decision was criticised by environmentalists who argued its revenues could range from roughly €5.3 billion to €13.6 billion under standard market pricing, spiking even higher during supply crises.
The proposal follows pressure from French President Emmanuel Macron, industry and the United States, the EU's biggest supplier of liquefied natural gas (LNG). It still requires approval by the European Parliament.

Fed’s Warsh sees AI boosting productivity but gives no signal on next rate hike
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:27:55 UTC
18:27:55 KST

US Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh said in Bangkok on Friday that the global economy has proved surprisingly resilient and called AI the most consequential change of his lifetime, but gave no hint on interest rates ahead of the Fed’s meeting this month.
The global economy has held up better than Kevin Warsh would have predicted earlier this year, the US central bank chief said on Friday, calling AI the biggest economic shift he had seen.
Speaking in Bangkok at the annual meetings of the IMF and the World Bank, Warsh offered no clue on the Federal Reserve’s next rate decision, due on 28 October.
Almost everywhere, the economy is showing a resilience "I’m not sure I would have predicted five or six months ago," Warsh said in a discussion on stage with IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva.
The Fed chair was most upbeat about the US, stating during the event that a broadening investment surge that "isn’t just AI" had given the economy "plenty of tailwinds", momentum "certainly not found everywhere in the world".
Energy prices have soared since the US and Israel went to war with Iran in late February. This, along with an AI investment boom, has fuelled inflation in many economies, forcing central banks to raise rates.
The Fed, which has seen inflation run above its 2% target for over five years, raised rates by a quarter point to 3.75-4% in September, its first hike since July 2023.
"At the Federal Reserve, we made very clear that we would deliver price stability," argued Warsh, who took over as chair in May.
He said he had heard the same "resolve" from central bankers in Bangkok, calling the wave of rate hikes, including two by the European Central Bank, a "synchronous tightening" that leaves "no free riders".
The IMF on Tuesday nudged up its 2026 global growth forecast to 3.1% but said risks were tilted to the downside. Rich countries also face soaring borrowing costs, with the 10-year US bond yield above 5% and the French bond yield trading around 4.8% at the time of writing.
A 'bumpy' road for AI
Much of Friday's discussion focused on AI, which Warsh said was "probably the most consequential change" for the US and global economies in his lifetime.
Before taking office, he had argued that an AI-driven productivity boom could curb inflation and make room for lower interest rates. On Friday, he acknowledged that for now, the investment frenzy was pushing prices up by fuelling demand.
Minutes of the Fed's September meeting noted that data centre construction had driven up the cost of chips, computer equipment and electrical components.
However, over time, Warsh expects AI to boost the economy’s capacity to produce, bringing a "huge benefit" at home and abroad.
He also expects it to change central banking as "we torture data with old-fashioned models," he said. "Not so long from now, it won’t be torture."
Despite the optimism, the Fed chair also warned that the road ahead was "likely to be a very bumpy one", both in understanding the technology and because "we really don’t know what the market structure is going to be".
Eyes on the next Federal Reserve meeting
Warsh, who has promised fewer hints about where policy is heading, kept to that pledge.
"I don’t prejudge meetings," he said, though he noted the world had "broadly conformed" to the Fed’s expectations since September.
US consumer price inflation rose to 3.7% in September from 3.4% as petrol prices surged, though core inflation, which excludes food and energy, was 2.6%.
Wholesale prices rose 6.3% year on year, the most since 2022, while the economy added just 29,000 jobs last month.
Bets on an October hike have swung this week, jumping from about 22% to around 50% after Wednesday’s inflation figures before falling back to about 30%, according to CME FedWatch, a tool that tracks market pricing.
Markets currently put the chance of a December hike at around 90%, while the September minutes showed that most Fed officials expect another hike this year.
New York Fed President John Williams, vice chair of the Fed’s committee, told Bloomberg on Tuesday that "it may be appropriate to have one more rate hike", but saw no need for more in 2027.
On the other hand, Fed Governor Michelle Bowman said at the Bangkok meetings on Wednesday that she felt no urgency to act.
The decision comes days before the 3 November US midterm elections.
September’s hike defied US President Donald Trump’s demands for lower rates, though he still backs Warsh, his pick for the job.
Friday’s remarks were among Warsh’s last before the Fed’s quiet period, which starts on Saturday and bars officials from discussing policy until after the meeting. Investors will next hear from him at his press conference after the decision.

The aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt (CVN 71) arrived at Yokosuka, Japan, on Oct. 16, 2026, with the cruiser USS Chosin (CG 65) and the destroyer USS Decatur (DDG 73), as the strike group prepares for the U.S.-Japan exercise Keen Sword.
The three ships of Carrier Strike Group 9 pulled into Commander, Fleet Activities Yokosuka, the U.S. Navy’s largest base in Japan and home of the forward-deployed carrier USS George Washington (CVN 73). The U.S. Navy said the stop will give crews time for routine maintenance and resupply before the strike group joins Keen Sword, a large joint field training exercise with the Japan Self-Defense Forces.
“Our crew is honored to visit Yokosuka and experience the rich culture and hospitality of Japan,” said Capt. Will Mathis, commanding officer of Theodore Roosevelt. “Port visits like this are vital for crew morale and mission readiness, allowing our Sailors to rest, recharge, and prepare to operate seamlessly alongside our allies during exercise Keen Sword.”
While in port, staff from Carrier Strike Group 9 will hold professional exchanges with officers from the Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force to align tactical procedures ahead of the exercise, which the U.S. Navy refers to as Keen Sword 2027. Keen Sword is held every two years and is designed to improve how Japanese and U.S. forces train, plan and fight together. The U.S. Navy did not give dates for this year’s exercise or say how many ships and aircraft will take part.
“The U.S.-Japan Alliance serves as the cornerstone of peace and security across the region,” said Rear Adm. Marcos Jasso, commander of Carrier Strike Group 9. “Every engagement with our JMSDF allies and the Japan community deepens the mutual trust vital to keeping this region free and open, especially as we transition to complex bilateral operations during Keen Sword.”
Before the visit, commanders reminded crews that they are expected to keep good order and discipline, follow the liberty policy and treat their Japanese hosts with respect. U.S. forces in Japan have tightened liberty rules in recent years after incidents involving service members, particularly on Okinawa, drew criticism from Japanese officials.
Theodore Roosevelt, a Nimitz-class carrier, carries an air wing of fighter jets, early warning aircraft, electronic attack jets and helicopters. Chosin is a Ticonderoga-class guided-missile cruiser and Decatur an Arleigh Burke-class destroyer, both armed with the Aegis air defense system and vertical launch cells for air defense and strike missiles.
The strike group is conducting routine operations in the U.S. 7th Fleet area, which covers the western Pacific and Indian Ocean, and will move from the Yokosuka port visit into bilateral operations with Japanese forces during Keen Sword.

Prime Minister of Ukraine Serhiy Koretsky states that 100% reservation for enterprises creates opportunities for significant manipulation, a problem that has grown to a large scale.
"100% reservation provides opportunities for major manipulations. If you have 100%, it means you can endlessly expand your staff and reserve people: and it doesn't matter whether a person is a repair worker or not, an energy worker or not. And this system has already reached a large scale, unfortunately. Therefore, this is the only reason why we are looking at the 100% barrier – to modify it or leave it as it is. Because, unfortunately, there are many abuses," Koretsky said during the "Question Time with the Government" in the Verkhovna Rada on Friday.
The Prime Minister noted that additional reservations continue to be granted by the tens of thousands monthly at such enterprises.
"It is necessary to separate criticality and the economic block. Because wages and the absence of tax debt do not always mean that an enterprise is critical. Criticality is the defense capability and life support of the state," he added.
To substantiate his words, Koretsky gave an example of a contractor performing work for an energy company, where only 20 out of 100 employees actually carry out the subcontract for that company, yet all 100 are reserved.

"The resolution is being processed, it will definitely be finalized, adopted, and published. There is no betrayal there. All details will follow once they are made public and all relevant decisions are made," he said.

Indian police launch New Delhi clampdown for Cockroach Party rally

Indian police launch New Delhi clampdown for Cockroach Party rally
Cockroach Janta Party standoff with government extended as youth-led movement calls protest over jailing of activists.
Authorities have tightened security in New Delhi after the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) called for a new protest over the jailing of two of its activists.
Thousands of additional police officers were deployed in the Indian capital on Friday as the Indian government appeared to prepare for further confrontations. The youth-led CJP movement has held a series of protests in recent weeks to demand India’s election chief resign. Its demonstrations have been met with a tough crackdown.
CJP supporters have been called to gather in New Delhi’s Central Park at 5pm (11:30am GMT). The rally was called after two of the movement’s leaders were jailed for five days this week for allegedly trespassing at a protest site.
Authorities have closed the park, citing “administrative reasons”, and set up metal barricades at key intersections.
CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke suggested police may try to arrest him before the protest but declared he and his supporters are “not afraid” and are “ready” to go to jail.
In a social media post, Dipke accused the government of hypocrisy and denounced police crackdowns against the movement.
Members of the government may never have come to power had they experienced similar protest restrictions, he asserted.
“The very party that is in power today spent decades organising protests, taking to the streets and questioning the governments of the day when it was in opposition,” Dipke said.
“Had the same restrictions, intimidation and police crackdowns been used against them, many of those who occupy positions of power today might never have reached where they are.”
The rally is just the latest facing a crackdown by the authorities.
The CJP has held almost daily demonstrations this month demanding electoral reforms and the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
The commissioner oversaw the removal of more than 130 million names from the electoral roll and is accused by the CJP of voter fraud. Election authorities said the changes were made to remove duplicate, deceased and fraudulent entries.
The CJP was founded in May amid anger over the leaking of exam papers and the poor prospects facing India’s youth.
The movement swiftly became a conduit for India’s Gen Z, many of whom feel disenfranchised during an unemployment crisis under Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s right-wing government. The movement has since forced the resignation of the education minister.
With the political opposition quick to support the protests, Modi has come under intense pressure with some analysts saying he is now facing the worst crisis since he came to office in 2014.

Liberman accuses Eisenkot of planning to join forces, create unity gov't with Netanyahu
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:16:44 UTC
18:16:44 KST

Yisrael Beytenu chairman Avigdor Liberman on Friday accused Yashar party leader and former IDF chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot of planning to join forces with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and the Likud party when forming a government after the upcoming elections.
"The campaign being run by Eisenkot is not intended to shift a single vote from the 'draft dodgers' bloc to the 'those who serve' bloc," Liberman said, referring to the issue of haredi (ultra-Orthodox) Israelis refusing to serve in the IDF as other citizens are made to serve months of reserve duty.
"This stands in complete contradiction with the agreements reached by the bloc's leaders during their last meeting, undermines unity, and raises one simple question: What lies behind this move?" Liberman asked.
Liberman said Eisenkot's strategy is to siphon votes from the parties that seek to enforce enlistment, then negotiate with Netanyahu to form a government once he has more mandates than Likud. To that end, on Thursday, Israeli journalist Ben Caspit reported that Eisenkot's Yashar party has recently decided to launch a campaign to draw votes from other parties in the opposition bloc, overtake Likud, and become the largest party in the Knesset. "The race to become the largest party is close. We must be the largest party and overtake Likud. Only then will we be the first to receive the mandate to form a government," read a message distributed to party activists.
"Regrettably, Gadi’s lack of political experience is reminiscent of a pattern we have seen before with IDF chiefs of staff who entered politics," added Liberman. "From Yigael Yadin and Ehud Barak to Benny Gantz, military rank and experience are no substitute for political experience. Even Yitzhak Rabin, following his first term as prime minister, needed many years to return, gain experience, and get re-elected."
'Ignore the spin...for the good of the State of Israel,' Eisenkot says
A short time later on Friday afternoon, Eisenkot shared his own comments, ostensibly in response to Liberman's accusations, although he did not mention Liberman -- or any other leaders -- by name.
"We are 11 days away from the [most] fateful elections since the founding of the state," Eisenkot wrote. "At this historic moment, we must keep a cool head and focus on the goal."
"I ask Israelis, those yearning for change, to ignore the spin and lift their heads toward the great victory we will bring for the good of the State of Israel," Eisenkot continued. "This is my mission, and it's the only thing I'm engaged in."
He then referenced the current administration, although he continued to do so without naming any particular politicians. "This [victory] must be the mission of...those who want to replace the leadership of October 7," wrote the former IDF chief of staff, "which must not continue in office for even one more day."
"After the heavy prices we have paid, the people of Israel will not forgive politicians who fail to rise to the occasion."
After decades in politics, Liberman 'hasn't done ten percent' of what Eisenkot has, Gantz says
Gantz, a former IDF chief of staff and defense minister whose Blue and White party has recently polled below the electoral threshold, responded to Liberman's remarks on social media.
"[After] 30 years in Israeli politics, Liberman hasn't done ten percent of what Gadi Eisenkot and I have done for the State of Israel," Gantz said.
"Ever since I exposed his plan to form a minority government with Bennett and the Arab parties, he's been under pressure and firing in all directions," he continued.
Liberman's original social media post insulted both Gantz and Eisenkot by calling the latter "Gantz II," attacking Gantz for running as an apparent opposition candidate before forming a unity government with Netanyahu in April 2020.
Eisenkot has repeatedly insisted he would not allow Abbas or Tibi’s Joint List to join his coalition, telling The Jerusalem Post that he did not consider them viable partners.
Yashar leads polls, Eisenkot criticizes Netanyahu
Yashar has been leading in recent polls and is part of the opposition bloc seeking to replace Netanyahu.
In a statement on Thursday, Eisenkot came out against Netanyahu, criticizing the prime minister for lacking strategic military objectives.
“Let it be clear: as long as Benjamin Netanyahu is in power, Hamas will remain in power,” Eisenkot said.
Shir Perets contributed to this report.

We are teaching children maths they will never use. Isn’t it better to help them speak fluently? | Simon Jenkins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:00:57 UTC
18:00:57 KST

At last the fourth R is born. Articulation – speaking – is to join reading, writing and arithmetic in the education canon. What has become the mighty struggle against the dictatorship of the screen can begin in earnest. The spoken word, human-to-human communication, must finally be recognised by the gods of reactionary schooling. The pundits call it oracy.
On Thursday, the education secretary, Lucy Powell, called the academics’ bluff. She wants a radical reform of the national curriculum in England to reduce “desktop” working in favour of verbal fluency and practical skills. This will take courage. For decades, education’s senior leaders have been ramming easily forgotten “subjects”, such as maths and French, into children’s brains so they can be judged and measured in league tables. These tables have grown ever more dominant as ministers seek to climb “global rankings”.
After the second world war, an “academic” secondary education was shaped by the increased demand for a university-educated workforce. Higher education was expanded, but Britain’s technical and vocational schools and colleges were relegated out of sight. Teaching became enslaved to exam quantification and lost contact with the real world.
But the act of excluding communication skills from this academic orthodoxy has come home to roost. Artificial intelligence and mobile phones are progressively distancing young people from adults and each other. I notice gatherings of young people who used to chatter, laugh and banter. They now stand gazing at their screens or they just shout at each other. Conversation – sharing, informing, discussing, sympathising – seems on the way out.
Speaking itself is going out of fashion. Research suggests that in the past two decades the number of words people say each day has shrunk by nearly a third. They prefer texting. A quarter of young people now say they never even answer the phone unless pre-arranged. They fear a phone call means bad news.
Powell’s promotion of oracy means teaching young people once again to use the spoken word to their advantage. It is about conveying what one means clearly; listening, debating and handling disagreement. Speaking well means using eye contact and appropriately adjusting your tone of voice. It means politeness and tolerance. Above all, it enables young people to present themselves to others effectively, whether in work, play, argument or friendship.
To the Greeks and Romans, oracy was the towering skill of rhetoric. It was central to citizenship. The New Education movement of Steiner and Montessori in early 20th-century Europe stressed building on the qualities of the individual child rather than imposing rote learning from above. It is significant that the movement has seen a revival in the Waldorf schools now favoured by California’s AI executives in Silicon Valley.
That such ideals of progressive education have long been drummed out of the English curriculum is outrageous. The aversion to the spoken word has corresponded with the increasing prominence of maths in the curriculum, its skills beyond foundational arithmetic irrelevant to all but a tiny minority of adults. Children need to master elementary maths in primary school. But after that they only need to know how to use a calculator. I wonder how many readers remember being able to answer this question from last year’s GCSE paper: “The volume of a sphere is 4/3πr³ where r is the radius. Work out the volume of a sphere with diameter 20cm in terms of π.”
It is extraordinary that passing this exam is still required for most apprenticeships. Yet while he was prime minister, Rishi Sunak wanted maths to be compulsory until the age of 18. Small wonder it has long headed the list of “most hated” school subjects.
Quite how the teaching profession will react to Powell is not clear. The hyper-centralisation of British government has meant ever more school time spent on exams. This has led to cutting back on individualised learning and creativity, which typically flourishes in teaching of the arts. Teachers are pressed to “teach to the test”, at peril of damnation from Ofsted. These days, only the private sector dares resist. Winchester college devotes an hour a day to its form of oracy: “div” and “forum” sessions, when pupils discuss contemporary topics not covered by the examination syllabus: scientific ideas, philosophy, politics, music, critical thinking and the acceptance of others’ opinions.
Such speech-centred concepts as group learning and peer tutoring are being pursued in some universities, and the cause was taken forward in the 2024 oracy commission report. But the catch is always resources. The essence of teaching people how to speak must lie in personal contact. It is in the human relationship of tutor and pupil, which was once the essence of teaching as a profession, not a mechanical skill.
One key might lie in killing maths. Leave it to its enthusiasts. For the rest, school should be about the world outside, a world of other human beings. It is about how to go about handling them that young people have most to learn.
- Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnist
