‘A direct cultural threat’: your questions on the rise of the right across Europe answered
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:00:56 UTC
18:00:56 KST

Support for far-right parties has been growing across Europe, with radical right, populist parties in coalition governments in Croatia, Czechia, Italy and Finland, and leading in the polls in Austria, Belgium, France and Germany.
The Guardian reported this year that nearly a quarter of voters in Europe voted for far-right parties in their most recent national elections, a fivefold increase since 1995.
In Germany, Alternative für Deutschland recently booked a historic state election victory in Saxony-Anhalt. Elsewhere, though – in the Netherlands, in Hungary and in Sweden, where the Sweden Democrats lost vote share – far-right parties have suffered defeats. But their ideas – and their influence on mainstream politics – are today clearly visible across the continent, notably on policies around immigration and law-and-order.
The coming months will see further crucial elections, beginning in Spain in November and continuing in France, Estonia, Finland, Greece, Slovakia, Poland and Italy next year.
How might these elections shape the political future of Europe? What is the impact of their policies – and what might prevent their continuing rise?
The Guardian’s Europe correspondent Jon Henley has reported for the Guardian from 23 of the EU’s 27 member states, while Europe community affairs correspondent Ashifa Kassam was on the ground in Sweden and Germany’s Saxony-Anhalt state to speak with people ahead of the elections.
Jon and Ashifa answered questions about their reporting and experiences. Read the Q&A below.
One user asked: It’s no secret in Europe that Donald Trump and his allies are funding far-right parties all over the continent. Trump is unpopular enough in Europe that even the majority of people planning to vote for the AfD et al despise him. So how can so many Europeans who hate Trump still vote for the far right?
Jon Henley: You’re absolutely right about the Trump administration’s efforts to promote far right parties in Europe. That was made very plain in the US National Security Strategy policy document last year – I wrote about that here.
But while there may be an ideological affinity between European far right and nationalist voters on issues like anti-immigration, hostility toward the EU, and softer stances on Russia, Trump’s “America First” policies (demands re Greenland, tariff threats, etc.) and constant unpredictability pose major problems for far-right leaders trying to look credible in Europe, because they scare all European voters – including far-right voters.
Leaders including Giorgia Meloni in Italy and Marine Le Pen in France have openly criticised Trump and distanced themselves from his more erratic pronouncements, conspiracy claims and hostility toward European security.
European far-right voters’ support for Trump varies from country to country but is broadly low – clearly peace and security in Europe matter more than anti-immigration sentiment. Ultimately, nation-first means putting your nation first, and Trump has made clear that the US’s interests are not Europe’s interests.
The evidence would seem to suggest that many of Europe’s far-right voters think their own far-right parties will be more responsible as regards (many of) those issues – though whether they actually will be or not is moot, of course.
00000000000000000000 asked: How do you measure when a grassroots movement represents a genuine structural shift versus an isolated vocal minority?
Ashifa Kassam: Our jobs involve covering a wide range of community actions, whether it’s people fighting back against datacentres, protests against tourism, or the vandalisation of mobile phone masts by people who seemingly linked them to the coronavirus pandemic.
Oftentimes the reporting starts small and local. For example, perhaps it’s focused tightly on a protest against tourists in Barcelona or a push to restrict cruise ship dockings in Dubrovnik. From there, myself and the editors often continue to watch these movements and their reach; are politicians responding in any way? Are others joining in? Will the movements lead to policy changes? These are the kinds of questions that I tend to consider when deciding how much to make of the grassroots movements and how much coverage to give them.
At times it’s been incredible to see just where these movements will go, whether it’s the housing protests in Spain that led to snap general elections or the opposition movement that coalesced around Péter Magyar in Hungary in 2024 and which, more than a year later, saw him oust Viktor Orbán from power.
Gramoun-kal asked: Can the EU survive the rise of the extreme right? What if AfD and RN get into power at the same time?
Jon Henley: One of the very few upsides of Brexit is that hardly any European far right parties now want their countries to leave the EU. Instead, they want to “transform it from within”, turning it more into a looser “Europe of nations”.
But that’s not to say the EU would not be considerably weakened by, say, a President Le Pen, who could paralyse decision-making, challenge the supremacy of EU law and push a “France First” agenda undermining the single market and Schengen free-travel zone and opposing EU expansion, climate action, etc.
I’m not sure there’s any imminent risk of the AfD coming to national power in Germany (and if Le Pen wins France’s presidential election, which isn’t certain but looks highly plausible, she is also unlikely to have a parliamentary majority, which will limit her room for manoeuvre).
Plus, the AfD is too extreme even for the RN – Le Pen’s outfit (which kicked the AfD out of its European parliament grouping a while ago over various issues including comments to the effect that not all Nazis were bad), has repeatedly made it clear it is not an ally of the German party and does not share its views on eg. “remigration” – the mass deportation of immigrants.
But for sure – if Spain, Italy, France and Poland all see far-right parties in government after elections due over the next 12 months or so, the EU will face some major challenges. I don’t think it will collapse, but it will certainly find it even harder to reach agreement on many major issues than it already does, and so move (even) more slowly. Natalie Tocci wrote a great comment piece about this.
OrangeSpaceMan5 asked: Do you see Nato and the EU disintegrating if we see Far-Right victories across Britain, Germany and France?
Jon Henley: No, I don’t see the EU and Nato disintegrating, just becoming a lot more complicated/difficult to run … The EU could be “eroded from within” above all by far right-led governments using their veto (as Orbán did with Hungary) in major decisions like the EU budget, EU enlargement, the green deal, etc. They may well also simply ignore EU law, as Orbán also did. And for Nato, see previous answer – it would survive but become more paralysed in terms of longer term decision making.
Ashifa Kassam: I think we saw a glimpse of how complicated things can become in the European parliament after an EU vote earlier this year aimed at increasing deportations. The immediate aftermath laid bare just how deeply polarised the EU has already become, as right-wing MEPs chanted “send them back” and centre-left and left-wing MEPs shot back with “Shame on you.”
ElendX asked: Why and how have the left and centre parties failed to respond to the concerns of the electorate? How do they now need to respond?
Ashifa Kassam: What comes to mind immediately is the housing crisis in Spain and beyond. It’s been just over two weeks now since the Spanish protests and encampments over the housing crisis burst into public view, laying bare the long-simmering anger over soaring housing costs.
I think it’s an issue that has long been overlooked by many left and centre parties across Europe, even as vulnerable people and minorities have been disproportionately affected, and analysts warn that the crisis could drive voters into the arms of the far right. Last year I spoke to Jaume Collboni, the Socialist mayor of Barcelona, who (along with 21 mayors across Europe) are urging the EU to treat the surging housing costs as a “new pandemic” by unleashing billions in funding to boost affordable housing and give mayors a seat at the table to ensure measures capable of tackling housing speculation. Speaking to me, Collboni warned: “We cannot remain stuck in the rhetoric of defending democracy, inclusive societies and equal opportunities if people’s standard of living is getting worse.”
I also think left and centre parties have done little to address the precariousness of the labour market, ie. the rise of gig jobs and, in many cases, the deterioration of public services. If you keep an eye on the Eurobarometer, the cost of living constantly ranks among the top concerns for people across Europe, hinting at the idea that this could be fertile territory for politicians to focus on. Immigration, in contrast, was in 7th place in the most recent survey.
Jon Henley: I think broadly speaking mainstream parties have failed to adequately address people’s concerns about the cost of living, declining public services (healthcare, education, transport), economic/job security, etc. – as I said above, fear of/anger at some kind of “loss of status” is one of the key drivers of the far right vote. (I’m not suggesting that’s easy – it clearly isn’t, economies are struggling.)
I’d also add that far-right parties are clearly extremely effective at exploiting voters’ concerns politically, including by pointing the finger at the group they think are most to blame and promising to fix things by getting rid of them.
And I’d also note that mainstream parties really have not helped themselves by adopting far-right parties’ framing on several issues in hopes of hanging on to disillusioned voters – electoral evidence shows that almost never works, mainly because, as Marine Le Pen’s father Jean-Marie put it, people tend to prefer the original to the copy.
Dc740 asked: Did you measure any change in online activity for extremist parties like Vox in Spain after the Yandex datacentre was targeted by Ukraine?
Ashifa Kassam: Funny you should ask – earlier this week, I sent out queries on this to several research groups, so it’s something we’re looking into. It’s a really interesting question. Last week, in an interview with news site Eldiario.es, the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez was asked whether he was worried about foreign interference in the elections given his high profile opposition to Israel’s war on Gaza and the US-Israeli attack on Iran. His answer: “Yes, and not only by nations, but also by non-state actors.”
Capitao_barbosa asked: How much foreign funding, especially from Russia and America, is being funnelled to these parties? And can we value how much indirect support (bots, disinformation by state actors, algorithm meddling on X, etc.) they are receiving?
Jon Henley: Our data team looked at this question a couple of years ago, before the last European parliament elections. They concluded a quarter of all private money donated to political parties in the EU was going to far-right, far-left and populist movements – aided by the fact that only a quarter of EU countries require parties to identify private donors – with €97m (about one in every seven private donation euros across the EU) going to far-right parties.
A European parliament report from 2023 estimated that about $1.18bn in funding towards organisations targeting LGBTQ+ rights and promoting traditional family policies flowed into Europe from 2019 to 2023, and a 2022 declassified US intelligence assessment found the Russian government had covertly funnelled at least $300m to foreign political parties, often in Europe, from 2014.
Ashifa Kassam: We’ve also had some recent reporting on the flow of funds from the US. In July, the Guardian reported that Donald Trump’s state department intended to allocate $12m to organisations in the UK founded by prominent conservatives. Of these funds, $7m was to go to 878, a thinktank that describes itself as being devoted to “the rediscovery of our ancient culture” and “ending mass migration.”
In July, the state department issued a notice of funding, offering grants for organisations and institutions interested in promoting what it described as “civilisational self-confidence in Europe”.
While research out of Europe, such as the Munich-based Ifo Institute, has found “no correlation” between migration and higher crime rates, the US state department notice suggested it was hoping the grants would lead to outcomes including reports on the impact of mass migration on local safety and tools to analyse impact of mass migration on democratic institutions.
One user asked: How serious would you describe the threat these far-right parties pose to democracy? And to what extent do you think there is a collaboration between them and powerful social media personalities or state sponsored online social media propaganda?
Jon Henley: Some far right parties definitely pose more of a threat to democracy than others. Political scientists divide far-right parties into those that essentially operate within basic democratic norms (“radical right” parties), and those that seek to overturn the system, to the extent even of condoning violence (“extreme right” parties).
If we take one example, AfD in Germany could be described as extreme right in some respects (and some local branches are indeed classified as such by German domestic intelligence). Some of its positions are in clear contradiction with liberal democracy: it is openly racist, homophobic, misogynistic. It believes citizens should be ranked by its own warped criteria, including ethnicity, gender and religious belief. It flirts continually with Nazi rhetoric, imagery and symbolism.
On this question I recommend this column by Cas Mudde, a top scholar of populism and the far right, after AfD won in the recent state elections in Saxony-Anhalt. He argues that mainstream parties have to wake up to the fact that they are not in a battle that’s about vote share and elections, it’s about democracy itself.
Ashifa Kassam: I would add that we’ve seen some fairly high-profile examples of collaboration, from Elon Musk’s repeated endorsements of the AfD on X to his 2025 X talk with the party’s co-leader, Alice Weidel. The Guardian has also regularly explored the interplay between the far right and social media, such as a 2025 investigation that looked at how a network of far-right Facebook groups had become an “engine of radicalisation” by exposing hundreds of thousands of people in Britain to racist and extremist disinformation.
KilmaSelth asked: Do you think the hard right parties tend to moderate as they approach power, or do they maintain their radicalism?
Jon Henley: Based on Meloni and Le Pen, I would for a long time have said yes – Meloni basically struck a bargain to get elected in which she promised to be responsible on the economy, in the EU and as regards foreign policy, as long as she could do her culture-wars stuff domestically. Le Pen has spent years “detoxifying” the National Rally and kicking out over-radical undesirables. But if you look at AfD, they haven’t moderated their language at all – if anything, they’ve hardened it – and it manifestly is not doing them any harm. And as Meloni and Le Pen have moderated their positions, we’ve started to see them being outflanked on their right, by the likes of Roberto Vannacci and his National Future in Italy and Eric Zemmour’s Reconquête in France. So I think we may be heading into a period where the former far right is effectively now part of the political landscape, like “regular” parties that will sometimes win and sometimes lose elections, and will be increasingly challenged on their right by more extreme elements.
Ashifa Kassam: Vox offers another way to look at this question, as the party was founded in 2013 by disgruntled members of the conservative People’s party (PP). Its leader, Santiago Abascal, is a career politician who was among those who saw an opportunity to push further on the right flank of Spanish politics when it came to Catalan separatism, immigration, abortion and LGBTQ+ rights. It was a hardline stance that was often (but not always) diluted when Abascal was part of the PP; now as a separate party, they’ve seized on their electoral momentum in some regions to push the party to heed their agenda.

Bulgaria seeks NATO anti-drone systems, says defence minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:00:23 UTC
18:00:23 KST

Bulgaria seeks NATO anti-drone systems, says defence minister
SOFIA, Oct 16 - Bulgaria has formally asked NATO to deploy combat aircraft and anti-drone systems to bolster its defences after a series of drone attacks on commercial shipping in the Black Sea, Defence Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said on Friday.
Drones hit two ships which caught fire off Romania's Black Sea coast this week. On Tuesday, a commercial vessel sank off Bulgaria's Black Sea coast following a drone attack, prompting Sofia to summon Russia's ambassador.
The attacks have highlighted the growing threat that drone warfare linked to the Russia-Ukraine conflict poses to commercial shipping near NATO's southeastern flank, prompting Bulgaria to push for stronger alliance defences in the Black Sea.
"We have sent letters and a request to the NATO Secretary General and the Supreme Allied Commander, urging them to strengthen our capabilities, which also means deploying additional forces on our territory. We are awaiting their decision," Stoyanov said.
NATO did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Stoyanov said he planned to meet his Romanian and Turkish counterparts soon to discuss coordinating action and a common approach to the situation in the Black Sea.
Bulgaria, which has proposed a moratorium on attacks on civilian ships in the Black Sea, also expects to join a NATO anti-drone initiative by the end of October. REUTERS

Why a new US–Israeli war against Iran could carry enormous risks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:00:22 UTC
18:00:22 KST

In recent days, three developments have emerged as key preliminary indicators that the US may be preparing to step up its military campaign against Iran. First, the dispatch of a third aircraft carrier strike group alongside additional American forces toward the waters surrounding Iran; second, the directive from the United States Central Command (CENTCOM) to achieve full operational readiness; and third, the continuation of economic pressure, sanctions, and blockades, alongside disputes over the Strait of Hormuz and diplomatic friction surrounding negotiations.
While these developments clearly signal an expansion of military options and an intensification of coercive pressure, they do not, on their own, constitute definitive proof of an executive decision to launch a broad war. This new force posture serves at least three strategic functions: deterrence, diplomatic leverage in negotiations, and operational preparation of a military option. Consequently, while a war posture increases the statistical probability of conflict, it does not in itself demonstrate a definitive decision to enter a major war.
Military power is not measured solely by the quantity of aircraft carriers, planes, or missile launchers. Rather, sustained combat power is a function of the equilibrium between consumption capacity, stockpiles, production, replenishment, human resources, logistics, and the ability to absorb the total costs of warfare.
Consequently, transforming a military posture into a major war requires the simultaneous presence of at least four structural capacities.
First, a sufficient reserve of munitions and weaponry must exist to execute initial operations and sustain subsequent engagements against Iran—a country that possesses the largest and most diverse missile arsenal in the region.
Second, robust equipment replenishment capacity is required, ensuring that if missiles, ammunition, aircraft, defence systems, or command assets are consumed or destroyed during hostilities, military industries can replace them at a commensurate rate—an outcome that appears practical implausible for the US regime.
These two requirements would appear to be unachievable at the moment. An April 21 report by the Center for Strategic and International Studies shows that in four out of the seven key categories of munitions analysed, expenditure during the 40-day conflict likely exceeded half of pre-war inventories, and replenishing some of these stockpiles could require between one to four years.
Alongside the depletion of ammunition stockpiles, the Ramadan War has imposed tangible costs upon the air fleet of the hostile United States administration. According to an official report by the US Congressional Research Service on 5 October, at least 81 US military aircraft, including fixed-wing planes, helicopters, and unmanned systems, have been destroyed or damaged.
Third, sufficient human resource and logistical capacity must exist to sustain long-term operations at a vast distance while simultaneously maintaining the US regime’s existing military commitments and global readiness across other regions.
Fourth, the capacity to absorb the economic and geopolitical fallout must be present, including the ability to withstand spikes in energy prices, supply chain disruptions and diminished oil transits through the Strait of Hormuz, fiscal strain, the depletion of strategic reserves, vulnerable military bases, and domestic political pressure ahead of the November elections.
Iran’s ability to disrupt confidence at the world’s primary energy chokepoint has become a strategic lever that substantially raises the cost of any military adventure for the global economy and decision-makers in Washington.
The cumulative weight of munitions constraints and the economic variables examined places enemy decision-makers before three plausible strategic trajectories:
In the first scenario, the American and Zionist regimes rely on the continuation of a heavy military posture, economic sanctions, maritime pressure, intelligence operations, and cognitive warfare without initiating a major new conflict. Operationally, this option is entirely feasible. Its primary appeal for Washington lies in avoiding further depletion of its vulnerable stockpiles of Patriot, THAAD, and Tomahawk missiles, as well as preventing additional aircraft losses. Nevertheless, evidence suggests that this path is not without cost or hazard: maintaining a state of neither war nor peace entails persistent insecurity in the Strait of Hormuz, oil flows remaining below normal capacity, recessionary pressure on global energy demand, continuous attrition of forces deployed to the region, and increasing difficulty in managing unintended maritime incidents.
In the second scenario, the US/Zionist axis considers executing limited, phased air and missile strikes against specific targets—including Iranian military, missile, nuclear, or energy infrastructure—rather than entering directly into an all-out war; an option cited by Axios sources as one of the plans under active consideration. Although the presence of three aircraft carrier strike groups and current stockpiles render such strikes operationally viable in the short term, the central dilemma of this scenario remains escalation control. When an actor initiates a limited attack under the assumption that the opponent’s response will remain bounded, it exposes itself to inadvertent escalation due to asymmetrical perceptions of thresholds and the absence of unilateral control over the defender’s decisions.
The third scenario—direct entry or a gradual slide into a full-scale regional war—represents the most costly and perilous trajectory facing the US regime and the genocidal Zionist entity. Should such a scenario materialise, the conflict is unlikely to remain unidimensional. Operationally, it could encompass, simultaneously or sequentially, high-intensity air combat, mass missile exchanges, severe disruption of the Strait of Hormuz, cyber operations, and strikes against enemy regional bases and energy infrastructure across the broader region. In such a context, a punitive operation could rapidly degrade into a multi-front war of attrition.
Alongside military variables, the autumn political and electoral calendar constitutes another factor influencing calculations regarding the timing and ceiling of escalation. The deployment of a third aircraft carrier and 10,000 additional troops toward the waters surrounding Iran coupled with the Pentagon’s directive to US Central Command to complete operational preparations explicitly demonstrates that the timing of potential operations within Washington and Tel Aviv’s decision-making circles is being weighed against the November congressional mid-terms, as well as the Zionist parliamentary elections scheduled just one week prior.
A further dimension concerns apprehension over Iran’s potential capacity to sever subsea internet cables, thereby completely severing connectivity across the Arabian Peninsula as well as the aggressor Zionist state, and disabling all exchange and financial markets dependent on this network infrastructure. Crucially, through the establishment of its National Information Network and its relative independence from western-dominated internet financial transactions, Iran has shifted the balance in this domain to its own strategic advantage.
From the standpoint of deterrence theory, inflicting costs that outweigh the scale of the initial strike often serves as a rational mechanism to fundamentally reshape the adversary’s cost-benefit calculus regarding subsequent actions. Given Iran’s documented capabilities, should such a miscalculation be committed by the US or the Zionist regime, a plausible strategic posture for Tehran would involve launching a multi-domain, asymmetrical, and extensive response designed to defy containment or mitigation. Consequently, even a limited military strike would impel Iran to formulate a response that far exceeds the initial scale of aggression. This underlying logic of an escalatory response to limited warfare significantly raises the calculative risks of any new military venture.
The principal danger in the current security environment is not necessarily a pre-planned decision to wage an all-out war, but rather the escalation—whether intended or unintended—of a small war into a major war through crisis instability.
If the deployment of military force as a pressure tactic leads to a miscalculation and a limited strike, and that limited strike is met with an asymmetric, multi-domain response, a cycle of reciprocal retaliation will take hold. This chain reaction could impose a war whose full consequences its initiators lack the capacity to absorb.

Flash floods destroy villages in central Nepal

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:51:27 UTC
17:51:27 KST

Flash floods have swept through Nepal’s central Gorkha district after a pre-dawn landslide on 11 October blocked the Budhi Gandaki River, triggering severe downstream flooding. Two villages in the worst-affected Chumanubri rural municipality were reportedly destroyed, with homes, roads and bridges washed away. Part of a hydropower station was also damaged.
After river levels surged from 2 metres to nearly 8.5 metres within hours, the national disaster risk reduction and management authority reported that 204 homes were damaged, and more than 650 people had been affected. More than 100 foreign trekkers were stranded in the popular hiking region. The floods come just two months after catastrophic flooding and landslides devastated parts of the country on the border with Tibet, leaving thousands dead or missing.
An exceptionally deep area of low pressure barrelled towards Iceland this week. The central pressure was measured at 931mb on 14 October. The pressure plummeted by 49mb in 24 hours, meeting the thresholds for explosive cyclogenesis, or a weather bomb. The system brought sustained winds of 55–60mph to the southern shores of the island before moving north-east through the North Atlantic towards Norway.
However, Iceland was spared the strongest winds as the track of the storm meant they remained out at sea. The system also affected areas beyond Iceland: a 108mph gust was recorded at Bealach Na Bà, in the Scottish Highlands, in association with a trailing 1,000-mile cold front that stretched from Norway to the mid-Atlantic.
Summer-like conditions have extended even further into meteorological autumn in Portugal. After temperatures of 40C at the end of September, on 14 October a maximum of 35.6C was recorded in the southern town of Mora, representing a climatological anomaly of more than 10C.
The heat was not localised, with numerous stations recording temperatures well into the mid-30s celsius. The latest forecasts show that the high pressure and unseasonably warm upper air temperatures will remain in place for the next few days. Looking further ahead, however, temperatures are expected to slowly return towards the average around the middle of next week.

New house sales in Türkiye rose 3.9 percent year-on-year to 51,519 in September, according to official data released on Oct. 16.
New homes accounted for 36.2% of total housing transactions during the month, data from the Turkish Statistical Institute (TÜİK) showed.
Overall house sales fell 9.3 percent from a year earlier to 142,390, as existing home sales dropped 15.3 percent to 90,871.
Adjusted for calendar effects, new house sales increased 3.8 percent annually. On a seasonally and calendar-adjusted basis, they rose 5.5 percent from August, while existing home sales remained unchanged.
Mortgaged house sales climbed 5.1 percent year-on-year to 23,397, accounting for 16.4 percent of total transactions.
Sales to foreign buyers increased 9.9 percent to 2,167, representing 1.5 percent of the total. Russian citizens purchased the most homes with 388, followed by Iraqis with 166 and Germans with 162.
In January-September, new house sales edged down 0.6 percent from the same period last year to 359,913, while total housing transactions declined 7.2 percent to 1.09 million.
In the first nine months of 2026, home sales to foreigners declined by 4.3 percent year-on-year to 15,308 units, according to TÜİK data.

Drone strikes in Black Sea raise fears of Russian escalation

2026-10-16
08:48:48 UTC

Romanian warships sail during a Romanian Navy led exercise outside Constanta, Romania, on April 16, 2024. (AP Photo/Andreea Alexandru, File)
A string of drone attacks on at least seven cargo vessels in the Black Sea this month, off the coasts of NATO members Romania and Bulgaria, has some members of the alliance wondering if Russian President Vladimir Putin is seeking escalation to test their support for Ukraine in its war against Moscow’s full-scale invasion.
The attacks in the two countries’ exclusive economic zones threaten a global shipping route and have left two people dead, with at least 25 still missing. They also run the risk of drawing other countries directly into the war for Ukraine.
Throughout the war, Russia has repeatedly bombarded Ukraine’s Black Sea and Danube River ports, leaving Kiev increasingly reliant on alternative routes to get its grain exports to markets in Africa and the Middle East. Russian drones have repeatedly violated Romanian airspace near some of Ukraine’s Danube ports.
In the latest incidents, fires broke out on two ships struck by drones on Oct. 14 and 15, one in Romania’s territorial waters.
Romanian President Nicusor Dan said on Oct. 15 in Brussels that “two drones” had hit the vessels but did not say whose drones they were. “There will be a reaction from the Romanian state,” he warned.
Increasingly, the suspicion falls on Russia.
“There is no logic in Ukraine attacking its own ships and crews, given that the outcome of all these attacks favors Russia, and indeed, the logic points in that direction,” Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev told his country’s Parliament.
“The problem is that we cannot prove it.”
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said on X on Oct. 15 that he met Radev and Dan to discuss security in the Black Sea and “the latest attacks on commercial shipping.”
“NATO has strengthened our posture along the eastern flank including with increasing counter-drone capabilities,” he said.
“NATO will continue to work closely with our Allies in the Black Sea, adjusting our deterrence and defense posture as needed.”
A source in Romania’s defense sector, who was not authorized to speak publicly about the incidents, told The Associated Press that the attacks are designed to hurt Ukraine economically and that “Romania is not the target right now.”
“All summer we’ve been hunting all kinds of [drone] debris, water drones, sea drones, air drones, debris in the water, on the beaches,” they said. “If this continues, someone should do something about that.”
The source added they have heard Türkiye “would like to summon all the riparian [Black Sea] states to plan a mission to escort these convoys” through a militarized safe corridor.
“I’m not sure about Turkish, but our Romanian vessels don’t have anti-air defense systems to protect against drones,” they said. “That would be a high risk for the Navy, for military vessels to escort this.”
In July, Romania, Bulgaria and Türkiye expanded the Black Sea Mine Countermeasures Task Force naval pact to “expand the missions to the protection of critical submarine infrastructure,” according to Romania’s Defense Ministry. It would include, it said, a permanent naval presence in Romania’s exclusive economic zone.
Bulgarian Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said on Oct. 14 that the country plans to join NATO’s Drone Edge project by the end of October. Launched in July, the initiative, which Romania also joined, aims to invest over $40 billion in “counter-drone capabilities” over the next five years.

Protecting property rights during wartime: is it possible to inherit property located in temporarily occupied territories?
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:47:39 EEST
17:47:39 KST

Protecting property rights during wartime: is it possible to inherit property located in temporarily occupied territories?
Kyiv • UNN
Occupation does not terminate property rights or inheritance rights. Heirs are advised not to delay submitting an application, to collect evidence, and, if necessary, to apply to court.
The full-scale armed aggression of the Russian Federation against Ukraine has presented the domestic legal system with a number of challenges that law-enforcement practice had not previously encountered systematically. One such challenge has been the formalization of inheritance rights to property located in temporarily occupied territories. This concerns tens of thousands of real estate properties, including residential buildings, apartments, and land plots, whose owners have died, while their heirs are forced to exercise their rights in the absence of physical access to the property, the loss of title documents, and the objective impossibility of carrying out some legally significant actions. Attorney Anastasiia Tsykalo, head of the administrative law practice at the "LOGIC Law Company," told UNN in a comment how property remaining in the TOTs is inherited.
The attorney explains that the starting point for any legal analysis of this category of cases is that the fact of a territory’s temporary occupation does not, in itself, terminate a citizen’s ownership rights to property and, accordingly, does not deprive their heirs of the right to inherit.
"This is consistent both with the constitutional guarantees of the right to private property and with the provisions of the Law of Ukraine "On Ensuring the Rights and Freedoms of Citizens and the Legal Regime in the Temporarily Occupied Territory of Ukraine," which expressly defines the occupied territories as an integral part of the territory of Ukraine. Thus, the legal problem faced in practice lies not in the very existence of the right, but in the difficulty of exercising, confirming, and formalizing it under conditions in which the usual mechanisms for interacting with government authorities and accessing documents have become significantly more complicated," Tsykalo states.
Do not put off inheritance until later
According to the attorney, one of the most common problems in cases involving the inheritance of property left in temporarily occupied territories is the passive position of heirs.
"In practice, situations are often encountered in which people postpone contacting a notary, waiting for the territory to be de-occupied, access to the real estate to be restored, or the possibility of obtaining documents that remain at its location. At the same time, such a position may create additional legal risks," says Anastasiia Tsykalo, head of the administrative law practice at the "LOGIC Law Company."
The attorney emphasizes that the Civil Code of Ukraine provides a six-month period for accepting an inheritance by submitting the relevant application. Missing this period does not in itself mean the loss of the right to inherit; however, it may subsequently require applying to court and proving the validity of the reasons why the heir was unable to exercise their right in a timely manner.
"When considering such cases, courts assess the specific circumstances of each situation, including the person’s ability to contact a notary, the existence of objective obstacles related to military actions or the occupation of the territory, as well as the heir’s conduct and actions aimed at accepting the inheritance. That is why, in cases of this category, it is important not only to formally comply with the established deadlines, but also to promptly record the person’s intention to accept the inheritance and take the necessary legal measures to protect their rights," the lawyer explains.
According to Tsykalo, in such cases the attorney’s primary task is to timely prevent risks arising for the heir and ensure that an application to accept the inheritance is submitted even in the absence of a complete set of documents for the property. It is important here that Ukrainian legislation provides special mechanisms for formalizing inheritance rights for internally displaced persons and citizens residing in areas of active hostilities or temporarily occupied territories, including the possibility of contacting a notary regardless of the place where the inheritance was opened in cases established by law.
The loss of the original property documents does not mean the loss of ownership rights
Another significant problem in cases in this category is proving the deceased’s ownership of the real estate in the absence of the original documents, which physically remained in the occupied territory, were lost, or were issued decades ago under procedures that do not correspond to modern registration systems.
"In such a situation, the absence of the original document is not tantamount to losing the ability to formalize an inheritance. The subject of an attorney’s professional legal work is a systematic search for alternative sources confirming ownership: information from the State Register of Real Rights to Real Estate and archival registers that existed before its introduction; sale and purchase, gift, and exchange agreements; privatization certificates; state acts confirming ownership of land; decisions of local self-government bodies on the allocation or assignment of land plots; technical documentation from the Bureau of Technical Inventory; and other written evidence that indirectly confirms the fact of possessing and disposing of the property," the lawyer lists possible ways to resolve the problem.
If the evidence is insufficient, go to court
If the totality of the available evidence is insufficient for the notarization of the inheritance, it becomes necessary to apply to the court to establish the relevant legal fact, in particular, the fact that a title document belongs to the deceased or the fact of the deceased’s ownership, which constitutes an independent category of cases in separate proceedings.
Established case law demonstrates that there is no universal algorithm, the attorney says.
The scope of legal support, the lawyer explains, depends on a combination of factors: whether documents are available, the circle of heirs and potential disputes between them, the nature of the real estate, and the date on which the inheritance was opened in relation to the beginning of the occupation of the particular territory. In some cases, standard notarial proceedings based on registry information are sufficient; in others, a full-fledged court process is necessary.
According to Tsykalo, the attorney’s task in this category of cases is a preliminary legal assessment: establishing the fact that the inheritance was accepted in a timely manner, evaluating the sufficiency of the evidentiary basis, determining whether legal facts need to be established through court proceedings, and forecasting the risk of future disputes between the heirs.
"Formalizing an inheritance involving property left in temporarily occupied territories is one of the most challenging areas of modern civil-law practice. The war has created significant obstacles to the exercise of inheritance rights, but it has not terminated citizens’ rights to the property belonging to them. The decisive principle in such cases should be the timeliness of action by the heir and their legal representative: contacting a notary, properly recording acceptance of the inheritance, and collecting and preserving evidence of ownership must be carried out regardless of the actual possibility of accessing the property itself. Protecting ownership rights in wartime consists not only in restoring violated rights, but also in taking measures in advance to prevent possible legal risks," the attorney concludes.

Mystery foreign buyer pays for its own custom F-35
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:38:38 UTC
17:38:38 KST

- An unnamed foreign customer is paying Lockheed Martin $18.8 million for development and integration work on an F-35 variant tailored to its requirements.
- The award continues a contract that funded similar work in 2022 and 2025, with the new effort running through December 2030.
An unnamed foreign government is paying Lockheed Martin another $18.8 million to develop and integrate a version of the F-35 fighter jet built to its own specifications, the U.S. Department of War said on Oct. 15.
The Pentagon’s daily contract announcement said the modification to an existing contract with Lockheed Martin Aeronautics in Fort Worth, Texas, adds scope for system development, demonstration and integration work on an F-35 variant tailored to the requirements of an unspecified Foreign Military Sales customer. The customer is covering the full $18.8 million, which was obligated when the contract was signed.
Foreign Military Sales is the government-to-government route Washington uses to sell weapons abroad, and Pentagon contract notices sometimes leave the buyer unnamed when the customer’s identity is considered sensitive.
About 80% of the work will take place in Fort Worth, where Lockheed builds the F-35, and the remaining 20% at undisclosed locations in the continental United States. The work is scheduled to run through December 2030, and Naval Air Systems Command at Patuxent River, Maryland, which handles F-35 contracting, awarded the sole-source deal.
The award is the latest step in a long-running effort on the same contract. The U.S. Navy awarded Lockheed a $53.4 million modification in August 2022 for continued engineering on the design and development of a Joint Strike Fighter variant tailored for an unspecified FMS customer, followed by a $12.9 million modification in August 2025, according to federal contracting records. The new action, numbered P00011, now combines cost-plus-incentive-fee and firm-fixed-price terms.
The F-35 comes in three versions: the conventional-takeoff F-35A, the short-takeoff and vertical-landing F-35B, and the carrier-based F-35C. Lockheed has delivered jets to more than a dozen foreign air forces, and some customers integrate national weapons, communications or electronic warfare gear on their aircraft. Israel’s F-35I Adir is the best-known example of a country-specific version, carrying Israeli-developed systems on the F-35A airframe.
When a similar tailored-variant contract surfaced in 2021, aviation analysts speculated about which country was behind it, with Key Aero pointing to customers such as Singapore that were then taking first deliveries. The Pentagon has never publicly named the customer under this contract.
The latest award comes as F-35 production remains near record levels. Lockheed delivered 191 F-35s in 2025, and recent long-lead contracts for Lots 20 and 21 cover nearly 200 more jets for U.S. services, partner nations and foreign buyers.
Work on the tailored variant under the new modification is set to continue for more than four years, through December 2030.

The achievement follows the group’s return to full-group activities after its seven members completed South Korea’s mandatory military service.

Spotify’s own newsroom said Arirang became the most-streamed K-pop album in the platform’s history on March 20.
In April, Spotify ranked BTS 12th on its list of the most-streamed artists of all time, based on data through that month.
The figures highlight BTS’s international reach and the global popularity of South Korean pop music, which has expanded through streaming platforms and social media.
After debuting in 2013, BTS became one of the world’s most successful K-pop groups.
Its international successes include topping the Billboard Hot 100 with songs such as “Dynamite” and “Butter,” helping expand the global reach of South Korean pop music.

No, this oil tanker didn’t carry Russian diesel to the United States
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:36:46 UTC
17:36:46 KST

No, this oil tanker didn’t carry Russian diesel to the United States
Following US President Donald Trump's October 9 announcement of an agreement signed with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel into the United States, a number of pro-Russian social media accounts began claiming that a Russian oil tanker was already carrying thousands of barrels of diesel to the United States. The ship was actually carrying fertiliser.
US President Donald Trump announced on Friday, October 9, that he had reached an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import millions of tons of Russian diesel.
“Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter. Additionally, based on the condition of their Diesel Refineries, Russia will then deliver, within a short period of time, 3,000,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel,” Trump wrote on his platform Truth Social.
The next day, the pro-Russian X account Russian Market (which uses the handle @runews) posted that Russian diesel was already being delivered to the United States, scarcely a day after the deal.
The account claimed that the Minerva Zen, an oil and chemical tanker, was carrying close to 280,000 barrels of diesel from Russia… and was bound for the United States. The post even featured a map of the route it was taking, starting with when the cargo was supposedly loaded on September 22 in Saint Petersburg, Russia.
The fake news spread quickly, appearing in different posts and garnering more than 570,000 views on X. It was also picked up by media outlets in Nigeria.
A ship carrying fertiliser, according to Tanker Trackers
This claim, however, is wrong. The Minerva Zen was not carrying diesel from Russia.
It is true that the Minerva Zen, an oil and chemical tanker (which means it is equipped to carry chemical products as well as petrol products), did leave the port in Saint Petersburg on September 23. You can see this on the site Global Fishing Watch, a site that makes it possible to follow marine traffic.
MarineTraffic, another site that tracks ships across the globe, shows that the Minerva Zen docked in Wilmington, North Carolina on the night of October 11 to 12.
The FRANCE 24 Observers team spoke to Tankertrackers.com, a company specialised in tracking oil tankers in particular, who said that the Minerva Zen wasn’t carrying diesel but fertiliser, specifically urea ammonium nitrate (UAN). This information was confirmed by the economic intelligence company Vortexa.
“When the US imposed sanctions on Russia back in February/March 2022, they banned the import of hydrocarbons such as crude oil, fuel oil, LNG, etc., but they allowed fertiliser,” Tanker Trackers said.
As you can see on a site that records imports, Russian fertiliser was also imported into Wilmington back in June. The June cargo was delivered to a company called Eurochem North America, which specialises in fertiliser production. According to Tankertrackers, the October 12 delivery was also bound for Eurochem North America.
Cargo not unloaded in the port’s petrol terminal
Another supporting the information that the Minerva Zen was not carrying diesel is that the tanker was not unloaded in the port’s "Apex Oil Co Wilmington" petrol terminal, which is located to the south of Wilmington port.
According to the data gathered by MarineTraffic, the tanker was unloaded in the “NSCPA” Terminal located to the north of the port. This terminal is where agricultural and chemical products as well as containers are unloaded.
Finally, Minerva Marine, the company that owns the Minerva Zen, told US local TV station Wwaytv3 that the tanker was carrying urea ammonium nitrate, not diesel.
This article has been translated from the original in French by Brenna Daldorph.

BRUSSELS, Belgium — Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis expressed his disdain for EU plans to earmark billions of euros of support for Ukraine in its next seven-year budget, in comments made to journalists at the Oct. 16 summit of EU leaders in Brussels.
The EU operates on a seven-year budget cycle that needs to be unanimously agreed upon, and leaders hope to reach consensus on the 2028-2034 budget before the end of the year, as 2027 will be a bumper year for elections across the bloc.
While consensus on the budget as a whole remains out of reach, support for Ukraine seemed like a consensus issue until Babis' latest comments.
"I don't like that there are 100 billion euros ($112 billion) from the European budget for Ukraine, that this money should be borrowed," Babis said.
"It should not be in the multi-year financial framework, where member states don't have enough money," he added.
The 100 billion euros figure is already outdated, reflecting the amount initially proposed for the budget by the European Commission earlier in the year.
That figure was reduced to 89 billion euros ($100 billion) in June as part of a first compromise proposal, and it remained unchanged in the second and latest compromise, published Oct. 10.
"In any case, Czechia will not guarantee for it," Babis added.
Surprising in the other direction was Babis' criticism of U.S. President Donald Trump, after portraying himself as aligned with Trump for several years.
"Trump effectively betrayed us by concluding the business deal with Putin, and we have to do something," Babis said, echoing President Volodymyr Zelensky's take on a set of recent pro-Russian moves made by the U.S. against Ukraine.
Babis said the day before that Europe needs to agree on how to proceed with issues such as peace talks, given that at the moment, "we are completely out."
His turn on Trump brings Babis closer to the European mainstream, with many EU leaders not holding back in condemning the U.S. president for his latest overtures towards Moscow.

====================================================================================================

Government agrees 60 million euro fuel-price relief package, rejects Finns Party proposal
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:24:02 EEST
17:24:02 KST

The government has reached an agreement on a 60 million euro package aimed at easing the impact of rising fuel prices.
Environment and Climate Minister Sari Multala (NCP) confirmed to reporters in Parliament on Thursday that a deal had been agreed, noting that all governing parties support the package as a whole.
The measures include a reduction in vehicle tax, an increase in the maximum commuting expense deduction, and fuel subsidies for the transport, agriculture and forestry sectors.
The government has also agreed to introduce flexibilities in the fuel distribution obligation, which sets requirements for the share of renewable fuels blended into transport fuels. The limits on cross-fulfilment and over-compliance will both rise from 30 percent to 100 percent, allowing companies to meet their obligations more cost-effectively, the government said.
However, the government has not adopted the broader reduction in the distribution obligation advocated by the Finns Party.
The package consists of: 30 million euros for fuel subsidies for businesses in the transport, agriculture and forestry sectors, 20 million euros to reduce vehicle tax, up from the previously agreed 10 million euros, and 10 million euros to raise the maximum commuting expense deduction from 7,000 euros to 7,800 euros in 2027.
Multala acknowledged that the measures would have only a limited impact on consumers’ fuel costs.
"We cannot afford to make tax cuts worth hundreds of millions, for example," she said.
According to a press release, published by the ministry on Friday, the 60 million euro package will be funded from within the government's spending limits.
Of the total, 40 million euros will be redirected from funding for biogenic carbon capture capacity that will go unused this year, with the remaining 20 million euros coming from the cutting of funding for basic transport infrastructure management.
Finns Party says measures are insufficient
The Finns Party has criticised the agreement, arguing that the package should have gone further in easing the fuel distribution obligation to bring down prices at the pump.
Jani Mäkelä, chair of the Finns Party parliamentary group, said his party had accepted the agreement because "some solution had to be found".
"The government seemed to be quite incapable of acting in this matter, and the prime minister also had to save face," Mäkelä said.
Mäkelä further argued that easing the distribution obligation, as proposed by his party, could have reduced fuel prices at the pump by a significant amount.
He said the fact that the government had agreed on the package was not sufficient reason to rule out that option.
"If the distribution obligation cannot be compromised in a situation where the price of fuel is so high, it reflects a certain mindset," Mäkelä said.
Multala was asked whether the Finns Party could have been persuaded to accept the agreement if the funding had come from money allocated to climate action. She replied that the question should be put to the party itself.
Orpo defends government’s decision
Speaking in Brussels on the sidelines of an EU meeting, Prime Minister Petteri Orpo (NCP) said that easing the distribution obligation would not have brought down fuel prices quickly.
"Being in the government means that when we are making decisions together, sometimes it is difficult to defend them, even if we have made the decision ourselves," Orpo said.
He stressed that the government had little room for manoeuvre during the negotiations, but noted he was pleased that the money had been directed towards commuters and professional transport.
Fuel prices are also on the agenda at the EU summit. Orpo said high prices at the pump were linked to the situation in the Strait of Hormuz and Russia’s war of aggression in Ukraine.
Relief measures will not lower pump prices directly
Hanna Kalenoja, a leading transport expert at the Central Chamber of Commerce, said the measures would not directly affect petrol and diesel prices.
Instead, they would ease costs for some motorists and businesses, but not all, she noted.
The vehicle tax reduction will be reflected in the tax bills of eligible car and van owners, rather than at the petrol station.
For example, a household whose vehicle tax period began in July would not see the reduction until its next tax period in July next year, Kalenoja said.
She estimated that the vehicle tax cut would save eligible motorists around 12 euros per year. The reduction applies to older cars and vans.
The increase in the maximum commuting expense deduction, meanwhile, could benefit people with high travel costs.
The government also plans to raise the maximum deduction, with Kalenoja estimating that the change would benefit people who commute more than 60 kilometres.
The deduction can be adjusted through a revised tax card, although eligibility depends on the circumstances of the commute. In some cases, expenses can be deducted based on the use of a private car if public transport is not reasonably accessible.
The fuel subsidies are aimed at businesses in the transport, agriculture and forestry sectors. A similar subsidy was made available retrospectively through the State Treasury in 2022.
Experts welcome decision to retain distribution obligation
Kalenoja said she was largely relieved by the government's decision, particularly because it did not ease the distribution obligation.
The requirement sets the minimum share of renewable fuels that must be included in transport fuels. Reducing it would lower the share of low-emission biofuels.
According to experts, easing the obligation would not necessarily have an immediate impact on pump prices. Kalenoja also warned that it could undermine planned investments in the biogas sector.
"It is a big relief that the decision not to lower the distribution obligation was made now," she said.
The Confederation of Finnish Industries (EK) also welcomed the decision in a statement on Thursday.
However, Kalenoja said it was disappointing that the government had not included a reduction in diesel excise duty in the package.

Russia’s Digital Development Ministry has proposed using artificial intelligence to analyze VPN services’ characteristics, aiming to detect and block them more effectively.
The proposal appears in one draft version of a national plan for implementing AI technologies through 2030, the Russian business daily Kommersant reported.
The plan’s drafters said AI could achieve 95% effectiveness in blocking VPN services.
The Digital Development Ministry told Kommersant that “the current version of the draft national plan for implementing AI technologies contains no such information.”
A source who spoke to the outlet, familiar with discussions around the initiative, said algorithms for intelligent traffic analysis are already in use, though these do not constitute AI.
“AI tools make it possible to find VPN servers relatively quickly based on indirect signs: how a node behaves, what hosting it uses, what neighboring addresses look like. And most importantly, this makes it possible to respond more quickly to changes in network activity,” a source in the industry told Kommersant.
However, several sources told the outlet that the use of AI, “especially during the initial stages of training,” would likely result in the erroneous blocking of “legitimate traffic.”
Demand for VPNs has surged in Russia amid blocks on popular social networks, services, and messaging apps. Russian authorities have responded by stepping up efforts to combat circumvention of these blocks. Russia’s budget for the next three years earmarked a record 60 billion rubles for traffic filtering. Reports have repeatedly said the Digital Development Ministry wants to charge higher rates for international traffic (operators treat VPN traffic as international).

"After about 10 minutes, they tried to make me get up; they pushed me back to the ground and continued kicking me," she said. "I tried to hold on to my cameras and my side bag, but in the end they just ripped everything from me and kept kicking me."
Mateh Binyamin Regional Council accuses PA of bringing terrorists to attack Israelis
The Mateh Binyamin Regional Council provided a different course of events.
According to the council, the Palestinian Authority "led hundreds of anarchists and terrorists into a direct confrontation with Israelis near Abu Falah, all under the cover of the olive harvest."
"Footage from the scene shows terrorists launching fireworks directly at people and hurling stones at Israelis, while journalists stand behind them, documenting this deliberate provocation," the council said.
"The event was orchestrated by the PA; its patrol vehicles were present and highly visible at the scene, even though it is in Area B, where Israel holds responsibility for security," it added.
"Clashes broke out between Arabs and Israelis, eventually being dispersed by Border Police officers who arrived at the location. According to reports, several activists were injured during the confrontations," the council said.
The council did not explicitly comment on Levine's reported wounds.
The event was part of four incidents of nationalist-motivated violence and clashes between Israelis and Palestinians which were reported overnight and on Friday morning at several locations across the West Bank, including several olive groves.
The incidents reportedly involved vehicles being set on fire, attacks on Palestinian olive harvesters, and attacks on Palestinian homes.
In the village of Burin, a confrontation broke out during the olive harvest. Additional incidents were reported in the village of Burqa, east of Ramallah, and in Turmus Ayya. The incidents reportedly included at least four vehicles being set on fire, one of which was a civil defense vehicle, and attacks on Palestinian olive harvesters.
In a separate incident, shortly before midnight, settlers reportedly attacked Palestinian homes in the Wadi al-Sheikh area of the town of Beit Ummar, north of Hebron.
The Palestinian Red Crescent said that two wounded Palestinians, a 63-year-old woman and a 40-year-old man, had been treated and taken to the hospital. Another Palestinian was reportedly shot in the knee.
Israel Police, Shin Bet launch manhunt for armed man in military uniform
Israeli security forces are working to chase down a possibly armed man in an olive grove near Kafr Kara, Israel Police announced on Friday.
The man is reportedly wearing a military uniform and carrying a rifle.
Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency), Israel Police (including aerial forces), Border Police, and emergency response squad volunteers are among the security forces conducting the manhunt.

Egypt has indefinitely suspended the passage of trucks bound for Sudan through the Qustul land port after two Egyptian drivers were killed and a third was injured in a shooting at a market south of the Sudanese capital, Khartoum.
The management of Egypt’s Qustul port, which operates under the General Authority for Land and Dry Ports at the Ministry of Transport, has ordered all trucks heading to the port to stop. Trucks will not be allowed to cross by ferry into Sudan until further instructions, citing “security developments in Sudan’s Northern State”.
The suspension does not apply to passenger traffic. Buses, private cars, minibuses and individual travellers are still allowed to cross, while the restrictions apply only to trucks.
An earlier decision by Egypt’s Land and International Transport Regulatory Authority banned Egyptian trucks from entering conflict zones in Sudan. It limited commercial transport to Wadi Halfa, Argeen and the city of Dongola in Sudan, as part of measures to protect drivers from security risks.
The authority stressed that truck drivers must comply with regulations governing transport within Sudan, exercise the utmost caution and avoid entering designated areas under any circumstances.
The instructions are based on directives issued by Egypt’s Ministry of Transport on 11th May 2025, requiring drivers to avoid conflict zones and unload goods only in safe areas of Sudan’s Northern State.
The suspension comes amid security risks affecting road transport between Egypt and Sudan as a result of the armed conflict. Two Egyptian drivers were killed and a third was injured in a shooting at a market south of Khartoum.

Protests rage in Albania; Prime Minister refuses to step down
Unknown

2026-10-16

17:03:59 KST

As student-led protests unfold in the Albanian capital—with windows being shattered and demonstrators clashing with police, who are deploying water cannons and tear gas—Prime Minister Edi Rama has stated that he has no intention of resigning, reports Reuters.
Protesters accuse officials of corruption and the neglect of the education sector. There is also persistent anger regarding the sale of a beach on Albania’s southern coast to developers of a luxury resort linked to Jared Kushner, the son-in-law of US President Donald Trump.
The streets of Tirana are littered with burnt-out trash bins; bus stop glass has been smashed, and traffic lights have been torn down. Police used tear gas, stun grenades, and water cannons against protesters who threw stones, set fire to a kiosk, and broke into a bank. The protesters are demanding Rama’s resignation, pointing out that their concerns went unheeded when the protests were still peaceful earlier in the summer.
Rama—whose government denies the corruption allegations—said he is prepared to discuss the rising costs of education, but he has no intention of stepping down. He stated that his duty is to listen, seek solutions, and continue moving Albania forward. The alternative would be to betray the Albanians who gave him a strong mandate to complete European Union accession negotiations.
A student identifying herself as Kiara told Reuters that the cost of living, poor job prospects, and corruption were the main issues. She remarked that 
the Albanian Prime Minister is the very definition of corruption, noting that one can only find a job if one "knows someone who knows someone else."
The protests, which entered their third day in Albania on the 15th of October, represent Rama's biggest challenge to date. He was elected to a fourth term last year, with EU accession at the heart of his campaign. As protests flared up near the parliament building, the session was cancelled.
Protester and lawyer Lulzim Tanushi stated that the Albanian government is corrupt and led by a corrupt Prime Minister. Since coming to power, Rama has allegedly abused his authority and ruined people's lives; this is precisely what people are angry about—that they have not been heard until now. The protests follow months of peaceful demonstrations sparked by plans to build a coastal resort. In July, residents of a village near the planned resort told Reuters that their land had been unfairly sold to developers. Reuters later reported that prosecutors were seeking the person who sold the land in connection with drug smuggling; his lawyers denied the allegations.
Albania’s image has long been tarnished by corruption scandals, and political analysts have noted that the country serves as a hub for gangs seeking to launder profits from drug and arms trafficking. This complicates Albania's path toward EU membership.
Rama stated that corruption must be combated, noting that the EU has recently acknowledged Albania is doing so more vigorously than ever before. He added that some—both at home and abroad—do not want Albania to be at the forefront of candidate countries, but he would not allow violence to stand in the way of the nation's European future.
The EU mission in Albania wrote on X that the only way forward is through constructive dialogue.

Russian drones violated Moldovan airspace five times overnight
Several Russian UAVs violated Moldovan airspace on the night of 15-16 October and on the morning of 16 October.
Source: European Pravda, citing TV8
Details: The drones crossed the border amid large-scale Russian attacks on Ukraine. The incidents were recorded in northern and south-eastern Moldova. No crashes or explosions were reported.
The first violation was recorded at 23:02. An object crossed the border from the direction of Tymkove in Ukraine's Odesa Oblast and headed towards the village of Ivanovca. Eighteen minutes later, it left Moldovan airspace and headed towards the Ukrainian settlement of Bronit.
The second incident was recorded at 03:37. A drone flew from the direction of the Ukrainian village of Starokozache in Odesa Oblast towards the village of Tudora in Ștefan Vodă District. One minute later, it returned to Ukrainian territory along the same route.
At 03:46, another drone crossed the border in the north from the direction of Mohyliv-Podilskyi, heading towards the town of Otaci. Two minutes later, it left Moldovan airspace near the village of Hădărăuți in Ocnița District.
The fourth violation was recorded at 05:59. A drone entered the country's airspace from the direction of Starokozache and headed towards the village of Căplani in Ștefan Vodă District. One minute later, the drone left Moldovan territory near the village of Olănești.
At 06:09, the same drone crossed the border again near the village of Purcari in Ștefan Vodă District. One minute later, it left the country's airspace via the Dnestrovsc area in the Transnistrian region, heading towards the Ukrainian settlement of Hradenytsi.
In less than seven hours, Moldova's Defence Ministry recorded five unauthorised incursions by aircraft into the country's airspace.
Background:
- On the night of 14-15 October, a drone once again violated Moldovan airspace during a Russian attack on Ukraine. Moldova's defence minister said the drone was "definitely" Russian.
- On the morning of 30 September, a drone flew through Moldovan airspace before crashing outside the village of Hîrbovăț in Anenii Noi District and exploding.

- He said nations are still “spending money on the wrong things”, with about US$2.6 trillion a year in public subsidies that damage nature and the climate.

AI generated
PARIS – UN chief Antonio Guterres on Oct 16 urged governments to stop subsidising the production of fossil fuels that are “boiling our planet and are the scourge of biodiversity”.
Addressing leaders in Armenia ahead of next week’s UN biodiversity summit, Guterres said governments were still “spending money on the wrong things” and singled out incentives for fossil fuels.
“Subsidising fossil fuels is subsidising suicide,” Guterres said at an event in Yerevan.
“They are boiling our planet and are the scourge of biodiversity. I urge governments everywhere to end these handouts once and for all, and to use the savings for people and planet instead.”
Nations have made little headway since pledging in 2022 to reduce public spending on activities that harm nature such as mining, fossil fuel extraction and intensive farming.
The United Nations says that for every dollar invested in protecting or restoring nature, about US$30 (S$38) still goes into activities that degrade it.
This includes an estimated US$2.6 trillion a year in public subsidies that negatively impact nature and the climate.
Nearly 200 nations are participating in the UN biodiversity negotiations in Yerevan starting on Oct 19, where a lack of finance for nature will be a core focus.
Guterres launched a report on Oct 16 showing that the world was off track to achieving the 2030 biodiversity targets enshrined in a landmark pact for nature. AFP

Saab, FMV and the Swedish Armed Forces launch uncrewed underwater vehicle
Unknown

Saab, FMV and the Swedish Armed Forces launch uncrewed underwater vehicle
Less than one year after contract award, Saab, the Swedish Defence Materiel Administration (FMV) and the Swedish Armed Forces have successfully developed, built and launched a demonstrator for a Large Uncrewed Underwater Vehicle (LUUV).
Developed at pace and according to plan, the demonstrator has progressed from concept to a fully functional vehicle. Following successful sea trials, the first phase of the project has been completed. The next phase is expected to focus on developing more advanced capabilities. The results will support the continued development of software, sensors and autonomous functions, while also contributing to future product development.
The vehicle illustrates how close collaboration between industry and government authorities can significantly reduce the time from identifying an operational need to testing a new capability.
“This project demonstrates how new technologies can be rapidly translated into practical operational value. The uncrewed underwater vehicle can contribute to increased endurance, enhanced situational awareness and strengthened underwater capabilities. The fact that we have also been able to develop and test the system in such a short timeframe demonstrates the strength of the collaboration between the Swedish Armed Forces, FMV and Saab,” says Mats Wicksell, head of Saab’s business area Naval.
The demonstrator has been developed to support the development and evaluation of future underwater capabilities and to enable operations alongside existing naval platforms, such as submarines.
The rapid development has been enabled by Saab’s software-centric approach and the integration of Autonomous Ocean Core, Saab’s autonomous control system that provides surface and subsurface vehicles with autonomous capabilities. Combined with Swedish expertise in submarine design and sensor integration, this has made it possible to take the project swiftly from concept to sea trials.
The LUUV project builds on Saab’s earlier investments and work in autonomous underwater systems and is now led by FMV in cooperation with the Swedish Armed Forces and Saab. The project provides a basis for Swedish authorities’ decisions regarding the future acquisition and operational use of autonomous underwater systems.

The exchange emerged in an undercover investigation by ITV Exposure, which has also shown councillors and election candidates for Reform making threats of extreme violence and expressing racist, Islamophobic and misogynistic views.
In the latest footage released by ITV, a senior Reform official is seen warning Farage that he was “protecting” a high-profile mayoral candidate accused of making racist comments about Lammy.
Sarah Pochin, one of two female MPs for Reform, is also seen complaining that other party officials “are so fucking chauvinistic” and that “they just exclude you if you are a woman”.
Jenrick, the party’s Treasury spokesperson and MP for Newark, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme on Friday: “[Farage] is the most heavily scrutinised figure in British politics, and he’s someone who’s probably done more than almost anybody else to stand against racism and the far right, and to protect our politics from that over the course of my lifetime.
“And this documentary failed to besmirch his character, which presumably was the ultimate objective.”
Farage has made repeated promises over the last two years to rid Reform of “extremists” and “bigots” and introduce vetting. The party says it carries out vetting checks on everyone who wants to stand for election.
However, the first clips from ITV’s year-long undercover investigation showed Alan Feeney, a Reform councillor and deputy mayor of Solihull, calling Asian homeowners “parasites”, and stating that “no more than 1% of [the] British population can be non-white”.
Further footage released on Thursday shows Farage discussing the case of Chris Parry, a retired rear admiral picked to contest the Hampshire and the Solent mayoral election for the party.
The party stood by Parry for months after it emerged he had said the former foreign secretary should “go home to the Caribbean” last year, and suggested that at least eight other politicians from minority ethnic backgrounds did not have a primary loyalty to the UK.
Reform eventually suspended him in March after the Guardian revealed other remarks by Parry, but clips from the ITV documentary show Farage pushing back against senior advisers who said the candidate had to be sacked. They included Ed Sumner, Reform’s head of communications, who had told another press officer in an earlier discussion that Parry was “clearly a racist”.
In a conversation between Farage and Sumner, which was recorded by the undercover reporter, the Reform leader said Parry “must apologise to Lammy” and was told that a text had been written for the candidate.
“He must do it and move on … Tell him that from me,” Farage said, to which Sumner said: “You’re protecting him.”
To laughter, Farage replied: “It’s showing a bit of … bit of sorrow. Look, ‘I’m sorry’ is probably a good thing to hear. Just take the fucking deal. Trouble is he’s a rear admiral. That’s the problem.”
Jenrick defended Reform’s vetting policy. “In my experience, all political parties have bad apples. I mean, you can see that’s plain to see from the conduct of other political parties. In fact, Councillor Feeney, the one that you presented before I came online, was for a short time a Reform councillor, but for a much greater time a Conservative councillor.”
He added: “We actually have very strong vetting, and we invest a huge amount in it, and it’s improving all the time. I don’t know what the vetting is like in every other political party. I can say in the Conservative party, because it was my former party, there is absolutely no vetting whatsoever by the central party for local councillors.”

UK and Germany strengthen defence ties in London talks
