Brethren Church member admits to 'brief' meeting with far-right figures during 2025 federal election campaign
In short:
The spiritual leader of the Plymouth Brethren Christian Church has denied allegations he coordinated church members to volunteer in the 2025 federal election campaign.
His son Gareth Hales says he encouraged members of the church, but did not instruct them to participate.
What's next?
A final report into the 2025 election is due by the end of the year.
The spiritual leader of the Plymouth Brethren Christian Church (PBCC) has denied coordinating a pro-Liberal campaign in the 2025 federal election, as his son acknowledged meeting far-right figures accused of targeting MPs.
Several politicians have alleged Brethren members intimidated rival candidates and campaigners, while Nine newspapers reported church members paid far-right influencers, including Neo-Nazi associates, to follow and heckle the prime minister.
Giving evidence before the Joint Standing Committee on Electoral Matters, senior elder Bruce Hales denied any knowledge of a coordinated campaign by the church.
"I did not coordinate such activities. I did not direct such activities. I did not fund such activities," he said.
"If anti-social acts were committed by any individual of any faith … I cannot answer for them".
Gareth Hales, Mr Hales's son, said he met with Chris De Bruyne and Morgan C Jonas, figures described by independent MP Andrew Gee as "far right", during the campaign.
But he described the encounters as "brief" business meetings, and said he was unaware of their political affiliations at the time.
Mr Hales Jnr also revealed he met then-opposition leader Peter Dutton at a petrol station media event, which he had heard about through "word of mouth".
"I don't recall, but I dare say it was probably a friend of a friend," he said.
He denied allegations that a company he formerly associated with, Sante Global, paid Neo-Nazi associates to disrupt Anthony Albanese's campaign.
Mr Hales Jnr said his own involvement in the election was limited to volunteering at four polling booths and maintained he had only a "very, very light-touch" role.
He admitted to encouraging some church members, but did not specify how many people he counselled, or the nature of his encouragement.
"I didn't direct or coordinate, but yes, if I was on a call, a leader is expected to encourage, inspire, if at all possible," he said.
It was also revealed members of the PBCC, which has a global congregation of 56,000, had met with US President Donald Trump in New York, although Mr Hale was not present.
The line of questioning of both senior PBCC men was likened to a "witch hunt" by Coalition members, with Nationals senator Bridget McKenzie going as far as accusing the committee of religious discrimination.
Where did 'Make Australia Smile Again' come from?
The committee spent considerable time litigating the origin of signs reported in several electorates that read "Make Australia Smile Again".
Mr Hales was questioned about the similarity to a sermon he gave the month before the election, in which he urged parishioners to pray for "good government" because Australia "needed to be happy again, smiling again".
He agreed that it was rare for his message, sent online to church members around the world, to be misinterpreted.
"Very, very rarely do I have to go back and explain what I meant," he said.
Asked whether his four sons, one of whom was later photographed campaigning, interpreted that as an endorsement for the Liberal Party, Mr Hales said he did not know.
"I think if they had asked me about them and asked permission [to campaign], I would have denied it," he said.
"The first indication I had that my eldest son was out on the polling booths was a photograph in the paper, and I was a bit surprised."
Mr Hales Jnr gave evidence he never saw the "Make Australia Smile Again" signs and was surprised when the Liberal Party's internal review described Brethren members involved in the campaign as a support group.
"I was not aware that was how the Liberals regarded us," he said.
When pressed on who he meant by "us", Mr Hales said he was referring simply to members of the Australian public.
Fiery Coalition members label questioning a 'witch hunt'
Chair Jerome Laxale said there had been "thousands and thousands" of church members who "flooded" polling booths during the campaign.
Mr Hales Jnr pushed back, asking how Mr Laxale knew those people at the polling booths were Brethren members.
"It was well documented," Mr Laxale said.
The inquiry was littered with interjections from Coalition members, who described the line of questioning as a "witch hunt".
Liberal senator Richard Colbeck repeatedly interrupted questioning and labelled the hearing "ridiculous".
"This is not the Spanish Inquisition," Senator Colbeck said.
Bruce Hales's role in the church
Mr Hales told the committee he succeeded his father, John Hales, as the senior elder and was not elected but assumed the position "spontaneously".
He said members followed his teachings, which they believed came from God.
"I would think that they would say that what I get, I get from the Lord," he said.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese previously described the Brethren as a cult, which Mr Hales rejected.
"We are not a cult. We are Christians,"
Mr Hales said.
Mr Hales said although he was the spiritual Brethren leader, he did not have authority over individual members, who were "entitled to make their own decisions".
Mr Hales Jnr said he did take part in the campaign as a volunteer for the Liberal Party in his capacity as a "private citizen".
He said campaigning alongside someone — in this case, fellow Brethren members — did not mean "adopting every opinion they have ever expressed".
"The committee chair is now taking a dangerous step, using a group of volunteers' religious identity to associate them publicly with ideologies apparently held by others," he said.

'I want children to know what it felt like to be held hostage': Keith Siegel speaks out
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
06:41:55 UTC
15:41:55 KST

Since returning from captivity in Gaza, I have been trying to relearn how to live. To be a husband, a father, a grandfather and a member of my family again. To return to the small things that once seemed obvious. Sitting with my family, leaving the house, making plans for tomorrow.
But coming home does not erase what happened, nor does it bring us back to the lives we had before October 7.
For 484 days, I was held hostage in Gaza. Days during which my freedom, my sense of security and even my ability to make the most basic decisions about my own life were taken from me.
During that time, my family was forced to confront an unimaginable reality. My wife, Aviva, who was abducted alongside me and released before I was, returned home but continued to live with the reality of my captivity every passing day.
I came home to a family that had been waiting for me, but also to a family that had endured an incredibly difficult period of its own. We have all changed. There is a deep desire to return to life, to enjoy simple moments and to be together again. But there are also memories, pain and struggles that do not end on the day you come home. Recovery is a long process, and even the smallest things can be challenging.
I share this because I want people to understand that the story of October 7 did not end when I was released from captivity. It continues to affect me and my family every day, just as it does thousands of others who experienced that terrible day and the difficult period that followed.
Each of them has a different story. Some lost the people they loved most. Others hid for hours as terrorists moved around their homes. Some survived the massacre at the Nova music festival. Others fought to defend their families and communities. There were also members of the security and emergency services who, during those terrible hours, risked their lives and struggled to save others.
Each carries a part of that day's story, a part that no one else can tell in their place.
There is no single story of October 7
Twenty years from now, when children in Israel learn about October 7, what will they know about what happened to us? They will certainly learn about the attack, those who were murdered, the abductions and the war. They will see photographs and videos and hear about decisions that were made and failures that occurred.
But I also want them to know what a mother felt as she sat with her children in a safe room, hearing terrorists outside the door. What a family went through when they did not know whether they would ever see their loved ones again. What it means to be held hostage, cut off from the world and the people you love, without knowing whether you will ever return.
Our national memory cannot be built solely on headlines, ceremonies and memorials. It must also be built on the voices of the people who were there, because there is no single story of October 7. There are thousands of stories, and each one is part of the truth.
In the coming years, books will be written, films will be made and memorial ceremonies will be held. All of these are important, but I believe that we, the people who experienced these events, must play a central role in shaping how they are remembered.
Not everyone who was affected is able or willing to speak, and the decision not to share or talk about what happened must also be respected. But those who choose to tell their stories must be given the space to do so in their own way and in their own words.
In captivity, I was stripped of control over my life. Today, as a free man once again, I can choose when to speak, what to share and how to tell the story of what I went through. That choice has enormous meaning for me.
More than just a date in the history books
This is one of the reasons I chose to take part in the "Salon Otef" initiative, led by the organization "255," of which I am a member. The organization brings together returned hostages and their families, supports them through the complex challenges that continue long after they return home, and works to ensure that our stories are heard in our own voices and told in the ways we choose.
Through Salon Otef, hundreds of survivors, returned hostages, family members and members of the security and emergency services meet with tens of thousands of people. Not through a television screen, but face to face. People sit together, listen and ask questions. It is precisely through these personal encounters that people can understand things that are difficult to convey in a newspaper headline.
This week, I will travel to Ethiopia, where I will hold a Salon Otef gathering with the Jewish and Israeli community in Addis Ababa. Alongside members of the public, diplomats, government representatives and civil society leaders will also attend. There, too, thousands of miles from Israel, I will speak about the abduction, captivity, coming home and life afterward.
October 7 is part of the history of the State of Israel, but it is also part of the collective memory of the entire Jewish people. It is important to me that our stories reach Jewish and Israeli communities around the world, and that they hear them directly from those who lived through them.
Three years have passed since October 7. For many of us, the struggle continues and will probably continue for many years to come. I do not know whether it is possible to become exactly the person I was before that day. But I do know that I want to keep living, to be with my family and to keep telling my story.
I do not want October 7 to become just another date in the history books 20 years from now. I want future generations to know the people behind the numbers, the lives they led, what they endured and the journeys they have been on ever since.
We cannot change what happened to us. But we have both a responsibility and a right to determine how our story is told and how it will be remembered.
Keith Siegel was abducted from his home in Kfar Aza on October 7 and returned from captivity in Gaza after 484 days. This week, he will hold a special Salon Otef gathering for the Jewish and Israeli community in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia.

In Israel, Netanyahu’s ultimate legacy is the opposition he has forged
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
06:41:15 UTC
15:41:15 KST

In Israel, Netanyahu’s ultimate legacy is the opposition he has forged
As Israel heads to the polls on October 27, Benjamin Netanyahu’s most enduring domestic legacy may be the right-wing opposition he faces, analysts say.
Benjamin Netanyahu had barely reached the United Nations podium when a sea of delegates jumped from their seats and began walking out in protest at the Israeli prime minister’s speech at the UN General Assembly in late September.
Undeterred, a grinning Netanyahu, who is seeking re-election later this month while being wanted by the International Criminal Court on charges of war crimes in Gaza, shot back: “If there are any other moral cowards who haven’t left the hall, please do so now.”
For his supporters watching in Israel, it was precisely what they wanted to hear.
“When they see Netanyahu at the United Nations,” his former aide, Mitchell Barak, told Al Jazeera, “that’s what they want – and it’s hard for them to imagine anyone else doing that.”
He added: “For many in Israel, but not all, he’s the only man that can truly lead Israel. He makes them proud to be Jewish.”
On October 27, Israel must choose between Netanyahu and an assorted number of rivals who are unified by little other than their absolute opposition to Israel’s longest-serving prime minister.
In the eyes of both his supporters and his opponents, as well as much of the world, Netanyahu has become the face of modern Israel.
Born in Tel Aviv in 1949 to Benzion Netanyahu and Tzila Segal, he spent his early years between Israel and the United States, the few constants in his life being the profoundly pessimistic views of his father – a right-wing historian who saw a world fundamentally opposed to the existence of Jews – and the military legacy of his brother, Yonatan, who was killed in 1976 while leading a raid to rescue hijacked Israeli hostages in Entebbe, Uganda.
Since then, Netanyahu has gone through numerous iterations.
In 1982, he was named deputy chief of mission at the Israeli embassy in Washington, DC. Two years later, he was appointed Israel’s ambassador to the UN, before returning to Israel to join the cabinet of then-Prime Minister Yitzhak Shamir as deputy foreign minister in 1988.
In 1996, Netanyahu became Israel’s youngest prime minister, leading the first in a series of coalitions that also saw him serving a record 12-year tenure from 2009 to 2021. He returned to power for a sixth term the next year, leading the most far-right government in Israel’s history.
From the outset of his political career, he faced growing accusations of having deliberately engineered division to further his own political and personal ends.
“Netanyahu is the perfect encapsulation of Israel’s political polarisation,” said political analyst Nimrod Flaschenberg. Describing Netanyahu as “always” being “in campaigning mode”, he said the Israeli leader “is very good at building coalitions that reflect public opinion, as well as steering that opinion in his own direction”.
Hardwired division
Under Netanyahu’s leadership, Israel has continued to lurch to the right, rejecting the path towards a two-state solution to the Israel-Palestine conflict set in motion by his predecessor, the assassinated Yitzhak Rabin. At the same time, vast swaths of the Israeli electorate have also grown accustomed to the violent expansion of illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank and reconciled themselves to the genocide in Gaza following the Hamas-led attack on October 7, 2023 – for which many still blame Netanyahu for alleged security failures – as well as the multiple wars waged at his direction since.
In July 2018, Netanyahu’s coalition passed the Nation-State Law, declaring the right to national self-determination “unique to the Jewish people”, stripping Arabic of its status as an official language and making the development of Jewish settlements a national value. In the law’s wake, settler violence in the occupied West Bank has surged, with the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) recording 1,291 attacks in 2023 and 1,835 in 2025. At least 1,071 Palestinians, including 233 children, have been killed in the West Bank by Israeli forces or settlers since October 7, 2023, according to OCHA, amid what a senior UN official called “virtually no accountability”.
More immediately, Netanyahu’s current coalition has seen some of Israel’s most controversial figures – such as National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, convicted of incitement to racism and support for a “terrorist” group, and the explicitly pro-settlement Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich – placed at the heart of power.
“Netanyahu didn’t create the racism and fascism in Israel, but he’s helped it,” said outgoing parliamentarian Aida Touma-Sliman, of the left-wing Hadash party. “He’s smart. He knows exactly what he’s doing when he includes people like Smotrich and Ben-Gvir in his government, and he knows the outcome of those appointments.”
“He thrives in chaos,” said Barak, Netanyahu’s former aide from the 1990s. “He’s all about the big picture, of ends justifying means.”
Running through the prime minister’s recent military campaigns have been his long-standing battles against any kind of domestic judicial restraint. Dogged by corruption cases dating back to 2019, which could see him serve time in prison if convicted, he has been locked in a confrontation with the same legal establishment attempting to hold him to account.
In January 2023, he and his right-wing allies sought to overhaul the judiciary, shaking off much of the oversight of the courts over government action. The proposals led to demonstrations on an unprecedented scale, with hundreds of thousands taking to the streets to protest against the contentious move. In June 2024, Netanyahu went so far as to appear to suggest that the division created by his reforms was somehow responsible for his own heavily criticised response to the October 7 attack.
The ‘devil’ you know
Still, while opinion polls show Netanyahu’s Likud party and its allies tied with the broad anti-Netanyahu bloc of similarly right-wing and militaristic parties, the prime minister’s support has weakened. Likud won 32 seats in the 2022 election, but most recent polls project a gain of about 20 to 22, with former supporters appearing to shift either to the opposition or to harder-line right-wing parties.
The alliance opposing Netanyahu has yet to nominate an official leader, but former army chief Gadi Eisenkot is widely seen as its most likely candidate for prime minister.
“We need to be clear about this,” said Barak. “He’s essentially running unopposed. It’s Netanyahu versus a coalition of opponents.”
“Think about it,” said Touma-Sliman, pointing out the double standards after the prominent leader of a party representing Palestinian citizens of Israel was forced to withdraw from the election over his remarks about the Gaza war. “He’s helped create a system where Arab MK Sami Abu Shehadeh is barred from running, and he, a war criminal who has led his country through a genocide, is not”.
For his supporters, noted Flaschenberg, Netanyahu “remains Israel’s only possible leader”. But for his opponents, “He’s the devil. He’s corruption personified, responsible for everything leading up to October 7 and everything afterwards.”
However, his ultimate legacy may still lie ahead, the analyst suggested, recalling the words of former British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher, who once cited the rightward tilt of the opposition as her greatest legacy.
“Netanyahu’s legacy lies with the opposition. All of the main contenders are right-wing, militaristic and ultimately racist,” said Flaschenberg. “That’s Netanyahu’s legacy.”

Estonia plans to bring back its blue passports from 2030
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
06:38:00 UTC
15:38:00 KST

Estonia plans to bring back its blue passports from 2030
The Interior Ministry plans to redesign Estonian passports and add new security features, with blue covers returning for citizen passports from 2030.
Security updates come sooner than that — those on "gray passport"-holders documents in January 2027, with those found on citizens' passports to follow in July. Existing passports remain valid until they expire.
The blue passport covers had been in use following the restoration of independence in 1991, but with accession to the EU in 2004 the familiar burgundy colored covers – an EU recommendation but not mandatory – came in.
Interior Minister Igor Taro (Eesti 200) said the idea of changing the cover color came up while preparing the updated passport.
"We had to review the design of the entire new generation of Estonian passports, and from there came the idea that, since the Estonian passport is a representative link between the state and its citizen in international communication and the main identity document when traveling, its visual form should also reflect the colors of the Estonian state," Taro told ERR.
Blue covers were first used on Estonian passports during the interwar period, when Estonia was first an independent state.
The security updates include a boulder-shaped, partly transparent window containing an oak-leaf-shaped chip antenna. The holder's signature image moves from the second page to the third.
Taro explained why the changes are being phased in rather than being done all at once:"This is because we have a so-called physical passport production contract valid until 2030. So that no additional cost or additional steps would need to be taken in connection with the color switch, it simply changes over naturally."
Personal data in the passport will not change, and applicants will not need to do anything extra. Existing passports remain valid until their original expiry date; the blue ones will enter circulation through natural renewal.
Opposition politicians: A cosmetic act ahead of elections
Some leading opposition politicians were critical of the changes.
Former interior minister Lauri Läänemets (SDE) said they were focusing on the wrong thing.
"Considering that we have to deal with preventing Russian hybrid attacks more and more, considering the challenges related to the staffing of the police and rescue services, considering the situation with migration, the interior minister's focus is in completely the wrong place," he told Postimees.
MEP Jüri Ratas (Isamaa), a former prime minister, said that while blue is a beautiful color and the EU's common color scheme is a recommendation rather than an obligation, the timing of dealing with passport color inevitably seems to him like pre-election distraction ahead of the Riigikogu election next March.

Is washing your face with water after outages dangerous? An immunologist explained what to watch out for
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:37:44 EEST
15:37:44 KST

Is washing your face with water after outages dangerous? An immunologist explained what to watch out for
Kyiv • UNN
After prolonged outages, it is recommended to let the water run because of possible rust and sediment. Boiling destroys microorganisms but not heavy metals.
After prolonged water supply outages, tap water may change color and acquire an unpleasant odor due to having remained in the pipes for a long time. At the same time, transparency and the absence of an odor do not guarantee that it is safe. UNN journalist was told in greater detail by immunologist Borys Donskyi why, after water service is restored, it is advisable to let the water run, whether boiling it is sufficient, and whether its quality can be determined independently.
Why water may become dirtier after outages
According to the doctor, water quality depends on the amount of impurities that may enter it at the water intake stage or while it is passing through pipes. In particular, after remaining in the water supply system for a long time, its condition may deteriorate.
There are certain standards governing what substances water may contain, and exceeding the permissible levels of these substances is already considered hazardous to health. As you understand, this is a quantitative issue: the cleaner the water, the better it will be. Certain impurities are added to this water: it picks them up while passing through the water supply system
The immunologist noted that after outages, water may come into contact with rust and other deposits in the pipes, which is why it sometimes has a characteristic color and odor when supply initially resumes. Therefore, after water service is restored, it is worth paying attention to its appearance and not using water with obvious signs of contamination.
Have you often observed the following after a water outage, even one lasting several hours: you turn on the tap, and rusty water flows out? This happens because a pocket of air has passed through the pipes, the water has stood in them and picked up rust, so it should be drained at first. If it remains in the pipes for even longer, it may become less clean and more contaminated
Can you wash your face with such water, and will boiling help?
In Borys Donskyi’s opinion, the risk of infection through intact skin should not be equated with the risk of consuming contaminated water. However, during hygiene procedures, water can still get into the mouth, eyes, or onto mucous membranes. Therefore, according to the doctor, if contamination is suspected, it is better not to use it for brushing your teeth or for other procedures during which water could enter the body.
I do not think it can be so contaminated that it would pose a risk through the skin. But if water remains in risers and pipes for a week, it is possible that it will contain more dangerous microorganisms and be more heavily contaminated
At the same time, according to the immunologist, boiling does help disinfect water, in particular by destroying many pathogenic microorganisms; however, it should be noted that it does not eliminate all possible contaminants.
Boiling disinfects water. But if it is also rusty and contains high levels of heavy metals, boil it or do not boil it—it will remain dirty. Therefore, it should at least be passed through household filters
At the same time, it is impossible to determine water quality solely by its color, odor, and taste, because even clear water may contain substances that cannot be detected without special testing.
You can independently determine that it is unfit for use. But you should not independently determine that it is definitely safe and can be consumed, because you do not have that capability. There are services that do this; they are supposed to regularly check water quality. And we hope they do so
Borys Donskyi also separately cautioned against trying to independently determine the cause of deteriorating health after contact with potentially contaminated water, because poisoning symptoms depend on the type of contamination: microorganisms, in particular, can cause intestinal infections, while chemical substances can cause other disorders.
Self-diagnosis is not advisable. Any deterioration in your health may indicate that something has entered your body. If the water is saturated with microorganisms, this will result in intestinal infections. If it contains heavy metals, the symptoms will be completely different
Moreover, according to the immunologist, some toxic effects may not appear immediately but as certain substances accumulate in the body, so the safety of water should not be assessed solely based on how you feel. If unusual symptoms occur after contact with suspicious water, it is advisable to consult a doctor directly.
ATTENTION! This material is for informational purposes only. If you are concerned about your health, consult a doctor.

Lithuania’s 2027 budget: 5% for defence, growing government deficit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
06:24:00 UTC
15:24:00 KST

Lithuania’s draft budget for 2027 allocates more than 4.8 billion euros to defence, equivalent to 5% of projected GDP, the Finance Ministry said Thursday. The government approved the proposal on Friday morning and will present the budget bill to the parliament, Seimas.
The proposed allocation would increase defence spending by nearly 35 million euros from this year. It includes funding for the Defence Ministry and the State Defence Fund, which is set to receive more than 896 million euros.
Although defence spending was lower in monetary terms this year, it accounted for a larger share of the economy, at 5.38% of GDP.
Early last year, Lithuania’s State Defence Council, which includes the country’s political leadership and representatives of its national defence system, agreed to allocate 5% to 6% of GDP to defence annually from 2026 through 2030. The increased spending is intended to help develop an army division and prepare Lithuania to host a German brigade.
The Finance Ministry on Thursday registered draft budgets for the state, municipalities and social funds for next year, projecting a general government deficit of 3.8% of GDP.
State budget revenue is expected to reach nearly 22.2 billion euros, including European Union funds, while expenditure is projected at 27.9 billion euros.
The projected deficit exceeds the European Union’s Maastricht criterion, which generally limits government deficits to 3% of GDP. Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said in an earlier interview that most spending beyond revenue was linked to the goal of allocating 5% of GDP to defence and to increases in benefits that are indexed.
The government is also proposing pay increases for statutory officers and cultural workers in 2027. Additional funding has been earmarked for a proposed package of measures to encourage families to have children.
Revenue for the Sodra state social insurance fund is projected at nearly 7 billion euros next year, with expenditure expected to exceed 5.5 billion euros.
The average pension is set to rise by 10.4% to 825 euros a month, increasing to 895 euros for people who meet the required length-of-service criteria. The budget allocates 715 million euros for the pension increases.
The Compulsory Health Insurance Fund is expected to collect nearly 3.3 billion euros in revenue in 2027 and spend almost 3.2 billion euros.
General government debt is projected to reach 48.2% of GDP next year.
Sinkevičius said Lithuania would continue to devote one of Europe’s largest shares of GDP to defence.
Finance Minister Taurimas Valys said the budget sought to balance stronger national security with income growth above inflation and the economy’s long-term growth potential.

====================================================================================================

Lisbon airport taxis: Fixed fares aim to end 'tourist trap'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
06:17:23 UTC
15:17:23 KST

Since Thursday, passengers landing at Lisbon airport who want to take a taxi can now rely on a fixed price for their trip.
Over the past few years, there have been many reports from tourists about excessive prices, scams and even drivers refusing to take passengers from Lisbon airport.
Faced with problems affecting both foreign visitors and locals, a protocol was signed last September to set fixed fares for taxi journeys.
Several complaints on social media describe allegedly tampered taximeters, mileage being diverted and cases in which taxi drivers will only accept cash payments.
Back in August, Josien Nation, a Dutch citizen living in Portugal, described the situation as a "tourist trap". In a video posted on the Facebook page Nations Without Borders, she said that "not all taxi drivers are 'crooks'", but that some try to negotiate the fare before setting off and then make the trip with the meter switched off, a practice expressly banned in Portugal.
In another account, posted in a Reddit group, a passenger says that on a journey from Lisbon airport to Rossio he was charged 18.50 euros, even though the meter showed 13 euros. According to the post, the driver justified the difference with an additional luggage fee. He also refused to let the passenger pay by card.
Most of these accounts come from tourists or foreign nationals living in Portugal who are allegedly treated as tourists. However, there are also testimonies from residents who use the service, such as a Portuguese man who shared his experience on the same platform.
"The last time I arrived in Lisbon, after a trip, I got into a taxi and immediately got back out again," he began. "The driver said he didn't take card payments. I asked him how much the journey from the airport to my home might cost, as I had some cash with me, but he replied that the price depended on a series of factors, such as traffic and how long the journey would take, among other nonsense."
Other users also say that some taxi drivers take less direct routes to reach their destination, in an attempt to make the journey longer and thus justify overcharging.
To prevent many of these situations, a fixed-fare mechanism came into force on Thursday, under which everyone will pay the same for trips to certain areas. Anyone travelling to areas within the so‑called "zone 1" (see image below) will pay 16 euros during the daytime, from 7:00 to 22:00, and 20 euros at night, from 22:00 to 7:00.
For trips to "zone 2", a daytime journey costs 19 euros and rises to 23 euros at night. These fares also apply at weekends and on public holidays.
Destinations not covered by the scheme will continue to be charged using the meter.
The fares include luggage, removing the additional fee of 1.60 euros that used to be charged for bags exceeding 55x35x20 centimetres.
Carlos Silva, president of the Portuguese Taxi Federation (FPT), explained in comments to Portuguese news agency Lusa that the system will only be fully operational from November and that a price still needs to be set for areas outside the capital, such as Moscavide, Sacavém and Prior Velho.
He believes "it is not fair for someone to pay 16 euros to Parque das Nações and, if the destination is a little further on but already in another municipality, Loures, and so close to the airport, for the service then to be paid according to the meter".
'Tourist prices'
Reactions to the new price list were quick to appear on social media, with many people branding the fares far too high and pointing to short journeys, such as trips from the airport to the parish of Alvalade or to Parque das Nações, both little more than two kilometres away.
An Instagram user says she usually takes a taxi to Oriente station, in Parque das Nações, and used to pay between 7.50 and 10 euros. "And now a fixed fare at such a high rate, why?", she asks. Among the comments, some argue that alternative transport platforms, such as TVDE services, will be the main beneficiaries of the new fares.
Some accuse the authorities of setting "tourist prices" or "rubber-stamping" the high fares and practices of many taxi drivers. "They are going to legalise what some have already been doing for years: turning off the meter," reads one comment.
Others, meanwhile, recognise the need for fixed prices in the name of transparency. "Having already seen this system in other countries, having the fares per destination set in advance without depending on the meter is actually useful," writes one user on Reddit.
The possibility of using public transport, such as the metro and the bus, is also mentioned in the comments, although users point to obstacles such as "large, heavy suitcases" or "travelling with children".
Protocol goes beyond fares
The new fares, which came into force on Thursday, will cover all taxi drivers in this first phase, even those not yet accredited to operate at the airport taxi rank. "Accreditation will also start to be carried out on Thursday," the official explained.
Carlos Silva also believes that these new rules could attract more drivers and ensure more taxis are available at the airport rank. "We know that many do not stop at the airport for various reasons, but that they are considering doing so if there are rules, because at the moment they do not feel comfortable. Fixed prices may be more advantageous, offsetting the time they might have to wait", he said.
If you arrive at Lisbon airport today, you can already expect these prices on taxi services. However, information panels are still missing in the arrivals area and outside, displaying this information so that it is visible to everyone. Transparency is one of the pillars of this new regulation, along with "improving the quality of the service and protecting users".
The protocol on fixed-price journeys, signed in September by Lisbon City Council, ANA - Aeroportos de Portugal, the Lisbon Tourism Association (ATL), the FPT (Portuguese Taxi Federation) and ANTRAL - National Association of Road Transport in Light Vehicles, also lays down other rules, such as the "non-refusal of services" by taxi drivers.
Taxi drivers are also obliged to accept vouchers and electronic payments, meaning the payment terminal must be operational.
PSP inspections confirmed need for regulation
The tightening of measures, even though they will only be fully implemented at the start of next month, also follows a major inspection operation by the Public Security Police (PSP) at the arrivals area of Humberto Delgado Airport in Lisbon at the end of August, during which 67 offences related to taxi activity were detected.
In a statement, Lisbon Metropolitan Command (COMETLIS) said that around 100 taxis were inspected at the site, resulting in 32 offences for "incorrect positioning of the taximeter", out of a total of 67.
Among the offences detected, eight related to lack of a CMT (Taxi Driver Certificate), six to lack of mandatory documents, six to fire extinguishers past their expiry date, three to lack of vehicle inspection and three to "lack of Group 2 on the taxi driver's licence" (the mandatory driving licence certification for taxi drivers).
Two offences were also recorded for a taximeter past its validity period, two for taxis in poor condition, one for failure to use restraint systems, one for lack of insurance, one for driving under the influence of alcohol and one for parking in a private car park.
The PSP also issued two warnings to present documents and complied with two requests for external action that were pending against one of the drivers.
Joana Mourão Carvalho contributed to the writing of this article.

SCALP, AASM Hammer, and Aster 30: France Has Granted Ukraine All the Promised Licenses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
06:16:29 UTC
15:16:29 KST

Ukraine has received all the licenses France promised for the domestic production of three types of weapons: Aster 30 air defense missiles, AASMHammer guided bombs, and SCALP cruise missiles.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced the development.
In July, French President Emmanuel Macron announced the licensing agreement following a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing in Paris. The agreement allows Ukraine to produce these weapons domestically under French licenses.
Ukrainian forces have been successfully employing Aster 30 missiles for an extended period as part of the SAMP/T surface-to-air missile systems supplied by France and Italy.
The modern Aster 30 Block 1 variant can engage aerodynamic targets, including aircraft, cruise missiles, and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), at ranges of up to 120 km and altitudes of up to 25 km.
In addition, the system can intercept tactical ballistic missiles at ranges of up to 30 km.
The French AASM Hammer is a guidance kit that converts conventional unguided Western-designed bombs into precision-guided munitions.
Unlike the American JDAM, AASM Hammer kits are equipped with an integrated rocket motor, enabling them to engage targets at ranges of up to 15 km when released from low altitudes and up to 70 km when released from high altitudes.
Currently, two versions are available: the Hammer 250, designed for 227 kg Mk 82 bombs, and the Hammer 1000, designed for 908 kg Mk 84 bombs. Both are available with different guidance systems.
The Franco-British SCALP EG / Storm Shadow is an air-launched cruise missile measuring 5.1 metres in length, weighing 1,300 kg, and equipped with a 450 kg warhead designed to destroy hardened, fixed targets.
The missile was developed by Matra and British Aerospace beginning in the late 1990s. It has been in service with France and the United Kingdom since 2003 and is manufactured by the MBDA consortium.
The French SCALP-EG and British Storm Shadow variants are essentially identical in design, differing primarily in their software and the specifics of their integration with carrier aircraft.

hollowed quartzite and steel form concav book, a magnetic bookend luminaire
concav book pairs an L-shaped support and a mobile C-element connected by hidden magnets to turn a functional bookend into an interactive luminary gesture.
prefer designboom on google

HOLLOWED BRAZILIAN QUARTZITE HOUSES HIDDEN LIGHTING ELEMENTS
The CONCAV collection, designed by Ignacio Martínez Todeschini and Ignacio Noel and produced in Argentina, explores geometric forms and lighting through Brazilian quartzite and galvanized steel. The central element of the series is a hollowed, curved quartzite module created through CNC milling and hand-finishing. This process houses the light source within the stone, creating a backlit linear element that contrasts the material’s inherent density. The piece pairs an L-shaped support and a mobile C-element connected by hidden magnets to turn a functional bookend into an interactive luminary gesture.
MAGNETIC light SWITCHING pairs WITH ADJUSTABLE BOOK SUPPORT
The inaugural release, CONCAV Book, functions as a hybrid bookend and luminaire. The design by Ignacio Martínez Todeschini and Ignacio Noel – Imto Deschini Studio comprises two distinct components: a fixed L-shaped steel base that houses the light source and acts as the main support, and a mobile C-shaped element. Hidden magnets regulate the internal circuitry, activating the light source when the two components are connected and turning it off when separated. This magnetic connection allows the user to adjust the configuration based on the arrangement and volume of books.

UK bookstores scramble as Sally Rooney's novels pulled over Palestine Action support
Critically acclaimed Irish novelist Sally Rooney's announcement that her books could no longer be sold in the UK due to her support for proscribed group Palestine Action has left British booksellers rushing to stock up on her works before distributors run out. The British government's ban on the group, which practiced non-violent direct action and sabotage against UK military assets believed to be working with the Israeli government, makes support for Palestine Action punishable by up to 14 years in prison.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
British booksellers are have been left scrambling after Irish novelist Sally Rooney said her books can no longer be sold in the UK because she financially supports the banned group Palestine Action.
The announcement by Rooney’s British publisher that it will no longer distribute her books has reignited debate over the UK government’s decision last year to outlaw the direct-action protest group as a terrorist organisation. The ban makes membership in – or, crucially, support for – Palestine Action a crime punishable by up to 14 years in prison.
Rooney, 35, is the critically praised author of four novels: “Conversations with Friends”, “Normal People”, “Beautiful World, Where are You” and “Intermezzo”. Her books have sold millions of copies, and both “Conversations with Friends” and “Normal People” were adapted for television by the BBC.
She supports the Palestinian-led Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement, which calls for boycotts of Israeli businesses, universities and cultural institutions over Israel’s treatment of the Palestinians.
Read moreWhat is Palestine Action, the protest movement banned under UK terror act?
After the UK banned Palestine Action in July 2025, Rooney said she would use proceeds from her books and their TV adaptations to support the group. On Wednesday her UK publisher, Faber, said that paying her royalties could violate the terror ban and it had “taken the decision that we can no longer supply her works in the UK in any format”.
"To sell a writer's work and not be able to pass on earnings is an unconscionable situation for a publisher," Faber said in a statement.
The publisher stressed the decision had been made with Rooney's agreement.
“I have made every effort to be honest with the public about my beliefs and intentions, and I am wholly prepared to accept the consequences,” the writer said in a statement.
Faber’s announcement left British bookstores scrambling to understand whether they were breaking the law by selling Rooney’s books.
The Booksellers Association later said it had “confirmed with Faber that whilst those titles are no longer available to UK bookshops to order, they can continue to sell their existing stock within the UK market”.
Some stores rushed to stock up on Rooney’s novels, but found distributors had already run out.
“We were thinking, we’ll just get a whole bunch before we stop being able to,” said Lucy Burke, a bookseller at London’s Camden Town Bookshop. “Because she’s a hugely popular seller here, and quite evergreen. But now it seems like what we have is all we’re going to have.”
Burke described the situation as “absolutely ridiculous” and said it amounted to censorship of “one of our most prominent writers”.
Palestine Action, founded in 2020, aims to stop UK military support for Israel, which it says is committing genocide against the Palestinians – a claim Israel strongly denies. An independent UN committee found in September 2025 that Israel was carrying out a genocide in the besieged Gaza Strip.
The group says it aims to stop genocide by disrupting “corporate enablers of the Israeli military-industrial complex".
In 2024 its activists broke into a factory owned by Israeli weapons manufacturer Elbit Systems UK, smashing equipment with sledgehammers and crowbars. The next year, activists broke into a Royal Air Force base in June 2025, sprayed red paint into the engines of two tanker planes and caused further damage with crowbars.
The group says it does not advocate violence against people, but a police officer suffered a fractured spine when she was hit with a sledgehammer as police tried to arrest members of the group during the factory break-in.
The British government says Palestine Action has “carried out acts of terrorism, celebrated those who took part in them and promoted the use of violence".
“The proscription of Palestine Action does not affect lawful protest in support of the Palestinian cause, which remains a fundamental democratic right,” the Home Office said in a statement.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Civil liberties groups say the ban unjustifiably restricts the rights to protest and free speech. In response to the government’s decision, thousands of people have tested the law by silently holding signs reading “I support Palestine Action.”
More than 3,000 people have been arrested, and more than 1,200 have been charged under the Terrorism Act, though no one has yet been convicted.
The scale of the arrests, and the profile of those detained – including retirees in their 80s and 90s – has put Britain’s Labour Party government under pressure.
The centre-left government has tried to rebuild bridges with pro-Palestinian supporters since Prime Minister Andy Burnham replaced Keir Starmer in July.
Last month the UK formally recognised a Palestinian state and banned goods from Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, which are illegal under international law. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said his message to people “moved and outraged by the plight of the Palestinian people” is: “We hear you. You were right.”
But the government has not lifted the ban on Palestine Action, and the group continues to challenge its proscription in court.
The High Court ruled in February that classing Palestine Action as a terror group alongside the likes of al Qaeda and Hamas was disproportionate and unlawful. The Court of Appeal overturned that decision in June, saying outlawing the group was “justified and proportionate”.
Next month the group’s lawyers will ask the country’s top court, the UK Supreme Court, to quash the ban.
John Clegg, a bookseller at the London Review Bookshop, told the Guardian that Rooney’s stance could help in changing the law.
“Good on her for taking a stand, it seems a ridiculous law. If this thing convinces the Home Office to move faster to get rid of it, I’m all for it.”
(FRANCE 24 with AP)

Four years after the promises of Cop15, our biodiversity targets are slipping away
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
06:00:53 UTC
15:00:53 KST

The world has lost its way on nature once again. Next week, biodiversity Cop17 begins in Yerevan, Armenia, and expectations are low. Very low.
Almost four years ago, governments reached an historic agreement at the biodiversity Cop15 to halt the destruction of Earth’s ecosystems – to rapturous applause in Montreal, Canada. I still remember the excitement in the hall in the early hours of that freezing December morning.
Governments had never met a self-mandated target on biodiversity loss, but there was a sense after the Covid-19 pandemic that this time really would be different. The 23-point deal included targets to protect 30% of the planet for nature, restore 30% of the planet’s degraded terrestrial, inland water, coastal and marine ecosystems, and tackle $500bn of environmentally damaging subsidies. Almost every country in the world, apart from the US and the Vatican, backed it.
Yes, the agreement was flawed, and barely matched what the science tells us we need to do to stop biodiversity loss. But it was a serious, considered plan to tackle the underlying causes of the largest loss of life since the dinosaurs (this time, humans are the asteroid).
Since then, though, action has fallen short. More on why that is, what it means and what is at stake at Cop17, after this week’s climate headlines.
Essential reads
- A perfect storm: how the super El Niño is devastating the fishing industry
- ‘We need less point scoring’: What party conference season taught us about UK climate action
- ‘I didn’t want to write about this’: the man who first saw chimps waging civil war
In focus
The summit in Yerevan is about assessing progress towards the targets, and the scorecard does not look good. In preparatory meetings governments have acknowledged (pdf) that they are way off track from meeting any of the targets. The traffic-light system used to rate actions towards the targets from countries is awash with yellow, orange and red.
“Unless collective implementation accelerates rapidly, the 2030 targets and mission will not be achieved,” the pre-Cop17 report reads. “Parties and other actors have taken action to address all 23 targets; however, no target presents a fully positive picture. The available evidence indicates that there are gaps in the collective progress. Without urgently addressing these gaps and barriers, it will not be possible to meet the 2030 targets and mission, in turn placing achievement of the 2050 goals and vision [to live in harmony with nature] in jeopardy.”
This time, it is hard to be too angry with some governments. Countries including Kazakhstan have used the agreement to drive a major rewilding effort, bringing back the caspian tiger. The EU did attempt to enact the targets with the nature restoration law – but it quickly became a culture-wars issue. Swathes of the world, though, have turned against action on the environment.
Donald Trump’s return to the White House has been catastrophic for the conservation sector, caught in his administration clampdown on the climate and “woke” policies. Through USAID and partner organisations, the US government provided, on average, 12.1% of the world’s biodiversity funding between 2015 and 2022, according to the OECD. Almost all of that has gone, hitting everything from anti-rhino poaching initiatives in east Africa, to efforts to combat illegal fishing in the Galápagos.
Power has also drained out of multilateral organisations such as the UN. Tech billionaires and the architects of AI are more powerful than many countries. Trump’s second term has seen a return to might-is-right politics that is dismissive of the international cooperation needed to make an agreement like this a reality.
So what next? Cop17 in Armenia is likely to be a moment where the calamity of the last four years crystallises – and governments must try to pick up the pieces.
“There’s a massive gap between countries agreeing to do something and actually doing it,” says Zac Goldsmith, who was UK environment minister when that landmark Cop15 deal was reached in 2022. “That’s where we are today.”

Tories call for 5-year freeze on minimum wage to tackle youth unemployment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
06:00:52 UTC
15:00:52 KST

A shadow minister has called for the government to freeze the minimum wage for five years, a move that could cost low-paid workers almost £9,000.
The call came in a report from the Prosperity Institute thinktank, which carries an endorsement from Andrew Sharpe, the shadow business minister. Sharpe said in his endorsement that it was time to take action to address the low rate of young people in work.
“With almost 1 million young people not in education, employment or training this report is timely and its recommendations very sound. The government should adopt them in full,” the Conservative MP said.
The paper recommends freezing the “national living wage” at £12.71 for five years and abolishing the Low Pay Commission (LPC), the independent body that recommends the yearly increase.
It also recommends returning employer national insurance contributions to pre-April 2025 levels and reinstating the two-year qualifying period for unfair dismissal, which was abolished under Labour’s Employment Rights Act.
The paper says a five-year freeze could result in an increase of about 270,000 young people in work, by suggesting that for every 1 percentage point increase in the minimum wage there is a a 0.37 percentage point decrease in the youth employment rate.
The report’s authors said they “do not present these findings as costless to workers” and that minimum wage workers’ purchasing power would be eroded by 9% to 12% over the five years due to projected inflation of 2% to 2.5%, a cumulative loss over five years of about £8,900.
The Labour business minister Kate Dearden said the recommendations were “tin-eared” and showed a pattern from the Conservatives of disparaging the minimum wage.
“It’s clear that Kemi Badenoch’s top team are determined that the lowest paid workers should be worse off,” she said. “The Conservatives opposed the minimum wage when the last Labour government introduced it, and now they’re showing again how little they understand the pressures facing people on the lowest pay. It’s the same old Tories, they haven’t changed.
“This Labour government believes that if you work hard, you should be able to get on in life. That’s why we’ve boosted work for the lowest paid, introduced more rights at work, and are giving people breathing space they deserve on the cost of living.”
Labour has previously said it intends to equalise the different rates of minimum wage – promising to give 18- to 20-year-olds the full rate. But rising youth unemployment has led to a debate at the top of government over how fast it should meet its promise.
The LPC last year recommended a 4.1% increase in the main rate of the minimum wage, and an 8.5% rise in the youth rate. The rates now stand at £12.71 and £10.85 respectively.
The commission will tell the government in October what it is recommending for the financial year starting on 1 April 2027, though ministers are not bound to accept the commission’s recommendations.
Earlier this year, ministers changed their guidance to the LPC to reflect the concerns in government over unemployment among young people, in the hope that it might recommend a lower level this year to make it easier for employers to take on younger staff.
The LPC has said it does not believe wage rises are contributing to higher youth unemployment rates. “While the commission recognises that labour market outcomes for young people have deteriorated over the past two years, we are not aware of any robust evidence that higher youth rates have contributed to these falls,” it said.

‘A haven of soft light, warm sunshine and sandy beaches’: readers’ favourite autumn escapes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
06:00:52 UTC
15:00:52 KST

Collioure is a Mediterranean dream
Last October, while I was cycling around south-west France, near the Spanish border, a tip from a local waiter led me to Collioure, near Perpignan. The town was like a Mediterranean dream, where the summer crowds had faded, leaving behind a peaceful, artistic haven of soft light, warm sunshine, cobbled streets, sandy beaches – and the Pyrenees as a backdrop. In the early evening, the still balmy autumn air was perfect for wandering through the quiet, pastel-coloured alleyways of the Le Mouré district to enjoy €5 off-season happy hour wine with fish tapas. I had planned to stay a weekend but ended up staying a week, seduced by Collioure’s perfect autumn cocktail of chilled Catalan culture and sunkissed seaside sensuality.
 
April
Peaceful Portuguese sunsets
Sitting outside in T-shirt and shorts on the deck of a boat gliding along the Tagus River in Lisbon, sipping a glass of crisp Portuguese wine as the setting autumn sun illuminated the pastel-coloured hills, is a lasting travel memory for me. October temperatures were still in the mid-20s, perfect for exploring fascinating areas on foot, or hanging out of trams as they rattled up and down the cobbled streets. In the evenings, I joined local people basking in the remaining warmth of the year at outdoor cafes or waterside tavernas like Ponto Final, enjoying coffee and pastries, or anchovies and beer, while watching magnificent sunsets without the summer masses.
 
Nicoletta
Wild times in St Davids, Pembrokeshire
My autumn escape is St Davids on the Pembrokeshire coast. Once the summer crowds disappear, it feels wonderfully wild and tranquil. We walk the coast path towards Whitesands, stopping to watch for seals below the cliffs, before heading back into tiny St Davids for something warm to eat. The beaches are often almost empty and, even when the weather turns, the dramatic sea and windswept coastline are part of the charm. My tip is to visit in early autumn; pack proper walking boots and layers, and embrace the weather – you get one of Britain’s loveliest coastlines almost to yourself.
 
Tess
Baroque beauty in eastern Germany
Görlitz makes for a fascinating autumnal base, with its location on the German-Polish border to the east of Dresden. The highlights were day excursions to Bad Muskau, where there is a wonderful baroque palace, and the Rakotzbrücke (Devil’s Bridge), reached by a narrow-gauge forest railway (waldeisenbahn.de). It’s a part of Germany rarely visited, but those who go there will be rewarded with amazing photographs.
 
Martin
Bliss on a lesser-visited Canary island
The Canary Islands are well-trodden choices for autumn sun, but the island of El Hierro remains a wilder alternative to Tenerife or Lanzarote. The scenery is beautiful and bizarrely varied: from pine forests to black volcanic lava flows – most of which you’ll have to yourself. You can pass hours exploring the rugged coastlines, where volcanic swimming holes such as Charco Azul can be found. We spent a blissful few hours there, relaxing on the rocks and looking out at the Atlantic. There are no big resorts but plenty of guest houses and smaller hotels, and sunshine is almost guaranteed into November.
 
Leo Mark
Dramatic Devon walks
We stayed in Woolacombe, north Devon, with our three-year-old in October 2023 and the off-season suited us well. The three-mile beach gave us room for proper sandcastle engineering, and the Atlantic offered drama rather than deckchair weather. We watched the sunset turn the sea orange and purple from the hill above the bay. We could walk into the village, then use Woolacombe as a base for Mortehoe and the South West Coast Path. Pack waterproofs as well as sunglasses: north Devon makes no promises. But on a bright autumn day, those enormous sands feel almost privately hired.
 
Katharina Parsons
Coast, culture and cable cars on Madeira
Funchal on Madeira is my pick for an autumn escape because it still feels properly alive after summer. The seafront is made for slow walks in the sunshine, with cafes and gardens open year-round. You can browse the colourful Mercado dos Lavradores, ride the cable car for views over the terracotta rooftops and Atlantic, then cool off at one of the city’s lidos. The weather is pleasantly warm rather than overpowering, while the mountains and levada (aqueduct) walks are within easy reach. It combines coast, culture and dramatic scenery without feeling like a resort that closes down for winter.
 
Bernice
Clifftops and crab rolls in the Scottish Borders
If you’re looking for a cracking wee coastal escape, head straight to St Abbs in the Scottish Borders. My wife and I absolutely fell in love with its rugged charm and bonny views. First off, Marvel fans will know it as New Asgard from Avengers: Endgame, and taking a selfie by the official sign set the right tone. Beyond the film fame, the dramatic clifftop walk up to St Abb’s Head is brilliant, packed with seabirds and proper fresh sea air. Afterwards, grab a fresh crab roll down at the harbour cafe – nae hassle, just proper good cheer.
 
Craig
Nonstop sun in a Cretan haven
Autumn came brutal and early to Crete this month. But the ferocious northerly that drenched the northern coast got stuck on the White Mountains. And on just one tiny south-west speck of the island, the sun shone all and every day. Palaiochora is a year-round magic place anyway. No big hotels. Still proudly Greek. A place where the town’s rhythms are set by the comings and goings of the Loutro ferry. But this past week, while thunder stalked the mountains, we swam and walked every day. “We’re unique,” said the man at the cafe. “Please don’t tell anyone.” What have I done?
 
Kay Jones
Winning tip: Fiestas and feasts in Zaragoza, Spain
For an autumn city break, Zaragoza comes alive during the Fiestas del Pilar in October. We spent a week there, wandering bustling streets lined with people, many in traditional dress, queueing to lay flowers at the vast floral tribute to the Virgin Mary in Plaza del Pilar. Along the river, food stalls served Aragonese specialities, from chistorra (sausage) and stews to roast chestnuts and sweet wine. Between festivities, we explored the stunning Aljafería Palace and discovered tiny tapas bars tucked down side streets. The city felt wonderfully local, lively and full of surprises.
 
Carrie

Ministers have been asked to extend Service Pupil Premium funding and wraparound childcare to the children of Royal Fleet Auxiliary personnel, and have replied that existing arrangements are kept under review, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Rachel Gilmour, the Liberal Democrat member for Tiverton and Minehead, asked what assessment had been made of the adequacy of welfare and family support for Royal Fleet Auxiliary personnel and their families, and whether eligibility for schemes open to armed forces families would be extended to them.
Calvin Bailey, Parliamentary Under-Secretary and Minister for Veterans and People, said: “The Ministry of Defence recognises the importance of supporting Royal Fleet Auxiliary (RFA) personnel and their families. Further support is delivered through the Employee Assistance Programme, the Defence Health and Wellbeing Portfolio, and Family and People Services, with the RFA workforce also benefitting from an extended welfare network under the umbrella of expert services, including the Navy Families Federation, ensuring holistic support for employees and their families.”
Royal Fleet Auxiliary personnel are civilians employed by the Ministry of Defence who crew the ships that fuel, supply and support the Royal Navy at sea, and their conditions sit outside the arrangements that cover service families.
The Royal Fleet Auxiliary employs around 1,800 people and crews the tankers and stores ships that keep the Royal Navy at sea, along with the Bay class landing ships and the aviation training ship Argus. Its sailors are civil servants and not service personnel, which is the distinction the question was aimed at. Pay and conditions have been a running problem, with members of the RMT and Nautilus International taking strike action in 2024 over a long period of below-inflation awards, and the service has struggled to hold on to qualified officers.

No breakthrough: EU budget talks have stalled
Kyiv • UNN
EU leaders failed to reach an agreement on the long-term budget at the summit in Brussels. The countries are arguing over cutting spending and increasing the budget.
European leaders failed to agree on the EU's long-term budget on the first day of the summit. UNN reports this with reference to DW.
Details
Talks among European leaders on the EU budget for the next seven years failed to produce a breakthrough and will continue in December, according to information received from sources in the German government overnight into Friday, October 16, by AFP. According to the publication's sources, several positions clashed during the summit of heads of state and government of EU member states in Brussels, leading to "controversial debates." As the agency notes, these positions were known even before the talks began. Some countries, including Germany, Austria, Sweden, Denmark, the Netherlands and Finland, are calling for spending cuts, while others, including France, Spain and Poland, are advocating an increase in the EU budget.
Last summer, the European Commission presented a draft long-term budget worth almost two trillion euros. Ireland, which holds the presidency of the Council of the EU, proposed cutting the budget by €140 billion (approximately 8%).
Ireland's proposal envisages cuts to EU budget spending in the areas of competitiveness, scientific research, defense and foreign policy.
The EU wants to agree on the budget by the end of the year
At the summit, France focused on introducing new pan-European levies that would make it possible to increase the budget without raising member states' contributions. In particular, the proposal concerns levies on digital services, crypto-assets and online gambling.

The next EU summit will take place in December. Many of the EU's 27 member states want to approve the long-term budget by the end of the year, since in 2027 euroskeptic and populist forces may come to power in several countries as a result of elections.
Thus, far-right politician Marine Le Pen may win the presidential election in France. As AFP reports, the country's current head, Emmanuel Macron, has already warned that in such a case reaching an agreement on the EU budget would be "difficult."
Before the talks began, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz called for the draft budget proposed by the European Commission to be "substantially" reduced and categorically rejected the idea of allocating additional funds to the traditional major spending areas—agriculture and cohesion policy.
Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker did not rule out the possibility that the talks could drag on and continue next year.

Ukraine pushes for European alternatives to US air defences and Starlink amid tensions with Washington
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
05:59:59 UTC
14:59:59 KST

As tensions between Kyiv and Washington deepen Ukraine is looking to Europe to help secure its long-term defence and technological independence. A senior Ukrainian presidential official told Euronews that concrete plans are already taking shape.
Ukraine is pushing ahead with plans to develop European alternatives to US-made air defence systems and Starlink satellite communications, with concrete discussions already under way and Kyiv expecting progress considerably sooner than sceptics anticipate, a senior Ukrainian presidential official has told Euronews.
In an exclusive interview with the Europe Today programme ahead of Friday's EU summit in Brussels, Ihor Zhovkva, deputy head of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's office, said Ukraine was seeking to reduce its reliance on American capabilities as uncertainty over Washington's support places growing pressure on Europe to strengthen its own defences.
"We are, of course, relying on the unique capabilities provided by the United States, whether air defence systems or Starlink," Zhovkva said.
"But Ukraine has already begun substantive discussions with European countries about a European air defence system."
He pointed to FREYJA, a European anti-ballistic missile programme launched in Paris in July, saying discussions had progressed to direct engagement between defence companies.
"We need a European equivalent of an air defence system," he said, adding that Ukraine intended to take a leading role in its development.
Kyiv is also pursuing talks on a European alternative to Starlink, with Zhovkva confirming that negotiations were under way but declining to disclose further details.
"European countries must have their own corresponding system," he said.
Zhovkva argued that both projects were essential not only to Ukraine's defence but also to Europe's wider security.
Asked whether developing these systems would take too long, Zhovkva dismissed such concerns.
"We have a clear timetable and deadlines," he said. "It will be much faster than ten or fifteen years, and even faster than five."
He declined to give a specific date.
Europe faces growing pressure to sustain Ukraine's defence
The plans come amid mounting tensions between Kyiv and Washington, including over US President Donald Trump's pressure on Ukraine to halt strikes against Russian oil infrastructure, and growing concerns about the reliability of American military support.
Russia has meanwhile intensified its aerial campaign against Ukraine, with fresh attacks on energy infrastructure raising fears of another difficult winter.
Zhovkva said securing additional air defence systems and interceptor missiles, alongside measures to protect Ukraine's energy infrastructure, would be among Zelenskyy's main priorities at the EU summit.
"Every country that can provide such assistance, whether systems or missiles, should do so," he said, adding that those unable to supply equipment should contribute financially.
Whether Europe can make up for any reduction in American military assistance, however, remains uncertain.
Zhovkva acknowledged that despite substantial contributions from countries such as Germany, European support was still falling short of Ukraine's needs.
With Kyiv facing a further funding shortfall next year, he stressed the importance of maintaining existing military commitments while securing additional European financial support.
Europe must have a seat at negotiating table
Zhovkva argued that European security guarantees should form the foundation of Ukraine's long-term security arrangements, identifying sustained support for its armed forces, joint defence production and EU membership as essential elements.
"The foundation of security guarantees for Ukraine is a strong, powerful army," he said, stressing the importance of reliable long-term financing.
"Without a clear understanding that Ukraine will become a member of the EU, we cannot speak about full-fledged security guarantees."
Yet despite growing tensions with Washington, Zhovkva acknowledged that European guarantees could not work alone.
"They cannot exist without support from the United States of America," he said.
With Washington seeking to revive diplomatic efforts to end the war, Zhovkva reaffirmed Kyiv's readiness to negotiate, while insisting that European partners must be involved at every stage, including any eventual talks between leaders.
"Ukraine is ready for negotiations now," he said.
"Europe, in the broader sense of the word, must be present at the table," he added, arguing that Ukraine's future security was inseparable from that of the wider continent.

Istanbul faces more rain as flood searches continue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
05:53:44 UTC
14:53:44 KST

Istanbul remains gripped by the aftermath of its heaviest rainfall in eight decades on Oct. 16, with municipal crews working to clear flood debris and repair damage as meteorologists warn of further downpours and renewed flooding.
Heavy rain began lashing Türkiye’s largest city on the morning of Oct. 14, intensifying throughout the day and triggering widespread disruption and flash floods. Footage showed cars being swept away by fast-flowing floodwaters.
Four people have been reported dead in the flooding. A 14-year-old was electrocuted after stepping into a puddle in a park in the Fatih district, while a 34-year-old slipped on a sidewalk in Sarıyer and suffered a fatal head injury.
Search operations later uncovered another body along a stream in Istanbul’s Kağıthane district, bringing the death toll to three.
On Oct. 16, rescue teams found the body of a person reported missing in Ayazağa, a neighborhood in Sarıyer. 
Among the hardest-hit locations was Sarıyer’s Ayazağa neighborhood, where power and natural gas outages persisted until noon on Oct. 15, leaving local bakeries and markets unable to operate.
On Oct. 16, Interior Minister Mustafa Çiftçi and Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change Minister Murat Kurum visited Ayazağa.
“We are experiencing the worst flood disaster since 1942,” Çiftçi told reporters during the visit.
Çiftçi said the number of people reported missing fell from five to four, adding that one of the missing individuals had lost contact with authorities after their phone battery ran out during the flooding.
Following the discovery of the body of a missing person, shortly after Çiftçi’s visit, search efforts were continuing for three other people.
“We experienced this problem because of inadequate infrastructure and haphazard urbanization. We will address the needs here. We will provide shelter for those who need accommodation and food for those who need food,” Kurum said.
Although the intensity of the downpour eased on Oct. 15, meteorological authorities warned that another spell of heavy rain was expected to reach Istanbul on Oct. 16 and 17, raising concerns about renewed flooding.
Rainfall recorded across Istanbul over the 48-hour period from Oct. 13 to 15 exceeded the long-term average for September and October. Precipitation reached 272 kilograms per square meter in some parts of the city, equivalent to approximately one-seventh of the area’s annual rainfall.
As the rain temporarily subsided on the morning of Oct. 16, Istanbul’s municipal crews began clearing the damage left behind by the floods.
Cleanup and repair operations were underway across the city, particularly in the districts of Beykoz, Şile, Sarıyer and Kağıthane, where torrential rain had caused flooding.
Response teams were active across the area, pumping water out of affected properties and removing ruined belongings. Crews also cleared streets of mud and debris before deploying washer trucks to clean the roadways.
Heavy rain caused a section of road outside Eyüpsultan to collapse. Crews cordoned off the area while heavy machinery worked to stabilize and clear the site.

G-7 to launch exercises to guard against AI cyberattacks
BANGKOK – Finance leaders of the Group of Seven (G-7) grouping agreed to hold tabletop exercises to guard against AI cyberattacks, Japanese Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama said, as policymakers increasingly seek to coordinate responses to growing cyber security risks.
The agreement comes after the International Monetary Fund warned this week that confidence could be undermined by an AI-enabled cyberattack on a critical service of a financial institution.
“The G7 finance deputies had been discussing the idea of doing tabletop exercises on frontier AI, which was signed off at the ministerial level,” Katayama told reporters on Oct 15.
She made the remarks after attending a meeting of finance ministers and central bank governors of the G-7 advanced economies held on the sidelines of the IMF’s annual gathering in Bangkok, the Thai capital.
The plan will feature simulations evolved by G-7 finance authorities to test how they can respond to AI-driven cyberattacks, said a Japanese finance ministry official who attended the finance leaders’ meeting.
The results will test effectiveness of existing protocols and be used to revise manuals to better tackle such incidents, the official told reporters.
The exercises by G-7 finance ministries and central banks could include private financial institutions depending on the nature of simulations, the official added.
Banking regulators globally are stepping up efforts to contain growing AI risks, Reuters reported, with some pointing to the potential for cyberattacks on banks or rogue agents undermining global financial stability.
Among them is the Bank of England, which is working with banks on deep cyber-recovery options, its deputy governor said on Oct 15, adding that they can no longer assume their defences are immune to AI-enabled cyberattacks. REUTERS

Kella 19.30 paiku sai politsei teate kahest mehest, kes seisid Valdeku tänaval ühe maja juures ja paistsid olevat eksinud. Politsei pidas mõlemad mehed kinni. Tegemist oli Sudaani kodanikega, kes viibisid Eestis ebaseaduslikult.

Droon märkas metsas liikuvaid inimesi ning politsei leidis sealt veel kaheksa meest. Üks meestest kukkus põgenedes ja vigastas kätt.
Kõik kümme meest viibisid Eestis ebaseaduslikult ning isikut tõendav dokument oli neist vaid ühel.
Hiiumaal ei saa naised enam sünnitada
Alates juulist ei saa Hiiumaa naised enam kodusaarel sünnitada. Endiselt pole selge, kuidas korraldada sünnitajate transport mandrile ja tagasi ning kes selle eest maksab.
Kärdlas elav Kärolyn Kivistik ootab oma viiendat last, kelle sünnitähtaeg on 8. novembril. Haiglakott on tal juba pakitud. Kuna ta ei soovi sünnituse ajal reisida, läheb ta tõenäoliselt nädal varem Tallinna. Pere hinnangul kaasneb sellega ligi 1000 eurot lisakulusid.
Hiiumaa haiglas on sünnitusabi osutamiseks vajalikud ruumid ja seadmed, kuid puuduvad töötajad. Lastearst läks juulist pensionile ning septembris puudus neljal päeval ka naistearst.
Haigla juhi Riina Tamme sõnul esitati esmaspäeval haigla nõukogule tegevuskava, kuid sünnitajate mandrile ja sealt tagasi toomise küsimus on endiselt lahendamata.
Tamme hinnangul on tegemist regionaalpoliitilise probleemiga, mis ei puuduta ainult Hiiumaad.
