Standardi koostanud komisjoni juhtinud Kristel Ressi sõnul tuleb teksti kirjutades kõigepealt mõelda sellele, kes seda lugema hakkab. Näiteks külmas paadis telefonist juhiste lugemine erineb kodus teksti lugemisest.
Ressi sõnul on standard abivahend, mitte rangete reeglite kogum. Ta sedastas, et esimest korda on kõik need soovitused koondatud ühte lühikesse juhendisse.
ERR-i keeletoimetaja Ester Põldma sõnul on soovitustest kasu kõigile, kes kirjutavad veebitekste. "Lugeja peaks juba esimesel lugemisel aru saama, mida lausega öelda tahetakse," ütles Põldma.

US sanctions leave Iranians facing flight cancellations and soaring costs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
05:51:40 UTC
14:51:40 KST

US sanctions leave Iranians facing flight cancellations and soaring costs
New US aviation sanctions force Iranians to take longer, costlier journeys as international flight routes disappear.
In late September, travellers could still fly directly from Tehran to Dubai in less than three hours, with a ticket costing between $100 and $200.
Less than a month later, it can take up to 18 hours to make the same journey and cost more than $1,000.
The change is the result of a new round of United States sanctions targeting Iranian airlines and foreign companies providing them with services. The restrictions intensified after a September 23 deadline for companies to stop servicing Iranian carriers, leading to the suspension of direct flights between Iran and the United Arab Emirates, as well as a number of other countries.
The United States has sought to block routes into and out of Iran and, more broadly, restrict access to the country. In August, the US announced Operation Economic Outcast as a means of increasing pressure on Iran, targeting the few remaining sectors of the Iranian economy still connected to the global economy.
As part of the campaign, the US sanctioned 27 airlines operating in Iran. Airports, fuel suppliers, ground-handling service providers and other foreign companies working with Iranian airlines were threatened with secondary sanctions, potentially cutting them off from the US financial system.
The first sign of the impact of the new sanctions came on September 24, when an Iranian flight travelling from Tehran to Dushanbe was forced to turn back mid-journey and return to Tehran after it was denied permission to enter Turkmenistan’s airspace.
The UAE, Azerbaijan, and Georgia also suspended services for Iranian flights. Flights between Iran and Muscat and Baghdad were halted, while a number of flights from Iran to neighbouring Turkiye were cancelled. Flights from Iran to the popular Shia pilgrimage destination of Najaf in Iraq were also briefly disrupted in late September.
All this was happening against the backdrop of the US-Israeli war on Iran, which had already caused widespread disruption to the country’s international air links. The vast majority of international airlines have yet to resume their services to Iran.
Flights to countries including China and Russia have continued despite the latest US measures, but restoring suspended routes will require negotiations with other governments.
Mass disruption
More than three weeks after the new aviation sanctions came into effect, routes to destinations including Moscow, Najaf, Istanbul, Yerevan and Guangzhou in China have continued operating. But Iran’s international flight network remains severely restricted.
The situation has created major disruption for both people travelling to Iran and those leaving the country.
Amir, 43, who lives in the US state of Illinois, described the challenges his ailing mother faced in attempting to travel to Iran.
“My mother lives in the United States, but her medical records are in Iran,” he said. “For months, her medical appointments have been delayed because of the war and the conditions it has created.
“A few weeks ago, we decided to take advantage of the relative calm and make a trip to Iran so she could receive medical care. But then the new sanctions were announced, effectively disrupting flights to Iran.
“Now, to get to Iran, we have to fly to Istanbul and wait there for several hours or even several days, depending on when a flight to Iran is available,” Amir said, adding that it was also difficult to purchase Iranian airline tickets from outside the country as a result of international sanctions.
“Making such a journey is extremely stressful for a woman travelling alone who is also ill. It is completely unfair.”
The sanctions have also had a significant impact on Iran’s domestic travel.
Majid Hosseini-Nejad, the founder of Alibaba Travel Group, one of the country’s largest online platforms for booking travel tickets and accommodation, told Al Jazeera that the new sanctions had affected ticket sales.
“As a result of the recent sanctions, around 20 percent of the flights operating from Iran to international destinations have been suspended,” Hosseini-Nejad said. “This has reduced revenues for airline ticket-booking services. Airlines’ revenues have also fallen significantly because of the sanctions.”
On October 11, Iran’s Foreign Ministry announced that its Department of Economic Affairs was continuing efforts to facilitate Iranian flights to destinations in other countries.
Flights to and from Iran continue to face lengthy delays, last-minute cancellations and, in some cases, even diversions back to their point of departure.
For now, Iranian travellers have little clarity about when the situation might change.
Another traveller named Amir, an Iranian national who flies regularly between Iran and Oman for work, said, “Beyond the other financial losses caused by the sanctions, flight cancellations have added another layer of difficulty to our lives. Every trip between Muscat and Tehran now takes several times longer and costs several times more than before.
“It is unclear when the situation will change, or whether it will improve at all.”

Russia takes control of more European corporate assets ahead of Zelenskiy's appearance at EU summit

Russia takes over more EU companies' assets over Ukraine support
MOSCOW, Oct 16 - Russia has seized control of the local assets of four companies from France, Germany, Sweden and Belgium, according to a decree by President Vladimir Putin, in retaliation for Europe's wartime support for Ukraine.
Thursday's decree listed assets belonging to French flooring maker Tarkett, German packaging maker Menshen, Swedish packaging maker Sverige International Holdings and Belgian hygiene product company Ontex.
The decree also listed Russian assets of former European metal-packaging business Eviosys acquired by US packaging group Sonoco in December 2024. The decree listed the assets as owned by Sonoco's Dutch unit.
EU leaders rallied around President Volodymyr Zelenskiy at a summit on Friday at one of the most difficult moments for Ukraine amid fears that the US could pull back intelligence sharing and weapons support from Kyiv.
The Kremlin said that the assets' takeover continued a trend after a similar move last month against food giant Nestle and retailers Auchan and Metro.
"Their country of origin was one of the factors taken into account in making the decision," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said, adding that these countries were involved in "illegal expropriations of Russian property."
Temporary administration of the European companies' properties was handed to Russian companies that had been largely unknown.
PUTIN NOTES 'DOWNSIDES'
Ontex, which employs 350 people in Russia and operates a factory outside Moscow, said it has been informed about the decree and will "consider appropriate actions to safeguard its assets and the continuity of Ontex Russia’s operations."
Sonoco said in its 2025 report that it had finalised its own exit from Russia in 2022 but acquired more assets, making up 0.5% of the company's total, as part of the Eviosys deal.
Tarkett said it was "losing effective control over its operations in Russia" and was assessing the situation.
The Kremlin said the measures responded to EU nations' involvement in "direct battlefield hostilities" but were also "reversible."
Speaking to Russian businessmen just before the decree was published on Thursday, Putin acknowledged that taking Western assets had "certain downsides" without giving more details.
He urged the Russian businesses taking over the assets to seek domestic financing sources instead.
Putin cited the 2008 global financial crisis, which had a profound impact on the Russian economy, as an example of the risks of excessive exposure to global markets. He said foreign countries pursued their own interests through investment.
There have been some reports that the US could seek control of some Russian assets frozen in Europe as part of efforts to provide incentives for Russia to negotiate with Ukraine.
Russia criticises the EU for freezing about €210 billion ($238 billion) of its sovereign assets in response to the war and for targeting assets belonging to Russian companies in Europe and other Western countries. REUTERS

Israeli airlines were operating 56 percent above pre-crisis levels.
Across the European network, arrival punctuality stood at 74.1 percent and departure punctuality at 69.8 percent, both lower than in the same week of 2025.
Air traffic flow management delays averaged 2.5 minutes per flight.
Jet fuel prices reached $4.82 per gallon on Oct. 9, up 2 percent over the preceding two weeks.

Four killed as Indonesia battles worst forest fires in more than a decade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
05:15:09 UTC
14:15:09 KST

Four killed as Indonesia battles worst forest fires in more than a decade
The deaths come as Jakarta says it will accept foreign help to tackle its worst forest fires in more than a decade.
Four people tackling a wildfire in a national park on Indonesia’s island of Java have been killed, the Forestry Ministry said, as the country battles its worst forest fires in more than a decade.
The victims were caught in the flames on Thursday in Bromo Tengger Semeru National Park in East Java, the ministry said on Friday.
Two others suffered serious burns and are receiving medical treatment. The forest fires have extended beyond Indonesia’s borders, blanketing neighbouring countries in haze, Reuters reported.
The ministry did not identify the victims. In a statement, it expressed “deep condolences” and paid tribute to the “courage and dedication” of the officers, volunteers and residents working on the fire lines.
The deaths, it said, were “a reminder that extinguishing forest and land fires is a high-risk operation”, adding that safety “must be the main concern”, including tracking how the fire is spreading and the wind direction, keeping evacuation routes ready and assessing conditions before and during operations.
The islands of Sumatra and Borneo, close to Singapore and Malaysia, are the worst affected.
Hotspots increase
The ministry said satellite monitoring detected 799 high-confidence hotspots nationwide as of Thursday night, up 427 from the day before. The ministry cautioned that hotspots are not the same as fires, as one blaze can register as several.
Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto has approved accepting help from neighbouring countries, Foreign Minister Arrmanatha Nasir said, according to Reuters.
Malaysia offered last month to send three helicopters, an aircraft and 52 personnel, but there has been no follow-up, Reuters reported. Singapore has also said it is ready to help.
Indonesia has faced heavy criticism over the fires, which have caused respiratory problems for hundreds of thousands of people and forced school closures in Malaysia and East Timor, according to Reuters.

US President Donald Trump has ruled out using nuclear weapons against Iran, saying Washington did not need them and emphasising that the "mother of all bombs" was non-nuclear.
Asked during an interview on Thursday with Newsmax about reports that his administration was considering using the bomb against Iran, potentially after the US midterm elections, Trump stressed that the weapon was conventional, not nuclear.
“The mother of all bombs is not nuclear,” he said, describing it as “just an extremely large bomb”.
He reiterated that the US did not need to use nuclear weapons.
“No, I wouldn't use nuclear. We don't have to,” he said.
Trump also raised the possibility of further strikes against Iran's nuclear facilities, including a suspected underground site known as Pickaxe Mountain.
"Now, we're looking at Pickaxe Mountain. We may have to go there," he said.
"We'll take a shot at that one. We'll knock it out fast."
Asked whether such an operation would involve American ground troops, Trump replied: "No, I don't see that. I don't see that."
He said withdrawing before ensuring Iran could not obtain nuclear weapons might require further US military action within a year.
"We want to make it so that they will never have a nuclear weapon," he said.
‘Iran war will be over very soon’
Trump also predicted that the war would end soon, saying Tehran was negotiating with Washington.
"The Iran war will be over very soon. It's going to end very soon," he said.
"One way or the other, it'll end very soon. And oil will go dropping like a rock — and gas prices as well."
Trump claimed Iranian officials had requested a halt to American and Israeli military operations.
"They've asked us to please stop. And we do, because we're negotiating with them," he said.
Asked whether he trusted Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Trump responded: "I don't trust anybody, honestly."

Finland to introduce mobile phone emergency alert system in November
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:13:54 EEST
14:13:54 KST

Emergency warnings will be sent directly to mobile phones in Finland under a new system called FI-Alert, according to the Ministry of Interior in a press release.
The system will complement Finland's existing emergency warnings by enabling authorities to send alerts almost instantly to phones in specific affected areas.
Currently, emergency warnings are available through the 112 Suomi and Yle apps, radio and television broadcasts, teletext page 112, and the 112.fi and yle.fi websites. Authorities can also use public warning sirens.
The new system is being introduced as authorities seek to improve their ability to reach the public quickly during emergencies, amid a changing security situation.
No app or personal information required
FI-Alert is based on Cell Broadcast technology and the EU Alert concept.
Such technology allows mobile phones to receive alerts without users having to share personal information, such as their phone number or location data.
The only requirements are that the phone is switched on and configured to receive Cell Broadcast messages. No app needs to be installed in advance, and users do not need to subscribe to the service.
The technology uses a distinctive sound to draw attention to alerts, even when a phone is set to silent. Messages appear on the phone screen automatically and remain there until the user acknowledges them.
The ministry has previously stated that the system is suited to emergency situations because it does not place the same strain on mobile networks as mass text-message distribution.
Similar systems are already in use or being developed in several European countries, and the Ministry of the Interior says the technology is becoming the most common way of using mobile phones to warn the public.
In August, the government proposed amending the law on emergency warnings to allow alerts to be sent using Cell Broadcast technology. President Alexander Stubb is expected to approve this legislation on Friday and bring it into force at the beginning of November.

PM Modi faces Gen Z revolt as anger spills onto India’s streets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
05:13:34 UTC
14:13:34 KST

Youth-led protests are mounting pressure on Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi as frustration over unemployment, alleged electoral manipulation and unfulfilled promises fuels demonstrations across the country.
Despite the deployment of tens of thousands of security personnel, young protesters scaled barricades, chanted anti-government slogans and clashed with police during demonstrations in New Delhi and elsewhere last week.
“Long live the revolution,” one protester shouted before police bundled him into a bus.
The independent Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (ACLED) says street protests in India this year are on course to reach their highest level in a decade. Analysts say the unrest, coupled with renewed opposition activity, represents Modi’s most serious political challenge since he took office in 2014.
“The nation has suddenly found its voice,” said activist Yogendra Yadav, who has played a leading role in the demonstrations. “I would not say this is the beginning of the end of the Modi regime, but this definitely is the beginning of a downward spiral.”
Modi’s government and his Bharatiya Janata Party declined to comment.
The latest demonstrations have centered on demands for the resignation of Election Commission chief Gyanesh Kumar over a voter-roll revision that opposition parties and activists allege favors the BJP and has helped it win recent state elections.
The government, the BJP and the Election Commission deny the accusations, with the ruling party attributing its electoral success to Modi’s popularity and economic growth.
But the protests reflect broader dissatisfaction with the government, including frustration over unemployment, examination paper leaks, crimes against women and the influence of wealthy businessmen alleged to have close ties to Modi.
Many young Indians also accuse the government of prioritizing Hindu nationalist politics over jobs and economic opportunities, while raising concerns about violence against religious minorities, particularly Muslims.
“The fear in us is gone,” said Ananya Raturi, a 21-year-old Delhi University student who joined protests in the capital.
Raturi said demonstrators were no longer deterred by the prospect of detention or police violence. Police have denied beating protesters and said officers followed established procedures.
The demonstrations have been energized by the Cockroach Janta Party, a youth-led movement that grew from online satire into a nationwide campaign in June after India's chief justice likened unemployed people to “cockroaches.”
Activists have used mobile phones and independent YouTube news channels to circulate footage of the protests, gaining audiences despite what critics describe as limited coverage by India's largely pro-government mainstream media.
CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke and left-wing activist Neha Bora have emerged as prominent online voices, while Congress Party leader Rahul Gandhi has joined demonstrations alongside tens of thousands of supporters.
The unrest has drawn comparisons with youth-led protests in neighboring Bangladesh and Nepal that brought down governments. However, analysts caution that India's political landscape and Modi's continuing support make direct comparisons difficult.
Employment remains a major source of anger among young people who grew up during Modi's rise to power and expected greater economic opportunity.
Although India has recorded strong economic growth, government figures put overall unemployment slightly above 5%. Unemployment among Indians aged 15 to 29 reached 9.9% in 2025, according to government data.
Azim Premji University's State of Working India 2026 report found that nearly 40% of graduates aged 15 to 25 were unemployed, while about one in five graduates aged 25 to 29 remained jobless.
Repeated examination paper leaks have added to the frustration. In May, protests erupted after the government invalidated examinations for admission to national medical colleges following leaked test papers.
Rubby Singh, a 30-year-old social activist in New Delhi, said the scandals had deepened young people's distrust of a system they believe is denying them opportunities despite years of study.
“This generation has been facing the brunt of not having proper education, which leads to not being able to get good opportunities,” she said.
The government, meanwhile, says the economy generated 168.3 million new jobs in the six years through 2024. Modi has repeatedly rejected allegations of religious bias, saying his administration serves all Indians.
India's next general election is not due until 2029, but elections in Uttar Pradesh, the country's most populous state, early next year could offer an indication of whether the growing discontent is weakening the BJP's electoral support.
Analysts caution that street protests do not necessarily translate into votes, and the ruling party retains considerable political strength.
“The BJP may not be as strong as it was a few months ago,” said Rahul Verma, a fellow at the Centre for Policy Research in New Delhi. “But whether there are going to be electoral implications, it is too early to say.”

Bank RBK to support World Wrestling Championships with record number of participating countries
Astana will host the World Wrestling Championships in Greco-Roman, freestyle, and women’s wrestling from October 24 to November 1, with Bank RBK serving as a partner of the event. Representatives from 135 countries have submitted applications to participate, setting a new record for the number of countries represented in the history of the senior World Wrestling Championships, Qazinform News Agency reports.
The championships will bring together the world’s top wrestlers in Kazakhstan. For fans, it will be an opportunity to watch world-class wrestling on home soil, while Astana will host one of the major events on the international sporting calendar.
“Hosting a World Championship of this magnitude is a great honor and a source of pride for Kazakhstan. When the world’s best athletes from 135 countries come to our country, Kazakhstan becomes the center of a major international sporting event, showcasing its strong traditions and great potential. For Bank RBK, it is important to be part of this event, which brings nations together, inspires young athletes and strengthens the belief that the greatest victories begin at home,” said Natalya Akentyeva, Chairwoman of the Management Board of Bank RBK.
Global scale in numbers
Interest in the championships has already surpassed previous records in terms of the number of participating countries. For comparison, the previous record was set in Istanbul in 2011, when 102 countries were represented.
According to the organizers' preliminary estimates, around 1,000 wrestlers are expected to compete. Over nine days, they will compete for medals across 30 weight categories. A total of 2,231 people have registered for the event, including athletes, coaches, heads of national federations and delegation members. More than 10,000 tourists are also expected to visit Astana during the championships.
Ahead of the competition, the United World Wrestling Congress will take place in Astana on October 23, bringing together representatives of the international wrestling community.
Opportunity to watch world champions on home soil
More than 51,000 children and teenagers train in wrestling at sports schools across Kazakhstan. For them, the World Championships will offer an opportunity to see the world’s top athletes compete in person, support the national team and experience the atmosphere of elite international competition.
“Hosting the World Wrestling Championships in Astana is a major event for Kazakhstan’s entire wrestling community. Over nine days, spectators will witness world-class competition, while our athletes will have the opportunity to compete for medals with the support of the home crowd. It is particularly important that such a tournament is being held in a country where wrestling has strong traditions and brings together tens of thousands of children and teenagers. We are grateful to Bank RBK for its partnership and support, which help make the World Championships more accessible to fans and encourage a new generation to take up the sport,” said Yerkin Okassov, Chairman of the Kazakhstan Wrestling Federation.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that Kazakhstan was hosting a stage of the World Aquatics Swimming World Cup for the first time.

Germany pressures Croatia to resolve bilateral disputes with Montenegro over EU accession
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
05:00:08 UTC
14:00:08 KST

The German government is pressuring Croatia to swiftly resolve its bilateral disputes with Montenegro, which would otherwise risk derailing Podgorica's accession process.
Berlin has stepped in, asking Croatia to constructively resolve the bilateral disputes that threaten to derail the accession of the EU’s most advanced candidate, four officials with direct knowledge of the matter told Euronews.
Earlier this week, Zagreb circulated an eight-point list of grievances that it wants resolved before Podgorica can finalise its accession bid. Behind the scenes, Berlin has been manoeuvring to ensure that enlargement does not lose momentum.
Berlin also recently offered to mediate, but the offer has not been put into practice. The government of Chancellor Friedrich Merz is positioning itself as an honest broker, fearing that unresolved bilateral problems could jeopardise the enlargement process.
“There are issues which we have signalled to our Montenegrin neighbours for years,” Croatian Prime Minister Andrej Plenković told reporters ahead of the European Council summit in Brussels on Thursday.
“In the last two years, there has been no progress whatsoever,” Plenković said, arguing that his country has been “extremely constructive” in the accession talks with Montenegro.
In recent weeks, the European Commission has been participating in the talks between the two countries, and several member states have worked to keep enlargement from stalling over bilateral issues.
In particular, France wants to avoid trouble with enlargement for domestic reasons, while Luxembourg has taken aim at using the accession process to resolve bilateral issues.
All three European governments have been actively talking with Croatia to pressure it into resolving the bilateral issues. But the strongest push comes from Germany, which is seeking to get the enlargement process going.
The disputes mostly stem from the legacy of the Yugoslav wars of the early 1990s, including property claims and contested borders. They threaten Montenegro’s ambition to become the EU’s 28th member state by 2028.
Croatia’s stance has also drawn public criticism, including from EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas, who said on the margins of the European Council that the accession process should not be hijacked by bilateral issues.
Zagreb has been accused of raising the disputes at the last minute to exert maximum pressure on Montenegro. Croatia counters that the issues are long-standing and that it has made only a handful of symbolic requests.
Zagreb points out that the investigation of war crimes and reparation of victims are targets Podgorica needs to fulfil to close its accession work. Still, EU officials fear the tide could quickly turn against enlargement if Montenegro’s accession is not finalised soon.
A string of elections is scheduled in key member states next year, including in France, where far-right leader Marine Le Pen, traditionally a sceptic of EU expansion, is the favourite to win the presidential race.
Germany has been pushing for new ways to enlarge the EU, including a special “associate candidate” status for Ukraine, the notion of “gradual integration” of candidate countries and stronger democratic safeguards for newcomers.
Montenegro would also be the first country to join the bloc under the current enlargement methodology.
The Berlin Process, an intergovernmental initiative launched in 2014 to promote regional cooperation among Western Balkan countries, is chaired this year by Podgorica, which has worked closely with the German government through the forum in recent months.
EU officials read Germany’s move on the bilateral matter as Berlin taking ownership of the process.
Montenegro’s accession also comes against a broader geopolitical backdrop, in which Brussels is increasingly using enlargement to anchor its immediate neighbours to the West amid growing tensions with Russia.
As Podgorica is first in line, a disruption caused by what some regard as futile bilateral issues could have a devastating effect on the other “frontrunners”, namely Albania, Moldova and, most notably, Ukraine, whose accession bid will likely be closely linked to the eventual peace negotiations with Moscow.
In other words, Germany believes it is time to move ahead with Montenegro’s accession, given the effort Podgorica has put in, and a geopolitical picture that demands enlargement keep its momentum.

Objects with Narratives presents collectible design that looks "found rather than fabricated"
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
05:00:01 UTC
14:00:01 KST

Objects with Narratives presents collectible design that looks "found rather than fabricated"
Belgian gallery Objects with Narratives has curated a texture-heavy exhibition at PAD London called What Remains?, featuring pieces from Ben Storms and Paul Cocksedge.
What Remains? marks the second show that Brussels platform Objects with Narratives has presented at design fair PAD London, which takes place annually in Mayfair's Berkley Square.
The emerging Brussels gallery's exhibition brings together a series of textured pieces united by amorphous shapes and patinated surfaces.
"Every piece was crafted in the present, yet many carry a sense of the past, as though found rather than fabricated," said Objects with Narratives.
Among the exhibitors is Belgian designer Ben Storms, who is known for his rough-hewn furniture that looks like jumbo pillows. Storms is presenting his most recent design, a cushion-like coffee table called Ex Hale, crafted from veiny red Mexican onyx decorated with mosaic veneer.
To create the piece, the designer used a hydroforming technique to blow up two pieces of metal sheet that were welded together and 3D-scanned to form a cushion shape.
After this, Storms used a CNC machine to mill the same shape from a block of stone.
"Ex Hale plays with our common notions of materiality," said the gallery. "The hard stone looks soft instead, an impression that is further enhanced by the delicate surface treatment."
Also on display is Critical Mass, a handmade Corten steel standing shelf by British designer Paul Cocksedge.
A trio of metal components were arranged to support three metal shelves, forming a piece that looks familiar to What Nelson Sees, a weathering steel installation by Cocksedge that was placed in Trafalgar Square for last year's London Design Festival.
"The Critical Mass series holds an energy, something on the edge of collapse or explosion," said Objects with Narratives.
Belgian designer Sofie Middernacht is showing a steel credenza, bench and duo of stools clad in gleaming crimson resin.
Middernacht works with discarded industrial materials to create her furniture, which is purposefully formed like archaeological artefacts.
Venezuelan artist Jojo Corväiá is presenting a trio of glazed vessels crafted from volcanic clay, a material central to his practice.
A host of other materials feature in the show, from shaggy mohair and wool lamps by Belgian practice KRJST Studio to lighting by Danish designer Karl Monies formed from patchwork slabs of copper.
"What Remains? asks what gives an object the sense that it might outlive the moment of its making: the material, the craft, or simply the possibility that some objects belong to no single time at all," Objects with Narratives concluded.
Objects with Narratives was founded by Nik and Robbe Vandewyngaerde and Oskar Eryatmaz, who opened their first permanent brick-and-mortar gallery inside a historic 1920s fur atelier in Brussels in 2023.
What Remains? is on until 18 October.
The photography is courtesy of Objects with Narratives.
PAD London 2026 takes place from 14 to 19 October 2026 at Berkeley Square, London W1J 6EN, UK. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

LRT English Newsletter – October 16, 2026.
Lithuania is planning to change the laws surrounding platform work. The changes aim to make the conditions better for the growing workforce who are named as “partners”, but have few – if any – possibilities to negotiate rates or even challenge automatic decisions taken by algorithms. Around 141,000 people worked for platforms like Wolt and Bolt in the country, according to data from 2024. The number is expected to rise to 157,000 by 2028.
Many of them are migrants or students, often from non-EU countries. They have also been at the centre of political efforts to point at the (allegedly) runaway migration taking place in the country. Amid a flurry of anti-migration rhetoric, the interior minister proposed limiting the right of foreign, non-EU students to work on a self-employed basis.
But who are the people that make up the immigrant community? Probably unsurprisingly, Belarusians and Ukrainians remain the two biggest nationalities. Meanwhile, Lithuania is at risk of increasing out-migration of its own citizens due to war fears and economic pressures.
DIESEL AND YANDEX
Donald Trump’s diesel-sucking deal with Russia received a bitter response even in Lithuania that normally backs Washington’s endeavours, with Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius saying the decision of the country’s strategic partner was “shameful and dishonourable”. The foreign minister, Kęstutis Budrys, tried to play it down, saying “this latest episode is not the worst we have seen in nearly two years”.
Speaking at the Warsaw Forum earlier this week, Sinkevičius also said Ukraine should strike more data centres, wink wink.
US TROOPS, BALTIC BORDERS
And speaking of America, the first US troops arrived in the country earlier this week. Up to 100 US troops are now here as part of a returning rotation, with the rest of the 1,000-strong force expected by mid-November.
Despite the returning Americans, the Baltic borders remain on edge. Last week, there was an armed incident on Latvia’s border with Belarus; the previously unknown “Black Russian” group claimed responsibility. But the whole announcement looked sus, with experts saying the group could be a front for security services. Or, this whole “group” could be a psyop product in the first place, seeing how Europe is bracing itself for “escalation” on Baltic borders. In any case, read more here.
In other defence updates, Lithuania is investing over 33 million euros into military fuel infrastructure. And if you’re feeling lost about all the different initiatives taking place in Lithuania to prepare for a potential conflict, we've got you covered.
SHOOTING IN VILNIUS
But it was an armed incident closer to home that proved deadly, when a former policeman shot a former kickboxing champion after an altercation outside an apartment block. They fled Russia, but the West sent them back
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
05:57:28 BST
13:57:28 KST

They fled Russia, but the West sent them back
- Published
Russian security services were waiting when the flight landed in Moscow in December. On board were Russians the US had deported, including activists denied political asylum.
"It was unbelievably frightening. My knees were shaking with fear," says Katya, one of the deportees. We have changed her name to protect her identity, as she remains in Russia.
Katya had left Russia and claimed asylum in the US two years earlier.
When Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, many countries publicly welcomed fleeing Russians. But more than four years later, attitudes have hardened. The numbers of anti-war Russians forcibly returned from Western countries is rising, and Katya's experience highlights the potential risks they face.
US authorities rejected her application for asylum, after she said she had provided evidence that she had taken part in protests and was a member of an opposition movement.
In Moscow, Katya says officers from the FSB security service handed all the male deportees military papers, requiring them to register with the local enlistment office, from where men are often sent to the war in Ukraine. Another passenger on the flight and an activist confirmed her account.
The officers interrogated her, and many others, for several hours.
"At one point, they found incriminating information on my phone," says Katya, "Their faces changed in a second. I was very afraid that they would simply bundle me off somewhere."
Katya was eventually released and allowed to stay with relatives. But she says police continue to call her and visit her at home.
"I feel as if I'm in a cage, like in a zoo," she says, "Whenever I see a police car, I feel terrified and start thinking, "What if they're coming for me?"
Katya showed the BBC documents and photographs confirming her story, which matches accounts from other deportees.
Removals from the US rose from 222 in 2023 to more than 1,200 in 2025, amid a wider increase in deportations under President Donald Trump's second term. Activists say Russian deportees included dissidents and Russian army deserters, some of whom were imprisoned or sent to war after returning to Russia.
One such case is Leonid Melekhin, an anti-war activist who sought asylum in the US after being arrested at protests in Russia. He had posted photographs of Russian President Vladimir Putin online with the message "Putin: murderer, fascist, usurper". After being deported back home last year, Melekhin was charged with "justifying terrorism" and sentenced to six years in prison.
"We have several examples of people who got eight years in prison when they crossed the [Russian] border," says Andrei Pivovarov, from Russia's exiled opposition Anti-War Committee.
And deportations are taking place from Europe too. His organisation has changed its advice to dissidents escaping Russia: the EU is no longer safe, it is better to seek refuge elsewhere.
Germany has sharply increased the number of Russian nationals it deports. Seven were sent back in 2023, rising to more than 110 in 2025, according to German government figures. More than 21,000 Russians sought asylum in Germany between 2022 and 2025, but the proportion of positive decisions fell from 29% in 2023 to just 6.8% in the first eleven months of 2025.
"Protection is only granted if there is an actual, well-founded fear of persecution," Germany's migration and asylum agency, BAMF, told the BBC.
Last year, Berlin suspended its humanitarian visa programme for Russians, and across the EU, the proportion of Russian applicants granted some form of asylum protection fell from 23% in 2024 to around 17% in the first nine months of 2025, according to EU data.
Russian opposition activists fleeing repression have become caught up in a wider crackdown on immigration, as governments across Europe and the US toughen rules amid political pressure over high numbers of irregular migrants and asylum applications, as well as over security concerns.
Western governments are "focused on limiting humanitarian programmes and asylum seekers", says lawyer Anastasia Burakova, founder of rights group Kovcheg (Ark), which helps anti-war Russians leave the country. The clampdown is "in response to public concerns and rising support for right-wing populist parties", she adds.
Following a negative asylum decision, Russian nationals are often given the chance to leave independently, but a rising number are being forcibly returned to Russia, usually escorted via third countries.
Several Russian activists in exile told the BBC that immigration officials had told them they faced "no danger" in Russia, and that officials often lacked an adequate understanding of the risks that activists face.
"I tried to explain that if they sent me back, I would be put in prison, or sent to war where I'd be killed," explains former soldier Artyom, who deserted from the Russian Army in 2022 after officers threatened to send him to Ukraine. "They just didn't believe me."
He says he provided US authorities with proof that a criminal investigation had been opened against him back in Russia for desertion. But he was put on a deportation flight back to Moscow via Egypt.
"I was preparing for death," says the former soldier, "I was thinking, 'how can I die without it being painful?'".
Back in Moscow, Artyom was held in a military detention facility but managed to escape. He is now in hiding abroad.
"Another country could investigate me better and give me asylum. Why didn't they give me that chance? Instead they deported me specifically to Russia," says the deserter. "It ruined my life."
The US Department of Homeland Security told the BBC: "All illegal aliens receive due process. If a judge finds an illegal alien has no right to be in this country, we are going to remove them."
The asylum clampdown comes as repression inside Russia has reached "an unprecedented level", according to Nobel Prize-winning Russian human rights group Memorial. Their list of political prisoners grew from 803 to 1,265 during 2025, a record increase.
The Russian Embassy in London did not respond to a request for comment.
Anti-war activist Mikhail says he and his wife Dasha are awaiting deportation from Finland "any day". Their names have been changed to protect their identity, as Mikhail fears for relatives back home.
Russian authorities blocked his social media accounts over anti-war posts, and police visited his mother and accused him of spreading "fake information".
Dasha is a Jehovah's Witness, an organisation banned as "extremist" in Russia. The couple provided Finnish authorities with evidence, seen by the BBC, including a video of Russian police telling his mother that more than 300 posts had violated Russian law. A single post can result in a long prison sentence.
The Finnish Immigration Service has rejected their asylum request five times, deciding there is "no reasonable basis to believe" the couple would face serious rights violations if returned.
"We're sitting here and someone could knock on our door at any moment, take us to the Russian border and simply hand us over to Russian officers," says Mikhail. "We fear for our lives!"
"We came to Finland for help, and they're refusing us," he adds. "My wife cries constantly."
Amnesty International, which is supporting the couple, says they could face a "real risk" of detention, prosecution, imprisonment and torture if returned.
The Finnish Immigration Service said all asylum decisions were based on international refugee law standards, and the share of Russian citizens receiving asylum was in line with EU averages.
For Mikhail and Dasha, the threat of deportation comes as more Russians may be considering leaving.
There are rumours that Vladimir Putin may announce a new wave of mobilisation to boost the ranks of his army in Ukraine, which the Kremlin denies. The last mobilisation in 2022 prompted hundreds of thousands of Russians to flee, many to ex-Soviet states such as Armenia and Georgia.
Anastasia Burakova's organisation says requests for help from Russians wanting to leave rose tenfold in August compared with May. For those now looking to escape, the question is whether the West will offer them refuge — or send them back.

Tesla unveiled a flying Roadster that accelerates to 100 km/h in 0.81 seconds

Unknown Publisher

07:57:00 EEST

Tesla unveiled a flying Roadster that accelerates to 100 km/h in 0.81 seconds
Kyiv • UNN
Tesla presented a Roadster with a brief flight and a flip in the air. Mass production is planned to begin in 2028.
Information has spread online about the presentation of the new Tesla Roadster electric sports car, which allegedly can lift off the ground, overcome obstacles, and accelerate to 100 km/h in just 0.81 seconds. At the same time, there is currently no official confirmation of these specifications or of the demonstration taking place, UNN writes.
Details
According to the description being circulated, the car is equipped with a fan system that generates downforce and allows the vehicle to remain on the surface even when upside down. Gas-powered engines for additional acceleration and maneuvering have also been claimed.
The authors of the report claim that the Roadster will have three versions: Performance, Thrust, and Rocket. The latter is allegedly designed for one person and capable of making short-duration flights.
What is known about the Tesla Roadster
Tesla first presented a prototype of the next-generation Roadster in 2017, promising to begin deliveries in 2020. However, the car's release has been postponed repeatedly.
The report being circulated also names 2028 as a possible start date for mass production and estimates the reservation cost at $50,000. This information requires separate confirmation.
According to Reuters and TechCrunch, Tesla did indeed hold a presentation of the Roadster in Texas. The car demonstrated a brief flight and a midair flip using a gas-engine system developed with the involvement of SpaceX. During the test, it was also claimed to have accelerated to 60 miles per hour (approximately 97 km/h) in 0.81 seconds. Mass production is planned to begin in 2028.
At the same time, a demonstration flight does not mean that the car is already certified for ordinary roads.

Children bear brunt as Ethiopia fighting fuels fears of wider war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
04:55:00 UTC
13:55:00 KST

Ten-year-old Iyerusalem lies in a hospital bed in northern Ethiopia, her amputated legs propped up by rolled blankets as she struggles with pain and the loss of her older brother, who was killed alongside their horse when fighting struck their home.
“I was in our compound with my older brother and our horse when we were hit. My brother and the horse died,” she told Agence France-Presse (AFP) from Ayder Comprehensive Specialised Hospital in Mekelle, the capital of the northern Tigray region.
Iyerusalem is among dozens of civilians wounded since fighting erupted between the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and Ethiopian federal forces on Sept. 23, reviving a conflict in a region still scarred by the devastating 2020-22 war.
Federal forces repelled the TPLF offensive and took control of Mekelle without resistance on Oct. 3 after rebel leaders and fighters abandoned the city.
The fighting has nevertheless left civilians, including children, with severe injuries and families mourning relatives killed in bombardments.
Many wounded people come from remote villages in southern Tigray, hours from medical care along difficult roads affected by fighting and shelling.
Iyerusalem, from Qarsole village in Alamata district, said her amputated legs were causing severe pain.
“If I get medical treatment and can walk again, I want to go back to school,” she said, as her father, Hiluf, watched anxiously.
Nearby, 12-year-old Hana was recovering from severe facial injuries and a broken leg. The explosion that wounded her killed her mother and brother.
“First I heard a loud explosion, and the whole house shook. I was scared and did not even know what had happened. I could not open my eyes or my mouth,” she said.
“The sound of the explosion keeps coming back in my head.”
In another room, Betelhem, 10, was being treated for a broken leg, while her 6-year-old sister, Melet, had suffered a neck injury. Their pregnant mother was killed when heavy artillery struck their home.
“The bomb hit our house directly, all these people have died, but no one is being held responsible. There is no government,” said their father, Haftom, a 39-year-old shopkeeper.
Birhanu Hailemariam, the emergency coordinator at Ayder hospital, said 34 people wounded by heavy artillery, drones, gunfire and explosives had arrived in recent days. Twenty-three were children, and one patient had died.
Medical staff lacked basic equipment and medicines, including anesthesia, he said.
“But we are doing our best to treat everyone,” he said.
Although the latest fighting had not reached the scale of the previous Tigray war, which the African Union (AU) estimates killed about 600,000 people, fear remained pervasive among patients and medical workers.
“Both are hurting people,” another doctor said of the TPLF and federal forces, asking not to be identified.
Families were reluctant to assign blame for attacks. Hiluf said he did not know who had bombarded his village and feared reprisals if he accused either side.
“I do not want to fight with anyone,” he said. “Let there be peace for us.”
Farther north, residents of the border town of Zalambessa say they are caught between Ethiopian and Eritrean troops as the risk of a broader conflict grows.
Eritrea has deployed thousands of troops to northern Tigray to support forces opposing Ethiopia's central government, according to a security source.
“Ethiopian troops are on one side, and Eritrean troops are on the other,” said Selam, 33, whose first name was changed for security reasons.
Eritrean soldiers initially advanced south before drone strikes forced them to retreat into the surrounding mountains, she said. Although the area was no longer seeing active fighting, her home and small shop had been without electricity or water for a week.
“We are caught in the middle and living in deep anxiety,” she said.
Conflict monitor ACLED reported that Ethiopian federal forces had moved heavy weapons toward Zalambessa in recent days. Eyewitnesses reported seeing a substantial convoy of tanks and other heavy weaponry advancing from the south, though AFP could not independently verify the reports.
Residents described deserted streets, closed businesses and growing shortages as blocked roads disrupted supplies.
“Most people only go out to attend church and pray,” said Hadush, 45, who also requested anonymity.
“Now there is no bread,” he said, describing the worsening hardship.
Selam said federal soldiers were preventing residents from traveling to Adigrat, about 30 kilometers (18 miles) south, making it difficult to visit relatives or obtain essential supplies.
Eritrean Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel did not respond to AFP questions about the reported presence of Eritrean troops.
The military buildup has raised international concern that the fighting in Tigray could draw the neighboring countries into another war.
On Wednesday, the United States urged Ethiopia and Eritrea to pursue “de-escalation,” calling on all countries to respect their neighbors' sovereignty and territorial integrity and avoid cross-border incursions.
Eritrea gained independence from Ethiopia in 1993. The countries fought a deadly border war from 1998 to 2000 before relations improved in 2018, when Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed took office and pursued closer ties with Asmara.
Relations have since deteriorated, with the two countries severing ties this month amid the renewed Tigray conflict.
Ethiopia accuses Eritrea of backing the TPLF, which launched its offensive on Sept. 23. Eritrea alleges that Ethiopia intends to exploit the fighting to invade its territory and seize Assab port on the Red Sea.
The TPLF initially made gains in the Afar region but has since retreated ahead of advancing federal forces, abandoning towns for the surrounding hills.
Federal troops took Mekelle without resistance on Oct. 3 and subsequently seized several other towns without encountering opposition. The latest reported advance brought government forces to Rama, about 7 kilometers (4 miles) from the Eritrean border, according to two residents.

Perceptible earthquake registered in Russia’s Kamchatka
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
04:51:46 UTC
13:51:46 KST

PETROPAVLOVSK-KAMCHATSKY, October 16. /TASS/. A perceptible earthquake with an intensity of up to four magnitude points has been registered in Kamchatka, the Kamchatka branch of the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Geophysical Service said.
"Instrumental intensity in Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky amounted to up to four points," scientists said.
Scientists estimated its magnitude at 6.5 first, but later revised it to 6.9. It was felt as a magnitude-5 earthquake in the region.
"According to verified information, the magnitude of this seismic event was 6.9. Its epicenter was located on land, 156 kilometers southwest of Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky, at the depth of 138 kilometers. In Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky, it was felt as a magnitude-5 earthquake," seismologists said.
A number of residents of the region’s administrative center evacuated from their apartments because of tremors. Inside residential buildings, the earthquake caused light fixtures to swing violently, doors to slam shut, and tableware to rattle, a TASS correspondent reported.
According to eyewitnesses, the tremor, which occurred at 3:36 p.m. local time (3:36 a.m. GMT), continued for about one minute.

'Symbol of filth': Delhi BJP MLA on why 30-foot 'cockroach' effigy is being burnt alongside Ravan

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
04:24:57 UTC
13:24:57 KST

Organisers say cockroaches symbolises filth and dirt in home and society
NEW DELHI: A 30-foot-tall cockroach effigy will be burnt alongside those of Ravan, Kumbhkaran and Meghnad during Dussehra celebrations in the national capital this year, with organisers saying the insect will symbolise filth and unhygienic conditions as part of their cleanliness message.The Shri Keshav Ramlila Committee, which organises the Ramlila in Pitampura, said the initiative aims to highlight the need to eliminate filth from homes, neighbourhoods and society at large, in keeping with the Swachh Bharat and Swachh Delhi campaigns.Ashok Goel Devaraha, president of the committee and Model Town BJP MLA, said the decision was intended to reinforce the message of the triumph of good over evil and was not politically motivated.Speaking to ANI, Devaraha said Vijayadashami symbolises the victory of truth over falsehood and righteousness over unrighteousness. He added that the committee had previously burnt effigies representing issues affecting the country, including Naxalism and terrorism.“Keeping these principles in mind, we have also, in the past, burned effigies representing various afflictions plaguing our nation, such as Naxalism or terrorism.
This year, our committee has decided to burn an effigy of a cockroach, a symbol of filth,” he said.
The effigy will be set alight at the committee grounds in Pitampura. Devaraha described it as a 30-foot-tall structure shaped like a cockroach, adding that the aim was to draw attention to the need to rid homes, neighbourhoods and society of dirt and unhygienic conditions.How did ‘cockroach’ become a political name?The choice of the insect comes amid protests by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) and opposition parties in Delhi, which had been campaigning against former Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan and is now demanding the resignation of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.The group staged protests against Pradhan in June and July, including a demonstration at Jantar Mantar and a march towards Parliament on July 20. Pradhan subsequently resigned as education minister in July, while Pralhad Joshi took over the portfolio.
The CJP has since returned to the streets over its allegations concerning the electoral roll revision process, joining opposition parties and student organisations in demonstrations. Several activists, students and journalists were detained during protests in the capital.The committee president, however, has denied that the cockroach effigy is politically motivated, maintaining that it is intended to convey a message about cleanliness.Also read: 6,000 cops, 200 CAPF companies: As CJP pushes ahead with Tiranga march, Delhi prepares for a high-security fridayOn May 15, while hearing a case in the Supreme Court, CJI Surya Kant had compared certain individuals with fraudulent degrees to “cockroaches” who become social media or RTI activists to attack the system. The remarks triggered widespread backlash among young people and inspired the satirical “Cockroach Janta Party” (CJP) movement.He later clarified that his oral remarks during a Supreme Court hearing were “misquoted” and later used with “malicious intent” to mislead the country’s youth.

Carney says US trying to break Canada amid vote for Alberta independence referendum
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
04:24:00 UTC
13:24:00 KST

Carney implies US trying to 'break' Canada as Alberta vote looms
October 16, 2026
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney warned the people of oil-rich Alberta against looming threats, suggesting that the United States was trying to "break" Canada so it could "own us."
Carney was speaking at a pro-Canada rally in Calgary, ahead of a vote which will decide if the disgruntled western province will begin a legal process toward separation from Canada.
"The world has become more dangerous and divided. Some outside our borders are working to break us so they can own us," he said, without naming the US or its president, Donald Trump.
This is not the first time Carney has made such a claim. His warning comes as Washington and Ottawa are in the middle of a trade war and Trump has threatened to make Canada the 51st US state.
Meanwhile, Carney's push toward making Canada less dependent on the US has irked Trump.
What is Alberta voting for?
Monday's vote in Alberta is not a direct referendum on independence. Rather, the province, which has the world's fourth-largest proven oil reserves, will vote to decide whether to remain a province or instruct the government to begin the legal process toward a referendum on separation.
Polling indicates less than a quarter of Alberta's roughly five million people want to break away from Canada.
Albertans have long held grievances with liberal governments in Ottawa, from concerns about immigration and federal power to oil industry management. While Carney, who grew up in Alberta, has attempted to address frustrations, a lot stands to be resolved.
"The frustrations that many Albertans have felt are real," Carney said, adding that Ottawa had made Albertans feel "like our resources weren't our own."
However, he urged the public there to not use the vote as a "message" to the federal government.
"Don't be fooled by the idea you can 'send a message' with your vote," Carney said. "This is not poker. A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep division and great uncertainty."
Mitch Sylvestre, who heads the Alberta Prosperity Project, a prominent separatist organization, told AFP that US interests "don't play a role" in Alberta "until we win and become a government." At that point, he would ensure free-flowing trade.
"There is no animosity toward America here," he said, adding that he didn't see a reason to stop trading with the world's largest economy.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has called Alberta a "natural partner" for the United States, and Alberta Prosperity Project leaders have held several meetings at the State Department.

The Expanded Scope of the Architect: Moving Windmills Innovation Center
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
04:00:00 UTC
13:00:00 KST

What do architects do? This age-old question reveals the perennial dichotomy between two aspects of building–how to construct, and why to build. Despite its ancient origins and its name deriving from Ancient Greek, the profession is one that has transformed over the centuries. Its present-day form, usually dated to the Italian Renaissance, makes a distinction between the act of building and the intellectual and aesthetic decision-making behind it. However, we may be in the midst of another nascent transformation. The commissioning of architecture has historically remained separate from the practice, but as can be seen in the work of MASS and projects like the Moving Windmills Innovation Center, this distinction is beginning to blur.
To achieve any level of sophistication and quality in construction, a modicum of planning is necessary. Fragments of papyrus with building plans have survived the millennia since their production during the Ancient Egypt. In medieval Europe, drawing became an indispensable part of the construction process of Gothic cathedrals, where master masons were in control of both planning and building. It was not until the Renaissance in Florence that the two processes began to diverge, and Brunelleschi, designer of the Duomo, is regarded as the first overseer of construction without engagement in the process, i.e., the first architect or engineer in the modern sense.
The separation of architecture from construction slowly spread across Europe, where it also became regarded as a learned discipline, often practiced by aristocrats. This further emphasized the social value of architecture as distinct from the practice of construction, and elevated the importance of drawing. Further events in Europe, such as the reconstruction after the Great Fire of London, solidified the role of the architect as planner and overseer. Building booms in the industrialized 1800s created speculative developers with only financial interests in construction, leading to an industry rife with fraud. The establishment of professional bodies and entry requirements for the profession followed to counter this, and it included a further separation of design from profiteering from the construction process.
Related Article
"Design Is Inseparable from Activism": In Conversation with Andrés Jaque at the UIA World Congress of Architects 2026
The next major rupture in Europe was the reconstruction after the Second World War. It was perhaps during this period that architecture's social value, and importance as a provider of amenity, came to the fore. The profession was brought into the mechanisms of the welfare state, mixing closely with the provision of housing, education, and healthcare. It was reliberalized after reconstruction ended and it returned to being a service provider, although the success of this period often comes into question, particularly when judged by its social value as compared to during reconstruction.
In response to this crisis, the role of the architect is beginning to transform again, with an expanded scope that begins to couple architecture once again with the provision of social amenity. This involves working directly with other professions outside the construction industry, and even blurring the lines between building commissioners and design service providers. Glimpses of these changes are apparent in ways of working and recognition. In 2025, the OBEL architecture award was given to a movement, rather than a single architectural office or project. In 2026, the AIA Architecture Firm Award was received by Mississippi-based architects Duvall Decker. The award recognizes how the approach moves beyond traditional practice to truly understand and provide for communities, often employing a multidisciplinary team.
Even more committed to this method of working and adopting new architectural roles is Model of Architecture Serving Society (MASS), based in Kigali, Rwanda, and Boston, Massachusetts. As its name suggests, MASS is an architecture firm. A closer look reveals that it is more than that. As a 'model of architecture,' MASS operates as a non-profit organization and includes a broad multidisciplinary team. It was set up to expand access to good design and to take direct action in societal and environmental upliftment. The model allows MASS to raise its own funds from donors, more than five million dollars annually, which is used to fund research, catalyst projects, and systems changes. Its direct involvement in the stories of communities' needs and solutions aligned it closely with the Moving Windmills project.
In 2009, inventor William Kamkwamba's story rose to global fame when he was interviewed in a TED Talk. At 14, his village in Kasungu, Malawi, faced a severe famine brought on by drought. In desperation, the young Kamkwamba devised a windmill from items available locally to pump water to irrigate the village's crop fields, with help from books in his school's library. The story inspired a movie production in 2019 titled "The Boy Who Harnessed the Wind," as well as a musical theater production later in 2026. Since building the windmill, Kamkwamba has set up the Moving Windmills initiative to support the youths of Kasungu, bringing resources to young inventors and problem-solvers in the rural agrarian community. This includes setting up workshops, stores for parts, and connecting locals with experts.
Partnering with MASS, the intention is to expand the initiative, creating the Moving Windmills Innovation Center. This project is distinguished by its overarching mission: to empower changemakers. The campus works as a living laboratory in which the architecture and design embody the Windmills pedagogy, engaging with the landscape and promoting sustainable, real-world values. Young people are treated not as beneficiaries but as innovation makers, learning to understand global and local systems and to develop homegrown solutions. The windmill model underpins the approach: a circular process of iterating, testing, applying practical solutions, and storytelling. Design is circular, regenerative, human and ecological, so the campus both embodies and facilitates the curriculum.
The machine shop will be built first, at the center of four quadrants which also include a field space and market, community and events space, and student housing. Staff housing, a football pitch, nursery, solar array, and regenerative agriculture follow. The campus will be a hub supporting existing work and the growing Moving Windmills network. The process is iterative, with testing of elements such as wall systems already under way. Using human-centered design, local materials, and on-site craftsmanship, it is built not just for the community but by it. Ecological practices, from water treatment to biodiversity, are part of the pedagogy.
Thus, the role of MASS is not simply to design a building for a pre-made brief set by a client. Their partnering model enables them to make a contribution to the planned activities of the innovation center, the research behind it, community engagement, and even the fundraising for the scheme. The traditional role of the architectural firm is expanded beyond its historical borders, and time will tell if this is a new direction for the profession.
This article is part of the ArchDaily Topic: The Architecture of Water: Territories, Tensions & Transformations. Every month we explore a topic in-depth through articles, interviews, news, and architecture projects. We invite you to learn more about our ArchDaily Topics. Twenty-two US lawmakers demand Trump immediately impose Russia sanctions under Graham Act

Twenty-two US lawmakers demand Trump immediately impose Russia sanctions under Graham Act
Twenty-two Democrat and Republican members of the US House of Representatives have written to President Donald Trump demanding the full and immediate implementation of the sanctions against Russia provided for under the Graham Act.
Source: Congressman Jim Costa's website; Ukrainian journalist in Washington Ostap Yarysh on Facebook
Details: The letter was authored by House Foreign Affairs Committee member Jim Costa, together with the co-chairs of the Congressional Ukraine Caucus in the House of Representatives: Mike Quigley, Marcy Kaptur, Brian Fitzpatrick and Joe Wilson. The lawmakers stressed that the first mandatory deadline for the key sanctions under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 to take effect expires on 18 October.
They emphasised the need to step up economic pressure on Moscow ahead of winter.
Quote: "As Russia prepares to wage a fifth winter campaign against Ukraine, the United States has an opportunity to reinvigorate peace efforts by placing maximum pressure on Vladimir Putin and the governments and networks that finance his war. Utilising the tools for economic pressure in this law will be decisive in forcing Putin to take peace talks seriously."
Details: In the letter, the lawmakers also expressed deep concern over the US Department of the Treasury's decision on 9 October to issue General Licence No. 135, which permits transactions involving the sale, delivery, offloading and import of Russian diesel fuel into the US.
They called on the administration to immediately revoke this permit and prevent any new exemptions that restore the flow of petrodollars into the Kremlin's war chest.
Furthermore, the House members have asked the administration five questions and demanded written answers by 18 October. They want to know what steps will be taken to ensure the full implementation of all mandatory sanctions, tariffs and bans, and whether the White House intends to delay any provisions or grant exemptions to them.
The lawmakers are also calling for the administration to publish a list of Russian officials, oligarchs, banks and state-owned companies targeted by the restrictions and to clarify whether foreign banks and Russia's shadow fleet operators will also be affected. They are further demanding details of which countries will face secondary tariffs for purchasing Russian energy, what safeguards will be in place for allies, how pressure on Putin will be measured, and why sanctions are being eased despite the existing legislative ban on Russian energy imports.
Among the 22 signatories to the letter are leading representatives of both parties, including Republicans Michael McCaul, Joe Wilson, Brian Fitzpatrick and Don Bacon, as well as Democrats Steny Hoyer, Jim Costa, Marcy Kaptur, Josh Gottheimer and Dina Titus.
Background:
- On 17 September, the US Congress passed bill H.R. 5334, the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026. The legislation authorises 500% tariffs on Russian goods, secondary tariffs of up to 100% on the largest buyers of Russian oil and gas, and mandatory sanctions against key sectors of the Russian economy.
- On 19 September, US President Donald Trump signed the Graham Act into law, setting the first 30-day deadline for the implementation of its provisions for 18 October.
- On 9 October, the US Department of the Treasury, through the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), issued General Licence No. 135, allowing transactions involving Russian-origin diesel fuel.
- On 14 October, a bipartisan group of 12 US senators sent a strongly worded letter to Donald Trump, calling the diesel deal with Moscow a "betrayal of the people of Ukraine" and urging him to immediately revoke the licence and move to full implementation of the Graham Act.

Nationals say Liberals oppose EU trade deal, Liberals beg to differ
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
03:53:42 UTC
12:53:42 KST

Liberals insist EU free trade position not settled, despite Canavan's assertion
In short:
Liberals insist they have not agreed to oppose the proposed Australia-EU trade deal, despite Nationals leader Matt Canavan claiming both parties are against it.
Some Liberals believe Trade Minister Don Farrell could renegotiate aspects of the deal, an idea strongly rebuffed by those on both sides of the negotiations.
What's next?
A joint parliamentary committee is expected to scrutinise the deal early next year.
Nationals leader Matt Canavan's claim that both Nationals and Liberals are against a slated European Union trade deal has angered some Liberals who privately insist the issue has not been settled.
In an opinion piece published in The Australian today, Senator Canavan said the deal landed by Trade Minister Don Farrell would "weaken Australia's sovereignty on climate change policy" and was bad for the steel industry and some farmers.
He said the deal, which parliament must approve, was opposed by both Coalition parties. That assertion was backed by his colleague, Bridget McKenzie.
"Don Farrell can try all he likes to find a Coalition senator willing to vote for it. He won't because we are absolutely united," she told ABC Radio National today.
But two Liberal senators subsequently told the ABC the proposed deal was better than the status quo and should be adopted. One cited the diplomatic importance of the deal at a time when the US was waging trade wars.
"As long as it's not a really bad free trade agreement, and I don't think it is, we should support it," the senator said. "It goes to what the Liberal Party stands for.
"There is a lot of internal disquiet about this."
'Opposed … subject to proper process'
Multiple senior Liberals told the ABC the matter had not been considered by shadow cabinet or discussed in the Coalition party room, and that could only happen after scrutiny by the parliament's joint standing committee on trade.
"You can't short-circuit that by [writing] an op-ed," one said, framing Senator Canavan's intervention as a clear attempt to strongarm Liberals, reigniting tensions between the parties that plagued the leadership of Angus Taylor's predecessor, Sussan Ley.
The joint standing committee process is still some time away. While the deal's text was agreed between leaders this year, it will not be signed until Australia and each EU member country complete the requisite legal checks, most likely early next year.
Some Liberals believe this leaves time to renegotiate aspects of the deal. Two Liberals seeking to downplay any disagreement said the agreed position was "opposed to the deal as it stands, subject to the proper parliamentary and Coalition process".
Senator Canavan used more cautious language in a press conference today, saying the opposition was "opposed to the deal in its current form".
Farrell says veto would be 'vandalism'
The government has rubbished the idea that renegotiation would be possible.
"There is no room … the deal is done," Senator Farrell said today.
The minister has projected confidence that the Senate, where the government does not have the numbers in its own right, will not stand in the way of the deal, telling the ABC on Wednesday he believed "enough senators … understand how important this is".
One interpretation of that comment is that Senator Farrell believes enough Liberals might cross the floor to vote for the deal, although none of those who spoke to the ABC suggested they would.
Another is that Senator Farrell is confident that the Coalition – or at least the Liberals – will eventually land in favour of the deal, a view shared among some European diplomats, who have directly lobbied Mr Taylor and other Liberals in recent weeks.
One diplomat from an EU nation told the ABC it would be "very damaging" if Australia did not ratify the deal and echoed Senator Farrell's comments: "There is no appetite [in Europe] to revisit this … the deal is done."
The deal broadens access to the European market for Australian beef and sheep meat exporters, although not by as much as those industries had hoped. It also secures access for Australian fruit, vegetable and seafood.
Senator Farrell told the ABC it was clear that the Nationals would vote against the deal.
"At a time when Australians are facing cost-of-living pressures, the National Party have chosen to block our farmers from 27 new export markets, lock in high tariffs on Aussie businesses, and kill local jobs," he said.
"Once a long-standing party of government, the Nationals have reduced themselves to desperate populism, dressed in fake fluoro."
The Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry supports the deal. Chief executive Andrew McKellar told the Insiders: On Background podcast it was not "perfect" but was in the national interest.
"From a business point of view, we are strongly supporting the fact that it should be ratified and passed into legislation in the Australian parliament," he said.
"If we lose that opportunity now, it's gone forever and, honestly, that would be very short-sighted."

Myanmar Establishes New Committee to Advance Normalization With ASEAN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
03:49:00 UTC
12:49:00 KST

Myanmar’s military-backed government has formed a new ASEAN Affairs Committee in order to support its efforts to reintegrate itself into the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.
The Southeast Asian bloc has excluded Myanmar from its summits and foreign ministers’ meetings since late 2021, due to its failure to implement ASEAN’s Five-Point Consensus plan. Promulgated in April 2021, two months after a military coup, the Consensus calls for an immediate cessation of violence, dialogue among “all parties” to the country’s conflict, and access for humanitarian aid.
The Irrawaddy reported yesterday that the new body, which met for the first time on Tuesday, ahead of the 49th ASEAN Summit next month, is intended to “regain the country’s original role and rights” in the 11-nation organization. Tuesday’s meeting was chaired by Foreign Minister Tin Maung Swe and attended by representatives from the President’s Office and ministries of Defense, Home Affairs, Information, and Social Welfare.
Tin Maung Swe told the meeting that Myanmar had suffered “discriminatory treatment” from ASEAN since 2021, The Irrawaddy reported. The meeting also discussed “Myanmar‑led approaches” for restoring the country’s position in the bloc.
Since taking office in April, Min Aung Hlaing’s quasi-civilian government has launched a diplomatic charm offensive, involving visits to India, China, Russia, Belarus, and Kazakhstan, aimed at consolidating key partnerships and seeking injections of much-needed foreign investment.
A priority has been the normalization of Myanmar’s relations with ASEAN. Many of the latter’s member states appear to be supportive of Naypyidaw’s goal, and five of them – Laos, Thailand, Cambodia, Vietnam, and Malaysia – have rolled out the red carpet for the coup leader in recent months, with Indonesia and Brunei possibly to come.
The Philippines also appears to be softening. In a recent interview, Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., who holds the rotating chairmanship of ASEAN for 2026, said that while the Five-Point Consensus was “absolutely correct,” the bloc needed to try a “new approach” on Myanmar.
At the same time as it has wooed individual ASEAN member states, the military-backed government has forcefully rejected the Five-Point Consensus. In July, Myanmar’s military proxy parliament adopted a motion rejecting the Consensus as an unwarranted interference in Myanmar’s internal affairs, which “does not align with the current political developments in Myanmar.” Min Aung Hlaing said in a speech the following month that some member states had “adopted positions and practices that it regarded as discriminatory towards Myanmar.”
While most member states are now leaning in the direction of reopening ASEAN’s door to Myanmar – Thailand and Malaysia have both explicitly stated that this is their goal, and Singapore and Timor-Leste appear to be the last hold-outs – full normalization, like all ASEAN decisions, will require a consensus among all 11 member states. As I noted earlier this week, however, there are “evidently still differences within ASEAN over how fast engagement should proceed, and to what end.”
Unless ASEAN agrees to abandon the Five-Point Consensus altogether, normalization would seem to require at least some effort to implement it, however nominal. With the Myanmar military ramping up its attacks on resistance groups and civilian populations accused of harboring them, this seems unlikely in the current circumstances.
