UN needs reform like never before — would-be secretary-general
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
03:42:00 UTC
12:42:00 KST

WASHINGTON, October 16. /TASS/. The United Nations needs reform like never before in order to correspond to modern challenges, Guyana's UN envoy Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett, who has been nominated to the post of the next UN secretary-general, said.
"Attention is <…> rightfully placed on reforms of the United Nations. It has never been louder to call for reform, in my view," she said at the Washington-based Stimson Center in Washington.
In her words, the question should be raised whether "the structures of 1945 are relevant to 2026 realities."
"And that brings in the issue or the matter of Security Council reform. Of course, the Secretary General doesn't have a role in that as such, that's for member states. But then you have the reform of the agencies, funds, and programs, and we have over 35 of them. Are they fit for today, and what do we need to do? Can we reduce the overlaps, or eradicate the overlaps, the duplication, so that we can deliver better on the ground," the diplomat continued.
In her view, there is also the need for a "reform of the UN Secretariat - that comes under the Secretary General as well - to be more effective, more efficient, and in lockstep with member states, and not the other way around."
She added that "the organization, as it currently is, must change."
"We are 19 years away from the centenary of the UN, and so now is the time to reform and to remake that UN," Rodrigues-Birkett concluded.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has called for reforming the UN Secretariat as it has been taken over by one group of states pursuing their own interests. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the organization has been under pressure for a reform. Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi believes that changes within the organization should start from a reform of the UN Security Council.
Currently, seven candidates are vying for the post of the UN secretary-general: Rafael Grossi (Argentina), head of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA); Rebeca Grynspan (Costa Rica), Secretary-General of the UN Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD); Macky Sall, former President of Senegal; Maria Fernanda Espinosa Garces, former Foreign Minister and Defense Minister of Ecuador; Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett, Guyana’s Permanent Representative to the UN; Ivonne Baki, former Ecuadorian Ambassador to the US and France; and Olara Otunnu, Uganda’s former Permanent Representative to the UN.
Antonio Guterres, who has headed the UN since 2017, will complete his term on December 31, 2026. Members of the Security Council select a candidate to recommend for the post of UN chief. The General Assembly then votes to formally appoint the new UN secretary-general.

A Tesla Flying Car? I Don’t Know, Man
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
03:18:30 UTC
12:18:30 KST

Where is my flying car? The enduring question sort of, kind of, might have an answer: In McGregor, Texas.
On Thursday, Tesla showed off a version of its new Roadster 2 sports car in a demonstration at SpaceX’s rocket development testing facility. And in its own way, with an awkward jerking maneuver, the Roadster flew a few dozen feet. The vehicle, which doesn’t yet have a price but is likely to be very expensive, is slated to go into production in 2028. The vehicle didn’t have a human occupant during the demo “to make sure we don’t kill anyone,” Tesla CEO Elon Musk said at the event.
Tesla’s Roadster “sort of, kind of, might” be an actual flying car because aviation experts say legally catching air in the vehicle will likely involve plenty of government permissions and red tape.
“The [Federal Aviation Administration] has jurisdiction over any machine that leaves the surface of the earth,” says Scott Miller, an airline pilot and a lecturer in the Aviation and Technology program at San José State University. The vehicle “is going to introduce a whole set of regulatory issues.”
At the event Thursday, Musk acknowledged as much. “I’m not sure it’s necessarily legal in all jurisdictions," he said. “This is not necessarily a safety-optimized car.”
The FAA did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Any flying vehicle that weighs more than 250 or so pounds would need to go through an FAA approval process and require clearance to operate in the national airspace, says Michael McCormick, a former FAA official who now heads the Air Traffic Management program at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University. Getting that certification, he predicts, could take “at least a year.” Your standard drivers license, meanwhile, wouldn’t cut it. Any Tesla owner piloting such a vehicle would likely have to obtain a recreational aviation license.
Actually taking off and landing the Roadster 2 would likely present its own set of issues. Most states require aircraft to take off from airports or designated helipads. Launching from the road to the air would fall under state or local rules, says Miller, and many places do not look kindly on the concept of sudden aircraft intrusions on their streets and highways. That’s the reason “it’s pretty rare to be able to jump in a helicopter and land at your favorite steakhouse to have a steak,” he says. Drivers might only be able to truly operate the vehicle on a large, private piece of land.
The FAA today is working on rules, regulations, and pilot projects around another sort of “flying car,” or what’s more commonly known as an electric vertical take-off and landing (eVTOL) vehicle. These aircraft use several smaller electric motors and propellers to carry up to four passengers between 20 and 150 miles, sometimes autonomously. The companies building the technology envision them taking off from small, local “vertipads,” allowing riders to skip urban traffic by floating above the fray.
The Trump administration this year launched a limited, three-year pilot project using the aircraft, where companies are able to test the tech in several states. It has taken years for the companies to receive certifications from the federal government.
When it comes to the Roadster 2, there are practical questions, too. True flying cars have struggled to take off because of the physics-led contradiction at the heart of the idea. What makes a car safe and durable enough to operate on roads is weight. But “weight is the enemy of an airplane,” says Miller. “Flying cars haven’t been able to find that balance of power versus weight.”
Still, Miller found himself impressed by Thursday’s demo. “If this does make it into production, that is a truly impressive engineering and production feat,” he says.

Taiwan’s former Army chief of staff punished over M1A2T procurement irregularities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
03:18:24 UTC
12:18:24 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Army Command Headquarters confirmed Thursday that seven military officials involved in the M1A2T main battle tank procurement project had been disciplined for what it described as “administrative oversight.”
KMT Legislator Ma Wen-chun (馬文君) pointed out in May that the budget for the M1A2T procurement project, which runs from 2019 through 2027, had unexpectedly increased by NT$4.8 billion (US$148 million) to NT$45.3 billion in the 2026 budget, per Storm Media. Defense Minister Wellington Koo (顧立雄) acknowledged the error at the time and said the officials responsible would be disciplined.
DPP Legislator Wang Ting-yu (王定宇) stressed that whether the Army had overlooked the issue or failed to inform the legislature, spending unauthorized funds was illegal. He called on the Ministry of National Defense to take responsibility for the violation.
Department of Strategic Planning Director-General Lieutenant General Huang Wen-chi (黃文啟) explained how the discrepancy arose. During the budgeting process, the Army removed certain items from its proposed procurement package to keep the project within the NT$40.5 billion budget.
However, Huang said the Army ultimately signed the A3 version of the letter of offer and acceptance which reinstated previously cut items, including six M1070 heavy equipment transporters and 14 M88A2 recovery vehicles.
Huang said the Army initially expected exchange rate fluctuations between 2019 and 2023 to help offset the additional costs. However, the strengthening of the US dollar since 2024 undermined the plan.
Ma criticized the Army’s handling, saying it should have requested additional funding if the existing budget was insufficient, per UDN. She argued that raising the cost issue after the US had delivered all the equipment effectively put the legislature under pressure to approve the additional funding.
Asked about the disciplinary action, Army Deputy Chief of Staff Major General Wu Sung-ling (吳松齡) said Thursday that the officials involved, including then-Army Chief of Staff Lieutenant General Chang Yuan-hsun (章元勳), had been disciplined in accordance with Army regulations, per Tai Sounds.
Retired Colonel Chou Yu-ping (周宇平), former head of the Air Force Surveillance Warning Center, said the case reflected the military’s long-standing failure to maintain a sufficient pool of qualified administrative specialists, compounded by overly restrictive procurement rules, per CMedia. He said the military’s practice of rotating personnel among service branches and positions prevented procurement officials from passing on expertise in negotiations, finance and project management.
Regarding procurement regulations, Chou proposed relaxing restrictions to give officials greater flexibility to negotiate time-sensitive deals while providing legal backing for them to seek better terms from the US. He also warned against relying on exchange rate fluctuations to cover budget shortfalls, calling for a more comprehensive exchange rate monitoring and hedging mechanism given that such projects often involve billions of Taiwan dollars.

Ursula von der Leyen suggests creating EU strategic gas reserves — Politico
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
03:12:01 UTC
12:12:01 KST

BRUSSELS, October 16. /TASS/. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has invited European leaders to consider creating the bloc-wide strategic gas reserves, three diplomats and two EU officials have told Politico.
The initiative was put forward amid concerns that the EU may face fuel shortages this winter.
The report says that the existing European gas storage facilities, normally refilled throughout the year by commercial actors, are running at record lows amid high summer prices, linked to the conflict in the Middle East.
The report says that the bloc was left "unprepared for winter."
It wasn't immediately clear to diplomatic officials what form the reserve idea would take, Politico wrote.
Earlier TASS reported that Europe risks starting the heating season with record-low gas stocks. By the traditional start of the autumn-winter period, EU countries may fill their storage facilities to only 70-75% capacity, marking an all-time low for the beginning of the heating season.
Under European Commission requirements, EU nations must ensure their gas storage facilities are 90% full between October 1 and December 1 each year. A 10% margin of flexibility is permitted in the event of challenging filling conditions. Consequently, net injections into European storage facilities must total at least 68 bcm by the start of the 2026-2027 autumn-winter season to meet the filling target. However, anticipating a very mild winter, the European Commission is prepared to lower this threshold to 80% for the current year.

US lifts some sanctions restrictions on overseas assets of Russia's Lukoil
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
06:03:00 EEST
12:03:00 KST

US lifts some sanctions restrictions on overseas assets of Russia's Lukoil
The US Department of the Treasury has extended until 24 April 2027 the validity of general licences authorising transactions involving some of the overseas assets of sanctioned Russian oil company Lukoil.
Source: a notice from the US Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC)
Details: According to the department, the licences cover Lukoil's petrol stations outside Russia and four Bulgarian entities, including an oil refinery in the city of Burgas.
The first licence governs the activities of Lukoil International GmbH, which holds the Russian oil giant's overseas assets. The authorisation also covers entities in which it holds a direct or indirect stake of 50% or more, including its US subsidiaries Lukoil North America and Lukoil Americas Corporation.
The licence allows customers to buy fuel and related goods at Lukoil petrol stations outside Russia. It also permits the provision of maintenance, measures to keep the stations operating or their gradual closure. OFAC said this move is intended to protect retail consumers from the adverse effects of sanctions. Permitted transactions include payments to suppliers, rent, insurance premiums and staff wages.
However, Washington has strictly prohibited the transfer of any funds to individuals or organisations in Russia or to accounts held with Russian banks. The licence also excludes any transactions involving the Central Bank of Russia, the Russian Finance Ministry or the National Wealth Fund.
The second general licence allows transactions involving four of the company's Bulgarian subsidiaries: the Lukoil Neftohim Burgas oil refinery as well as Lukoil Bulgaria, Lukoil Aviation Bulgaria and Lukoil Bulgaria Bunker. The exemptions also cover subsidiaries in which these entities hold a stake of at least 50%, but do not extend to other sanctioned assets belonging to the group.
According to Reuters estimates, the easing of restrictions covers a network of around 2,000 petrol stations across Europe, Central Asia, the Middle East and North America. These include around 200 stations in the US states of New York, New Jersey and Pennsylvania, 600 in Türkiye and more than 300 in Romania. Lukoil also holds leading positions in the retail fuel markets of Moldova and Bulgaria.
Background:
- On 22 October 2025, the US Department of the Treasury added Rosneft, Lukoil and 34 of their subsidiaries to its sanctions list. Washington said the decision reflected Moscow's unwillingness to take meaningful steps towards ending the war in Ukraine.
- In late October 2025, the Russian oil group announced plans to sell its foreign assets and agreed to sell Lukoil International to commodities trader Gunvor. However, the deal fell through after the US regulator refused to approve the transaction.
- On 10 December 2025, OFAC introduced a special licence allowing Lukoil's overseas assets to be sold to companies not subject to sanctions.
- On 14 April 2026, the US extended the licences allowing the company's foreign petrol station network and Bulgarian businesses to operate until 29 October 2026.
- In early October 2026, The New York Times posted a report saying that negotiations between Donald Trump's administration and the Kremlin had expanded to include discussions about a multi-billion-dollar deal involving Lukoil's international assets. According to sources, a group of investors with links to White House special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner is seeking to acquire the portfolio of oil fields, refineries and petrol stations.

China tells Israel to stop ‘forced establishment’ of West Bank settlements
“The Palestinian question is the greatest historical injustice of this century,” China’s foreign minister said.
China’s Foreign Minister Wang Yi has told Israeli President Isaac Herzog during a meeting in Azerbaijan that Israel should stop and reverse its “forced establishment” of West Bank settlements, China’s foreign ministry said in a statement.
Wang told Herzog that China has consistently viewed the Palestinian question as the greatest historical injustice of this century, the ministry said in the statement on Friday.
Wang emphasised that the “two-state solution” is the right path to a resolution and said the immediate priority is to fully open access to the Gaza Strip so a humanitarian “catastrophe” is not allowed to spread.
Wang added that China is willing to work with the international community to push all parties to return to dialogue as soon as possible and seek a political settlement.
Wang is attending the Seventh Summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence-Building Measures in Asia, held in Baku, Azerbaijan, as the special representative of President Xi Jinping, China’s state news agency Xinhua reported.
China urges new Middle East framework
In September, Chinese President Xi Jinping visited Cairo for the first time in a decade and called on Middle East countries to oppose external influence and consider reshaping the region’s security order.
Xi’s rare visit arrived as Beijing seeks to expand its influence in the region amid the US-Israel war on Iran.
The talks covered the US-Israel war on Iran, with both presidents urging “diplomatic solutions” to reach a “comprehensive agreement to end the war”, according to a statement from Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi’s spokesperson.
In March, China criticised the US and Israeli attacks on Iran, with Beijing demanding an immediate halt to the joint attacks. Wang told his Israeli counterpart, Gideon Saar, that the attack on Iran came as negotiations between Washington and Tehran had “made significant progress, including addressing Israel’s security concerns”, China’s foreign ministry said in a statement following the start of the war.
China was Iran’s largest trading partner, buying up to 90 percent of its oil, according to the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission. In 2021, Beijing signed a 25-year “comprehensive strategic partnership agreement” with Tehran.
At the same time, Beijing has spent the past decade cultivating closer ties with Gulf countries, including Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, and remains a top trade partner of both the US and Israel.

Argentine students protest on campus over Milei’s austerity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
02:11:33 UTC
11:11:33 KST

Argentine students protest on campus over Milei’s austerity
Judge fines government for failing to fund universities as protests over Milei’s cuts turn violent.
“This cannot go on!” students shout during an assembly in the middle of the central hall of the University of Buenos Aires Exact and Natural Sciences building.
It is part of Argentina’s prestigious public university system.
The faculty’s central hall is covered with dozens of banners protesting President Javier Milei’s spending cuts. Students have called an assembly to announce the occupation of the university, a traditional form of protest in Argentina meant to raise public awareness and pressure the government.
They say they will take over the building for a day. Many students and professors here are concerned about the impact of Milei’s austerity policies on public universities and say the future of free higher education is at risk.
“Our best professors are leaving en masse. With salaries that cannot cover their basic needs, they are leaving for private universities,” Emiliano Gato, a physics student who is part of the group, told Al Jazeera.
“I dream of doing research and teaching at the public University of Buenos Aires. It’s a prestigious school. But now, with this austerity plan, I don’t know what will happen.”
Public universities in Argentina have become a major battleground of Milei’s austerity plan. Students and professors are protesting the lack of funding and the erosion of salaries, which they say is a major threat to the country’s public education.
Milei is implementing one of the harshest austerity plans in Argentina’s history.
Since taking office in 2023, he has laid off thousands of state employees, shut down ministries, reduced subsidies and cut government-funded programmes. The measures were meant to fight high inflation, which was a major problem in Argentina. Almost three years later, inflation has fallen to around 2 percent a month. Milei says his plan is going well.
“Argentina is growing at a remarkable pace. We have now recorded 27 consecutive months of sustained growth, and today the country is expanding at four times its historical rate. This growth is being felt across almost every sector of the economy,” said Milei during a recent visit to Washington.
Ripple effects
But not everyone agrees. His plan is also having a profound impact on public education, welfare plans for people with disabilities, pensioners and others who depend on state support. The opposition has tried to block many of Milei’s reforms.
Last year, Congress overturned presidential vetoes and approved two laws, one increasing funding for public universities and another declaring a disability emergency. But Milei’s government has refused to implement them, arguing that Congress failed to identify how they would be financed.
A federal judge has now begun fining the government 100,000 pesos (around $70) a day for failing to implement parts of the financing law, which requires Milei’s government to restore university salaries and student scholarships lost to inflation, regularly update budgets and provide funding for research, hospitals and infrastructure.
And that’s why thousands of people took to the streets on Thursday to demand that the government implement it. All around Buenos Aires, long columns of people blocked the centre of the city as they called for a general strike. Although the protest was meant to be peaceful, it soon turned violent. Police fired tear gas and rubber bullets as protesters threw rocks.
The plaza in front of Congress resembled a battleground. At least 25 people were detained, and several others were injured, including members of the security forces.
Maria Teresa de Jesus is a professor in the University of Buenos Aires chemistry department. She says she makes around $700 a month and it has become difficult to make ends meet. “I have come to this protest as a last resort. I am professor. I love teaching, doing research. I shouldn’t be here,” she told Al Jazeera. “Public education is crucial in this country, to make education accessible to all. And the government is ignoring it.”
Many in Argentina continue to support Milei’s economic plan. They are hoping the government’s plan to exploit the country’s vast natural resources will pay off and translate into more jobs, higher wages and improved living standards.
But many others have stopped believing and are prepared to raise the stakes. They accuse Milei’s government of protecting the interests of a privileged few while asking the rest of the country to bear the cost of his economic plan.

thessaloniki’s layered historic center weaves into expandable pedestrian network
linked by a neutral urban skin, apostolopoulos tasoulis’ masterplan establishes an expandable urban network designed to unify over seventy monuments and archaeological sites across thessaloniki, greece.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
EXPANDABLE city NETWORK UNIFIES THESSALONIKI’S HISTORICAL layers
The Armosi (Άρμοση) masterplan, designed by Apostolopoulos Tasoulis, establishes an expandable urban network to unify over seventy monuments and archaeological sites across Thessaloniki, Greece. Structured along the historic Egnatia Street axis and its intersection with Aristotelous Street, the design framework integrates Roman, Byzantine, Ottoman, Jewish, and modern historical layers into a cohesive public landscape informed by UNESCO’s Historic Urban Landscape approach.
NEUTRAL MATERIAL TOOLKIT REDEFINES SITE BOUNDARIES AND URBAN AXES
To improve urban legibility without adding visual complexity, the proposal by Apostolopoulos Tasoulis architectural studio applies a unified design toolkit. A continuous, light-colored paved surface creates a neutral backdrop, supported by standardized lighting, signage, and discreet street furniture. Site boundaries are reconfigured through subterranean facilities, new public access points, and light enclosures, with targeted interventions restoring the historic imperial axis at the Rotunda and Galerian Complex and introducing a new axial entry at the Roman Forum.
GREEN PEDESTRIAN CORRIDORS LINK ARCHAEOLOGY WITH PUBLIC TRANSIT
Pedestrian movement and climate resilience dictate the ground plane. Existing vegetation is expanded into continuous green corridors connected to the city’s metro network and public transport system, establishing traffic-calmed routes that allow Thessaloniki’s historical stratification to operate as an active part of daily urban mobility.

Tesla launches flying Roadster concept car
Electric car company Tesla has unveiled its flying Roadster vehicle with a demonstration in which the car drove upside down, flipped off a ramp and briefly flew, using compressed-air thrusters that Tesla claims will make it the world's quickest production car.
During a live event in Texas, the two-seat Roadster model drove up a half-pipe ramp and launched off the top, remaining in the air for a few seconds before landing
It also became airborne after building up speed on flat ground, launching over a row of parked vehicles. It then lifted off from a stationary position.
A series of thrusters in the bottom and back propelled the car into the air and cushioned the landings.
It was designed by Tesla and SpaceX, both companies led by businessman Elon Musk, who called the second-generation Roadster "a collaboration with the world's best car company and the world's best rocket company".
The thrusters can also fire rearward to boost acceleration. Tesla demonstrated the car reaching 60 miles per hour in a claimed 0.81 seconds, and said it would be the "quickest" production vehicle to 60 miles per hour.
On the half-pipe ramp, the vehicle was able to remain upside down due to a fan suction system. The air tanks in the vehicle are rechargeable and can be recompressed without fuel, according to Tesla.
Long term, Musk said the car will be the "only manual" vehicle in its lineup, referencing plans for driverless vehicles. Though the demonstration used a pre-programmed sequence with no driver.
Tesla chief designer Franz von Holzhausen said the car was designed with an "aerospace aesthetic". It has an angular supercar exterior with scissor doors and a deployable spoiler, and is a coupe with a hard top.
The seats are moulded directly to the chassis, and it features wire steering, which replaces the mechanical link between the steering wheel and wheels with electronic controls.
Musk referenced the uncertainty of street legality for the flying capabilities and said that "success is not guaranteed" before the test.
Production on the vehicle is set for 2028, according to Tesla. The company first unveiled a second-generation Roadster in 2017, with deliveries planned for 2020.
Tesla's last major launch was the Cybertruck, unveiled in 2019.
Other recent concept cars include Alef's concept vehicle.
The imagery is courtesy of Tesla.

Missiles supplied to Ukraine sold on ‘open market’ – Trump

In an interview with Newsmax aired on Thursday, Trump lashed out at Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky, accusing him of exploiting Washington’s generosity, while refusing to negotiate an end to the conflict with Russia.
“Where is the cash that we gave to Ukraine? Where is all the equipment? Biden was giving them missiles, and they were being sold on the open market,” Trump said.

An RT investigation in 2022 found a variety of Western-supplied weapons such as anti-tank rockets, drones, and small arms for sale on the “dark web.”
According to a report by Small Arms Survey, the Ukrainian authorities intercepted a vehicle carrying 18 US-made Javelin anti-tank missiles and other hardware in Kiev-controlled part of Russia’s Donetsk People’s Republic in 2024. The driver lacked the proper paperwork to transport the weapons, which suggested that they could have been intended for sale, it said.
Ukraine has also been rocked by numerous corruption scandals in military procurement involving officials close to Zelensky. In August, the country’s National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) reported losses of 254 million hryvnias ($6 million) as a result of an alleged embezzlement scheme which revolved around purchases of drones for Ukrainian forces.
Last year, investigators uncovered a $100 million corruption scheme in the Ukrainian energy sector allegedly run by a former close associate of Zelensky, businessman Timur Mindich, who fled the country before he could be detained. Former Ukrainian Defense Minister Rustem Umerov has been questioned as a witness in the case.
Zelensky has faced criticism from the West and street protests in 2025 over his attempts to put Ukraine’s independent anti-corruption watchdogs under the control of the government. The pressure eventually forced him to reverse course.
Trump has repeatedly criticized Biden for providing Ukraine with weapons and funds without preconditions and proper oversight. During Thursday’s interview, the US president compared Zelensky to P.T. Barnum, a 19th-century American showman and traveling circus-owner, known for publicity stunts and sensational attractions.
“Zelensky is not a good guy for us to deal with. Biden gave him billions and billions of dollars,” he said.
Trump also questioned the Ukrainian leader’s willingness to reach a diplomatic resolution to the conflict with Moscow.
“He says he wants to settle but he [doesn’t],” he said, adding: “No, I’m not a big fan of Zelensky. They’ve destroyed that country.”
The remarks followed Zelensky’s criticism of Trump’s decision last week to ease sanctions on Russian diesel exports in order to contain surging energy prices ahead of the November 3 US midterm elections. The Ukrainian leader said he felt betrayed by Washington’s move and defied Trump’s demand to halt attacks on Russian oil refineries.
The US president, meanwhile, made clear that Washington would prioritize rebuilding its own depleted weapons inventories rather than continuing to supply Kiev.
“Once we are really stocked, we will start letting our allies buy them [the arms] from us,” he said.

Sharing care for my son is hard. But I'm learning
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
02:01:03 UTC
11:01:03 KST

perspective
How I'm learning to share the invisible load of being a carer
At 27, Dimity's son Stu moved into his own home.
Stu, who is autistic and requires substantial levels of support, has been living in the purpose-built house with 24/7 care for almost two years.
The transition has been an opportunity for independence that Stu craved, and a shift in responsibilities for mum Dimity.
But like for many carers, there is an invisible caring load that remains.
Dimity still recruits and trains support workers, meets regularly with a team leader, oversees Stu's support program, advocates for him and acts as his nominee.
"It's the hardest thing to do, to share that load. Even with other people in your family," 67-year-old Dimity says.
"To trust another person to take on that responsibility."
But Dimity is learning to share Stu's care with others.
These are her words.
A determined young man
Stuart is my fourth child. I always say it was as if I had three children and then I got 10, because of the energy that he had.
He's an individual. There can be a tendency to think all autistic people are the same. And that is not true.
He has his own temperament and personality.
He is a very determined person. He is very perfectionistic, very focused. He loves cooking, crafting and creating things.
He micromanages; he observes. He has learned to knit simply by watching me knit.
On top of that, he struggles with issues of his autism: being non-verbal, illiterate, issues with emotional regulation, a need for predictable routines and rituals, problems with sensory overload, minimal social awareness, and intellectual disability.
Planning for the future
When Stu lived with us, it became apparent that, like all young men, he wanted more independence. He wanted to "divorce" his mother, as most sons eventually do.
It's the goal of every parent for children to reach independence; it was no different from my other sons.
He became resentful of my interference in his life.
We started to consider the process of creating a life for him where he had more control, more of a sense of agency over his own life.
Of course, in the background I still manage it, but it's not in his face.
Sign up to the ABC Lifestyle newsletter
In the couple of months prior to him actually moving, it was frenetic because I had a million ducks in a row.
I kept worrying that the degree to which this was working depended on me.
What would happen if his support workers weren't there? All sorts of worries started encroaching.
I actually had a medical event related to the stress, and from that time forward I started planning for a future of becoming somewhat redundant in his life.
I needed to work out how he was going to be supported when I'm not here. In a positive way.
Articulating my invisible load
Now I negotiate a lot with the disability support agency we work with, working to expand their responsibilities and what they are willing to share. Also forward planning for Stuart’s future, including other people in his circle of support, like siblings and extended family, for them to share caring responsibilities.
I'm developing a working document that explains in detail everything I do as Stu's mother and advocate and manager.
When he lived at home, I was definitely like the boss.
Now I look to his care team to guide me, too. It's not just me teaching, guiding and managing; I'm part of the team, and we're learning together the best ways to support Stu.
I look after grandchildren for three half-days a week, on top of what I do with Stu.
It's busy.
As his mother, my job is to look after him. No-one else is ever going to love him like I do.
And while being a carer is a lot of work and most of my life has been devoted to caring for my children and now my grandchildren, that's OK. That's my job.
What I'm trying to work on by working with a circle of support, creating the working document, is the space for people in that circle to then volunteer to take on that responsibility.
The running joke is "If I end up under a bus, would you be willing to take on this role?"
While I cover it all now, there will come a time when multiple people need to cover it.
Our relationship has improved
I remember one night talking to my husband and deeply realising and feeling the loss of Stuart from my home. And really having a big cry about it.
That was hard.
However, my relationship with Stuart has improved vastly since he moved into his own home.
When home life is challenging, often overwhelming, it's easy over a period to start to diminish the degree you feel or engage in affection for someone.
To have relieved both of us of that has been such a gift.
Now when he visits, he sits next to me and holds my hand. He puts his head on my shoulder. He touches my cheek. He cuddles me.
I've always been devoted to him.

Extreme warmth drives plant extinctions, diversity booms: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:48:07 CST
10:48:07 KST

MELBOURNE, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- Extreme global warmth drove both mass extinctions and explosions in plant diversity during two periods over the past 140 million years, offering new insights into how flowering plants became dominant on Earth, a new study has found.
The study examined fossilized pollen and spores to show that the mid-Cretaceous and early Cenozoic periods of extreme global warmth were central to plant evolution, both for flowering plants and the other main types on Earth, according to a statement released Thursday by Australia's University of Tasmania (UTAS).
Researchers said that land plants sustain almost all terrestrial animals, fungi and bacteria, while flowering plants are the most productive and diverse group, with about 400,000 species worldwide.
The team examined more than 60,000 fossil occurrences and applied methods that overcome the major biases in the fossil record, generating revised estimates of fossil pollen and spore diversity over the past 130 million years, according to the study published in Nature Plants.
Both plant extinctions and the emergence of new but evolutionarily related plant groups occurred mostly during the two periods of extreme global warmth, said the study's co-author, UTAS Professor Greg Jordan.
Each interval lasted several million years, with warming simultaneously destroying and promoting plant diversity "over million-year timescales," Jordan said. In contrast, cooler periods were marked by little change in plant diversity.
However, the researchers warned that human-driven warming is likely to cause plant extinctions much faster than past extreme warming events. ■

BEIJING, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- Brazil's Rafael Camara will make his Formula 1 debut with Haas in 2027 after signing a multi-year contract with the American team, replacing the outgoing Esteban Ocon.
The 21-year-old Ferrari academy driver, who currently leads the Formula 2 championship, was selected following an evaluation process involving four candidates, including reigning F2 champion Leonardo Fornaroli and Haas reserve drivers Jack Doohan and Ryo Hirakawa.
Camara impressed Haas during a test at Portugal's Portimao circuit in August, driving the team's 2025 F1 car. Team principal Ayao Komatsu said the Brazilian's pace had been the decisive factor in securing the seat.
"I always said we would choose a driver by performance. He showed incredible speed. That was the fully overriding factor above everything else," Komatsu said.
"In Portimao, he was just simply outstanding. We really wanted to go for someone who had that natural speed."
Camara joined Ferrari's driver academy in 2021 and has established himself as one of the most promising talents in junior single-seater racing.
He won the Formula Regional European Championship in 2024 before claiming the Formula 3 title in his rookie season in 2025.
The Brazilian has continued his rapid progress in Formula 2 this year, winning three races and holding a seven-point championship lead over Red Bull junior Nikola Tsolov with two scheduled rounds remaining in Qatar and Abu Dhabi.
Should Camara secure the F2 crown, he would become the first driver since Oscar Piastri to win consecutive titles in Formula Regional, F3 and F2.
Komatsu praised Camara's ability to adapt quickly to F1 machinery despite his limited experience.
"He showed that he could handle himself very well with not a huge amount of time to learn the car. He showed us more than just raw speed," Komatsu said.
Camara expressed his gratitude to Haas and Ferrari, while acknowledging the challenges awaiting him in his debut season.
"It's an important step in my career and I want to thank [team founder] Gene Haas and Ayao Komatsu for the trust they have placed in me," he said.
"Now my focus is on preparing myself in the best possible way for this new challenge. There will be a lot to learn, and I'm looking forward to working closely with the team, understanding the car and continuing to develop as a driver."
Camara will replace Ocon, whose departure was confirmed last month after two seasons with Haas. The Frenchman has struggled to match the performances of teammate Oliver Bearman during his time with the team.
Haas has yet to formally confirm its second driver for 2027, although Bearman is widely expected to remain for a third season, potentially giving the team an all-Ferrari academy lineup.
"It is our intention to continue with Ollie. It is just a matter of timing and finalising certain details," Komatsu said.
Camara is the first rookie confirmed for the 2027 F1 grid. His promotion also ensures Brazil will have at least two representatives in the championship next season for the first time since 2016, with Gabriel Bortoleto set to continue at Audi. ■

Why has "China Haul" become new buzzword on social media worldwide?
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:47:47 CST
10:47:47 KST

Foreign tourists buy handheld camera equipment at a flagship store of DJI in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province, June 24, 2026. (Xinhua/Liang Xu)
By Liu He
More and more foreign visitors are arriving in China with empty suitcases and returning home with bags full of Chinese goods. What is behind this trend? British YouTuber Elliot Page offered a glimpse of the appeal with a shopping vlog filmed in Guangzhou, south China's Guangdong Province. Exploring Chinese sportswear brands such as Li-Ning and Anta, Page was impressed not only by their affordability, but also by their design and quality.
Sportswear is just the tip of the iceberg. As "China Haul" gains traction on social media worldwide, an increasing number of international visitors are traveling to China not only to explore its attractions, but also to discover and shop for products that catch their eye.
In the first seven months of 2026, people from overseas spent 263.6 billion yuan (about 39 billion U.S. dollars) in China, an increase of 27.8 percent year on year, according to the Ministry of Commerce.
What is drawing international consumers to Chinese goods?
The growing appeal of homegrown Chinese brands is giving international consumers more reasons to take notice. "Chinese products, like clothes, accessories and daily necessities, are not only competitively priced, but also feature trendy designs that are hard to find in stores in my home country," said Carlos Alvarado, an international student from Guatemala, now a seasoned shopper in China.
An increasingly visitor-friendly shopping environment is making it easier for international tourists to spend in China. Visa-free entry arrangements and expanded departure tax refund services have further enhanced the country's appeal as a shopping destination.
From sprawling shopping malls and efficient delivery services to delivery robots that bring orders right to hotel doors, China offers a seamless shopping experience that lowers the barriers for foreign visitors. "Foreign tourists now account for 30 percent of our daily customer flow," said Zhou Man, manager of a Xiaomi store in Chengdu, southwest China's Sichuan Province.
Chinese cultural products are broadening the appeal of shopping in China, giving visitors more opportunities to connect purchases with the stories and creativity behind them.
From globally popular designer toys such as Labubu to the animated blockbuster Ne Zha 2, Chinese cultural products are capturing international attention. As international audiences become more familiar with Chinese cultural creations, shopping in China can offer another way to discover the country's contemporary culture and everyday life.
China Haul, at its core, reflects a simple shift: foreign visitors are discovering China's global appeal firsthand, exploring its products and brands for themselves rather than relying on secondhand impressions. By sharing their shopping finds online, they are introducing the world to a more diverse and appealing side of China.

“Every feeling of hardship is inseparable from the desire to escape from it; every…

“Every feeling of hardship is inseparable from the desire to escape from it; every idea of pleasure from the desire to enjoy it. All desire implies a want, and all wants are painful; hence our wretchedness consists in the disproportion between our desires and our powers. A conscious being whose powers were equal to his desires would be perfectly happy.”

Trump press secretary Katie Zacharia defends ‘lawyer’ title, downplays bar exam results
- Katie Zacharia acknowledged she did not pass the California bar exam, calling the result “inconsequential” because she did not need it in China.
- She said legal experts told her she could call herself a lawyer because she has a JD and international transaction law experience, but not “an attorney at law.”
- Her legal title has drawn scrutiny after Trump called her “an attorney”; the White House defended her and said she is “uniquely qualified,” while the ABA says bar admission is needed to practise law.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – White House press secretary Katie Zacharia appeared to acknowledge on Oct 15 that she did not pass the California bar exam, calling the results “inconsequential” as she sought to tamp down mounting questions over her legal credentials.
Zacharia said that when she sat for the exam, she was preparing to marry her now husband and move with him to China, where he worked for a private equity company.
She called herself “obviously incredibly distracted and overwhelmed and excited” at the time, in an interview on Oct 15 with conservative outlet Real America’s Voice.
“I had already pre-registered to take the bar, and I didn’t want to withdraw from that,” she said, adding that she decided to take the exam “and see what happens”.
She downplayed the exam results, calling them “somewhat inconsequential because I knew I wouldn’t need the bar in China” and the couple left soon thereafter.
“After moving to China, I think I didn’t really think much of the bar results or consider that something that I needed to focus on,” Zacharia said.
The new press secretary, whom US President Donald Trump described as “an attorney” when announcing her appointment, has faced scrutiny over her legal career.
The Wall Street Journal reported on Oct 14 that Zacharia had failed the bar exam in her home state of California before moving to China.
She has said that while living in China she “practiced international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials”.
Zacharia on Oct 15 said she had sought advice from legal professionals who told her it was acceptable to call herself a lawyer and provide legal analysis instead of legal advice.
“They said: ‘absolutely, absolutely across the board. You can call yourself a lawyer. You have a JD, and to buffer that, you have international legal experience in transactional law, which gives you the ability to analyse it, not necessarily give advice’,” she said in the interview.
“The truth is, is I was very careful how I executed this, and I never came across as someone who was an attorney at law.”
A JD or Juris Doctor is a graduate-level degree for people seeking to practice law in the US.
Zacharia earned her degree from Pepperdine Law School in 2011, according to an announcement from the university.
The White House has defended Zacharia over the questions over her legal career but did not address Zacharia’s status as a lawyer when asked about the Journal report.
“Katie is a fabulous and wonderful addition to the team,” White House communications director Steven Cheung said in a statement.
“She is uniquely qualified and whip smart to help inform the American people about all the great things President Trump and his Administration have been doing, and she will do an incredible job as Press Secretary.”
According to the American Bar Association, someone in the US who graduates from law school cannot practice law or present themselves as an attorney before passing a bar exam and being admitted to a state bar.

Police reveal identity of man found in a barrel in drought-stricken Lake Mead
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
01:34:53 UTC
10:34:53 KST

After four years, a piece of the haunting mystery uncovered in the waning waters of drought-stricken Lake Mead has been solved.
Since the remains of an unknown homicide victim were discovered stuffed inside a barrel in 2022, Las Vegas investigators have been searching not for his killer – but for his identity. At a press conference on Thursday, Clark county coroner Melanie Rouse shared his name publicly for the first time: Edward Lelburian Jackson.
“He also went by the name ‘Buddy’,” Rouse said, as a grainy picture of a smiling and bearded man holding a baby flashed on a screen behind her. They believe he was in his mid to late-50s.
The decades-old murder sparked nationwide attention after the remains were discovered in the shallow waters by boaters in 2022 near Hemenway Harbor at Lake Mead National Recreation area. An initial autopsy revealed the man had been killed by a single shot to the head. Investigators determined he was likely killed in the mid-1970s to early 1980s – an era when organized crime ran rampant in Las Vegas – due to the style of his clothing.
In the years since he was found, authorities revealed he had been wearing a button-down short-sleeve shirt, light blue jeans, a silver wristwatch and blue-and-white tennis shoes. They also released composite renderings of what he may have looked like, in the hopes that someone might come forward with information.
Behind the scenes though, they searched for his DNA in crime databases, uploaded his description into a national missing persons database, and sent bone samples to a lab to obtain a genealogy profile.
A break in the case didn’t come until this year, when a forensics team at Oklahoma State University, which had partnered with investigators, received a strong lead. With a DNA sample from Jackson and his believed family member, “we were able to confirm that the remains were, in fact, Mr. Jackson,” Rouse said.
Jackson was from Arkansas, Las Vegas Metropolitan police department Lt Robert Price said, adding that detectives have not yet found a single thing that would tie him to the Las Vegas area. His family last saw him in the early 80s and there are records of him in California, where he briefly lived with his wife, and in Utah, where he was charged with aggravated arson and a conspiracy fraud case.
“There has been speculation in the past that the homicide had ties to an organized criminal group,” Price said. “At this point of our investigation, we don’t have any information to support those theories.”
Now that he has been identified, Price added, the investigation into what happened – and who was responsible – for Jackson’s murder can continue.
Jackson’s remains weren’t the only ones uncovered from Lake Mead in recent years, as its water levels reached historic lows due to years of overuse, longstanding drought and increasing temperatures. The water level of the 90-year-old reservoir has continually dropped, exposing areas that were previously underwater and leading historians to predict more bodies will be found.
A few days after the barrel was discovered, a second barrel was found by a KLAS-TV news crew, not far from the first. It was empty. Shortly after that, paddleboarders discovered human remains on a newly surfaced sand bar, but officials found no evidence of foul play.
In August, more human remains were discovered and police again determined there was no evidence of foul play.
Lake Mead and the upstream Lake Powell are the largest human-made reservoirs in the US, part of a system that provides Colorado River water to more than 40 million people, tribes, agriculture and industry in Arizona, California, Colorado, Nevada, New Mexico, Utah, Wyoming and across the southern border in Mexico.
The Associated Press and Uwa Ede-Osifo contributed reporting

Myanmar’s coup leader-turned-president wins back neighbours despite war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
01:34:47 UTC
10:34:47 KST

Myanmar’s coup leader-turned-president wins back neighbours despite war
From Thailand to Malaysia, ASEAN leaders are embracing Min Aung Hlaing, but critics warn it emboldens a military that is still bombing civilians.
Rohingya activist says it’s unfair to send refugees back to Myanmar
Yangon, Myanmar – When Malaysia invited Myanmar’s coup leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing for a visit in September, it insisted the trip did not amount to recognition. The purpose, an official said, was to address the “longstanding issue” of refugees and migrants from Myanmar in Malaysia.
But when Min Aung Hlaing arrived in Kuala Lumpur last week, the former general – whose power grab in 2021 triggered a devastating civil war – received a red carpet welcome, complete with an honour guard.
After an official luncheon on Thursday, Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said Myanmar was prepared to take its nationals back at its own cost, a message with appeal in a country where anti-refugee sentiment is growing. Malaysia hosts about 193,000 Myanmar nationals, most of them from the persecuted Rohingya Muslim minority.
“Because the weather is favourable, I will dispatch Navy ships to repatriate them,” Min Aung Hlaing said.
For his part, Anwar pledged to help reintegrate Myanmar into the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), the 11-member regional bloc that has barred Min Aung Hlaing from its high-level meetings for refusing to carry out its peace plan. Malaysia was a vocal supporter of the plan, which is known as the Five Point Consensus and calls for an end to violence and “constructive dialogue” between the warring parties.
The civil war in Myanmar is now in its fifth year and has killed as many as 100,000 people and displaced at least 3.5 million, according to monitoring groups.
“Malaysia will do whatever is possible to make sure that we … ultimately, take Myanmar as part of our community of nations, without prejudice, and particularly in the context of ASEAN,” Anwar told reporters.
Malaysia is the fifth ASEAN nation to host Min Aung Hlaing since he became president in April, after an election held in December and January, which major opposition parties were barred from participating in. In recent months, he has visited Thailand, Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos.
Following his return from Malaysia, his spokesperson said Indonesia and Brunei could be next.
“Malaysia’s reversal on Min Aung Hlaing has broken a dam of opposition to the junta,” said Bridget Welsh, an honorary research associate at the University of Nottingham’s Asia Research Institute in Kuala Lumpur. She said regional leaders who have welcomed Min Aung Hlaing, despite accusations that he has committed crimes against humanity, were putting pragmatism ahead of human rights.
“It is a step back for ASEAN as an organisation, and for Myanmar,” she said. “It does not offer any concrete path to the resolution of the Myanmar crisis, and in fact, arguably worsens it by giving the military legitimacy internationally, a legitimacy it does not have in Myanmar itself.”
‘Convenience plays a part’
Min Aung Hlaing’s rehabilitation extends beyond Southeast Asia.
Since April, the former general has also visited India, China, Russia and Belarus. At each stop, he has tried to present his government as stable and “on the path to democracy”, while pitching trade and infrastructure deals.
Even the United States appears to have opened the door.
Washington has begun direct talks with Min Aung Hlaing’s government, the Reuters news agency reported last week, despite sanctions on him over human rights abuses. These include the 2017 crackdown on the Rohingya, which sent more than 700,000 people fleeing into Bangladesh and which the US has called a genocide.
Reuters said the latest talks have focused on shutting down scam centres operating from Myanmar that have defrauded Americans of billions of dollars.
Khin Zaw Win, director of the Tampadipa Institute in Yangon, said Min Aung Hlaing’s quest for international legitimacy has been aided by a coordinated push from China, India and Thailand, all of which share borders with Myanmar. The three neighbours have experienced spillover from the war, such as fighting near their borders, disrupted trade and influxes of refugees.
Khin Zaw Win said the three countries “have the biggest stakes in how Myanmar pans out” and want the military-installed government recognised. Russia and Belarus, meanwhile, are both major arms suppliers to Myanmar, and Naypyidaw has backed Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
“Convenience plays a part for all of them,” he said.
The growing diplomatic recognition, however, has done little to resolve the conflict.
While Min Aung Hlaing has invited all armed groups to peace talks, fighting continues to rage across much of the country. His forces have launched offensives to retake territory lost to opposition armed rebels and ethnic armed groups in Rakhine, Chin, Kachin and Karen states and the Sagaing region. They have been aided by an intensified air campaign and a recruitment drive that has added tens of thousands to their ranks. China, too, has helped by brokering ceasefires between the military and powerful ethnic armed groups on its border.
Still, Laetitia van den Assum, a former Dutch diplomat, said the military is unlikely to regain control of the whole country.
“That would require a huge occupation army and not – as now – a garrison army that controls a particular location,” she said. “That is why Min Aung Hlaing… bets on an increasing number of temporary ceasefires in some parts of the country so that troops can be directed to areas where he wants to continue fighting”.
Van den Assum said she found it “quite surprising” that ASEAN nations are seeking Rohingya repatriation from the very man accused of orchestrating crimes against them.
Myanmar has long denied the Rohingya citizenship, so it is unclear whether it would accept them as nationals. And with much of Rakhine State – their homeland – now held by the ethnic Arakan Army, it is far from clear where they would go.
“It is the blind speaking to the blind,” she said.
‘Low-cost, high optics’
Min Aung Hlaing has made other gestures.
Shortly before his trip to Thailand in August, he allowed the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) to see Aung San Suu Kyi, the civilian leader he deposed in 2021. The 81-year-old Nobel laureate has been held incommunicado since the coup, and the ICRC visit on August 3 produced her first photographs in years.
Sai Kyi Zin Soe, a research fellow at the University of Sydney, called the move a “low-cost, high-optics gesture rather than a real political opening”. The visit confirmed only that Aung San Suu Kyi is alive, “nothing more”, he said.
He noted that the military’s air raids have continued unabated even as ASEAN leaders roll out the red carpet, including a September 28 strike on a market in Rakhine State that killed an estimated 50 people.
The continuing attacks, he said, were the “strongest evidence that soft diplomacy hasn’t produced any deterrent effect”.
Sai Kyi Zin Soe also warned that the legitimacy conferred by the foreign visits would embolden the military further.
“Given the near-total absence of deterrence, no meaningful sanctions enforcement, an ASEAN pivoting toward re-engagement, and continued arms and fuel access via China and Russia, the military has every structural incentive to keep escalating, particularly in contested zones like Sagaing and Rakhine, where its grip is weakest,” he said.
Much now depends on the Philippines and Singapore, ASEAN’s current and incoming chairs.
Phil Robertson, director of Asia Human Rights and Labor Advocates, said the two countries must set an agenda that pushes back hard on entreaties from others in the region to allow “Myanmar fully back into the fold” and keep pressing the bloc’s five-point peace plan.
He also urged the US, the United Kingdom, Canada, Australia and the European Union to adopt targeted sanctions, such as an aviation fuel ban, rather than leaving “the whole Myanmar conundrum” to the regional bloc.
“International accountability is now more urgent than ever, whether that comes through additional universal jurisdiction cases or some sort of breakthrough to refer Myanmar’s generals to the International Criminal Court,” he added.
Zaheena Rasheed reported and wrote from Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia.

A 16-year-old opened fire at an elementary school in Bend, Oregon, on Thursday, killing three children and a teacher before he was shot by a person at the scene who pursued him into the school, authorities said.
Authorities found the suspect dead inside the school minutes after the shooting was first reported, Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said.
The three children killed were aged 5, 8 and 11. Another child, 7, and a teacher, 54, were injured and taken to a hospital in critical condition, Krantz said.
The attacker, identified as a Bend resident, forced his way into the school by shooting at locked doors, police said. He was shot and went down inside the school shortly after officers arrived, police spokesperson Sheila Miller said.
The first 911 call came just before 1pm from a person in a vehicle outside Silver Rail Elementary who reported being shot at by someone with a long gun, Krantz said.
Further 911 calls came from inside the school, and officers arrived on scene within minutes, Miller said.
Police said they did not know if the attacker knew anyone at the school or whether he had attended.

The attacker used a pump-action shotgun that was purchased by his mother, according to a law enforcement official briefed on the shooting. The official spoke to The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to publicly discuss the investigation.

WELLINGTON, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- New Zealand petrol and diesel prices rose in September from a month earlier, while annual food price inflation accelerated, official data showed on Friday.
Petrol prices increased 6.4 percent and diesel prices grew 7.8 percent in September compared with August, according to the statistics department Stats NZ.
Supply disruptions that began in late February contributed to higher fuel prices in March and April. Prices then declined through July before rising again in August and September, Stats NZ prices and deflators spokesperson Nicola Growden said in a statement.
"Although prices in September were above March levels, they were still below the peak recorded in April," Growden was quoted as saying.
In the year to September 2026, petrol prices rose 24.3 percent and diesel prices increased 55.8 percent, statistics showed.
Meanwhile, food prices increased 2.4 percent in the year to September, up from a 1.9-percent annual rise in the year to August 2026, Stats NZ said. ■

Budget showdown slips to November as Costa pushes for quick deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
00:56:56 UTC
09:56:56 KST

European Council President António Costa with Commission President Ursula von der Leyen at the EU headquarters in Brussels, on Oct. 15, 2026. | Ludovic Marin/AFP via Getty Images
BRUSSELS — EU leaders will go back to the drawing board in November as they race to finalize a deal on the bloc's next seven-year budget by the end of the year.
During the first day of a two-day summit in Brussels on Thursday, European Council President António Costa announced he was convening an additional gathering on Nov. 26 in a bid to overcome disagreements and lay the ground for a final deal in December. To bring the sides closer to an agreement, he will present new budget figures before the meeting, according to an EU official, who was granted anonymity to discuss the confidential planning.
Costa is pressing leaders to finalize negotiations by the end of the year — before elections in France, Italy and Poland in 2027 threaten to derail the talks.
Advertisement
In a speech to the leaders, Costa warned that going past the end-of-year deadline will delay EU payments to farmers and researchers past Jan. 1, 2028, when the new budget is scheduled to come into force.
If leaders fail to reach a deal in December, the electoral calendar might push an agreement to May or even October 2027, Costa warned leaders in his concluding remarks, according to two EU diplomats briefed on the discussions.
Pressure on governments
Costa's plan received a major boost on Thursday from French President Emmanuel Macron, who told fellow leaders that he won’t have a political mandate to sign a deal close to the French presidential elections in April 2027.
European Council President António Costa, Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever and French President Emmanuel Macron pictured at the European Council Summit on Oct. 15, 2026. | Nicolas Maeterlinck/Belga/AFP via Getty Images
This is a major reversal for France, which has previously been unwilling to commit to the end-of-year deadline.
Macron’s words put more pressure on governments to advance the talks over the coming weeks — although some cast doubt on his good intentions.
“There are so many elections next year. [French far-right leader Marine] Le Pen herself [said] it's undemocratic if we were now to agree,” said one EU diplomat.
Advertisement
Just hours before the leaders’ gathering, Le Pen renewed calls to halve France’s contributions to the EU budget if she wins the presidential elections next year.
She said that rushing the budget agreement before the French elections would be "a democratic scandal."
The new frugal
Costa is stuck between messy domestic politics across Europe and hardening stances among the EU’s 27 leaders.
The so-called frugal EU countries pushing for major budget cuts — Germany, Netherlands, Austria, Sweden, Denmark and Finland — have publicly said that an Irish proposal envisioning €159 billion cuts doesn’t go far enough.
On Thursday, the six hardliners were joined by Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever, who joked in a press conference after the summit that “I’m married to a Dutch person so I’m very frugal also in my personal life.”
However, behind closed doors the budget hardliners employed a more conciliatory tone.
Advertisement
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz — the unofficial leader of the frugal camp — said that the Irish proposal has achieved progress despite reductions still being needed, said two EU diplomats briefed on the discussions.
He pointed to EU payouts to poorer regions, as opposed to farmer's subsidies, as an avenue for cuts.
On the other side of the spectrum, Spanish Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez — who will try to cling on to power in an election on Nov. 29 — insisted that the budget is way too small.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez addresses journalists upon arriving at the European Council Summit on Oct. 15, 2026. | Nicolas Tucat/AFP via Getty Images
“It is a distribution of misery,” he told fellow leaders during the discussions, according to the diplomats. He was joined by Italy’s right-wing Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni — an ideological foe on most issues, but an ally of sorts in the budget battle. She insisted that no further cuts to the budget will be accepted.
To bring sides together closer to a deal, Costa promised to advance progress on EU-wide taxes, or own resources, to finance the next seven-year budget and reduce national contributions.
He will explore the European Parliament’s proposed taxes on crypto firms, online gambling and tech giants as well as a Greek idea to funnel future national sales of 6G mobile spectrum to the EU budget.
But given the level of opposition, getting EU countries to agree to any of these options will be no mean feat.
“It is time to be realistic and work on what is plausible and reasonable, instead of wishful thinking,” said another EU diplomat.

FBI, US Postal Service investigate suspicious mailings to election officials, lawmakers
- FBI and USPS are investigating suspicious letters sent to election officials and lawmakers, including some with an unknown or white powder substance, before the Nov 3 midterms.
- Several letters were intercepted in states such as Pennsylvania, Ohio and Idaho, while officials like Alex Padilla said the threats show the “very real dangers” facing election workers.
- USPS said it is “absolutely ready” for millions of ballots and plans extra measures, after a Supreme Court setback for a rule tied to mail-in ballots and Donald Trump’s push to tighten voting by mail.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – The FBI and US Postal Service’s law enforcement arm said on Oct 15 they were investigating suspicious mailings, including some sent to state election officials and lawmakers’ offices ahead of the Nov 3 midterm elections.
The FBI said some of the letters contained an unknown substance.
The investigation come less than three weeks before the midterms, which will determine control of the US Congress, as the Postal Service prepares to handle millions of mailed ballots.
Spokespeople for Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, Alex Padilla, a California Democrat, and Chris Murphy, a Connecticut Democrat, all said the US Postal Service intercepted letters containing a suspicious substance mailed to their offices.
“This incident is a stark reminder of the very real dangers facing those who serve the public and who help administer our elections,” Padilla said in a statement.
The US House of Representatives sergeant at arms, the House’s chief law enforcement officer, told staff in an e-mail seen by Reuters that some public officials had received letters containing suspicious white powder substances.
Brendan Donahue, a deputy chief inspector with the US Postal Inspection Service, said some suspicious letters had been intercepted and that an investigation was ongoing.
“We are committed to protecting our nation’s election officials from threatening and dangerous mail. Any threat or attack on an election official is unacceptable,” Donahue told reporters.
The National Association of Secretaries of State and the National Association of State Election Directors said late on Oct 14 that a series of suspicious letters was sent to state election offices.
Letters bound for several state election offices were intercepted before they were delivered, including in Pennsylvania, Ohio and Idaho.
The Wisconsin Elections Commission said on Oct 15 it received a suspicious letter with an unidentified powdery substance that was deemed not hazardous.
“Let this be very clear: this incident will not shake us,” said Meagan Wolfe, the state’s chief election official.
An email to Senate staff said suspicious letters could have postmarks that do not match the return address and included an image of an envelope with a return address labelled “DSA” and a New York City address.
Postal service plans new measures
Earlier on Oct 15, US Postmaster General David Steiner said USPS was “absolutely ready” to handle millions of ballots for the midterm elections.
USPS said in October it would take “extraordinary measures” for the 2026 election, including extending hours at some retail locations and expediting handling, extra deliveries and special pickups of ballots.
On Sept 14, the US Supreme Court declined to let USPS enforce a rule targeting mail-in ballots, dealing a setback to President Donald Trump’s effort to restrict voting by mail. USPS said it would not enforce the rule under the order.
The agency adopted the measure after Trump issued a March executive order aimed at tightening rules governing mail voting.
In 2024, USPS delivered 99.2 million ballots to and from voters in the presidential election. About 30% of votes were cast by mail in the November 2024 presidential election, down from 46% in 2020.
Trump’s fellow Republicans are locked in a tight battle to retain control of Congress in the midterms. Democratic voters disproportionately use mail-in ballots, according to various surveys, so restricting them could benefit Republicans.
Under the rule that was blocked, states would have had to provide lists of mail-ballot recipients to USPS and use agency-approved outbound and return ballot mail envelopes outfitted with unique barcodes.
The Postal Service could then have refused to send out ballots that did not comply or were associated with voters not appearing on the lists. REUTERS

09:07:02 KST

Nickolay Mladenov, director-general of the Board of Peace, said on Thursday that he had received a letter from the Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories (COGAT) informing him of the suspension of coordination for private-sector goods entering Gaza following reports of threats and coercion by Hamas.
In a post on X/Twitter, Mladenov condemned the reported intimidation of merchants and interference with commercial supply chains.
“As I have warned repeatedly, such practices are unacceptable and must end immediately. The intimidation of merchants and interference in the supply chain only deepen the suffering of Gaza's civilians,” Mladenov posted.
He stressed the urgent need to establish new governance and security arrangements in the Gaza Strip.
“These developments demonstrate why the rapid deployment of the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG) supported by the International Stabilization Force (ISF), is urgently needed,” he wrote.
“Civilian supplies, humanitarian assistance and commercial activity must be protected from coercion, exploitation and interference,” Mladenov added.
He called on all parties to work with the Board of Peace to implement US President Donald Trump's comprehensive peace plan for Gaza, endorsed by the UN Security Council in Resolution 2803, without delay.
Mladenov emphasized the need to move forward with the arrangements required for NCAG and ISF operations in Gaza.
“This includes the decommissioning of weapons, the transition to legitimate transitional governance and the protection of humanitarian and commercial supply chains,” he concluded.
Commercial goods banned from entering Gaza over tax dispute between local merchants and Hamas
Israel said commercial goods were no longer entering Gaza over what it said was a dispute over taxes between local merchants and Hamas, shutting off a vital source of food and other goods in the territory where the population is dependent on aid.
COGAT, which oversees humanitarian affairs in Gaza, made the announcement in a statement on Wednesday, citing what it said was a decision by Gazan merchants to stop coordinating with COGAT on the entry of commercial goods.
It said the Gazan merchants had told COGAT that they had made the decision in response to a NIS 10,000 ($3,220) fee imposed by Hamas on each truck entering Gaza and a demand for 30% of all of their sales in Gaza to be carried out in cash.
Hamas later claimed that the NIS 10,000 fee was a voluntary payment by wealthy Gazans to a national fund that seeks to provide for those in need, such as widows and orphans. It also said that cash payments were encouraged due to what it described as an acute cash shortage in the war-torn territory.
Nahed Shhaibar, the head of the private transport union in Gaza, claimed that not a single truck carrying commercial products from Israel entered Gaza on Thursday. However, he said trucks carrying humanitarian aid had entered, as had trucks carrying commercial goods from Egypt via an Israeli-controlled crossing.
COGAT said the decision by Gazan merchants would cut the total number of trucks, which carry both humanitarian and commercial goods, entering Gaza each day to around 300, or half.
Diplomats say that far fewer than 600 trucks normally enter Gaza each day. Shhaibar claimed the figure was closer to 300, with two-thirds carrying commercial goods.
Israel is obliged under a US-mediated agreement to allow a minimum of 600 trucks carrying humanitarian aid to enter Gaza each day. However, it says it is required to allow only 600 trucks and that commercial goods are needed to supplement aid supplies.
