====================================================================================================

Costa angers EU leaders as splits mar summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
00:03:30 UTC
09:03:30 KST

European Council President António Costa and France's President Emmanuel Macron speak together ahead of a round table in Brussels, on Oct. 15, 2026. | Ludovic Marin/AFP via Getty Images
BRUSSELS ― António Costa is supposed to be the dealmaker who brings European leaders together. Increasingly, his efforts are going unrewarded.
At a summit of the bloc’s national leaders on Thursday, Costa — who, unlike most of the EU’s current big beasts, is a Socialist — suffered his most stinging criticism since taking the role of European Council president nearly two years ago. The ire centered on his handling of unrelated negotiations over curbing energy prices and the EU’s next seven-year budget.
Governments were looking for both debates to show signs of progress at the two-day gathering, which was scheduled to continue on Friday. What they got was, at best, stalemate ― at worst, mounting division. And a day of talking that dragged on for 14 hours with little to show for it.
Advertisement
The longer budget negotiations last, the “more difficulties we will have,” Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo told POLITICO. “So we have to work to find a solution this year. I understand very well that it is difficult. A huge challenge.”
The stakes could barely be higher. The EU is desperate to ease the cost of living crisis and get a deal on the budget before national elections next year make finding an agreement much tougher. Disunity between the bloc’s 27 members looks even starker when Donald Trump makes moves to take Russia’s side in the Ukraine war, the economy is struggling to match the might of China and anti-EU nationalists get closer to power in Europe’s biggest capitals.
All 16 diplomats and officials who POLITICO spoke to for this article were granted anonymity to allow them to speak on a sensitive issue. They were all either in the summit room on Thursday or were immediately briefed by leaders who were. While most were critical of Costa, others spoke more positively.
Costa’s spokesperson declined to comment.
European Council President António Costa, Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever, Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten and French President Emmanuel Macron in conversation at the European Council Summit on Oct. 15, 2026. | Nicolas Maeterlinck/Belga Mag/AFP via Getty Images
Bogged down
Costa, a former Portuguese prime minister, is appointed by leaders to chair their summits and corral them into agreement. As Brussels Playbook reported on Thursday, EU officials judge he’s entering a defining period of his presidency, racing against time to overcome huge divisions on the budget. He is widely expected to push for reappointment for a second two-and-a-half-year term next year, officials said.
Thursday’s summit was dominated by discussions unraveling on the second phase of the bloc’s carbon pricing regime, known as ETS2.
Advertisement
The showdown over the Emissions Trading System — both the current one, and the second iteration which is already legislated and will put a carbon price on heating and transport from 2028 — became so bogged down it forced Costa to cancel the summit’s planned press conference and delay further talks until after dinner, because they had become a “mess,” three EU diplomats told POLITICO.
With German Chancellor Friedrich Merz incensed by what Berlin saw as his Italian counterpart Giorgia Meloni’s intransigence, fiery negotiations pitted a coalition made up of Germany, Spain, France, Portugal, the Nordics and the Netherlands against a stubborn bloc of Italy with Hungary, Czechia, Slovakia and Poland (known as the Visegrád Four). Rome and the V4 group wanted the EU to postpone ETS2 because of the burden it would place on energy bills, according to five diplomats.
Leaders were fuming at Costa for allowing talks to go off the rails, two EU diplomats from different member countries said. While the pre-summit conclusions didn’t point to any rethink of ETS2, the countries tried to unpick the legislation in the summit room, leaving Costa flustered, one of them said.
Costa “wants to have conclusions ready from [pre-summit meetings of ambassadors] and not to open them during EUCO,” the diplomat said. “He is not a fan of drafting on the spot.”
Another said there was “huge frustration,” calling the tug-of-war over the wording of the energy policy “insane chaos.”
“They just went on with Italian drafts and disregarded texts that were handed in before by others, seemingly not understanding the political nuances of the whole ETS discussion,” they added.
Another accused Costa of “losing control of the room,” saying he had failed to keep track of proposed amendments and present them to EU leaders in time for the discussions. As a result, leaders were left debating without them, contributing to negotiations going on past midnight.
One diplomat and one EU official separately compared Costa with his immediate predecessors, Charles Michel ― who governments frequently criticized for a lack of dealmaking know-how ― and Donald Tusk, who enjoyed broad support throughout his term in office.
Advertisement
Costa performed “worse than Charles Michel” on Thursday, the diplomat said. The official said “there is frustration that things are not being dealt with a bit more Tusk-style.”
Honest broker
The annoyance went beyond the energy debate. While governments weren’t expecting a breakthrough on the EU budget on Thursday, they have started raising questions about Costa’s handling of that topic too.
High Representative Kaja Kallas addresses the press on Oct. 15, 2026. | Nicolas Maeterlincl/Belga/AFP via Getty Images
Costa is determined to secure an agreement by the end of the year. In his job, the Council president must act as a honest broker and facilitate a deal among 27 governments.
Northern EU countries are worried he’s favoring southern countries, according to a further four EU diplomats.
One EU diplomat accused Costa of being two-faced and not acting as an honest broker in the budget negotiations.
Another diplomat, from a country that wants the budget to be smaller, said: “Costa personally and politically belongs to the other camp.”
Advertisement
“There is some skepticism on how he will take the process further from here,” they said. The so-called frugal countries are calling on Costa to propose further cuts ahead of a special EU summit on the budget that was confirmed Thursday for Nov. 26.
‘Superb deal maker’
Many governments still believe Costa may succeed over the long term. Even those who acknowledge that his honeymoon is over ― a period when he was roundly praised for being a safe pair of hands and avoiding diplomatic faux-pas ― retain faith in him.
Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever defended Costa as “capable” and “shrewd” after the first day of the summit — praising the Council president for largely avoiding drafting on the day, unlike Michel.
Costa “avoids negotiation about the wording on the table which happened all the time under his predecessor and which annoyed the hell out of everybody because then you are here until three o’clock to discuss about syllables, commas and words that the next morning you cannot see the difference anymore,” De Wever said. “You don’t even know anymore what you are negotiating about.”
Other diplomats said the disarray wasn’t Costa’s fault, and blamed the leaders who tried to unpick the energy legislation, notably Meloni. “He did not want to reopen the conclusions, it was the V4 and Italy who did so,” one said. “I don’t see what he could have done differently.”
Another EU official defended the sheer difficulty of the task faced by the Council president. “Discussing drafting at leaders’ level is not the most straightforward thing in general.” On energy, the official said leaders wanted to have “proper consideration” of the different proposals by countries, which had “opposing interests.”
One of the diplomats more critical of his political leanings on the budget said Costa was “impeccable” in his behavior. “He’s a superb deal maker.”
The next few weeks will show how true that turns out to be.
Hanne Cokelaere, Camille Gijs, Sebastian Starcevic, Gerardo Fortuna and Hans von der Burchard contributed to this article.

Are student protests being manipulated ahead of France's presidential election?
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
00:25:06 BST
08:25:06 KST

Are student protests being manipulated ahead of France's presidential election?
- Published
The French passion for protest is legendary in Europe.
Over the last few years, we have regularly witnessed farmers angry about costly regulations lobbing manure at local mayoral offices, while masked youths periodically hurl homemade grenades at riot police in disadvantaged city suburbs.
For over three weeks now, thousands of students have barricaded entry to high schools and taken their grievances to the streets.
This Saturday, hundreds of new demonstrations have been announced across France.
Students are expected to be joined by workers' unions and key figures from the so-called "yellow vest" movement.
France's Prime Minister, Sébastien Lecornu, suggested this week that student anger was being manipulated as politics heats up ahead of next year's presidential election.
The gilets jaunes (yellow vests) demonstrated against cost-of-living hikes for over a year from 2018 - becoming one of the longest-lived protest movements in French history.
Jérôme Rodrigues, a prominent gilets jaunes activist, has used Instagram to encourage people to join Saturday's demonstrations.
The protests should give a voice to those who "want to be able to live decently, no longer have to count every cent, and no longer have to choose between eating and driving", he said in a video.
"Anger has no political party. An empty fridge has no political party," he added.
So what is going on in the EU's second largest economy?
Social unrest, government borrowing costs at eye-watering highs, a deeply divided French parliament and an apparent revolving door of exasperated French prime ministers - six prime ministers over the last five years - all claiming to want to reduce their country's public debt.
Is France at breaking-point - and what does this all mean for the eurozone currency the French are such a huge part of?
"You can't compare France to the Greece debt crisis of 2012 or Argentina in 2001. And the financial markets know it," economist Anne-Laure Delatte told me.
She is a CNRS Tenured Researcher at the Economics Department of Paris Dauphine University; a well-known face in debates on French media on the parlous state of the country's public debt.
"The markets recognised already in 2024 that we would have a budgetary problem after [snap] elections left parliament deeply divided between three [opposing political] blocs but they also realise France is a big country with the ability to raise taxes if necessary."
"Our situation is more like the UK in 2023 with Liz Truss," suggests Delatte, referring to the then UK prime minister's so-called mini budget, which triggered a sharp drop in the pound, a spike in government bond yields and soaring mortgage rates.
"The crisis was relatively short-lived because the markets recognised the UK had the financial tools to right itself."
"Here in France it would be painful, but a 4% increase in VAT would raise the 120bn euros needed to plug government debt. Investors know that," she concludes.
Maybe, in theory. And, as Delatte also points out, the European Central Bank would likely intervene if France's finances nosedived to the point where other European economies would be affected.
But with so many French citizens already visibly unhappy with the status quo, imagine the reaction if taxes were to increase, or welfare and education budgets decrease, further.
France's national motto is liberté, égalité, fraternité (freedom, equality and fraternity), but that is certainly not the sense you get on seething streets and in viral social media posts.
I met 17-year-olds Maxime, Madeleine and Elodie this week, perched on big green dustbins that have been used to block the entrance to their high school as part of the weeks' long protest.
They told me things were bad enough here, in the 3rd district of Paris, with holes in classroom walls, swelling class sizes and a dearth of teaching staff, but the teenagers were more than aware, they said, that the situation was far worse in their capital city's disadvantaged suburbs.
"France likes to speak of égalité," they told me "but the reality is the poor here are prejudiced against, while the rich benefit."
None of them will be old enough to vote in the presidential election in France next spring but they questioned whether the changing face of politicians in power made all that much difference anyway.
The three young women told me large-scale protests seemed the only way to get heard by French authorities.
- France's school protests: What lies behind the anger 
  - Published8 October
They are part of a defiant French tradition.
Cultural icon Victor Hugo, the 19th-Century author of French Revolution classic Les Misérables, also an activist for the French Republic, proclaimed: "Si vous n'êtes pas contents, manifestez, criez, hurlez, mais ne subissez pas."
("If you are not happy, protest, shout, scream but do not give up and give in.")
Amongst crowds of protesting students walking through Paris on Thursday, I came across a number of mums, with placards around their necks, reading: "Mums in solidarity."
Were they there to protest or to protect their kids, I asked? "Both!" was the emphatic response.
Gwen, 37, said she and other mothers were taking it in turns every morning to co-ordinate between students and police at their local school lock-in.
This came after mounting accusations of police brutality, denied by France's interior ministry, during protests earlier this month in which hundreds were injured and a 15-year-old boy in the town of Lens lost a hand.
France's interior minister has since suspended the use of stun grenades by police at high school demonstrations.
Gwen told me she did not mind that her son was missing weeks of school as a result of the lock-ins. "It's a far better education for him to wake up to his civic duty and to fight for what is just in society," she said.
At Thursday's demo I also came across 17-year-old Lola and her mother, Sandrine, sharing a placard that said revolution was the most beautiful expression of humanity.
"My mum took to the streets in '68," Lola said proudly. "Now it's my turn. No point in waiting for the presidential election in France. We want change now."
Student protests in Paris in May 1968 are the stuff of legend in France. Demands for better education inspired workers to join the marches which turned into the biggest general strike in French history. It set the standard for revolutionary upheaval for a generation and is credited with creating new opportunities for the French left.
Now, though, with six months to go before an already fraught presidential election in France, there are accusations that the hard left, under presidential hopeful Jean-Luc Mélenchon, is weaponising student frustration.
"Members of [Mélenchon's] France Insoumise (LFI) are instrumentalising the high school movement for their electoral advantage," said Sébastien Lecornu on Wednesday. He accused them of encouraging protests, then going through the motions of condemning any violence.
"This hypocrisy damages France," said Lecornu.
But "Mélenchon for President!" is a chant you often hear amongst the students in the streets.
Supporters applaud his desire for a wealth tax in France, for lowering the voting age to 16 and for being the only presidential candidate to turn up to French schools to examine the state of them, several demonstrators told me.
For Marine Le Pen, the nationalist anti-immigration favourite in France's presidential race, the solution is cutting the country's €11bn contribution to the EU's budget.
There is, though, reason to doubt that any new French president, from the left or the right, will be able to break the impasse over France's finances.
France is far from alone in Europe right now faced with an ageing population, a generous welfare state to run and a national economy squeezed by outside pressures such as US President Donald Trump's trade tariffs and the war in the Gulf.
Whether in France, Germany, Sweden or Italy, there is an inherent tension between politicians who hesitate to tell voters the truth about shrinking public finances, the defence establishment's demand for higher defence spending and citizens' insistence on improved public services.
In France, that pressure is particularly acute. French public expenditure, at about 57% GDP, is one of the steepest amongst wealthy nations worldwide.
Social spending, particularly on pensions, is exceptionally large, while French citizens pay one of the highest overall tax and social contribution burdens in Europe. Simply put, they expect a welfare and public service bang for their buck.
But economist Anne-Laure Delatte does not believe having a new president will ease her country's financial migraine.
"We need constitutional change. A new system. A new Republic," she told me.
"Our Fifth Republic is centred around a powerful president. Parliament is there to block him or her rather than to find consensus or to make new laws."
For France to progress, she says, that has to change.
The French parliamentary election that follows the 2027 presidential vote is likely to be as divided as ever, she believes: "We need a system where MPs have more power and should learn consensus and coalition-building from our European neighbours."
In her opinion, education had to be protected and funds better distributed. It was an investment in France's financial future, she told me.
"Our current system of inequality in schooling and low wages for teachers means we lose out from benefiting from the best and brightest across French society. That is not only unfair on individuals but our economy ultimately loses out on innovation and productivity."
Re-writing France's constitution is not on the cards, at the moment. So, what about the here and now, I asked centrist politician Anne-Catherine Loisier.
She's a senator for the Centrist Union in France's upper house of parliament and vice president of the parliamentary group for sciences and technology.
Loisier, along with pretty much every leading French politician across the political spectrum, says the protesting students "must feel heard".
"Our budgets are limited," she admitted, "but you don't necessarily need more money. You can make improvements by redistributing funding better. Education is a regional competence in France. Every region should take a look at local needs and address priorities accordingly. That action can be taken immediately."
I asked Loisier if she agreed with UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, the former mayor of Greater Manchester, that regions should be given greater powers. "Absolutely," she replied. "France has traditionally been very Paris-centric but so much could be improved by decentralising the country."
"My France isn't broken. I don't recognise that image you see portrayed in the media. My country is made up of lots of Frances. Paris, the regions; northern and southern France. We need to give power back to the people. Local governments can look people in the eye directly, so voters feel they have power over their own future, rather than politicians handing them their fate from up high in Paris."
"That way I hope we can restore voters' - and students' - faith in politics."
It's a promise you hear from politicians - right and left - ahead of France's huge elections next year.
But opinion polls here, as across most of Europe, indicate public faith in the political class is in dwindling supply.

A Neanderthal was killed with a spear 75,000 years ago: scientists found traces of ancient violence

Unknown Publisher

A Neanderthal was killed with a spear 75,000 years ago: scientists found traces of ancient violence
Kyiv • UNN
Traces of a fatal injury to a Neanderthal caused by a sharp weapon were found in Shanidar Cave. A year before his death, he had also suffered a facial injury.
Scientists from the University of Cambridge examined the remains of a Neanderthal who lived about 75,000 years ago. Analysis of the bones showed that he likely died from a blow from a sharp weapon to the chest. Haaretz reports this, citing a study in Scientific Reports, UNN writes.
Details
The remains of the man, known as Shanidar A, were found in Shanidar Cave in Iraqi Kurdistan. He was approximately 45 years old at the time of his death.
Researchers led by Emma Pomeroy discovered a hole in his left shoulder blade. A sharpened stick likely penetrated his chest, passed through his lung, and damaged the bone. Similar marks have previously been found on animal remains.
What else the scientists discovered
Approximately one year before his death, the Neanderthal also sustained facial injuries and lost a front tooth.
Earlier, researchers examined the remains of another Neanderthal in the cave, Shanidar 3, who lived about 50,000 years ago. He had a rib injury and a foot disease that required long-term care.
According to Pomeroy, these findings demonstrate the complexity of ancient human behavior.
I think we should see the same complexity in Neanderthals that we see in people today. Some are violent, some are caring

Cuba is scheduled to submit a resolution to the UN General Assembly on Oct. 29 for the 34th time, calling for an end to the U.S. economic, commercial and financial blockade imposed on the island for more than six decades.
According to Cuban government figures, the blockade has caused nearly 179 billion U.S. dollars in economic losses. ■

Order to limit Starshield for Ukraine came from inside White House, sources say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Order to limit Starshield for Ukraine came from inside White House, sources say
NEW YORK/WASHINGTON – The order to limit a satellite system used by Ukraine for battlefield communications and drone operations came from inside the White House, according to two US officials and a Western official briefed on the matter.
The officials said leaders at the Defense Department received a message that the SpaceX Starshield service for the Ukrainian military needed to be slowed.
The officials, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, did not specify who in the White House made the decision or who was responsible for implementing the order. 
The Pentagon is the biggest customer of Starshield, which is the military-grade version of the Starlink service.
Ukrainian officials said this week that military-grade Starlink receptors stopped working in Ukraine when mounted on fast-moving objects, interfering with the performance of Ukrainian drones that rely on them for onboard guidance systems over Ukrainian territory.
A person in Ukraine’s Defence Ministry said on Oct 15 that the receptors were now working when in motion, but only at speeds of up to 160kmh.
US pressures Ukraine over refinery attacks
The move to temporarily restrict the vital communications system came as US President Donald Trump has pressured Kyiv to stop its attacks on Russian refineries, which he has blamed for the soaring energy prices that are denting his Republican Party’s prospects in the November midterm elections.
But experts say that surge in energy costs is mainly the result of the US-Israeli war with Iran, which brought Iranian attacks on energy facilities and has largely shut the vital Strait of Hormuz.
In response to a request for comment about the order to limit Starshield, a senior US official said: “No such request was ever made by the president.”
The White House did not respond to questions about whether other administration officials might have made the request.
Starshield was developed by SpaceX specifically for government and national-security customers, particularly the US Department of Defense. Starshield uses the Starlink constellation as its backbone.
Ukrainian officials said the restrictions complicated strike missions against Russian forces and logistics in occupied territory and slowed interceptor drones used to shoot down incoming Russian Shahed drones.
Elon Musk, the chief executive of SpaceX, said on X on Oct 15 that because Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government, any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military or the president.
SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment.
The Department of Defense and the Ukrainian embassy in Washington also did not respond to requests for comment.
Decline in relations
Relations between Kyiv and Washington have deteriorated in recent days following a meeting in Miami on Oct 9 that convened representatives from both countries as well as Europe and the World Bank.
Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, the Trump administration’s Middle East envoy, struck a tough tone with Ukraine in the meeting, according to a separate person familiar with the matter. 
They told Ukrainian officials that the US was frustrated with Kyiv’s continued strikes on Russian refineries despite repeated requests from Washington to stop.
The US delegation also explained Washington’s decision to strike a diesel deal with Russia, saying the White House hoped it would soften Moscow’s stance on peace talks.
That deal, under which Russia will supply more than 2.25 million barrels of diesel to US and global markets, has triggered a backlash from some US lawmakers, who say it will give Moscow cash to pursue its war without forcing Russian President Vladimir Putin to make concessions to end the conflict.
In the days that followed, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and Trump criticised each other, with Zelensky calling the US decision on the Russian diesel deal “weak”.
Trump called for elections in Ukraine and Zelensky’s ouster.
Behind the scenes, American officials threatened to stop providing intelligence to Kyiv about Russian missile launches that Ukraine uses to thwart attacks, as Reuters previously reported. On Oct 14, Trump said Washington was still sharing intelligence with Ukraine.
Following the move to restrict Ukraine’s access to Starshield, the Ukrainians made calls on Oct 14-15 to find answers from senior officials at the White House, State Department and Pentagon, a senior Ukrainian official said, adding that Kyiv was told it was a White House decision.
The Pentagon has spent billions of dollars on the Starlink and Starshield services.  
It has also bought dedicated Starshield satellites, including communications spacecraft for missile-warning missions and a spy constellation for the National Reconnaissance Office, Reuters reported in 2024. REUTERS

Army Building Up New Space Operations Branch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
22:37:27 UTC
07:37:27 KST

The Army has long been dependent on space capabilities to navigate terrain, communicate in hard-to-reach areas, and identify and strike targets. Now, the service wants to deepen its space operations expertise and is making plans to expand its own cadre of operators in the coming years.
In June, the service established its a Space Operations Branch, consolidating space-related career paths and created to train Soldiers to operate and deploy space systems.
This week, during the annual Association of the U.S. Army Annual Meeting in Washington, after transverring 600 enlisted Soldiers into the branch Oct. 1, Army officials predicted the Space Operations Branch will eventually include thousands of officers and troops.
The 600 transfers were reclassified as 40D Tactical Space Operations Specialists, the Army’s Military Occupational Specialty code for space troops—uniting them with 40A Space Operations Officers. The enlisted Soldiers had previously been temporarily reassigned to space-related units from Air Defense Artillery, Signal, and Military Intelligence fields.
Speaking with reporters Oct. 14 during the conference, Col. Joseph Mroszczyk, director of the Army’s Transformation Integration Directorate for Space Superiority and High Altitude, said the service’s space operations cadre has almost doubled since 2012, and he expects that to continue within the new Space Operations Branch.
“When we talk about the branch and the targets, having a couple thousand dedicated folks within the branch, between the enlisted and the officer side, is a significant contribution across the service,” Mroszczyk said when asked if the Army has a target level of growth for the branch. He didn’t offer more specifics on how long it might take the service to get there.
After the Space Force was created in 2019, space operators and units transferred from the Air Force, Navy, and Army, with the bulk of Space Force operators coming from the Air Force. Army officials have continued to make the case that they need to have their own space-focused Soldiers. While critics charge that this risks duplicating effort and blurring roles and missions, the Army says the difference is that while the Space Force is focused on maintaining space superiority in orbit, its role is integrating space capability and effects into tactical multidomain operations from the ground.
Lt. Gen. John Rafferty, commander of the Army’s Space and Missile Defense Command, told Air & Space Forces Magazine in an Oct. 13 interview that as demand for these capabilities grows, the Army needs to provide the same professional pathways and training for space operators that it does for other specializations, like artillery, infantry, and aviation.
“Training, education, experience, and talent management is how you create great leaders, and that’s how you build great units with great leaders,” Rafferty said. “It became apparent to the Army that in order to capitalize on the momentum, the gains that we’ve made in Army space-delivered capabilities, we need to professionalize the branch and do it fast.”
Rafferty highlighted a few areas where the Army expects to need more space personnel and effects in the coming years.
The service on Oct. 8 activated its a new Multi-Domain Task Force at Fort Carson, Colo., one of four elements stationed around the world and designed to integrate air, land, sea, space, and cyber operations in theater. A fifth is slated for activation in 2028. Each task force incorporates space effects, and Rafferty said that as the service adds more MDTFs, it will naturally need more space personnel and systems.
He also pointed to the creation of a new Theater Strike Effects Group at U.S. Army Pacific, which will require space support. The service also wants to expand the focus of its 1st Space Brigade—headquartered at Fort Carson, but distributed across six countries—beyond GPS, theater missile warning, and satellite communications into new capability areas. He did not provide details.
As for space systems, the Army hasn’t revealed plans to field its own satellites, but Rafferty and others said the service has an interest in building out an architecture of stratospheric platforms in the “near-space” region—between 60,000 and 100,000 feet in altitude.
“That’s a—no pun intended—space that is just ripe with potential, and the opportunities for various payloads to be on those is remarkable right now,” Rafferty said. “It’s affordable and scalable, and we’ve just got to really pursue that as part of the space branch growth.”
Mroszczyk described the region as a sort of transition point between the air and space domains where platforms could host a variety of payloads supporting missions like sensing and communications, and even serve as platforms for “launched effects”—the Army’s term for small, air- or ground-launched autonomous systems.
As an example, Mroszczyk said high-altitude platforms could form a “complementary” layer for some of the Space Force’s data transport efforts, like the Space Development Agency’s Proliferated Warfighter Space Architecture or the Space Data Network. Systems in that layer could help distribute data during a conflict and provide resiliency should space systems be targeted.
He told reporters the Army is looking at a range of systems—from smaller platforms to larger balloons—and is planning multiple experiments in the coming year.
“That operational space allows some persistence and broad coverage in an area where you can deliver space-like capabilities in terms of payloads, but then also take advantage of the deep access that you get from a stratospheric balloon,” he said.

UN warns of food shortages if Hormuz fertiliser crisis continues
A failure by the United States and Iran to agree within weeks on a UN-backed plan for moving fertiliser through the Strait of Hormuz could cause a food security crisis in parts of Asia and Africa, an official overseeing the proposed scheme said on Wednesday.
The United Nations set up a taskforce in March to facilitate passage of fertilisers through the strait. It is yet to implement the mechanism it drew up, but United Nations Under-Secretary-General Jorge Moreira da Silva said this could be activated within 7-10 days of an agreement between Washington and Tehran.
"It's absolutely crucial to get the deal in the next few weeks. Otherwise, we will miss the planting season," he said in an interview in Bangkok, on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank annual meetings.
In response to questions from Reuters, a US State Department spokesman said the US military has assisted thousands of commercial vessels with transiting the strait.
"The United States will continue to take decisive action against Iran's attempts to disrupt freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and hold the global economy hostage," he said.
The White House and Iran's Embassy in Bangkok did not immediately reply to a request for comment.
Iran has sought to tighten its grip on the Strait of Hormuz since US and Israeli strikes on 28 February, using the chokepoint to pressure Washington, which has been pressing its own naval blockade of Iranian ports.
Before the war, the waterway handled roughly a third of globally traded urea - the world's most widely used fertiliser - and nearly half of seaborne sulphur, a key input. It is also a major conduit for global oil supplies.
Fertiliser shipments out of the Gulf region remained largely halted more than six months after the start of the conflict, the Washington-based International Food Policy Research Institute said in a note last month. Fertiliser products accounted for a "very negligible" share of the resumption of some shipping during a ceasefire between mid-June and mid-July, it said.
Five vessels a day
If the Hormuz disruption continues, commodity prices could rise by up to 81% for cereals, 66% for oil crops and 30% for animal products, according to an August report by the International Chamber of Commerce.
"If we miss that planting season, the productivity of agriculture would significantly drop and the impact on prices will significantly increase," said Moreira da Silva, who is also the executive director of the United Nations Office for Project Services.
The proposed operation would use a coordination centre in Oman to register vessels and coordinate safe passage, with UN monitors working alongside local authorities at Gulf ports to verify cargo loading.
The passage of only five vessels per day through Hormuz could keep fertiliser supplies flowing to countries in critical need, Moreira da Silva said.
Ships would be tracked during transit, and additional inspections could be carried out if countries raised concerns about a vessel or its cargo, he added.
Multiple shipping chokepoints
Iran and the United States have exchanged proposals through intermediaries since a June interim ceasefire collapsed, but efforts to reopen the Strait of Hormuz have stalled over Tehran's conditions and Washington's insistence on addressing Iran's nuclear programme from the outset.
The proposed UN mechanism could operate alongside negotiations on a comprehensive deal aimed at securing lasting peace and freedom of navigation, Moreira da Silva said.
"What we are telling them is, while you continue your discussions towards a comprehensive deal, let us work, let us do our job," he said, declining to specify the exact bottlenecks to a deal as discussions continue with both sides.
Beyond the Hormuz crisis, a deteriorating situation in the Black Sea region, where cargo vessels have come under attack, and an offensive by Iran-backed Houthi militants along a key Red Sea shipping route are compounding the threat to global food security.
"What we are witnessing now is a concentration of factors," Moreira da Silva said. "Climate crisis, simultaneous disruption of maritime chokepoints on the Black Sea, on the Red Sea and on Hormuz."
(Reuters)

Putin orders seizure of Tarkett and four other European companies' Russian assets
Russian leader Vladimir Putin has signed a decree ordering the takeover of Russian assets owned by French flooring manufacturer Tarkett and four other European companies, which together generate more than RUB 50 billion (about US$596 million) in annual revenue.
Source: Russia's official legal information portal; The Moscow Times, an independent Amsterdam-based news outlet
Details: Under Putin's decree, assets belonging to French flooring manufacturer Tarkett have been transferred to the temporary management of Centre Capital Management Company.
According to the document, European owners have been forcibly stripped of 187,500 ordinary shares and 500,000 preference shares in Tarkett. The shares belonged to Tarkett's Serbian subsidiary in Bačka Palanka as well as an equivalent block of shares in Tarkett's parent company.
In addition, 100 ordinary shares in Tarkett RU and 100% of the ownership interests in Tarkett Sommer, both owned by Russian company Tarkett, have been transferred to Centre Capital.
Under the same decree, Putin ordered the seizure of assets belonging to four other European companies that had continued operating in Russia for years. The assets placed under Russian control include 12,565 shares in paper packaging manufacturer Kappa RU and the entire stakes in hygiene products maker Ontex RU, metal packaging producer Eviosys Packaging Kuban and packaging manufacturer Menshen Packaging CIS.
Tarkett is an international flooring manufacturer serving the residential, commercial, industrial and sports sectors. In its 2024 report, the company said it was the world's third-largest flooring seller and the global leader in vinyl flooring. Despite Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, it continued operating two factories in Russia, out of 34 production sites worldwide, and paying taxes to the Russian state.
According to sources in the Russian government and business community who spoke to Reuters, major European companies that chose to remain in Russia have become a tool for the Kremlin to put pressure on the EU in response to sanctions and its support for Ukraine.
"The time has come for asymmetric measures. Let them think about what measures they are taking and what sanctions they are introducing," a senior Russian government official familiar with the situation told Reuters on condition of anonymity.
Commenting on potential targets, including the Russian subsidiaries of the Italian banking group UniCredit and the Austrian banking group Raiffeisen, the Russian official openly threatened foreign investors: "Let them be scared."
Background:
- On 25 April 2023, Putin signed Decree No. 302, On the temporary management of certain assets. The document justified the forced seizure of businesses as "retaliatory measures" in response to the "confiscation" of Russian property in the US and countries that had joined it. The first companies affected were the Russian subsidiaries of energy groups Uniper and Fortum.
- In July 2023, the Kremlin used the same mechanism to seize the Russian assets of French food producer Danone and Danish brewing group Carlsberg. The businesses were subsequently transferred to entities linked to the Russian authorities.
- In September 2026, the Kremlin launched a new large-scale wave of takeovers targeting European businesses. On 17 September, Putin transferred the Russian assets of Swiss food manufacturer Nestlé, French retail chain Auchan, logistics operator FM Logistics and DIY superstore chain Lemana PRO (the new brand name for the chain formerly known in Russia as Leroy Merlin). to the temporary management of an obscure company called LEV Management.
- On 21 September, a manufacturer of plastic packaging and dispensing systems owned by French holding company Aptar Europe Holding was placed under temporary management in Russia.
- On 28 September, Putin signed a decree transferring the Russian assets of German hypermarket chain Metro to the management of UK Torg Rus, a company registered just three weeks earlier with a share capital of RUB 10,000 (about US$119).

USAFA Board Calls for Opening Part of Long-Closed Chapel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
22:02:49 UTC
07:02:49 KST

The U.S. Air Force Academy’s Board of Visitors wants the service academy to partially reopen its iconic chapel ahead of schedule next year when it sheds the “big white box” that has enclosed it through years of renovations.
The idea is one of more than a dozen recommendations the board made in its semiannual report released Oct. 15, ahead of a planned Oct. 16 meeting.
The Cadet Chapel, designed by architect Walter Netsch Jr. and opened in 1962, is a National Historic Landmark, renowned for its use of tetrahedrons and its 17 spires. But it has been closed since 2019 for repairs due to leaks and water damage. Originally expected to cost $158 million and to be completed by 2023, renovation costs more than doubled to $335 million due to asbestos removal, among other problems, and the job won’t be finished until 2028.
The chapel has been enclosed in the “the box,” as cadets call it, for seven years. Locals and alums describe the scene as an “eyesore” and President Donald Trump has decried the troubled project, saying last October, “this mess should be investigated.”
At one point, officials feared the renovations wouldn’t be complete until spring 2029. But this summer, the Air Force Civil Engineer Center announced the box would start coming down in August 2027 and be fully deconstructed by January 2028. Chaplains will be allowed back in around April 2028, and the building will fully reopen to the public in August 2028. The news was hailed by local media.
USAFA’s Board of Visitors—a congressionally mandated oversight committee—called the new timeline “highly commendable,” but the board argues more can be done.
The board is “deeply concerned that the spiritual and character development of an entire generation of future officers is being compromised by the extended renovation timeline of the Cadet Chapel,” the report states. Members want to reopen the lower level of the chapel by December 2027, even as work continues on the upper level.
A white paper attached to the report makes the case that removing “the box”is a “strategic opportunity” to give cadets at least some access to the building, reorienting the eyesore to its spiritual purpose. To make that happen, the paper argues for:
- Accelerating the removal of the box by one month
- Prioritizing repairs and renovations for the lower level
- Creating “safe and isolated” access points for cadets to enter and exit the lower level
- Updating any legal and administrative frameworks to support the effort
The lower level of the building hosts Catholic and Jewish chapels, while the upper level has a Protestant chapel. The white paper argues that the lower chapels “can be dynamically time-shared” while the upper chapel is finished to “provide an immediate, centralized home for worship for all faith groups across the cadet wing.”
Assignments and Accreditation
Other Board of Visitors’ recommendations touch on USAFA’s role as an academic institution. One recommendation calls for the Air Force to “elevate the value” of an officer assignment to USAFA as a “career-enhancing duty” for Air Force and Space Force officers.
“While the Board fundamentally considers instructing and working at USAFA to be a premier developmental assignment, Career Field Managers are often reluctant to promote this duty,” the board report states. “Most positions at USAFA are not career-field-specific and therefore CFMs must ‘release’ officers to perform these duties. Career field management teams frequently view these releases as a ‘tax’ and perceive them negatively, as the individual is temporarily leaving their primary specialty.”
The issue is common to special duties such as recruiting, which also takes Airmen and Guardians out of their career field. To overcome the problem, the board wants the academy and Air Force Personnel Center to incentivize Academy duty by rewarding personnel who take USAFA assignments. They also recommend the Air Force examine promotion rates for officers who served as instructors to see whether the assignments improve or hurt career advancement.
More than 2,000 Airmen and Guardians work at USAFA, in jobs ranging from faculty to administration and support roles. In recent times, the number of uniformed faculty has grown as more military instructors have arrived in the wake of a rash of departures by civilian staff spurred by cuts to the federal workforce.
The exodus of civilian staff last year led one alumnus to file a complaint with the Higher Learning Commission, the academy’s accrediting institution. The complaint was settled without affecting the school’s accreditation. Meanwhile, the board report is calling for USAFA to sever its relationship with the HLC and instead join the other service academies and the Air Force’s other degree-granting institutions—including the Air Force Institute of Technology and Air University—to band together under a single accreditor.
A board working group favor joining the new Commission for Public Higher Education, founded by six states’ public university systems whose political leaders argue the new commission is needed to combat liberal bias and burdensome bureaucracy among current accreditors. The working group says CPHE “guarantees an apolitical baseline and alignment with requirements specific to the military education system.”
Previous Recommendations
The Board of Visitors is chaired Rep. August Pfluger (R-Texas), a former by former F-22 pilot and academy alumnus. The boarfd’s previous report, released in February, called for the academy to grow its cadet wing by 10 percent and build a new “tri-complex” of buildings to house a new “Air, Space, and Cyber Education Center,” including a new “home” base for the U.S. Space Force.
The bulk of the recommendations in that February report remain open, awaiting action from Congress. Decisions could come in the 2027 National Defense Authorization bill, but the measure remains stalled and will not be resolved until after the midterm elections.

Family genetics study questions the role of genetic nurture in ADHD
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
22:00:31 UTC
07:00:31 KST

A large study of families suggests that a child’s overall attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder traits are primarily driven by their own genetics by mid-childhood, rather than by the indirect environmental influence of their parents’ genes. Researchers found a lack of evidence for parental genetic nurture effects at both age five and age eight, though they note that statistical limitations might obscure more subtle influences. The research was published in Behavior Genetics.
Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder, or ADHD, is a neurodevelopmental condition involving patterns of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity. Decades of twin studies indicate that ADHD is highly heritable. This means a child’s own DNA plays a major role in whether they develop these behavioral traits.
However, genetic and environmental factors do not operate in isolation. In recent years, scientists have focused on how an individual’s traits might be shaped by the genes of the people around them. Because biological parents provide both their children’s DNA and their rearing environment, it is notoriously difficult to separate nature from nurture.
When parents’ genes influence their child’s environment, this process is known as an indirect genetic effect, or genetic nurture. For instance, a parent’s genetic makeup might influence their patience, parenting style, or the general household environment they create. This environment then affects the child’s development, meaning the parent’s genes have shaped the child’s traits from the outside in.
When indirect genetic effects are not accounted for, researchers risk overestimating the direct impact of a child’s own DNA. To better understand the origins of ADHD traits, researchers set out to untangle these direct and indirect genetic influences. Daniel L. Wechsler, a researcher at King’s College London, led a team to investigate whether parents’ genetic profiles exert indirect effects on a child’s ADHD traits over and above the child’s own direct genetic risks.
The researchers also wanted to see how these influences might shift as children grow. Previous research has explored these dynamics for specific traits like hyperactivity at single time points. The current project instead focused on overall ADHD scores across two distinct developmental stages, early and mid-childhood.
Wechsler and his colleagues utilized data from the Norwegian Mother, Father and Child Cohort Study, a population-based registry. They analyzed genetic data from mother, father, and child trios alongside survey data. The questionnaires asked parents to rate the frequency of specific behaviors, such as difficulty paying attention to tasks or acting without thinking.
A method called trio genome-wide complex trait analysis was used to examine around a million genetic variations across all three family members. These genetic variations, known as single-nucleotide polymorphisms, are tiny changes in the genetic code that can influence various physical and behavioral traits. Humans share the vast majority of their DNA, but these small variations make each person unique.
Unlike some genetic approaches that only look at specific genes tied to a known condition, this method captures the cumulative influence of all measured genetic variations. By modeling the genetic data from the whole family at once, the researchers could estimate the child’s direct genetic effects alongside the cumulative indirect environmental effects of both parents’ genes.
The first analysis focused on a large study sample of 12,374 family trios when the children were five years old. The initial statistical models at this age suggested that maternal indirect genetic effects accounted for nearly five percent of the variation in children’s ADHD traits. At the same time, the child’s direct genetic effects appeared to account for less than two percent.
However, when the researchers tested these findings against more stringent statistical models, the results failed to hold up. The model comparisons ultimately favored a scenario in which neither direct nor indirect genetic effects were present at age five. Large margins of error in the data prevented the team from confirming specific genetic effects at this age.
This lack of measurable direct genetic influence at early childhood was unexpected. ADHD is widely recognized as highly heritable, even in young children. The researchers suggested that ADHD traits might not fully manifest in a measurable way for many children by age five.
Alternatively, it is possible that children’s individual genetic propensities simply account for more variation in their behavior as they grow older. This pattern has been observed in other developmental traits, where the influence of a child’s own genetics becomes more apparent over time. In previous research utilizing an even larger sample of the same cohort, scientists found evidence for direct genetic effects on specific traits like hyperactivity and inattention as early as age three.
Next, the team conducted a similar analysis on an overlapping large study sample of 12,714 family trios when the children were eight years old. The preliminary models for this mid-childhood stage showed increased genetic influence overall. These early estimates pointed to roughly equal contributions, with the child’s own genes and the mother’s indirect genetic effects each accounting for about eight percent of the variation.
Once again, the researchers applied rigorous model comparisons to see which scenario best fit the data. At age eight, the most accurate model indicated that the child’s direct genetics played a role in their ADHD traits. This model, however, showed no evidence of indirect genetic effects from either parent.
Across both age groups, the team found no robust evidence that a mother or father’s genetic profile indirectly influences a child’s overall ADHD traits through the environment. The results at age eight suggest that a child’s own DNA is the primary biological driver of their overall ADHD traits by mid-childhood.
While the results appear to rule out genetic nurture for total ADHD traits, the researchers caution against drawing absolute conclusions. The statistical models were hampered by large margins of error, meaning the results were not statistically significant enough to firmly distinguish direct from indirect effects in the more complicated models. The study might simply have lacked the mathematical power to detect subtle indirect influences.
The decision to analyze total ADHD scores rather than breaking them down into specific categories might have also obscured important details. Past studies have successfully detected indirect genetic effects on specific behaviors like hyperactivity and inattention. This suggests that genetic nurture might operate on certain specific behaviors rather than the overarching condition.
Another limitation is that the survey data relied solely on the mothers’ assessments of their children. Mothers’ ratings could be influenced by their own perceptions or biases based on their specific interactions with the children. Utilizing teacher reports or formal clinical diagnoses could provide a more rounded perspective in future investigations.
Additionally, the genetic data came exclusively from families of European ancestry. This demographic focus limits how well the findings might apply to more diverse populations worldwide. Future research could benefit from even more massive study samples across diverse demographics to better separate these intertwined genetic signals.
The study, “Direct and Indirect Genetic Effects on Child ADHD Traits in Early and Mid-Childhood: Trio Genome-Wide Complex Trait Analyses in a Large Norwegian Birth Registry Cohort,” was authored by Daniel L. Wechsler, Espen M. Eilertsen, Yasmin I. Ahmadzadeh, Rosa Cheesman, Nicoletta Adamo, Laurie J. Hannigan, Eivind Ystrom, and Tom A. McAdams. Their work adds new context to the ongoing scientific effort to untangle the developmental roots of behavioral traits.

The China decoupling paradox: why the world still needs its manufacturing machine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
22:00:15 UTC
07:00:15 KST

In FocusThe China decoupling paradox: why the world still needs its manufacturing machine
Chinese parts, machinery and know-how remain deeply embedded in countries seeking to build manufacturing industries of their own
Talk of global decoupling from China has persisted for years, as has speculation that emerging economies such as India and Vietnam could soon replace it as the “world’s factory”.
But for Indian hardware engineer Neeraj Arora, the growth of India’s electronics manufacturing industry has not eliminated the need to source components from China. Instead, it has changed the nature of those imports.
A decade ago, Arora imported finished phone chargers from the world’s second-largest economy. Today, more of these products can be made in India, even as manufacturers there still rely on Chinese parts for assembly.
“They don’t have a single industry; they have created an ecosystem,” said Arora, who has travelled repeatedly to Shenzhen, Dongguan and Guangzhou – southern China’s manufacturing hubs that offer a wide range of competitively priced parts, from power-switching transistors to charging chips.

Israel halts commercial goods from entering Gaza; Hamas denies tax claims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
21:57:58 UTC
06:57:58 KST

Israel halts commercial goods from entering Gaza; Hamas denies tax claims
The halt to commercial shipments, including fruit and winter clothing, cuts off a key source of critical supplies.
Israeli authorities say no commercial goods have entered Gaza for two days, citing what they claim is a tax dispute between local merchants and Hamas.
COGAT, or the Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories, the Israeli military body that “oversees humanitarian affairs” in Gaza, announced the halt on Wednesday.
COGAT claimed that local merchants “made the decision in response to a 10,000 shekel ($3,220) fee imposed by Hamas on each truck entering Gaza” as well as a demand for 30 percent of all sales in Gaza to be carried out in cash.
This decision is expected to impact a crucial source of food and goods for the 2.1 million people in the Strip, who are completely reliant on Israel’s border crossings in a territory that is still suffering from famine.
Gaza’s government media office refuted the claims on Thursday and condemned the “blatant disinformation campaign and false statement”.
The media office instead said it was an attempt “to hold the government apparatus in Gaza responsible for the disruption of truck entry” and that the fee was a voluntary payment to a fund providing aid for those in need, such as widows and orphans.
It also said that cash payments were encouraged due to what it described as an acute cash shortage in the war-torn territory, but were never a mandatory requirement.
An already dire humanitarian crisis
The halt to commercial shipments, including fruit and winter clothing, cuts off a key source of food and other critical supplies as fears mount ahead of the encroaching winter.
Aid groups generally bring in staples such as flour, while merchants import more perishable foods like fruits and meat, according to data released earlier this year by COGAT.
The suspension is raising fears about affordability, with humanitarian workers saying a combination of aid and a robust commercial market is needed to keep prices under control.
“The humanitarian sector on its own cannot meet the needs of all the people,” said Shaina Low, a spokesperson for the Norwegian Refugee Council. “The markets need to be functioning.”
Local merchants step in
The head of Gaza’s private truckers union, Nahed Sheheiber, denied the Israeli narrative, saying: “The Israeli coordinator is claiming that Gaza’s merchants are responsible, but the truth is that the Israelis are the ones who imposed the restrictions.”
Following COGAT’s announcement, Sheheiber’s union met with Gaza’s Ministry of Economy to express concern and say Israel was citing fees levied by the ministry as a pretext to cut off commercial goods.
A global hunger monitor in July warned that more than two-thirds of people in Gaza could face acute hunger by the year-end.
Israel is obliged under a US-mediated agreement to allow a minimum of 600 trucks carrying humanitarian aid to enter Gaza each day.
Diplomats say that far fewer than 600 trucks normally enter Gaza each day. Sheheiber said the figure was closer to 300, with two-thirds carrying commercial goods.

U.S. sues California in fight over checking citizenship of mail voters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
21:24:57 UTC
06:24:57 KST

The federal government sued the state of California on Thursday in an escalating battle over how to prevent non-U.S. citizens from voting by mail in federal elections.
The lawsuit is the latest action by the Department of Justice targeting state administration of elections, which President Donald Trump has often criticized as susceptible to fraud and voting by noncitizens.
The civil complaint, which the DOJ had threatened to file, asks a judge to prevent California officials from tabulating mail-in ballots "from likely non-citizens in the upcoming federal election until the voter's citizenship status can be determined."
The Department of Justice asks that a judge order the state to set aside mail ballots from voters "identified by the Federal Government likely to be noncitizens," and to verify their citizenship status before their ballot is counted.
Non-citizens are barred from voting in federal elections.
California Gov. Gavin Newsom, in a post on X on Wednesday, said, in anticipation of the suit, "More dangerous nonsense from a President losing his grip on reality."
"Trump is now demanding that California election officials VIOLATE federal law," Newsom wrote. "Apparently, the rule of law only matters when it's convenient for MAGA's dear leader. California's elections are NOT Donald Trump's to control. We will ensure EVERY California voter can participate in a free and fair election.
The suit in U.S. District Court in Los Angeles came two days after acting U.S. Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter, in a letter to California Secretary of State Shirley Weber, gave the state 48 hours to determine whether any U.S. citizens were on a list of people the DOJ believes are likely noncitizens who were sent ballots for the Nov. 3 election.
The DOJ previously gave officials in Los Angeles County a thumb drive containing the questioned names to officials in Los Angeles County.
McCotter told Weber the state needed to tell local election officials to segregate mail ballots until the citizenship status of their voters could be determined, and not send a ballot to anyone who had not yet received one.
"If you cannot implement this process by then, given the ongoing federal election, the United States will have no choice but to seek emergency relief," McCotter said in his letter.
Weber's office, in a statement on Thursday, said, "In July of this year, President Trump and DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullen made (still) unsubstantiated claims that California had 190,000 non-citizens on its voter rolls."
"Given the many high-profile examples of states purging US citizens from their voter rolls based on DHS/SAVE data, SOS immediately requested written information about their methodology and data sources to back up their claims," Weber's office said. "They refused and provided California with nothing."
"Now the USDOJ, under threat of 'emergency' litigation, demands that California blindly trust this administration without any evidence or legal authority to justify its request."
Weber, in a statement Thursday, said the DOJ's "relentless efforts to unlawfully gain access to states' protected voter data and purge voter rolls serve only to cause chaos and fuel public distrust in our elections."
She also said that California "has robust state law requirements that only U.S. citizens can register to vote and that any non-eligible registrants are removed from the State's voter rolls."
"My office and California election officials remain committed – as always – to ensuring a fair and smooth 2026 General Election," Weber said.
Weber's office declined to comment on the lawsuit Thursday, but pointed to a letter she had sent McCotter in response to his letter.
Weber, in her letter, said, "California's election administration will continue to be governed by applicable federal and state law, not by unsubstantiated claims and outrageous demands."
She said that "despite failing to send the list of alleged non-citizens to my office, you demand that we request transmittal of the list, review and confirm the citizenship status of each of the approximately 20,000 individuals on the list on the eve of an election and within a mere 48 hours."
"This is an emergency of the DOJ's creation," Weber said.

F-35 Drops 8 Bombs in Quick Succession During ‘Ripple’ Test
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
21:17:47 UTC
06:17:47 KST

The Marine Corps recently conducted its first-ever “ripple” release of eight Small Diameter Bomb IIs from an F-35B, a key early step in proving out the capability for all F-35 variants.
A “ripple release” refers to munitions all being released in one pass instead of multiple go-arounds. Marine aviators from the Marine Operational Test and Evaluation Squadron 1 at Yuma Proving Ground, Ariz., conducted the test Sept. 15, retired Air Force Maj. Gen. Jon Norman, Raytheon’s vice president for air and space systems, told Air & Space Forces Magazine.
SDB II, also called “StormBreaker,” is a 250-pound, low-yield, precision-guided munition that can hit moving targets in all weather conditions at ranges of at least 46 miles. It is a joint effort between the Air Force and Department of the Navy and is built by RTX’s Raytheon.
While software and other issues have delayed fielding StormBreaker on the F-35, the “ripple” capability could be critical to the Lockheed Martin-made stealthy fighter down the line, Norman argued.
“From a pilot perspective, it’s nice because you’re not sitting there exposing yourself when you have eight targets to address,” he said.
It also eliminates the need to do hands-on weaponeering for each bomb.
“You address the entire target set, so it’s less workload in the cockpit, and you’re able to achieve an effect that I think the pilots are really going to appreciate,” Norman said.
The networked missiles can also be confined to a defined kill box to ensure they strike only a specific area on the battlefield.
“We’re able to set boundaries,” Norman said. “So, you give it a kill box, and it’ll exclude everything outside of that and only hit within that kill box.”
That’s a key upgrade for the StormBreaker compared to what the bomb is replacing—cluster munitions. SDB II was developed to give pilots an option to replace legacy-era cluster munitions following the 2008 DOD policy directive, which set a 2019 deadline to stop using the area-saturation weapons that had high failure rates and could produce swaths of unexploded ordnance on battlefields.
So, a pilot could spot a boat swarm, quickly set the parameters, and then launch eight 250-pound missiles to destroy the mini-fleet in one pass, Norman said.
“Through automated target recognition software that’s built into it, we can hit prioritized threats,” Norman said. “So, if one fails or one gets shot down, then they just reorder the prioritization.”
F-35 Tests
Low-rate initial production on the StormBreaker started in 2015, and the Air Force cleared the bomb to go on its “objective” aircraft, the F-15E, in 2020. But the service hopes to integrate the munition onto many more platforms, including the F-35A. The Navy, meanwhile, cleared the SDB II to go on its F/A-18E/F this February, though its objective aircraft remains the F-35B and C.
But while the F-15 and F/A-18 carry the StormBreaker externally, the F-35 uses its internal weapons bays to maintain stealthiness, offering a new wrinkle to the ripple release process. The F-35B has the smallest internal capacity of the variants, to accommodate the fan that enables vertical landings.
The next ripple release test is planned for this quarter over a small range in Texas, Norman said.
“We’ll take those results then to the Air Force and to the Navy and the Marines and say, “we’ve demonstrated this capability, is this something you’re interested in?’” Norman told Air & Space Forces Magazine.
Future tests could include striking moving targets at sea with multiple munitions, Norman said—a particularly relevant capability, given reports of swarming boat attacks by the Iranian military in the Strait of Hormuz.
As Raytheon works on refining the “ripple eight” capability for operational use, the F-35 fleet is awaiting rolling software patches to fully incorporate the StormBreaker into its arsenal.
A July report from the Government Accountability Office noted that “SDB II initial capability on the F-35 is delayed 2 years, and program officials said that it might be delayed 2 more years due to F-35 software development issues.”
The F-35 fleet has undergone its third technology refresh, or TR-3, which upgraded the L3Harris core processor, replaced the aircraft’s memory storage unit, and installed multicore processors. But while a “truncated” version of TR-3 was completed in 2025, the fleet is still getting software patches to continue upgrades.
“Development on TR-3 was completed in 2025,” Lockheed Martin spokesperson Mireya Villarreal told Air & Space Forces Magazine in an email. “We continue to build on this baseline through the Block 4 modernization program, which implements upgrades including additional weapons, electronic warfare capabilities and improved sensor technology to ensure the warfighter can defeat any threat.”
StormBreaker’s Future
in addition to the ripple release test, Norman said Raytheon is working to extend the StormBreaker’s 46-mile range by exploring engine efficiencies and design work on the bomb’s body.
“We don’t want to constrain pilots,” Norman said. “We want to give them their full operating envelope to be able to release this.”
At the program’s inception, the Pentagon planned to acquire 21,160 StormBreakers, but that figure has now risen to 31,800, according to the GAO report
“Last year we produced and delivered 1,500 StormBreakers. This year we’re increasing that,” Norman said. He could not provide specific numbers for this year’s deliveries.
“But it’s a significant increase, and we have capacity in the factory to increase more,” he said.

Congo Ebola outbreak spreads to new province bordering Central African Republic

Congo Ebola outbreak spreads to new province bordering Central African Republic
DAKAR, Senegal – The ongoing Ebola outbreak in Democratic Republic of Congo has spread to a new province bordering Central African Republic, two health officials said on Oct 15, posing a fresh challenge for authorities struggling to contain it.
North Ubangi becomes the eighth province to be affected by the outbreak of the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which was announced in mid-May and has become the second-largest Ebola outbreak on record, with more than 9,000 cases and more than 4,000 deaths confirmed.
Two cases have been confirmed in North Ubangi, the officials said. They have not been officially announced by the Congolese authorities.
Ituri province remains the epicentre of the outbreak though cases have increased recently in North Kivu province. Cases have also been confirmed in South Kivu, Tshopo, Haut-Uele, Bas-Uele and South Ubangi provinces.
A health official in North Ubangi told Reuters on Oct 15 there had been a series of suspect deaths recently in a mining area in Wapinda health zone, close to the border with Bas-Uele, prompting samples to be analysed at a provincial laboratory and in Kinshasa.
In addition to spreading within Congo, the outbreak has also resulted in cases in Uganda, which was declared Ebola-free in August, and in Kenya, which announced its first Ebola infection earlier in October and announced a second case - a close family member of the first one – on Oct 14. REUTERS

Iraq parliament fills Cabinet posts, naming a US-sanctioned deputy prime minister
Unknown

Breadcrumb
Iraq parliament fills Cabinet posts, naming a US-sanctioned deputy prime minister
Iraq's parliament voted Thursday to appoint ministers to previously vacant Cabinet posts and complete the country's government - including a deputy prime minister who is under S sanctions.
Laith al-Khazali, appointed to that post, is the brother of Qais al-Khazali, leader of the Iran-backed Asaib Ahl al-Haq militia. Laith al-Khazali was arrested by US forces in 2007 over allegations related to an attack targeting American forces in Karbala in January of that year, which resulted in the deaths of five US soldiers.
He was released from US custody in June 2009. In 2019, the US Treasury Department imposed sanctions on him, citing his leadership role in Asaib Ahl al-Haq and allegations involving human rights abuses as well as the 2007 attack.
His appointment to a senior government position raises questions about its potential implications for relations between Baghdad and Washington. Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi was backed by US President Donald Trump when he took the post and has strong relations with Washington, but he has also sought to maintain relations with Iran.
Past Iraqi governments have also sought to balance relations with Washington and Tehran, but the balancing act has become more difficult since the US and Iran went to war on Feb. 28.
There was no immediate official statement from the US on the appointment.
Republican US Rep. Joe Wilson wrote on X that al Khazali “is a designated terrorist and Iranian puppet whose militia AAH killed Americans and Iraqis.”
“He is no better than ISIS, maybe even worse,” Wilson said. "It is outrageous but sadly not shocking that he has been appointed deputy PM of Iraq.”
The parliament also appointed two other deputy prime ministers, as well as a new interior minister, defense minister, planning minister, minister of higher education and scientific research, and culture minister.
The other Cabinet posts had been appointed five months earlier.
Al-Zaidi said in a statement that with the vacant posts filled, “we are embarking on a phase of accelerated, diligent work” and pledged to "move forward in implementing our government’s priorities and program, and in fulfilling the aspirations of all Iraqis.”
He said the government had worked over the past several months amid complicated domestic and international circumstances, noting that the war in the region had imposed exceptional economic challenges on Iraq, in addition to security challenges.
Al-Zaidi has vowed to fight corruption and strengthen Iraq's sovereignty, both by completing the withdrawal of US forces from the country and by disarming non-state armed groups.
Some of the most powerful militias have said they have no intention of giving up their weapons, although Asaib Ahl al-Haq is one of a handful that have agreed to hand over their arms.
(The Associated Press)

Ukraine Accuses Captured Russian Soldier of Executing Five Unarmed Troops, Killing Civilian
Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU) has charged a captured Russian soldier with killing five unarmed Ukrainian servicemen and a civilian, according to the Security Service of Ukraine on October 15.
The suspect was identified as 36-year-old St. Petersburg resident Leonid Ryzhikov, call sign “Yula.” He served in the 2nd Battalion of Russia’s 1009th Motorized Rifle Regiment, part of the 68th Motorized Rifle Division.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The SBU stated that Ryzhikov fled Russian positions near Starytsia in the Kharkiv region after coming under Ukrainian fire on October 5-6. Armed with an AK-74, he moved toward Kharkiv on foot and stole civilian clothing from an abandoned house.
Investigators allege that on October 13, Ryzhikov shot and killed a 60-year-old civilian fishing near Mykhailivka before pushing his body into the water. Later that day, he allegedly entered a house in Momotove and killed five Ukrainian servicemen who were unarmed and wearing civilian clothes. Some were asleep at the time.
The SBU noted that the five servicemen were not participating in hostilities at the time and were protected under the Geneva Convention. Ryzhikov allegedly hid his rifle near a gardening community and continued toward Kharkiv while concealing himself in forest belts.
The SBU, National Police, and National Guard detained Ryzhikov in Kharkiv’s Saltivskyi district on October 14 and recovered his AK-74. He was charged under Article 438 of Ukraine’s Criminal Code for war crimes resulting in deaths and faces life imprisonment.
Violence by Russian servicemen in the Kharkiv region has also turned inward.
On October 25, 2025, Alexey Korolev, a soldier recruited from prison after seven criminal convictions, allegedly shot dead six fellow troops and wounded two others near Lyman Pershyi during Russia's offensive around Kupiansk.
Among the dead was a specialist from the FSB's highly classified 16th Center, a unit focused on signals intelligence and cyber espionage. Korolev now faces murder and extortion charges in a closed-door military court in temporarily occupied Donetsk.
