Ahead of US midterms, voters are frustrated with Trump, want change: Poll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
18:17:57 UTC
03:17:57 KST

Ahead of US midterms, voters are frustrated with Trump, want change: Poll
Widespread voter disillusionment and pocketbook anxieties set a volatile stage for the GOP weeks before election night.
Voter sentiment across the United States is increasingly negative towards US President Donald Trump’s domestic and foreign policies, according to a new Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll.
In the closing weeks before the November 3 US congressional midterm elections, 80 percent of Americans polled said the country needs substantial change or “complete and total upheaval” in how it is run, according to the survey of over 1,100 US adults released on Thursday.
Democrats and independents are much more likely than Republicans to want a total overhaul of the country’s direction, the survey found, but even Republican voters are still looking for some change. Slightly fewer than half, 45 percent, want substantial change, while 13 percent are seeking upheaval.
The results point to a pervasive appetite for legislative realignment that poses a risk to the Republican Party’s power as it looks to keep control of both houses of the US Congress.
Fuelled by soaring living costs, everyday economics is driving a majority of the electorate, with 85 percent of respondents saying the economy is one of the most significant issues in weighing their vote in the upcoming election. About eight in 10 registered voters disapprove of how Trump is handling the cost of living, and about three-quarters disapprove of his performance on the economy.
Only about one-third of registered voters overall have a “very” or “somewhat” favourable view of the Republican president, and a similar share approve of his performance as president.
More voters want Democrats to win control of Congress and have a more negative view of Republicans.
Immigration and crime rates are also top concerns for some voters, according to the survey results, with 45 percent of voters identifying them as top priorities, though the two issues are prioritised disproportionately by Republican voters who reference them more frequently than Democrats. Conversely, Democratic voters are more prone to name healthcare as their top priority.
Emerging cultural and technological concerns drew less immediate alarm across the board: 35 percent of voters ranked artificial intelligence as a substantial issue, while transgender issues sit significantly lower at 12 percent.
Healthcare is also considered a top issue for 69 percent of voters, while 64 percent cite the war on Iran as top-of-mind.
Despite their grievances, a majority of voters across both major American parties still value civic engagement.
About two-thirds of registered voters in the survey say it’s “extremely” important to vote in the upcoming election, while about two in 10 say it’s “very” important. Seventy-five percent of Democratic voters view it as “extremely” important, compared to roughly 60 percent of Republican respondents.

Why Data Centers Have Become Military Targets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
18:17:04 UTC
03:17:04 KST

When the U.S. and Israel launched attacks against Iran earlier this year, Tehran responded by striking energy infrastructure across the Gulf. The result was a severe shock to global energy markets that continues to this day. Less publicized at the time were its strikes on another kind of infrastructure: data centers.
Similar attacks have since taken place in Russia and Ukraine, where both sides have been trading tit-for-tat strikes on data centers.
Experts say these attacks represent a new front in warfare, in which facilities powering the technology behind many critical industries have become military targets.
The AI boom has led to a surge in demand for computing power, data storage and cloud services, making the data centers that provide them a crucial part of modern infrastructure. A mass of data center construction is currently underway in the U.S., and tech companies are investing hundreds of billions of dollars a year to meet AI demand. Telecommunications companies, banks, hospitals and energy suppliers all rely on them.
“Data centers are now on the critical path for modern digital infrastructure,” Kirk Cameron, founding director of the Institute for Advanced Computing at Virginia Tech, tells TIME. “The loss of key data centers could collapse economies, disrupt public and private transportation with loss of GPS, and affect government essential services for health, emergency dispatch, and power grids.”
Military use of AI for targeting and information processing has made data centers crucial to fighting a war. Ukraine uses AI for an array of battlefield functions such as drone targeting, battle planning, and missile analyzing Russian missile attacks. U.S. tech companies such as Palantir now work closely with Ukraine’s military to develop new AI-powered weaponry, taking advantage of the ability to immediately test their technology on the battlefield. The U.S. military also uses Palantir’s Maven system to help identify targets for strikes.
“Data centers are competitive advantages in warfare,” Cameron says. “Knocking out capabilities means potentially crippling combat operations for an adversary. It’s also a form of economic warfare and could lead to longer-term competitive challenges for the target.”
Where have data centers been attacked?
The first wave of attacks on data centers was carried out in March this year by Iran, when it launched strikes on two Amazon facilities in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and another in Bahrain was damaged by a nearby drone strike.
Those facilities have been mostly offline ever since; Amazon said on Sept. 15 that it had been “unable to restore access to the resources and data” hosted in those two regions.
Russian attacks on Ukrainian data centers in late September disrupted television broadcasts and internet access. Russia’s Defense Ministry said it was striking data centers because they “process and transmit intelligence data for the Ukrainian Armed Forces.”
Ukraine’s response began on Oct. 8, and it has since carried out drone strikes on three data centers belonging to tech giant Yandex, often called Russia’s version of Google. The first site hit, in Sasovo, houses two of the three supercomputers Yandex uses to develop its AI models, Meduza reported, and the outage disrupted several companies relying on Yandex’s cloud services, including Russian Railways, MegaFon, T-Bank, and several media outlets.
Following the first strike, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky defended the retaliation: "We always respond in kind. You all know that they are hitting and hitting our data centers; we responded to them.”
How have tech companies responded?
The spate of attacks over the last year has already caused tech companies to rethink how and where they build data centers.
The United Arab Emirates is reportedly revising plans for a 5-gigawatt AI data center project following the Iranian strikes. The original plan envisioned a 10-square-mile campus in Abu Dhabi, to be built in partnership with American tech companies like Oracle, Nvidia, and Cisco. Now the data centers will likely be spread out across the UAE, according to officials who spoke to Reuters.
Emily Harding, director of the Intelligence, National Security, and Technology Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, believes that data centers have become a new frontline in warfare—and that may require new strategies.
“If you’re Russia and you attack a Microsoft data center, is that an attack on Ukraine? Is that an attack on Microsoft? Is that an attack on a U.S. company and, by extension, the U.S.?” she asks.
The U.S. has largely followed a policy that attacks on American companies do not constitute an attack on the United States, but Harding says the government may need to decide on a new approach “that creates deterrence not just to protect life and health, but also data.”
And while the threat to data centers in the U.S. may be relatively low compared to the Gulf and Ukraine or Russia, tech companies will also have to think more about the security of their facilities when building, while trying to keep pace with massive demand.
“The knock-on effect is that the companies that own the data centers are realizing they can't protect them, and that kind of calls into question the cloud model in general,” Harding says. “They're having to make big adjustments. You could see a time in the future where Amazon starts losing business to Microsoft because Microsoft does a better job of hiding where their data centers are.”

Clean Energy Must Avoid the Mistake of Overdependence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
18:17:00 UTC
03:17:00 KST

For decades, energy security has meant oil. Countries worried about their dependence on the Middle East and Russia, the security of shipping lanes, and the geopolitical consequences of relying on a small number of producers for the oil that powered global economies. The transition to renewable energy was supposed to rebalance that equation. Yet in doing so, we may be creating a potentially greater vulnerability, since the clean energy supply chain is dominated by China.
Take Europe as an example. The year before Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Russia supplied 45 percent of the EU’s natural gas imports. The war has forced European countries to scramble for new energy sources.
The war in the Middle East showed again how quickly concentrated energy supplies can become an economic liability. Roughly one-fifth of global oil consumption passes through the Strait of Hormuz – or did, before the strait was effectively closed by the conflict.
Clean energy can reduce exposure to these specific chokepoints, but the world must diversify its energy dependence without simply relocating it.
China leads in the industries powering the next phase of the global economy. It is the world’s largest supplier and exporter of green technology. In July 2026, China’s green energy exports rose 51 percent year-on-year, with new energy vehicles rising an astonishing 90 percent.
China dominates the clean energy value chain. Today, the country provides roughly 85 percent of global solar production capacity and 80 percent of lithium-ion batteries. This is essentially a monopoly. In electric vehicles, China accounted for almost three-quarters of global production in 2025.
Its control also extends upstream. China holds critical positions in processing and refining the minerals essential to new energy technologies, from batteries to electric motors and wind turbines. It also possesses much of the manufacturing expertise – and increasingly the equipment – needed to turn those materials into finished products.
Therefore, clean energy dependence extends across an entire industrial ecosystem – from processing through technology, components and manufacturing equipment to the finished product. A disruption at any point in the supply chain could reverberate through the entire system.
The International Energy Agency (IEA) estimated that each month of a halt in Chinese battery supply chain exports could reduce output from EV factories elsewhere by some $17 billion, with more than half of those losses occurring in Europe.
The risk is not hypothetical. China’s use of export controls on rare earths and other critical materials has demonstrated how concentrated supply chains translate into strategic leverage. China mines roughly 60 percent of the world’s rare earths but produces about 90 percent of its rare earth permanent magnets, leaving downstream manufacturers with few immediate alternatives.
Oil reserves are fixed by geology, while China’s dominance in clean technology is the product of industrial policy, capital investment, and accumulated manufacturing expertise. That should, in theory, make clean energy dependence more reversible. In practice, however, diversification is difficult.
A critical part of China’s advantage is manufacturing efficiency. The IEA attributed more than 40 percent of China’s battery cost edge over Europe to automation and efficiency. In critical mineral mining and refining, China’s position also rests on decades of accumulated processing capacity and a willingness to bear environmental costs that many other countries have been reluctant to accept. None of this can be replicated quickly.
China’s enormous investment and innovation in clean technology has helped drive down costs and accelerate deployment. Attempting to exclude China entirely would make the energy transition slower and more expensive. Interdependence is not the problem, and energy security has never required producing everything at home. It requires enough diversity that no single supplier can disrupt the system.
As with trade, the answer is not decoupling but diversification.
Countries should identify where domestic capacity is strategically necessary, build alternative sources of supply with allies and emerging markets, and continue trading and investing with China where it makes economic sense.
It can be done, but it takes time, capital, and political will. Las Vegas-based MP Materials operates North America’s only rare earth mine of scale, producing more than 10 percent of global rare earth supply. The company is building heavy rare earth processing capacity and investing more than $1.25 billion in a magnet manufacturing campus. Importantly, its strategy is becoming international: in 2025, MP Materials, the U.S. government, and Saudi Arabia’s Maaden agreed to develop a Saudi rare earth refinery to supply rare earth oxides to U.S., Saudi, and allied manufacturers.
This one refinery is not, on its own, a solution, but it points to the kind of allied, government-supported investment in processing that rebalancing requires.
While the world will remain dependent upon fossil fuels for the foreseeable future, the diversification to clean energy will continue, and the stakes will rise as demand grows. The world should not spend decades reducing its dependence on Middle Eastern and Russian hydrocarbons only to discover that it has exchanged one form of strategic dependence for another – this time on China.

PM Carney urges Canadian unity ahead of Alberta secession vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
17:46:00 UTC
02:46:00 KST

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney made a push for national unity in oil-rich Alberta on Thursday as the province prepared to vote on whether to pursue a binding referendum on independence from Canada.
Polling indicates less than a quarter of Alberta's roughly five million people want to break away from Canada, but Carney, who grew up in the western province, said: "polls don't vote."
"We need people to show up and vote and stand up for Alberta, stand up for Canada," he said during a television interview in Calgary.
Speaking later with local business leaders, Carney said he couldn't think of a "worse time to have a referendum," citing a "more dangerously divided world" and friction with the United States.
Alberta's right-wing Premier Danielle Smith says she is against independence but called Monday's non-binding vote to settle a divisive issue.
If a majority votes for independence, she has committed to launching a legally binding separation process. If a majority votes to stay, Smith says she won't approve another referendum.
Mitch Sylvestre, who heads the Alberta Prosperity Project, a prominent separatist organization, told AFP his side might "actually win this referendum."
"I would be very surprised if we got less than 40%," he said in an interview on Tuesday.
Carney has put Alberta's oil industry at the center of his plans to solidify Canada's economy and reduce dependence on the United States, warning close economic ties have been permanently fractured by President Donald Trump.
Carney has backed a new pipeline and other projects to increase crude production, marking a clear break from his predecessor, Justin Trudeau, who was broadly reviled in Alberta over allegations he stifled oil industry growth in favor of environmental policies.
Carney has repeatedly cited the proposed pipeline to argue for Alberta's future prosperity within a united Canada.
Alberta separatists voice familiar conservative frustrations, from concerns about immigration levels to generalized fears about fraying individual liberty, but their grievances often hinge on oil industry management.
Smith told the CBC that Alberta separatists stepped up mobilization because Trudeau, who left office last year, was "actively trying to kill" the oil industry.
Oil's dominance in separatist discussion makes Alberta "mostly an outlier," said Syracuse University professor Ryan Griffiths, an expert on global secessionist groups.
Secessionist movements regularly have "economic motivations," but typically those are married to a linguistic or nationalist component, Griffiths said.
"There's no magic line" dictating what defines a nation, he told AFP, but noted Alberta's case for nationhood appears harder to make than that of other groups, like Catalans, Scots and French-speaking Canadians in Quebec.
The alleged influence of Trump allies in Alberta has attracted intense scrutiny in Canada.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has called Alberta a "natural partner" for the United States, and Alberta Prosperity Project leaders held several meetings at the State Department.
Earlier this month, Canada's Globe and Mail newspaper detailed contacts between Sylvestre, his team and Republican Party operatives.
Sylvestre told AFP that, for him, U.S. interests "don't play any role" in Alberta "until we win and become government," at which point he would work to ensure free-flowing trade.
"There's no animosity towards America here," he said. "I can't see why we wouldn't want to continue trading with the biggest economy in the world."
Asked about alleged foreign interference on Thursday, Carney said: "our expectation is – to be absolutely clear on foreign governments, United States included – we don't get ourselves involved in their elections, they don't get themselves involved in our elections."

Saudi Arabia accuses Iran of encouraging Houthis in latest escalation
Saudi Arabia on Thursday accused Iran of encouraging Yemen's Houthis in the dramatic escalation of their fight with the kingdom, adding that the Islamic republic continued to arm and train the group.
In a virtual briefing with reporters including AFP journalists, Saudi Arabia's deputy minister for public diplomacy at the foreign ministry said Riyadh was still in touch with Iran, but that Tehran did not appear ready to make concessions.
Saudi Arabia, the world's top crude oil exporter, has come under sustained attack by the Houthis in recent days, shifting the focus of the Middle East war that erupted with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in February.
It has launched retaliatory strikes on Houthi strongholds in Yemen - one of the world's poorest countries - but the Iran-backed group remains undeterred.
"Iran continues to arm, train and support the Houthi militia in violation of UN security council resolutions," said Dr. Rayed Krimly, the deputy minister.
"We think that the escalation by the Houthis at this latest stage of the conflict is encouraged by Iran," he added.
The official said the kingdom continued "to have direct communications with Iran", but added: "Overall, it doesn't seem yet that the Iranians are able to provide the necessary concessions for a solution."
In 2023, regional rivals Iran and Saudi Arabia reached a deal mediated by China to thaw a longstanding freeze in ties, but the latest violence might threaten to upend the entente.
The Saudi official went on to accuse the Houthis of refusing to meet in Oman in recent weeks as fighting ramped up between the two sides.
"At the beginning of this escalation, we asked them to meet in Muscat, Oman and they refused," he added.
"This was the last communication which happened a few weeks ago."
Airport strikes
On Saturday, a strike hit Riyadh's international airport, killing 13 people and wounding around 300 others, in the deadliest attack on Saudi Arabia in a decade.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis on Thursday said the group had attacked Riyadh's airport 20 times in October.
During a presentation in Riyadh covering the strikes, coalition spokesman Turki Al-Malki said "the Houthis must immediately cease all terrorist operations targeting civilians and civilian facilities, including airports, ports, oil facilities, and infrastructure".
"The terrorist Houthi militias have worked to obtain advanced technologies with the help of regional actors," he said, adding that the group now had "ballistic missiles, attack and suicide drones, and fast explosive-laden boats".
Yemen's civil war reignited in July after a years-long UN-brokered truce collapsed, months into a wider Middle East war that has rocked the region and roiled energy supplies and markets.
The situation took a sharp turn for the worse in September, when the Houthis launched a lightning offensive that saw them capture swathes of new territory in Yemen, including along the Red Sea coast where a waterway crucial to global energy flows is located.
On Thursday, the Houthis fired missiles at the presidential palace in Aden, which also serves as the headquarters of the internationally recognised government, security sources told AFP, while a journalist saw smoke rising from the site.
"Houthi missiles targeted the Al-Maashiq presidential palace in Aden," the government's interim capital, three local police sources said on condition of anonymity, after residents of the southern city reported hearing explosions.
Since their offensive began, the Houthis have also repeatedly targeted Saudi Arabia, which backs the internationally recognised government whose forces they are battling on the ground.
The attacks on Saudi Arabia have tested the country's infrastructure and resilience, the energy minister acknowledged earlier this week.
Riyadh usually hosts a packed calendar of events this time of year, including its flagship investment conference drawing foreign leaders and business titans.
In Yemen, the conflict has caused what the United Nations calls one of the world's worst humanitarian crises, leaving most of the nation's population dependent on aid.

A mother’s touch helps premature babies grow strong in Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
17:43:01 UTC
02:43:01 KST

A mother’s touch helps premature babies grow strong in Gaza
At Nasser Hospital, a kangaroo mother care pilot programme helps vulnerable newborns as Gaza’s healthcare system struggles with shortages.
Khan Younis, Gaza Strip – For 11 days after giving birth last month, Rania Fadel could not hold her newborn son.
The 24-year-old gave birth to twin boys, Ilyas and Yahya, on September 25.
While Yahya was born healthy, Ilyas was admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit at Nasser Medical Complex in Khan Younis, in southern Gaza, where he remained for nearly two weeks.
Born prematurely, Ilyas weighed just 1.4 kilogrammes (3 pounds) at birth, according to his mother. He had medical issues affecting his blood and lungs, she said, and needed specialised care in an incubator.
Rania herself was recovering from a Caesarean section when her son was taken into intensive care. For days, she could not hold him.
“When they called me to hold him, I rushed over,” she recalled. “I was in a hurry to get to him. It was such a feeling.”
As Ilyas’s condition improved and he moved from intensive care to the hospital’s neonatal care unit, Rania was able to hold him against her bare chest, introducing her to a form of care for low-birthweight newborns known as kangaroo mother care, part of a newly-launched programme at the hospital.
It involves prolonged skin-to-skin contact between a caregiver – ideally the mother – and baby, with exclusive breast milk feeding, and has been shown to have important health benefits for premature and low-birthweight babies.
“I was so happy. It was such a beautiful feeling,” Rania said.
During the session, a nurse helped Rania position Ilyas against her chest, with his skin touching hers. Rania said he remained there for about 90 minutes.
“He started breastfeeding from me, and he stayed a little longer,” she said. “I felt he was improving.”
For Rania, the contact also brought a sense of closeness after days of separation.
“The baby feels that his mother is there,” she said. “He feels safe. Honestly, it makes me very happy.”
Skin-to-skin
Kangaroo mother care involves placing a baby against a parent’s bare chest for skin-to-skin contact, alongside breastfeeding and appropriate medical care.
For premature and low-birthweight babies, it can help regulate body temperature, support breastfeeding and improve health outcomes.
World Health Organization (WHO) guidance says that kangaroo mother care has been shown to reduce neonatal mortality by 32 percent, and mortality by six months of age by 25 percent, compared with conventional care.
At Nasser Medical Complex, Khawla al-Madhoun, director of nursing at the hospital’s maternity and neonatal departments, described it as an integrated approach to newborn care that supports growth and strengthens the bond between mother and baby.
“When we place a baby on the mother’s chest, it helps the baby grow,” she said.
“We have seen babies who were unwell or underweight begin to grow faster with kangaroo care. This can help them leave the hospital sooner.”
The hospital has begun introducing kangaroo care through a pilot programme supported by WHO, the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), and the UN Population Fund (UNFPA). The agencies announced the initiative at Nasser Hospital in September, but the practice is being introduced gradually in its external neonatal care unit, where babies stay with their mothers, and in maternity wards after delivery.
Al-Madhoun said the team was also preparing a dedicated room and seeking equipment to make the sessions more comfortable.
The team aims for longer periods of skin-to-skin contact – WHO recommends at least eight hours per day – although its immediate target is at least two hours, depending on each family’s circumstances.
At Nasser, the team is currently prioritising babies who are medically stable and do not require oxygen support. Nurses monitor their vital signs and assess them throughout the process.
Al-Madhoun stressed that the technique cannot replace an incubator or other treatment when a baby needs intensive care.
“It can help babies grow, gain weight and leave the hospital earlier, but some babies need other interventions, such as respiratory support,” she said. “Those babies still need the incubator and the care it provides.”
Shortage of neonatal equipment
The need for specialised newborn care comes as Gaza’s health system continues to struggle with damaged facilities, shortages of equipment and overcrowded neonatal units.
Before Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began in October 2023, Gaza had eight neonatal intensive care units with a total of 178 incubators, according to UNICEF.
By November 2024, three of those units had been destroyed by Israel, and the number of available incubators had fallen to about 54, a reduction of 70 percent. The shortage of equipment, compounded by limited supplies of fuel and electricity as a result of Israeli restrictions, put premature newborns at serious risk.
Israeli strikes have continued since an October 2025 “ceasefire”. Despite this supposed truce, and despite the delivery of some new equipment, the shortage of incubators and other equipment has persisted.
In May, UNICEF said it and its partners had supplied incubators and ventilators to hospitals in Gaza, while warning that neonatal units were still managing large numbers of fragile infants with limited equipment, space and power.
The war in Gaza has worsened living conditions for pregnant women with economic hardship, food shortages, poor nutrition and the harsh realities of displacement, including cooking over open fires and carrying water.
“These conditions have contributed to the rise in premature births and babies born with low birth weight who need specialised neonatal care,” al-Madhoun said.
Meanwhile, repeated displacement and overcrowding have placed further pressure on hospitals, including Nasser Medical Complex, which is already struggling with limited space and shortages of incubators and other essential neonatal equipment.
Newborn in a tent
Linda Abu Nasira’s baby girl is only three days old.
The infant initially developed a fever, which has since subsided, according to 23-year-old Linda.
As her daughter was being treated and breastfed, Linda was learning how to hold her against her chest under the guidance of the medical team.
The sessions were brief. Linda said she held her daughter against her chest for about 30 minutes at a time, repeating the process roughly every two hours, according to the instructions she had received.
“She is a little better than yesterday,” Linda said. “Little by little.”
Away from the hospital, Linda lives in a tent in al-Mawasi, in Khan Younis, where she is raising her two older children – aged three and two – while caring for her newborn.
She described the conditions as difficult, particularly when it comes to securing food and drinking water.
“We try to manage,” she said. “But it is not like before, or like the conditions you would expect when giving birth.”
She does not know how long the baby will need to remain under observation in the hospital’s external neonatal care unit.
“As a mother, it means a lot to me to feel that I am helping my daughter recover,” Linda said. “I hope she will recover and be discharged as soon as possible.”

In 100th lawsuit against Trump, California challenges immigration arrests near courthouses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
17:41:13 UTC
02:41:13 KST

In 100th lawsuit against Trump, California challenges immigration arrests near courthouses
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- California is challenging the practice of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents arresting people for alleged civil immigration violations at or near state courthouses.
- State Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta said such arrests have long been barred because they are unconstitutional and deeply disruptive to the rule of law and the rights of victims, witnesses, defendants and other parties to court proceedings.
- Bonta said his office having to take the Trump administration to court 100 times in less than two years, often alongside other Democrat-led states, was a ‘sobering milestone.’
California sued the Trump administration for the 100th time in under two years Thursday, challenging the practice of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents arresting people for alleged civil immigration violations at or near state courthouses.
California Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta said such arrests have long been barred because they are unconstitutional and deeply disruptive to the rule of law and the rights of victims, witnesses, defendants and other parties to court proceedings.
“We’ve seen serious criminal charges dropped and entire cases jeopardized because victims and witnesses are too scared to come to the courthouse to testify,” Bonta said. “Our justice system cannot function this way.”
Bonta said his office having to take the Trump administration to court 100 times in less than two years, often alongside other Democrat-led states, was a “sobering milestone” and a reflection not of political interference on California’s part — as the president and his supporters have cast it — but of Trump’s nearly unbridled lawlessness.
“It’s very troubling when the most powerful person on the planet and the president of our country is the one trampling over the Constitution, breaking the law so blatantly and brazenly, so consistently, so frequently,” Bonta said.
Independent legal experts said several factors have driven the wave of lawsuits.
Federal officials have given California election officials 48 hours to prove the citizenship of voters flagged as potential noncitizens, or withhold their ballots.
Presidents from both parties have increasingly flexed their executive power, and state attorneys general have increasingly sued in response. During Trump’s first term in office, California — under the leadership of then-Atty. Gen. Xavier Becerra, a current gubernatorial candidate — sued the Trump administration more than 120 times over four years. Texas Atty. Gen. Ken Paxton — now a Republican candidate for Senate — sued the Biden administration just over 100 times in four years.
Trump in this term quickly began implementing an array of policies left over from his first term or outlined in the Project 2025 policy blueprint, many of which Bonta and other Democratic attorneys general were prepared to sue over, experts said.
Trump was also able to appoint a host of loyalists with the help of the Republican-controlled Congress, who helped advance policies that less loyal agency heads would have balked at, and which were sure to draw additional legal challenges, experts said.
Daniel Farber, a professor at UC Berkeley Law School and author of “Contested Ground: How to Understand the Limits of Presidential Power,” said California’s raft of lawsuits is a result of the current Trump administration “doing more aggressive things right off the starting block” — but also repeatedly targeting California specifically.
Bonta claimed in August that his lawsuits had saved California more than $200 billion, namely by reversing Trump cuts to federal funding meant for the state.
The White House has consistently derided Bonta’s litigation against the administration as baseless and misguided. White House spokesperson Lauren Bis on Thursday said Bonta should stop bragging about “filing frivolous lawsuits” and “focus on addressing problems in his own state.”
“The reality is, with well over 25 Supreme Court victories, the administration’s policies have been consistently upheld as lawful, despite some lower courts issuing an unprecedented number of lawless injunctions,” Bis said.
ICE, which did not immediately respond to a request for comment, has defended its arrests near courthouses as a “common sense” approach to apprehending offenders at times and locations where authorities know they will be.
The 100th case
Bonta’s lawsuit argues that such arrests are arbitrary and capricious given the chilling effect they have on justice in the state. They violate the Immigration and Nationality Act as intended by Congress, and interfere with California’s rights under the 10th Amendment to execute its “core sovereign judicial and police functions,” Bonta’s office said.
His arguments echo those made by other state officials in the past. During Trump’s first term, for example, then-California Supreme Court Chief Justice Tani G. Cantil-Sakauye called the arrests “disruptive, shortsighted and counterproductive.”
Arrests at or near courthouses began to rise again after Trump took office in January 2025. An ICE memo, issued in May 2025, said agents could conduct “civil immigration enforcement actions in or near courthouses when they have credible information that leads them to believe the targeted alien(s) is or will be present at a specific location.”
Incidents quickly began cropping up. In June 2025, ICE agents arrested two women outside a Los Angeles County courthouse after a hearing in a local criminal case. The same unfolded across the state.
Alejandro Barraza, a criminal defense and immigration attorney, said he has witnessed the effect firsthand.
In October 2025, a client was arrested driving home from a hearing at the Riverside County Hall of Justice. In December, another client was arrested leaving the Rancho Cucamonga courthouse. And a third client chose to plead guilty in his criminal case rather than go to jury trial, despite Barraza’s advice that the case was worth fighting, for fear of being arrested by ICE.
“The victims are losing,” Barraza said. “Our clients are losing their rights to due process. Everyone is losing.”
In June, U.S. District Judge P. Casey Pitts in San Francisco struck down ICE’s expanded courthouse arrest policies nationwide. Although the lawsuit focused on immigration courthouses, the ruling also covered state criminal courthouses, restoring earlier restrictions that barred civil immigration arrests in or near courthouses except in limited circumstances. The Trump administration is appealing the ruling.
Since then, California court officials have tracked arrests by federal agents and reported them to the Judicial Council of California. Thirty people were taken into custody in June, 29 in July, 19 in August and 14 in September.
Three lawsuits filed Friday challenge the Trump administration’s rollback of vehicle mileage rules as illegal, including one led by California.
State legislators have tried to push back. Last month, Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a law strengthening California’s protections against civil arrests for people traveling to, attending or leaving courthouses for lawful purposes. The measure extends those protections to public ways within 1,000 feet of court facilities, while preserving an exception for arrests made under a valid judicial warrant.
Bonta said his lawsuit is necessary despite the new California law, in part because the Trump administration thinks that “no state law applies to them,” and courts have in some cases agreed — including the U.S. 9th Circuit Court of Appeals, which this week blocked a state law that would have required federal immigration agents to display identification while working in the state.
The wider legal battle
Bonta’s office has had substantial success in halting some of the Trump administration’s biggest policy moves — including its plans to end birthright citizenship for the U.S.-born children of immigrants, its worldwide tariffs, its deployment of National Guard troops in Los Angeles and other U.S. cities, and its withholding of billions of dollars in federal funding allocated to the state by Congress.
Michael McConnell, director of the Constitutional Law Center at Stanford Law School, said many of California’s lawsuits have been “legally meritorious,” as there is a “whole lot of legal error” coming out of the Trump administration — with a “lot of the overreach” having been “facilitated by the lack of internal checks” from loyal Trump agency heads.
However, he also said that as a California taxpayer, he doesn’t “appreciate having government using my tax dollars for what essentially are in many cases ideological lawsuits, even if meritorious,” because private litigants can and often do bring lawsuits of their own. He said he felt the same way about many of the lawsuits brought against the Biden administration by Republican states.
Bonta said he is proud of his team for challenging the Trump administration every time they believed it had broken the law and harmed California, despite Trump’s intentional effort to make that difficult.
“It was a shock and awe,” he said. “It was flood the zone. It was trying to overwhelm with speed and volume, and we kept pace every time.”
What happens next, he said, will depend on Trump. If he keeps breaking the law in ways that hurt the state or its residents, Bonta said he’ll keep getting sued by California.

Britain funds Chornobyl repairs after Russian drone hit
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
18:16:57 BST
02:16:57 KST

Britain is putting £17 million towards repairing the protective shelter over the Chornobyl nuclear power plant, which was punctured by a Russian drone strike last year, according to the government.
The money forms part of an international programme coordinated by the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development alongside the Ukrainian government and G7 donors, and will pay for work to restore the structure’s confinement and ventilation functions and protect its intended lifespan. Corrosion threatens to undermine decades of international investment and create longer term environmental and safety risks if the damage is left.
John Healey, the Chancellor of the Exchequer, said: “As the full-scale invasion of Ukraine by Putin continues, our commitment to the Ukrainian people is unshakeable. We are curtailing the war chest funding Putin so desperately wants and backing the reconstruction of Ukraine that has suffered at the hands of his barbaric attacks.”
Ed Miliband, the Foreign Secretary, said: “Our message to Putin is clear, we stand shoulder to shoulder with Ukraine and will do so until they prevail. Working with our allies, we are strengthening Ukraine’s security, raising the cost of Russia’s aggression and working towards a just and lasting peace.”
The structure in question is the New Safe Confinement, the arch built over the remains of reactor four and the Soviet-era sarcophagus around it, which was slid into position in 2016 and handed over in 2019 after an international effort costing around €1.5 billion. It was designed to hold for a century while the reactor underneath is dismantled, and its outer skin and ventilation system are what keep moisture out of the space where that work has to happen. A drone strike that breaches it turns a sealed structure into one that corrodes.
Attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure have continued through the autumn at a heavy rate. Between 5 and 11 October Russia carried out more than two hundred strikes on electricity infrastructure and a further seventeen on oil and gas facilities, six of them after President Trump announced an energy ceasefire on Sunday. On 13 October Russia fired thirty-nine ballistic missiles at Ukraine in one of the largest such attacks of the war, much of it aimed at energy targets, leaving six hundred thousand civilians without power.
Britain has been involved in nuclear safety at the site for years. It was a founding donor to the International Chornobyl Cooperation Account in 2020, when that account took over responsibility for safety in the exclusion zone, and has given €8 million to it, making it the third largest individual donor behind Norway and France.
The Foreign Secretary visited Kyiv last week for the first time since taking office and announced £54 million of winter support, including £20 million in energy funding. The Prime Minister hosted President Zelensky in Downing Street on Wednesday, where he set out a further package of Lightweight Multirole Missiles built by Thales in Belfast.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.

How Israel's policies exposed Zionism's racist foundations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
17:12:17 UTC
02:12:17 KST

The UK's Green Party, whose leader Zack Polanski is Jewish, recently described Zionism as an ethnonationalist political project, triggering a fierce debate about the nature of Israel's founding ideology.
Zionism emerged in the late 19th century, shaped by European Jewish intellectuals like Moses Hess, Theodor Herzl and Nathan Birnbaum, partly in response to Western antisemitism.
Yet it has paradoxically embraced Jewish supremacy over Palestine’s native population, denying Palestinian self-determination and their national aspirations.
Israel’s atrocities in Gaza and the occupied West Bank since October 7, which some leading international bodies and political scientists have described as genocide, have led analysts to argue that Zionism has increasingly taken a racist turn.
This is a particularly stark accusation against a state that has drawn much of its historical legitimacy from the Holocaust, in which Nazi Germany murdered millions of European Jews during World War II.
“In the aftermath of the Gaza genocide in response to the October 7 Hamas attack, the racist character of Israel has again surfaced,” seriously discrediting Zionism, according to Richard Falk, a prominent Jewish-American professor of international law.
Growing international criticism of Zionism has been reinforced by racist and genocidal statements from senior Israeli leaders, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, since October 7.
Pro-Israel groups, meanwhile, have sought to equate criticism of Zionism with antisemitism, a move critics see as an attempt to shield Israel from international accountability.
From the British Green Party's characterisation of Zionism to the findings of the UN Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese on the occupied Palestinian territories and the UN Human Rights Council's Commission of Inquiry, chaired by Navi Pillay, these developments “have deepened the perception of Zionism as an aggressive ideology,” Falk tells TRT World.
Zionism's growing aggressiveness has become “abhorrent to many countries in the world as testified to by the walkout of many delegations when it came time for Netanyahu to address the recent UN General Assembly,” he says.
The UK Green Party episode has also revived memories of the UN General Assembly Resolution 3379, adopted on November 10, 1975, which determined that Zionism was a form of racism. The resolution passed by 72 votes to 32, with 35 states abstaining.
It received overwhelming support from countries in the Global South, though Latin American nations were divided and Western countries largely opposed it.
“The resolution was withdrawn in response to Israel/US lobbying leverage in 1991, but without any language explaining the withdrawal, or exonerating Israel from the earlier charges,” Falk tells TRT World.
In a 2017 report commissioned by the UN Economic and Social Commission for Western Asia (ESCWA), Falk and Virginia Tilley, an American political scientist specialising in ethnic and racial conflict, concluded that Israel had established a system of racial discrimination against Palestinians.
“Despite Israel's strenuous objections to being labeled an apartheid state, it virtually acknowledged the allegation in the Knesset of a 2018 Basic Law which proclaimed Jewish preeminence in Israel, and vesting the right of self-determination exclusively in the Jewish people with Hebrew designated as the only official language,” Falk says.
Many see the Basic Law, enacted by the Netanyahu government, as the codification of Zionist principles within Israel's constitutional framework.
Has Zionism always been racist?
Beyond the developments since October 7, some Israeli historians argue that Zionism has been a racist ideology since Israel's establishment in 1948, rejecting the notion that different versions of Zionism have existed.
While a more recent narrative suggests that Israel's racist and discriminatory policies have emerged under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his far-right coalition partners, Israeli historian and political scientist Ilan Pappe argues that racism has always been central to the Jewish state's identity, describing “liberal Zionism” as an “illusion”.
In a recent interview, Pappe rejected this distinction, saying that “the problem is Zionism in its all varieties”, which was “behind the ethnic cleansing of 1948 and the military rule on Palestinians” as Israel's state ideology.
According to Pappe, the intimidation of Palestinians within Israel since 1948, as well as the tactics used against Palestinians and support for illegal settlers in territories occupied since 1967, have been “the results and the implementation of the Zionist ideology”.
British-Israeli historian Avi Shlaim, who identifies as an Arab Jew, argues that even if “liberal Zionism” once existed in Israel, it is now “dead” under Netanyahu, particularly following the adoption of far-right policies since October 7.
“This promise was never fulfilled. It was just one of many examples of the huge gap between the liberal Zionist rhetoric on universal values and the discriminatory, racist reality, a gap that was filled by Israel’s leaders with hypocrisy and humbug,” Shlaim wrote in an article last month.
“One of the very few things that can be said in favour of the present, far-right Israeli Government is that it has dispensed with the liberal rhetoric and exposed the ugly reality of contemporary Israeli society for all to see,” he added.
However, Alon Liel, a former director-general of Israel's foreign ministry, offers a different perspective, arguing that his country “had a different kind of Zionism” three decades ago.
“The comeback of equating Zionism as racism is definitely an outcome of the last war, especially because of the number of casualties and the destruction in Gaza,” Liel tells TRT World.
Over the years, Zionism, originally regarded as a secular ideology, “has become more nationalistic and messianic”, according to Liel.
He points to the growing influence of far-right groups in Israel, a development some analysts associate with the convergence of revisionist and messianic Zionism.
Zionism: settler colonialism
Western imperial powers ruled much of the world, from the Americas and Africa to Southeast Asia and the Middle East, drawing many of today's international borders. But colonial rule largely receded after World War II, as former colonies gained independence.
Despite this wave of decolonisation, Israel emerged as a settler-colonial state in Palestine, a land inhabited by its native population for centuries, following the armed campaigns of Zionist militant groups such as Haganah and Irgun.
Against this historical backdrop, experts argue that Zionism constitutes a settler-colonial project.
“Zionism is a self-avowed settler-colonial movement, and its principal political progeny – the State of Israel – is a settler-colonial state. The logic of settler-colonialism is the elimination of the natives in order to take over the land and its resources. Ethnic cleansing is the means by which this goal is achieved,” Shlaim viewed.
Zionist leaders also drew on European Orientalist attitudes and the continent's colonial history to gain support for their project, presenting themselves as representatives of Western civilisation in the Muslim-majority Middle East.
While Zionism was originally “a movement among Jews countering the racism embedded in European antisemitism”, it also “had its own racist outlook that can be associated with an Orientalist version of Western cultural superiority and a disregard for the rights of inferior non-Europeans, especially as embedded in Islamic majority countries of the MENA,” Falk says.
“In the aftermath of WW II, Orientalist attitudes combined with liberal guilt associated with allowing Hitler to get away with extreme forms of antisemitism eventuated in a Zionist settler colonial project to establish a state of their own within Palestine, pretending to accept partition as a solution but never giving up their vision of unified Israeli sovereignty over the whole of Palestine.”
Future of Zionism
If Zionism continues on its current aggressive path, what does the future hold for Israel?
The Netanyahu government, which has launched military campaigns in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran, appears confident in its approach, claiming it is changing “the face of the Middle East.”
But some historians argue that Israel's embrace of an increasingly aggressive form of Zionism, driven by ambitions pursued on a shorter timetable than those of earlier Zionist generations, could signal the ideology's final phase.
“Historically, I’m willing to say with some caution that this is the last phase of Zionism. Such developments in ideological movements, whether they are colonial or empires, it’s usually the final chapter [that is] the ruthless one, the most ambitious one. And then it’s too much and then they fall and collapse,” Pappe said in an interview last year.
Like Pappe, Gregory Simmons, an independent researcher and academic, sees a bleak future for Zionism beyond Israel and its Western supporters.
Simmons argues that Israel's actions in Gaza and its military campaigns across the Middle East have eroded public support and sympathy, even in Western countries, while alienating Jewish communities abroad and turning Zionism into “a globally toxic ideology”.
Liel, however, takes a more cautious view. The former Israeli diplomat says he wants to wait for the results of the October 27 election before assessing Zionism's future.
He considers the ideology “very solid” within Israel, while acknowledging that it has been “more rejected” internationally.
Nathan Birnbaum, the Austrian-Jewish writer and journalist credited with coining the term Zionism, offers a historical example of how attitudes towards the ideology can change.
Despite helping organise the First Zionist Congress in Basel in 1897 and serving as secretary-general of the Zionist Organisation, Birnbaum later became a staunch opponent of Zionism and the establishment of a Jewish state in Palestine.

UK scraps three planned Boxer variants after budget cut
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
17:10:07 UTC
02:10:07 KST

- The British Army has dropped armored mortar, repair and recovery, and anti-tank overwatch versions of Boxer, Defence Minister Luke Pollard told Parliament.
- Pollard said Boxer will not be used for armored cavalry and will form the spine of the mechanized infantry force.
The British Army has dropped plans for armored mortar, repair and recovery, and anti-tank overwatch versions of its Boxer wheeled armored vehicle, and has ruled out using Boxer in the armored cavalry role, Defence Minister Luke Pollard told Parliament.
Pollard, the minister for defence readiness and industry, gave the answers in response to written questions from Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member of Parliament for Huntingdon, the UK Defence Journal reported. Obese-Jecty asked what had been cut from the Mechanised Infantry Vehicle programme after the government’s major projects watchdog, the National Infrastructure and Service Transformation Authority, recorded £1.86 billion ($2.47 billion) coming out of the programme in its annual report for 2025 to 2026.
“As part of reprioritisation within the Military Strategic Headquarters, the Armoured Mortar, Repair and Recovery and Mounted Close Combat Overwatch capabilities of the Mechanised Infantry Vehicle programme are no longer being pursued,” said Pollard.
He added that the Army is considering how the underlying capability requirements will be addressed, meaning the need for those three jobs remains even though the Boxer versions designed to fill them are gone.
Each of the cancelled variants was meant to cover a different gap in the British Army’s mechanized infantry brigades. The armored mortar would have given battlegroups their own 120 mm indirect fire that could move with the infantry, and Rheinmetall BAE Systems Land test-fired a mortar module on a Boxer on Salisbury Plain in 2022. The repair and recovery vehicle was intended to tow and fix damaged Boxers, which weigh well over 30 tonnes and need a purpose-built recovery vehicle to move once disabled. Mounted Close Combat Overwatch was the long-range anti-tank version, and Rheinmetall BAE Systems Land and MBDA had shown a Boxer concept carrying Brimstone missiles for the role.
Earlier Army planning had pointed to initial operating capability for the recovery vehicle in 2029, the armored mortar in 2030 and the overwatch variant in the early 2030s, EDR Magazine reported.
Asked how many Boxers would go to armored cavalry units and how many to mechanized infantry, Pollard said Boxer will not be used for armored cavalry at all.
“Boxer vehicles will not be used in the Armoured Cavalry role. Boxer will form the spine of the Mechanised Infantry force,” said Pollard.
Under current plans, he said, Boxer is being fielded in supporting roles across 3rd (UK) Division, including command and control, specialist troop carrier and medical vehicles, with detailed fielding plans and vehicle allocations still being refined. Armored cavalry, the British Army’s reconnaissance and screening role, is being equipped with the tracked Ajax family built by General Dynamics Land Systems UK, which carries a stabilized 40 mm cannon.
Britain rejoined the multinational Boxer program in 2018, 15 years after leaving it, and has ordered more than 600 of the 8×8 vehicles in infantry carrier, specialist carrier, command and ambulance versions. The vehicles are built under license in Britain by Rheinmetall BAE Systems Land at Telford and by KNDS UK, formerly WFEL, at Stockport, with the rest coming from German production lines.

Venezuela’s Maduro and wife plead not guilty to US torture charges
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:51:10 UTC
01:51:10 KST

Venezuela’s Maduro and wife plead not guilty to US torture charges
NEW YORK – Ousted Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores pleaded not guilty on Oct 15 to a new US indictment accusing them of conspiring to torture political opponents.
The additional charges, brought on Oct 15, significantly expanded the US criminal case against Maduro, 63, and Flores, 70. They previously pleaded not guilty to charges that they abused their power to help drug traffickers ship cocaine.
Maduro and Flores, captured by the US military in a January raid ordered by US President Donald Trump and flown to New York, entered their pleas at an arraignment before District Judge Alvin Hellerstein in Manhattan federal court. They wore tan prison garb and were shackled at the ankles during the hearing.
When Hellerstein asked for his plea, Maduro said the accusations had been made previously and were false.
“I have seen it in its entirety, Judge Hellerstein,” Maduro said, referring to the indictment. “I reject this document in its entirety.”
The judge cut Maduro off as he spoke and said a plea of not guilty would be entered on his behalf.
Flores said: “I am completely innocent. I am not guilty.”
Maduro and Flores are not accused of personally carrying out any acts of torture. They would each face a mandatory minimum sentence of 50 years in prison if convicted on all charges.
Hellerstein postponed the trial start date by two weeks to June 14, 2027, due to the new charges.
‘Squeeze them harder’
Prosecutors with the Manhattan US Attorney’s office say Maduro directed Venezuelan officials to torture opposition politicians and military personnel accused of plotting against him to maintain power in the South American country.
In one alleged incident described in the indictment, Maduro in 2014 directed officials to kidnap military personnel to draw information out of them about possible dissidents, and told officials to “squeeze them harder” when some remained defiant.
Flores agreed with the plan in the meeting, and dismissed a suggested alternative plan to glean information by infiltrating the ranks, according to the indictment.
Relations between Maduro, a socialist, and the US were tense during his 13 years in power leading the oil-rich country.
Successive US administrations imposed sanctions on top Venezuelan officials and key state companies, citing alleged human rights violations, corruption and election-rigging. Maduro accused the US of seeking his ouster to gain greater control of the South American country’s natural resources.
Captured at home
The pressure campaign culminated in the Jan 3 raid, when the US military captured Maduro and Flores at their Caracas home and brought them to the US to face drug trafficking charges announced that same day. Since then, they have been held at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn.
Maduro’s former vice-president, Delcy Rodriguez, has led Venezuela since his capture and has ramped up cooperation with the US. Trump has touted Maduro’s capture and the reset of relations with Venezuela as a key foreign policy success heading into the Nov 3 midterm elections in which his fellow Republicans are fighting to retain control of Congress. Farmer's discovery in Egypt leads to pieces of statues for ancient king
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:51:08 UTC
01:51:08 KST

An Egyptian farmer found "an unusual stone." It led archaeologists to pieces of statues for an ancient king.
Cairo — Egyptian farmer Khaled al-Shahat was working on his land when he came across something he hadn't seen before. The unusual pink rock led archaeologists to unearth pieces of statues for King Ramses II, who ruled Egypt from 1279 B.C. to 1213 B.C.
"I was working on my land on Friday when I came across an unusual stone," al-Shahat told CBS News. "I informed the relevant authorities, and they came to examine it."
The stone turned out to be an ancient pink granite block measuring approximately 1.3 meters long (around 4.26 feet) and bearing two royal titles of Ramses II: "Nesw-Bity" (King of Upper and Lower Egypt) and "Sa-Ra" (Son of Ra, the sun god), the Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities said.
Archaeologists began excavations, and near the block they uncovered a colossal head of a statue of Ramses II, measuring approximately 1.6 meters high (around 5.25 feet). The king is depicted wearing the double crown, a symbol of the unification of Upper and Lower Egypt around 3100 B.C.
On Wednesday, Minister of Tourism and Antiquities Sherif Fathy visited al-Shahat's hometown in Al Gharbia Governorate in the Nile Delta to honor him.
The minister presented al-Shahat and his wife with certificates of appreciation, and awarded them a trip to Saudi Arabia to perform the Umrah pilgrimage in recognition of his honesty and responsible conduct for not keeping the discovery to himself.
"The minister insisted that the citizen be honored in his village, on his own land, and among his family and fellow villagers, in recognition of his honesty, awareness, and sense of responsibility," the ministry said in a statement.
Archaeologists also unearthed the remains of the upper part of the statue's back pillar, bearing Ramses II's formal royal title, or Horus name: Hor Ka Nakht Mery Maat.
The size of the head suggests the complete statue was about 28 feet tall, according to archaeologists.
"I was surprised and happy when they discovered more antiquities," al-Shahat told CBS News. "They told me this might change the history of the area."
Most of a second royal statue, also believed to depict Ramses II, was uncovered. Measuring approximately 2.4 meters long (around 7.87 feet), it is missing its legs and base, as well as part of the upper section of its royal nemes headdress. Its head has clearly visible, well-preserved facial features resembling those of the first statue, the ministry said.
Excavations and archaeological studies are continuing on al-Shahat's land to learn more about the statues, the area's history and its architectural development in ancient Egypt.

At least 5 killed in Houthi attack on Yemen’s presidential palace in Aden

At least five people have been killed in the vicinity of the al-Maashiq presidential palace in Yemen’s port city of Aden after Houthi missile strikes.
Yemeni health minister says five people were killed and 16 others injured in the Houthi missile attack that targeted the al-Maashiq Presidential Palace in Yemen’s Aden on Thursday.
The Yemeni Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani said in a social media post on Thursday that Houthis had targeted the al-Maashiq presidential palace with five missiles.

The palace is considered the headquarters and the seat of power for the Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government.
Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry, reporting from the Houthi-controlled capital Sanaa, said the attacks on the headquarters of the internationally recognised government are the “first of their kind” by the Houthis.

On Sunday, the Ministry of Public Health warned of a “humanitarian catastrophe” there.
Meanwhile, the Saudi-led coalition says Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport has come under at least 20 Houthi attacks over the past 11 days with dozens of other airports, oil facilities and ports also targeted.
Major-General Turki al-Maliki, the spokesperson for the alliance, released footage showing strikes on the main airport with passengers seen fleeing for safety, during a news conference in the Saudi capital,
The coalition says the Houthi attacks have killed 17 people and injured more than 300.
Al-Maliki also accused the Houthis of obtaining ballistic missiles from other countries in the region.
Mohamad Elmasry, a professor at the Doha Institute for Graduate Studies, said the Saudi-led coalition’s news conference was intended as a response “to some of the, perhaps, military and security failures”.
“There’s kind of an image problem there because this is maybe affecting the perception of Saudi deterrence, the fact that missiles are getting through,” he told Al Jazeera.
Elmasry said the Houthis also have an image crisis, with the global community viewing their actions as “reprehensible, in particular these targeting civilian infrastructure”.

How RSF defections are reshaping Sudan's fragmented battlefield
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:49:50 UTC
01:49:50 KST

Breadcrumb
How RSF defections are reshaping Sudan's fragmented battlefield
On 8 October, Mohamed Azraq al-Fangari defected from the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and joined the Sudanese Armed Forces, the national army.
The special forces commander was accompanied by some 300 fighters from Kordofan, a region in central Sudan where the army has made advances in recent weeks.
Al-Fangari’s forces played a key role in besieging North Darfur’s capital of El-Fasher in April 2024.
The chokehold lasted 18 months and culminated in the mass killing of sedentary farming ‘non-Arab’ civilians. A UN probe found that the atrocities bore the ‘hallmarks of genocide’.
By then, al-Fangari had long been living in neighbouring Chad, where he was lobbying the RSF’s leadership for better equipment, higher salaries, and medical treatment for his fighters, according to Ahmed Gouja, a local journalist who hails from the same nomadic ‘Arab’ Hawzama tribe as al-Fangari.
“Al-Fangari had a lot of fighters who were injured in his special forces, but the RSF’s leaders treated them as an afterthought,” Gouja told The New Arab. “For those reasons, he defected.”
Dozens of disgruntled RSF officers have defected to the SAF in recent months, a trend that could fragment the RSF across tribal lines, according to local journalists and analysts from Darfur.
Like al-Fangari, most defected fighters hail from nomadic Arab tribes that the RSF’s top brass excludes from powerful positions. The RSF’s leadership is made up almost entirely of the Dagalo family, which hails from the nomadic ‘Arab’ Mahariya tribe.
The family’s grip on power has exacerbated tensions between its own tribe and other Arab communities, which the RSF leans on to fight the SAF.
The SAF’s warm embrace of RSF defectors is also stoking tensions within its own camp, which includes dozens of militias from various ethnic backgrounds and ideological leanings.
Defectors have been awarded impunity, arms and vehicles as a way to tempt other RSF commanders to change sides.
This has agitated some SAF-aligned militias who fear losing power and resources to RSF defectors, analysts say.
Favouritism and neglect
Throughout the war, the RSF’s leaders have sidelined ground commanders despite their role in spearheading major battlefield victories, which they achieved by committing systematic atrocities.
Former RSF commander Al-Nour ‘al-Gubba’ Ahmed Adam expected to be appointed governor of North Darfur for playing a substantial role in the RSF’s genocidal campaign to capture El-Fasher in October 2025.
Yet as a member of the nomadic ‘Arab’ Mahamid tribe - a community divided over its support between the RSF and the SAF – he was passed over for a fighter from the Mahariya.
In April 2026, al-Gubba defected to the SAF, partially because he was denied that powerful post. Many others have followed suit for similar reasons.
“Many [Arab] community leaders have come out and said publicly that these defections don’t represent the position of their tribes, but merely the self-interest of the officers who defected,” said Gouja.
Despite these statements, Gouja added that the RSF has stigmatised these communities, often arresting young men based on unfounded allegations that they are collaborating with the SAF by helping commanders defect.
This has compounded grievances among many nomadic Arab communities, who believe they are shouldering an unfair burden in the war against the SAF.
Many have sent their sons and fathers to either die or suffer life-altering injuries on the front lines, according to Abdel Nasser Suluk Hamid, an analyst from Darfur who is in touch with many Arab tribal leaders and civilians across the region.
“Fighters belonging to [the Mahariya] are sent abroad for life-saving hospital treatment, while the rest of the fighters are abandoned in South Darfur’s capital of Nyala or in Kordofan,” Suluk Hamid told The New Arab.
Despite the discriminatory treatment, Suluk Hamid believes that nomadic Arab tribes won’t turn against the RSF any time soon. Most still fear that the army will subject them to collective punishment if it recaptures Darfur - a fear the RSF stokes to keep them aligned and to attract new recruits.
“Arab communities in Darfur are told that SAF will rape their mothers and loot their lands,” Suluk Hamid told The New Arab.
The irony is that while both sides have committed atrocities such as torture and summary executions, the RSF is disproportionately responsible for systemic sexual violence and mass looting, according to human rights groups and media reports.
Simmering tensions
The wave of RSF defections could also lead to infighting within the delicate alliance of armed groups fighting under the banner of the SAF.
On 8 October, Minni Arko Minnawi, the leader of the SAF-aligned Joint Forces, which is composed of non-Arab militias that rebelled against the state in 2003, warned that he would rebel again if the army supported the creation of new militias.
“We are against any militias that are supported by the state with our money and taxes,” he said during an address to reporters from his residence in Khartoum.
Noon al-Baramkee, a journalist from Darfur, said that many of the RSF’s defectors are present across Sudan’s capital of Khartoum and in eastern Sudan. She said that Minnawi’s speech was likely prompted by fear that these groups would be empowered at the expense of the Joint Forces.
In addition, she believes Minnawi is agitated by the racist rhetoric of vocal SAF supporters, who are calling on the SAF to replace non-Arab armed groups with a new force.
Still, al-Baramkee said that Minnawi’s speech had exacerbated ethnic tensions.
“His speech was very dangerous and poorly timed. Many people now believe that Minnawi may be planning another rebellion [against the army again],” she told The New Arab.
A day after Minnawi’s speech, he walked back his threat of rebelling against the state, saying that he supports one state and one army. However, Gouja believes that Minnawi succeeded in warning the SAF against diluting his power and influence.
He noted that the Joint Forces remain a pivotal force, leading ground battles against the RSF in the broader Kordofan region, and that the SAF can’t afford to betray them.
“There are members of the SAF and of Sudan’s deep state that don’t view Minnawi as a trusted partner,” Gouja told The New Arab.
“But the leadership in the SAF knows that they would be weaker without him.”

Fiji is enlisting New Zealand’s intelligence agency to help overhaul its fragmented security sector, Suva said on Wednesday, as US warnings of suspected China-linked cyberintrusions highlight concerns about vulnerabilities in the nation.
The Fijian Cabinet approved a six-month partnership with the New Zealand Security Intelligence Service (NZSIS), funded by Wellington, to assess Fiji’s intelligence structure and recommend reforms, Fiji’s government said in a statement.

Fiji did not identify a specific threat behind the review.

Hackers linked to China maintained access to the organization’s network for several days, while Washington had provided technical recommendations to help Fiji and the affected entity protect their systems, the embassy said.

Stolen data could expose sensitive communications among Pacific island countries and territories, it added.
China’s embassy in Suva rejected the allegations, saying on Tuesday that Beijing opposed hacking and the politicization of cybersecurity.
“China firmly opposes and combats hacking activities in accordance with law,” the Chinese embassy said, accusing the US of making allegations without evidence and calling for dialogue to manage cyberrisks.

TSMC eyes adding facilities in Texas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:43:40 UTC
01:43:40 KST

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC, 台積電) yesterday said it is in discussions with a customer to secure wafer capacity supply in Texas, potentially extending its US manufacturing footprint beyond Arizona to satisfy surging demand from customers for artificial intelligence (AI) chips.
“Recently, we did expand our capacity consideration to see whether we can get another chance to expand our capacity outside Arizona, and Texas is the one,” TSMC chief executive officer C.C. Wei (魏哲家) said at the company’s earnings conference.
“So we sent our teams to Texas to do all the evaluation and we also talked to one of our customers who is trying to build a fab, TeraFab. And we are discussing with them to see whether we can utilize that actual capacity,” Wei said.
Photo: Cheng I-hwa, AFP
The main principle is that “the fab [has] got to be run by TSMC,” no matter the framework — whether it is similar to the company’s joint venture in Japan or the structure adopted in Europe, he said.
TSMC believes accelerating capacity in the US is “necessary,” he said, citing demand to ramp up onshore production from major customers there.
The company in July increased its US investment to US$265 billion.
TSMC yesterday said it remains committed to the AI mega trend, rebuffing skepticism over the profitability and sustainability of such investments.
“We observe increasing AI demand fueled by the rising adoption of agentic AI as we transition from chatbots to AI assistants,” Wei said.
“In addition, we are observing greater adoption of open-source AI models. This will drive greater efficiency and help lower the barrier to future AI usage, and result in more and more demand for leading-edge silicon,” he added.
Customer demand is far higher than what TSMC can supply, the company said, adding that it is adopting many approaches to maximize capacity support. "The AI demand is a very extremely robust. And we did not see any sign of slowdown," Wei said. “We have no intention to leave food on the table for others and we want to capture every piece of business possible."
Addressing competition from Intel Corp’s EMIB-T packaging technology, Wei highlighted TSMC’s unmatched market position, saying that the company offers highly competitive packaging technologies — producing 5.5-reticle size chip-on-wafer-on-substrate (CoWoS) and planning larger versions.
“I don’t believe that any company can do that today except TSMC. And the yield is excellent,” he said, adding that the company’s CoWoS products are the “No. 1 choice” for customers.
Asked if TSMC would provide CoWoS capacity as a contingency for customers should Intel fail to deliver its EMIB-T solutions, Wei said that it would.
TSMC’s ultimate priority is ensuring customers have smooth product rollouts, he said.
The company said it expects revenue this quarter to expand to US$52.3 billion to US$54.3 billion due to increasing demand for its leading-edge technologies, including the 2-nanometer process.
The mid-point of the revenue projection would represent sequential growth of 14 percent from US$46.72 billion last quarter.
Revenue is expected to expand about 44 percent in US dollar terms annually for the whole of this year, TSMC said.
It said it expects its 2-nanometer capacity to more than double next year from this year.
The company said it plans to build one more 3-nanometer plant in Tainan, with volume production scheduled in the first half of 2028.
Gross margin is forecast at 65 to 67 percent, compared with 66.4 percent last quarter, due to dilution from the steep ramp-up of 2-nanometer technology, TSMC said.
Net profit last quarter hit a new record at NT$763.06 billion (US$23.65 billion), up 8 percent from NT$706.56 billion a quarter earlier and 68.7 percent from NT$452.3 billion in the same period last year.
Earnings per share advanced to NT$29.43 from NT$27.25 in the second quarter and NT$17.44 a year earlier.
