====================================================================================================

‘Misty Green’ nicely skewers Hollywood
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:43:38 UTC
01:43:38 KST

Ten years ago moviegoers got a love letter to Los Angeles in the achingly sweet La La Land, where characters danced on air. Gravity arrives a decade later in Chris Rock’s terrific poison pen letter to the city, Misty Green.
Rock, who directs and stars in the film as well as having written the screenplay, holds a mirror up to modern-day Los Angeles and shows us a metropolis that acts as a meat-grinder for a never-ending wave of wannabes. The city may as well use that mirror to cut another line of coke and snort it off someone’s thigh in a dingy bathroom.
Misty Green is an almost noirish take on Hollywood and the chase for fame. The result is one of Rock’s best projects, boosted by the ferocious abilities of Rosalind Eleazar as Misty. She turns a star-seeking character into a star-making part.
Photo: AP
Eleazar’s Misty Green is a mess when we first meet her: A once white-hot actor-singer who won a supporting Emmy trophy years before but is now approaching 40 and struggling to keep her career going.
Misty has poor impulse control, a long line of grudges and finds herself somewhat trapped: “Too Black to be with Leo (Leonardo DiCaprio), not Black enough to be with Damson (Idris), not a nepo baby or a Brit,” she says, which is a little meta because Eleazar is, in fact, a Brit.
Topher Grace, who plays Misty’s unhelpful agent, is out of ideas for his struggling client.
“You’re not exactly unknown,” he tells her. “I don’t know if I could get you on Law & Order.”
Hope arrives in Rock, who plays a movie director trying to recover from his last flop, starring Nicolas Cage, one of several celebs who catch strays in this movie. (Others include Victoria Beckham, J. Lo and Nicole Kidman. Speaking of celebs, look for a hysterical Ice-T cameo and, in an apparent nod to nepo babies, Rock’s daughter, Zahra, also has a small part.)
Rock’s easygoing director fired Misty years ago when she assaulted a makeup artist while coked up during his remake of Cinderella. Misty chalks up the incident to “creative differences,” and Rock may be willing to give her a second chance in his remake of the musical Dreamgirls.
Adding to Misty’s stress levels are the need to find new housing, stat, and the arrival of her bipolar brother, heartbreakingly played by Daniel Kaluuya. His character can be very dangerous when not on his meds and he has an irritating tendency of throwing plastic spiders at people.
Others in Misty’s orbit include an actor friend played by Anna Kendrick, who’s growing disillusioned by show biz.
“I really can’t do this anymore. I love acting, but riding the line between ’ho and hostess, I’m out,” she says.
Then there’s Misty’s hook-up/drug dealer friend played by Adam Driver. Both actors are terrific. Rock, bless him, is out of his depth, showing a lot of Progressive car insurance actor energy.
Rock puts Misty in a city divided by haves and have-nots — homeless encampments on one side juxtaposed by men in suits who keep telling people experiencing homelessness that they’re not carrying any cash. Everyone here is cheating, gossiping and judging. A Birkin bag is the coin of the realm.
It’s the kind of town where the emergency room doctor tending to your wounds confesses that she’s a fan of your TV work and wants a selfie, or the young woman auditioning for the same part as you are remarking that her dad — her dad — really loves your work.
Early on, the widow of Misty’s sugar daddy bursts into their love nest apartment, demanding she leave immediately and cursing up a storm, but soon offers to run dialogue with Misty ahead of her audition. “Memorize your lines,” she advises. Hollywood, right?
Rock has created a complicated character in Misty, a talented singer and actor who delivers a brave cover of Radiohead’s Creep at a piano lounge, but who is also an egotistical, party-loving starlet. She really should stay home and memorize her scenes, yet ends up lured to a nightclub all night. Eleazar shows us all her flaws and yet we root for her; it’s a stunning performance from the Slow Horses star.
Rock slyly examines race in this setting, too, with a casting agent blurting out to Misty: “Are you mixed?” Seemingly every role for Black women is exploitative. Rock notes wryly that wherever you go, at some point in history, Black people weren’t allowed there. The TV news is blaring about a dead white college student and a manhunt for her killer; Misty’s brother suspects they’ll railroad a Black man.
Misty’s money, family and career woes all build to an almost-operatic decision — follow her craft and career or debase herself and earn a lot of money. Whatever happens, no one in this tawdry town will be dancing on air.

US to account for over 20% of LNG imports: minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:43:36 UTC
01:43:36 KST

US liquefied natural gas (LNG) is expected to account for more than 20 percent of Taiwan’s LNG imports this year, up from 10 percent last year, and rise to 25 percent by 2029, Minister of Economic Affairs Kung Ming-hsin (龔明鑫) said yesterday.
If talks to purchase LNG from an Alaskan project proceed smoothly, supply could begin as early as 2032, potentially raising the US share in Taiwan’s LNG imports to 30 percent or more, Kung said.
Under a planned investment of up to US$4.4 billion in the project, CPC Corp, Taiwan (台灣中油) would purchase 6 million tonnes of LNG from Alaska annually once production begins, the ministry said.
Photo: Lin Jing-hua, Taipei Times
As Taiwan’s natural gas demand continues to rise, with 25 additional large gas-fired power units expected to be added by 2035, the government needs to secure supplies in advance and diversify procurement sources to strengthen energy resilience, Kung said.
In addition, securing stable supplies through long-term contracts could help reduce price volatility in LNG imports, he said.
Alaska is also relatively close to Taiwan, with a shipping time of about 10 days, which could reduce transportation time and shipping risks, Kung said.
For the US$4.4 billion investment, the government has a preliminary plan and an investment ceiling, but the actual amount, equity stake and other terms still need to be determined through negotiations, he said.
Kung said he is confident in CPC’s ability to negotiate favorable investment terms, but declined to disclose pricing because of commercial confidentiality.
The source of funding for the investment would depend on the final investment structure, timetable and CPC’s financial position, and could include capital injections, capitalization of retained earnings or loans, he said.
Funds would also be committed in stages in line with project progress rather than paid in a lump sum, he said.
As Taiwan’s trade surplus with the US has widened, increasing energy purchases from the US could also help narrow the imbalance, Kung said.
Separately, asked about Pegatron Corp (和碩) chairman Tung Tzu-hsien’s (童子賢) suggestion of developing an artificial intelligence (AI) park in the Danhai New Town (淡海新市鎮) area of New Taipei City’s Tamsui District (淡水), Kung said it was “a pretty good idea.”
The area has advantages including large contiguous parcels of land, convenient transportation and access to labor, he said.
The Danjiang Bridge would also improve access to the Port of Taipei and provide links to Taiwan Taoyuan International Airport, improving the area’s transportation advantages, he said.
In contrast, Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an’s (蔣萬安) proposal to develop an AI park on the site of Taipei International Airport (Songshan airport) could remain in the discussion phase for another decade because opinions remain divided, Kung said.
Taiwan’s AI industry cannot afford to wait for a consensus before moving ahead, he added.

A Thai influencer working illegally in Taiwan who was posting videos of her work and daily life drew the attention of National Immigration Agency (NIA) officers, leading to the arrest of 20 Thai nationals who had overstayed their visas and five people suspected of illegally employing them, the agency said yesterday.
The influencer, who had overstayed her visa, was working illegally at a farm in a remote area of Kaohsiung.
She posted TikTok videos of her work and of herself dancing, using them to recruit fellow Thai nationals, with one video drawing more than 100,000 views, the agency’s Southern Taiwan Administration Corps said.
Photo courtesy of a member of the public
The videos also helped officers track her down.
Investigators from the agency’s Kaohsiung City Specialized Operation Brigade pieced together clues about the farm’s surroundings and terrain from the footage, despite its secluded location, the brigade said.
After multiple stakeouts at suspected locations, officers arrested 20 Thai nationals and five people suspected of illegally employing them, the agency said, adding that it would investigate whether an illegal labor brokerage was involved.
Chao Chih-cheng (趙志成), captain of the Kaohsiung brigade, said employers who illegally hire foreign workers face fines of up to NT$750,000 (US$23,384).
Those who employ them illegally for profit face a prison sentence of up to three years, as well a maximum fine of NT$1.2 million, he added.

====================================================================================================

New life on Kaohsiung’s old cemetery slopes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:43:08 UTC
01:43:08 KST

Just 10 years ago, the site of Shuanghu Forest Park (雙湖森林公園) was a blight on the Kaohsiung landscape. Motorists on the nearby freeway were treated to a view of a weedy hill covered in scattered graves, with a few corrugated steel buildings thrown in for good measure. Things got worse before they got better.
It was decided to turn this public land into a park, but in order for that to happen, all the human remains had to be moved and the existing mess of weeds and patchy tree growth had to be landscaped. After nearly 30,000 burials were relocated to a nearby columbarium, the whole area was razed clean and the new park laid out. Old photos from 2018 show what looks like a desert landscape of bare earth, the unsightly chrysalis of the beautifully landscaped park that is still emerging today.
Thousands of trees were planted, and detention ponds were created, both for flood protection and to create a water ecosystem. Last year, as part of a major upgrade, nectar-producing plants were added to encourage butterflies to settle here, and even more trees were planted. Frogs, dragonflies and several butterfly species now call this place home, and there is more and more shade among the maturing trees.
Photo by Tyler Cottenie
Lastly, the entire slope leading up to the adjacent Kaohsiung Green Park, formerly the site of a golf course, has been transformed. Where a mishmash of tombs once lay, terraced pathways now run along the length of the hill, adorned with rows of trees, including Taiwanese golden rain trees, currently displaying their gorgeous pink fall color.
WALK, RUN, CLIMB
There are a few benches scattered throughout, but the park is, above all, a place for walking or jogging. If you want a large open space where you can sit down for a picnic or to let children run around, take a walk through Shuanghu Forest Park first and then hike up the hill along one of three trails to Kaohsiung Green Park for its open, grassy spaces.
Dingjin 1st Lane runs right through the length of the park from south to north and is its main transportation artery. It was recently widened and paved with asphalt, so it is also a nice lane for walking, especially thanks to the ample shade from the trees on either side.
Alongside Dingjin 1st Lane itself, there are five smaller parking lots, with spaces for cars and/or scooters. Right across from the first parking lot at the south end is the site of the Islamic burial section in the old cemetery. This was the last section to be cleared out, as the remains could not be cremated and moved to a columbarium, but had to await the opening of a new cemetery in far-away Shanlin District (杉林區) before they could be moved. Nowadays, the area is newly landscaped and there is no hint of its former function.
Wherever you start your walk in the park, check out one of the signs in these parking lots if you need a quick overview of the park’s layout. The “Sunset Walkway” is not a single trail but the interconnected walkways on the terraces going up the hill to Kaohsiung Green Park. These provide the best view of the surrounding city by far and are west-facing so they are a perfect spot to end your day around sunset. The “Green Hiking Trails” are newly built connectors providing access to Kaohsiung Green Park above.
The “Ecological Walkway” takes visitors around the new detention ponds that several egrets have already decided to call home, and among nectar-rich plants that have attracted numerous species of butterflies. The newly planted trees still have some filling out to do, but this area is already far more beautiful and ecologically diverse than 10 years ago. One final item worth noting on the sign is the “pavilion.”
It would be a grave mistake to visit the park without taking a walk over to this spot. Perched conspicuously up on a hill behind one of the detention ponds in the shade of two enormous banyan trees, this “pavilion” is actually a tomb dating back to 1938, and one of only three that was spared during the dismantling of the former cemetery.
THE TOMBS
Surrounded by a low, ornamented concrete wall, with a central staircase flanked by three pairs of stone lanterns, the tomb is distinctively Japanese in its style, and is likely one of the best-preserved examples still remaining in Taiwan.
It is visually stunning in its symmetry, beautifully framed by the banyans and provides an excellent view of the surrounding cityscape from the top, next to the tall stone monument. It was preserved not only for its aesthetic value but also for its historical significance.
Originally the tomb of Japanese businessman and longtime Kaohsiung (Takao) resident Sugimoto Otokichi, it later became the repository for the remains of approximately 3,000 Japanese. After World War II, Japanese graves scattered throughout the country were subject to abandonment and vandalism, so three locations were selected and the remains of Japanese from the colonial era were relocated to these locations.
The Sugimoto family, in keeping with Otokichi’s reputation as a man of justice, allowed his spacious tomb to become the designated repository for southern Taiwan. Over 50 years later, the remains were moved to a columbarium along with those in the rest of the cemetery, but the tomb’s structure was preserved.
Two other tombs of identical style were also preserved from the old cemetery and are easily accessible near the main road. One is right next to the second roadside parking lot from the south and belonged to Taiwanese businessman and local credit union co-founder Huang Ching-yun (黃慶雲). Much smaller in scale but equally well preserved, this tomb represents the inclination of some Taiwanese to adopt the customs and aesthetics of their colonizers.
The final tomb is directly east of the nearby incinerator’s smokestack, at a bend in the road. Slightly larger in scale, this one belonged to Japanese businessman Otsubo Yoichi and is notable for having been moved here from another location during the Japanese era.
GETTING THERE
Using public transit, take Bus Red 33 from the Aozihdi MRT stop, get off at the Benguan Rd. (Funeral Interment Management Office) stop, and walk north along the freeway to Dingjin 1st Lane, which takes you to the park’s south entrance. Alternatively, you can take Bus Green 2 from the Cultural Center or near any light rail stop on Dashun Road counterclockwise up to Minzu Road. Get off at the Jixian Park stop and walk south on Dafeng St. to the park’s north entrance. By scooter or car, approach from Benguan Road and then turn to follow the east side of the freeway to Dingjin 1st Lane to enter the park, or continue further north to a large parking lot and then walk up to the park entrance.
However, the easiest way may be to visit as a side trip from Kaohsiung Green Park, and it is recommended to combine these two into one excursion. Look for the marked trails down from Holes 13, 14 and 17.
Shuanghu Forest Park is open 24 hours a day but has no toilet facilities. The adjacent Kaohsiung Green Park has plenty, but the opening hours are 5am to 6pm in winter.

EDITORIAL: Beware Beijing’s expanding lawfare
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:43:06 UTC
01:43:06 KST

China’s revised National Defense Mobilization Law took effect on Oct. 1, allowing the government to mobilize civilians and redirect resources for military purposes, and ensures a rapid transition from peacetime to wartime. It has a wide scope of “national interests” pretexts, which would likely be used against Taiwan.
The amendment incorporates Chinese President Xi Jinping’s (習近平) “Military-Civil Fusion” principle into law, and stipulates that once the state initiates national defense mobilization, “the people’s governments at or above the county level may expropriate and requisition civilian resources,” and “all organizations and individuals shall have the obligation to accept the lawful expropriation and requisition of civilian resources.” It massively expands China’s national mobilization, including drafting men aged 18 to 60 and women aged 18 to 55 into the armed forces, and allows it to legally and forcibly seize private property.
Given that most top Chinese political officials and military commanders have been purged under Xi’s corruption crackdown, the revised law was widely seen as a legislation to further consolidate Xi and his ruling clique’s control of public and civilian forces, paving the way for his five-year term or even to extend his leadership indefinitely.
As the new law aims to convert all peacetime resources, including energy, media and cutting-edge technologies, such as drones and artificial intelligence, into wartime supplies under government control, Taiwanese and international firms and assets in China could also be targeted. All cross-strait and cross-border business cooperation, supply chains, data flows and personnel could be incorporated into China’s national mobilization system, transforming them from commercial assets into warfare resources. Taiwan and other democracies should be vigilant and ensure Beijing is not using the law to expand its war preparations from just the military to the entire society.
The law has turned Xi’s aggressive and expansionary foreign policies into national legislation. While most countries’ military and social mobilization primarily focuses on crisis response, China’s law states that mobilization can take place if the nation’s sovereignty, unification, territorial integrity, security or development interests are threatened. This is the first time “unification” and “development interests” have been included in China’s legal framework for mobilization. The law also expands the discretionary power of the Chinese Communist Party, its government and military over what constitutes a threat.
The legislation could be used as “legal warfare” against Taiwan; Beijing could define an invasion of the nation as a “unification” mission to be safeguarded through defense mobilization. For example, the Chinese People’s Liberation Army could mobilize more civilian forces in its “gray zone” operations, cognitive warfare, cross-border repression or even a military conflict against Taiwan.
China could also use the law to send political signals, putting pressure on countries along the First Island Chain — including Taiwan, Japan and the Philippines — as well as Australia, the US and the EU.
American Foreign Policy Council Asian security senior fellow Larry Wortzel warned that “the wording of the legislation suggests a scope that is larger still,” as Beijing could invoke the law under the pretext of national development interests. It could mobilize warfare actions if it believes areas it “controls” — such as the South China Sea, East China Sea, or islands and territorial borders in dispute with other countries — are being threatened, or even just to secure overseas economic investments or foreign interests.
As Beijing strengthens its peacetime-wartime transition capabilities through legal and institutional adjustments, Taiwan must accelerate the enhancement of its national resilience and countermeasure capabilities. As a democratic country, it must consider how to integrate public and private “social powers” into collective “national resilience” based on democratic constitutionalism, cross-sectoral collaboration and social trust.
Dennis Blair, former US director of national intelligence and a retired commander of US forces in the Pacific, has praised the transformation of the annual Han Kuang military drill into a whole-of-society defense exercise, calling it a “great decision.” People and parties in Taiwan need to transcend political divisions, promote more social cooperation and shared determination to safeguard the security and sustainability of the nation.
Faced with China’s legalization of “military-civil fusion” for “national development interests,” which could pose a profound threat to regional stability and international order, democratic countries must foster more and stronger multilateral alliances to jointly counter Beijing’s aggression, and safeguard global democratic rules and peace.

China-North Korea border bridge opens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:43:05 UTC
01:43:05 KST

China and North Korea yesterday officially opened their most significant land border crossing, aiming to rejuvenate trade and commerce.
Trucks festooned with the national flags of the neighbors drove across the long-delayed 3km New Yalu River Bridge, its towering pylons also decked in flags, linking the Chinese city of Dandong with North Korea.
Knots of spectators crowded a road on the Chinese side overlooking the cable-stayed bridge completed in 2014, but unused while North Korea left its approach roads and customs compound unfinished.
Photo: Reuters
Bilateral “relations are entering a new phase, embarking on a new chapter,” Chinese Premier Li Qiang (李強) said in a video address at the opening, the official Xinhua news agency reported.
The border crossing would “strongly promote” economic and trade cooperation, and further strengthen exchanges between their people, Li said.
It also offers an opportunity to improve border clearance procedures, boost connectivity and build cooperation in border areas, he said.
North Korean Premier Pak Thae-song also delivered a video address, Xinhua said, but North Korea’s state media were yet to report on the event.
The opening is the latest sign of warming ties between Beijing and Pyongyang after two summits between their leaders in the past year.
However, despite the potential economic boost from trade, analysts said North Korea remains cautious of greater dependence on China.
“The bridge is unlikely to lead immediately to a full-scale return to pre-sanctions trade,” said Lim Eul-chul at Kyungnam University’s Institute for Far Eastern Studies.
The bridge will help move heavy equipment, raw materials and energy products that North Korea needs for development efforts, Lim said.
China is by far Pyongyang’s largest trading partner, even after a series of UN sanctions banned the flow of goods and workers with the North over the latter’s missile and nuclear weapons development.
China and Russia, permanent members of the UN Security Council that voted to approve sanctions resolutions until 2017, have since questioned the legitimacy and efficacy of such bans.
Russia is accused by countries such as the US and South Korea of supplying sensitive military assistance to the North in return for Pyongyang’s help in fighting the war in Ukraine.
The delay in opening the bridge was a setback for Dandong, whose economy thrived in the early 21st century as the primary trade gateway to North Korea’s isolated economy.
Until now, most goods have crossed about 10km upstream, using an 83-year-old bridge with a rail track and a single-lane road. That remains the busiest of about 15 crossing points along the roughly 1,350km shared border.
Dandong residents welcomed the opening.
“It’s been more than a decade since they first said the bridge would open ... but coming here today and seeing it for myself makes me incredibly happy,” said a 50-year-old resident surnamed He.
“Once the bridge opens, this place will become much livelier, attracting more tourists,” said another Dandong resident, surnamed Xie.
The bridge opening was “effectively the first visible case” of adoption of agreements struck at a June summit of leaders, a South Korean Ministry of Unification official said.

Navigating the strategic path ahead
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:43:04 UTC
01:43:04 KST

Europe’s interest in strategic autonomy has been reignited as uncertainty surrounding US policy has reached a level that can no longer be covered up with diplomatic niceties. Repeated flip-flopping on tariffs, military aid, NATO and policy toward Russia have forced European countries to confront a harsh reality: Security frameworks dependent on a single provider are vulnerable to changes in political winds that can quickly translate into military, energy and industrial risks.
Increasing defense spending is the first step, not a complete solution. Europe has long struggled with fragmented weapons standards, lengthy procurement cycles, slow cross-border decisionmaking and insufficient defense manufacturing capacity. If countries increase their individual budgets, but continue purchasing and maintaining equipment independently, all that additional spending would only result in more variation in equipment models and higher logistical costs. Genuine European autonomy would require establishing shared requirements, joint procurements, interoperable components and wartime resupply mechanisms.
France’s proposal to link nuclear deterrence with European defenses mainly reflects Paris’ ambition to translate its existing capabilities into political leadership. Other member states have misgivings about concentrating decisionmaking power, as well as the possibility that France’s nuclear arsenal would ultimately serve French national interests. Such concerns cannot be dispelled by summit declarations alone. Europe must clarify who can initiate collective defense, who foots the bill, how non-nuclear states can participate in oversight and which institution takes command during a crisis.
Fiscal constraints present another major obstacle. Many European countries are grappling with aging populations, social welfare commitments, energy transitions and debt pressures. If defense budgets are financed solely through borrowing, their political support could be eroded within a few years. A more viable approach would be to integrate military procurement with industrial policy. Through joint financing, long-term contracts and regional specialization, additional spending could be converted into sustainable production capacity rather than one-off purchases.
European strategic autonomy should not be seen simply as a break from the US. It would minimize the potential fallout of any ally abandoning its commitments, while preserving NATO’s advantages in intelligence, nuclear deterrence and joint operations. Autonomy and alliance are not mutually exclusive. Indeed, a Europe capable of shouldering greater responsibility would be better positioned to coordinate with the US on equal footing.
Taiwan should draw two lessons from the debate in Europe.
First, rather than a weapons shopping list, increases in defense spending must meaningfully translate into production and maintenance capacity, ammunition supplies and personnel. Second, security cooperation commitments must be operable in peacetime, including intelligence sharing, supply chain contingencies, joint training and crisis communications.
If Europe turns strategic autonomy into nothing more than a budget race, its military system is likely to end up expensive and fragmented. Only by translating shared threats into common standards, pooled funding and joint decisionmaking can Europe develop genuinely effective security capabilities.
Similarly, Taiwan’s defense self-reliance does not mean producing everything domestically. It means ensuring that domestic capabilities are sufficient to sustain key operations even when external support is held up.
Taiwan must also be alert to the market changes that might result from Europe’s pursuit of strategic autonomy. As Europe looks elsewhere for defense procurements, it might toughen its requirements on local manufacturing, cybersecurity certifications and supply chain disclosures. Taiwanese manufacturers of drones, communications equipment and electronic components seeking to enter these markets cannot rely on competitive prices and delivery times alone. They must also be prepared to provide long-term maintenance, technology protections and establish local partnerships across Europe.
Security alliances are increasingly becoming a prerequisite for industrial involvement, and the government should help businesses understand the relevant standards and establish credible track records well in advance.
These steps are also a measure by which Taiwan can assess its strategic autonomy. The number of weapons procured is a single variable; the capabilities that can be sustained during a crisis are the real measure of success. Defense reform should include regular public reporting of non-sensitive indicators — such as equipment serviceability rates, training volumes and replenishment progress — so that the public can see what actual capabilities additional spending has delivered.
Edwin Yang is an associate professor at National Taiwan Normal University and chairman of the Central Taiwan Association of University Professors.
Translated by Gilda Knox Streader

Taiwan Blocks Coinbase, Kalshi Over Suspected Election Bets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:43:04 UTC
01:43:04 KST

Taiwan has blocked the websites of Coinbase Global Inc. and Kalshi Inc. over suspected election betting, weeks before local polls that will test support for President Lai Ching-te’s government.
A New Taipei court authorized the Taiwanese communications regulator and internet registry to bar domestic access to the platforms, according to a ruling seen by Bloomberg News. Some Coinbase users in Taiwan reported being unable to access the site since Wednesday.
The Criminal Investigation Bureau, which sought the order, said in response to questions from Bloomberg that the websites were suspected of violating the Public Officials Election and Recall Act. The law prohibits operating gambling for profit based on the outcome of an election or recall.
Photo: Reuters
Coinbase and Kalshi didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
The bureau said it requested the restrictions to protect election integrity and prevent “overseas interference,” without giving further details. Taiwanese authorities have separately warned that money from mainland China could enter the island through underground financial channels and be used to influence elections.
The government has stepped up scrutiny of illicit financial flows ahead of the Nov. 28 vote, including underground gambling operations. Authorities haven’t alleged that Coinbase or Kalshi handled funds from China.
China’s Taiwan Affairs Office didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment sent outside normal office hours.
Taiwan is among the jurisdictions that criminalize election wagering. Under a 2023 amendment to the election act, bettors can face as long as six months in prison, while gambling operators can receive up to five years.
Authorities have increasingly targeted election wagering on prediction markets. Polymarket, the main rival to Kalshi, has also been blocked in Taiwan. Cryptocurrencies are often used to place bets on such platforms.
Taiwanese voters will choose local officials ranging from mayors and city councilors to village chiefs. The elections will be the first island-wide electoral test for Lai since he took office in 2024 and could offer an early indication of the political landscape ahead of the 2028 presidential election.

Army to open Chengkungling base to public Oct. 24
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:43:02 UTC
01:43:02 KST

The army is to open its Chenggong Ling (成功嶺) base to the public on Saturday next week, showcasing new equipment including M1A2T tanks and the High Mobility Artillery Rocket System (HIMARS), while offering rides in eight-wheeled armored vehicles and other hands-on military experiences, the Ministry of National Defense (MND) said yesterday.
The event, part of the military’s efforts to promote public understanding of national defense, is to run from 8am to 3pm and is free, said Major General Wang Chun-chin (王俊欽), chief of staff of the 10th Army Corps.
Visitors are required to bring a photo ID for identity checks. Foreign spouses must be accompanied by their Taiwanese spouses, while foreign caregivers must be accompanied by their care recipient, and present valid documents, Wang said.
Photo: CNA
The static display is to feature 24 types of ground equipment, including M1A2T tanks and HIMARS systems, as well as the navy’s mobile missile launchers and the air force’s Patriot and Tien Kung (天弓) air defense missile systems.
The program would also include an aerial formation by AH-1W Cobra helicopters, fast-rope descents from UH-60M Black Hawk helicopters, helicopter-borne assault demonstrations using CH-47SD helicopters, drone displays, mixed martial arts demonstrations and a precision parachute landing by the army’s Shen Long parachute team, he said.
Visitors can also ride in eight-wheeled armored vehicles and try pulling the firing mechanism of a towed 155mm howitzer.
Other activities include military recruitment booths, civil defense education, air rifle shooting and a fair, the ministry said.
No private vehicles would be allowed inside the base, and traffic controls would be implemented on nearby roads.
Free shuttle buses are to run between the venue and designated stops at Chengkung Station, Xinwuri Station, Shuinan Transit Center, the Jingmao 6 free parking lot and Chenggong military supply station.
With the Nov. 28 local elections approaching, Wang reminded visitors that military events must remain politically neutral, with election-related clothing and the distribution or posting of campaign materials prohibited.
Military officials said they would also urge visitors not to display campaign sashes worn as hair accessories or other ornaments.

Trump cannot figure out peace in Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:43:01 UTC
01:43:01 KST

US President Donald Trump’s deal to purchase diesel fuel from Russia is a moral outrage: It rewards an aggressor that is terrorizing Ukrainian cities with drones and missiles, while punishing the victim for fighting back. Its economic benefits for the US would be modest at best. Above all, the deal is sadly indicative of a deeper failing in Trump’s Ukraine policy. The president genuinely desires peace in that country, but his strategic blinders and indiscipline keep making that task harder.
The details of the deal are dispiriting. The US has agreed to temporarily lift sanctions so Russia can bring about 2 million barrels of diesel to market immediately (with about 13 million barrels committed in total), in hopes of driving down prices at the pump in the US before the midterm elections next month. The deal follows growing US frustration with Ukraine’s drone and missile strikes on Russian energy infrastructure, which have added to stress on global markets. It is not clear if the agreement would ease that pressure, given that the volumes involved are relatively small and the real problem in global energy markets is the president’s war with Iran.
However, the deal would have a strategic impact, by weakening the push to cut Western purchases of Russian energy. It threatens to undo a year’s worth of European efforts to convince Trump that Russia, not Ukraine, is the primary obstacle to peace. And it creates a perverse scenario in which Trump fills the coffers of a neo-fascist autocracy while penalizing Ukraine for targeting Russian President Vladimir Putin’s war economy in self-defense.
Illustration: Mountain People
A bipartisan group of senators has already condemned the deal. Trump has defended it and announced an “energy ceasefire” between Ukraine and Russia — a breakthrough more imagined than real.
Whatever comes of this episode, it illustrates how election-year incentives and economic blowback from the Iran war are affecting US foreign policy in theaters far beyond the Middle East. It is also a window into the frustrations of Trump’s bid to end the war in Ukraine.
Trump seems genuinely appalled by the killing. He has strong strategic incentives to seek a peace deal, amid a potential forever-war in the Persian Gulf and a rising Chinese threat in the Pacific — but his approach to peacemaking has done more harm than good.
To be fair, a realistic strategy would have included some of Trump’s initiatives, such as pushing the Europeans to take primary responsibility for aiding Ukraine. It would also involve quietly urging Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy’s government to accept that it would not recapture all the territory it has lost to Russia or become a member of NATO.
Yet the other half of this strategy would have involved a concerted effort to ratchet up sanctions pressure on Russia, consistent support for Ukraine’s punishing deep-strike campaign, and strong measures to convince Putin that he cannot simply outlast US support for Ukraine or wait for the Western coalition to fracture. Here, the record is bleak.
Since his Oval Office showdown with Zelenskiy in February last year, Trump has repeatedly feuded with the Ukrainian leader in public and threatened to withdraw US intelligence and military support. He has brawled with European allies not just in good causes (burden sharing), but also in bad ones (acquiring Greenland). His administration has sometimes taken Russia’s side in seeking to influence European elections; it might withdraw significant US forces from the continent just as Moscow’s hybrid warfare campaign intensifies. Trump and his aides also convey the strong impression that they want to get back to business with Moscow, once the pesky war in Ukraine is cleared away.
All this has surely encouraged Putin to think he can divide the US from Ukraine and from Europe if he shows enough bloody-minded patience. It gives him confidence he can win the war in Washington even if he cannot win it on the battlefield in Donetsk. Even when the administration seeks peace by offering up major Ukrainian concessions — as Trump did at his summit with Putin in Alaska last year — these efforts cannot satiate Moscow’s sweeping demands.
Trump’s Ukraine peacemaking has been a self-defeating experience that reflects two of his worst strategic flaws.
First, he has consistently misdiagnosed the source of the deadlock. He often seems more frustrated with Ukraine’s insistence on surviving as an independent nation than with Russia’s obsessive drive to snuff that independence out. He insists, against all evidence to the contrary, that Putin wants peace more than Zelenskiy.
That view might reflect Trump’s spheres-of-influence mentality, which holds that smaller powers must accommodate larger powers, but it blinds him to the fact that Putin seeks Ukrainian surrender as part of his larger geopolitical assault on the West. The Russian leader would only quit when the price of persistence becomes too high.
Second, a president who prioritizes quick fixes fails at the hard work of strategy. Peacemaking in Ukraine was never going to be easy. It demands deftly mixing pressure and diplomacy with Moscow; it requires sustaining Western solidarity while moving toward unsatisfying compromises.
However, Trump lacks the patience for careful, coordinated statecraft; he disdains consultation with allies. So he has repeatedly launched ill-considered peace initiatives that panic Kyiv and Europe, but fail to move Putin.
Now, Trump has struck a diesel deal that would have scant economic benefits and serious strategic costs. He is, reportedly, threatening to abandon Ukraine unless it drops its deep-strike campaign against Russian energy targets — that is, its best tool for making the price of Putin’s war prohibitive.
In the process, Trump is depleting US leverage, by encouraging Putin to continue his onslaught, and squandering US influence in Kyiv. Peace in Ukraine is a worthy destination. Alas, Trump has no idea how to get there.
Hal Brands is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist and the Henry Kissinger distinguished professor at Johns Hopkins University’s School of Advanced International Studies. Brands is also a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, the author of The Landscape of Power: Geography and the Rise and Fall of Nations, and a senior adviser to Macro Advisory Partners. This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.
Taiwan might just give up. That’s the argument Simon Shuster made in The Atlantic’s October issue. The US is unreliable, the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) leadership is aligned with the Chinese Communist Party (CCP), and Taiwan does not have the military capability to defend itself in a prolonged war without help. What hope does Taiwan have? Quite a bit more, in fact, than Shuster lets on. Shuster points to genuine problems. The first Donald Trump administration had a mostly positive record on Taiwan policy. It regularized the arms sales process, enhanced the military-to-military relationship, and treated Taiwan more like a normal

EU-GCC summit postponed due to Houthi militia attacks on Saudi Arabia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:28:56 UTC
01:28:56 KST

The second European Union-Gulf Cooperation Council (EU-GCC) Summit, scheduled for October 24 in Riyadh, has been postponed amid escalating attacks by the Houthi militia on Saudi Arabia.
The GCC announced the postponement on Thursday, saying both sides would agree on a new date.
GCC Secretary-General Jasem Albudaiwi said the decision reflected “the continued attempts by the terrorist Houthi militia to target Saudi Arabia and its civilian objects, threatening the security and safety of civilians”, as well as the extended suspension of operations at King Khalid International Airport and concerns over the safety of participating delegations.
In a separate statement on Thursday, the EU reaffirmed the strategic importance of its partnership with the GCC and its commitment to strengthening ties and maintaining the momentum established since the first summit in October 2024.
Rise in attacks
Albudaiwi said both sides remained determined to create suitable conditions for holding the summit and advancing cooperation across various fields.
The postponement comes as attacks by the Houthi militia on Saudi Arabia have intensified since July. Riyadh’s airport has been targeted several times in recent days, prompting a suspension of operations.
Five Saudi airports have been targeted by the Houthi militia since October 5, leaving 20 people dead and hundreds injured, damaging property and disrupting air traffic.
The latest developments are part of a military escalation that began in July and is the most extensive since the relative calm in Yemen following a truce that began in April 2022.
Saudi Arabia has led a military coalition supporting Yemen’s internationally recognised government against the Houthi militia since 2015. The militia has controlled the capital, Sanaa, and several provinces since 2014.

Why are eight US states suing OpenAI?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:28:44 UTC
01:28:44 KST

Why are eight US states suing OpenAI?
They allege ChatGPT has caused harm to their residents, coaching its users — including teenagers — to harm themselves or others.
Eight US states have filed the most significant coordinated state action against tech giant OpenAI, adding to a wave of legal challenges that the firm is facing as it prepares for a public listing.
Recent legal and regulatory challenges have highlighted concerns about how AI chatbots and social media platforms are used and triggered discussions on policies for identifying and addressing user conversations that threaten violence.
Calls have been growing for AI companies to be held accountable for the impact of their digital platforms on users, specifically children, who are particularly susceptible to addiction and other harms.
What is this legal action about?
Florida filed the first lawsuit in June, alleging that the platform has harmed children by enabling information to be gathered by school shooters, providing access to guidance on self-harm and using addictive algorithms to keep young users hooked.
It cited a shooting at Florida State University in Tallahassee in April 2025, when a 20-year-old gunman shot dead two adults and wounded five others. According to the lawsuit, gunman Phoenix Ikner consulted OpenAI’s ChatGPT programme about what type of weapon and ammunition to use and at what time campus would be busiest.
On Wednesday, attorneys general from eight states – Iowa, Kansas, Arizona, Arkansas, Idaho, Montana, Nebraska and West Virginia – said they had also sued OpenAI in courts across the country.
They all claim ChatGPT has caused harm to their residents, alleging the chatbot has coached its users – including teenagers – to harm themselves or others.
Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird said in a statement that OpenAI was “hurting kids and they are lying to Iowans.”
“OpenAI claims ChatGPT is safe while it’s giving dangerous medical advice, encouraging people to hurt others, and coaching people to commit suicide—all while pretending to be their fake friend,” she said.
West Virginia Attorney General JB McCuskey said the chatbot lacks adequate safeguards for sensitive conversations involving suicide, school shootings and self-harm. “We must do all we can to protect kids,” McCuskey said.
What are the allegations?
The legal action alleges that ChatGPT has been designed to be “agreeable and engaging to earn the trust of users”. In doing so, it reinforces delusions, encourages dangerous behaviour and assists users in planning violence like mass shootings.
Additionally, the suits accuse OpenAI of violating state consumer protection laws by misleading users about the safety of their AI tool, which in fact poses a danger to the health of the states’ residents.
The states are seeking orders forcing OpenAI to make substantial changes to how ChatGPT works, as well as measures barring the company from developing AI models that can improve themselves until it can ensure those models are aligned with human values.
Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers said the lawsuit “simply holds OpenAI to the same standards under Nebraska law as any other company”.
How has OpenAI responded?
OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri gave a statement to the media, saying that the company has “built industry-leading age-specific protections into our product that many other AI products lack”.
“While no system can be perfect, we’ll continue to work with experts to inform our work and build additional safeguards, such as the parental controls, break reminders and age-appropriate model protections that exist today,” Pusateri said.
“We’re committed to working with states on advancing pragmatic AI policies that apply to the entire AI industry, not just one company.”
What other lawsuits is the tech giant facing?
OpenAI is also facing dozens of lawsuits by private plaintiffs alleging ChatGPT helped users plan mass shootings or other violence.
A mother, whose two children use the chatbot, alleged in a proposed class action lawsuit filed on Tuesday in San Francisco federal court that OpenAI illegally profits from the personal information and data that minors share with ChatGPT.
The lawsuit claims the chatbot is designed to collect data and information from minors, which is then used to train OpenAI’s AI models. Minors can’t consent to the use of their data under California law.
In July, a Florida pastor sued OpenAI and its chief executive, Sam Altman, claiming ChatGPT’s inaccurate medical advice kept him from seeking treatment for recurrent dizzy spells, leading him to suffer a pulmonary embolism that nearly killed him.
OpenAI is also facing a series of lawsuits over its failure to alert authorities to threats made on ChatGPT in advance of one of the worst mass shootings in Canada’s history.
The province of British Columbia filed a lawsuit against OpenAI in a California court in September, seven months after 18-year-old Jesse Van Rootselaar shot eight people in the small Canadian town of Tumbler Ridge, including his mother and half-brother, before dying by suicide.
The lawsuit alleges that OpenAI had failed to notify authorities about concerning user interactions on ChatGPT, accusing the company of “aiding and abetting a mass shooting”.
Victims of that shooting and their families filed 30 lawsuits against OpenAI in the Northern District of California in the San Francisco division at the start of September, alleging that “ChatGPT played a role in the mass shooting and OpenAI could have, and should have, prevented it”.
OpenAI said it had flagged a ChatGPT account linked to Van Rootselaar for abuse eight months before the shooting, and deactivated it, but did not alert police at the time because the user’s content “did not meet the higher threshold required for referral” – meaning the company did not believe it indicated a credible, imminent risk of a plan for violent acts.

A senior UN official warned on Thursday that the situation in the Gaza Strip and the occupied West Bank is dangerously fragile, saying a return to war must be avoided at all costs, Anadolu reports.
Briefing the UN Security Council on Palestine, Ramiz Alakbarov, UN acting special coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process, marked the anniversary of the Oct. 7 events, saying Palestinians and Israelis need a political horizon.
“Palestinians and Israelis deserve more than short-term fixes. They deserve a credible path to peace and finally an end to this conflict,” he said. “The international community must move beyond words and take concrete actions to ensure the future of security and dignity of the people. It is time to return to a genuine peace process.”
Turning to Gaza, Alakbarov noted that one year has passed since a ceasefire was completed. “While some progress has been made, the situation remains extremely fragile,” he said.
He said Israeli military operations have continued, “causing some 1,500 fatalities, including more than 320 children.”
Alakbarov described families in Gaza living in worn-out tents, overcrowded displacement sites and badly damaged buildings, with water and sanitation systems devastated. “Most of Gaza still lives in darkness,” he said.
“People in Gaza must not be forced to endure another winter without safe shelter and basic services,” he stressed.
Highlighting the needs of children, he said, “Emergency assistance alone is not enough. Sustainable recovery and political progress must advance together.”
On the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, Alakbarov said the situation continues to deteriorate amid Israeli military operations, movement restrictions, displacement and Palestinian attacks. He said settler violence persists at “extremely high levels,” with daily attacks on Palestinians.
Describing his assessment as “realistic,” Alakbarov said he felt compelled to raise concerns before the council.
“Today, I feel obliged to sound the alarm. In Gaza, desperation is palpable,” he said.
He warned that frustration among Gaza’s population cannot continue to build indefinitely and described the risk of a return to war as extremely high. “This must be avoided at all costs,” he said.
“The West Bank is also at a boiling point,” he added.

Egypt becomes first country to retain WHO gold-tier Hep C status
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:23:16 UTC
01:23:16 KST

Breadcrumb
Egypt becomes world's first to retain WHO hepatitis C elimination status
Egypt has become the first country in the world to receive certification for maintaining the World Health Organization’s gold-tier status in its efforts to eliminate hepatitis C, following a review of its achievements in combating the virus between 2023 and 2025.
Until the 2010s, Egypt had the highest prevalence of Hep C globally, affecting roughly 10% of the population, largely due to historical public health campaigns involving unsterilised medical needles in the 20th century.
But on Wednesday, the country received the certificate from the WHO after the organisation confirmed that it had met the requirements for retaining the status, which it first obtained in October 2023.
WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus presented the certificate to Egyptian Health Minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar during a news conference in Cairo, held on the sidelines of the 73rd session of the WHO Regional Committee for the Eastern Mediterranean.
The WHO said the recognition reflected Egypt’s continued progress in tackling Hep C. The review of the country’s efforts between 2023 and 2025 confirmed that it had fulfilled the requirements for maintaining the gold-tier status.
The decision had previously been approved in July 2026 by the WHO Regional Committee for the Validation of the Elimination of HIV, Hepatitis and Sexually Transmitted Infections.
Egypt's Health Minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar said the country’s achievements were built on the 100 Million Health campaign, launched in 2018. The campaign screened 68 million Egyptians and provided free treatment to around 4.5 million people living with the virus, using locally produced medicines.
In a statement, the WHO said Egypt had moved away from large-scale screening campaigns towards a sustainable and integrated approach to combating Hep C during the period in which it maintained its gold-tier status.
The approach includes strengthening routine screening, diagnosis, treatment, surveillance and prevention, while expanding access to services for people living with the virus.
The organisation highlighted Egypt’s expansion of screening, diagnosis and treatment services, as well as efforts to strengthen governance and oversight between 2025 and 2030.
Other measures include drawing up a national plan to sustain the elimination of Hep C and continuing to integrate hepatitis services into primary healthcare and the country’s comprehensive health insurance system.
Egypt has also worked to improve laboratory quality and disease surveillance systems, while maintaining high standards for blood and injection safety, according to the WHO.
The WHO first awarded Egypt gold-tier status in October 2023, making it the first country in the world to receive the recognition for its progress towards eliminating Hep C.
Over roughly a decade, Egypt, a country of more than 120 million people today, reduced the prevalence of the virus from 10% to 0.38%.
During that period, the country diagnosed 87% of people living with the virus and provided treatment to 93% of those diagnosed.
These figures exceeded the WHO’s gold-tier benchmarks, which require countries to diagnose at least 80% of people living with Hep C and treat at least 70% of those diagnosed.

Santa Ana Winds Trigger Wildfire Warnings in Southern California. Here's What To Know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:22:13 UTC
01:22:13 KST

Southern California towns are on high alert as the first Santa Ana winds of the season are set to arrive.
The red flag warning put out by the National Weather Service (NWS) Wednesday evening follows a relatively quiet wildfire season so far in California. Only 300,000 acres have burned since Jan. 1, compared to the over one million acres that fires have usually burned by mid-October.
Why are Santa Ana winds so dangerous?
Santa Ana winds blow in from the desert, typically between the months of September and May. The winds bring warmer temperatures and drier air to Southern California. They also greatly increase the risk of wildfires—warm winds coupled with summer drought can often make for a dangerous combination. The January 2025 fires that tore through the Pacific Palisades and Altadena were fueled by Santa Ana wind gusts that reached 100 m.p.h.
This week’s winds will not be as strong, according to NWS predictions. But that doesn’t mean the area is in the clear. The NWS has warned that, if any fires ignite, “conditions are favorable for extreme fire behavior.”
What areas of Southern California are under fire warnings?
The NWS has issued a red flag warning for the Los Angeles County San Gabriel Valley forecast zone that will stay in effect until Saturday evening. The most extreme conditions are expected in the Ventura and Los Angeles County valleys and mountains, particularly Santa Clarita, Thousand Oaks, and Simi Valley.
Southern California Edison is considering shutting off power to some 250,000 customers. Areas in Northern and Central California, including parts of Alameda county, Fresno County, and Napa County could also face power outages. Shutting down power helps stop downed power lines or aging infrastructure from sparking fires.
Recent rain means that San Diego and Orange County will face less of a fire risk, though the areas should still expect to see strong winds.
If you live in an impacted area, sign up for local emergency alerts, plan for power outages, and avoid any outdoor activities that might ignite sparks like BBQs, campfires, or improperly discarding cigarette butts.
One Southern California town is even encouraging residents to secure hallowed decorations—the giant skeleton and inflatable pumpkins haunting front lawns. High winds can turn Halloween decorations into hazards,” the city of Pasadena said in a Facebook post. “Secure them before winds pick up.”

Russia’s New Drone Base Could Launch Over 100 Jet-Powered Drones Daily, Expert Warns
Unknown

- World
Russia’s New Drone Base Could Launch Over 100 Jet-Powered Drones Daily, Expert Warns
Russia has nearly completed a major new base for launching jet-powered attack drones near Ukraine after just six weeks of construction, according to Reuters on October 15.
Satellite imagery from Planet Labs and Airbus, reviewed by Reuters, shows the facility in Russia’s Rostov region expanding from an empty field on August 31 into a complex covering approximately 0.9 square kilometers, equivalent to roughly 126 soccer fields.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the Reuters investigation, DroneSec founder Mike Monnik assessed that the facility could launch Russia’s newer Geran-4 and Geran-5 jet-powered drones.
Satellite images reveal eight launch platforms on the western side, with rails installed on two and construction continuing on others. Monnik estimated that the base could potentially launch 100 or more jet-powered drones within 24 hours, depending on operational requirements and available weapons.
“The speed of construction … demonstrates the ease with which Russia can bring now-established offensive capabilities to bear rapidly,” Monnik stated, as quoted by Reuters. He assessed that the facility could become fully operational within weeks, if not sooner.
The installation is located approximately 3.5 kilometers from Russia’s Millerovo air base, which hosts the 31st Guards Fighter Aviation Regiment. DroneSec assessed that the new facility likely benefits from the air defense systems protecting the military airfield, potentially complicating Ukrainian efforts to strike it, Reuters reported.
Russia increased its deployment of jet-powered drones roughly sixfold during a three-month period this summer, according to Ukrainian military data previously examined by Reuters. These drones can reach speeds of up to 600 kilometers per hour, making them substantially harder for Ukrainian interceptor drones to engage.
Drone infrastructure around Millerovo has already drawn repeated Ukrainian strikes.
On August 30, Ukrainian forces hit a facility in the area used to store, prepare and launch Russian attack drones, roughly 170 kilometers from the front line.
The overnight strike sparked a fire and coincided with an attack on the Yeysk military airfield in Krasnodar Krai. Earlier, Ukrainian drones targeted a Nebo-U radar station at the Millerovo airfield, a site used to launch Shahed drones and other UAVs against Ukraine.

Comprising 54 solar panels, three inverters and six batteries, the system is intended to support more than 1,800 students by providing a cleaner and more reliable electricity supply.
The "Yunnan Hand in Hand Program" comprises small-scale, practical and effective public welfare projects designed to benefit communities across South Asia, Southeast Asia and the Indian Ocean region.
Since the launch of the program in 2022, 56 projects have been carried out in Myanmar in areas including infrastructure, clean energy, safe drinking water, agricultural technology, environmental conservation, educational support, cultural exchange, capacity building and healthcare. BEIJING, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- China's online literature market revenue more than doubled from 26.72 billion yuan (about 3.97 billion U.S. dollars) in 2021 to 57.47 billion yuan in 2025, according to a report released Thursday at a national online literature conference held in Beijing.
The report, released by the China Audio-video and Digital Publishing Association at the conference's opening ceremony, said the online literature sector had maintained steady growth during the 14th Five-Year Plan period (2021-2025), with progress in content development, overseas expansion and industry governance.
Revenue from overseas online literature markets rose from 2.91 billion yuan in 2021 to 6.98 billion yuan in 2025, outpacing domestic market growth, the report said. The number of works distributed overseas, including original works created by overseas authors, increased from 314,600 to 933,100.
The report noted that the total number of authors registered on online literature platforms climbed from 23.41 million in 2021 to 33.73 million in 2025, while the user base expanded from 460 million to 646 million.
In 2025 alone, China's online literature market revenue grew 15.99 percent year on year, while overseas market revenue surged 45.03 percent, the report showed. The overseas expansion of adaptations across multiple formats, including films, television productions and short dramas, was a major growth driver.
In recent years, Chinese films, TV series, web novels and video games have gained growing popularity overseas. The country's online literature has reached hundreds of millions of readers in more than 200 countries and regions.
In the next five years, China will enhance copyright protection and transaction rules in online literature and arts, while also improving its international IP protection system and stepping up IP cooperation through multilateral international mechanisms, according to the country's 15th five-year plan for intellectual property protection and utilization.
The plan set the goal of making decisive progress in building China into an IP powerhouse by 2030, with its IP competitiveness ranking among the world's best by 2035. Another target is to raise the share of copyright industries' value added in GDP to 7.53 percent by 2030. ■

Israel says commercial goods not entering Gaza over Hamas tax dispute
JERUSALEM - Israel on Oct 15 said commercial goods usually delivered into Gaza by private merchants had not entered the beleaguered territory for days because of Hamas threats and a taxation scheme, an accusation the group rejected.
Despite a fragile ceasefire observed since October 2025, the Gaza Strip remains engulfed in a severe humanitarian crisis and the alleged dispute between Hamas and merchants threatens to further cut off supplies to the territory.
Gaza, a tiny territory surrounded by Israel, Egypt and the Mediterranean Sea, has been under blockade even before Hamas’s Oct 7, 2023 attack sparked the most recent war.
But COGAT, the Israeli defence ministry agency responsible for civilian affairs in the Palestinian territories, said it told senior international officials that merchants had suspended coordination for the entry of goods into Gaza “until further notice” because of what it described as Hamas coercion.
In a letter to international representatives involved in implementing the ceasefire, COGAT said merchants reported that Hamas demanded about 10,000 shekels (S$4,132) for every truck into Gaza and that traders sell around 30 per cent of goods in cash instead of bank transfers.
The agency also cited reports that Hamas security personnel had arrested the son of a merchant who refused to comply with the demands, prompting traders to suspend operations out of fear for their safety.
Hamas rejected the allegations in a letter addressed to mediators including Egypt, Qatar and Turkey, saying it “categorically” denied imposing taxes or government fees on commercial trucks.
It said it had not collected taxes or fees on commercial activity in the past three years of war because of the humanitarian and economic conditions in Gaza.
Hamas said the 10,000-shekel figure referred to a “voluntary community initiative” by Gaza’s businesspeople to put money into a “national fund” for relief projects, while the transaction requirement was to inject “cash liquidity” into the territory.
COGAT said the private sector accounted for roughly half of all trucks entering Gaza each week and warned the suspension could undermine the ceasefire agreement.
COGAT said Israel had not initiated the suspension of coordination, but the merchants.
Nickolay Mladenov, the Gaza representative of the US-backed Board of Peace tasked with implementing the ceasefire, said he had received COGAT’s letter and condemned reported “threats and coercion” against merchants.
“Such practices are unacceptable and must end immediately,” Mladenov wrote on X, adding that interference in supply chains increased the suffering of Gaza’s civilians.
The International Organisation for Migration (IOM) last week called for Israel to ease the “constraints” on the entry of critical supplies into Gaza. AFP

According to govt, 8,133 gigawatt hour of solar power was curtailed or restricted during April-June 2026 due to transmission constraints and to maintain grid security. NEW DELHI: New Delhi: India needs to align power generation plans with the time required to build transmission infrastructure to meet future electricity demand reliably and affordably, energy sector experts said at RE: DIALOGUES 2026 in the capital.They flagged right-of-way constraints, the availability of transformers and the distance between renewable energy generation centres and consumption hubs as key challenges for power sector planning.The mismatch between renewable energy generation and transmission readiness has emerged as a major concern. According to ICRA data for May 2026, about 18.1 GW, or 33% of the 54.8 GW of recently commissioned renewable energy capacity, was relying on temporary grid access because permanent transmission infrastructure was incomplete. Delays in transmission lines and substations can leave completed solar and wind projects unable to evacuate their full generation capacity.
The constraints are also leading to power curtailment. According to govt, 8,133 gigawatt hour of solar power was curtailed or restricted during April-June 2026 due to transmission constraints and to maintain grid security. The mismatch highlights the need to synchronise the commissioning of generation projects with transmission lines and substations to ensure electricity reaches consumption centres.
The discussion, organised by Policy Perspectives Foundation and Orange Circle Energy, also highlighted the need to strengthen electricity distribution infrastructure, ensure regulatory stability and direct investments towards supporting infrastructure to meet rising demand.Bhupinder Bhalla, former secretary in the ministry of new and renewable energy, said India’s energy transition must be aligned with its wider development priorities, including domestic manufacturing, technology development, investment and job creation. He called for coordinated planning between the Centre and states to address infrastructure and regulatory challenges.Nikesh Sinha, founder of Orange Circle Energy, said India needs to look beyond its ability to generate electricity and assess how much power it will need, where demand will emerge and how reliably it can be delivered.
“Transmission infrastructure takes time to build, and generation and consumption centres are not always in the same locations. Anticipating these requirements and aligning transmission planning with generation, while also considering decentralised solutions, will be critical to meeting India’s future electricity needs,” Sinha said.The experts also discussed the need to channel existing public resources towards priorities such as renewable energy and disaster resilience. Safi Ahsan Rizvi, former adviser to the National Disaster Management Authority and associated with the Policy Perspectives Foundation, said better allocation of existing resources could help unlock investment.

The 2025 clashes erupted in Syria's Sweida province between armed Druze factions and Bedouin fighters, with government security forces and some tribal groups then intervening on the side of the Bedouins.
More than 2,000 people were killed, including 789 Druze civilians, according to the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights watchdog.
A committee set up by the Syrian government said it had documented 1,760 deaths.
At the time, government forces and their allies were accused of executing civilians and other abuses.
Israel, which also has a Druze population, intervened militarily during the clashes, with strikes in Sweida and against government targets in Damascus, saying it was defending the minority community.
Government-aligned forces later withdrew from Sweida city, leaving a fragile ceasefire in place, and in July of this year Damascus said it had begun trying suspects over the violence.
Since the December 2024 ouster of longtime Syrian ruler Bashar al-Assad, Israel has carried out hundreds of strikes in Syria and sent troops into a UN-patrolled buffer zone that had separated Israeli and Syrian forces in the Golan since 1974.
It has also carried out repeated incursions deeper into Syrian territory and has vowed to keep troops in a so-called "security zone" in southern Syria, where it seeks a broader demilitarised area.
Syria's new leaders have condemned Israeli military action in the country's south but have refrained from responding with force.
Despite the tensions, Syria and Israel have held several rounds of direct talks as they edge towards a security agreement.

Fewer than one in thirty reservists deployed last year
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:30:15 BST
00:30:15 KST

Just under three per cent of Britain’s reservists were mobilised for operations in the last financial year, with the proportion falling for a second year running as overall reserve strength declined, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Gordon McKee, the Labour member for Glasgow South, asked what proportion of reservists had been mobilised for operations in each of the last five years.
Calvin Bailey, Parliamentary Under-Secretary and Minister for Veterans and People, said: “Our Reservists make a vital contribution to the nation’s security, supporting operations at home and overseas.”
The figures he supplied cover Future Reserves 2020 personnel and serving ex-regular reserves. Strength stood at 39,400 at the end of the 2021/22 financial year, 37,460 a year later, 36,220 at the end of 2023/24, 35,940 at the end of 2024/25 and 36,280 at the end of 2025/26, the first rise in the series.
Deployments over the same period moved on a different curve. In 2021/22 a total of 920 reservists deployed, which was 2.3 per cent of the force. That rose to 1,730 in 2022/23, or 4.6 per cent, and peaked at 1,850 in 2023/24, or 5.1 per cent. The figure then dropped to 1,160 in 2024/25, which was 3.2 per cent, and to 1,060 in 2025/26, or 2.9 per cent.
The peak years coincide with the heaviest period of British support to Ukraine, including Operation Interflex, the training mission for Ukrainian recruits run from sites across the UK, which drew on reservists alongside regulars and allied instructors.
Reserve strength has been a persistent problem for the department for well over a decade. The Future Reserves 2020 programme set a target of 30,000 trained Army Reserve soldiers that proved difficult to hit, and the services have struggled with the recruitment and retention of part-time personnel for most of the past decade. The Strategic Defence Review last year committed to growing the reserves and gave them a larger role in homeland defence, including the protection of critical national infrastructure, and the department has since set out investment in equipment for reserve units.
Mobilisation of a reservist can be compulsory or voluntary, and employers have statutory obligations and rights around it.
