Last weekend, Taiwan celebrated Double Ten National Day, marking 115 years since the Wuchang Uprising.
An Army CH-47SD Chinook carried a massive 12-by-18-meter ROC flag across downtown Taipei, accompanied by two UH-60M Black Hawk helicopters, passing over vibrant celebrations in front of the Presidential Office Building.
The spectacle made global headlines, with Reuters even titling its report “Giant Taiwan flag flies from helicopter for national day, defying Beijing.”
Yet the irony is that the flag is not originally Taiwanese, and its display hardly represents defiance of Beijing given that ROC flags have filled Double Ten celebrations in Taiwan for decades.
There is a deeper paradox. Double Ten commemorates an event that did not take place in Taiwan and did not significantly involve Taiwanese people.
Double Ten commemorates the 1911 Wuchang Uprising in Wuhan, China. It took place while Taiwan was under Japanese rule.
A historical event fundamentally external to Taiwan’s own historical narrative and collective memory will inevitably struggle to resonate widely with Taiwanese.
The uprising helped overthrow the Qing dynasty and paved the way for the establishment of the Republic of China. It was not until 1949 that the ROC government relocated to Taiwan.
Although Double Ten distinguishes Taiwan’s national commemoration from the People’s Republic of China’s Oct. 1 National Day, it continues to tie Taiwan to an outdated pan-Chinese political ideology.
To solidify Taiwan’s identity, break free from historical constraints, and signal its separate sovereignty to the international community, the country should establish a new and genuinely Taiwanese national day.
More troubling is that the giant flags flown over Taipei last Saturday still serve as a stark reminder to many Taiwanese of the KMT’s authoritarian legacy.
The upper-left “blue sky, white sun” portion of the ROC flag is also used by the KMT as its party emblem. After the ROC took control of Taiwan in 1945 and the KMT government relocated there in 1949, the party-state embedded ROC institutions and symbols throughout Taiwan.
As a minority regime ruling over a largely local Taiwanese population, the KMT imposed martial law to maintain political control and suppress threats to its rule.
Its central narrative for justifying the suspension of constitutional democracy, freezing elections, and almost four decades of authoritarian one-party rule was that the ROC government remained the sole legitimate government of all China and Taiwan was merely a temporary base from which it would eventually launch a counteroffensive to recover the “mainland.”
No other day of the year displayed that narrative more vividly.
To project legitimacy, the authoritarian KMT government gathered foreign dignitaries and overseas Chinese delegates for grand Double Ten celebrations in Taipei.
Outside this elite circle, many of whom had little or no connection to Taiwan, many Taiwanese looked on with indifference or quietly shook their heads for fear of the repercussions of disrupting the regime’s manufactured narrative.
Many local Taiwanese also felt alienated by Double Ten celebrations during martial law, which centered on a China-focused national narrative expressed overwhelmingly in Mandarin.
This excluded Hoklo, Hakka, and Indigenous Taiwanese communities, many of whose members did not speak Mandarin. For many, authoritarian ROC governance represented language erasure and suppression of culture and identity rather than national liberation.
Although the holiday can counter Beijing’s narrative by emphasizing the distinction between the ROC and PRC, Double Ten nevertheless commemorates the founding story of a political system born in China.
Celebrating a national day with origins in the heart of China continues to tie Taiwan to a Greater China political framework. Beijing can exploit this ambiguity to bolster its narrative that Taiwan is an integral part of China that must ultimately be “unified,” by force if necessary.
It also reinforces the international ambiguity Beijing has worked to shape.
When international media report that Taiwan is celebrating a Chinese uprising as its national day, it can blur the reality of Taiwan’s current de facto independence and its existence as a sovereign political entity separate from China.
Breaking free of this Greater China framework will require a new national anchor.
Double Ten represents to many Taiwanese an imported historical narrative and a dark authoritarian past. Taiwan deserves better.
The country is no longer an authoritarian regime in exile, but a vibrant modern democracy. Celebrating a violent historical event that did not even take place in Taiwan sits awkwardly beside the democratic values that distinguish modern Taiwan so sharply from China.
While Taiwan’s government and civil society promote those values, celebrating a date tied to bloodshed in China more than a century ago risks confusing the story Taiwan tells about itself to the world.
A national day should also belong to the land and the people living on it. The Wuchang Uprising obviously did not take place in Taiwan.
Without the coercive machinery that once imposed a singular national narrative, it is difficult to expect Taiwan’s diverse communities to rally around a commemoration so distant from their own histories.
The national fabric would be better woven around a Taiwan-centered cause that people of different languages, cultures, backgrounds, generations, and newer immigrant communities can share. It would also help disentangle Taiwan’s statehood from the ROC’s founding history in China.
Taiwan needs a forward-looking national day that celebrates its democratic progress.
March 23 or May 20 could serve as alternatives. March 23 marks Taiwan’s first direct presidential election in 1996, while May 20 is the traditional inauguration day for Taiwan’s democratically elected presidents.
Either could serve as a reminder of the democratic mandate of Taiwan’s people and their collective journey toward self-government. May 20 could even allow national celebrations to coincide with presidential inaugurations every four years.
With China increasing pressure to distort Taiwan’s political reality, there is an even greater need for the country to step out of Double Ten’s Chinese shadow and tell the world that Taiwan is Taiwan.
A genuinely Taiwanese national day would make clear that Taiwan’s modern identity is rooted in the history, democratic choices, and political sovereignty of the people who live here.
Rath Wang is a political commentator based in Taipei focusing on Taiwan’s politics, media, civil society, and key issues influencing Taiwan’s future. He is a media producer and host of current affairs talk shows and podcasts and has worked on political campaigns and lived in Taiwan, Japan, Thailand, and the US.

El Nino a 'terrifying' threat to coral reefs: UN biodiversity expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
15:23:16 UTC
00:23:16 KST

El Nino a ‘terrifying’ threat to coral reefs: UN biodiversity expert
PARIS, France – A super El Nino fuelling record ocean temperatures poses a “terrifying” threat to the world’s fragile coral reefs, the chair of the UN’s expert nature panel told AFP.
Marine scientist David Obura said the exceptional El Nino pattern building strength in the tropical Pacific could drive vulnerable coral species even closer toward extinction.
Corals are heat sensitive and particularly vulnerable to climate change, which is heating the world’s oceans and increasing the frequency and intensity of damaging bleaching events.
But 2026’s El Nino layers “a terrifying level of additional risk”, said Obura, a Kenyan reef expert and chair of IPBES, the UN’s expert scientific panel on biodiversity.
The warming phase of a natural climate cycle, El Nino events temporarily elevate global temperatures, altering cloud and wind patterns, and raise the risk of damaging weather.
Global forecasters expect this episode to be the strongest on record, and sea surface temperatures in parts of the Pacific have already hit all-time highs months before its expected peak.
That greatly concerns Obura, who recalled the damaging impact of a previous super El Nino episode in 1997/98.
“That this coming event is worse than that, after three intervening global bleaching events ... is a terrifying reality,” he said.
Significant worsening
Obura led a major reassessment of coral health published in Nature on Thursday that reported a sharp deterioration in reef-building species since the last global census in 2008.
“Our results show that by 2020, nearly half of coral species were at elevated relative risk of extinction” with climate change the main driver of this decline, wrote Obura and dozens of top scientists.
The review covered hundreds of species on the IUCN’s “red list” – icons like staghorn and table corals whose mineral skeletons give reefs their dazzling three-dimensional complexity.
This “indicates conditions for corals are worsening significantly... not at all surprising given the accelerated warming and lack of abatement of global drivers of coral decline”, said Obura.
But the study was completed in 2020 and the findings today would be even bleaker, he said.
Since then, global ocean temperatures have soared to unprecedented highs and the worst coral bleaching episode on record between 2023 and 2025 caused widespread mortality across reefs.
“It is entirely possible that reassessing the status of corals just after this coming El Nino may show them to have crossed the 50 percent mark of the proportion of species at elevated risk of extinction,” said Obura.
In 2025, scientists warned that warm-water coral reefs had almost certainly crossed a point of no return as oceans warm beyond a level most can survive.
The study in Nature said that projected rises in ocean temperatures and other pressures “primarily determined when and where, rather than if, conditions will become unviable for corals”.
“When they hit their threshold the collapse of reefs in that region could be precipitous and we don’t know if that is five, 15 or 30 years into the future, or maybe this year with the super El Nino ramping up,” said Obura. AFP

Man with suitcase full of snakes stopped at German airport
- Published
A man has been stopped at Cologne Bonn Airport in Germany after trying to smuggle in more than 90 lizards and venomous snakes.
Customs officials said the 45-year-old Mexican firefighter had looked "conspicuously nervous" as he tried to go through the green - nothing to declare - exit at the airport.
They conducted a drugs test on the man - which came back positive for cocaine - before proceeding to check his suitcase.
They did not find any drugs, but vipers, rattlesnakes and other species of snakes and lizards, including iguanas, hidden in shampoo and cream bottles, plastic containers and balls of socks.
"My colleagues at the airport are used to a lot when it comes to souvenirs in suitcases, but we've never had 37 live venomous snakes and 55 lizards from Mexico before," said Jens Ahland, spokesman for the Cologne Customs office.
Some were being kept "in inhumane conditions", Ahland said. Others had died during the journey from Mexico City via Istanbul.
The man, who has not been named, told officers that he had brought the animals back as a favour for a Brazilian acquaintance.
He was denied entry to Germany and flown back to Istanbul.
As for the surviving animals, they are being looked after at a snake farm in Germany.
"Last year, we had over 1,300 seizures nationwide involving more than 56,600 protected animals and plants or products made from them," the Customs spokesman said.
Six years ago, 26 rare reptiles - 10 of them dead - smuggled inside parcels of toys and sweets from Mexico, were found by customs officials at Cologne Bonn Airport.
They were destined for private buyers in Germany.

Jaguar Trafficking in Latin America Persists Through Bone Paste and Pet Smuggling
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
15:04:00 UTC
00:04:00 KST

Reported by
Skins in markets, fangs turned into jewelry, and bones processed into paste: the illegal trade in jaguars persists in Latin America. An investigation spanning seven countries points to a primarily local, small-scale business, with evidence of international trafficking in Peru and Suriname.
Between 2023 and 2025, the Wildlife Justice Commission (WJC) investigated the trade of these big cats in Bolivia, Brazil, Colombia, Chile, Panama, Peru, and Suriname. Its findings—shared with OCCRP—describe a market that often relies on sporadic sales opportunities, though the investigation also identified a network trafficking multiple species.
The latest WJC report "The Illegal Jaguar Trade in Latin America: An Updated Picture," published Thursday, found that a significant portion of the demand stems from local buyers, including members of Asian communities residing in the region. These results add nuance to alarms raised in the early 2010s regarding a new international market for jaguar parts targeting China, while not ruling out the continued existence of those connections.
Wildlife Justice Commission Executive Director Olivia Swaak-Goldman told OCCRP that the investigation identified two main types of trade: a local market for handicrafts and jaguar parts, observed in Colombia and Bolivia, and a higher-priced market linked to international demand, including for jaguar bone paste, observed in Suriname.
There, operatives identified suppliers of jaguar bone paste and retailers selling jewelry made from jaguar fangs in the capital, Paramaribo.
Swaak-Goldman said Suriname remained a high-risk country because of its proximity to large jaguar populations and porous borders that facilitate smuggling with neighboring countries, including Brazil and Guyana. She also pointed to demand from certain foreign nationals and the difficulties local authorities face in detecting international trafficking networks.
“Even so, the trade we observed was relatively low-volume and discreet. What made Suriname particularly important was the evidence of links between local wildlife products and international demand.”
The founder of Probios—an environmental organization based in Paramaribo—Erlan Sleur, also described the production of jaguar bone paste. “They make a black paste from it that is sold at an exorbitant price in China,” Sleur confirmed to OCCRP.
Sleur has raised awareness regarding the illegal hunting of jaguars in Suriname’s forested interior—animals targeted for years for use in Asian medicine and luxury goods. When OCCRP visited Sleur in Paramaribo in 2022, he displayed a cage he planned to use to capture jaguars that had accidentally wandered into agricultural fields, hoping to save them from poachers. “Those jaguars—those animals are simply shot,” he said.
According to the WJC report, transactions appeared infrequent, were carried out on demand, and provided supplementary income for the sellers. Records compiled by the organization included the seizure of at least 29 fangs and 16 kilograms of jaguar bone paste in Suriname between 2019 and 2025. At least four suspects were arrested, with two receiving prison sentences.
In Peru, the WJC identified a network of Peruvian citizens and individuals of Chinese origin operating between Lima and Iquitos. Its members offered jaguar parts and trafficked in other wildlife and marine species.
In Bolivia, investigators found vendors selling small quantities of skins, paws, claws, fangs, and handicrafts in La Paz, Santa Cruz, and Trinidad. “Temporary Chinese migrants working as independent contractors on large infrastructure projects are present in some sectors of the illegal trade in Bolivia. Specifically in Trinidad, some local traders stated that there were now fewer buyers of jaguar products, and [noted] that prices had dropped since the completion of a major road construction project, as foreign workers had moved to projects underway in other areas,” the report details.
The WJC found indications that law enforcement pressure had pushed some traders to operate more covertly or abandon the business entirely. However, it also noted gaps in information regarding subsequent judicial proceedings, the demand for live animals, and the ultimate destination of the products in Asia.
Meanwhile, a supplementary review of seizures between 2019 and 2025 revealed a dynamic that field investigations had barely captured: live jaguars were the most frequently seized category, accounting for 38 percent of the records. The majority of these seizures took place in Mexico.
Swaak-Goldman described Mexico as both a source and a destination market for the illegal pet trade in jaguars. She noted that jaguars are harder to breed in captivity than other big cats, such as tigers, and that their rarity makes them prestige animals in that market.
“So we know there is a signal in the seizure data, but we still need to understand how this market operates and what is driving the demand.”
For Swaak-Goldman, the findings offer grounds for cautious optimism.
“The report is not a reason for complacency, but it does provide an encouraging lesson: sustained, targeted enforcement can change the behaviour of traffickers and make an illegal market harder and less profitable to operate.”

International Energy Agency (IEA) members have agreed to accelerate the release of around 100 million barrels of remaining emergency oil stocks, including more than 20 million barrels of diesel, as soon as possible amid continued tightness in global energy markets.
The agency's Governing Board said on Thursday its latest assessments pointed to persistent tightness in oil markets, particularly diesel, following a meeting on energy markets and security.
Approximately 330 million barrels have already been released under the collective action launched in March in response to the Strait of Hormuz crisis.
Total releases will exceed the original commitment of 400 million barrels, as some members have released more than initially pledged and others intend to do so, the board said.
Members agreed to take all necessary steps to complete the remaining releases promptly, consistent with national circumstances, with specific acceleration plans already in place.
The board also encouraged members with oil production and refining capacity to boost supplies of crude and refined products, particularly diesel, and emphasised the importance of the free flow of energy trade.
Reaffirming their commitment to international energy security, members expressed willingness to take further action to address global energy market challenges, building on the G7 statement of October 2.
The IEA Secretariat will monitor progress and inform G7 leaders and the Governing Board of further action needed, drawing on an updated oil market assessment focused on diesel.

More than two hundred Ajax vehicles now accepted

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
16:00:14 BST
00:00:14 KST

The Ministry of Defence had accepted 227 Ajax Capability Drop 3 vehicles as of 15 September, including 41 taken on since 17 April, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked for the overall total of each variant now held, mapped against the current production schedule, following an answer of 8 September.
Luke Pollard, the Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, gave the headline figure but declined the breakdown. “The Department does not routinely disclose fleet holdings by variant, nor provide variant-level delivery information against production schedules,” he said. “Such information is directly linked to military readiness and operational capability, and its disclosure could prejudice operational effectiveness by enabling assessments to be made about the availability, preparedness and deployment of capability.”
He added: “The Ajax programme remains on track to deliver all 589 vehicles as contracted.”
Forty one vehicles accepted in five months gives a run rate of roughly eight a month. At that pace the remaining 362 vehicles would take around three and a half years, though the answer gives no delivery profile and no completion date.
Ajax is a family of tracked armoured vehicles built by General Dynamics Land Systems UK, with hulls from Spain and final assembly at Merthyr Tydfil. The reconnaissance variant carries a stabilised 40mm cased telescoped cannon, and the family covers six variants in all. The programme was contracted for 589 vehicles at a firm price of £5.5 billion, and trials were suspended for a period after crews reported hearing damage and joint injuries linked to noise and vibration.

Fico’s Slovakia Revives Moscow Ties With Energy and Trade Talks Set for November
Slovakia is preparing to revive a dormant cooperation forum with Moscow, with Russian energy supplies, nuclear fuel, and the treatment of Russian athletes expected to feature prominently, POLITICO reported on October 15.
According to a Russian government note obtained by POLITICO, Slovak Foreign Minister Juraj Blanár agreed during an August 20 video call to hold a meeting of the Russian-Slovak Intergovernmental Commission in Moscow. Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico announced that the meeting is scheduled for November 25.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Slovakia under Prime Minister Robert Fico has repeatedly taken positions closer to Moscow than most EU governments, including halting state military aid to Ukraine, criticizing sanctions on Russia, and maintaining energy ties with Moscow. In May, Fico visited Putin, in Moscow and described himself as the EU’s “black sheep” for supporting dialogue with Russia.
The Russian-Slovak Intergovernmental Commission covers economic, scientific, and technical cooperation and has been dormant since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Its previous session was held in Bratislava in November 2021.
POLITICO reported that the Russian note was written by Science and Higher Education Minister Valery Falkov and dated September 10. The outlet could not independently verify the document but noted that it bore the hallmarks of a legitimate Russian ministerial communication.
Blanár had raised Slovakia’s opposition to the EU phaseout of Russian gas imports and requested that energy supplies be discussed at the Moscow meeting, according to the note.
Slovak representatives also emphasized continued Russian oil deliveries through the Druzhba pipeline and welcomed regular shipments of Russian nuclear fuel to Slovak power plants, POLITICO reported.
Fico has argued that ending Russian energy imports would increase costs for Slovakia, which remains heavily dependent on Russian oil and gas. During a May 9 meeting in Moscow, the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin, stated that Russia would continue working to meet Slovakia’s energy needs.
The planned agenda extends beyond energy. According to POLITICO, the two sides are considering cooperation on culture, tourism, agriculture, and environmental protection, as well as the status of the Russian Center for Science and Culture in Bratislava.
The Russian note also recorded Blanár’s opposition to what it described as “discrimination against Russian athletes” in international competitions. That issue is expected to be discussed at the November meeting.
“We pursue a policy in all directions and maintain dialogue with all countries that are interested in pragmatic cooperation with us for the benefit of the Slovak Republic’s national interests,” Blanár stated after the August 20 call, POLITICO wrote.
The renewed Slovak-Russian dialogue follows Fico’s May visit to Moscow and comes after Viktor Orbán’s defeat in Hungary’s April election. POLITICO noted that Orbán had previously been one of Putin’s closest partners inside the EU.
Before leaving office, Orbán’s government had also revived Hungary’s own intergovernmental economic cooperation commission with Russia. Budapest and Moscow later agreed on a 12-point plan covering energy, trade, and cultural ties.
The Slovak initiative now mirrors parts of that approach, with energy cooperation serving as a central component of renewed ties with Moscow.
POLITICO also linked the effort to Russia’s broader attempts to expand energy relationships abroad.
After speaking with Putin, US President Donald Trump recently announced a deal under which Russia would supply diesel to US and global markets, potentially providing Moscow with additional revenue while Ukraine continues striking Russian oil infrastructure.

Russia’s Drone Attack on Lutsk Damages World’s Largest Painting—Ukraine’s 2,000-Square-Meter “Cosmogony”

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
14:36:01 UTC
23:36:01 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia’s Drone Attack on Lutsk Damages World’s Largest Painting—Ukraine’s 2,000-Square-Meter “Cosmogony”
Russia’s drone attack on the Ukrainian city of Lutsk on October 13 damaged Cosmogony, the largest work of painting in Ukraine and the largest painting in the world, after falling drone debris sparked a fire at the Adrenalin City entertainment complex, according to Suspilne on October 15.
The artwork was damaged after falling drone debris sparked a fire at the Adrenalin City entertainment complex, which houses the Museum of Modern Ukrainian Art.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Museum director Tetiana Repnytska told Suspilne that the fire damaged The Future, the final section of the six-part artwork, while the other thematic sections remained intact.
“By destroying art and culture, they are also trying to destroy Ukrainians. This is the largest painting in the world. Cosmogony covers an area of 2,000 square meters,” Repnytska said.
Despite the damage to the monumental painting, museum staff managed to protect much of the institution’s collection from the consequences of the attack.
According to art historian and the museum’s chief curator, Oles Tomakh, employees were forced to evacuate artworks during the fire, including pieces from an exhibition dedicated to Ukrainian artist Emma Andiievska .
“We had an exhibition of Emma Andiievska at Cosmogony, featuring more than 300 works. We began quickly removing them, but we couldn't get to some in time. However, only the glass was broken. Fortunately, all the other museum halls were undamaged,” Tomakh said.
The museum has yet to determine whether the damaged section of Cosmogony will be restored or replaced with a newly created segment.
Repnytska said the decision would be made by the artwork’s creators, emphasizing that the museum intends to continue its cultural activities despite Russian attacks.
“Despite the shelling, we will continue to develop contemporary Ukrainian art and preserve it,” the museum director said.
Cosmogony, by Ukrainian artist Petro Antyp, is one of Ukraine’s most ambitious contemporary art projects. Created over nearly two years at the Museum of Modern Ukrainian Art in Lutsk, the painting was officially recognized in September 2024 as the largest work of painting in Ukraine, surpassing the previous world record. Covering 2,086.5 square meters, the artwork exceeds the nearly 1,600-square-meter The Journey of Humanity, created by British artist Sasha Jafri in 2020.
The painting consists of six main thematic sections. These include The Beginning, depicting the origins of the universe; The Creation of Earth, illustrating the formation of the planet; The Creation of Nature, exploring the emergence of life; The Creation of Humanity, portraying human origins and development; The Creation of Society, examining the evolution of communities and civilization; and The Future, reflecting on humanity's relationship with the world and its future.
The project was launched in November 2022. Originally from Horlivka in the Donetsk region, Antyp relocated to the Kyiv region following the outbreak of Russia’s war against Ukraine in 2014 before settling in Lutsk after the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022.
While Ukrainian cultural institutions continue to face damage from Russian attacks, art is also being used internationally to support those affected by the war, including Ukrainian children.
In a separate initiative, Beatles musician Paul McCartney contributed a lyric from his 1973 song Band on the Run to inspire a charity exhibition and auction featuring original works by more than 60 contemporary artists. Proceeds will support children affected by armed conflicts worldwide, including Russia’s war against Ukraine.
According to The Art Newspaper on October 8, McCartney selected the line “Well the rain exploded with a mighty crash as we fell into the sun” from Band on the Run, the title track of the 1973 album released by McCartney and his band Wings.

Meta said its safeguards would have flagged and blocked the advertisements before they reached voters.

Why Teach Philosophy is a new series of interviews with philosophers known for their teaching, their research on philosophy pedagogy, or their work on curriculum design.
Created by Russell Marcus, professor of philosophy at Hamilton College, the interviews, he says, are “an offshoot of a larger research project about philosophical learning goals.”
Currently there are interviews with David W. Concepción (Ball State), Mo Janzen (Anoka Ramsey CC), László Kőszeghy (International Baccalaureate), Tommy Curry (Edinburgh), Rebecca Scott (Harper College), and L.A. Paul (Yale), with eleven more coming soon.
Professor Marcus says, “the interviews are tightly edited audio, typically under an hour, extracted from much longer (typically 3-4 hour) conversations that I had over the past year with renowned philosophy teachers. We’re not flashy, but I think the content is pretty good and the audience really should be philosophers.”
He adds, “I think that the podcasts could be especially good resources for grad schools to use in whatever teacher training they do. Typically, they do minimal such training. Listening to good teachers talk about their craft can be enlightening and useful.”
The Why Teach Philosophy interviews are available on YouTube, Spotify, Apple Podcasts, etc., and transcripts of the longer conversations are posted on the project’s site.

U.S. Navy teaches drones to land on ships without GPS
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
14:32:59 UTC
23:32:59 KST

- A U.S. Navy drone completed mission tasks and landed on a pitching ship without GPS or a pilot, using its own cameras and software.
- NAWCAD says the software is ready for fleet testing and is working to transition it to Navy drone programs, Collaborative Combat Aircraft and DARPA’s EVADE.
The U.S. Navy has flown a drone through mission tasks and landed it on a pitching ship at sea with GPS jammed or unavailable and no pilot at the controls, using only the aircraft’s own cameras, motion sensors and onboard software, the Naval Air Warfare Center Aircraft Division said.
NAWCAD, the U.S. Navy’s main aviation test and engineering center at Patuxent River, Maryland, said the live-flight demonstration showed a tactical drone can carry out its tasks and recover aboard a moving vessel without satellite navigation. The software is now ready for operational testing on fleet platforms.
“In contested areas where satellites and communications are jammed, autonomy gives significant advantage to our sailors,” said Rear Adm. Todd Evans, commander of NAWCAD.
Landing a drone on a ship has usually depended on extra hardware. Shipboard recoveries rely on radar systems that cost millions of dollars, along with flight deck recovery gear and ship modifications that can take months to install. When the U.S. Navy’s RQ-8A Fire Scout made the service’s first autonomous drone landings on a moving ship aboard USS Nashville in 2006, it used a radar sensor on the ship to track the aircraft’s position relative to the deck.
NAWCAD’s approach moves that job into software. Engineers at the center’s Maritime Autonomous Guidance-Navigation-Control Intelligent Coupled Systems Lab paired the drone’s existing mission cameras with guidance, navigation and control algorithms. In flight, the aircraft recognizes the ship’s shape and visual cues and steers toward it much as a human pilot would, while the software predicts how the deck is rising and falling so the drone can time a smooth touchdown.
“In a high-end maritime conflict, GPS is the first operational link an adversary attempts to sever,” said Peter Arslanian, a NAWCAD aerospace engineer.
The system runs on commercial-standard cameras, motion sensors and electronics, and NAWCAD says the software works with nearly any drone flight computer. That means it can be added through a software upgrade instead of costly changes to ships with little spare room, and it can scale from small tactical quadcopters up to large combat drones.
NAWCAD plans to apply the technology next to larger uncrewed aircraft, including tactical resupply drones. The center is working to move the capability into the U.S. Navy’s Small Tactical Unmanned Aircraft Systems program office, the Collaborative Combat Aircraft program for drone wingmen, and DARPA’s EVADE effort.
EVADE, short for Early VTOL Aircraft Demonstration, is a DARPA project to field drones that can take off from and land on ship decks without launch or recovery equipment, with five companies including AeroVironment and Sikorsky building designs for it.
The Naval Innovative Science and Engineering Program and the Office of Naval Research funded the NAWCAD work, which now moves to operational testing on fleet aircraft.

NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Thursday sought responses from the Centre, Delhi Police and others on a plea seeking to hold organisers of protests personally or jointly liable for loss of life, injuries, damage to public or private property and the costs incurred by the authorities.A bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justice Joymalya Bagchi was hearing the petition, which also sought a direction that protests, dharnas, demonstrations, processions and public assemblies in the national capital should not be held without prior written permission from the competent authority.
The plea sought to make organisers, callers, leaders or convenors of protests liable for losses arising from unlawful acts or omissions, including when an assembly is held without permission or violates the conditions imposed for its approval.The bench issued notices to the Centre, Delhi Police and other parties, seeking their responses to the petition, according to news agency PTI.
Plea seeks designated protest sites in Delhi
The petition also sought directions to the authorities to identify and notify designated locations for protests, dharnas, demonstrations and public assemblies in Delhi. These sites, it said, should be situated away from densely populated, commercial and central areas.
It further proposed that every application seeking permission for a protest, demonstration, procession or public assembly should be accompanied by an affidavit from the organiser disclosing the source of funding.The declaration should also specify whether any part of the funds had been received, or was expected to be received, from a foreign source or an unidentified source, the plea said.According to the petition, a false or incomplete declaration should provide grounds for revoking permission, recovering compensation and costs from the organiser and those found to have financed the assembly, and initiating prosecution in accordance with the law.
Supreme Court hears multiple pleas linked to Delhi protests
The hearing came as the Supreme Court considered several petitions connected to protests in Delhi, including pleas concerning alleged assaults on journalists and lawyers, police action and restrictions on demonstrations.In a separate matter, the bench issued notices to the Centre and the Delhi government on a plea challenging the Delhi Police’s decision to de-notify Jantar Mantar as a designated protest site.The petitioner, advocate Swaty Malik, argued that removing the designation violated the fundamental right to protest. The plea maintained that demonstrations should be permitted at a location where protesters could make their grievances heard by the state administration.Justice Bagchi observed that the concept of being heard should also be considered in the context of technology.“The word ‘heard’ must be used in the perspective of technology also”, Justice Bagchi remarked.The court agreed to examine the petition and sought responses from the authorities.In other pleas linked to the protests, the Supreme Court sought responses from the authorities over allegations involving journalists and lawyers. It also directed law-enforcement agencies to preserve CCTV footage and other digital records relating to the demonstrations.The bench further directed that the order issued under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) be placed on record. The provision empowers authorised executive magistrates to issue urgent prohibitory orders to prevent public danger, disturbances or riots.The court indicated that the Union government would file a consolidated response to the batch of petitions while relevant material relating to individual cases was preserved.
Court also takes up pleas on voter roll revision
Separately, the Supreme Court issued notices to the Election Commission and chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar on a petition filed by Congress leader Rahul Gandhi and 12 other opposition leaders over alleged large-scale voter deletions and irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.The bench also took note of submissions concerning the October 12 march to the Supreme Court by Rahul and other opposition leaders.“Nobody can browbeat us (judiciary),” CJI Surya Kant said during the hearing, adding that the court was aware of statements made both inside and outside the courtroom.
The court said it would ask one of the petitioners about his conduct at the next hearing, without naming the individual.The petition by Rahul and the other opposition leaders sought an independent audit of deletions and modifications made during the SIR, to be conducted by a committee headed by a retired Supreme Court judge and assisted by technical experts and other prominent citizens.It also sought safeguards against deleting voters’ names without notice and a reasonable opportunity to be heard, along with measures to allow eligible voters in Punjab and other poll-bound states to seek inclusion in electoral rolls within the time permitted by law.

Technology company Apple has released a screen that consolidates the functions of its app products and its home-management software into one device.
HomeView is a seven-inch display meant to function as a centralised location for home controls, signalling a step forward in Apple's home integration and smart home services.
The screens come in two versions. One sits on its own, standing on a base with an integrated speaker, while the other is wall-mounted.
HomeView works similarly to other Apple touchscreen products, with a home screen, apps, widgets and a built-in front-facing camera. It has many of the same functions, including FaceTime video calling.
The product creates a physical dashboard for the Apple Home app, which was released in 2022 to control integrated functions such as smart locks, appliances, cameras and thermostats.
HomeView uses face recognition for up to six people per device in a household with personalised settings for each user, instead of the app sitting on personalised devices.
The product also includes an intercom system that can connect multiple devices within one household.
The tabletop version of the device has a distinct form, with a case and a thick base made from recycled aluminium. Its rounded base and movable screen evoke the design of the 2002 iMac G4 desktop computer.
Apple emphasised the device's potential as decor, calling it "the perfect addition to a kitchen counter, nightstand, or side table."
It comes in four colour options: silver, starlight, rose pink, and space grey.
The company also noted the integration of its next-generation AI, called Siri AI.
"HomeView features Siri AI, an entirely new version of Siri powered by the next generation of Apple Intelligence and advanced Apple silicon," said Apple.
"Siri AI is a profoundly more capable and conversational assistant with personal context understanding and onscreen awareness."
The release also included a lineup of updated home products such as cameras, locks and thermostats.
HomeView comes after a slate of recent releases from Apple, including the brand's first foldable smartphone.

‘Boiling point’: Why students are protesting against Albania’s Edi Rama
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
14:22:13 UTC
23:22:13 KST

‘Boiling point’: Why students are protesting against Albania’s Edi Rama
Experts say Albania’s protests reflect ignored student grievances and growing frustration.
Student protests against poor conditions in Albania’s education system have continued for a third day in the capital, Tirana, as Prime Minister Edi Rama insists he will not resign.
Demonstrators have called on Rama to quit in often violent protests since Tuesday. They have set fire to several buildings across the city, including the prime minister’s office, ministry buildings and branches of several banks.
Dozens of police officers and protesters have been injured amid attempts to disperse the crowds using water cannon and tear gas.
“What you are seeing is the boiling point of months of suppressed grievances,” Albanian journalist Arlis Alikaj told Al Jazeera.
Students have complained for months about the high cost of education and their limited employment prospects after graduation.
Afrim Krasniqi, a professor and researcher at the Institute for Political Studies in Tirana, told Al Jazeera that students and young people protested peacefully for nearly three months, “yet their demands were largely ignored, while the government often responded with discrediting campaigns rather than genuine dialogue”.
He added that the current escalation reflects “frustration not only with the government itself, but also with the lack of institutional accountability and responsiveness.”
The protests represent one of the most serious waves of public discontent directed at Rama, who won a fourth term last May but has since faced public anger over corruption allegations involving senior officials.
The unrest in Tirana coincides with a broader wave of student protests across Europe. In France, secondary school students have spent weeks protesting and blockading schools, demanding more teachers and better learning facilities. They have warned that deteriorating school buildings and overcrowded classrooms are undermining the quality of education.
Protests against Rama’s government began a few months ago, fuelled by plans to build a luxury resort along Albania’s largely unspoilt southern coast. Jared Kushner, US President Donald Trump’s son in law, is involved in the project.
Local media reported that the protests spread from Tirana to universities in Elbasan and Shkoder on Wednesday.
Albania is among the economies of the Western Balkans seeking to catch up with European living standards. However, the gap with the European Union average remains evident in purchasing power, wages, productivity and the quality of public services. Despite economic progress, the country continues to face challenges including emigration, regional inequalities and the need for stronger institutions and the rule of law.
After Montenegro, Albania stands out as one of the countries that has made the most progress towards full EU membership. However, behind the optimistic political rhetoric, frustration is growing among citizens over the slow pace of European integration and the lack of tangible improvements in their daily lives.
While opposition groups seek to support the demonstrators and capitalise on the moment to strengthen their own position, Alikaj said the protests are being driven by young people and students demanding systemic change.
On Thursday, Rama – who has been PM since 2013 – told Reuters, “As for calls for my resignation, governments change through democratic elections. Last year, we had elections, not a revolution.”
Sokol Lleshi, a lecturer at the University of New York Tirana specialising in political science, said social change is more likely to emerge from a broader coalition of different social groups, rather than mass mobilisation limited to university and secondary school students.
“Elite defection from the current ruling political elite could enable the institutional means to channel societal dissatisfaction or resentment into political and policy changes. Yet, the current student protest does not seem to replicate the December 2018 mass movement of university students and its effects”, Lleshi said.
The student protests that shook Albania in December 2018 began over rising education costs and forced Rama to dismiss eight ministers as part of a cabinet reshuffle and announce a package of measures known as the “Pact for the University”.
But some of the students’ demands remained unmet.
Lleshi drew some more positive conclusions from Albania’s past experience of social unrest.
Albanian society is polarised and unequal, “with hollowed intermediary political institutions”, he said, but the legacy of unrest and political confrontation will serve as a “warning to avoid destabilisation”, he said.

Johns Hopkins lab gets up to $500M for DARPA research
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
14:22:04 UTC
23:22:04 KST

- DARPA awarded Johns Hopkins APL a sole-source contract worth up to $499.8 million for engineering, development and research work through October 2031.
- The award continues a DARPA-APL arrangement that began with a $225 million contract in 2021 and later grew to about $1.1 billion.
The Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, the Pentagon’s advanced research arm, has awarded the Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory a contract worth up to $499.8 million to keep the lab working on DARPA engineering, development and research projects through October 2031.
The U.S. Department of War announced the award on Oct. 14. Under the indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity contract, DARPA will place individual task orders with the Laurel, Maryland, laboratory as work is needed, paying costs plus a fixed fee, up to the $499.8 million ceiling. No money was obligated at signing, and the minimum guaranteed amount will be funded with the first task order.
The contract covers what the Pentagon describes as an essential capability for engineering and developmental work that puts scientific and technical findings into practical use. DARPA awarded it on a sole-source basis, without a competition, which is standard for work assigned to a university affiliated research center.
APL is one of the Pentagon’s university affiliated research centers, a small group of nonprofit laboratories tied to universities that the U.S. Department of War keeps on long-term contracts for engineering work it considers too important to compete for each time. Based in Laurel, between Washington and Baltimore, the lab works for several defense customers, including the U.S. Navy, which holds a separate APL contract for fiscal 2023 through 2032 with a potential value of up to $10.6 billion.
The new award continues a long-running arrangement between DARPA and APL. DARPA gave the lab a $225 million sole-source contract in November 2021 for the same kind of engineering and development support, then raised its value to $740 million with a $515 million modification in May 2024. A later $388.8 million modification lifted the total to about $1.1 billion, with task orders running into November 2027, ExecutiveGov reported.
Under the earlier contract, DARPA issued task orders for support services on programs it often identifies only by code names. Two such orders placed in April 2026, labeled Ibiza and Bratislava, were worth about $6.1 million and $5.3 million, according to federal contracting data.
DARPA runs research programs across areas ranging from hypersonics and space to biotechnology and artificial intelligence, and relies on outside laboratories such as APL for engineering analysis, prototyping and technical support as those projects move from research toward practical systems.
Work under the new contract will be performed primarily in Laurel, and DARPA can place orders under it until October 2031.

====================================================================================================

Israel ended Iran war with more interceptors than it started with, Rafael CEO says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
14:21:16 UTC
23:21:16 KST

WASHINGTON - Rafael Advanced Defense Systems emerged from Israel’s recent wars with Iran with more Tamir interceptors in stock than it had when the fighting began, despite thousands of interceptors being fired to defend the country against missiles, rockets, and drones, according to CEO Yoav Tourgeman.
"We ended the war with more Tamir interceptors than before," Tourgeman told Defense & Tech by The Jerusalem Post in an exclusive interview at the Association of the United States Army (AUSA) Annual Meeting & Exposition in Washington, DC.
For decades, air-defense development focused primarily on improving the performance of individual systems with greater range, better accuracy, and higher interception rates. But recent conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East have exposed a significant challenge where even the most advanced interceptor is of limited value if a defending country cannot produce enough of them to sustain operations through a prolonged campaign.
For Rafael, the Israeli defense company behind the famous Iron Dome and David’s Sling, industrial capacity is becoming inseparable from operational effectiveness.
The challenge is building an architecture that can handle them all, including simultaneous attacks designed to overwhelm defenses through sheer volume. The company’s answer is a layered approach to air defense, matching different systems to different threats, from inexpensive drones and rockets to ballistic missiles and emerging hypersonic weapons.
No single interceptor can economically or effectively address every threat, Tourgeman argued, adding that “we are building the right solution for the right threat.”
The Israeli company's combat credentials remain central to that argument. According to Tourgeman, Iron Dome and David's Sling have intercepted more than 11,000 threats together since becoming operational.
“There would have been a lot more blood in the streets without the Iron Dome,” he said. “These systems have proven themselves in situations we once thought impossible.”
1,000 interceptors a year
But intercepting incoming weapons is only part of the equation. Replenishing inventories during a sustained conflict requires manufacturing capacity, reliable supply chains, skilled workers, and the ability to expand output without compromising quality.
That has been driving Rafael’s international expansion across 48 different countries, and with governments increasingly looking not only for advanced technology but also for confidence that suppliers can deliver when demand surges, Rafael has subsidiaries worldwide.
Rafael has also increased automation across its manufacturing operations and is expanding production partnerships overseas. Its new facility in Arkansas is expected to have the capacity to produce roughly 1,000 interceptors annually for both the United States and Israel. It will also provide a US-based manufacturing source as Washington and its allies seek to rebuild munitions stockpiles and strengthen domestic defense production.
Tourgeman also told D&T that Rafael is willing to transfer intellectual property and deepen cooperation with American industry. And for end-users, that appeal extends beyond delivery timelines because domestic production can reduce dependence on overseas supply chains and give governments greater control over critical defense capabilities during a crisis.
As European governments confront a more threatening security environment and the prospect of sustained high-intensity warfare, the continent is another major market. Germany, in particular, has been rebuilding its long-term air and missile-defense requirements.
In September, the German state of Lower Saxony, Rafael Advanced Defense Systems, and Aurelius Capital signed a letter of intent to purchase Volkswagen’s Osnabrück plant, allowing the Israeli defense company to establish the production of Iron Dome components in Germany.
That, Tourgeman confirmed, was the first step towards Berlin acquiring the Iron Dome.
“What we’re doing in Germany is bringing confidence and safety to the population,” he said.
He also suggested that civilian industrial sectors, particularly automotive manufacturing, could play a larger role in defense production. Car plants already possess expertise in high-volume manufacturing, quality control, and supply-chain management, which could help governments rapidly scale weapons production during periods of crisis.
Staying ahead of the next generation of threats
Beyond today's missile threats, Rafael is preparing for the next generation of challenges.
At AUSA the company showcased a full-size model of Sky Sonic, its interceptor designed to counter hypersonic missiles. The interceptor was first announced over three years and Tourgeman dismissed the idea that hypersonic weapons represent an entirely new category of threat, arguing that many of the technologies needed to defeat advanced missiles already exist within Rafael's portfolio.
More pressing, he suggested, is the rise of coordinated attacks involving large numbers of inexpensive drones operating alongside traditional missiles.
Such attacks can expose critical infrastructure and create a difficult economic and operational problem for defenders, and the West has already seen how using costly interceptors against cheap drones can quickly strain inventories.
Countering the threat will require systems that can coordinate sensors, weapons, and decision-making across a network rather than operate as isolated platforms.
At AUSA, the company showcased solutions designed to operate within networked defense architectures and is advancing concepts such as Hunter Eagle, which Tourgeman described as a platform capable of functioning within a mesh network against drone swarms, both offensively and defensively.
That approach reflects a broader change in the economics of air warfare. The side launching an attack can increasingly draw on large numbers of relatively cheap, expendable weapons. The defender, meanwhile, must preserve enough interceptors and other capabilities to protect cities, military assets, and critical infrastructure over days, weeks, or longer.
For Rafael, the next contest in air defense will therefore be measured not only by interception rates or technological sophistication, but also by production lines, supply chains, and the ability to replenish stocks while fighting continues.
In a prolonged war, the decisive advantage may belong not simply to the country with the best interceptor, but to the one that can keep producing it at scale.

J&amp;K HC restricts motorboat operations on Dal Lake
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
14:20:01 UTC
23:20:01 KST

The high court of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh has ordered a ban on fuel-powered motorboats and jet skis on Dal Lake.
The high court of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh has prohibited the operation of fuel-powered motorboats and jet skis on Dal Lake until further orders.A division bench comprising chief justice Pushpendra Singh Bhati and Justice Rajesh Sekhri passed the directive on Wednesday while hearing a petition filed by Mohammad Rafiq Mir.The court directed the authorities, including the lakes conservation and management authority (LCMA), the tourism department and the police, to ensure strict implementation of the ban.
“In the larger interest of justice, taking a comprehensive view of the submissions made, it is directed that the respondent authorities LCMA, tourism, and police shall ensure that no motor boat, whether it be a shikara motorboat or Jet Ski which operates by fuel, is operated in the Dal Lake until further orders,” the bench said.The court also warned that any violation of its directive would amount to contempt of court, instructing the concerned officials to strictly prohibit such operations, according to the new agency PTI.
Court stresses need to protect Dal Lake from pollution
The bench observed that protecting lake ecosystems has become increasingly important, making it necessary to restrict activities that contribute to pollution.It also emphasised that the policy governing motorised boats should strike a reasonable balance between tourism-related activities, environmental protection and ensuring uniform rules for all operators.
The judges suggested that solar-powered and electric boats could provide a viable alternative, allowing tourism operators to continue their activities while safeguarding the lake's ecological health.
Solar-powered boats suggested as an alternative
The court asked the government to examine whether conventional motorisation could be replaced with solar-powered systems or electric engines.
Senior additional advocate general Mohsin Qadri was asked to explore the possibility of replacing existing motorised boats with solar-powered electric engines and present the findings before the court.The government had earlier been directed to submit a comprehensive policy on the operation of motorised boats.However, the court clarified that the prohibition would not apply to boats used for emergency services, law and order, disaster management and safety-related operations.The matter has been listed for the next hearing on October 30.

The student organisation ASAP in Britain and its partners are preparing to hold a protest outside the Azerbaijani Embassy in London on Friday 16 October, in opposition to restrictions on the wearing of hijab in Azerbaijani schools and in solidarity with Muslim pupils and teachers who face measures preventing them from attending school or continuing their work because they wear the hijab.
The demonstration is scheduled to take place from 4pm to 6pm outside the Azerbaijani Embassy at 66 Holland Park, London, W11 3SJ, near Holland Park station. It will be held under the slogan “Hands Off My Hijab”.
The protest comes amid renewed opposition to restrictions in Azerbaijan, where school uniform rules have sparked widespread controversy following reports that hijab-wearing pupils have been prevented from entering classrooms. The developments have brought questions surrounding the hijab, the right to education and freedom of religious belief back into the spotlight.
Call for Solidarity and a Strong Turnout
The organisers are hoping for a substantial turnout that reflects the level of solidarity with women and girls affected by the restrictions and sends a clear message against making access to education conditional on adhering to a uniform policy that excludes the hijab.
Participants have been asked to bring handmade solidarity placards, featuring messages in support of pupils and teachers in Azerbaijan. The signs are intended to reinforce the message that women and girls should have the right to education without discrimination on the grounds of religious belief or appearance.
The demonstration is expected to highlight the principle that education is a fundamental right and that preventing pupils from attending school because they wear the hijab raises serious questions about religious freedom, equality and equal access to educational opportunities.
The protest will also provide an opportunity to call for a review of restrictions that have reportedly resulted in some pupils being barred from entering their schools.
Background: Hijab Restrictions in Azerbaijani Schools
The controversy surrounding the hijab in Azerbaijani schools dates back to December 2010, when the then education minister, Misir Mardanov, announced on 9 December that the wearing of hijab would be prohibited in primary and secondary schools, citing school uniform requirements and the country’s secular education system.
READ: An estimated quarter of a million join London march marking three years of Gaza genocide
Although no explicit law banning the hijab was enacted at the time, the implementation of school uniform rules effectively imposed restrictions on its wearing.
The decision prompted a series of protests. On 10 December 2010, hundreds of people reportedly demonstrated outside the Ministry of Education in the capital, Baku, while further gatherings took place in other parts of the country. In May 2011, police dispersed another protest in Baku and arrested several participants, according to media and human rights reports.
The issue resurfaced in September 2026, following reports that Azerbaijan’s Cabinet of Ministers approved amendments to school uniform regulations on 21 September. The changes reportedly included restrictions on clothing considered inconsistent with uniform requirements or the principle of secular education.
Although the amendments did not explicitly mention a ban on the hijab, recent reports indicate that some schools have prevented hijab-wearing pupils from entering classrooms. Objections have also emerged from pupils, parents and teachers over the implementation of the new rules.
The current opposition therefore extends beyond a debate about school uniforms. It raises broader questions about how education regulations can be reconciled with freedom of religion and how pupils can be protected from being denied an education because they wear the hijab.
As opposition continues and solidarity campaigns emerge both within Azerbaijan and abroad, the planned demonstration outside the Azerbaijani Embassy in London forms part of wider efforts to challenge the restrictions, highlight their educational and social consequences, and call for women and girls to be able to study and work without discrimination.

Puberty may mark a turning point for sex differences in the brain’s emotion and memory centers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
14:00:08 UTC
23:00:08 KST

Differences between males and females in the fine-grained tissue structure of deep brain regions are minimal at ages 9 to 12 but emerge and widen during adolescence, according to a new brain imaging study. The timing coincides with puberty and with the period when sex differences in conditions like anxiety and depression begin to appear, though the study could not determine what drives the brain changes. The findings were published in Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience.
Deep gray matter refers to a collection of structures located beneath the outer layer of the brain. These areas include the amygdala, which processes emotions, the hippocampus, which is central to memory, and the nucleus accumbens, which plays a role in reward and motivation. The study also examined the thalamus, a relay hub for sensory signals, and the caudate and putamen, which help control movement and habits. In human populations, many mental health conditions tied to these brain functions show different rates of diagnosis between men and women, but the biological reasons behind these differences remain poorly understood.
Animal research points to puberty as a key period for these changes: a 2008 study in rats found that sex hormones during puberty drive the addition of new cells to brain regions that differ between the sexes. In humans, a 2014 study that followed young people over time found that pubertal development was linked to the size of these deep brain regions in both boys and girls, independent of age.
While overall volume provides part of the picture, scientists have sought to understand the microscopic layout of brain tissue. Earlier work by the same research team, covered by PsyPost in 2024, found large differences between young adult men and women in measures of tissue microstructure, with men showing signs of more densely packed cells in regions like the hippocampus. The new research, led by Christopher G. Filippi of The Hospital for Sick Children and Richard Watts of the University of Canterbury, aimed to pinpoint when those microscopic differences first develop.
The research team examined brain scan data from 1,643 individuals aged 9 to 35. The participants were drawn from two large public databases: the Human Connectome Project Development dataset for children and teens, and the Young Adult dataset for older participants. In their analyses, the scientists statistically controlled for age and body mass index, and they accounted for family relationships among the many twins included in the adult sample.
To evaluate tissue microstructure, the researchers used an advanced magnetic resonance imaging technique called Restriction Spectrum Imaging. This method measures how water molecules diffuse through brain tissue. Water trapped inside a cell encounters barriers, producing a restricted diffusion signal that reflects cell packing. Water in the spaces between cells encounters fewer obstacles, producing a hindered diffusion signal that reflects the extracellular environment.
For the youngest participants, aged 9 to 12, the researchers observed no statistically significant differences between boys and girls in these diffusion measures. Across the deep gray matter structures, the tissue composition in childhood appeared similar between the sexes.
However, differences began to emerge between ages 13 and 16, first in the hippocampus, amygdala, and thalamus. Restricted diffusion rose with age in both sexes, but from puberty onward it was consistently higher in males, a pattern the researchers suggest may reflect more densely packed cells or larger cell bodies. By ages 17 to 21, sex accounted for roughly 13 to 33 percent of the variation in restricted diffusion across all six regions, and in adults it explained 32 to 37 percent in the hippocampus and amygdala.
Females, in turn, showed a larger hindered component, meaning a greater share of the water signal came from the spaces between cells. Because both measures are expressed as shares of the total signal, the two patterns largely mirror each other.
In regions such as the nucleus accumbens, caudate, and putamen, females showed a slowing in development in their late teens before accelerating again in their early 20s, while males followed a more steady progression. By the mid-20s, the size of the sex difference in the hippocampus and amygdala had leveled off, though the measures themselves were still changing in both sexes. In the thalamus, the divergence between the sexes continued to widen up to age 35.
“Sex differences in the brain have so far been primarily investigated at the macro-structural level (i.e., differences in overall brain size or differences in the size of specific regions),” said Yumnah Khan, a doctoral scientist at the Autism Research Centre at the University of Cambridge who was not involved in the research. “What is interesting about this work is it provides evidence for differences in brain microstructure (i.e., what is happening at a finer level within brain tissue), which gives us a more detailed picture of sex differences in the brain.”
Marco Balducci, a senior researcher at the University of Turku who was not involved in the study, said the findings build on earlier work. “Earlier studies had identified sex differences in subcortical brain structure and, more recently, in diffusion-derived microstructure in young adults,” Balducci told PsyPost. “This study extends that work by showing that the differences emerge during adolescence rather than simply being present in adulthood.”
The timing of these changes aligns with the pubertal transition, leading the study authors to speculate about biological drivers. Earlier animal work indicates that sex hormones can influence synapses and dendrites, the connection points and branching extensions of nerve cells. Because these adolescent brain shifts occur alongside the emergence of sex-biased mental health conditions, identifying typical developmental paths could help clarify underlying vulnerabilities.
Khan told PsyPost that considering human imaging alongside animal research helps connect biology to observation. “Animal studies can provide much stronger evidence about causality and specific mechanisms, while human studies are generally observational and correlational,” she said. “However, when both of these lines of research are considered and interpreted together, we get a better picture of the mechanisms underlying sex differences in brain development.”
Balducci noted that the broad descriptive findings appear well-supported. “The main descriptive finding appears robust because the study uses a large combined sample, finds a consistent developmental pattern across several brain regions, and applies correction for multiple comparisons,” he said. “However, the reasons for these differences remain uncertain because the data are cross-sectional, and in this setting it is difficult to distinguish age-related changes from pubertal development or establish a hormonal cause.”
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The study relied on cross-sectional data from different individuals at each age, rather than following the same individuals across their development. Additionally, puberty was measured using ratings of physical development, which rose so closely with age that the researchers could not separate the effects of puberty from those of getting older, and hormone levels were not measured. The researchers did find an association between a girl’s first menstrual period and a specific measure in the thalamus, but they describe any role of sex hormones as speculative.
The researchers also had to combine two projects that used different scanners and imaging settings. Because one covered ages 9 to 21 and the other ages 22 to 36, the statistical adjustments for those differences fall at the same point as the transition into adulthood, so features of the age trajectories near that point, such as the slowdown seen in females, should be read with some caution. Comparisons between males and females within each age group are less affected.
“I think the biggest risk is interpreting these findings as showing that male and female brains are fundamentally different,” Khan said. “In reality, sex differences in the brain tend to be relatively small, with a lot of overlap between the sexes.”
She added that the timing of differences depends on which ages a study covers. “It is also important not to assume that adolescence is when these differences necessarily begin,” Khan noted. “Although the study found minimal differences early in childhood, sex-by-age effects can be highly sensitive to the particular age range that is being studied. As such, the findings do not necessarily mean that differences are entirely absent earlier in development.”
Balducci also cautioned against reading too much into what the scans can show.
“The findings do not show that differences in water diffusion directly cause differences in behavior or mental health,” Balducci pointed out. “Diffusion MRI provides an indirect measure of tissue microstructure.”
“Also, as with many sex differences, males and females vary on average,” Balducci added. “However, when multiple small differences are considered together, the overall profiles of males and females can become considerably more distinct.”
To address these remaining questions, both outside researchers point toward the need for investigations that capture earlier and more detailed developmental data.
“The most important next step would be a longitudinal study that repeatedly scans the same individuals before, during, and after puberty, while also measuring pubertal hormones and developmental phases,” Balducci told PsyPost. “That would help determine whether the observed diffusion changes track individual pubertal development and whether they are related to later mental-health outcomes.”
“It would be very interesting to see this approach being used in earlier stages of development, such as the prenatal period,” Khan said. “The prenatal period is another critical window for the emergence of sex differences in the brain. Moreover, male and female fetuses are exposed to different levels of sex hormones, which may contribute to differences in early brain development.”
The researchers say the sex-specific trajectories they describe could serve as a reference point for future studies exploring how departures from typical development might relate to mental health conditions.
The study, “Sex Differences in Human Deep Grey Matter Microstructure Emerge During Adolescence,” was authored by Christopher G. Filippi, Jay N. Giedd, Aziz M. Uluğ, and Richard Watts.

LONDON – A “severe drought” was declared in parts of southern England on Oct 15 by the British government, which said it took the decision following an “unprecedented period of extreme weather”.
The United Kingdom experienced its hottest summer on record in 2026, featuring several heatwaves and an exceptional drought that resulted from a lack of rainfall not seen since records began in 1836.
More than 80% of England is currently in a state of drought as it continues to experience below average levels of rainfall into the autumn months.
“Record-breaking summer heat and severe drought have put our water resources under immense pressure,” said Environment Agency head Philip Duffy.
The “severe drought” status was declared in the English counties of Cornwall, Devon, Dorset, Somerset, East Sussex and West Sussex. It is the worst stage triggered by “exceptionally low indicators over a long period of time”.
The declaration came as two major reservoirs in south-west England serving nearly 400,000 properties were below 20% of their storage capacity.
The Environment Agency said it “would expect reservoir storage to be around 75% for this time of year”.
South-east and south-west England have experienced their driest April to September period in more than a century, according to the government.
Scientists say climate change is intensifying weather events such as drought and heatwaves, resulting in records being broken more frequently.
As of last week, average reservoir levels across England stood at 54%, with the nation receiving just 10% of average October rainfall.
The government has urged water companies to monitor their water intake from natural resources and encouraged customers to cut their consumption, with usage restrictions already imposed in several regions.
“This level of drought is something we have not experienced for decades,” environment minister Angela Eagle said.
Months of drought have piled pressure on everyone from farmers and anglers to firefighters, who say tinder-dry conditions resulted in challenging wildfires this summer.
Since August, the government has convened a weekly National Drought Group, involving the weather agency, water companies, experts and farmers’ representatives.
