From underground wealth to diplomatic power: Azerbaijan’s energy strategy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:53:03 UTC
22:53:03 KST

Azerbaijani oil passes through Turkiye to Israel, its gas reaches European markets, and Emirati and Saudi capital finances its power plants. This network places Azerbaijan at the intersection of interests that do not always align. Baku has made itself relevant to several competing actors. Its harder task is to turn those relationships into lasting influence while preserving strategic autonomy.
Continued oil deliveries to Israel, despite Ankara’s trade restrictions, illustrate the challenge. Infrastructure, contracts and commercial interests can sustain connections across political divisions. Azerbaijan gains revenue and strategic importance, while becoming exposed to disputes among its partners.
Ankara and Tel Aviv: Two relationships, one route
Turkiye is both a political partner and Azerbaijan’s gateway to overseas markets. The Baku–Tbilisi–Ceyhan pipeline carries Caspian oil to the Mediterranean, while the Trans-Anatolian pipeline forms part of the Southern Gas Corridor, connecting Azerbaijani gas to Europe. These assets give the Baku–Ankara relationship a durability extending beyond immediate political positions.
The route’s importance to Israel is measurable. Azerbaijani crude accounted for 46.4 per cent of Israeli oil imports in 2025. Reuters reported in January 2026, citing Kpler data, that imports through Ceyhan reached approximately 94,000 barrels a day, up 31 per cent from the previous year. It also described vessels declaring alternative destinations and switching off tracking systems.
These shipments expose a gap between Ankara’s declared restrictions and the operation of a multinational oil supply chain. Cargo ownership, pipeline operations and final delivery involve different commercial and regulatory arrangements. In November 2024, Turkiye’s energy ministry stated that BTC operates under the 1999 intergovernmental agreement and associated host government agreements, and that its Turkish operator has no involvement in oil purchases or sales. It also denied loading cargoes with Israel as their declared destination.
The contrast with final-destination tracking data raises questions about enforcement and oversight. Distinguishing transit operations from oil sales explains part of the commercial structure; it does not settle the extent of the Turkish state’s authority or responsibility.
Energy supplies and defence cooperation give Baku’s relationship with Israel strategic depth. According to SIPRI, Israel supplied 69 per cent of Azerbaijan’s imports of major arms in 2016–2020. Azerbaijan occupies an important place in Israel’s oil supply, while Israeli arms have contributed to Baku’s military capabilities.
These interests raise the cost of political disengagement for both sides.
For Baku, the benefits come with political costs. Against the backdrop of the Gaza war, supplying Israel with oil raises serious ethical and political questions. Azerbaijan must manage a partnership important to its trade and defence while facing scrutiny from regional publics.
Iran: Geography needs workable agreements
Iran demonstrates another feature of Baku’s energy diplomacy: neighbours with political differences can still need each other’s infrastructure. The November 2021 gas swap agreement envisaged Iran receiving 1.5–2 billion cubic metres of Turkmen gas annually and delivering an equivalent volume to Azerbaijan. Existing networks enabled cooperation without constructing a new pipeline along the entire route.
READ: Azerbaijani president approves financial aid for Palestinian Embassy
The arrangement’s temporary suspension in early 2024 exposed its commercial limits. Trend reported at the time that Baku and Ashgabat had not agreed the terms for that year. Geography creates an opportunity for exchange; prices and contracts determine whether gas flows.
This lesson also applies to proposed connections with Nakhchivan. Routes through Iran and southern Armenia involve different geographical and legal arrangements. Their value depends on sovereignty, security and investment. For Tehran and Baku, durable cooperation requires clearly shared benefits and reliable implementation.
Gulf capital expands Baku’s options
Emirati and Saudi investment has widened Azerbaijan’s energy partnerships. Masdar announced the inauguration of the 230-megawatt Garadagh solar plant in October 2023. The 240-megawatt Khizi–Absheron wind plant, developed by Saudi Arabia’s ACWA Power, was officially inaugurated in January 2026. These projects anchor Gulf relationships in long-term economic assets.
Baku gains capital and a broader choice of partners. Gulf investors gain opportunities to expand in the Caucasus. The practical value of these partnerships will emerge through electricity production, grid development and domestic capabilities.
Renewables offer another benefit. The International Energy Agency notes that their expansion could conserve gas for exports and petrochemical production. Green investment therefore also supports the management of Azerbaijan’s export resources.
Europe and the credibility test
Europe adds weight to this network. The 2022 energy memorandum set an ambition to expand corridor capacity to deliver at least 20 billion cubic metres annually to the EU by 2027. Achieving it requires additional gas production, infrastructure and commercial commitments.
TAP’s March 2026 announcement confirmed that its first expansion phase was operational, adding 1.2 billion cubic metres of annually booked long-term capacity. This is a concrete advance, but it does not by itself establish a delivery pathway to the 2027 ambition. Meeting that target requires further transport capacity, additional exportable gas and firm purchasing commitments.
Reliable delivery strengthens Baku’s bargaining position. Political promises unsupported by the necessary investment risk weakening the credibility on which that position depends.
Today’s wealth, tomorrow’s power
The World Bank’s 2023 assessment placed oil and gas at around 90 per cent of Azerbaijan’s exports. Such concentration leaves the economy exposed to market volatility and the global energy transition.
Baku has made its resources matter abroad. Its next test is to build an economy that can sustain that influence as hydrocarbon revenues decline. Diplomatic power will endure only if Azerbaijan converts today’s resource income into productive capacity beyond the extractive sector.

The World Health Organization (WHO) said Thursday that 1,282 people had been killed and 5,891 injured in Yemen as a result of the military escalation between Aug. 6 and Oct. 11.
The figures were included in the UN agency’s seventh report on the escalation of the conflict in Yemen, which put the total number of casualties during the period at 7,173, including those killed and injured.
According to the report, the death toll stood at 1,282, accounting for 17.9% of all casualties, while 5,891 people were injured.
The report also recorded 2,007 additional casualties between Oct. 3 and 11, including 323 deaths and 1,684 injuries. The daily average rose to around 223 people killed or injured, up from 114 in the preceding period, according to the report.
The escalation comes amid the Dawn of Yemen military operation launched by Yemen’s internationally recognized government earlier this month to retake Houthi-held areas, including the national capital, Sanaa.
The offensive, backed by a Saudi-led coalition, has intensified fighting on several fronts, particularly in Taiz, where government forces and the Houthis have battled for control of strategic positions and supply routes.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis seized Sanaa in 2014, forcing the internationally recognized government from the capital. A Saudi-led coalition intervened militarily in support of the government in 2015.

JUBA, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- The 14th batch of the Chinese medical team in South Sudan delivered healthcare services to communities at the latest weekly clinical outreach session on Wednesday.
Conducted at the University of Juba clinic in the capital city, the session benefited not only enrolled students but also vulnerable people from surrounding communities.
Sonia Laku, 25, a medical student at the University of Juba, returned to the outreach clinic for follow-up care two months after her first visit.
Laku sought pain-relief plasters for her knee. Although the plasters she sought were temporarily unavailable, doctors prescribed alternative pain medication.
"Whenever I come here, I find not only students but also people from neighboring communities. The Chinese medical team has been providing great services to vulnerable people who are unable to access proper medical care due to the prevailing economic hardship," she said.
Chinese medicated pain plasters are widely utilized to provide temporary relief for minor muscle aches, joint stiffness, backaches, sprains, and bruises.
Margret Tabu Tereza, an engineering student who sought treatment for a severe headache, said Chinese doctors reassessed an elderly woman who had previously been diagnosed with diabetes at a private clinic.
"It was my first time visiting the clinic, and I saw Chinese doctors helping our people. I met an elderly woman who had been wrongly diagnosed with diabetes. The Chinese doctors noticed the anomaly and rectified this grave mistake," Tabu said.
The medical team's evaluation found that the woman did not have diabetes, and doctors prescribed medication for her actual condition.
Alfred Angwet Gai, a waste management supervisor at the University of Juba, returned to the campus clinic for a follow-up visit after receiving treatment for severe chest pain in the last session.
"I came here last week with terrible chest pain. The Chinese doctors examined me and gave me medicine that relieved the pain," Angwet said.
He said the team's outreach efforts also extend beyond the university, bringing health care services to communities in other parts of the country.

Individuals seeking care at the outreach clinics frequently present with a wide range of ailments, including chronic abdominal discomfort, joint and musculoskeletal pain, hypertension, and diabetes, Li added.

Chinese navy hospital ship arrives in Cote d'Ivoire on medical mission
China

21:33:38 CST
22:33:38 KST

Local honor guards welcome the Chinese People's Liberation Army Navy hospital ship Auspicious Ark upon its arrival in Abidjan, Cote d'Ivoire, Oct. 14, 2026. Auspicious Ark arrived in Abidjan, the economic capital of Cote d'Ivoire, on Wednesday to begin a friendly visit and provide medical services, marking the first visit by a Chinese naval hospital ship to the country. The hospital ship, which is carrying out Mission Harmony-2026, docked at Abidjan at about 10:00 a.m. local time (1000 GMT). (Photo by Yvan Sonh/Xinhua)
ABIDJAN, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- The Chinese People's Liberation Army Navy hospital ship Auspicious Ark arrived in Abidjan, the economic capital of Cote d'Ivoire, on Wednesday to begin a friendly visit and provide medical services, marking the first visit by a Chinese naval hospital ship to the country.
The hospital ship, which is carrying out Mission Harmony-2026, docked at Abidjan at about 10:00 a.m. local time (1000 GMT).
Ivorian military and government officials, China's ambassador to Cote d'Ivoire, the defense attache and embassy staff, as well as representatives of the Chinese community and Chinese enterprises welcomed the ship at the port.
On board, Chinese naval personnel and civilian staff stood in formation and waved to the welcoming crowd at the port.
At the welcoming ceremony, local residents held banners and waved the national flags of China and Cote d'Ivoire to welcome the Chinese naval hospital ship. After the ceremony, the Chief of Staff of the Ivorian Navy boarded the Auspicious Ark and toured the hospital ship.
During the seven-day visit, the hospital ship will provide medical treatment for local patients aboard the vessel, while medical personnel will visit the Abidjan Military Hospital and a local university, among other places, for medical exchanges and medical services.
The mission will also organize a deck reception to strengthen friendship and mutual trust with the Ivorian side.
China and Cote d'Ivoire established diplomatic relations in March 1983 and formally established a strategic partnership in September 2024. ■

China Focus: Long March legacy takes root in greener landscapes of revolutionary heartlands
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
21:33:31 CST
22:33:31 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- Perched on a hillside in Changting County of southern China, visitors soak in lush scenery stretching beside the glistening Tingjiang River.
But things weren't always so picturesque.
Changting, an old revolutionary base area in Fujian Province, was among the counties hardest hit by soil erosion in China's red-soil region, which threatened local people's livelihoods and left the landscape degraded.
Efforts to improve the local environment began nearly a century ago.
In November 1931, the Communist Party of China (CPC) established the Provisional Central Government of the Chinese Soviet Republic in Ruijin, Jiangxi Province, where the CPC put its revolutionary ideals into governance experimentation. The following year, it launched a tree-planting campaign to protect farmland from floods and droughts, reclaim barren hills and benefit local people.
During this campaign, CPC-led Red Army soldiers in Changting, which neighbors Ruijin, taught residents how to plant trees. In turn, residents brought food and seedlings to the soldiers and joined the planting campaign voluntarily.
"Even amid the turmoil of war, the Party still called for tree planting with great vigor," said Chen Liping, a researcher of CPC history and local chronicles in the county. "It reflects the Party's commitment to putting people's interests first and laying the foundations for future development."
As the war intensified, however, the tree-planting campaign had to be halted. The Red Army then embarked on the Long March, an epic military trek from 1934 to 1936 that broke through the encirclement of Kuomintang (Nationalist Party) forces. With some marching as far as 12,500 kilometers, the arduous journey helped lay the foundation for the eventual victory of the Chinese revolution.
As one of the starting points of the Long March, Changting has carried forward the Red Army's legacy in its decades-long efforts to combat soil erosion.
Tree planting, as the Red Army had practiced earlier, remained an effective method to tackle the problem. However, in severely eroded areas, ground temperatures can soar above 70 degrees Celsius, making it difficult for trees to survive.
Through experimentation, the county developed a phased approach suited to its natural conditions: first planting grass, then shrubs, and next trees, bringing the barren hills back to life step by step.
"Grass helps lower ground temperatures and create favorable conditions for other vegetation, allowing a mix of tree species to take root," said Shangguan Yuanbin, deputy head of the county's soil and water conservation station.
Over the years, local people adapted to changing conditions and met emerging problems with determination, patience and ingenuity.
Years of effort have paid off. To date, Changting has reduced the area affected by soil erosion by about 1.17 million mu (about 78,000 hectares), while its soil erosion rate fell from 31.47 percent to 6.31 percent, according to local authorities.
"Had we given up at any point over these decades, we would not have achieved such results today," said Shangguan. "We've applied the fearless Long March spirit to soil and water conservation."
Changting's transformation epitomizes a broader greening trend in China, which marks a national tree-planting day annually. Official data showed that between 2021 and 2025, China accounted for roughly one-quarter of the world's increase in green vegetation, while its forest and grass coverage rate exceeded 56 percent in 2025.
China's greening endeavor has gained international recognition. In 2021, Changting's comprehensive soil erosion control and ecological restoration practices were selected as a model case at the 15th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (COP15).
But restoring the land is not the end of the story. The next challenge is to turn environmental recovery into lasting economic opportunities for local communities.
One of these places is Xikuangshan, an old mining area in central China's Hunan Province. During the Long March, about 1,500 well-disciplined Red Army soldiers were stationed there for a week. Through their words and deeds, they gained the trust of locals, who went from hiding from the Red Army to following it.
Dubbed the "World's Capital of Antimony," Xikuangshan has witnessed decades of intensive underground mining dating back to 1897, which led to vegetation loss, air and water pollution, and ground subsidence. Some even joked that "a white bird flying across Xikuangshan could turn black."
In 2004, local people mounted an all-out campaign for ecological restoration. Inspired by the perseverance shown by the Red Army, a research team conducted countless experiments and finally achieved a breakthrough in the treatment of harmful residue generated during antimony refining, a challenge that has long confronted the industry worldwide.
The once-scarred mining landscape gradually regained its vitality. The improved environment, together with its revolutionary history and mining culture, helped Xikuangshan to develop into a well-known tourist destination with around 300 million yuan (about 44.6 million U.S. dollars) in tourism revenue annually.
Yang Lijun is among those who have benefited. After more than a decade, he decided to return home in 2021 upon seeing his hometown's blue skies and clear waters. He rented an abandoned rural house and opened a tourist restaurant featuring local specialties, which now generates an annual income of more than 100,000 yuan.
"In the past, many residents, myself included, left home because of worsening environmental conditions," he recalled. "Now, with the environment improving, more tourists are coming, bringing new opportunities for a better life."
For places like Changting and Xikuangshan, ecological restoration is therefore not simply about bringing back greenery, but also about higher-quality lives and new development paths for former revolutionary base areas.
Earlier this year, China issued guidelines on accelerating the development of such areas, with measures to support systematic environmental protection and encourage eco-tourism.
For Yue Hui, director of the soil and water conservation center in Changting, the changes are encouraging, but the work is far from over.
"Combating soil erosion requires sustained effort. We will continue our march toward a greener future," Yue said. ■

Fifth Congress of Chinese Archaeology opens in north China's Shanxi Province
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
21:33:30 CST
22:33:30 KST

TAIYUAN, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- The Fifth Congress of Chinese Archaeology opened on Thursday in Yuncheng, north China's Shanxi Province, under the theme of "Archaeology: The Past and the Future."
Scheduled to run through Saturday, the congress draws hundreds of archaeologists from home and abroad, featuring keynote speeches and 28 parallel sessions, with more than 570 academic presentations and 22 public lectures.
Yuncheng, the host city, is where the Xiyin site in Xia County was excavated 100 years ago. The site dates back to the Neolithic Age. The excavation unearthed thousands of pottery fragments and other artifacts associated with the Yangshao culture, which originated around the middle reaches of the Yellow River and dates back 4,700 to 7,000 years.
Led by Chinese archaeologist Li Ji and geologist Yuan Fuli, it was the first modern scientific archaeological excavation independently conducted by Chinese scholars, ushering in a new era for Chinese archaeology and becoming a landmark in modern Chinese archaeology.
Marie Louise Stig Sørensen, professor of Prehistoric Europe and Heritage Studies at the University of Cambridge's Department of Archaeology and a guest at the congress, said she became interested in archaeology related to the Yangshao Culture after working with some young scholars about the importance of the culture.
"It is such a fascinating part of our world history, and at the same time, its archaeology is so similar in some way to what I do in Europe," she said.
Established in 2016, the Congress of Chinese Archaeology aims to showcase the current state and achievements of Chinese archaeology, promote greater openness and international academic exchanges, and advance the overall development of Chinese archaeology. ■

Estonia fears Russia will erode Western support for Ukraine, minister says
WARSAW, Oct 15 - The risk that Russia could erode Western support for Ukraine through hybrid attacks, sabotage and disinformation campaigns is a key concern for Estonia, the Baltic nation's top diplomat said.
European officials have warned that Moscow is intensifying such attacks across the continent in an effort to sow opposition to the wide-ranging support that Ukraine's European neighbours and NATO provide to Kyiv to help it resist Russia's invasion.
"Russia is looking very carefully how we react. What is our political unity in practice," Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna told Reuters in a brief interview on the sidelines of a conference in Warsaw.
"I think the Baltic states, Finland, Poland ... have prepared mentally for decades that Russia may commit different levels of attacks," he said. "But my main concern is that the Western part of European societies, they are not ready."
The Kremlin consistently denies European allegations of drone attacks on land and at sea, cyberattacks, arson and other covert operations in NATO countries.
Tsahkna reiterated concerns that Moscow may step up hybrid efforts, with a likely focus on critical infrastructure and defence industry companies, to divide Western societies.
Ties between Ukraine and the United States have come under strain and opponents of aid to Ukraine have been gaining ground in Europe.
On Wednesday, Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the small leftist BSW party joined forces to pass a symbolic motion in the state parliament of Saxony-Anhalt calling for an end to Berlin's military support for Ukraine.
In France, National Rally leader Marine Le Pen, who is leading in opinion polls ahead of next year's presidential vote, has said France can no longer afford to finance Ukraine. REUTERS

NEW DELHI: President Droupadi Murmu has accepted the resignation of Union minister of state L Murugan from the Union Council of Ministers, the Rashtrapati Bhavan said on Thursday.The resignation fuelled speculation about an imminent Union Cabinet reshuffle.Murugan had resigned as the minister of state for Information and Broadcasting and Parliamentary Affairs on Tuesday, said he wanted to return to Tamil Nadu to strengthen the BJP’s grassroots organisation ahead of the 2029 Lok Sabha elections. He also sought permission to relinquish his Rajya Sabha membership.“I requested our Prime Minister to relieve me from the Council of Ministers and the Rajya Sabha because I want to go to Tamil Nadu to strengthen our party,” Murugan said.His exit marks the third resignation by a minister of state after George Kurian and Ravneet Singh Bittu quit in June and July, respectively, following the BJP’s decision not to renominate them for Rajya Sabha elections.
"The President of India, as advised by the prime minister, has accepted the resignation of Dr L Murugan from the Union Council of Ministers, with immediate effect, under clause (2) of Article 75 of the Constitution of India," a communique issued by the Rashtrapati Bhavan on Wednesday said.
In his letter to Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Murugan described his tenure in the Union government as a privilege.“With humility and grateful heart, I therefore request you to relieve me of my responsibility as MoS and permit me to relinquish my membership of the Rajya Sabha, so that I may dedicate full time to strengthening the party in Tamil Nadu,” he wrote.
Murugan said his journey from a family of daily wage labourers to the Union Council of Ministers had been a defining experience.“Now, I wish to return to the grassroots, stand with our 'karyakartas' and dedicate myself full-time to strengthening the BJP in Tamil Nadu ahead of the 2029 Lok Sabha elections. Nation First. Party Next. Self Last,” he said.Murugan has been a Rajya Sabha member since September 2021 and was re-elected from Madhya Pradesh in April 2024. His tenure is due to end in April 2030.Several ministers who were not renominated to the Upper House, including Hardeep Singh Puri and BL Verma, continue to hold office. Pankaj Chaudhary and Harsh Malhotra, who were appointed heads of the BJP’s Uttar Pradesh and Delhi units, respectively, have also retained their ministerial responsibilities.

In a statement, the ministry warned that the continued closure had led to a “dangerous and rapidly growing accumulation of critical cases,” with waiting lists for treatment abroad increasing by the day.
It said the number of people awaiting evacuation far exceeds the capacity of Gaza’s deteriorating and besieged hospitals to accommodate them or provide even the minimum level of treatment.
The ministry described the continued closure as a “grave violation of international humanitarian law and a deliberate deprivation of patients and wounded people of their right to treatment.”
It called on relevant parties to “exert serious and urgent pressure on Israel to reopen the Rafah crossing and all other crossings and facilitate the departure of critically ill patients for treatment abroad.”
The continued closure comes as more than 20,000 patients and wounded people in Gaza await evacuation for treatment abroad, amid severe shortages of medicines, medical equipment, and specialized medical services following Israel’s destruction of the healthcare system during its genocidal war on the enclave.
More than 1,344 patients have died while waiting for treatment since the ceasefire agreement took effect on Oct. 10, 2025, according to the Gaza Health Ministry.
On Feb. 2, 2026, Israel reopened the crossing on a limited basis, allowing small numbers of patients and wounded people to leave under tight restrictions.
According to Health Ministry statistics, a total of 2,480 patients and wounded people left Gaza through the crossing between Feb. 2 and Sept. 2.
This amounts to an average of about 12 patients and wounded people per day, compared with the agreed arrangement of 50 patients and 50 companions daily.
According to Health Ministry figures from October 2025, Israel’s war destroyed or rendered inoperable 25 of Gaza’s 38 hospitals, leaving 13 operating partially under difficult conditions.
The Israeli army also destroyed 103 of the enclave’s 157 primary healthcare centers during the genocide, while the remaining 54 continued to operate partially.
Israeli violations of the ceasefire had killed 1,501 Palestinians and injured 5,323 others as of Monday, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry.
Since October 2023, more than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed and over 175,000 injured in Gaza in Israel’s genocide, while around 90% of the enclave’s infrastructure has been damaged or destroyed.

How Chinese Clean Tech Is Reshaping Ukraine’s Wartime Energy Security
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:16:00 UTC
22:16:00 KST

Russia’s war against Ukraine has shown that energy security is no longer just about access to fuels, pipelines, and large power stations. It also depends on solar panels, batteries, and other distributed energy equipment that can keep homes, businesses, and critical services operating when the electricity grid is under attack.
Ironically, most of the equipment helping Ukraine keep the lights on comes from China.
Beijing has maintained close strategic ties with Russia. Yet through trade and global supply chains, Chinese-made clean energy technologies are helping Ukraine reduce the vulnerability created by Russian attacks on its energy system.
Russia’s attacks exposed the vulnerability of Ukraine’s highly centralized power system. The International Energy Agency (IEA) estimated that around half of Ukraine’s generation capacity was occupied, damaged or destroyed during 2022-23, while around half of its large network substations were damaged by missiles and drones. After another wave of attacks in spring 2024, Ukraine lost a further 9 GW of generation capacity, leaving it with only around one-third of its pre-war capacity. On January 20, 2026, another major Russian attack on energy infrastructure left almost half of Kyiv without heat and power.
Such attacks turned Ukraine’s large, fixed energy assets into major points of vulnerability, making energy decentralization an increasingly important source of resilience. Consequently, there has been a resurgence of solar power in Ukraine.
The country was already a significant solar market before Russia’s full-scale invasion, ranking ninth globally for new solar capacity addition in 2019. But deployment and trade collapsed after February 2022. Chinese module exports to Ukraine fell from 83.9 MW in February 2022 to just 7.5 MW in March, and totaled only 15.8 MW in 2023.
Since then, the market has recovered. The Solar Energy Association of Ukraine estimated that around 800 MW of solar was installed in 2024 and 1.5 GW in 2025. Businesses and households have been installing solar power to reduce their dependence on the grid. Distributed solar PV, often combined with battery storage, has therefore become an important part of Ukraine’s wartime energy security.
International organizations, such as the IEA and the Center for Strategic and International Studies, have recently examined Ukraine’s energy reconstruction, covering aspects such as decentralization, solar power, battery storage, financing, and electricity-market reform. However, these reports tell us remarkably little about the sources of the equipment needed for this transition.
In particular, the role of Chinese-made equipment in this shift has received much less attention. According to the IEA, China accounts for around 85 percent of global solar supply-chain production capacity and around 80 percent of lithium-ion battery production capacity. Its share in some specific segments is even higher – for example, China supplies around 95 percent of global PV wafer capacity.
Currently there is no authoritative estimate on the specific share of Chinese-made equipment in Ukraine’s solar and battery markets, not least because some products reach Ukraine through third countries, international procurement channels, and aid programs. Still, given China’s dominance of these supply chains, Chinese-made equipment is likely to have played an important role in Ukraine’s decentralized energy expansion and will probably continue to do so.
This raises an intriguing question. Does China’s position in these supply chains give Beijing significant leverage over Ukraine? Could China, particularly given its close relations with Russia, use access to clean energy equipment as a coercive geopolitical tool?
Supply chain concentration undoubtedly creates structural influence. But as I argued in an article in September 2025 in The Diplomat, it does not translate automatically into the kind of coercive power historically associated with oil and gas.
In Ukraine’s case, three factors are particularly relevant.
First, clean energy equipment moves through complex international commercial networks. A substantial volume of Chinese products can reach Ukraine indirectly through third countries, distributors, international procurement, and aid programs. This makes it difficult for Beijing to control the ultimate destination or end user. Blocking such flows would require much wider restrictions and would be commercially and politically difficult.
Second, weaponizing clean-energy supply would impose considerable costs on China’s own industries. It could expose Chinese companies to greater regulatory and compliance risks while strengthening Western arguments for supply chain diversification, domestic manufacturing, and “friend-shoring.” In the long run, that could accelerate precisely the reduction in dependence that Chinese manufacturers would prefer to avoid.
Third, such restrictions would contradict Beijing’s stated approach to the Russia-Ukraine war. China has repeatedly called for promoting peace talks while maintaining civilian trade. Deliberately restricting technologies important to civilian electricity supply would be difficult to reconcile with that position and could carry diplomatic and reputational costs.
When it comes to clean energy, China’s industrial dominance does not necessarily translate into the ability to exercise political control. Global commercial networks can significantly constrain a government’s ability to determine where clean technologies ultimately go and how they are used.
A further question is how the Chinese government and Chinese companies might participate constructively in Ukraine’s ongoing energy transformation and eventual reconstruction.
The potential market is substantial. The IEA estimates that Ukraine would need to add around 4 GW of distributed solar PV each year through 2030 to build a more decentralized and secure electricity system while meeting its national energy and climate objectives. It would also require an additional 5.6 GW of battery energy capacity by 2030.
For Chinese companies, the opportunities extend beyond exporting more solar modules and batteries. There is considerable scope for cooperation in system integration, energy management, technology transfer, joint project development, local assembly and production, and operations and maintenance.
But such involvement would not be straightforward. Chinese firms would have to navigate wartime risks, technical standards, financing constraints, supply chain security screening, and an increasingly complex geopolitical environment. Companies seeking to participate will therefore need to create value locally, build trusted partnerships, and adapt to an institutional and regulatory environment, particularly as Ukraine becomes more deeply integrated into European energy markets.
Ukraine’s experience offers a broader lesson about the geopolitics of clean energy. Countries still need secure fuel supplies and reliable power grids, but they also need access to the equipment used to produce and store electricity locally. China’s lead in manufacturing gives it considerable influence, though not complete control. Once solar panels and batteries enter global trading networks, they can contribute to energy security in ways that go beyond the intentions or expectations of their country of origin.

====================================================================================================

Gaza’s future is not Washington’s to decide, says rights chief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:14:50 UTC
22:14:50 KST

Nearly a year after the UN Security Council endorsed the Board of Peace to oversee Gaza’s transition, questions over who controls it, and in whose interest, have not gone away. For Anouar El Gharbi, president of the Geneva Centre for Democracy and Human Rights (GCDHR), the problem begins with the Board’s origin. It was not born of an independent international process grounded in the freely expressed will of the Palestinian people, he told MEMO in an interview, but of a political initiative led by the US. That origin, he argues, shapes everything that follows: the scope of the Board’s mandate, the powers it holds and the people it answers to.
The Board emerged from the “Comprehensive Plan to End the Gaza Conflict” advanced by US President Donald Trump. The Security Council endorsed the plan on 17 November 2025 through Resolution 2803, adopted by 13 votes with Russia and China abstaining. The resolution recognised the Board as a transitional administration with international legal personality and authorised a set of operational arrangements on the ground.
El Gharbi rejects any suggestion that this grants the Board permission to place itself above the law. Its work, he insists, “must respect the Palestinian people’s right to self-determination, the prohibition on acquiring territory by force and the obligations of international humanitarian law”.
Asked whether the backing of the Security Council settles the question of legitimacy, he points to the sequence of events in the formation of the board. “Washington designed the initiative and shaped the framework under which the Board operates, and the Council’s endorsement came afterwards.” This, he says, “raises serious questions about the Board’s independence, about how far Palestinians take part in its decisions and about whether there is adequate international oversight to hold it to account”.
El Gharbi draws a clear distinction. A temporary international framework to support reconstruction, humanitarian aid and transitional administration is one thing; a political trusteeship over Gaza is another. The right to self-determination, he says, belongs to Palestinians, and no outside power can exercise it on their behalf.
READ: Trump’s Gaza board accused of creating legal black hole to protect officials and contractors
International law, El Gharbi explains, gives no state or international body an unrestricted right to impose permanent political arrangements on a people under occupation. “Transitional arrangements must stay within their mandate, be subject to effective oversight and must not displace legitimate Palestinian institutions or weaken the ability of Palestinians to exercise their political rights,” he says.
Accountability is a recurring concern. Although Resolution 2803 gives the Board an international legal framework, the Board is not a subsidiary organ of the UN. That, El Gharbi says, makes it crucial to spell out who is responsible for what among the Board, the participating states, the operational bodies and the international institutions involved. Legal personality, he stresses, does not exempt an entity from its obligations under international law, nor does it grant unlimited immunity from the courts.
“The scope of any privileges and immunities must be determined by the relevant legal instruments,” El Gharbi says. “They cannot simply be presumed to extend to every act or every official associated with the transitional arrangements.” He warns that Palestinians would pay the price if this is not resolved. “Excessively broad immunities, inadequate accountability, or decisions about public resources and property taken without proper legal safeguards could seriously endanger the rights of Gaza’s population, including their access to justice and to effective remedies.”
On the role of Palestinians themselves, El Gharbi is unequivocal. The Palestinian people, he says, remain the holders of the right to decide their political future and how their territory is governed. Resolution 2803 does provide for a Palestinian technocratic committee to run day-to-day administration, but in his view meaningful participation must go well beyond administrative tasks. It must shape the decisions that determine Gaza’s governance, its reconstruction and its long-term political future. “Shutting Palestinians out of real decision-making,” he argues, “would undermine the political legitimacy of the whole arrangement and raise serious doubts about whether it is consistent with the right to self-determination.”
READ: From Count Bernadotte to the ‘Gaza Board of Peace’
Nor, in El Gharbi’s view, does the new arrangement relieve Israel of its responsibilities as the occupying power. “Setting up an international transitional mechanism or a local administrative committee does not, by itself, end Israel’s obligations under international law towards the occupied Palestinian territory,” he says. “The obligations arising from the law of occupation must be judged against the relevant legal criteria and the facts on the ground, and new governance arrangements cannot wipe out existing responsibilities or absolve any party of accountability for violations it has committed.”
El Gharbi also points out that international humanitarian law requires the protection of civilians and the delivery of essential aid. Access to food, medicine, shelter and basic services, he says, must not be made subject to unlawful political conditions that put civilian lives and dignity at risk.
El Gharbi is concerned, too, that continuing violence and obstacles to reconstruction raise questions about the practical effectiveness of the transitional framework, and whether it can protect civilians, support humanitarian recovery and ensure compliance with international law.
This is not, he insists, an argument against international help for Gaza. The danger, he says, is that a mechanism of this kind could reduce the Palestinian question to a humanitarian and security matter and sideline the core legal and political issues of occupation, self-determination and national rights.
READ: Why the recent UNSC Resolution 2803 “Board of Peace” violates the UN Charter
“Transitional powers must not become a way of entrenching prolonged external rule over Gaza, or of cementing its separation from the rest of the occupied Palestinian territory,” he stresses. “Resolution 2803 grants only a time-limited authorisation, subject to further action by the Security Council, and this time limit must be respected in practice. It cannot be used to justify open-ended foreign control without the meaningful participation and consent of Palestinians.”
The resolution itself, El Gharbi maintains, must be read and implemented in line with the UN Charter and international law, including peremptory norms and the right of Palestinians to self-determination. It cannot reasonably be treated as a blank cheque for any state or body to decide the permanent political future of Palestinian territory regardless of the rights of its people.
El Gharbi calls for clear and effective international oversight of the Board, greater transparency in how it takes decisions and a precise definition of the powers and responsibilities of everybody involved, and of how each will be held to account. He also urges human rights organisations, legal institutions and independent monitors to scrutinise how the arrangements are carried out, particularly where they affect Palestinian rights, public property, humanitarian access, access to justice and the ability of Palestinians to run their own affairs.
In the end, El Gharbi returns to the point where he began. No political initiative led by the US, he says, can take the place of the freely expressed will of the Palestinian people. A Security Council resolution is not enough on its own to make an international arrangement legitimate; that arrangement must also comply with international law and respect fundamental rights. A lasting peace, he argues, requires three things: respect for international law, the Palestinian people’s right to self-determination and a lawful end to the occupation. Without them, he warns, any transitional arrangement will remain fragile, no matter how many powerful states stand behind it.

Several leaders voiced opposing positions on the bloc’s proposed multiannual financial framework as they arrived for a European Council meeting, with disagreements centering on the budget’s size, spending priorities, and contributions from member states.
Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten called on European countries to increase their financial and military support for Ukraine, saying some member states were lagging behind.
“A lot of European countries are lagging behind in the support for Ukraine. So let's step up our game and make sure that they can win this senseless war,” Jetten said.

Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson also rejected the proposed budget, saying it would increase Sweden’s net contribution by around 60%.
"A 60% increase of the Swedish contribution is simply not acceptable. It's a no-go zone," he said, adding that Sweden would not accept a further increase in its contributions.
Kristersson said the negotiations would be tense and questioned whether an agreement could be reached before the end of the year, stressing the need for a budget that balances modernization, support for Ukraine, and traditional spending priorities.
Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda, meanwhile, welcomed the Irish presidency’s proposal, describing it as well-balanced, but expressed concern over cuts to the Connecting Europe Facility, particularly military mobility, and the competitiveness fund.
He stressed that an ambitious budget with sufficient funding was necessary to implement the bloc’s priorities, adding that reaching a consensus by the end of the year would be difficult.
Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal said security, connectivity and competitiveness were among his country’s main priorities, particularly given its location on the EU’s eastern border.
He also called for reducing bureaucracy to help the bloc compete with China and the US, while saying he did not expect major compromises during the summit.
Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin defended the proposal, saying the presidency had sought to facilitate negotiations by balancing the positions of member states.
He said the proposal preserved cohesion funding and maintained key elements of the competitiveness fund, while acknowledging that issues remained to be resolved before the end of the year.
"My view all along has been a larger budget is required for Europe to attain its objectives," Martin added.
Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs stressed the importance of agreeing on the next seven-year budget, noting that "strong economy can only bring a strong defense."
He said eastern European countries needed additional economic support to keep the bloc’s eastern borders safe.
He also called for further measures to help Ukraine export its agricultural products and implement sanctions against Russia.
Kulbergs described the coming winter as critical for Ukraine, saying the country’s ability to remain resilient was closely linked to Europe’s own security.
"We should think a little bit less about the comfort, a little bit less about ourselves and think further what is best for Europe in general," he added.
"It is one beer less for a European a year. We can afford that, but Ukraine needs it now. That one beer is just the cost. There it's the cost of life," Kulbergs further said.

Taiwan's ITRI and eJoule improve drone battery manufacturing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
12:57:44 UTC
21:57:44 KST

TAIPEI (TAIPEI NEWS) – Hsinchu-based Industrial Technology Research Institute said Thursday that it has partnered with local battery maker eJoule to make high-capacity batteries for drones and electric vehicles.
Medium-and high-lithium ternary batteries use nickel, cobalt, and manganese. Higher lithium content means greater storage capacity, making them suitable for drones, robotics, and electric vehicles.
According to a press release, drones and EVs are driving demand for lighter, longer-lasting batteries. Although ternary batteries are valued for their capacity, there are lifecycle and safety bottlenecks that need to be addressed before commercialization.
ITRI and eJoule co-developed a solution using single-crystal structures, electrode fabrication, and power cell certification to speed commercialization for drones, robotics, and storage applications. The project also aims to achieve production and supply chain self-reliance.
Electrode fabrication combines raw materials with metal foils to create the positive and negative charges required for batteries to function. The common method involves mixing the materials with additives and solvents such as water for coating onto the foils, which are then vacuumed and pressed into batteries.
ITRI Material and Chemical Research Laboratories Director Chiu Kuo-chan (邱國展) said eJoule provided the material while ITRI designed battery specifications and conducted performance tests. He noted that the material proved stable after extensive, repetitive cycles of charging and discharging, making it a suitable candidate comparable to lithium iron phosphate batteries in terms of lifespan as well as safer than traditional ternary materials.
ITRI said eJoule’s patented dynamic crystallization process yields simple, high-performing structures without using toxic precursors. eJoule Vice President Liu Min-tuan (劉敏端) said the initiative would combine ITRI's battery expertise to speed material applications from laboratory settings to commercially viable products.

Obama says Israel has ‘ceded moral ground’ in Middle East conflict

Berk Kutay Gökmen
15 October 2026•Update: 15 October 2026
Former US President Barack Obama has criticized Israel’s handling of the Middle East conflict, warning that military strength cannot guarantee lasting security and that refusing concessions to Palestinians risks undermining its moral standing.
The former president made the remarks on Tuesday during a discussion with award-winning writer and journalist Susan McKay at Belfast, northern Ireland, according to the Belfast Telegraph.
Speaking about the Israeli war on Gaza, Obama said the violence should “pain everybody”, describing it as a destructive cycle driven by historical grievances, hardened attitudes and deep divisions.
He acknowledged the long history of persecution faced by Jewish people in Europe. However, he also stressed that Palestinians had suffered injustice through the loss of their land.
“That is undeniable. What is also undeniable is that they took land off people and they were excessive. And those people understandably said: ‘This is injustice and I want my land back,’” he said.
Obama argued that the stronger side carries a greater responsibility to help break the cycle of violence, rather than relying solely on its military and technological superiority.
“If the attitude of Israel is, now that we are the strongest, the most technologically advanced in the region, then our security will depend on us simply doing whatever we need and taking whatever we want, and not making any concessions to anyone,” he said.
“That may work short-term... but you have ceded moral ground if that is the position you take.”
He said the current Israeli government appeared to have adopted that approach and urged it to recognize that millions of Palestinians would remain in the region.
“I would say the current Israeli government appears to have taken that. It is incumbent on them to recognise that 7 million Palestinians are not going anywhere,” Obama said.
“It is not sustainable to press upon them a condition that no-one would accept for themselves.”
Earlier on Tuesday, Obama received an honorary doctorate from Queen’s University Belfast.

DeepSeek offers user refunds after suffering another major outage
Chinese AI firm apologises and offers one-week refund after its chatbot and API services went offline for nearly five hours
Chinese artificial intelligence firm DeepSeek apologised and promised compensation to users after its services suffered a nearly five-hour outage on Thursday.
DeepSeek will issue users a full refund for any consumption between October 8 and October 14 in the form of credits, according to a notice posted on the Hangzhou-based start-up’s application programming interface (API) platform.
DeepSeek’s namesake chatbot and API services for its V4 Pro and V4.1 Flash models went offline on Thursday morning, affecting users globally, before being restored over four hours and 50 minutes later at around 1pm.
Some users turned to social media to share the error messages they had encountered when trying to use DeepSeek, such as “server temporarily unavailable”.

Egypt, Qatar stress need to halt hostilities against Saudi Arabia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
12:54:26 UTC
21:54:26 KST

Egypt and Qatar stressed the need to halt all hostilities against Saudi Arabia and expressed solidarity with the kingdom, according to the Egyptian Foreign Ministry on Thursday, Anadolu reports.
The position was expressed during a phone call late Wednesday between Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty and his Qatari counterpart, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, the ministry said in a statement.
The call came as part of “continuous communication and coordination between the two brotherly countries on various issues of common interest,” the statement said.
The two officials discussed bilateral relations and areas of cooperation, including exchanges of high-level visits. They praised the progress in ties and affirmed their commitment to further strengthening them, according to the statement.
On regional developments, the officials discussed the latest situation and agreed on the importance of supporting ongoing efforts and coordinating action to ease tensions and prevent the conflict from spreading.
They stressed the need to halt all hostilities against Saudi Arabia, strongly condemned the attacks and expressed solidarity with the kingdom.
The officials also called for activating political and diplomatic channels to resolve the current crisis and strengthen regional security and stability.
READ: Pakistan reiterates ‘unwavering’ commitment to Saudi Arabia’s protection under Makkah defense pact
The call came amid an ongoing military escalation between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthi group, involving missile and drone attacks on airports and critical infrastructure in the kingdom in recent days.
Since Oct. 5, five Saudi airports have come under attack, leaving 20 people dead and hundreds injured, in addition to material damage and disruptions to air traffic, according to the report.
Meanwhile, the military operation known as Dawn of Yemen has continued. Yemeni Presidential Leadership Council Chairman Rashad al-Alimi said the operation aims to restore state institutions from Houthi control and retake the capital, Sanaa.
The developments in Yemen are part of a military escalation that began in July and is the most extensive since a period of relative calm following a UN-brokered truce that began in April 2022.
Saudi Arabia has led a military coalition supporting Yemen’s internationally recognized government since 2015 against the Houthis, who have controlled Sanaa and several other provinces since 2014.

A brilliant reflection on the links between craftsmanship and contemporary art, particularly on the Murano glass tradition. This was the lecture delivered at the Indian Museum by Italian master Jean Blanchaert as part of the “Contemporary Art Days” promoted by the Consulate General of Italy in Kolkata.
Blanchaert, a curator, art critic, and contemporary art gallery owner specializing in glass and ceramics, spoke about how artisanal expertise can become a tool for contemporary artistic expression, while today’s artists are able to imbue traditional techniques with new potential and unprecedented meanings. These concepts resonate both in Italy and in West Bengal, especially as the celebrations for the Hindu festival of Durga Puja begin and its extraordinary pandals are erected.

all they have done and continue to do for him," the Vatican
Press Office reported, as it released photos of Leo.

Extra levies on financial sector won't kill anyone says Giorgetti
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
14:19:13 CEST
21:19:13 KST

Economy Minister Giancarlo Giorgetti
said Friday that the additional taxes the government intends to
impose on banks and insurers in the 2027 budget law will not be
too severe.
                                    
"I confirm that a contribution will be requested from the
financial system because we believe it can afford it," Giorgetti
said.
                                    
"We also believe the terms will be sustainable," he added,
stressing that "keeping the (bond) spread under control is in
everyone's interest" and that banks hold billions of euros in
Italian BTP bonds on their balance sheets.
                                    
When asked about possible legal challenges by the banks, the
minister commented: "every Italian could take the government to
court for raising taxes. We'll try to figure out the right
course of action; I don't think anyone will die over it."
The government's Draft Budgetary Plan (DBP) says the financial
sector will make a contribution of five billion euros to the
2027 budget package, and an additional three billion euros in
2028 and two billion in 2029.
                                    
The 2026 budget law included extra levies on banks and insurers
worth around 4.4 billion euros.

Students throw rocks, eggs, firecrackers at cops amid anti-govt protests across Italy
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
14:05:00 CEST
21:05:00 KST

Rocks and eggs were thrown at police
by high-school students in Turin and firecrackers against
security officers and the education ministry in Rome on Friday
amid anti-government protests across Italy demanding more
funding for schools and less for arms.
                                    
"Money for schools, not for war" and "Fewer weapons, more
rights" were  some of the slogans chanted by students who have
taken to the streets in various Italian cities, following the
recent occupations of their schools.
                                    
In Turin, several hundred young people marched, shouting slogans
against the government, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, Minister
of Education Giuseppe Valditara, and general-turned-politician
Roberto Vannacci, the leader of the new far-right party National
Future (FnV).
                                    
Demonstrations also took place in Genoa, Venice, Padua, and
Treviso.
                                    
In Cagliari, the protest was dubbed a "No Meloni Day."
During the tudent march currently underway in Rome, near Via
Marmorata, several hooded individuals threw improvised explosive
devices (firecrackers and small homemade bombs) and pushed waste
containers into the middle of the street to block it.
                                    
Bottles, improvised explosive devices, and the contents of fire
extinguishers were hurled toward the security personnel
overseeing the student march in Rome. According to the police
headquarters, this action was carried out by a small group of
masked protesters.
                                    
In Verona, a group of students from the Giorgi State Institute
set fire to five waste containers and an electric scooter parked
nearby.
                                    
Reports indicate that this was not merely a prank, but an act of
protest following disciplinary measures imposed by the school
administration in response to several fights that had broken out
in the classrooms. 
                                    
ALL RIGHTS RESERVED © Copyright ANSA

In Accra, Ambassador Ranalli Unveils a Mural Dedicated to Ghanaian Artist Kofi Antubam
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
14:04:15 CEST
21:04:15 KST

The Italian Ambassador to Ghana, Laura Ranalli, unveiled a mural dedicated to the Ghanaian artist Kofi Antubam at Achimota School in Accra. A Ghanaian sculptor, painter, art theorist, educator, and social activist, Antubam was one of the founders of the Ghanaian National School of Painting. In the 1950s, he created carved wooden reliefs that adorn the facades of the parliament building in the Ghanaian capital; during the same period, he painted part of the walls of the UN building in Geneva. 
The mural dedicated to him was created by Italian artist Francesco Ferreri (Chekos) together with students from the institute; the work is part of the “Artitude” project, born from a collaboration between the Puglia Region, the Random Association (Lecce), and ArtLifeMatters.
                                    
In her remarks, Ambassador Ranalli emphasized how cultural initiatives of this kind build a solid bridge between Italy and Ghana.
                                    
In the days leading up to the event, representatives from the institutions and associations involved met with the ambassador at her residence to take stock of the collaborative project.

Douglas Alexander welcomes defence skills investment boost
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:47:41 BST
21:47:41 KST

Douglas Alexander welcomes defence skills investment boost
Two Defence Technical Excellence Colleges are coming to Scotland after the Scottish Government confirmed it will match fund the UK Government's £10 million,
- The Colleges in the East and West of Scotland will upskill young people, enabling them to benefit from good, well-paid jobs in Scotland’s growing defence sector.
- Scotland already benefits from over £2 billion a year in MoD spending, which supports more than 12,000 jobs.
Scottish Secretary Douglas Alexander today welcomed the Scottish Government’s decision to match fund the UK Government’s £10 commitment to create two Defence Technical Excellence Colleges (DTECs) in Scotland, as part of a £50 million Scottish Defence Growth Deal.
The DTECs will help provide young people with new specialist pathways into high-skilled, well-paid careers in defence engineering, advanced manufacturing and maritime technology are coming to Scotland.
The colleges will be located to support Scotland’s defence clusters in the East and West of the country and will benefit from the engineering and innovation centres previously announced as part of the Scottish Defence Growth Deal.
Scottish Secretary Douglas Alexander said:
  In March we announced a £10 million commitment to develop two Defence Technical Excellence Colleges in Scotland. I’m pleased that the Scottish Government has now agreed to match fund these colleges to give our young people the skills they need to secure high-skilled, well-paid careers in Scotland’s defence sector in the years to come.
  Scotland is a defence industrial powerhouse and is already benefiting from increased UK Government investment as we deliver a defence dividend for Scotland, creating new skilled jobs, new training places and new opportunities for communities while keeping us and our allies secure. It is crucial that we continue to develop the skilled workforce needed to support this growing sector.
Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, Luke Pollard MP said:
  Finally matching DTEC funding is welcome news for Scottish careers. The colleges will provide routes into high-skilled, well-paid roles in the defence sector which is crucial to the work of keeping the UK safe around the clock.
This is an important part of our £50 million Defence Growth Deal - announced back in March - to boost growth opportunities for Scotland that supports our Armed Forces.
Industry analysis suggests there could be demand for up to 50,000 additional defence jobs across the UK by 2034/35.
Scotland already benefits from over £2.5 billion a year in Ministry of Defence spending, which directly supports 12,200 jobs.
The Scottish Secretary launched the UK Government’s Defence Growth Deal on 12 March, committing £10 million towards the creation of two DTECs — one in the East and one in the West of Scotland — as part of a wider £50 million deal.
The offer remained conditional on the Scottish Government providing match funding. More here: https://www.gov.uk/government/news/scotland-set-for-skills-and-innovation-boost-as-50-million-defence-growth-deal-unveiled
Scottish Government Innovation minister Alyn Smith on October 15th confirmed that Holyrood ministers would “partner with the UK Government” on the project.

Experts: Cyberattack on French supermarkets serves as a warning sign for Estonia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:48:05 UTC
21:48:05 KST

Cybersecurity experts believe that the cyberattack on French supermarkets on the night of the 12th of September—which resulted in the destruction of a large quantity of food—serves as a warning sign for Estonia, reports ERR News.
During the cyberattack, the perpetrators gained access to temperature control systems and raised the temperature in refrigerators and freezers to 50 degrees Celsius. As a result, a large amount of food was spoiled, causing significant financial losses. Estonia, too, must be prepared for such threats.
Toomas Lepik, a cybersecurity analyst at Tallinn University of Technology, stated that such incidents are possible and that the threat is very real. Fortunately, Estonia has not yet encountered problems of the kind seen in France; however, this does not mean that such an event could not occur due to a mistake or lax adherence to cybersecurity protocols.
Estonian Minister of Justice Liisa Pakosta, who is currently attending a cybersecurity conference in Singapore, described the incident in France as shocking. She pointed out that society must adapt to a new reality: cyberattacks no longer affect only computers and information systems. At the same time, the Minister emphasized that Estonia adheres to some of the strictest cybersecurity regulations in the world. She noted that companies providing essential services—including those involved in food security—are subject to stringent cybersecurity requirements, which must be met. 
Businesses must ensure that software is updated in a timely manner, systems are properly connected, and access is restricted so that unauthorized individuals cannot gain entry. 
Regarding entities such as grocery stores, the Minister stated that regular audits are conducted at major companies responsible for food security.
However, these requirements do not apply to all grocery stores. Pakosta added that both the government and businesses need to invest more in cybersecurity to ensure the security of their systems. She explained that while Estonia faces financially motivated cyberattacks on one hand, there are also attacks specifically targeting the state and society as a whole. As a digital nation, Estonia must pay greater attention to this issue. The Estonian supermarket chain Selver is closely monitoring events in France to prevent similar situations in its own stores. It is currently unknown who orchestrated the cyberattack on the French stores or whether a ransom will be demanded. Selver’s Communications Manager, Mariann Järvela, confirmed that the chain has not faced such attacks. She emphasized that the supermarket chain is doing everything possible to prevent such an occurrence, noting that every company and retail chain has its own strict protocols and systems in place to manage these matters. Järvela stated that, overall, Selver is well-protected against such threats.
Järvela added that the consequences of the incident in France do not differ significantly from those caused by a power outage—scenarios for which the supermarket chain already conducts training exercises.

'Thanks a lot, Trump': Wyoming conservatives divided ahead of US midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:48:00 UTC
21:48:00 KST

'Thanks a lot, Trump': Wyoming conservatives divided ahead of US midterms
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on: Modified:
Famous for its cowboy culture, Wyoming is the least populated, the most rural and the most conservative of all the US states. With two weeks to go until the midterm elections, our reporters James André and Sylvain Rousseau travelled across this Republican stronghold and found that the party of US President Donald Trump is deeply divided in the Cowboy State.
Come election season in the United States, news networks tend to flock to the swing states, the battlegrounds that shape the outcome of the vote. Two weeks ahead of the US midterm elections, FRANCE 24 decided to go in the opposite direction and visit the reddest of the red states: Wyoming.
US President Donald Trump carried 70 percent of the vote in Wyoming in his three presidential runs. The state is so overwhelmingly Republican that the decisive vote is not the midterm election there, but rather the Republican primaries that took place on August 18. The results are very clear.
In 2024, Wyoming voters had given an outright majority to the ultra-conservative Freedom Caucus, a hard-right organisation that emerged in the wake of Trump's MAGA movement. Wyoming was the first and only state to offer this national movement a majority. In the 2026 primaries, the Freedom Caucus was aiming for a supermajority in both chambers of the Wyoming Congress. But it got a spectacular rebuke from voters, losing its majority in the state House of Representatives and official posts across the board.
This electoral defeat is significant because the Freedom Caucus is the local incarnation of a form of "ultra-Trumpism". For two years, its lawmakers imported a hardline version of Trump's methods and agenda to Wyoming. They cut budgets and passed bills aligned with their conservative views. They sought to reform education, abortion and LGBTQ+ rights. They also constantly attacked the state's rare Democrats, and what they call RINOs (Republicans in Name Only): traditional, old-school Republicans whom they accuse of betraying the party's values.
In the meantime, the more traditional forces within the Republican establishment got organised to take their party back. During the campaign, political action committees spent millions trying to sway Wyoming's 580,000 residents. The state is a perfect target with a very small, already conservative population and two US Senate seats in Washington – just as many as California or Texas.
This report goes inside the battle within the Republican Party between the ultra-conservative bloc and the more moderate traditionalists. It also explores a paradox: Wyomingites are turning on Trump, but will carry on voting Republican – no matter what.
